Direct inference on external datasets. AI models trained on a specific dataset often struggle to generalize to novel datasets when a domain gap exists. While domain adaptation and generalization are research strategies to mitigate this, we assume the domain gap between CT volumes from different hospitals is less pronounced than in computer vision due to the standardized nature of CT imaging, where pixel intensity conveys consistent anatomical meaning. AbdomenAtlas 1.1 offers impressive diversity, covering variations in contrast enhancement, reconstruction kernels, scanner types, and acquisition parameters. This study definitively examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models pre-trained on 3D annotated datasets and fine-tuned on 3D image segmentation tasks. We begin by constructing AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an extensive collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes with high-quality, per-voxel annotations. The scale of this dataset is unprecedented in data volume (2,789,975 images), annotation granularity (251,323 masks), and diversity (88 hospitals). This dataset enables development of a suite of pre-trained models, SuPreM, that can be effectively transferred to a broad spectrum of 3D image segmentation tasks. Notably, SuPreM transfers better than all existing 3D models by a large margin, especially on under-annotated datasets. The model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability identical to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, proving the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training. Title: How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks? A Comprehensive Investigation into Large-Scale Annotated Pre-Training

Abstract
The paradigm of pre-training models on large, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuning them for specific target tasks has become a cornerstone of modern transfer learning in computer vision. For instance, a model pre-trained on the extensive ImageNet dataset and then fine-tuned for the PASCAL VOC challenge consistently and significantly outperforms a model trained exclusively on PASCAL from a random initialization. While ImageNet pre-training has demonstrated enormous success across numerous 2D vision applications, it is fundamentally limited to two-dimensional imagery and is primarily designed for image classification objectives. Consequently, when transferring these learned features to more diverse and complex three-dimensional tasks, such as volumetric medical image segmentation, performance is inevitably compromised due to the substantial deviation from the original ImageNet context. A pivotal and long-standing challenge in the field of 3D medical imaging has been the stark absence of large-scale, meticulously annotated 3D datasets that can rival the scale and impact of ImageNet for foundational model pre-training. To decisively overcome this critical challenge, this work makes two major and transformative contributions. Firstly, we construct and introduce AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an unprecedented dataset that comprises a vast collection of 9,262 three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, each accompanied by high-quality, per-voxel annotations for 25 distinct anatomical structures and pseudo-annotations for seven clinically significant tumor types. Secondly, we develop and release a comprehensive suite of models, pre-trained on our expansive AbdomenAtlas 1.1, specifically designed for transfer learning in 3D medical imaging. Our rigorous preliminary analyses definitively indicate that a supervised model trained with a remarkably small set of just 21 CT volumes, 672 segmentation masks, and 40 GPU hours achieves a transfer learning ability virtually identical to a state-of-the-art self-supervised model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and a massive 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, we conclusively demonstrate that the transfer learning ability of supervised models exhibits a powerful scaling law, improving substantially and consistently as the size of the annotated pre-training dataset increases, thereby achieving significantly and uniformly better performance than all preexisting pre-trained models, irrespective of their underlying pre-training methodologies or data sources. We are confident that this foundational study will catalyze and facilitate collective, global efforts in constructing even larger 3D medical datasets and accelerate the widespread release of powerful supervised pre-trained models, ultimately driving progress in medical AI.

1 INTRODUCTION

The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm stands as a widely adopted and profoundly effective framework for transfer learning in artificial intelligence. Given the intrinsic relationships and shared visual primitives across different computer vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one large, diverse dataset is expected to confer substantial benefits when adapted to another. Over the past several decades, pre-training has been undeniably important and instrumental in the rapid development of AI capabilities. For conventional 2D vision tasks, practitioners typically have two principal options: (i) supervised pre-training and (ii) self-supervised pre-training. However, for the critically important domain of 3D vision tasks, option (i) has historically been largely unavailable, primarily due to the profound and persistent lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets of sufficient scale and quality.

Supervised pre-training possesses the inherent capability to learn rich, discriminative image features that are highly transferable to a wide array of downstream target tasks. It has been the established common practice for years to pre-train models using the ImageNet dataset and then fine-tune the model on target tasks which often possess limited training data, such as PASCAL VOC. However, two fundamental and well-documented challenges arise with ImageNet-based pre-training for 3D medical applications. Firstly, ImageNet is predominantly composed of 2D natural images, leaving a palpable and significant void in the availability of large-scale 3D datasets and consequently, a lack of systematic investigation into 3D-specific transfer learning dynamics. Secondly, since ImageNet is explicitly intended for image classification, its benefit for pixel-wise prediction tasks like segmentation (and other dense prediction vision tasks) can be somewhat compromised and suboptimal. If such an ImageNet-like dataset existed—but formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models are unequivocally expected to transfer far more effectively to 3D medical image segmentation than self-supervised ones, for two compelling and fundamental reasons.

1. Supervised pre-training is dramatically more efficient in terms of both data and computational resource consumption because of its explicit and well-defined learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training offers the advantage of learning features without manual annotation, it invariably requires an enormous corpus of unlabeled data to achieve competitive performance. Extracting meaningful and generalizable features directly from raw, unlabeled data is an inherently challenging and noisy process. Unlabeled data often contain a high degree of redundancy and significant noise, which can substantially complicate and slow down the feature learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training consistently calls for vastly greater computational resources and time to match the superior outcomes achieved by efficient supervised pre-training. We have definitively quantified this improved data and computational efficiency from the dual perspectives of both the pre-training phase (Figure 2a; demonstrating a 99.6% reduction in required data) and the fine-tuning phase (Figure 2b; showing 66% less computation). Specifically, our supervised model trained with merely 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates a transfer learning ability essentially equivalent to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, irrefutably highlighting the remarkable and unparalleled efficiency of the supervised pre-training approach.

2. Supervised pre-training directly enables the model to learn image features that are intrinsically relevant and optimally suited for the target task of image segmentation. In contrast, self-supervised pre-training must indirectly extract image features from raw, unlabeled data using various pretext tasks such as mask image modeling, instance discrimination, and others. Despite their demonstrated efficacy in learning representations, these pretext tasks share no obvious or direct semantic relation to the ultimate target task of image segmentation. In stark contrast, supervised pre-training utilizes semantically meaningful and precise annotations (e.g., organ and tumor segmentation maps) as direct supervision, enabling the model to effectively mimic the expert behavior of medical professionals—specifically, identifying the edges, boundaries, and spatial extents of specific anatomical structures. As a direct result, the pre-training process is highly interpretable, and the learned features are unequivocally expected to be maximally relevant and beneficial for downstream image segmentation tasks. We have conclusively demonstrated that the features learned through supervision can be used for direct inference to perform accurate organ segmentation on completely unseen CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; rigorously evaluated on three novel hospital datasets). Furthermore, these supervised features can also be efficiently fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (for classes completely unseen during pre-training) with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned through self-supervision (Table 4; comprehensively evaluated on 63 novel classes).

This seminal paper seeks to definitively answer the pivotal question: how well does a model transfer to diverse 3D medical imaging tasks IF it is pre-trained on large-scale, annotated 3D datasets? Naturally, to address this question, we must begin by creating the essential IF condition—a dataset of massive scale. Firstly, we construct a groundbreaking dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas 1.1) comprising 9,262 CT volumes with exhaustive per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven clinically critical tumor types. This large-scale, fully-annotated dataset uniquely enables us to train models in a fully supervised manner using multi-organ segmentation as the direct pretext task. As meticulously reviewed in Table 1, this dataset is vastly more extensive—considering both the sheer number of CT volumes and the diversity of annotated classes—than any previously available public dataset. Our scaling experiments in §3.1 definitively suggest that pre-training models on progressively larger annotated datasets can further and consistently improve transfer learning ability. Secondly, we develop and release a comprehensive suite of Supervised Pre-trained Models, termed SuPreM, that synergistically combine the advantages of large-scale data and precise per-voxel annotations, demonstrating their unequivocal efficacy across a broad range of target segmentation tasks. As reported in §3.2, several of the dominant segmentation model backbones have been pre-trained using our dataset and will be made publicly available to the research community. The current suite of pre-trained backbones includes U-Net (a CNN-type architecture), SegResNet (another CNN-type architecture), and Swin UNETR (a Transformer-type architecture), with plans to incorporate more backbones over time.

In prospective endeavors, we confidently anticipate that the continued expansion of such datasets and their annotations will not only powerfully enhance feature learning capabilities, as conclusively demonstrated in this study, but will also actively promote the development of more advanced AI algorithms and establish new benchmarks for the state of the art in terms of segmentation accuracy, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability, thereby accelerating the entire field.

2 BRIEF HISTORY: SUPERVISED PRE-TRAINING

In the major and ongoing initiative aimed at developing widely transferable and foundational AI models for the medical domain—increasingly known as Medical Foundation Models—one faces a critical and foundational decision: should the primary focus of pre-training be supervised or self-supervised? While human annotations undeniably and dramatically improve task-specific performance, such as for semantic segmentation, the optimal strategy for learning generic, transferable image features that can generalize across a wide spectrum of tasks has been a subject of intense debate. For 2D vision tasks, the seminal advent of ImageNet made it feasible to rigorously debate the comparative merits and limitations of supervised pre-trained models for transfer learning against their self-supervised counterparts. The learning objective of supervised pre-training is to explicitly minimize the discrepancy between AI predictions and the semantic labels provided by human annotators. Over the years, supervised pre-training on ImageNet has shown marked and consistent success in transfer learning across numerous domains. Moreover, this transfer learning ability can be further and substantially enhanced when models are trained on increasingly expansive and diverse datasets. In general, supervised pre-training exhibits clear and demonstrated advantages over self-supervised pre-training when sizable, high-quality annotated datasets are available. However, acquiring millions of manual annotations is notoriously labor-intensive, time-consuming, and challenging to scale—though certainly not impossible, as evidenced by several recent influential and large-scale annotation endeavors.

On the other hand, self-supervised pre-training offers a powerful alternative by enabling AI models to learn directly from vast quantities of raw, unlabeled data, thereby reducing the dependency on costly manual annotation. Self-supervised pre-training has historically lagged behind the state-of-the-art performance achieved by supervised pre-training on standard benchmarks. However, the recent rapid pace of progress in self-supervised methodologies has yielded models whose performance not only matches but, in certain contexts, surpasses those achieved by supervised pre-training. This progress has raised hopes that self-supervised pre-training could potentially replace the ubiquitous supervised paradigm in advanced computer vision. The significant caveat, however, remains the substantial demand for both data volume and computational power, often exceeding the resources typically available in academic research settings.

Supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated clear benefit for 2D medical image tasks after transfer learning. Unfortunately, its application has been severely constrained for 3D medical imaging tasks due to the fundamental lack of a true 3D counterpart to ImageNet. Although there exists a great number of raw, unlabeled medical images available in archives and repositories, annotating these 3D volumes at voxel-level precision remains a profoundly labor-intensive undertaking for medical professionals. Our foundational contribution of a large, annotated 3D dataset is poised to spark and inform the crucial debate of whether self-supervised or supervised pre-training leads to superior performance and data/computational efficiency—a debate that would simply not be possible without the invention of a dataset of such unprecedented scale and quality.

3 MATERIAL & METHOD

We constructed the groundbreaking AbdomenAtlas 1.1 dataset, comprising an extensive collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes and over 251,323 high-quality segmentation masks spanning 25 anatomical structures and 7 types of tumors. In parallel, we developed and released a comprehensive suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM) specifically designed to confer significant benefits for a wide array of 3D medical imaging tasks through transfer learning.

3.1 EXTENSIVE DATASET: ABDOMENATLAS 1.1

The creation of AbdomenAtlas 1.1 employed an interactive segmentation framework, which represents an advanced integration of cutting-edge AI algorithms and specialized human expertise, executed in a sophisticated semi-automatic procedure. We recruited a dedicated team of ten board-certified radiologists to perform and oversee manual annotations, ensuring the highest possible standard of annotation quality. Given the inherent complexity of annotating 3D volumetric data, rather than annotating the entire massive dataset voxel by voxel—an impractical endeavor—we directed the radiologists to focus their efforts on the most important CT volumes and the most clinically relevant regions therein. An importance score for each volume was intelligently computed, derived from quantitative metrics of model uncertainty, inter-annotator consistency, and regional overlap. Six junior radiologists meticulously revised the annotations initially predicted by the AI under the direct supervision of four senior radiologists, and in turn, the AI system improved its predictive capabilities by learning from these expert-revised annotations. This iterative, interactive procedure continued in cycles to systematically enhance the quality of annotations until no major revisions were required from the radiologist team. Subsequently, the four senior radiologists conducted a final comprehensive review of visualizations for all annotations, detecting and revising any major errors as needed before the dataset was finalized for release. The annotation tools employed in this rigorous process included both a licensed commercial platform from Pair and the open-source MONAI Label toolkit.

Table 1: Contribution #1: An extensive and unprecedented dataset of 9,262 CT volumes with exhaustive per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures. This dataset is truly unprecedented in terms of both data volume and annotation scale, providing over 251,323 precise organ/tumor masks and 2,789,975 annotated 2D slices that are sourced from a globally diverse set of 88 hospitals worldwide. In 2009, before the seminal advent of ImageNet, it was profoundly challenging to empower an AI model with generalized image representation using a small or even medium size of labeled data; we firmly believe the same limiting situation presents itself in 3D medical image analysis today. As clearly seen in the table, the annotations of existing public datasets are often limited, partial, and incomplete, and the CT volumes in these datasets are frequently biased toward specific populations, medical centers, and countries. Our meticulously constructed dataset directly mitigates these critical gaps, representing a significant and substantial leap forward for the entire field. The CT volumes integrated from datasets 1–17 form the comprehensive foundation of AbdomenAtlas 1.1.

AbdomenAtlas 1.1 presents an exceptional level of clinical and technical diversity because the CT volumes are sourced from 88 hospitals across the globe, encompassing various contrast enhancement phases including pre-contrast, portal venous, arterial, and delayed phases. Furthermore, we provide exhaustive per-voxel annotations for 25 distinct anatomical structures, including 16 abdominal organs, two thorax organs, five vascular structures, and two skeletal structures. We also provide high-quality pseudo annotations for seven critical types of tumors, namely liver, kidney, pancreatic, hepatic vessel, lung, and colon tumors, as well as kidney cysts. In total, more than 272.7 billion voxels are annotated in AbdomenAtlas 1.1, marking a monumental leap compared with the 4.3 billion voxels annotated in all the constituent public datasets combined, thereby amplifying the total annotation volume by a factor of 63.2. We are fully committed to releasing AbdomenAtlas 1.1 to the public to foster research. However, it is crucial to note that this dataset, while the largest public per-voxel annotated CT collection by a wide margin, still accounts for only approximately 0.01% of the CT volumes annually acquired in the United States alone. Therefore, continued and expanded cross-institutional collaboration remains absolutely crucial for accelerating data sharing, annotation efforts, and overall AI development in medicine.

3.2 A SUITE OF PRE-TRAINED MODELS: SUPREM

The unprecedented magnitude of our AbdomenAtlas 1.1, in terms of both data volume and annotation quality, provides a unique and powerful advantage: it enables the training of AI models using both supervised and self-supervised methodologies on a scale previously unimaginable. At the time of this writing, neither supervised nor self-supervised pre-training has been performed on a 3D medical dataset of this scale (9,262 volumetric scans). We have developed a comprehensive suite of models (termed SuPreM) pre-trained on the data and annotations from AbdomenAtlas 1.1, which leverage established and widely recognized CNN backbones, such as U-Net and SegResNet, as well as modern Transformer backbones, such as Swin UNETR. With the growing and undeniable trend of utilizing pre-trained models as foundational components, we have established and maintain a standardized, easily accessible model repository for sharing public model weights, including our full suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM). Releasing these pre-trained models constitutes a marked and valuable contribution in itself, as they offer a powerful alternative mechanism for knowledge sharing while rigorously protecting patient privacy and data confidentiality. In this study, all models within the SuPreM suite follow consistent and clearly defined pre-training and fine-tuning configurations as detailed below.

This observation aligns with findings from the broader medical imaging community, suggesting that significant exploration is still needed to advance the fundamental capabilities of segmentation backbones themselves. In summary, our SuPreM surpasses all existing 3D pre-trained models by a large and significant margin in transfer learning performance, irrespective of their underlying pre-training methodologies or data sources.

4 EXPERIMENT & ANALYSIS

4.1 DATA, ANNOTATION, AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY

Summary. We conclusively demonstrate the remarkable and multifaceted efficiency of supervised pre-training: (1) SuPreM trained with a minimal set of 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability essentially identical to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. (2) SuPreM requires 50% fewer manual annotations for achieving high-quality organ/tumor segmentation performance compared to self-supervised pre-training approaches.

Data efficiency for pre-training. As shown definitively in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires orders of magnitude less data (21 vs. 5,050 CT volumes) for the pretext task than state-of-the-art self-supervised pre-training. This profound discrepancy arises from the inherent and fundamental differences in their learning objectives and the information they leverage during training. Supervised pre-training benefits directly from explicit human annotations, which provide clear, unambiguous guidance for the specific task—in this case, semantic segmentation. The model learns rich features from both the image data and the accompanying annotations, which together offer strong and precise supervisory signals. On the other hand, self-supervised learning relies on various pretext tasks derived solely from the raw data structure itself, which may offer a more ambiguous and indirect learning signal, therefore necessitating a vastly larger number of examples to capture similarly meaningful and transferable features. Importantly, our finding establishes that supervised pre-training is also more scalable with increased data. When the supervised pre-training data is increased from 21 to 1,575 volumes, the transfer learning performance on TotalSegmentator improves substantially from 90.4% to 91.3%. In stark comparison, for self-supervised pre-training, an increase in data from 1,000 to 5,050 volumes yields only a marginal performance improvement from 89.7% to 89.9%. Therefore, supervised pre-training not only requires significantly less data than self-supervised pre-training but is also demonstrably more scalable and effective as the volume of annotated data increases.

Annotation efficiency for fine-tuning. We have rigorously assessed the annotation efficiency by fine-tuning both our SuPreM models and leading self-supervised models on the TotalSegmentator dataset. Specifically, SuPreM fine-tuned on 512 per-voxel annotated CT volumes can achieve segmentation performance similar to a self-supervised model fine-tuned on 1,024 annotated CT volumes. The performance advantage and annotation savings of SuPreM become even more pronounced and significant when the number of annotated volumes available for the target task is severely limited (e.g., 64, 128, or 256 volumes).

Computational efficiency for both pre-training and fine-tuning. This superior efficiency stems, in significant part, from the dramatically reduced data requirements inherent to supervised pre-training, as discussed above. As shown conclusively in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires only 40 GPU hours to achieve a transfer learning performance comparable to that of self-supervised pre-training, which requires 1,152 GPU hours—representing a computational increase factor of 28.8x. This implies that the image features learned by supervised pre-training are intrinsically more expressive and task-relevant, enabling the model to seamlessly and efficiently adapt across a myriad of challenging 3D image segmentation tasks with minimal annotated data required for fine-tuning. This computational efficiency makes supervised pre-training a compelling and practical choice for 3D medical image segmentation without compromising final model performance, especially when a large, high-quality annotated dataset is available for pre-training.

4.2 ENHANCED FEATURES FOR NOVEL DATASETS, CLASSES, AND TASKS

Summary. The features learned through our supervised pre-training paradigm manifest considerable generalizability and adaptability. These features can be used for direct inference to perform accurate organ segmentation on completely external datasets of CT volumes taken from different hospitals without any fine-tuning. Furthermore, these features can be efficiently fine-tuned to segment novel organ/tumor classes and to classify fine-grained tumor sub-types with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned by state-of-the-art self-supervision.

Direct inference on external datasets. AI models trained on a specific dataset often encounter significant challenges in generalizing to novel datasets when a marked distributional difference—referred to as a domain gap—exists between the training and test environments. While domain adaptation and generalization are active research areas to mitigate this challenge, we posit that the domain gap between CT volumes from different hospitals, while present, may not be as extreme as those encountered in general computer vision. This is largely due to the relatively standardized nature of computed tomography as an imaging modality, where Hounsfield unit (pixel) intensity conveys consistent and physically meaningful anatomical information. AbdomenAtlas 1.1 presents impressive intrinsic diversity, covering CT volumes with wide variations in contrast enhancement protocols, reconstruction kernels, CT scanner manufacturers and models, and acquisition parameters. This exceptional breadth and diversity are imperative for developing an AI model with the robustness required to accommodate the realistic variations present in novel, unseen clinical datasets. We conduct rigorous external validation on several novel datasets sourced from hospitals in Switzerland and East Asia to stringently challenge the AI model on data distributions it has never encountered during training. This result is referred to as out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For a strong comparison, we also report the result achieved by dataset-specific AI models—those individually trained from scratch on each specific target dataset—referred to as independently and identically distributed (IID) performance, often considered an upper bound in domain transfer literature. As shown conclusively in Table 3, our SuPreM generalizes exceptionally well to novel data distributions without requiring any further fine-tuning or adaptation, consistently delivering OOD performance that matches or even exceeds that of its IID counterparts.

[Table 3 description placeholder]
Table 3: Direct inference performance on three completely external datasets. We conduct comprehensive external validation across four hospitals worldwide. Specifically, our SuPreM—trained on the full 9,262 CT volumes—is directly applied (without any fine-tuning) for inference on three external datasets: TotalSegmentator (representing a Central European population from Switzerland), DAP Atlas (a Central European population from Germany), and a proprietary dataset (a North American population from the United States), with performance measured by DSC scores. For each target dataset, we compare the out-of-distribution (OOD) performance obtained by SuPreM with the independently and identically distributed (IID) performance obtained by AI models trained directly on that specific dataset. We find definitively that SuPreM can generalize remarkably well across these external datasets, yielding comparable or even superior performance to the IID counterparts, as evidenced by rigorous one-sample t-test results.

Fine-tuning on novel classes. The core value of transfer learning lies in the ability to efficiently fine-tune pre-trained models on novel scenarios, such as novel anatomical classes, image modalities, or vision tasks that were completely unseen during the original pre-training phase. In this study, we rigorously evaluate the proficiency of SuPreM when transferred to a wide and challenging variety of novel classes for 3D image segmentation tasks. These novel classes include 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from the TotalSegmentator dataset, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor subtypes from our proprietary dataset. As shown conclusively in Table 4, our SuPreM, supervised pre-trained on 25 classes, transfers significantly better to these diverse novel classes than state-of-the-art self-supervised models pre-trained on raw, unlabeled data. We find that the pretext task of segmentation itself powerfully enhances the model's inherent capability for segmenting novel classes. The benefit of this same-task transfer learning—where segmentation serves as both the pretext and the target task—is much more straightforward, interpretable, and effective than transfer from other, less related pretext tasks such as contextual prediction, mask image modeling, or instance discrimination. Through full supervision in segmentation tasks, the model learns a deep and generalizable understanding of the fundamental "concept of objectness," wherein the model gains a profound understanding of what universally characterizes an object in an image. The model does not merely memorize predefined objects but begins to understand the foundational visual factors that define objects in general. Such factors include texture, boundary, shape, size, and other low-level visual cues that are universally essential for image segmentation. This resonates strongly with our core assertion in the introduction: just as classification-based features from ImageNet transfer optimally for classification tasks, segmentation-based features are unequivocally optimal for segmentation tasks. Our findings do not negate the potential future value of self-supervised pre-training. Should self-supervised pre-training on 9,262 CT volumes eventually outperform supervised pre-training in model transferability, its value would be further highlighted by eliminating the need for manual annotations altogether.

Table 4: Fine-tuning SuPreM on 66 novel, unseen classes. Following the standard transfer learning paradigm, we fine-tune our SuPreM on segmentation tasks for novel classes that were completely absent during pre-training. These tasks include segmenting 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from TotalSegmentator, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor types from the proprietary dataset. It is critical to note that none of these 66 classes were part of the original 25-class pre-training of SuPreM. The results demonstrate that the pretext task of segmentation itself powerfully enhances the model's capability for segmenting novel-class objects. This benefit is much more direct and understandable than transfer from self-supervised tasks like contextual prediction or instance discrimination. We hypothesize this is because the model learns a general concept of "objectness" through full supervision. This diversity in texture patterns is reflected in the values of the Area Under the Curve (AUC) that we obtained. For all three sub-types of pancreatic tumors, SuPreM (in red) demonstrates superior and more robust performance over the leading self-supervised model (in gray), conclusively showcasing its effectiveness even for fine-grained tumor classification tasks.

Fine-tuning on novel tasks. We have further investigated the cross-task transfer learning ability of SuPreM between the primary task of organ segmentation and the distinct, challenging task of fine-grained tumor classification. The semantic and functional distance between these two tasks is much larger than transferring among different segmentation tasks, presenting a stringent test of feature generality. Benchmarking fine-grained tumor classification is particularly challenging due to the extreme scarcity of detailed annotations in public datasets. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we employed our large-scale proprietary dataset, which comprises 3,577 meticulously annotated pancreatic tumors, including detailed subtypes: 1,704 PDACs, 945 Cysts, and 928 PanNETs. This extensive and unique dataset enabled us to thoroughly and rigorously assess the cross-task transfer learning ability of SuPreM. Figure 3 shows conclusively that supervised models (SuPreM) transfer substantially better to the target classification tasks than leading self-supervised models, leading to consistently improved Area Under the Curve (AUC) for identifying each specific tumor type. Detailed analysis reveals a sensitivity of 86.1% and specificity of 95.4% for PDAC detection using SuPreM. This performance notably surpasses the average radiologist's performance in PDAC identification as reported in recent literature, demonstrating a substantial 27.6% improvement in sensitivity and a 4.4% improvement in specificity. This performance leap is particularly critical for tumor imaging tasks because annotating tumors at this level of detail requires significantly more expert effort and often depends on the availability of confirmatory pathology reports.

5 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION

This foundational study comprehensively examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models that are pre-trained on large-scale annotated 3D datasets and subsequently fine-tuned for diverse 3D medical image segmentation tasks. We begin by constructing and introducing AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an extensive and unprecedented collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes accompanied by high-quality, per-voxel annotations. The magnitude of this dataset is truly unprecedented regarding data volume (2,789,975 images), granularity of annotations (251,323 masks), and inclusive clinical diversity (spanning 88 hospitals worldwide). This dataset directly facilitates the development and release of a comprehensive suite of pre-trained models, termed SuPreM, which can be effectively and efficiently transferred to a broad spectrum of 3D medical image segmentation tasks. Notably, SuPreM transfers significantly better than all existing 3D pre-trained models by a large and consistent margin, especially when transferred to challenging, under-annotated target datasets. The supervised model trained with a minimal set of just 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates a transfer learning ability essentially equivalent to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, irrefutably highlighting the remarkable and unparalleled efficiency of the supervised pre-training paradigm. We also conclusively demonstrate that the features learned through supervision can be used for direct inference with high effectiveness on completely external datasets and can be fine-tuned to segment novel anatomical classes and classify multiple types of tumors with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned by state-of-the-art self-supervision.

Title: How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks? A Comprehensive Investigation into Large-Scale Annotated Pre-Training

Abstract
The paradigm of pre-training models on large, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuning them for specific target tasks has become a cornerstone of modern transfer learning in computer vision. For instance, a model pre-trained on the extensive ImageNet dataset and then fine-tuned for the PASCAL VOC challenge consistently and significantly outperforms a model trained exclusively on PASCAL from a random initialization. While ImageNet pre-training has demonstrated enormous success across numerous 2D vision applications, it is fundamentally limited to two-dimensional imagery and is primarily designed for image classification objectives. Consequently, when transferring these learned features to more diverse and complex three-dimensional tasks, such as volumetric medical image segmentation, performance is inevitably compromised due to the substantial deviation from the original ImageNet context. A pivotal and long-standing challenge in the field of 3D medical imaging has been the stark absence of large-scale, meticulously annotated 3D datasets that can rival the scale and impact of ImageNet for foundational model pre-training. To decisively overcome this critical challenge, this work makes two major and transformative contributions. Firstly, we construct and introduce AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an unprecedented dataset that comprises a vast collection of 9,262 three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, each accompanied by high-quality, per-voxel annotations for 25 distinct anatomical structures and pseudo-annotations for seven clinically significant tumor types. Secondly, we develop and release a comprehensive suite of models, pre-trained on our expansive AbdomenAtlas 1.1, specifically designed for transfer learning in 3D medical imaging. Our rigorous preliminary analyses definitively indicate that a supervised model trained with a remarkably small set of just 21 CT volumes, 672 segmentation masks, and 40 GPU hours achieves a transfer learning ability virtually identical to a state-of-the-art self-supervised model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and a massive 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, we conclusively demonstrate that the transfer learning ability of supervised models exhibits a powerful scaling law, improving substantially and consistently as the size of the annotated pre-training dataset increases, thereby achieving significantly and uniformly better performance than all preexisting pre-trained models, irrespective of their underlying pre-training methodologies or data sources. We are confident that this foundational study will catalyze and facilitate collective, global efforts in constructing even larger 3D medical datasets and accelerate the widespread release of powerful supervised pre-trained models, ultimately driving progress in medical AI.

1 INTRODUCTION

The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm stands as a widely adopted and profoundly effective framework for transfer learning in artificial intelligence. Given the intrinsic relationships and shared visual primitives across different computer vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one large, diverse dataset is expected to confer substantial benefits when adapted to another. Over the past several decades, pre-training has been undeniably important and instrumental in the rapid development of AI capabilities. For conventional 2D vision tasks, practitioners typically have two principal options: (i) supervised pre-training and (ii) self-supervised pre-training. However, for the critically important domain of 3D vision tasks, option (i) has historically been largely unavailable, primarily due to the profound and persistent lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets of sufficient scale and quality.

Supervised pre-training possesses the inherent capability to learn rich, discriminative image features that are highly transferable to a wide array of downstream target tasks. It has been the established common practice for years to pre-train models using the ImageNet dataset and then fine-tune the model on target tasks which often possess limited training data, such as PASCAL VOC. However, two fundamental and well-documented challenges arise with ImageNet-based pre-training for 3D medical applications. Firstly, ImageNet is predominantly composed of 2D natural images, leaving a palpable and significant void in the availability of large-scale 3D datasets and consequently, a lack of systematic investigation into 3D-specific transfer learning dynamics. Secondly, since ImageNet is explicitly intended for image classification, its benefit for pixel-wise prediction tasks like segmentation (and other dense prediction vision tasks) can be somewhat compromised and suboptimal. If such an ImageNet-like dataset existed—but formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models are unequivocally expected to transfer far more effectively to 3D medical image segmentation than self-supervised ones, for two compelling and fundamental reasons.

1. Supervised pre-training is dramatically more efficient in terms of both data and computational resource consumption because of its explicit and well-defined learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training offers the advantage of learning features without manual annotation, it invariably requires an enormous corpus of unlabeled data to achieve competitive performance. Extracting meaningful and generalizable features directly from raw, unlabeled data is an inherently challenging and noisy process. Unlabeled data often contain a high degree of redundancy and significant noise, which can substantially complicate and slow down the feature learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training consistently calls for vastly greater computational resources and time to match the superior outcomes achieved by efficient supervised pre-training. We have definitively quantified this improved data and computational efficiency from the dual perspectives of both the pre-training phase (Figure 2a; demonstrating a 99.6% reduction in required data) and the fine-tuning phase (Figure 2b; showing 66% less computation). Specifically, our supervised model trained with merely 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates a transfer learning ability essentially equivalent to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, irrefutably highlighting the remarkable and unparalleled efficiency of the supervised pre-training approach.

2. Supervised pre-training directly enables the model to learn image features that are intrinsically relevant and optimally suited for the target task of image segmentation. In contrast, self-supervised pre-training must indirectly extract image features from raw, unlabeled data using various pretext tasks such as mask image modeling, instance discrimination, and others. Despite their demonstrated efficacy in learning representations, these pretext tasks share no obvious or direct semantic relation to the ultimate target task of image segmentation. In stark contrast, supervised pre-training utilizes semantically meaningful and precise annotations (e.g., organ and tumor segmentation maps) as direct supervision, enabling the model to effectively mimic the expert behavior of medical professionals—specifically, identifying the edges, boundaries, and spatial extents of specific anatomical structures. As a direct result, the pre-training process is highly interpretable, and the learned features are unequivocally expected to be maximally relevant and beneficial for downstream image segmentation tasks. We have conclusively demonstrated that the features learned through supervision can be used for direct inference to perform accurate organ segmentation on completely unseen CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; rigorously evaluated on three novel hospital datasets). Furthermore, these supervised features can also be efficiently fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (for classes completely unseen during pre-training) with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned through self-supervision (Table 4; comprehensively evaluated on 63 novel classes).

This seminal paper seeks to definitively answer the pivotal question: how well does a model transfer to diverse 3D medical imaging tasks IF it is pre-trained on large-scale, annotated 3D datasets? Naturally, to address this question, we must begin by creating the essential IF condition—a dataset of massive scale. Firstly, we construct a groundbreaking dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas 1.1) comprising 9,262 CT volumes with exhaustive per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven clinically critical tumor types. This large-scale, fully-annotated dataset uniquely enables us to train models in a fully supervised manner using multi-organ segmentation as the direct pretext task. As meticulously reviewed in Table 1, this dataset is vastly more extensive—considering both the sheer number of CT volumes and the diversity of annotated classes—than any previously available public dataset. Our scaling experiments in §3.1 definitively suggest that pre-training models on progressively larger annotated datasets can further and consistently improve transfer learning ability. Secondly, we develop and release a comprehensive suite of Supervised Pre-trained Models, termed SuPreM, that synergistically combine the advantages of large-scale data and precise per-voxel annotations, demonstrating their unequivocal efficacy across a broad range of target segmentation tasks. As reported in §3.2, several of the dominant segmentation model backbones have been pre-trained using our dataset and will be made publicly available to the research community. The current suite of pre-trained backbones includes U-Net (a CNN-type architecture), SegResNet (another CNN-type architecture), and Swin UNETR (a Transformer-type architecture), with plans to incorporate more backbones over time.

In prospective endeavors, we confidently anticipate that the continued expansion of such datasets and their annotations will not only powerfully enhance feature learning capabilities, as conclusively demonstrated in this study, but will also actively promote the development of more advanced AI algorithms and establish new benchmarks for the state of the art in terms of segmentation accuracy, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability, thereby accelerating the entire field.

2 BRIEF HISTORY: SUPERVISED PRE-TRAINING

In the major and ongoing initiative aimed at developing widely transferable and foundational AI models for the medical domain—increasingly known as Medical Foundation Models—one faces a critical and foundational decision: should the primary focus of pre-training be supervised or self-supervised? While human annotations undeniably and dramatically improve task-specific performance, such as for semantic segmentation, the optimal strategy for learning generic, transferable image features that can generalize across a wide spectrum of tasks has been a subject of intense debate. For 2D vision tasks, the seminal advent of ImageNet made it feasible to rigorously debate the comparative merits and limitations of supervised pre-trained models for transfer learning against their self-supervised counterparts. The learning objective of supervised pre-training is to explicitly minimize the discrepancy between AI predictions and the semantic labels provided by human annotators. Over the years, supervised pre-training on ImageNet has shown marked and consistent success in transfer learning across numerous domains. Moreover, this transfer learning ability can be further and substantially enhanced when models are trained on increasingly expansive and diverse datasets. In general, supervised pre-training exhibits clear and demonstrated advantages over self-supervised pre-training when sizable, high-quality annotated datasets are available. However, acquiring millions of manual annotations is notoriously labor-intensive, time-consuming, and challenging to scale—though certainly not impossible, as evidenced by several recent influential and large-scale annotation endeavors.

On the other hand, self-supervised pre-training offers a powerful alternative by enabling AI models to learn directly from vast quantities of raw, unlabeled data, thereby reducing the dependency on costly manual annotation. Self-supervised pre-training has historically lagged behind the state-of-the-art performance achieved by supervised pre-training on standard benchmarks. However, the recent rapid pace of progress in self-supervised methodologies has yielded models whose performance not only matches but, in certain contexts, surpasses those achieved by supervised pre-training. This progress has raised hopes that self-supervised pre-training could potentially replace the ubiquitous supervised paradigm in advanced computer vision. The significant caveat, however, remains the substantial demand for both data volume and computational power, often exceeding the resources typically available in academic research settings.

Supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated clear benefit for 2D medical image tasks after transfer learning. Unfortunately, its application has been severely constrained for 3D medical imaging tasks due to the fundamental lack of a true 3D counterpart to ImageNet. Although there exists a great number of raw, unlabeled medical images available in archives and repositories, annotating these 3D volumes at voxel-level precision remains a profoundly labor-intensive undertaking for medical professionals. Our foundational contribution of a large, annotated 3D dataset is poised to spark and inform the crucial debate of whether self-supervised or supervised pre-training leads to superior performance and data/computational efficiency—a debate that would simply not be possible without the invention of a dataset of such unprecedented scale and quality.

3 MATERIAL & METHOD

We constructed the groundbreaking AbdomenAtlas 1.1 dataset, comprising an extensive collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes and over 251,323 high-quality segmentation masks spanning 25 anatomical structures and 7 types of tumors. In parallel, we developed and released a comprehensive suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM) specifically designed to confer significant benefits for a wide array of 3D medical imaging tasks through transfer learning.

3.1 EXTENSIVE DATASET: ABDOMENATLAS 1.1

The creation of AbdomenAtlas 1.1 employed an interactive segmentation framework, which represents an advanced integration of cutting-edge AI algorithms and specialized human expertise, executed in a sophisticated semi-automatic procedure. We recruited a dedicated team of ten board-certified radiologists to perform and oversee manual annotations, ensuring the highest possible standard of annotation quality. Given the inherent complexity of annotating 3D volumetric data, rather than annotating the entire massive dataset voxel by voxel—an impractical endeavor—we directed the radiologists to focus their efforts on the most important CT volumes and the most clinically relevant regions therein. An importance score for each volume was intelligently computed, derived from quantitative metrics of model uncertainty, inter-annotator consistency, and regional overlap. Six junior radiologists meticulously revised the annotations initially predicted by the AI under the direct supervision of four senior radiologists, and in turn, the AI system improved its predictive capabilities by learning from these expert-revised annotations. This iterative, interactive procedure continued in cycles to systematically enhance the quality of annotations until no major revisions were required from the radiologist team. Subsequently, the four senior radiologists conducted a final comprehensive review of visualizations for all annotations, detecting and revising any major errors as needed before the dataset was finalized for release. The annotation tools employed in this rigorous process included both a licensed commercial platform from Pair and the open-source MONAI Label toolkit.

Table 1: Contribution #1: An extensive and unprecedented dataset of 9,262 CT volumes with exhaustive per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures. This dataset is truly unprecedented in terms of both data volume and annotation scale, providing over 251,323 precise organ/tumor masks and 2,789,975 annotated 2D slices that are sourced from a globally diverse set of 88 hospitals worldwide. In 2009, before the seminal advent of ImageNet, it was profoundly challenging to empower an AI model with generalized image representation using a small or even medium size of labeled data; we firmly believe the same limiting situation presents itself in 3D medical image analysis today. As clearly seen in the table, the annotations of existing public datasets are often limited, partial, and incomplete, and the CT volumes in these datasets are frequently biased toward specific populations, medical centers, and countries. Our meticulously constructed dataset directly mitigates these critical gaps, representing a significant and substantial leap forward for the entire field. AbdomenAtlas 1.1 presents an exceptional level of clinical and technical diversity because the CT volumes are sourced from 88 hospitals across the globe, encompassing various contrast enhancement phases including pre-contrast, portal venous, arterial, and delayed phases. Furthermore, we provide exhaustive per-voxel annotations for 25 distinct anatomical structures, including 16 abdominal organs, two thorax organs, five vascular structures, and two skeletal structures. We also provide high-quality pseudo annotations for seven critical types of tumors, namely liver, kidney, pancreatic, hepatic vessel, lung, and colon tumors, as well as kidney cysts. In total, more than 272.7 billion voxels are annotated in AbdomenAtlas 1.1, marking a monumental leap compared with the 4.3 billion voxels annotated in all the constituent public datasets combined, thereby amplifying the total annotation volume by a factor of 63.2. However, it is crucial to note that this dataset, while the largest public per-voxel annotated CT collection by a wide margin, still accounts for only approximately 0.01% of the CT volumes annually acquired in the United States alone. Therefore, continued and expanded cross-institutional collaboration remains absolutely crucial for accelerating data sharing, annotation efforts, and overall AI development in medicine.

3.2 A SUITE OF PRE-TRAINED MODELS: SUPREM

The unprecedented magnitude of our AbdomenAtlas 1.1, in terms of both data volume and annotation quality, provides a unique and powerful advantage: it enables the training of AI models using both supervised and self-supervised methodologies on a scale previously unimaginable. At the time of this writing, neither supervised nor self-supervised pre-training has been performed on a 3D medical dataset of this scale (9,262 volumetric scans). We have developed a comprehensive suite of models (termed SuPreM) pre-trained on the data and annotations from AbdomenAtlas 1.1, which leverage established and widely recognized CNN backbones, such as U-Net and SegResNet, as well as modern Transformer backbones, such as Swin UNETR. With the growing and undeniable trend of utilizing pre-trained models as foundational components, we have established and maintain a standardized, easily accessible model repository for sharing public model weights, including our full suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM). Releasing these pre-trained models constitutes a marked and valuable contribution in itself, as they offer a powerful alternative mechanism for knowledge sharing while rigorously protecting patient privacy and data confidentiality. In this study, all models within the SuPreM suite follow consistent and clearly defined pre-training and fine-tuning configurations as detailed below.

This observation aligns with findings from the broader medical imaging community, suggesting that significant exploration is still needed to advance the fundamental capabilities of segmentation backbones themselves. 4 EXPERIMENT & ANALYSIS

4.1 DATA, ANNOTATION, AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY

Summary. We conclusively demonstrate the remarkable and multifaceted efficiency of supervised pre-training: (1) SuPreM trained with a minimal set of 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability essentially identical to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. (2) SuPreM requires 50% fewer manual annotations for achieving high-quality organ/tumor segmentation performance compared to self-supervised pre-training approaches.

Data efficiency for pre-training. As shown definitively in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires orders of magnitude less data (21 vs. 5,050 CT volumes) for the pretext task than state-of-the-art self-supervised pre-training. This profound discrepancy arises from the inherent and fundamental differences in their learning objectives and the information they leverage during training. Supervised pre-training benefits directly from explicit human annotations, which provide clear, unambiguous guidance for the specific task—in this case, semantic segmentation. The model learns rich features from both the image data and the accompanying annotations, which together offer strong and precise supervisory signals. On the other hand, self-supervised learning relies on various pretext tasks derived solely from the raw data structure itself, which may offer a more ambiguous and indirect learning signal, therefore necessitating a vastly larger number of examples to capture similarly meaningful and transferable features. Importantly, our finding establishes that supervised pre-training is also more scalable with increased data. When the supervised pre-training data is increased from 21 to 1,575 volumes, the transfer learning performance on TotalSegmentator improves substantially from 90.4% to 91.3%. In stark comparison, for self-supervised pre-training, an increase in data from 1,000 to 5,050 volumes yields only a marginal performance improvement from 89.7% to 89.9%. Therefore, supervised pre-training not only requires significantly less data than self-supervised pre-training but is also demonstrably more scalable and effective as the volume of annotated data increases.

Annotation efficiency for fine-tuning. We have rigorously assessed the annotation efficiency by fine-tuning both our SuPreM models and leading self-supervised models on the TotalSegmentator dataset. Specifically, SuPreM fine-tuned on 512 per-voxel annotated CT volumes can achieve segmentation performance similar to a self-supervised model fine-tuned on 1,024 annotated CT volumes. The performance advantage and annotation savings of SuPreM become even more pronounced and significant when the number of annotated volumes available for the target task is severely limited (e.g., 64, 128, or 256 volumes).

Computational efficiency for both pre-training and fine-tuning. This superior efficiency stems, in significant part, from the dramatically reduced data requirements inherent to supervised pre-training, as discussed above. As shown conclusively in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires only 40 GPU hours to achieve a transfer learning performance comparable to that of self-supervised pre-training, which requires 1,152 GPU hours—representing a computational increase factor of 28.8x. This implies that the image features learned by supervised pre-training are intrinsically more expressive and task-relevant, enabling the model to seamlessly and efficiently adapt across a myriad of challenging 3D image segmentation tasks with minimal annotated data required for fine-tuning. This computational efficiency makes supervised pre-training a compelling and practical choice for 3D medical image segmentation without compromising final model performance, especially when a large, high-quality annotated dataset is available for pre-training.

4.2 ENHANCED FEATURES FOR NOVEL DATASETS, CLASSES, AND TASKS

Summary. The features learned through our supervised pre-training paradigm manifest considerable generalizability and adaptability. These features can be used for direct inference to perform accurate organ segmentation on completely external datasets of CT volumes taken from different hospitals without any fine-tuning. Furthermore, these features can be efficiently fine-tuned to segment novel organ/tumor classes and to classify fine-grained tumor sub-types with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned by state-of-the-art self-supervision.

Direct inference on external datasets. AI models trained on a specific dataset often encounter significant challenges in generalizing to novel datasets when a marked distributional difference—referred to as a domain gap—exists between the training and test environments. While domain adaptation and generalization are active research areas to mitigate this challenge, we posit that the domain gap between CT volumes from different hospitals, while present, may not be as extreme as those encountered in general computer vision. This is largely due to the relatively standardized nature of computed tomography as an imaging modality, where Hounsfield unit (pixel) intensity conveys consistent and physically meaningful anatomical information. AbdomenAtlas 1.1 presents impressive intrinsic diversity, covering CT volumes with wide variations in contrast enhancement protocols, reconstruction kernels, CT scanner manufacturers and models, and acquisition parameters. This exceptional breadth and diversity are imperative for developing an AI model with the robustness required to accommodate the realistic variations present in novel, unseen clinical datasets. We conduct rigorous external validation on several novel datasets sourced from hospitals in Switzerland and East Asia to stringently challenge the AI model on data distributions it has never encountered during training. This result is referred to as out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For a strong comparison, we also report the result achieved by dataset-specific AI models—those individually trained from scratch on each specific target dataset—referred to as independently and identically distributed (IID) performance, often considered an upper bound in domain transfer literature. As shown conclusively in Table 3, our SuPreM generalizes exceptionally well to novel data distributions without requiring any further fine-tuning or adaptation, consistently delivering OOD performance that matches or even exceeds that of its IID counterparts.

[Table 3 description placeholder]
Table 3: Direct inference performance on three completely external datasets. We conduct comprehensive external validation across four hospitals worldwide. Specifically, our SuPreM—trained on the full 9,262 CT volumes—is directly applied (without any fine-tuning) for inference on three external datasets: TotalSegmentator (representing a Central European population from Switzerland), DAP Atlas (a Central European population from Germany), and a proprietary dataset (a North American population from the United States), with performance measured by DSC scores. For each target dataset, we compare the out-of-distribution (OOD) performance obtained by SuPreM with the independently and identically distributed (IID) performance obtained by AI models trained directly on that specific dataset. We find definitively that SuPreM can generalize remarkably well across these external datasets, yielding comparable or even superior performance to the IID counterparts, as evidenced by rigorous one-sample t-test results.

Fine-tuning on novel classes. The core value of transfer learning lies in the ability to efficiently fine-tune pre-trained models on novel scenarios, such as novel anatomical classes, image modalities, or vision tasks that were completely unseen during the original pre-training phase. In this study, we rigorously evaluate the proficiency of SuPreM when transferred to a wide and challenging variety of novel classes for 3D image segmentation tasks. These novel classes include 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from the TotalSegmentator dataset, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor subtypes from our proprietary dataset. As shown conclusively in Table 4, our SuPreM, supervised pre-trained on 25 classes, transfers significantly better to these diverse novel classes than state-of-the-art self-supervised models pre-trained on raw, unlabeled data. We find that the pretext task of segmentation itself powerfully enhances the model's inherent capability for segmenting novel classes. The benefit of this same-task transfer learning—where segmentation serves as both the pretext and the target task—is much more straightforward, interpretable, and effective than transfer from other, less related pretext tasks such as contextual prediction, mask image modeling, or instance discrimination. Through full supervision in segmentation tasks, the model learns a deep and generalizable understanding of the fundamental "concept of objectness," wherein the model gains a profound understanding of what universally characterizes an object in an image. The model does not merely memorize predefined objects but begins to understand the foundational visual factors that define objects in general. Such factors include texture, boundary, shape, size, and other low-level visual cues that are universally essential for image segmentation. This resonates strongly with our core assertion in the introduction: just as classification-based features from ImageNet transfer optimally for classification tasks, segmentation-based features are unequivocally optimal for segmentation tasks. Our findings do not negate the potential future value of self-supervised pre-training. Should self-supervised pre-training on 9,262 CT volumes eventually outperform supervised pre-training in model transferability, its value would be further highlighted by eliminating the need for manual annotations altogether.

[Table 4 description placeholder]
Table 4: Fine-tuning SuPreM on 66 novel, unseen classes. Following the standard transfer learning paradigm, we fine-tune our SuPreM on segmentation tasks for novel classes that were completely absent during pre-training. These tasks include segmenting 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from TotalSegmentator, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor types from the proprietary dataset. It is critical to note that none of these 66 classes were part of the original 25-class pre-training of SuPreM. The results demonstrate that the pretext task of segmentation itself powerfully enhances the model's capability for segmenting novel-class objects. This benefit is much more direct and understandable than transfer from self-supervised tasks like contextual prediction or instance discrimination. We hypothesize this is because the model learns a general concept of "objectness" through full supervision. An independent two-sample t-test was performed between the self-supervised and supervised pre-trained models, with significant results highlighted.

[Figure 3 description placeholder]
Figure 3: Fine-tuning SuPreM for the challenging task of fine-grained tumor classification. We plot receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to evaluate the transfer learning performance for discriminating between tumor subtypes. Detecting Cysts and PanNETs presents additional challenges for AI because these lesions exhibit a greater variety of texture and appearance patterns than PDACs. This diversity in texture patterns is reflected in the values of the Area Under the Curve (AUC) that we obtained. For all three sub-types of pancreatic tumors, SuPreM (in red) demonstrates superior and more robust performance over the leading self-supervised model (in gray), conclusively showcasing its effectiveness even for fine-grained tumor classification tasks.

Fine-tuning on novel tasks. We have further investigated the cross-task transfer learning ability of SuPreM between the primary task of organ segmentation and the distinct, challenging task of fine-grained tumor classification. The semantic and functional distance between these two tasks is much larger than transferring among different segmentation tasks, presenting a stringent test of feature generality. Benchmarking fine-grained tumor classification is particularly challenging due to the extreme scarcity of detailed annotations in public datasets. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we employed our large-scale proprietary dataset, which comprises 3,577 meticulously annotated pancreatic tumors, including detailed subtypes: 1,704 PDACs, 945 Cysts, and 928 PanNETs. This extensive and unique dataset enabled us to thoroughly and rigorously assess the cross-task transfer learning ability of SuPreM. Figure 3 shows conclusively that supervised models (SuPreM) transfer substantially better to the target classification tasks than leading self-supervised models, leading to consistently improved Area Under the Curve (AUC) for identifying each specific tumor type. Detailed analysis reveals a sensitivity of 86.1% and specificity of 95.4% for PDAC detection using SuPreM. This performance notably surpasses the average radiologist's performance in PDAC identification as reported in recent literature, demonstrating a substantial 27.6% improvement in sensitivity and a 4.4% improvement in specificity. This performance leap is particularly critical for tumor imaging tasks because annotating tumors at this level of detail requires significantly more expert effort and often depends on the availability of confirmatory pathology reports.

5 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION

This foundational study comprehensively examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models that are pre-trained on large-scale annotated 3D datasets and subsequently fine-tuned for diverse 3D medical image segmentation tasks. We begin by constructing and introducing AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an extensive and unprecedented collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes accompanied by high-quality, per-voxel annotations. The magnitude of this dataset is truly unprecedented regarding data volume (2,789,975 images), granularity of annotations (251,323 masks), and inclusive clinical diversity (spanning 88 hospitals worldwide). This dataset directly facilitates the development and release of a comprehensive suite of pre-trained models, termed SuPreM, which can be effectively and efficiently transferred to a broad spectrum of 3D medical image segmentation tasks. Notably, SuPreM transfers significantly better than all existing 3D pre-trained models by a large and consistent margin, especially when transferred to challenging, under-annotated target datasets. The supervised model trained with a minimal set of just 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates a transfer learning ability essentially equivalent to a self-supervised model trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, irrefutably highlighting the remarkable and unparalleled efficiency of the supervised pre-training paradigm. We also conclusively demonstrate that the features learned through supervision can be used for direct inference with high effectiveness on completely external datasets and can be fine-tuned to segment novel anatomical classes and classify multiple types of tumors with higher accuracy and requiring less annotated data than features learned by state-of-the-art self-supervision.
