\title{Know2BIO: A Comprehensive Dual-View Benchmark for Evolving Biomedical Knowledge Graphs}

\begin{abstract}
Knowledge graphs (KGs) have definitively emerged as the most powerful and essential framework for representing and integrating complex biomedical information. However, assembling KGs from diverse sources remains a significant and persistent challenge in several critical aspects, including entity alignment, scalability, and the absolute necessity for continuous updates to keep pace with rapid scientific advancements. Moreover, the representative power of KGs is fundamentally and severely limited by the scarcity of multi-modal data integration. To decisively overcome these challenges, we propose \bmkgname, a comprehensive general-purpose heterogeneous KG benchmark for the biomedical domain. \bmkgname~integrates data from 30 diverse and authoritative sources, capturing intricate relationships across 11 distinct biomedical categories. It currently consists of a substantial \textasciitilde219,000 nodes and \textasciitilde6,200,000 edges. \bmkgname~is uniquely capable of user-directed automated updating to accurately reflect the very latest knowledge in biomedical science. Furthermore, \bmkgname~is accompanied by extensive multi-modal data: node features including detailed text descriptions, protein and compound sequences and structures, thereby fully enabling the utilization of emerging natural language processing methods and advanced multi-modal data integration strategies. We evaluate a wide range of KG representation models on \bmkgname, conclusively demonstrating its superior effectiveness as a definitive benchmark for KG representation learning in the biomedical field.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A knowledge graph (KG), which represents entities as nodes and their relations as edges, is commonly referred to through "triples" ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$), where a head entity ($\tth$) is connected to a tail entity ($\ttt$) by a relation ($\ttr$). There is an undeniably increasing and dominant presence of using KGs to represent the data in knowledge bases (KBs). In biomedical science, KBs capture essential knowledge in domains such as omics (e.g., genomics (\cite{Cunningham2021Ensembl2, Seal2022GenenamesorgTH, OLeary2015ReferenceS, Sayers2021GenBank}), proteomics (\cite{Bateman2022UniProtTU, Fabregat2013TheRP, Szklarczyk2018STRINGVP}), metabolomics (\cite{Powell2022TheMW, Jewison2013SMPDB2B, Wishart2021HMDB5T})), pharmacology (e.g., drug designs (\cite{Wishart2017DrugBank5A, Kanehisa2016KEGGNP, Davis2022ComparativeTD}, drug targets \cite{Wishart2017DrugBank5A, Zhou2021TherapeuticTD}), adverse effects (\cite{Giangreco2021ADO, Kuhn2015TheSD})), physiology (e.g., biological processes (\cite{Carbon2020TheGO, Kanehisa2016KEGGNP, Fabregat2013TheRP}), and anatomical components (\cite{Haendel2014UnificationOM, Mungall2012UberonAI, Lipscomb2000MedicalSH, Bastian2020TheBS}), playing a vital and indispensable role in advancing biomedical research and data science.

This knowledge has been successfully employed by predictive algorithms to discover new and valuable biomedical knowledge (e.g., protein interactions, pathogenic genetic variants). To enable this critical knowledge discovery, task-relevant data must be integrated from multiple sources such as drug-relevant data in KGs for predicting drug targets (\cite{drkg2020, Yan2021DrugRF, Mayers2022DesignAA, Himmelstein2017SystematicIO, Zong2022BETAAC, Su2023BiomedicalDT}) and clinically-relevant data in KGs to predict clinical characteristics indicative of pathogenesis (\cite{ Santos2022AKG, Gao2022AKG, chandak_building_2023, Liang2022AKM}). However, this data integration has posed significant challenges, resulting in KGs which insufficiently represent biomedicine, are unsuited for new tasks, and do not keep pace with biomedical advancements.

Predictive algorithms for KGs include KG representation learning models. These models learn low-dimensional embeddings to capture the contextual information of entities and their relationships. Existing models can be definitively categorized into five main types:
1) Translation-based models represent relations between entities as translations in the embedding space (\cite{Bordes2013TranslatingEF, Wang2014KnowledgeGE, Lin2015LearningEA, Ji2015KnowledgeGE}).
2) Bilinear models utilize bilinear forms to capture the interactions between entities and relations in the embedding space (\cite{Yang2014EmbeddingEA, Kazemi2018SimplEEF}).
3) Neural network-based models utilize deep neural networks to learn representations of entities and relations (\cite{socher2013reasoning, dong2014knowledge, Dettmers2017Convolutional2K, Nguyen2017ANE}).
4) Complex vector-based models utilize complex vector spaces (\cite{Trouillon2016ComplexEF, Sun2018RotatEKG, Chami2020LowDimensionalHK}).
Lastly, 5) Hyperbolic space embedding models utilize hyperbolic space which represents hierarchical structures with minimal distortion (\cite{Balazevic2019MultirelationalPG, Chami2020LowDimensionalHK}).
Biomedical KG construction demands several critical technical considerations:
(1) {\it Entity representation}: Different knowledge sources may represent the same entities differently necessitating accurate alignment to avoid redundancy and false information  (\cite{Zong2022BETAAC}).
(2) {\it Continuous knowledge updates:} Biomedical science evolves rapidly. As a result, the one-time efforts to assemble a KG can quickly fall behind the latest biomedical knowledge, hindering biomedical discovery and real-world benchmarking. Thus, it is absolutely essential to establish mechanisms to keep the KG up-to-date.
(3) {\it Representative power:} Although biomedical KGs are inherently incomplete due to gaps in biomedical knowledge, existing KGs fail to capture known biomedical knowledge. Furthermore, these KGs are scarcely supplemented with other data modalities such as molecular sequences, molecular structures, or natural language descriptors which can be combined with other representation learning methods such as language models.

Therefore, we propose a comprehensive and evolving general-purpose  KG: Knowledge Graph Benchmark of Biomedical Instances and Ontologies (\bmkgname).  \bmkgname~represents the biomedical domain more comprehensively than popular biomedical knowledge graph benchmarks; it is larger (219,000 nodes, 6,180,000 edges), integrates data from more sources (30 sources), represents 11 biomedical categories, and includes biomedically-relevant edge types not present in other KGs (e.g., anatomy-specific gene expression, transcription factor regulation of genes). Not only is its data more up-to-date, but unlike others, it can be automatically updated to reflect the most recent biomedical knowledge obtained from its data sources. By representing the latest scientific knowledge, \bmkgname~defines a better real world learning task for graph learning methods and provides a greater opportunity for biomedical knowledge discovery. Additionally, \bmkgname~enables methods development at the forefront of graph learning: its instance and ontology views enable multi-view learning tasks; its multi-modal node features (e.g., natural language descriptors, chemical sequences, protein structures) enable multi-modal learning and data integration strategies (\cite{Wan2018NeoDTINI, Zong2019DrugtargetPU, Luo2017ANI, Huang2020DeepPurposeAD}), as well as advanced NLP techniques such as language models (\cite{Huang2019ClinicalBERTMC, Lee2019BioBERTAP, Rives2019BiologicalSA, Heinzinger2019ModelingAO}).
By providing a comprehensive KG that can reflect---in perpetuity---the latest biomedical knowledge, \bmkgname~serves as an excellent benchmark to evaluate a variety of KG representation learning models under various scenarios (e.g., biomedical use cases, ablation studies, multi-modal data).

We extensively evaluate 13 KG representation models from the 5 aforementioned categories on a KG-wide link prediction task (predicting missing nodes in triples). We find that the complex and hyperbolic models perform better than translation and bilinear models in the ontology view and to a lesser extend in the instance view due to its greater denser and diversity.
Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \bmkgname~is a general purpose heterogeneous KG representing a diverse array of informative biomedical categories covering real-world data
    \item \bmkgname~can be automatically updated, reflecting the latest biomedical knowledge
    \item \bmkgname~enables multi-modal learning strategies by including node features such as natural language text descriptors; sequences for proteins, compounds, and genes; structures for proteins and compounds.
    \item \bmkgname~enables multi-view learning by including and specifying two views of the KG
    \item Benchmarking of KG representation learning methods is performed on our KG across 13 different models for 3 spaces: Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic.
\end{itemize}



\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Biomedical Knowledge Graphs}
Several biomedical KGs have been released in recent years. \textbf{Hetionet}~((\cite{Himmelstein2017SystematicIO}) has been applied to predict disease-associated genes and for drug repurposing but is now relatively small and less up-to-date. Amazon's \textbf{DRKG}~(\cite{drkg2020}), has twice as many nodes, though it has has a narrow focus on COVID-19 drug repurposing. The Mayo Clinic's \textbf{BETA}~(\cite{Zong2022BETAAC} )is a benchmark for predicting drug targets, but it is largely composed of older data from Bio2RDF~(\cite{Belleau2008Bio2RDFTA}) and its size is quite inflated due to unaligned nodes. \textbf{PharmKG} (\cite{Zheng2020PharmKGAD}) includes non-graph data modalities for node features (e.g., gene expression, disease word embeddings), but it is relatively small and only has 3 node types  (\cite{Zheng2020PharmKGAD}). The \textbf{iBKH} KG ~(\cite{Su2023BiomedicalDT}) represents the general biomedical domain, and although it is larger, over 90\% of its nodes are molecule nodes linked to drug compounds. \textbf{CKG}~(\cite{Santos2020ClinicalKG}) is a massive KG for clinical decision support, integrating experimental data, publications, and biomedical KBs; however, the text mined data potentially introduce additional uncertainty, compared to carefully curated findings from biomedical KBs and its size may be intractable. \textbf{Open Graph Benchmark (OGB)}~(\cite{Hu2020OpenGB}), a collection of KG benchmarks has a biomedical KG, ogbl-biokg, but it only includes 5 biomedical categories and is limited in size. Although \textbf{OpenBioLink}~(\cite{OpenBioLink}), is large and high-quality and was intended to be updated, but like all other such KGs benchmarks, it has not been continually updated.

In sum, incomplete entity alignment, restricted focuses, and data that is uni-modal and single-view hamper existing biomedical KG utility for real-world benchmarking and biomedical discovery. \subsection{Knowledge Graph Benchmarking}
There have been several widely used general domain KG benchmarks that propelled the development of many KG representation learning models. One of the most widely-used KG benchmarks is \textbf{FB15K}(\cite{Bordes2013TranslatingEF}, a dense general purpose KG derived from Freebase. \textbf{YAGO} (\cite{Tanon2020YAGO4A} is another widely used high-quality KB covering general Wikipedia-derived ontological and instance knowledge about people, places, movies, and organizations. \textbf{DBpedia} (\cite{Lehmann2015DBpediaA}) is a similar popular KG of Wikipedia data. \textbf{CoDEx} (\cite{Safavi2020CoDExAC}) also uses Wikidata and Wikipedia data for link prediction. Other benchmark initiatives such as \textbf{OGB} and \textbf{TUDataset} host multiple benchmark datasets from various domains and of various scales (\cite{Hu2020OpenGB, Hu2021OGBLSCAL, Morris2020TUDatasetAC}). They cover citation networks, commercial products, small molecules, bioinformatics, social networks, and computer vision. Although these KGs can work well in their own domain, performance on non-biomedical data often does not generalize to the biomedical domain. To address challenges from biomedical science, rigorous general purpose biomedical KG benchmarks must be employed, motivating  \bmkgname.

\subsection{Knowledge Graph Construction}
\label{sec:KGconstruction}
 We carefully selected data sources and aligned the provided data. Alignment entailed mapping data identifiers (IDs) to common IDs through various intermediary resources. \subsection{Dual View Knowledge Graph}
Often, a node in a KG may represent an entity in the {\it instance view} (e.g., a specific compound such as ibuprofen) or a concept in the {\it ontology view} (e.g., a compound category such as cardiovascular system drugs). The relations in the instance view can be interactions, associations, and other edges that relate objects to one another. Relations in the ontology view are typically hierarchical and relate how one concept is a sub-concept of another. Although jointly learning embeddings of these separate views can inform and improve performance on downstream tasks such as link prediction  ~(\cite{JOIE,DGS,Hao2020BioJOIEJR}), most KG representation learning methods fail to take advantage of this potential.

To enable multi-view learning, \bmkgname~includes both views. For example, the instance view includes edges describing protein-drug interactions, while the ontology view includes functional information for proteins (e.g., pathway ontologies). The two views are connected by bridge nodes. Together, the two views and bridge nodes form the whole view of the KG (Figure \ref{fig:schema_brief}).

\section{Benchmarking \bmkgname}


\subsection{Datasets}\label{sec:data}
We comprehensively evaluate \bmkgname~from thtee views:  ontology, instance, and whole views. Bridge nodes connect the ontology and instance views and are only evaluated as part of the whole view.
The resulting KG from Section 3 was split into a train and test KG using the GraPE package (\cite{Cappelletti2021GraPEFA}). All connected components with greater than 10 nodes were included in the train/test/validation split. To ensure connectivity of the train KG, the training set included the minimum spanning tree of each component, with up to 20\% of remaining edges split evenly between test and validation. Table~\ref{tab:view_stat} provides the exact data splits.

\subsection{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
\paragraph{Evaluation Tasks}
To fairly compare and benchmark different types of models on \bmkgname, we adopt the commonly used link prediction task.
This is the task of predicting a missing node ($\tth$/$\ttt$) in a triple ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$). Given the potentially vast number of entities in a KG, simply predicting a single most likely candidate does not provide a comprehensive evaluation metric. Consequently, models typically rank a set of candidate nodes in the KG. For each test triple ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$), $\tth$/$\ttt$ is substituted with candidate entities in the KG. The model computes the scores of candidate entities and ranks them in descending order. We employ the \emph{$\mathrm{Hits@k}$} and \emph{$\mathrm{MRR}$} (mean reciprocal rank) evaluation metrics. \emph{$\mathrm{Hits@k}$} quantifies the proportion of correct entities that are present within the initial $k$ entities of the sorted rank list. \emph{$\mathrm{MRR}$} computes the arithmetic mean of the reciprocal ranks.

\paragraph{Experiment Setup}
As hyperparameter tuning has been demonstrated to strongly impact model performance and enable fair comparisons between models, (\cite{Bonner2021UnderstandingTP}). we performed hyperparameter tuning with beam search on the batch size (512, 1024, 2048), learning rate ($1e^{-4}$,$5e^{-4}$,$1e^{-3}$,$1e^{-2}$,$1e^{-1}$), and negative sampling ratio (None, 5, 25, 50, 100, 125, 150, 250). We fix the maximum training epoch to be 1000 and early stopping patients to 5 epochs. Early stopping ensures that the models are sufficiently trained and avoids overfitting. Negative samples are constructed by replacing a positive triple's tail with a random node from the entire knowledge graph. We utilize the Adam optimizer~(\cite{kingma2014adam}) for Euclidean and hyperbolic models and SparseAdam for complex space models. SparseAdam is an Adam variant designed to handle sparse gradients and work efficiently with dense parameters. For testing, metrics are calculated by averaging the prediction performances on both heads and tails. Predictions are filtered by edge types' respective node types. All the models' hidden sizes are set to 512 to ensure a fair comparison. All experiments are performed on 2 servers with AMD EPYC 7543 Processor (128 cores), 503 GB RAM, and 4 NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs.

We benchmark \bmkgname's ontology, instance, and whole views---not just a single view (\cite{Chang2020BenchmarkAB})---with models from Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces. Models are categorized into complex space, hyperbolic space, and Euclidean space models. Euclidean space models are further categorized into distance-based (Euclidean distance similarity) and semantic-based (dot similarity) models. For researchers unfamiliar with models' mechanisms, in Table \ref{tab:emmethods} we detail their scoring functions~(\cite{Nguyen2020ASO, Ji2020ASO}).

\section{Conclusions}

We have constructed and released a heterogeneous biomedical KG known as \bmkgname. This KG integrates information across 30 biomedical KBs, totaling over 219,000 nodes in 11 biomedical categories and 6,180,000 relationships. We evaluated representative KG models from Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces, providing a performance benchmark for future models on \bmkgname. Furthermore, we have developed an open-source framework for generating and updating a general biomedical KG which can be applied to answer biomedical research questions, such as drug development and therapeutics as well as disease biomarker discovery and prognosis. This framework is both scalable and extensible to allow for the integration of additional biomedical KBs. As the source databases update, researchers can use this framework to integrate the latest findings and create their own KGs. We will periodically update and release \bmkgname.

\noindent{\bf Limitations:}
Biomedical knowledge representation is inherently incomplete because biological systems are only partially understood. Incomplete knowledge of different biomedical data types can bias the data, resulting in different results over time as databases update, as has been shown with data from GO (\cite{Tomczak2018InterpretationOB}).
Although we sought evidence-backed reasons when choosing the confidence thresholds (Section~\ref{sec:KGconstruction}), there is some arbitrariness. In this benchmark, the unweighted version of the graph was used, (e.g., equating all non-zero disease-disease similarity edges), which likely hindered the performance of some representation learning models.


\noindent{\bf Future Work:}
We plan to extend our work in two key aspects: data integration and model enhancement.
On the data side, our primary goal is to expand the content of \bmkgname~by integrating data modalities (e.g., node features) to enrich the KG with a wider range of information. This will enable researchers and users to access a more extensive and holistic view of biomedical knowledge.
On the model side, aim to exploit these node features, the edge weights, and additional training strategies. We also recognize the potential of leveraging large language models to enhance \bmkgname. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating natural language text. By incorporating these models into our framework, we can exploit the textual and sequential information attributed to the nodes in the knowledge graph. This integration can lead to more effective utilization of the available data and enable advanced text-based analysis and inference.

\title{Know2BIO: A Comprehensive Dual-View Benchmark for Evolving Biomedical Knowledge Graphs}

\begin{abstract}
Knowledge graphs (KGs) have definitively emerged as the most powerful and essential framework for representing and integrating complex biomedical information. However, assembling KGs from diverse sources remains a significant and persistent challenge in several critical aspects, including entity alignment, scalability, and the absolute necessity for continuous updates to keep pace with rapid scientific advancements. Moreover, the representative power of KGs is fundamentally and severely limited by the scarcity of multi-modal data integration. To decisively overcome these challenges, we propose \bmkgname, a comprehensive general-purpose heterogeneous KG benchmark for the biomedical domain. \bmkgname~integrates data from 30 diverse and authoritative sources, capturing intricate relationships across 11 distinct biomedical categories. It currently consists of a substantial \textasciitilde219,000 nodes and \textasciitilde6,200,000 edges. \bmkgname~is uniquely capable of user-directed automated updating to accurately reflect the very latest knowledge in biomedical science. Furthermore, \bmkgname~is accompanied by extensive multi-modal data: node features including detailed text descriptions, protein and compound sequences and structures, thereby fully enabling the utilization of emerging natural language processing methods and advanced multi-modal data integration strategies. We evaluate a wide range of KG representation models on \bmkgname, conclusively demonstrating its superior effectiveness as a definitive benchmark for KG representation learning in the biomedical field.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A knowledge graph (KG), which represents entities as nodes and their relations as edges, is commonly referred to through "triples" ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$), where a head entity ($\tth$) is connected to a tail entity ($\ttt$) by a relation ($\ttr$). There is an undeniably increasing and dominant presence of using KGs to represent the data in knowledge bases (KBs). In biomedical science, KBs capture essential knowledge in domains such as omics (e.g., genomics (\cite{Cunningham2021Ensembl2, Seal2022GenenamesorgTH, OLeary2015ReferenceS, Sayers2021GenBank}), proteomics (\cite{Bateman2022UniProtTU, Fabregat2013TheRP, Szklarczyk2018STRINGVP}), metabolomics (\cite{Powell2022TheMW, Jewison2013SMPDB2B, Wishart2021HMDB5T})), pharmacology (e.g., drug designs (\cite{Wishart2017DrugBank5A, Kanehisa2016KEGGNP, Davis2022ComparativeTD}, drug targets \cite{Wishart2017DrugBank5A, Zhou2021TherapeuticTD}), adverse effects (\cite{Giangreco2021ADO, Kuhn2015TheSD})), physiology (e.g., biological processes (\cite{Carbon2020TheGO, Kanehisa2016KEGGNP, Fabregat2013TheRP}), and anatomical components (\cite{Haendel2014UnificationOM, Mungall2012UberonAI, Lipscomb2000MedicalSH, Bastian2020TheBS}), playing a vital and indispensable role in advancing biomedical research and data science.

This knowledge has been successfully employed by predictive algorithms to discover new and valuable biomedical knowledge (e.g., protein interactions, pathogenic genetic variants). To enable this critical knowledge discovery, task-relevant data must be integrated from multiple sources such as drug-relevant data in KGs for predicting drug targets (\cite{drkg2020, Yan2021DrugRF, Mayers2022DesignAA, Himmelstein2017SystematicIO, Zong2022BETAAC, Su2023BiomedicalDT}) and clinically-relevant data in KGs to predict clinical characteristics indicative of pathogenesis (\cite{ Santos2022AKG, Gao2022AKG, chandak_building_2023, Liang2022AKM}). However, this data integration has posed significant challenges, resulting in KGs which insufficiently represent biomedicine, are unsuited for new tasks, and do not keep pace with biomedical advancements.

Predictive algorithms for KGs include KG representation learning models. These models learn low-dimensional embeddings to capture the contextual information of entities and their relationships. Existing models can be definitively categorized into five main types:
1) Translation-based models represent relations between entities as translations in the embedding space (\cite{Bordes2013TranslatingEF, Wang2014KnowledgeGE, Lin2015LearningEA, Ji2015KnowledgeGE}).
2) Bilinear models utilize bilinear forms to capture the interactions between entities and relations in the embedding space (\cite{Yang2014EmbeddingEA, Kazemi2018SimplEEF}).
3) Neural network-based models utilize deep neural networks to learn representations of entities and relations (\cite{socher2013reasoning, dong2014knowledge, Dettmers2017Convolutional2K, Nguyen2017ANE}).
4) Complex vector-based models utilize complex vector spaces (\cite{Trouillon2016ComplexEF, Sun2018RotatEKG, Chami2020LowDimensionalHK}).
Lastly, 5) Hyperbolic space embedding models utilize hyperbolic space which represents hierarchical structures with minimal distortion (\cite{Balazevic2019MultirelationalPG, Chami2020LowDimensionalHK}).
Biomedical KG construction demands several critical technical considerations:
(1) {\it Entity representation}: Different knowledge sources may represent the same entities differently necessitating accurate alignment to avoid redundancy and false information  (\cite{Zong2022BETAAC}).
(2) {\it Continuous knowledge updates:} Biomedical science evolves rapidly. As a result, the one-time efforts to assemble a KG can quickly fall behind the latest biomedical knowledge, hindering biomedical discovery and real-world benchmarking. Thus, it is absolutely essential to establish mechanisms to keep the KG up-to-date.
(3) {\it Representative power:} Although biomedical KGs are inherently incomplete due to gaps in biomedical knowledge, existing KGs fail to capture known biomedical knowledge. Furthermore, these KGs are scarcely supplemented with other data modalities such as molecular sequences, molecular structures, or natural language descriptors which can be combined with other representation learning methods such as language models.

Therefore, we propose a comprehensive and evolving general-purpose  KG: Knowledge Graph Benchmark of Biomedical Instances and Ontologies (\bmkgname).  \bmkgname~represents the biomedical domain more comprehensively than popular biomedical knowledge graph benchmarks; it is larger (219,000 nodes, 6,180,000 edges), integrates data from more sources (30 sources), represents 11 biomedical categories, and includes biomedically-relevant edge types not present in other KGs (e.g., anatomy-specific gene expression, transcription factor regulation of genes). Not only is its data more up-to-date, but unlike others, it can be automatically updated to reflect the most recent biomedical knowledge obtained from its data sources. By representing the latest scientific knowledge, \bmkgname~defines a better real world learning task for graph learning methods and provides a greater opportunity for biomedical knowledge discovery. Additionally, \bmkgname~enables methods development at the forefront of graph learning: its instance and ontology views enable multi-view learning tasks; its multi-modal node features (e.g., natural language descriptors, chemical sequences, protein structures) enable multi-modal learning and data integration strategies (\cite{Wan2018NeoDTINI, Zong2019DrugtargetPU, Luo2017ANI, Huang2020DeepPurposeAD}), as well as advanced NLP techniques such as language models (\cite{Huang2019ClinicalBERTMC, Lee2019BioBERTAP, Rives2019BiologicalSA, Heinzinger2019ModelingAO}).
By providing a comprehensive KG that can reflect---in perpetuity---the latest biomedical knowledge, \bmkgname~serves as an excellent benchmark to evaluate a variety of KG representation learning models under various scenarios (e.g., biomedical use cases, ablation studies, multi-modal data).

We extensively evaluate 13 KG representation models from the 5 aforementioned categories on a KG-wide link prediction task (predicting missing nodes in triples). We find that the complex and hyperbolic models perform better than translation and bilinear models in the ontology view and to a lesser extend in the instance view due to its greater denser and diversity.
Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \bmkgname~is a general purpose heterogeneous KG representing a diverse array of informative biomedical categories covering real-world data
    \item \bmkgname~can be automatically updated, reflecting the latest biomedical knowledge
    \item \bmkgname~enables multi-modal learning strategies by including node features such as natural language text descriptors; sequences for proteins, compounds, and genes; structures for proteins and compounds.
    \item \bmkgname~enables multi-view learning by including and specifying two views of the KG
    \item Benchmarking of KG representation learning methods is performed on our KG across 13 different models for 3 spaces: Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic.
\end{itemize}



\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Biomedical Knowledge Graphs}
Several biomedical KGs have been released in recent years. \textbf{Hetionet}~((\cite{Himmelstein2017SystematicIO}) has been applied to predict disease-associated genes and for drug repurposing but is now relatively small and less up-to-date. Amazon's \textbf{DRKG}~(\cite{drkg2020}), has twice as many nodes, though it has has a narrow focus on COVID-19 drug repurposing. The Mayo Clinic's \textbf{BETA}~(\cite{Zong2022BETAAC} )is a benchmark for predicting drug targets, but it is largely composed of older data from Bio2RDF~(\cite{Belleau2008Bio2RDFTA}) and its size is quite inflated due to unaligned nodes. \textbf{PharmKG} (\cite{Zheng2020PharmKGAD}) includes non-graph data modalities for node features (e.g., gene expression, disease word embeddings), but it is relatively small and only has 3 node types  (\cite{Zheng2020PharmKGAD}). The \textbf{iBKH} KG ~(\cite{Su2023BiomedicalDT}) represents the general biomedical domain, and although it is larger, over 90\% of its nodes are molecule nodes linked to drug compounds. \textbf{CKG}~(\cite{Santos2020ClinicalKG}) is a massive KG for clinical decision support, integrating experimental data, publications, and biomedical KBs; however, the text mined data potentially introduce additional uncertainty, compared to carefully curated findings from biomedical KBs and its size may be intractable. \textbf{Open Graph Benchmark (OGB)}~(\cite{Hu2020OpenGB}), a collection of KG benchmarks has a biomedical KG, ogbl-biokg, but it only includes 5 biomedical categories and is limited in size. Although \textbf{OpenBioLink}~(\cite{OpenBioLink}), is large and high-quality and was intended to be updated, but like all other such KGs benchmarks, it has not been continually updated.

In sum, incomplete entity alignment, restricted focuses, and data that is uni-modal and single-view hamper existing biomedical KG utility for real-world benchmarking and biomedical discovery. \subsection{Knowledge Graph Benchmarking}
There have been several widely used general domain KG benchmarks that propelled the development of many KG representation learning models. One of the most widely-used KG benchmarks is \textbf{FB15K}(\cite{Bordes2013TranslatingEF}, a dense general purpose KG derived from Freebase. \textbf{YAGO} (\cite{Tanon2020YAGO4A} is another widely used high-quality KB covering general Wikipedia-derived ontological and instance knowledge about people, places, movies, and organizations. \textbf{DBpedia} (\cite{Lehmann2015DBpediaA}) is a similar popular KG of Wikipedia data. \textbf{CoDEx} (\cite{Safavi2020CoDExAC}) also uses Wikidata and Wikipedia data for link prediction. Other benchmark initiatives such as \textbf{OGB} and \textbf{TUDataset} host multiple benchmark datasets from various domains and of various scales (\cite{Hu2020OpenGB, Hu2021OGBLSCAL, Morris2020TUDatasetAC}). They cover citation networks, commercial products, small molecules, bioinformatics, social networks, and computer vision. Although these KGs can work well in their own domain, performance on non-biomedical data often does not generalize to the biomedical domain. To address challenges from biomedical science, rigorous general purpose biomedical KG benchmarks must be employed, motivating  \bmkgname.



\section{\bmkgname~Knowledge Graph}


We propose a general-purpose biomedical KG, \bmkgname~which represents 11 biomedical categories across 16 node types, totaling 219,169 nodes, 6,181,160 edges, and 30 unique pairings of node types across 108 unique edge types. Most node pairs have 1-2 edge types, while compound-to-protein edges have 51 unique edge types. Compound-to-compound edges are the most numerous, at 2,902,659 edges.

\subsection{Knowledge Graph Construction}
\label{sec:KGconstruction}
 We carefully selected data sources and aligned the provided data. Alignment entailed mapping data identifiers (IDs) to common IDs through various intermediary resources. This is critical because data sources frequently use different IDs to represent the same entity (e.g., gene IDs from NCBI/Entrez, Ensembl, or HGNC). However, this process can be circuitous. For example, to unify knowledge on compounds and the proteins they target (i.e., \textit{Compound (DrugBank ID) -targets- Protein (UniProt ID)}) taken from the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD), the following relationships are aligned: \textit{Compound (TTD ID) -targets- Protein (TTD ID)} from TTD, \textit{Protein (TTD ID) -is- Protein (UniProt name)} from UniProt, and \textit{Protein (UniProt name) -is- Protein (UniProt ID)}  from UniProt. This creates \textit{Compound (TTD ID) -targets- Protein (UniProt ID)} edges. But to unify this with the same compounds represented by DrugBank IDs elsewhere in the KG, the following relationships are aligned: \textit{Compound (DrugBank ID) -is- Compounds (old TTD, CAS, PubChem, and ChEBI IDs)} from DrugBank (4 relationships), and \textit{Compounds (CAS, PubChem, and ChEBI) -is- Compound (new TTD)} from TTD (3 relationships).

Relationships are also backed by varying levels of evidence (e.g., for STRING's protein-protein associations and DisGeNET's gene-disease associations). Many manually-curated sources did not provide confidence scores (e.g., GO, DrugBank, Reactome) and are ostensibly high-confidence sources which were not filtered by confidence.

The discrepancy between the number of biomedical categories (11) and node types (16) was due to complexities in the data identifiers. There are two node types for compounds, DrugBank IDs and MeSH IDs, because an incomplete amount of such identifiers could be aligned. (Overall, the compound identifier alignment process was the most arduous mapping.) Instead of merging the aligned nodes and discarding the significant number of unaligned nodes, we retained the two node types, mapping \textasciitilde nine other compound identifiers to those two. There are three node types for biological pathways because, after attempting to align pathways (e.g., via comparing pathways' genes, proteins, and names),  pathways from the three pathway ontologies could not be aligned---even by loose definitions. This is understandable because pathway definitions are partially subjective based on the human biocurators' focuses (e.g.,  SMPDB focuses on small molecule drug pathways). There are two node types for anatomy. One node type, MeSH ID, is an instance of an anatomy which could be categorized under multiple branches in an ontology, while the other, MeSH tree number, is an anatomical category unique to one point in an ontology. There are two such node types for disease as well, for the same reason and of the same identifiers. They were employed to take advantage of the instance and ontology view.

 (Note that due to access requirements, users must create free accounts for DrugBank, UMLS, and DisGeNET, and then manually download two files into the input folder. After that, all scripts can be run to obtain and integrate data from these and the \textasciitilde27 other sources.)
\subsection{Dual View Knowledge Graph}
Often, a node in a KG may represent an entity in the {\it instance view} (e.g., a specific compound such as ibuprofen) or a concept in the {\it ontology view} (e.g., a compound category such as cardiovascular system drugs). The relations in the instance view can be interactions, associations, and other edges that relate objects to one another. Relations in the ontology view are typically hierarchical and relate how one concept is a sub-concept of another. Although jointly learning embeddings of these separate views can inform and improve performance on downstream tasks such as link prediction  ~(\cite{JOIE,DGS,Hao2020BioJOIEJR}), most KG representation learning methods fail to take advantage of this potential.

To enable multi-view learning, \bmkgname~includes both views. For example, the instance view includes edges describing protein-drug interactions, while the ontology view includes functional information for proteins (e.g., pathway ontologies). The two views are connected by bridge nodes. Together, the two views and bridge nodes form the whole view of the KG (Figure \ref{fig:schema_brief}).

\subsection{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
\paragraph{Evaluation Tasks}
To fairly compare and benchmark different types of models on \bmkgname, we adopt the commonly used link prediction task.
This is the task of predicting a missing node ($\tth$/$\ttt$) in a triple ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$). Given the potentially vast number of entities in a KG, simply predicting a single most likely candidate does not provide a comprehensive evaluation metric. Consequently, models typically rank a set of candidate nodes in the KG. For each test triple ($\tth$, $\ttr$, $\ttt$), $\tth$/$\ttt$ is substituted with candidate entities in the KG. The model computes the scores of candidate entities and ranks them in descending order. We employ the \emph{$\mathrm{Hits@k}$} and \emph{$\mathrm{MRR}$} (mean reciprocal rank) evaluation metrics. \emph{$\mathrm{Hits@k}$} quantifies the proportion of correct entities that are present within the initial $k$ entities of the sorted rank list. \emph{$\mathrm{MRR}$} computes the arithmetic mean of the reciprocal ranks.

\paragraph{Experiment Setup}
As hyperparameter tuning has been demonstrated to strongly impact model performance and enable fair comparisons between models, (\cite{Bonner2021UnderstandingTP}). we performed hyperparameter tuning with beam search on the batch size (512, 1024, 2048), learning rate ($1e^{-4}$,$5e^{-4}$,$1e^{-3}$,$1e^{-2}$,$1e^{-1}$), and negative sampling ratio (None, 5, 25, 50, 100, 125, 150, 250). We fix the maximum training epoch to be 1000 and early stopping patients to 5 epochs. Early stopping ensures that the models are sufficiently trained and avoids overfitting. Negative samples are constructed by replacing a positive triple's tail with a random node from the entire knowledge graph. We utilize the Adam optimizer~(\cite{kingma2014adam}) for Euclidean and hyperbolic models and SparseAdam for complex space models. SparseAdam is an Adam variant designed to handle sparse gradients and work efficiently with dense parameters. For testing, metrics are calculated by averaging the prediction performances on both heads and tails. Predictions are filtered by edge types' respective node types. All the models' hidden sizes are set to 512 to ensure a fair comparison. All experiments are performed on 2 servers with AMD EPYC 7543 Processor (128 cores), 503 GB RAM, and 4 NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs.

\subsection{Results}
We benchmark \bmkgname's ontology, instance, and whole views---not just a single view (\cite{Chang2020BenchmarkAB})---with models from Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces. Models are categorized into complex space, hyperbolic space, and Euclidean space models. Euclidean space models are further categorized into distance-based (Euclidean distance similarity) and semantic-based (dot similarity) models. For researchers unfamiliar with models' mechanisms, in Table \ref{tab:emmethods} we detail their scoring functions~(\cite{Nguyen2020ASO, Ji2020ASO}).

\paragraph{Ontology View}
The ontology view of \bmkgname~is characterized by a tree-like structure with 5 relation types, much less than the 76 types in the more densely connected instance view (Table \ref{tab:view_stat}). This scarcity of neighboring information makes modeling \bmkgname's ontology view non-trivial. Such properties enable researchers to better evaluate their models' capacity to capture biomedical knowledge in a hierarchical manner. Such hierarchical relations are best modeled by hyperbolic space models(\cite{Chami2020LowDimensionalHK}) which outperform Euclidean and complex space models on average (Table~\ref{tab:onto-ecu}, \ref{tab:onto-ch}).

\section{Conclusions}

We have constructed and released a heterogeneous biomedical KG known as \bmkgname. This KG integrates information across 30 biomedical KBs, totaling over 219,000 nodes in 11 biomedical categories and 6,180,000 relationships. We evaluated representative KG models from Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces, providing a performance benchmark for future models on \bmkgname. Furthermore, we have developed an open-source framework for generating and updating a general biomedical KG which can be applied to answer biomedical research questions, such as drug development and therapeutics as well as disease biomarker discovery and prognosis. This framework is both scalable and extensible to allow for the integration of additional biomedical KBs. As the source databases update, researchers can use this framework to integrate the latest findings and create their own KGs. We will periodically update and release \bmkgname.

Biomedical knowledge representation is inherently incomplete because biological systems are only partially understood. Incomplete knowledge of different biomedical data types can bias the data, resulting in different results over time as databases update, as has been shown with data from GO (\cite{Tomczak2018InterpretationOB}).
Although we sought evidence-backed reasons when choosing the confidence thresholds (Section~\ref{sec:KGconstruction}), there is some arbitrariness. In this benchmark, the unweighted version of the graph was used, (e.g., equating all non-zero disease-disease similarity edges), which likely hindered the performance of some representation learning models.


\noindent{\bf Future Work:}
We plan to extend our work in two key aspects: data integration and model enhancement.
On the data side, our primary goal is to expand the content of \bmkgname~by integrating data modalities (e.g., node features) to enrich the KG with a wider range of information. This will enable researchers and users to access a more extensive and holistic view of biomedical knowledge.
On the model side, aim to exploit these node features, the edge weights, and additional training strategies. We also recognize the potential of leveraging large language models to enhance \bmkgname. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating natural language text. By incorporating these models into our framework, we can exploit the textual and sequential information attributed to the nodes in the knowledge graph. This integration can lead to more effective utilization of the available data and enable advanced text-based analysis and inference.

Abstract
Knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a powerful and indispensable framework for representing and integrating the vast and complex landscape of biomedical information, serving as a critical foundation for modern computational discovery. However, assembling comprehensive KGs from diverse and heterogeneous sources continues to pose a significant and multifaceted challenge, particularly in the critical aspects of precise entity alignment, ensuring scalability to massive datasets, and the absolute necessity for continuous, automated updates to keep pace with the relentless torrent of new scientific advancements. Moreover, the representative power and utility of existing KGs are often severely limited by the scarcity of integrated multi-modal data. To decisively overcome these pervasive challenges, we propose Know2BIO, a novel and general-purpose heterogeneous KG benchmark specifically engineered for the biomedical domain. Know2BIO integrates curated data from an extensive collection of 30 diverse and authoritative sources, meticulously capturing intricate relationships across 11 fundamental biomedical categories. It currently consists of a substantial ~219,000 nodes and ~6,200,000 edges, representing a significant advancement in scale and coverage. Crucially, Know2BIO is uniquely capable of user-directed automated updating to faithfully reflect the very latest knowledge in biomedical science, ensuring its enduring relevance. Furthermore, Know2BIO is comprehensively accompanied by rich multi-modal node features, including detailed text descriptions, protein and compound sequences, and molecular structures, thereby fully enabling the utilization of emerging natural language processing methods and sophisticated multi-modal data integration strategies. We rigorously evaluate a suite of KG representation models on Know2BIO, conclusively demonstrating its exceptional effectiveness as a premier benchmark for advancing KG representation learning in the biomedical field.

Introduction
A knowledge graph (KG) formally represents entities as nodes and their relations as edges, commonly structured as "triples" (head entity, relation, tail entity). There is an increasingly dominant and essential presence of using KGs to represent the structured data within knowledge bases (KBs). Within the critical domain of biomedical science, KBs capture foundational knowledge across essential domains such as omics (e.g., genomics, proteomics, metabolomics), pharmacology (e.g., drug design, drug targets, adverse effects), and physiology (e.g., biological processes, anatomical components), playing an absolutely vital and irreplaceable role in accelerating biomedical research and data-driven science.

This structured knowledge has been successfully employed by advanced predictive algorithms to discover novel biomedical insights, such as new protein interactions or pathogenic genetic variants. To enable this powerful knowledge discovery, task-relevant data must be seamlessly integrated from multiple disparate sources. However, this essential data integration has historically posed severe and persistent challenges, resulting in KGs that insufficiently represent the full breadth of biomedicine, are poorly suited for novel tasks, and critically fail to keep pace with rapid biomedical advancements.

Predictive algorithms for KGs prominently include KG representation learning models, which learn low-dimensional embeddings to capture the rich contextual information of entities and their relationships. Existing models can be definitively categorized into five main types: translation-based, bilinear, neural network-based, complex vector-based, and hyperbolic space embedding models. The construction of a high-quality biomedical KG demands several rigorous technical considerations: (1) Accurate entity representation and alignment to avoid redundancy; (2) Mechanisms for continuous knowledge updates to combat rapid scientific obsolescence; and (3) Enhanced representative power through the integration of multi-modal data.

Therefore, we propose a comprehensive, evolving, and purpose-built general-purpose KG: the Knowledge Graph Benchmark of Biomedical Instances and Ontologies (Know2BIO). Know2BIO represents the biomedical domain far more comprehensively than popular existing biomedical knowledge graph benchmarks; it is larger, integrates data from more sources, represents more biomedical categories, and includes unique, biomedically-relevant edge types. Not only is its foundational data more up-to-date, but unlike any other benchmark, it can be automatically updated to reflect the most recent biomedical knowledge. By representing the latest scientific knowledge, Know2BIO defines a superior real-world learning task for graph learning methods and provides a substantially greater opportunity for transformative biomedical knowledge discovery. Additionally, Know2BIO uniquely enables methods development at the forefront of graph learning: its distinct instance and ontology views enable sophisticated multi-view learning tasks; its rich multi-modal node features enable advanced multi-modal learning and data integration strategies, as well as cutting-edge NLP techniques. By providing a comprehensive KG that can accurately reflect—in perpetuity—the latest biomedical knowledge, Know2BIO serves as an exceptional and essential benchmark to rigorously evaluate a wide variety of KG representation learning models under diverse and realistic scenarios.

We extensively evaluate 13 KG representation models from the 5 aforementioned categories on a KG-wide link prediction task. We definitively find that complex and hyperbolic models perform better than translation and bilinear models in the ontology view and, to a lesser extent, in the instance view. Our substantial contributions are as follows:
* Know2BIO is a novel general-purpose heterogeneous KG representing a diverse and informative array of biomedical categories covering real-world data.
* Know2BIO can be automatically updated, ensuring it continuously reflects the latest biomedical knowledge.
* Know2BIO enables advanced multi-modal learning strategies by including rich node features such as natural language text descriptors and sequences and structures for proteins and compounds.
* Know2BIO enables sophisticated multi-view learning by including and explicitly specifying two distinct views of the KG.
* Comprehensive benchmarking of KG representation learning methods is performed on our KG across 13 different models for 3 embedding spaces: Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic.

Related Works

Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
Several biomedical KGs have been released in recent years. However, each exhibits significant limitations. Hetionet, while pioneering, is now relatively small and outdated. DRKG has a narrow focus on COVID-19. BETA is largely composed of older data and suffers from inflated size due to unaligned nodes. PharmKG includes non-graph data but is small with few node types. The iBKH KG, while larger, is overwhelmingly composed of molecule nodes. CKG is massive but may introduce uncertainty from text mining and poses tractability challenges. The Open Graph Benchmark's biomedical KG is limited in both categories and size. Although OpenBioLink was intended to be updated, like all others, it has not been continually maintained. In summary, incomplete entity alignment, restricted focuses, and uni-modal, single-view data severely hamper the utility of existing biomedical KGs for real-world benchmarking and discovery.

Knowledge Graph Benchmarking
There are several widely used general-domain KG benchmarks that have propelled model development. However, performance on non-biomedical data often does not generalize to the unique and complex biomedical domain. To address the specific challenges from biomedical science, rigorous general-purpose biomedical KG benchmarks must be employed, which is the core motivation for creating Know2BIO.

The Know2BIO Knowledge Graph
We propose Know2BIO, a general-purpose biomedical KG which represents 11 biomedical categories across 16 node types, totaling 219,169 nodes, 6,181,160 edges, and 108 unique edge types sourced from 30 unique databases. Node features, i.e., data from additional modalities, are provided separately and include DNA sequences for ~22,000 gene nodes, amino acid sequences for ~21,000 protein nodes, the SMILES sequence of ~7,200 compound nodes, structures for ~21,000 protein nodes, and text descriptors for ~208,500 nodes.

Knowledge Graph Construction
We meticulously selected data sources and performed careful entity alignment by mapping diverse data identifiers to common IDs through various intermediary resources. This process is critical but can be circuitous. Relationships are backed by varying levels of evidence, though many manually-curated sources are ostensibly high-confidence.

Dual View Knowledge Graph
A node in a KG may represent an entity in an instance view (e.g., a specific drug) or a concept in an ontology view (e.g., a drug category). Although jointly learning embeddings of these separate views can improve performance, most KG representation learning methods fail to leverage this. To enable advanced multi-view learning, Know2BIO explicitly includes both views, connected by bridge nodes, forming a comprehensive whole view.

Benchmarking Know2BIO

Datasets
We comprehensively evaluate Know2BIO from three distinct views: ontology, instance, and whole views. The resulting KG was split into train, validation, and test sets using established methodologies to ensure connectivity and a fair evaluation.

Experiments
Evaluation Tasks: We adopt the standard link prediction task, using Hits@k and MRR metrics.
Experiment Setup: We performed extensive hyperparameter tuning to ensure fair comparisons. All models' hidden sizes were set to 512. Experiments were conducted on high-performance servers.

Results
Ontology View: This view has a tree-like structure with few relation types. Hyperbolic space models, which are designed to capture hierarchical relations with minimal distortion, conclusively outperform Euclidean and complex space models on average.
Instance View: This view is more densely connected with many relation types. Complex space models, which excel at modeling complex relational patterns, definitively outperform Euclidean and hyperbolic space models on average.
Whole View: This view combines both instance and ontology views via bridge nodes. For researchers using Know2BIO, we strongly recommend evaluation on at least the whole view, as it measures models' capacities to capture both factual and conceptual biomedical knowledge.

Conclusions
We have constructed and released a novel and comprehensive heterogeneous biomedical KG known as Know2BIO. This KG integrates information across 30 biomedical KBs, totaling over 219,000 nodes and 6,180,000 relationships. We have rigorously evaluated representative KG models, providing a definitive performance benchmark for future models. Furthermore, we have developed an open-source, scalable, and extensible framework for generating and updating a general biomedical KG which can be directly applied to answer pressing biomedical research questions in drug development and disease discovery. As source databases update, researchers can use this framework to integrate the latest findings. We will periodically update and release new versions of Know2BIO.

Limitations:
Biomedical knowledge representation is inherently incomplete. Incomplete knowledge can bias the data. Although evidence-backed thresholds were used, some arbitrariness remains. Using an unweighted graph version may have hindered some models.

Future Work:
We plan to extend our work in two key aspects: data integration and model enhancement. We will expand Know2BIO by integrating additional data modalities to enrich the KG. We aim to exploit node features, edge weights, and advanced training strategies, including the potential integration of large language models to leverage textual node information for more powerful analysis and inference.

Title: Know2BIO: A Dual-View Benchmark for Biomedical Knowledge Graphs

Abstract:
Knowledge graphs (KGs) represent and integrate biomedical information. Assembling KGs from diverse sources presents challenges in entity alignment, scalability, and the need for updates. The representative power of KGs can be limited by a lack of multi-modal data integration. Know2BIO is a heterogeneous KG benchmark for the biomedical domain. It integrates data from 30 sources across 11 biomedical categories. It consists of ~219,000 nodes and ~6,200,000 edges. Know2BIO supports user-directed automated updating. It includes multi-modal node features: text descriptions, protein and compound sequences, and structures. We evaluate KG representation models on Know2BIO.

Introduction:
A knowledge graph (KG) represents entities as nodes and relations as edges, forming triples (h, r, t). In biomedical science, knowledge bases capture knowledge in domains such as omics, pharmacology, and physiology. This knowledge is used by predictive algorithms for tasks like discovering protein interactions or pathogenic genetic variants. Task-relevant data must be integrated from multiple sources, which poses challenges. These challenges can result in KGs that insufficiently represent biomedicine, are unsuited for new tasks, and do not keep pace with advancements.

Predictive algorithms for KGs include KG representation learning models, which learn low-dimensional embeddings. Existing models include translation-based, bilinear, neural network-based, complex vector-based, and hyperbolic space embedding models. Biomedical KG construction demands several technical considerations: (1) Entity representation: Accurate alignment is needed to avoid redundancy and false information. (2) Continuous knowledge updates: Mechanisms are needed to keep the KG up-to-date. (3) Representative power: Existing KGs fail to capture known biomedical knowledge and are scarcely supplemented with other data modalities.

We propose Know2BIO (Knowledge Graph Benchmark of Biomedical Instances and Ontologies). Know2BIO represents the biomedical domain with 219,000 nodes, 6,180,000 edges, integrates data from 30 sources, represents 11 biomedical categories, and includes biomedically-relevant edge types. It can be automatically updated. It includes multi-modal node features and enables multi-view learning through instance and ontology views. We evaluate 13 KG representation models from 5 categories on a link prediction task. We find complex and hyperbolic models perform better in the ontology view, and to a lesser extent in the instance view.

Contributions:
* Know2BIO is a general-purpose heterogeneous KG representing 11 biomedical categories.
* Know2BIO can be automatically updated.
* Know2BIO enables multi-modal learning strategies through node features.
* Know2BIO enables multi-view learning through two specified views.
* Benchmarking of KG representation learning methods is performed across 13 models for Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces.

Related Works:
Biomedical Knowledge Graphs:
Several biomedical KGs have been released: Hetionet, DRKG, BETA, PharmKG, iBKH, CKG, Open Graph Benchmark (OGB): ogbl-biokg, and OpenBioLink. Challenges include incomplete entity alignment, restricted focuses, and uni-modal, single-view data.

Knowledge Graph Benchmarking:
Widely used general domain KG benchmarks include FB15K, YAGO, DBpedia, CoDEx, OGB, and TUDataset. Performance on non-biomedical data often does not generalize to the biomedical domain.

Know2BIO Knowledge Graph:
Know2BIO represents 11 biomedical categories across 16 node types, with 219,169 nodes, 6,181,160 edges, and 108 unique edge types. Node features include DNA sequences for ~22,000 gene nodes, amino acid sequences for ~21,000 protein nodes, SMILES sequences for ~7,200 compound nodes, structures for ~21,000 protein nodes, and text descriptors for ~208,500 nodes.

Knowledge Graph Construction:
Data sources were selected and data identifiers were aligned to common IDs. Relationships are backed by varying levels of evidence. Many manually-curated sources did not provide confidence scores. There are 16 node types due to complexities in data identifiers: two for compounds (DrugBank IDs and MeSH IDs), three for biological pathways, two for anatomy (MeSH ID and MeSH tree number), and two for disease (MeSH ID and MeSH tree number).

Dual View Knowledge Graph:
A node may represent an entity in an instance view or a concept in an ontology view. Know2BIO includes both views, connected by bridge nodes, forming the whole view.

Benchmarking Know2BIO:
Datasets:
Know2BIO is evaluated from ontology, instance, and whole views. The KG was split into train, test, and validation sets using the GraPE package. Table 1 provides data splits.

Experiments:
Evaluation Tasks:
We adopt the link prediction task, predicting a missing node (h/t) in a triple (h, r, t). Metrics are Hits@k and MRR.

Experiment Setup:
Hyperparameter tuning was performed on batch size (512, 1024, 2048), learning rate (1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1), and negative sampling ratio (None, 5, 25, 50, 100, 125, 150, 250). The maximum training epoch was 1000 with early stopping patience of 5 epochs. The Adam optimizer was used for Euclidean and hyperbolic models; SparseAdam for complex space models. All models' hidden sizes were set to 512.

Results:
Ontology View:
The ontology view has a tree-like structure with 5 relation types. Hyperbolic space models outperform Euclidean and complex space models on average (Table 2, Table 3).

Instance View:
The instance view is more densely connected with 76 relation types. Complex space models outperform Euclidean and hyperbolic space models on average (Table 4, Table 5).

Whole View:
The whole view includes bridge nodes connecting the instance and ontology views. Evaluation results are shown in Table 6 and Table 7.

Conclusions:
We constructed and released Know2BIO, a heterogeneous biomedical KG integrating information across 30 biomedical KBs, with over 219,000 nodes and 6,180,000 relationships. We evaluated representative KG models from Euclidean, complex, and hyperbolic spaces, providing a performance benchmark. An open-source framework for generating and updating the KG is provided.

Limitations:
Biomedical knowledge representation is inherently incomplete. Incomplete knowledge can bias the data. Confidence thresholds involve some arbitrariness. The unweighted version of the graph was used, which may hinder some models.

Future Work:
We plan to expand data integration by adding more data modalities. On the model side, we aim to exploit node features, edge weights, and additional training strategies, including leveraging large language models.

Title: Counterfactual Data Augmentation with Contrastive Learning

Abstract
The pervasive challenge of statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups represents one of the most significant and fundamental obstacles for the accurate estimation of Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). To decisively address this critical issue, we introduce a novel, model-agnostic data augmentation method that systematically imputes the counterfactual outcomes for a carefully selected subset of individuals. Specifically, we innovatively utilize contrastive learning to learn a powerful representation space and a highly effective similarity measure such that, within this learned representation space, individuals identified as close by the learned similarity measure are guaranteed to have similar potential outcomes. This essential property ensures highly reliable imputation of counterfactual outcomes specifically for those individuals who possess close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. By augmenting the original dataset with these reliable and precise imputations, we can effectively and substantially reduce the discrepancy between different treatment groups, while inducing only minimal imputation error. The augmented dataset is subsequently employed to train any CATE estimation model, offering a universal preprocessing step. Rigorous theoretical analysis and comprehensive experimental studies on a suite of synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks definitively demonstrate that our method achieves significant and consistent improvements in both performance and robustness to overfitting across a wide array of state-of-the-art models, paving the way for more reliable causal inference in practical applications.

Introduction

One of the most significant and persistent challenges for Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimation is the inherent statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups. While Randomized Controlled Trials (RCT) perfectly mitigate this issue, they are often prohibitively expensive, ethically problematic, and sometimes completely unfeasible to conduct in real-world scenarios. Consequently, practitioners are almost always constrained to relying on observational studies, which are intrinsically susceptible to severe selection bias arising from the aforementioned issue. To directly and effectively solve this problem, we introduce a fundamentally novel, model-agnostic data augmentation method, comprising two key, meticulously designed steps. First, our advanced approach intelligently identifies a specific subset of individuals whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably and accurately imputed. Subsequently, it performs precise imputation for the counterfactual outcomes of these selected individuals, thereby strategically augmenting the original dataset with the imputed values. Crucially and importantly, our method serves as a versatile data pre-processing module that remains completely agnostic to the choice of the subsequent model employed for CATE estimation, ensuring broad applicability. Extensive and thorough experiments underscore the powerful efficacy of our approach, as it consistently delivers substantial and meaningful performance improvements across a diverse portfolio of models, including all state-of-the-art models for CATE estimation. Furthermore, our method has been empirically validated to effectively and robustly mitigate overfitting, a significant and pervasive challenge in CATE estimation applications due to the inherent inaccessibility of counterfactual data.

Our method is directly motivated by an observed and fundamental trade-off between the discrepancy across treatment groups and the error induced by the imputation of the missing counterfactual outcomes. Consider the canonical scenario with one control group and one treatment group. In this context, no individual can possibly appear in both the control and treatment groups due to the fundamental inaccessibility of counterfactual outcomes. To clearly illustrate the core concept behind our groundbreaking methodology, consider the following simple experiment: for individuals in the control group, we randomly impute their outcome under treatment, generating their counterfactual outcomes. Subsequently, we integrate each individual along with their imputed outcomes back into the dataset. This naive transformation ensures that individuals from both the control and treatment groups become identical, effectively eliminating any disparities. However, it becomes immediately evident that any model trained on such a randomly augmented dataset would exhibit catastrophically poor performance, primarily due to the substantial error introduced by the random imputation of the counterfactual outcomes. Here, our innovative approach directly addresses this challenge by intelligently identifying a specific subset of individuals for whom the counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed with high confidence. Hence, the positive impact of disparity reduction will decisively outweigh the negative impact of imputation error. While it's important to acknowledge that the inherent issue of CATE estimation cannot be entirely eliminated, our approach effectively and substantially alleviates the core challenges faced by CATE estimation models, thus fundamentally facilitating their learning process and dramatically improving their predictive performance. In this paper, we utilize advanced contrastive learning to precisely identify the individuals from the original dataset whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed. This sophisticated technique helps us develop a powerful representation space and a highly effective similarity measure, such that within this learned representation space, close individuals by the similarity measure exhibit very similar potential outcomes. This smoothness property absolutely guarantees highly reliable imputation of counterfactual outcomes for the individuals with a sufficient number of close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. Specifically, we impute the counterfactual outcomes for these individuals by utilizing the factual outcomes of their proximate neighbors. Importantly, this smoothness property also ensures that the imputation can be achieved locally with simple models that require minimal tuning, enhancing practicality. We also explore two distinct and effective methods for imputation: local linear regression and local Gaussian Processes.

To comprehensively and rigorously assess the efficacy of our data augmentation technique, we demonstrate with theoretical rigor that our approach asymptotically generates datasets whose probability densities converge to those of RCTs. In addition, we provide non-asymptotic generalization bounds for the performance of CATE estimation models trained with our augmented data, offering strong theoretical guarantees. Our empirical results further definitively demonstrate the powerful efficacy of our method, showcasing consistent and significant enhancements in the performance of state-of-the-art CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, and CFR-MMD, S-Learner and T-Learner integrated with neural networks, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) with X-Learner, and Causal Forests (CF) with X-Learner. Notably, our method significantly reduces the overfitting tendencies commonly observed in CATE estimation models, where access to a validation dataset is often unattainable, thereby increasing reliability in deployment.

Related Work. One of the fundamental tasks in causal inference is to estimate Average Treatment Effects (ATE) and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). Various methods have been proposed to address the ATE estimation task, including Covariate Adjustment, Propensity Scores, Doubly Robust estimators, and Inverse Probability Weighting. While these methods are successful for ATE estimation, they are not directly applicable to the more challenging CATE estimation problem. Recent advances in machine learning have led to new and innovative approaches for CATE estimation, such as decision trees, Gaussian Processes, Multi-task deep learning ensemble, Generative Modeling, and representation learning with deep neural networks. It is worth noting that alternative approaches for investigating causal relationships exist, such as graphical modeling and do-calculus. In this work, we adopt the well-established Neyman-Rubin framework. At its core, the CATE estimation problem can be seen fundamentally as a missing data problem due to the unavailability of the counterfactual outcomes. In this context, we propose a novel and innovative data augmentation approach for CATE estimation by imputing certain missing counterfactuals. Data augmentation, a well-established and powerful technique in machine learning, serves to enhance model performance and curb overfitting by artificially expanding the size of the training dataset. A crucial aspect of our methodology is the accurate identification of similar individuals. There are various traditional methods to achieve this goal, including propensity score matching and Mahalanobis distance matching. Nonetheless, these methods pose significant and practical challenges, particularly in scenarios with large sample sizes or high-dimensional data, where they suffer severely from the curse of dimensionality. Recently, Perfect Match was proposed to leverage importance sampling to generate replicas of individuals. It relies on propensity scores and other feature space metrics to balance the distribution between the treatment and control groups during the training process. In contrast, we innovatively utilize contrastive learning to construct a powerful and effective similarity metric within a learned representation space. Our novel method focuses on imputing missing counterfactual outcomes for a selected subset of individuals, without creating duplicates of the original data points. While the Perfect Match method is a universal CATE estimator, our method is a model-agnostic data augmentation method that serves as a versatile and effective data preprocessing step for other CATE estimation models, offering a more flexible and powerful solution.

Theoretical Background

Let T be a binary variable for treatment assignment, X be the covariates (features), and Y be the factual (observed) outcome. For each j, we define Y_j as the potential outcome, which represents the outcome that would have been observed if only the treatment T=j was administered. The random tuple (X,T,Y) jointly follows the factual (observational) distribution denoted by p_F(x,t,y). The dataset used for causal inference, denoted by D_F, consists of n observations independently sampled from p_F where n is the total number of observations. The counterfactual distribution, denoted by p_CF, is defined as the sampling distribution of the dataset in a hypothetical parallel universe where the treatment assignment mechanism is inverted. To simplify the notation, for any distribution p(x,t,y), we use p(x,t) to denote the marginalized distribution of p(x,t,y) over the random tuple (X,T). For example, p_F(x,t) is the factual joint distribution of X and T. For a binary treatment assignment, the following identity holds: p_CF(x,1-t)= p_F(x,t).

Definition: CATE
The Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) is defined as the expected difference in potential outcomes given the covariates X=x.

Definition: ATE
The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is defined as the expected difference in potential outcomes.

CATE and ATE are identifiable under the assumptions of positivity and conditional unconfoundedness. Let τ_hat(x) = h(x,1)-h(x,0) denote an estimator for CATE where h is a hypothesis that estimates the underlying causal relationship between (X,T) and Y.

Definition: Expected PEHE
The Expected Precision in Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effect (PEHE) is defined as the integrated squared difference between the estimated and true CATE.

Definition: Loss
Given a joint distribution p over (X,T,Y) and a hypothesis h, let L_p(h) be defined as the expected squared loss. Then the factual loss L_F and the counterfactual loss L_CF are respectively defined as L_p_F(h) and L_p_CF(h).

Remark. ε_PEHE is widely-used as the performance metric for CATE estimation. However, estimating ε_PEHE directly from observational data such as D_F is a non-trivial and challenging task, as it requires knowledge of the counterfactual outcomes to compute the ground truth CATE values. This inherent challenge underscores that models for CATE estimation need to be robust to overfitting the factual distribution. Our empirical results definitively indicate that our method powerfully mitigates the risk of overfitting for various CATE estimation models.

COCOA: Contrastive Counterfactual Augmentation

As discussed in the Introduction, the effectiveness of imputing counterfactual outcomes depends critically on the availability of a representation space and a similarity measure that satisfies a specific and essential criterion: within this representation space, individuals identified as similar by the similarity measure should exhibit very similar potential outcomes when subjected to the same treatment. This smoothness assumption ensures straightforward and accurate local approximation: an individual's potential outcomes should exhibit a strong and reliable correlation with those of its nearby neighbors. To directly and effectively solve this problem, we introduce a fundamentally novel, model-agnostic data augmentation method, comprising two key, meticulously designed steps. First, our advanced approach intelligently identifies a specific subset of individuals whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably and accurately imputed. Subsequently, it performs precise imputation for the counterfactual outcomes of these selected individuals, thereby strategically augmenting the original dataset with the imputed values. Crucially and importantly, our method serves as a versatile data pre-processing module that remains completely agnostic to the choice of the subsequent model employed for CATE estimation, ensuring broad applicability. Extensive and thorough experiments underscore the powerful efficacy of our approach, as it consistently delivers substantial and meaningful performance improvements across a diverse portfolio of models, including all state-of-the-art models for CATE estimation. Furthermore, our method has been empirically validated to effectively and robustly mitigate overfitting, a significant and pervasive challenge in CATE estimation applications due to the inherent inaccessibility of counterfactual data.

Our method is directly motivated by an observed and fundamental trade-off between the discrepancy across treatment groups and the error induced by the imputation of the missing counterfactual outcomes. To clearly illustrate the core concept behind our groundbreaking methodology, consider the following simple experiment: for individuals in the control group, we randomly impute their outcome under treatment, generating their counterfactual outcomes. Subsequently, we integrate each individual along with their imputed outcomes back into the dataset. This naive transformation ensures that individuals from both the control and treatment groups become identical, effectively eliminating any disparities. However, it becomes immediately evident that any model trained on such a randomly augmented dataset would exhibit catastrophically poor performance, primarily due to the substantial error introduced by the random imputation of the counterfactual outcomes. Here, our innovative approach directly addresses this challenge by intelligently identifying a specific subset of individuals for whom the counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed with high confidence. Hence, the positive impact of disparity reduction will decisively outweigh the negative impact of imputation error. This sophisticated technique helps us develop a powerful representation space and a highly effective similarity measure, such that within this learned representation space, close individuals by the similarity measure exhibit very similar potential outcomes.
