This concept is formally captured in the following Theorem.

Theorem
Let x and let {X_k} be iid samples of X. Under positivity, we have that for any treatment t, the probability that none of M samples fall within an ε-ball around x converges to zero as M increases.

This implies definitively that with a sufficient number of samples, the probability of not encountering data points in close proximity to any given point x becomes very small. Hence, positivity ensures that within the big data regime, we will encounter densely populated regions, enabling us to approximate counterfactual distributions locally. This fundamentally facilitates the practical application of our methods.

Generalization Bound for Data Augmentation Methods

Let p_F(x,t,y) denote the factual distribution of the datasets and p_CF(x,t,y) the counterfactual distribution. Counterfactual data augmentation is essentially sampling from an estimated counterfactual distribution p_hat_CF(x,t,y). The distribution of the augmented factual dataset can be defined as a mixture.
where α represents the ratio of the number of generated counterfactual samples to the total number of samples in the augmented dataset. Let p_RCT(x,t,y) represent the distribution when the observations are sampled from randomized controlled trials.

Next, we present powerful generalization bounds for the performance of a hypothesis trained with the augmented dataset. To establish the generalization bound, we assume that there is a true potential outcome function f such that Y = f(X,T) + η with η having zero mean. Let A denote the process of data augmentation such that A(x,t, D) denotes the imputed outcome for the individual x under treatment t where D is the original dataset. Let n=|D| denote the total number of samples in the original dataset. Let f_tilde_n(x,t) denote the expected imputation when the dataset D consists of n samples independently sampled from p_F.

Theorem: Generalization Bound
Let H denote all the measurable functions for potential outcome estimation. Let L_AF be the loss under the augmented distribution. Then the expected imputation function minimizes the augmented loss. Moreover, for any measurable hypothesis function h, its ε_PEHE is upper bounded by a sum of three terms: the training loss on the augmented data, the L1 distance between the covariate-treatment distributions of RCT and augmented data, and a bias term scaled by α.

Interpretation of the Generalization Bound. We first note that the first term in the Theorem L_AF(h) is essentially the training loss of a hypothesis h on the augmented dataset. The second term, which is independent of Y, characterizes the statistical similarity between the individuals and treatment assignments in the augmented dataset and those generated from an RCT. As there is no statistical disparity across treatment groups when (X,T) follows p_RCT, the closer p_AF is to p_RCT the less is the statistical disparity in the augmented dataset. Meanwhile, the third term characterizes the accuracy of the data augmentation method. Hence, this theorem provides a rigorous and clear illustration of the fundamental trade-off between the statistical disparity across treatment groups and the imputation error. It underscores that by simultaneously minimizing disparity and imputation error, we can dramatically enhance the performance of CATE estimation models. Also note that as α, i.e., the ratio of imputed data points to all the data points, increases, the third term increases while the second decreases. This rigorously captures another important trade-off between the precision of data imputation and the discrepancy across treatment groups. It is also essential to highlight that if the local regression module can achieve more accurate estimation with more samples, the bias term will converge to 0 as n increases. Hence, ε_PEHE will converge to 0. This result aligns perfectly with our asymptotic analysis, indicating that as the augmented dataset grows in size, it converges toward RCT. In our experiments, we demonstrate convincingly that even small datasets can substantially benefit from augmenting the training data with just a few additional data samples using our powerful approach.

Experimental Studies

We test our proposed methods on various benchmark datasets: the IHDP dataset, the News dataset, and the Twins dataset. Additionally, we apply our methods to two synthetic datasets: one with linear functions for potential outcomes and the other with non-linear functions. To estimate the variance of our method, we randomly divide each of these datasets into a train (70%) dataset and a test (30%) dataset with varying seeds, and record the results from experiments with these different splits of data. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of our methods across a wide variety of CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, CFR-MMD, T-Learner, S-Learner, BART, and Causal Forests (CF).

Performance Improvements.
The experimental results to verify the effect of COCOA on improving the performance of CATE estimation models are summarized in two tables. These tables showcase the performance of various CATE estimation models, including the state-of-the-art ones, with and without data augmentation. It can be definitively observed that COCOA leads to consistent and significant performance improvement for a wide variety of CATE estimation models. Moreover, the improvements achieved by our method are consistent across all the datasets. We also observe that COCOA significantly and consistently outperforms Perfect Match as shown in the tables.

Robustness Improvements. In the context of CATE estimation, it is essential to notice the absence of a validation dataset due to the unavailability of the counterfactual outcomes. This poses a significant and practical challenge in preventing the models from overfitting to the factual distribution. Our proposed data augmentation technique effectively and powerfully addresses this challenge, as illustrated in the figure, resulting in a significant enhancement of the overall effectiveness and reliability of various CATE estimation models.
Notably, counterfactual balancing frameworks significantly benefit from COCOA. This improvement can be directly attributed to the fact that data augmentation in dense regions helps narrow the discrepancy between the distributions of the control and the treatment groups. By reducing this disparity, our approach enables better generalization and minimizes the balancing distance, leading to more stable and robust outcomes.
Ablation Studies. Additionally, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to assess the impact of two key parameters on the performance of different CATE estimation models trained with the IHDP dataset. Specifically, we investigate the influence of the epsilon ball size (R) in the embedding space and the number of neighbors (K) on the models' performance, as shown in the figure. These experiments clearly illustrate the trade-off between the quality of imputation and the discrepancy of the treatment groups. Finally, we provide ablations comparing our proposed contrastive learning method to other standard similarity measures: propensity scores and Euclidean distance in the feature space, presented in a table, confirming the superiority of our approach.

Conclusion

In this paper, we present a novel, model-agnostic data augmentation method for CATE estimation that combines strong theoretical guarantees with practical and effective implementation. Our innovative method utilizes advanced contrastive learning to learn a powerful representation space where it is possible to accurately identify a subset of individuals for which it can reliably impute their counterfactual outcomes. By adopting this powerful approach, we substantially enhance the performance and robustness of various CATE estimation models across a wide range of benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant practical value. We also present rigorous theoretical analysis and powerful generalization bounds strongly supporting our methods. This work establishes a new and effective paradigm for improving causal inference from observational data.

Title: Counterfactual Data Augmentation with Contrastive Learning

Abstract:
Statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups is a challenge for estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). A model-agnostic data augmentation method is introduced that imputes counterfactual outcomes for a selected subset of individuals. Contrastive learning is used to learn a representation space and a similarity measure such that individuals identified as close by the learned similarity measure have similar potential outcomes. This property enables imputation of counterfactual outcomes for individuals with close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. Augmenting the original dataset with these imputations can reduce the discrepancy between treatment groups while inducing minimal imputation error. The augmented dataset is used to train CATE estimation models. Theoretical analysis and experimental studies on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks show that the method can improve performance and robustness to overfitting across state-of-the-art models.

1. Introduction
A challenge for Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimation is statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups (Goldsmith et al., 2022). Randomized Controlled Trials (RCT) mitigate this issue (Rubin, 1974; Imbens & Rubin, 2015) but can be expensive, unethical, or unfeasible. Observational studies are susceptible to selection bias. A model-agnostic data augmentation method is introduced, comprising two steps. First, it identifies a subset of individuals whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed. Second, it performs imputation for these individuals, augmenting the original dataset. The method is a data pre-processing module agnostic to the subsequent CATE estimation model. Experiments show the method can deliver performance improvements across various models, including state-of-the-art models for CATE estimation. The method can also mitigate overfitting, a challenge in CATE estimation due to the inaccessibility of counterfactual data.

The method is motivated by a trade-off between (i) the discrepancy across treatment groups and (ii) the error induced by imputation of missing counterfactual outcomes. In a scenario with one control and one treatment group, no individual appears in both groups due to the inaccessibility of counterfactual outcomes (Holland, 1986). If counterfactual outcomes were randomly imputed for all individuals and added to the dataset, disparity would be eliminated, but model performance would be poor due to substantial imputation error. The approach addresses this by identifying a subset of individuals for whom counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed, so the positive impact of disparity reduction outweighs the negative impact of imputation error. The approach alleviates challenges faced by CATE estimation models.

Contrastive learning is used to identify individuals from the original dataset whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed. This technique develops a representation space and a similarity measure such that within this space, close individuals by the similarity measure exhibit similar potential outcomes. This smoothness property guarantees reliable imputation of counterfactual outcomes for individuals with a sufficient number of close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. Counterfactual outcomes for these individuals are imputed using the factual outcomes of their proximate neighbors. The smoothness property also ensures imputation can be achieved locally with simple models that require minimal tuning. Two distinct methods for imputation are explored: local linear regression and local Gaussian Processes.

To assess the efficacy of the data augmentation technique, it is shown that the approach asymptotically generates datasets whose probability densities converge to those of RCTs. Non-asymptotic generalization bounds are provided for the performance of CATE estimation models trained with the augmented data. Empirical results show the method can enhance the performance of state-of-the-art CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, and CFR-MMD (Shalit et al., 2017), S-Learner and T-Learner integrated with neural networks, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) (Hill, 2011; Chipman et al., 2010; Hill, 2020) with X-Learner (Künzel et al., 2019), and Causal Forests (CF) (Athey & Imbens, 2016) with X-Learner. The method can reduce overfitting tendencies in CATE estimation models.

Related Work.
A fundamental task in causal inference is to estimate Average Treatment Effects (ATE) and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE) (Neyman, 1923; Rubin, 2005). Methods for ATE estimation include Covariate Adjustment (Rubin, 1974), Propensity Scores (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983), Doubly Robust estimators (Robins et al., 1994), and Inverse Probability Weighting (Hirano et al., 2003). These methods are not directly applicable to CATE estimation. Recent approaches for CATE estimation include decision trees (Athey & Imbens, 2016), Gaussian Processes (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2017), Multi-task deep learning ensemble (Jiang et al., 2023), Generative Modeling (Yoon et al., 2018), and representation learning with deep neural networks (Shalit et al., 2017; Johansson et al., 2016). Alternative approaches for investigating causal relationships exist, such as graphical modeling and do-calculus (Pearl, 2009). The Neyman-Rubin framework is adopted. The CATE estimation problem can be seen as a missing data problem (Rubin, 1974; Holland, 1986; Ding et al., 2018). A new data augmentation approach for CATE estimation is proposed by imputing certain missing counterfactuals. Data augmentation is a technique in machine learning to enhance model performance and curb overfitting by artificially expanding the training dataset (van Dyk & Meng, 2001; Chawla et al., 2002; Han et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2021).

A crucial aspect is the identification of similar individuals. Methods include propensity score matching (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983) and Mahalanobis distance matching (Imai et al., 2008). These methods pose challenges in scenarios with large sample sizes or high-dimensional data. Perfect Match (Schwab et al., 2018) leverages importance sampling to generate replicas of individuals, relying on propensity scores and other feature space metrics to balance the distribution between treatment and control groups during training. In contrast, contrastive learning is used to construct a similarity metric within a representation space. The method focuses on imputing missing counterfactual outcomes for a selected subset of individuals, without creating duplicates. While Perfect Match is a universal CATE estimator, this method is a model-agnostic data augmentation method that serves as a data preprocessing step for other CATE estimation models.

2. Theoretical Background
Let T ∈ {0,1} be a binary variable for treatment assignment, X ∈ X ⊂ ℝ^d be the covariates (features), and Y ∈ Y ⊂ ℝ be the factual (observed) outcome. For each j ∈ {0,1}, Y_j is the potential outcome (Rubin, 1974), representing the outcome that would have been observed if only treatment T=j was administered. The random tuple (X,T,Y) jointly follows the factual (observational) distribution denoted by p_F(x,t,y).
The dataset used for causal inference, denoted by D_F = {(x_i, t_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n, consists of n observations independently sampled from p_F where n is the total number of observations.
The counterfactual distribution, denoted by p_CF, is defined as the sampling distribution of the dataset in a hypothetical parallel universe where the treatment assignment mechanism is inverted. For any distribution p(x,t,y), p(x,t) (respectively, p(x)) denotes the marginalized distribution of p(x,t,y) over (X,T) (respectively, X). For a binary treatment assignment, p_CF(x,1-t)= p_F(x,t) (Shalit et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2017).

Definition 1 (CATE).
The Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) is defined as the expected difference in potential outcomes given the covariates X=x:
τ(x) = 𝔼[Y_1 - Y_0 | X=x].

Definition 2 (ATE).
The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is defined as:
τ_ATE = 𝔼[Y_1 - Y_0].

CATE and ATE are identifiable under the assumptions of positivity, i.e., 0 < p_F(T=1|X) < 1, and conditional unconfoundedness, i.e., (Y_1, Y_0) ⫫ T | X (Robins, 1986; Imbens & Rubin, 2015).
Let τ̂(x) = h(x,1) - h(x,0) denote an estimator for CATE where h is a hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y that estimates the underlying causal relationship between (X,T) and Y.

Definition 3 (Expected PEHE).
The Expected Precision in Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effect (PEHE) (Hill, 2011) is defined as:
ε_PEHE(h) = ∫_X (τ̂(x) - τ(x))^2 p_F(x) dx = ∫_X (h(x,1) - h(x,0) - τ(x))^2 p_F(x) dx.

Definition 4 (Loss).
Given a joint distribution p over (X,T,Y) and a hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y, let L_p(h) be defined as:
L_p(h) = ∫ (y - h(x,t))^2 p(x,t,y) dx dt dy.
Then the factual loss L_F and the counterfactual loss L_CF are respectively defined as:
L_F(h) = L_p_F(h), L_CF(h) = L_p_CF(h).

Remark. ε_PEHE is widely-used as the performance metric for CATE estimation. Estimating ε_PEHE directly from observational data such as D_F is non-trivial, as it requires knowledge of counterfactual outcomes to compute ground truth CATE values. Models for CATE estimation need to be robust to overfitting the factual distribution. Empirical results indicate the method can mitigate the risk of overfitting for various CATE estimation models.

3. COCOA: Contrastive Counterfactual Augmentation
The effectiveness of imputing counterfactual outcomes depends on the availability of a representation space and a similarity measure that satisfies a criterion: within this representation space, individuals identified as similar by the similarity measure should exhibit similar potential outcomes when subjected to the same treatment. This smoothness assumption ensures straightforward local approximation: an individual's potential outcomes should exhibit a strong correlation with those of its nearby neighbors. For individuals who possess a sufficient number of close neighbors from the alternative treatment group, their counterfactual outcomes can be imputed using the factual outcomes of their nearby neighbors.

COntrastive COunterfactual Augmentation (COCOA) is proposed, consisting of two key components. The first component is a classifier g_θ*, trained using contrastive learning (Le-Khac et al., 2020; Jaiswal et al., 2020) to predict whether two individuals have similar outcomes when subjected to the same treatment. The second component is a local regressor ψ, which imputes the counterfactual outcome for a given individual after being fitted to the close neighbors.
The trained classifier g_θ* first identifies the close neighbors of a given individual. These close neighbors are individuals who are likely to have similar potential outcomes. Subsequently, the non-parametric regressor ψ utilizes the factual outcomes of these identified individuals to estimate the counterfactual outcome of the target individual. For example, if the target individual x belongs to the control group, g_θ* is used to select a subset of individuals from the treatment group who may exhibit outcomes similar to those of x. Then, ψ uses the factual outcomes of these selected individuals from the treatment group to estimate the counterfactual outcome of x under treatment. The imputed outcome of x is incorporated into the original dataset. The minimal error of the counterfactual imputation plays a crucial role. To ensure reliability, imputations are only performed for individuals who possess a sufficient number of close neighbors. In experiments, the minimum required number of close neighbors is set to 5. In the worst case, no individuals meet these criteria, resulting in no augmentation. This approach guarantees the method does not compromise the information inherent in the original dataset.

Remark. COCOA differs from standard CATE estimation models: it does not generalize to unseen samples. Its objective is to identify individuals within a given dataset and impute their counterfactual outcomes. COCOA serves as a tool to augment the dataset for other CATE models.

3.1. Contrastive Learning Module
Contrastive learning methods (Wu et al., 2018; Bojanowski & Joulin, 2017; Dosovitskiy et al., 2014; Caron et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Trinh et al., 2019; Misra & Maaten, 2020; Tian et al., 2020) are based on the principle that similar individuals should be associated with closely related representations within an embedding space. This is achieved by training models to predict whether two individuals are similar or dissimilar. In the context of CATE estimation, two individuals with similar outcomes under the same treatment are considered similar individuals. The degree of similarity between outcomes is measured using a metric in the potential outcome space Y. The Euclidean norm in ℝ^1 is employed. Given the factual dataset D_F = {(x_i, t_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n, a positive dataset D^+ is constructed that includes pairs of similar individuals. Specifically, D^+ = {(x_i, x_j): i,j ∈ [n], i ≠ j, t_i = t_j, ||y_i - y_j|| ≤ ε} where ε is a user-defined sensitivity parameter. A negative dataset D^- = {(x_i, x_j): i,j ∈ [n], i ≠ j, t_i = t_j, ||y_i - y_j|| > ε} is also created. Let ℓ: {0,1} × {0,1} → ℝ be any loss function for classification task. A parametric classifier g_θ: X × X → ℝ is trained where θ is the parameter vector that minimizes:
θ* ∈ argmin_θ Σ_{(x,x') ∈ D^+} ℓ(g_θ(x,x'),1) + Σ_{(x,x') ∈ D^-} ℓ(g_θ(x,x'),0).

Selection of the Nearest Neighbors for imputation.
For a given individual x with treatment t, g_θ* is used to identify a group of individuals from the factual dataset suitable for counterfactual imputation. Specifically, iterate over all individuals who received treatment 1-t and employ g_θ* to predict whether their potential outcomes are close to the potential outcome of x under treatment 1-t. Let x be the individual who received treatment t and whose counterfactual outcome will be imputed. Its selected neighbors D_{x,t} is defined as:
D_{x,t} ≐ {i ∈ [n]: t_i = 1-t, g_θ*(x,x_i) = 1}.
To ensure quality, the counterfactual outcome of x is estimated only if |D_{x,t}| ≥ K, where K is a pre-determined parameter. The approach ensures augmentation of the counterfactual outcome for an individual solely when there exists a sufficient number of closely related neighbors.

3.2. Local Regression Module
After identifying the nearest neighbors, a local regression module ψ is employed to impute the counterfactual outcomes. ψ has two arguments (i) x: the individual whose counterfactual outcome needs to be imputed; (ii) D_x = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^{n_x}: a set of close neighbors to x from the alternative treatment group with y_i their factual outcomes and n_x the number of close neighbors.
Two different types of local regression modules are explored: linear regression and Gaussian Process (GP). These function classes are chosen motivated by three principles:
1. Local Approximation: complex functions can be locally estimated with simple functions, e.g., continuous functions can be approximated by a linear function (Rudin, 1953) and complex distributions by Gaussian distributions.
2. Sample Efficiency: if the class of the local linear regression module can estimate the true target function locally, then a class with less complexity will require fewer close neighbors for good approximations.
3. Practicality: A simpler class of ψ requires less hyper-parameter tuning.

Gaussian Process.
Gaussian Processes (Seeger, 2004) offer a non-parametric approach to regression. Consider φ(x) ∼ GP(m(x), k(x,x')), for x,x' ∈ X. It is a collection of random variables indexed by a set X such that any finite collection follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Consider a finite index set of n elements X ≐ {x_i}_{i=1}^n, then the n-dimensional random variable φ(X) ≐ [φ(x_1), φ(x_2), ..., φ(x_n)] follows a Gaussian distribution:
φ(X) ∼ N(m(X), K(X))
where m(X) ≐ [m(x_1),..., m(x_n)] is the mean and K(X) is an n × n covariance matrix with element K(X)_{ij} ≐ k(x_i, x_j). A GP imposes a prior over functions φ: X → ℝ, characterized by a mean function m: X → ℝ and a kernel k: X × X → ℝ.

Based on the principle of Local Approximation, it is assumed that, given the construction of D_{x,t}, the counterfactual outcome of an individual x and the factual outcomes of individuals within D_{x,t} follow a GP. If x received treatment t, after locating the group of close neighbors, the imputed counterfactual outcome for x is:
ŷ_x^{1-t} ≐ 𝔼[y^{1-t} | x, {y_i^{1-t}}], i ∈ D_{x,t}.
Let σ(i) denote the i-th smallest index in D_{x,t} and k denote the kernel of GP. The imputed counterfactual outcome has the following close-form formula:
ŷ_x^{1-t} = 𝔼[y^{1-t} | x, y_i^{1-t}, i ∈ D_{x,t}] = K_x^T K_{xx}^{-1} y
where y = [y^{1-t}_{σ(1)}, ..., y^{1-t}_{σ(|D_{x,t}|)}], K_x = [k(x, x_{σ(1)}), ..., k(x, x_{σ(|D_{x,t}|)})] and K_{x,x} is a |D_{x,t}| × |D_{x,t}| matrix with element k(x_{σ(i)}, x_{σ(j)}). The tuple (x, 1-t, ŷ_x^{1-t}) is appended to the factual dataset.

4. Theoretical Analysis
Two main theoretical results are presented. The first characterizes the asymptotic behavior of COCOA, demonstrating that the distribution of the augmented dataset converges towards the distribution of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The second establishes a generalization bound for the performance of CATE estimation models trained using the augmented dataset. The generalization bound is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of data augmentation techniques.

4.1. Asymptotic Analysis
To establish the asymptotic behavior of COCOA, a notion of consistency for data augmentation is defined. It is demonstrated that the proposed consistency is equivalent to emulating RCTs. Convergence guarantees for COCOA under the positivity assumption are provided to be asymptotically consistent.

Definition 5 (Consistency of Factual Distribution).
A factual distribution p_F is consistent if for every hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y, L_F(h) = L_CF(h).

Definition 6 (Consistency of Data Augmentation).
A data augmentation method is said to be consistent if the augmented data follows a factual distribution that is consistent.

Theorem 1 (Consistency is Equivalent to RCT).
The factual distribution of any randomized controlled trial is consistent. Suppose we have a consistent factual distribution, then the data must originate from a distribution that is equivalent to one generating a randomized controlled trial.

Theorem 1 suggests that any consistent data augmentation is equivalent to collecting data from an RCT. Next, asymptotic consistency of COCOA is established. It is demonstrated that for any given individual x, the likelihood of encountering neighboring data points is sufficiently high as the number of data points grows, which guarantees reliable imputation of its counterfactual outcome.

Theorem 2.
Let x ∈ X and let {X_k}_{k=1}^M be iid samples of X. Under positivity, for t ∈ {0,1}:
P(∩_{k=1}^M X_k ∉ B_ε(x) | T=t) ≤ (1 - P(X ∈ B_ε(x) | T=t))^M →_{M→∞} 0
where B_ε(x) = {x' ∈ X | ||x - x'|| < ε} is the ε-ball around x.

This implies that with a sufficient number of samples, the probability of not encountering data points in close proximity to any given point x becomes very small. Positivity ensures that within the big data regime, densely populated regions are encountered, enabling approximation of counterfactual distributions locally.

4.2. Generalization Bound for Data Augmentation Methods
Let p_F(x,t,y) denote the factual distribution of the datasets and p_CF(x,t,y) the counterfactual distribution. Counterfactual data augmentation is essentially sampling from an estimated counterfactual distribution p̂_CF(x,t,y). The distribution of the augmented factual dataset can be defined as:
p_AF(x,t,y) = (1 - α) · p_F(x,t,y) + α · p̂_CF(x,t,y),
where α ∈ [0, ½] represents the ratio of the number of generated counterfactual samples to the total number of samples in the augmented dataset. Let p_RCT(x,t,y) represent the distribution of (X,T,Y) when the observations are sampled from randomized controlled trials.

Generalization bounds for the performance of a hypothesis trained with the augmented dataset are presented. To establish the generalization bound, it is assumed that there is a true potential outcome function f such that Y = f(X,T) + η with η verifying 𝔼[η] = 0. Let A denote the process of data augmentation such that A(x,t, D) denotes the imputed outcome for the individual x under treatment t where D is the original dataset. Let n = |D| denote the total number of samples in the original dataset. Let
f̃_n(x,t) = 𝔼_D[A(X,T,D) | X=x, T=t]
denote the expected imputation when the dataset D consists of n samples independently sampled from p_F.

Theorem 3 (Generalization Bound).
Let H = {h: X × {0,1} → Y} denote all the measurable functions for potential outcome estimation. Let L_AF = L_p_AF be defined as in Definition 4. Then
f̃ ∈ argmin_{h ∈ H} L_AF(h).
Moreover, for any measurable hypothesis function h ∈ H, its ε_PEHE is upper bounded as follows:
ε_PEHE(h) ≤ 4 · ( L_AF(h) + V(p_RCT(X,T), p_AF(X,T)) + α · b_A(n) )
where V(p,q) = ∫_S |p(s) - q(s)| ds is the L_1 distance between two distributions,
b_A(n) = 𝔼_{X,T ∼ p̂_CF(x,t)}[ ||f(X,T) - f̃_n(X,T)||^2 ]
is the expected bias of A with n samples.

Interpretation of the Generalization Bound.
The first term L_AF(h) is the training loss of a hypothesis h on the augmented dataset. The second term characterizes the statistical similarity between the individuals and treatment assignments in the augmented dataset and those generated from an RCT. As there is no statistical disparity across treatment groups when (X,T) follows p_RCT, the closer p_AF is to p_RCT the less is the statistical disparity in the augmented dataset. The third term characterizes the accuracy of the data augmentation method. The theorem illustrates the trade-off between the statistical disparity across treatment groups and the imputation error. By simultaneously minimizing disparity and imputation error, performance of CATE estimation models can be enhanced. As α increases, the third term increases while the second decreases. This captures another trade-off between the precision of data imputation and the discrepancy across treatment groups. If the local regression module can achieve more accurate estimation with more samples (e.g., local Gaussian Process and local linear regression) b_A(n) will converge to 0 as n increases. Hence, ε_PEHE will converge to 0. This result aligns with asymptotic analysis, indicating that as the augmented dataset grows in size, it converges toward RCT. Experiments demonstrate that even small datasets can substantially benefit from augmenting the training data with just a few additional data samples.

5. Experimental Studies
The methods are tested on benchmark datasets: the IHDP dataset (Ramey et al., 1992; Hill, 2011), the News dataset (Johansson et al., 2016; Newman et al., 2008), and the Twins dataset (Louizos et al., 2017). Additionally, methods are applied to two synthetic datasets: one with linear functions for potential outcomes and the other with non-linear functions. To estimate variance, each dataset is randomly divided into a train (70%) dataset and a test (30%) dataset with varying seeds, and results from experiments with these different splits are recorded. Efficacy is demonstrated across a variety of CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, CFR-MMD, T-Learner, S-Learner, BART, and Causal Forests (CF).

Performance Improvements.
Experimental results to verify the effect of COCOA on improving the performance of CATE estimation models are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. These tables showcase the performance of various CATE estimation models, with and without data augmentation. COCOA can lead to consistent performance improvement for a variety of CATE estimation models. Improvements are consistent across all datasets. COCOA can outperform Perfect Match (Schwab et al., 2018) as shown in Table 2.

Robustness Improvements.
In CATE estimation, the absence of a validation dataset due to the unavailability of counterfactual outcomes poses a challenge in preventing models from overfitting to the factual distribution. The proposed data augmentation technique can address this challenge, as illustrated in Figure 1, resulting in enhancement of the overall effectiveness of various CATE estimation models.
Counterfactual balancing frameworks (Johansson et al., 2016; Shalit et al., 2017) can benefit from COCOA. This improvement can be attributed to data augmentation in dense regions helping narrow the discrepancy between the distributions of the control and the treatment groups.

Ablation Studies.
Ablation studies were conducted to assess the impact of two key parameters on the performance of different CATE estimation models trained with the IHDP dataset. Specifically, the influence of the epsilon ball size (R) in the embedding space and the number of neighbors (K) on the models' performance is investigated, as shown in Figure 2. These experiments illustrate the trade-off between the quality of imputation and the discrepancy of the treatment groups. Ablations comparing the proposed contrastive learning method to other standard similarity measures: propensity scores and Euclidean distance in the feature space, are presented in Table 3.

6. Conclusion
A model-agnostic data augmentation method for CATE estimation is presented. The method combines theoretical guarantees with practical implementation, utilizing contrastive learning to learn a representation space where it is possible to identify a subset of individuals for which it can reliably impute their counterfactual outcomes. This approach can enhance the performance and robustness of various CATE estimation models across benchmark datasets. Theoretical analysis and generalization bounds supporting the methods are presented.

Title: Counterfactual Data Augmentation with Contrastive Learning

Abstract:
Statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups is a challenge for estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). A model-agnostic data augmentation method is introduced that imputes counterfactual outcomes for a selected subset of individuals. Contrastive learning is used to learn a representation space and a similarity measure such that individuals identified as close by the learned similarity measure have similar potential outcomes. This property enables imputation of counterfactual outcomes for individuals with close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. Augmenting the original dataset with these imputations can reduce the discrepancy between treatment groups while inducing minimal imputation error. The augmented dataset is used to train CATE estimation models. Theoretical analysis and experimental studies on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks show that the method can improve performance and robustness to overfitting across state-of-the-art models.

1. Introduction
A challenge for Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimation is statistical disparity between distinct treatment groups (Goldsmith et al., 2022). Randomized Controlled Trials (RCT) mitigate this issue (Rubin, 1974; Imbens & Rubin, 2015) but can be expensive, unethical, or unfeasible. Observational studies are susceptible to selection bias. A model-agnostic data augmentation method is introduced, comprising two steps. First, it identifies a subset of individuals whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed. Second, it performs imputation for these individuals, augmenting the original dataset. The method is a data pre-processing module agnostic to the subsequent CATE estimation model. Experiments show the method can deliver performance improvements across various models, including state-of-the-art models for CATE estimation. The method can also mitigate overfitting, a challenge in CATE estimation due to the inaccessibility of counterfactual data.

The method is motivated by a trade-off between (i) the discrepancy across treatment groups and (ii) the error induced by imputation of missing counterfactual outcomes. In a scenario with one control and one treatment group, no individual appears in both groups due to the inaccessibility of counterfactual outcomes (Holland, 1986). If counterfactual outcomes were randomly imputed for all individuals and added to the dataset, disparity would be eliminated, but model performance would be poor due to substantial imputation error. The approach addresses this by identifying a subset of individuals for whom counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed, so the positive impact of disparity reduction outweighs the negative impact of imputation error. The approach alleviates challenges faced by CATE estimation models.

Contrastive learning is used to identify individuals from the original dataset whose counterfactual outcomes can be reliably imputed. This technique develops a representation space and a similarity measure such that within this space, close individuals by the similarity measure exhibit similar potential outcomes. This smoothness property guarantees reliable imputation of counterfactual outcomes for individuals with a sufficient number of close neighbors from the alternative treatment group. Counterfactual outcomes for these individuals are imputed using the factual outcomes of their proximate neighbors. The smoothness property also ensures imputation can be achieved locally with simple models that require minimal tuning. Two distinct methods for imputation are explored: local linear regression and local Gaussian Processes.

To assess the efficacy of the data augmentation technique, it is shown that the approach asymptotically generates datasets whose probability densities converge to those of RCTs. Non-asymptotic generalization bounds are provided for the performance of CATE estimation models trained with the augmented data. Empirical results show the method can enhance the performance of state-of-the-art CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, and CFR-MMD (Shalit et al., 2017), S-Learner and T-Learner integrated with neural networks, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) (Hill, 2011; Chipman et al., 2010; Hill, 2020) with X-Learner (Künzel et al., 2019), and Causal Forests (CF) (Athey & Imbens, 2016) with X-Learner. The method can reduce overfitting tendencies in CATE estimation models.

Related Work.
A fundamental task in causal inference is to estimate Average Treatment Effects (ATE) and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE) (Neyman, 1923; Rubin, 2005). Methods for ATE estimation include Covariate Adjustment (Rubin, 1974), Propensity Scores (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983), Doubly Robust estimators (Robins et al., 1994), and Inverse Probability Weighting (Hirano et al., 2003). These methods are not directly applicable to CATE estimation. Recent approaches for CATE estimation include decision trees (Athey & Imbens, 2016), Gaussian Processes (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2017), Multi-task deep learning ensemble (Jiang et al., 2023), Generative Modeling (Yoon et al., 2018), and representation learning with deep neural networks (Shalit et al., 2017; Johansson et al., 2016). Alternative approaches for investigating causal relationships exist, such as graphical modeling and do-calculus (Pearl, 2009). The Neyman-Rubin framework is adopted. The CATE estimation problem can be seen as a missing data problem (Rubin, 1974; Holland, 1986; Ding et al., 2018). A new data augmentation approach for CATE estimation is proposed by imputing certain missing counterfactuals. Data augmentation is a technique in machine learning to enhance model performance and curb overfitting by artificially expanding the training dataset (van Dyk & Meng, 2001; Chawla et al., 2002; Han et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2021).

A crucial aspect is the identification of similar individuals. Methods include propensity score matching (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983) and Mahalanobis distance matching (Imai et al., 2008). These methods pose challenges in scenarios with large sample sizes or high-dimensional data. Perfect Match (Schwab et al., 2018) leverages importance sampling to generate replicas of individuals, relying on propensity scores and other feature space metrics to balance the distribution between treatment and control groups during training. In contrast, contrastive learning is used to construct a similarity metric within a representation space. The method focuses on imputing missing counterfactual outcomes for a selected subset of individuals, without creating duplicates. While Perfect Match is a universal CATE estimator, this method is a model-agnostic data augmentation method that serves as a data preprocessing step for other CATE estimation models.

2. Theoretical Background
Let T ∈ {0,1} be a binary variable for treatment assignment, X ∈ X ⊂ ℝ^d be the covariates (features), and Y ∈ Y ⊂ ℝ be the factual (observed) outcome. For each j ∈ {0,1}, Y_j is the potential outcome (Rubin, 1974), representing the outcome that would have been observed if only treatment T=j was administered. The random tuple (X,T,Y) jointly follows the factual (observational) distribution denoted by p_F(x,t,y).
The dataset used for causal inference, denoted by D_F = {(x_i, t_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n, consists of n observations independently sampled from p_F where n is the total number of observations.
The counterfactual distribution, denoted by p_CF, is defined as the sampling distribution of the dataset in a hypothetical parallel universe where the treatment assignment mechanism is inverted. For any distribution p(x,t,y), p(x,t) (respectively, p(x)) denotes the marginalized distribution of p(x,t,y) over (X,T) (respectively, X). For a binary treatment assignment, p_CF(x,1-t)= p_F(x,t) (Shalit et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2017).

Definition 1 (CATE).
The Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) is defined as the expected difference in potential outcomes given the covariates X=x:
τ(x) = 𝔼[Y_1 - Y_0 | X=x].

Definition 2 (ATE).
The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is defined as:
τ_ATE = 𝔼[Y_1 - Y_0].

CATE and ATE are identifiable under the assumptions of positivity, i.e., 0 < p_F(T=1|X) < 1, and conditional unconfoundedness, i.e., (Y_1, Y_0) ⫫ T | X (Robins, 1986; Imbens & Rubin, 2015).
Let τ̂(x) = h(x,1) - h(x,0) denote an estimator for CATE where h is a hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y that estimates the underlying causal relationship between (X,T) and Y.

Definition 3 (Expected PEHE).
The Expected Precision in Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effect (PEHE) (Hill, 2011) is defined as:
ε_PEHE(h) = ∫_X (τ̂(x) - τ(x))^2 p_F(x) dx = ∫_X (h(x,1) - h(x,0) - τ(x))^2 p_F(x) dx.

Definition 4 (Loss).
Given a joint distribution p over (X,T,Y) and a hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y, let L_p(h) be defined as:
L_p(h) = ∫ (y - h(x,t))^2 p(x,t,y) dx dt dy.
Then the factual loss L_F and the counterfactual loss L_CF are respectively defined as:
L_F(h) = L_p_F(h), L_CF(h) = L_p_CF(h).

Remark. ε_PEHE is widely-used as the performance metric for CATE estimation. Estimating ε_PEHE directly from observational data such as D_F is non-trivial, as it requires knowledge of counterfactual outcomes to compute ground truth CATE values. Models for CATE estimation need to be robust to overfitting the factual distribution. Empirical results indicate the method can mitigate the risk of overfitting for various CATE estimation models.

3. COCOA: Contrastive Counterfactual Augmentation
The effectiveness of imputing counterfactual outcomes depends on the availability of a representation space and a similarity measure that satisfies a criterion: within this representation space, individuals identified as similar by the similarity measure should exhibit similar potential outcomes when subjected to the same treatment. This smoothness assumption ensures straightforward local approximation: an individual's potential outcomes should exhibit a strong correlation with those of its nearby neighbors. For individuals who possess a sufficient number of close neighbors from the alternative treatment group, their counterfactual outcomes can be imputed using the factual outcomes of their nearby neighbors.

COntrastive COunterfactual Augmentation (COCOA) is proposed, consisting of two key components. The first component is a classifier g_θ*, trained using contrastive learning (Le-Khac et al., 2020; Jaiswal et al., 2020) to predict whether two individuals have similar outcomes when subjected to the same treatment. The second component is a local regressor ψ, which imputes the counterfactual outcome for a given individual after being fitted to the close neighbors.
The trained classifier g_θ* first identifies the close neighbors of a given individual. These close neighbors are individuals who are likely to have similar potential outcomes. Subsequently, the non-parametric regressor ψ utilizes the factual outcomes of these identified individuals to estimate the counterfactual outcome of the target individual. For example, if the target individual x belongs to the control group, g_θ* is used to select a subset of individuals from the treatment group who may exhibit outcomes similar to those of x. Then, ψ uses the factual outcomes of these selected individuals from the treatment group to estimate the counterfactual outcome of x under treatment. The imputed outcome of x is incorporated into the original dataset. The minimal error of the counterfactual imputation plays a crucial role. To ensure reliability, imputations are only performed for individuals who possess a sufficient number of close neighbors. In experiments, the minimum required number of close neighbors is set to 5. In the worst case, no individuals meet these criteria, resulting in no augmentation. This approach guarantees the method does not compromise the information inherent in the original dataset.

Remark. COCOA differs from standard CATE estimation models: it does not generalize to unseen samples. Its objective is to identify individuals within a given dataset and impute their counterfactual outcomes. COCOA serves as a tool to augment the dataset for other CATE models.

3.1. Contrastive Learning Module
Contrastive learning methods (Wu et al., 2018; Bojanowski & Joulin, 2017; Dosovitskiy et al., 2014; Caron et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Trinh et al., 2019; Misra & Maaten, 2020; Tian et al., 2020) are based on the principle that similar individuals should be associated with closely related representations within an embedding space. This is achieved by training models to predict whether two individuals are similar or dissimilar. In the context of CATE estimation, two individuals with similar outcomes under the same treatment are considered similar individuals. The degree of similarity between outcomes is measured using a metric in the potential outcome space Y. The Euclidean norm in ℝ^1 is employed. Given the factual dataset D_F = {(x_i, t_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n, a positive dataset D^+ is constructed that includes pairs of similar individuals. Specifically, D^+ = {(x_i, x_j): i,j ∈ [n], i ≠ j, t_i = t_j, ||y_i - y_j|| ≤ ε} where ε is a user-defined sensitivity parameter. A negative dataset D^- = {(x_i, x_j): i,j ∈ [n], i ≠ j, t_i = t_j, ||y_i - y_j|| > ε} is also created. Let ℓ: {0,1} × {0,1} → ℝ be any loss function for classification task. A parametric classifier g_θ: X × X → ℝ is trained where θ is the parameter vector that minimizes:
θ* ∈ argmin_θ Σ_{(x,x') ∈ D^+} ℓ(g_θ(x,x'),1) + Σ_{(x,x') ∈ D^-} ℓ(g_θ(x,x'),0).

Selection of the Nearest Neighbors for imputation.
For a given individual x with treatment t, g_θ* is used to identify a group of individuals from the factual dataset suitable for counterfactual imputation. Specifically, iterate over all individuals who received treatment 1-t and employ g_θ* to predict whether their potential outcomes are close to the potential outcome of x under treatment 1-t. Let x be the individual who received treatment t and whose counterfactual outcome will be imputed. Its selected neighbors D_{x,t} is defined as:
D_{x,t} ≐ {i ∈ [n]: t_i = 1-t, g_θ*(x,x_i) = 1}.
To ensure quality, the counterfactual outcome of x is estimated only if |D_{x,t}| ≥ K, where K is a pre-determined parameter. The approach ensures augmentation of the counterfactual outcome for an individual solely when there exists a sufficient number of closely related neighbors.

3.2. Local Regression Module
After identifying the nearest neighbors, a local regression module ψ is employed to impute the counterfactual outcomes. ψ has two arguments (i) x: the individual whose counterfactual outcome needs to be imputed; (ii) D_x = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^{n_x}: a set of close neighbors to x from the alternative treatment group with y_i their factual outcomes and n_x the number of close neighbors.
Two different types of local regression modules are explored: linear regression and Gaussian Process (GP). These function classes are chosen motivated by three principles:
1. Local Approximation: complex functions can be locally estimated with simple functions, e.g., continuous functions can be approximated by a linear function (Rudin, 1953) and complex distributions by Gaussian distributions.
2. Sample Efficiency: if the class of the local linear regression module can estimate the true target function locally, then a class with less complexity will require fewer close neighbors for good approximations.
3. Practicality: A simpler class of ψ requires less hyper-parameter tuning.

Gaussian Process.
Gaussian Processes (Seeger, 2004) offer a non-parametric approach to regression. Consider φ(x) ∼ GP(m(x), k(x,x')), for x,x' ∈ X. It is a collection of random variables indexed by a set X such that any finite collection follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Consider a finite index set of n elements X ≐ {x_i}_{i=1}^n, then the n-dimensional random variable φ(X) ≐ [φ(x_1), φ(x_2), ..., φ(x_n)] follows a Gaussian distribution:
φ(X) ∼ N(m(X), K(X))
where m(X) ≐ [m(x_1),..., m(x_n)] is the mean and K(X) is an n × n covariance matrix with element K(X)_{ij} ≐ k(x_i, x_j). A GP imposes a prior over functions φ: X → ℝ, characterized by a mean function m: X → ℝ and a kernel k: X × X → ℝ.

Based on the principle of Local Approximation, it is assumed that, given the construction of D_{x,t}, the counterfactual outcome of an individual x and the factual outcomes of individuals within D_{x,t} follow a GP. If x received treatment t, after locating the group of close neighbors, the imputed counterfactual outcome for x is:
ŷ_x^{1-t} ≐ 𝔼[y^{1-t} | x, {y_i^{1-t}}], i ∈ D_{x,t}.
Let σ(i) denote the i-th smallest index in D_{x,t} and k denote the kernel of GP. The imputed counterfactual outcome has the following close-form formula:
ŷ_x^{1-t} = 𝔼[y^{1-t} | x, y_i^{1-t}, i ∈ D_{x,t}] = K_x^T K_{xx}^{-1} y
where y = [y^{1-t}_{σ(1)}, ..., y^{1-t}_{σ(|D_{x,t}|)}], K_x = [k(x, x_{σ(1)}), ..., k(x, x_{σ(|D_{x,t}|)})] and K_{x,x} is a |D_{x,t}| × |D_{x,t}| matrix with element k(x_{σ(i)}, x_{σ(j)}). The tuple (x, 1-t, ŷ_x^{1-t}) is appended to the factual dataset.

4. Theoretical Analysis
Two main theoretical results are presented. The first characterizes the asymptotic behavior of COCOA, demonstrating that the distribution of the augmented dataset converges towards the distribution of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The second establishes a generalization bound for the performance of CATE estimation models trained using the augmented dataset. The generalization bound is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of data augmentation techniques.

4.1. Asymptotic Analysis
To establish the asymptotic behavior of COCOA, a notion of consistency for data augmentation is defined. It is demonstrated that the proposed consistency is equivalent to emulating RCTs. Convergence guarantees for COCOA under the positivity assumption are provided to be asymptotically consistent.

Definition 5 (Consistency of Factual Distribution).
A factual distribution p_F is consistent if for every hypothesis h: X × {0,1} → Y, L_F(h) = L_CF(h).

Definition 6 (Consistency of Data Augmentation).
A data augmentation method is said to be consistent if the augmented data follows a factual distribution that is consistent.

Theorem 1 (Consistency is Equivalent to RCT).
The factual distribution of any randomized controlled trial is consistent. Suppose we have a consistent factual distribution, then the data must originate from a distribution that is equivalent to one generating a randomized controlled trial.

Theorem 1 suggests that any consistent data augmentation is equivalent to collecting data from an RCT. Next, asymptotic consistency of COCOA is established. It is demonstrated that for any given individual x, the likelihood of encountering neighboring data points is sufficiently high as the number of data points grows, which guarantees reliable imputation of its counterfactual outcome.

Theorem 2.
Let x ∈ X and let {X_k}_{k=1}^M be iid samples of X. Under positivity, for t ∈ {0,1}:
P(∩_{k=1}^M X_k ∉ B_ε(x) | T=t) ≤ (1 - P(X ∈ B_ε(x) | T=t))^M →_{M→∞} 0
where B_ε(x) = {x' ∈ X | ||x - x'|| < ε} is the ε-ball around x.

This implies that with a sufficient number of samples, the probability of not encountering data points in close proximity to any given point x becomes very small. Positivity ensures that within the big data regime, densely populated regions are encountered, enabling approximation of counterfactual distributions locally.

4.2. Generalization Bound for Data Augmentation Methods
Let p_F(x,t,y) denote the factual distribution of the datasets and p_CF(x,t,y) the counterfactual distribution. Counterfactual data augmentation is essentially sampling from an estimated counterfactual distribution p̂_CF(x,t,y). The distribution of the augmented factual dataset can be defined as:
p_AF(x,t,y) = (1 - α) · p_F(x,t,y) + α · p̂_CF(x,t,y),
where α ∈ [0, ½] represents the ratio of the number of generated counterfactual samples to the total number of samples in the augmented dataset. Let p_RCT(x,t,y) represent the distribution of (X,T,Y) when the observations are sampled from randomized controlled trials.

Generalization bounds for the performance of a hypothesis trained with the augmented dataset are presented. To establish the generalization bound, it is assumed that there is a true potential outcome function f such that Y = f(X,T) + η with η verifying 𝔼[η] = 0. Let A denote the process of data augmentation such that A(x,t, D) denotes the imputed outcome for the individual x under treatment t where D is the original dataset. Let n = |D| denote the total number of samples in the original dataset. Let
f̃_n(x,t) = 𝔼_D[A(X,T,D) | X=x, T=t]
denote the expected imputation when the dataset D consists of n samples independently sampled from p_F.

Theorem 3 (Generalization Bound).
Let H = {h: X × {0,1} → Y} denote all the measurable functions for potential outcome estimation. Let L_AF = L_p_AF be defined as in Definition 4. Then
f̃ ∈ argmin_{h ∈ H} L_AF(h).
Moreover, for any measurable hypothesis function h ∈ H, its ε_PEHE is upper bounded as follows:
ε_PEHE(h) ≤ 4 · ( L_AF(h) + V(p_RCT(X,T), p_AF(X,T)) + α · b_A(n) )
where V(p,q) = ∫_S |p(s) - q(s)| ds is the L_1 distance between two distributions,
b_A(n) = 𝔼_{X,T ∼ p̂_CF(x,t)}[ ||f(X,T) - f̃_n(X,T)||^2 ]
is the expected bias of A with n samples.

Interpretation of the Generalization Bound.
The first term L_AF(h) is the training loss of a hypothesis h on the augmented dataset. The second term characterizes the statistical similarity between the individuals and treatment assignments in the augmented dataset and those generated from an RCT. As there is no statistical disparity across treatment groups when (X,T) follows p_RCT, the closer p_AF is to p_RCT the less is the statistical disparity in the augmented dataset. The third term characterizes the accuracy of the data augmentation method. The theorem illustrates the trade-off between the statistical disparity across treatment groups and the imputation error. By simultaneously minimizing disparity and imputation error, performance of CATE estimation models can be enhanced. As α increases, the third term increases while the second decreases. This captures another trade-off between the precision of data imputation and the discrepancy across treatment groups. If the local regression module can achieve more accurate estimation with more samples (e.g., local Gaussian Process and local linear regression) b_A(n) will converge to 0 as n increases. Hence, ε_PEHE will converge to 0. This result aligns with asymptotic analysis, indicating that as the augmented dataset grows in size, it converges toward RCT. Experiments demonstrate that even small datasets can substantially benefit from augmenting the training data with just a few additional data samples.

5. Experimental Studies
The methods are tested on benchmark datasets: the IHDP dataset (Ramey et al., 1992; Hill, 2011), the News dataset (Johansson et al., 2016; Newman et al., 2008), and the Twins dataset (Louizos et al., 2017). Additionally, methods are applied to two synthetic datasets: one with linear functions for potential outcomes and the other with non-linear functions. To estimate variance, each dataset is randomly divided into a train (70%) dataset and a test (30%) dataset with varying seeds, and results from experiments with these different splits are recorded. Efficacy is demonstrated across a variety of CATE estimation models, including TARNet, CFR-Wass, CFR-MMD, T-Learner, S-Learner, BART, and Causal Forests (CF).

Performance Improvements.
Experimental results to verify the effect of COCOA on improving the performance of CATE estimation models are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. These tables showcase the performance of various CATE estimation models, with and without data augmentation. COCOA can lead to consistent performance improvement for a variety of CATE estimation models. Improvements are consistent across all datasets. COCOA can outperform Perfect Match (Schwab et al., 2018) as shown in Table 2.

Robustness Improvements.
In CATE estimation, the absence of a validation dataset due to the unavailability of counterfactual outcomes poses a challenge in preventing models from overfitting to the factual distribution. The proposed data augmentation technique can address this challenge, as illustrated in Figure 1, resulting in enhancement of the overall effectiveness of various CATE estimation models.
Counterfactual balancing frameworks (Johansson et al., 2016; Shalit et al., 2017) can benefit from COCOA. This improvement can be attributed to data augmentation in dense regions helping narrow the discrepancy between the distributions of the control and the treatment groups.

Ablation Studies.
Ablation studies were conducted to assess the impact of two key parameters on the performance of different CATE estimation models trained with the IHDP dataset. Specifically, the influence of the epsilon ball size (R) in the embedding space and the number of neighbors (K) on the models' performance is investigated, as shown in Figure 2. These experiments illustrate the trade-off between the quality of imputation and the discrepancy of the treatment groups. Ablations comparing the proposed contrastive learning method to other standard similarity measures: propensity scores and Euclidean distance in the feature space, are presented in Table 3.

6. Conclusion
A model-agnostic data augmentation method for CATE estimation is presented. The method combines theoretical guarantees with practical implementation, utilizing contrastive learning to learn a representation space where it is possible to identify a subset of individuals for which it can reliably impute their counterfactual outcomes. This approach can enhance the performance and robustness of various CATE estimation models across benchmark datasets. Theoretical analysis and generalization bounds supporting the methods are presented.

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flows Modeling for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection

Abstract
Unified anomaly detection (AD) represents a critical frontier in machine learning, where a single model is trained on normal samples from multiple classes to detect anomalies across all of them. For this challenging task, popular normalizing flow (NF) based AD methods often fall into a "homogeneous mapping" issue, where they generate similar latent representations for both normal and abnormal features, leading to a high rate of missed anomalies. In this paper, we propose a novel Hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for unified Anomaly Detection, called HGAD. Our HGAD consists of two key components: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and intra-class mixed class centers learning. Compared to previous NF-based AD methods, this hierarchical approach provides a significantly stronger representation capability for the latent space of normalizing flows. This design definitively avoids mapping different class distributions into a single Gaussian prior, thereby effectively mitigating the "homogeneous mapping" issue. We further establish that more distinguishable class centers are more conducive to avoiding this bias. Thus, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to better structure the latent feature space. We evaluate our method on four real-world AD benchmarks, where it significantly improves upon previous NF-based AD methods and also outperforms state-of-the-art unified AD methods.

Introduction

Anomaly detection has received increasingly wide attention and applications in diverse scenarios, such as industrial defect detection, video surveillance, medical lesion detection, and road anomaly detection. Given the scarcity of anomalies and the diversity of normal classes, most previous AD studies have focused on unsupervised one-class learning, training a specific model for each class using only its normal samples. However, this one-for-one paradigm requires substantial human labor, time, and computation costs when dealing with many product categories and can underperform when a single normal class has high intra-class diversity.

This work tackles the more practical and scalable task of unified anomaly detection. Here, a single model is trained with normal samples from multiple classes and must detect anomalies for all these classes without fine-tuning. Solving this task is challenging. Current reconstruction-based unified AD methods, such as UniAD and PMAD, can fall into an "identical shortcut reconstruction" dilemma, where anomalies are also well-reconstructed, causing detection failure. While these methods use masking strategies, the diverse scale and shape of anomalies mean abnormal information leakage during reconstruction remains a risk. Therefore, we approach unified AD from a normal data distribution learning perspective, which in principle avoids the risk of abnormal information leakage as it is based solely on normal data and eschews reconstruction. Specifically, we employ normalizing flows (NF) to learn the normal data distribution.

However, we find that standard NF-based AD methods perform unsatisfactorily on the unified AD task. They typically encounter a "homogeneous mapping" issue, where the models are biased to generate large log-likelihoods for both normal and abnormal inputs. We explain this issue as follows: standard NF-based AD methods use a uni-modal Gaussian prior to model a multi-class (multi-modal) distribution. This forces a mapping from a heterogeneous feature space to a homogeneous latent space. To learn this mapping, the network may bias towards concentrating on coarse-grained common characteristics (e.g., local pixel correlations) and suppressing fine-grained distinguishable characteristics (e.g., semantic content) among different classes. Consequently, the network homogeneously maps different class features to similar latent embeddings, making anomalies less distinguishable.

To address this issue, we first empirically confirm that mapping to a multi-modal latent distribution is effective in preventing this bias. Accordingly, we propose an inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling approach for NF-based networks to better capture the complex multi-class distribution. Second, we argue that inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling alone ensures features are drawn to the overall distribution but lacks inter-class repulsion, which can still result in weak discriminative ability and cause class centers to collapse. To increase inter-class discriminability, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to introduce class repulsion, pushing class centers apart. Third, we introduce an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy to help the model learn diverse normal patterns within a single class. Together, these form our hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for unified anomaly detection (HGAD). In summary, our main contributions are:

1. We propose HGAD, a novel unified AD method where hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling provides a stronger representation capability for the latent space of normalizing flows.
2. We specifically propose three key designs: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling, a mutual information maximization loss, and an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy.
3. Under the unified AD task, our method dramatically improves the performance of previous one-for-one NF-based AD methods (e.g., boosting CFLOW-AD's AUROC from 89.0%/94.0% to 98.4%/97.9%) and also outperforms state-of-the-art unified AD methods (e.g., UniAD).

Related Work

GMM in Anomaly Detection. Previous methods like DAGMM and PEDENet also use GMMs. However, our method is significantly different: 1) Task Difference: DAGMM is for non-image data, and PEDENet is for one-class image AD. Applying them to unified AD is non-trivial, whereas our method is designed for and achieves superiority in this task. 2) Approach Difference: DAGMM and PEDENet predict membership to calculate GMM parameters directly. Our method uses learnable class centers and weights, which is more beneficial for hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling.

Method

Preliminary of Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection
Normalizing flow models fit an arbitrary distribution p(X) using a tractable latent base distribution p(Z) and a bijective mapping φ. The log-likelihood of x is estimated as log p_θ(x) = log p_Z(φ_θ(x)) + log|det J|. The model is trained by maximizing log-likelihoods across the training distribution. In AD, Z for normal features is typically assumed to follow N(0, I). The anomaly score is derived as s(x) = 1 - p_θ(x).

Revisiting Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection Methods
Under the unified AD task, we observe that NF-based methods suffer a performance drop after training, with losses becoming very small and log-likelihoods becoming large for both normal and abnormal features. We attribute this to the "homogeneous mapping" issue. A rough analysis using a simple coupling layer model shows that with a maximum likelihood loss pushing all z to fit N(0, I), the model can bias towards predicting transformation coefficients that allow it to fit abnormal features well too, failing detection. Mapping different class features to different class centers makes this biased solution harder to achieve.

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flow Modeling

Overview. HGAD consists of a feature extractor, a normalizing flow model, and hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling. Multi-level feature maps are processed, and the NF model transforms features into latent embeddings, which are then fitted using our hierarchical modeling.

Inter-Class Gaussian Mixture Modeling. To better fit the multi-class distribution, we use a Gaussian mixture model with class-dependent means μ_y and unit covariance matrices as the prior for latent variables Z: p_Z(z) = Σ_y p(y) N(z; μ_y, I). Class weights p(y) are parameterized via a learnable vector ψ. The corresponding loss function is derived as L_g.

Mutual Information Maximization. To introduce class repulsion and prevent center collapse, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to increase I(Y, Z). The practical loss format is L_mi. We also introduce an entropy loss L_e to minimize inter-class entropy.

Learning Intra-Class Mixed Class Centers. To model diverse intra-class patterns, we extend the Gaussian prior per class to a mixture Gaussian prior. To avoid numerical issues during optimization, we decouple the learning of inter-class and intra-class centers. We learn a main class center μ_1^y and delta vectors Δμ_i^y for other intra-class centers. The main center is optimized via L_g, while the delta vectors are optimized via a detached loss L_in.

Overall Loss Function. The total training loss is L = λ_1 L_g + λ_2 L_mi + L_e + L_in, with λ_1=1 and λ_2=100 by default.

Anomaly Scoring
For a test feature x^k from level k, we calculate its intra-class log-likelihood and inter-class negative entropy. These are converted to likelihoods and upsampled to image resolution. The final anomaly score map S is the element-wise product of the score maps derived from likelihoods (S_l) and entropy (S_e). This combined criterion helps ensure anomalies are identified as out-of-distribution.

Further Discussions

Explicitly Distinguishing Classes. Our method uses image class labels y, which does not introduce extra data collection cost compared to one-class AD models, as existing AD datasets are already organized by class. The key advantage is training one model for all classes, reducing resource costs. While PMAD also uses class information, and UniAD/OmniAL use extra information for anomaly simulation, our method achieves superior results, suggesting class information is a practical and effective resource for unified AD modeling.

Experiment

Datasets and Metrics
We evaluate on four real-world industrial AD datasets: MVTecAD, BTAD, MVTec3D-RGB, and VisA. We also form a combined 40-class Union dataset. Performance is measured using the AUROC metric.

Main Results

Setup. We train one unified model per dataset. We use EfficientNet-b6 as a frozen feature extractor. The NF model has 12 layers. The number of inter-class centers equals the number of dataset classes. The number of intra-class centers is set to 10. Models are trained for 100 epochs.

Baselines. We compare against one-class AD baselines (PaDiM, MKD, DRAEM), SOTA unified AD methods (PMAD, UniAD, OmniAL), and SOTA one-class NF-based methods (CFLOW, FastFlow).

Quantitative Results. On MVTecAD, HGAD outperforms all baselines under the unified setting. It improves upon one-class NF-based methods (FastFlow, CFLOW) by large margins (e.g., from 91.8%/96.0% to 98.4%/97.9% image/pixel AUROC) and surpasses SOTA unified methods PMAD and UniAD. Results on BTAD, MVTec3D-RGB, VisA, and the Union dataset consistently show HGAD's superiority.

Qualitative Results. Visual comparisons show HGAD generates more accurate anomaly score maps than the CFLOW baseline across various anomaly types.

Ablation Studies

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Modeling. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of each component: using multiple centers improves performance; inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling provides further gains; mutual information maximization boosts detection; intra-class mixed centers learning increases performance. The full hierarchical combination achieves the best results.

Number of Intra-Class Centers. A moderate number of 10 intra-class centers yields the best performance.

Anomaly Criterion. Combining log-likelihood and entropy for scoring outperforms using either criterion alone.

Hyperparameters. A larger weight λ_2 for the mutual information loss leads to better performance, underscoring the importance of class discrimination.

Optimization Strategy. A two-stage optimization strategy that decouples inter-class and intra-class learning brings stability and better results.

Conclusion

This paper addresses the challenge of unified anomaly detection across multiple classes. Standard normalizing flow based AD methods suffer from a "homogeneous mapping" issue in this setting. To counter this, we propose HGAD, which incorporates inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling, mutual information maximization, and intra-class mixed class centers learning. Under the unified AD setting, our method delivers substantial improvements over NF-based AD methods and surpasses state-of-the-art unified AD methods.
