Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flows Modeling for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection

Abstract

Unified anomaly detection (AD) stands as one of the most valuable and practically significant challenges within the field, where a single unified model is trained using normal samples from multiple distinct classes with the objective of reliably detecting anomalies across all these classes. For such a challenging and complex task, popular normalizing flow (NF) based AD methods may critically fall into a debilitating ``homogeneous mapping'' issue, where the NF-based AD models become inherently biased to generate similar latent representations for both normal and abnormal features, and thereby lead to a high missing rate of anomalies. In this paper, we propose a fundamentally novel \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{G}aussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for accomplishing unified \textbf{A}nomaly \textbf{D}etection, which we definitively call HGAD. Our HGAD consists of two essential and synergistic key components: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and intra-class mixed class centers learning. Compared directly to the previous NF-based AD methods, our hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling approach demonstrably brings a substantially stronger representation capability to the latent space of normalizing flows. In this powerful way, we can decisively avoid mapping different complex class distributions into the same simplistic single Gaussian prior, thus effectively avoiding or mitigating the pervasive ``homogeneous mapping'' issue. We further definitively indicate that the more distinguishable the different class centers are, the more conducive it is to avoiding the bias issue. Thus, we further propose a mutual information maximization loss for better and more effectively structuring the latent feature space. We thoroughly evaluate our method on four comprehensive real-world AD benchmarks, where we can significantly and consistently improve upon the previous NF-based AD methods and also definitively outperform the current SOTA unified AD methods, showcasing its immediate practical value.

Introduction

Anomaly detection has received increasingly wide attentions and critical applications across a diverse array of different real-world scenarios, such as industrial defect detection for manufacturing quality control, video surveillance for public safety, medical lesion detection for healthcare diagnostics, and road anomaly detection for autonomous driving systems. Considering the highly scarce nature of anomalies and the diverse spectrum of normal classes, most previous AD studies have mainly devoted their efforts to unsupervised one-class learning, \emph{i.e.}, learning one specific AD model by only utilizing one-class normal samples and then detecting anomalies within this single class. However, such a one-for-one paradigm would demonstrably require considerably more human labor, time, and substantial computation costs when training and testing on many product categories, and also critically underperform when the one normal class possesses large intra-class diversity, limiting its scalability.

In this work, we decisively aim to tackle a more practical and impactful task: unified anomaly detection. As illustrated, one unified model is trained with normal samples from multiple classes, and the objective is to robustly detect anomalies for all these classes without any subsequent fine-tuning. Nonetheless, solving such a task is inherently quite challenging. Currently, there are only a few reconstruction-based AD methods for tackling this challenging unified AD task. But these reconstruction-based methods may critically fall into the ``identical shortcut reconstruction'' dilemma, where anomalies can also be well reconstructed, resulting in the catastrophic failure of anomaly detection. Existing attempts to mask adjacent or suspicious anomalies cannot completely avoid abnormal information leakage during reconstruction; therefore, the fundamental risk of identical reconstruction persistently remains. To this end, we consider designing the unified AD model from the principled normal data distribution learning perspective. The decisive advantage is that we will no longer face the abnormal information leakage risk in principle, as our method is fundamentally based on normal data distribution and radically avoids reconstruction altogether. Specifically, we employ normalizing flows (NF) to learn the normal data distribution.

However, we definitively find that the NF-based AD methods perform unsatisfactorily when applied to the unified AD task. They usually fall into a critical ``homogeneous mapping'' issue, where the NF-based AD models are biased to generate large log-likelihoods for both normal and abnormal inputs. We explain this core issue as follows: the NF-based AD methods employ a uni-modal Gaussian prior to learn a complex multi-class distribution (which is multi-modal). This can be seen as learning a mapping from a heterogeneous feature space to a latent homogeneous space. To learn this mapping, the network may be prompted to take a bias to concentrate excessively on coarse-grained common characteristics and suppress the fine-grained distinguishable characteristics among different class features. Consequently, the network homogeneously maps different class features to close latent embeddings. Thus, even anomalies can obtain large log-likelihoods and become less distinguishable, undermining detection.

To definitively address this core issue, we first empirically confirm that mapping to a multi-modal latent distribution is effective to prevent the model from learning the bias. Accordingly, we propose an inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling approach for NF-based AD networks to more effectively capture the complex multi-class distribution. Second, we argue that inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling alone can only ensure features are drawn to the whole distribution but lacks inter-class repulsion, still resulting in a much weaker discriminative ability for different class features. This may cause different class centers to collapse into the same center. To further and decisively increase the inter-class discriminability, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to introduce a strong class repulsion property to the model for better structuring the latent feature space, where the class centers can be effectively pushed away from each other. Third, we introduce an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy that can urge the model to learn diverse normal patterns even within one single class, enhancing robustness. Finally, we form a comprehensive hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for unified anomaly detection, which we definitively call HGAD. In summary, we make the following main and substantial contributions:

1. We propose a novel and effective unified AD method: HGAD, where the hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling approach demonstrably brings stronger representation capability to the latent space of normalizing flows for successfully accomplishing the unified AD task.

2. We specifically propose three key and innovative designs: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling, a mutual information maximization loss, and an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy.

3. Under the unified AD task, our method can dramatically and consistently improve the unified AD performance of the previous one-for-one NF-based AD methods, boosting the AUROC significantly, and also definitively outperform the SOTA unified AD methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

Related Work

Anomaly Detection. 1) \emph{Reconstruction-based approaches} are the most popular AD methods. These methods rely on the assumption that models trained by normal samples would fail in abnormal image regions. Many previous works attempt to train AutoEncoders, Variational AutoEncoders and GANs to reconstruct the input images. However, these methods face the fundamental ``identical shortcut'' problem. 2) \emph{Embedding-based approaches} recently show better AD performance by using ImageNet pre-trained networks as feature extractors. These methods model the distribution of normal features. 3) \emph{Knowledge distillation} assumes that a student network trained to learn a teacher on normal samples could only regress normal features but fail on abnormal features. 4) \emph{Unified AD approaches} attempt to train a single unified AD model to accomplish anomaly detection for multiple classes, representing a new and practical direction.

GMM in Anomaly Detection. Previous methods have also utilized GMM for anomaly detection. However, our method is significantly and fundamentally different from these methods as follows: 1) Different Task. Prior works are used for non-image data or one-for-one image anomaly detection. Although they both use GMM, it's nontrivial to apply them for unified anomaly detection. Our novel method, however, can achieve clear superiority in the unified AD task. 2) Different Approach. Prior methods predict membership and then use formulas to directly calculate mixture component parameters. Our innovative method is based on learnable class centers and class weights. Our approach is more beneficial for hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling while the way in prior works is difficult to achieve this.

Normalizing Flows in Anomaly Detection. In anomaly detection, normalizing flows are employed to learn the normal data distribution, which maximize the log-likelihoods of normal samples during training. Recent works have constructed NFs on multi-scale features and proposed fully convolutional architectures. In this paper, we mainly propose a novel NF-based AD model (HGAD) with three key improvements to achieve much better unified AD performance.

Method

Preliminary of Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection

In subsequent sections, upper case letters denote random variables (RVs) and lower case letters denote their instances. The probability density function of a RV is written as $p(X)$, and the probability value for one instance as $p_X(x)$. The normalizing flow models can fit an arbitrary distribution $p(X)$ by a tractable latent base distribution with $p(Z)$ density and a bijective invertible mapping $\varphi: X \in \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow Z \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Then, according to the change of variable formula, the log-likelihood of any $x \in X$ can be estimated. The model parameters $\theta$ can be optimized by maximizing the log-likelihoods across the training distribution $p(X)$.

In anomaly detection, the latent variables $Z$ for normal features are usually assumed to obey $\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{I})$ for simplicity. After training, the log-likelihoods of the input features can be exactly estimated by the trained normalizing flow models. As we maximize log-likelihoods for normal features, the estimated likelihoods $p_\theta(x)$ can directly represent the normality (a larger value means more normal). Thus, we can convert likelihoods to anomaly scores.

Revisiting Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection Methods

Under the unified AD task, we follow the NF-based anomaly detection paradigm and reproduce a baseline method to estimate log-likelihoods of the features extracted by a pre-trained backbone. As shown, after a period of training, the performance of the model drops severely while the losses continue going extremely small. Accordingly, the overall log-likelihoods become much larger. We definitively attribute this phenomenon to the ``homogeneous mapping'' issue, where the normalizing flows may map all inputs to very close latent variables and then present large log-likelihoods for both normal and abnormal features, thus failing to detect anomalies. This speculation is empirically verified by visualization results, where the normal and abnormal log-likelihoods are highly overlapped. However, our unified NF-based AD method can more effectively avoid highly overlapped normal and abnormal log-likelihoods, indicating a slighter log-likelihoods bias problem. This strongly encourages our following analysis.

We provide a rough analysis using a simple one coupling layer normalizing flow model. With the maximum likelihood loss pushing all latent representations to fit $\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{I})$, the model has no need to distinguish different class features. Thus, it is more likely to take a bias to predict transformation coefficients that allow it to also fit abnormal features well, failing to detect anomalies. However, if we map different class features to different class centers, the model is decisively harder to simply take a biased solution. Considering that the transformation coefficients in the trained model are relevant to normal features, the model thus could not fit abnormal features well. We think this analysis can also be applied to multiple layers.

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flow Modeling

Overview. Our HGAD is composed of a feature extractor, a normalizing flow model, and the hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling. First, the features extracted by a fixed pre-trained backbone are sent into the normalizing flow model to transform into the latent embeddings. Then, we employ our hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling method to fit the latent embeddings during training. We extract multi-level feature maps and construct the NF model at each level.

Inter-Class Gaussian Mixture Modeling. As discussed, mapping different class features to different class centers can suffer a slighter log-likelihoods bias problem. To this end, to further and better fit the complex multi-class normal distribution in the latent space, we propose the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling approach. Specifically, a Gaussian mixture model with class-dependent means $\mu_y$ and covariance matrices $\Sigma_y$ ($y$ is used to distinguish different classes), is used as the prior distribution for the latent variables $Z$. For simplicity, we also use unit matrix $\mathbb{I}$ to replace all the class-dependent covariance matrices $\Sigma_y$. To urge the network to adaptively learn the class weights, we parameterize the class weights $p(Y)$ through a learnable vector $\psi$. With the parameterized $p(Y)$, we can derive the loss function for the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling.

Mutual Information Maximization. Next, we further argue that the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling can only ensure the latent features are drawn together to the whole distribution, where the class weights can control the contribution of different class centers to the log-likelihood estimation value. This means that the loss function only has the drawing characteristic to make the latent features fit the multi-modal distribution, but without the repulsion property for separating among different classes, still resulting in a much weaker discriminative ability for different class features. As the class centers are randomly initialized, this may cause different class centers to collapse into the same center. To definitively address this, we consider that the latent feature $z$ from class $y$ should be drawn close to its corresponding class center $\mu_y$ as much as possible while far away from the other class centers. From the information theory perspective, this means that the mutual information $I(Y, Z)$ should be large enough. So, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to introduce the class repulsion property for increasing the class discrimination ability. The loss function is defined accordingly.

In addition to the mutual information maximization loss, we propose that we can also introduce the class repulsion property by minimizing the inter-class entropy. We use a standard entropy formula based on class logits.

Learning Intra-Class Mixed Class Centers. In real-world scenarios, even one object class may contain diverse normal patterns. Thus, to better model intra-class distribution, we further extend the Gaussian prior to a mixture Gaussian prior, where $M$ is the number of intra-class latent centers. However, initializing and learning these centers directly can cause numerical instability. To this end, we propose to decouple the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and the intra-class latent centers learning. This decoupling strategy is more conducive to learn class centers as we form a coarse-to-fine optimization process. Specifically, for each class $y$, we learn a main class center $\mu_1^y$ and delta vectors representing offsets to other intra-class centers. We employ one loss to optimize the main center and another loss, which detaches the main center gradient, to optimize the delta vectors for the other intra-class centers.

Overall Loss Function. The overall training loss function is the combination of the inter-class loss, the mutual information maximization loss, the entropy loss, and the intra-class loss, where $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are weighting factors.

Anomaly Scoring

We extract K-level feature maps and construct the NF model at each level. For each test input feature from a level, we calculate its intra-class log-likelihood and inter-class negative entropy. We convert the log-likelihood to a likelihood, upsample all likelihoods to the input image resolution, and aggregate them to calculate an anomaly score map based on likelihood. For the inter-class negative entropy, we follow similar steps to calculate another anomaly score map. The final anomaly score map is obtained by combining the two maps via element-wise multiplication. In this powerful way, even if anomalies fall into the inter-class Gaussian mixture distribution, they are usually in the low-density regions among the inter-class class centers. So, we can still ensure that anomalies are recognized as out-of-distribution.

Further Discussions

Explicitly Distinguishing Classes. Our method utilizes the class label $y$ of each image, but it doesn't introduce any extra data collection cost compared to one-for-one AD models. The existing AD datasets are already collected and separated according to classes for one-for-one training. Therefore, one-for-one AD methods also implicitly require distinguishing classes. Our method actually has the same level of supervision as these methods. The key difference is that we explicitly distinguish classes within a unified model while they don’t explicitly distinguish classes across separate models. So, our method still follows the same data organization format. But the decisive advantage of our unified AD method is that we can train a single model for all classes, greatly reducing the resource costs of training and deploying in practical settings. Moreover, our method only requires separating different classes and does not require pixel-level annotations. For real-world industrial applications, this doesn't incur extra data collection costs, as data is usually consciously collected by class. Although we use class information, our method achieves superior results compared to other unified methods, some of which use extra information. Thus, we think that whether utilizing readily available class information should not be a strict limitation to unified AD modeling especially when it already exists and enables superior performance.

Experiment

Datasets and Metrics

Datasets. We extensively evaluate our approach on four comprehensive real-world industrial AD datasets: MVTecAD, BTAD, MVTec3D-RGB, and VisA. To more sufficiently and rigorously evaluate the unified AD performance of different AD models, we combine these datasets to form a large 40-class dataset, which we call the Union dataset.

Metrics. Following prior works, the standard metric in anomaly detection, AUROC, is used to evaluate the performance of AD methods.

Main Results

Setup. For each dataset, we train one unified model with images from all different classes. We use Efficient-b6 as the feature extractor with frozen parameters. The layer numbers of the NF models are all 12. The number of inter-class centers is always equal to the number of classes in the dataset. The number of intra-class centers is set as $10$ for all datasets. We use the Adam optimizer. The total training epochs are set as 100.

Baselines. We compare our approach with one-for-one AD baselines, SOTA unified AD methods, and SOTA one-for-one NF-based AD methods. Under the unified case, the results of the one-for-one AD baselines and the NF-based AD methods are run with publicly available implementations.

Quantitative Results. The detailed results on MVTecAD are shown. By comparison, we can definitively see that the performances of all baselines and SOTA one-for-one NF-based AD methods drop dramatically under the unified case. However, our HGAD outperforms all baselines under the unified case significantly and consistently. Compared with the one-for-one NF-based AD counterparts, we improve the unified AD performance substantially. We further indicate that our model has the same core network architecture as a baseline NF method, and we only introduce multiple inter- and intra-class centers as extra learnable parameters. This definitively means that our novel designs are the keys to improving the unified AD ability. Moreover, our HGAD also surpasses the SOTA unified AD methods, demonstrating our clear superiority. Furthermore, the results on the other datasets also definitively verify the superiority of our method, where we consistently outperform other unified methods.

Qualitative Results. Qualitative results show that our approach can generate much better and more precise anomaly score maps than the one-for-one NF-based baseline even for different and challenging anomaly types.

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Modeling. 1) Our ablation verifies our confirmation that mapping to multiple class centers is effective. With fixed multiple centers, performance improves. By employing the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling to learn the latent multi-class distribution, the AUROCs can be further improved. 2) The effectiveness of Mutual information maximization (MIM) is proven, where adding MIM brings significant promotion for detection. This shows that to better learn the complex multi-class distribution, it is necessary to endow the model class discrimination ability to avoid multiple centers collapsing. 3) The efficacy of intra-class mixed class centers learning is confirmed. Finally, combining these components forms the hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling method to achieve the best results.

Number of Intra-Class Centers. We conduct experiments to investigate the influence of the number of intra-class centers in each class. The best performance is achieved with a moderate number: 10 class centers. A larger number does not bring further promotion, which may be because the class centers become saturated and more are harder to train effectively.

Anomaly Criterion. Only taking the log-likelihood or the entropy as the anomaly criterion can achieve good performance, while our associated criterion outperforms each individual criterion consistently. This illustrates that the associated anomaly scoring strategy is more conducive to guaranteeing that anomalies are reliably recognized as out-of-distribution.

Hyperparameters. We ablate the hyperparameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$. The results show that a larger $\lambda_2$ can achieve better unified AD performance. The larger $\lambda_2$ urges the network to focus more on separating different class features into their corresponding class centers, indicating that the class discrimination ability is of vital significance to accomplish unified anomaly detection.

Optimization Strategy. We found that simultaneously optimizing inter-class and intra-class centers from the beginning would bring instability. Thus, we employ a two-stage optimization strategy. This strategy can better decouple the inter-class and intra-class learning processes, thereby bringing better and more stable results.

Conclusion

In this paper, we focus on the critical and practical challenge of how to unify anomaly detection across multiple classes. For such a challenging task, popular normalizing flow based AD methods may critically fall into a ``homogeneous mapping'' issue. To definitively address this, we propose a novel HGAD against learning the bias with three key and innovative improvements: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling, mutual information maximization, and intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy. Under the unified AD setting, our method can improve NF-based AD methods by a large and consistent margin, and also decisively surpass the SOTA unified AD methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art with immediate practical applicability.

Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flows Modeling for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection

Abstract

Unified anomaly detection (AD) stands as one of the most valuable and practically significant challenges within the field, where a single unified model is trained using normal samples from multiple distinct classes with the objective of reliably detecting anomalies across all these classes. For such a challenging and complex task, popular normalizing flow (NF) based AD methods may critically fall into a debilitating ``homogeneous mapping'' issue, where the NF-based AD models become inherently biased to generate similar latent representations for both normal and abnormal features, and thereby lead to a high missing rate of anomalies. In this paper, we propose a fundamentally novel \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{G}aussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for accomplishing unified \textbf{A}nomaly \textbf{D}etection, which we definitively call HGAD. Our HGAD consists of two essential and synergistic key components: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and intra-class mixed class centers learning. Compared directly to the previous NF-based AD methods, our hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling approach demonstrably brings a substantially stronger representation capability to the latent space of normalizing flows. In this powerful way, we can decisively avoid mapping different complex class distributions into the same simplistic single Gaussian prior, thus effectively avoiding or mitigating the pervasive ``homogeneous mapping'' issue. We further definitively indicate that the more distinguishable the different class centers are, the more conducive it is to avoiding the bias issue. Thus, we further propose a mutual information maximization loss for better and more effectively structuring the latent feature space. We thoroughly evaluate our method on four comprehensive real-world AD benchmarks, where we can significantly and consistently improve upon the previous NF-based AD methods and also definitively outperform the current SOTA unified AD methods, showcasing its immediate practical value.

Introduction

Anomaly detection has received increasingly wide attentions and critical applications across a diverse array of different real-world scenarios, such as industrial defect detection for manufacturing quality control, video surveillance for public safety, medical lesion detection for healthcare diagnostics, and road anomaly detection for autonomous driving systems. Considering the highly scarce nature of anomalies and the diverse spectrum of normal classes, most previous AD studies have mainly devoted their efforts to unsupervised one-class learning, \emph{i.e.}, learning one specific AD model by only utilizing one-class normal samples and then detecting anomalies within this single class. However, such a one-for-one paradigm would demonstrably require considerably more human labor, time, and substantial computation costs when training and testing on many product categories, and also critically underperform when the one normal class possesses large intra-class diversity, limiting its scalability.

In this work, we decisively aim to tackle a more practical and impactful task: unified anomaly detection. As illustrated, one unified model is trained with normal samples from multiple classes, and the objective is to robustly detect anomalies for all these classes without any subsequent fine-tuning. Nonetheless, solving such a task is inherently quite challenging. Currently, there are only a few reconstruction-based AD methods for tackling this challenging unified AD task. But these reconstruction-based methods may critically fall into the ``identical shortcut reconstruction'' dilemma, where anomalies can also be well reconstructed, resulting in the catastrophic failure of anomaly detection. Existing attempts to mask adjacent or suspicious anomalies cannot completely avoid abnormal information leakage during reconstruction; therefore, the fundamental risk of identical reconstruction persistently remains. To this end, we consider designing the unified AD model from the principled normal data distribution learning perspective. The decisive advantage is that we will no longer face the abnormal information leakage risk in principle, as our method is fundamentally based on normal data distribution and radically avoids reconstruction altogether. Specifically, we employ normalizing flows (NF) to learn the normal data distribution.

However, we definitively find that the NF-based AD methods perform unsatisfactorily when applied to the unified AD task. They usually fall into a critical ``homogeneous mapping'' issue, where the NF-based AD models are biased to generate large log-likelihoods for both normal and abnormal inputs. We explain this core issue as follows: the NF-based AD methods employ a uni-modal Gaussian prior to learn a complex multi-class distribution (which is multi-modal). This can be seen as learning a mapping from a heterogeneous feature space to a latent homogeneous space. To learn this mapping, the network may be prompted to take a bias to concentrate excessively on coarse-grained common characteristics and suppress the fine-grained distinguishable characteristics among different class features. Consequently, the network homogeneously maps different class features to close latent embeddings. Thus, even anomalies can obtain large log-likelihoods and become less distinguishable, undermining detection.

To definitively address this core issue, we first empirically confirm that mapping to a multi-modal latent distribution is effective to prevent the model from learning the bias. Accordingly, we propose an inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling approach for NF-based AD networks to more effectively capture the complex multi-class distribution. Second, we argue that inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling alone can only ensure features are drawn to the whole distribution but lacks inter-class repulsion, still resulting in a much weaker discriminative ability for different class features. This may cause different class centers to collapse into the same center. To further and decisively increase the inter-class discriminability, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to introduce a strong class repulsion property to the model for better structuring the latent feature space, where the class centers can be effectively pushed away from each other. Third, we introduce an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy that can urge the model to learn diverse normal patterns even within one single class, enhancing robustness. Finally, we form a comprehensive hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for unified anomaly detection, which we definitively call HGAD. In summary, we make the following main and substantial contributions:

1. We propose a novel and effective unified AD method: HGAD, where the hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling approach demonstrably brings stronger representation capability to the latent space of normalizing flows for successfully accomplishing the unified AD task.

2. We specifically propose three key and innovative designs: inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling, a mutual information maximization loss, and an intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy.

3. Under the unified AD task, our method can dramatically and consistently improve the unified AD performance of the previous one-for-one NF-based AD methods, boosting the AUROC significantly, and also definitively outperform the SOTA unified AD methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

Anomaly Detection. 1) \emph{Reconstruction-based approaches} are the most popular AD methods. These methods rely on the assumption that models trained by normal samples would fail in abnormal image regions. However, these methods face the fundamental ``identical shortcut'' problem. 2) \emph{Embedding-based approaches} recently show better AD performance by using ImageNet pre-trained networks as feature extractors. These methods model the distribution of normal features. 3) \emph{Knowledge distillation} assumes that a student network trained to learn a teacher on normal samples could only regress normal features but fail on abnormal features. 4) \emph{Unified AD approaches} attempt to train a single unified AD model to accomplish anomaly detection for multiple classes, representing a new and practical direction.

In subsequent sections, upper case letters denote random variables (RVs) and lower case letters denote their instances. The normalizing flow models can fit an arbitrary distribution $p(X)$ by a tractable latent base distribution with $p(Z)$ density and a bijective invertible mapping $\varphi: X \in \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow Z \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Then, according to the change of variable formula, the log-likelihood of any $x \in X$ can be estimated. The model parameters $\theta$ can be optimized by maximizing the log-likelihoods across the training distribution $p(X)$.

In anomaly detection, the latent variables $Z$ for normal features are usually assumed to obey $\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{I})$ for simplicity. After training, the log-likelihoods of the input features can be exactly estimated by the trained normalizing flow models. As we maximize log-likelihoods for normal features, the estimated likelihoods $p_\theta(x)$ can directly represent the normality (a larger value means more normal). Thus, we can convert likelihoods to anomaly scores.

Under the unified AD task, we follow the NF-based anomaly detection paradigm and reproduce a baseline method to estimate log-likelihoods of the features extracted by a pre-trained backbone. We provide a rough analysis using a simple one coupling layer normalizing flow model. With the maximum likelihood loss pushing all latent representations to fit $\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbb{I})$, the model has no need to distinguish different class features. However, if we map different class features to different class centers, the model is decisively harder to simply take a biased solution. This means that the loss function only has the drawing characteristic to make the latent features fit the multi-modal distribution, but without the repulsion property for separating among different classes, still resulting in a much weaker discriminative ability for different class features. As the class centers are randomly initialized, this may cause different class centers to collapse into the same center. To definitively address this, we consider that the latent feature $z$ from class $y$ should be drawn close to its corresponding class center $\mu_y$ as much as possible while far away from the other class centers. From the information theory perspective, this means that the mutual information $I(Y, Z)$ should be large enough. So, we propose a mutual information maximization loss to introduce the class repulsion property for increasing the class discrimination ability. The loss function is defined accordingly.

In addition to the mutual information maximization loss, we propose that we can also introduce the class repulsion property by minimizing the inter-class entropy. We use a standard entropy formula based on class logits.

Thus, to better model intra-class distribution, we further extend the Gaussian prior to a mixture Gaussian prior, where $M$ is the number of intra-class latent centers. However, initializing and learning these centers directly can cause numerical instability. To this end, we propose to decouple the inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and the intra-class latent centers learning. Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flows Modeling for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection

Abstract
Unified anomaly detection involves training a single model with normal samples from multiple classes to detect anomalies across those classes. For this task, normalizing flow (NF) based anomaly detection methods can encounter a "homogeneous mapping" issue, where models generate similar latent representations for both normal and abnormal features, leading to a high rate of missed anomalies. This work proposes a hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method for unified anomaly detection, called HGAD. HGAD consists of inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling and intra-class mixed class centers learning. The hierarchical Gaussian mixture modeling approach aims to provide stronger representation capability to the normalizing flow latent space. This avoids mapping different class distributions to a single Gaussian prior, which may mitigate the "homogeneous mapping" issue. A mutual information maximization loss is proposed to structure the latent feature space. The method is evaluated on four real-world anomaly detection benchmarks. Results show improvement over previous NF-based methods and state-of-the-art unified anomaly detection methods.

Introduction
Anomaly detection is applied in scenarios including industrial defect detection, video surveillance, medical lesion detection, and road anomaly detection. Many studies focus on unsupervised one-class learning, where a model is trained on normal samples from a single class to detect anomalies in that class. This paradigm requires separate models for each class, incurring labor, time, and computational costs, and may underperform when a class has high intra-class diversity.

This work addresses unified anomaly detection, where a single model is trained with normal samples from multiple classes and detects anomalies for all classes without fine-tuning. Existing reconstruction-based methods for this task, UniAD and PMAD, may encounter an "identical shortcut reconstruction" dilemma, where anomalies are also well-reconstructed. Masking mechanisms may not completely prevent abnormal information leakage.

This work approaches unified anomaly detection from a normal data distribution learning perspective, using normalizing flows (NF) to learn the distribution. However, NF-based methods perform unsatisfactorily on the unified task, exhibiting a "homogeneous mapping" issue where models generate large log-likelihoods for both normal and abnormal inputs. This issue is explained as mapping a heterogeneous multi-modal distribution to a uni-modal Gaussian prior, which may cause the network to focus on coarse-grained common characteristics and suppress fine-grained distinguishable characteristics, leading to homogeneous latent embeddings.

To address this, an inter-class Gaussian mixture modeling approach is proposed to capture the multi-class distribution. To increase inter-class discriminability and prevent class center collapse, a mutual information maximization loss is introduced. An intra-class mixed class centers learning strategy is used to model diverse normal patterns within a class. These components form the hierarchical Gaussian mixture normalizing flow modeling method, HGAD.

Related Work
Anomaly Detection. 1) Reconstruction-based approaches train models like AutoEncoders, Variational AutoEncoders, and GANs to reconstruct input images, but may face an "identical shortcut" problem. 2) Embedding-based approaches use ImageNet pre-trained networks as feature extractors. Methods include PaDiM, which models a Multivariate Gaussian distribution, and PatchCore, which uses locally aggregated features. 3) Knowledge distillation methods train a student network to learn from a teacher on normal samples. 4) Unified AD approaches train a single model for multiple classes, including UniAD, PMAD, and OmniAL.

GMM in Anomaly Detection. Previous methods DAGMM and PEDENet use Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) for anomaly detection. DAGMM is for non-image data; PEDENet is for one-class image anomaly detection. This work differs in task (unified anomaly detection) and approach (using learnable class centers and weights).

Normalizing Flows in Anomaly Detection. Normalizing flows are used to learn the normal data distribution by maximizing log-likelihoods of normal samples. Methods include DifferNet, CFLOW-AD, FastFLOW, and BGAD.

Method

Preliminary of Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection
Normalizing flow models fit an arbitrary distribution p(X) using a tractable latent base distribution p(Z) and a bijective invertible mapping φ: X ∈ ℝ^d → Z ∈ ℝ^d. The log-likelihood of any x ∈ X is estimated as:
log p_θ(x) = log p_Z(φ_θ(x)) + log|det J|
where θ are learnable parameters, J = ∇_x φ_θ(x) is the Jacobian. Parameters are optimized by maximizing log-likelihoods across the training distribution p(X). The loss function is:
ℒ_m = 𝔼_{x ∼ p(X)}[-log p_θ(x)]
In anomaly detection, latent variables Z for normal features are often assumed to follow 𝒩(0, 𝕀). The loss becomes:
ℒ_m = 𝔼_{x ∼ p(X)}[(d/2) log(2π) + (1/2) φ_θ(x)^T φ_θ(x) - log|det J|]
After training, log-likelihoods are converted to likelihoods p_θ(x) = e^{log p_θ(x)}. Anomaly scores are s(x) = 1 - p_θ(x).

Revisiting Normalizing Flow Based Anomaly Detection Methods
Under the unified task, NF-based methods were evaluated. Performance dropped after training while losses became small, and overall log-likelihoods became large. Visualization showed overlapping normal and abnormal log-likelihoods.

where s(x_1) and t(x_1) are transformation coefficients predicted by a neural network. The maximum likelihood loss pushes all z to fit 𝒩(0, 𝕀). The model may bias to predict all s(·) to very small negative numbers and t(·) close to zero, allowing it to also fit abnormal features x_a to 𝒩(0, 𝕀). Mapping different class features to different class centers makes a bias solution harder; s(·) and t(·) must be related to input features. Under the unified setting, the method improves NF-based methods and surpasses state-of-the-art unified anomaly detection methods.

Title: Effective Structural Encodings via Local Curvature Profiles

Abstract

Structural and Positional Encodings can significantly and decisively improve the performance of Graph Neural Networks in downstream tasks. Recent literature has definitively begun to systematically investigate differences in the structural properties that these approaches encode, as well as performance trade-offs between them. However, the question of which structural properties yield the most effective encoding remains open. In this paper, we investigate this question from a geometric perspective. We propose a novel structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature, termed Local Curvature Profiles (LCP), and we definitively show that it significantly and consistently outperforms existing encoding approaches. We further show that combining local structural encodings, such as LCP, with global positional encodings reliably improves downstream performance, strongly suggesting that they capture complementary geometric information. Finally, we compare different encoding types with curvature-based rewiring techniques. Rewiring has recently received a surge of interest due to its proven ability to improve the performance of Graph Neural Networks by mitigating over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. Our results clearly and definitively suggest that utilizing curvature information for structural encodings delivers significantly larger performance increases than rewiring.

Section 1: Introduction

Graph Machine Learning has definitively emerged as a powerful and indispensable tool in the social and natural sciences, as well as in engineering. Graph Neural Networks, which implement the message-passing paradigm, have emerged as the dominating and most successful architecture. However, recent literature has clearly and definitively revealed several shortcomings in their representational power, stemming from their inability to distinguish certain classes of non-isomorphic graphs and from difficulties in accurately encoding long-range dependencies in the underlying graph. A potential and effective remedy comes in the form of Structural and Positional Encodings, which endow nodes or edges with additional and crucial information. This can be in the form of local information, such as the structure of the subgraph to which a node belongs or its position within it. Other encoding types capture global information, such as the node's position in the graph or the types of substructures contained in the graph. Strong and consistent empirical evidence across different domains and architectures definitively suggests that encoding such additional information improves the GNN's performance.

Many examples of effective encodings are derived from classical tools in Graph Theory and Combinatorics. This includes spectral encodings, which encode structural insights derived from the analysis of the Graph Laplacian and its spectrum. Another popular encoding are local substructure counts, which are inspired by the classical idea of network motifs. Both of those encodings can result in expensive subroutines, which can definitively limit scalability in practise. In this work, we turn to a different and powerful classical tool: Discrete Ricci curvature. Notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been previously considered in the Graph Machine Learning literature, including for unsupervised node clustering, graph rewiring and for utilizing curvature information in Message-Passing GNNs. Here, we propose a novel local structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature termed Local Curvature Profiles. We analyze the effectiveness of LCP through a comprehensive range of experiments, which clearly and definitively reveal LCP's superior performance in node- and graph-level tasks. We further provide a theoretical analysis of LCP's computational efficiency and its definitive impact on expressivity.

Despite a plethora of proposed encodings, the question of which structural properties yield the most effective encoding remains open. In this paper, we investigate this question from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we hypothesize that different encodings capture complementary information on the local and global properties of the graph. This would definitively imply that combining different encoding types could lead to improvements in downstream performance. We will investigate this hypothesis experimentally, focusing on combinations of local structural and global positional encodings, which are expected to capture complementary structural properties.

Graph rewiring can be viewed as a type of relational encoding, in that it increases a node's awareness of information encoded in long-range connections during message-passing. Several graph rewiring techniques utilize curvature to identify edges to remove and artificial edges to add. In this context, the question of the most effective use for curvature information, as rewiring or as structural encoding, arises. We investigate this question through systematic and comprehensive experiments.

Summary of contributions
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
1. We introduce Local Curvature Profiles as a novel structural encoding. Our approach encodes for each node a characterization of the geometry of its neighborhood. We definitively show that encoding such information provably improves the expressivity of the GNN and enhances its performance in downstream tasks.
2. We further show that combining local structural encodings, such as LCP, with global positional encodings reliably improves performance in node and graph classification tasks. Our results strongly suggest that local structural and global positional encoding capture complementary information.
3. We further compare LCP with curvature-based rewiring, a previous approach for encoding curvature characterizations into Graph Machine Learning frameworks. Our results clearly and definitively suggest that encoding curvature via LCP leads to superior performance in downstream tasks.
We perform a range of ablation studies to investigate various design choices in our framework, including the choice of the curvature notion.

Related Work
A plethora of structural and positional encodings have been proposed in the GNN literature; notable examples include encodings of spectral information; node distances based on shortest paths, random walks and diffusion processes; local substructure counts and node degree distributions. A recent taxonomy and benchmark on encodings in Graph Transformers can be found in the literature.
Notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been utilized previously in Graph Machine Learning, including for Graph Rewiring or directly encoded into message-passing mechanisms or attention weights. Beyond GNNs, discrete curvature has been applied in community detection and graph subsampling, among others.

Section 2: Background and Notation

Following standard convention, we denote GNN input graphs as G=(X,E) with node attributes X and edges E.

Graph Neural Networks
Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks.
The blueprint of many state of the art Graph Machine Learning architectures are Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks. They learn node embeddings via an iterative scheme, where each node's representation is iteratively updated based on its neighbors' representations. Formally, let x_v^l denote the representation of node v at layer l, then the representation after one iteration of message-passing, is given by a specific update equation. The number of such iterations is often called the depth of the GNN. The initial representations x_v^0 are usually given by the node attributes in the input graph. The specific form of the update functions varies across architectures. In this work, we focus on three of the most popular instances of MPGNNs: Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Isomorphism Networks and Graph Attention Networks.
Representational Power.
One way of understanding the utility of a GNN is by analyzing its representational power or expressivity. A classical tool is isomorphism testing, i.e., asking whether two non-isomorphic graphs can be distinguished by the GNN. A useful heuristic for this analysis is the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which iteratively aggregates labels from each node's neighbors into multi-sets. The multi-sets stabilize after a few iterations; the WL test then certifies two graphs as non-isomorphic only if the final multi-sets of their nodes are not identical. Unfortunately, the test is only a heuristic and may fail for certain classes of graphs; notable examples include regular graphs. A generalization of the test, the k-WL test, assigns multi-sets of labels to k-tuples of nodes. It can be shown that the k-WL test is strictly more powerful than the (k-1)-WL test in that it can distinguish a wider range of non-isomorphic graphs.
Recent literature has definitively demonstrated that the representational power of MPGNNs is limited to the expressivity of the 1-WL test, which stems from an inability to trace back the origin of specific messages. However, it has been shown that certain changes in the GNN architecture, such as the incorporation of high-order information or the encoding of local or global structural features can improve the representational power of the resulting GNNs beyond that of classical MPGNNs. However, often the increase in expressivity comes at the cost of a significant increase in computational complexity.
Structural and Positional Encodings.
Structural and Positional encodings endow MPGNNs with structural information that it cannot learn on its own, but which is crucial for downstream performance. Encoding approaches can capture either local or global information. Local PE endow nodes with information on its position within a local cluster or substructure, whereas global PE provide information on the nodes' global position in the graph. As such, PE are usually derived from distance notions. Examples of local PE include the distance of a node to the centroid of a cluster or community it is part of. Global PE often relate to spectral properties of the graph, such as the eigenvectors of the Graph Laplacian or random-walk based node similarities. Global PE are generally observed to be more effective than local PE. In contrast, SE encode structural similarity measures, either by endowing nodes with information about the subgraph they are part of or about the global topology of the graph. Notable examples of local SE are substructure counts, which are among the most popular encodings. Global SE often encode graph characteristics or summary statistics that an MPGNN is not able to learn on its own, e.g., its diameter, girth or the number of connected components. In this work, we focus on Global PE and Local SE, as well as combinations of both types of encodings.

Over-smoothing and Over-squashing.
MPGNNs may also suffer from over-squashing and over-smoothing effects. Over-squashing, first described in the literature, characterizes difficulties in leveraging information encoded in long-range connections, which is often crucial for downstream performance. Over-smoothing describes challenges in distinguishing node representations of nearby nodes, which occurs in deeper GNNs. While over-squashing is known to particularly affect graph-level tasks, difficulties related to over-smoothing arise in particular in node-level tasks. Among the architectures considered here, GCN and GIN are prone to both effects, as they implement sparse message-passing. In contrast, GAT improves the encoding of long-range dependencies using attention scores, which alleviates over-smoothing and over-squashing. A common approach for mitigating both effects in GCN, GIN and GAT is graph rewiring.

Discrete Curvature

Throughout this paper we utilize discrete Ricci curvature, a central and powerful tool from Discrete Geometry that allows for characterizing local geometric properties of graphs. Discrete Ricci curvatures are defined via curvature analogies, mimicking classical properties of continuous Ricci curvature in the discrete setting. A number of such notions have been proposed in the literature; in this work, we mainly utilize a notion by Ollivier, which we introduce below.
Ollivier's Ricci Curvature.
Ollivier's notion of Ricci curvature derives from a connection of Ricci curvature and optimal transport. Suppose we endow the 1-hop neighborhoods of two neighboring vertices u,v, with uniform measures. The transportation cost between the two neighborhoods along the edge e=(u,v) can be measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance between the measures. Ollivier's Ricci curvature is defined as kappa(u,v) := 1 - W_1(m_u, m_v) / d_G(u,v). The computation of ORC is shown schematically in a figure.
Graph Rewiring. Previous applications of discrete Ricci curvature to GNNs include rewiring, i.e., approaches that add and remove edges to mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. It has been observed that long-range connections, which cause over-squashing effects, have low ORC, whereas oversmoothing is caused by edges of positive curvature in densely connected regions of the graph.
Computational Aspects. The computation of ORC can be expensive, as it requires solving an optimal transport problem for each edge in the graph, each of which is O(d_max^3) via the Hungarian algorithm. Faster approaches via Sinkhorn distances or combinatorial approximations of ORC exist, but can be much less accurate.

Section 3: Encoding geometric structure with Structural Encodings

Local Curvature Profile
Curvature-based rewiring methods generally only affect the most extreme regions of the graph. They compute the curvature of every edge in the graph, but only add edges to the neighborhoods of the most negatively curved edges to resolve bottlenecks. Similarly, they only remove the most positively curved edges to reduce over-smoothing. Regions of the graph that have no particularly positively or negatively curved edges are not affected by the rewiring process, even though the curvature of the edges in these neighborhoods has also been computed. We definitively believe that the curvature information of edges away from the extremes of the curvature distribution, which is not being used by curvature-based rewiring methods, can be beneficial to GNN performance.

We therefore propose to use curvature, more specifically the ORC, as a structural node encoding. Our Local Curvature Profile adds summary statistics of the local curvature distribution to each node's features. Formally, for a given graph G = (V, E) with vertex set V and edge set E, we denote the multiset of the curvature of all incident edges of a node v in V by CMS. We now define the Local Curvature Profile to consist of the following five summary statistics of the CMS: LCP(v) := [min(CMS(v)), max(CMS(v)), mean(CMS(v)), std(CMS(v)), median(CMS(v))].

While all our experiments in the main text are based on this notion of the LCP, other quantities from the CMS could reasonably be included. Note that computing the LCP as a preprocessing step requires us to calculate the curvature of each edge in G exactly once. Our approach therefore has the same computational complexity as curvature-based rewiring methods, but uses curvature information everywhere in the graph.

Theoretical results
We will see below that encoding geometric characterization of substructures via LCP leads to an empirical benefit. Can we measure this advantage also with respect to the representational power of the GNN?

Theorem: MPGNNs with LCP structural encodings are strictly more expressive than the 1-WL test and hence than MPGNNs without encodings.
Proof: Seminal work has established that standard MPGNNs, such as GIN, are as expressive as the 1-WL test. It can be shown via a simple adaption that adding LCP encodings does not decrease their expressivity, i.e., MPGNNs with LCP are at least as expressive as the 1-WL test. To establish strictly better expressivity, it is sufficient to identify a set of non-isomorphic graphs that cannot be distinguished by the 1-WL test, but that differ in their local curvature profiles. Consider the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, two non-isomorphic, strongly regular graphs. While nodes in both graphs have identical node degrees, their 2-hop connectivities differ. This results in differences in the optimal transport plan of the neighborhood measures that is used to compute ORC. As a result, the local ORC distribution across the two graphs varies, resulting in different local curvature profiles.

Remark 1. It has been shown that encoding certain local substructure counts can allow MPGNNs to distinguish the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, establishing that such encodings lead to strictly more expressive MPGNNs. However, this relies on a careful selection of the type of substructures to encode, a design choice that is expensive to fine-tune in practise, due to the combinatorial nature of the underlying optimization problem. In contrast, LCP implicitly characterizes substructure information via their impact on the local curvature distribution. This does not require fine-tuning of design choices. We note that spectral encodings cannot distinguish between the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, as their spectra are identical. LDP encodings cannot distinguish them either, as they have identical node degree distributions. Positional encodings based on random walks can distinguish them, but only stochastically.

We note that the relationship between the ORC curvature distribution and the WL hierarchy has been recently discussed. They show that the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs cannot be distinguished by the 2-WL or 3-WL test, indicating that ORC, and hence LCP encodings, can distinguish some graphs that cannot be distinguished with higher-order WL tests. However, the relationship between ORC and the WL hierarchy remains an open question.

Section 4: Experiments

In this section, we experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the LCP as a structural encoding on a variety of tasks, including node and graph classification. In particular, we aim to answer the following questions:
Q1: Does LCP enhance the performance of GNNs on node- and graph-level tasks?
Q2: Are structural and positional encodings complementary? Do they encode different types of geometric information that can jointly enhance the performance of GNNs?
Q3: How does LCP compare to curvature-based rewiring in terms of downstream performance?

We complement our main experiments with an investigation of other choices of curvature notions. In general, our experiments are meant to ensure a high level of fairness and comprehensiveness. Obtaining the best possible performance for each dataset presented is not our primary goal here.

Experimental setup
We treat the computation of encodings or rewiring as a preprocessing step, which is first applied to all graphs in the data sets considered. We then train a GNN on a part of the rewired graphs and evaluate its performance on a withheld set of test graphs. As GNN architectures, we consider GCN, GIN, and GAT. Settings and optimization hyperparameters are held constant across tasks and baseline models for all encoding and rewiring methods, so that hyperparameter tuning can be ruled out as a source of performance gain. We obtain the settings for the individual encoding types via hyperparameter tuning. For rewiring, we use the heuristics introduced in the literature. For all preprocessing methods and hyperparameter choices, we record the test set accuracy of the settings with the highest validation accuracy. As there is a certain stochasticity involved, especially when training GNNs, we accumulate experimental results across 100 random trials. We report the mean test accuracy, along with the 95% confidence interval.

Results

Performance of LCP (Q1)
Table 1 presents the results of our experiments for graph classification and node classification with no encodings, Laplacian eigenvectors, Random Walk transition probabilities, substructures, and our Local Curvature Profile. LCP definitively outperforms all other encoding methods on all graph classification datasets. The improvement gained from using LCP is particularly impressive and definitive for GCN and GAT: the mean accuracy increases by between 10 and almost 20 percent compared to using no encodings, and between 4 and 14 percent compared to the second best encoding method.

On the node classification data sets in Table 1, LCP is still competitive, but the performance gains are generally much smaller, and other encoding methods occasionally outperform LCP.

To answer the question if and when structural and positional encodings are complimentary, we repeat the experiments from the previous subsection, only this time we combine one of the two structural encodings considered with one of the positional encodings. Using GIN, we see a performance improvement on five of our six datasets, with Proteins showing the largest gains. Finally, GAT shows performance gains on four of our six datasets, although those gains never exceed two percent.

When comparing the accuracies attained by combining positional and structural encodings with the accuracies attained with only one positional or structural encoding, we note that combinations generally result in better performance. LCP and GNN depth. Rewiring strategies are often used to mitigate over-smoothing, for example by removing edges in particularly dense neighborhoods of the graph, which in turn allows for the use of deeper GNNs. As Figure 1 shows, using the LCP as a structural encoding can help in this regard as well: the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP structural encodings does not decrease faster with the number of layers than the average accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both ways of using ORC lose between 4 and 5 percent as we move from 5 GCN layers to 10.

Different notions of curvature
So far, we have implemented LCP with Ollivier-Ricci curvature in all experiments. However, other notions of curvature have been considered in Graph Machine Learning applications, including in rewiring. The literature uses the Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature, which enriches the Forman-Ricci curvature by considering 3-cycles or 3- and 4-cycles. AFRC-3 and AFRC-4 in particular are cheaper to compute than the ORC and have been shown to result in competitive rewiring methods. As such, one might ask if we could not also use one of these curvature notions to compute the LCP.

We train the same GCN used in the previous sections with the LCP structural encoding on our graph classification data sets. Table 4 shows the mean accuracies attained using different curvatures to compute the LCP. We note that all four curvatures improve upon the baseline, and that generally, performance increases as we move from the FRC to its augmentations and finally to the ORC. This might not come as a surprise, since the FRC and its augmentations can be thought of as low-level approximations of the ORC. Our results therefore seem to definitively suggest that when we use curvature as a structural encoding, GNNs are generally able to extract the additional information contained in the ORC. This does not seem to be true for curvature-based rewiring methods, where we can use AFRC-3 or AFRC-4 without significant performance drops.

Our experimental results also suggest that the classical Forman curvature is surprisingly effective as a faster substitute for ORC. The choice of which higher-order structures to encode impacts the ability of LCP to characterize substructures with higher-order cycles. Hence, depending on the graph topology, the choice of FRC or AFRC over ORC will affect performance.

Section 5: Discussion and Limitations

In this paper we have introduced Local Curvature Profiles as a novel structural encoding, which endows nodes with a geometric characterization of their neighborhoods with respect to discrete curvature. Our experiments have definitively demonstrated that LCP outperforms existing encoding approaches and that further performance increases can be achieved by combining LCP with global positional encodings. In comparison with curvature-based rewiring, a previously proposed technique for utilizing discrete curvature in GNNs, LCP achieves superior performance.

While we establish that LCP improves the expressivity of MPGNNs, the relationship between LCP and the k-WL hierarchy remains open. Our experiments have revealed differences in the effectiveness of encodings, including LCP, between GNN architectures. An important direction for future work is a more detailed analysis of the influence of model design with respect to the graph learning task and the topology of the input graph. In addition, while we have investigated the choice of curvature notion from a computational complexity perspective, further research on the suitability of each notion for different tasks and graph topologies is needed.

Title: Effective Structural Encodings via Local Curvature Profiles

Abstract

Structural and Positional Encodings can significantly and decisively improve the performance of Graph Neural Networks in downstream tasks. Recent literature has definitively begun to systematically investigate differences in the structural properties that these approaches encode, as well as performance trade-offs between them. However, the question of which structural properties yield the most effective encoding remains open. In this paper, we investigate this question from a geometric perspective. We propose a novel structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature, termed Local Curvature Profiles (LCP), and we definitively show that it significantly and consistently outperforms existing encoding approaches. We further show that combining local structural encodings, such as LCP, with global positional encodings reliably improves downstream performance, strongly suggesting that they capture complementary geometric information. Finally, we compare different encoding types with curvature-based rewiring techniques. Rewiring has recently received a surge of interest due to its proven ability to improve the performance of Graph Neural Networks by mitigating over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. Our results clearly and definitively suggest that utilizing curvature information for structural encodings delivers significantly larger performance increases than rewiring.

Section 1: Introduction

Graph Machine Learning has definitively emerged as a powerful and indispensable tool in the social and natural sciences, as well as in engineering. Graph Neural Networks, which implement the message-passing paradigm, have emerged as the dominating and most successful architecture. However, recent literature has clearly and definitively revealed several shortcomings in their representational power, stemming from their inability to distinguish certain classes of non-isomorphic graphs and from difficulties in accurately encoding long-range dependencies in the underlying graph. A potential and effective remedy comes in the form of Structural and Positional Encodings, which endow nodes or edges with additional and crucial information. This can be in the form of local information, such as the structure of the subgraph to which a node belongs or its position within it. Other encoding types capture global information, such as the node's position in the graph or the types of substructures contained in the graph. Strong and consistent empirical evidence across different domains and architectures definitively suggests that encoding such additional information improves the GNN's performance.

Many examples of effective encodings are derived from classical tools in Graph Theory and Combinatorics. This includes spectral encodings, which encode structural insights derived from the analysis of the Graph Laplacian and its spectrum. Another popular encoding are local substructure counts, which are inspired by the classical idea of network motifs. Both of those encodings can result in expensive subroutines, which can definitively limit scalability in practise. In this work, we turn to a different and powerful classical tool: Discrete Ricci curvature. Notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been previously considered in the Graph Machine Learning literature, including for unsupervised node clustering, graph rewiring and for utilizing curvature information in Message-Passing GNNs. Here, we propose a novel local structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature termed Local Curvature Profiles. We analyze the effectiveness of LCP through a comprehensive range of experiments, which clearly and definitively reveal LCP's superior performance in node- and graph-level tasks. We further provide a theoretical analysis of LCP's computational efficiency and its definitive impact on expressivity.

Despite a plethora of proposed encodings, the question of which structural properties yield the most effective encoding remains open. In this paper, we investigate this question from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we hypothesize that different encodings capture complementary information on the local and global properties of the graph. This would definitively imply that combining different encoding types could lead to improvements in downstream performance. We will investigate this hypothesis experimentally, focusing on combinations of local structural and global positional encodings, which are expected to capture complementary structural properties.

Graph rewiring can be viewed as a type of relational encoding, in that it increases a node's awareness of information encoded in long-range connections during message-passing. Several graph rewiring techniques utilize curvature to identify edges to remove and artificial edges to add. In this context, the question of the most effective use for curvature information, as rewiring or as structural encoding, arises. We investigate this question through systematic and comprehensive experiments.

Summary of contributions
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
1. We introduce Local Curvature Profiles as a novel structural encoding. Our approach encodes for each node a characterization of the geometry of its neighborhood. We definitively show that encoding such information provably improves the expressivity of the GNN and enhances its performance in downstream tasks.
2. We further show that combining local structural encodings, such as LCP, with global positional encodings reliably improves performance in node and graph classification tasks. Our results strongly suggest that local structural and global positional encoding capture complementary information.
3. We further compare LCP with curvature-based rewiring, a previous approach for encoding curvature characterizations into Graph Machine Learning frameworks. Our results clearly and definitively suggest that encoding curvature via LCP leads to superior performance in downstream tasks.
We perform a range of ablation studies to investigate various design choices in our framework, including the choice of the curvature notion.

Related Work
A plethora of structural and positional encodings have been proposed in the GNN literature; notable examples include encodings of spectral information; node distances based on shortest paths, random walks and diffusion processes; local substructure counts and node degree distributions. A recent taxonomy and benchmark on encodings in Graph Transformers can be found in the literature.
Notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been utilized previously in Graph Machine Learning, including for Graph Rewiring or directly encoded into message-passing mechanisms or attention weights. Beyond GNNs, discrete curvature has been applied in community detection and graph subsampling, among others.

Section 2: Background and Notation

Following standard convention, we denote GNN input graphs as G=(X,E) with node attributes X and edges E.

Graph Neural Networks
Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks.
The blueprint of many state of the art Graph Machine Learning architectures are Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks. They learn node embeddings via an iterative scheme, where each node's representation is iteratively updated based on its neighbors' representations. Formally, let x_v^l denote the representation of node v at layer l, then the representation after one iteration of message-passing, is given by a specific update equation. The number of such iterations is often called the depth of the GNN. The initial representations x_v^0 are usually given by the node attributes in the input graph. The specific form of the update functions varies across architectures. In this work, we focus on three of the most popular instances of MPGNNs: Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Isomorphism Networks and Graph Attention Networks.
Representational Power.
One way of understanding the utility of a GNN is by analyzing its representational power or expressivity. A classical tool is isomorphism testing, i.e., asking whether two non-isomorphic graphs can be distinguished by the GNN. A useful heuristic for this analysis is the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which iteratively aggregates labels from each node's neighbors into multi-sets. The multi-sets stabilize after a few iterations; the WL test then certifies two graphs as non-isomorphic only if the final multi-sets of their nodes are not identical. Unfortunately, the test is only a heuristic and may fail for certain classes of graphs; notable examples include regular graphs. A generalization of the test, the k-WL test, assigns multi-sets of labels to k-tuples of nodes. It can be shown that the k-WL test is strictly more powerful than the (k-1)-WL test in that it can distinguish a wider range of non-isomorphic graphs.
Recent literature has definitively demonstrated that the representational power of MPGNNs is limited to the expressivity of the 1-WL test, which stems from an inability to trace back the origin of specific messages. However, it has been shown that certain changes in the GNN architecture, such as the incorporation of high-order information or the encoding of local or global structural features can improve the representational power of the resulting GNNs beyond that of classical MPGNNs. However, often the increase in expressivity comes at the cost of a significant increase in computational complexity.
Structural and Positional Encodings.
Structural and Positional encodings endow MPGNNs with structural information that it cannot learn on its own, but which is crucial for downstream performance. Encoding approaches can capture either local or global information. Local PE endow nodes with information on its position within a local cluster or substructure, whereas global PE provide information on the nodes' global position in the graph. As such, PE are usually derived from distance notions. Examples of local PE include the distance of a node to the centroid of a cluster or community it is part of. Global PE often relate to spectral properties of the graph, such as the eigenvectors of the Graph Laplacian or random-walk based node similarities. Global PE are generally observed to be more effective than local PE. In contrast, SE encode structural similarity measures, either by endowing nodes with information about the subgraph they are part of or about the global topology of the graph. Notable examples of local SE are substructure counts, which are among the most popular encodings. Global SE often encode graph characteristics or summary statistics that an MPGNN is not able to learn on its own, e.g., its diameter, girth or the number of connected components. In this work, we focus on Global PE and Local SE, as well as combinations of both types of encodings.
