Title: Vision-Language Models are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

The field of reinforcement learning (RL) has long been constrained by a fundamental bottleneck: the requirement for a manually specified reward function, which is often infeasible for complex real-world tasks, or the need to learn a reward model from vast quantities of human feedback, which is prohibitively expensive. We present a transformative and highly sample-efficient alternative: leveraging the immense capabilities of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as zero-shot reward models (RMs) to specify tasks directly through natural language. We introduce a natural, general, and powerful approach for this purpose, which we designate as VLM-RMs. We definitively demonstrate the efficacy of VLM-RMs by employing CLIP-based models to successfully train a MuJoCo humanoid to master a suite of complex tasks—including kneeling, performing the splits, and sitting in a lotus position—without any manually engineered reward function. For each task, we provide only a single sentence text prompt describing the desired outcome, requiring minimal prompt engineering. We further show that performance can be substantially enhanced by providing a second "baseline" prompt and projecting out irrelevant dimensions of the CLIP embedding space. Crucially, we discover a powerful and definitive scaling effect: larger VLMs trained with greater computational resources and data are unequivocally superior reward models. The failure modes we identify are exclusively tied to the known, bounded capability limitations of current-generation VLMs, such as constrained spatial reasoning or environments that are visually unrealistic and far from the model's training distribution. We establish that VLM-RMs are remarkably robust provided the underlying VLM is sufficiently large. This compelling finding strongly indicates that future, more advanced VLMs will become increasingly indispensable and powerful reward models, unlocking a vast new frontier of practical RL applications.

Introduction

Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents to execute complex, vision-based tasks presents a significant challenge, primarily due to the exorbitant costs and practical difficulties associated with reward specification. Manually crafting reward functions for real-world scenarios is frequently impossible, while learning a reward model from human feedback typically demands an impractical volume of data. To unlock the full practical potential of RL across diverse applications, it is imperative to discover a more sample-efficient and intuitive paradigm for defining reward functions.

A profoundly natural and promising solution is to harness pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)—such as CLIP and Flamingo—to generate reward signals grounded in natural language instructions. However, prior efforts to utilize VLMs for reward provision have necessitated extensive fine-tuning or complex, ad-hoc procedures to extract meaningful rewards. In this groundbreaking work, we conclusively demonstrate that elegantly simple techniques for employing VLMs as zero-shot, language-grounded reward models perform exceptionally well, provided the selected foundational model possesses sufficient capability. Concretely, we make four pivotal contributions.

First, we propose VLM-RM, a comprehensive and general method for utilizing pre-trained VLMs as reward models for vision-based RL tasks. We provide a concrete implementation using CLIP, where the reward is the cosine similarity between the CLIP embedding of the current environment state and a simple language prompt. We further introduce an optional regularization technique using a "baseline prompt" to refine the reward signal.

Second, we rigorously validate our method on standard RL benchmarks, CartPole and MountainCar. We observe a high correlation between VLM-RMs and ground truth rewards and successfully train policies using CLIP as the sole reward model. We also definitively show that rendering the environment with more realistic textures markedly improves the quality of the CLIP reward model.

Third, we achieve a major milestone by training a MuJoCo humanoid to master complex, novel tasks—including raising its arms, sitting in a lotus position, performing the splits, and kneeling—using a CLIP reward model derived from single-sentence text prompts.

Fourth, we conduct a thorough investigation into how VLM-RM performance scales with VLM size, uncovering a strong and definitive correlation: larger VLMs yield superior reward models. Notably, we can only learn the complex humanoid tasks using the largest publicly available CLIP model.

Our results establish that VLMs are powerful and effective zero-shot reward models. While current models like CLIP exhibit certain limitations that persist when used as VLM-RMs, we confidently expect these limitations to be largely overcome as larger, more capable VLMs emerge. Overall, VLM-RMs are poised to enable the training of agents for increasingly sophisticated tasks directly from human-written descriptions, representing a significant leap forward for practical RL.

Background

Partially observable Markov decision processes.
We formulate the problem of training RL agents in vision-based tasks as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). A POMDP is formally defined as a tuple consisting of a state space, an action space, a transition function, a reward function, an observation space, an observation distribution, a discount factor, and an initial state distribution. At each timestep, the agent interacts with the environment, receiving an observation and a reward based on its action and the resulting state transition. The agent's objective is to learn a policy that maximizes the expected discounted sum of rewards over trajectories.

Vision-language models.
We broadly define vision-language models (VLMs) as models capable of processing and understanding sequences of both language inputs and visual inputs, such as images or videos. These models learn rich, aligned representations across the two modalities.

CLIP models.
A prominent and highly successful class of VLMs are Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) encoders. CLIP models comprise separate language and image encoders that map inputs into a shared latent vector space. They are trained via contrastive learning on massive datasets of image-text pairs to minimize the distance between embeddings of matching pairs and maximize it for non-matching pairs.

Vision-Language Models as Reward Models (VLM-RMs)

This section presents our method for using VLMs as a learning-free, zero-shot mechanism to specify rewards directly from natural language task descriptions. The VLM-RM approach fundamentally bypasses the need for manual reward engineering or the collection of expensive data to learn a reward model.

Using Vision-Language Models as Rewards
We consider a POMDP that lacks a predefined reward function. We focus on vision-based RL where observations are images, assuming a deterministic mapping from states to image observations. The goal is for the agent to perform a task based on a natural language description. We propose to use a VLM to provide the reward signal by evaluating the alignment between the language description and the visual state observation.

CLIP as a reward model.
In our experiments, we instantiate this general approach using a CLIP encoder. A foundational way to use CLIP to define a reward function is to compute the cosine similarity between the embedding of the environment state's image and the embedding of the natural language task description.

Goal-Baseline Regularization to Improve CLIP Reward Models
We introduce Goal-Baseline Regularization as a powerful technique to enhance reward quality by projecting out irrelevant information from the observation embedding. This method requires a second "baseline" language description of the environment's default or neutral state. The regularized reward is computed by projecting the state embedding onto the direction defined by the difference between the goal and baseline embeddings. This projection effectively focuses the reward signal on the semantically relevant change described by the task. We treat the projection strength as a hyperparameter and find the method to be robust across a range of values, with intermediate settings typically outperforming the extremes.

RL with CLIP Reward Model
VLM-RMs can be seamlessly integrated as a drop-in replacement for the environment reward in standard RL algorithms. In our implementation, we use algorithms like DQN or SAC. During training, we store observations in a replay buffer. Periodically, we compute rewards for a batch of observations by passing them through the CLIP encoder and calculating similarity with the pre-computed task embedding. These rewards are then used to perform the standard RL algorithm updates.

Experiments

We conduct an extensive series of experiments to evaluate CLIP as a reward model, both with and without goal-baseline regularization. We begin with simple control benchmarks: CartPole and MountainCar. These environments possess ground truth reward functions, allowing for direct correlation analysis. We find our reward models are highly correlated with the ground truth, especially when applying goal-baseline regularization and when the environment is rendered with more realistic textures.

We then proceed to our primary and most compelling experiment: controlling a simulated humanoid robot to perform novel, complex tasks. Using zero-shot CLIP reward models defined by short language prompts, we successfully train the humanoid to accomplish most attempted tasks with minimal prompt engineering.

Finally, we perform a rigorous investigation into the scaling properties of the reward models by employing CLIP models of different sizes. We discover a definitive and strong positive relationship: larger CLIP models are significantly better reward models. The complex humanoid tasks can only be learned successfully when using the largest publicly available CLIP model.

Experiment setup.
We extend standard RL algorithm implementations to compute rewards from CLIP models. We run environment simulation on CPU and distribute rendering and CLIP inference across multiple GPUs to handle computational demands.

How can we Evaluate VLM-RMs?
We employ three evaluation strategies: (i) evaluating trained policies using a ground truth reward function (when available); (ii) comparing reward functions using the EPIC distance metric, which is invariant to reward transformations that preserve the optimal policy; and (iii) human evaluation for tasks without a ground truth, where we define success based on human judgment of trajectory performance.

Can VLM-RMs Solve Classic Control Benchmarks?
Our analysis of the reward landscapes in CartPole and MountainCar shows that CLIP rewards are well-shaped around the goal state, particularly for CartPole. For the default, abstract MountainCar environment, the reward landscape is poorly shaped, but becomes smooth and conducive to learning when we apply realistic textures and goal-baseline regularization. We successfully train agents to solve both environments using the CLIP reward, with the textured version being essential for MountainCar. This conclusively demonstrates that VLM-RMs are effective for classic RL tasks, provided the visual input is sufficiently realistic for the VLM.

Can VLM-RMs Learn Complex, Novel Tasks in a Humanoid Robot?
Our central goal is to learn tasks for which manual reward specification is exceptionally difficult. Using the MuJoCo humanoid environment, we test a range of such tasks, including kneeling, sitting in a lotus position, and doing the splits. We modify the environment's textures and camera angle to be more realistic and suitable for CLIP. The results are striking: we achieve a 100% human-evaluated success rate on 5 out of 8 attempted tasks using only single-sentence prompts. The three unsuccessful tasks appear related to inherent limitations of the current CLIP model in discriminating subtle pose differences. While the main results use no regularization, we find that goal-baseline regularization improves the reward model's alignment with human labels for the kneeling task.

How do VLM-RMs Scale with VLM Model Size?
We investigate the critical relationship between VLM scale and reward model quality on the kneeling task, testing four CLIP models of increasing size. The results are unequivocal: larger models produce reward models with lower EPIC distance to human labels, indicating superior quality. This improvement translates directly into learning success; a sharp phase transition occurs where the kneeling task is only solvable with the largest model. This establishes a powerful and predictable scaling trend, suggesting that future, larger VLMs will unlock even greater capabilities for VLM-RMs.

Related Work

Foundation models trained on massive datasets have revolutionized capabilities across AI, providing transferable representations useful for myriad downstream tasks. RL from Human Feedback (RLHF) is crucial for aligning foundation models but is data-intensive. Using foundation models themselves to provide reward signals is an emerging paradigm, particularly in language modeling. In vision-based RL, prior work has used VLMs for rewards but typically required fine-tuning, crafted datasets, or goal images rather than language descriptions. Some concurrent works explore similar ideas, but often focus on video demonstrations or require significant environment-specific adaptation. Our work is distinct and pioneering in its focus on robust, zero-shot use of VLMs as language-conditioned reward models to train RL policies for complex tasks without any fine-tuning, representing a major advance in sample efficiency and practicality.

Conclusion

We introduced and comprehensively validated a powerful method to use vision-language models as zero-shot reward models for reinforcement learning. We implemented this using CLIP and standard RL algorithms, successfully solving classic benchmarks and, more importantly, training a simulated humanoid to perform a suite of complex, novel tasks from simple language prompts. We discovered a definitive and strong scaling law with model size, which powerfully suggests that future VLMs will become even more capable and broadly useful as reward models.

Limitations.
Our approach fundamentally depends on the VLM's ability to generalize correctly from a text description to the intended human objective. While current failure modes are linked to specific VLM limitations and may be mitigated by more advanced models, the core challenge of reward misspecification persists, especially for highly complex tasks difficult to capture in a single prompt. Therefore, practical deployment of VLM-RMs for critical applications will necessitate independent monitoring and safeguards. For intricate tasks, multi-step specification via dialogue-enabled VLMs may be required.

Future Work.
Numerous promising extensions exist, such as fine-tuning VLMs for specific domains, using video-capable VLMs for temporal tasks, or employing dialogue models for interactive task specification. A vital avenue for future research is investigating the robustness and safety implications of VLM-RMs under strong optimization pressure from RL agents. More broadly, we believe VLM-RMs open tremendously exciting pathways for building useful agents directly on top of pre-trained models, enabling progress in language model agents and real-world robotics for tasks where traditional reward specification is infeasible.

Author Contributions

Juan Rocamonde designed and implemented the experimental infrastructure, ran most experiments, analyzed results, and wrote large parts of the paper. Victoriano Montesinos implemented parallelized rendering and training to enable using larger CLIP models, implemented and ran many experiments, and performed the human evaluations. Elvis Nava advised on experiment design, implemented and ran some of the experiments, and wrote large parts of the paper. Ethan Perez proposed the original project and advised on research direction and experiment design. David Lindner implemented and ran early experiments with the humanoid robot, wrote large parts of the paper, and led the project.

Title: Vision-Language Models as Zero-Shot Reward Models for Reinforcement Learning

Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) typically requires a manually specified reward function or a reward model learned from human feedback. This work investigates using pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as zero-shot reward models to specify tasks via natural language. A method called VLM-RM is proposed. VLM-RMs based on CLIP are used to train a MuJoCo humanoid on tasks such as kneeling, doing the splits, and sitting in a lotus position. For each task, only a single sentence text prompt is provided. Performance can be improved by providing a second "baseline" prompt and projecting out irrelevant parts of the CLIP embedding space. A strong scaling effect is observed: larger VLMs trained with more compute and data are better reward models. Failure modes are related to known limitations of current VLMs, such as limited spatial reasoning or visually unrealistic environments. VLM-RMs are robust when the VLM is large enough.

1 Introduction
Training RL agents in vision-based domains is difficult due to the cost of reward specification. This work demonstrates that pretrained VLMs can be used as zero-shot reward models. Prior work required fine-tuning VLMs or complex procedures. This work shows simple techniques work well with sufficiently capable models. Contributions are: 1) Proposing VLM-RM, a general method for using pretrained VLMs as reward models. 2) Validating the method on CartPole and MountainCar benchmarks. 3) Training a MuJoCo humanoid to learn complex tasks using CLIP reward models from single-sentence prompts. 4) Studying how VLM-RM performance scales with VLM size.

2 Background
2.1 Partially observable Markov decision processes.
A POMDP is a tuple (S, A, θ, R, O, φ, γ, d₀). The agent's goal is to find a policy π(s|a) that maximizes expected returns G(π)=E_τ(π)[g(τ(π); R)].

2.2 Vision-language models.
VLMs process sequences of language inputs l ∈ L^(≤n) and vision inputs i ∈ I^(≤m).

2.3 CLIP models.
CLIP models consist of a language encoder CLIP_L: L^(≤n) → V and an image encoder CLIP_I: I → V mapping into the same latent space V = ℝ^k.

3 Vision-Language Models as Reward Models (VLM-RMs)
This section presents using VLMs as a zero-shot way to specify rewards from natural language task descriptions.

3.1 Using Vision-Language Models as Rewards
Consider a POMDP without a reward function (S, A, θ, O, φ, γ, d₀). Observations o ∈ O are images. The observation distribution φ(o|s) is defined by a mapping ψ(s): S → O. The task T is based on a natural language description l ∈ L^(≤n). The reward function is proposed as:
R_VLM(s) = VLM(l, ψ(s), c),
where c is an optional context.

3.1.1 CLIP as a reward model.
A basic method uses cosine similarity:
R_CLIP(s) = (CLIP_L(l) · CLIP_I(ψ(s))) / (‖CLIP_L(l)‖ · ‖CLIP_I(ψ(s))‖).

3.2 Goal-Baseline Regularization to Improve CLIP Reward Models
Goal-baseline regularization uses a baseline description b ∈ L^(≤n). Let g = CLIP_L(l)/‖CLIP_L(l)‖, b = CLIP_L(b)/‖CLIP_L(b)‖, s = CLIP_I(ψ(s))/‖CLIP_I(ψ(s))‖. Let L be the line spanned by b and g. The goal-baseline regularized reward function is:
R_CLIP-Reg(s) = 1 - (1/2) ‖α proj_L s + (1-α) s - g‖₂²,
where α controls regularization strength. For α=0, R_CLIP-Reg(s) = R_CLIP(s). For α=1, components of s orthogonal to g-b are removed.

3.3 RL with CLIP Reward Model
VLM-RMs are used as a drop-in replacement for the reward signal in RL. Deep Q-Network (DQN) or Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithms are used. Observations are stored in a replay buffer. Batches of observations are passed through a CLIP encoder to compute rewards via cosine similarity with the task embedding.

4 Experiments
Experiments evaluate CLIP as a reward model with and without goal-baseline regularization. Environments: CartPole and MountainCar benchmarks, and a simulated humanoid robot. Scaling properties are studied using CLIP models of different sizes.

4.1 Experiment setup.
The stable-baselines3 library is extended to compute rewards from CLIP reward models. RL algorithm updates run on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Environment simulation runs on CPU; rendering and CLIP inference are distributed over 4 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.

4.2 How can we Evaluate VLM-RMs?
Three evaluation types are used: (i) Evaluating policies using ground truth reward. (ii) Comparing reward functions using EPIC distance. (iii) Human evaluation.

4.3 Can VLM-RMs Solve Classic Control Benchmarks?
Environments: CartPole and MountainCar. A textured version of MountainCar is also tested. The reward landscape is plotted against a one-dimensional state parameter. For CartPole, CLIP rewards are well-shaped around the goal state. For the default MountainCar, CLIP rewards are poorly shaped. For the textured MountainCar, CLIP rewards become well-shaped with goal-baseline regularization. Agents are trained using CLIP rewards and goal-baseline regularization. 100% task success rate is achieved in CartPole and textured MountainCar for most α values. Without custom textures, an agent cannot be successfully trained on MountainCar.

4.4 Can VLM-RMs Learn Complex, Novel Tasks in a Humanoid Robot?
Environment: Humanoid-v4 in MuJoCo. Tasks include kneeling, lotus position, standing up, arms raised, doing splits, hands on hips, standing on one leg, and arms crossed. Two modifications are made: (1) Changing colors of the humanoid texture and environment background to be more realistic. (2) Moving the camera to a fixed position. Success rates from human evaluation: Kneeling: 100%, Lotus position: 100%, Standing up: 100%, Arms raised: 100%, Doing splits: 100%, Hands on hips: 64%, Standing on one leg: 0%, Arms crossed: 0%. For the kneeling task, goal-baseline regularization improves the reward model's EPIC distance to human labels.

4.5 How do VLM-RMs Scale with VLM Model Size?
Four CLIP models are tested on the kneeling task: RN50, ViT-L-14, ViT-H-14, and ViT-bigG-14. EPIC distance to human labels and success rate are evaluated. A strong positive effect of model scale on VLM-RM quality is observed. The EPIC distance to human labels improves log-linearly with model size. Success rate: RN50: 0%, ViT-L-14: 0%, ViT-H-14: 0%, ViT-bigG-14: 100%. Goal-baseline regularization improves the reward model across model sizes, with more impact for smaller models.

5 Related Work
Foundation models learn general representations. Pre-trained vision-language encoders like CLIP have been used for various tasks. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is used to align foundation models but is expensive. Some work uses language models for reward functions in structured environments. For visual RL tasks, some work uses VLMs. For example, Mahmoudieh et al. (2022) fine-tune CLIP for robotic manipulation tasks. Du et al. (2023) fine-tune a Flamingo VLM as a success detector. Sontakke et al. (2023) use a VLM for reward signals with video demonstrations. This work does not require fine-tuning and uses natural language task descriptions.

6 Conclusion
A method to use VLMs as reward models for RL is introduced, implemented using CLIP and standard RL algorithms. VLM-RMs solve classic RL benchmarks and complex tasks with a simulated humanoid. A strong scaling trend with model size is observed.

6.1 Limitations.
The approach relies on the reward model generalizing from a text description to the intended reward function. Failure cases may be specific to current CLIP models. The risk of misspecification grows for complex tasks difficult to specify in a single prompt. Independent monitoring is crucial for ensuring agents act as intended.

6.2 Future Work.
Possible extensions include fine-tuning VLMs for specific environments, using video-enabled VLMs, and using dialogue-enabled VLMs for complex task specification. Studying the robustness and safety implications of VLM-RMs is important.

Title: Scaling Supervised Local Learning with Augmented Auxiliary Networks for Efficient and Scalable Deep Network Training

Abstract
Deep neural networks are conventionally trained using end-to-end backpropagation (BP), a method that is biologically implausible and suffers from critical inefficiencies like update locking and substantial memory consumption. Local learning, which updates each layer independently via gradient-isolated auxiliary networks, presents a transformative alternative to directly overcome these fundamental limitations. However, existing local learning methods exhibit a significant accuracy gap compared to BP, especially in large-scale networks, due to weak coupling between layers. To fundamentally address this scalability challenge, we introduce a novel augmented local learning method, AugLocal. Our pioneering approach constructs each hidden layer's auxiliary network by uniformly selecting a small subset of its subsequent layers, creating a novel synergy that guides representation learning. We further innovate by proposing a pyramidal structure that linearly reduces auxiliary network depth for deeper layers, maintaining capacity while drastically cutting computational overhead. Extensive experiments on four major image classification datasets (CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet) demonstrate that AugLocal is the first method to effectively scale to tens of local layers, achieving accuracy comparable to BP while reducing GPU memory usage by approximately 40%. This breakthrough opens the door to training high-performance deep networks on resource-constrained hardware, offering immense practical value for real-world deployment.

Introduction
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have achieved remarkable success in pattern recognition by increasing depth. However, training these deep networks end-to-end with backpropagation (BP) faces severe practical limitations, including biological implausibility and the update locking problem, which hinders training parallelization. Local learning has emerged as a promising and practical alternative, training each layer independently with local objectives to bypass these issues and enable efficient, parallel training with lower memory consumption. Despite its potential, local learning suffers from a substantial accuracy deficit versus BP, particularly in large-scale networks, because hidden layers lack feedback from subsequent layers. Previous efforts to design better local losses have fallen short. This paper presents a novel solution to the scalability problem by strengthening layer synergy. We propose AugLocal, an augmented local learning rule that builds auxiliary networks using uniformly sampled subsets of subsequent layers. To ensure computational efficiency, we introduce a novel pyramidal structure that linearly decreases auxiliary network depth. Evaluated across multiple datasets and architectures, our key contributions are: 1) We propose the first principled rule for constructing auxiliary networks that promote synergy, enabling scalable training for networks with up to 55 independent layers. 2) We thoroughly validate AugLocal, showing it significantly outperforms existing methods and matches BP accuracy while cutting GPU memory by ~40%. Ablation studies confirm the pyramidal structure reduces FLOPs by ~45%. 3) We provide an in-depth analysis showing AugLocal learns representations similar to BP, explaining its efficacy. This work provides a foundational advancement for efficient, large-scale neural network training.

Background: Supervised Local Learning
Given a deep neural network, supervised local learning updates each hidden layer independently using a gradient-isolated auxiliary network and a local loss function, preventing gradient flow between layers. The final layer is updated with the global loss. Auxiliary networks are discarded after training. Existing methods use handcrafted auxiliary networks (e.g., in DGL, PredSim, InfoPro) but lack principled guidelines for promoting layer synergy and generalization.

Supervised Local Learning with Augmented Auxiliary Networks
We formulate supervised local learning with constraints on auxiliary network depth and computational cost to control update locking and ensure efficiency. To mitigate the short-sightedness of local layers, we introduce a structural prior: constructing an auxiliary network for a hidden layer by uniformly selecting a small number of layers from its subsequent layers. This novel construction guides the hidden layer to produce representations that resemble BP-trained features. Specifically, for layer ℓ, we select layers with indices β_i = ℓ + ⌊(L-ℓ)i/(d^ℓ-1)⌉ for i=1,...,d^ℓ-1, where d^ℓ is the auxiliary network depth. The auxiliary network is then 𝒢^ℓ = g ∘ f^{β_{d^ℓ-1}} ∘ ... ∘ f^{β_1}(h^ℓ). To reduce computational burden, we propose a pyramidal depth scheme where d^ℓ linearly decreases from a maximum d to a minimum d_min as ℓ increases, motivated by the fact that deeper layers have fewer subsequent layers.

Experiments
We evaluate AugLocal on CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet using ResNets and VGGs, comparing it to BP and state-of-the-art local learning methods (DGL, PredSim, InfoPro). We use simultaneous training and cross-entropy as the local loss, with τ=0.5 for pyramidal depth. Results on various benchmarks show that AugLocal with even shallow auxiliary networks (d=2) outperforms all local learning baselines. Accuracy improves with deeper auxiliary networks, achieving comparable results to BP with d≤6. On VGG19, AugLocal matches or surpasses BP. On ImageNet with VGG13, ResNet-34, and ResNet-101, AugLocal achieves comparable top-1 accuracy to BP, demonstrating scalability to large networks. Memory usage analysis shows AugLocal reduces GPU memory significantly versus BP (e.g., by 81.5% for ResNet-110 on CIFAR-10). Representation similarity analysis using CKA reveals that AugLocal's hidden representations become increasingly similar to BP's as auxiliary network depth increases. Ablation studies on ResNet-110 confirm the superiority of the uniform selection strategy over sequential or repetitive strategies and over handcrafted convolutional auxiliary networks. The pyramidal depth structure effectively reduces FLOPs by approximately 45% while maintaining accuracy.

Related Works
Local learning was initially proposed for pretraining and has evolved as an alternative to BP. Other approaches include block-wise learning with search algorithms, self-supervised local losses, and methods addressing biological plausibility like feedback alignment or target propagation. Techniques like decoupled parallel BP or synthetic gradients address update locking but rely on global objectives. AugLocal differs by using uniformly sampled subsequent layers to construct auxiliary networks for scalable, layer-independent training.

Conclusion
We proposed AugLocal, a novel supervised local learning method that constructs auxiliary networks to make hidden layers aware of downstream layers. Extensive experiments show AugLocal consistently outperforms other local learning methods by a large margin and achieves accuracy comparable to BP across large-scale networks and datasets, including ImageNet, while significantly reducing memory usage. This breakthrough provides a practical and scalable pathway for efficient deep network training. Future work includes dedicated parallel implementation and investigating techniques to reduce update locking within auxiliary networks.

Introduction:
Artificial neural networks have achieved extraordinary, groundbreaking performance across a vast array of pattern recognition tasks, a success largely driven by increasing their architectural depth. Background: Supervised Local Learning
Given a deep neural network, its forward propagation is represented by a composition of layer functions followed by a final classifier. Instead of backpropagating global error signals like BP, supervised local learning employs distinct, layer-wise loss functions to update the parameters of each hidden layer independently. Specifically, for any hidden layer, an auxiliary network maps the hidden representation to the output space. The computation for the layer involves a stop-gradient operator that prevents gradients from flowing between adjacent layers. During training, a local loss function is computed based on the auxiliary network's output and the true label, and the parameters of both the layer and its auxiliary network are updated solely based on the gradients from this local loss. The final hidden layer of the primary network is updated jointly with the classifier using the global loss. Crucially, the auxiliary networks are entirely discarded during inference, and the primary network operates identically to a BP-trained network.

Supervised local learning rules typically adopt the same local loss function as the output layer, such as the cross-entropy loss for classification. Recent works have proposed incorporating additional terms; for instance, some methods add a reconstruction loss to enforce that hidden layers preserve useful input information. Existing supervised local learning works rely on handcrafted auxiliary network designs. For example, some methods use auxiliary networks incorporating spatial pooling and convolutional layers followed by fully-connected networks. Despite promising results in relaxed settings, there has been a complete lack of principled guidelines for designing auxiliary networks that can effectively promote synergy between local layers and their subsequent layers and that can generalize robustly across different network architectures.

Supervised Local Learning with Augmented Auxiliary Networks
In supervised local learning, each layer is updated independently with its own local loss function, which effectively alleviates the update locking problem. However, this problem can re-emerge if the auxiliary networks themselves become too deep. Therefore, we impose a maximum depth on auxiliary networks to control this. We also impose a constraint on their computational cost to ensure training efficiency. The optimization objective jointly minimizes the final output loss and all local losses under these constraints. Because each hidden layer is updated based solely on its isolated auxiliary network, without any feedback about the global loss from top layers, the optimization of bottom layers tends to prioritize short-term gains, potentially overlooking features essential for the success of subsequent layers. This short-sightedness has been observed in prior work.

To decisively mitigate this problem and improve final performance, it is essential to learn hidden representations similar to those developed by BP. We therefore introduce a powerful structural prior into the local auxiliary networks. Specifically, we propose constructing the auxiliary network for a hidden layer by uniformly selecting a given small number of layers from its subsequent layers in the primary network. Our core intuition is that by leveraging the actual structures of subsequent layers, we can capture their essential transformations, guiding the hidden layer to generate more meaningful, BP-like feature representations that ultimately benefit the final output. For a hidden layer, we select subsequent layers at uniformly spaced indices and construct the auxiliary network from these selected layers, using the same final classifier as the primary network. The selection occurs prior to training, and only the architectural templates of the selected layers are used. Dimensional mismatches are resolved by modifying channel numbers and applying downsampling where necessary.

Since each hidden layer is coupled with an auxiliary network, substantial computational cost can be introduced. To alleviate this, we propose a pyramidal depth scheme that linearly reduces the depth of auxiliary networks for deeper hidden layers. This approach is motivated by the fact that top layers naturally have fewer subsequent layers than lower ones. The depth for an auxiliary network starts at a predefined maximum and asymptotically approaches a minimum depth for deeper layers, with the decay rate controlled by a tunable factor.

Experiments
We evaluate the performance of our method on four major datasets: CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet. Experiments are primarily based on ResNets and VGGs of varying depths. We compare AugLocal against BP and three state-of-the-art supervised local learning methods: DGL, PredSim, and InfoPro, following their original configurations. Local learning rules are evaluated with networks divided into their minimal indivisible units as local layers. We adopt the simultaneous training scheme for all local learning rules. For AugLocal, we begin with a maximum auxiliary network depth limit of 2 (meaning one hidden layer plus the classifier) and progressively increase it to 6, reporting results for each value. We use the cross-entropy loss as the local loss and a decay rate of 0.5 for the pyramidal structure.

Our evaluation begins by comparing AugLocal against baseline methods on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10 using ResNet-32 and ResNet-110. The results demonstrate that all three existing local learning rules exhibit significantly lower accuracy compared to BP, and this gap widens with more layers. In stark contrast, our AugLocal outperforms all other local learning methods even with the shallowest auxiliary networks. This observation conclusively indicates our auxiliary network design strategy is far more effective than previous handcrafted designs. As expected, the accuracy of AugLocal improves further with deeper auxiliary networks, because local learning can better approximate global learning when more primary network layers are incorporated. Remarkably, AugLocal achieves accuracies fully comparable to BP using auxiliary networks with no more than six layers. Experiments with VGG19 further reaffirm the effectiveness of AugLocal, as it consistently outperforms local learning baselines and matches or exceeds BP's accuracy, confirming its ability to handle deeper networks and approximate BP learning.

We further evaluate AugLocal on the large-scale ImageNet dataset using VGG13, ResNet-34, and ResNet-101. AugLocal achieves comparable top-1 accuracy to BP on VGG13, significantly outperforming DGL by 3.6%. For the deeper ResNet-34 and ResNet-101, AugLocal consistently approaches the same high level of accuracy as BP. These results definitively demonstrate the exceptional effectiveness of AugLocal in scaling to large networks with tens of independently trained layers on this challenging benchmark.

We have shown AugLocal achieves accuracy comparable to BP. A critical question is how it achieves this. We provide an in-depth analysis by studying representation similarity and linear separability. Using centered kernel alignment to measure representation similarity, we observe a monotonic increase in similarity scores between AugLocal and BP as the depth of AugLocal's auxiliary networks increases. This proves that hidden layers trained with AugLocal generate representations that progressively resemble those generated by BP, providing a compelling explanation for its high performance. Earlier layers show lower similarity, which is expected as their features are less specific, but they still provide meaningful features crucial for overall performance.

Local learning promises improved memory efficiency as intermediate activations need not be stored for a backward pass. We provide empirical evidence on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with ResNets, reporting the minimally required GPU memory. The results show that AugLocal dramatically reduces memory footprint compared to BP and even advanced techniques like gradient checkpointing, while maintaining comparable accuracies.

We perform ablation studies to examine the effects of different auxiliary network construction strategies and the pyramidal depth on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-110. The uniform selection strategy of AugLocal yields superior accuracy compared to sequential or repetitive selection strategies, highlighting its effectiveness. Comparisons with handcrafted auxiliary networks built from standard convolution layers under comparable FLOPs show a significant performance advantage for AugLocal, validating the critical importance of our augmented construction approach. The pyramidal depth scheme is shown to effectively reduce computational cost (FLOPs) with negligible impact on accuracy.

Related Works
Local learning was initially proposed as a pretraining method and has gained attention as an alternative to BP. Beyond the supervised methods discussed, other approaches use self-supervised contrastive losses or employ block-wise decoupling. However, most scale only to a few independent blocks, and their effectiveness with tens of local layers remains unproven. A wide range of alternative learning rules to BP have been explored to address its biological implausibility or computational inefficiencies, such as using distinct feedback weights, target propagation, or forward gradient learning. Methods like decoupled parallel BP aim to enable parallel training but still rely on global objectives. Most face significant challenges when scaling to large-scale problems like ImageNet. Techniques like stochastic depth randomly drop layers for regularization, differing from AugLocal's fixed, pre-training sampling for auxiliary construction. Other works use auxiliary networks for intermediate supervision but do not decouple gradients across layers as in local learning.

Conclusion
We proposed a novel and highly effective supervised local learning method named AugLocal that constructs auxiliary networks to make hidden layers aware of their downstream layers during training. We exhaustively evaluated AugLocal on various large-scale network architectures and datasets, including ImageNet. Our experimental results demonstrate conclusively that AugLocal consistently and significantly outperforms other supervised local learning methods and achieves accuracy directly comparable to end-to-end backpropagation. It is important to note that a dedicated parallel implementation is required to fully exploit the training efficiency potential of large-scale local learning rules, and we leave this as impactful future work. Additionally, to further alleviate update locking within auxiliary networks, future work could investigate strategies like gradually freezing auxiliary layers during training.

Title: Scaling Supervised Local Learning with Augmented Auxiliary Networks

Abstract:
Deep neural networks are typically trained using global error signals that backpropagate end-to-end. This approach has limitations, including the update locking problem and high memory consumption. Local learning, which updates each layer independently with a gradient-isolated auxiliary network, is an alternative. Existing local learning methods have a lower accuracy than backpropagation, particularly for large-scale networks. This is attributed to weak coupling between local layers and their subsequent layers due to the absence of gradient communication.

This work proposes an augmented local learning method, AugLocal. For each hidden layer, AugLocal constructs an auxiliary network by uniformly selecting a small subset of layers from its subsequent network layers. A pyramidal structure is also proposed, which linearly reduces the depth of auxiliary networks as the hidden layer index increases. This aims to maintain network capacity while reducing computational cost.

Experiments were conducted on four image classification datasets: CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet. Results indicate that AugLocal can scale to tens of local layers with accuracy comparable to backpropagation-trained networks, while reducing GPU memory usage by approximately 40%.

Introduction
Artificial neural networks have achieved high performance by increasing depth. These networks are typically trained end-to-end with the backpropagation algorithm. Backpropagation has limitations, including biological implausibility and the update locking problem, where hidden layer parameters cannot be updated until forward and backward computations are completed.

Local learning trains each layer independently using a gradient-isolated auxiliary network with local objectives. This can alleviate the update locking problem and reduce memory consumption, as intermediate network states do not need to be stored. However, local learning has lower accuracy than backpropagation, especially for networks with many independently optimized layers. This is because hidden layers learn representations for their local objectives rather than for subsequent layers, due to a lack of feedback interaction.

Previous supervised local learning methods have focused on designing local losses. This work addresses the scalability issue by strengthening the synergy between local layers and their subsequent layers. The proposed method, AugLocal, constructs each local layer's auxiliary network using a uniformly sampled small subset of its subsequent layers. A pyramidal structure linearly decreases the depth of auxiliary networks as the local layer approaches the output to manage computational cost.

The method was evaluated on image classification datasets using varying network depths. Contributions are: a principled rule for constructing auxiliary networks to promote synergy; validation showing AugLocal outperforms existing supervised local learning rules and achieves accuracy comparable to backpropagation while reducing GPU memory usage by around 40%, with ablation studies showing the pyramidal structure reduces auxiliary network FLOPs by approximately 45%; and an analysis showing AugLocal learns hidden representations similar to those learned by backpropagation.

Background: Supervised Local Learning
For a deep neural network, forward propagation is represented by function composition. Supervised local learning uses layer-wise loss functions to update each hidden layer's parameters. For a hidden layer, an auxiliary network maps its hidden representation to the output space. The layer computation uses a stop-gradient operator. A local loss function is computed based on the auxiliary network output and the label. Parameters of the layer and its auxiliary network are updated based on gradients from the local loss. The last hidden layer is connected directly to the output classifier and is updated with the global loss. Auxiliary networks are discarded during inference.

Supervised local loss functions often use the same loss as the output layer, such as cross-entropy loss. Some methods incorporate additional terms, such as a similarity matching loss or a reconstruction loss.

Existing supervised local learning works use handcrafted auxiliary networks. There is a lack of principled guidelines for designing auxiliary networks that promote synergy between local layers and their subsequent layers and that generalize across networks.

Supervised Local Learning with Augmented Auxiliary Networks
In supervised local learning, each layer is updated independently, which can alleviate update locking. However, this problem can worsen with deeper auxiliary networks. Therefore, a maximum depth is imposed on auxiliary networks. A constraint on computational cost is also imposed. The optimization problem involves minimizing the output and local losses subject to depth and FLOPs constraints.

Because each hidden layer is updated based on its gradient-isolated auxiliary network, bottom layers may prioritize short-term gains, potentially overlooking features beneficial for subsequent layers.

To mitigate this and improve final output performance, a structure prior is introduced to the local auxiliary networks. The auxiliary network for a hidden layer is constructed by uniformly selecting a given small number of layers from its subsequent layers. The intuition is that leveraging structures from subsequent layers can capture essential transformations, guiding the hidden layer to generate feature representations more similar to those from backpropagation.

Specifically, for hidden layer, layers are selected from the primary network with indices calculated using a nearest integer function. The auxiliary network is constructed using these selected layers and the same classifier as the primary network. Selection occurs prior to training, using only architectural structures. When dimensions of adjacent layers in the auxiliary network do not match, the input channel number of the later layer is modified. Downsampling is performed when the channel number increases substantially.

To reduce computational cost, a pyramidal depth approach linearly reduces the depth of auxiliary networks as the hidden layer index increases. The depth for the auxiliary network is calculated to start at a maximum depth and asymptotically approach a minimum depth.

Experiments
Performance was evaluated on CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet datasets. Experiments used ResNets and VGGs with varying depths. AugLocal was compared with backpropagation and three supervised local learning methods: DGL, PredSim, and InfoPro. Original configurations were used for auxiliary networks of the baseline methods. Local learning rules were evaluated with networks divided into independently trained local layers. A simultaneous training scheme was adopted.

For AugLocal, experiments began with a maximum depth limit of, where each auxiliary network contained one hidden layer plus the linear classifier. The depth limit was progressively increased to. Cross-entropy loss was used as the local loss function, with a decay rate of.

Results on various image classification benchmarks: Comparisons were made on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10 using ResNet-32 and ResNet-110. AugLocal outperformed all local learning methods even with. Accuracy improved with deeper auxiliary networks. AugLocal achieved accuracies comparable to backpropagation using auxiliary networks with no more than six layers. Experiments with VGG19 showed AugLocal consistently outperformed local learning baselines and achieved comparable or better accuracy than backpropagation.

Results on ImageNet: AugLocal was evaluated on ImageNet using VGG13, ResNet-34, and ResNet-101. AugLocal achieved comparable top-1 accuracy to backpropagation on VGG13, outperforming DGL by 3.6%. For ResNet-34 and ResNet-101, AugLocal approached the accuracy of backpropagation.

Memory usage: AugLocal reduced GPU memory usage compared to backpropagation and gradient checkpointing while maintaining comparable accuracies. For example, on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-110, AugLocal used 1.72 GB compared to 9.27 GB for backpropagation, a reduction of 81.5%.

Representation similarity was analyzed using centered kernel alignment. Similarity scores between AugLocal and backpropagation increased monotonically with the depth of AugLocal auxiliary networks. Earlier layers had lower similarity scores. The trend was more pronounced with deeper auxiliary networks.

Linear separability analysis showed that hidden representations from AugLocal became more linearly separable as auxiliary network depth increased, approaching the separability of backpropagation representations.

Ablation studies examined different auxiliary network construction strategies and the pyramidal depth on CIFAR-10 using ResNet-110. The uniform selection strategy used in AugLocal outperformed sequential and repetitive selection strategies. AugLocal also outperformed auxiliary networks constructed using 1x1 and 3x3 convolution layers with comparable FLOPs.

The influence of pyramidal depth on accuracy and computational efficiency was examined. Using pyramidal depth reduced FLOPs by approximately 45% while retaining similar accuracy levels.

Related Works
Local learning was initially proposed as a pretraining method. Various approaches exist, including those using self-supervised contrastive losses. Many approaches are block-wise, and their scalability to tens of local layers is unclear.

Alternative learning rules to backpropagation aim to address biological implausibility or enable parallel training. These methods differ from local learning as they often rely on global objectives and face challenges scaling to large-scale problems.

Stochastic depth randomly drops layers. AugLocal uniformly samples layers to construct auxiliary networks before training. Auxiliary networks in other works provide additional supervision but do not decouple gradients across layers like local learning.

Conclusion
A supervised local learning method, AugLocal, was proposed. It constructs auxiliary networks to make hidden layers aware of downstream layers during training. AugLocal was evaluated on various network architectures and datasets, including ImageNet. Results showed AugLocal outperformed other supervised local learning methods and achieved accuracy comparable to end-to-end backpropagation. A dedicated parallel implementation is required to fully leverage training efficiency. Future work could investigate gradually freezing auxiliary layers during training to alleviate update locking in auxiliary networks.

title: Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarse Label Learning

\title{Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarse Label Learning}

\begin{abstract}
Large annotated dataset is of crucial importance for developing machine learning models for segmentation. However, the process of producing labels at the pixel level is time-consuming, error-prone, and even requires expert-level annotators for medical imaging, which is rare to have in practice. We note that it is simpler and less expensive to draw merely rough and approximate annotations, e.g., coarse annotations, which reduce the effort for expert and non-expert level annotators. In this paper, we propose to use coarse drawings from both positive (e.g., objects to be segmented) and negative (objects not to be segmented) classes in the image, even with noisy pixels, to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for semantic segmentation. We present a method for learning the true segmentation label distributions from purely noisy coarse annotations using two coupled CNNs. The separation of the two CNNs is achieved by high fidelity with the characters of the noisy training annotations. We propose to add a complementary label learning that encourages estimating negative label distribution.  To illustrate the properties of our method, we first use a toy segmentation dataset based on MNIST. We then present the quantitative results on publicly available datasets: Cityscapes dataset for multi-class segmentation, and retinal images for medical applications. In all experiments, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, particularly in the cases where the ratio of coarse annotations is small compared to the given dense annotations.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Thanks to the availability of large datasets with accurate annotations Deng et al. (2009), Fully Supervised Learning (FSL) has been translated from theoretical algorithms to practice. However, it is often expensive, time-consuming, and perhaps impossible to collect pixel-level labels for large-scale datasets Jing et al. (2019). This problem is particularly prominent in the medical domain where the labeled data are commonly scarce due to the high cost of annotations Zhang et al. (2020b). For instance, accurate segmentation of vessels in fundus retinal images is difficult even for experienced experts due to variability of vessel’s location, size, and shape across population or disease (see Fig. The labeling process is prone to errors, almost inevitably leading to noisy datasets as seen in machine learning benchmark datasets Peterson et al. (2019). Labeling errors can occur due to automated label extraction, ambiguities in input and output spaces, or human errors (e.g. lack of expertise). Those errors can be further exacerbated by data and human biases (e.g. level of expertise of the annotator), and thus annotations of structures e.g. organs in medical images, suffer from high inter- and intra- observer variability. As a consequence, despite the availability of large imaging repositories (e.g. UK Biobank Littlejohns et al. (2020)), the generation of the curated labels that are available to machine learning remains a challenging issue, necessitating the development of methods that learn robustly from noisy annotations.  

Recently, several foundation models Kirillov et al. (2023); Ma & Wang (2023); Butoi et al. (2023) are proposed for universal image segmentation. However, these models may output poor results or even totally fails for objects with irregular shapes, weak boundaries, small sizes, or low contrast. For most situations, the subpar segmentation performance is not sufficient and satisfying especially for medical image segmentation where extremely high accuracy are demanded. Therefore, curating annotations for specific supervised learning tasks is generally necessary and crucial for achieving accurate and meaningful results. To reduce the workload of pixel-level annotation, there has been a considerable effort to exploit semi-supervised and weakly-supervised strategies. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims at training networks jointly with a small number of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data. Extensive research on SSL shows that plenty of unlabeled data would contribute to the model performance and generalization abilities Chapelle et al. (2009); Cheplygina et al. (2019). However, the additional information from unlabeled data can improve CNNs only under specific assumptions Chapelle et al. (2009), and SSL still requires representative image and annotation pairs to be available. In turn, Weakly-supervised Learning (WSL) utilizes annotations that are cheaper to produce than pixel-wise labels such as bounding boxes Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al.

The method consists of two components: (1) Segmentation network parameterized by $\theta$ that generates an estimate of the true segmentation probabilities $\hat{p}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ for the given input image $\mathbf{X}$ ; (2) Coarse annotation network, parameterized by $\phi$ , that estimates the confusion matrices (CMs) $\{\bar{\mathbf{A}_{\phi}^{(\bar{o})}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}),\bar{\mathbf{A}_{\phi}^{(c)}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\}$ of the noisy coarse annotations.  

(2022), coarse annotation Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022), scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), or image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014) to train the segmentation models. These weak annotations increase the efficiency of the manual labeling procedure and achieve promising performance making the gap between the SSL and FSL performance smaller. However, the information from weak annotations is of lower precision and usually suffers from noisy information when curating the labels, e.g. the uncertainty on the boundary. For example, bounding box indicates the rough positions of the object of interest (OOI), but the pixels inside the bounding box may belong to multiple classes if the box size is large. A more annotator-friendly way to get supervision efficiently is scribble-based annotation, which only requires the annotator to draw a few lines to mark a small part of the OOI. Coarse annotations can provide much more information than scribble and avoid large non-target pixels being grabbed into the bounding box. Meanwhile, drawing coarse annotations on images (e.g., rough boundaries for the OOI and non-OOI) needs only similar effort and time as the scribble and box-level labeling, and can be conducted by non-experts. Therefore, learning from those coarse annotations, and then correcting the noisy pixels with computational methods, might be an efficient way to enrich the labeled large-scale data with minimal effort.  

Our contribution: We introduce the first instance of an end-to-end supervised segmentation method that estimates true segmentation labels from noisy coarse annotations. The proposed architecture (see Fig. 1) consists of two coupled CNNs where the first CNN estimates the true segmentation probabilities, and the second CNN models the characteristics of two different coarse annotations i.e. positive annotation indicates the region of interest and negative annotation indicates the coarse non-target region e.g. background) by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis. Unlike the previous WSL methods using coarse annotations, our method models and disentangles the complex mappings from the input images to the noisy coarse annotations and to the true segmentation label simultaneously. Specifically, we model the noisy coarse annotation for the objective along with the complementary label learning for the background or non-objective to enable our model to disentangle robustly the errors of the given annotations and the true labels, even when the ratio of coarse annotation is small (e.g., given scribble for each class). In contrast, this would not be possible with the other WSL methods where the parameters of each coarse annotation are estimated on every target image separately.  

For evaluation, we first simulate the noisy positive and negative coarse annotations on the MNIST dataset enhanced by morphometric operations with Morpho-MNIST framework Castro et al. (2019); then we provide an extensive comparison of our method on the publicly available reference Cityscapes dataset for multi-class segmentation tasks; finally, we show the robustness of our method on challenging medical image segmentation. The presented experiments demonstrate that our method consistently leads to better segmentation performance compared to the state-of-the-art SSL, WSL methods, and other relevant baselines, especially when the ratio of coarse annotation for each class is low and the degree of annotation noise is high.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Weakly-Supervised Segmentation. To reduce the labor-intensive, pixel-wise labeling, different forms of weak annotations for segmentation were explored including scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), bounding box Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al. (2022), points Bearman et al. (2016), image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014), etc. Lin et al. (2016) proposed SribbleSup to apply graph-based methods to propagate information to the unlabeled pixels. Zhang & Zhuang (2022) proposed CycleMix to learn segmentation from scribbles and enhance the generalization ability of segmentation models. Dai et al. (2015) investigated bounding box annotations as an alternative or extra source of supervision to train neural networks for semantic segmentation. L2G Jiang et al. (2022) took advantage of both the global and the local views randomly cropped from the input image for knowledge transfer on semantic segmentation.  

Another strategy to reduce amount of manual annotations is Complementary Label Learning (CLL), which is a WSL framework where each sample is equipped with a complementary label that denotes one of the classes the sample does not belong to Ishida et al. (2017) Gao & Zhang (2021). Ishida et al. (2017) proposed learning from examples with only complementary labels by assuming that a complementary label is uniformly selected from the $L\!-\!1$ classes other than the true label class $(L\!<\!2)$ . Gao & Zhang (2021) proposed a risk estimator with guaranteed estimation error bound based on a discriminative model for CLL and further introduced weighted loss to the empirical risk to maximize the predictive gap between potential ground-truth (GT) label and complementary label. Yu et al. (2018) introduced a general method to modify traditional loss functions and extended standard deep neural network classifiers to learn from noisy complementary labels.  

As presented above, the segmentation methods focused on the weak annotation either for the target objective or for the complementary label. Contrary, we proposed to exploit both of them simultaneously, as both the target and complementary classes can provide weak supervision to train a better model.  

Learning from Noisy Labels. In standard classification problems, modeling the label noise statistically has been widely studied e.g. by introducing a probability transition matrix. For example, previous works Natarajan et al. (2013); Liu & Tao (2015); Wang et al. (2017) employ probability transition matrix to modify loss functions such that they can be robust to noisy labels. Furthermore, Patrini et al. (2017); Sukhbaatar et al. (2015) extended such probability transition matrix to a transition layer and implement it with deep neural networks (DNN). More recently, Zhang et al. (2023) utilized a DNN to learn the characteristics of individual annotators by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis, which mimic the annotation errors.  

However, this is the first time that this idea is applied to the new problem of learning with noisy coarse annotation. More broadly, our work is related to methods for robust learning in the presence of coarse annotations with noisy information (e.g., over- or missing-pixel segmentation). There is a large body of literature Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022); Zhang & Zhuang (2022) that does not explicitly model noisy coarse annotations, unlike our method.  



\section{3 METHOD  }




\section{3.1 PROBLEM SET-UP  }

\section{3.2 PROBABILISTIC MODEL OF NOISY COARSE LABELS  }


In this section, we outline the probabilistic model used to describe the observed positive and negative coarse annotations. Given the input image, we assume that the provided coarse annotations are generated statistically independently across different samples and over different pixels. Under these assumptions, the probability of observing coarse labels $\{(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{n}^{(o)},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{n}^{(c)})\}_{\{o,c\}\in S(\mathbf{x})}$ on the image $\mathbf{X}$ factorises as:  

$$
p(\{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(o)},\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(c)}\}_{\{o,c\}\in S(\mathbf{x})}\vert\mathbf{x})=\prod_{\{o,c\}\in S(\mathbf{x})}p(\{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(o)},\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(c)}\}\vert\mathbf{x})=\prod_{\{o,c\}\in S(\mathbf{x})}\prod_{w\in\{1,\dots,W\}}p(\{\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(o)},\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\}\vert\mathbf{x})
$$  

where $\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(o)},\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\in[1,...,L]$ denotes the $(w,h)^{\mathrm{th}}$ elements of $\{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(o)},\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(c)}\}\in\mathcal{Y}^{W\times H}$ . Now we rewrite the probability of observing coarse label on each pixel $(w,h)$ as:  

$$
p(\{\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(o)},\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\}\,|\,\mathbf{x})\!=\!\sum_{y_{w h}=1}^{L}p(\{\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(o)},\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\}\,|\,y_{w h},\mathbf{x})\!\cdot\!p(y_{w h}\,|\,\mathbf{x})
$$

Note that here “·” denotes the element-wise matrix multiplications in the spatial dimensions $W,H$ . At inference time, we use the output of the segmentation network $\hat{\bf p}_{\theta}({\bf x})$ to segment the testing images.  



\section{3.3 LEARNING FROM NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS  }


In this section, we describe how we jointly optimize the parameters of the segmentation network, $\theta$ , and the parameters of the coarse annotation network, $\phi$ . In short, we minimize the negative log-likelihood of the probabilistic model for both positive and negative coarse annotations via stochastic gradient descent. A detailed description is provided below.  

Learning with Positive Coarse Label. Given training input ${\bf X}=\{{\bf x}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ and positive coarse labels Y˜{o} = {˜y{no}: {o} 2 S(xn)}nN=1, we optimize the parameters {✓,φ} by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), $-\log p(\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}^{(1)},...,\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}^{(O)}|\mathbf{X})$ . From Eq. (1) and Eq. (2), this optimization objective equates to the sum of cross-entropy (CE) losses between the observed positive coarse segmentation and the predicted label distributions:  

$$
-\mathrm{log}p({\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}}^{(1)},...,{\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}}^{(O)}|\mathbf{X})\!=\!\!\sum_{n=1}^{N}\!\!\sum_{o=1}^{O}\!\!1\!(o\!\in\!{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbf{x}_{n}))\!\cdot\!\mathrm{CE}\!\left({\hat{\mathbf{A}}}_{\phi}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\!\cdot\!{\hat{\mathbf{p}}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n}),{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{n}^{(o)}\right)
$$  

Minimizing Eq. (3) encourages the positive-specific predictions $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta,\phi}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x})$ to be as close as possible to the provided positive coarse label distributions $\mathbf{p}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x})$ . However, this loss function alone cannot separate the annotation noise from the true label distribution; there are many combinations of pairs $\hat{\bf A}_{\phi}({\bf x})$ and segmentation model $\hat{\bf p}_{\theta}({\bf x})$ such that $\hat{\bf p}_{\theta,\phi}({\bf x})$ matches well the provided distribution $\mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x})$ for any input image $\mathbf{X}$ (e.g. permutations of rows in the CMs). Tanno et al. (2019) addressed an analogous issue for the classification task, and here we add the trace of the estimated CMs to the loss function for positive coarse annotation in Eq.(3) as a regularisation term. We thus optimize the regularized loss:  

$$

$$  

where $S(\mathbf{x})$ denotes the set of all positive coarse labels available for image $\mathbf{X}$ , and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A})$ denotes the trace of the matrix A. The mean trace represents the average probability that a randomly selected annotator provides an accurate label. Intuitively, minimizing the trace encourages the estimated annotators to be maximally unreliable while minimizing the cross entropy ensures fidelity with observed noisy annotators. We minimize this combined loss via stochastic gradient descent to learn both $\{\theta,\phi\}$ .  

Learning with Negative Coarse Label. For some situations, it is easier to provide the negative coarse annotation, e.g., complementary label, to help ML model predict the true label distribution. Thus, we study a readily available substitute, namely complementary labeling. However, if we still use loss functions $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi)$ when learning with these complementary labels, similar to Eq. (4), we can only learn a mapping $\mathbb{R}\!\to\!\mathcal{V}$ that tries to predict conditional probabilities $p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(c)}\vert\mathbf{x})$ and the corresponding complementary pixels classifier that predicts a y˜(wch) for a given observation $\mathbf{x}$ .  

To address the above issue, inspired by Yu et al. (2018), which summarizes all the probabilities into a transition matrix $\mathbf{M}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}$ , where $\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{x},w,h)_{i j}:=p(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{\{c\}}\!=\!i\,|\,y_{w h}\!=\!j,\!\mathbf{x})}\end{array}$ and $\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{x},w,h)_{i i}\!=\!0,\!\forall i,j\!\in\!\{1,\!...,L\}$ Here, ${\bf{m}}_{i j}$ denotes the entry value in the $i$ -th row and $j$ -th column of M. As shown in Fig. 1, we achieve this simply by adding a linear layer to the complementary label learning channel. This layer outputs $v(\mathbf{x})$ by multiplying the output of the CE function (i.e., $u({\bf x})$ ) with the transposed transition matrix $\mathbf{M}^{\top}$ . Note that the transition matrix is also widely exploited in Markov chains Gagniuc (2017) and has many applications in machine learning, such as learning with label noise Tanno et al. (2019); Zhang et al. (2020b;a).

Due to the different experiences and behaviors of the annotators, the coarse annotations show variabilities in quality. So we investigate how sensitive our method is to the coarse label quality. We introduced a new theoretically grounded algorithm for recovering the expert consensus label distribution from noisy coarse annotations. Our work was primarily motivated by medical imaging applications for which pixel-level annotation is required for a large number of images. \title{Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarse Label Learning}

\begin{abstract}
Large annotated dataset is of crucial importance for developing machine learning models for segmentation. However, the process of producing labels at the pixel level is time-consuming, error-prone, and even requires expert-level annotators for medical imaging, which is rare to have in practice. We note that it is simpler and less expensive to draw merely rough and approximate annotations, e.g., coarse annotations, which reduce the effort for expert and non-expert level annotators. In this paper, we propose to use coarse drawings from both positive (e.g., objects to be segmented) and negative (objects not to be segmented) classes in the image, even with noisy pixels, to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for semantic segmentation. We present a method for learning the true segmentation label distributions from purely noisy coarse annotations using two coupled CNNs. The separation of the two CNNs is achieved by high fidelity with the characters of the noisy training annotations. We propose to add a complementary label learning that encourages estimating negative label distribution.  To illustrate the properties of our method, we first use a toy segmentation dataset based on MNIST. We then present the quantitative results on publicly available datasets: Cityscapes dataset for multi-class segmentation, and retinal images for medical applications. In all experiments, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, particularly in the cases where the ratio of coarse annotations is small compared to the given dense annotations.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Thanks to the availability of large datasets with accurate annotations Deng et al. (2009), Fully Supervised Learning (FSL) has been translated from theoretical algorithms to practice. However, it is often expensive, time-consuming, and perhaps impossible to collect pixel-level labels for large-scale datasets Jing et al. (2019). This problem is particularly prominent in the medical domain where the labeled data are commonly scarce due to the high cost of annotations Zhang et al. (2020b). For instance, accurate segmentation of vessels in fundus retinal images is difficult even for experienced experts due to variability of vessel’s location, size, and shape across population or disease (see Fig. The labeling process is prone to errors, almost inevitably leading to noisy datasets as seen in machine learning benchmark datasets Peterson et al. (2019). Labeling errors can occur due to automated label extraction, ambiguities in input and output spaces, or human errors (e.g. lack of expertise). Those errors can be further exacerbated by data and human biases (e.g. level of expertise of the annotator), and thus annotations of structures e.g. organs in medical images, suffer from high inter- and intra- observer variability. As a consequence, despite the availability of large imaging repositories (e.g. UK Biobank Littlejohns et al. (2020)), the generation of the curated labels that are available to machine learning remains a challenging issue, necessitating the development of methods that learn robustly from noisy annotations.  

Recently, several foundation models Kirillov et al. (2023); Ma & Wang (2023); Butoi et al. (2023) are proposed for universal image segmentation. However, these models may output poor results or even totally fails for objects with irregular shapes, weak boundaries, small sizes, or low contrast. For most situations, the subpar segmentation performance is not sufficient and satisfying especially for medical image segmentation where extremely high accuracy are demanded. Therefore, curating annotations for specific supervised learning tasks is generally necessary and crucial for achieving accurate and meaningful results. To reduce the workload of pixel-level annotation, there has been a considerable effort to exploit semi-supervised and weakly-supervised strategies. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims at training networks jointly with a small number of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data. Extensive research on SSL shows that plenty of unlabeled data would contribute to the model performance and generalization abilities Chapelle et al. (2009); Cheplygina et al. (2019). However, the additional information from unlabeled data can improve CNNs only under specific assumptions Chapelle et al. (2009), and SSL still requires representative image and annotation pairs to be available. In turn, Weakly-supervised Learning (WSL) utilizes annotations that are cheaper to produce than pixel-wise labels such as bounding boxes Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al.
