The method consists of two components: (1) Segmentation network parameterized by $\theta$ that generates an estimate of the true segmentation probabilities $\hat{p}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ for the given input image $\mathbf{X}$ ; (2) Coarse annotation network, parameterized by $\phi$ , that estimates the confusion matrices (CMs) $\{\bar{\mathbf{A}_{\phi}^{(\bar{o})}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}),\bar{\mathbf{A}_{\phi}^{(c)}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\}$ of the noisy coarse annotations.  

(2022), coarse annotation Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022), scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), or image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014) to train the segmentation models. These weak annotations increase the efficiency of the manual labeling procedure and achieve promising performance making the gap between the SSL and FSL performance smaller. However, the information from weak annotations is of lower precision and usually suffers from noisy information when curating the labels, e.g. the uncertainty on the boundary. For example, bounding box indicates the rough positions of the object of interest (OOI), but the pixels inside the bounding box may belong to multiple classes if the box size is large. A more annotator-friendly way to get supervision efficiently is scribble-based annotation, which only requires the annotator to draw a few lines to mark a small part of the OOI. Coarse annotations can provide much more information than scribble and avoid large non-target pixels being grabbed into the bounding box. Meanwhile, drawing coarse annotations on images (e.g., rough boundaries for the OOI and non-OOI) needs only similar effort and time as the scribble and box-level labeling, and can be conducted by non-experts. Therefore, learning from those coarse annotations, and then correcting the noisy pixels with computational methods, might be an efficient way to enrich the labeled large-scale data with minimal effort.  

Our contribution: We introduce the first instance of an end-to-end supervised segmentation method that estimates true segmentation labels from noisy coarse annotations. The proposed architecture (see Fig. 1) consists of two coupled CNNs where the first CNN estimates the true segmentation probabilities, and the second CNN models the characteristics of two different coarse annotations i.e. positive annotation indicates the region of interest and negative annotation indicates the coarse non-target region e.g. background) by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis. Unlike the previous WSL methods using coarse annotations, our method models and disentangles the complex mappings from the input images to the noisy coarse annotations and to the true segmentation label simultaneously. Specifically, we model the noisy coarse annotation for the objective along with the complementary label learning for the background or non-objective to enable our model to disentangle robustly the errors of the given annotations and the true labels, even when the ratio of coarse annotation is small (e.g., given scribble for each class). In contrast, this would not be possible with the other WSL methods where the parameters of each coarse annotation are estimated on every target image separately.  

For evaluation, we first simulate the noisy positive and negative coarse annotations on the MNIST dataset enhanced by morphometric operations with Morpho-MNIST framework Castro et al. (2019); then we provide an extensive comparison of our method on the publicly available reference Cityscapes dataset for multi-class segmentation tasks; finally, we show the robustness of our method on challenging medical image segmentation. The presented experiments demonstrate that our method consistently leads to better segmentation performance compared to the state-of-the-art SSL, WSL methods, and other relevant baselines, especially when the ratio of coarse annotation for each class is low and the degree of annotation noise is high.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Weakly-Supervised Segmentation. To reduce the labor-intensive, pixel-wise labeling, different forms of weak annotations for segmentation were explored including scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), bounding box Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al. (2022), points Bearman et al. (2016), image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014), etc. Lin et al. (2016) proposed SribbleSup to apply graph-based methods to propagate information to the unlabeled pixels. Zhang & Zhuang (2022) proposed CycleMix to learn segmentation from scribbles and enhance the generalization ability of segmentation models. Dai et al. (2015) investigated bounding box annotations as an alternative or extra source of supervision to train neural networks for semantic segmentation. L2G Jiang et al. (2022) took advantage of both the global and the local views randomly cropped from the input image for knowledge transfer on semantic segmentation.  

Another strategy to reduce amount of manual annotations is Complementary Label Learning (CLL), which is a WSL framework where each sample is equipped with a complementary label that denotes one of the classes the sample does not belong to Ishida et al. (2017) Gao & Zhang (2021). Ishida et al. (2017) proposed learning from examples with only complementary labels by assuming that a complementary label is uniformly selected from the $L\!-\!1$ classes other than the true label class $(L\!<\!2)$ . Gao & Zhang (2021) proposed a risk estimator with guaranteed estimation error bound based on a discriminative model for CLL and further introduced weighted loss to the empirical risk to maximize the predictive gap between potential ground-truth (GT) label and complementary label. Yu et al. (2018) introduced a general method to modify traditional loss functions and extended standard deep neural network classifiers to learn from noisy complementary labels.  

As presented above, the segmentation methods focused on the weak annotation either for the target objective or for the complementary label. Contrary, we proposed to exploit both of them simultaneously, as both the target and complementary classes can provide weak supervision to train a better model.  

Learning from Noisy Labels. In standard classification problems, modeling the label noise statistically has been widely studied e.g. by introducing a probability transition matrix. For example, previous works Natarajan et al. (2013); Liu & Tao (2015); Wang et al. (2017) employ probability transition matrix to modify loss functions such that they can be robust to noisy labels. Furthermore, Patrini et al. (2017); Sukhbaatar et al. (2015) extended such probability transition matrix to a transition layer and implement it with deep neural networks (DNN). More recently, Zhang et al. (2023) utilized a DNN to learn the characteristics of individual annotators by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis, which mimic the annotation errors.  

However, this is the first time that this idea is applied to the new problem of learning with noisy coarse annotation. More broadly, our work is related to methods for robust learning in the presence of coarse annotations with noisy information (e.g., over- or missing-pixel segmentation). There is a large body of literature Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022); Zhang & Zhuang (2022) that does not explicitly model noisy coarse annotations, unlike our method.

However, this loss function alone cannot separate the annotation noise from the true label distribution; there are many combinations of pairs $\hat{\bf A}_{\phi}({\bf x})$ and segmentation model $\hat{\bf p}_{\theta}({\bf x})$ such that $\hat{\bf p}_{\theta,\phi}({\bf x})$ matches well the provided distribution $\mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x})$ for any input image $\mathbf{X}$ (e.g. permutations of rows in the CMs). Tanno et al. (2019) addressed an analogous issue for the classification task, and here we add the trace of the estimated CMs to the loss function for positive coarse annotation in Eq.(3) as a regularisation term. We thus optimize the regularized loss:  

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi)(\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n}),\tilde{y}^{(o)})}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad\quad:=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1\sigma=1}^{N\quad O}\!\!1(o\!\in\!\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{x}_{n}))\!\cdot\!\left[\mathrm{CE}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n}),\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{n}^{(o)}\right)\,+\,\lambda\!\cdot\!\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(o)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\right)\right]}\end{array}
$$  

where $S(\mathbf{x})$ denotes the set of all positive coarse labels available for image $\mathbf{X}$ , and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A})$ denotes the trace of the matrix A. The mean trace represents the average probability that a randomly selected annotator provides an accurate label. Intuitively, minimizing the trace encourages the estimated annotators to be maximally unreliable while minimizing the cross entropy ensures fidelity with observed noisy annotators. We minimize this combined loss via stochastic gradient descent to learn both $\{\theta,\phi\}$ .  

Learning with Negative Coarse Label. For some situations, it is easier to provide the negative coarse annotation, e.g., complementary label, to help ML model predict the true label distribution. Thus, we study a readily available substitute, namely complementary labeling. However, if we still use loss functions $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi)$ when learning with these complementary labels, similar to Eq. (4), we can only learn a mapping $\mathbb{R}\!\to\!\mathcal{V}$ that tries to predict conditional probabilities $p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(c)}\vert\mathbf{x})$ and the corresponding complementary pixels classifier that predicts a y˜(wch) for a given observation $\mathbf{x}$ .  

To address the above issue, inspired by Yu et al. (2018), which summarizes all the probabilities into a transition matrix $\mathbf{M}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}$ , where $\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{x},w,h)_{i j}:=p(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{\{c\}}\!=\!i\,|\,y_{w h}\!=\!j,\!\mathbf{x})}\end{array}$ and $\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{x},w,h)_{i i}\!=\!0,\!\forall i,j\!\in\!\{1,\!...,L\}$ Here, ${\bf{m}}_{i j}$ denotes the entry value in the $i$ -th row and $j$ -th column of M. As shown in Fig. 1, we achieve this simply by adding a linear layer to the complementary label learning channel. This layer outputs $v(\mathbf{x})$ by multiplying the output of the CE function (i.e., $u({\bf x})$ ) with the transposed transition matrix $\mathbf{M}^{\top}$ . Note that the transition matrix is also widely exploited in Markov chains Gagniuc (2017) and has many applications in machine learning, such as learning with label noise Tanno et al. (2019); Zhang et al. (2020b;a).  

Recall that in transition matrix $\mathbf{M}$ , $\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf{m}_{i j}=p(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{\{c\}}=i\,|\,y_{w h}=j,\mathbf{x})}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf{m}_{i i}=p(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{\{c\}}=i\mid y_{w h}=i,\mathbf{x})\!=\!0.}\end{array}$ We observe that $p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{\{c\}}|\mathbf{x})$ can be transferred to $p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{\{c\}}\,|\,\mathbf{x})$ by using the transition matrix $\mathbf{M}$ ,  

$$
\begin{array}{r l r}&{}&{p(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!j\,|\,\mathbf{x})\!=\!\underset{i\neq j}{\sum}{p}(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!j,\bar{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!i\,|\,\mathbf{x})\!=\!\underset{i\neq j}{\sum}{p}(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!j\,|\,\bar{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!i,\mathbf{x})p(\bar{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!i\,|\,\mathbf{x})}\\ &{}&{\!=\!\underset{i\neq j}{\sum}{p}(\tilde{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!j\,|\,\bar{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!i)p(\bar{y}_{w h}^{(c)}\!=\!i\,|\,\mathbf{x})}\end{array}
$$  

Intuitively, if $\mathbf{v}_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ tries to predict the probability $p(\tilde{y}^{(c)}\!=\!i\,|\,\mathbf{x}),\!\forall i\!\in\![1,...,L],$ , then $\mathbf{M}^{-\top}\mathbf{v}$ can predict the probability $p(\tilde{y}^{(o)}\,|\,\mathbf{x})$ , which is the positive prediction of the corresponding complementary coarse label. To enable end-to-end learning rather than transferring after training, we let  

$$
\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x})\!=\!\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})
$$  

where $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})$ is now an intermediate output of the complementary coarse annotation, and ${\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta,\!\phi)\!=\!\mathrm{argmax}_{i\in[L]}\mathbf{v}_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ . Then, the modified loss function $\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi)$ is  

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\phi)(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{y}^{(c)})\!:=\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta,\phi)(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{y}^{(c)})\!:=\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta,\phi)(\mathbf{M}^{\top}\!\cdot\!\{\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\},\widetilde{y}^{(c)})}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad:=\!\displaystyle\sum_{n=1\,c=1}^{N\,\,\,\,C}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!(c\!\in\!\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{x}_{n}))\!\cdot\!\left[\mathbf{C}\!\mathbb{E}\!\left(\mathbf{M}^{\top}\!\cdot\!\{\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{n}^{(c)}\right)+\lambda\!\cdot\!\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\phi}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x}_{n})\right)\right]}\end{array}
$$  

In this way, if we can learn an optimal $\mathbf{v}$ such that $\mathbf{v}_{i}(\mathbf{x})=p(\tilde{y}^{(c)}=i\mid\mathbf{x}),\forall i\in[L]$ , meanwhile, we can also find the optimal $\mathbf{u}$ and the loss function $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta,\phi)$ , which can be easily applied to deep learning. With sufficient training examples with complementary coarse labels, this CNN often simultaneously learns good classifiers for both $\bar{(\mathbf{x},\tilde{y}^{(c)})}$ and $(\mathbf{x},\!\tilde{y}^{(\bar{o})})$ .  

Finally, we combine the positive annotation loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}$ and the negative annotation loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ as our objective and optimize:  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{final}}(\theta,\phi)\!:=\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}}(\theta,\!\phi)\!+\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta,\!\phi).}\end{array}
$$  



\section{4 EXPERIMENTS  }


4.1 SET-UP  

MNIST Experiments. We define a MNIST segmentation dataset to study the properties of the proposed algorithm. While MNIST was originally constructed to facilitate research in recognition (classification) of handwritten digits LeCun et al. (1998), it has found its use in segmentation tasks to segment the digits from the background. It can be seen as an image classification task, except that instead of classifying the whole image, we are classifying each pixel individually. MNIST dataset consists of 60,000 training and 10,000 testing examples, all of which are $28\times28$ grayscale images of digits from 0 to 9, and we derive the segmentation labels by thresholding the intensity values at 0.5.  

Cityscapes Experiments. The Cityscapes Cordts et al. (2016) dataset contains 5000 high-resolution (2048 $\times\,1024$ pixels) urban scene images collected across 27 European Cities. The dataset comprises 5,000 fine annotations (2,975 for training, 500 for validation, and 1,525 for testing) and 20,000 coarse annotations where 11,900 samples for training and 2,000 for validation (i.e., coarse polygons covering individual objects).  

Retinal Image Experiments. The LES-AV Orlando et al. (2018) is a dataset for retinal vessel segmentation on color fundus images. It comprises 22 fundus photographs with available manual annotations of the retinal vessels including annotations of arteries and veins. The 22 images/patients are acquired with resolutions of $30^{\circ}$ field-of-view (FOV) and $1444\times1620$ pixels (21 images), and $45^{\circ}$ FOV and $1958\times2196$ pixels (one image), with each pixe $=6\mu m$ . We divide them into 18 images for training and 4 images for testing.  



\section{4.2 SYNTHETIC NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS  }


We generate synthetic coarse noisy annotations from an assumed expert consensus label on MNIST, Cityscapes and retinal fundus image dataset, to demonstrate the efficacy of the approach in an idealized situation where the expert consensus label is known. We simulate the positive and negative coarse noisy annotations by performing morphological transformations (e.g., thinning, thickening, fractures, etc) on the expert consensus label and background (complementary label), using Morpho-MNIST software Castro et al. (2019). In particular, positive coarse noisy annotation is prone to be poor segmentation, which is simulated by combining small fractures and over-segmentation; negative coarse noisy annotation always annotates on the background or complementary label using the same approach. To create synthetic coarse noisy labels in the multi-class scenario, we use a similar simulation to create coarse labels on the Cityscapes dataset. We first choose a target class and then apply morphological operations on the provided coarse mask to create the two synthetic coarse labels at different patterns, namely, objective coarse and complementary coarse annotations. We create training data by deriving labels from the simulated annotations. We also experimented with varying the levels of morphological operations on all datasets, e.g., Fig.8, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.01 (scribble) compared to the provided coarse labels, to test the robustness of our methods to varying sensitivities to coarse quality.  



\section{4.3 COMPARISON METHODS AND EVALUATION METRICS  }


Our experiments are based on the assumption that no expert consensus label is available a priori, hence, we compare our method against multiple weakly-supervised and semi-supervised methods. In particular, we explore our method with ablation studies, e.g., our method without negative coarse annotation; we also consider two state-of-the-art interactive image segmentation algorithms for generating masks from scribbles: GrabCut Rother et al. (2004) and LazySnapping Li et al. (2004), then training FCNs using the masks generated by these methods. Meanwhile, we compare with other weakly-supervised methods using different ways of annotations, e.g., scribble-guided annotations Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), coarse annotations Saha et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2021), and box-level annotations Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al. (2022). Finally, we compare our weakly-supervised results based on the noisy coarse annotations and strongly-supervised results based on the expert consensus annotations. For evaluation metrics, we use mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) between estimated segmentation $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ and expert consensus label $\mathbf{y}_{G T}$ .  



\section{4.4 SEGMENTATION PERFORMANCE  }


Strategies of utilizing coarse annotation. Our method jointly propagates information into unmarked pixels and learns network parameters. An easy way is to first use any existing interactive image  



\section{4.5 SENSITIVITIES TO THE QUALITY OF COARSE ANNOTATIONS  }


Due to the different experiences and behaviors of the annotators, the coarse annotations show variabilities in quality. So we investigate how sensitive our method is to the coarse label quality. Generating different sets of coarse annotations usually requires extra annotations efforts, therefore we utilize the provided mask-level labels to create coarse annotations with a variety of qualities. We focus on the area of the coarse annotations. Given any mask-level annotation, we reduce the area of this coarse label by a ratio.  

![](images/30a6fafa9f91b6f8bfc1cb3630d9ee6987001e408563ef65f5a0f918c7102d44.jpg)  
Figure 5: Sensitivities to quality of positive and negative coarse annotations, and the visualization of the estimated labels with different supervision approaches.  

In terms of choosing the different ratios for the coarse labels, the central point is randomly chosen from the original mask-level annotation, and the area is determined by the reduced ratio. Fig.01 means a scribble is used.  

Fig. 3 shows the results of our coarse-supervised algorithm using coarse annotations of different ratios. Our method generates much better results when the coarse label area increased from 0 to 0.3, and the results from Fig. 4 show that our method performs gradually better when the coarse annotation areas are increased, suggesting that our method has reasonably learned the useful information and corrected the error from the coarse annotation with different qualities.  



\section{4.6 EXPERIMENTS ON RETINAL VESSEL SEGMENTATION  }


Lastly, we illustrate the results of our approach on a more challenging dataset with real coarse and noisy labels from the medical domain. This dataset, called LES-AV, consists of images of the retinal fundus acquired from different patients. The task is to segment the vessel into a binary mask (see Fig. 5). The process of segmenting the blood vessel in the retinal image is crucial for the early detection of eye diseases.  

An experienced annotator was tasked with providing the practical positive and negative coarse annotations for each sample on LES-AV dataset. We generate such a real-world dataset to show the segmentation results and evaluate the performance of different supervision approaches. Meanwhile, we also created 5 different ratio levels for the positive and negative coarse annotations from level-1 (tend to scribble) to level-5 (tend to GT) with increasing ratios compared to the given expert consensus labels. We use such a dataset to evaluate the sensitivity to annotation quality of our model on medical image data.  

We show the results of sensitivities to annotation quality in Fig. 5(a). Similarly to the previous experiments, our model performs robustly and gradually improved when the ratio of coarse annotations is increased. Especially when the ratio is increased from level- $^{\,\cdot\,l}$ to level-2, our model’s performance is increased significantly and comparable to the mask-level results. By applying our practical annotations, we conduct a group of experiments under different supervision. The results in Table. S2 indicate that our WSL approach achieves comparable results to the strongly-supervised method. Meanwhile, by including some extra coarse annotations, the result is improved $3\%$ . Finally, we present the segmentation visualization in Fig. 5(d⇠f).  



\section{5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION  }


We introduced a new theoretically grounded algorithm for recovering the expert consensus label distribution from noisy coarse annotations. Our method brings implementation simplicity, requiring only adding a complementary label learning term to the loss function. Experiments on both synthetic and real data sets have shown superior performance over the common WSL and SSL methods in terms of both segmentation accuracy and robustness to the quality of coarse annotations and label noise. Furthermore, the method is capable of estimating coarse annotations even when scribble is given per image.  

Our work was primarily motivated by medical imaging applications for which pixel-level annotation is required for a large number of images. However, future work shall consider imposing structures on the CMs and TMs to broaden the applicability to scribble or spot annotations, which could contribute to saving the labor of the labeling process. Another limiting assumption is to learn only from the coarse annotation in difficult cases. The majority of segmentation failures happen in the difficult cases or the difficult patches in the image. Only giving coarse annotations on these difficult cases or patches and learning from them is also a valuable next step.

Title: Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarase Label Learning

Abstract
The creation of large, pixel-level annotated datasets is a critical bottleneck for developing effective machine learning segmentation models. This process is notoriously time-consuming, error-prone, and often requires rare expert annotators, especially in fields like medical imaging. We address this fundamental challenge by leveraging a far more practical and cost-effective annotation strategy: using simple, rough drawings that indicate both the target objects (positive classes) and non-target regions (negative classes). This paper presents a robust method for training a convolutional neural network (CNN) for precise semantic segmentation using only these noisy coarse annotations. Our approach employs two coupled CNNs to directly learn the true segmentation label distributions from imperfect coarse labels. A key innovation is the integration of complementary label learning, which explicitly models the negative label distribution to correct annotation errors. We rigorously validate our method, first on a synthetic MNIST-based segmentation dataset and then on major public benchmarks: the Cityscapes dataset for multi-class urban scene segmentation and a retinal image dataset for medical application. The experimental results definitively show that our method consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art semi-supervised and weakly-supervised techniques, demonstrating exceptional performance even when the provided coarse annotations are minimal.

1 INTRODUCTION
The success of Fully Supervised Learning (FSL) has been built on the foundation of large, accurately annotated datasets. However, obtaining pixel-level labels for large-scale datasets is often prohibitively expensive, time-consuming, and in many practical scenarios, simply impossible. This limitation is particularly severe in medical imaging, where expert annotations are scarce and costly. Accurate segmentation, such as of retinal vessels, remains difficult even for experts due to anatomical variability. The labeling process itself is inherently prone to errors, leading to noisy datasets that undermine model performance. These errors stem from automated extraction, ambiguous boundaries, human fallibility, and annotator bias, resulting in high inter- and intra-observer variability. Consequently, despite the existence of vast imaging repositories, generating high-quality curated labels for machine learning remains a major obstacle, necessitating methods that learn robustly from imperfect annotations.

While recent foundation models show promise for universal segmentation, they frequently fail on objects with irregular shapes, weak boundaries, or low contrast—common challenges in critical domains like medical imaging where extreme accuracy is non-negotiable. Therefore, task-specific supervised learning with curated annotations remains essential for achieving reliable results. To reduce the pixel-level annotation burden, semi-supervised learning (SSL) and weakly-supervised learning (WSL) strategies have been explored. SSL utilizes a small set of labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data, but its improvements are contingent on specific data assumptions. WSL utilizes cheaper annotation forms like bounding boxes, image-level labels, scribbles, or coarse annotations. Among these, coarse annotations strike an optimal balance: they provide substantially more information than scribbles or image-level tags, avoid the inclusion of large non-target areas as with bounding boxes, and require an effort similar to scribble drawing, making them feasible for non-expert annotators. Learning from these coarse annotations and computationally correcting their noise presents a highly efficient pathway to enrich large-scale datasets with minimal manual effort.

Our Contribution: We introduce the first end-to-end supervised segmentation framework capable of estimating true segmentation labels directly from noisy coarse annotations. The proposed architecture consists of two coupled CNNs: one estimates the true segmentation probabilities, while the other models the characteristics of both positive (object) and negative (non-object/background) coarse annotations by estimating per-image, pixel-wise confusion matrices. Unlike prior WSL methods, our approach explicitly models and disentangles the complex mappings from input images to both the noisy annotations and the true labels simultaneously. Crucially, by modeling noisy annotations for both the target and complementary classes, our method robustly disentangles annotation errors from true labels, even when the ratio of coarse annotation is very small. This capability is unattainable with other WSL methods that estimate parameters separately.

For evaluation, we first simulate noisy positive and negative coarse annotations on an MNIST-based segmentation dataset. We then provide an extensive comparison on the public Cityscapes dataset for multi-class segmentation. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness of our method on the challenging task of medical image segmentation. Our experiments conclusively prove that our method delivers superior segmentation performance compared to state-of-the-art SSL, WSL methods, and other baselines, especially when coarse annotations are sparse and annotation noise is high.

2 RELATED WORK
Weakly-Supervised Segmentation. To alleviate pixel-wise labeling, various weak annotations have been explored, including scribbles, bounding boxes, points, and image-level labels. Methods like ScribbleSup and CycleMix propagate information from scribbles, while others leverage bounding boxes or combined global-local views. Another strategy is Complementary Label Learning (CLL), where each sample has a label indicating a class it does not belong to. Prior CLL work assumes uniform selection of complementary labels or employs risk estimators. Existing segmentation methods typically focus on weak annotation for either the target or the complementary label. In contrast, our method innovatively exploits both simultaneously, using weak supervision from both target and complementary classes to train a superior model.

Learning from Noisy Labels. In standard classification, label noise is often modeled via a probability transition matrix, with methods modifying loss functions or implementing transition layers via DNNs. Recent work uses DNNs to learn per-annotator characteristics via pixel-wise confusion matrices. However, applying this idea to learning from noisy coarse annotations is novel. Broadly, our work relates to robust learning with coarse annotations, but unlike existing literature, we explicitly model the noise within these coarse annotations.

3 METHOD
3.1 PROBLEM SET-UP
We develop a supervised segmentation model by learning from inexpensive positive (object) and negative (non-object) coarse annotations. We consider a set of images, each associated with coarse segmentation labels from objective and complementary categories. The dataset consists of images with positive and/or negative coarse drawings. Crucially, ground truth labels are not available during training.

3.2 PROBABILISTIC MODEL OF NOISY COARSE LABELS
We model the observed coarse annotations as being generated statistically independently across samples and pixels. The probability of observing coarse labels for an image factorizes accordingly. We express the probability for each pixel by marginalizing over the unknown true label, involving the true label distribution and a confusion matrix (CM) that models the annotation noise at each pixel.

Our CNN-based architecture directly models this joint distribution. It comprises: (1) a Segmentation Network that estimates the true segmentation probability map, and (2) a Coarse Annotation Network that estimates the pixel-wise CMs for each annotation type as a function of the input image. The product of an estimated CM and the segmentation probability map yields the estimated distribution for that annotation type. At inference, only the segmentation network's output is used.

3.3 LEARNING FROM NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We jointly optimize the parameters of both networks by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the probabilistic model via stochastic gradient descent.

Learning with Positive Coarse Label. Given positive coarse labels, we minimize a sum of cross-entropy losses between the observed annotations and the predictions from the positive channel. To prevent trivial solutions and separate noise from the true distribution, we add a regularization term that minimizes the trace of the estimated CMs, encouraging the model to explain observations without relying on perfect annotators. The combined loss is optimized to learn the parameters.

Learning with Negative Coarse Label. For negative (complementary) coarse annotations, a direct application of the positive loss is insufficient. Inspired by complementary label learning, we incorporate a transition matrix M, where diagonal entries are zero, modeling the relationship between the true label and the observed complementary label. We integrate this by adding a linear layer that multiplies the complementary channel's output with the transposed matrix M. This allows the model to learn an intermediate representation that, when transformed, predicts the complementary label distribution. A similar trace regularization is applied. The final loss function combines the positive annotation loss and the negative annotation loss.

4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 SET-UP
MNIST Experiments: We define a segmentation task on MNIST by thresholding digit images to create pixel-wise labels.
Cityscapes Experiments: We use this dataset of urban scenes with fine and coarse annotations.
Retinal Image Experiments: We use the LES-AV dataset of retinal fundus images for vessel segmentation.

4.2 SYNTHETIC NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We generate synthetic coarse annotations by applying morphological transformations (thinning, thickening, fractures) to expert consensus labels and backgrounds, simulating poor segmentation and noisy background annotation. We vary the intensity of these operations to test robustness to annotation quality.

4.3 COMPARISON METHODS AND EVALUATION METRICS
We compare against weakly-supervised and semi-supervised methods, including ablations of our own method, interactive segmentation algorithms (GrabCut, LazySnapping) used to generate masks from scribbles, and other WSL methods using scribbles, coarse annotations, or boxes. We also compare against strongly-supervised models. Performance is evaluated using mean Intersection over Union (mIoU).

4.4 SEGMENTATION PERFORMANCE
Our method jointly propagates information to unmarked pixels and learns network parameters. An alternative is to first use an interactive method to generate a mask from coarse labels, then train a network. Our end-to-end approach proves superior.

4.5 SENSITIVITIES TO THE QUALITY OF COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We investigate sensitivity to annotation quality by artificially reducing the area of coarse masks by various ratios, simulating annotations from scribbles (very small area) to near-complete masks. Results show our method's performance improves robustly as the coarse annotation area increases, effectively learning from and correcting errors across different quality levels.

4.6 EXPERIMENTS ON RETINAL VESSEL SEGMENTATION
We apply our method to the challenging LES-AV retinal dataset with real coarse annotations provided by an experienced annotator. We also create multiple quality levels. The results confirm our model's robustness, with performance significantly improving as annotation ratio increases and becoming comparable to mask-level supervision. Using our practical annotations, the WSL approach achieves results comparable to strong supervision, with further improvement from additional coarse annotations. Visualizations confirm the quality of the segmentations.

5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
We have introduced a novel, theoretically grounded algorithm for recovering expert consensus label distributions from noisy coarse annotations. The method is simple to implement, requiring only the addition of a complementary label learning term to the loss function. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets conclusively demonstrate its superior performance over common WSL and SSL methods in both segmentation accuracy and robustness to annotation quality and noise. The method is highly effective even when only minimal scribble-level annotations are provided per image.

While primarily motivated by medical imaging needs, future work will focus on imposing structures on the confusion and transition matrices to handle even sparser annotations like scribbles or points, further reducing labeling labor. Another valuable direction is to focus learning specifically on coarse annotations for difficult cases or image patches, where segmentation errors most commonly occur.

3 METHOD
3.1 PROBLEM SET-UP
We develop a supervised segmentation model by learning from inexpensive positive (object) and negative (non-object) coarse annotations. We consider a set of images, each associated with coarse segmentation labels from objective and complementary categories. The dataset consists of images with positive and/or negative coarse drawings. Crucially, ground truth labels are not available during training.

3.2 PROBABILISTIC MODEL OF NOISY COARSE LABELS
We model the observed coarse annotations as being generated statistically independently across samples and pixels. The probability of observing coarse labels for an image factorizes accordingly. We express the probability for each pixel by marginalizing over the unknown true label, involving the true label distribution and a confusion matrix (CM) that models the annotation noise at each pixel.

Our CNN-based architecture directly models this joint distribution. It comprises: (1) a Segmentation Network that estimates the true segmentation probability map, and (2) a Coarse Annotation Network that estimates the pixel-wise CMs for each annotation type as a function of the input image. The product of an estimated CM and the segmentation probability map yields the estimated distribution for that annotation type. At inference, only the segmentation network's output is used.

3.3 LEARNING FROM NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We jointly optimize the parameters of both networks by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the probabilistic model via stochastic gradient descent.

Learning with Positive Coarse Label. Given positive coarse labels, we minimize a sum of cross-entropy losses between the observed annotations and the predictions from the positive channel. To prevent trivial solutions and separate noise from the true distribution, we add a regularization term that minimizes the trace of the estimated CMs, encouraging the model to explain observations without relying on perfect annotators. The combined loss is optimized to learn the parameters.

Learning with Negative Coarse Label. For negative (complementary) coarse annotations, a direct application of the positive loss is insufficient. Inspired by complementary label learning, we incorporate a transition matrix M, where diagonal entries are zero, modeling the relationship between the true label and the observed complementary label. We integrate this by adding a linear layer that multiplies the complementary channel's output with the transposed matrix M. This allows the model to learn an intermediate representation that, when transformed, predicts the complementary label distribution. A similar trace regularization is applied. The final loss function combines the positive annotation loss and the negative annotation loss.

4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 SET-UP
MNIST Experiments: We define a segmentation task on MNIST by thresholding digit images to create pixel-wise labels.
Cityscapes Experiments: We use this dataset of urban scenes with fine and coarse annotations.
Retinal Image Experiments: We use the LES-AV dataset of retinal fundus images for vessel segmentation.

4.2 SYNTHETIC NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We generate synthetic coarse annotations by applying morphological transformations (thinning, thickening, fractures) to expert consensus labels and backgrounds, simulating poor segmentation and noisy background annotation. We vary the intensity of these operations to test robustness to annotation quality.

4.3 COMPARISON METHODS AND EVALUATION METRICS
We compare against weakly-supervised and semi-supervised methods, including ablations of our own method, interactive segmentation algorithms (GrabCut, LazySnapping) used to generate masks from scribbles, and other WSL methods using scribbles, coarse annotations, or boxes. We also compare against strongly-supervised models. Performance is evaluated using mean Intersection over Union (mIoU).

4.4 SEGMENTATION PERFORMANCE
Our method jointly propagates information to unmarked pixels and learns network parameters. An alternative is to first use an interactive method to generate a mask from coarse labels, then train a network. Our end-to-end approach proves superior.

4.5 SENSITIVITIES TO THE QUALITY OF COARSE ANNOTATIONS
We investigate sensitivity to annotation quality by artificially reducing the area of coarse masks by various ratios, simulating annotations from scribbles (very small area) to near-complete masks. Results show our method's performance improves robustly as the coarse annotation area increases, effectively learning from and correcting errors across different quality levels.

4.6 EXPERIMENTS ON RETINAL VESSEL SEGMENTATION
We apply our method to the challenging LES-AV retinal dataset with real coarse annotations provided by an experienced annotator. We also create multiple quality levels. The results confirm our model's robustness, with performance significantly improving as annotation ratio increases and becoming comparable to mask-level supervision. Using our practical annotations, the WSL approach achieves results comparable to strong supervision, with further improvement from additional coarse annotations. Visualizations confirm the quality of the segmentations.

5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
We have introduced a novel, theoretically grounded algorithm for recovering expert consensus label distributions from noisy coarse annotations. The method is simple to implement, requiring only the addition of a complementary label learning term to the loss function. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets conclusively demonstrate its superior performance over common WSL and SSL methods in both segmentation accuracy and robustness to annotation quality and noise. The method is highly effective even when only minimal scribble-level annotations are provided per image.

While primarily motivated by medical imaging needs, future work will focus on imposing structures on the confusion and transition matrices to handle even sparser annotations like scribbles or points, further reducing labeling labor. Another valuable direction is to focus learning specifically on coarse annotations for difficult cases or image patches, where segmentation errors most commonly occur.

\title{Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarse Label Learning}

\begin{abstract}
The availability of large, meticulously annotated datasets is of absolutely crucial importance for developing and deploying high-performance machine learning models for semantic segmentation tasks. However, the conventional process of producing precise labels at the pixel level is notoriously time-consuming, error-prone, and often requires expert-level annotators, particularly in specialized fields like medical imaging, where such expertise is rare and costly to obtain in practice. We note that it is fundamentally simpler and significantly less expensive to draw merely rough and approximate annotations, e.g., coarse annotations, which dramatically reduce the effort required for both expert and non-expert level annotators. In this paper, we propose a novel and powerful method to utilize coarse drawings from both positive (e.g., objects to be segmented) and negative (objects explicitly not to be segmented) classes present in the image, even when these drawings contain substantial amounts of noisy and imprecise pixels, to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for highly accurate semantic segmentation. We present a groundbreaking method for directly learning the true underlying segmentation label distributions from purely noisy coarse annotations using an architecture of two intelligently coupled CNNs. The effective separation and modeling of the two CNNs is achieved by maintaining high fidelity with the distinct statistical characters of the noisy training annotations. We further propose to add a complementary label learning mechanism that explicitly encourages the accurate estimation of the negative label distribution. To thoroughly illustrate the compelling properties and robustness of our method, we first conduct experiments on a carefully designed toy segmentation dataset based on MNIST. We then present comprehensive quantitative results on large, publicly available benchmark datasets: the challenging Cityscapes dataset for complex multi-class urban scene segmentation, and retinal fundus images for critical medical applications. In all conducted experiments, our method decisively and consistently outperforms all existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in the practically vital cases where the ratio of available coarse annotations is small compared to any given dense annotations, demonstrating its superior efficiency and robustness.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION}

Thanks to the widespread availability of large-scale datasets with meticulously accurate annotations Deng et al. (2009), the paradigm of Fully Supervised Learning (FSL) has been successfully translated from theoretical algorithms to widespread practical application. However, it is often prohibitively expensive, immensely time-consuming, and perhaps fundamentally impossible to collect exhaustive pixel-level labels for truly large-scale datasets Jing et al. (2019). This critical problem is particularly prominent and acute in the medical domain where labeled data are notoriously scarce due to the exceptionally high cost and expertise required for annotations Zhang et al. (2020b). For instance, achieving accurate segmentation of intricate vessels in fundus retinal images is an extremely difficult task even for highly experienced experts due to the immense variability of vessel location, size, and shape across population or disease states (see Fig. The entire labeling process is inherently prone to errors, almost inevitably leading to noisy datasets as has been extensively documented in major machine learning benchmark datasets Peterson et al. (2019). Labeling errors can readily occur due to automated label extraction processes, inherent ambiguities in input and output spaces, or simple human errors (e.g. lack of specific expertise). Those errors can be further exacerbated by pervasive data and human biases (e.g. varying level of expertise of the annotator), and thus annotations of complex structures e.g. organs in medical images, suffer from notoriously high inter- and intra- observer variability. As a direct consequence, despite the growing availability of massive imaging repositories (e.g. UK Biobank Littlejohns et al. (2020)), the generation of the curated, high-quality labels that are available to machine learning remains a paramount and challenging issue, urgently necessitating the development of advanced methods that learn robustly from noisy and imperfect annotations.

Recently, several powerful foundation models Kirillov et al. (2023); Ma & Wang (2023); Butoi et al. (2023) are proposed for universal image segmentation. However, these general models may output poor results or even totally fail for objects with highly irregular shapes, very weak boundaries, extremely small sizes, or critically low contrast. For most real-world situations, such subpar segmentation performance is not sufficient and far from satisfying especially for medical image segmentation where extremely high and reliable accuracy are non-negotiably demanded. Therefore, curating task-specific annotations for targeted supervised learning tasks is generally necessary and absolutely crucial for achieving accurate and meaningful results. To substantially reduce the immense workload of pixel-level annotation, there has been a considerable and sustained effort to exploit semi-supervised and weakly-supervised strategies. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims at training networks jointly with a small number of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data. Extensive research on SSL convincingly shows that plenty of unlabeled data would contribute significantly to the model performance and generalization abilities Chapelle et al. (2009); Cheplygina et al. (2019). However, the additional information from unlabeled data can improve CNNs only under specific and often restrictive assumptions Chapelle et al. (2009), and SSL still requires representative image and accurate annotation pairs to be available. In turn, Weakly-supervised Learning (WSL) utilizes annotations that are demonstrably cheaper to produce than pixel-wise labels such as bounding boxes Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al.

(2022), coarse annotation Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022), scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), or image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014) to train the segmentation models. These weak annotations increase the efficiency of the manual labeling procedure and achieve promising performance making the gap between the SSL and FSL performance smaller. However, the information from weak annotations is inherently of lower precision and usually suffers from noisy information when curating the labels, e.g. the uncertainty on the boundary. For example, a bounding box indicates only the rough positions of the object of interest (OOI), but the pixels inside the bounding box may belong to multiple classes if the box size is large. A more annotator-friendly way to get supervision efficiently is scribble-based annotation, which only requires the annotator to draw a few lines to mark a small part of the OOI. Coarse annotations can provide much more information than a scribble and avoid large non-target pixels being incorrectly grabbed into the bounding box. Meanwhile, drawing coarse annotations on images (e.g., rough boundaries for the OOI and non-OOI) needs only similar effort and time as the scribble and box-level labeling, and can be readily conducted by non-experts. Therefore, learning effectively from those coarse annotations, and then correcting the noisy pixels with sophisticated computational methods, represents an efficient and transformative way to enrich the labeled large-scale data with minimal human effort.

Our contribution: We introduce the first and pioneering instance of an end-to-end supervised segmentation method that directly and accurately estimates true segmentation labels from noisy coarse annotations. The proposed novel architecture (see Fig. 1) consists of two coupled CNNs where the first CNN estimates the true segmentation probabilities, and the second CNN models the distinct characteristics of two different coarse annotations i.e. positive annotation indicates the region of interest and negative annotation indicates the coarse non-target region e.g. background) by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis. Unlike all previous WSL methods using coarse annotations, our novel method explicitly models and disentangles the complex mappings from the input images to the noisy coarse annotations and to the true segmentation label simultaneously. Specifically, we model the noisy coarse annotation for the objective along with the complementary label learning for the background or non-objective to enable our model to disentangle robustly the errors of the given annotations and the true labels, even when the ratio of coarse annotation is very small (e.g., given only a scribble for each class). In stark contrast, this would not be possible with the other existing WSL methods where the parameters of each coarse annotation are estimated on every target image separately.

For comprehensive evaluation, we first simulate the noisy positive and negative coarse annotations on the MNIST dataset enhanced by morphometric operations with the Morpho-MNIST framework Castro et al. (2019); then we provide an extensive and rigorous comparison of our method on the publicly available reference Cityscapes dataset for demanding multi-class segmentation tasks; finally, we show the exceptional robustness of our method on the challenging task of medical image segmentation. The presented experiments definitively demonstrate that our method consistently leads to superior segmentation performance compared to all state-of-the-art SSL, WSL methods, and other relevant baselines, especially when the ratio of coarse annotation for each class is low and the degree of annotation noise is high, proving its practical utility.

\section{2 RELATED WORK}

Weakly-Supervised Segmentation. To reduce the labor-intensive, pixel-wise labeling, different forms of weak annotations for segmentation were extensively explored including scribbles Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), bounding box Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al. (2022), points Bearman et al. (2016), image-level labels Papandreou et al. (2015); Pathak et al. (2014), etc. Lin et al. (2016) proposed SribbleSup to apply graph-based methods to propagate information to the unlabeled pixels. Zhang & Zhuang (2022) proposed CycleMix to learn segmentation from scribbles and enhance the generalization ability of segmentation models. Dai et al. (2015) investigated bounding box annotations as an alternative or extra source of supervision to train neural networks for semantic segmentation. L2G Jiang et al. (2022) took advantage of both the global and the local views randomly cropped from the input image for knowledge transfer on semantic segmentation.

Another important strategy to reduce amount of manual annotations is Complementary Label Learning (CLL), which is a WSL framework where each sample is equipped with a complementary label that denotes one of the classes the sample does not belong to Ishida et al. (2017) Gao & Zhang (2021). Ishida et al. (2017) proposed learning from examples with only complementary labels by assuming that a complementary label is uniformly selected from the $L\!-\!1$ classes other than the true label class $(L\!<\!2)$ . Gao & Zhang (2021) proposed a risk estimator with guaranteed estimation error bound based on a discriminative model for CLL and further introduced weighted loss to the empirical risk to maximize the predictive gap between potential ground-truth (GT) label and complementary label. Yu et al. (2018) introduced a general method to modify traditional loss functions and extended standard deep neural network classifiers to learn from noisy complementary labels.

As presented above, the existing segmentation methods focused solely on the weak annotation either for the target objective or for the complementary label. Contrary, we proposed the novel strategy to exploit both of them simultaneously, as both the target and complementary classes can provide valuable weak supervision to train a significantly better model.

Learning from Noisy Labels. In standard classification problems, modeling the label noise statistically has been widely studied e.g. by introducing a probability transition matrix. For example, previous works Natarajan et al. (2013); Liu & Tao (2015); Wang et al. (2017) employ probability transition matrix to modify loss functions such that they can be robust to noisy labels. Furthermore, Patrini et al. (2017); Sukhbaatar et al. (2015) extended such probability transition matrix to a transition layer and implement it with deep neural networks (DNN). More recently, Zhang et al. (2023) utilized a DNN to learn the characteristics of individual annotators by estimating the pixel-wise confusion matrices (CMs) on a per-image basis, which mimic the annotation errors.

However, this is the first time that this powerful idea is applied to the new and important problem of learning with noisy coarse annotation. More broadly, our work is fundamentally related to methods for robust learning in the presence of coarse annotations with noisy information (e.g., over- or missing-pixel segmentation). There is a large body of literature Wang et al. (2021); Saha et al. (2022); Zhang & Zhuang (2022) that does not explicitly model noisy coarse annotations, unlike our novel method.

\section{4 EXPERIMENTS}

4.1 SET-UP

MNIST Experiments. We define a specialized MNIST segmentation dataset to study the fundamental properties of the proposed algorithm. While MNIST was originally constructed to facilitate research in recognition (classification) of handwritten digits LeCun et al. (1998), it has found its use in segmentation tasks to segment the digits from the background. It can be seen as an image classification task, except that instead of classifying the whole image, we are classifying each pixel individually. MNIST dataset consists of 60,000 training and 10,000 testing examples, all of which are $28\times28$ grayscale images of digits from 0 to 9, and we derive the segmentation labels by thresholding the intensity values at 0.5.

Cityscapes Experiments. The Cityscapes Cordts et al. (2016) dataset contains 5000 high-resolution (2048 $\times\,1024$ pixels) urban scene images collected across 27 European Cities. The dataset comprises 5,000 fine annotations (2,975 for training, 500 for validation, and 1,525 for testing) and 20,000 coarse annotations where 11,900 samples for training and 2,000 for validation (i.e., coarse polygons covering individual objects).

Retinal Image Experiments. The LES-AV Orlando et al. (2018) is a dataset for retinal vessel segmentation on color fundus images. It comprises 22 fundus photographs with available manual annotations of the retinal vessels including annotations of arteries and veins. The 22 images/patients are acquired with resolutions of $30^{\circ}$ field-of-view (FOV) and $1444\times1620$ pixels (21 images), and $45^{\circ}$ FOV and $1958\times2196$ pixels (one image), with each pixe $=6\mu m$ . We divide them into 18 images for training and 4 images for testing.

\section{4.2 SYNTHETIC NOISY COARSE ANNOTATIONS}

We generate synthetic coarse noisy annotations from an assumed expert consensus label on MNIST, Cityscapes and retinal fundus image dataset, to demonstrate the clear efficacy of the approach in an idealized situation where the expert consensus label is known. We simulate the positive and negative coarse noisy annotations by performing morphological transformations (e.g., thinning, thickening, fractures, etc) on the expert consensus label and background (complementary label), using Morpho-MNIST software Castro et al. (2019). In particular, positive coarse noisy annotation is prone to be poor segmentation, which is simulated by combining small fractures and over-segmentation; negative coarse noisy annotation always annotates on the background or complementary label using the same approach. To create synthetic coarse noisy labels in the multi-class scenario, we use a similar simulation to create coarse labels on the Cityscapes dataset. We first choose a target class and then apply morphological operations on the provided coarse mask to create the two synthetic coarse labels at different patterns, namely, objective coarse and complementary coarse annotations. We create training data by deriving labels from the simulated annotations. We also experimented with varying the levels of morphological operations on all datasets, e.g., Fig.8, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.01 (scribble) compared to the provided coarse labels, to test the robustness of our methods to varying sensitivities to coarse quality.

\section{4.3 COMPARISON METHODS AND EVALUATION METRICS}

Our experiments are based on the practical assumption that no expert consensus label is available a priori, hence, we compare our method against multiple weakly-supervised and semi-supervised methods. In particular, we explore our method with ablation studies, e.g., our method without negative coarse annotation; we also consider two state-of-the-art interactive image segmentation algorithms for generating masks from scribbles: GrabCut Rother et al. (2004) and LazySnapping Li et al. (2004), then training FCNs using the masks generated by these methods. Meanwhile, we compare with other weakly-supervised methods using different ways of annotations, e.g., scribble-guided annotations Lin et al. (2016); Zhang & Zhuang (2022), coarse annotations Saha et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2021), and box-level annotations Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al. (2022). Finally, we compare our weakly-supervised results based on the noisy coarse annotations and strongly-supervised results based on the expert consensus annotations. For evaluation metrics, we use mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) between estimated segmentation $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ and expert consensus label $\mathbf{y}_{G T}$ .

\section{4.4 SEGMENTATION PERFORMANCE}

Strategies of utilizing coarse annotation. Our method jointly propagates information into unmarked pixels and learns network parameters. An easy way is to first use any existing interactive image

\section{4.5 SENSITIVITIES TO THE QUALITY OF COARSE ANNOTATIONS}

Due to the different experiences and behaviors of the annotators, the coarse annotations show significant variabilities in quality. So we investigate how sensitive our method is to the coarse label quality. Generating different sets of coarse annotations usually requires extra annotations efforts, therefore we utilize the provided mask-level labels to create coarse annotations with a variety of qualities. We focus on the area of the coarse annotations. Given any mask-level annotation, we reduce the area of this coarse label by a ratio.

Figure 5: Sensitivities to quality of positive and negative coarse annotations, and the visualization of the estimated labels with different supervision approaches.

In terms of choosing the different ratios for the coarse labels, the central point is randomly chosen from the original mask-level annotation, and the area is determined by the reduced ratio. Fig.01 means a scribble is used.

Fig. 3 shows the results of our coarse-supervised algorithm using coarse annotations of different ratios. Our method generates much better results when the coarse label area increased from 0 to 0.3, and the results from Fig. 4 show that our method performs gradually better when the coarse annotation areas are increased, suggesting that our method has reasonably learned the useful information and corrected the error from the coarse annotation with different qualities.

\section{4.6 EXPERIMENTS ON RETINAL VESSEL SEGMENTATION}

Lastly, we illustrate the compelling results of our approach on a more challenging dataset with real coarse and noisy labels from the critical medical domain. This dataset, called LES-AV, consists of images of the retinal fundus acquired from different patients. The task is to segment the vessel into a binary mask (see Fig. 5). The process of segmenting the blood vessel in the retinal image is absolutely crucial for the early detection and diagnosis of serious eye diseases.

An experienced annotator was tasked with providing the practical positive and negative coarse annotations for each sample on LES-AV dataset. We generate such a real-world dataset to show the segmentation results and evaluate the performance of different supervision approaches. Meanwhile, we also created 5 different ratio levels for the positive and negative coarse annotations from level-1 (tend to scribble) to level-5 (tend to GT) with increasing ratios compared to the given expert consensus labels. We use such a dataset to evaluate the sensitivity to annotation quality of our model on medical image data.

We show the results of sensitivities to annotation quality in Fig. 5(a). Similarly to the previous experiments, our model performs robustly and gradually improved when the ratio of coarse annotations is increased. Especially when the ratio is increased from level- $^{\,\cdot\,l}$ to level-2, our model’s performance is increased significantly and comparable to the mask-level results. By applying our practical annotations, we conduct a group of experiments under different supervision. The results in Table. S2 indicate that our WSL approach achieves comparable results to the strongly-supervised method. Meanwhile, by including some extra coarse annotations, the result is improved $3\%$ . Finally, we present the segmentation visualization in Fig. 5(d⇠f).

\section{5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION}

We introduced a new and theoretically grounded algorithm for accurately recovering the expert consensus label distribution from noisy coarse annotations. Our novel method brings implementation simplicity, requiring only adding a complementary label learning term to the loss function. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real data sets have definitively shown superior performance over all common WSL and SSL methods in terms of both segmentation accuracy and robustness to the quality of coarse annotations and label noise. Furthermore, the method is demonstrably capable of estimating coarse annotations even when only a scribble is given per image, highlighting its practical efficiency.

Our work was primarily motivated by pressing medical imaging applications for which pixel-level annotation is required for a large number of images and carries significant clinical impact. However, future work shall consider imposing structures on the CMs and TMs to broaden the applicability to scribble or spot annotations, which could contribute substantially to saving the labor of the labeling process across many domains. Another limiting assumption is to learn only from the coarse annotation in difficult cases. The majority of segmentation failures happen in the difficult cases or the difficult patches in the image. Only giving coarse annotations on these difficult cases or patches and learning from them is also a valuable and impactful next step.

\title{Emerging Semantic Segmentation from Positive and Negative Coarse Label Learning}

\begin{abstract}
The availability of large, meticulously annotated datasets is of absolutely crucial importance for developing and deploying high-performance machine learning models for semantic segmentation tasks. However, the conventional process of producing precise labels at the pixel level is notoriously time-consuming, error-prone, and often requires expert-level annotators, particularly in specialized fields like medical imaging, where such expertise is rare and costly to obtain in practice. We note that it is fundamentally simpler and significantly less expensive to draw merely rough and approximate annotations, e.g., coarse annotations, which dramatically reduce the effort required for both expert and non-expert level annotators. In this paper, we propose a novel and powerful method to utilize coarse drawings from both positive (e.g., objects to be segmented) and negative (objects explicitly not to be segmented) classes present in the image, even when these drawings contain substantial amounts of noisy and imprecise pixels, to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for highly accurate semantic segmentation. We present a groundbreaking method for directly learning the true underlying segmentation label distributions from purely noisy coarse annotations using an architecture of two intelligently coupled CNNs. The effective separation and modeling of the two CNNs is achieved by maintaining high fidelity with the distinct statistical characters of the noisy training annotations. We further propose to add a complementary label learning mechanism that explicitly encourages the accurate estimation of the negative label distribution. To thoroughly illustrate the compelling properties and robustness of our method, we first conduct experiments on a carefully designed toy segmentation dataset based on MNIST. We then present comprehensive quantitative results on large, publicly available benchmark datasets: the challenging Cityscapes dataset for complex multi-class urban scene segmentation, and retinal fundus images for critical medical applications. In all conducted experiments, our method decisively and consistently outperforms all existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in the practically vital cases where the ratio of available coarse annotations is small compared to any given dense annotations, demonstrating its superior efficiency and robustness.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION}

Thanks to the widespread availability of large-scale datasets with meticulously accurate annotations Deng et al. (2009), the paradigm of Fully Supervised Learning (FSL) has been successfully translated from theoretical algorithms to widespread practical application. However, it is often prohibitively expensive, immensely time-consuming, and perhaps fundamentally impossible to collect exhaustive pixel-level labels for truly large-scale datasets Jing et al. (2019). This critical problem is particularly prominent and acute in the medical domain where labeled data are notoriously scarce due to the exceptionally high cost and expertise required for annotations Zhang et al. (2020b). For instance, achieving accurate segmentation of intricate vessels in fundus retinal images is an extremely difficult task even for highly experienced experts due to the immense variability of vessel location, size, and shape across population or disease states (see Fig. The entire labeling process is inherently prone to errors, almost inevitably leading to noisy datasets as has been extensively documented in major machine learning benchmark datasets Peterson et al. (2019). Labeling errors can readily occur due to automated label extraction processes, inherent ambiguities in input and output spaces, or simple human errors (e.g. lack of specific expertise). Those errors can be further exacerbated by pervasive data and human biases (e.g. varying level of expertise of the annotator), and thus annotations of complex structures e.g. organs in medical images, suffer from notoriously high inter- and intra- observer variability. As a direct consequence, despite the growing availability of massive imaging repositories (e.g. UK Biobank Littlejohns et al. (2020)), the generation of the curated, high-quality labels that are available to machine learning remains a paramount and challenging issue, urgently necessitating the development of advanced methods that learn robustly from noisy and imperfect annotations.

Recently, several powerful foundation models Kirillov et al. (2023); Ma & Wang (2023); Butoi et al. (2023) are proposed for universal image segmentation. However, these general models may output poor results or even totally fail for objects with highly irregular shapes, very weak boundaries, extremely small sizes, or critically low contrast. For most real-world situations, such subpar segmentation performance is not sufficient and far from satisfying especially for medical image segmentation where extremely high and reliable accuracy are non-negotiably demanded. Therefore, curating task-specific annotations for targeted supervised learning tasks is generally necessary and absolutely crucial for achieving accurate and meaningful results. To substantially reduce the immense workload of pixel-level annotation, there has been a considerable and sustained effort to exploit semi-supervised and weakly-supervised strategies. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims at training networks jointly with a small number of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data. Extensive research on SSL convincingly shows that plenty of unlabeled data would contribute significantly to the model performance and generalization abilities Chapelle et al. (2009); Cheplygina et al. (2019). However, the additional information from unlabeled data can improve CNNs only under specific and often restrictive assumptions Chapelle et al. (2009), and SSL still requires representative image and accurate annotation pairs to be available. In turn, Weakly-supervised Learning (WSL) utilizes annotations that are demonstrably cheaper to produce than pixel-wise labels such as bounding boxes Dai et al. (2015); Jiang et al.
