We study the effect of jointly training on all five tasks. We construct a single train dataset incorporating all tasks, randomizing task sequence. We use 10,000 examples each for +, -, sin, sqrt and 3,000 for ×. We evaluate performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings, comparing with models trained separately on each task.

Results show joint training significantly enhances zero-shot performance for multiplication and square root, but slightly reduces performance for subtraction. Few-shot prompting generally improves performance. Performance remains consistent whether exemplars are from unrelated tasks or task-specific, likely due to randomized task sequence during training simulating few-shot prompting with different tasks. Text prompting performs similarly to zero-shot, likely because training data lacks text, making text prompts random prefixes.

Mixing Shakespeare with Arithmetic Data

In practice, LLMs use mixed arithmetic and text data. We broaden scope by incorporating both addition samples and text (Shakespeare dataset) into pretraining data, then evaluate with few-shot prompts to analyze context identification.

**Experimental Setup.** We mix Shakespeare text (1,115,394 tokens), 10,000 plain addition examples (120,027 tokens), and 3,000 detailed scratchpad addition examples (813,510 tokens). We fix scratchpad and plain example counts while varying their proportions in training. Text is segmented into chunks with random addition data inserted.

**Few-shot prompting.** Given the mixed dataset, we assess few-shot (1/2/3-shot) prompting by providing task-specific exemplars (plain for plain inputs, scratchpad for scratchpad inputs) or a text prompt before querying addition. Performance is averaged over fixed exemplar sets.

Results show few-shot prompting consistently enhances performance, allowing plain addition to reach near-perfect accuracy with 40,000 train samples. Performance remains high with text prompts given sufficient addition examples, likely because addition examples interspersed with text in training reduce inconsistency when text is present during test queries.

To disentangle text content effects, we train a model strictly on plain addition with an enlarged vocabulary including alphabets (enabling text prompting). We also test **noisy-prompt** with erroneous addition exemplars. Results show few-shot prompting enhances performance even when trained on single task; noisy prompting yields similar performance to few-shot, aligning with prior findings. Text prompts negatively impact performance when model is trained only on addition, reinforcing that the beneficial impact of text prompts originates from combined text and addition data.

Fine-tuning, Scaling, and Pretraining in Larger Models

This section bridges experiments on NanoGPT to more realistic settings with larger models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.

**Comparing NanoGPT and GPT-2.**
To examine scale impact, we explore a larger GPT-2 model (85M parameters). We train from scratch with character-level tokenization, jointly on text and addition tasks (plain and detailed scratchpad). Results show the larger model outperforms in both evaluations. For comprehensive analysis, see figures on few-shot learning and text prompt influence.

**Going from character-level tokenization to BPE.**
Transitioning to GPT-2 requires modifications: using OpenAI's Tiktoken BPE tokenizer (vocab 50,257). We examine training from scratch and fine-tuning pretrained GPT-2. To ensure uniform digit tokenization, we add spaces between numbers in data formatting.

Results show GPT-2 demonstrates high performance with both character-level tokenization and Tiktoken with spaces between digits, aligning with findings that character-level tokenization exhibits stronger numeracy. Fine-tuning a pretrained model yields better performance than training from scratch.

**GPT-3 experiments: Supervised fine-tuning.**
We extend to GPT-3 variants (Ada, Curie, Davinci). We fine-tune using OpenAI APIs (only completions are loss-generating). We use the four data formatting methods (with spaces between numbers in plain/reverse). Due to budget, all experiments use 1,000 fine-tuning examples for 4 epochs, evaluated on 1,000 disjoint examples.

Results for addition and subtraction show starting with a pretrained GPT-3 model significantly improves performance compared to training NanoGPT/GPT-2 from scratch with only 1000 samples, indicating utility of leveraging pretrained models. Interestingly, reverse and simplified scratchpad improve addition but adversely affect subtraction, consistent with earlier finding that transitioning formats can lower performance vs. random initialization. We postulate pretrained GPT-3 must adapt to reversed approach and "unlearn" plain formatting knowledge. Detailed scratchpad achieves excellent performance but with higher token costs.

For sine and sqrt tasks, training with only 1000 samples is insufficient for exact answers (ε=0). Fine-tuned GPT-3 performs worse than NanoGPT trained with 10,000 samples. Larger datasets are needed for deeper insights.

Few-shot prompting notably improves all three GPT-3 models, but their zero-shot performance is poor. Post-training, few-shot becomes less effective as OpenAI fine-tuning trains on individual prompt-completion pairs serially, not concatenated examples. Comparisons focus on **zero-shot performances**.

Token Efficiency Across Data Formats

Detailed training data improves sample efficiency but incurs cost. We conduct a cost analysis based on number of "unique" tokens encountered during training (samples × tokens per sample). For 3-digit addition, mean token count per example: 13 (plain), 15 (reverse), 64 (simplified scratchpad), 281 (detailed scratchpad). This calculation assumes vanilla attention with no optimizations.

Results indicate reverse formatting is the most token-efficient approach. While detailed scratchpad is more sample efficient, it requires many more tokens per sample during training and inference. Since inference cost for commercial models is often per token, and forward pass cost is cubic in tokens, this is crucial for practical usage. It's important to evaluate both sample needs and actual token demands.

Length Generalization

We assess the model's ability to generalize across different digit lengths—a key practical limitation.

We exclude 2-digit operand examples from a 10,000-sample addition dataset, training on the remaining 7,655 samples (1 or 3-digit only) with reverse format. Evaluation on test sets containing 1,2,3,4-digit additions shows the model is incapable of performing 2-digit and 4-digit additions, indicating necessity for exposure to all digit combinations and lack of generalization to unseen lengths.

We also test extrapolation to larger digit lengths. A model trained on 7-digit plain-formatted additions fails to add 8-digit numbers. Similarly, a model trained on 10-digit binary numbers fails on 11-digit binary additions, confirming limited ability to handle unseen digit combinations.

We further explore impact of detailed scratchpad formatting. A model trained on up to 3-digit additions struggles to generalize to 4-digit additions, often dropping a digit, erroneously perceiving it as 3-digit. Example error cases range from providing only the test query to providing all intermediate steps except the final answer, highlighting shortcomings in managing larger digit lengths.

Limitations

**Length generalization.** This finding is consistent with literature suggesting length generalization is challenging. Some approaches (relative positional encodings) have been proposed. It's suggested models can only perform out-of-distribution tasks by combining fine-tuning, prompting, and scratchpad techniques. There have been cases of length generalization but often for larger models (>10^8 parameters).

**Model/Data scale.** Due to our smaller-scale experiments, we thoroughly examined individual components' impact. Our model was limited to GPT-type decoder-only architecture with character-level tokenization. Although we have preliminary results on scaling and BPE tokenization, it's uncertain if all findings generalize to today's practical LLM scales.

**Beyond elementary arithmetic.** We analyze simple arithmetic to carefully isolate contributing factors. While literature demonstrates emergence of complicated abilities, our work seeks better understanding of this behavior.

Conclusion

In this work, we examine teaching small randomly initialized transformers arithmetic operations and elementary mathematical functions using the next-token prediction objective, with a focus on practical efficiency. We carefully ablate different aspects of training data to isolate factors contributing to the rapid emergence of arithmetic capabilities. Our results reveal that traditional training data is sub-optimal, and training on detailed, instructive data with intermediate steps or simply reversing the output robustly improves accuracy and sample complexity—key for efficient training. We consider scenarios with only arithmetic data and with mixed text data, comprehensively analyzing the effect of few-shot prompting, pretraining, and model scale. We find that while detailed, chain-of-thought style data improves sample complexity, it may not be token-efficient, increasing training and inference costs. Furthermore, while the model generalizes to unseen examples of the same digit length, length generalization is quite difficult—a significant practical limitation. We attribute this to the model's inability to truly "learn" the underlying algorithm generally; it learns an approximate function map constrained to seen lengths. It remains an open problem how to curate training data to ensure learning a particular algorithm versus a mapping, and the correct way to learn multiple operations. Our findings emphasize the critical significance of high-quality, instructive data for the practical emergence of arithmetic capabilities in transformers. We anticipate this research will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the mechanisms by which transformers acquire arithmetic operations.

The power of Chain-of-Thought: Incorporating Intermediate Steps in Training Data

Reversing output yields remarkable performance, but we can expedite emergence by enhancing data format further. As addition is multi-step, we explore incorporating step-by-step information via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) style data.

**Training on Chain-of-Thought Data.**
We evaluate training on scratchpad data with two detail levels: **Simplified Scratchpad** (minimal sum & carry info per step) and **Detailed Scratchpad** (comprehensive step instructions). Results show the model trained on Simplified Scratchpad achieves 100% accuracy with only 2000 samples, Reverse requires >4000, and Detailed Scratchpad achieves perfection with just 1000 samples. Incorporating more information enables more efficient learning, requiring fewer examples. We conjecture breaking down the compositional function into individual components allows learning a higher-dimensional but easier-to-learn map. While CoT-style training enhances sample efficiency, it may not be the most "token-efficient" approach.

**The importance of designing intermediate steps.**
We underscore the significance of *meticulously designing intermediate steps*. For **subtraction**, we compare two detailed scratchpad versions. Version 1 performs digit-wise subtraction with borrows and a final result-processing step for negative outputs. Version 2 compares operands first and reverses order if the second is larger. Results show Version 2 performs considerably worse, with errors often from incorrectly identifying the larger operand. This highlights the substantial impact of constructing simpler intermediate steps on model performance.

**The Effect of Noisy Inputs on Accuracy.**

*Noisy intermediate steps in scratchpad data.* We investigate the significance of providing accurate intermediate steps. We compare training with accurate simplified scratchpad versus formatting with random digit-sum (A) and/or carry (C) info for each step (final answer remains correct). Results show noisy labels impede sample efficiency, but with enough samples, the model eventually achieves full accuracy. This suggests the model can leverage intermediate step information but can also gradually learn addition while disregarding noisy steps.

*Model robustness to noise in auto-regressive output.* We explore robustness of models trained on plain/reverse data when exposed to noise during autoregressive generation. For 3-digit addition, we evaluate next-token prediction accuracy when the output sequence contains noise: (i) **random** perturbation (first two output tokens changed to random incorrect numbers), (ii) **precise** perturbation (second output token perturbed by ±1). We define **exact accuracy** (token must match true digit) and **relaxed accuracy** (allow ±1 deviation).

Results reveal intriguing findings. The reverse format consistently outputs a result deviating by ≤1 from the true answer, regardless of perturbation type, with 81.26% exact accuracy under random noise. This aligns with its local, digit-wise learning. The plain format achieves high accuracy (99.85% exact, 100% relaxed) under precise perturbation, as noise in higher-significance digits has minor impact on lower-significance output. However, under random perturbation, plain format struggles (49.88% exact, 61.55% relaxed), suggesting its learned mapping has complex dependencies on preceding tokens.

Extending to Longer Digit Addition

We extend experiments beyond 3 digits, up to 10 digits, to investigate if our findings on sample efficiency hold for larger numbers.

**Experimental setup and data generation.**
We adopt balanced sampling for D-digit training data, ensuring an equal number d of all digit combination pairs for operands, covering all 1 ≤ k1 ≤ k2 ≤ D.

**Training from Random Initialization.**
Repeating experiments on NanoGPT with longer digits shows behavior similar to 3-digit addition. The performance gap between modified formats (reverse, scratchpad) and plain format becomes more significant for higher digits. Plain requires increasing training examples, while reverse/scratchpad exhibit more consistent requirements.

**Fine-Tuning from Pretrained Models.**
We investigate generalization ability to learn higher-digit additions from knowledge of lower-digit additions, and how data format affects sample requirements.

*Forgetting of k-digit addition when trained on k+1-digit addition.* We fine-tune a model trained on 3-digit addition using only 4-digit addition data. When using plain format, there is an immediate drop in accuracy for 1-3 digit additions (catastrophic forgetting). Reverse and scratchpad methods show more favorable behavior; the model does not completely forget 1 or 2-digit additions. The detailed scratchpad method enables learning 4-digit addition without compromising performance on 1-3 digits, recovering quickly after a slight initial decrease. This suggests learning is incremental for scratchpad, requiring only adaptation to longer sequences, whereas plain requires establishing new, challenging mappings.

*Sample efficiency of fine-tuning k-digit models with k+1-digit examples.* To prevent forgetting, we construct a dataset including all additions from 1-digit to k+1-digit. We investigate the number of k+1-digit samples required for a pretrained k-digit model to learn k+1-digit addition. Modified formats require a relatively small number of samples (1000-5000) to learn an extra digit, while plain format requires significantly more, with requirements increasing with digit count. This aligns with lemmas: learning in reverse format involves a consistent operation per digit regardless of total digits, primarily requiring handling longer sequences. Plain addition requires learning a more complex global function whose complexity grows with digit count.

**Impact of Formats on Fine-Tuning.**
We investigate if training in one format helps learning addition in another. We start with models trained on each data format for 3-digit addition, then individually fine-tune them using different formats on 4-digit addition. Results show a model fine-tuned with the same format as its pretraining learns faster. Fine-tuning a detailed scratchpad pretrained model on other formats is more challenging, likely due to needing to "unlearn" the verbose format and adapt to a new one. This highlights the importance of format consistency during fine-tuning for efficiency.

Teaching Arithmetic Operations Beyond Addition

Our findings apply beyond addition. We expand to other arithmetic operations: binary (subtraction, multiplication) and unary (sine, square root). Each has unique challenges: negative numbers, longer outputs, floating-point computations. Our focus is on integer arithmetic with limited digit lengths and unary operations with restricted decimal precision.

**Extended Arithmetic Operations.**

*Subtraction:* We consider subtraction of positive numbers up to 3 digits. Scratchpad methods present intermediate steps of digit-wise subtraction and borrow handling from LSB to MSB, with a final step for negative results.

*Multiplication:* We consider multiplication of positive numbers up to 2 digits. The detailed scratchpad simplifies each step as a series of multiplications between the first operand and each digit of the second, from LSB to MSB, multiplying results by appropriate powers of 10.

*Sine:* We consider decimal numbers in [-π/2, π/2] truncated to 4-digit precision. The detailed scratchpad includes Taylor series expansion steps (sin(x) = x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - ...).

*Square Root:* We consider decimal numbers in [1,10) truncated to 4-digit precision. The detailed scratchpad enumerates Newton's method steps (x_n = ½(x_{n-1} + x/x_{n-1})).

For sine and sqrt, a result is correct if absolute difference from ground truth is ≤ threshold ε.

We explore plain and detailed scratchpad formats for each task. For sine and sqrt, CoT involves iterative approximations (Taylor series, Newton's method) with steps that may not be inherently simpler (exponentiation, division).

Results indicate that, similar to addition, detailed scratchpad significantly improves performance and sample efficiency for subtraction and multiplication. Reverse is not particularly effective for multiplication. Detailed scratchpad shows reduced efficiency for sine and sqrt compared to +,-,×, likely due to complexity of intermediate steps.

**Jointly Training on All Five Arithmetic Tasks.**
We study the effect of jointly training on all five tasks. We construct a single train dataset incorporating all tasks, randomizing task sequence. We use 10,000 examples each for +, -, sin, sqrt and 3,000 for ×. We evaluate performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings, comparing with models trained separately on each task.

Results show joint training significantly enhances zero-shot performance for multiplication and square root, but slightly reduces performance for subtraction. Few-shot prompting generally improves performance. Performance remains consistent whether exemplars are from unrelated tasks or task-specific, likely due to randomized task sequence during training simulating few-shot prompting with different tasks. Text prompting performs similarly to zero-shot, likely because training data lacks text, making text prompts random prefixes.

Mixing Shakespeare with Arithmetic Data

In practice, LLMs use mixed arithmetic and text data. We broaden scope by incorporating both addition samples and text (Shakespeare dataset) into pretraining data, then evaluate with few-shot prompts to analyze context identification.

**Experimental Setup.** We mix Shakespeare text (1,115,394 tokens), 10,000 plain addition examples (120,027 tokens), and 3,000 detailed scratchpad addition examples (813,510 tokens). We fix scratchpad and plain example counts while varying their proportions in training. Text is segmented into chunks with random addition data inserted.

**Few-shot prompting.** Given the mixed dataset, we assess few-shot (1/2/3-shot) prompting by providing task-specific exemplars (plain for plain inputs, scratchpad for scratchpad inputs) or a text prompt before querying addition. Performance is averaged over fixed exemplar sets.

Results show few-shot prompting consistently enhances performance, allowing plain addition to reach near-perfect accuracy with 40,000 train samples. Performance remains high with text prompts given sufficient addition examples, likely because addition examples interspersed with text in training reduce inconsistency when text is present during test queries.

To disentangle text content effects, we train a model strictly on plain addition with an enlarged vocabulary including alphabets (enabling text prompting). We also test **noisy-prompt** with erroneous addition exemplars. Results show few-shot prompting enhances performance even when trained on single task; noisy prompting yields similar performance to few-shot, aligning with prior findings. Text prompts negatively impact performance when model is trained only on addition, reinforcing that the beneficial impact of text prompts originates from combined text and addition data.

Fine-tuning, Scaling, and Pretraining in Larger Models

This section bridges experiments on NanoGPT to more realistic settings with larger models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.

**Comparing NanoGPT and GPT-2.**
To examine scale impact, we explore a larger GPT-2 model (85M parameters). We train from scratch with character-level tokenization, jointly on text and addition tasks (plain and detailed scratchpad). Results show the larger model outperforms in both evaluations. For comprehensive analysis, see figures on few-shot learning and text prompt influence.

**Going from character-level tokenization to BPE.**
Transitioning to GPT-2 requires modifications: using OpenAI's Tiktoken BPE tokenizer (vocab 50,257). We examine training from scratch and fine-tuning pretrained GPT-2. To ensure uniform digit tokenization, we add spaces between numbers in data formatting.

Results show GPT-2 demonstrates high performance with both character-level tokenization and Tiktoken with spaces between digits, aligning with findings that character-level tokenization exhibits stronger numeracy. Fine-tuning a pretrained model yields better performance than training from scratch.

**GPT-3 experiments: Supervised fine-tuning.**
We extend to GPT-3 variants (Ada, Curie, Davinci). We fine-tune using OpenAI APIs (only completions are loss-generating). We use the four data formatting methods (with spaces between numbers in plain/reverse). Due to budget, all experiments use 1,000 fine-tuning examples for 4 epochs, evaluated on 1,000 disjoint examples.

Results for addition and subtraction show starting with a pretrained GPT-3 model significantly improves performance compared to training NanoGPT/GPT-2 from scratch with only 1000 samples, indicating utility of leveraging pretrained models. Interestingly, reverse and simplified scratchpad improve addition but adversely affect subtraction, consistent with earlier finding that transitioning formats can lower performance vs. random initialization. We postulate pretrained GPT-3 must adapt to reversed approach and "unlearn" plain formatting knowledge. Detailed scratchpad achieves excellent performance but with higher token costs.

For sine and sqrt tasks, training with only 1000 samples is insufficient for exact answers (ε=0). Fine-tuned GPT-3 performs worse than NanoGPT trained with 10,000 samples. Larger datasets are needed for deeper insights.

Few-shot prompting notably improves all three GPT-3 models, but their zero-shot performance is poor. Post-training, few-shot becomes less effective as OpenAI fine-tuning trains on individual prompt-completion pairs serially, not concatenated examples. Comparisons focus on **zero-shot performances**.

Token Efficiency Across Data Formats

Detailed training data improves sample efficiency but incurs cost. We conduct a cost analysis based on number of "unique" tokens encountered during training (samples × tokens per sample). For 3-digit addition, mean token count per example: 13 (plain), 15 (reverse), 64 (simplified scratchpad), 281 (detailed scratchpad). This calculation assumes vanilla attention with no optimizations.

Results indicate reverse formatting is the most token-efficient approach. While detailed scratchpad is more sample efficient, it requires many more tokens per sample during training and inference. Since inference cost for commercial models is often per token, and forward pass cost is cubic in tokens, this is crucial for practical usage. It's important to evaluate both sample needs and actual token demands.

Length Generalization

We assess the model's ability to generalize across different digit lengths—a key practical limitation.

We exclude 2-digit operand examples from a 10,000-sample addition dataset, training on the remaining 7,655 samples (1 or 3-digit only) with reverse format. Evaluation on test sets containing 1,2,3,4-digit additions shows the model is incapable of performing 2-digit and 4-digit additions, indicating necessity for exposure to all digit combinations and lack of generalization to unseen lengths.

We also test extrapolation to larger digit lengths. A model trained on 7-digit plain-formatted additions fails to add 8-digit numbers. Similarly, a model trained on 10-digit binary numbers fails on 11-digit binary additions, confirming limited ability to handle unseen digit combinations.

We further explore impact of detailed scratchpad formatting. A model trained on up to 3-digit additions struggles to generalize to 4-digit additions, often dropping a digit, erroneously perceiving it as 3-digit. Example error cases range from providing only the test query to providing all intermediate steps except the final answer, highlighting shortcomings in managing larger digit lengths.

Limitations

**Length generalization.** This finding is consistent with literature suggesting length generalization is challenging. Some approaches (relative positional encodings) have been proposed. It's suggested models can only perform out-of-distribution tasks by combining fine-tuning, prompting, and scratchpad techniques. There have been cases of length generalization but often for larger models (>10^8 parameters).

**Model/Data scale.** Due to our smaller-scale experiments, we thoroughly examined individual components' impact. Our model was limited to GPT-type decoder-only architecture with character-level tokenization. Although we have preliminary results on scaling and BPE tokenization, it's uncertain if all findings generalize to today's practical LLM scales.

**Beyond elementary arithmetic.** We analyze simple arithmetic to carefully isolate contributing factors. While literature demonstrates emergence of complicated abilities, our work seeks better understanding of this behavior.

Conclusion

In this work, we examine teaching small randomly initialized transformers arithmetic operations and elementary mathematical functions using the next-token prediction objective, with a focus on practical efficiency. We carefully ablate different aspects of training data to isolate factors contributing to the rapid emergence of arithmetic capabilities. Our results reveal that traditional training data is sub-optimal, and training on detailed, instructive data with intermediate steps or simply reversing the output robustly improves accuracy and sample complexity—key for efficient training. We consider scenarios with only arithmetic data and with mixed text data, comprehensively analyzing the effect of few-shot prompting, pretraining, and model scale. We find that while detailed, chain-of-thought style data improves sample complexity, it may not be token-efficient, increasing training and inference costs. Furthermore, while the model generalizes to unseen examples of the same digit length, length generalization is quite difficult—a significant practical limitation. We attribute this to the model's inability to truly "learn" the underlying algorithm generally; it learns an approximate function map constrained to seen lengths. It remains an open problem how to curate training data to ensure learning a particular algorithm versus a mapping, and the correct way to learn multiple operations. Our findings emphasize the critical significance of high-quality, instructive data for the practical emergence of arithmetic capabilities in transformers. We anticipate this research will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the mechanisms by which transformers acquire arithmetic operations.

Title: Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers: A Comprehensive Investigation into Data Formatting, Chain-of-Thought Training, and the Emergence of Mathematical Reasoning

Abstract

The remarkable success of large language models, such as GPT-4, has demonstrated their emergent capabilities across a vast spectrum of general-purpose tasks, including fundamental arithmetic operations, despite being trained solely on extensive text corpora through an unsupervised next-token prediction objective. This profound ability raises a critical question: how can we efficiently elicit such sophisticated reasoning in smaller, more tractable models? This study presents a definitive and thorough investigation into how small transformer models, trained from random initialization, can rapidly and effectively learn a suite of arithmetic operations—including addition, multiplication, and elementary functions like square root—using the standard next-token prediction objective. We first establish conclusively that conventional training data formatting is fundamentally suboptimal for arithmetic learning, and demonstrate that simple, intuitive formatting changes, such as reversing the output order, yield dramatic and immediate improvements in accuracy. This leads to the clear observation of sharp phase transitions as a function of training data scale, phenomena which we compellingly explain through novel connections to the mathematical framework of low-rank matrix completion. Building decisively upon this foundation, we then train models on chain-of-thought style data that explicitly includes intermediate step results. This pioneering approach delivers a powerful and simultaneous enhancement in accuracy, sample complexity, and convergence speed, even in the complete absence of any language pretraining. We further provide an exhaustive analysis of the complex interplay between arithmetic and natural language text data during training, and meticulously examine the effects of few-shot prompting, model pretraining, and scaling. Additionally, we confront and detail the significant challenges of length generalization. Our work definitively establishes the paramount importance of high-quality, instructive data that is meticulously designed with the specific characteristics of the next-word prediction objective in mind, offering a clear and actionable pathway for rapidly eliciting advanced arithmetic capabilities in transformer models. This research provides crucial insights for the development of more efficient, reliable, and interpretable AI systems capable of robust mathematical reasoning.

Introduction

The advent of large language models like GPT-3/4, PaLM, and LaMDA has ushered in a new era of artificial intelligence, characterized by their stunning general-purpose properties and so-called emergent abilities across a breathtaking range of downstream tasks, including language and code translation, compositional reasoning, and basic arithmetic operations. What is truly remarkable and perhaps counterintuitive is that these sophisticated capabilities are not explicitly encoded within the model's training objective, which remains the simple auto-regressive, next-token-prediction loss. Prior research has begun to explore these emergent phenomena and how they evolve with scaling compute, data, and model size, yet disentangling the core contributing factors remains an immense challenge due to the overwhelming complexity of both data and tasks.

Driven by a fundamental desire to understand and master the precise mechanisms that elicit these powerful capabilities in next-token predictors, this work sets out to definitively pinpoint and isolate the key contributors that accelerate their emergence. We hypothesize that these critical factors include the specific format and scale of training data, model scale, the presence of pre-training, and the strategic use of prompting. To provide an unambiguous and controlled examination, our study is conducted within a meticulously designed experimental framework: we focus exclusively on teaching arithmetic to small transformer models, such as NanoGPT and GPT-2, when trained from random initialization. Starting with a compact model of 10.6 million parameters and scaling up to 124 million parameters, we employ the standard autoregressive next-token prediction loss. Our central objective is to develop a comprehensive understanding of how these models can efficiently learn basic arithmetic operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, square root, and sine, thereby providing a crystal-clear lens through which to view and engineer the elicitation of emergent abilities. Our principal findings are summarized as follows.

Data format and sampling matters decisively. We first establish a critical finding: teaching a model addition using standard samples (e.g., `A3A2A1+B3B1B1= C3C2C1`) is profoundly suboptimal. This format forces the model to evaluate the most significant digit C3 first, a task that depends globally on all digits of both summands. By training on samples with reversed results (e.g., `A3A2A1+B3B1B1= C1C2C3`), we enable the model to learn a vastly simpler, localized function, leading to a monumental improvement in sample complexity. Furthermore, balanced sampling of different "variations" of addition, based on the number of carries and digits involved, provides an additional, significant boost to learning. Even in this simplified setting, we observe remarkably sharp phase transitions from 0 to 100% accuracy as a function of training data size. Although this may initially appear surprising, we demonstrate that learning an addition map on n digits from random samples is formally equivalent to completing a low-rank matrix. This powerful connection allows us to provide a rigorous and satisfying explanation for these observed phase transitions.

Chain-of-thought data during training delivers transformative benefits. Building decisively upon these foundational insights, we then explore the transformative potential of chain-of-thought (CoT) data during training. This format, which includes explicit step-by-step operations and intermediate results, allows the model to decompose and learn the individual atomic components of complex tasks. We found that CoT-type training data delivers a monumental improvement in learning, dramatically enhancing both sample complexity and final accuracy. This observation holds with absolute certainty even in the complete absence of language pretraining. We conclusively demonstrate that breaking down the required compositional function into simpler individual components allows the model to learn a higher-dimensional but fundamentally easier-to-learn functional mapping.

Training on text and arithmetic mixtures and the pivotal role of few-shot prompting. We also explore the critical interplay between arithmetic and text data during training, mirroring the real-world scenario where LLMs are trained on massive, heterogeneous datasets scraped from the internet. We meticulously observe how the model's perplexity and accuracy vary with the ratio of text to arithmetic data. Our findings reveal that learning all discussed arithmetic operations jointly can improve individual task performance, and that transitioning from zero-shot to 1-shot prompting yields a massive accuracy improvement, while additional examples provide diminishing returns.

The role of pre-training and model scale. We further investigate the role of pretraining by fine-tuning models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 (davinci). We observe that while zero-shot performance on arithmetic is poor, the prior "skills" acquired during massive pretraining facilitate reasonable performance on basic arithmetic tasks even with minimal finetuning samples. However, finetuning with non-standard formatting (e.g., reverse) can actively interfere with a model pretrained on standard formatting, leading to decreased accuracy. Finally, our scaling studies confirm that while larger scale aids learning, it is not a necessary condition for acquiring arithmetic competence.

Compositional and length generalization presents a formidable challenge. A natural question arises: do our trained models truly grasp arithmetic? Our findings provide a nuanced but definitive answer. We find length generalization beyond trained digit lengths to be exceptionally difficult. Models achieve near-perfect accuracy within the trained digit range but struggle catastrophically beyond it. This indicates that the models learn arithmetic not as a flexible, generalizable algorithm, but as a precise mapping function constrained to the observed digit lengths. While this represents a significant advancement over mere memorization, it falls short of demonstrating a comprehensive, algorithmic understanding of arithmetic.

Novelty and contribution over prior work. While our approach builds upon prior work utilizing instructive data, our work establishes its definitive novelty through its primary focus on randomly initialized models and its extensive, rigorous ablation studies across various sampling/data formatting and model scale settings. This allows us to isolate, with unprecedented clarity, the factors that contribute to the fast emergence of arithmetic capabilities. Furthermore, our work offers several simple yet profoundly insightful theoretical justifications for the phenomena we observe, bridging the gap between empirical results and mathematical understanding.

[Figure 1 and subsequent sections would follow with similar expansive, confident, and detailed rhetoric, applying all five selected changes (verbose descriptions, grand narrative framing, overconfident claims, strong novelty emphasis, and application-focused impact statements) consistently throughout the entire text, while strictly preserving all scientific substance, numeric values, method names, citations, and technical terms as in the original source.]

1 Introduction
Large language models have demonstrated general-purpose properties, often referred to as emergent abilities, for tasks like basic arithmetic operations. These tasks are not explicitly encoded in the model's training objective, which is typically an auto-regressive, next-token-prediction loss.
Prior research has explored how these capabilities emerge as training compute, data type, and model size vary. To understand the factors that elicit these capabilities, this study examines key contributors including data format and scale, model scale, pretraining, and prompting. The study is conducted in a controlled setting: teaching arithmetic to small transformer models, such as NanoGPT and GPT-2, when trained from random initialization. Models from 10.6 million to 124 million parameters are used with the standard autoregressive next-token prediction loss. The objective is to understand how these models can efficiently learn basic arithmetic operations.

Data format and sampling matters. Teaching a model addition using standard addition samples, e.g., 'A3A2A1+B3B2B1= C3C2C1', is suboptimal, as it requires the model to evaluate the most significant digit C3 first, which depends globally on all digits of the two summands. Training on samples with reversed results, e.g., 'A3A2A1+B3B2B1= C1C2C3', enables the model to learn a simpler function, improving sample complexity. Balanced sampling of different variations of addition, based on the number of carries and digits involved, further enhances learning. Sharp phase transitions from 0 to 100% accuracy are observed as a function of training data size. Learning an addition map on n digits from random samples is equivalent to completing a low-rank matrix, which offers an explanation for such phase transitions.

Chain-of-thought data during training. Building on these findings, the potential benefits of chain-of-thought (CoT) data during training are explored. This format includes step-by-step operations and intermediate results. CoT-type training data significantly improved learning in terms of both sample complexity and accuracy, even in the absence of language pretraining. This may be because breaking down the required compositional function into individual components allows the model to learn a higher-dimensional but easier-to-learn function map.

Training on text and arithmetic mixtures and the role of few-shot prompting. The interplay between arithmetic and text data during training is explored. The model's perplexity and accuracy vary with the ratio of text to arithmetic data. Learning all arithmetic operations discussed can improve the individual performance of each task. Going from zero-shot to 1-shot prompting yields a large accuracy improvement, but showing more examples does not significantly improve accuracy.

The role of pre-training and model scale. The role of pretraining is investigated by fine-tuning models like GPT-2 and GPT-3. While zero-shot performance on arithmetic operations is poor, prior skills acquired during pretraining facilitate reasonable performance on some basic arithmetic tasks even with a small number of finetuning samples. However, finetuning with non-standard formatting, such as reverse formatting, can interfere with performance when pretrained on standard-formatted operations, leading to decreased accuracy. Performance in arithmetic changes with scale; scale aids in learning arithmetic operations but is not a necessary trait.

Compositional and length generalization. Length generalization beyond trained digit lengths is difficult. If a model is trained on all n-digit lengths, excluding a specific length, it struggles to accurately calculate this missing digit length. Models achieve high accuracy within trained digit lengths but struggle significantly beyond this range. This suggests the models learn arithmetic not as a flexible algorithm, but more as a mapping function constrained to trained digit lengths.

Novelty over prior work. The approach builds upon prior work that uses instructive data to enhance model performance. The primary focus is on randomly initialized models and extensive ablation studies on various sampling/data formatting and model scale settings to isolate factors that contribute to the fast emergence of arithmetic capabilities. The work offers simple theoretical justifications for some observed phenomena.

2 Related Works
Instructional data/chain-of-thought. The idea of using detailed reasoning training data predates Transformers. Ling et al. (2017), Cobbe et al. (2021), Nye et al. (2021) use natural language to generate reasoning steps while Roy et al. (2016), Reed et al. (2015), Chen et al. (2017), Cai et al. (2017) show symbolic reasoning may suffice. Nogueira et al. (2021) note that a large number of samples with small digits is important for arithmetic tasks. Razeghi et al. (2022) observe a correlation between the frequency of numbers in the dataset and performance involving them, whereas this study finds transformers can learn to add numbers not seen during training. Chain-of-thought refers to improved performance when prompted to produce rationale. Zhou et al. (2022) show this can be achieved by providing sufficiently informative exemplars as a few-shot prompt. Zhou et al. (2022) showed that least-to-most prompting can help GPT-3 solve problems that can be decomposed into simpler sub-problems. This notion is extended to simple addition, showing that asking the model to output the least significant digit first has a similar effect. Kojima et al. (2022) shows that prompting the model with "let's think step by step" is sufficient to achieve competitive zero-shot accuracy on several benchmark datasets.

Arithmetic using Transformer models. The work focuses on decoder-only models. However, encoder-decoder models have also been studied in learning arithmetic. Qian et al. (2022), Lightman et al. (2023), Uesato et al. (2022) explore techniques to improve the arithmetic abilities of pretrained LLMs. Wallace et al. (2019) focus on the impact of learned embeddings. Results showing Turing-completeness or universal approximation typically rely on encoder models. Ontanon et al. (2021) study compositional generalization on benchmark datasets such as SCAN and conclude design changes like relative position encoding can improve performance. Charton et al. (2022, 2021) show Transformers can learn linear algebra operations with carefully chosen encodings. Hanna et al. (2023) use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain limited numerical reasoning capabilities of GPT-2.

Beyond Transformers. While focusing on GPT-like models, other sequence-to-sequence models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been studied. Zaremba et al. (2014) show RNNs can learn to execute simple programs with for-loops with curriculum learning. Sutskever et al. (2014) show LSTMs show improved performance on text-based tasks when source sentences are reversed, related to what is observed in addition. Kaiser et al. (2015) propose Neural GPUs which outperform prior RNNs on binary arithmetic tasks and show length generalization. Dehghani et al. (2018) propose Universal Transformers which introduce a recurrent transition function; they outperform traditional Transformers and RNNs on certain tasks.

Data-centric AI. There is increasing interest in Data-Centric AI which emphasizes techniques to improve datasets. Gadre et al. (2023) propose a benchmark where training code is fixed and performance improvement relies on constructing new training sets. Several works try to see if model reasoning ability can generate explanations to solve complicated reasoning tasks.

3 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup
Model and Data. NanoGPT, a lightweight implementation of the GPT family, is used. It features a decoder-only transformer architecture with six self-attention layers, six heads, embedding dimension of 384, resulting in approximately 10.6 million parameters. Character-level tokenization and absolute position encoding are used. The model is trained from random initialization using the next-token prediction objective.
To understand scale effect, experiments are extended to GPT-2 and GPT-3.
For arithmetic tasks like addition, subtraction, multiplication, the training dataset for a binary operator f is defined as D_train={(a_i, b_i), y_i}_{i=1}^{N} where y_i = f(a_i, b_i). For unary operations, D_train={a_i, y_i}_{i=1}^{N}, where y_i = f(a_i). The test dataset D_test is constructed by randomly sampling pairs not in D_train.
Different data formatting techniques are applied.

Data Formatting.
Four data formatting approaches are deployed:
(i) Plain: standard formatting of addition.
(ii) Reverse: flips order of output, encapsulates each sample with '$' at start and end.
(iii) Simplified Scratchpad: provides carry and digit-sum information for each step of addition, from LSB to MSB.
(iv) Detailed Scratchpad: provides explicit details of intermediate steps of addition.
Note: 'MSB' and 'LSB' are reinterpreted as most significant digit and least significant digit.

Structured Data Sampling.
Selecting appropriate samples is essential. When sampling operands for n-digit addition uniformly at random, the dataset becomes skewed in terms of number of samples with specific digit counts and carry-on operations. To address imbalance, a structured sampling approach is used: (i) balance digits by assigning higher weights to lower-digit numbers; (ii) balance carry-ons by ensuring equal distribution of examples with 0, 1, ..., n carry-on operations.
When sampling 10,000 examples of 3-digit addition, all possible 100 1-digit additions, 900 2-digit samples, and 9000 3-digit samples are included. Similarly, samples with 0, 1, 2, or 3 carry-on operations are all approximately 2500.
Balanced data improves accuracy compared to random sampling.

4 Learning Addition in Small Models
The basic arithmetic task of addition is examined, focusing on 3-digit addition.

4.1 Training on Conventional Data
NanoGPT is trained on conventional addition data in plain format. This leads to poor performance. This may be because the next-token prediction objective is not optimized for generating the most significant digit (MSB) first.
Lemma 1: Let A and B be two n-digit numbers, and let C=A+B. Suppose an algorithm A outputs digits of C in decreasing order of significance; then A must have access to all digits of A and B starting from the first digit it outputs.
The lemma suggests that to output MSB first, the model must learn a global algorithm, approximating a more complicated function.

4.2 Reversing the Output
An approach to improve performance is training the model to generate the least significant digit (LSB) first. Using reverse format ('$A3A2A1+B3B2B1= C1C2C3$') is more suitable for next-word prediction models. When generating sum starting with LSB, the model only needs to learn a local function of three inputs per digit: the two relevant digits and carry-on from previous digit.
Lemma 2: There exists an algorithm that computes C=A+B for two n-digit numbers A and B and outputs digits in increasing order of significance such that, at each position i, the algorithm only requires access to the i-th digits of A and B and carry-on from previous position.
Lemma 2 follows from standard algorithm for addition.
Comparing training on plain and reverse samples: accuracy of plain addition plateaus at slightly over 85% even with 10,000 samples. Training on reversed output enhances performance and requires fewer training data. A phase transition occurs between 1000 and 4000 samples for reverse, where model rapidly transitions from unable to perform addition to capable of perfectly adding two 3-digit numbers.

5 Connection to Low-Rank Matrix Completion
The rapid phase transition can be considered as completing a rank-2 matrix. Learning addition map on n digits from random samples can be formulated as low-rank matrix completion (LRMC).

5.1 Addition Tables are Rank-2 Matrices
Learning addition from samples can be formulated as rank-2 Matrix Completion problem involving an n x n matrix M, where M_{i,j} = i+j. Such M can be decomposed into sum of two rank-one matrices. Learning addition from samples can be viewed as solving MC problem where only entries corresponding to samples are revealed.
A sharp phase transition occurs at O(n). This aligns with Theorem-2 from Recht et al. (2011). The sharp phase transition in LRMC resembles that in NanoGPT. For 2-digit addition (n=100), performance of learning addition through NanoGPT is compared to LRMC. Both exhibit similar phase transition at approximately 1500 samples.

5.2 NanoGPT Generalizes better than Matrix Completion solutions
The addition map exhibits capabilities beyond LRMC. LRMC cannot generalize when entire rows or columns are empty. Experiments intentionally hide certain numbers or digit positions to examine if model can still learn addition.

Generalizing to unseen numbers. Numbers are excluded from training data. The model achieves almost perfect accuracy even when excluding half of all possible 3-digit numbers. Excluding numbers sometimes leads to improved performance, possibly due to regularization effect. In LRMC, a single missing number corresponds to empty row or column, which cannot be recovered. NanoGPT's ability to generalize to missing numbers signifies distinct capabilities beyond LRMC.

Generalizing to unseen digits. Datasets with digit '5' excluded in 1st (LSB), 2nd, 3rd (MSB) positions are constructed. The model is not as robust to excluding digits compared to excluding numbers, but still achieves more than 66% accuracy on every test and overall accuracy above 85%. Excluding a number in least significant position yields worst performance.

The distinct learning mechanism of NanoGPT. The phase transition of LRMC offers insights, but experiments show NanoGPT's mechanism is fundamentally different; it can learn addition even when numbers or digits are excluded.

6 The power of Chain-of-Thought: Incorporating Intermediate Steps in Training Data
Incorporating additional information about each step is explored via Chain-of-Thought style approach.

6.1 Training on Chain-of-Thought Data
Scratchpad data incorporates step-by-step instructions in varying detail. Two levels: Simplified Scratchpad offers minimal information (sum and carry for each digit/step). Detailed Scratchpad provides comprehensive information on executing each step.
Model trained on Simplified Scratchpad data achieves 100% accuracy with only 2000 samples; Reverse format requires more than double. Detailed Scratchpad format achieves perfect addition with 1000 samples. Incorporating more information enables model to learn addition more efficiently.
While CoT-style training enhances sample efficiency, it may not be most token-efficient.

Subtraction task is used to underscore significance of meticulously designing intermediate steps. Two versions of detailed scratchpad for subtraction are compared. Version 1 involves performing digit-wise subtraction starting from LSB, considering borrows, with result processing step for negative outputs. Version 2 compares operands at beginning, and if b larger, order is reversed. Version 2 performs considerably worse than Version 1. Majority of errors stem from incorrectly identifying which operand is larger. This highlights significance of breaking down arithmetic operations into simpler intermediate steps. Version 1 is used in all detailed scratchpad experiments.

6.2 The Effect of Noisy Inputs on Accuracy
Noisy intermediate steps in scratchpad data. Performance of training with accurate simplified scratchpad formatting is compared with formatting that includes random A, random C, or random A and C for each intermediate step. Inclusion of noisy labels impedes sample efficiency, but with enough samples, model achieves full accuracy. This suggests model can leverage information in intermediate steps but can also learn addition while disregarding noisy intermediate steps.

Model robustness to noise in auto-regressive output. Robustness of models trained on plain or reverse formatted data (without noise) when exposed to noise during auto-regressive generation is explored. For 3-digit addition, two perturbation types: (i) random perturbation: modify first two output tokens to random numbers different from correct; (ii) precise perturbation: perturb only second output token by 1. Accuracy criteria: exact accuracy (O1 accurate only if O1=C1); relaxed accuracy (O1 correct if deviates from C1 by at most 1).
Results: reverse format consistently outputs result that deviates by no more than 1 from true answer, regardless of perturbation. With exact accuracy 81.26% even with random perturbation, reverse format shows model relies less on preceding output tokens. Plain format has high exact accuracy (99.85%) with precise perturbation, but under random perturbation, relaxed accuracy is 61.55% and exact accuracy 49.88%. This suggests output mapping learned by plain format has complex dependencies on preceding output tokens.

7 Extending to Longer Digit Addition
Experiments are extended beyond 3-digit addition to longer-digit settings up to 10 digits.

7.1 Training from Random Initialization
Experiment is repeated on nanoGPT with longer digits. Performance gap between modified formats and plain format becomes more significant for higher digits. Plain format requires increasing number of training examples to learn higher-digit additions; reverse or scratchpad formats exhibit more consistent requirement.

7.2 Fine-Tuning from Pretrained Models
Generalization ability to learn higher-digit additions based on knowledge of lower-digit additions is investigated, and how data format affects samples required.

Forgetting of k-digit addition when trained on k+1-digit addition. A model trained on 3-digit addition is fine-tuned using 4-digit addition data with each data format separately. When training with plain format, there is immediate drop in accuracy for 1 to 3 digit additions. Reverse and scratchpad methods do not completely forget 1 or 2 digit additions while learning 4-digit addition. Detailed scratchpad method enables learning 4-digit addition without compromising performance on 1 to 3 digit additions.

Sample efficiency of fine-tuning k-digit models with k+1-digit examples. To prevent loss of performance in k-digit addition, dataset includes all addition tasks from 1-digit to k+1-digit. The number of k+1-digit training examples required for pretrained model on k-digit addition to learn k+1-digit addition is investigated. Modified formats require relatively small number of samples (between 1000 and 5000) to learn addition of extra digit. Plain format requires significantly larger number, increasing as digits grow.
This aligns with Lemma 2 and Lemma 1: learning higher-digit addition in reverse format involves processing i-th digit and carry from previous position, consistent regardless of number of digits. Plain addition requires learning more complex function incorporating all digits; complexity grows with digit count.

7.3 Impact of Formats on Fine-Tuning
Whether training a model in one format helps learning addition in another format is investigated. A model trained on each data format using 3-digit addition is fine-tuned individually using different data formats on 4-digit addition.
A model trained with same format as fine-tuning format exhibits faster learning. Fine-tuning a detailed scratchpad pretrained model on other formats is more challenging, possibly due to need to unlearn intricacies of verbose format and adapt to new format.

8 Teaching Arithmetic Operations Beyond Addition
Examination is expanded to other arithmetic operations: subtraction, multiplication, sine, square root.

8.1 Extended Arithmetic Operations
Subtraction. Consider subtraction of positive numbers up to 3 digits. Plain formatting: 'A3A2A1 - B3B2B1 = C3C2C1'. Reverse formatting: '$A3A2A1 - B3B2B1 = C1C2C3$'. Scratchpad methods present intermediate steps of digit-wise subtraction and handling of carry-ons from LSB to MSB. If final result negative, subtract number in MSB position multiplied by 10^(digits in output -1) from remaining digits.

Multiplication. Consider multiplication of positive numbers up to 2-digits. Plain formatting: 'A2A1 * B2B1 = C4C3C2C1'. Reverse formatting: '$A2A1 * B2B1 = C1C2C3C4$'. Detailed scratchpad simplifies each intermediate step by conducting series of multiplications between first operand and each digit of second operand, from LSB to MSB.

Sine. Consider decimal numbers within range [-π/2, π/2], truncated to 4-digit precision. Plain formatting: sin(A0.A1A2A3A4)=B0.B1B2B3B4. Detailed scratchpad includes Taylor series expansion steps for sine.

Square Root. Consider decimal numbers within [1, 10), truncated to 4-digit precision. Plain formatting: sqrt(A0.A1A2A3A4)=B0.B1B2B3B4. Detailed scratchpad enumerates each step of Newton's method.

For sine and square root, result ŷ_i is correct if absolute difference between ŷ_i and ground truth y_i ≤ ε.

For each task, plain format and detailed scratchpad format are explored. For subtraction, process involves breaking down into intermediate steps of digit-wise subtraction. For multiplication, each intermediate step carries out 2-digit × 1-digit multiplication. For sine and square root, iterative approximations (Taylor's series, Newton's method) are used. Note: CoT for sine and square root requires intermediate steps involving operations like exponentiation or division, which might not be simpler.

Similar to addition findings, detailed scratchpad format improves performance over plain or reverse formats for subtraction and multiplication. Reverse is not particularly effective in multiplication. Detailed scratchpad exhibits reduced efficiency for sin and sqrt compared to +,-,×, possibly due to complexity of intermediate steps.

8.2 Jointly Training on All Five Arithmetic Tasks
Effect of jointly training on all five arithmetic tasks is studied. Single train dataset incorporating all tasks is constructed, randomizing sequence of tasks in train samples. Model performance after training on joint dataset is evaluated in zero-shot and few-shot settings, compared with models trained separately on each dataset.
Joint training significantly enhances zero-shot performance for multiplication and square root tasks, slightly reduces performance for subtraction. Few-shot prompting exhibits improved performance. Performance remains consistent regardless of whether exemplars are from unrelated tasks or task-specific, possibly due to randomized task sequence during training. Text prompting performs similar to zero-shot, possibly because training data does not include text data.

9 Mixing Shakespeare with Arithmetic Data
Both addition samples and text are incorporated into pretraining data. Shakespeare dataset is used. Number of detailed scratchpad examples and plain addition examples are fixed while varying each type in training. Shakespeare text is segmented into dialogue chunks, with random number of addition data inserted.
Few-shot prompting is assessed by providing task-specific exemplars. Plain addition formatted exemplars are used for testing plain addition inputs; detailed scratchpad formatted exemplars for detailed scratchpad formatted inputs. For each 1/2/3-shot and text prompting, average performance is reported over fixed set of exemplars.
Few-shot prompting directs enhancement of performance, allowing plain addition to perform almost perfectly with 40,000 train samples. Performance remains high on plain addition even with text prompt given substantial addition examples, possibly due to structure of mixed dataset where addition examples are interspersed within Shakespeare data.
To disentangle effects of textual content, a model is trained strictly on plain addition with enlarged vocabulary including alphabet characters. Few-shot prompting contributes to performance enhancement even when model is confined to training on single plain addition task. Noisy prompting (erroneous addition exemplars) yields performance nearly identical to few-shot prompting. Text prompts negatively influence performance when model is trained only on addition.

10 Fine-tuning, Scaling, and Pretraining in Larger Models
Focus is on bridging gap between experiments on NanoGPT and larger language models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.

Comparing NanoGPT and GPT-2. GPT-2 model with 85 million parameters is trained from scratch using character-level tokenization, jointly on text and addition tasks, adopting plain and detailed scratchpad formats. Larger model outperforms in both plain and detailed scratchpad evaluations.

Going from character-level tokenization to BPE. Transition to GPT-2 setup uses OpenAI's Tiktoken BPE tokenizer. Two training approaches: training from random initialization and fine-tuning pretrained model from Huggingface. To ensure uniform digit tokenization, spaces are included between numbers.
GPT-2 demonstrates high performance with both character-level tokenization and Tiktoken with spaces between digits. Fine-tuning pretrained model results in better performance compared to training from scratch.

GPT-3 experiments: Supervised fine-tuning. Experiments are extended to GPT-3 variants: Ada, Curie, Davinci. Models are fine-tuned using four data formatting methods: plain, reverse, simplified scratchpad, detailed scratchpad. Spaces between numbers are introduced in plain and reverse formatting for consistent tokenization.
Due to budget constraints, experiments used fine-tuning dataset of 1,000 examples, trained for 4 epochs. Performance evaluated on 1,000 disjoint examples.
Initiating with pretrained GPT-3 model significantly improves performance compared to training NanoGPT or GPT-2 from random initialization with 1000 samples. Reverse formatting and simplified scratchpad improve addition performance but adversely affect subtraction performance, possibly due to pretrained model needing to adapt to reversed approach and unlearn knowledge of plain formatting. Detailed scratchpad achieves excellent performance but with increased training and inference costs.
For sine and square root, training with 1000 samples is insufficient to generate exact answers. GPT-3 fine-tuned with 1,000 samples performs worse than NanoGPT trained with 10,000 samples.
Few-shot prompting improves performance of all three GPT-3 models, but zero-shot performance is poor. Comparisons focus on zero-shot performances.

11 Token Efficiency Across Data Formats
Cost analysis based on number of unique tokens encountered during training is conducted. Number of unique tokens is derived by multiplying number of samples with tokens per sample. Mean token count for single training example in 3-digit addition: 13 for plain, 15 for reverse, 64 for simplified scratchpad, 281 for detailed scratchpad.
Reverse formatting is most token-efficient approach. Detailed scratchpad training is more sample efficient but necessitates larger number of tokens per sample. For practical usage, both number of samples needed and token demands during training and inference should be evaluated.

12 Length Generalization
Model's ability to generalize across different digit lengths is assessed.
Training examples featuring 2-digit operands are excluded from 10,000-sample addition dataset, yielding reduced dataset of 7,655 samples with 1 or 3-digit operands. Model trained with reverse format is evaluated on test dataset containing 100 random samples of 1-digit, 2-digit, 3-digit, 4-digit additions. NanoGPT model is incapable of performing 2-digit and 4-digit additions, suggesting necessity for exposure to all digit combinations.
Model trained on 7-digit plain-formatted additions is tested on adding 8-digit numbers. Model is unable to generalize to greater number of digits beyond trained on. Similarly, model trained on 10-digit binary numbers fails to generalize to 11-digit binary additions.
Impact of detailed scratchpad formatting is explored. Model trained on additions up to 3 digits struggles to generalize to 4-digit additions; it randomly drops a single digit, erroneously perceiving it as 3-digit number.

13 Limitations
Length generalization. Finding is consistent with literature suggesting length generalization is challenging. Shaw et al. (2018), Sun et al. (2022) reported similar difficulties. Anil et al. (2022) suggests models can only perform out-of-distribution tasks by combining fine-tuning, prompting, scratchpad. Nye et al. (2021) demonstrated length generalization but only for models with >10^8 parameters.

Model/Data scale. Due to smaller scale, impact of individual components could be examined. Model limited to GPT-type decoder-only architecture, focusing on character-level tokenization. It remains uncertain if findings generalize to scale of LLMs in practice.

Beyond elementary arithmetic. Simple arithmetic operations are analyzed to isolate factors contributing to emergence.

14 Conclusion
The problem of teaching small randomly initialized transformers arithmetic operations and elementary mathematical functions using next-token prediction objective is examined. Different aspects of training data are ablated to isolate factors contributing to emergence of arithmetic capabilities.
Traditional training data is sub-optimal; training on detailed, instructive data with intermediate steps or simply reversing output improves accuracy and sample complexity. Scenarios with only arithmetic data and with text data are considered; effect of few-shot prompting, pretraining, model scale is analyzed. Detailed, chain-of-thought style data improves sample complexity but may not be efficient in terms of training and inference costs due to higher token requirements. Model generalizes to unseen examples of same number of digits, but length generalization is difficult, possibly due to inability to truly learn underlying arithmetic operation in all generality. It remains open how to curate training data to ensure model learns a particular algorithm versus approximate function map. Correct way to learn multiple operations is unclear; learning in increasing order of complexity may be beneficial if catastrophic forgetting can be circumvented.
Findings emphasize significance of high-quality, instructive data for emergence of arithmetic capabilities in transformers.
