Previous linear attention methods have limitations. They cannot be easily swapped into existing fine-tuned models. After replacing the quadratic attention mechanism, they require training new attention relations and cannot directly learn the full range of attention relations during knowledge distillation, leading to unpredictable accuracy degradation on downstream tasks. For example, Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) outperforms other baselines on MNLI (Williams et al., 2018) but shows the worst performance on Wikitext2 (Merity et al., 2016). Also, previous linear attention methods may hinder interpretability of the attention matrix or token merging/pruning (Kim et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Bolya et al., 2022) as they do not produce the full attention matrix.

The proposed method, SEA: Sparse linear attention with Estimated Attention mask, focuses on estimating the attention matrix from a pretrained teacher transformer model with O(T) complexity at inference instead of O(T²). The estimator distills knowledge (Hinton et al., 2015) from the teacher and estimates the attention matrix with O(T) complexity by fixing the second dimension to a constant value K where K << T. This results in a compressed attention matrix which can be decompressed via interpolation into an approximation of the full attention matrix during distillation. By distilling from the full attention matrix into the compressed matrix, SEA can use complex and dynamic attention information from the pretrained model and preserve task performance.
Because SEA distills knowledge from a full attention matrix, the resulting compressed and sparse attention matrices can provide interpretable attention, allowing analysis of token relationships and importance. SEA reduces the space and time complexity of attention from O(T²) to O(T) at test-time, with reduced memory and computational cost while maintaining performance similar to the original pretrained transformer model.

The method's inference stage first estimates a compressed attention matrix $\mathbf{\hat{A}}$ with O(T) complexity, then performs sparse attention after choosing O(T) important relationships inferred from $\mathbf{\hat{A}}$. Specifically, the output features of the kernel-based linear attention method Performer (Choromanski et al., 2020) are decoded to form $\mathbf{\hat{A}}$. A top-$\hat{k}$ selection is performed on $\mathbf{\hat{A}}$ to form a compressed attention mask used to generate a sparse attention mask for the final sparse attention operation. Using both kernel-based and sparse attention takes advantage of their diverse token embedding spaces (Chen et al., 2021a). The compressed estimated attention matrix $\mathbf{\hat{A}}$ is trained via knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2019) from a pretrained quadratic teacher model. Linear complexity is achieved by controlling sparsity and compression ratio in the compressed attention mask.

SEA is validated by applying it to BERT for text classification (Devlin et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018) and to OPT for causal language modeling (Zhang et al., 2022; Merity et al., 2016). Empirical results show SEA retains the performance of the quadratic teacher model in both tasks, while previous methods do not. SEA significantly outperforms the best linear attention baselines, such as Performer, in language modeling with 47.7% lower perplexity while consuming 54.2% less memory than quadratic attention.

Contributions:
* A novel, test-time linear attention mechanism (SEA) that distills knowledge from a pretrained quadratic transformer into a compressed estimated attention matrix, which is then used to create a sparse attention mask for the final attention operation. SEA is O(T) at test time.
* Demonstration of the method's efficiency and effectiveness on natural language processing tasks: text classification on GLUE and language modeling on Wikitext-2, where competitive performance with the vanilla transformer baseline is maintained.
* Proposal and code for a novel CSR tensor operation, called FlatCSR, which handles non-contiguous flatten tasks within a GPU kernel.
* Showcasing of the method's interpretability by visualizing the estimated sparse attention matrix and comparing it to the teacher's attention matrix. The estimator can estimate both self-attention and causal attention.

Related Work

Sparse Attention for Efficient Transformers.
Sparse attention uses static and dynamic attention masks. Static mask methods include Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) and BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) which introduce heuristic patterns. Other methods learn to sort or cluster tokens to better fit static masks (Tay et al., 2020a; Kitaev et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020b). TDSA (Zhu et al., 2021) learns to estimate an attention mask but still performs quadratic attention when generating dynamic sparse attention masks.

Kernel and Low-rank Methods for Efficient Transformers.
Recent works use kernel-based methods (Choromanski et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2022) or combine kernel and sparse methods (Chen et al., 2021a). Performer (Choromanski et al., 2020) uses a positive-definite kernel approximation to approximate softmax attention but has approximation errors. Cosformer (Qin et al., 2022) replaces Performer's non-linear approximate softmax with a linear operation containing a non-linear cosine-based re-weighting mechanism, but the cosine weighting is a heuristic. Scatterbrain (Chen et al., 2021a) combines sparse and low-rank methods to approximate attention but cannot straightforwardly benefit from direct attention matrix distillation.

Method: SEA

Preliminaries.
Notations: $\mQ, \mK, \mV \in \R^{T \times d}$. The attention matrix $\mA$ is $\mA = \text{softmax}(\mQ \mK^\top) \in \R^{T \times T}$. Context feature $\mC = \mA \mV \in \R^{T \times d}$. T is sequence length, d is head embedding dimension. $\odot$ denotes elementwise multiplication. K is the width of the compressed matrix. k controls the sparsity of an attention matrix. The matrix superscript $*$ (e.g., $\mA^*$) indicates a sparse matrix. Superscript $\hat{}$ (e.g., $\hat{\mA}$) refers to the compressed $T \times K$ space. $\mathbb{KL}(p, q)$ and $\text{MSE}(x, y)$ are standard KL divergence and mean-squared error. Batch and head dimensions are omitted for simplicity.

Performer (FAVOR+).
Simplified notation: $\text{FAVOR+}(\mQ, \mK, \mV) = \phi(\mQ) \times (\phi(\mK)^\top \phi(\mV)) \in \R^{T \times d}$. The mechanism scales linearly.

SEA Attention
SEA has two main phases: (1) Attention Estimation (kernel-based), and (2) Sparse Attention Mask Generation and Subsequent Sparse Attention.
In step (1), a compressed attention matrix $\hat{\mA}$ is estimated by fixing one dimension size to K, where K << T, using Performer and a decoder.
In step (2), an attention mask is built from values in $\hat{\mA}$ using a novel grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection method. The mask is interpolated to form a sparse mask on the full attention matrix $\mA$, resulting in a sparse attention matrix $\mA^*$. Then, sparse $\mA^* \mV$ multiplication is performed. Using a kernel-based estimator and a sparse attention matrix takes advantage of complementary aspects of their representation spaces (Chen et al., 2021a).

Attention Matrix Estimation.
The intuition is to compress one dimension of the matrix. The compressed attention matrix values should be similar to the full attention matrix. Performer (Choromanski et al., 2020) and a decoder are used, treating the output as the estimated attention matrix. This matrix can be interpolated to decompress into an approximation of the full attention matrix for distillation during training, or top-$\hat{k}$ selection can be performed on the compressed matrix to construct a mask for sparse attention.
Estimation starts by passing $\mQ$, $\mK$, $\mV_{\text{cat}}$ to Performer, where $\mV_{\text{cat}} = [\mV_I; \mV] \in \R^{T \times 2d}$ and $\mV_I$ is obtained by performing nearest neighbor interpolation on the identity matrix $\mI \in \R^{d \times d}$ to modify the first dimension, resulting in $\mV_I \in \R^{T \times d}$. $\mV_I$ is included because the output of Performer can be considered as the attention matrix when $\mV = \mI \in \R^{T \times T}$. Passing $\mV_I$ with $\mV$ may enable more accurate estimation by the decoder. This results in $\mC_{\text{perf}} = \text{FAVOR+}(\mQ, \mK, \mV_{\text{cat}}) \in \R^{T \times 2d}$.

CNN Decoder.
Performer's estimated output $\mC_{\text{perf}}$ is transformed with an MLP and CNN. The CNN is necessary because convolutions provide fine-grained detail among local features, which is crucial for dynamically representing complex patterns in the attention matrix. The attention matrix can be considered as a compressed 'image'.
For the decoder, $\mC_{\text{perf}}$ and the previous context $\mV$ are concatenated as $\mV^\prime_{\text{cat}}=[\mC_{\text{perf}}; \mV] \in \R^{T \times 3d}$. An MLP $\mu: \R^{3d} \mapsto \R^{d^\prime}$ is applied to obtain $\mZ = \mu(\mV^\prime_{\text{cat}}) \in \R^{T \times d^\prime}$, where $d^\prime$ is a hyperparameter for the shared hidden state size. $\mZ$ is used for estimating the attention matrix and for scalers ($\mS_{\text{mix}}$ and $\mS_{\text{prob}}$). Then, before applying the CNN on $\mZ$, MLP $\nu: \R^{d^\prime} \mapsto \R^{K c_h/c_s}$ is applied, where $c_s$ and $c_h$ are width reduction and channel expansion factors. The output $\hat{\mZ} = \nu(\mZ)$ is transposed and reshaped into $\R^{H c_h \times T \times K / c_s}$. Finally, a 2D CNN $f_\text{dec}$ is applied, treating the extra head dimension H as a channel dimension, resulting in the compressed attention matrix $\hat{\mA} = f_\text{dec}(\hat{\mZ}) \in \R^{T \times K}$. The decoder $f_\text{dec}$ results in a fixed width $\hat{\mA}$, enabling generation of dynamic patterns with linear time and space complexity. The CNN captures local patterns of the estimated compressed attention matrix. A fixed 3-layer CNN is used in experiments.

Grouped Top-$\hat{k}$ Selection.
Once the compressed attention matrix $\hat{\mA}$ is obtained, k critical values are selected for use in the final $T \times T$ sparse attention. Since top-$\hat{k}$ selection is held in the compressed $\hat{\mA}$, k is transformed to $\hat{k}$, the number of selected values in the compressed $T \times K$ attention space.
Four methods for top-$\hat{k}$ selection are proposed: per-query, per-head, per-batch, and causal-per-batch, where each method performs the top-$\hat{k}$ selection along different dimensions. For clarity, the head dimension H is included so that $\hat{\mA} \in \R^{H \times T \times K}$.
For per-query, per-head, and per-batch, the dimension of the group is gradually extended, starting from the last dimension of ${\hat A}$, so that top-$\hat{k}$ selection is held in $\R^{K}$, $\R^{T \times K}$, and $\R^{H \times T \times K}$ space for each grouping method, respectively. Consequently, $\hat{k}$ is adjusted to $\hat{k}_{\text{\tiny per-query}} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{k}_{\text{\tiny per-head}} = T\times\hat{k}$, and $\hat{k}_{\text{\tiny per-batch}} = H\times T \times\hat{k}$.
For causal-per-batch for causal attention, top-$\hat{k}$ is performed in $\R^{H \times K}$ space, with $\hat{k}_{\text{\tiny causal-per-batch}} = H\times\hat{k}$. For this, $\hat{\mA}$ is transposed to $\R^{T \times H \times K}$ and the last two dimensions are grouped without the T dimension, to avoid temporal information exchange across the time dimension.
In experiments, causal-per-batch is used, which shows strong performance in an ablation study on GLUE-MNLI (K=128, 5 epochs).

Linear Sparse Attention Mask Generation.
With $\hat{\mA}$, a sparse formatted binary mask $\mM^* \in \{0,1\}^{T \times T}$ is generated in two steps: 1) Performing grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection from the compressed $\hat{\mA}$ to generate a binary mask $\hat{\mM} \in \{0,1\}^{T \times K}$, and 2) Interpolating $\hat{\mM}$ to the sparse formatted $\mM^* \in \{0, 1\}^{T\times T}$.
For grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection, k is a hyperparameter determining the number of selected indices in each block of $\mM^*$, depending on the top-$\hat{k}$ strategy and attention matrix size. Each selection strategy has a different block shape.
Since top-$\hat{k}$ is performed on the smaller $\hat{\mA} \in \R^{T \times K}$, k is converted to a compressed $\hat{k}$ with $\hat{k}=\max(1, \round(k * K / T))$.
Once the compressed mask $\hat{\mM} \in \{0,1\}^{T \times K}$ is obtained, it is interpolated into the sparse formatted ${\mM^*} \in \{0,1\}^{T \times T}$. For very long sequences, if $\max(1, \round(k * K / T))$ evaluates to 1, interpolation to create $\mM^*$ could result in a block larger than k being computed, losing linear complexity. To avoid this, the number of pixel duplications in the block of $\mM^*$ is enforced to be $\min(k, \ceil{T/K})$, and the resulting pixels are uniformly spaced within the larger block. Since only indices where values are 1 in $\hat{\mM}$ need to be checked and 1 put in corresponding indices in $\mM^*$, the interpolation has linear complexity.

Sparse Attention and Final Output Calculation within Linear Cost

Sparse Attention Mechanism.
A re-weighted sparse attention probability $\mA^*$ is calculated by first applying a sparse masked matrix multiplication $\rho$, where $\rho(\mQ, \mK^\top, \mM^*) = \mQ\mK^\top \odot \mM^*$ followed by a softmax operation $\sigma$. The $\mQ$ and $\mK$ matrices are the same as inputs to Performer. Weights are re-scaled using $\bm{s}_{\text{prob}} \in \R^{T}$, so that $\mA^* = \bm{s}_{\text{prob}} \odot \sigma(\rho(\mQ, \mK^\top, \mM^*)) \in \R^{T \times T}$. $\rho$ is a sparse operation and $\mM^* \in \{0, 1\}^{T \times T}$ is the sparse binary mask using FlatCSR. The output of $\rho$ stores only non-zero values and indices where $\mM^*$ has value 1. The softmax $\sigma(\rho(\mQ, \mK^\top, \mM^*))$ calculates the softmax probability of non-zero values in the sparse input. After $\sigma$, each row of $\mA^*$ sums to 1. Due to high sparsity of $\mM^*$, resulting non-zero values after $\sigma$ will be higher than the ground truth attention matrix from the teacher. To account for this, the attention probability is scaled using a learned weight $\bm{s}_{\text{prob}} \in \R^{T}$, where $\bm{s}_{\text{prob}} = f_{\text{prob}}(\mZ)$ and $f_{\text{prob}}$ is a linear projection from $\R^{d^\prime} \mapsto \R$ followed by a sigmoid activation. The sparse calculation of $\rho$ is only performed where $\mM^*$ has 1, so complexity follows that of $\mM^*$, which is O(T). $\mA^*$ remains in a sparse matrix format. The context feature is calculated as $\mC = \mA^* \mV \in \R^{T \times d}$, which has linear complexity due to linear complexity of $\mA^*$ and $\mV$. $\mC$ is stored in a dense matrix format.

FlatCSR: A Modified Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) Format.
FlatCSR is an efficient implementation of the sparse attention mask generation and attention operations utilizing grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection. Initial attempts used the Coordinate List (COO) sparse format. COO is not ideal because it stores every coordinate of each non-zero point and does not take advantage of the structure from grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection. CSR sparse format is adopted instead, as it uses less memory and schedules per-row computations wisely using pre-constructed rows from grouped top-$\hat{k}$ selection.

Output Calculation.
The final output $\mC_{\text{sea}}$ combines the output of Performer and the sparse attention operation to improve the ability of the highly sparse attention matrix to look up global information. $\mC_{\text{sea}}$ is computed as a summation of two terms $\mC$ and $\mC_{\text{avg}}$, obtained from $\mA^*$ and $\hat{\mA}$ respectively.
First, the importance score of each token is calculated by averaging every row of $\hat{\mA}$, resulting in $\hat{\vi} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=0}^{T}{\hat{\mA}_{t, :}} \in \R^{K}$. $\hat{\vi}$ is interpolated to $\vi \in \R^{T}$ and then weighted average pooling is performed: $\mC_{\text{avg}} = \vi^\top \mV \in \R^{d}$. In causal attention, $\mC_{\text{avg}}$ is replaced with an accumulated average of tokens in $\mV$ such that $\mV_j = \frac{1}{j} \sum_{i=1}^j \mV_i$.
$\mC_{\text{avg}}$ and $\mC$ are mixed using learned weight $\bm{s}_{\text{mix}} = f_{\text{pool}}(\mZ) \in \R^{T}$, with $f_{\text{pool}}$ composed of a linear transformation and sigmoid activation $f_{\text{pool}}: \R^{d^\prime} \mapsto \R$. $\mC_{\text{sea}}$ is calculated as $\mC_{\text{sea}} = \bm{s}_{\text{mix}} \odot \mC + (1-\bm{s}_{\text{mix}}) \odot \mC^\top_{\text{avg}}$.

Training SEA Attention
For training SEA, the attention mechanism of a pretrained teacher transformer model is replaced with the SEA attention mechanism. Knowledge distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015) is used to train the newly added SEA attention parameters while adapting original weights to SEA attention. The training scheme is similar to previous transformer KD work (Jiao et al., 2019) as context features and attention matrices are approximated. An objective is added for the compressed estimated attention matrix $\hat{\mA}$ to match the teacher attention matrix.
With $\mathcal{L}^{(i)}$ signifying a loss for layer i, the overall training loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sea}}$ is:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sea}} = \frac{1}{L}\left(\sum_{i=1}^L \mathcal{L}_{\text{approx}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{prob}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{context}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{kd}}^{(i)} \right) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{kd\_task}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$

To calculate $\mathcal{L}_{\text{approx}}$, nearest neighbor interpolation is performed on the estimated attention matrix $\hat{\mA}_i$ to get $\mA^\prime_i \in \R^{T \times T}$ to match the shape of teacher attention matrix $\tilde{\mA}_i \in \R^{T \times T}$. Then KL divergence and MSE loss are applied between $\mA^\prime_i$ and $\tilde{\mA}_i$: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{approx}}^{(i)} = \mathbb{KL}(\mA^\prime_i, \tilde{\mA}_i) + \text{MSE}(\mA^\prime_i, \tilde{\mA}_i)$.
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{prob}}^{(i)} = \mathbb{KL}(\mA_i, \tilde{\mA}_i) + \text{MSE}(\mA_i, \tilde{\mA}_i)$ minimizes error between student's $\mA_i$ and teacher's $\tilde{\mA}_i$ attention matrices. For $\mathcal{L}_{\text{prob}}^{(i)}$, dense student attention $\mA_i = \sigma(\mQ_i \mK_i^\top)$ is calculated during training.
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{context}}^{(i)} = \text{MSE}(\mC_{\text{sea}}^{(i)}, \tilde{\mC}^{(i)})$ minimizes error between attention context feature $\mC_{\text{sea}}^{(i)}$ and teacher context feature $\tilde{\mC}^{(i)} \in \R^{T \times d}$.
To minimize error of each transformer layer (after attention layer and MLP), outputs of each layer $\mO_{\text{sea}}^{(i)}, \tilde{\mO}^{(i)} \in \R^{N \times T \times H*d}$ for SEA and teacher are gathered and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{kd}}^{(i)} = \text{MSE}(\mO_{\text{sea}}^{(i)}, \tilde{\mO}^{(i)})$ is calculated.
The loss for training the i-th layer is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sea}}^{(i)}$, a weighted sum of each layerwise loss: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sea}}^{(i)} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{approx}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{prob}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{context}}^{(i)} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{kd}}^{(i)}$. Weight terms on each sub-task loss are omitted for simplicity.
Knowledge distillation loss from model output logits is calculated: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{kd\_task}} = \mathbb{KL}(\mP, \tilde{\mP})$, where $\mP \in \R^z$ is model output logit.
Finally, the average layer-wise loss and downstream task loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$ are summed into the SEA training loss.

Experiments

Causal Language Modeling
SEA was evaluated on language modeling on Wikitext2 (Merity et al., 2016) with various OPT (Zhang et al., 2022) variants, which involves causal attention.
Baselines: Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) and Performer (Choromanski et al., 2020), representing sparse attention and kernel-based linear attention methods.
Reformer shows unpredictable performance between tasks, exhibiting strong performance in text classification and the worst result in causal language modeling. SEA performs best in both cases with the closest perplexity score to vanilla OPT and surpasses the quadratic attention model on OPT-125M. A trade-off between computational cost and perplexity is shown. SEA exhibits more latency because it uses both kernel-based and sparse attention. The latency and memory trade-off is discussed. Even though SEA uses both Performer and sparse attention modules, the convergence rate is much faster than both solo baselines due to direct attention distillation from the quadratic teacher.

Text Classification
Text classification evaluation of SEA was performed on the GLUE (Wang et al., 2018) benchmark with BERT (Devlin et al., 2018). SEA attention was trained by adapting to the fine-tuned model.
A trade-off between computational costs and various performance scores is shown. Baseline methods tested: Reformer, Sinkhorn (Tay et al., 2020b), Performer, Cosformer (Qin et al., 2022), and Synthesizer (Tay et al., 2020a). In all tested subsets, SEA achieves top performance and maintains competitive latency and memory costs. Results of tested baselines within the same constraints are shown by limiting all baselines and the method to have the same bucket size in sparse attentions and the same number of random projection feature sizes in kernel-based attentions. The method achieves higher accuracy than all linear baselines while maintaining competitive performance in latency and memory usage. SEA comes within 0.1% accuracy of quadratic attention on MNLI. It is shown that k can be dynamically adjusted after training to outperform quadratic attention.

Dynamically Adjusting k
Experiments with dynamically adjusting k after training with a fixed value of k on Wikitext2 and MNLI dataset show that increasing k also increases accuracy without further training. This means after fine-tuning SEA, the model still preserves pretrained knowledge and increases accuracy when the constraint on k is relaxed. This characteristic helps design flexible and dynamic models that adapt to real-time service demands and cost constraints by dynamically adjusting k. Lower k leads to lower computational cost. If a situation calls for lower computational cost, k can be minimized; if accuracy is more important, k can be set higher in real-time. Increasing k after training makes the model perform better than the vanilla quadratic model. The vanilla baseline shows a perplexity score of 29.2, but all SEA models (k=32, 64,128) surpass this when k is increased after training.

Efficiency of SEA Attention Computation
Memory usage and latency experiment results with different sequence lengths T are provided. Resource usage tendency is O(T). SEA attention was tested with the causal per-batch top-$\hat{k}$ grouping mode with FlatCSR implementation.

Peak Memory Usage.
Peak memory usage in megabytes for each attention method is compared. Compared to baselines, SEA shows competitive peak memory usage. There is an 81.05% reduction in peak memory usage compared to quadratic attention at sequence length 2¹³. The method consumes memory only about 78.81% compared to Reformer, while consistently maintaining higher accuracy. The method operates with a competitive memory budget with other linear attention methods on all sequence lengths, while quadratic attention exceeds memory capacity above 2¹³. The method reduces memory complexity to O(T) and exhibits less memory usage than Reformer.

Latency.
Latency between SEA and linear attention baselines is compared, showing that SEA scales linearly. The model incurs 32.72% of the latency cost of quadratic attention for a sequence length of 2¹³ where quadratic attention runs out of memory. SEA shows better performance with similar latency to Reformer. A latency-accuracy trade-off exists where some baselines such as Sinkhorn, Cosformer, and Performer show better latency but worse accuracy than SEA.
Latency of each component is broken down. Dense operations use 47.45%, FlatCSR sparse operations use 46.28%, and other operations (mainly permute and reshape) comprise 6.27% of latency. In the COO sparse format, dense operations use 13.31%, and COO sparse operations comprise 86.68% of latency cost. The COO format is 6.63× slower than FlatCSR format.

Visualization of Estimated Attention from SEA Attention
Using BERT and the MNLI dataset, the interpolated estimated attention matrix $\hat{\mA}$ from SEA is visualized and compared with the attention matrix of the teacher model $\tilde{\mA}$. The learned estimator shows ability to predict various attention shapes from the original fine-tuned BERT model. The estimator learns well-known fixed patterns, such as the diagonal, and dynamic patterns that require contextual interpretation.
Visualization of causal attention commonly used in generative models shows a diagonal attention probability with wavy or chunked diagonal lines, patterns not handled by previous heuristic linear attention mask patterns. The estimator shows predictions on such highly variant patterns.
The compressed attention $\hat{\mA}$, top-k compressed mask $\hat{\mM}$, sparse mask $\mM^*$, and sparse attention $\mA^*$ are shown.
The model can perform well even if estimated attention is slightly different from the teacher's, thanks to grouped top-k, which drops all values not selected in the top-k procedure. For example, a sparse attention matrix after masking the estimated matrix with grouped top-k selection masks is shown. Although the estimated attention matrix seems somewhat different from the teacher's, the resulting sparse attention pattern is quite similar to the teacher's after applying the top-k mask.

Conclusion and Discussion
The proposed method, SEA attention, shows state-of-the-art performance for integrating linear attention with pretrained transformers. The critical change over existing works is estimating the attention matrix in a compressed size using kernel-based linear attention to form a compressed sparse attention mask which can be decompressed into a full sparse attention mask to overcome quadratic cost. This preserves dynamic and complex attention patterns of the pretrained teacher transformer model through direct attention matrix distillation. SEA also provides interpretable attention patterns. SEA performs similarly to vanilla attention while existing works could not. Future research may apply a learnable masking method instead of top-$\hat{k}$ selection, such as concrete masking (Pan et al., 2021), or improve uniform interpolation by non-uniform or learnable interpolation for further performance increases.

Title: Training Dynamics of Graph Neural Networks in Function Space

Abstract:
A goal in deep learning is to characterize the learning behavior of models. For graph neural networks (GNNs), work has formalized what functions they can represent, but whether GNNs learn desired functions during optimization is less clear. This work studies their training dynamics in function space. Gradient descent optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages the graph structure to update the learned function, as quantified by a phenomenon called kernel-graph alignment. Theoretical explanations for this phenomenon are provided for the overparameterized regime, with empirical validation on real-world GNNs. This finding offers insights into when and why the learned GNN functions generalize, highlighting limitations in heterophilic graphs. A parameter-free algorithm is proposed that directly uses a sparse adjacency matrix to update the learned function. This approach can be as effective as GNNs while being orders-of-magnitude faster.

1 Introduction
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [gori2005new, scarselli2008graph, bruna2014spectral, kipf2016semi] are network architectures for learning on entities with relations. Theoretical work has dissected GNNs in terms of representation power or expressiveness [maron2019provably, xu2018powerful, oono2019graph, chen2019equivalence], which aims to answer what families of functions GNNs can represent. However, it remains unclear whether GNNs will learn the desired function during training. This gap calls for attention to the optimization of GNNs and effects of graph structures that bias the learning process. This paper analyzes the training dynamics of GNNs in function space, aiming to answer: Do GNNs indeed learn the desired function that can generalize during the training process, and if so, how?

The exact mathematical characterization of neural network optimization is prohibitive due to non-linearity. Existing work resorts to simplifications, such as removing activations (e.g., [xu2021optimization] for GNNs) or training a single neuron (e.g., [bai2019beyond, frei2020agnostic]). Insights from different angles exist for illuminating certain mechanisms (e.g., [cao2019towards, papyan2020prevalence, he2019local]). This work provides initial answers by studying the role of graph structures. Informally: The optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages the graph structure, as quantified by kernel-graph alignment, to learn functions that can generalize.

Formally, Kernel-Graph Alignment characterizes a graph implicit bias during training, where the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [jacot2018neural] that controls the evolution of the learned GNN function tends to align with the message passing matrix (typically graph adjacency) used in GNNs' forward pass. This result is useful for understanding GNN optimization and allows explaining previously unresolved theoretical questions and developing practical algorithms.

Contributions are summarized:
Warm-Up Example: Residual Propagation. A class of learning algorithms is proposed that replaces the NTK matrix in training dynamics with a sparse adjacency matrix, representing an extreme case of perfect kernel-graph alignment. This method is called Residual Propagation (RP) as it minimizes loss and yields predictions by propagating residuals without trainable parameters or back-propagation. The algorithm has connections with label propagation [zhou2003learning] and kernel regression [shawe2004kernel]. Empirical evidence across 15 benchmarks, including three OGBN datasets, shows this method has generalization performance competing with non-linear GNNs. It offers up to thousands of times speedup and requires ten times less memory due to linear complexity. This algorithm serves as an example illustrating the inner mechanism of GNNs' optimization. (Section 2)
Implicit Leverage of Graphs in Optimization. The training dynamics of GNNs are formally studied. To make analysis tractable, the training dynamics are examined in the overparameterized regime [jacot2018neural, lee2019wide], where the model asymptotically converges to its first-order Taylor expansion around initialization. Message passing modules and non-linearities are preserved. Explicit mathematical formulas are provided for recurrently computing the NTK of GNNs (node-level GNTK) with arbitrary model depth and inputs. The formula demonstrates how graph structure integrates into the kernel function, inducing kernel-graph alignment. Additional examples of shallow GNNs with fixed inputs show cases where the kernel function becomes equivalent to special forms of adjacency. (Section 3)
Generalization and Failure Modes. Interpretable explanations are provided for how graph implicit bias in optimization leads to generalization, and why GNNs struggle with problems such as heterophily. An optimal kernel matrix is introduced, which denotes if a pair of instances share the same label. The alignment of this matrix with the adjacency matrix quantifies the homophily level of the graph [zhu2020beyond], a data characteristic relevant to GNNs' generalization. For homophilic graphs, a larger homophily level with good kernel-graph alignment indicates the kernel function approaches the optimal one (kernel-target alignment [cristianini2001kernel]); this is desired for favorable generalization, as labels of training instances tend to flow to testing instances with the same label during optimization. Theoretically, a strong correlation between generalization and homophily is established by deriving a data-dependent generalization bound that depends on graph heterophily, and showing GNNs are the Bayesian optimal prior model architecture that minimizes population risk on homophilic graphs. (Section 4)
Empirical Verification. The evolution of real-world GNNs during GD-based training is numerically studied on synthetic and real-world datasets. Their NTKs align with the message passing matrix used in the forward pass. On homophilic graphs, alignment with the graph promotes alignment with the optimal kernel matrix and improves generalization, whereas on heterophilic graphs, it adversely affects generalization. GNNs are capable of gradually adapting to align with the optimal kernel regardless of different graph structures. (Section 5)
The analysis may explain a limited part of a complex problem. The analytical framework may pave the way for dissecting other graph learning tasks and gaining insights into other GNN issues. (Section 6)

2 Preliminary
Notation and Setup. Given a training set with n_l labeled instances X = {x_i}_{i=1}^{n_l} ∈ R^{n_l× d} and Y = {y_i}_{i=1}^{n_l} ∈ R^{n_l}, the aim is to learn a predictive function f(x) parameterized by weights W. For (semi-)supervised learning, the squared loss L is minimized using Gradient Descent (GD),
L = ‖ F_t - Y ‖^2/2, ∂ W_t/∂ t = - η ∇_W L,
where W_t and F_t = {f_t(x)}_{x ∈ X} ∈ R^{n_l} are weights and predictions for the training set at optimization time index t, and η is the learning rate. Temporal discretization with time-step Δ t = 1 yields fixed step-size GD. Let X' and Y' denote testing instances, and X̄ = [X, X'] ∈ R^{n× d} (resp. Ȳ) the concatenation of training and testing inputs (resp. labels), where n is the full dataset size. f_t(x) is prediction for a single data point, allowed to depend on other nodes' information. F_t and F'_t are predictions for training and testing sets.
The focus is on learning node representations, where instances (nodes) and relations (edges) are described by an undirected graph G = (V, E), |V|=n. The graph defines a symmetric adjacency matrix A ∈ R^{n× n} where A_{ij} = 1 for connected nodes (x_i, x_j) otherwise 0. Based on data split, submatrices of A are denoted A_{XX} and A_{X'X}.
Insights apply to both transductive and inductive settings, focusing on the former unless stated.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of network architectures for learning representations on graphs. For GNNs with ReLU activation, each layer can be written as
Z^{(ℓ)} = ReLU(A Z^{(ℓ-1)} W^{(ℓ)}) ∈ R^{n× m},
where Z^{(ℓ)} are node representations at the ℓ-th layer with Z^{(0)} = X̄, and m is model width. The definition of A could differ for different GNNs. Analysis applies to arbitrary A and will not differentiate adjacency and the actual message passing matrix used.
GNN prediction for a single data point is denoted f(x; A).
Label Propagation (LP) represents a class of algorithms for semi-supervised learning, where labels Y propagate along edges to predict F'. From [zhou2003learning], the LP update equation can be written as LP(Y; k, α) =
[F_k, F'_k] = α A [F_{k-1}, F'_{k-1}] + (1-α) [Y, 0],
where [·,·] is concatenation, k is iteration number, and α is a hyperparameter. Initialization [F_0, F'_0] = [Y, 0], and after convergence [F_∞, F'_∞] ∝ (I_n - α A)^{-1} [Y, 0]. LP algorithms have efficiency and scalability.

3 Graph Implicit Bias in Training
A label propagation perspective on the evolution of a general parameterized model during GD-based optimization is provided, whereby a simple non-parametric algorithm for semi-supervised learning is proposed. The algorithm shows that explicitly leveraging graph structure in training dynamics to update the learned function leads to satisfactory generalization performance comparable to non-linear GNNs. This serves as an illustrative example, later contributing to understanding GNN optimization where they implicitly leverage graph structures.
3.1 Label Propagation View of Gradient Descent
On the training set, the evolution of a general parameterized model f(·), induced by GD-based optimization that updates weights W_t, is characterized as [jacot2018neural]:
∂F_t /∂ t = η Θ_t(X, X) R_t
Θ_t(X, X) ≜ ∇_W F_t^⊤ ∇_W F_t ∈ R^{n_l× n_l},
where R_t = Y - F_t ∈ R^{n_l} denotes residuals (errors). The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [jacot2018neural] Θ_t(X, X) is produced by the product of Jacobians, dependent on network architecture and evolves over time. It quantifies similarity between instances based on how differently their outputs change by an infinitesimal perturbation of weights. If the kernel is constant, the dynamics reduce to kernel regression [shawe2004kernel].
Residual Dynamics. While the equation has found usage for analyzing convergence of empirical risk [du2019gradientb, arora2019fine] and spectral bias [mei2019mean, cao2019towards], it is restricted to training samples. To see how the model evolves on arbitrary inputs, the equation is extended to accommodate unseen samples:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η Θ_t(X̄, X̄) [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t],
where Θ_t(X̄, X̄) ≜ ∇_W [F_t, F'_t]^⊤ ∇_W [F_t, F'_t] ∈ R^{n× n} is the NTK matrix between training and testing sets. The n× n matrix is abbreviated Θ_t. The equation can be viewed as propagating residuals unidirectionally from training to arbitrary unseen samples based on a similarity measure.
To provide intuitions, rewrite for an arbitrary unseen data point x':
f_{t+1}(x') = f_{t}(x') + η ∑_{x ∈ X} Θ_t(x, x')( y(x) - f_t(x) ),
where y(x) is ground-truth label for x, and Θ_t(x, x') = ∇_W f(x)^⊤ ∇_W f(x'). For an unseen instance x' more similar to x, more ground-truth label information y(x) propagates to x'. For f_t(x)≠ 0, ground-truth label is adjusted by subtracting current prediction, enabling propagation to diminish as residuals are minimized.
Drawing an analogy between the equation induced by optimization and instance-wise propagation schemes in graph learning, the hypothesis is: For GNNs, its optimization process implicitly leverages graph structure to update the learned function by aligning their Θ_t with certain forms of A, which is a key factor contributing to generalization.
3.2 Residual Propagation
To test this hypothesis, a toy algorithm is proposed that explicitly introduces graph structure into training dynamics, by replacing NTK matrix Θ_t with high-order graph adjacency matrix A^K. Such replacement allows implementing it as a practically useful semi-supervised algorithm that can efficiently run, taking advantage of A sparsity. This algorithm is called Residual Propagation (RP), with update equation:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^K [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t].
At initialization, F_0 and F'_0 are 0, and unknown testing labels Y' = 0. Predictions can be converted from R'_t. More generally, A^K can be replaced with other matrices indicating similarity.
RP has connections with LP [zhou2003learning] and kernel regression [shawe2004kernel].
Proposition 1 (Connection with Label Propagation). The first step of RP yields identical classification results as LP (with α = 1 and k = K):
(First Step of RP): [F_1, F'_1] = η A^K [Y, 0],
(Label Propagation): LP(Y;K, 1) = A^K [Y, 0],
and each subsequent step of RP can be viewed as LP on adjusted ground-truth labels, i.e. Y - F_t = R_t.
Each subsequent step can be written as:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η LP^*(R_t) + [R_t, R'_t],
where LP^*(·): R^{n_l} → R^{n} is a general LP function.
Theorem 1 (Convergence & Connection with Kernel Regression). For RP and sufficiently small step size η < 2 σ^{-1}_{max}[A^K_{XX}], where A^K_{XX} is a submatrix of A^K, and σ_{max} is its largest eigenvalue, R_t and R'_t converge for positive definite A^K_{XX} or positive semi-definite A^K. Upon convergence in the former case, predictions are equivalent to kernel regression solution w.r.t. kernel κ(x, x') ≜ A^K_{xx'}
F_∞ = Y, F'_∞ = A^K_{X'X}(A^K_{XX})^{-1} Y.
Different from kernel regression, RP might not necessarily converge since it does not restrict propagation matrix to be PSD or symmetric. It can achieve generalization by stopping at step with peak validation performance.
3.3 Preliminary Empirical Verification
Since RP represents an extreme case of perfect kernel-graph alignment, its performance is tested against GNNs to verify whether graph implicit bias in optimization is crucial for performance.
Setup. RP is compared with standard GNN architectures (LinearGNN [wu2019simplifying] and GCN [kipf2016semi]) on 15 datasets, including three OGB [hu2020open] datasets Arxiv, Proteins, Products with up to millions of nodes.
Results. RP demonstrates competitive performance. RP achieves same performance as LP using one step, and increases until peak performance, often surpassing GNNs. On Proteins, a single step of RP exceeds a well-trained deep GNN. In Products, four steps exceed GNN. RP does not require trainable parameters and boosts speed, each step more than 10 times faster than each GD step for training GNN. Overall takes significantly less time (up to 1000 times less) to attain GNN-level performance. RP consumes up to 10 times less memory.
Generalized RP combines with kernels (e.g. Gaussian) to incorporate node features. Update equation can be re-written as [R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^K K(X̄, X̄) A^K [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t], where K(X̄, X̄) could be arbitrary kernel functions. Tests on 12 datasets including homophilic and heterophilic ones show RP can outperform most popular GNNs.

4 Analysis in Overparameterized Regime
It is theoretically verified that optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages graph structure for updating learned function.
4.1 Insights from Explicit Formula of GNNs' NTK
Training dynamics of GNNs in node-level tasks is characterized by their NTK:
Definition 1 (Node-Level GNTK). For a ℓ-layer GNN in node-level tasks, the NTK is defined as
Θ^{(ℓ)}_t(x, x'; A) = ∇_W f(x; A)^⊤ ∇_W f(x'; A),
referred to as Node-Level Graph Neural Tangent Kernel (GNTK).
GNN evolution during training follows the extended dynamics equation. To show mathematical characterization and connection with A is impossible due to complexity. To make analysis tractable, node-level GNTK is studied in overparameterized regimes, where model width m tends to infinity, and neural networks asymptotically converge to first order Taylor expansion around initialization (e.g. [jacot2018neural, lee2019wide]), i.e. a kernel regression predictor. In this case, node-level GNTK is constant kernel Θ^{(ℓ)}. The explicit mathematical formula applies to arbitrary layer number ℓ, input features X, graph structure G, and GNN architectures conforming to definition.
Similar to fully-connected neural networks, NTK of ℓ-layer GNN can be recursively computed based on NTK of (ℓ-1)-layer GNNs. Layer-wise formula decomposes into two steps: Transformation (i.e. Z← ReLU(ZW)) and Propagation (i.e. Z← A Z) in GNN architecture. Additional elements: node-level GNTK for GNN without propagation at ℓ-th layer as Θ̄^{(ℓ)}, covariance matrix of ℓ-th layer outputs with (and w/o) propagation as Σ^{(ℓ)} (and Σ̄^{(ℓ)}), covariance matrix of derivative to ℓ-th layer as Σ̇^{(ℓ)}
(Transformation) Θ̄^{(ℓ)} = Θ^{(ℓ-1)} ⊙ Σ̇^{(ℓ)} + Σ̄^{(ℓ)}
(Propagation) { Σ^{(ℓ)}= A Σ̄^{(ℓ)} A ; Θ^{(ℓ)}=A Θ̄^{(ℓ)} A. }
Implications. Compared with NTK of fully-connected neural network [jacot2018neural], node-level GNTK has equivalent transformation step, while uniqueness stems from propagation step, whereby adjacency matrix A naturally integrates into kernel similarity measure. Consequently, kernel function inherently accommodates graph implicit bias, and gradient descent optimization of GNNs tends to follow trajectory regulated by graph, similar to RP behavior. Case studies show how training dynamics of certain shallow GNNs, given fixed inputs, can be exactly described by generalized RP framework.
Analysis for real-world finite width GNNs' NTK is provided in Section 5 to empirically corroborate insights.
4.2 Illustrative Examples
Focus is on role of graphs; external node features are excluded. Inputs defined as: 1) identity matrix X̄ ≜ I_{n} assigning each node one-hot vector as unique identity (as assumed in practice [kipf2016semi, zhu2021graph]), treating first-layer weights as embedding table; 2) fixed node embeddings from graph spectral decomposition X̄ ≜ argmin_B ‖ A - B B^⊤ ‖_F^2, aligning with network embedding approaches [qiu2018network].
Two-Layer GNN. Training of two-layer GNNs where first-layer weights are optimized:
Theorem 2 (Two-Layer GNN). For infinite width two-layer GNN defined as [F, F'] = A ReLU(A X̄ W^{(1)}) W^{(2)} / √m with X̄ = I_{n} and standard NTK parameterization, training dynamics by optimizing W^{(1)} can be written as generalized RP process
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A (A^2 ⊙ S) A [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t],
S_{ij} = (π - arccos( (A_i^⊤ A_j)/(‖ A_i ‖ ‖ A_j ‖) ))/(2π).
Matrix S reweights each element in A^2 by similarity of neighborhood distributions.
Deep and Wide GNNs. Evolution of arbitrarily deep GNNs where feature propagation applied at last layer (e.g. [klicpera2018predict, liu2020towards, spinelli2020adaptive, chien2020adaptive]), i.e. f(X;A, W) = A^{ℓ} MLP(X; W).
Theorem 3 (Deep and Wide GNN Dynamics). For arbitrarily deep and infinitely-wide GNNs with feature propagation deferred to last layer, i.e. [F, F'] = A^{ℓ} MLP(X̄) with X̄ = I_{n}, training dynamics from optimizing MLP weights can be written as generalized RP process [R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^{ℓ} (I_n + c 1 1^⊤) A^{ℓ} [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t], where c ≥ 0 constant determined by model depth, 1 all-1 column vector.
Linear GNNs. Linear GNN (SGC [wu2019simplifying]) training dynamics equivalent to special case of RP:
Corollary 1 (One-Layer GNN). Training dynamics of linear GNN [F, F'] = A^ℓ X̄ W is identical to basic RP with K = 2ℓ for input features X̄ = I_{n}, and K = 2ℓ + 1 for X̄ = argmin_B ‖ A - B B^⊤ ‖_F^2 and positive semi-definite A.
Remark. This linear GNN parameter number scales with dataset size, and full-rank spectral decomposition of A is computationally expensive (n^3) for large graphs. RP efficiently yields identical results without training parameters or decomposing matrix. In practice, RP consistently performs better than linear GNN, since real-world input feature is tall matrix.
Other examples exist where NTK of GNNs identical to special forms of adjacency.

5 Generalization and Heterophily
Interpretable explanations of when and why GNNs generalize and pathological training behavior on heterophilic graphs are offered. Time evolution of real-world GNN NTKs is studied to empirically verify theoretical results.
5.1 When and Why GNNs Generalize?
Discussions revolve around graph adjacency matrix A and NTK matrix Θ_t. An optimal kernel matrix [cristianini2001kernel] is introduced, defined as Θ^* ≜ Ȳ Ȳ^⊤ ∈ R^{n× n} to indicate whether two instances have same label, and a metric to quantify alignment:
Definition 2 (Alignment, [cristianini2001kernel]). Given two matrices K_1 and K_2, alignment defined as A(K_1, K_2)≜⟨ K_1, K_2⟩_F/(‖ K_1 ‖_F ‖ K_2 ‖_F) ∈[0,1]. This generalizes cosine similarity from vectors to matrices.
Homophily Level: A(A, Θ^*). Alignment between A and Θ^* quantifies homophily level of graph structure, i.e. whether connected nodes have same label, determined by dataset. High homophily level is important for GNN performance [zhu2020beyond].
Kernel-Target Alignment: A(Θ_t, Θ^*). Alignment between kernel matrix and optimal Θ^* studied and used as objective for learning kernels [cristianini2001kernel, kwok2003learning, lanckriet2004learning, gonen2011multiple]. Better kernel-target alignment leads to favorable generalization for classic non-parametric models. Substituting Θ^* to training dynamics leads to perfect generalization.
Kernel-Graph Alignment: A(Θ_t, A). Alignment between NTK and graph is novel; prior sections show GNN NTK matrices naturally tend to align with A. RP serves as extreme case.
Implications. Two cases. For homophilic graphs where A(A, Θ^*) is large, better kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) leads to better kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*). NTK of GNNs approaches optimum as graph possesses homophily, leveraging it in optimization encourages training residuals to flow to unseen samples with same label for better generalization. For heterophilic graphs where A(A, Θ^*) small, better kernel-graph alignment hinders kernel-target alignment, explaining pathological learning behavior on heterophilic graphs.
5.2 Theoretical Results
Generalization behavior of infinitely-wide neural networks examined in extreme case where NTK matrix governed by graph, e.g., lim_{k→∞} ∑_{i=0}^{k}(α A)^i with α ∈ (0,1) as adopted by converged LP. With assumption training instances drawn i.i.d, generalization bound:
O( √(1 - c n_l^{-1} A(A, Θ^*)) + √(n_l^{-1} log (δ^{-1})) ),
where c = α ‖ Θ^* ‖_F ‖ A ‖_F constant, A(A, Θ^*) homophily level for training set. Bound demonstrates: for A(Θ_t, A) fixed as 1, higher graph homophily A(A, Θ^*) plays dominant role in better generalization. Analysis can be extended to infinitely-wide GNNs with assumptions on condition number of NTK.
In complementary setting, where objective is to find optimal a priori kernel for minimizing population risk without access to input features or ground-truth labels, when homophily assumptions imposed on graph, infinitely-wide GNNs and RP yield optimal kernel regression predictor with provably best generalization:
Theorem 4 (Bayesian Optimality of GNN). Assume underlying data generation distribution P such that probability of pair of instances having same label P(y(x_i) = y(x_j)) proportional to A_{ij} - 1/2. Then optimal kernel regression predictor minimizing population risk with squared loss has kernel matrix A.
Remark. Matrix A could vary depending on assumptions on P(y(x_i) = y(x_j)), such as A^K for basic RP, or A(A^2 ⊙ S) A for infinitely-wide two-layer GNNs. If privileged access to labels of all instances, optimal matrix is optimal kernel Θ^* and perfect generalization achieved. Result verifies interpretation: for A(A, Θ^*) fixed large, better A(Θ_t, A) leads to favorable generalization.

6 Empirical Verification
Empirically verified whether real-world GNN NTKs align with graph during training and effect on generalization.
Results reflected by alignment between Θ_t, A and Θ^*.
Synthetic Dataset. Stochastic block models [holland1983stochastic] generate synthetic dataset. Kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) for GNNs stays high regardless of graph structures, as natural result of network architecture. As homophily level A(A, Θ^*) decreases, kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*) decreases and testing accuracy drops.
Real-World Datasets. On real-world homophilic and heterophilic datasets, graph progressively coarsened until GNN degrades to MLP, analyzing effects of feature propagation. Kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) overall decreases with less graph structure, verifying results. Impact depends on homophily levels A(A, Θ^*): on homophilic dataset, more graph structure and better A(Θ_t, A) optimizes NTK matrix reflected by better kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*), but worsens on heterophilic. Results in distinct generalization behavior.
Can and How (G)NNs Handle Heterophily? Discussion on whether standard GNNs handle heterophily with diverging conclusions [zhu2020beyond, ma2021homophily, luan2022revisiting, platonov2023critical]. From training dynamics perspective:
1) Infinitely-wide GNNs sub-optimal on heterophilic graphs, MLPs have no guarantee of kernel-target alignment (since both A(A, Θ^*) and A(Θ_t, A) not well-aligned), indicating they could either generalize better or worse without clearcut (dis)advantages, as opposed to homophilic graphs where GNN provably at advantage, explaining diverse empirical results.
2) NTK time evolution shows overall increase of kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*) during training. Training enables real-world GNNs to adjust NTK feature space such that kernel matrix leans towards homophilic graph structure (Θ^*) to adapt to heterophilic datasets (consequently different evolutionary trends of A(Θ_t, A) for homophilic and heterophilic datasets). Phenomenon found for other models in vision tasks [baratin2021implicit].
Analysis applies to other forms of A for feature propagation, potentially explaining how specialized models with different A (e.g. signed propagation) mitigate heterophily.

7 Discussions
Abridged Related Work. Existing work on theoretical aspects of GNNs focuses on representation and generalization (see [jegelka2022theory]) while optimization properties under-explored [zhang2020fast, xu2021optimization, yadati2022convex, huang2023graph]. Representation work does not provide answers to what GNN functions are found during optimization. Generalization prior work insufficient to explain effects of training, and does not connect to heterophily.
Applicability and Future Directions. Analytical framework could be extended to other tasks; for graph classification, definition of GNTK modified to graph-level [du2019graph]; for link prediction and self-supervised learning, loss function adjusted. Similar message passing process in function space would hold. Framework could be adapted to analyze other GNN issues, such as over-smoothing and over-squashing. Framework can be used to study effects of different model architectures by noting definition of A associated with GNN architectures.
