Title: Training Dynamics of Graph Neural Networks in Function Space

Abstract:
A goal in deep learning is to characterize the learning behavior of models. For graph neural networks (GNNs), work has formalized what functions they can represent, but whether GNNs learn desired functions during optimization is less clear. This work studies their training dynamics in function space. Gradient descent optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages the graph structure to update the learned function, as quantified by a phenomenon called kernel-graph alignment. Theoretical explanations for this phenomenon are provided for the overparameterized regime, with empirical validation on real-world GNNs. This finding offers insights into when and why the learned GNN functions generalize, highlighting limitations in heterophilic graphs. A parameter-free algorithm is proposed that directly uses a sparse adjacency matrix to update the learned function. This approach can be as effective as GNNs while being orders-of-magnitude faster.

1 Introduction
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [gori2005new, scarselli2008graph, bruna2014spectral, kipf2016semi] are network architectures for learning on entities with relations. Theoretical work has dissected GNNs in terms of representation power or expressiveness [maron2019provably, xu2018powerful, oono2019graph, chen2019equivalence], which aims to answer what families of functions GNNs can represent. However, it remains unclear whether GNNs will learn the desired function during training. This gap calls for attention to the optimization of GNNs and effects of graph structures that bias the learning process. This paper analyzes the training dynamics of GNNs in function space, aiming to answer: Do GNNs indeed learn the desired function that can generalize during the training process, and if so, how?

The exact mathematical characterization of neural network optimization is prohibitive due to non-linearity. Existing work resorts to simplifications, such as removing activations (e.g., [xu2021optimization] for GNNs) or training a single neuron (e.g., [bai2019beyond, frei2020agnostic]). Insights from different angles exist for illuminating certain mechanisms (e.g., [cao2019towards, papyan2020prevalence, he2019local]). This work provides initial answers by studying the role of graph structures. Informally: The optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages the graph structure, as quantified by kernel-graph alignment, to learn functions that can generalize.

Formally, Kernel-Graph Alignment characterizes a graph implicit bias during training, where the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [jacot2018neural] that controls the evolution of the learned GNN function tends to align with the message passing matrix (typically graph adjacency) used in GNNs' forward pass. This result is useful for understanding GNN optimization and allows explaining previously unresolved theoretical questions and developing practical algorithms.

Contributions are summarized:
Warm-Up Example: Residual Propagation. A class of learning algorithms is proposed that replaces the NTK matrix in training dynamics with a sparse adjacency matrix, representing an extreme case of perfect kernel-graph alignment. This method is called Residual Propagation (RP) as it minimizes loss and yields predictions by propagating residuals without trainable parameters or back-propagation. The algorithm has connections with label propagation [zhou2003learning] and kernel regression [shawe2004kernel]. Empirical evidence across 15 benchmarks, including three OGBN datasets, shows this method has generalization performance competing with non-linear GNNs. It offers up to thousands of times speedup and requires ten times less memory due to linear complexity. This algorithm serves as an example illustrating the inner mechanism of GNNs' optimization. (Section 2)
Implicit Leverage of Graphs in Optimization. The training dynamics of GNNs are formally studied. To make analysis tractable, the training dynamics are examined in the overparameterized regime [jacot2018neural, lee2019wide], where the model asymptotically converges to its first-order Taylor expansion around initialization. Message passing modules and non-linearities are preserved. Explicit mathematical formulas are provided for recurrently computing the NTK of GNNs (node-level GNTK) with arbitrary model depth and inputs. The formula demonstrates how graph structure integrates into the kernel function, inducing kernel-graph alignment. Additional examples of shallow GNNs with fixed inputs show cases where the kernel function becomes equivalent to special forms of adjacency. (Section 3)
Generalization and Failure Modes. Interpretable explanations are provided for how graph implicit bias in optimization leads to generalization, and why GNNs struggle with problems such as heterophily. An optimal kernel matrix is introduced, which denotes if a pair of instances share the same label. The alignment of this matrix with the adjacency matrix quantifies the homophily level of the graph [zhu2020beyond], a data characteristic relevant to GNNs' generalization. For homophilic graphs, a larger homophily level with good kernel-graph alignment indicates the kernel function approaches the optimal one (kernel-target alignment [cristianini2001kernel]); this is desired for favorable generalization, as labels of training instances tend to flow to testing instances with the same label during optimization. Theoretically, a strong correlation between generalization and homophily is established by deriving a data-dependent generalization bound that depends on graph heterophily, and showing GNNs are the Bayesian optimal prior model architecture that minimizes population risk on homophilic graphs. (Section 4)
Empirical Verification. The evolution of real-world GNNs during GD-based training is numerically studied on synthetic and real-world datasets. Their NTKs align with the message passing matrix used in the forward pass. On homophilic graphs, alignment with the graph promotes alignment with the optimal kernel matrix and improves generalization, whereas on heterophilic graphs, it adversely affects generalization. GNNs are capable of gradually adapting to align with the optimal kernel regardless of different graph structures. (Section 5)
The analysis may explain a limited part of a complex problem. The analytical framework may pave the way for dissecting other graph learning tasks and gaining insights into other GNN issues. (Section 6)

2 Preliminary
Notation and Setup. Given a training set with n_l labeled instances X = {x_i}_{i=1}^{n_l} ∈ R^{n_l× d} and Y = {y_i}_{i=1}^{n_l} ∈ R^{n_l}, the aim is to learn a predictive function f(x) parameterized by weights W. For (semi-)supervised learning, the squared loss L is minimized using Gradient Descent (GD),
L = ‖ F_t - Y ‖^2/2, ∂ W_t/∂ t = - η ∇_W L,
where W_t and F_t = {f_t(x)}_{x ∈ X} ∈ R^{n_l} are weights and predictions for the training set at optimization time index t, and η is the learning rate. Temporal discretization with time-step Δ t = 1 yields fixed step-size GD. Let X' and Y' denote testing instances, and X̄ = [X, X'] ∈ R^{n× d} (resp. Ȳ) the concatenation of training and testing inputs (resp. labels), where n is the full dataset size. f_t(x) is prediction for a single data point, allowed to depend on other nodes' information. F_t and F'_t are predictions for training and testing sets.
The focus is on learning node representations, where instances (nodes) and relations (edges) are described by an undirected graph G = (V, E), |V|=n. The graph defines a symmetric adjacency matrix A ∈ R^{n× n} where A_{ij} = 1 for connected nodes (x_i, x_j) otherwise 0. Based on data split, submatrices of A are denoted A_{XX} and A_{X'X}.
Insights apply to both transductive and inductive settings, focusing on the former unless stated.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of network architectures for learning representations on graphs. For GNNs with ReLU activation, each layer can be written as
Z^{(ℓ)} = ReLU(A Z^{(ℓ-1)} W^{(ℓ)}) ∈ R^{n× m},
where Z^{(ℓ)} are node representations at the ℓ-th layer with Z^{(0)} = X̄, and m is model width. The definition of A could differ for different GNNs. Analysis applies to arbitrary A and will not differentiate adjacency and the actual message passing matrix used.
GNN prediction for a single data point is denoted f(x; A).
Label Propagation (LP) represents a class of algorithms for semi-supervised learning, where labels Y propagate along edges to predict F'. From [zhou2003learning], the LP update equation can be written as LP(Y; k, α) =
[F_k, F'_k] = α A [F_{k-1}, F'_{k-1}] + (1-α) [Y, 0],
where [·,·] is concatenation, k is iteration number, and α is a hyperparameter. Initialization [F_0, F'_0] = [Y, 0], and after convergence [F_∞, F'_∞] ∝ (I_n - α A)^{-1} [Y, 0]. LP algorithms have efficiency and scalability.

3 Graph Implicit Bias in Training
A label propagation perspective on the evolution of a general parameterized model during GD-based optimization is provided, whereby a simple non-parametric algorithm for semi-supervised learning is proposed. The algorithm shows that explicitly leveraging graph structure in training dynamics to update the learned function leads to satisfactory generalization performance comparable to non-linear GNNs. This serves as an illustrative example, later contributing to understanding GNN optimization where they implicitly leverage graph structures.
3.1 Label Propagation View of Gradient Descent
On the training set, the evolution of a general parameterized model f(·), induced by GD-based optimization that updates weights W_t, is characterized as [jacot2018neural]:
∂F_t /∂ t = η Θ_t(X, X) R_t
Θ_t(X, X) ≜ ∇_W F_t^⊤ ∇_W F_t ∈ R^{n_l× n_l},
where R_t = Y - F_t ∈ R^{n_l} denotes residuals (errors). The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [jacot2018neural] Θ_t(X, X) is produced by the product of Jacobians, dependent on network architecture and evolves over time. It quantifies similarity between instances based on how differently their outputs change by an infinitesimal perturbation of weights. If the kernel is constant, the dynamics reduce to kernel regression [shawe2004kernel].
Residual Dynamics. While the equation has found usage for analyzing convergence of empirical risk [du2019gradientb, arora2019fine] and spectral bias [mei2019mean, cao2019towards], it is restricted to training samples. To see how the model evolves on arbitrary inputs, the equation is extended to accommodate unseen samples:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η Θ_t(X̄, X̄) [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t],
where Θ_t(X̄, X̄) ≜ ∇_W [F_t, F'_t]^⊤ ∇_W [F_t, F'_t] ∈ R^{n× n} is the NTK matrix between training and testing sets. The n× n matrix is abbreviated Θ_t. The equation can be viewed as propagating residuals unidirectionally from training to arbitrary unseen samples based on a similarity measure.
To provide intuitions, rewrite for an arbitrary unseen data point x':
f_{t+1}(x') = f_{t}(x') + η ∑_{x ∈ X} Θ_t(x, x')( y(x) - f_t(x) ),
where y(x) is ground-truth label for x, and Θ_t(x, x') = ∇_W f(x)^⊤ ∇_W f(x'). For an unseen instance x' more similar to x, more ground-truth label information y(x) propagates to x'. For f_t(x)≠ 0, ground-truth label is adjusted by subtracting current prediction, enabling propagation to diminish as residuals are minimized.
Drawing an analogy between the equation induced by optimization and instance-wise propagation schemes in graph learning, the hypothesis is: For GNNs, its optimization process implicitly leverages graph structure to update the learned function by aligning their Θ_t with certain forms of A, which is a key factor contributing to generalization.
3.2 Residual Propagation
To test this hypothesis, a toy algorithm is proposed that explicitly introduces graph structure into training dynamics, by replacing NTK matrix Θ_t with high-order graph adjacency matrix A^K. Such replacement allows implementing it as a practically useful semi-supervised algorithm that can efficiently run, taking advantage of A sparsity. This algorithm is called Residual Propagation (RP), with update equation:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^K [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t].
At initialization, F_0 and F'_0 are 0, and unknown testing labels Y' = 0. Predictions can be converted from R'_t. More generally, A^K can be replaced with other matrices indicating similarity.
RP has connections with LP [zhou2003learning] and kernel regression [shawe2004kernel].
Proposition 1 (Connection with Label Propagation). The first step of RP yields identical classification results as LP (with α = 1 and k = K):
(First Step of RP): [F_1, F'_1] = η A^K [Y, 0],
(Label Propagation): LP(Y;K, 1) = A^K [Y, 0],
and each subsequent step of RP can be viewed as LP on adjusted ground-truth labels, i.e. Y - F_t = R_t.
Each subsequent step can be written as:
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η LP^*(R_t) + [R_t, R'_t],
where LP^*(·): R^{n_l} → R^{n} is a general LP function.
Theorem 1 (Convergence & Connection with Kernel Regression). For RP and sufficiently small step size η < 2 σ^{-1}_{max}[A^K_{XX}], where A^K_{XX} is a submatrix of A^K, and σ_{max} is its largest eigenvalue, R_t and R'_t converge for positive definite A^K_{XX} or positive semi-definite A^K. Upon convergence in the former case, predictions are equivalent to kernel regression solution w.r.t. kernel κ(x, x') ≜ A^K_{xx'}
F_∞ = Y, F'_∞ = A^K_{X'X}(A^K_{XX})^{-1} Y.
Different from kernel regression, RP might not necessarily converge since it does not restrict propagation matrix to be PSD or symmetric. It can achieve generalization by stopping at step with peak validation performance.
3.3 Preliminary Empirical Verification
Since RP represents an extreme case of perfect kernel-graph alignment, its performance is tested against GNNs to verify whether graph implicit bias in optimization is crucial for performance.
Setup. RP is compared with standard GNN architectures (LinearGNN [wu2019simplifying] and GCN [kipf2016semi]) on 15 datasets, including three OGB [hu2020open] datasets Arxiv, Proteins, Products with up to millions of nodes.
Results. RP demonstrates competitive performance. RP achieves same performance as LP using one step, and increases until peak performance, often surpassing GNNs. On Proteins, a single step of RP exceeds a well-trained deep GNN. In Products, four steps exceed GNN. RP does not require trainable parameters and boosts speed, each step more than 10 times faster than each GD step for training GNN. Overall takes significantly less time (up to 1000 times less) to attain GNN-level performance. RP consumes up to 10 times less memory.
Generalized RP combines with kernels (e.g. Gaussian) to incorporate node features. Update equation can be re-written as [R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^K K(X̄, X̄) A^K [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t], where K(X̄, X̄) could be arbitrary kernel functions. Tests on 12 datasets including homophilic and heterophilic ones show RP can outperform most popular GNNs.

4 Analysis in Overparameterized Regime
It is theoretically verified that optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages graph structure for updating learned function.
4.1 Insights from Explicit Formula of GNNs' NTK
Training dynamics of GNNs in node-level tasks is characterized by their NTK:
Definition 1 (Node-Level GNTK). For a ℓ-layer GNN in node-level tasks, the NTK is defined as
Θ^{(ℓ)}_t(x, x'; A) = ∇_W f(x; A)^⊤ ∇_W f(x'; A),
referred to as Node-Level Graph Neural Tangent Kernel (GNTK).
GNN evolution during training follows the extended dynamics equation. To show mathematical characterization and connection with A is impossible due to complexity. To make analysis tractable, node-level GNTK is studied in overparameterized regimes, where model width m tends to infinity, and neural networks asymptotically converge to first order Taylor expansion around initialization (e.g. [jacot2018neural, lee2019wide]), i.e. a kernel regression predictor. In this case, node-level GNTK is constant kernel Θ^{(ℓ)}. The explicit mathematical formula applies to arbitrary layer number ℓ, input features X, graph structure G, and GNN architectures conforming to definition.
Similar to fully-connected neural networks, NTK of ℓ-layer GNN can be recursively computed based on NTK of (ℓ-1)-layer GNNs. Layer-wise formula decomposes into two steps: Transformation (i.e. Z← ReLU(ZW)) and Propagation (i.e. Z← A Z) in GNN architecture. Additional elements: node-level GNTK for GNN without propagation at ℓ-th layer as Θ̄^{(ℓ)}, covariance matrix of ℓ-th layer outputs with (and w/o) propagation as Σ^{(ℓ)} (and Σ̄^{(ℓ)}), covariance matrix of derivative to ℓ-th layer as Σ̇^{(ℓ)}
(Transformation) Θ̄^{(ℓ)} = Θ^{(ℓ-1)} ⊙ Σ̇^{(ℓ)} + Σ̄^{(ℓ)}
(Propagation) { Σ^{(ℓ)}= A Σ̄^{(ℓ)} A ; Θ^{(ℓ)}=A Θ̄^{(ℓ)} A. }
Implications. Compared with NTK of fully-connected neural network [jacot2018neural], node-level GNTK has equivalent transformation step, while uniqueness stems from propagation step, whereby adjacency matrix A naturally integrates into kernel similarity measure. Consequently, kernel function inherently accommodates graph implicit bias, and gradient descent optimization of GNNs tends to follow trajectory regulated by graph, similar to RP behavior. Case studies show how training dynamics of certain shallow GNNs, given fixed inputs, can be exactly described by generalized RP framework.
Analysis for real-world finite width GNNs' NTK is provided in Section 5 to empirically corroborate insights.
4.2 Illustrative Examples
Focus is on role of graphs; external node features are excluded. Inputs defined as: 1) identity matrix X̄ ≜ I_{n} assigning each node one-hot vector as unique identity (as assumed in practice [kipf2016semi, zhu2021graph]), treating first-layer weights as embedding table; 2) fixed node embeddings from graph spectral decomposition X̄ ≜ argmin_B ‖ A - B B^⊤ ‖_F^2, aligning with network embedding approaches [qiu2018network].
Two-Layer GNN. Training of two-layer GNNs where first-layer weights are optimized:
Theorem 2 (Two-Layer GNN). For infinite width two-layer GNN defined as [F, F'] = A ReLU(A X̄ W^{(1)}) W^{(2)} / √m with X̄ = I_{n} and standard NTK parameterization, training dynamics by optimizing W^{(1)} can be written as generalized RP process
[R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A (A^2 ⊙ S) A [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t],
S_{ij} = (π - arccos( (A_i^⊤ A_j)/(‖ A_i ‖ ‖ A_j ‖) ))/(2π).
Matrix S reweights each element in A^2 by similarity of neighborhood distributions.
Deep and Wide GNNs. Evolution of arbitrarily deep GNNs where feature propagation applied at last layer (e.g. [klicpera2018predict, liu2020towards, spinelli2020adaptive, chien2020adaptive]), i.e. f(X;A, W) = A^{ℓ} MLP(X; W).
Theorem 3 (Deep and Wide GNN Dynamics). For arbitrarily deep and infinitely-wide GNNs with feature propagation deferred to last layer, i.e. [F, F'] = A^{ℓ} MLP(X̄) with X̄ = I_{n}, training dynamics from optimizing MLP weights can be written as generalized RP process [R_{t+1}, R'_{t+1}] = -η A^{ℓ} (I_n + c 1 1^⊤) A^{ℓ} [R_t, 0] + [R_t, R'_t], where c ≥ 0 constant determined by model depth, 1 all-1 column vector.
Linear GNNs. Linear GNN (SGC [wu2019simplifying]) training dynamics equivalent to special case of RP:
Corollary 1 (One-Layer GNN). Training dynamics of linear GNN [F, F'] = A^ℓ X̄ W is identical to basic RP with K = 2ℓ for input features X̄ = I_{n}, and K = 2ℓ + 1 for X̄ = argmin_B ‖ A - B B^⊤ ‖_F^2 and positive semi-definite A.
Remark. This linear GNN parameter number scales with dataset size, and full-rank spectral decomposition of A is computationally expensive (n^3) for large graphs. RP efficiently yields identical results without training parameters or decomposing matrix. In practice, RP consistently performs better than linear GNN, since real-world input feature is tall matrix.
Other examples exist where NTK of GNNs identical to special forms of adjacency.

5 Generalization and Heterophily
Interpretable explanations of when and why GNNs generalize and pathological training behavior on heterophilic graphs are offered. Time evolution of real-world GNN NTKs is studied to empirically verify theoretical results.
5.1 When and Why GNNs Generalize?
Discussions revolve around graph adjacency matrix A and NTK matrix Θ_t. An optimal kernel matrix [cristianini2001kernel] is introduced, defined as Θ^* ≜ Ȳ Ȳ^⊤ ∈ R^{n× n} to indicate whether two instances have same label, and a metric to quantify alignment:
Definition 2 (Alignment, [cristianini2001kernel]). Given two matrices K_1 and K_2, alignment defined as A(K_1, K_2)≜⟨ K_1, K_2⟩_F/(‖ K_1 ‖_F ‖ K_2 ‖_F) ∈[0,1]. This generalizes cosine similarity from vectors to matrices.
Homophily Level: A(A, Θ^*). Alignment between A and Θ^* quantifies homophily level of graph structure, i.e. whether connected nodes have same label, determined by dataset. High homophily level is important for GNN performance [zhu2020beyond].
Kernel-Target Alignment: A(Θ_t, Θ^*). Alignment between kernel matrix and optimal Θ^* studied and used as objective for learning kernels [cristianini2001kernel, kwok2003learning, lanckriet2004learning, gonen2011multiple]. Better kernel-target alignment leads to favorable generalization for classic non-parametric models. Substituting Θ^* to training dynamics leads to perfect generalization.
Kernel-Graph Alignment: A(Θ_t, A). Alignment between NTK and graph is novel; prior sections show GNN NTK matrices naturally tend to align with A. RP serves as extreme case.
Implications. Two cases. For homophilic graphs where A(A, Θ^*) is large, better kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) leads to better kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*). NTK of GNNs approaches optimum as graph possesses homophily, leveraging it in optimization encourages training residuals to flow to unseen samples with same label for better generalization. For heterophilic graphs where A(A, Θ^*) small, better kernel-graph alignment hinders kernel-target alignment, explaining pathological learning behavior on heterophilic graphs.
5.2 Theoretical Results
Generalization behavior of infinitely-wide neural networks examined in extreme case where NTK matrix governed by graph, e.g., lim_{k→∞} ∑_{i=0}^{k}(α A)^i with α ∈ (0,1) as adopted by converged LP. With assumption training instances drawn i.i.d, generalization bound:
O( √(1 - c n_l^{-1} A(A, Θ^*)) + √(n_l^{-1} log (δ^{-1})) ),
where c = α ‖ Θ^* ‖_F ‖ A ‖_F constant, A(A, Θ^*) homophily level for training set. Bound demonstrates: for A(Θ_t, A) fixed as 1, higher graph homophily A(A, Θ^*) plays dominant role in better generalization. Analysis can be extended to infinitely-wide GNNs with assumptions on condition number of NTK.
In complementary setting, where objective is to find optimal a priori kernel for minimizing population risk without access to input features or ground-truth labels, when homophily assumptions imposed on graph, infinitely-wide GNNs and RP yield optimal kernel regression predictor with provably best generalization:
Theorem 4 (Bayesian Optimality of GNN). Assume underlying data generation distribution P such that probability of pair of instances having same label P(y(x_i) = y(x_j)) proportional to A_{ij} - 1/2. Then optimal kernel regression predictor minimizing population risk with squared loss has kernel matrix A.
Remark. Matrix A could vary depending on assumptions on P(y(x_i) = y(x_j)), such as A^K for basic RP, or A(A^2 ⊙ S) A for infinitely-wide two-layer GNNs. If privileged access to labels of all instances, optimal matrix is optimal kernel Θ^* and perfect generalization achieved. Result verifies interpretation: for A(A, Θ^*) fixed large, better A(Θ_t, A) leads to favorable generalization.

6 Empirical Verification
Empirically verified whether real-world GNN NTKs align with graph during training and effect on generalization.
Results reflected by alignment between Θ_t, A and Θ^*.
Synthetic Dataset. Stochastic block models [holland1983stochastic] generate synthetic dataset. Kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) for GNNs stays high regardless of graph structures, as natural result of network architecture. As homophily level A(A, Θ^*) decreases, kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*) decreases and testing accuracy drops.
Real-World Datasets. On real-world homophilic and heterophilic datasets, graph progressively coarsened until GNN degrades to MLP, analyzing effects of feature propagation. Kernel-graph alignment A(Θ_t, A) overall decreases with less graph structure, verifying results. Impact depends on homophily levels A(A, Θ^*): on homophilic dataset, more graph structure and better A(Θ_t, A) optimizes NTK matrix reflected by better kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*), but worsens on heterophilic. Results in distinct generalization behavior.
Can and How (G)NNs Handle Heterophily? Discussion on whether standard GNNs handle heterophily with diverging conclusions [zhu2020beyond, ma2021homophily, luan2022revisiting, platonov2023critical]. From training dynamics perspective:
1) Infinitely-wide GNNs sub-optimal on heterophilic graphs, MLPs have no guarantee of kernel-target alignment (since both A(A, Θ^*) and A(Θ_t, A) not well-aligned), indicating they could either generalize better or worse without clearcut (dis)advantages, as opposed to homophilic graphs where GNN provably at advantage, explaining diverse empirical results.
2) NTK time evolution shows overall increase of kernel-target alignment A(Θ_t, Θ^*) during training. Training enables real-world GNNs to adjust NTK feature space such that kernel matrix leans towards homophilic graph structure (Θ^*) to adapt to heterophilic datasets (consequently different evolutionary trends of A(Θ_t, A) for homophilic and heterophilic datasets). Phenomenon found for other models in vision tasks [baratin2021implicit].
Analysis applies to other forms of A for feature propagation, potentially explaining how specialized models with different A (e.g. signed propagation) mitigate heterophily.

7 Discussions
Abridged Related Work. Existing work on theoretical aspects of GNNs focuses on representation and generalization (see [jegelka2022theory]) while optimization properties under-explored [zhang2020fast, xu2021optimization, yadati2022convex, huang2023graph]. Representation work does not provide answers to what GNN functions are found during optimization. Generalization prior work insufficient to explain effects of training, and does not connect to heterophily.
Applicability and Future Directions. Analytical framework could be extended to other tasks; for graph classification, definition of GNTK modified to graph-level [du2019graph]; for link prediction and self-supervised learning, loss function adjusted. Similar message passing process in function space would hold. Framework could be adapted to analyze other GNN issues, such as over-smoothing and over-squashing. Framework can be used to study effects of different model architectures by noting definition of A associated with GNN architectures.

title: Rep-Adapter: Parameter-free Automatic Adaptation of Pre-trained ConvNets via Re-parameterization

\title{Rep-Adapter: Parameter-free Automatic Adaptation of Pre-trained ConvNets via Re-parameterization}

\begin{abstract}
Recent advances in visual pre-training have demonstrated the advantage of transferring pre-trained models to target tasks. However, different transfer learning protocols have distinctive advantages regarding target tasks, and are nontrivial to choose without repeated trial and error. This paper presents a parameter-free automatic model adaptation protocol for ConvNets, aiming at automatically balancing between fine-tuning and linear probing, by using adaptive learning rate for each convolution filters on target tasks. First, we propose Rep-Adapter, an adapter module with re-parameterization scheme, which can achieve soft balancing between the pre-trained and fine-tuned filters, and can be equivalently converted to a single weight layer, without introducing additional parameters to the inference phase. We show by theoretical analysis that Rep-Adapter can simulate a ConvNet layer with each filter fine-tuning at different learning rate. We present a simple adapter tuning protocol with Rep-Adapter to achieve automatic adaptation of pretrained models without additional search cost. Extensive experiments on various datasets with ResNet and CLIP demonstrate the superiority of our Rep-Adapter on semi-supervised, few-shot and full dataset transfer learning scenarios.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Recent advances in both computer vision and neural language processing field have demonstrated the advantage of transferring large-scale pre-trained models to downstream tasks. To leverage the information of the pre-trained models, there emerges different transfer learning protocols such as fine-tuning directly on the new task (Girshick et al., 2014), feature-based methods (Turian et al., 2010) that only update the parameters of the task-specific head, and adapter tuning (Houlsby et al., 2019) that introduces new learnable modules to adapt some layers in the original model.  

The most suitable choice of the protocols depends on many factors, including target dataset size, label fraction, etc. For instance, fine-tuning is usually more powerful on fully-supervised ImageNet, while linear probing are sometimes better on semi-supervised ImageNet (Zhou et al., 2022a). We also observe a similar trend on Caltech101 dataset. As in shown in Figure 1, fine-tuning outperforms linear probing for full dataset transfer on Caltech101 (dataset B in the figure), while linear probing performs better for low-shot (1000 examples) scenario. Moreover, when taking partial fine-tuning and layer-wise learning rate adjustment into consideration, the option space becomes computationally prohibitive for an extensive search. Therefore, we believe there is an urgent need of designing an automatic transfer learning protocol that can combine the advantages of these protocols without tediously searching for hyper-parameter settings.  

There exists some preliminary attempts to avoid manually tuning layer-wise and filter-wise hyperparameter settings. SpotTune (Guo et al., 2019) and AdaFilter (Guo et al., 2020b) dynamically route between frozen and learnable weights, at a cost of having more than twice the original model size during inference. AutoLR (Ro & Choi, 2021) searches for layer-wise fine-tuning learning rate via repeated trial. However, these methods introduce either policy networks or repeated training loops, increasing the training or inference cost. We thus explore a simple model adaptation method, without introducing extra training steps or extra parameters during inference.  

In this paper, we introduce Rep-Adapter, a novel adapter module that achieves soft balancing between the pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each adapter module has two branches, a frozen branch with the pre-trained parameters, and a learnable branch that adapts on the target tasks. During inference, we leverage the re-parameterization scheme to equivalently convert the two branches into one, avoiding the increase in model size and computational cost.  

In addition, we prove that, during training, our RepAdapter is equivalent to a layer fine-tuned by a finegrained transfer learning protocol with different learning rate for each fliter. This eliminates the need of tedious hyper-parameter search for learning rate configurations like previous methods. By optimizing a network stacked by Rep-Adapter, the pre-trained model can be transferred with adaptive learning rate for each filter. As such, finetuning and linear probing can be achieved by learning the learning rate to a certain value or zero.  

![](images/12bb18b4718e6ff9b15bb8d739f52ccb88bc89774790055c43deb1fccaad2d7a.jpg)  
Figure 1: Comparison of fine-tuning, linear probing and our proposed RepAdapter. Dataset A: DTD for texture classification; B: Caltech101 for object identification; C: EuroSAT for satellite image classification. Models are pre-trained on ImageNet with a selfsupervised method, PIRL.  

We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate and analysis our method. We use VISSL (Goyal et al., 2021) library to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on full dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning scenarios. We adapt models from several different pre-training protocols (fully-supervised pre-training and three state-of-the-art self-supervised pre-training methods on ImageNet, CLIP pre-training with text supervision), to various downstream datasets, and on fullshot, low-shot (1000 examples) or few-shot (16-shot) scenarios. We also perform experiments on semi-supervised ImageNet, by adapting models pre-trained by 3 different self-supervised learning methods to ImageNet with $1\%$ and $10\%$ label fraction. Moreover, we explore the transferability to VOC object detection and Cityscapes, COCO instance segmentation tasks. Our Rep-Adapter tuning protocol consistently surpasses the baselines across tasks and scenarios, which clearly evidences the effectiveness and generalization ability of our method.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Transfer Learning via Model Adaptation. Model adaptation methods modify a pre-trained model to achieve higher performance on a target task. Figure 2 illustrates popular model adaptation methods in computer vision field. Feature-based methods (Figure 2 (a)), including linear classification, directly learn task specific head on frozen features (Turian et al., 2010). Fine-tuning (Girshick et al., 2014) is the most generally used transfer learning protocol (Figure 2 (b)). Some works regularize the distance between the fine-tuned model and the pretrained model on the network parameters (e.g., $L^{2}$ -SP (Li et al., 2018)) or the output features (e.g., DELTA (Li et al., 2019)) to improve the performance, but the weight of the regularization comes a hand-crafted hyper-parameter. Some works (Furlanello et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2017) use network ensemble to boost the performance by combining the frozen and learnable weights, at a cost of using $M\times$ model size $M$ is the number of ensemble models) during inference. Adapter tuning (Yin et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Houlsby et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2020) (Figure 2 (c)) adds light-weight modules on the pre-trained network to adapt the model without changing its original parameters. Previous works on convolution adapter modules (Rebuffi et al., 2017; 2018; Rosenfeld & Tsotsos, 2018) perform incremental learning by adding small point-wise convolution adapter modules, at a cost of about $11\%$ increase in model size for each tasks. Our Rep-Adapter is also related to ensemble methods. However, an ensemble of models can not be directly converted to a single model due to the non-linearity in the models and thus much larger than us in terms of parameters and computation complexity. Different from previous methods, Rep-Adapter does not increase inference model size, which accelerates the deployment and removes the size constraint of the adapter modules.  

Table 1: Comparison of different model adaptation protocols. (orig. weight: accessible to original weight; auto.: automatic protocol; no ext. train: no extra training steps; no ext. infer.: no extra inference cost)   

![](images/7ee56245ae3b93c14259de7cd899bda40b110f0b6519dab69beb5a64b68a1766.jpg)  

![](images/bd41d68efe768d196af58f4117be9c0b6c2555009b90523a5dbad0ddee754230.jpg)  
Pretrained Model(a) Feature-based. (b) Fine-tuning. (c) Adapter tuning.  

Some methods including LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) and Progressive Networks (Rusu et al., 2016) also adopt the idea of using both frozen branches and learnable branches in the network. The main differences between Rep-Adapter and these works are summarized in Tab. 2. First, different from LoRA and Progressive Networks, the added branch in Rep-Adapter is non-linear during training and linear during inference. This is in line with vision re-parameterization works which benefit from the unique property of BN layer. Second, unlike these works, we add two scaling factor layers to the two branches and prove that our module achieves an automatic learning rate adjustment to avoid manual hyper-parameter search. Third, different from LoRA, Rep-Adapter does not aim at parameter-efficient tuning of large pretrained models, but aims at the transfer learning performance, in line with works such as L2-SP (Li et al., 2018), DELTA (Li et al., 2019), etc.  

AutoML on transfer learning. There exists some preliminary attempts on automating transfer learning. Dynamic tuning methods (Guo et al., 2019; 2020b; Yang et al., 2021) introduce more than $2\times$ parameters during inference, with additional policy networks or gating modules to achieve dynamic routing among frozen and fine-tuning weights. AutoLR (Ro & Choi,  

Table 2: Comparison of Rep-Adapter, Progressive Network and LoRA.   

![](images/dc0a4c4e79bd0d8fdda9b9c8ed09b95c7513848169b2610812ea0e63bcb5f769.jpg)  

2021) presents auto-tuning of layer-wise learning rates, at a cost of performing repeated learning rate trial during training. Different from these methods, we solve automatic model adaptation problem in a much simpler way, without introducing extra training steps, or extra model size during inference. A comprehensive comparison of different model adaptation schemes is shown in Tab. 1. We consider four aspects including: preservation of original weight, automatic method, no extra training steps and no extra inference cost. Among these methods, only ours could cover all aspects.  

Traditional Re-parameterization. Traditional Re-parameterization (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017) parameterize weight as a combination of a set of parameters for optimization of deep neural networks. Traditional Re-parameterization has also been used for AutoML. (Chen et al., 2019) uses meta kernels with re-parameterization to denote a neural architecture search space. SCC (Yang et al., 2019b) and CondConv (Yang et al., 2019a) derive a kernel as the weighted sum of multiple generated kernels, to perform a conditionally parameterized convolution. Differently, we focus on automating the optimization of learning rate during transfer learning.  

Structural Re-parameterization. Structural Re-parameterization, proposed by (Ding et al., 2021c), is a method that parameterizes a network structure with the parameters transformed from another network structure. This method has recently been used to boost the training phase of ConvNets (Luo et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2021b; 2019; Guo et al., 2020a; Cao et al., 2020) and MLP models (Ding et al., 2021a) by introducing merge-able branches with different architectures, without changing the whole network architecture in the inference phase. In this paper, we use reparameterization to represent structural re-parameterization. Different from these works that merge branches with different architecture, we use re-parameterization to merge frozen branch and tuning branch (with the same architecture), and simulate a layer with arbitrary learning rate. This is the first time that re-parameterization is proved to be able to represent different learning rate, and also the first time that scaling factors are introduced to re-parameterization for learning rate optimization.  



\section{3 METHODOLOGY  }


In this section, we first formulate the automatic model adaptation problem and analyze the downside of baseline methods, then introduce Rep-Adapter, a novel adapter module with re-parameterization technique. We prove that our adapter can simulate a fine-tuning layer with arbitrary learning rate for each filter, and further present a simple adapter tuning protocol to achieve automatic adaptation of pre-trained models without additional search cost.  

3.1 PRELIMINARIES  

Model Adaptation. Let $\psi$ denote a pre-trained model equipped with a random initialized task specific head. Given a target task with objective $\{\operatorname*{min}\mathcal{L}\}$ , model adaptation yields a target model $\psi^{\star}$ by executing certain transfer protocol $\zeta$ :  

$$
\psi^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\psi}\mathcal{L}(\psi,\zeta).
$$  

In computer vision field, most of the transfer learning protocols for ConvNets use the same network architecture of the pre-trained model on the target task, where the network parameters $\omega$ inherit from the pre-trained ones $\omega_{\mathrm{0}}$ . As discussed in Section 1, most of these protocols fall in two categories, fine-tuning and linear probing.The essential difference between these protocols is the learning rate of each network parameters. Without loss of generality, let $\eta_{m}$ be a reference learning rate, and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{|i|}$ be the learning rate multipliers $\eta^{(i)}\in\bar{\mathbb{R}}$ for all the $|i|$ filters (where $i$ indexes network filters and $|i|$ denotes total filter number). Given the hyper-parameter $\eta$ , the objective of these protocols is:  

$$
\omega^{\star}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\omega}\mathcal{L}(\omega,\eta).
$$  

In this framework, the fine-tuning protocol is equivalent to setting a global $\eta$ for all parameters, while linear probing is equivalent to setting $\eta=0$ .  

Automatic Model Adaptation. Intuitively, the optimal learning rate of each parameter is influenced by factors like data distribution, model architectures. To this end, another line of work aims to learn the proper transfer protocol $\zeta$ for the target task in an automatic fashion. Following the previous discussion, the objective of automatic model adaptation can be denoted as:  

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{\omega,\eta}\mathcal{L}(\omega,\eta).
$$  

In the following sections, we first introduce a novel parameter-free adapter module, and then present a carefully designed tuning protocol that is equivalent to a bi-level optimization (Anandalingam & Friesz, 1992) of the learning rate and network parameters.  

Intuitively, a soft balancing between a frozen filter and a fine-tuning filter can represent an intermediate state between them, i.e., a filter tuning at a smaller learning rate. Motivated by the intuition, we set to solve this problem by first proposing an adapter module to achieve this balance. This intuition will be further analysed in Sec. 3.3.  

Rep-Adapter. To make a soft balancing between a ConvNet layer with frozen filters and a ConvNet layer with tuned filters, we present the Rep-Adapter module that comprises a frozen branch and a tuning branch, both initialized with pre-trained network parameters. We explicitly introduce the scaling factors $\pmb{\delta},\pmb{\zeta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for each filter of the two branches, where $d$ denotes filter number for a network layer. As shown in Figure 3 (a), Rep-Adapter can be defined as:  

![](images/fbdc90602c9e9a74bb9a57148a117c53352de044eea4241bcc1429dc4315e028.jpg)  
Figure 3: A Rep-Adapter can be equivalently converted to a single weight layer, and can also simulate a layer fine-tuning with certain filter-wise learning rate by setting the value of $\zeta$ accordingly.  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\psi^{\mathcal{R}}(\omega_{0},\omega^{\mathcal{R}}):=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\psi(\omega_{0})+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)\psi(\omega^{\mathcal{R}}),}\end{array}
$$  

where $\omega_{0},\,\omega^{\mathcal{R}}$ denote pre-trained network parameters and parameters of the tuning branch, and $\mathrm{diag(\cdot)}$ denotes the corresponding diagonal matrix constructed from a vector. Such soft weighting with factors $\{\delta,\zeta\}$ in the adapter would generally introduce twice model size and computation, leading to high inference cost and model size. Accordingly, we introduce a re-parameterization scheme to merge the two branches in Rep-Adapter.  

Re-parameterization. Considering a pre-trained ConvNet, a Rep-Adapter $\psi^{\mathcal{R}}$ for the ConvNet contains a frozen branch and an adapting branch, both of which consist of a convolution (Conv) layer and a batch normalization (BN) layer. The weights and optional bias of a Conv layer can be denoted by $\pmb{w}$ and $^{b}$ . A BN layer performs per-channel normalization and scaling. Let $\pmb{\mu}$ and $\pmb{\sigma}$ denote running mean and variance of training samples, and let $\gamma$ and $\beta$ be the channel-wise scaling factor and bias. A Conv-BN branch can be converted to a single Conv layer as:  

$$
\psi(\pmb{x})=(\pmb{w}\star\pmb{x}-\pmb{\mu})\frac{\gamma}{\sigma}+\beta=(\underbrace{\pmb{w}\cdot\frac{\gamma}{\sigma}}_{w^{\prime}})\star\pmb{x}+(\underbrace{\beta-\pmb{\mu}\frac{\gamma}{\sigma}}_{b^{\prime}}),
$$  

where $\star$ denotes convolution operator, $w^{\prime}$ and $b^{\prime}$ are the equivalent weights and bias after the merge.  

After merging Conv-BN, we consider to merge the two Conv branches in Rep-Adapter. When the outputs of two or more Conv layers with the same configurations are added up, we can merge them into a single Conv. Let $\pmb{w}_{0}$ , $b_{\mathrm{0}}$ be the pre-trained weights and bias of a merged Conv-BN branch, and $\pmb{w}^{\mathcal{R}}$ , $\breve{\b{b}}^{\mathcal{R}}$ be the merged weights and bias of the tuning Conv-BN branch in Rep-Adapter. The adapter, i.e., weighted sum of two branches, can be converted as:  

$$
\boldsymbol\psi^{\mathcal{R}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)(\boldsymbol{w}_{0}\star\boldsymbol{x}+b_{0})+\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol\zeta)(\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathcal{R}}\star\boldsymbol{x}+b^{\mathcal{R}}).
$$  

Thus, the adapter can be merged to a single convolution layer by setting:  

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\boldsymbol{w}_{0}+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathcal{R}},\quad\widetilde{\boldsymbol{b}}=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\boldsymbol{b}_{0}+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathcal{R}}.
$$  

In this way, a Rep-Adapter $\psi^{\mathcal{R}}$ with two branches can be converted to a single weight layer $\psi(\widetilde{\omega})$ during inference (Figure 3), enabling parameter-free model adaptation.  

In Sec. 3.2 we intuitively use our proposed Rep-Adapter as a balance between fine-tuning and frozen weights. Here we show by theoretical analysis that Rep-Adapter can indeed simulate a layer finetuning at a different learning rate.  

Proposition 3.1. Given a pre-trained linear network layer $\psi(\omega_{0})$ . Let $\psi^{\mathcal{R}}({\pmb x})=d i a g(\delta)\psi(\omega_{\mathcal{Q}})+$ $d i a\bar{g}(\zeta)\psi(\omega^{\mathcal{R}})$ denotes this layer under adapter tuning scheme at learning rate $\eta_{m}$ , and $\mathring{\psi}^{\mathcal{F}}(\omega)$ denotes this layer with each of the d filters fine-tuning at a certain learning rate $\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Suppose the network functions of the two schemes are identical before tuning step $t$ , then there always exists scaling factor $\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for each filter such that after one step of tuning, $\dot{\psi}^{\mathcal{F}}(\pmb{x})=\psi^{\mathcal{R}}(\pmb{x})$ still holds.  

Proof. Suppose the network functions of the two schemes are identical at step $t$ . We have $\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{F}}(\pmb{x})=$ $\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}(x)$ and $\partial{\mathcal{L}}_{t}/\partial\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}=\partial{\mathcal{L}}_{t}/\partial\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{F}}$ . First, we calculate the weight change of $\omega^{\mathcal{R}}$ in the adapter:  

$$
\Delta\pmb{\omega}_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}=-\eta_{m}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial\pmb{\omega}_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}}=-\eta_{m}\cdot\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial\pmb{\psi}_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}}.
$$  

Let $\begin{array}{r}{\widetilde{\omega}_{t}=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\omega_{0}+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)\omega_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}}\end{array}$ , this layer function after one-step adapter tuning is:  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\psi_{t+1}^{\mathcal{R}}(\pmb{x})=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\omega_{0}\pmb{x}+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)(\omega^{\mathcal{R}}+\Delta\omega^{\mathcal{R}})\pmb{x}}\\ {=(\widetilde{\omega}_{t}-\eta_{m}\cdot\mathrm{diag}(\zeta_{1}^{2},\dots,\zeta_{d}^{2})\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}_{t}}{\partial\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}})\pmb{x}.}\end{array}
$$  

As for the fine-tuned case:  

$$
\boldsymbol{\psi}_{t+1}^{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\omega_{t+1}\boldsymbol{x}=(\omega_{t}-\mathrm{diag}(\eta)\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\psi}_{t}^{\mathcal{F}}})\boldsymbol{x}.
$$  

Recall that $\pmb{\psi}_{t}^{\mathcal{F}}(\pmb{x})=\pmb{\psi}_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}(\pmb{x})$ , and $\partial{\mathcal{L}}_{t}/\partial\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}=\partial{\mathcal{L}}_{t}/\partial\psi_{t}^{\mathcal{F}}$ . Thus, there exists:  

$$
\zeta=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\eta_{i}}{\eta_{m}}}\right)_{i=1}^{d},\quad\mathrm{such\;that}\;\;\psi_{t+1}^{\mathcal{F}}(\pmb{x})=\psi_{t+1}^{\mathcal{R}}(\pmb{x}),
$$  

which proves that after one step of tuning, $\psi^{\mathcal{F}}({\pmb x})=\psi^{\mathcal{R}}({\pmb x})$ still holds.  

Based on Proposition 3.1, we have two corollaries. First, as in Figure 3, if a Rep-Adapter and a network layer with filter-wise fine-tuning $l r$ are identical before training $(\psi_{0}^{\mathcal{F}}(\pmb{x})^{\bot}=\psi_{0}^{\mathcal{\dot{R}}}(\pmb{x}))$ , by properly setting scaling factors $\zeta$ in Rep-Adapter based on the filter-wise learning rate $\eta$ , the RepAdapter can represent this layer in every steps $(\psi^{\mathcal{F}}({\pmb x})=\psi^{\mathcal{R}}({\pmb x}))$ . Second, when using the optimal scaling factors $\zeta$ at each training step, the Rep-Adapter represents a layer fine-tuning with optimal filter-wise $l r$ . Therefore, the optimization of $l r$ can be relaxed to the optimization of $\zeta$ .1  

3.4 AUTOMATIC MODEL ADAPTATION VIA REP-ADAPTER TUNING  

Rep-Adapter tuning. We present a simple Rep-Adapter tuning scheme, by adding the RepAdapter to every layer of a pre-trained model, and making the factors $\delta$ and $\zeta$ in the adapters learnable. In Rep-Adapter tuning protocol, adapter parameters $\omega^{\mathcal{R}}$ and factors $\{\delta\}\,=\,\{\delta^{(l)}\bar{\}_{l=0}^{|l|}$ $\{\zeta\}~=~\{\zeta^{(l)}\}_{l=0}^{|l|}$ of all the layers are jointly optimized. Based on Proposition 3.1, we have $\begin{array}{r}{\omega=\mathrm{diag}(\delta)\omega_{0}+\mathrm{diag}(\zeta)\omega^{\mathcal{R}}}\end{array}$ , $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(\zeta^{2})\eta_{m}$ . Thus, the original objective of automatic model adaptation in Equation (3) can be converted to:  

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{\omega^{\mathcal{R}},\{\delta\},\{\zeta\}}\mathcal{L}(\omega_{0},\omega^{\mathcal{R}},\{\delta\},\{\zeta\},\eta_{m}),
$$  

where pre-trained $\omega_{\mathrm{0}}$ and reference learning rate $\eta_{m}$ are task-agnostic hyper-parameters. Since $\zeta$ participates in loss calculation, it can be simply optimized by back-propagation together with $\omega^{\mathcal{R}}$ .2 Thus, Rep-Adapter tuning simulates a model fine-tuning with adaptive learning rate for each filter without introducing additional training loops or searching phase. In practice, the weight $\gamma$ of BN layer of the two branches have the same shape and play a similar role to the scaling factors $\delta$ and $\zeta$ . Thus, we directly use $\gamma$ as the scaling factor for convenience in our implementation.  

After the tuning phase, the model can be deployed efficiently by re-parameterization following the scheme in Sec. 3.2. The model size and computation complexity are exactly the same as in finetuning scheme, without introducing any additional parameters during inference. This scheme avoids the issue of catastrophic forgetting during training, and the tuned model can also be used for further transfer as the original weights are not modified.  



\section{4 EXPERIMENTS  }


We evaluate our Rep-Adapter on various settings to demonstrate its effectiveness, including manyshot and low-shot transfer learning with supervised and unsupervised ImageNet pre-training, fewshot transfer learning of CLIP, and semi-supervised learning.  



\section{4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS  }


We implement the cross-domain transferring with the popular computer vision library VISSL (Goyal et al., 2021), which is inspired by the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) (Zhai et al., 2020). VISSL contains 14 diverse classification downstream datasets, and two settings for tuning phase, 1) many shot transfer learning setting, where all training labels of the downstream tasks are used; 2) low-shot transfer learning setting that only trains on 1000 labeled images sampled from the downstream datasets. For few-shot learning with CLIP, we adopt 16-shot settings on 10 transfer learning datasets. See the supplementary for more details.  

Pre-Training Protocol. We evaluate Rep-Adapter on self-supervised models, fully supervised models, and text-supervised models. We use two representative self-supervised methods, PIRL (Misra & Maaten, 2020), MoCoV2 (Chen et al., 2020b) on cross domain transfer learning and an additional self-supervised learning method SwAV (Caron et al., 2020) for semi-supervised learning on ImageNet, and use CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) for experiments with text-supervised pre-training.Please check the supplementary for more details.  

Baseline methods. As our method aims to combine the advantage of the prevalent feature-based methods, e.g. linear probing, and fine-tuning. we choose these two method as our baseline methods. value for the classification layer, while fine-tuning is setting a same $\eta$ for all the network parameters.

We first evaluate our method on many-shot transfer learning setting. We use all training data with labels from all 14 target datasets during the tuning phase. Results are presented in Tab. 3. Our Rep-Adapter generally outperforms the baseline methods, on 37 out of 42 scenarios. As shown in Tab. 8, enabling learnable weight of BN, i.e., learnable $\delta$ in Rep-Adapter, slightly increase network performance on all the five datasets. Thus, we enabling it be default, though it does not affect the simulated learning rate of Rep-Adapter.  

(b) Effect of joint optimization of $\delta,\zeta$ with $\omega$ . In Sec. 3.3, we discussed Rep-Adapter under the situation when the scaling factors $\delta,\zeta$ of the frozen branch and the fine-tuning branch are fixed when updating $\omega$ , i.e., $\delta,\zeta$ and network parameter $\omega$ are updated iteratively in separate steps. To save the training cost and simplify the pipeline, we jointly optimize $\delta,\zeta$ and $\omega$ in each single step as in Equation (12). As shown in Tab. 8, joint and iterative optimization achieve comparable performance.  

(c) Effect of the batch-wise statistics ${\pmb\sigma},{\pmb\mu}$ . In Sec. 3.3, we discussed Rep-Adapter on linear case, which covers using BN with running statistics ${\pmb\sigma},{\pmb\mu}$ . However, its a common practice in reparameterization literature to enable the batch-wise statistics in BN during training (Ding et al., 2021c;b). Here, we explore how will the non-linearity and stochasticity brought by batch-wise statistics affect the performance. As shown in Tab. 8, enabling the batch-wise statistics (ours) consistently outperforms the case using frozen $\pmb{\sigma},\pmb{\mu}$ .  

(d) Effect of the BN position. In Rep-Adapter, we use BN in both branches, before adding the output of the branches together. Alternatively, the BN can also be used after addition, where only Conv layers are in the branches. The results of the two cases is shown in Tab. 8. Using BN in the branches clearly improves the performance of Rep-Adapter.  

(e) Effect of $\omega_{\mathrm{0}}$ weight initialization. In Rep-Adapter, the weight of the frozen branch is initialized with the pretrained weight $\omega_{0}$ . As shown in Tab. 8, random initializing the frozen branch would drastically damage the performance of Rep-Adapter (e.g., from $90.3\%$ to $17.0\%$ on Pets), demonstrating that Rep-Adapter do make use of the information in the frozen branch and the importance of pretrained weight initialization in the frozen branch.  

(f) Effect of weight frozen in frozen branch. Tab. 8 also shows the result of not freezing the weight in the frozen branch of Rep-Adapter. The performance drop considerably on all the five datasets (up to $4.8\%$ on Pets) when making the frozen branch learnable, and is comparable to finetuning baseline. This demonstrate that the performance gain achieved by Rep-Adapter over finetuning is not caused by re-parameterization and not by increasing the network complexity during training. The frozen weights are critical for Rep-Adapter to achieve the performance improvement.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


Model adaptation is a long-standing problem in transfer learning. We notice the fact that most previous model adaptation baselines have several downsides, such as tedious manual tuning of learning rate and extra computational cost during inference phase. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to formulate automatic model adaptation into a bi-level optimization problem. We propose a parameter-free protocol that can jointly optimize the learning rate and model parameters during tuning phase with a theoretical basis. Our experiments empirically evidence the effectiveness and generalization ability of our method. We hope our work can benefit future works on model adaptation and reduce the human effort to manually tuning the hyper-parameters during transfer learning.

\title{Rep-Adapter: Parameter-free Automatic Adaptation of Pre-trained ConvNets via Re-parameterization}

\begin{abstract}
Recent advances in visual pre-training have demonstrated the advantage of transferring pre-trained models to target tasks. However, different transfer learning protocols have distinctive advantages regarding target tasks, and are nontrivial to choose without repeated trial and error. This paper presents a parameter-free automatic model adaptation protocol for ConvNets, aiming at automatically balancing between fine-tuning and linear probing, by using adaptive learning rate for each convolution filters on target tasks. First, we propose Rep-Adapter, an adapter module with re-parameterization scheme, which can achieve soft balancing between the pre-trained and fine-tuned filters, and can be equivalently converted to a single weight layer, without introducing additional parameters to the inference phase. We show by theoretical analysis that Rep-Adapter can simulate a ConvNet layer with each filter fine-tuning at different learning rate. We present a simple adapter tuning protocol with Rep-Adapter to achieve automatic adaptation of pretrained models without additional search cost. Extensive experiments on various datasets with ResNet and CLIP demonstrate the superiority of our Rep-Adapter on semi-supervised, few-shot and full dataset transfer learning scenarios.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Recent advances in both computer vision and neural language processing field have demonstrated the advantage of transferring large-scale pre-trained models to downstream tasks. To leverage the information of the pre-trained models, there emerges different transfer learning protocols such as fine-tuning directly on the new task (Girshick et al., 2014), feature-based methods (Turian et al., 2010) that only update the parameters of the task-specific head, and adapter tuning (Houlsby et al., 2019) that introduces new learnable modules to adapt some layers in the original model.  

The most suitable choice of the protocols depends on many factors, including target dataset size, label fraction, etc. For instance, fine-tuning is usually more powerful on fully-supervised ImageNet, while linear probing are sometimes better on semi-supervised ImageNet (Zhou et al., 2022a). We also observe a similar trend on Caltech101 dataset. As in shown in Figure 1, fine-tuning outperforms linear probing for full dataset transfer on Caltech101 (dataset B in the figure), while linear probing performs better for low-shot (1000 examples) scenario. Moreover, when taking partial fine-tuning and layer-wise learning rate adjustment into consideration, the option space becomes computationally prohibitive for an extensive search. Therefore, we believe there is an urgent need of designing an automatic transfer learning protocol that can combine the advantages of these protocols without tediously searching for hyper-parameter settings.  

There exists some preliminary attempts to avoid manually tuning layer-wise and filter-wise hyperparameter settings. SpotTune (Guo et al., 2019) and AdaFilter (Guo et al., 2020b) dynamically route between frozen and learnable weights, at a cost of having more than twice the original model size during inference. AutoLR (Ro & Choi, 2021) searches for layer-wise fine-tuning learning rate via repeated trial. However, these methods introduce either policy networks or repeated training loops, increasing the training or inference cost. We thus explore a simple model adaptation method, without introducing extra training steps or extra parameters during inference.  

In this paper, we introduce Rep-Adapter, a novel adapter module that achieves soft balancing between the pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each adapter module has two branches, a frozen branch with the pre-trained parameters, and a learnable branch that adapts on the target tasks. During inference, we leverage the re-parameterization scheme to equivalently convert the two branches into one, avoiding the increase in model size and computational cost.  

In addition, we prove that, during training, our RepAdapter is equivalent to a layer fine-tuned by a finegrained transfer learning protocol with different learning rate for each fliter. This eliminates the need of tedious hyper-parameter search for learning rate configurations like previous methods. By optimizing a network stacked by Rep-Adapter, the pre-trained model can be transferred with adaptive learning rate for each filter. As such, finetuning and linear probing can be achieved by learning the learning rate to a certain value or zero.  

![](images/12bb18b4718e6ff9b15bb8d739f52ccb88bc89774790055c43deb1fccaad2d7a.jpg)  
Figure 1: Comparison of fine-tuning, linear probing and our proposed RepAdapter. Dataset A: DTD for texture classification; B: Caltech101 for object identification; C: EuroSAT for satellite image classification. Models are pre-trained on ImageNet with a selfsupervised method, PIRL.  

We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate and analysis our method. We use VISSL (Goyal et al., 2021) library to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on full dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning scenarios. We adapt models from several different pre-training protocols (fully-supervised pre-training and three state-of-the-art self-supervised pre-training methods on ImageNet, CLIP pre-training with text supervision), to various downstream datasets, and on fullshot, low-shot (1000 examples) or few-shot (16-shot) scenarios. We also perform experiments on semi-supervised ImageNet, by adapting models pre-trained by 3 different self-supervised learning methods to ImageNet with $1\%$ and $10\%$ label fraction. Moreover, we explore the transferability to VOC object detection and Cityscapes, COCO instance segmentation tasks. Our Rep-Adapter tuning protocol consistently surpasses the baselines across tasks and scenarios, which clearly evidences the effectiveness and generalization ability of our method.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Transfer Learning via Model Adaptation. Model adaptation methods modify a pre-trained model to achieve higher performance on a target task. Figure 2 illustrates popular model adaptation methods in computer vision field. Feature-based methods (Figure 2 (a)), including linear classification, directly learn task specific head on frozen features (Turian et al., 2010). Fine-tuning (Girshick et al., 2014) is the most generally used transfer learning protocol (Figure 2 (b)). Some works regularize the distance between the fine-tuned model and the pretrained model on the network parameters (e.g., $L^{2}$ -SP (Li et al., 2018)) or the output features (e.g., DELTA (Li et al., 2019)) to improve the performance, but the weight of the regularization comes a hand-crafted hyper-parameter. Some works (Furlanello et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2017) use network ensemble to boost the performance by combining the frozen and learnable weights, at a cost of using $M\times$ model size $M$ is the number of ensemble models) during inference. Adapter tuning (Yin et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Houlsby et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2020) (Figure 2 (c)) adds light-weight modules on the pre-trained network to adapt the model without changing its original parameters. Previous works on convolution adapter modules (Rebuffi et al., 2017; 2018; Rosenfeld & Tsotsos, 2018) perform incremental learning by adding small point-wise convolution adapter modules, at a cost of about $11\%$ increase in model size for each tasks. Our Rep-Adapter is also related to ensemble methods. However, an ensemble of models can not be directly converted to a single model due to the non-linearity in the models and thus much larger than us in terms of parameters and computation complexity. Different from previous methods, Rep-Adapter does not increase inference model size, which accelerates the deployment and removes the size constraint of the adapter modules.

Some methods including LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) and Progressive Networks (Rusu et al., 2016) also adopt the idea of using both frozen branches and learnable branches in the network. AutoML on transfer learning. There exists some preliminary attempts on automating transfer learning. Dynamic tuning methods (Guo et al., 2019; 2020b; Yang et al., 2021) introduce more than $2\times$ parameters during inference, with additional policy networks or gating modules to achieve dynamic routing among frozen and fine-tuning weights.
