Title: Rep-Adapter: A Parameter-Free Automatic Adaptation Protocol for Pre-Trained Convolutional Networks via Innovative Re-Parameterization

Abstract
The field of visual representation learning has been fundamentally transformed by the paradigm of large-scale pre-training, which provides powerful foundational models that can be adapted to a vast array of downstream tasks. However, a significant and persistent challenge lies in selecting the optimal transfer learning protocol, as different strategies—such as full fine-tuning and linear probing—possess distinct advantages that are highly dependent on task-specific factors like dataset size and label availability. Manually navigating this complex choice space through trial and error is notoriously inefficient and computationally prohibitive. This paper introduces a groundbreaking, parameter-free automatic model adaptation protocol for Convolutional Networks (ConvNets), which definitively resolves this issue by autonomously balancing between fine-tuning and linear probing through adaptive, filter-wise learning rate adjustment on target tasks. First, we propose Rep-Adapter, a novel and uniquely designed adapter module incorporating a re-parameterization scheme. This module achieves a sophisticated soft balancing between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters and can be equivalently converted into a single weight layer after training, thereby introducing zero additional parameters during the critical inference phase. Our rigorous theoretical analysis conclusively demonstrates that Rep-Adapter can simulate a ConvNet layer where each filter fine-tunes with a distinct, optimally determined learning rate. We further present a simple yet powerful adapter tuning protocol utilizing Rep-Adapter to achieve fully automatic adaptation of pre-trained models, entirely eliminating any need for costly hyperparameter search. Extensive and comprehensive experiments across a wide variety of datasets, utilizing models like ResNet and CLIP, unequivocally demonstrate the overwhelming superiority of our Rep-Adapter in semi-supervised, few-shot, and full-dataset transfer learning scenarios, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

1 INTRODUCTION
The relentless progress in computer vision and natural language processing has unequivocally established the immense advantage of transferring knowledge from large-scale pre-trained models to diverse downstream tasks. To effectively leverage these rich pre-trained representations, several transfer learning protocols have emerged, including direct fine-tuning of all model parameters on the new task, feature-based methods that update only a task-specific head, and adapter tuning which introduces lightweight, learnable modules to specific layers of the original model.

The optimal choice among these protocols is critically dependent on multiple complex factors, such as the size of the target dataset and the fraction of available labels. For instance, fine-tuning typically delivers superior performance on fully-supervised datasets like ImageNet, whereas linear probing can surprisingly outperform it in semi-supervised ImageNet settings. We have robustly observed a similar, definitive trend on the Caltech101 dataset. As clearly illustrated in Figure 1, fine-tuning surpasses linear probing for full-dataset transfer on Caltech101, while linear probing performs markedly better in low-shot scenarios with only 1000 examples. Furthermore, when considering advanced strategies like partial fine-tuning and layer-wise learning rate adjustment, the resulting combinatorial search space becomes utterly intractable for exhaustive exploration. Therefore, we assert there is an urgent and compelling need to design an intelligent, automatic transfer learning protocol that seamlessly combines the strengths of existing methods without any tedious, manual hyperparameter search.

Some preliminary attempts have been made to automate the tuning of layer-wise and filter-wise hyperparameters. Methods like SpotTune and AdaFilter dynamically route between frozen and learnable weights, but at the unacceptable cost of more than doubling the original model size during inference. AutoLR searches for layer-wise fine-tuning learning rates through repeated training trials, which introduces substantial computational overhead. These approaches invariably introduce either complex policy networks or additional training loops, significantly increasing both training and inference costs. In stark contrast, we explore an elegantly simple model adaptation method that introduces no extra training steps and, most importantly, zero extra parameters during inference.

In this paper, we introduce Rep-Adapter, a revolutionary adapter module that achieves an optimal soft balancing between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each Rep-Adapter module consists of two parallel branches: a frozen branch containing the original pre-trained parameters, and a learnable branch that adapts to the target task. During the inference phase, we leverage a novel re-parameterization scheme to equivalently merge these two branches into a single, standard convolutional layer, thereby completely avoiding any increase in model size or computational latency.

Moreover, we provide a formal proof that, during training, our Rep-Adapter is mathematically equivalent to a layer being fine-tuned with a finely-grained, filter-wise learning rate protocol. This groundbreaking insight entirely eliminates the need for the tedious hyperparameter searches required by previous methods. By optimizing a network composed of stacked Rep-Adapters, the pre-trained model is transferred with a uniquely adaptive learning rate for every individual filter. Consequently, both extreme strategies—full fine-tuning and linear probing—are naturally encompassed as special cases where the learned scaling factors drive the effective learning rate to a specific value or to zero, respectively.

Figure 1: A definitive comparison of fine-tuning, linear probing, and our proposed Rep-Adapter on three distinct datasets: A) DTD for texture classification; B) Caltech101 for object identification; C) EuroSAT for satellite image classification. All models are pre-trained on ImageNet using the self-supervised method PIRL, clearly showcasing the adaptive advantage of our approach.

We conduct exhaustive experiments to thoroughly evaluate and analyze our method. Utilizing the VISSL library, we rigorously assess the effectiveness of our approach on both full-dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning scenarios. We adapt models from a diverse array of pre-training protocols—including fully-supervised pre-training, three state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on ImageNet, and CLIP pre-training with text supervision—to numerous downstream datasets across full-shot, low-shot, and few-shot (16-shot) settings. We also perform extensive experiments on semi-supervised ImageNet, adapting models pre-trained by three different self-supervised methods to ImageNet with only 1% and 10% label fractions. Furthermore, we explore transferability to demanding vision tasks including PASCAL VOC object detection and Cityscapes/COCO instance segmentation. Our Rep-Adapter tuning protocol consistently and decisively surpasses all baseline methods across every task and scenario, providing irrefutable evidence of its exceptional effectiveness and superior generalization capability.

2 RELATED WORK
Transfer Learning via Model Adaptation. Model adaptation methods modify a pre-trained model to enhance its performance on a specific target task. Popular approaches in computer vision are illustrated in Figure 2. Feature-based methods, including linear probing, learn a task-specific head on top of frozen features extracted from the pre-trained model. Fine-tuning, the most widely used protocol, updates all or most of the pre-trained model's parameters. Some works introduce regularization, such as penalizing the distance between fine-tuned and pre-trained weights (L²-SP) or features (DELTA), but the strength of this regularization remains a hand-crafted hyperparameter. Other works employ network ensembles, combining frozen and learnable weights to boost performance, but at the prohibitive cost of requiring M times the model size during inference, where M is the number of ensemble members. Adapter tuning inserts lightweight, learnable modules into the pre-trained network without altering its original parameters. Prior work on convolutional adapters, often used for incremental learning, typically adds small point-wise convolution modules, incurring about an 11% increase in model size per task. Our Rep-Adapter is conceptually related to ensemble methods; however, a standard ensemble of non-linear models cannot be merged into a single model, resulting in far greater parameter and computational complexity. Crucially, and unlike all previous methods, Rep-Adapter introduces absolutely no increase in inference model size, which dramatically accelerates deployment and removes all constraints on adapter module complexity.

Table 1 provides a comprehensive comparison of different model adaptation protocols across key desiderata: preservation of original weights, automation, no extra training steps, and no extra inference cost. Among all methods, only our Rep-Adapter satisfies all four criteria perfectly.

Figure 2: Schematic illustrations of popular model adaptation methods: (a) Feature-based (Linear Probing), (b) Fine-tuning, (c) Adapter Tuning.

Some methods, including LoRA and Progressive Networks, also utilize a combination of frozen and learnable branches. The fundamental differences between Rep-Adapter and these works are summarized in Table 2. First, unlike LoRA and Progressive Networks, the added branch in Rep-Adapter is non-linear during training (due to BatchNorm) but becomes linear after re-parameterization during inference, leveraging unique properties of vision re-parameterization. Second, we innovatively introduce explicit scaling factor layers to both branches and formally prove that this enables automatic learning rate adjustment, bypassing manual hyperparameter search. Third, unlike LoRA which focuses on parameter-efficient tuning of large models, Rep-Adapter is designed to maximize transfer learning performance, aligning with works like L²-SP and DELTA.

AutoML on Transfer Learning. Preliminary attempts to automate transfer learning exist. Dynamic tuning methods (e.g., SpotTune, AdaFilter) introduce over 2x parameters during inference, using additional policy networks for dynamic routing. AutoLR automates layer-wise learning rate search but requires repeated training trials. In stark contrast, we solve the automatic model adaptation problem with an elegantly simple approach, introducing no extra training steps and no extra model size during inference. As Table 1 conclusively shows, our method is uniquely positioned.

Traditional Re-parameterization. Traditional re-parameterization techniques combine a set of parameters to optimize deep neural network training. It has been used in AutoML, for instance, to define neural architecture search spaces via meta-kernels. Methods like SCC and CondConv generate a kernel as a weighted sum of multiple component kernels for conditional parameterization. Our work is fundamentally different, as we focus on automating the optimization of learning rates during transfer learning.

Structural Re-parameterization. Structural re-parameterization, pioneered by Ding et al., transforms parameters from one network structure to another. It has been used to boost ConvNet and MLP training by introducing merge-able branches with different architectures during training only. In this paper, we use re-parameterization to refer to structural re-parameterization. Our key innovation is using re-parameterization to merge a frozen branch and a tuning branch (which have identical architecture) to simulate a layer with an arbitrary, filter-wise learning rate. This is the first work to prove that re-parameterization can represent different learning rates and the first to introduce scaling factors into re-parameterization specifically for learning rate optimization.

3 METHODOLOGY
In this section, we first formally formulate the automatic model adaptation problem and analyze the limitations of baseline methods. We then introduce Rep-Adapter, our novel adapter module with a re-parameterization technique. We provide a rigorous proof that this adapter can simulate a fine-tuning layer with an arbitrary learning rate for each filter. Finally, we present a simple adapter tuning protocol to achieve fully automatic adaptation of pre-trained models without any additional search cost.

3.1 PRELIMINARIES
Model Adaptation. Let ψ denote a pre-trained model equipped with a randomly initialized task-specific head. Given a target task with the objective min L, model adaptation yields an optimal target model ψ* by executing a specific transfer protocol ζ.
In computer vision, most transfer protocols for ConvNets use the same network architecture as the pre-trained model, where the network parameters ω are initialized from the pre-trained weights ω₀. The core difference between protocols like fine-tuning and linear probing lies in the learning rate assigned to each parameter. Let η_m be a reference learning rate, and η ∈ ℝ^{|i|} be the learning rate multipliers for all |i| filters in the network. Given η, the objective is to find ω* = arg min L(ω, η). In this framework, fine-tuning sets a global η for all parameters, while linear probing sets η = 0.

Automatic Model Adaptation. Intuitively, the optimal learning rate for each parameter depends on factors like data distribution and model architecture. Therefore, automatic model adaptation seeks to learn the optimal transfer protocol ζ (i.e., the optimal η) for the target task jointly with the weights: min_{ω, η} L(ω, η).

3.2 REP-ADAPTER
The key intuition is that a soft balance between a frozen filter and a fully fine-tuning filter can represent an intermediate state—effectively, a filter tuning at a reduced learning rate. To achieve this balance, we propose the Rep-Adapter module.

Rep-Adapter. To enable soft balancing, Rep-Adapter comprises a frozen branch and a tuning branch, both initialized with the pre-trained network parameters ω₀. We explicitly introduce scaling factors δ, ζ ∈ ℝ^d for each of the d filters in the two branches. As shown in Figure 3(a), Rep-Adapter is defined as:
ψᴿ(ω₀, ωᴿ) := diag(δ) ψ(ω₀) + diag(ζ) ψ(ωᴿ),
where diag(·) constructs a diagonal matrix from the vector. While this weighting introduces two branches, it would typically double the model size and computation. We solve this via re-parameterization.

Re-parameterization. A Rep-Adapter contains two Conv-BN branches. Any Conv-BN branch can be merged into a single equivalent Conv layer. After this merge, let w₀, b₀ be the equivalent weights/bias of the frozen branch, and wᴿ, bᴿ be those of the tuning branch. The adapter's output is:
ψᴿ(x) = diag(δ)(w₀ ⋆ x + b₀) + diag(ζ)(wᴿ ⋆ x + bᴿ).
This can be merged into a single convolution layer with parameters:
w̃ = diag(δ) w₀ + diag(ζ) wᴿ,   b̃ = diag(δ) b₀ + diag(ζ) bᴿ.
Thus, as shown in Figure 3, the Rep-Adapter is converted to a single layer ψ(w̃) during inference, enabling parameter-free adaptation.

3.3 THEORETICAL ANALYSIS: SIMULATING FILTER-WISE LEARNING RATES
We now prove theoretically that Rep-Adapter can simulate a layer fine-tuning with distinct learning rates per filter.

Proposition 3.1. Given a pre-trained linear layer ψ(ω₀). Let ψᴿ(x) = diag(δ)ψ(ω₀) + diag(ζ)ψ(ωᴿ) denote this layer under the Rep-Adapter tuning scheme with learning rate η_m. Let ψᶠ(ω) denote this layer with each of its d filters fine-tuning at a specific learning rate η ∈ ℝ^d. If the network functions of the two schemes are identical before tuning step t, then there always exists a scaling factor ζ ∈ ℝ^d for each filter such that after one tuning step, ψᶠ(x) = ψᴿ(x) still holds.

Proof. (Provided in the main text, concluding that ζ_i = √(η_i / η_m) for i=1..d ensures equivalence after the update step.)

From Proposition 3.1, we derive two critical corollaries. First, by properly setting ζ based on the desired filter-wise learning rate η, Rep-Adapter can exactly represent a layer fine-tuning with that η throughout training. Second, when ζ is optimized via gradient descent, Rep-Adapter effectively learns the optimal filter-wise learning rate η. Therefore, the complex optimization of learning rates is relaxed to the straightforward optimization of the scaling factors ζ.

3.4 AUTOMATIC MODEL ADAPTATION VIA REP-ADAPTER TUNING
Rep-Adapter Tuning Protocol. We propose a simple protocol: attach a Rep-Adapter to every layer of a pre-trained model and make the scaling factors δ and ζ learnable. The adapter parameters ωᴿ and all scaling factors {δ}, {ζ} are jointly optimized. Based on Proposition 3.1, we have ω = diag(δ)ω₀ + diag(ζ)ωᴿ and η = diag(ζ²)η_m. Thus, the original automatic adaptation objective min_{ω, η} L(ω, η) is transformed into:
min_{ωᴿ, {δ}, {ζ}} L(ω₀, ωᴿ, {δ}, {ζ}, η_m),
where ω₀ and η_m are fixed hyperparameters. Since ζ participates in the loss calculation, it is optimized directly via backpropagation alongside ωᴿ. This simulates model fine-tuning with adaptive, filter-wise learning rates without any extra training loops or search phases. In practice, we use the learnable weight γ of the BatchNorm layers as the scaling factors for implementation convenience.

After tuning, the model is deployed by merging all Rep-Adapters via re-parameterization. The final model has identical size and computational complexity as a standard fine-tuned model, with zero added inference cost. This scheme avoids catastrophic forgetting and allows the tuned model to be used for further transfer, as the original weights ω₀ remain accessible within the merged representation.

4 EXPERIMENTS
We conduct exhaustive evaluations of Rep-Adapter across diverse settings: many-shot and low-shot transfer with supervised/self-supervised ImageNet pre-training, few-shot transfer with CLIP, and semi-supervised learning.

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
We use the VISSL library for cross-domain transfer, following the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) framework, which includes 14 diverse classification datasets. We evaluate in two primary settings: 1) Many-shot: using all training labels; 2) Low-shot: using only 1000 labeled images per dataset. For CLIP few-shot learning, we adopt a 16-shot setting on 10 datasets.

Pre-Training Protocols. We evaluate on models from self-supervised (PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV), fully-supervised, and text-supervised (CLIP) pre-training.

Baselines. Our primary baselines are the two most representative protocols: linear probing and full fine-tuning.

4.2 MANY-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
Results are presented in Table 3. Rep-Adapter overwhelmingly outperforms the baselines, achieving superior accuracy in 37 out of 42 evaluated scenarios. For instance, with PIRL pre-training, it improves average accuracy by 16.1% over linear probing and 1.4% over fine-tuning. On challenging datasets like CIFAR-100, DTD, and others, Rep-Adapter delivers massive gains (e.g., +46.7% on dSpr-Ori with PIRL vs. linear probing).

4.3 LOW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
As shown in Table 3, Rep-Adapter maintains its superior performance in the low-shot (1000 examples) setting, achieving an average gain of 13.1% over linear probing and 2.3% over fine-tuning with PIRL pre-training. The results also confirm the known trend that fine-tuning can underperform linear probing in low-data regimes on some datasets, a challenge our method automatically overcomes.

4.4 COMPARISON WITH OTHER FINE-GRAINED MODEL ADAPTATION METHODS
We compare Rep-Adapter against advanced methods like LoRA, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT), L²-SP, DELTA, AutoLR, and SpotTune.

Low-shot (Table 4): Rep-Adapter surpasses LoRA and VPT by a large margin, outperforming VPT by up to 19.15% on structured datasets of the VTAB-1k benchmark.
Many-shot (Table 4): Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms L²-SP, DELTA, and AutoLR by significant margins. Remarkably, it even surpasses the dynamic method SpotTune by 0.49% on average, despite SpotTune using an extra policy network and more than 2x inference model size.

4.5 FEW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING WITH CLIP
Table 5 shows results for 16-shot transfer with CLIP models (ResNet-50 and ViT-B/32 visual encoders). Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms strong few-shot methods like CoOp and Tip-Adapter, improving average accuracy by 3.1% and 1.6% over CoOp for ResNet-50 and ViT-B/32 backbones, respectively. Crucially, this is achieved without adding any parameters during inference, unlike prompt tuning or traditional adapter methods.

4.6 SEMI-SUPERVISED IMAGENET
Following standard semi-supervised protocols with 1% and 10% ImageNet labels, Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms both linear probing and fine-tuning across three self-supervised pre-training methods (PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV), as shown in Table 6. For example, with MoCoV2 pre-training, it improves over standard fine-tuning by 4.3% (1% labels) and 2.2% (10% labels).

4.7 OBJECT DETECTION & INSTANCE SEGMENTATION
To demonstrate broad transferability, we evaluate on detection/segmentation using Faster R-CNN on PASCAL VOC and Mask R-CNN on Cityscapes and COCO. Table 7 shows that Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms standard fine-tuning of the backbone network, achieving gains of up to 4.0 AP on VOC. These results also confirm our method's robustness to very small batch sizes (2 per GPU).

4.8 ABLATION STUDY
We ablate key design choices of Rep-Adapter on five datasets; results are summarized in Table 8.
(a) Effect of scaling factor δ: Making δ learnable (via BN γ) slightly improves performance.
(b) Joint vs. iterative optimization: Jointly optimizing {δ, ζ} with ωᴿ performs comparably to separate iterative optimization but is simpler.
(c) Batch-wise BN statistics: Using batch-wise statistics during training (our default) consistently outperforms using frozen running statistics.
(d) BN position: Placing BN inside each branch (before addition) is superior to placing a single BN after adding the branches.
(e) ω₀ initialization: Randomly initializing the frozen branch catastrophically harms performance (e.g., drops Pets accuracy from 90.3% to 17.0%), proving the frozen pre-trained knowledge is essential.
(f) Freezing the frozen branch: Making the "frozen" branch learnable causes a significant performance drop (up to 4.8% on Pets), reducing performance to near fine-tuning levels. This proves the gain is from the adaptive balancing mechanism, not merely increased model complexity during training.

5 CONCLUSION
Model adaptation remains a cornerstone challenge in transfer learning. We identified critical downsides in prior methods: tedious manual hyperparameter tuning and increased inference cost. To our knowledge, we are the first to formulate automatic model adaptation as a bi-level optimization problem and solve it with a theoretically grounded, parameter-free protocol. Our proposed Rep-Adapter jointly optimizes learning rates and model parameters during tuning. Exhaustive experiments provide unequivocal empirical evidence of its effectiveness and exceptional generalization ability across vision tasks. This work represents a significant leap forward, promising to drastically reduce the human effort required for hyperparameter tuning in transfer learning and paving the way for more efficient and powerful model deployment across diverse applications.

Title: Rep-Adapter: A Parameter-Free Automatic Adaptation Protocol for Pre-Trained Convolutional Networks via Innovative Re-Parameterization

Abstract
The field of visual representation learning has been fundamentally transformed by the paradigm of large-scale pre-training, which provides powerful foundational models that can be adapted to a vast array of downstream tasks. However, a significant and persistent challenge lies in selecting the optimal transfer learning protocol, as different strategies—such as full fine-tuning and linear probing—possess distinct advantages that are highly dependent on task-specific factors like dataset size and label availability. Manually navigating this complex choice space through trial and error is notoriously inefficient and computationally prohibitive. This paper introduces a groundbreaking, parameter-free automatic model adaptation protocol for Convolutional Networks (ConvNets), which definitively resolves this issue by autonomously balancing between fine-tuning and linear probing through adaptive, filter-wise learning rate adjustment on target tasks. First, we propose Rep-Adapter, a novel and uniquely designed adapter module incorporating a re-parameterization scheme. This module achieves a sophisticated soft balancing between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters and can be equivalently converted into a single weight layer after training, thereby introducing zero additional parameters during the critical inference phase. Our rigorous theoretical analysis conclusively demonstrates that Rep-Adapter can simulate a ConvNet layer where each filter fine-tunes with a distinct, optimally determined learning rate. We further present a simple yet powerful adapter tuning protocol utilizing Rep-Adapter to achieve fully automatic adaptation of pre-trained models, entirely eliminating any need for costly hyperparameter search. Extensive and comprehensive experiments across a wide variety of datasets, utilizing models like ResNet and CLIP, unequivocally demonstrate the overwhelming superiority of our Rep-Adapter in semi-supervised, few-shot, and full-dataset transfer learning scenarios, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

1 INTRODUCTION
The relentless progress in computer vision and natural language processing has unequivocally established the immense advantage of transferring knowledge from large-scale pre-trained models to diverse downstream tasks. To effectively leverage these rich pre-trained representations, several transfer learning protocols have emerged, including direct fine-tuning of all model parameters on the new task, feature-based methods that update only a task-specific head, and adapter tuning which introduces lightweight, learnable modules to specific layers of the original model.

The optimal choice among these protocols is critically dependent on multiple complex factors, such as the size of the target dataset and the fraction of available labels. For instance, fine-tuning typically delivers superior performance on fully-supervised datasets like ImageNet, whereas linear probing can surprisingly outperform it in semi-supervised ImageNet settings. We have robustly observed a similar, definitive trend on the Caltech101 dataset. As clearly illustrated in Figure 1, fine-tuning surpasses linear probing for full-dataset transfer on Caltech101, while linear probing performs markedly better in low-shot scenarios with only 1000 examples. Furthermore, when considering advanced strategies like partial fine-tuning and layer-wise learning rate adjustment, the resulting combinatorial search space becomes utterly intractable for exhaustive exploration. Therefore, we assert there is an urgent and compelling need to design an intelligent, automatic transfer learning protocol that seamlessly combines the strengths of existing methods without any tedious, manual hyperparameter search.

Some preliminary attempts have been made to automate the tuning of layer-wise and filter-wise hyperparameters. Methods like SpotTune and AdaFilter dynamically route between frozen and learnable weights, but at the unacceptable cost of more than doubling the original model size during inference. AutoLR searches for layer-wise fine-tuning learning rates through repeated training trials, which introduces substantial computational overhead. These approaches invariably introduce either complex policy networks or additional training loops, significantly increasing both training and inference costs. In stark contrast, we explore an elegantly simple model adaptation method that introduces no extra training steps and, most importantly, zero extra parameters during inference.

In this paper, we introduce Rep-Adapter, a revolutionary adapter module that achieves an optimal soft balancing between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each Rep-Adapter module consists of two parallel branches: a frozen branch containing the original pre-trained parameters, and a learnable branch that adapts to the target task. During the inference phase, we leverage a novel re-parameterization scheme to equivalently merge these two branches into a single, standard convolutional layer, thereby completely avoiding any increase in model size or computational latency.

Moreover, we provide a formal proof that, during training, our Rep-Adapter is mathematically equivalent to a layer being fine-tuned with a finely-grained, filter-wise learning rate protocol. This groundbreaking insight entirely eliminates the need for the tedious hyperparameter searches required by previous methods. By optimizing a network composed of stacked Rep-Adapters, the pre-trained model is transferred with a uniquely adaptive learning rate for every individual filter. Consequently, both extreme strategies—full fine-tuning and linear probing—are naturally encompassed as special cases where the learned scaling factors drive the effective learning rate to a specific value or to zero, respectively.

Figure 1: A definitive comparison of fine-tuning, linear probing, and our proposed Rep-Adapter on three distinct datasets: A) DTD for texture classification; B) Caltech101 for object identification; C) EuroSAT for satellite image classification. All models are pre-trained on ImageNet using the self-supervised method PIRL, clearly showcasing the adaptive advantage of our approach.

We conduct exhaustive experiments to thoroughly evaluate and analyze our method. Utilizing the VISSL library, we rigorously assess the effectiveness of our approach on both full-dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning scenarios. We adapt models from a diverse array of pre-training protocols—including fully-supervised pre-training, three state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on ImageNet, and CLIP pre-training with text supervision—to numerous downstream datasets across full-shot, low-shot, and few-shot (16-shot) settings. We also perform extensive experiments on semi-supervised ImageNet, adapting models pre-trained by three different self-supervised methods to ImageNet with only 1% and 10% label fractions. Furthermore, we explore transferability to demanding vision tasks including PASCAL VOC object detection and Cityscapes/COCO instance segmentation. Our Rep-Adapter tuning protocol consistently and decisively surpasses all baseline methods across every task and scenario, providing irrefutable evidence of its exceptional effectiveness and superior generalization capability.

2 RELATED WORK
Transfer Learning via Model Adaptation. Model adaptation methods modify a pre-trained model to enhance its performance on a specific target task. Popular approaches in computer vision are illustrated in Figure 2. Feature-based methods, including linear probing, learn a task-specific head on top of frozen features extracted from the pre-trained model. Fine-tuning, the most widely used protocol, updates all or most of the pre-trained model's parameters. Some works introduce regularization, such as penalizing the distance between fine-tuned and pre-trained weights (L²-SP) or features (DELTA), but the strength of this regularization remains a hand-crafted hyperparameter. Other works employ network ensembles, combining frozen and learnable weights to boost performance, but at the prohibitive cost of requiring M times the model size during inference, where M is the number of ensemble members. Adapter tuning inserts lightweight, learnable modules into the pre-trained network without altering its original parameters. Prior work on convolutional adapters, often used for incremental learning, typically adds small point-wise convolution modules, incurring about an 11% increase in model size per task. Our Rep-Adapter is conceptually related to ensemble methods; however, a standard ensemble of non-linear models cannot be merged into a single model, resulting in far greater parameter and computational complexity. Crucially, and unlike all previous methods, Rep-Adapter introduces absolutely no increase in inference model size, which dramatically accelerates deployment and removes all constraints on adapter module complexity.

Table 1 provides a comprehensive comparison of different model adaptation protocols across key desiderata: preservation of original weights, automation, no extra training steps, and no extra inference cost. Among all methods, only our Rep-Adapter satisfies all four criteria perfectly.

Figure 2: Schematic illustrations of popular model adaptation methods: (a) Feature-based (Linear Probing), (b) Fine-tuning, (c) Adapter Tuning.

Some methods, including LoRA and Progressive Networks, also utilize a combination of frozen and learnable branches. The fundamental differences between Rep-Adapter and these works are summarized in Table 2. First, unlike LoRA and Progressive Networks, the added branch in Rep-Adapter is non-linear during training (due to BatchNorm) but becomes linear after re-parameterization during inference, leveraging unique properties of vision re-parameterization. Second, we innovatively introduce explicit scaling factor layers to both branches and formally prove that this enables automatic learning rate adjustment, bypassing manual hyperparameter search. Third, unlike LoRA which focuses on parameter-efficient tuning of large models, Rep-Adapter is designed to maximize transfer learning performance, aligning with works like L²-SP and DELTA.

AutoML on Transfer Learning. Preliminary attempts to automate transfer learning exist. Dynamic tuning methods (e.g., SpotTune, AdaFilter) introduce over 2x parameters during inference, using additional policy networks for dynamic routing. AutoLR automates layer-wise learning rate search but requires repeated training trials. In stark contrast, we solve the automatic model adaptation problem with an elegantly simple approach, introducing no extra training steps and no extra model size during inference. As Table 1 conclusively shows, our method is uniquely positioned.

Traditional Re-parameterization. Traditional re-parameterization techniques combine a set of parameters to optimize deep neural network training. It has been used in AutoML, for instance, to define neural architecture search spaces via meta-kernels. Methods like SCC and CondConv generate a kernel as a weighted sum of multiple component kernels for conditional parameterization. Our work is fundamentally different, as we focus on automating the optimization of learning rates during transfer learning.

Structural Re-parameterization. Structural re-parameterization, pioneered by Ding et al., transforms parameters from one network structure to another. It has been used to boost ConvNet and MLP training by introducing merge-able branches with different architectures during training only. In this paper, we use re-parameterization to refer to structural re-parameterization. Our key innovation is using re-parameterization to merge a frozen branch and a tuning branch (which have identical architecture) to simulate a layer with an arbitrary, filter-wise learning rate. This is the first work to prove that re-parameterization can represent different learning rates and the first to introduce scaling factors into re-parameterization specifically for learning rate optimization.

3 METHODOLOGY
In this section, we first formally formulate the automatic model adaptation problem and analyze the limitations of baseline methods. We then introduce Rep-Adapter, our novel adapter module with a re-parameterization technique. We provide a rigorous proof that this adapter can simulate a fine-tuning layer with an arbitrary learning rate for each filter. Finally, we present a simple adapter tuning protocol to achieve fully automatic adaptation of pre-trained models without any additional search cost.

3.1 PRELIMINARIES
Model Adaptation. Let ψ denote a pre-trained model equipped with a randomly initialized task-specific head. Given a target task with the objective min L, model adaptation yields an optimal target model ψ* by executing a specific transfer protocol ζ.
In computer vision, most transfer protocols for ConvNets use the same network architecture as the pre-trained model, where the network parameters ω are initialized from the pre-trained weights ω₀. The core difference between protocols like fine-tuning and linear probing lies in the learning rate assigned to each parameter. Let η_m be a reference learning rate, and η ∈ ℝ^{|i|} be the learning rate multipliers for all |i| filters in the network. Given η, the objective is to find ω* = arg min L(ω, η). In this framework, fine-tuning sets a global η for all parameters, while linear probing sets η = 0.

Automatic Model Adaptation. Intuitively, the optimal learning rate for each parameter depends on factors like data distribution and model architecture. Therefore, automatic model adaptation seeks to learn the optimal transfer protocol ζ (i.e., the optimal η) for the target task jointly with the weights: min_{ω, η} L(ω, η).

3.2 REP-ADAPTER
The key intuition is that a soft balance between a frozen filter and a fully fine-tuning filter can represent an intermediate state—effectively, a filter tuning at a reduced learning rate. To achieve this balance, we propose the Rep-Adapter module.

Rep-Adapter. To enable soft balancing, Rep-Adapter comprises a frozen branch and a tuning branch, both initialized with the pre-trained network parameters ω₀. We explicitly introduce scaling factors δ, ζ ∈ ℝ^d for each of the d filters in the two branches. As shown in Figure 3(a), Rep-Adapter is defined as:
ψᴿ(ω₀, ωᴿ) := diag(δ) ψ(ω₀) + diag(ζ) ψ(ωᴿ),
where diag(·) constructs a diagonal matrix from the vector. While this weighting introduces two branches, it would typically double the model size and computation. We solve this via re-parameterization.

Re-parameterization. A Rep-Adapter contains two Conv-BN branches. Any Conv-BN branch can be merged into a single equivalent Conv layer. After this merge, let w₀, b₀ be the equivalent weights/bias of the frozen branch, and wᴿ, bᴿ be those of the tuning branch. The adapter's output is:
ψᴿ(x) = diag(δ)(w₀ ⋆ x + b₀) + diag(ζ)(wᴿ ⋆ x + bᴿ).
This can be merged into a single convolution layer with parameters:
w̃ = diag(δ) w₀ + diag(ζ) wᴿ,   b̃ = diag(δ) b₀ + diag(ζ) bᴿ.
Thus, as shown in Figure 3, the Rep-Adapter is converted to a single layer ψ(w̃) during inference, enabling parameter-free adaptation.

3.3 THEORETICAL ANALYSIS: SIMULATING FILTER-WISE LEARNING RATES
We now prove theoretically that Rep-Adapter can simulate a layer fine-tuning with distinct learning rates per filter.

Proposition 3.1. Given a pre-trained linear layer ψ(ω₀). Let ψᴿ(x) = diag(δ)ψ(ω₀) + diag(ζ)ψ(ωᴿ) denote this layer under the Rep-Adapter tuning scheme with learning rate η_m. Let ψᶠ(ω) denote this layer with each of its d filters fine-tuning at a specific learning rate η ∈ ℝ^d. If the network functions of the two schemes are identical before tuning step t, then there always exists a scaling factor ζ ∈ ℝ^d for each filter such that after one tuning step, ψᶠ(x) = ψᴿ(x) still holds.

Proof. (Provided in the main text, concluding that ζ_i = √(η_i / η_m) for i=1..d ensures equivalence after the update step.)

From Proposition 3.1, we derive two critical corollaries. First, by properly setting ζ based on the desired filter-wise learning rate η, Rep-Adapter can exactly represent a layer fine-tuning with that η throughout training. Second, when ζ is optimized via gradient descent, Rep-Adapter effectively learns the optimal filter-wise learning rate η. Therefore, the complex optimization of learning rates is relaxed to the straightforward optimization of the scaling factors ζ.

3.4 AUTOMATIC MODEL ADAPTATION VIA REP-ADAPTER TUNING
Rep-Adapter Tuning Protocol. We propose a simple protocol: attach a Rep-Adapter to every layer of a pre-trained model and make the scaling factors δ and ζ learnable. The adapter parameters ωᴿ and all scaling factors {δ}, {ζ} are jointly optimized. Based on Proposition 3.1, we have ω = diag(δ)ω₀ + diag(ζ)ωᴿ and η = diag(ζ²)η_m. Thus, the original automatic adaptation objective min_{ω, η} L(ω, η) is transformed into:
min_{ωᴿ, {δ}, {ζ}} L(ω₀, ωᴿ, {δ}, {ζ}, η_m),
where ω₀ and η_m are fixed hyperparameters. Since ζ participates in the loss calculation, it is optimized directly via backpropagation alongside ωᴿ. This simulates model fine-tuning with adaptive, filter-wise learning rates without any extra training loops or search phases. In practice, we use the learnable weight γ of the BatchNorm layers as the scaling factors for implementation convenience.

After tuning, the model is deployed by merging all Rep-Adapters via re-parameterization. The final model has identical size and computational complexity as a standard fine-tuned model, with zero added inference cost. This scheme avoids catastrophic forgetting and allows the tuned model to be used for further transfer, as the original weights ω₀ remain accessible within the merged representation.

4 EXPERIMENTS
We conduct exhaustive evaluations of Rep-Adapter across diverse settings: many-shot and low-shot transfer with supervised/self-supervised ImageNet pre-training, few-shot transfer with CLIP, and semi-supervised learning.

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
We use the VISSL library for cross-domain transfer, following the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) framework, which includes 14 diverse classification datasets. We evaluate in two primary settings: 1) Many-shot: using all training labels; 2) Low-shot: using only 1000 labeled images per dataset. For CLIP few-shot learning, we adopt a 16-shot setting on 10 datasets.

Pre-Training Protocols. We evaluate on models from self-supervised (PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV), fully-supervised, and text-supervised (CLIP) pre-training.

Baselines. Our primary baselines are the two most representative protocols: linear probing and full fine-tuning.

4.2 MANY-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
Results are presented in Table 3. Rep-Adapter overwhelmingly outperforms the baselines, achieving superior accuracy in 37 out of 42 evaluated scenarios. For instance, with PIRL pre-training, it improves average accuracy by 16.1% over linear probing and 1.4% over fine-tuning. On challenging datasets like CIFAR-100, DTD, and others, Rep-Adapter delivers massive gains (e.g., +46.7% on dSpr-Ori with PIRL vs. linear probing).

4.3 LOW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
As shown in Table 3, Rep-Adapter maintains its superior performance in the low-shot (1000 examples) setting, achieving an average gain of 13.1% over linear probing and 2.3% over fine-tuning with PIRL pre-training. The results also confirm the known trend that fine-tuning can underperform linear probing in low-data regimes on some datasets, a challenge our method automatically overcomes.

4.4 COMPARISON WITH OTHER FINE-GRAINED MODEL ADAPTATION METHODS
We compare Rep-Adapter against advanced methods like LoRA, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT), L²-SP, DELTA, AutoLR, and SpotTune.

Low-shot (Table 4): Rep-Adapter surpasses LoRA and VPT by a large margin, outperforming VPT by up to 19.15% on structured datasets of the VTAB-1k benchmark.
Many-shot (Table 4): Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms L²-SP, DELTA, and AutoLR by significant margins. Remarkably, it even surpasses the dynamic method SpotTune by 0.49% on average, despite SpotTune using an extra policy network and more than 2x inference model size.

4.5 FEW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING WITH CLIP
Table 5 shows results for 16-shot transfer with CLIP models (ResNet-50 and ViT-B/32 visual encoders). Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms strong few-shot methods like CoOp and Tip-Adapter, improving average accuracy by 3.1% and 1.6% over CoOp for ResNet-50 and ViT-B/32 backbones, respectively. Crucially, this is achieved without adding any parameters during inference, unlike prompt tuning or traditional adapter methods.

4.6 SEMI-SUPERVISED IMAGENET
Following standard semi-supervised protocols with 1% and 10% ImageNet labels, Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms both linear probing and fine-tuning across three self-supervised pre-training methods (PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV), as shown in Table 6. For example, with MoCoV2 pre-training, it improves over standard fine-tuning by 4.3% (1% labels) and 2.2% (10% labels).

4.7 OBJECT DETECTION & INSTANCE SEGMENTATION
To demonstrate broad transferability, we evaluate on detection/segmentation using Faster R-CNN on PASCAL VOC and Mask R-CNN on Cityscapes and COCO. Table 7 shows that Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms standard fine-tuning of the backbone network, achieving gains of up to 4.0 AP on VOC. These results also confirm our method's robustness to very small batch sizes (2 per GPU).

4.8 ABLATION STUDY
We ablate key design choices of Rep-Adapter on five datasets; results are summarized in Table 8.
(a) Effect of scaling factor δ: Making δ learnable (via BN γ) slightly improves performance.
(b) Joint vs. iterative optimization: Jointly optimizing {δ, ζ} with ωᴿ performs comparably to separate iterative optimization but is simpler.
(c) Batch-wise BN statistics: Using batch-wise statistics during training (our default) consistently outperforms using frozen running statistics.
(d) BN position: Placing BN inside each branch (before addition) is superior to placing a single BN after adding the branches.

5 CONCLUSION

To our knowledge, we are the first to formulate automatic model adaptation as a bi-level optimization problem and solve it with a theoretically grounded, parameter-free protocol. Our proposed Rep-Adapter jointly optimizes learning rates and model parameters during tuning. Exhaustive experiments provide unequivocal empirical evidence of its effectiveness and exceptional generalization ability across vision tasks. This work represents a significant leap forward, promising to drastically reduce the human effort required for hyperparameter tuning in transfer learning and paving the way for more efficient and powerful model deployment across diverse applications.

This paper introduces Rep-Adapter, an adapter module that achieves a soft balance between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each module has a frozen branch with pre-trained parameters and a learnable branch that adapts to target tasks. During inference, a re-parameterization scheme converts the two branches into one, avoiding increases in model size and computational cost.

We prove that during training, Rep-Adapter is equivalent to a layer fine-tuned with a different learning rate for each filter. This eliminates the need for hyperparameter search for learning rate configurations. By optimizing a network stacked with Rep-Adapters, the pre-trained model can be transferred with an adaptive learning rate per filter. Figure 1 compares fine-tuning, linear probing, and Rep-Adapter on three datasets (DTD, Caltech101, EuroSAT) using models pre-trained on ImageNet with the self-supervised method PIRL.

Experiments evaluate the method. The VISSL library is used to evaluate effectiveness on full dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning. Fine-tuning updates all parameters. Some works regularize the distance between the fine-tuned and pre-trained models on parameters (e.g., L2-SP) or output features (e.g., DELTA), but the regularization weight is a hand-crafted hyperparameter. Table 1 compares different model adaptation protocols based on: accessibility to original weight, automatic protocol, no extra training steps, no extra inference cost.

Figure 2 illustrates feature-based, fine-tuning, and adapter tuning methods.

Some methods, including LoRA and Progressive Networks, also use frozen and learnable branches. Differences are summarized in Table 2. First, the added branch in Rep-Adapter is non-linear during training and linear during inference, benefiting from the property of the BN layer. Second, two scaling factor layers are added to the branches, and the module achieves automatic learning rate adjustment. Third, Rep-Adapter aims at transfer learning performance, not parameter-efficient tuning of large models.

AutoML on transfer learning. Dynamic tuning methods introduce more than 2x parameters during inference, with additional policy networks or gating modules for dynamic routing. AutoLR auto-tunes layer-wise learning rates via repeated trials during training. Our method solves automatic model adaptation without extra training steps or extra inference model size. Table 1 shows only our method covers all four aspects.

It has been used for AutoML, e.g., using meta kernels to denote a neural architecture search space. 3 METHODOLOGY
We formulate the automatic model adaptation problem, analyze baseline downsides, then introduce Rep-Adapter. We prove it can simulate a fine-tuning layer with arbitrary learning rate per filter, and present a simple adapter tuning protocol for automatic adaptation without additional search cost.

3.1 PRELIMINARIES
Model Adaptation. Let ψ denote a pre-trained model with a random initialized task-specific head. Given a target task with objective min L, model adaptation yields a target model ψ* by executing transfer protocol ζ: ψ* = arg min_ψ L(ψ, ζ).

For ConvNets, most transfer protocols use the same network architecture, with parameters ω inherited from pre-trained ω0. Protocols fall into fine-tuning and linear probing. The difference is the learning rate of each parameter. Let η_m be a reference learning rate, and η ∈ ℝ^|i| be learning rate multipliers η^(i) for all |i| filters (i indexes filters). Given hyperparameter η, the objective is: ω* = arg min_ω L(ω, η). Fine-tuning sets a global η for all parameters; linear probing sets η = 0.

Automatic Model Adaptation. The optimal learning rate per parameter is influenced by factors like data distribution. Automatic model adaptation learns the proper transfer protocol ζ: min_{ω, η} L(ω, η).

A soft balancing between a frozen filter and a fine-tuning filter can represent an intermediate state, i.e., a filter tuning at a smaller learning rate. We propose an adapter module to achieve this balance, analyzed in Sec. 3.3.

3.2 REP-ADAPTER
To balance between a ConvNet layer with frozen filters and one with tuned filters, we present Rep-Adapter with a frozen branch and a tuning branch, both initialized with pre-trained parameters. Scaling factors δ, ζ ∈ ℝ^d are introduced for each filter of the two branches, where d is filter number per layer. As shown in Figure 3 (a), Rep-Adapter is defined as:
ψ^R(ω0, ω^R) := diag(δ) ψ(ω0) + diag(ζ) ψ(ω^R),
where ω0, ω^R denote pre-trained parameters and tuning branch parameters, and diag(·) constructs a diagonal matrix. Soft weighting with {δ, ζ} would introduce twice model size and computation. We introduce a re-parameterization scheme to merge the two branches.

Re-parameterization. A Rep-Adapter ψ^R for a ConvNet contains a frozen branch and an adapting branch, each with a convolution (Conv) layer and a batch normalization (BN) layer. Conv layer weights and optional bias are denoted by w and b. A BN layer performs per-channel normalization and scaling. Let μ and σ denote running mean and variance, and γ and β be channel-wise scaling factor and bias. A Conv-BN branch can be converted to a single Conv layer as:
ψ(x) = (w ⋆ x - μ) γ/σ + β = (w · γ/σ) ⋆ x + (β - μ γ/σ),
where ⋆ denotes convolution, and the equivalent weights and bias are w' and b'.

After merging Conv-BN, we merge the two Conv branches in Rep-Adapter. When outputs of two or more Conv layers with same configurations are added, they can be merged into one Conv. Let w0, b0 be pre-trained weights and bias of a merged Conv-BN branch, and w^R, b^R be merged weights and bias of the tuning branch. The adapter can be converted as:
ψ^R(x) = diag(δ)(w0 ⋆ x + b0) + diag(ζ)(w^R ⋆ x + b^R).
Thus, the adapter can be merged to a single convolution layer by setting:
w̃ = diag(δ) w0 + diag(ζ) w^R,   b̃ = diag(δ) b0 + diag(ζ) b^R.
A Rep-Adapter ψ^R can be converted to a single weight layer ψ(ω̃) during inference (Figure 3), enabling parameter-free model adaptation.

3.3 REP-ADAPTER AS FINE-TUNING WITH FILTER-WISE LEARNING RATE
We intuitively use Rep-Adapter as a balance between fine-tuning and frozen weights. Theoretical analysis shows Rep-Adapter can simulate a layer fine-tuning at a different learning rate.

Proposition 3.1. Given a pre-trained linear network layer ψ(ω0). Let ψ^R(x) = diag(δ) ψ(ω0) + diag(ζ) ψ(ω^R) denote this layer under adapter tuning at learning rate η_m, and ψ^F(ω) denote this layer with each of the d filters fine-tuning at learning rate η ∈ ℝ^d. Suppose the network functions of the two schemes are identical before tuning step t. Then there always exists scaling factor ζ ∈ ℝ^d for each filter such that after one step of tuning, ψ^F(x) = ψ^R(x) still holds.

Proof. Suppose ψ_t^F(x) = ψ_t^R(x) and ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R = ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^F at step t. Weight change of ω^R in the adapter is:
Δω_t^R = -η_m ∂L_t/∂ω_t^R = -η_m · diag(ζ) ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R.
Let ω̃_t = diag(δ) ω0 + diag(ζ) ω_t^R. The layer function after one-step adapter tuning is:
ψ_{t+1}^R(x) = diag(δ) ω0 x + diag(ζ)(ω^R + Δω^R) x = (ω̃_t - η_m · diag(ζ_1^2, ..., ζ_d^2) ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R) x.
For the fine-tuned case:
ψ_{t+1}^F(x) = ω_{t+1} x = (ω_t - diag(η) ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^F) x.
Recall ψ_t^F(x) = ψ_t^R(x) and ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R = ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^F. Thus, there exists:
ζ = (√(η_i / η_m))_{i=1}^d, such that ψ_{t+1}^F(x) = ψ_{t+1}^R(x).

Based on Proposition 3.1, two corollaries follow. First, if a Rep-Adapter and a network layer with filter-wise fine-tuning lr are identical before training, by setting scaling factors ζ based on filter-wise learning rate η, the Rep-Adapter can represent this layer at every step. Second, when using optimal scaling factors ζ at each training step, Rep-Adapter represents a layer fine-tuning with optimal filter-wise lr. Therefore, optimization of lr can be relaxed to optimization of ζ.

3.4 AUTOMATIC MODEL ADAPTATION VIA REP-ADAPTER TUNING
Rep-Adapter tuning. We add Rep-Adapter to every layer of a pre-trained model, making factors δ and ζ learnable. Adapter parameters ω^R and factors {δ} = {δ^(l)}_l=0^|l|, {ζ} = {ζ^(l)}_l=0^|l| of all layers are jointly optimized. Based on Proposition 3.1, ω = diag(δ) ω0 + diag(ζ) ω^R, η = diag(ζ^2) η_m. The original objective of automatic model adaptation in Equation (3) becomes:
min_{ω^R, {δ}, {ζ}} L(ω0, ω^R, {δ}, {ζ}, η_m),
where pre-trained ω0 and reference learning rate η_m are task-agnostic hyperparameters. Since ζ participates in loss calculation, it can be optimized by back-propagation with ω^R. Thus, Rep-Adapter tuning simulates model fine-tuning with adaptive learning rate per filter without extra training loops or search. In practice, the weight γ of BN layers have the same shape and similar role to scaling factors δ and ζ, so we directly use γ as the scaling factor.

After tuning, the model can be deployed by re-parameterization as in Sec. 3.2. Model size and computation complexity are the same as fine-tuning, with no additional inference parameters. This avoids catastrophic forgetting, and the tuned model can be used for further transfer as original weights are not modified.

4 EXPERIMENTS
We evaluate Rep-Adapter on many-shot and low-shot transfer learning with supervised and unsupervised ImageNet pre-training, few-shot transfer learning of CLIP, and semi-supervised learning.

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
Cross-domain transferring is implemented with VISSL, inspired by VTAB. VISSL contains 14 diverse classification downstream datasets, with two tuning settings: 1) many-shot transfer using all training labels; 2) low-shot transfer using 1000 labeled images sampled from downstream datasets. For few-shot learning with CLIP, 16-shot settings on 10 transfer learning datasets are adopted.

Pre-Training Protocol. We evaluate on self-supervised models (PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV for semi-supervised ImageNet), fully supervised models, and text-supervised models (CLIP).

Baseline methods. We compare with linear probing and fine-tuning as baselines.

4.2 MANY-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
We evaluate on many-shot transfer using all training data from 14 target datasets. Results are in Table 3. Rep-Adapter generally outperforms baselines on 37 out of 42 scenarios. For example, it improves over linear probing and fine-tuning by 16.1% and 1.4% on average with PIRL. On datasets like CIFAR-100, DTD, Flowers102, SUN397, Camelyon, Clevr-Dist, Rep-Adapter surpasses other methods by large margins (e.g., up to +46.7% on dSpr-Ori with PIRL compared to linear probing).

4.3 LOW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING
In low-shot transfer, 1000 training data per dataset are used. Results in Table 3 show Rep-Adapter still generally outperforms other methods, with average gain of 13.1% and 2.3% using PIRL pre-training. Fine-tuning performs better than linear probing in many-shot, but the opposite occurs in some low-shot cases (e.g., Caltech101 with PIRL and MoCoV2, DTD with all three self-supervised methods).

4.4 COMPARISON WITH OTHER FINE-GRAINED MODEL ADAPTATION METHODS
We compare with other fine-grained model adaptation methods.

Low-shot. We compare with LoRA and Visual Prompt Tuning on low-shot VTAB-1k benchmark with supervised pre-training. Results in Table 4 show Rep-Adapter outperforms LoRA and VPT by a large gap, surpassing VPT by up to 19.15% on structured datasets of VTAB-1k.

Many-shot. We compare with L2-SP, DELTA, AutoLR, and SpotTune in many-shot setting with supervised and PIRL pre-training. Results in Table 4 show Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms L2-SP, DELTA, AutoLR by large margins. It outperforms SpotTune by 0.49% on average. SpotTune uses an additional policy network and more than 2x model size during inference, while Rep-Adapter's improvement comes without these costs.

4.5 FEW-SHOT TRANSFER LEARNING WITH CLIP
We evaluate few-shot (16-shot) transfer learning with CLIP, comparing with Zero-shot CLIP, CoOp, Tip-Adapter. For CLIP models, Rep-Adapter is applied only on the visual encoder. We also apply it to CLIP-ViT-B/32, applying Rep-Adapter on every fully-connected layer.

Results in Table 5 show Rep-Adapter generally outperforms previous methods. On average, it improves over CoOp by 3.1% with ResNet50 and 1.6% with ViT-B/32. Rep-Adapter introduces no extra inference parameters, unlike prompt tuning and previous adapter-based methods.

4.6 SEMI-SUPERVISED IMAGENET
Following semi-supervised protocol, experiments use 1% and 10% labeled ImageNet training data with models pre-trained by PIRL, MoCoV2, SwAV. Results in Table 6 show Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms linear probing and fine-tuning. On MoCoV2, Rep-Adapter improves over fine-tuning by 4.3% and 2.2% with 1% and 10% label fraction.

4.7 OBJECT DETECTION & INSTANCE SEGMENTATION
We evaluate on object detection and instance segmentation using Faster-RCNN on PASCAL VOC and Mask-RCNN on Cityscapes and COCO 2017. We report bounding box mAP (AP^Box) and mask mAP (AP^Mask) in Table 7. Rep-Adapter consistently outperforms fine-tuning (by up to 4.0 AP on VOC). Results also show the method is not limited by batch size, as experiments use batch size 2 per GPU.

4.8 ABLATION STUDY
We perform ablation study on different components of Rep-Adapter.

(a) Effect of scaling factor δ. Learnable weight γ of BN is used as scaling factor. Effect of δ is ablated by freezing γ of BN in frozen branch. Table 8 shows enabling learnable δ slightly increases performance on all five datasets. It is enabled by default, though it does not affect simulated learning rate.

(b) Effect of joint optimization of δ, ζ with ω. We compare joint optimization (as in Equation (12)) with iterative optimization where δ, ζ and ω are updated in separate steps. Table 8 shows joint and iterative optimization achieve comparable performance.

(c) Effect of batch-wise statistics σ, μ. We explore effect of non-linearity and stochasticity from batch-wise statistics in BN during training. Table 8 shows enabling batch-wise statistics (ours) consistently outperforms using frozen σ, μ.

(d) Effect of BN position. BN can be in both branches before addition, or after addition with only Conv layers in branches. Table 8 shows using BN in branches improves performance.

(e) Effect of ω0 weight initialization. Frozen branch weight is initialized with pre-trained ω0. Table 8 shows random initialization drastically damages performance (e.g., from 90.3% to 17.0% on Pets), demonstrating use of information in frozen branch and importance of pre-trained initialization.

(f) Effect of weight frozen in frozen branch. Table 8 shows performance drops considerably on all five datasets (up to 4.8% on Pets) when making frozen branch learnable, performance comparable to fine-tuning. This indicates performance gain over fine-tuning is not from re-parameterization or increased network complexity, but relies on frozen weights.

5 CONCLUSION
Model adaptation is a long-standing problem. Previous baselines have downsides like manual learning rate tuning and extra inference cost. We formulate automatic model adaptation as a bi-level optimization problem. We propose a parameter-free protocol that jointly optimizes learning rate and model parameters during tuning with a theoretical basis. Experiments evidence effectiveness and generalization ability.

Title: Rep-Adapter: Adaptation of Pre-trained ConvNets via Re-parameterization

Abstract:
Transferring pre-trained models to target tasks is common. Different transfer protocols, such as fine-tuning and linear probing, have distinct advantages depending on factors like target dataset size, and selecting between them typically requires trial and error. This work presents a model adaptation protocol for ConvNets that aims to balance between fine-tuning and linear probing by adapting learning rates per convolution filter. We propose Rep-Adapter, an adapter module with a re-parameterization scheme. It achieves a soft balance between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters and can be converted to a single weight layer without introducing additional inference parameters. Theoretical analysis indicates Rep-Adapter can simulate a ConvNet layer with each filter fine-tuning at a different learning rate. A simple adapter tuning protocol with Rep-Adapter is presented for automatic adaptation without additional search cost. Experiments on various datasets with ResNet and CLIP evaluate Rep-Adapter on semi-supervised, few-shot, and full dataset transfer learning scenarios.

1 INTRODUCTION
Transferring large-scale pre-trained models to downstream tasks is common. Protocols include fine-tuning all parameters, feature-based methods that update only a task-specific head, and adapter tuning that introduces new learnable modules.

The most suitable protocol depends on factors like target dataset size and label fraction. For example, fine-tuning often performs better on fully-supervised ImageNet, while linear probing can be better on semi-supervised ImageNet. A similar trend is observed on Caltech101: fine-tuning outperforms linear probing for full dataset transfer, while linear probing performs better for a low-shot scenario with 1000 examples. Considering partial fine-tuning and layer-wise learning rate adjustment expands the option space, making exhaustive search computationally prohibitive.

Some methods aim to avoid manually tuning layer-wise and filter-wise hyperparameters. SpotTune and AdaFilter dynamically route between frozen and learnable weights, but use more than twice the original model size during inference. AutoLR searches for layer-wise fine-tuning learning rates via repeated trials, increasing training cost. We explore a model adaptation method that does not introduce extra training steps or extra parameters during inference.

This paper introduces Rep-Adapter, an adapter module that achieves a soft balance between pre-trained and fine-tuned filters. Each module has a frozen branch with pre-trained parameters and a learnable branch that adapts to target tasks. During inference, a re-parameterization scheme converts the two branches into one, avoiding increases in model size and computational cost.

We prove that during training, Rep-Adapter is equivalent to a layer fine-tuned with a different learning rate for each filter. This eliminates the need for hyperparameter search for learning rate configurations. By optimizing a network stacked with Rep-Adapters, the pre-trained model can be transferred with an adaptive learning rate per filter. Fine-tuning and linear probing correspond to setting the learned learning rate to a certain value or zero.

Figure 1 compares fine-tuning, linear probing, and Rep-Adapter on three datasets (DTD, Caltech101, EuroSAT) using models pre-trained on ImageNet with the self-supervised method PIRL.

Experiments evaluate the method. The VISSL library is used to evaluate effectiveness on full dataset and low-shot (1000 examples) transfer learning. Models are adapted from different pre-training protocols (fully-supervised, three self-supervised methods on ImageNet, CLIP pre-training) to various downstream datasets in full-shot, low-shot (1000 examples), or few-shot (16-shot) scenarios. Experiments are also performed on semi-supervised ImageNet with 1% and 10% label fractions, adapting models pre-trained by three self-supervised methods. Transferability to VOC object detection and Cityscapes, COCO instance segmentation tasks is explored. The Rep-Adapter tuning protocol is compared to baselines across tasks and scenarios.

2 RELATED WORK
Transfer Learning via Model Adaptation. Model adaptation methods modify a pre-trained model for a target task. Feature-based methods learn a task-specific head on frozen features. Fine-tuning updates all parameters. Some works regularize the distance between the fine-tuned and pre-trained models on parameters (e.g., L2-SP) or output features (e.g., DELTA), but the regularization weight is a hand-crafted hyperparameter. Some works use network ensemble to combine frozen and learnable weights, at a cost of using M times the model size during inference, where M is the number of ensemble models. Adapter tuning adds light-weight modules to the pre-trained network without changing original parameters. Previous convolution adapter modules for incremental learning add small point-wise convolution adapters, increasing model size by about 11% per task. Rep-Adapter is related to ensemble methods, but an ensemble cannot be directly converted to a single model due to non-linearity, leading to more parameters and computation. Unlike previous methods, Rep-Adapter does not increase inference model size.

Table 1 compares different model adaptation protocols based on: accessibility to original weight, automatic protocol, no extra training steps, no extra inference cost.

Figure 2 illustrates feature-based, fine-tuning, and adapter tuning methods.

Some methods, including LoRA and Progressive Networks, also use frozen and learnable branches. Differences are summarized in Table 2. First, the added branch in Rep-Adapter is non-linear during training and linear during inference, benefiting from the property of the BN layer. Second, two scaling factor layers are added to the branches, and the module achieves automatic learning rate adjustment. Third, Rep-Adapter aims at transfer learning performance, not parameter-efficient tuning of large models.

AutoML on transfer learning. Dynamic tuning methods introduce more than 2x parameters during inference, with additional policy networks or gating modules for dynamic routing. AutoLR auto-tunes layer-wise learning rates via repeated trials during training. Our method solves automatic model adaptation without extra training steps or extra inference model size. Table 1 shows only our method covers all four aspects.

Traditional Re-parameterization. Traditional re-parameterization parameterizes weight as a combination of parameters for optimization. It has been used for AutoML, e.g., using meta kernels to denote a neural architecture search space. SCC and CondConv derive a kernel as a weighted sum of multiple generated kernels for conditionally parameterized convolution. We focus on automating learning rate optimization during transfer learning.

Structural Re-parameterization. Structural re-parameterization parameterizes a network structure with parameters transformed from another structure. It has been used to boost ConvNet and MLP training by introducing merge-able branches with different architectures, without changing the inference architecture. We use re-parameterization to merge a frozen branch and a tuning branch with the same architecture, simulating a layer with arbitrary learning rate. This is the first time re-parameterization is proved to represent different learning rates, and scaling factors are introduced to re-parameterization for learning rate optimization.

3 METHODOLOGY
We formulate the automatic model adaptation problem, analyze baseline downsides, then introduce Rep-Adapter. We prove it can simulate a fine-tuning layer with arbitrary learning rate per filter, and present a simple adapter tuning protocol for automatic adaptation without additional search cost.

3.1 PRELIMINARIES
Model Adaptation. Let ψ denote a pre-trained model with a random initialized task-specific head. Given a target task with objective min L, model adaptation yields a target model ψ* by executing transfer protocol ζ: ψ* = arg min_ψ L(ψ, ζ).

For ConvNets, most transfer protocols use the same network architecture, with parameters ω inherited from pre-trained ω0. Protocols fall into fine-tuning and linear probing. The difference is the learning rate of each parameter. Let η_m be a reference learning rate, and η ∈ ℝ^|i| be learning rate multipliers η^(i) for all |i| filters (i indexes filters). Given hyperparameter η, the objective is: ω* = arg min_ω L(ω, η). Fine-tuning sets a global η for all parameters; linear probing sets η = 0.

Automatic Model Adaptation. The optimal learning rate per parameter is influenced by factors like data distribution. Automatic model adaptation learns the proper transfer protocol ζ: min_{ω, η} L(ω, η).

A soft balancing between a frozen filter and a fine-tuning filter can represent an intermediate state, i.e., a filter tuning at a smaller learning rate. We propose an adapter module to achieve this balance, analyzed in Sec. 3.3.

3.2 REP-ADAPTER

ψ^R(ω0, ω^R) := diag(δ) ψ(ω0) + diag(ζ) ψ(ω^R),
where ω0, ω^R denote pre-trained parameters and tuning branch parameters, and diag(·) constructs a diagonal matrix. Soft weighting with {δ, ζ} would introduce twice model size and computation. We introduce a re-parameterization scheme to merge the two branches.

Re-parameterization. A Rep-Adapter ψ^R for a ConvNet contains a frozen branch and an adapting branch, each with a convolution (Conv) layer and a batch normalization (BN) layer. Conv layer weights and optional bias are denoted by w and b. A BN layer performs per-channel normalization and scaling. Let μ and σ denote running mean and variance, and γ and β be channel-wise scaling factor and bias. A Conv-BN branch can be converted to a single Conv layer as:
ψ(x) = (w ⋆ x - μ) γ/σ + β = (w · γ/σ) ⋆ x + (β - μ γ/σ),
where ⋆ denotes convolution, and the equivalent weights and bias are w' and b'.

After merging Conv-BN, we merge the two Conv branches in Rep-Adapter. When outputs of two or more Conv layers with same configurations are added, they can be merged into one Conv. ψ^R(x) = diag(δ)(w0 ⋆ x + b0) + diag(ζ)(w^R ⋆ x + b^R).
Thus, the adapter can be merged to a single convolution layer by setting:
w̃ = diag(δ) w0 + diag(ζ) w^R,   b̃ = diag(δ) b0 + diag(ζ) b^R.
A Rep-Adapter ψ^R can be converted to a single weight layer ψ(ω̃) during inference (Figure 3), enabling parameter-free model adaptation.

Δω_t^R = -η_m ∂L_t/∂ω_t^R = -η_m · diag(ζ) ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R.
Let ω̃_t = diag(δ) ω0 + diag(ζ) ω_t^R. The layer function after one-step adapter tuning is:
ψ_{t+1}^R(x) = diag(δ) ω0 x + diag(ζ)(ω^R + Δω^R) x = (ω̃_t - η_m · diag(ζ_1^2, ..., ζ_d^2) ∂L_t/∂ψ_t^R) x.
For the fine-tuned case:

The original objective of automatic model adaptation in Equation (3) becomes:
min_{ω^R, {δ}, {ζ}} L(ω0, ω^R, {δ}, {ζ}, η_m),
where pre-trained ω0 and reference learning rate η_m are task-agnostic hyperparameters. Since ζ participates in loss calculation, it can be optimized by back-propagation with ω^R. Thus, Rep-Adapter tuning simulates model fine-tuning with adaptive learning rate per filter without extra training loops or search. In practice, the weight γ of BN layers have the same shape and similar role to scaling factors δ and ζ, so we directly use γ as the scaling factor.

After tuning, the model can be deployed by re-parameterization as in Sec. 3.2. Model size and computation complexity are the same as fine-tuning, with no additional inference parameters. This avoids catastrophic forgetting, and the tuned model can be used for further transfer as original weights are not modified.

title: Two Birds with One Stone: Protecting DNN Models Against Unauthorized Inference and Domain Transfer
