Title: Two Birds with One Stone: A Comprehensive Framework for Protecting DNN Models Against Unauthorized Inference and Domain Transfer

Abstract

Deep neural network (DNN) models constitute immensely valuable intellectual property (IP) assets due to their remarkable and impressive performance, which malicious actors might seek to extract and exploit for unauthorized and illegal use. While existing model protection schemes have primarily focused on preventing attackers from obtaining a well-performing model, the critical issue of transferability for such extracted models has been largely and unfortunately under-explored. In this scenario, attackers could easily transfer the stolen model to another, potentially lucrative, domain while maintaining good performance, thereby compounding the infringement. For the very first time, this pioneering work jointly and comprehensively considers these two paramount security concerns. We propose DeTrans, an innovative and robust DNN model protection framework that strategically utilizes bi-level optimization to meticulously modify the weights of highly transferable filters. This approach definitively prevents both unauthorized inference on the source domain and subsequent cross-domain transfer following model extraction. Furthermore, DeTrans crucially ensures that the full, original model functionality is perfectly preserved for authorized users through specialized hardware support. Our extensive experimental evaluations conclusively demonstrate that DeTrans can dramatically reduce inference accuracy in the source domain to the level of random guessing and simultaneously achieve an impressive reduction in transferability to target domains of up to 81.23%.

1 INTRODUCTION

The widespread success and adoption of on-device machine learning (ML) can be directly attributed to the deployment of high-performance deep neural networks (DNNs). Given the monumental effort required for model training—encompassing massive data labeling campaigns and substantial computational resources—pre-trained DNNs are undeniably valuable intellectual property (IP) assets for model owners. However, model extraction has been definitively demonstrated to be both practical and successful for on-device ML, where the exact DNN models can be completely extracted via sophisticated run-time attacks. Such attacks constitute a clear IP violation and can potentially lead to significant financial and competitive losses for model owners. As a primary countermeasure, previous works have almost exclusively focused on preventing unauthorized inference for the victim models within their original source domain. However, these works have critically neglected another, equally serious attack objective that follows model leakage: cross-domain transfer.

Why would attackers be motivated to conduct cross-domain transfer on stolen victim models? In practical terms, model IP attackers are strongly motivated to transfer a maliciously extracted model to other domains of interest. They can exploit the common, valuable features already learned by the pre-trained model to overcome data scarcity and save considerable effort compared to the prohibitive cost of training a model from scratch. This act represents a further and significant infringement of model owners’ rights and has been previously identified in the literature. While some defense strategies have been suggested, they predominantly and restrictively rely on training models from scratch specifically to safeguard against transferability, which severely limits their applicability to general, already pre-trained models. Moreover, employing these specialized training strategies to obtain a pre-trained model is certainly not the optimal approach. This could negatively impact not only the model’s core accuracy but also other desirable attributes, such as causing model owners to lose their own transferability advantage. Despite their inapplicability to pre-trained models, the models produced by these methods still consistently exhibit high performance on the source domain, rendering them inherently vulnerable to unauthorized inference by attackers. Importantly, addressing this dual vulnerability is not as straightforward as simply merging existing methods, since techniques designed to tackle these distinct issues utilize disparate training strategies and typically start from scratch. Consequently, model owners cannot sequentially apply different, incompatible methods to a model and expect it to concurrently and effectively address both critical vulnerabilities.

Considering that both unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer are undeniably practical and common attack objectives, we are therefore motivated to propose a comprehensive, unified protection method that can intelligently post-process pre-trained models to achieve two definitive goals: (i) significant accuracy degradation on the source domain for any unauthorized use, and (ii) substantially reduced transferability to potential target domains. However, implementing such a holistic solution faces several non-trivial challenges. First, the potential target domains that attackers might choose are completely uncertain and unknown during protection. Second, we must implicitly yet accurately measure the performance of possible model transfers during the protection process itself, thereby ensuring the protected model remains robust against a wide range of cross-domain transfer attempts. Finally, it is absolutely essential to maintain the original high performance on the source domain for legitimate, authorized users.

To decisively address these challenges, we propose DeTrans, a novel and powerful approach that provides double-layered protection for pre-trained DNN models. For the first challenge, while we cannot predict the specific target domain, we make a reasonable and well-supported assumption that the distribution of any potential target domain is likely to be close to that of the source domain. With this key assumption, we generate multiple auxiliary domains based on the source domain, inspired by techniques from single domain generalization, to effectively solve the problem of target domain uncertainty. To address the second challenge, we formulate an elegant bi-level optimization problem, where the lower level explicitly assesses the model's current transferability.

Furthermore, DeTrans leverages trusted hardware support in the form of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) to perfectly address the final challenge. Specifically, DeTrans only optimizes the weights of the single filter identified with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer of the victim DNN model. Since these particular weights capture the most common and transferable features between the source and potential target domains, strategically perturbing them can effectively degrade performance on both domains simultaneously. Therefore, when the protected model is deployed on a device, attackers cannot achieve high performance on either domain, thus achieving the desired double protection. Meanwhile, the original values of these perturbed weights are compact enough to be stored within the stringent secure memory of a TEE. These stored values can be used to seamlessly restore the high performance on the source domain exclusively for authorized users. The major contributions of this transformative work are definitively summarized as follows:

• To the best of our knowledge, this is the inaugural work that successfully mitigates the multifaceted risk of model leakage by preventing attackers from both unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer, thereby achieving truly comprehensive protection for pre-trained DNN models.
• By leveraging generated auxiliary domains, DeTrans optimizes a critical subset of the victim model's weights through a sophisticated bi-level optimization process. The resulting protected model exhibits nearly random guessing performance for attackers on the source domain and reduces transferability by a remarkable margin of up to 81.23% on potential target domains.
• Extensive experiments conclusively demonstrate that DeTrans significantly outperforms state-of-the-art model protection works and exhibits strong robustness against various fine-tuning methods that attackers might employ.

2 BACKGROUND

2.1 THREAT MODEL

Attackers. To achieve comprehensive protection, we assume a strong and knowledgeable model IP attacker who possesses knowledge of the domain in which the victim model was originally trained. We also assume the attacker is capable of extracting the complete DNN model—including its architecture and all pre-trained weights—from unsecured memory, for instance by using a run-time attack. As illustrated, attackers could exploit the extracted model in two primary ways: 1) they directly use the model for inference tasks that align perfectly with the source domain; or 2) they fine-tune the extracted model to achieve successful cross-domain transfer after collecting a small set of labeled data from a new target domain, while keeping the model architecture unchanged.

Model IP Owners. To protect pre-trained models against illegal exploitation while perfectly preserving model performance for authorized users, model owners can employ defense solutions integrated with trusted hardware support (e.g., a TEE). This hardware can block all unauthorized access to critical data stored in secure memory. Specifically, owners will generate a protected model for deployment on devices, while the crucial original data (the pristine values of the perturbed weights) is safeguarded exclusively within the TEE. During authorized inference, users can utilize this data but cannot extract it, thanks to the fundamental security properties of the TEE. It is important to note that our intention is not to block all conceivable target domains, as this would be entirely impractical. Instead, we consider a common and highly practical scenario where the target domains are distributionally close to the source domain and share the same label space.

2.2 SINGLE DOMAIN GENERALIZATION

To protect models from illegal cross-domain transfer, we face the significant challenge that the target domains are completely unknown during the model protection phase. This identical challenge exists in the field of single domain generalization, where the objective is to allow a model learned from a single source to generalize well to a series of unknown target distributions. Furthermore, it also assumes that the unknown target domain is close to the source, which aligns perfectly with our own core assumption. A common and effective practice in single domain generalization is to augment the source domain data to approximate the unknown domain distributions. For example, some methods add adversarially perturbed samples to the data space, while others generate fictitious domains using auto-encoders to encourage large domain discrepancy in the input space.

Given the shared challenge and assumption, we generate auxiliary domains by augmenting the source domain using conceptually similar methods. However, it is crucial to note that our design objective is precisely the opposite of domain generalization: we intentionally and systematically reduce the victim model’s generalization ability, thereby impeding its ease of transfer to any unknown target domains.

2.3 TRUSTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT

The Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) has been successfully used in prior model protection schemes to create hardware-based isolation between the secure and normal memory of a device, thereby isolating sensitive information. However, the secure memory space is relatively limited compared to the size of typical DNNs. To address this critical constraint, we aim to identify a minimal subset of critical model weights that disproportionately affect the model’s performance on both the source and potential target domains. Without authorized access to these critical weights stored securely within the TEE, the extracted portion of the model will perform poorly due to the lack of this essential data. It is also noted that even during authorized inference, the data inside the TEE remains a black box for users; they can leverage it to achieve high accuracy but cannot extract it. Since the effectiveness of TEE has been firmly established in other studies, this work will not delve into its implementation details.

2.4 DISCUSSION ON RELATED WORKS

As model IP protection is critically important for model owners, several studies have explored methods to degrade a model’s performance to mitigate the risk of model leakage. For example, some propose key-dependent training algorithms to obfuscate the weight space, causing accuracy to drop significantly if the model is extracted. Others introduce protection for pre-trained models by obfuscating a small set of model weights using a fine-grained mask. However, these methods focus primarily on degrading accuracy on the source domain and cannot naturally reduce the model's inherent transferability to prevent cross-domain transfer by attackers.

Conversely, other works have proposed training strategies specifically designed to restrict model transferability by capturing exclusive data representations or emphasizing private style features. However, these methods cannot be extended to general pre-trained models, and using them to train a model would inherently restrict its transferability even for the legitimate owners. More importantly, these methods are designed for cloud-based scenarios where high source-domain performance must be maintained for users, rendering them completely ineffective at preventing attackers from making unauthorized inferences on the source domain itself.

3 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK: DETRANS

Aiming to achieve the best possible protection against both illegal usages—unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer—we propose an extensive and novel model IP protection scheme that can provide simultaneous accuracy degradation on the source domain and transferability reduction on target domains. The workflow of our proposed method, DeTrans, is illustrated. We first generate auxiliary domains by augmenting the source domain, then select a critical set of weights via a filter-wise mask designed to fit within small secure memory. Finally, we obtain the protected model by modifying the selected weights through a sophisticated bi-level optimization process. These modifications decisively hinder attackers from leveraging the victim model, thereby successfully protecting the model IP.

3.1 AUXILIARY DOMAINS

We introduce a generative domain augmentation method to produce multiple auxiliary domains based on the source domain. The fundamental rationale behind this approach is that attackers are far more likely to attempt model transfer when the target domain closely aligns with the source domain. This choice provides them with the well-known advantages of transfer learning while avoiding potential drawbacks. Therefore, even though we cannot precisely predict the specific target domain attackers may select, we can effectively approximate its distribution by intelligently augmenting the source domain.

Inspired by prior work, we build a Wasserstein Auto-Encoder (WAE) to introduce controlled domain discrepancy between the source domain and the generated auxiliary domains. However, to accurately simulate the cross-domain transfer process attackers use, we need to generate fully labeled samples, mimicking how attackers use limited labeled data to fine-tune an extracted model. To this end, we enhance the WAE by incorporating the label as a conditioning signal during the decoding phase. Specifically, it consists of an encoder and a conditional decoder. We employ Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to quantify the distance between the encoded distribution and a Gaussian prior. The conditional WAE is optimized accordingly.

After optimization, we can generate labeled samples to construct auxiliary domains via the decoder. To encourage a wider range of domain discrepancies that better align with unseen target distributions, we introduce feature augmentation by incorporating a latent vector sampled from a Gaussian distribution into the feature embedding. This proven augmentation technique effectively enhances domain discrepancy through variations in the distribution parameters. As a result, we can generate diverse and representative auxiliary domains. Each auxiliary domain is then divided into a training set and a validation set for use in the lower-level and upper-level optimization steps, respectively.

3.2 MASK DESIGN

To overcome the stringent limitations of secure memory in the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), DeTrans introduces an innovative filter-wise mask design, allowing for the modification of weights exclusively for a carefully selected subset of filters. The filter selection strategy is centered on identifying the single filter with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer. This selection is based on the understanding that filters with higher transferability capture the shared, common patterns between domains, making them intrinsically more transferable. By adjusting the weights of these high-transferability filters, we directly disrupt the shared features learned by both the source and target domains, thus achieving concurrent and significant accuracy degradation and transferability reduction. Since the true target domains are unknown, we substitute them with our generated auxiliary domains for this measurement.

To quantify filter transferability, we adopt a discrepancy-based approach. We first measure the discrepancy between the source domain and each auxiliary domain for each channel (the output of a filter). The distance-based probability for each channel is then calculated, where a higher score indicates greater transferability of that filter. We calculate these scores for each source-auxiliary domain pair and take the average to definitively rank the filters. Consequently, a binary mask is generated, with a value of 1 indicating the selected filter with the highest transferability in each corresponding layer.

3.3 BI-LEVEL OPTIMIZATION

We consider a pre-trained model with weights as the victim model, trained on labeled data from the source domain. We selectively modify a small set of weights corresponding to the chosen filters, while keeping the rest of the model weights completely fixed. A basic protection method would involve adding weight changes to degrade performance on the source domain, thus preventing unauthorized inference. The optimization of these modified weights follows a straightforward maximization of the loss on the source domain data.

Given that our protection ambitiously extends to preventing cross-domain transfer, we significantly improve upon the basic method by formulating a powerful bi-level optimization framework. This advanced framework enables us to comprehensively address the model protection challenge by alternating optimization stages while implicitly considering the transferability of the protected model through the use of our auxiliary domains.

Lower-level Optimization. In this stage, we explicitly emulate how an attacker would optimize the extracted model for transfer to a new domain. We find an optimal weight update on the extracted model to enhance its performance on the training data of an auxiliary domain, simulating the attacker's fine-tuning process.

Upper-level Optimization. To leverage the knowledge gained from the lower-level optimization about the model's current transferability, we then optimize the protected model's weights further. The explicit goal here is to diminish the model's transferability across all auxiliary domains, guided by a maximization of the loss on the validation sets of these domains. Notably, we also incorporate the source domain itself as one of the auxiliary domains during this bi-level optimization to ensure that accuracy degradation is rigorously maintained on the source domain.

3.4 SUMMARY OF DETRANS

Integrating all the aforementioned strategies, we present the complete DeTrans algorithm, with the following key operational points: (i) Given a pre-trained model, DeTrans first identifies the most critical filters for transfer learning and generates a corresponding mask for optimization; (ii) DeTrans implements basic protection as a warm-up to initialize the modified weights; (iii) DeTrans then employs the bi-level optimization to further and more effectively optimize these weights, incorporating the source domain to maintain accuracy degradation. The optimal protected model is generated upon convergence, which successfully prevents attackers from both direct use and model transfer. Furthermore, the small set of original weights is stored in TEE secure memory, which corrects the functionality of the protected model exclusively for authorized users.

4 EXPERIMENTS

We thoroughly evaluate the performance of DeTrans on multiple DNN models and datasets for classification tasks, conclusively demonstrating its superior effectiveness compared to other methods. As DeTrans specifically targets the protection of on-device DNN models—where memory and computational capability are limited—we examine it on relatively small DNNs and datasets in line with practical deployment scenarios. Additionally, we conduct detailed ablation studies to examine the influence of DeTrans's important constituent modules.

4.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP

Dataset. We examine our method on two primary types of datasets following previous related works. One category is digits datasets, including MNIST, USPS, and SVHN. The other is natural image datasets, including CIFAR-10 and STL-10.

DNN Models. We train VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on different datasets as our victim models, selected to match the models used in previous comparative works. The victim models are trained using the Adam optimizer.

Settings. We generate auxiliary domains based on the source domain using specified parameter ranges. The true target domain remains completely unseen during the model protection phase. We assume attackers hold only 5% of the training data from the target domain to conduct cross-domain transfer. The ratio of modified parameters is kept constant and minimal (0.07% for VGG-11 and 0.18% for ResNet-18). The corresponding storage size is compact enough to meet the secure memory constraints of a TEE. We use top-1 inference accuracy as the evaluation metric for all experiments.

4.2 COMPARISON METHODS

As DeTrans is the first approach to provide dual protection, there are no previous works fully comparable. However, to rigorously evaluate its effectiveness, we adopt state-of-the-art (SOTA) works for comparison on each individual aspect. For preventing unauthorized inference, we select the SOTA method NNSplitter. For defending against model transfer, we compare against recent works NTL and CUTI. We also include a Baseline (no protection) and a Supervised Learning (SL) baseline where attackers train from scratch with only 5% of data.

4.3 PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

Based on our threat model, we consider two attack scenarios and demonstrate definitively that DeTrans can defend against both attacks simultaneously, while SOTA works can only achieve one aspect.

Scenario I: Unauthorized Inference. When attackers' target aligns with the source domain, they can directly use the extracted model. DeTrans aims to degrade accuracy on the source domain to prevent this. From the results, we observe that applying DeTrans causes a dramatic drop in top-1 inference accuracy compared to the baseline (from over 90% to approximately 10%). This degraded accuracy is comparable to the SOTA method NNSplitter and is even lower than what an attacker could achieve by training a new model from scratch with very limited data (SL). In stark contrast, methods designed for restraining transferability (NTL, CUTI) completely fail to prevent unauthorized inference, as their accuracy on the source domain remains high.

Scenario II: Model Transfer. We form several domain pairs to demonstrate that models protected by DeTrans have significantly reduced transferability. As shown in the results, while NNSplitter is optimal for defending against unauthorized inference, it shows almost no reduction in transferability. DeTrans, however, proves to be highly effective in reducing transferability, achieving up to an 81.23% accuracy drop. It achieves protection comparable to the SOTA transferability-reduction methods (NTL, CUTI), with a difference of less than 4%. Importantly, unlike NTL and CUTI, DeTrans does not require any input-level modifications (like adding a patch) to achieve this reduction.

Furthermore, in cases where transferring to a more complex domain yields relatively low accuracy even without protection, attackers may still be motivated to extract and transfer the model, as training from scratch with limited data would yield even worse performance. In such scenarios, DeTrans successfully reduces the transferred performance to a level lower than the SL baseline, rendering the attacker's effort futile.

Overall, DeTrans achieves comprehensive model protection by successfully defending against unauthorized inference and model transfer at the same time, filling a critical gap in SOTA methods. It reduces source-domain accuracy to random-guessing levels while restraining performance on unseen target domains below what an attacker could achieve by training from scratch with very limited data.

4.4 ABLATION STUDIES

Filter Selection. The filter selection strategy in DeTrans is based on measuring channel transferability. To measure its influence, we replace it with a random filter selection strategy. Results show that random selection can also reduce transferability, but DeTrans performs significantly better, providing an extra 14.95% accuracy drop on average, validating the importance of our targeted selection strategy.

Optimization Method. Our bi-level optimization considers the potential attack surface (malicious transfer) during protection. To demonstrate its necessity, we compare it to a naive, alternating optimization scheme where a protector and attacker alternately optimize against each other with knowledge of the target domain. The model performance after this naive optimization shows only a 1.3% accuracy drop, while our bi-level optimization achieves over 80% drop. The reason is that in the naive scheme, each party can counteract the other's last step, resulting in minimal net effect, especially since the attacker makes the final modification. This conclusively demonstrates the superior effectiveness of our bi-level formulation.

5 DISCUSSION

5.1 MODIFICATION AND FINE-TUNING RANGE

We explore different ranges for protector modifications (e.g., modifying only the first layer vs. one filter per layer) and attacker fine-tuning (no fine-tuning, fine-tuning last layer, or fine-tuning the whole model). Evaluation on VGG-11 shows that modifying one filter per layer (p2) outperforms modifying only the first layer (p1) when defending against unauthorized inference. Furthermore, when using p2, attackers achieve very low accuracy (~20%) on a target domain regardless of their fine-tuning range. This demonstrates the clear advantage of spreading the weight modifications strategically across all layers of the network.

5.2 APPLICABILITY BEYOND SMALLER MODELS

While this work focuses on on-device models, our proposed methodology is generic and can be applied to larger models if the device can accommodate them. As a case study, we applied DeTrans to a pre-trained ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10. By modifying only 0.14% of the weights, DeTrans degraded unauthorized inference accuracy to 10% and reduced cross-domain transfer accuracy to 10.5%, which also outperforms SOTA methods in reducing transferability, confirming the scalability of our approach.

6 CONCLUSION

In this work, we introduce DeTrans, a novel and comprehensive framework for protecting on-device DNN models against the dual threats of unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer, while perfectly preserving model performance for authorized users via a TEE. By selectively modifying a minimal subset of weights in the pre-trained model, DeTrans achieves near-random guess performance on the source domain and substantial transferability reduction for potential target domains (exceeding 80% for ResNet-18). The original values of these modified weights are stored securely within a TEE, accessible only to authorized users. Moreover, DeTrans remains robust regardless of how attackers attempt to fine-tune the protected model and is applicable to larger model architectures. Overall, DeTrans decisively fills a critical gap in SOTA model protection works, which have previously either failed to prevent unauthorized inference or overlooked the serious risk of cross-domain transfer by attackers.

Title: Two Birds with One Stone: A Comprehensive Framework for Protecting DNN Models Against Unauthorized Inference and Domain Transfer

Abstract

Deep neural network (DNN) models constitute immensely valuable intellectual property (IP) assets due to their remarkable and impressive performance, which malicious actors might seek to extract and exploit for unauthorized and illegal use. While existing model protection schemes have primarily focused on preventing attackers from obtaining a well-performing model, the critical issue of transferability for such extracted models has been largely and unfortunately under-explored. In this scenario, attackers could easily transfer the stolen model to another, potentially lucrative, domain while maintaining good performance, thereby compounding the infringement. For the very first time, this pioneering work jointly and comprehensively considers these two paramount security concerns. We propose DeTrans, an innovative and robust DNN model protection framework that strategically utilizes bi-level optimization to meticulously modify the weights of highly transferable filters. This approach definitively prevents both unauthorized inference on the source domain and subsequent cross-domain transfer following model extraction. Furthermore, DeTrans crucially ensures that the full, original model functionality is perfectly preserved for authorized users through specialized hardware support. Our extensive experimental evaluations conclusively demonstrate that DeTrans can dramatically reduce inference accuracy in the source domain to the level of random guessing and simultaneously achieve an impressive reduction in transferability to target domains of up to 81.23%.

1 INTRODUCTION

The widespread success and adoption of on-device machine learning (ML) can be directly attributed to the deployment of high-performance deep neural networks (DNNs). Given the monumental effort required for model training—encompassing massive data labeling campaigns and substantial computational resources—pre-trained DNNs are undeniably valuable intellectual property (IP) assets for model owners. However, model extraction has been definitively demonstrated to be both practical and successful for on-device ML, where the exact DNN models can be completely extracted via sophisticated run-time attacks. Such attacks constitute a clear IP violation and can potentially lead to significant financial and competitive losses for model owners. As a primary countermeasure, previous works have almost exclusively focused on preventing unauthorized inference for the victim models within their original source domain. However, these works have critically neglected another, equally serious attack objective that follows model leakage: cross-domain transfer.

Why would attackers be motivated to conduct cross-domain transfer on stolen victim models? In practical terms, model IP attackers are strongly motivated to transfer a maliciously extracted model to other domains of interest. They can exploit the common, valuable features already learned by the pre-trained model to overcome data scarcity and save considerable effort compared to the prohibitive cost of training a model from scratch. This act represents a further and significant infringement of model owners’ rights and has been previously identified in the literature. While some defense strategies have been suggested, they predominantly and restrictively rely on training models from scratch specifically to safeguard against transferability, which severely limits their applicability to general, already pre-trained models. Moreover, employing these specialized training strategies to obtain a pre-trained model is certainly not the optimal approach. This could negatively impact not only the model’s core accuracy but also other desirable attributes, such as causing model owners to lose their own transferability advantage. Despite their inapplicability to pre-trained models, the models produced by these methods still consistently exhibit high performance on the source domain, rendering them inherently vulnerable to unauthorized inference by attackers. Importantly, addressing this dual vulnerability is not as straightforward as simply merging existing methods, since techniques designed to tackle these distinct issues utilize disparate training strategies and typically start from scratch. Consequently, model owners cannot sequentially apply different, incompatible methods to a model and expect it to concurrently and effectively address both critical vulnerabilities.

Considering that both unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer are undeniably practical and common attack objectives, we are therefore motivated to propose a comprehensive, unified protection method that can intelligently post-process pre-trained models to achieve two definitive goals: (i) significant accuracy degradation on the source domain for any unauthorized use, and (ii) substantially reduced transferability to potential target domains. However, implementing such a holistic solution faces several non-trivial challenges. First, the potential target domains that attackers might choose are completely uncertain and unknown during protection. Second, we must implicitly yet accurately measure the performance of possible model transfers during the protection process itself, thereby ensuring the protected model remains robust against a wide range of cross-domain transfer attempts. Finally, it is absolutely essential to maintain the original high performance on the source domain for legitimate, authorized users.

To decisively address these challenges, we propose DeTrans, a novel and powerful approach that provides double-layered protection for pre-trained DNN models. For the first challenge, while we cannot predict the specific target domain, we make a reasonable and well-supported assumption that the distribution of any potential target domain is likely to be close to that of the source domain. With this key assumption, we generate multiple auxiliary domains based on the source domain, inspired by techniques from single domain generalization, to effectively solve the problem of target domain uncertainty. To address the second challenge, we formulate an elegant bi-level optimization problem, where the lower level explicitly assesses the model's current transferability.

Furthermore, DeTrans leverages trusted hardware support in the form of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) to perfectly address the final challenge. Specifically, DeTrans only optimizes the weights of the single filter identified with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer of the victim DNN model. Since these particular weights capture the most common and transferable features between the source and potential target domains, strategically perturbing them can effectively degrade performance on both domains simultaneously. Therefore, when the protected model is deployed on a device, attackers cannot achieve high performance on either domain, thus achieving the desired double protection. Meanwhile, the original values of these perturbed weights are compact enough to be stored within the stringent secure memory of a TEE. These stored values can be used to seamlessly restore the high performance on the source domain exclusively for authorized users. The major contributions of this transformative work are definitively summarized as follows:

• To the best of our knowledge, this is the inaugural work that successfully mitigates the multifaceted risk of model leakage by preventing attackers from both unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer, thereby achieving truly comprehensive protection for pre-trained DNN models.
• By leveraging generated auxiliary domains, DeTrans optimizes a critical subset of the victim model's weights through a sophisticated bi-level optimization process. The resulting protected model exhibits nearly random guessing performance for attackers on the source domain and reduces transferability by a remarkable margin of up to 81.23% on potential target domains.
• Extensive experiments conclusively demonstrate that DeTrans significantly outperforms state-of-the-art model protection works and exhibits strong robustness against various fine-tuning methods that attackers might employ.

2 BACKGROUND

2.1 THREAT MODEL

Attackers. To achieve comprehensive protection, we assume a strong and knowledgeable model IP attacker who possesses knowledge of the domain in which the victim model was originally trained. We also assume the attacker is capable of extracting the complete DNN model—including its architecture and all pre-trained weights—from unsecured memory, for instance by using a run-time attack. As illustrated, attackers could exploit the extracted model in two primary ways: 1) they directly use the model for inference tasks that align perfectly with the source domain; or 2) they fine-tune the extracted model to achieve successful cross-domain transfer after collecting a small set of labeled data from a new target domain, while keeping the model architecture unchanged.

Model IP Owners. To protect pre-trained models against illegal exploitation while perfectly preserving model performance for authorized users, model owners can employ defense solutions integrated with trusted hardware support (e.g., a TEE). This hardware can block all unauthorized access to critical data stored in secure memory. Specifically, owners will generate a protected model for deployment on devices, while the crucial original data (the pristine values of the perturbed weights) is safeguarded exclusively within the TEE. During authorized inference, users can utilize this data but cannot extract it, thanks to the fundamental security properties of the TEE. It is important to note that our intention is not to block all conceivable target domains, as this would be entirely impractical. Instead, we consider a common and highly practical scenario where the target domains are distributionally close to the source domain and share the same label space.

2.2 SINGLE DOMAIN GENERALIZATION

To protect models from illegal cross-domain transfer, we face the significant challenge that the target domains are completely unknown during the model protection phase. This identical challenge exists in the field of single domain generalization, where the objective is to allow a model learned from a single source to generalize well to a series of unknown target distributions. Furthermore, it also assumes that the unknown target domain is close to the source, which aligns perfectly with our own core assumption. A common and effective practice in single domain generalization is to augment the source domain data to approximate the unknown domain distributions. For example, some methods add adversarially perturbed samples to the data space, while others generate fictitious domains using auto-encoders to encourage large domain discrepancy in the input space.

Given the shared challenge and assumption, we generate auxiliary domains by augmenting the source domain using conceptually similar methods. However, it is crucial to note that our design objective is precisely the opposite of domain generalization: we intentionally and systematically reduce the victim model’s generalization ability, thereby impeding its ease of transfer to any unknown target domains.

2.3 TRUSTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT

The Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) has been successfully used in prior model protection schemes to create hardware-based isolation between the secure and normal memory of a device, thereby isolating sensitive information. However, the secure memory space is relatively limited compared to the size of typical DNNs. To address this critical constraint, we aim to identify a minimal subset of critical model weights that disproportionately affect the model’s performance on both the source and potential target domains. Without authorized access to these critical weights stored securely within the TEE, the extracted portion of the model will perform poorly due to the lack of this essential data. It is also noted that even during authorized inference, the data inside the TEE remains a black box for users; they can leverage it to achieve high accuracy but cannot extract it. Since the effectiveness of TEE has been firmly established in other studies, this work will not delve into its implementation details.

2.4 DISCUSSION ON RELATED WORKS

As model IP protection is critically important for model owners, several studies have explored methods to degrade a model’s performance to mitigate the risk of model leakage. For example, some propose key-dependent training algorithms to obfuscate the weight space, causing accuracy to drop significantly if the model is extracted. Others introduce protection for pre-trained models by obfuscating a small set of model weights using a fine-grained mask. However, these methods focus primarily on degrading accuracy on the source domain and cannot naturally reduce the model's inherent transferability to prevent cross-domain transfer by attackers.

Conversely, other works have proposed training strategies specifically designed to restrict model transferability by capturing exclusive data representations or emphasizing private style features. However, these methods cannot be extended to general pre-trained models, and using them to train a model would inherently restrict its transferability even for the legitimate owners. More importantly, these methods are designed for cloud-based scenarios where high source-domain performance must be maintained for users, rendering them completely ineffective at preventing attackers from making unauthorized inferences on the source domain itself.

3 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK: DETRANS

Aiming to achieve the best possible protection against both illegal usages—unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer—we propose an extensive and novel model IP protection scheme that can provide simultaneous accuracy degradation on the source domain and transferability reduction on target domains. The workflow of our proposed method, DeTrans, is illustrated. We first generate auxiliary domains by augmenting the source domain, then select a critical set of weights via a filter-wise mask designed to fit within small secure memory. Finally, we obtain the protected model by modifying the selected weights through a sophisticated bi-level optimization process. These modifications decisively hinder attackers from leveraging the victim model, thereby successfully protecting the model IP.

3.1 AUXILIARY DOMAINS

We introduce a generative domain augmentation method to produce multiple auxiliary domains based on the source domain. The fundamental rationale behind this approach is that attackers are far more likely to attempt model transfer when the target domain closely aligns with the source domain. This choice provides them with the well-known advantages of transfer learning while avoiding potential drawbacks. Therefore, even though we cannot precisely predict the specific target domain attackers may select, we can effectively approximate its distribution by intelligently augmenting the source domain.

Inspired by prior work, we build a Wasserstein Auto-Encoder (WAE) to introduce controlled domain discrepancy between the source domain and the generated auxiliary domains. However, to accurately simulate the cross-domain transfer process attackers use, we need to generate fully labeled samples, mimicking how attackers use limited labeled data to fine-tune an extracted model. To this end, we enhance the WAE by incorporating the label as a conditioning signal during the decoding phase. Specifically, it consists of an encoder and a conditional decoder. We employ Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to quantify the distance between the encoded distribution and a Gaussian prior. The conditional WAE is optimized accordingly.

After optimization, we can generate labeled samples to construct auxiliary domains via the decoder. To encourage a wider range of domain discrepancies that better align with unseen target distributions, we introduce feature augmentation by incorporating a latent vector sampled from a Gaussian distribution into the feature embedding. This proven augmentation technique effectively enhances domain discrepancy through variations in the distribution parameters. As a result, we can generate diverse and representative auxiliary domains. Each auxiliary domain is then divided into a training set and a validation set for use in the lower-level and upper-level optimization steps, respectively.

3.2 MASK DESIGN

To overcome the stringent limitations of secure memory in the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), DeTrans introduces an innovative filter-wise mask design, allowing for the modification of weights exclusively for a carefully selected subset of filters. The filter selection strategy is centered on identifying the single filter with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer. This selection is based on the understanding that filters with higher transferability capture the shared, common patterns between domains, making them intrinsically more transferable. By adjusting the weights of these high-transferability filters, we directly disrupt the shared features learned by both the source and target domains, thus achieving concurrent and significant accuracy degradation and transferability reduction. Since the true target domains are unknown, we substitute them with our generated auxiliary domains for this measurement.

To quantify filter transferability, we adopt a discrepancy-based approach. We first measure the discrepancy between the source domain and each auxiliary domain for each channel (the output of a filter). The distance-based probability for each channel is then calculated, where a higher score indicates greater transferability of that filter. We calculate these scores for each source-auxiliary domain pair and take the average to definitively rank the filters. Consequently, a binary mask is generated, with a value of 1 indicating the selected filter with the highest transferability in each corresponding layer.

3.3 BI-LEVEL OPTIMIZATION

We consider a pre-trained model with weights as the victim model, trained on labeled data from the source domain. We selectively modify a small set of weights corresponding to the chosen filters, while keeping the rest of the model weights completely fixed. A basic protection method would involve adding weight changes to degrade performance on the source domain, thus preventing unauthorized inference. The optimization of these modified weights follows a straightforward maximization of the loss on the source domain data.

Given that our protection ambitiously extends to preventing cross-domain transfer, we significantly improve upon the basic method by formulating a powerful bi-level optimization framework. This advanced framework enables us to comprehensively address the model protection challenge by alternating optimization stages while implicitly considering the transferability of the protected model through the use of our auxiliary domains.

Lower-level Optimization. In this stage, we explicitly emulate how an attacker would optimize the extracted model for transfer to a new domain. We find an optimal weight update on the extracted model to enhance its performance on the training data of an auxiliary domain, simulating the attacker's fine-tuning process.

Upper-level Optimization. To leverage the knowledge gained from the lower-level optimization about the model's current transferability, we then optimize the protected model's weights further. The explicit goal here is to diminish the model's transferability across all auxiliary domains, guided by a maximization of the loss on the validation sets of these domains. Notably, we also incorporate the source domain itself as one of the auxiliary domains during this bi-level optimization to ensure that accuracy degradation is rigorously maintained on the source domain.

3.4 SUMMARY OF DETRANS

Integrating all the aforementioned strategies, we present the complete DeTrans algorithm, with the following key operational points: (i) Given a pre-trained model, DeTrans first identifies the most critical filters for transfer learning and generates a corresponding mask for optimization; (ii) DeTrans implements basic protection as a warm-up to initialize the modified weights; (iii) DeTrans then employs the bi-level optimization to further and more effectively optimize these weights, incorporating the source domain to maintain accuracy degradation. The optimal protected model is generated upon convergence, which successfully prevents attackers from both direct use and model transfer. Furthermore, the small set of original weights is stored in TEE secure memory, which corrects the functionality of the protected model exclusively for authorized users.

4 EXPERIMENTS

We thoroughly evaluate the performance of DeTrans on multiple DNN models and datasets for classification tasks, conclusively demonstrating its superior effectiveness compared to other methods. As DeTrans specifically targets the protection of on-device DNN models—where memory and computational capability are limited—we examine it on relatively small DNNs and datasets in line with practical deployment scenarios. Additionally, we conduct detailed ablation studies to examine the influence of DeTrans's important constituent modules.

4.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP

Dataset. We examine our method on two primary types of datasets following previous related works. One category is digits datasets, including MNIST, USPS, and SVHN. The other is natural image datasets, including CIFAR-10 and STL-10.

DNN Models. We train VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on different datasets as our victim models, selected to match the models used in previous comparative works. The victim models are trained using the Adam optimizer.

Settings. We generate auxiliary domains based on the source domain using specified parameter ranges. The true target domain remains completely unseen during the model protection phase. We assume attackers hold only 5% of the training data from the target domain to conduct cross-domain transfer. The ratio of modified parameters is kept constant and minimal (0.07% for VGG-11 and 0.18% for ResNet-18). The corresponding storage size is compact enough to meet the secure memory constraints of a TEE. We use top-1 inference accuracy as the evaluation metric for all experiments.

4.2 COMPARISON METHODS

As DeTrans is the first approach to provide dual protection, there are no previous works fully comparable. However, to rigorously evaluate its effectiveness, we adopt state-of-the-art (SOTA) works for comparison on each individual aspect. For preventing unauthorized inference, we select the SOTA method NNSplitter. For defending against model transfer, we compare against recent works NTL and CUTI. We also include a Baseline (no protection) and a Supervised Learning (SL) baseline where attackers train from scratch with only 5% of data.

4.3 PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

Based on our threat model, we consider two attack scenarios and demonstrate definitively that DeTrans can defend against both attacks simultaneously, while SOTA works can only achieve one aspect.

Scenario I: Unauthorized Inference. When attackers' target aligns with the source domain, they can directly use the extracted model. DeTrans aims to degrade accuracy on the source domain to prevent this. From the results, we observe that applying DeTrans causes a dramatic drop in top-1 inference accuracy compared to the baseline (from over 90% to approximately 10%). This degraded accuracy is comparable to the SOTA method NNSplitter and is even lower than what an attacker could achieve by training a new model from scratch with very limited data (SL). In stark contrast, methods designed for restraining transferability (NTL, CUTI) completely fail to prevent unauthorized inference, as their accuracy on the source domain remains high.

Scenario II: Model Transfer. We form several domain pairs to demonstrate that models protected by DeTrans have significantly reduced transferability. As shown in the results, while NNSplitter is optimal for defending against unauthorized inference, it shows almost no reduction in transferability. DeTrans, however, proves to be highly effective in reducing transferability, achieving up to an 81.23% accuracy drop. It achieves protection comparable to the SOTA transferability-reduction methods (NTL, CUTI), with a difference of less than 4%. Importantly, unlike NTL and CUTI, DeTrans does not require any input-level modifications (like adding a patch) to achieve this reduction.

Furthermore, in cases where transferring to a more complex domain yields relatively low accuracy even without protection, attackers may still be motivated to extract and transfer the model, as training from scratch with limited data would yield even worse performance. In such scenarios, DeTrans successfully reduces the transferred performance to a level lower than the SL baseline, rendering the attacker's effort futile.

Overall, DeTrans achieves comprehensive model protection by successfully defending against unauthorized inference and model transfer at the same time, filling a critical gap in SOTA methods. It reduces source-domain accuracy to random-guessing levels while restraining performance on unseen target domains below what an attacker could achieve by training from scratch with very limited data.

4.4 ABLATION STUDIES

Filter Selection. The filter selection strategy in DeTrans is based on measuring channel transferability. To measure its influence, we replace it with a random filter selection strategy. Results show that random selection can also reduce transferability, but DeTrans performs significantly better, providing an extra 14.95% accuracy drop on average, validating the importance of our targeted selection strategy.

Optimization Method. Our bi-level optimization considers the potential attack surface (malicious transfer) during protection. To demonstrate its necessity, we compare it to a naive, alternating optimization scheme where a protector and attacker alternately optimize against each other with knowledge of the target domain. The model performance after this naive optimization shows only a 1.3% accuracy drop, while our bi-level optimization achieves over 80% drop. The reason is that in the naive scheme, each party can counteract the other's last step, resulting in minimal net effect, especially since the attacker makes the final modification. This conclusively demonstrates the superior effectiveness of our bi-level formulation.

5 DISCUSSION

5.1 MODIFICATION AND FINE-TUNING RANGE

We explore different ranges for protector modifications (e.g., modifying only the first layer vs. one filter per layer) and attacker fine-tuning (no fine-tuning, fine-tuning last layer, or fine-tuning the whole model). Evaluation on VGG-11 shows that modifying one filter per layer (p2) outperforms modifying only the first layer (p1) when defending against unauthorized inference. Furthermore, when using p2, attackers achieve very low accuracy (~20%) on a target domain regardless of their fine-tuning range. This demonstrates the clear advantage of spreading the weight modifications strategically across all layers of the network.

5.2 APPLICABILITY BEYOND SMALLER MODELS

While this work focuses on on-device models, our proposed methodology is generic and can be applied to larger models if the device can accommodate them. As a case study, we applied DeTrans to a pre-trained ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10. By modifying only 0.14% of the weights, DeTrans degraded unauthorized inference accuracy to 10% and reduced cross-domain transfer accuracy to 10.5%, which also outperforms SOTA methods in reducing transferability, confirming the scalability of our approach.

6 CONCLUSION

In this work, we introduce DeTrans, a novel and comprehensive framework for protecting on-device DNN models against the dual threats of unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer, while perfectly preserving model performance for authorized users via a TEE. By selectively modifying a minimal subset of weights in the pre-trained model, DeTrans achieves near-random guess performance on the source domain and substantial transferability reduction for potential target domains (exceeding 80% for ResNet-18). The original values of these modified weights are stored securely within a TEE, accessible only to authorized users. Moreover, DeTrans remains robust regardless of how attackers attempt to fine-tune the protected model and is applicable to larger model architectures. Overall, DeTrans decisively fills a critical gap in SOTA model protection works, which have previously either failed to prevent unauthorized inference or overlooked the serious risk of cross-domain transfer by attackers.
