Title: Protecting DNN Models Against Unauthorized Inference and Domain Transfer

Abstract:
Deep neural network (DNN) models are intellectual property. Model extraction attacks can obtain these models for unauthorized use. Existing protection schemes primarily focus on preventing unauthorized inference on the source domain. The transferability of extracted models to other domains has been less explored. This work proposes DeTrans, a DNN model protection framework that uses bi-level optimization to modify weights of highly transferable filters. The objective is to prevent both unauthorized inference on the source domain and cross-domain transfer following model extraction. DeTrans is designed to preserve model functionality for authorized users with specialized hardware support. Experiments show DeTrans can reduce source domain accuracy to near random guessing and achieve up to an 81.23% reduction in transfer accuracy to a target domain.

1 INTRODUCTION
On-device machine learning uses high-performance deep neural networks (DNNs) Dhar et al. (2021). Pre-trained DNNs are intellectual property assets Xue et al. (2021). Model extraction attacks can obtain DNN models via run-time attack Sun et al. (2021). As a countermeasure, previous works focus on preventing unauthorized inference on the source domain Chakraborty et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2019); Zhou et al. (2023). These works have not addressed cross-domain transfer as an attack objective following model leakage.

Attackers may transfer an extracted model to other domains to exploit learned features and overcome data scarcity Zhuang et al. (2020). This is an infringement of model owners’ rights Wang et al. (2022; 2023). Existing defense strategies against transferability rely on training models from scratch, which restricts applicability to general pre-trained models Wang et al. (2022; 2023). These strategies could impact model accuracy and transferability for the owner. Models produced by these methods maintain high performance on the source domain, making them vulnerable to unauthorized inference. Methods designed for these distinct issues use disparate training strategies from scratch Wang et al. (2022; 2023); Chakraborty et al. (2020). Model owners cannot sequentially apply different methods to address both vulnerabilities.

Unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer are practical attack objectives. A protection method is needed that can post-process pre-trained models to achieve: (i) accuracy degradation on the source domain for unauthorized use, and (ii) reduced transferability to target domains. Challenges include: First, the potential target domains of attackers are uncertain. Second, the performance of possible model transfers should be implicitly measured during protection to ensure robustness. Third, high performance on the original domain should be maintained for authorized users.

To address these challenges, DeTrans is proposed. For the first challenge, it is assumed the distribution of a potential target domain is likely close to that of the source domain, following the threat model of cross-domain transfer Torrey & Shavlik (2010). Auxiliary domains are generated based on the source domain, inspired by single domain generalization Qiao et al. (2020); Volpi et al. (2018). For the second challenge, a bi-level optimization problem is formulated, with the lower level assessing model transferability. For the third challenge, DeTrans uses hardware support in the form of a trusted execution environment (TEE) Ngabonziza et al. (2016); Truong et al. (2021). DeTrans optimizes the weights of the filter with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer. These weights capture common features between source and potential target domains. Perturbing these weights can degrade performance on both domains. The original values of the perturbed weights are stored in the secure memory of the TEE Ngabonziza et al. (2016) to restore performance for authorized users.

2 BACKGROUND

2.1 THREAT MODEL
Attackers. A strong model IP attacker is assumed with knowledge of the source domain. The attacker can extract the DNN model, including architecture and pre-trained weights, using a run-time attack Sun et al. (2021). Attackers could: 1) use the model directly on the source domain; or 2) fine-tune the extracted model for cross-domain transfer using a small set of target domain data, keeping the architecture unchanged.

Model IP owners. Defense solutions with hardware support (e.g., TEE) can protect pre-trained models while preserving performance for authorized users. A protected model is deployed on devices. Critical data (the original values of perturbed weights) is safeguarded by TEE. During inference, users can access this data but cannot extract it Chakrabarti et al. (2020). The intention is not to block all potential target domains. A common scenario is considered where target domains are close to the source domain and share the same label space.

2.2 SINGLE DOMAIN GENERALIZATION
Single domain generalization assumes an unknown target domain close to the source Zhou et al. (2022). Its objective is to allow a model learned from a single source to generalize over unknown distributions. A common practice is to augment the source domains to approximate unknown domain distributions Qiao et al. (2020); Volpi et al. (2018); Fan et al. (2021). For example, Volpi et al. add adversarially perturbed samples Volpi et al. (2018). Qiao et al. generate fictitious domains using a Wasserstein Auto-Encoder Qiao et al. (2020).

Given the shared challenge and assumption, auxiliary domains are generated by augmenting the source domain using similar methods. The design objective is opposite of domain generalization: to reduce the victim model’s generalization ability to impede transfer to unknown target domains.

2.3 TRUSTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT
TEE (e.g., ARM TrustZone Ngabonziza et al. (2016)) creates hardware-based isolation between secure and normal memory to isolate sensitive information Sun et al. (2023); Chakraborty et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2019); Zhou et al. (2023). Secure memory space is limited, e.g., 3-5MB in TrustZone Amacher & Schiavoni (2019), compared to normal DNNs Chen et al. (2019). A subset of critical model weights is identified that affect performance on both source and target domains. Without authorized access to these weights stored in TEE, the extracted model performs poorly. Authorized users can leverage data within TEE for high inference accuracy but cannot extract it. The effectiveness of TEE has been established in other studies Chen et al. (2019); Sun et al. (2023).

2.4 DISCUSSION ON RELATED WORKS
Several studies explore methods to degrade model performance to mitigate model leakage risk. Chakraborty et al. propose a key-dependent training algorithm to obfuscate the weight space Chakraborty et al. (2020). Zhou et al. introduce a protection approach for pre-trained models that obfuscates a small set of weights using a fine-grained mask designed by a reinforcement learning-based controller Zhou et al. (2023). These methods focus on degrading accuracy on the source domain and do not reduce transferability to prevent cross-domain transfer.

Considering transferability, Wang et al. propose a training strategy to restrict model transferability by capturing exclusive data representation in the source domain Wang et al. (2022). A compact un-transferable isolation domain is proposed to prevent cross-domain transfers by emphasizing private style features Wang et al. (2023). These methods cannot be extended to general pre-trained models. Using such methods restricts the model’s transferability for the owner. Wang et al. (2022; 2023) are designed for machine-learning-as-a-service (MLaaS), where service providers guarantee good performance on the source domain. The preserved high performance makes them ineffective in preventing unauthorized inference.

3 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK: DETRANS
DeTrans is a model IP protection scheme designed to provide accuracy degradation on the source domain and transferability reduction on the target domain. The workflow: first, generate auxiliary domains by augmenting the source domain; second, select critical weights via a filter-wise mask; third, obtain the protected model by modifying the selected weights via bi-level optimization.

3.1 AUXILIARY DOMAINS
A generative domain augmentation method generates auxiliary domains $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ based on the source domain. The rationale is that attackers are more likely to transfer a model when the target domain closely aligns with the source domain Pan & Yang (2010); Wang et al. (2019b). The specific target domain cannot be predicted, but its distribution can be approximated by augmenting the source domain.

Inspired by Qiao et al. (2020), a Wasserstein Auto-Encoder (WAE) parameterized by $\theta$ is built to introduce domain discrepancy between the source domain $\boldsymbol{S}$ and auxiliary domains $\mathcal{D}_{i}$. To generate labeled samples simulating how attackers use limited labeled data, the WAE is enhanced by incorporating the label as a condition in the decoding phase. It consists of an encoder $Q(x|\bar{z})$ and a decoder $G(z,y)$, where $x$ and $y$ are the input and its label, and $z$ is the bottleneck embedding. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) quantifies the distance between $Q(x)$ and the Gaussian prior $P(z)$ Tolstikhin et al. (2018). The conditional WAE is optimized according to:
$$
\operatorname*{min}_{\theta}||G(Q(x),y))-x||_{2}+\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{D}(Q(x),P(z))
$$
After optimization, samples are generated to construct auxiliary domains via the decoder $G$. To encourage a range of domain discrepancies, feature augmentation incorporates a latent vector $h$ sampled from ${\mathcal{N}}\left(\mu,\sigma\right)$ into the feature embedding Qiao & Peng (2021). Variations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$ enhance domain discrepancy. Diverse auxiliary domains $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ are generated. Each is divided into a training set and a validation set for the lower-level and upper-level optimization, respectively.

3.2 MASK DESIGN
A filter-wise mask design modifies weights exclusively for selected filters to overcome TEE secure memory limitations. The filter with the highest transferability in each layer is selected. Filters with higher transferability capture shared patterns between domains. Adjusting weights of these filters disrupts shared features learned by both source and target domains, achieving concurrent accuracy degradation and transferability reduction. Auxiliary domains replace unknown target domains.

Filter transferability is quantified following Wang et al. (2019a). The discrepancy $d$ between the source domain $\boldsymbol{S}$ and each auxiliary domain $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ for each channel $c$ (output of a filter) is measured with Eq. 2, omitting $i$ for simplicity.
$$
d^{(c)}=\left|\frac{\mu_{S}^{(c)}}{\sqrt{{\sigma_{S}^{2}}^{(c)}}}-\frac{\mu_{D}^{(c)}}{\sqrt{{\sigma_{D}^{2}}^{(c)}}}\right|,\mathrm{~where~}\mu^{(c)}=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^{b}x_{j}^{(c)},\mathrm{~}{\sigma^{2}}^{(c)}=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^{b}(x_{j}^{(c)}-\mu^{(c)}).
$$
Here, $b$ is the batch size and $\textbf{\em x}$ is the feature map of convolutional layers. $\textbf{\em x}$ is from the source domain for $\mu_{S}$ and $\sigma_{S}^{2}$, and from $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ otherwise. The distance-based probability $\pmb{\alpha}$ for each channel c is:
$$
\pmb{\alpha}^{(c)}=\frac{K(1+d^{(c)})^{-1}}{\sum_{n=1}^{K}(1+d^{(n)})^{-1}},\quad c=1,2,...,K
$$
where $K$ is the channel size. A higher $\pmb{\alpha}$ score indicates greater filter transferability. $\pmb{\alpha}$ scores are calculated for each source-auxiliary domain pair and averaged to rank filters. A binary mask $\mathbf{M}$ is generated, with 1 indicating the selected filter with the highest transferability in each layer.

3.3 BI-LEVEL OPTIMIZATION
A pre-trained model $\mathcal{M}$ with weights $\mathbf{W}$ is the victim model, trained on labeled data pairs $(x_{s},\,y_{s})$ from source domain $\boldsymbol{S}$. A small set of weights $\mathbf{W_{P}}$ corresponding to chosen filters is modified, while the rest $\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{W_{P}}$ is fixed. A basic protection method adds weight changes $\Delta\mathbf{W_{P}}$ to $\mathbf{W_{P}}$ to degrade performance (accuracy drop) to prevent unauthorized inference. The optimization of modified weights $\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}$ ( $:=$ $\mathbf{W_{P}}+\Delta\mathbf{W_{P}}$) follows:
$$
\operatorname*{max}_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{s};\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}\cup\left(\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)\right),y_{s}\right),
$$
where $f$ is the DNN functionality, and $\mathcal{L}$ is the loss function of the source task.

To also prevent cross-domain transfer, a bi-level optimization is formulated.

Lower-level Optimization. This stage emulates how attackers optimize the extracted model for transfer by finding an optimal weight update $\Delta\mathbf{W}$ to enhance performance in the target domain. This is done using training data $(x_{i}^{t r},y_{i}^{t r})$ in auxiliary domain $\mathcal{D}_{i}$. $\Delta\mathbf{W}$ is optimized with:
$$
\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}^{*}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{i}^{t r};\mathbf{W}^{\prime}+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}\right),y_{i}^{t r}\right)
$$
where $\mathbf{W}^{\prime}$ is the weights of the protected model from the upper-level optimization.

Upper-level Optimization. To diminish model transferability across all auxiliary domains, weights $\mathbf{W}^{\prime}$ are further optimized. The process is guided by:
$$
\operatorname*{max}_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{Z}\lambda_{i}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{i}^{v a l};\mathbf{W}^{\prime}+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}^{*}\right),y_{i}^{v a l}\right),\;s.t.\;\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}\cup\left(\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)=\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}\odot\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{W}\odot\left(\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{M}\right)
$$
where $\lambda_{i}$ is the scaling factor of the loss on $(x_{i}^{v a l},y_{i}^{v a l})$, the validation set in auxiliary domain $\mathcal{D}_{i}$, and $\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{Z}\lambda_{i}=1$. The source domain is incorporated as one $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ during bi-level optimization to ensure accuracy degradation on the source domain.

3.4 SUMMARY OF DETRANS
Integrating these strategies, DeTrans: (i) identifies the most critical filters for transfer learning and generates a corresponding mask M; (ii) implements basic protection as a warm-up to initialize $\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}$; (iii) employs bi-level optimization to further optimize $\mathbf{W_{P}^{\prime}}$, adding $\boldsymbol{S}$ as one $\mathcal{D}_{i}$. The optimal protected model is generated upon convergence. The protected original weights $\mathbf{W_{P}}$ are stored in TEE secure memory to correct functionality for authorized users.

4 EXPERIMENTS
DeTrans is evaluated on multiple DNN models and datasets for classification tasks. As DeTrans targets on-device DNN models with limited memory and computational capability, relatively small DNNs and datasets are examined. Ablation studies examine the influence of important modules.

4.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP
Dataset. Two types of datasets are examined following Wang et al. (2022; 2023). One is digits datasets: MNIST (MN) Lecun et al. (1998), USPS (US) Hull (1994), and SVHN (SV) Netzer et al. (2011). Training and test sets are unbalanced. The other is natural image datasets: CIFAR10 (CF10) Krizhevsky et al. (2009) and STL10 Coates et al. (2011).

DNN Models. VGG-11 Simonyan & Zisserman (2015) and ResNet-18 He et al. (2016) are trained on different datasets as victim models. These DNNs match victim models in previous works Wang et al. (2022); Zhou et al. (2023). Victim models are trained using the Adam optimizer Kingma & Ba (2015).

Settings. Auxiliary domains are generated based on the source domain, with $\mu$ from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.25 and $\sigma$ set to 0.5 and 1. The target domain remains unseen during protection. Attackers hold $5\%$ of training data in the target domain for cross-domain transfer. The ratio of modified parameters is unchanged: $0.07\%$ and $0.18\%$ of total parameters for VGG-11 and ResNet-18, respectively. Corresponding storage size is 79KB and 122KB, meeting TEE secure memory constraints. Top-1 inference accuracy $(\%)$ is the evaluation metric. Experiments are implemented using PyTorch on a machine with an NVIDIA A10 GPU.

4.2 COMPARISON METHODS
DeTrans is the first approach for simultaneous prevention of unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer. State-of-the-art (SOTA) works are compared on a single aspect. For preventing unauthorized inference, NNSplitter Zhou et al. (2023) is selected. For defending against model transfer, NTL Wang et al. (2022) and CUTI Wang et al. (2023) are used for comparison. Since they did not experiment with ResNet-18, comparison is only on VGG11. Baseline applies no protection. Supervised Learning $(S L)$ trains from scratch with limited data ($5\%$ of training data).

4.3 PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
Two attack scenarios are considered.

Scenario I: Unauthorized Inference. Attackers directly use the extracted model on the source domain. DeTrans aims to degrade accuracy on the source domain. Results are in Table 1. Applying DeTrans, top-1 inference accuracy drops significantly compared to baseline (from over $90\%$ to $\mathord{\sim}10\%$). The success results from misclassifying all images into a random class. For CF10 and STL10 with balanced classes, accuracy degrades to $10\%$ with no variance. DeTrans achieves comparable degraded accuracy to NNSplitter. The degraded accuracy is lower than victim DNN trained with supervised learning $(S L)$. NTL Wang et al. (2022) and CUTI Wang et al. (2023) fail in preventing unauthorized inference as their accuracy on the source domain remains high.

Scenario II: Model Transfer. Several domain pairs demonstrate reduced transferability. Results are in Table 2. NNSplitter shows almost no reduction in transferability compared to baseline, with $0.46\%$ and $0.39\%$ accuracy drop on VGG-11 and ResNet-18, respectively. Accuracy reduction on the source domain does not necessarily impact model transferability. DeTrans is effective in reducing transferability, e.g., up to $81.23\%$ accuracy drop on ResNet-18. It achieves comparable protection to NTL and CUTI on transferability reduction, with difference less than $4\%$. Unlike NTL and CUTI, DeTrans does not require additional input-level modification. When transferring to a more complex domain (e.g., $\mathrm{MN}\Rightarrow$ SV), transferred accuracy is relatively low without protection ($81.53\%$ for baseline). Attackers may still be motivated as training from scratch with limited data yields lower accuracy ($20.12\%$ for $S L$). The model under DeTrans protection achieves performance lower than $S L$.

Overall, DeTrans achieves comprehensive model protection, reducing source domain accuracy to near random-guessing level (${\sim}10\%$ for ten-class tasks) and restraining performance on unseen target domains below attackers training from scratch using $S L$.

4.4 ABLATION STUDIES
Filter Selection. The filter selection strategy is based on transferability measurement. To measure its influence, it is replaced with a random filter selection strategy. Comparison experiments on VGG-11 are shown in Figure 3. Random filter selection reduces transferability compared to baseline, but DeTrans performs better with an extra $14.95\%$ accuracy drop on average.

Optimization Method. Bi-level optimization considers the potential attack surface (malicious model transfer). To demonstrate effectiveness, a stronger protector is assumed who: (i) has knowledge of the target domain as the attacker (a small set of target domain data); (ii) applies a naive model protection scheme where protector and attacker conduct "defense-attack-defense-..." in an alternative optimization manner as described in Eq. (7) and Eq. (8):
$$
\left(\mathrm{attack}\right)\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{t};\mathbf{W}^{\prime}+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}\right),y_{t}\right)
$$
$$
(\operatorname{defense})\,\operatorname*{max}_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{t};\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}\cup\left(\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}\right),y_{t}\right)
$$
where $\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}$ is weights modification by attackers via transfer learning, $\mathbf{W_{P}^{\prime}}$ is optimization from the protector, and $(\pmb{x}_{t},\pmb{y}_{t})$ denotes $5\%$ labeled data from the target domain.

Model performance after 50-step naive optimization is reported in Table 3. Compared to baseline, naive optimization shows $1.3\%$ accuracy drop, while bi-level optimization achieves over $80\%$ accuracy drop. In naive optimization, the influence of one equation can be nullified by the other, resulting in minimal impact on model accuracy. As the attacker makes the final modification, they can improve accuracy to a level comparable to baseline.

5 DISCUSSION

5.1 MODIFICATION AND FINE-TUNING RANGE
Different modification ranges for protectors and model fine-tuning ranges for attackers are explored. For protectors: p1) modify the first layer; p2) modify one filter per layer. For attackers: a1) fine-tune the last layer; a2) fine-tune the whole extracted model for transfer; or conduct unauthorized inference without fine-tuning. Performance is evaluated on VGG-11 trained on MN. Results in Table 4 show p2 outperforms p1 when defending against unauthorized inference. When adopting p2, attackers achieve low accuracy ($\sim\!20\%$) whether fine-tuning the last layer or whole model. Results demonstrate the advantage of spreading weights modification across all layers.

5.2 APPLICABILITY BEYOND SMALLER MODELS
This work focuses on securing IP of on-device DNN models vulnerable to extraction Sun et al. (2021), so models with fewer layers are chosen as victim models. As a generic defense strategy, the methodology can be applied to larger models if the device accommodates them. ResNet-50 is used as a case study, as in Wang et al. (2022; 2023). A pre-trained ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10 has inference accuracy of $93.65\%$. Applying DeTrans protection with $0.14\%$ of weights modified degrades unauthorized inference accuracy to $10\%$. As shown in Table 5, cross-domain transfer achieves $10.5\%$ with DeTrans, which outperforms SOTA in reducing transferability.

6 CONCLUSION
DeTrans is a framework for protecting on-device DNN models against unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer while preserving model performance for users using TEE. By selectively modifying a small subset of weights in the pre-trained model, DeTrans achieves near-random guess performance on the source domain and transferability reduction for potential target domains ($>80\%$ for ResNet-18). The original values of modified weights are stored in TEE, accessible only to authorized users. DeTrans remains effective regardless of how attackers fine-tune the protected model and is applicable to larger models. It addresses a gap in SOTA model protection works, which either fail to prevent unauthorized inference or overlook cross-domain transfer.

Title: Protecting DNN Models Against Unauthorized Inference and Domain Transfer

Abstract:
Deep neural network (DNN) models are intellectual property. Model extraction attacks can obtain these models for unauthorized use. Existing protection schemes primarily focus on preventing unauthorized inference on the source domain. The transferability of extracted models to other domains has been less explored. This work proposes DeTrans, a DNN model protection framework that uses bi-level optimization to modify weights of highly transferable filters. The objective is to prevent both unauthorized inference on the source domain and cross-domain transfer following model extraction. DeTrans is designed to preserve model functionality for authorized users with specialized hardware support. Experiments show DeTrans can reduce source domain accuracy to near random guessing and achieve up to an 81.23% reduction in transfer accuracy to a target domain.

1 INTRODUCTION
On-device machine learning uses high-performance deep neural networks (DNNs) Dhar et al. (2021). Pre-trained DNNs are intellectual property assets Xue et al. (2021). Model extraction attacks can obtain DNN models via run-time attack Sun et al. (2021). As a countermeasure, previous works focus on preventing unauthorized inference on the source domain Chakraborty et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2019); Zhou et al. (2023). These works have not addressed cross-domain transfer as an attack objective following model leakage.

Attackers may transfer an extracted model to other domains to exploit learned features and overcome data scarcity Zhuang et al. (2020). This is an infringement of model owners’ rights Wang et al. (2022; 2023). Existing defense strategies against transferability rely on training models from scratch, which restricts applicability to general pre-trained models Wang et al. (2022; 2023). These strategies could impact model accuracy and transferability for the owner. Models produced by these methods maintain high performance on the source domain, making them vulnerable to unauthorized inference. Methods designed for these distinct issues use disparate training strategies from scratch Wang et al. (2022; 2023); Chakraborty et al. (2020). Model owners cannot sequentially apply different methods to address both vulnerabilities.

Unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer are practical attack objectives. A protection method is needed that can post-process pre-trained models to achieve: (i) accuracy degradation on the source domain for unauthorized use, and (ii) reduced transferability to target domains. Challenges include: First, the potential target domains of attackers are uncertain. Second, the performance of possible model transfers should be implicitly measured during protection to ensure robustness. Third, high performance on the original domain should be maintained for authorized users.

To address these challenges, DeTrans is proposed. For the first challenge, it is assumed the distribution of a potential target domain is likely close to that of the source domain, following the threat model of cross-domain transfer Torrey & Shavlik (2010). Auxiliary domains are generated based on the source domain, inspired by single domain generalization Qiao et al. (2020); Volpi et al. (2018). For the second challenge, a bi-level optimization problem is formulated, with the lower level assessing model transferability. For the third challenge, DeTrans uses hardware support in the form of a trusted execution environment (TEE) Ngabonziza et al. (2016); Truong et al. (2021). DeTrans optimizes the weights of the filter with the highest transferability in each convolutional layer. These weights capture common features between source and potential target domains. Perturbing these weights can degrade performance on both domains. The original values of the perturbed weights are stored in the secure memory of the TEE Ngabonziza et al. (2016) to restore performance for authorized users.

2 BACKGROUND

2.1 THREAT MODEL
Attackers. A strong model IP attacker is assumed with knowledge of the source domain. The attacker can extract the DNN model, including architecture and pre-trained weights, using a run-time attack Sun et al. (2021). Attackers could: 1) use the model directly on the source domain; or 2) fine-tune the extracted model for cross-domain transfer using a small set of target domain data, keeping the architecture unchanged.

Model IP owners. Defense solutions with hardware support (e.g., TEE) can protect pre-trained models while preserving performance for authorized users. A protected model is deployed on devices. Critical data (the original values of perturbed weights) is safeguarded by TEE. During inference, users can access this data but cannot extract it Chakrabarti et al. (2020). The intention is not to block all potential target domains. A common scenario is considered where target domains are close to the source domain and share the same label space.

2.2 SINGLE DOMAIN GENERALIZATION
Single domain generalization assumes an unknown target domain close to the source Zhou et al. (2022). Its objective is to allow a model learned from a single source to generalize over unknown distributions. A common practice is to augment the source domains to approximate unknown domain distributions Qiao et al. (2020); Volpi et al. (2018); Fan et al. (2021). For example, Volpi et al. add adversarially perturbed samples Volpi et al. (2018). Qiao et al. generate fictitious domains using a Wasserstein Auto-Encoder Qiao et al. (2020).

Given the shared challenge and assumption, auxiliary domains are generated by augmenting the source domain using similar methods. The design objective is opposite of domain generalization: to reduce the victim model’s generalization ability to impede transfer to unknown target domains.

2.3 TRUSTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT
TEE (e.g., ARM TrustZone Ngabonziza et al. (2016)) creates hardware-based isolation between secure and normal memory to isolate sensitive information Sun et al. (2023); Chakraborty et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2019); Zhou et al. (2023). Secure memory space is limited, e.g., 3-5MB in TrustZone Amacher & Schiavoni (2019), compared to normal DNNs Chen et al. (2019). A subset of critical model weights is identified that affect performance on both source and target domains. Without authorized access to these weights stored in TEE, the extracted model performs poorly. Authorized users can leverage data within TEE for high inference accuracy but cannot extract it. The effectiveness of TEE has been established in other studies Chen et al. (2019); Sun et al. (2023).

2.4 DISCUSSION ON RELATED WORKS
Several studies explore methods to degrade model performance to mitigate model leakage risk. Chakraborty et al. propose a key-dependent training algorithm to obfuscate the weight space Chakraborty et al. (2020). Zhou et al. introduce a protection approach for pre-trained models that obfuscates a small set of weights using a fine-grained mask designed by a reinforcement learning-based controller Zhou et al. Considering transferability, Wang et al. propose a training strategy to restrict model transferability by capturing exclusive data representation in the source domain Wang et al. (2022). A compact un-transferable isolation domain is proposed to prevent cross-domain transfers by emphasizing private style features Wang et al. (2023). When transferring to a more complex domain (e.g., $\mathrm{MN}\Rightarrow$ SV), transferred accuracy is relatively low without protection ($81.53\%$ for baseline). Attackers may still be motivated as training from scratch with limited data yields lower accuracy ($20.12\%$ for $S L$). The model under DeTrans protection achieves performance lower than $S L$.

Overall, DeTrans achieves comprehensive model protection, reducing source domain accuracy to near random-guessing level (${\sim}10\%$ for ten-class tasks) and restraining performance on unseen target domains below attackers training from scratch using $S L$.

4.4 ABLATION STUDIES
Filter Selection. The filter selection strategy is based on transferability measurement. To measure its influence, it is replaced with a random filter selection strategy. Comparison experiments on VGG-11 are shown in Figure 3. Random filter selection reduces transferability compared to baseline, but DeTrans performs better with an extra $14.95\%$ accuracy drop on average.

Optimization Method. Bi-level optimization considers the potential attack surface (malicious model transfer). To demonstrate effectiveness, a stronger protector is assumed who: (i) has knowledge of the target domain as the attacker (a small set of target domain data); (ii) applies a naive model protection scheme where protector and attacker conduct "defense-attack-defense-..." in an alternative optimization manner as described in Eq. (7) and Eq. (8):
$$
\left(\mathrm{attack}\right)\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{t};\mathbf{W}^{\prime}+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}\right),y_{t}\right)
$$
$$
(\operatorname{defense})\,\operatorname*{max}_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{L}\left(f\left(x_{t};\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}^{\prime}\cup\left(\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)+\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}\right),y_{t}\right)
$$
where $\Delta\mathbf{W}_{a}^{*}$ is weights modification by attackers via transfer learning, $\mathbf{W_{P}^{\prime}}$ is optimization from the protector, and $(\pmb{x}_{t},\pmb{y}_{t})$ denotes $5\%$ labeled data from the target domain.

Model performance after 50-step naive optimization is reported in Table 3. Compared to baseline, naive optimization shows $1.3\%$ accuracy drop, while bi-level optimization achieves over $80\%$ accuracy drop. In naive optimization, the influence of one equation can be nullified by the other, resulting in minimal impact on model accuracy. As the attacker makes the final modification, they can improve accuracy to a level comparable to baseline.

5 DISCUSSION

5.1 MODIFICATION AND FINE-TUNING RANGE
Different modification ranges for protectors and model fine-tuning ranges for attackers are explored. For protectors: p1) modify the first layer; p2) modify one filter per layer. For attackers: a1) fine-tune the last layer; a2) fine-tune the whole extracted model for transfer; or conduct unauthorized inference without fine-tuning. Performance is evaluated on VGG-11 trained on MN. Results in Table 4 show p2 outperforms p1 when defending against unauthorized inference. When adopting p2, attackers achieve low accuracy ($\sim\!20\%$) whether fine-tuning the last layer or whole model. Results demonstrate the advantage of spreading weights modification across all layers.

5.2 APPLICABILITY BEYOND SMALLER MODELS
This work focuses on securing IP of on-device DNN models vulnerable to extraction Sun et al. (2021), so models with fewer layers are chosen as victim models. As a generic defense strategy, the methodology can be applied to larger models if the device accommodates them. ResNet-50 is used as a case study, as in Wang et al. (2022; 2023). A pre-trained ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10 has inference accuracy of $93.65\%$. Applying DeTrans protection with $0.14\%$ of weights modified degrades unauthorized inference accuracy to $10\%$. As shown in Table 5, cross-domain transfer achieves $10.5\%$ with DeTrans, which outperforms SOTA in reducing transferability.

6 CONCLUSION
DeTrans is a framework for protecting on-device DNN models against unauthorized inference and cross-domain transfer while preserving model performance for users using TEE. By selectively modifying a small subset of weights in the pre-trained model, DeTrans achieves near-random guess performance on the source domain and transferability reduction for potential target domains ($>80\%$ for ResNet-18). The original values of modified weights are stored in TEE, accessible only to authorized users. DeTrans remains effective regardless of how attackers fine-tune the protected model and is applicable to larger models. It addresses a gap in SOTA model protection works, which either fail to prevent unauthorized inference or overlook cross-domain transfer.

Title: MissDiff: A Practical Framework for Training Diffusion Models on Tabular Data with Missing Values to Enhance Real-World Data Synthesis

Abstract

Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable performance in modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing high-quality data, holding significant potential for practical applications. However, a critical limitation of the standard diffusion model is its requirement for complete or fully observed data during training. Incomplete data is an extremely common and challenging issue across numerous real-world applications, including healthcare diagnostics, financial forecasting, and recommendation systems, particularly when dealing with tabular datasets. This work presents a unified and principled diffusion-based framework designed specifically for learning from data containing missing values under various missing mechanisms, addressing a key practical bottleneck. We first identify that the widely adopted "impute-then-generate" pipeline, a common practical workaround, can lead to a biased learning objective, compromising model fidelity. To resolve this, we propose to mask the regression loss of Denoising Score Matching during the training phase. We provide a theoretical proof that the proposed method is consistent in learning the true score of the underlying data distributions, and we demonstrate that the proposed training objective serves as an upper bound for the negative log-likelihood in certain cases, offering solid theoretical grounding. The proposed framework is rigorously evaluated on multiple real-world tabular datasets using realistic and efficacious metrics for assessing synthetic data quality. It is demonstrated to outperform the state-of-the-art diffusion model for tabular data when used with the "impute-then-generate" pipeline by a large and practically significant margin, showcasing its substantial practical value.

Introduction

Diffusion models have emerged as a highly effective and versatile tool for modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing various types of data, such as images, videos, point clouds, and tabular data. It is well-known that such powerful machine learning models typically rely on access to high-quality training data, which is usually expected to be free of missing values to function optimally. In practical reality, however, it is often exceptionally challenging to obtain complete datasets, particularly in high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, recommendation systems, and social networks. This incompleteness arises from a multitude of real-world constraints including stringent privacy concerns, the high cost or inherent difficulties of certain measurements, and the skewed nature of user-generated content. For a concrete example, the respiratory rate of a patient in a clinical setting may not have been measured, either because it was deemed unnecessary at the time or was accidentally not recorded. Additionally, some critical information may be difficult or even dangerous to acquire, such as diagnostic information obtained through an invasive biopsy, which may not have been gathered for various practical or ethical reasons.

In this work, we focus on the highly relevant and practical problem of learning a robust generative model directly from training data containing a significant proportion of missing values. This problem has been largely overlooked in the literature despite its widespread practical implications and applications. Deep generative models, particularly diffusion models, have proven valuable for augmenting training data and enhancing the performance of downstream tasks like image classification and improving adversarial robustness. Following this impactful idea, we can achieve substantially better performance for critical downstream tasks by utilizing a generative model trained effectively on incomplete data for high-quality synthetic data generation, a capability with direct real-world utility. We will primarily utilize tabular data as our central example, especially for the numerical experiments, as tabular data is a ubiquitous and commonly encountered data type that very frequently contains missing values in various practical applications. Moreover, by considering tabular data as our exemplar, we simultaneously study the missing value scenarios for both categorical and continuous variables, which are both contained in this general and practically important data type.

To deal with missing values in training data, numerous previous studies propose to use various imputation methods as a preliminary step and then train the model on the imputed data. Taking tabular data as a specific example, some basic approaches involve simply deleting entire instances (rows) or features (columns) with missing data or replacing missing values with simple statistics like the mean of observed values for that feature. Other, more sophisticated methods employ advanced machine learning approaches or deep generative models specifically for the imputation task. It has been shown, however, that imputation may inadvertently reduce the diversity of the training data and can lead to biased and suboptimal performances in downstream tasks, highlighting a significant practical drawback. In addition to imputation or simple deletion methods, previous work has also studied learning from data with missing values and synthesizing complete data using GAN or VAE architectures. Compared with our proposed framework, these methods often involve training additional and complex networks, impose certain restrictive assumptions on the missing mechanisms, and the unique challenges associated with mixed-type tabular data are less thoroughly investigated.

In this work, we propose a novel and practical diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, specifically designed for learning directly from data with missing values. We present detailed theoretical justifications for MissDiff regarding its capability for recovering the oracle score function and for upper bounding the negative log-likelihood of the data under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that learns a generative model directly from mixed-type data containing missing values, where the missing values are used explicitly in the training process without any prior imputation step, offering a more streamlined and principled approach. We conduct a comprehensive suite of numerical experiments on mixed-type tabular data, comprising both continuous and categorical variables, under various missing mechanisms. Evaluated under several realistic and efficacious metrics, MissDiff consistently outperforms other baseline methods by a considerable and practically meaningful margin, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.
Our contributions can be summarized in a detailed manner as follows.
*   We propose a novel and practical diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, for generative model training directly from incomplete data. We mainly focus on the highly applicable domain of tabular data generation, which contains both categorical and continuous variables.
*   We provide rigorous theoretical justifications for MissDiff concerning its recovery of the oracle score function and its role in upper bounding the negative log-likelihood of the data under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms.
*   We conduct extensive and thorough numerical experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets under different missing mechanisms to convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness and practical superiority of MissDiff.

The rest of the paper is organized in a structured manner as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary setup of the missing data mechanism and the diffusion model. Section 3 introduces the proposed method in detail. Section 4 theoretically characterizes the effectiveness of the proposed method. Numerical results are presented and discussed in Section 5. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 6.

Related Work

One line of research focuses on developing different types of generative models trained directly on data with missing values. These studies carefully modify the architecture and training objectives of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to learn from incomplete data.

Another distinct research direction explores learning generative models specifically for the task of imputing missing values in observed data. For example, one study proposes a conditional score-based generative model for time series imputation. Moreover, another work adapts this conditional score-based diffusion model for imputing tabular data. It is important to note that these imputation methods are not easily used for the broader and often more valuable task of generating entirely new complete data, which is the main difference from the first line of works and a key focus of our approach.

Tabular data, as a mixed-type data format that typically contains both categorical and continuous variables, has attracted significant and growing attention in the field of machine learning due to its practical prevalence. Tabular data synthesis has been a long-standing research topic in this important area. The presence of mixed variable types and class imbalance for discrete variables makes it a particularly challenging task to model tabular data accurately. Recently, several deep learning-based models have been proposed for generating high-quality tabular data. Among these advanced methods, one employs Gaussian transitions for continuous variables and multinomial transitions for discrete random variables, while another proposes a self-paced learning technique and a fine-tuning strategy for score-based models and achieves state-of-the-art performance in tabular data generation. Moreover, the discrete Score Matching methods proposed in other recent works can also be employed to handle discrete variables in tabular data effectively.

Problem Setup and Preliminaries

Training with Missing Data

We aim to learn a diffusion-based generative model from training data that may contain a certain proportion of missing values, a common practical scenario.
Following established settings in the literature, we denote the underlying complete d-dimensional data as x and assume it is sampled from the unknown true data-generating distribution p0(x). Here, each variable xi can be either categorical or continuous. For each data point x, suppose there is a corresponding binary mask m which indicates the missing entry for the current sample. Then, the observed data xobs is defined accordingly, where na indicates the missing value.
Suppose we have n complete (but unobservable) training data points and simultaneously n corresponding masks generated from a specific missing data mechanism detailed later. Then the observed data values are the set Sobs.
The missing mechanisms can be categorized based on the relationships between the mask m and the complete data x as follows:
*   Missing Completely At Random (MCAR): mask m is independent of the completed data x.
*   Missing At Random (MAR): mask m only depends on the observed value xobs.
*   Not Missing At Random (NMAR): m depends on both the observed value xobs and the missing value.

Compared with previous work which typically develops algorithms and theoretical foundations under the restrictive MCAR assumption, our method and theoretical guarantees aim to provide a more general and practical framework for learning on incomplete data and generating complete data under broader conditions.

Our objective is to train a generative model pφ, parametrized by neural network parameters φ, using only the observed data Sobs, such that pφ is close to the true distribution p0(x) and we can efficiently generate synthetic data from pφ. The optimal model is the one that maximizes the likelihood of the data sampling from the true data-generating distribution p(x). In the following, we mainly consider the score-based generative model as pφ.

Score-Based Generative Model

In this work, we adopt the diffusion model as the prototype for developing our proposed method, aiming to train the model with missing values directly without the need for prior imputation, which offers a more direct and potentially less biased approach. We first briefly review the key components of score-based generative models.

Score-based generative models are a powerful class of generative models that learn the score function, which is the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. Following the standard notation, the score-based generative models are based on a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). The solution of this SDE is a continuous trajectory of random variables. When constructing the SDE, we let p0(x) be the true data distribution, and after perturbing the data according to the SDE, the data distribution becomes pT(x) which is close to a tractable noise distribution, usually set as the standard Gaussian distribution.

The data generation process is performed via the reverse SDE. We can generate new data by running backward the reverse-time SDE when the score of each marginal distribution is known. Score Matching can be used for training a score-based model sθ(x(t), t) to estimate the score accurately. The local consistency of score matching is a well-established property.

Method

In general, there are two broad approaches to learn a generative model from incomplete data. The first approach is to construct a complete training dataset first and then learn a generative model on the completed data. We can either delete instances or features with missing data or adopt the "impute-then-generate" paradigm, i.e., we complete the data either by traditional imputation methods or by training machine learning imputation models or deep generative models specifically for imputation tasks. However, this pipeline may introduce bias into the training objective. We clarify this important claim in the following remark. Moreover, some of the more advanced imputation methods require ground truth for the missing values and significantly increase the computational costs due to learning additional networks, which highlights the practical need for alternative unbiased approaches that can handle missing data directly and more efficiently.

The second way is to learn the generative model to deal with the incomplete data directly. In previous works, learning from incomplete data with GAN or VAE is proposed, which often require training some additional networks and have restrictive assumptions on the missing mechanism. Moreover, the practically important case of tabular data that contains mixed-type variables was not fully considered in those previous works. Therefore, a general and practical framework for learning on missing data and generating complete data on tabular data is clearly needed.

The standard diffusion model typically requires complete data for training, which is not practical for various real-world applications. To address this significant limitation, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework specifically designed for training diffusion models on tabular data with missing values, making it more suitable and applicable for real-world scenarios where incomplete data is a common and persistent challenge.

Remark (Challenges when training generative models with missing data)
Inspired by the analysis pipeline of "impute-then-regress" for the prediction task, we can study a corresponding framework for the generation task. The generative model pφ represents the probability distribution of the synthetic data x. Under the maximum likelihood framework, the optimal parameters φ* are defined. When data has missing values, the general approach, known as "impute-then-generate", may be used in practice. In this approach, the observed data xobs is first imputed using an imputation model fφ. Then, the generative model is trained by maximizing the likelihood of the imputed data. However, this pipeline is biased because with single imputation, the conditional distribution over the missing data is discarded, and the optimal single imputation can no longer capture the full data variability, leading to suboptimal generative performance.

Motivated by the above critical observation, we instead propose to train the model parameters φ by maximizing the likelihood of the full joint distribution pφ(xobs, xmiss). Therefore, we propose MissDiff, a novel diffusion-based framework for learning directly on missing data. This approach aims to address the limitations of traditional impute-then-generate methods by incorporating the uncertainty in missing data directly into the learning process, resulting in a more accurate and robust generative model that better reflects the true underlying data distribution.
We propose the following Denoising Score Matching method for data with missing values.
Instead of using the standard objective for learning the score-based model sθ(x(t), t), we propose MissDiff as the solution to a modified objective where the loss is masked according to the observed entries.

More specifically, we mainly adopt the Variance Preserving (VP) SDE in this paper although the Variance Exploding (VE) SDE is also applicable. The forward diffusion process of the Variance Preserving SDE is defined accordingly. The provided algorithms demonstrate the Denoising Score Matching objective on missing data and the sampling procedure of MissDiff.

Theory

In this section, we rigorously examine the effectiveness of MissDiff by theoretically characterizing the Score Matching objective under mild and realistic conditions on the missing mechanisms and we build a further connection between Score Matching and the maximum likelihood objective for training the diffusion model.

In the following theorem, we present our first theoretical result that verifies that Denoising Score Matching on missing data can learn the oracle score, i.e., the score on the complete data. Theorem 1 states that the global optimal solution of Denoising Score Matching on missing data obtained by MissDiff is the same as the oracle score.

Theorem 1
Denote ρi as the percentage of missing samples for the i-th entry in the training data. Suppose ρmax is less than 1. Let θ* be the solution to the training objective of MissDiff. Then we have that the learned score function equals the true score.

It is well known that with careful design of the weighting function, Denoising Score Matching can upper bound the negative log-likelihood of the diffusion model on complete data. Therefore, it is straightforward to extend such a connection to incomplete data scenarios, which is detailed in the following theorem. These results provide insightful connections between the training objective of MissDiff and the maximum likelihood objective of the generative model on observed data.

Theorem 2
The negative expected log-likelihood is upper bounded by a scaled version of the Denoising Score Matching objective plus a constant.

When there are missing values, Theorem 2 shows that the Denoising score matching on incomplete data still upper bounds the likelihood of the incomplete data up to a constant coefficient. When there is no data missing, the coefficient becomes 1 and Theorem 2 degenerates to the known result for complete data.

Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate the effectiveness and practical utility of the proposed method MissDiff using simulations and two real-world tabular datasets. We introduce the experimental setup, including datasets, baseline models, and evaluation criteria, in Section 5.1. The detailed experiment results under different designs of MCAR are presented in Section 5.2. The detailed experiment results under the missing mechanisms MAR and NMAR are shown in Section 5.3.

Experimental Setup

Datasets
We present a comprehensive suite of numerical evaluations of the proposed MissDiff approach on a simulated Bayesian Network data, a real Census tabular dataset, and the MIMIC4ED tabular dataset, with various proportions of missing values. The primary and practical goal is to compare the effectiveness in synthetic data generation of the proposed MissDiff with the alternative baselines detailed later in this subsection.

The detailed description of the dataset can be found in Table 1, which specifies the number of training data, the number of testing data, the number of categorical variables in the tabular dataset, and the number of continuous variables. Moreover, the last column shows the evaluation task we adopted as detailed later.

Choice of Masks under Different Missing Mechanisms
To evaluate the performance of MissDiff on different missing mechanisms, we give a detailed explanation of the practical implementation of MCAR, MAR, and NMAR.

*   MCAR: there are three specific types of missing mechanisms in MCAR.
    *   Row Missing. For a given missing ratio α, we have the number of elements missing in each row is a function of α and d, and the location of the missing entries is randomly chosen.
    *   Column Missing. For a given missing ratio α, we have the number of elements missing in each column is a function of α and n, and the location of the missing entries is randomly chosen.
    *   Independent Missing. Each entry in the table is masked missing according to the realization of a Bernoulli random variable with parameter α.
*   MAR: a fixed subset of variables that cannot have missing values is first sampled. Then, the remaining variables will have missing values according to a logistic model with random weights, which takes the non-missing variables as inputs. The outcome is scaled to attain a given missing ratio α.
*   NMAR: the same pipeline as MAR with the inputs of the logistic model are masked by the MCAR mechanism.

Remark 1 gives the guarantee that MissDiff can recover the oracle score under MCAR with high probability. In the following tables in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, we adopt the missing ratio α=0.2 and XGBoost for the downstream tasks unless specified otherwise.

Baseline Methods

We compare the proposed method with several baseline methods for synthetic data generation trained on data with missing values. The baseline methods are described in a detailed manner as follows:
1.  Diff-delete: Learn a vanilla diffusion model after deleting rows containing missing values.
2.  Diff-mean: Learn a vanilla diffusion model after imputing missing values using the mean value in that column.
3.  STaSy with the above two data completion methods. STaSy is the state-of-the-art diffusion model on tabular data, which outperforms other generative models by a large margin.

We use the variance-preserving SDE with specific time durations for different datasets. We use the standard pre/post-processing of tabular data to deal with mixed-type data. We train the diffusion model for 250 epochs with a batch size of 64.

Evaluation Criterion
Following established practices, we use two types of criterion, fidelity and utility, to thoroughly evaluate the quality of the synthetic data generated. To evaluate the fidelity of synthetic data compared with real data, we adopt a model-agnostic library, SDMetrics. The result is a float number ranging from 0 to 100%. The larger the score, the better the overall quality of synthetic data is, indicating higher fidelity.

To evaluate the practical utility of synthetic data, we follow the same pipeline of training various machine learning models on synthetic data, and validating the model on original training data, and testing them with real test data. All the experiments are obtained from 3 repetitions to ensure reliability.

Experiment Results

Simulation Study
Q1: How does MissDiff perform on different missing ratios against the vanilla diffusion model learned on the data completed by two baseline methods mentioned in section 5.1?

Figure 1 summarizes the SDMetrics score on the simulated Bayesian Network dataset example. With the same diffusion model architecture and the same training hyperparameters, MissDiff achieves consistently better results against the vanilla diffusion model deleting the incomplete row or using the mean value for imputation when the missing ratio varies from 0.1 to 0.9. Moreover, the advantage of MissDiff becomes more obvious and pronounced for large missing ratios. These experimental results verify the motivation of MissDiff proposed earlier that the learning objective of impute-then-generate is biased. Directly learning on the missing data can significantly enhance the performance of the learned generative model in a practical setting.

Real Tabular Datasets
Q2: How does MissDiff perform on more complicated real-world data and compared with the state-of-the-art generative model on tabular data?

Table 2 and Table 3 demonstrate the effectiveness of MissDiff on the Census dataset under MCAR. STaSy is a state-of-the-art generative model for tabular data, which means MissDiff achieves quite good performance on learning from incomplete data and generating complete data. More importantly, MissDiff achieves better performance than STaSy-delete and STaSy-mean even without adopting the self-paced learning technique and the fine-tuning strategy used by STaSy. Moreover, the results of STaSy-delete and STaSy-mean are obtained by training the diffusion model for 1000 epochs, compared with only 250 epochs for MissDiff, Diff-delete, and Diff-mean. Compared with the state-of-the-art performance of STaSy for complete tabular data generation, its relatively worse performance here indicates that STaSy could be susceptible to missing data, whereas MissDiff is robust to it.

Q3: How does MissDiff perform on a real application of large-scale Electronic Health Records data?

Table 4 and Table 5 show the performance of MissDiff on the MIMIC4ED dataset under MCAR. On this large and complex dataset with dozens of continuous and discrete variables, MissDiff gives consistently better performance with the same training epochs (250 epochs), demonstrating its scalability and effectiveness.

Ablation Study
Q4: How does MissDiff perform on other missing mechanisms beyond MCAR, i.e., MAR and NMAR?

Table 6 and Table 7 demonstrate the effectiveness of MissDiff on the Census dataset beyond MCAR. The results show the great potential and practical value of learning directly on the missing data when the missing mechanism is not MCAR, which cannot be easily dealt with by previous methods that often assume MCAR.

Q5: How does MissDiff perform on the imputation task?

Furthermore, we validate the performance of the proposed MissDiff on imputation tasks for the Census dataset. We compare MissDiff with state-of-the-art imputation approaches in Table 8. The result shows that although primarily designed for generation tasks, MissDiff also performs very well for imputation tasks, showcasing its versatility.

Conclusion and Discussion

We propose a novel and practical diffusion-based generative framework, called MissDiff, for synthetic data generation trained directly on data with missing values. Compared with traditional methods of handling missing data, such as deletion or imputation, which may lead to reduced data diversity and biased performance, MissDiff offers a promising and effective alternative that directly handles missing data without the need for imputation or deletion, providing significant practical advantages. Theoretical justification for MissDiff's effectiveness is provided, grounding the method in solid principles. Moreover, extensive and thorough numerical experiments demonstrate strong empirical evidence for the effectiveness and practical superiority of MissDiff across various datasets and missing mechanisms.

Limitations and broader impact
Overall, this research presents a promising and impactful direction for handling missing data in generative model training, a problem with wide-reaching implications. The proposed framework, MissDiff, has potential applications in a wide range of domains where missing data is a common and persistent issue, such as healthcare, finance, and social science. A potential limitation of this work is that it has only been empirically validated on tabular data, though the framework is general. For important future directions, it would be interesting and valuable to see how MissDiff performs empirically with more complicated data types such as video or language data. Furthermore, further research could explore the theoretical effectiveness of MissDiff from a utility perspective or a differential privacy perspective, enhancing its applicability in sensitive domains.

Yidong Ouyang and Liyan Xie are partially supported by UDF01002142 through The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen. Guang Cheng is partially supported by Office of Naval Research, ONR (N00014-22-1-2680), NSF – SCALE MoDL (2134209), and Meta gift fund.
