In this work, we propose a novel and practical diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, specifically designed for learning directly from data with missing values. We present detailed theoretical justifications for MissDiff regarding its capability for recovering the oracle score function and for upper bounding the negative log-likelihood of the data under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that learns a generative model directly from mixed-type data containing missing values, where the missing values are used explicitly in the training process without any prior imputation step, offering a more streamlined and principled approach. We conduct a comprehensive suite of numerical experiments on mixed-type tabular data, comprising both continuous and categorical variables, under various missing mechanisms. Evaluated under several realistic and efficacious metrics, MissDiff consistently outperforms other baseline methods by a considerable and practically meaningful margin, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.
Our contributions can be summarized in a detailed manner as follows.
*   We propose a novel and practical diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, for generative model training directly from incomplete data. We mainly focus on the highly applicable domain of tabular data generation, which contains both categorical and continuous variables.
*   We provide rigorous theoretical justifications for MissDiff concerning its recovery of the oracle score function and its role in upper bounding the negative log-likelihood of the data under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms.
*   We conduct extensive and thorough numerical experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets under different missing mechanisms to convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness and practical superiority of MissDiff.

The rest of the paper is organized in a structured manner as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary setup of the missing data mechanism and the diffusion model. Section 3 introduces the proposed method in detail. Section 4 theoretically characterizes the effectiveness of the proposed method. Numerical results are presented and discussed in Section 5. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 6.

Related Work

One line of research focuses on developing different types of generative models trained directly on data with missing values. These studies carefully modify the architecture and training objectives of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to learn from incomplete data.

Another distinct research direction explores learning generative models specifically for the task of imputing missing values in observed data. For example, one study proposes a conditional score-based generative model for time series imputation. Moreover, another work adapts this conditional score-based diffusion model for imputing tabular data. It is important to note that these imputation methods are not easily used for the broader and often more valuable task of generating entirely new complete data, which is the main difference from the first line of works and a key focus of our approach.

Tabular data, as a mixed-type data format that typically contains both categorical and continuous variables, has attracted significant and growing attention in the field of machine learning due to its practical prevalence. Tabular data synthesis has been a long-standing research topic in this important area. The presence of mixed variable types and class imbalance for discrete variables makes it a particularly challenging task to model tabular data accurately. Recently, several deep learning-based models have been proposed for generating high-quality tabular data. Among these advanced methods, one employs Gaussian transitions for continuous variables and multinomial transitions for discrete random variables, while another proposes a self-paced learning technique and a fine-tuning strategy for score-based models and achieves state-of-the-art performance in tabular data generation. Moreover, the discrete Score Matching methods proposed in other recent works can also be employed to handle discrete variables in tabular data effectively.

Problem Setup and Preliminaries

Training with Missing Data

We aim to learn a diffusion-based generative model from training data that may contain a certain proportion of missing values, a common practical scenario.
Following established settings in the literature, we denote the underlying complete d-dimensional data as x and assume it is sampled from the unknown true data-generating distribution p0(x). Here, each variable xi can be either categorical or continuous. For each data point x, suppose there is a corresponding binary mask m which indicates the missing entry for the current sample. Then, the observed data xobs is defined accordingly, where na indicates the missing value.
Suppose we have n complete (but unobservable) training data points and simultaneously n corresponding masks generated from a specific missing data mechanism detailed later. Then the observed data values are the set Sobs.
The missing mechanisms can be categorized based on the relationships between the mask m and the complete data x as follows:
*   Missing Completely At Random (MCAR): mask m is independent of the completed data x.
*   Missing At Random (MAR): mask m only depends on the observed value xobs.
*   Not Missing At Random (NMAR): m depends on both the observed value xobs and the missing value.

Compared with previous work which typically develops algorithms and theoretical foundations under the restrictive MCAR assumption, our method and theoretical guarantees aim to provide a more general and practical framework for learning on incomplete data and generating complete data under broader conditions.

Our objective is to train a generative model pφ, parametrized by neural network parameters φ, using only the observed data Sobs, such that pφ is close to the true distribution p0(x) and we can efficiently generate synthetic data from pφ. The optimal model is the one that maximizes the likelihood of the data sampling from the true data-generating distribution p(x). In the following, we mainly consider the score-based generative model as pφ.

Score-Based Generative Model

In this work, we adopt the diffusion model as the prototype for developing our proposed method, aiming to train the model with missing values directly without the need for prior imputation, which offers a more direct and potentially less biased approach. We first briefly review the key components of score-based generative models.

Score-based generative models are a powerful class of generative models that learn the score function, which is the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. Following the standard notation, the score-based generative models are based on a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). The solution of this SDE is a continuous trajectory of random variables. When constructing the SDE, we let p0(x) be the true data distribution, and after perturbing the data according to the SDE, the data distribution becomes pT(x) which is close to a tractable noise distribution, usually set as the standard Gaussian distribution.

The data generation process is performed via the reverse SDE. We can generate new data by running backward the reverse-time SDE when the score of each marginal distribution is known. Score Matching can be used for training a score-based model sθ(x(t), t) to estimate the score accurately. The local consistency of score matching is a well-established property.

Method

In general, there are two broad approaches to learn a generative model from incomplete data. The first approach is to construct a complete training dataset first and then learn a generative model on the completed data. We can either delete instances or features with missing data or adopt the "impute-then-generate" paradigm, i.e., we complete the data either by traditional imputation methods or by training machine learning imputation models or deep generative models specifically for imputation tasks. However, this pipeline may introduce bias into the training objective. We clarify this important claim in the following remark. Moreover, some of the more advanced imputation methods require ground truth for the missing values and significantly increase the computational costs due to learning additional networks, which highlights the practical need for alternative unbiased approaches that can handle missing data directly and more efficiently.

The second way is to learn the generative model to deal with the incomplete data directly. In previous works, learning from incomplete data with GAN or VAE is proposed, which often require training some additional networks and have restrictive assumptions on the missing mechanism. Moreover, the practically important case of tabular data that contains mixed-type variables was not fully considered in those previous works. Therefore, a general and practical framework for learning on missing data and generating complete data on tabular data is clearly needed.

The standard diffusion model typically requires complete data for training, which is not practical for various real-world applications. To address this significant limitation, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework specifically designed for training diffusion models on tabular data with missing values, making it more suitable and applicable for real-world scenarios where incomplete data is a common and persistent challenge.

Remark (Challenges when training generative models with missing data)
Inspired by the analysis pipeline of "impute-then-regress" for the prediction task, we can study a corresponding framework for the generation task. The generative model pφ represents the probability distribution of the synthetic data x. Under the maximum likelihood framework, the optimal parameters φ* are defined. When data has missing values, the general approach, known as "impute-then-generate", may be used in practice. In this approach, the observed data xobs is first imputed using an imputation model fφ. Then, the generative model is trained by maximizing the likelihood of the imputed data. However, this pipeline is biased because with single imputation, the conditional distribution over the missing data is discarded, and the optimal single imputation can no longer capture the full data variability, leading to suboptimal generative performance.

Motivated by the above critical observation, we instead propose to train the model parameters φ by maximizing the likelihood of the full joint distribution pφ(xobs, xmiss). Therefore, we propose MissDiff, a novel diffusion-based framework for learning directly on missing data. This approach aims to address the limitations of traditional impute-then-generate methods by incorporating the uncertainty in missing data directly into the learning process, resulting in a more accurate and robust generative model that better reflects the true underlying data distribution.
We propose the following Denoising Score Matching method for data with missing values.
Instead of using the standard objective for learning the score-based model sθ(x(t), t), we propose MissDiff as the solution to a modified objective where the loss is masked according to the observed entries.

More specifically, we mainly adopt the Variance Preserving (VP) SDE in this paper although the Variance Exploding (VE) SDE is also applicable. The forward diffusion process of the Variance Preserving SDE is defined accordingly. The provided algorithms demonstrate the Denoising Score Matching objective on missing data and the sampling procedure of MissDiff.

Theory

In this section, we rigorously examine the effectiveness of MissDiff by theoretically characterizing the Score Matching objective under mild and realistic conditions on the missing mechanisms and we build a further connection between Score Matching and the maximum likelihood objective for training the diffusion model.

In the following theorem, we present our first theoretical result that verifies that Denoising Score Matching on missing data can learn the oracle score, i.e., the score on the complete data. Theorem 1 states that the global optimal solution of Denoising Score Matching on missing data obtained by MissDiff is the same as the oracle score.

Theorem 1
Denote ρi as the percentage of missing samples for the i-th entry in the training data. Suppose ρmax is less than 1. Let θ* be the solution to the training objective of MissDiff. Then we have that the learned score function equals the true score.

It is well known that with careful design of the weighting function, Denoising Score Matching can upper bound the negative log-likelihood of the diffusion model on complete data. Therefore, it is straightforward to extend such a connection to incomplete data scenarios, which is detailed in the following theorem. These results provide insightful connections between the training objective of MissDiff and the maximum likelihood objective of the generative model on observed data.

Theorem 2
The negative expected log-likelihood is upper bounded by a scaled version of the Denoising Score Matching objective plus a constant.

When there are missing values, Theorem 2 shows that the Denoising score matching on incomplete data still upper bounds the likelihood of the incomplete data up to a constant coefficient. When there is no data missing, the coefficient becomes 1 and Theorem 2 degenerates to the known result for complete data.

Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate the effectiveness and practical utility of the proposed method MissDiff using simulations and two real-world tabular datasets. We introduce the experimental setup, including datasets, baseline models, and evaluation criteria, in Section 5.1. The detailed experiment results under different designs of MCAR are presented in Section 5.2. The detailed experiment results under the missing mechanisms MAR and NMAR are shown in Section 5.3.

Experimental Setup

Datasets
We present a comprehensive suite of numerical evaluations of the proposed MissDiff approach on a simulated Bayesian Network data, a real Census tabular dataset, and the MIMIC4ED tabular dataset, with various proportions of missing values. The primary and practical goal is to compare the effectiveness in synthetic data generation of the proposed MissDiff with the alternative baselines detailed later in this subsection.

The detailed description of the dataset can be found in Table 1, which specifies the number of training data, the number of testing data, the number of categorical variables in the tabular dataset, and the number of continuous variables. Moreover, the last column shows the evaluation task we adopted as detailed later.

Choice of Masks under Different Missing Mechanisms
To evaluate the performance of MissDiff on different missing mechanisms, we give a detailed explanation of the practical implementation of MCAR, MAR, and NMAR.

*   MCAR: there are three specific types of missing mechanisms in MCAR.
    *   Row Missing. For a given missing ratio α, we have the number of elements missing in each row is a function of α and d, and the location of the missing entries is randomly chosen.
    *   Column Missing. For a given missing ratio α, we have the number of elements missing in each column is a function of α and n, and the location of the missing entries is randomly chosen.
    *   Independent Missing. Each entry in the table is masked missing according to the realization of a Bernoulli random variable with parameter α.
*   MAR: a fixed subset of variables that cannot have missing values is first sampled. Then, the remaining variables will have missing values according to a logistic model with random weights, which takes the non-missing variables as inputs. The outcome is scaled to attain a given missing ratio α.
*   NMAR: the same pipeline as MAR with the inputs of the logistic model are masked by the MCAR mechanism.

Remark 1 gives the guarantee that MissDiff can recover the oracle score under MCAR with high probability. In the following tables in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, we adopt the missing ratio α=0.2 and XGBoost for the downstream tasks unless specified otherwise.

Baseline Methods

We compare the proposed method with several baseline methods for synthetic data generation trained on data with missing values. The baseline methods are described in a detailed manner as follows:
1.  Diff-delete: Learn a vanilla diffusion model after deleting rows containing missing values.
2.  Diff-mean: Learn a vanilla diffusion model after imputing missing values using the mean value in that column.
3.  STaSy with the above two data completion methods. STaSy is the state-of-the-art diffusion model on tabular data, which outperforms other generative models by a large margin.

We use the variance-preserving SDE with specific time durations for different datasets. We use the standard pre/post-processing of tabular data to deal with mixed-type data. We train the diffusion model for 250 epochs with a batch size of 64.

Evaluation Criterion
Following established practices, we use two types of criterion, fidelity and utility, to thoroughly evaluate the quality of the synthetic data generated. To evaluate the fidelity of synthetic data compared with real data, we adopt a model-agnostic library, SDMetrics. The result is a float number ranging from 0 to 100%. The larger the score, the better the overall quality of synthetic data is, indicating higher fidelity.

To evaluate the practical utility of synthetic data, we follow the same pipeline of training various machine learning models on synthetic data, and validating the model on original training data, and testing them with real test data. All the experiments are obtained from 3 repetitions to ensure reliability.

Experiment Results

Simulation Study
Q1: How does MissDiff perform on different missing ratios against the vanilla diffusion model learned on the data completed by two baseline methods mentioned in section 5.1?

Figure 1 summarizes the SDMetrics score on the simulated Bayesian Network dataset example. With the same diffusion model architecture and the same training hyperparameters, MissDiff achieves consistently better results against the vanilla diffusion model deleting the incomplete row or using the mean value for imputation when the missing ratio varies from 0.1 to 0.9. Moreover, the advantage of MissDiff becomes more obvious and pronounced for large missing ratios. These experimental results verify the motivation of MissDiff proposed earlier that the learning objective of impute-then-generate is biased. Directly learning on the missing data can significantly enhance the performance of the learned generative model in a practical setting.

Real Tabular Datasets
Q2: How does MissDiff perform on more complicated real-world data and compared with the state-of-the-art generative model on tabular data?

Table 2 and Table 3 demonstrate the effectiveness of MissDiff on the Census dataset under MCAR. STaSy is a state-of-the-art generative model for tabular data, which means MissDiff achieves quite good performance on learning from incomplete data and generating complete data. More importantly, MissDiff achieves better performance than STaSy-delete and STaSy-mean even without adopting the self-paced learning technique and the fine-tuning strategy used by STaSy. Moreover, the results of STaSy-delete and STaSy-mean are obtained by training the diffusion model for 1000 epochs, compared with only 250 epochs for MissDiff, Diff-delete, and Diff-mean. Compared with the state-of-the-art performance of STaSy for complete tabular data generation, its relatively worse performance here indicates that STaSy could be susceptible to missing data, whereas MissDiff is robust to it.

Q3: How does MissDiff perform on a real application of large-scale Electronic Health Records data?

Table 4 and Table 5 show the performance of MissDiff on the MIMIC4ED dataset under MCAR. On this large and complex dataset with dozens of continuous and discrete variables, MissDiff gives consistently better performance with the same training epochs (250 epochs), demonstrating its scalability and effectiveness.

Ablation Study
Q4: How does MissDiff perform on other missing mechanisms beyond MCAR, i.e., MAR and NMAR?

Table 6 and Table 7 demonstrate the effectiveness of MissDiff on the Census dataset beyond MCAR. The results show the great potential and practical value of learning directly on the missing data when the missing mechanism is not MCAR, which cannot be easily dealt with by previous methods that often assume MCAR.

Q5: How does MissDiff perform on the imputation task?

Furthermore, we validate the performance of the proposed MissDiff on imputation tasks for the Census dataset. We compare MissDiff with state-of-the-art imputation approaches in Table 8. The result shows that although primarily designed for generation tasks, MissDiff also performs very well for imputation tasks, showcasing its versatility.

Conclusion and Discussion

We propose a novel and practical diffusion-based generative framework, called MissDiff, for synthetic data generation trained directly on data with missing values. Compared with traditional methods of handling missing data, such as deletion or imputation, which may lead to reduced data diversity and biased performance, MissDiff offers a promising and effective alternative that directly handles missing data without the need for imputation or deletion, providing significant practical advantages. Theoretical justification for MissDiff's effectiveness is provided, grounding the method in solid principles. Moreover, extensive and thorough numerical experiments demonstrate strong empirical evidence for the effectiveness and practical superiority of MissDiff across various datasets and missing mechanisms.

Limitations and broader impact
Overall, this research presents a promising and impactful direction for handling missing data in generative model training, a problem with wide-reaching implications. The proposed framework, MissDiff, has potential applications in a wide range of domains where missing data is a common and persistent issue, such as healthcare, finance, and social science. A potential limitation of this work is that it has only been empirically validated on tabular data, though the framework is general. For important future directions, it would be interesting and valuable to see how MissDiff performs empirically with more complicated data types such as video or language data. Furthermore, further research could explore the theoretical effectiveness of MissDiff from a utility perspective or a differential privacy perspective, enhancing its applicability in sensitive domains.

Title: MissDiff: A Unified and Principled Diffusion-Based Framework for Training Generative Models on Tabular Data with Missing Values

Abstract

Diffusion models have demonstrated truly remarkable and unparalleled performance in modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing high-fidelity data across numerous domains. However, a fundamental and critical limitation of the vanilla diffusion model is its strict requirement for complete or fully observed data during the training phase. Incomplete data constitutes a pervasive and significant issue across a vast array of real-world applications, including healthcare, finance, and social science, particularly when dealing with ubiquitous tabular datasets. This pioneering work presents a unified, principled, and highly effective diffusion-based framework specifically designed for learning from data containing missing values under various missing mechanisms. We first make the crucial observation that the widely adopted yet simplistic "impute-then-generate" pipeline inherently leads to a biased and suboptimal learning objective. To directly address this core limitation, we propose a novel method that strategically masks the regression loss within the Denoising Score Matching objective during the training phase. We definitively prove that the proposed method is consistent in learning the true score of the underlying data distributions, and we further establish that the proposed training objective serves as a rigorous upper bound for the negative data likelihood under general conditions. The proposed framework is exhaustively evaluated on multiple real-world tabular datasets using realistic and highly efficacious metrics and is conclusively demonstrated to outperform the state-of-the-art diffusion model applied with the "impute-then-generate" pipeline by a substantial and decisive margin.

Introduction

Diffusion models have rapidly emerged as an exceptionally powerful and versatile tool for modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing high-quality samples across various data types, including images, videos, point clouds, and tabular data. It is well-understood that such advanced machine learning models typically rely on access to high-quality, complete training data, which is conventionally expected to be entirely free of missing values. In practical reality, it is frequently challenging and often impossible to obtain pristine, complete datasets, particularly in critical fields such as healthcare, finance, recommendation systems, and social network analysis. This challenge arises from a confluence of factors including stringent privacy concerns, prohibitive data acquisition costs, inherent sampling difficulties, and the naturally skewed distribution of user-generated content. For a concrete illustration, consider the respiratory rate of a patient in a clinical setting, which may not have been measured due to a clinical decision, an accidental omission during recording, or resource constraints. Furthermore, certain types of information can be exceptionally difficult, invasive, or even dangerous to acquire, such as data obtained through an invasive biopsy procedure, which may be deliberately omitted for a subset of patients due to associated risks.

In this seminal work, we decisively focus on the pivotal problem of learning a robust generative model directly from training data containing a significant proportion of missing values. This problem has been largely and surprisingly overlooked in the contemporary literature despite its immense and widespread practical significance. Deep generative models, and diffusion models in particular, have proven instrumental for data augmentation, substantially enhancing performance in tasks like image classification and improving adversarial robustness. By extending this powerful paradigm, we can achieve superior performance for critical downstream tasks by utilizing generative models trained directly on incomplete data to produce high-quality synthetic data. We will primarily utilize tabular data as our central exemplar, especially for the numerical experiments, as tabular data represents one of the most commonly encountered and practically important data types, and it frequently contains missing values across diverse applications. Moreover, by considering tabular data, we simultaneously and effectively address the challenging missing value scenarios for both categorical and continuous variables, which are inherently mixed within this data type.

To handle missing values in training data, numerous existing studies propose to employ various imputation methods as a preprocessing step before training the model on the imputed data. Common simplistic approaches for tabular data involve deleting entire instances (rows) or features (columns) with missing data, or replacing missing values with simple statistics like the column mean. More sophisticated methods employ advanced machine learning techniques or deep generative models specifically for the imputation task. However, it has been clearly shown that imputation can artificially reduce the intrinsic diversity of the training data and may consequently lead to biased and unreliable performances in downstream tasks. Beyond imputation or simple deletion, previous work has also explored learning from incomplete data using GAN or VAE architectures for synthetic data generation. Compared to our proposed, comprehensive framework, these methods often necessitate training additional auxiliary networks, impose restrictive assumptions on the missing data mechanisms, and have not thoroughly investigated the unique challenges posed by mixed-type tabular data.

In this groundbreaking work, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, for principled learning from data with missing values. We present rigorous theoretical justifications for MissDiff, proving its capability in recovering the oracle score function and establishing its objective as an upper bound for the negative data likelihood under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that successfully learns a generative model directly from mixed-type data containing missing values, where the missing values are incorporated into the training process without any prior imputation step. We conduct an extensive suite of numerical experiments on mixed-type tabular data, comprising both continuous and categorical variables, under a comprehensive range of missing mechanisms. Evaluated under several realistic and highly efficacious metrics, MissDiff consistently and decisively outperforms all other baseline methods by a considerable and significant margin.

Our fundamental and substantial contributions are decisively summarized as follows.
* We propose MissDiff, a novel and principled diffusion-based framework for generative model training directly from incomplete data. We primarily focus on the highly practical and challenging task of tabular data generation, which contains a complex mixture of categorical and continuous variables.
* We provide rigorous and comprehensive theoretical justifications for MissDiff, proving its consistency in recovering the oracle score function and establishing that its training objective upper bounds the negative data likelihood under mild assumptions on the missing mechanisms.
* We conduct extensive and thorough numerical experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets under different missing mechanisms to conclusively demonstrate the superior effectiveness and practical utility of MissDiff.

The rest of the paper is systematically organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the essential setup of missing data mechanisms and the diffusion model. Section 3 introduces the proposed MissDiff method in detail. Section 4 provides the theoretical characterization of the method's effectiveness. Comprehensive numerical results are presented in Section 5. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 6.

Related Work

One prominent line of research focuses on adapting different types of generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), to train directly on data with missing values. These studies carefully modify the model architecture and training objectives to accommodate incomplete data.

Another significant research direction explores the use of generative models specifically for the task of imputing missing values within observed data. For instance, conditional score-based diffusion models have been adapted for time series and tabular data imputation. A key distinction is that these imputation methods are not inherently designed for generating entirely new, complete data samples, which is the primary focus of the first line of work and our own contribution.

Tabular data, as a mixed-type format containing both categorical and continuous variables, has attracted considerable attention in machine learning. Tabular data synthesis is a long-standing research challenge due to the presence of mixed variable types and potential class imbalance. Recently, several deep learning-based models have been proposed for generating high-quality tabular data. Among these, state-of-the-art methods employ Gaussian diffusion for continuous variables and multinomial transitions for discrete variables, with advanced techniques like self-paced learning further pushing performance boundaries. Furthermore, recent developments in discrete Score Matching methods provide additional tools for handling discrete variables within a score-based framework.

Problem Setup and Preliminaries

Training with Missing Data

We aim to learn a powerful diffusion-based generative model from training data that may contain a significant proportion of missing values. Following established statistical frameworks, we denote the underlying complete d-dimensional data vector and assume it is sampled from an unknown true data-generating distribution. Each variable can be either categorical or continuous. For each data point, we assume there exists a corresponding binary mask vector which explicitly indicates which entries are observed and which are missing. The observed data is then constructed by an element-wise multiplication with this mask. Suppose we have n independent complete (but unobservable) training data points and simultaneously n corresponding masks generated from a specific missing data mechanism. The observed dataset consists of these partially masked samples.

Missing data mechanisms are classically categorized based on the relationship between the mask and the complete data as follows:
* Missing Completely At Random (MCAR): The mask is statistically independent of the complete data.
* Missing At Random (MAR): The mask depends only on the observed values within the data point.
* Not Missing At Random (NMAR): The mask depends on both the observed and the missing values.

Compared to previous work which often develops algorithms and theory primarily under the restrictive MCAR assumption, our proposed method and its theoretical guarantees are designed to provide a general and flexible framework for learning from incomplete data under broader conditions, with the ultimate goal of generating high-quality, complete synthetic data.

Our core objective is to train a generative model, parameterized by neural network weights, using only the observed data, such that the model's distribution closely approximates the true data distribution, allowing for efficient and accurate synthetic data generation. The optimal model is the one that maximizes the expected log-likelihood of data from the true distribution, which is equivalent to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true and model distributions. In the following, we specifically consider the powerful score-based generative model as our foundational architecture.

Score-Based Generative Model

In this work, we adopt the highly flexible diffusion model as the prototype for developing our proposed method. We propose to train the model directly on data with missing values, eliminating the need for any prior imputation step. We first provide a concise review of the key components of score-based generative models.

Score-based generative models are a powerful class of generative models that learn the score function, defined as the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. These models are based on a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) that gradually perturbs the data distribution over time. The solution to this SDE is a continuous trajectory of random variables. The forward process is constructed so that the initial distribution is the true data distribution, and the final distribution after perturbation is a simple, tractable noise distribution, typically a standard Gaussian.

The crucial data generation process is performed by reversing this diffusion process via a corresponding reverse-time SDE. Generating new data involves sampling from the simple noise distribution and then simulating this reverse SDE backwards in time. The reverse SDE depends critically on the score function of the perturbed data distributions at each timestep. Therefore, the central learning problem is to train a time-dependent score-based model to accurately estimate these scores. This is achieved through objectives like Denoising Score Matching, which have been proven to yield consistent estimators of the true score function under appropriate conditions.

Method

In general, there are two predominant approaches to learn a generative model from incomplete data. The first approach is to construct a complete training dataset as a preprocessing step and then learn a generative model on this completed data. This can involve deleting incomplete rows/columns or adopting an "impute-then-generate" paradigm, using either simple statistical imputation or sophisticated machine learning models trained for imputation. However, this pipeline can introduce significant bias into the training objective, as we formally clarify. Moreover, many advanced imputation methods require additional computational resources to train separate networks, highlighting the pressing need for alternative, unbiased approaches that can handle missing data directly and more efficiently.

The second approach is to learn the generative model to inherently deal with incomplete data directly. Previous works have proposed learning from incomplete data with GANs or VAEs, but these methods often require training auxiliary networks, make strong assumptions about the missing mechanism, and have not fully addressed the complexities of mixed-type tabular data. Therefore, a general, principled framework for learning from missing data and generating complete tabular data is urgently needed.

The standard diffusion model described previously requires complete data for training, which is a severe practical limitation for numerous real-world applications. To decisively address this critical limitation, we propose MissDiff, a novel diffusion-based framework specifically designed for training diffusion models directly on tabular data with missing values, making it exceptionally suitable for real-world scenarios where incomplete data is the norm rather than the exception.

Motivated by the analysis of biased pipelines, we propose to train the model parameters by targeting the likelihood of the full data. The standard "impute-then-generate" approach maximizes a different, biased objective. Therefore, we introduce MissDiff, a diffusion-based framework for learning on missing data. This innovative approach aims to directly address the limitations of traditional methods by incorporating the inherent uncertainty of missing data directly into the learning process, resulting in a more accurate and reliable generative model that better reflects the true underlying data distribution.

We propose the following modified Denoising Score Matching objective for data with missing values. Instead of the standard objective, we define MissDiff as the solution to a masked version of the loss. In this formulation, the mask vector, which indicates missing entries in the original observed data, is used to element-wise mask the regression loss. To ensure the transition kernel and its gradient are well-defined for mixed-type data, we apply standard preprocessing: missing continuous values are replaced with 0, and for discrete variables, a new category is introduced to represent missingness, followed by one-hot encoding.

We primarily adopt the Variance Preserving SDE in this work. The detailed training algorithm for MissDiff and the corresponding sampling procedure are provided in the algorithmic descriptions. The training algorithm involves sampling noisy versions of the observed data, applying the mask to the score-matching loss, and performing gradient descent. The sampling procedure follows the standard reverse diffusion process for the VP-SDE, using the learned score network.

Theory

In this section, we rigorously examine the effectiveness of MissDiff by theoretically characterizing its Score Matching objective under mild conditions on the missing mechanisms. We further establish a fundamental connection between this objective and the maximum likelihood framework for training the diffusion model on incomplete data.

Our first major theoretical result verifies that Denoising Score Matching on missing data, as performed by MissDiff, can successfully learn the oracle score function of the complete data. The theorem definitively states that the global optimal solution of the MissDiff objective is identical to the true score of the underlying complete data distribution, provided the maximum missing rate across features is less than one.

It is well-established that with a careful design of the weighting function, Denoising Score Matching on complete data can upper bound the negative log-likelihood of the diffusion model. We directly extend this profound connection to the incomplete data scenario. Our second theorem provides insightful connections between the training objective of MissDiff and the maximum likelihood objective on the observed data. It shows that the Denoising Score Matching objective on incomplete data still serves as an upper bound for the negative log-likelihood of the observed data, scaled by a factor related to the maximum missing rate. When no data is missing, this result gracefully reduces to the known bound for complete data, confirming the consistency and generality of our framework.

Experiments

In this section, we comprehensively demonstrate the superior effectiveness of the proposed MissDiff method using simulations and two real-world tabular datasets. We introduce the experimental setup, including datasets, baseline models, and evaluation criteria. Detailed results under different MCAR designs are presented, followed by results under the more complex MAR and NMAR mechanisms.

Experimental Setup

Datasets
We present an extensive suite of numerical evaluations of MissDiff on a simulated Bayesian Network dataset, a real U.S. Census tabular dataset, and the large-scale MIMIC4ED electronic health records dataset, each with various proportions of artificially introduced missing values. The primary goal is to compare the effectiveness in synthetic data generation of MissDiff against the alternative baselines detailed next.

Choice of Masks under Different Missing Mechanisms
To thoroughly evaluate MissDiff under different missing mechanisms, we implement practical versions of MCAR, MAR, and NMAR. For MCAR, we consider three variants: missing entire rows, missing entries per column, and independent Bernoulli missing per entry. For MAR, missingness for a subset of variables is determined by a logistic model based on other, fully observed variables. NMAR follows a similar logistic model pipeline, but the inputs to the model are themselves partially masked via an MCAR mechanism. A key remark provides a probabilistic guarantee that the condition for our main consistency theorem holds with high probability under the MCAR mechanisms when the sample size is sufficiently large.

Baseline Methods
We compare MissDiff with several strong baseline methods for synthetic data generation trained on data with missing values:
1. Diff-delete: A vanilla diffusion model trained after deleting all rows containing any missing values.
2. Diff-mean: A vanilla diffusion model trained after imputing missing values using the column mean/mode.
3. The state-of-the-art tabular diffusion model STaSy, applied after the two data completion methods above (STaSy-delete, STaSy-mean). STaSy itself significantly outperforms a wide range of prior generative models for tabular data.

We use a variance-preserving SDE and follow standard preprocessing techniques for mixed-type tabular data, including min-max normalization for continuous variables and one-hot encoding with rounding for discrete variables. All diffusion models are trained for 250 epochs unless specified otherwise.

Evaluation Criterion
Following established benchmarks, we use two complementary criteria, fidelity and utility, to holistically evaluate synthetic data quality. Fidelity is assessed using a comprehensive model-agnostic library (SDMetrics) that produces a score between 0% and 100%, where higher scores indicate better overall resemblance to real data. Utility is evaluated by training a variety of downstream machine learning models (e.g., Decision Tree, XGBoost, MLP) on the synthetic data, validating them on the original real training data, and testing their performance on held-out real test data. All reported results are averaged over multiple repetitions.

Experiment Results

Simulation Study
Q1: How does MissDiff perform across different missing ratios compared to vanilla diffusion models trained on data completed by baseline methods?
Results on the simulated Bayesian Network dataset consistently show that MissDiff achieves superior fidelity scores compared to models using deletion or mean imputation, across a wide range of missing ratios from 0.1 to 0.9. The performance advantage of MissDiff becomes increasingly pronounced as the missing ratio grows larger. These results provide strong empirical validation for our core motivation: directly learning on missing data significantly enhances generative model performance compared to the biased impute-then-generate approach.

Real Tabular Datasets
Q2: How does MissDiff perform on complex real-world data compared to the state-of-the-art generative model for tabular data?
Results on the Census dataset under MCAR mechanisms demonstrate that MissDiff achieves excellent fidelity and utility performance. Crucially, MissDiff outperforms both STaSy-delete and STaSy-mean, even though the STaSy baselines were trained for four times as many epochs (1000 vs. 250) and incorporate advanced techniques like self-paced learning. This indicates that the state-of-the-art STaSy model is highly susceptible to degradation when faced with missing data, whereas MissDiff handles it natively and effectively.

Q3: How does MissDiff perform on a large-scale Electronic Health Records application?
Results on the large MIMIC4ED dataset under MCAR show that MissDiff delivers consistently superior fidelity and utility (lower regression error) compared to the baseline methods, even with the same limited training budget of 250 epochs. This confirms the scalability and practical effectiveness of MissDiff on real-world, high-dimensional data with numerous mixed-type variables.

Ablation Study
Q4: How does MissDiff perform under missing mechanisms beyond MCAR, i.e., MAR and NMAR?
Experiments on the Census dataset under MAR and NMAR mechanisms demonstrate the strong potential of MissDiff. It achieves the best fidelity and utility scores, outperforming methods that rely on deletion or mean imputation. This shows the general applicability of MissDiff, as it can effectively handle more complex, real-world missing data patterns that cannot be easily addressed by previous methods which often assume MCAR.

Q5: How does MissDiff perform on the imputation task?
We further validate MissDiff on the classic data imputation task for the Census dataset. Although primarily designed for generation, MissDiff also performs remarkably well for imputation, achieving a lower root mean square error (RMSE) than several state-of-the-art dedicated imputation methods, including mean/mode imputation, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and a recent diffusion-based imputation method.

Conclusion and Discussion

We propose MissDiff, a novel and principled diffusion-based generative framework for synthetic data generation trained directly on data with missing values. Compared to traditional methods like deletion or imputation, which can reduce data diversity and introduce bias, MissDiff offers a powerful and promising alternative that handles missing data natively without requiring preprocessing. We provide rigorous theoretical justification for its effectiveness. Furthermore, extensive and comprehensive numerical experiments on multiple real-world datasets provide decisive empirical evidence for the superior performance and broad utility of MissDiff.

Limitations and Broader Impact
Overall, this research presents a highly promising and impactful direction for handling the ubiquitous problem of missing data in generative model training. The proposed MissDiff framework has immediate and significant potential applications across a wide range of domains where missing data is a common and critical issue, such as healthcare analytics, financial modeling, and social science research. A potential limitation is that the empirical validation in this work has been conducted primarily on tabular data. For future work, it would be highly interesting and valuable to investigate how MissDiff performs empirically with more complex data types such as video, audio, or natural language data. Furthermore, additional research could explore the theoretical effectiveness of MissDiff from perspectives such as downstream task utility or its properties under differential privacy constraints.

Title: MissDiff: A Unified and Principled Diffusion-Based Framework for Training Generative Models on Tabular Data with Missing Values

Abstract

Diffusion models have demonstrated truly remarkable and unparalleled performance in modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing high-fidelity data across numerous domains. However, a fundamental and critical limitation of the vanilla diffusion model is its strict requirement for complete or fully observed data during the training phase. Incomplete data constitutes a pervasive and significant issue across a vast array of real-world applications, including healthcare, finance, and social science, particularly when dealing with ubiquitous tabular datasets. This pioneering work presents a unified, principled, and highly effective diffusion-based framework specifically designed for learning from data containing missing values under various missing mechanisms. We first make the crucial observation that the widely adopted yet simplistic "impute-then-generate" pipeline inherently leads to a biased and suboptimal learning objective. To directly address this core limitation, we propose a novel method that strategically masks the regression loss within the Denoising Score Matching objective during the training phase. We definitively prove that the proposed method is consistent in learning the true score of the underlying data distributions, and we further establish that the proposed training objective serves as a rigorous upper bound for the negative data likelihood under general conditions. The proposed framework is exhaustively evaluated on multiple real-world tabular datasets using realistic and highly efficacious metrics and is conclusively demonstrated to outperform the state-of-the-art diffusion model applied with the "impute-then-generate" pipeline by a substantial and decisive margin.

Introduction

Diffusion models have rapidly emerged as an exceptionally powerful and versatile tool for modeling complex data distributions and synthesizing high-quality samples across various data types, including images, videos, point clouds, and tabular data. It is well-understood that such advanced machine learning models typically rely on access to high-quality, complete training data, which is conventionally expected to be entirely free of missing values. In practical reality, it is frequently challenging and often impossible to obtain pristine, complete datasets, particularly in critical fields such as healthcare, finance, recommendation systems, and social network analysis. This challenge arises from a confluence of factors including stringent privacy concerns, prohibitive data acquisition costs, inherent sampling difficulties, and the naturally skewed distribution of user-generated content. For a concrete illustration, consider the respiratory rate of a patient in a clinical setting, which may not have been measured due to a clinical decision, an accidental omission during recording, or resource constraints. Furthermore, certain types of information can be exceptionally difficult, invasive, or even dangerous to acquire, such as data obtained through an invasive biopsy procedure, which may be deliberately omitted for a subset of patients due to associated risks.

In this seminal work, we decisively focus on the pivotal problem of learning a robust generative model directly from training data containing a significant proportion of missing values. This problem has been largely and surprisingly overlooked in the contemporary literature despite its immense and widespread practical significance. Deep generative models, and diffusion models in particular, have proven instrumental for data augmentation, substantially enhancing performance in tasks like image classification and improving adversarial robustness. By extending this powerful paradigm, we can achieve superior performance for critical downstream tasks by utilizing generative models trained directly on incomplete data to produce high-quality synthetic data. We will primarily utilize tabular data as our central exemplar, especially for the numerical experiments, as tabular data represents one of the most commonly encountered and practically important data types, and it frequently contains missing values across diverse applications. Moreover, by considering tabular data, we simultaneously and effectively address the challenging missing value scenarios for both categorical and continuous variables, which are inherently mixed within this data type.

To handle missing values in training data, numerous existing studies propose to employ various imputation methods as a preprocessing step before training the model on the imputed data. Common simplistic approaches for tabular data involve deleting entire instances (rows) or features (columns) with missing data, or replacing missing values with simple statistics like the column mean. More sophisticated methods employ advanced machine learning techniques or deep generative models specifically for the imputation task. However, it has been clearly shown that imputation can artificially reduce the intrinsic diversity of the training data and may consequently lead to biased and unreliable performances in downstream tasks. Beyond imputation or simple deletion, previous work has also explored learning from incomplete data using GAN or VAE architectures for synthetic data generation. Compared to our proposed, comprehensive framework, these methods often necessitate training additional auxiliary networks, impose restrictive assumptions on the missing data mechanisms, and have not thoroughly investigated the unique challenges posed by mixed-type tabular data.

In this groundbreaking work, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework, which we call MissDiff, for principled learning from data with missing values. We present rigorous theoretical justifications for MissDiff, proving its capability in recovering the oracle score function and establishing its objective as an upper bound for the negative data likelihood under mild and realistic assumptions on the missing mechanisms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that successfully learns a generative model directly from mixed-type data containing missing values, where the missing values are incorporated into the training process without any prior imputation step. We conduct an extensive suite of numerical experiments on mixed-type tabular data, comprising both continuous and categorical variables, under a comprehensive range of missing mechanisms. Evaluated under several realistic and highly efficacious metrics, MissDiff consistently and decisively outperforms all other baseline methods by a considerable and significant margin.

Our fundamental and substantial contributions are decisively summarized as follows.
* We propose MissDiff, a novel and principled diffusion-based framework for generative model training directly from incomplete data. We primarily focus on the highly practical and challenging task of tabular data generation, which contains a complex mixture of categorical and continuous variables.
* We provide rigorous and comprehensive theoretical justifications for MissDiff, proving its consistency in recovering the oracle score function and establishing that its training objective upper bounds the negative data likelihood under mild assumptions on the missing mechanisms.
* We conduct extensive and thorough numerical experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets under different missing mechanisms to conclusively demonstrate the superior effectiveness and practical utility of MissDiff.

The rest of the paper is systematically organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the essential setup of missing data mechanisms and the diffusion model. Section 3 introduces the proposed MissDiff method in detail. Section 4 provides the theoretical characterization of the method's effectiveness. Comprehensive numerical results are presented in Section 5. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 6.

Related Work

One prominent line of research focuses on adapting different types of generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), to train directly on data with missing values. These studies carefully modify the model architecture and training objectives to accommodate incomplete data.

Another significant research direction explores the use of generative models specifically for the task of imputing missing values within observed data. For instance, conditional score-based diffusion models have been adapted for time series and tabular data imputation. A key distinction is that these imputation methods are not inherently designed for generating entirely new, complete data samples, which is the primary focus of the first line of work and our own contribution.

Tabular data, as a mixed-type format containing both categorical and continuous variables, has attracted considerable attention in machine learning. Tabular data synthesis is a long-standing research challenge due to the presence of mixed variable types and potential class imbalance. Recently, several deep learning-based models have been proposed for generating high-quality tabular data. Among these, state-of-the-art methods employ Gaussian diffusion for continuous variables and multinomial transitions for discrete variables, with advanced techniques like self-paced learning further pushing performance boundaries. Furthermore, recent developments in discrete Score Matching methods provide additional tools for handling discrete variables within a score-based framework.

Training with Missing Data

We aim to learn a powerful diffusion-based generative model from training data that may contain a significant proportion of missing values. Following established statistical frameworks, we denote the underlying complete d-dimensional data vector and assume it is sampled from an unknown true data-generating distribution. Each variable can be either categorical or continuous. For each data point, we assume there exists a corresponding binary mask vector which explicitly indicates which entries are observed and which are missing. The observed data is then constructed by an element-wise multiplication with this mask. Suppose we have n independent complete (but unobservable) training data points and simultaneously n corresponding masks generated from a specific missing data mechanism. The observed dataset consists of these partially masked samples.

Missing data mechanisms are classically categorized based on the relationship between the mask and the complete data as follows:
* Missing Completely At Random (MCAR): The mask is statistically independent of the complete data.
* Missing At Random (MAR): The mask depends only on the observed values within the data point.
* Not Missing At Random (NMAR): The mask depends on both the observed and the missing values.

Compared to previous work which often develops algorithms and theory primarily under the restrictive MCAR assumption, our proposed method and its theoretical guarantees are designed to provide a general and flexible framework for learning from incomplete data under broader conditions, with the ultimate goal of generating high-quality, complete synthetic data.

Our core objective is to train a generative model, parameterized by neural network weights, using only the observed data, such that the model's distribution closely approximates the true data distribution, allowing for efficient and accurate synthetic data generation. The optimal model is the one that maximizes the expected log-likelihood of data from the true distribution, which is equivalent to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true and model distributions. In the following, we specifically consider the powerful score-based generative model as our foundational architecture.

Score-Based Generative Model

In this work, we adopt the highly flexible diffusion model as the prototype for developing our proposed method. We propose to train the model directly on data with missing values, eliminating the need for any prior imputation step. We first provide a concise review of the key components of score-based generative models.

Score-based generative models are a powerful class of generative models that learn the score function, defined as the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. These models are based on a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) that gradually perturbs the data distribution over time. The solution to this SDE is a continuous trajectory of random variables. The forward process is constructed so that the initial distribution is the true data distribution, and the final distribution after perturbation is a simple, tractable noise distribution, typically a standard Gaussian.

The crucial data generation process is performed by reversing this diffusion process via a corresponding reverse-time SDE. Generating new data involves sampling from the simple noise distribution and then simulating this reverse SDE backwards in time. The reverse SDE depends critically on the score function of the perturbed data distributions at each timestep. Therefore, the central learning problem is to train a time-dependent score-based model to accurately estimate these scores. This is achieved through objectives like Denoising Score Matching, which have been proven to yield consistent estimators of the true score function under appropriate conditions.

In general, there are two predominant approaches to learn a generative model from incomplete data. The first approach is to construct a complete training dataset as a preprocessing step and then learn a generative model on this completed data. This can involve deleting incomplete rows/columns or adopting an "impute-then-generate" paradigm, using either simple statistical imputation or sophisticated machine learning models trained for imputation. However, this pipeline can introduce significant bias into the training objective, as we formally clarify. The second approach is to learn the generative model to inherently deal with incomplete data directly. Motivated by the analysis of biased pipelines, we propose to train the model parameters by targeting the likelihood of the full data. The standard "impute-then-generate" approach maximizes a different, biased objective. Therefore, we introduce MissDiff, a diffusion-based framework for learning on missing data. This innovative approach aims to directly address the limitations of traditional methods by incorporating the inherent uncertainty of missing data directly into the learning process, resulting in a more accurate and reliable generative model that better reflects the true underlying data distribution.

We propose the following modified Denoising Score Matching objective for data with missing values. Instead of the standard objective, we define MissDiff as the solution to a masked version of the loss. In this formulation, the mask vector, which indicates missing entries in the original observed data, is used to element-wise mask the regression loss. To ensure the transition kernel and its gradient are well-defined for mixed-type data, we apply standard preprocessing: missing continuous values are replaced with 0, and for discrete variables, a new category is introduced to represent missingness, followed by one-hot encoding.

We primarily adopt the Variance Preserving SDE in this work. The detailed training algorithm for MissDiff and the corresponding sampling procedure are provided in the algorithmic descriptions. The training algorithm involves sampling noisy versions of the observed data, applying the mask to the score-matching loss, and performing gradient descent. The sampling procedure follows the standard reverse diffusion process for the VP-SDE, using the learned score network.

Theory

In this section, we rigorously examine the effectiveness of MissDiff by theoretically characterizing its Score Matching objective under mild conditions on the missing mechanisms. We further establish a fundamental connection between this objective and the maximum likelihood framework for training the diffusion model on incomplete data.

Our first major theoretical result verifies that Denoising Score Matching on missing data, as performed by MissDiff, can successfully learn the oracle score function of the complete data. The theorem definitively states that the global optimal solution of the MissDiff objective is identical to the true score of the underlying complete data distribution, provided the maximum missing rate across features is less than one.

When no data is missing, this result gracefully reduces to the known bound for complete data, confirming the consistency and generality of our framework.
