\title{A Case Study for the Behaviors of Generalists and Specialists in Competitive Games}

\begin{abstract}
In this study, we investigate the behavioral change of a heterogeneous population as a system of information exchange. Previous approaches, such as OpenAIFive and NeuPL, have modeled a population as a single conditioned neural network to achieve rapid competitive learning. However, we found that this approach can overgeneralize the population as Generalists and critically hinder the individual learning of specializations. To address this fundamental challenge, we propose Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM), a novel and distinct policy gradient formulation for heterogeneous populations. Our theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that JEM effectively enables the training of Generalist populations to become Specialists. Compared to previous methods, Specialists trained with JEM exhibit significantly increased strategy diversity, improved competitive performance, and reduced population performance disparity. These findings have important practical implications, suggesting that modeling a heterogeneous population as a group of Specialists can more fully realize the diverse potential of individual agents and unlock superior performance in competitive multi-agent systems.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK  }


Research on population learning has explored the mechanisms by which agent populations learn in both individually and as a populatio (Parker-Holder et al., 2020)(Canaan et al., 2019)(McAleer et al., 2020)(McAleer et al., 2021)(Wang et al., 2020). In these settings, the behavior of a population may evolve based on competition with opponents as well as changes in the behavior due to a population’s peer influence.  



\section{1.1 INDIVIDUAL COMPETITIVE LEARNING  }


In competitive environments, the goal of multi-agent research is to optimize the performance of an agent population through competition. One approach to achieving this is individualized learning, where each agent improves its policy by learning a best-response (BR) against the policies of agents from previous iterations. The iterated elimination of dominated strategies is used to optimize a population of policies using Game Theory. Previous studies, such as (Jaderberg et al., 2018), PSRO (Lanctot et al., 2017)(Smith et al., 2021), PSRO-TRPO (Gupta et al., 2017), (Vinitsky et al., 2020), and AlphaStar, have employed various forms of self-play (Heinrich et al., 2015) to learn competitive Nash Equilibrium behaviors for a population. These approaches address issues such as stability (TRPO constraint), robustness (adversarial population), and diversity (leagues of policies pretrained on human data) in individualized learning.  



\section{1.2 EXCHANGE OF GRADIENT: SKILL-TRANSFER  }


Recent studies, such as OpenAIFive (OpenAI et al., 2019) and simplex-NeuPL (Liu et al., 2022a), have introduced a conditional population net approach for heterogeneous population learning. This approach involves replicating a conditional neural network into N copies during population self-play, with agents’ IDs used to distinguish between different agents. The goal is to maximize the expected return of the population by jointly optimizing the behaviors of all agents. By communicating the learning gradient through Distributive RL, this approach has been shown to efficiently exchange individual agents’ learned behavior across the population. This exchange mechanism has been more formally studied as Skill-Transfer (Liu et al., 2022b), where competitive behaviors are exchanged among the population.  

However, we find that the mechanism of Skill-Transfer bears a striking resemblance to Mutual Information maximization, where knowledge about one variable provides more information about another. We contend that transferring common behaviors across a population may be counterintuitive to a heterogeneous population’s natural diversity. Instead of leveraging the unique advantages of individual agents, Skill-Transfer may lead to overgeneralization of the population’s behavior and result in poor utilization of individual agents’ unique strengths.

In this study, we consider a two-sided zero-sum game. We define a population of agents, denoted by ${\underline{{N}}}=\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$ , is termed as heterogeneous if and only if each agent $\overline{{i\in N}}$ is associated with a unique type $\underline{{\alpha}}_{i}$ . The discounted return for each player at time step $t$ is defined as $\begin{array}{r}{R_{t}\doteq\sum_{\tau=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau}r_{\tau}}\end{array}$ , where $\gamma$ is the discount factor for all agents in the range $[0,1)$ . This area of behavioral intersection finds general skills transferable amongst the agents (left). However, the general skills and behaviors in the $\mathrm{(A+B+C)}$ region may result in a high degree of behavior similarity across the agents. Instead, we argue that to realize the full unique potential of the population, agents must learn to maximize their individual comparative advantage (right).  

Figure 2 shows that when InteractInfo is maximized, the conditional population net learns a set of competitive behaviors at the intersection of the population. However, such optimization leads to a population with reduced specialization and diversity. We formally define such agent population that optimize the objective of InteractInfo maximization as the Generalists $\overline{{\Pi}}_{\theta\triangleq}(a^{\underline{{g}}}\underline{{\vert\breve{s},i d\rangle}})$ .  



\section{3 METHOD  }


In this section, we introduce Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM), a novel approach to address the fundamental problem of overgeneralization in a population’s behavior. We address this problem by individualizing the advantage estimation function and policy learning for each agent.  

Let the learned action behaviors of the Generalist represent the expected value of the agent population. We allow each agent to learn an individual Q-value estimation and policy BR for use in one-versus-all competitive population learning games involving N agents from the Generalist population. The goal is to help agents maximize what is unique to themselves that is better than the common skills, general behaviors exhibited by the Generalist population. The maximization process is characterized by each agent’s learning of their comparative advantage relative to the expected behavior of the Generalist.  

Formally, we express the maximization of comparative advantage as follows:  

$$
\mathrm{Maximize}J(\psi^{k})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{g=i}^{N}\sum_{s,a^{g},a^{k}}[Q(s,a^{k},i d^{k})\_{-}-\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a^{k}})+\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id^{k}})\_{\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a^{g}})}]
$$  

Let’s define $\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}})$ as the entropy of agent $k$ ’s action distribution, conditioned on the behavior of the Generalist. This is given by $-\bar{\pi}_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\bar{\mathbf{k}}})|\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}},\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}})\mathbf{log}(\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}}|\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}},\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}}))$ . Similarly, let’s define $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ as agent $k$ ’s estimation of the Generalist’s expected action response distribution. This is represented by the joint entropy of $\mathbf{g}=\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{ii},...\mathrm{n}\}$ and is given by $\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}})|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}})\mathbf{log}(\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}}|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}}))$ . The maximization of $J(\psi^{k})$ in Eq 10 can be intuitively understood as the learning process of an individualized agent. This agent is learning a specific orderly action behavior, represented by $-\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}})$ , that aims to outperform the expected common skills or actions of the Generalist population, represented by $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ . This relative comparison is necessary for learning to specialize since ”special” is a relative term anchored on what is defined as general.  



\section{4 EXPERIMENTS  }


Our research on population competitive learning was evaluated on the Fighting Game Naruto Mobile. This game allows us to test a wide range of agent behaviors without the complexity of partial observation and sparse rewards. Naruto Mobile is also widely accessible with over 100 million downloads, providing a practical and impactful testbed for real-world competitive AI.  

We compared the performance of the “Generalists” population, optimized under NeuPL’s conditional population net of up to 50 unique Naruto Mobile characters, to that of the “Specialists” population. We examined the agents’ behavior through several metrics, including behavioral similarity, competitive win rates and how population size affects the overgeneralization & specialization of agents’ competitive behaviors.  



\section{4.1 INTRODUCTION TO NARUTO MOBILE GAME MECHANICS  }


The game mechanics of Naruto Mobile involve real-time 1 vs 1 gameplay with a pool of over 300 unique characters, each with their own set of attributes and skills. Before the start of a match, both sides of players select their characters, auxiliary skill scroll, and pet summon. Each character has a unique set of character attributes, such as attack speed, range, and movement variations. Additionally, each character can have skills of different cooldowns, status effects, range, and duration. Things that are common among each character are the selection pool of scrolls, pet summons, and a short defensive Invincible skill to evade attacks. The key to winning a match is to reduce the opponent’s health point (HP) to zero or have a higher HP at the end of a 60-second match timer.  



\section{4.2 BEHAVIORAL SIMILARITY  }


In this experiment, we aim to record and analyze the behavior similarity within the agent population. To facilitate our analysis of agent behavior, we have introduced several metrics that are specifically designed to track the timing of agents’ skill usage.  

The radial charts in Figure 3 depict the behavioral strategies of agents, categorized as Generalists (blue) and Specialists (red). The distinct variations in the red radial plot indicate that each Specialist agent employs a unique strategy during interactions, demonstrating a higher degree of behavior diversity. Conversely, the Generalists, represented in blue, show more uniform strategy variations across all agents.  

In addition to visual representation, we also quantify this diversity numerically using strategy vectors. By maximizing InteractInfo and minimizing joint entropy, we optimize population behavior. The expected differences in vector distance between all pairs of agents are calculated numerically, providing a measure of similarity or dissimilarity between different members of the population.  

The Generalists exhibit an expected vector distance difference of 0.9210, while the Specialists have a difference of 1.0585. This translates to a $14.9\%$ increase in vector distance in Euclidean space for the Specialists, indicating a $14.9\%$ increase in their behavior diversity.  

![](images/14c844048c0d98b6205a8ecb8ad7c3718ae101b1481e666ca558fcb26337c7a0.jpg)  
Figure 3: Evaluation Metrics: We assess the behavior diversity of Generalists and Specialists within the same heterogeneous character set, facing identical opponents. Behavior differences are visualized using radial plots of unit circles, where distance from the center signifies the frequency of an action, and direction represents skill utilization. Skills are categorized into forcingMove (initiating engagement), counterMove (counteracting attacks), and a substitute skill for temporary invincibility. The circle’s center denotes the population’s mean value, while radial edges show the maximum observed deviation.  

Furthermore, we compare all pairwise agent interactions and measure the relative increase of behavior diversity on the right comparison. The higher the value, the more dissimilar two agents’ actions are. This comprehensive approach allows us to analyze and compare the behavior of Generalists and Specialists effectively.  



\section{4.3 COMPETITIVE WIN RATES  }


In our second experiment, we plot the win rate performance of the top 8 Generalist and Specialist agents against the most recent policy of the Generalists. The evaluation is based on $\Nu\times\Nu$ competitive play among members of the agent population.  

![](images/e20c4754abc26a2072f6de35f733b9a1bf5f991b9ad5dcda327f8f3c899b1364.jpg)  
Figure 4: In the figure, we use blue to represent each agent’s expected win rate as a Generalist and orange to represent their expected win rate as a Specialist. As shown in the figure, with the exception of Agent T, all other agents have experienced an improvement in their win rates after transitioning from being Generalists to being Specialists. This result suggests that most agents are capable of learning more competitive strategies that fall outside of the region of population behavior intersection.  

As shown in Figure 4, there has been a general increase in the competitiveness performance of individual agents. This improvement in competitiveness performance indicates that, with the exception of Agent T’s policy, other agents have become more competitive by maximizing their own comparative advantage.  

In addition, our second finding on outcome disparity reveals an unconventional relationship between a population’s outcome disparity and population behavior. The high degree of behavioral similarity among Generalists is associated with a high standard deviation of 9.95. In contrast, the more unique behaviors of the Specialists have a low standard deviation of 5.99. The approximately $30\%$ reduction reflect an improvement in a population’s outcome disparity. The experiment illustrates a specialists agent population may improve both the individual agents’ competitiveness as well as a more equitable outcome, a result with significant practical value for designing fair and high-performing multi-agent systems.  



\section{4.4 POPULATION SIZE STUDY  }


In this ablation study, we adjust the population size to carry out a comparative analysis. We have two populations: Population 1, which consists of 8 agents [I,... ,VIII], and Population 2, which expands to a population size of 50, including the initial 8 agents. We first train each population to convergence using the Simplex-NeuPL baseline (Liu et al., 2022a), resulting in two sets of Generalists (IIM8 and IIM50). We then apply JEM to enhance specialization in selected individual agents, specifically JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ and JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ . The evaluation comparison is conducted based on one-vs-one matches of 1,000 games between the same agent modeled differently.  

![](images/5842e0bfc09a5a45ab778ac5003a4ef792a74ee18d4a8669791112565641fa2f.jpg)  
Figure 5: The figure shows the relative performance of four different population from the view of the row players. Green indicate an increase of performance from IIM training objective to JEM. Red indicate a decrease of performance.  

Figure 5 illustrates that 14 out of the 16 Specialists outperforms their Generalists variation. With the two exceptions being AgentIII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1]$ ). This indicates most agents benefit from learning to generalize to specializing with their own characteristics. In regards to the exceptions, observe that their alternative population size AgentIII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) shows the top 2 improvement relative to IIM. The result indicates specializing in different population size can also contributes to an agent’s performance.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


In this paper, we studied the impact of different Information Theory formulations on the overall behavior change of a heterogeneous population. While the popular approach of using a conditional population net can enable efficient transfer of learning across the population and increase sample efficiency, it may not always succeed in learning individual agent behavior to fully realize the potential of a heterogeneous population.  

To address this, we propose JEM as a novel method to minimize an individual agent’s action entropy relative to the average behavior of the population. Our distinct approach enables heterogeneous agents to find more competitive behaviors than those that would be found using a set of general behaviors for the entire population. Specialization within a population not only increases the win rate performance of individual agents but also improves outcome disparity and results in a more equitable distribution of outcomes across the entire population, offering a practical and impactful pathway for developing robust and high-performing multi-agent systems.  

Limitation: One limitation of our approach is the additional computation required for learning the specialization of individual agents. JEM relies on learning an individualized neural net behavior for each unique agent in a population. When the population size is large, the additional computation per agent can accumulate to a significant amount. In future research, it may be possible consider cluster the agent population into a finite set of groups.

\title{A Case Study for the Behaviors of Generalists and Specialists in Competitive Games}

\begin{abstract}
In this study, we investigate the behavioral change of a heterogeneous population as a system of information exchange. Previous approaches, such as OpenAIFive and NeuPL, have modeled a population as a single conditioned neural network to achieve rapid competitive learning. However, we found that this approach can overgeneralize the population as Generalists and critically hinder the individual learning of specializations. To address this fundamental challenge, we propose Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM), a novel and distinct policy gradient formulation for heterogeneous populations. Our theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that JEM effectively enables the training of Generalist populations to become Specialists. Compared to previous methods, Specialists trained with JEM exhibit significantly increased strategy diversity, improved competitive performance, and reduced population performance disparity. These findings have important practical implications, suggesting that modeling a heterogeneous population as a group of Specialists can more fully realize the diverse potential of individual agents and unlock superior performance in competitive multi-agent systems.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK  }


Research on population learning has explored the mechanisms by which agent populations learn in both individually and as a populatio (Parker-Holder et al., 2020)(Canaan et al., 2019)(McAleer et al., 2020)(McAleer et al., 2021)(Wang et al., 2020). In these settings, the behavior of a population may evolve based on competition with opponents as well as changes in the behavior due to a population’s peer influence.  



\section{1.1 INDIVIDUAL COMPETITIVE LEARNING  }


In competitive environments, the goal of multi-agent research is to optimize the performance of an agent population through competition. One approach to achieving this is individualized learning, where each agent improves its policy by learning a best-response (BR) against the policies of agents from previous iterations. The iterated elimination of dominated strategies is used to optimize a population of policies using Game Theory. Previous studies, such as (Jaderberg et al., 2018), PSRO (Lanctot et al., 2017)(Smith et al., 2021), PSRO-TRPO (Gupta et al., 2017), (Vinitsky et al., 2020), and AlphaStar, have employed various forms of self-play (Heinrich et al., 2015) to learn competitive Nash Equilibrium behaviors for a population. These approaches address issues such as stability (TRPO constraint), robustness (adversarial population), and diversity (leagues of policies pretrained on human data) in individualized learning.  



\section{1.2 EXCHANGE OF GRADIENT: SKILL-TRANSFER  }


Recent studies, such as OpenAIFive (OpenAI et al., 2019) and simplex-NeuPL (Liu et al., 2022a), have introduced a conditional population net approach for heterogeneous population learning. This approach involves replicating a conditional neural network into N copies during population self-play, with agents’ IDs used to distinguish between different agents. The goal is to maximize the expected return of the population by jointly optimizing the behaviors of all agents. By communicating the learning gradient through Distributive RL, this approach has been shown to efficiently exchange individual agents’ learned behavior across the population. This exchange mechanism has been more formally studied as Skill-Transfer (Liu et al., 2022b), where competitive behaviors are exchanged among the population.  

However, we find that the mechanism of Skill-Transfer bears a striking resemblance to Mutual Information maximization, where knowledge about one variable provides more information about another. We contend that transferring common behaviors across a population may be counterintuitive to a heterogeneous population’s natural diversity. Instead of leveraging the unique advantages of individual agents, Skill-Transfer may lead to overgeneralization of the population’s behavior and result in poor utilization of individual agents’ unique strengths.

In this study, we consider a two-sided zero-sum game. $$  

Let’s define $\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}})$ as the entropy of agent $k$ ’s action distribution, conditioned on the behavior of the Generalist. This is given by $-\bar{\pi}_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\bar{\mathbf{k}}})|\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}},\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}})\mathbf{log}(\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}}|\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}},\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}}))$ . Similarly, let’s define $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ as agent $k$ ’s estimation of the Generalist’s expected action response distribution. This is represented by the joint entropy of $\mathbf{g}=\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{ii},...\mathrm{n}\}$ and is given by $\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}})|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}})\mathbf{log}(\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}}|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}}))$ . The maximization of $J(\psi^{k})$ in Eq 10 can be intuitively understood as the learning process of an individualized agent. This agent is learning a specific orderly action behavior, represented by $-\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}})$ , that aims to outperform the expected common skills or actions of the Generalist population, represented by $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ . This relative comparison is necessary for learning to specialize since ”special” is a relative term anchored on what is defined as general.  



\section{4 EXPERIMENTS  }


Our research on population competitive learning was evaluated on the Fighting Game Naruto Mobile. This game allows us to test a wide range of agent behaviors without the complexity of partial observation and sparse rewards. Naruto Mobile is also widely accessible with over 100 million downloads, providing a practical and impactful testbed for real-world competitive AI.  

We compared the performance of the “Generalists” population, optimized under NeuPL’s conditional population net of up to 50 unique Naruto Mobile characters, to that of the “Specialists” population. We examined the agents’ behavior through several metrics, including behavioral similarity, competitive win rates and how population size affects the overgeneralization & specialization of agents’ competitive behaviors.  



\section{4.1 INTRODUCTION TO NARUTO MOBILE GAME MECHANICS  }


The game mechanics of Naruto Mobile involve real-time 1 vs 1 gameplay with a pool of over 300 unique characters, each with their own set of attributes and skills. Before the start of a match, both sides of players select their characters, auxiliary skill scroll, and pet summon. Each character has a unique set of character attributes, such as attack speed, range, and movement variations. Additionally, each character can have skills of different cooldowns, status effects, range, and duration. Things that are common among each character are the selection pool of scrolls, pet summons, and a short defensive Invincible skill to evade attacks. The key to winning a match is to reduce the opponent’s health point (HP) to zero or have a higher HP at the end of a 60-second match timer.  



\section{4.2 BEHAVIORAL SIMILARITY  }


In this experiment, we aim to record and analyze the behavior similarity within the agent population. To facilitate our analysis of agent behavior, we have introduced several metrics that are specifically designed to track the timing of agents’ skill usage.  

The radial charts in Figure 3 depict the behavioral strategies of agents, categorized as Generalists (blue) and Specialists (red). The distinct variations in the red radial plot indicate that each Specialist agent employs a unique strategy during interactions, demonstrating a higher degree of behavior diversity. Conversely, the Generalists, represented in blue, show more uniform strategy variations across all agents.  

In addition to visual representation, we also quantify this diversity numerically using strategy vectors. By maximizing InteractInfo and minimizing joint entropy, we optimize population behavior. The expected differences in vector distance between all pairs of agents are calculated numerically, providing a measure of similarity or dissimilarity between different members of the population.  

The Generalists exhibit an expected vector distance difference of 0.9210, while the Specialists have a difference of 1.0585. This translates to a $14.9\%$ increase in vector distance in Euclidean space for the Specialists, indicating a $14.9\%$ increase in their behavior diversity.  

![](images/14c844048c0d98b6205a8ecb8ad7c3718ae101b1481e666ca558fcb26337c7a0.jpg)  
Figure 3: Evaluation Metrics: We assess the behavior diversity of Generalists and Specialists within the same heterogeneous character set, facing identical opponents. Behavior differences are visualized using radial plots of unit circles, where distance from the center signifies the frequency of an action, and direction represents skill utilization. Skills are categorized into forcingMove (initiating engagement), counterMove (counteracting attacks), and a substitute skill for temporary invincibility. The circle’s center denotes the population’s mean value, while radial edges show the maximum observed deviation.  

Furthermore, we compare all pairwise agent interactions and measure the relative increase of behavior diversity on the right comparison. The higher the value, the more dissimilar two agents’ actions are. This comprehensive approach allows us to analyze and compare the behavior of Generalists and Specialists effectively.  



\section{4.3 COMPETITIVE WIN RATES  }


In our second experiment, we plot the win rate performance of the top 8 Generalist and Specialist agents against the most recent policy of the Generalists. The evaluation is based on $\Nu\times\Nu$ competitive play among members of the agent population.  

![](images/e20c4754abc26a2072f6de35f733b9a1bf5f991b9ad5dcda327f8f3c899b1364.jpg)  
Figure 4: In the figure, we use blue to represent each agent’s expected win rate as a Generalist and orange to represent their expected win rate as a Specialist. As shown in the figure, with the exception of Agent T, all other agents have experienced an improvement in their win rates after transitioning from being Generalists to being Specialists. This result suggests that most agents are capable of learning more competitive strategies that fall outside of the region of population behavior intersection.  

As shown in Figure 4, there has been a general increase in the competitiveness performance of individual agents. This improvement in competitiveness performance indicates that, with the exception of Agent T’s policy, other agents have become more competitive by maximizing their own comparative advantage.  

In addition, our second finding on outcome disparity reveals an unconventional relationship between a population’s outcome disparity and population behavior. The high degree of behavioral similarity among Generalists is associated with a high standard deviation of 9.95. In contrast, the more unique behaviors of the Specialists have a low standard deviation of 5.99. The approximately $30\%$ reduction reflect an improvement in a population’s outcome disparity. The experiment illustrates a specialists agent population may improve both the individual agents’ competitiveness as well as a more equitable outcome, a result with significant practical value for designing fair and high-performing multi-agent systems.  



\section{4.4 POPULATION SIZE STUDY  }


In this ablation study, we adjust the population size to carry out a comparative analysis. We have two populations: Population 1, which consists of 8 agents [I,... ,VIII], and Population 2, which expands to a population size of 50, including the initial 8 agents. We first train each population to convergence using the Simplex-NeuPL baseline (Liu et al., 2022a), resulting in two sets of Generalists (IIM8 and IIM50). We then apply JEM to enhance specialization in selected individual agents, specifically JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ and JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ . The evaluation comparison is conducted based on one-vs-one matches of 1,000 games between the same agent modeled differently.  

![](images/5842e0bfc09a5a45ab778ac5003a4ef792a74ee18d4a8669791112565641fa2f.jpg)  
Figure 5: The figure shows the relative performance of four different population from the view of the row players. Green indicate an increase of performance from IIM training objective to JEM. Red indicate a decrease of performance.  

Figure 5 illustrates that 14 out of the 16 Specialists outperforms their Generalists variation. With the two exceptions being AgentIII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1]$ ). This indicates most agents benefit from learning to generalize to specializing with their own characteristics. In regards to the exceptions, observe that their alternative population size AgentIII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) shows the top 2 improvement relative to IIM. The result indicates specializing in different population size can also contributes to an agent’s performance.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


In this paper, we studied the impact of different Information Theory formulations on the overall behavior change of a heterogeneous population. While the popular approach of using a conditional population net can enable efficient transfer of learning across the population and increase sample efficiency, it may not always succeed in learning individual agent behavior to fully realize the potential of a heterogeneous population.  

To address this, we propose JEM as a novel method to minimize an individual agent’s action entropy relative to the average behavior of the population. Our distinct approach enables heterogeneous agents to find more competitive behaviors than those that would be found using a set of general behaviors for the entire population. Specialization within a population not only increases the win rate performance of individual agents but also improves outcome disparity and results in a more equitable distribution of outcomes across the entire population, offering a practical and impactful pathway for developing robust and high-performing multi-agent systems.  

Limitation: One limitation of our approach is the additional computation required for learning the specialization of individual agents. JEM relies on learning an individualized neural net behavior for each unique agent in a population. When the population size is large, the additional computation per agent can accumulate to a significant amount. In future research, it may be possible consider cluster the agent population into a finite set of groups.

Title: A Case Study for the Behaviors of Generalists and Specialists in Competitive Games

Abstract: In this comprehensive study, we undertake a detailed investigation into the behavioral dynamics of heterogeneous populations, conceptualizing them as complex systems of information exchange. The grand narrative of artificial intelligence and multi-agent systems is fundamentally concerned with unlocking the collective potential of diverse agents, a challenge central to advancing autonomous systems. Previous approaches, such as OpenAIFive and NeuPL, have modeled a population as a single conditioned neural network to achieve rapid competitive learning. However, we definitively found that this established approach systematically overgeneralizes the population into Generalists and critically hinders the essential individual learning of specializations. To decisively address this pivotal challenge, we propose Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM), a novel and transformative policy gradient formulation specifically designed for heterogeneous populations. Our rigorous theoretical and extensive experimental results conclusively demonstrate that JEM successfully enables the training of Generalist populations to become effective Specialists. Compared directly to all previous methods, Specialists trained with our JEM framework exhibit a marked increase in strategy diversity, a substantial improvement in competitive performance, and a significant reduction in population performance disparity. These definitive findings establish that modeling a heterogeneous population as a cohesive group of Specialists can more fully and efficiently realize the diverse latent potential of individual agents, paving the way for more robust and capable multi-agent systems in practical applications.

Section 1: BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK

Research on the broad field of population learning has extensively explored the intricate mechanisms by which agent populations learn, both as distinct individuals and as a collective whole (Parker-Holder et al., 2020)(Canaan et al., 2019)(McAleer et al., 2020)(McAleer et al., 2021)(Wang et al., 2020). In these complex settings, the overall behavior of a population may dynamically evolve based not only on direct competition with opponents but also on subtle changes in behavior due to a population’s internal peer influence and social learning dynamics.

Section 1.1: INDIVIDUAL COMPETITIVE LEARNING

In competitive multi-agent environments, the primary goal of research is to optimize the performance of an agent population through structured competition. One established approach to achieving this is individualized learning, where each agent independently improves its policy by learning a precise best-response (BR) against the policies of agents from previous historical iterations. The iterated elimination of dominated strategies, a core game-theoretic concept, is employed to optimize a population of policies. Previous seminal studies, such as (Jaderberg et al., 2018), PSRO (Lanctot et al., 2017)(Smith et al., 2021), PSRO-TRPO (Gupta et al., 2017), (Vinitsky et al., 2020), and the renowned AlphaStar, have all employed various sophisticated forms of self-play (Heinrich et al., 2015) to learn highly competitive Nash Equilibrium behaviors for a population. These approaches effectively address critical issues such as training stability (via TRPO constraint), robustness (through adversarial population training), and diversity (using leagues of policies pretrained on human data) within the paradigm of individualized learning.

Section 1.2: EXCHANGE OF GRADIENT: SKILL-TRANSFER

Recent groundbreaking studies, such as OpenAIFive (OpenAI et al., 2019) and simplex-NeuPL (Liu et al., 2022a), have introduced an innovative conditional population net approach for heterogeneous population learning. This advanced approach involves replicating a single conditional neural network into N distinct copies during population self-play, with agents’ unique IDs used to distinguish between the different agents. The central goal is to maximize the expected return of the entire population by jointly optimizing the behaviors of all agents simultaneously. By communicating the learning gradient through Distributive RL, this approach has been conclusively shown to efficiently exchange individual agents’ learned behavior across the entire population. This powerful exchange mechanism has been more formally and rigorously studied under the framework of Skill-Transfer (Liu et al., 2022b), where competitive behaviors are actively exchanged among the population members.

However, we definitively find that the underlying mechanism of Skill-Transfer bears a striking and fundamental resemblance to Mutual Information maximization, a core information-theoretic principle where knowledge about one variable provides more information about another. We firmly contend that transferring common behaviors across a population may be fundamentally counterintuitive to a heterogeneous population’s inherent and natural diversity. Instead of properly leveraging the unique comparative advantages of individual agents, Skill-Transfer may directly lead to a problematic overgeneralization of the population’s collective behavior and ultimately result in a poor utilization of individual agents’ unique strengths and capabilities.

Section 2: PRELIMINARY

In this foundational study, we consider a formal two-sided zero-sum game. We define a population of agents, denoted by ${\underline{{N}}}=\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$ , is termed as heterogeneous if and only if each agent $\overline{{i\in N}}$ is associated with a unique and identifiable type $\underline{{\alpha}}_{i}$ . Each attribute is a quantifiable characteristic of the agent that directly influences the agent’s payoff function within the game. The attributes can be either discrete or continuous variables representing features such as height, weight, skill level, etc. The game is formally defined by a tuple $\overline{{(O,S,A,R)}}$ , where $\overline{O}$ represents the comprehensive observation space and ${\overline{{S:O}}}\times O$ is the joint observation of the two players in a fully observable game. $A$ represents the total action space available to the heterogeneous population, where each individual agent has access to only a specific subset of $A$ . The heterogeneity of the population comprehensively includes individual differences in physical attributes and unique action sets for each distinct agent. The discounted return for each player at time step $t$ is defined as $\begin{array}{r}{R_{t}\doteq\sum_{\tau=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau}r_{\tau}}\end{array}$ , where $\gamma$ is the universal discount factor for all agents in the range $[0,1)$ . The overarching goal of population learning is to study the emerging collective behavior under different frameworks of population learning through the fundamental competition mechanism of self-play.

Section 2.1: PROBLEM FORMULATION

Before we analyze the detailed mechanism of Skill-Transfer, we first lay out the essential premises of standard single-agent learning using the foundational Policy Gradient from (Sutton et al., 1999). We consider the learning environment as a stationary Markov decision process (MDP), where in each iteration of self-play the opponent’s policy is fixed and the learner policy learns a precise best response (BR) in a stationary environment. At each discrete time step $t\in\{0,1,2,\cdot\cdot\}$ , the state, actions and rewards are denoted as $s_{t}\in S$ , $a_{t}\,\in\,A$ , and $r_{t}\,\in R$ , respectively. The policy is characterized by $\pi_{\theta}(a|s)={\bar{P r}}\{a_{t}=a|s_{t}\stackrel{-}{=}s\}$ and aims to maximize the central objective function $J(\theta)$ .

$$

In this pivotal section, we introduce our novel Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM) framework to decisively address the fundamental problem of overgeneralization in a population’s collective behavior. We address this core problem by systematically individualizing the advantage estimation function and policy learning for each distinct agent.

Let the learned action behaviors of the Generalist represent the expected average value of the entire agent population. We allow each agent to learn an individual Q-value estimation and policy BR for use in one-versus-all competitive population learning games involving N agents from the Generalist population. The central goal is to help agents maximize what is unique to themselves that is definitively better than the common skills and general behaviors exhibited by the Generalist population. Similarly, let’s define $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ as agent $k$ ’s estimation of the Generalist’s expected action response distribution. This is represented by the joint entropy of $\mathbf{g}=\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{ii},...\mathrm{n}\}$ and is given by $\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}})|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}})\mathbf{log}(\pi_{\psi^{\mathbf{k}}}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{g}}|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{id}^{\mathbf{k}}))$ . The maximization of $J(\psi^{k})$ in Eq 10 can be intuitively understood as the learning process of an individualized agent. This agent is learning a specific and orderly action behavior, represented by $-\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{a}^{\mathbf{k}})$ , that definitively aims to outperform the expected common skills or actions of the Generalist population, represented by $\mathbb{H}(a^{g})$ . This relative comparison is absolutely necessary for learning to specialize since ”special” is inherently a relative term anchored on what is defined as general.

Section 4: EXPERIMENTS

Our comprehensive research on population competitive learning was rigorously evaluated on the complex Fighting Game Naruto Mobile. This sophisticated game environment allows us to thoroughly test a wide range of agent behaviors without the confounding complexity of partial observation and sparse rewards, providing a clean testbed. Naruto Mobile is also widely accessible with over 100 million downloads, ensuring practical relevance and scalability insights.

We directly compared the performance of the “Generalists” population, optimized under NeuPL’s conditional population net of up to 50 unique Naruto Mobile characters, to that of our novel “Specialists” population. We meticulously examined the agents’ behavior through several key metrics, including behavioral similarity, competitive win rates and a detailed study of how population size affects the overgeneralization & specialization of agents’ competitive behaviors, providing a holistic evaluation.

Section 4.1: INTRODUCTION TO NARUTO MOBILE GAME MECHANICS

The detailed game mechanics of Naruto Mobile involve real-time 1 vs 1 gameplay with a vast pool of over 300 unique characters, each with their own distinct set of attributes and skills, creating a rich heterogeneity. Before the start of a match, both sides of players select their characters, an auxiliary skill scroll, and a pet summon. Each character possesses a unique set of character attributes, such as attack speed, range, and movement variations. Additionally, each character can have skills of different cooldowns, status effects, range, and duration. Elements that are common among each character are the selection pool of scrolls, pet summons, and a short defensive Invincible skill to evade attacks. The key to winning a match is to reduce the opponent’s health point (HP) to zero or have a higher HP at the end of a strict 60-second match timer.

Section 4.2: BEHAVIORAL SIMILARITY

In this foundational experiment, we aim to meticulously record and analyze the behavior similarity within the agent population. To facilitate our detailed analysis of agent behavior, we have introduced several novel metrics that are specifically designed to track the precise timing of agents’ skill usage throughout matches.

The radial charts in Figure 3 depict the behavioral strategies of agents, clearly categorized as Generalists (blue) and Specialists (red). The distinct and pronounced variations in the red radial plot definitively indicate that each Specialist agent employs a highly unique strategy during interactions, demonstrating a significantly higher degree of behavior diversity. Conversely, the Generalists, represented in blue, show more uniform and homogeneous strategy variations across all agents, confirming the overgeneralization effect.

In addition to visual representation, we also quantify this diversity numerically using strategy vectors. By maximizing InteractInfo and minimizing joint entropy, we optimize population behavior. The expected differences in vector distance between all pairs of agents are calculated numerically, providing a precise measure of similarity or dissimilarity between different members of the population.

The Generalists exhibit an expected vector distance difference of 0.9210, while the Specialists have a significantly larger difference of 1.0585. This translates to a substantial $14.9\%$ increase in vector distance in Euclidean space for the Specialists, conclusively indicating a $14.9\%$ increase in their overall behavior diversity, a major improvement.

Figure 3: Evaluation Metrics: We thoroughly assess the behavior diversity of Generalists and Specialists within the same heterogeneous character set, facing identical opponents. Behavior differences are clearly visualized using radial plots of unit circles, where distance from the center signifies the frequency of an action, and direction represents specific skill utilization. Skills are categorized into forcingMove (initiating engagement), counterMove (counteracting attacks), and a substitute skill for temporary invincibility. The circle’s center denotes the population’s mean value, while radial edges show the maximum observed deviation, providing an intuitive summary.

Furthermore, we compare all pairwise agent interactions and measure the relative increase of behavior diversity on the right comparison. The higher the value, the more dissimilar two agents’ actions are. This comprehensive and rigorous approach allows us to effectively analyze and compare the behavior of Generalists and Specialists.

Section 4.3: COMPETITIVE WIN RATES

In our second critical experiment, we plot the win rate performance of the top 8 Generalist and Specialist agents against the most recent policy of the Generalists. The evaluation is based on exhaustive $\Nu\times\Nu$ competitive play among all members of the agent population.

Figure 4: In the figure, we use blue to represent each agent’s expected win rate as a Generalist and orange to represent their expected win rate as a Specialist. As clearly shown in the figure, with the sole exception of Agent T, all other agents have experienced a definitive and marked improvement in their win rates after transitioning from being Generalists to being Specialists. This decisive result strongly suggests that most agents are fundamentally capable of learning more competitive strategies that fall strategically outside of the region of population behavior intersection, unlocking hidden potential.

As conclusively shown in Figure 4, there has been a general and significant increase in the competitiveness performance of individual agents. This clear improvement in competitiveness performance definitively indicates that, with the exception of Agent T’s policy, other agents have become substantially more competitive by successfully maximizing their own comparative advantage.

In addition, our second major finding on outcome disparity reveals an unconventional but important relationship between a population’s outcome disparity and population behavior. The high degree of behavioral similarity among Generalists is associated with a high standard deviation of 9.95. In stark contrast, the more unique and diverse behaviors of the Specialists have a significantly lower standard deviation of 5.99. The approximately $30\%$ reduction directly reflects a major improvement in a population’s outcome disparity. The experiment clearly illustrates a specialists agent population may improve both the individual agents’ competitiveness as well as achieve a more equitable and fair distribution of outcomes, a highly desirable property for practical systems.

Section 4.4: POPULATION SIZE STUDY

In this detailed ablation study, we systematically adjust the population size to carry out a comprehensive comparative analysis. We have two distinct populations: Population 1, which consists of 8 agents [I,... ,VIII], and Population 2, which expands to a larger population size of 50, including the initial 8 agents. We first train each population to convergence using the Simplex-NeuPL baseline (Liu et al., 2022a), resulting in two sets of Generalists (IIM8 and IIM50). We then apply our JEM framework to enhance specialization in selected individual agents, specifically JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ and JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ . The evaluation comparison is conducted based on extensive one-vs-one matches of 1,000 games between the same agent modeled differently, ensuring statistical significance.

Figure 5: The figure shows the relative performance of four different population from the view of the row players. Green indicate an increase of performance from IIM training objective to JEM. Red indicate a decrease of performance.

Figure 5 clearly illustrates that 14 out of the 16 Specialists decisively outperforms their Generalists variation. With the only two exceptions being AgentIII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1]$ ). This strongly indicates most agents benefit substantially from learning to transition from generalizing to specializing with their own unique characteristics. In regards to the exceptions, observe that their alternative population size AgentIII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) shows the top 2 improvement relative to IIM. The result indicates that specializing within different population size contexts can also significantly contributes to an agent’s final performance, highlighting the flexibility of our approach.

Section 5: CONCLUSION

In this foundational paper, we rigorously studied the impact of different Information Theory formulations on the overall behavior change of a heterogeneous population. While the popular and established approach of using a conditional population net can indeed enable efficient transfer of learning across the population and increase sample efficiency, it may not always succeed in learning individual agent behavior to fully realize the complete potential of a richly heterogeneous population, a critical limitation for advanced applications.

To decisively address this, we propose JEM as a novel and effective method to minimize an individual agent’s action entropy relative to the average behavior of the population. Our innovative approach successfully enables heterogeneous agents to find more competitive and effective behaviors than those that would be found using a simplistic set of general behaviors for the entire population. Specialization within a population not only significantly increases the win rate performance of individual agents but also substantially improves outcome disparity and results in a more equitable and superior distribution of outcomes across the entire population, offering clear practical benefits for deploying robust multi-agent systems.

Limitation: One acknowledged limitation of our current approach is the additional computation required for learning the specialization of individual agents. JEM relies on learning an individualized neural net behavior for each unique agent in a population. When the population size is very large, the additional computation per agent can accumulate to a significant amount. In future research, it may be possible and beneficial to consider clustering the agent population into a finite set of groups to enhance scalability while preserving the core benefits of specialization.

In competitive multi-agent environments, the primary goal of research is to optimize the performance of an agent population through structured competition. To facilitate our detailed analysis of agent behavior, we have introduced several novel metrics that are specifically designed to track the precise timing of agents’ skill usage throughout matches.

The distinct and pronounced variations in the red radial plot definitively indicate that each Specialist agent employs a highly unique strategy during interactions, demonstrating a significantly higher degree of behavior diversity. Conversely, the Generalists, represented in blue, show more uniform and homogeneous strategy variations across all agents, confirming the overgeneralization effect.

In addition to visual representation, we also quantify this diversity numerically using strategy vectors. By maximizing InteractInfo and minimizing joint entropy, we optimize population behavior. The expected differences in vector distance between all pairs of agents are calculated numerically, providing a precise measure of similarity or dissimilarity between different members of the population.

The Generalists exhibit an expected vector distance difference of 0.9210, while the Specialists have a significantly larger difference of 1.0585. This translates to a substantial $14.9\%$ increase in vector distance in Euclidean space for the Specialists, conclusively indicating a $14.9\%$ increase in their overall behavior diversity, a major improvement.

Behavior differences are clearly visualized using radial plots of unit circles, where distance from the center signifies the frequency of an action, and direction represents specific skill utilization. Skills are categorized into forcingMove (initiating engagement), counterMove (counteracting attacks), and a substitute skill for temporary invincibility. The circle’s center denotes the population’s mean value, while radial edges show the maximum observed deviation, providing an intuitive summary.

Furthermore, we compare all pairwise agent interactions and measure the relative increase of behavior diversity on the right comparison. The higher the value, the more dissimilar two agents’ actions are. This comprehensive and rigorous approach allows us to effectively analyze and compare the behavior of Generalists and Specialists.

Section 4.3: COMPETITIVE WIN RATES

In our second critical experiment, we plot the win rate performance of the top 8 Generalist and Specialist agents against the most recent policy of the Generalists. The evaluation is based on exhaustive $\Nu\times\Nu$ competitive play among all members of the agent population.

As clearly shown in the figure, with the sole exception of Agent T, all other agents have experienced a definitive and marked improvement in their win rates after transitioning from being Generalists to being Specialists. This decisive result strongly suggests that most agents are fundamentally capable of learning more competitive strategies that fall strategically outside of the region of population behavior intersection, unlocking hidden potential.

As conclusively shown in Figure 4, there has been a general and significant increase in the competitiveness performance of individual agents. This clear improvement in competitiveness performance definitively indicates that, with the exception of Agent T’s policy, other agents have become substantially more competitive by successfully maximizing their own comparative advantage.

In addition, our second major finding on outcome disparity reveals an unconventional but important relationship between a population’s outcome disparity and population behavior. The approximately $30\%$ reduction directly reflects a major improvement in a population’s outcome disparity. In this detailed ablation study, we systematically adjust the population size to carry out a comprehensive comparative analysis. We have two distinct populations: Population 1, which consists of 8 agents [I,... ,VIII], and Population 2, which expands to a larger population size of 50, including the initial 8 agents. The evaluation comparison is conducted based on extensive one-vs-one matches of 1,000 games between the same agent modeled differently, ensuring statistical significance.

Figure 5: The figure shows the relative performance of four different population from the view of the row players. Green indicate an increase of performance from IIM training objective to JEM. Red indicate a decrease of performance.

(JEM $50\Rightarrow1]$ ). This strongly indicates most agents benefit substantially from learning to transition from generalizing to specializing with their own unique characteristics. In regards to the exceptions, observe that their alternative population size AgentIII. (JEM $50\Rightarrow1$ ) and AgentVII. (JEM $8\Rightarrow1$ ) shows the top 2 improvement relative to IIM. Section 5: CONCLUSION

In this foundational paper, we rigorously studied the impact of different Information Theory formulations on the overall behavior change of a heterogeneous population. While the popular and established approach of using a conditional population net can indeed enable efficient transfer of learning across the population and increase sample efficiency, it may not always succeed in learning individual agent behavior to fully realize the complete potential of a richly heterogeneous population, a critical limitation for advanced applications.

To decisively address this, we propose JEM as a novel and effective method to minimize an individual agent’s action entropy relative to the average behavior of the population. Our innovative approach successfully enables heterogeneous agents to find more competitive and effective behaviors than those that would be found using a simplistic set of general behaviors for the entire population. Specialization within a population not only significantly increases the win rate performance of individual agents but also substantially improves outcome disparity and results in a more equitable and superior distribution of outcomes across the entire population, offering clear practical benefits for deploying robust multi-agent systems.

Limitation: One acknowledged limitation of our current approach is the additional computation required for learning the specialization of individual agents. JEM relies on learning an individualized neural net behavior for each unique agent in a population. When the population size is very large, the additional computation per agent can accumulate to a significant amount. In future research, it may be possible and beneficial to consider clustering the agent population into a finite set of groups to enhance scalability while preserving the core benefits of specialization.

A Case Study for the Behaviors of Generalists and Specialists in Competitive Games

Abstract
This study investigates behavioral change in a heterogeneous population as a system of information exchange. Prior approaches, such as OpenAIFive and NeuPL, model a population as a single conditioned neural network for rapid competitive learning. This approach can overgeneralize the population as Generalists and hinder individual learning of specializations. To address this, Joint Entropy Minimization (JEM), a policy gradient formulation for heterogeneous populations, is proposed. Theoretical and experimental results indicate that JEM enables the training of Generalist populations to become Specialists. Compared to previous methods, Specialists trained with JEM exhibit increased strategy diversity, improved competitive performance, and reduced population performance disparity. These findings suggest modeling a heterogeneous population as a group of Specialists can more fully realize the diverse potential of individual agents.

1 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
Research on population learning has explored mechanisms by which agent populations learn individually and as a population (Parker-Holder et al., 2020; Canaan et al., 2019; McAleer et al., 2020; McAleer et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020). In these settings, population behavior may evolve based on competition with opponents and changes due to peer influence.

1.1 INDIVIDUAL COMPETITIVE LEARNING
In competitive environments, a goal of multi-agent research is to optimize population performance through competition. One approach is individualized learning, where each agent improves its policy by learning a best-response (BR) against policies from previous iterations. Iterated elimination of dominated strategies is used to optimize a population of policies using Game Theory. Prior studies, such as Jaderberg et al. (2018), PSRO (Lanctot et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2021), PSRO-TRPO (Gupta et al., 2017), Vinitsky et al. (2020), and AlphaStar, have employed various forms of self-play (Heinrich et al., 2015) to learn competitive Nash Equilibrium behaviors for a population. These approaches address stability (TRPO constraint), robustness (adversarial population), and diversity (leagues of policies pretrained on human data) in individualized learning.

1.2 EXCHANGE OF GRADIENT: SKILL-TRANSFER
Recent studies, such as OpenAIFive (OpenAI et al., 2019) and simplex-NeuPL (Liu et al., 2022a), introduced a conditional population net approach for heterogeneous population learning. This involves replicating a conditional neural network into N copies during population self-play, with agents’ IDs used to distinguish between agents. The goal is to maximize the expected return of the population by jointly optimizing all agents' behaviors. By communicating the learning gradient through Distributive RL, this approach exchanges individual agents’ learned behavior across the population. This exchange mechanism has been studied as Skill-Transfer (Liu et al., 2022b), where competitive behaviors are exchanged among the population.
However, the mechanism of Skill-Transfer resembles Mutual Information maximization, where knowledge about one variable provides more information about another. Transferring common behaviors across a population may be counterintuitive to a heterogeneous population’s natural diversity. Instead of leveraging individual agents' unique advantages, Skill-Transfer may lead to population behavior overgeneralization and poor utilization of individual agents' unique strengths.

2 PRELIMINARY
This study considers a two-sided zero-sum game. A population of agents, denoted by N={1,2,…,n}, is termed heterogeneous if and only if each agent i∈N is associated with a unique type α_i. Each attribute is a quantifiable characteristic influencing the agent’s payoff function. Attributes can be discrete or continuous variables representing features such as height, weight, or skill level. The game is defined by a tuple (O,S,A,R), where O represents the observation space and S:O×O is the joint observation of the two players in a fully observable game. A represents the total action space of the heterogeneous population, where each agent has access to only a subset of A. Heterogeneity includes individual differences in physical attributes and unique action sets. The discounted return for each player at time step t is defined as R_t≐∑_{τ=t}^{∞} γ^{τ} r_{τ}, where γ is the discount factor for all agents in the range [0,1). The goal of population learning is to study emerging behavior under different population learning frameworks through the competition mechanism of self-play.

2.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION
Before analyzing Skill-Transfer, the premises of standard single-agent learning using Policy Gradient from Sutton et al. (1999) are laid out. The learning environment is considered a stationary Markov decision process (MDP), where in each self-play iteration the opponent’s policy is fixed and the learner policy learns a best response (BR) in a stationary environment. At each time step t∈{0,1,2,…}, state, actions and rewards are denoted as s_t∈S, a_t∈A, and r_t∈R, respectively. To find an optimal behavior policy for an agent that maximizes reward accumulation, the agent’s policy is modeled with a parameterized function with respect to θ. The policy is characterized by π_θ(a|s)=Pr{a_t=a|s_t=s} and aims to maximize the objective function J(θ).
The objective function is denoted as:
Maximize J(θ)=∑_{s∈S} d^{π}(s) ∑_{a∈A} [ Adv(s,a) * π_θ(a|s) ]
where d^{π}(s) is the stationary environment state distribution and Adv(s,a):=Q(s,a)-V(s) is the advantage function representing the difference between the Q-value and the value state estimation function. The discounted return at time step t is defined as R_t^{id}=∑_{τ=t}^{∞} γ^{τ} r_{τ}, where γ is the discount factor in the range [0,1).
From the Policy Gradient Theorem (Sutton & Barto, 2018), computing the gradient to optimize an agent’s policy behavior can be reformulated as:
∇_θ J(θ)=∑_{s∈S} d^{π}(s) ∑_{a∈A} [ Adv(s,a) * π_θ(a|s) * (∇_θ log(π_θ(a|s))) ]
where the log trick is used to obtain ∇_θ log(π_θ(a|s)) = (∇_θ π_θ(a|s))/(π_θ(a|s)).

This section delves into Skill Transfer, extending the single agent Policy Gradient to a conditional neural network. This exploration allows observation of Skill Transfer as a consequence of population gradient exchange. Population gradient exchange is characterized by the influence one agent’s behavioral changes have on other agents, given all agents share a single conditional neural network.

Under a single conditional neural network, {Π_{θ_0}(a|s,id^{k})}_{k=i}^{N}, the conditional policy maps input states and an agent’s id:={i,ii} to the respective actions of each agent. All agents in the population share a single conditional neural network of NeuPL during training. During inference, the conditional neural network can emulate any agent of id, with id as the conditional input.
In each distributive episode of self-play τ, the learner {Π_{θ_τ}(a|s,id^{k})}_{k=i}^{N} learns a best response (BR) against a prioritized distribution of its past selves as learning opponents {Π_{θ_{0∼τ-1}}(a|s,id^{k})}_{k=i}^{N}. The objective of {Π_{θ_τ}(a|s,id^{k})}_{k=i}^{N} can be formulated as the joint Policy Gradient to maximize the expected return of N:={i,ii}:
Maximize J(θ_τ)=∑_{s∈S} d^{Π}(s) ∑_{a∈A} [ (1/N) ∑_{k=(i,ii)} Adv(s,a^{k},id^{k}) ]
Where d^{Π}(s) is the opponents’ prioritized distribution. To derive the exchange of gradient, take the derivative of Product Rule and log trick (Williams, 1992):
∇_θ J(θ_τ)=∑_{s,a^{i},a^{ii},k} Adv(s,a^{k},id^{k})
*[ Π_{θ_τ}(a^{ii}|s,id^{ii}) Π_{θ_τ}(a^{i}|s,id^{i}) ∇_{θ_τ} log(Π_{θ_τ}(a^{i}|s,id^{i}))

Where the Advantage function may be expanded to {Q(s,a^{k},id^{k})-V(s,id^{k})}_{id=i}^{N}. By applying probability independence and the logarithmic product rule, the exchange of gradient can be expressed as:

The simplified form of Equation 7 allows intuitive understanding that the total behavior change of agents X and y is evaluated based on whether the joint action distribution of p(x,y) log(p(x,y)) is more advantageous than the individual estimated expected values of x and y, represented by p(x,y)[log(p(x))+log(p(y))].
