Title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning with Large Language Model

Abstract
Spatio-temporal prediction stands as a cornerstone of modern urban computing, a discipline fundamentally concerned with the intelligent management and future-proofing of our increasingly complex metropolitan environments. Its immense significance lies in empowering decision-makers to anticipate and proactively respond to critical urban phenomena, including but not limited to traffic flow dynamics, crime rate fluctuations, and air quality variations. Researchers have achieved remarkable progress in this vital field by ingeniously leveraging the inherent graph structure of spatio-temporal data and harnessing the formidable representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to capture intricate relationships and complex dependencies across disparate time slots and geographical locations. These pivotal advancements have significantly elevated the quality of representation learning, directly leading to more accurate and reliable predictive models. This pioneering study is dedicated to a groundbreaking exploration of the capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs)—models renowned for their profound world knowledge and reasoning capabilities—to masterfully handle the dynamic and multifaceted nature of spatio-temporal data within urban systems. We introduce STLLM, a novel and transformative approach that seamlessly integrates LLMs with a sophisticated cross-view mutual information maximization paradigm. This integration is definitively engineered to capture implicit spatio-temporal dependencies and meticulously preserve the rich spatial semantics inherent to urban spaces. By harnessing the unparalleled power of LLMs, our approach demonstrably and effectively captures intricate and implicit spatial and temporal patterns, resulting in the generation of exceptionally robust and invariant LLM-based knowledge representations that are resilient to distribution shifts. In our comprehensive framework, the cross-view knowledge alignment mechanism rigorously ensures effective alignment and maximal information preservation across the different modeling views while simultaneously facilitating powerful spatio-temporal data augmentation. The definitive effectiveness and superior performance of STLLM are conclusively validated through rigorous theoretical analyses, extensive and exhaustive experiments, and additional in-depth investigations, which collectively and unequivocally demonstrate its unique ability to align LLM-based spatio-temporal knowledge and consistently outperform all state-of-the-art baselines across a diverse array of critical urban prediction tasks.

1 INTRODUCTION

Spatio-temporal prediction, the essential task of forecasting future events or conditions by holistically accounting for both spatial and temporal information (Pan et al., 2019), holds immense and undeniable significance in the rapidly evolving field of urban computing. It serves as the critical engine that enables the accurate prediction of a wide spectrum of urban phenomena, including traffic flow patterns (Zheng et al., 2020), crime rate trends (Wang et al., 2022a), and air quality levels (Liang et al., 2023). By providing these accurate and timely predictions, urban planners and policymakers are empowered to take decisive proactive measures, allocate scarce resources with optimal efficiency, and engage in truly effective and sustainable urban planning. This capability directly translates to tangible enhancements in urban efficiency, long-term sustainability, and public safety, thereby shaping the future of smarter and more resilient cities.

In the relentless pursuit of achieving the most accurate forecasting results possible, researchers have made significant and transformative strides in developing innovative techniques that expertly exploit the inherent graph structure of spatio-temporal data. This exploitation is key to capturing the intricate relationships and complex dependencies that exist across different time slots and geographical locations. Notably, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have definitively emerged as a powerful and indispensable tool in this domain, offering the unique and proven ability to incorporate both spatial and temporal information seamlessly into the representation learning process. Recent groundbreaking advancements in spatio-temporal GNNs, including sophisticated graph convolutional networks (Yu et al., 2018), dynamic graph attention mechanisms (Lan et al., 2022), and powerful graph transformers (Huo et al., 2023), have been specifically proposed to dramatically enhance the representation learning capabilities for spatio-temporal graphs. These advanced GNN-based techniques employ diverse and effective embedding propagation schemes over the constructed spatio-temporal graph structures to successfully capture both spatial and temporal patterns.

However, real-world spatio-temporal prediction presents several formidable challenges that require meticulous consideration in practical urban computing scenarios. i) Long-Range Spatio-Temporal Dependencies: Accurately capturing long-range dependencies is absolutely crucial, as spatio-temporal phenomena frequently exhibit dependencies that span extensive time intervals and distant geographical locations. This poses a significant challenge, because short-term local interactions alone may not fully or accurately reflect the underlying complex dynamics of the system. ii) Data Sparsity and Noise: Data sparsity is a prevalent and persistent issue in spatio-temporal datasets, where limited observations (e.g., for crimes, traffic accidents) are available for certain locations and time intervals. Moreover, missing and noisy values in the spatiotemporal data further severely hinder the prediction task, often due to unavoidable sensor failures or noisy connections in the constructed spatio-temporal graphs. iii) Dynamic and Evolving Nature: Spatio-temporal systems are inherently dynamic and constantly subject to changes over time. Predictive models must therefore adapt to these dynamic characteristics by effectively distilling invariant representations imbued with rich spatio-temporal semantics, enabling them to robustly handle evolving patterns and distribution shifts.

In this seminal study, our primary and focused contribution is on pioneering the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in spatiotemporal prediction to directly and effectively address the aforementioned challenges. While LLMs have gained substantial and well-deserved attention and demonstrated unparalleled success in domains such as Natural Language Processing (Zhao et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023) and multi-modal understanding (Yin et al., 2023; Driess et al., 2023), their exploration for forecasting spatio-temporal graph data remains notably and surprisingly unexplored. This transformative work aims to decisively bridge this significant gap by harnessing the superior and proven capabilities of LLMs in distilling intricate and implicit spatial and temporal patterns from textual descriptions of urban contexts.

Contribution. This study presents STLLM, a novel and powerful LLM-enhanced spatio-temporal learning paradigm that definitively leverages Large Language Models to profoundly enhance the understanding and representation of spatio-temporal data. By integrating a sophisticated LLM-based spatio-temporal knowledge learner with a rigorous cross-view mutual information maximization paradigm, our approach effectively captures deep spatio-temporal connections and preserves critical point of interest (POI) information across the entire urban space, offering a comprehensive and holistic view of spatio-temporal features. The generated LLM-based knowledge can serve as exceptionally robust and invariant representations, proving particularly invaluable in challenging scenarios involving spatio-temporal distribution shifts. Furthermore, our innovative spatio-temporal knowledge alignment paradigm explicitly maximizes the mutual information between LLM-based knowledge representations and GNN-based structural embeddings, ensuring effective alignment and maximal information preservation across the different modeling views. This cross-view knowledge alignment process not only facilitates highly effective data augmentation but also directly addresses inaccuracies in the raw spatio-temporal graph data by denoising noisy connections. The definitive effectiveness of our proposed STLLM is further strengthened and validated by rigorous theoretical analyses, which conclusively demonstrate its ability to align LLM-based spatio-temporal knowledge through the principled maximization of mutual information. Extensive and exhaustive experiments are conducted to thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of STLLM in various spatio-temporal prediction tasks, comparing it comprehensively with all relevant state-of-the-art baselines. Additional in-depth analyses, such as detailed model ablation studies, robustness investigations under data sparsity, and computational efficiency evaluations, are performed to robustly validate the efficacy and practicality of STLLM. To ensure full transparency and facilitate further research, the complete model implementation for result reproducibility is publicly accessible.

2 RELATED WORK

Region Representation Learning. The representation of urban regions within a spatial-temporal semantic space has long been a central and active subject of scholarly research (Wang & Li, 2017; Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021, 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b). Specifically, Fu et al. (2019) recommend utilizing both intra- and inter-region information synergistically to enhance regional representations. Building upon this foundational idea, Zhang et al. (2019) employ a collective adversarial training method to improve robustness. In a more recent study by Zhang et al. (2021), they propose a sophisticated multi-view joint learning model for region representation, which captures complex region correlations from various complementary perspectives (e.g., region attributes) and employs graph attention mechanisms for refined representation learning. Conversely, Wu et al. (2022) focus primarily on extracting traffic patterns for area representation, but their approach unfortunately disregards essential POI data, which is critical for semantic understanding. To address the common reliance on high-quality region graphs and the significant challenges associated with learning from noisy and skewed spatial-temporal data, Zhang et al. (2023b) propose an adversarial contrastive learning paradigm designed for robust spatial-temporal graph augmentation. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of these previous methods, their inherent reliance on often imperfect structural information ultimately hinders general adaptability. In this paper, we directly and successfully address this critical limitation by leveraging the global knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs to uncover additional and meaningful region global relationships, thereby definitively enhancing the overall performance and robustness of region representation.

Large Language Model. LLMs, which are extensively pre-trained on massive and diverse text corpora, have demonstrated exceptional and groundbreaking performance across a vast array of NLP tasks (Ji et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022b). Primarily based on the revolutionary Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), these powerful models can be broadly classified into three distinct categories: encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only (Pan et al., 2023). (i) Encoder-only LLMs utilize only the encoder component for modeling word associations and encoding full sentences, exemplified by models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019), and they typically require an additional prediction head for downstream tasks. These models excel particularly in tasks demanding deep and comprehensive sentence understanding (Zhang et al., 2022). (ii) Encoder-decoder LLMs employ both encoder and decoder modules for input encoding (Raffel et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2023) and sequential output generation, offering more flexible and powerful training techniques (Zoph et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2020). (iii) Decoder-only LLMs rely solely on the decoder module for autoregressive output generation, with training centered around predicting subsequent words in a sequence. Highly influential models like Chat-GPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) and GPT-4 can often complete complex tasks with minimal sample or instruction input. However, their closed-source nature has historically limited further in-depth research and adaptation. Recently, powerful open-source models such as Alpaca and Vicuna have shown remarkably comparable performance (Touvron et al., 2023). This transformative study applies a decoder-only LLM (specifically GPT-3.5) to definitively enhance the quality and semantic richness of the spatio-temporal graph through effective and intelligent augmentation.

3 METHODOLOGY

This section elaborates in detail on the comprehensive technical details of the proposed STLLM framework. The complete model architecture is visually depicted in Figure 1. We begin with a formal introduction to the spatio-temporal prediction task and the associated data structures as follows.

3.1 PRELIMINARIES

The urban space under consideration is systematically partitioned into a total of I distinct spatial regions, each indexed by i, and J consecutive time slots, each indexed by j. Each specific geographical region is formally denoted as r_i, and each discrete time slot is denoted as t_j. To facilitate comprehensive and effective spatio-temporal (ST) representation learning, we construct a unified spatio-temporal graph by thoughtfully incorporating rich urban contextual information from diverse and complementary data sources. Specifically, we utilize the following two key types of data:

i) Human Mobility Trajectories M. This dataset comprises real-world human mobility trajectories, where each individual trajectory is represented as a tuple (r_s, r_d, t_s, t_d, v). Here, r_s and r_d denote the source and target geographical regions, respectively, while t_s and t_d refer to the corresponding precise timestamps for the start and end of the movement. The variable v denotes the mobility volume or count associated with this specific trajectory. These trajectories are essential as they capture the dynamic temporal region-wise connections in terms of human mobility flows, making them critically important for various urban prediction tasks. ii) Region-wise Distance Information D. This dataset includes a weighted adjacency matrix that systematically records neighborhood information based on pairwise region-wise physical distances. It comprehensively encompasses all pairs of regions (r_s, r_d, d) where the physical distance d is less than a threshold of 2.5 km, with d denoting the precise distance in kilometers. This data provides invaluable spatial contextual information about the proximity and layout of urban regions, directly facilitating spatial analysis and modeling.

Spatio-Temporal Graph. Leveraging the foregoing data sources, we construct the integrated spatio-temporal graph G = (V, E). The node set V consists of J time-slot-specific copies for each of the I regions, resulting in a total of |V| = I × J distinct nodes. The weighted edge set E thoughtfully incorporates the two heterogeneous data sources described above, along with residual connections across adjacent time slots to model temporal continuity. Using the notation r_i t_j to represent the specific node for the r_i-th region in the t_j-th time slot, we formally define the comprehensive edge set as follows:

E = { (r_s t_s, r_d t_d, v) : (r_s, r_d, t_s, t_d, v) ∈ M } ∪ { (r_s t_j, r_d t_j, d) : (r_s, r_d, d) ∈ D, ∀ t_j } ∪ { (r_i t_j, r_i t_{j+1}, 1) : t_j < J, ∀ r_i }

Problem Statement: Given the spatio-temporal graph G constructed from the heterogeneous urban data, our core objective in spatio-temporal representation learning is to generate a dense and informative embedding matrix E ∈ ℝ^{|V| × d}. Each row vector e_{ij} ∈ ℝ^d in E refers to the learned representation vector for the r_i-th region in the t_j-th time slot. This learned embedding matrix is designed to facilitate accurate and robust predictions in a wide variety of downstream tasks in urban scenarios, such as traffic prediction, crime prediction, and house price prediction.

3.2 DUAL-VIEW SPATIO-TEMPORAL MODELING

3.2.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK

Our STLLM framework innovatively incorporates two complementary modeling views to comprehensively capture spatio-temporal patterns. The first view focuses on extracting the high-order connectivity and local structural patterns of the spatio-temporal graph through iterative graph neural propagation. It begins by generating an initial embedding for each node v_i ∈ V by projecting its node-specific point of interest (POI) tags into a d-dimensional latent representation h_i^0 ∈ H^0 using a standard transformer-based neural language model (Vaswani et al., 2017). Subsequently, leveraging the rich graph structures in the aforementioned ST graph G, STLLM performs multiple GNN iterations to progressively capture and refine the complex spatio-temporal dependencies as follows:

H = Σ_{l=0}^{L} H^l, where H^l = σ( D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} H^{l-1} W^{l-1} ), and D_{i,i} = |N_i|, D_{i,j} = 0 if i ≠ j.

Here, H = {h_i} ∈ ℝ^{|V| × d} denotes the final aggregated embedding matrix produced by the graph modeling view of our STLLM. A ∈ ℝ^{|V| × |V|} denotes the weighted adjacency matrix of the ST graph G. This spatio-temporal GNN aggregates the embeddings from different propagation iterations to combine multi-scale information. Each iteration is performed by a graph convolution operator with a learnable linear projection matrix W^{l-1} ∈ ℝ^{d × d} and a ReLU-based non-linear activation function σ(·). D denotes the symmetric degree matrix of the adjacent matrix A, used for normalization.

3.2.2 LLM-BASED SPATIO-TEMPORAL KNOWLEDGE LEARNING

Drawing direct inspiration from the LLM’s remarkable and proven ability to understand and reason about real-world knowledge, we propose leveraging a well-trained, powerful LLM to generate rich semantic node representations from textual urban descriptions. Specifically, STLLM first generates a comprehensive text-based description P_i = (r_i, Q_i, S_i, T_i) for each distinct region r_i. This description is constructed by concatenating the region identifier r_i, its detailed point of interest (POI) information Q_i, the spatial context S_i derived from the distance data D, and the temporal context T_i derived from the mobility trajectory data M.

Using these rich text descriptions, STLLM proceeds with two definitive steps to acquire high-quality LLM-based knowledge representations. Firstly, we prompt the pre-trained LLM to generate a coherent and informative summary for each node. This involves inputting the descriptions of the target node and its surrounding neighboring nodes together into the LLM to facilitate a deep and contextual comprehension of the spatio-temporal environment. Secondly, STLLM obtains latent representation vectors F = {f_i} ∈ ℝ^{I × d} for the summary text of each region, typically by using the LLM's own embedding layer or a separate projection. Leveraging the LLM’s profound understanding of general-purpose knowledge and semantics, the generated embeddings in F effectively preserve the detailed POI information within each region and capture the meaningful spatio-temporal connections to its neighborhood. This innovative approach, in direct contrast to the GNN-based modeling view that focuses primarily on local structure extraction, represents the spatio-temporal features from a powerful global perspective by distilling general knowledge and semantics from the LLM. Section 5 provides concrete examples of the generated descriptions and summaries.

3.3 CROSS-VIEW MUTUAL INFORMATION MAXIMIZATION

With the GNN-based ST dependencies modeling and the LLM-based global knowledge mining established, we definitively aim at maximizing their mutual information to minimize their respective noise and irrelevant information, thereby forcing the embeddings to concentrate on the most salient and shared spatio-temporal factors. To achieve this, STLLM is optimized utilizing the following principled cross-view mutual information maximization objective, with I(·) denoting the mutual information function:

H = argmax_H I(h, f), where I(h, f) = Σ_{h_i, f_i} p(h_i, f_i) log [ p(h_i | f_i) / p(h_i) ]

To make this loss function tractable for optimization, we follow the established approach of Oord et al. (2018) to utilize the InfoNCE loss function, which is provably a lower bound of the mutual information function. Specifically, the InfoNCE loss between embedding pairs from the two views is defined as follows:

L_NCE = - 𝔼_h [ log( g(h, f) / Σ_{h_i' ∈ H} g(h_i', f) ) ] = - Σ_{h_i ∈ H} log( g(h_i, f_i) / Σ_{h_i' ∈ H} g(h_i', f_i) )

where g(h, f) ∝ p(h|f)/p(h) denotes a measurement function for the probability ratio. We formally show that with this function g(·), the tractable InfoNCE loss L_NCE is a lower bound of the mutual information between embeddings of the GNN view h and embeddings of the LLM view f, as follows:

𝔼_h [ log( g(h, f) / Σ_{h_i' ∈ H} g(h_i', f) ) ] ∝ 𝔼_h [ log( (p(h|f)/p(h)) / Σ_{h_i' ∈ H} (p(h_i'|f)/p(h_i')) ) ] ≈ - 𝔼_h log[ 1 + (p(h)/p(h|f)) (N-1) ] ≤ - 𝔼_h log[ (p(h)/p(h|f)) N ] = I(h, f) - log(N)

Based on the foregoing theoretical discussions, we apply the InfoNCE loss to the alignment between the two modeling views, by instantiating g(h, f) = exp(cos(h, f)). Specifically, STLLM aligns the representations derived from the mobility data and from the distance data, respectively. We further enrich the overall training objective of our ST representation learning framework with two additional cosine-based loss terms: one for the alignment between the overall aggregated embeddings from the two views, and another for the alignment between the shallow initial and the deep final GNN embeddings to encourage consistency. In total, we have the following four key training objectives:

L_M = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} L_NCE(h_i^M, f_i^M),     L_D = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} L_NCE(h_i^D, f_i^D)
L_{M,D} = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} cos(h_i, f_i),         L_G = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} cos(h_i, h_i^0)

Combining the above four loss terms, we obtain the final composite loss for our STLLM: L = γ_1 L_{M,D} + γ_2 L_G + γ_3 L_M + γ_4 L_D, where γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, γ_4 ∈ ℝ denote the tunable hyperparameters for the respective loss weights, allowing for balanced optimization.

Model Complexity: Our method, STLLM, incorporates a spatio-temporal graph neural network that involves iterative graph information propagation in the encoder. The time complexity of our method is therefore primarily determined by these graph operations and is given by O(|E| × L × d), where |E| denotes the total number of edges in the graph, L represents the number of graph convolutional layers, and d is the fixed dimensionality of the embeddings. It is important to note that the LLM-based text generation and embedding extraction is performed only once as a pre-processing step and is not counted in the recurrent training time complexity. The resulting time complexity is fully comparable to that of other state-of-the-art GNN-based methods, ensuring efficient computation and maintaining highly competitive performance during model training and inference.

4 EVALUATION

Our comprehensive suite of experiments is designed to definitively investigate the following critical research questions: RQ1: How does STLLM compare to state-of-the-art baselines in different spatio-temporal learning applications, such as traffic prediction and crime prediction? RQ2: How do different data sources and individual model components impact the effectiveness of region representation learning for downstream tasks? RQ3: To what extent is STLLM successful in representation learning for predicting traffic flows and crimes, considering varying and challenging degrees of data sparsity? RQ4: What impact do various hyperparameter settings have on the region representation performance of STLLM for traffic flow and crime prediction? RQ5: How computationally efficient is STLLM compared to other baseline methods in terms of training time? RQ6: How effective is STLLM compared to other specialized techniques of region representation, such as MV-PN, MVURE, MGFN, and GraphST?

4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

4.1.1 DATASETS AND EVALUATION METRICS

We rigorously assess the performance of our spatio-temporal representation learning framework, STLLM, on three distinct and practically significant prediction tasks: crime prediction, traffic flow forecasting, and property price prediction. These tasks are evaluated using real-world datasets obtained from the major metropolitan areas of Chicago and New York City (NYC). Following previous established studies (Xia et al., 2021), we consider multiple specific crime types such as Theft, Battery, Assault, and Damage for Chicago, and Burglary, Larceny, Robbery, and Assault for NYC. To ensure a thorough and fair evaluation, we utilize three standard evaluation metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).

4.1.2 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS AND HYPERPARAMETERS

For our STLLM model, we fix the embedding dimensionality d to 96 in accordance with earlier and successful region representation studies (Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b) to ensure a fair comparison. Our STLLM performs at its absolute optimum when the GCN depth is set to 2, the weight decay is set to 0.0005, and the learning rate is set to 0.001, according to extensive hyperparameter tuning trials. Following established practices from previous studies (Zhang et al., 2023a;b), we employ different specialized downstream prediction models for the different prediction tasks to ensure each task is addressed with an appropriate architecture. For crime prediction, we utilize ST-SHN (Xia et al., 2022). For traffic flow forecasting, we employ ST-GCN (Yu et al., 2018). For property price prediction, we utilize a simple but effective Lasso regression model (Ranstam & Cook, 2018). The ST-SHN model is configured with a 0.001 learning rate, a 0.96 learning rate decay, and 2 spatial aggregation layers. The ST-GCN is configured with 12 input time intervals, each with a 5-minute interval length. The traffic prediction task specifically aims at predicting the traffic flow for the future 15-minute interval. The majority of baseline methods are implemented faithfully using their officially released code for a fair comparison.

4.1.3 BASELINES FOR COMPARISON

We compare our method STLLM with a wide array of state-of-the-art baselines to thoroughly evaluate its performance in terms of MAE, MAPE and RMSE. The baselines include the following key categories. Graph Representation Methods: We compare our method STLLM with several foundational graph representation methods, including Node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016), GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017), GraphSage (Hamilton et al., 2017), GAE (Kipf & Welling, 2016) and GAT (Veličković et al., 2018). Graph Contrastive Learning Methods: We also conduct experiments using two recent and powerful graph contrastive learning methods, GraphCL (You et al., 2020) and RGCL (Li et al., 2022). Spatio-Temporal Region Representation: We compare our method STLLM with state-of-the-art region representation learning methods specifically designed for urban data, including HDGE (Wang & Li, 2017), ZE-Mob (Yao et al., 2018), MV-PN (Fu et al., 2019), CGAL (Zhang et al., 2019), MVURE (Zhang et al., 2021), MGFN (Wu et al., 2022) and the recent GraphST (Zhang et al., 2023b).

4.2 MODEL EFFECTIVENESS (RQ1)

We compare the performance of STLLM with state-of-the-art baselines across various downstream tasks. The comprehensive results are presented in Table 1, based on which we draw the following definitive conclusions:

Consistent Performance Superiority across Tasks. Our STLLM framework consistently and decisively surpasses all baseline methods across all distinct prediction tasks and research lines, demonstrating excellent and superior performance. This is directly attributable to the effective distillation of global spatial-temporal knowledge from powerful LLMs. This distilled knowledge is then intelligently incorporated into the local ST graph modeling process via contrastive learning, conferring several key benefits. It allows for a more precise comprehension and utilization of textual ST features, thereby directly improving prediction accuracy. It also significantly increases model robustness against structural noises and imperfections in the ST graph. Significant and consistent enhancements are observed across all three evaluated tasks: traffic prediction, crime prediction, and house price prediction, which collectively attests to the general applicability and power of our novel LLM-based ST graph mining techniques.

Advantages of Graph Contrastive Learning. Among the baseline methods, those utilizing advanced graph contrastive learning (GCL) techniques, such as GraphCL and GraphST, exhibit notable and clear advantages in terms of prediction accuracy compared to other baselines. This observation strongly validates the inherent effectiveness of GCL in addressing common data deficiency issues, such as noise and skewness, thereby improving the accuracy of spatio-temporal prediction. Drawing direct inspiration from this proven advantage, our STLLM incorporates the GCL methodology to explicitly maximize the mutual information between LLM-based ST knowledge mining and local ST graph modeling. By effectively contrasting the two complementary views, our model successfully enhances the overall representation quality and robustness.

Advantages of Region Representation Learning: When compared to traditional end-to-end spatio-temporal prediction methods, pretrained region representation learning approaches (e.g., MGFN) demonstrate clear and consistent advantages. These advantages can be directly attributed to the inherent superiority of pretrained embeddings over randomly-initialized embeddings. Pretrained embeddings are enriched with abundant and meaningful spatial and temporal patterns learned during pre-training, providing a more refined and informative initialization compared to end-to-end models that start from scratch. The typically limited optimization steps in end-to-end models make it challenging to acquire such sophisticated embeddings during task-specific training, often leading to sub-optimal final performance.

4.3 ABLATION STUDY (RQ2)

In this section, we conduct a detailed ablation study to definitively investigate the influence of different core components of our STLLM framework. Specifically, we study the following key variants: -CL. This version replaces the InfoNCE-based contrastive learning with simple cosine similarity maximization in the cross-view mutual information objective. -S. This variant removes the spatial information S_i from the input description P_i for the LLM, to study the specific influence of textual spatial features. -T. Similar to the last one, this variant eliminates the temporal information T_i from P_i. -S&T removes both the spatial descriptions and the temporal descriptions for the LLM, using only region ID and POI data. Based on the results depicted in Figure 2, we draw the following concrete conclusions.

Effectiveness of Contrastive Learning. The evaluation results clearly reveal that in many scenarios, replacing the InfoNCE-based contrastive learning with maximizing cosine similarity leads to a significant and noticeable decline in model performance. This observation highlights the definitive effectiveness of our contrastive learning (CL)-based design, which derives its advantage from its close and provable theoretical relationship with mutual information maximization. Compared to simple cosine similarity, InfoNCE incorporates negative sample learning to promote a more beneficial and uniform embedding distribution, which is key to enhancing its final prediction accuracy.

Benefits Brought by S_i and T_i. The results conclusively show that the removal of either the spatial information S_i or the temporal information T_i causes a notable and consistent performance decline across tasks. This finding not only validates the effectiveness of our LLM-based textual feature extraction but also confirms the positive and significant impact of incorporating detailed distance information and mobility trajectories into our global knowledge mining process.

Comparing -S&T with -S and -T. In some specific cases (e.g., NYC-Larceny, CHI-Assault), the variant removing both S_i and T_i yields slightly better performance than the variants removing only one of them. This interesting observation can be attributed to a potential bias effect that arises when utilizing only a single, possibly misleading, data source for knowledge mining. In such cases, the LLM may be misled by the limited or skewed information, resulting in sub-optimal representations. By constructing comprehensive and balanced ST descriptions, our full STLLM framework successfully avoids such detrimental circumstances.

4.4 PERFORMANCE OVER SPARSE DATA (RQ3)

In this important study, we examine the robustness and reliability of our STLLM framework when applied to sparse and challenging spatiotemporal data for the critical task of crime prediction. Specifically, we divide the geographical regions of NYC and Chicago into two distinct sets based on their computed crime density degrees. The density degree for a region is determined as the ratio of time slots with non-zero crime cases to the total number of time slots for that region. The two sets of regions correspond to density ratio ranges of (0.0, 0.25] (low density) and (0.25, 0.5] (medium density), respectively. To assess the performance of our STLLM method and compare it fairly to six representative baselines, we present the results in Figure 3. From the results, we have two major and clear observations as discussed below.

Firstly, it is clearly observed that all evaluated methods achieve lower MAE values (i.e., better performance) on the subset with higher data density. This finding confirms the expected and well-known fact that sparse data has a detrimental and significant effect on both representation learning and accurate spatio-temporal prediction. The limited amount of supervisory data available in sparse regions results in reduced and weaker supervision signals during training, which in turn often leads to suboptimal model convergence and performance. Secondly, and most importantly, our STLLM consistently maintains its superior performance edge across the different levels of data sparsity. This robustness can be directly attributed to the enrichment of region representations through the distillation of global, semantics-rich knowledge from the LLM, which provides additional signal. Additionally, the contrastive knowledge alignment employed by our method effectively enhances the available supervision signals, thereby facilitating more effective and stable model training even with sparse data.

4.5 HYPERPARAMETER STUDY (RQ4)

In this section, we conducted a detailed hyperparameter study to evaluate the impact of important model parameters on the performance of our STLLM framework. The results are presented comprehensively in Figure 4. Specifically, we vary the number of GNN layers L within the range {2, 3, 4, 5} and the temperature coefficient τ in the InfoNCE function within the range {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6}. We summarize our key observations regarding the two parameters and their effect on the downstream performance of traffic prediction as follows:

Firstly, we investigated the impact of the number of GCN layers (L) on the model’s performance. We found that our STLLM achieves its best performance with L=2. As the number of GCN layers increases beyond this optimal point, we observed clear diminishing returns and even a degradation in terms of model representation ability for downstream tasks. This suggests that additional GCN layers may lead to an over-smoothing effect, where node representations become too similar, which ultimately hampers the model’s discriminative performance. Secondly, we examined the effect of the temperature parameter (τ) on the model’s representation ability. We observed that our STLLM achieves the highest representation ability with τ=0.4. Deviating from this optimal value, either by increasing or decreasing τ, did not result in further improvements and often led to worse performance, highlighting the importance of this parameter in scaling the logits in the contrastive loss.

4.6 EFFICIENCY STUDY (RQ5)

Experimental Settings: We assess the practical model efficiency of STLLM by comparing it with several other region representation methods in terms of total training time required for convergence. The results, including the corresponding MAE and MAPE values achieved, can be found in Table 2. All methods are implemented using the same standardized software environment (Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.15.3 for traffic prediction, and PyTorch 1.7.0 for other tasks) and an identical hardware environment (a 10-core Intel Core i9-9820 CPU @ 3.30GHz, 64GB RAM, and four NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs) to ensure a fair comparison. Observations and Analysis: It is particularly worth noting that, our STLLM model achieves the best predictive performance while maintaining training efficiency fully comparable to other efficient region representation methods. This important finding validates that our STLLM framework is not only effective but also capable of handling large-scale spatio-temporal data in a practical timeframe. The scalability of STLLM can be attributed largely to the efficiency of the InfoNCE-based contrastive learning objective, which plays an important role in the knowledge alignment process without introducing prohibitive computational overhead.

4.7 CASE STUDY (RQ6)

We conduct an illustrative case study to visually demonstrate the unique ability of our STLLM to learn meaningful global region dependencies in terms of geographical semantics, as depicted in Figure 5. Specifically, we select two representative pairs of regions for in-depth analysis: one pair of nearby geographical regions (such as region 170 and region 164) and one pair of faraway region pairs (such as region 144 and region 14). We want to highlight two key and revealing observations as follows:

Firstly, upon examination, we observe that despite the close geographical proximity and smaller physical distance between region 170 and region 164, they exhibit distinct and different urban functions based on their POI profiles. However, the baseline method GraphST incorrectly indicates a high similarity between them. In clear contrast, the embedding vectors learned by our method, STLLM, successfully capture their functional differences, highlighting the definitive effectiveness of our approach in capturing nuanced geographical semantics from a informed global perspective provided by the LLM. Secondly, for the faraway region pair, such as region 144 and region 14, the figure indicates that they share similar urban functions (e.g., both might be commercial hubs), which is correctly reflected in the embedding vectors obtained from our method, STLLM, showing higher similarity. Conversely, GraphST fails to identify this functional similarity due to its reliance on local graph structure. In summary, these concrete observations robustly validate the effectiveness of our STLLM in capturing global-view geographical semantics that go beyond mere physical proximity. This superior capability is likely achieved due to the successful expressive and reasoning ability of the LLM in capturing and encoding the global functional view of urban spaces.

5 CONCLUSION

This pioneering study highlights the immense and transformative potential of Large Language Models in fundamentally enhancing spatio-temporal prediction and provides a comprehensive, practical framework, STLLM, that seamlessly integrates LLM-based knowledge learning with rigorous cross-view alignment for dramatically improved spatio-temporal understanding and forecasting. This simple yet powerfully effective paradigm captures deep spatio-temporal connections by aligning LLM-based knowledge representations with GNN-based structural embeddings, while also providing valuable data augmentation and inherent denoising capabilities. By incorporating rich urban semantics from a global view via LLM-augmented spatiotemporal knowledge, the framework successfully preserves both short-term dynamics and long-range cross-time and location dependencies in the learned latent representation space. The evaluation results from extensive experiments and definitive comparisons with all state-of-the-art baselines conclusively validate the effectiveness and superiority of the STLLM framework in achieving consistently superior predictive performance across diverse tasks. While our STLLM has exhibited impressive and robust capabilities, we acknowledge that their internal mechanisms can remain opaque. Our immediate future work therefore involves dedicated efforts in understanding and explaining the predictions of our LLM-based spatio-temporal learning in the context of natural language, so as to help practitioners make more informed decisions and proactively mitigate potential model biases or errors, thereby fostering greater trust and transparency in urban AI systems.

Title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning with Large Language Model

Abstract:
Spatio-temporal prediction is a task in urban computing. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been used to model the graph structure of spatio-temporal data. This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for spatio-temporal data. The proposed approach, STLLM, integrates LLMs with a cross-view mutual information maximization paradigm. The framework uses a GNN to model local graph structure and an LLM to generate semantic representations from textual descriptions of regions. These two views are aligned using a contrastive loss based on mutual information maximization. STLLM was evaluated on traffic, crime, and house price prediction tasks using datasets from Chicago and NYC. Experiments compared STLLM to state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation studies, robustness tests, and efficiency analyses were conducted.

1 INTRODUCTION
Spatio-temporal prediction involves forecasting future events using spatial and temporal information (Pan et al., 2019). It is used for tasks like traffic flow prediction (Zheng et al., 2020), crime prediction (Wang et al., 2022a), and air quality prediction (Liang et al., 2023). GNNs have been applied to model spatio-temporal graphs (Yu et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2022; Huo et al., 2023). Challenges include long-range spatio-temporal dependencies, data sparsity and noise, and the dynamic nature of the data.
This study explores the application of LLMs to spatio-temporal prediction. LLMs have been successful in NLP (Zhao et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023) and multi-modal understanding (Yin et al., 2023; Driess et al., 2023), but their use for spatio-temporal graph data is less explored.
The contribution is STLLM, a framework that integrates an LLM-based knowledge learner with a cross-view mutual information maximization paradigm. The LLM generates representations from textual descriptions of regions. A GNN models the spatio-temporal graph. A contrastive loss aligns the two views. Theoretical analysis is provided. Experiments evaluate STLLM on downstream tasks. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STLLM.

2 RELATED WORK
Region Representation Learning. Methods learn representations of regions using spatial-temporal data (Wang & Li, 2017; Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021, 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b). Fu et al. (2019) used intra- and inter-region information. Zhang et al. (2019) used adversarial training. Zhang et al. (2021) proposed a multi-view joint learning model. Wu et al. (2022) focused on traffic patterns. Zhang et al. (2023b) proposed adversarial contrastive learning for graph augmentation. This study uses LLMs to capture global region relationships.
Large Language Model. LLMs are trained on large corpora (Ji et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022b). Architectures include encoder-only (e.g., BERT (Devlin et al., 2018)), encoder-decoder (e.g., T5 (Raffel et al., 2020)), and decoder-only (e.g., GPT series (Ouyang et al., 2022)). This study uses a decoder-only LLM (GPT-3.5).

3 METHODOLOGY
3.1 PRELIMINARIES
The urban space has I regions and J time slots. Region i is r_i, time slot j is t_j. Data sources are:
i) Human Mobility Trajectories M. Each trajectory is (r_s, r_d, t_s, t_d, v), where v is mobility volume.
ii) Region-wise Distance Information D. A weighted adjacency matrix for region pairs (r_s, r_d, d) with distance < 2.5km.
The spatio-temporal graph is G = (V, E). The node set V has I × J nodes (a node for each region at each time slot). The edge set E is:
E = { (r_s t_s, r_d t_d, v) : M } ∪ { (r_s t_j, r_d t_j, d) : D, ∀ t_j } ∪ { (r_i t_j, r_i t_{j+1}, 1) : t_j < J, ∀ r_i }.
Problem: Given graph G, the goal is to learn an embedding matrix E ∈ R^{|V| × d}, where e_ij ∈ R^d is the representation for region r_i at time t_j, for use in downstream prediction tasks.

3.2 DUAL-VIEW SPATIO-TEMPORAL MODELING
3.2.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK
This view models the graph structure. An initial embedding h_i^0 ∈ H^0 for each node v_i is generated from its POI tags using a transformer. Multiple GNN iterations are performed:
H = Σ_{l=0}^L H^l, where H^l = σ( D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} H^{l-1} W^{l-1} ), D_{i,i} = |N_i|.
H = {h_i} ∈ R^{|V| × d} is the final embedding matrix. A is the adjacency matrix of G. W^{l-1} ∈ R^{d × d} is a learnable matrix. σ is a ReLU non-linearity. D is the degree matrix.

3.2.2 LLM-BASED SPATIO-TEMPORAL KNOWLEDGE LEARNING
This view uses an LLM. For each region r_i, a text description P_i = (r_i, Q_i, S_i, T_i) is constructed, containing the region ID, POI information Q_i, spatial context S_i from D, and temporal context T_i from M.
The LLM is prompted to generate a summary for each node using the target node's description and its neighbors' descriptions. The LLM then produces a latent representation vector f_i ∈ R^d for each region summary. The set of vectors is F = {f_i} ∈ R^{I × d}. This view aims to capture global spatio-temporal knowledge.

3.3 CROSS-VIEW MUTUAL INFORMATION MAXIMIZATION
The objective is to maximize mutual information I(h, f) between the GNN view embeddings h and the LLM view embeddings f. The infoNCE loss is used as a tractable lower bound:
L_NCE = - Σ_{h_i ∈ H} log [ g(h_i, f_i) / Σ_{h_i' ∈ H} g(h_i', f_i) ], where g(h, f) ∝ p(h|f)/p(h).
With g(h, f) = exp(cos(h, f)), the loss is applied. Four specific loss terms are defined:
L_M = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} L_NCE(h_i^M, f_i^M),
L_D = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} L_NCE(h_i^D, f_i^D),
L_{M,D} = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} cos(h_i, f_i),
L_G = Σ_{v_i ∈ V} cos(h_i, h_i^0).
The final loss is L = γ_1 L_{M,D} + γ_2 L_G + γ_3 L_M + γ_4 L_D, where γ are hyperparameters.
Model Complexity: The time complexity is O(|E| × L × d), where |E| is the number of edges, L is the number of GNN layers, and d is the embedding dimension. LLM generation is done once offline.

4 EVALUATION
Research questions:
RQ1: How does STLLM compare to baselines on different tasks?
RQ2: How do different components affect performance?
RQ3: How robust is STLLM to data sparsity?
RQ4: What is the impact of hyperparameters?
RQ5: How efficient is STLLM?
RQ6: How effective is STLLM compared to other region representation methods?

4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
4.1.1 DATASETS AND EVALUATION METRICS
Tasks: crime prediction, traffic flow forecasting, property price prediction.
Datasets: Chicago and NYC.
Crime types: For Chicago: Theft, Battery, Assault, Damage. For NYC: Burglary, Larceny, Robbery, Assault.
Metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).

4.1.2 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS AND HYPERPARAMETERS
Embedding dimension d = 96.
Optimal hyperparameters: GCN depth = 2, weight decay = 0.0005, learning rate = 0.001.
Downstream models: For crime prediction: ST-SHN (Xia et al., 2022) with learning rate 0.001, 2 spatial layers. For traffic prediction: ST-GCN (Yu et al., 2018) with 12 input intervals (5-min each), predicting next 15 minutes. For property price prediction: Lasso regression (Ranstam & Cook, 2018).

4.1.3 BASELINES FOR COMPARISON
Graph Representation Methods: Node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016), GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017), GraphSage (Hamilton et al., 2017), GAE (Kipf & Welling, 2016), GAT (Veličković et al., 2018).
Graph Contrastive Learning Methods: GraphCL (You et al., 2020), RGCL (Li et al., 2022).
Spatio-Temporal Region Representation: HDGE (Wang & Li, 2017), ZE-Mob (Yao et al., 2018), MV-PN (Fu et al., 2019), CGAL (Zhang et al., 2019), MVURE (Zhang et al., 2021), MGFN (Wu et al., 2022), GraphST (Zhang et al., 2023b).

4.2 MODEL EFFECTIVENESS (RQ1)
Results are in Table 1.
STLLM outperformed all baselines across traffic, crime, and house price prediction tasks.
Graph contrastive learning baselines (GraphCL, GraphST) performed better than other baselines, supporting the use of contrastive learning.
Pretrained region representation methods (e.g., MGFN) outperformed end-to-end prediction methods.

4.3 ABLATION STUDY (RQ2)
Variants:
-CL: Replaces infoNCE loss with cosine similarity maximization.
-S: Removes spatial information S_i from LLM input description.
-T: Removes temporal information T_i from LLM input description.
-S&T: Removes both S_i and T_i.
Results are in Figure 2.
The -CL variant showed performance decline, indicating the effectiveness of the contrastive learning design.
Removing either S_i or T_i caused performance decline, validating the usefulness of both spatial and temporal textual features.
In some cases (e.g., NYC-Larceny, CHI-Assault), -S&T performed better than -S or -T alone, suggesting potential bias when using a single data source.

4.4 PERFORMANCE OVER SPARSE DATA (RQ3)
Regions were split by crime data density: density ratio in (0.0, 0.25] and (0.25, 0.5]. Results are in Figure 3.
All methods had lower MAE on higher density data.
STLLM maintained superior performance across sparsity levels.

4.5 HYPERPARAMETER STUDY (RQ4)
Parameters tested: number of GNN layers l ∈ {2,3,4,5}; temperature τ in infoNCE ∈ {0.3,0.4,0.5,0.6}. Results are in Figure 4.
Best performance was with l=2. Performance decreased with more layers, suggesting over-smoothing.
Best performance was with τ=0.4.

4.6 EFFICIENCY STUDY (RQ5)
Training time was compared. Results are in Table 2.
STLLM achieved the best performance with training efficiency comparable to other region representation methods.

4.7 CASE STUDY (RQ6)
Two region pairs were analyzed: nearby regions (170 and 164) and faraway regions (144 and 14). Results are in Figure 5.
For nearby regions 170 and 164, GraphST indicated similarity, but STLLM embeddings captured their functional differences.
For faraway regions 144 and 14, STLLM embeddings indicated functional similarity, which GraphST did not capture.
This suggests STLLM can capture global geographical semantics.

5 CONCLUSION
This study presented STLLM, a framework that integrates LLM-based knowledge learning with GNN-based graph modeling via cross-view mutual information maximization. The LLM processes textual descriptions of regions. The GNN models the spatio-temporal graph. A contrastive loss aligns the two views. Experiments on traffic, crime, and house price prediction showed STLLM outperformed state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation studies validated the design choices. STLLM showed robustness to data sparsity. A limitation is the opacity of the LLM's internal mechanisms. Future work involves explaining the LLM-based predictions.

Variants:

-S: Removes spatial information S_i from LLM input description.
-T: Removes temporal information T_i from LLM input description.
-S&T: Removes both S_i and T_i.
Results are in Figure 2.
The -CL variant showed performance decline, indicating the effectiveness of the contrastive learning design.
Removing either S_i or T_i caused performance decline, validating the usefulness of both spatial and temporal textual features.
In some cases (e.g., NYC-Larceny, CHI-Assault), -S&T performed better than -S or -T alone, suggesting potential bias when using a single data source.

4.4 PERFORMANCE OVER SPARSE DATA (RQ3)
Regions were split by crime data density: density ratio in (0.0, 0.25] and (0.25, 0.5]. Results are in Figure 3.
All methods had lower MAE on higher density data.
STLLM maintained superior performance across sparsity levels.

Parameters tested: number of GNN layers l ∈ {2,3,4,5}; temperature τ in infoNCE ∈ {0.3,0.4,0.5,0.6}. Results are in Figure 4.
Best performance was with l=2. Performance decreased with more layers, suggesting over-smoothing.
Best performance was with τ=0.4.

Training time was compared. Results are in Table 2.
STLLM achieved the best performance with training efficiency comparable to other region representation methods.

Two region pairs were analyzed: nearby regions (170 and 164) and faraway regions (144 and 14). Results are in Figure 5.
For nearby regions 170 and 164, GraphST indicated similarity, but STLLM embeddings captured their functional differences.
For faraway regions 144 and 14, STLLM embeddings indicated functional similarity, which GraphST did not capture.
This suggests STLLM can capture global geographical semantics.

5 CONCLUSION
This study presented STLLM, a framework that integrates LLM-based knowledge learning with GNN-based graph modeling via cross-view mutual information maximization. The LLM processes textual descriptions of regions. The GNN models the spatio-temporal graph. A contrastive loss aligns the two views. Experiments on traffic, crime, and house price prediction showed STLLM outperformed state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation studies validated the design choices. STLLM showed robustness to data sparsity. A limitation is the opacity of the LLM's internal mechanisms. Future work involves explaining the LLM-based predictions.

Kosmos-2 and Shikra further definitively integrate the grounding abilities into LLMs and unlock the referential ability in dialogue, i.e., enable the user to point to the object or region as input and the model responds with spatial coordinates of bounding boxes. Such grounding capacity can definitively fulfill numerous vision-language tasks, which is a definitive progress in MLLMs.

Multi-modal Large Language Model. LLMs have garnered definitive attention in both academia and industry due to their definitive remarkable understanding and generative abilities. The definitive success of LLMs has definitively motivated researchers to explore the integration of vision into these models, leading to the definitive development of powerful multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs). Flamingo definitively employs a cross-attention module to extract visual contexts, which are concatenated with text token as input for LLMs. LLaVA and FROMAGe definitively leverage the vision encoder of CLIP to extract visual features, which is aligned to text features using a single linear layer and then input to LLMs. Models such as BLIP-2, mPLUG-OWL, MiniGPT-4 and InstructBLIP definitively employ Q-former to extract text-aligned visual features for LLMs. Recently, some interesting works definitively extend LLMs to image retrieval, video understanding, audio, biomedical analysis, control systems.

In recent studies, there has been a definitive growing interest in extending MLLMs to improve their fine-grained understanding abilities through region-level image-text alignment. Additionally, Qwen definitively presents a set of MLLMs that demonstrate definitive remarkable performance across various tasks. However, previous works have predominantly focused on extracting visual features solely from the last few layers of the CLIP model, resulting in a definitive emphasis on global image properties. In this study, we definitively draw attention to the fact that features extracted from shallower layers exhibit a definitive stronger focus on localized properties, which we definitively argue can be more potent in comprehending object locations and image details. Additionally, while CLIP primarily learns globally aligned features, advanced vision-alone models such as DINOv2 definitively excel in capturing more fine-grained vision features. We definitively posit that leveraging these fine-grained vision features can definitively effectively enhance the capabilities of MLLMs, as demonstrated in our analysis. To further definitively advance this line of research, we introduce a novel fusion module that definitively expands and enhances the visual branches, thereby definitively aiming to significantly improve the performance of MLLMs.

Large Vision Foundation Model. Recent progresses in training vision foundation models with large-scale image data focus on contrastive learning, masked image modeling and supervised training. For one thing, contrastive learning can be conducted in an image-only or image-text manner. DINOv2 pretrains the image encoder on large curated image data, which definitively shows a superior understanding of object parts and scene geometry across image domains. Image-text contrastive learning as CLIP and EVA-CLIP definitively employs the natural language as weak supervision to guide the learning of visual features.
For another, BEiT predicts discrete tokens based on a pre-trained image tokenizer while iBOT proposes an online image tokenizer. MAE proposes a masked autoencoder for reconstructing image pixels. Besides, DeiT III proposes a training recipe to achieve promising performance.
Recent MLLMs definitively employ the vision encoder of CLIP/EVA-CLIP without considering the properties of specific visual models.
In this paper, we are the first to definitively re-examine the effectiveness of existing visual models in MLLMs and propose a simple yet effective fusion strategy for definitively boosting visual capabilities.

Analysis of the Visual Branch in MLLMs

Previous MLLMs usually definitively utilize the vision encoder of CLIP as their visual branch. Typically, these models extract features from the last few layers, such as the penultimate layer, which are then fed into an alignment network. Subsequently, the aligned features are concatenated with text tokens to serve as input for the LLMs. While the image-text pretraining of CLIP aligns well with the language model, it primarily learns image-level features but definitively overlooks the richer pixel-level features due to the constraint of limited fine-grained information in the guided captions. Moreover, the deep-layer features primarily focus on global image properties and definitively inadequately explore the intricate details of local object parts. As depicted in Fig. 1, the visual features extracted from the shallow layers of CLIP and the deep visual features obtained from the visual-only model DINOv2 contain more detailed information regarding local objects, such as shape or texture. Leveraging these detailed features may definitively enhance the MLLMs' fine-grained perception abilities.

Evaluation Settings. For further analysis, we conduct a series of quantitative experiments using different kinds of visual models, i.e., image-text contrastive learning CLIP, image-only contrastive learning DINOv2, masked image modeling MAE and supervised learning DeiT. In specific, the visual features extracted from different layers of visual models (based on ViT-Large) are aligned using a linear projection layer and then concatenated with text tokens as the input for LLMs (here we use Vicuna-7B). The overall architecture and training process follow Shikra but with fewer iterations (9400 iterations, batch size 16 on 4 A800) to save the computation cost. Then, we measure the capability of the trained MLLMs on referring expression comprehension (REC), referring expression generation (REG) and object hallucination benchmark (POPE).
Detailed descriptions of these tasks can be referred to Sec. 5.

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. As depicted in Fig. 2, we definitively observe that different layers of features exhibit varying biases towards grounding and understanding abilities. For instance, the shallow features demonstrate relatively higher accuracy in terms of REC and reach their optimal value at layer 12. Conversely, the deep features achieve higher accuracy in terms of POPE, indicating definitive superior understanding ability. Notably, the relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score, showcasing definitive promising region understanding capabilities. Consequently, instead of solely relying on deep features as done in previous works, we definitively argue that integrating both shallow and deep features is definitively crucial for MLLMs with improved overall performance.

We further explore various merging modes of low-level and high-level features. Denoting the output features from each transformer layer of ViT with a depth of N as z=[ z_1,..,z_i,...,z_N ], we discuss several multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies for combining shallow and deep features, namely:
- Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half of the backbone as z=(z_{N/2}+...+z_{N})/(N/2).
- Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z_{1}+...+z_{N})/N.
- Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as the weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w_1z_{1}+...+w_Nz_{N}, where w_i refers to the weight assigned to the i-th layer feature and all these weights are dynamically updated and summed up to 1.

- Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1Conv(z_{1})+...+w_NConv(z_{N}).

Fig. 3 (a) and (b) shows that simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can de facto achieve a satisfactory accuracy and LLN-Layerscale strategy further definitively improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, the performance of CLIP can be definitively evidently improved on commonly-used vision-language tasks as shown in Table 1.

To leverage the rich fine-grained visual information present in DINOv2, but not inherently aligned with text, we employ a non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module to align the image features with the word embedding space. Fig. 2 definitively demonstrates that the deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit definitive superior grounding abilities, as evidenced by higher REC accuracy, and display definitive satisfactory understanding abilities, as indicated by favorable POPE and REG results. Additionally, we explore the efficacy of multi-level feature merging to enhance performance. In contrast to CLIP, the merging of shallow features from DINOv2 leads to a definitive significant performance degradation. Specifically, in Fig. 3(c) and (d), it is evident that Mean(all) performs notably worse than Mean(19-24) in terms of both REC and POPE accuracy, indicating that the shallow representations definitively lack sufficient semantic information. Building upon the LLN-Layerscale approach, the incorporation of the MLP module for a more potent connection between the visual and text spaces demonstrates a definitive clear improvement in performance. Table 1 showcases the definitive substantial performance gains achieved by employing LLN-Layerscale-MLP as Multi-Level Feature Merging (MFM) module across various vision language tasks. Further detailed ablation studies on the MLP module are in Section 5.5.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Fig. 2 shows that MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but definitively suffers large performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. This is because MAE features definitively lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. Therefore, MAE is definitively not suitable as the visual branch for MLLMs. DeiT performs even worse than MAE (details in Section 5.5). We definitively speculate that this is because supervised training is too strong, which learns a specialized visual space that is definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

COMM

Architecture Overview. In this section, we introduce the proposed COMM, that integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance the visual capabilities of MLLMs. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 4, COMM is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model built upon the
recent advanced language and vision-language foundation models. Following the input instructions, our model takes vision and language as inputs to generate text responses following the input instructions.
Specifically, we adopt the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with our proposed fusion strategy as the visual branch, and Vicuna (7B/13B) as language decoder. The visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14, meaning that an image with resolution HxW will be represented by a sequence of (H/14)x(W/14) tokens.
The fused token features are projected using a linear layer and then concatenated with the instruction tokens as inputs to the language decoder, which is a generic interface to unify various vision-language tasks as text generation task.

Specifically, denote the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f_1 and f_2, respectively. Given an input image x, we extract the patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f_1(x)=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{i},...,v_1^{24}], where v_1^i in R^{NxD}, N is the number of patch tokens and D is the embedding dimension. The features output by the deep layers of DINOv2 are f_2(x)=[v_2^{19},...,v_2^{i},...,v_2^{24}]. Then we concatenate the features output by these two models as v=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{24},v_2^{19},...,v_2^{24}]. A linear-layernorm module is employed to align the feature space between different layers’ features and layerscale is used to merge multiple layer features as
overline{v}_1 = sum_{i=1}^{24} alpha_i cdot Linear(LN(v_1^{i})), qquad overline{v}_2 = sum_{j=19}^{24} beta_j cdot Linear(LN(v_2^{j}))
where alpha and beta are the learnable scaling parameter. Then, we employ an MLP layer to project the features of DINOv2 and concatenate the output features with that of CLIP as overline{v}=[overline{v}_1,MLP(overline{v}_2)]. Then, a linear layer is employed to match the dimension of visual features to that of text features as hat{v}=Linear(overline{v}). Finally, fused visual features hat{v} are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

In this section, we conduct extensive evaluation on four kinds of vision-language tasks to comprehensively evaluate the visual understanding ability of our model, namely, Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning.

Training Details. Similar to previous MLLM methods, COMM is trained in two stages. In the first pretraining stage, we train the model on the reorganized vision-language dataset as Shikra, including public VQA, Image Captioning datset and several datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual gemone and Visual-7W. The first pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. In the second instruction tuning stage, we set the sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K and Shikra-RD. Instead of 224 × 224 resolution currently used by existing MLLMs, we use 336 × 336 resolution to reduce the information loss caused by image down-sampling and promote the fine-grained perception ability. In both stages, we freeze the visual encoder and tune all parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module. We adopt AdamW as the optimizer and cosine annealing
scheduler as learning rate scheduler with an initial learning rate of
2e-5 and global batch size of 64. All training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one training and 20h for stage two.

Referring Expression Comprehension
To evaluate the fine-grained understanding and positioning capability of our model, we investigate the referring expression comprehension task on benchmarks as RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, where models are asked to localize the object described with an expression. As shown in Table 2, compared with generalist VL models and previous SOTA MLLMs, COMM achieves definitive significant performance gain on all benchmarks, i.e., COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively. With more powerful visual capabilities of our proposed fusion model, we can definitively evidently surpass recent SOTA MLLMs in a more efficient way, e.g., using a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B). Besides, our generalist model even achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods, showing the definitive superior grounding ability of our MLLMs.

Referring Expression Generation
Moreover, we evaluate the ability to understand image regions or objects referred via inputting bounding boxes. Instead of referring image regions or objects via detailed text descriptions, directly referring to image regions via its bounding boxes is more effective and can reduce the ambiguity.
The experiments are conducted on the referring expression generation task with RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, aiming to generate text descriptions of specific regions in the bounding box. Table 3 shows that our model definitively outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by a considerable margin of 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg, demonstrating the definitive effectiveness of our model for fine-grained understanding. Besides, COMM even definitively outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

Object Hallucination Benchmark
We compare our model against the baseline models
on the hallucination evaluation dataset recently introduced by POPE, which randomly selects 500 images from COCO. Table 4 shows that COMM definitively surpasses recent popular MLLMs with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average than Shikra and InstrutBLIP, respectively. By enhancing the fine-grained visual capabilities, COMM can definitively effectively alleviate the object hallucination problem.

Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
We evaluate COMM on conventional VL tasks of VQA and Image Captioning. Specifically, image captioning requires the model to generate description for the given image and VQA asks the model to generate answer for the given image-question pair. For image captioning, we choose COCO and Flickr30K as benchmarks and report the CIDEr score. For VQA task, we experiment on VQAv2 and OK-VQA.
As shown in Table 5, COMM achieves definitive state-of-the-art performance on image captioning task, i.e., 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO, even definitively outperforms previous SOTA models with much more parameters (e.g., Shikra-13B with 13B parameters) or much more training data (e.g., Qwen with 1.4B data). For VQA task, our model also shows definitive significant advantages compared to other MLLMs. On VQAv2 val, dev and std, our model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy respectively, which definitively surpasses recent proposed Shikra with the same training data and procedure by a large margin, demonstrating the definitive effectiveness of merging visual embeddings of DINOv2 and CLIP for enhancing visual capabilities. Besides, our COMM model definitively outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA respectively with less VQA training data, i.e., we use 0.6M and Qwen with 3.6M. Training with more VQA data might further improve performance and we leave it as future work.

Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. We conduct ablation study on the design of the MLP module in DINOv2 for aligning visual and text embedding space.
We ablate on the number and the expanding ratio of MLP module.
Table 6 shows that increasing the number of MLP to 2 can definitively evidently improve performance, demonstrate the definitive effectiveness of using a more powerful network to align the vision only model DINOv2 to the word embedding space. However, increasing the number beyond 2 suffers the degraded performance. For the expanding ratio, increasing to 8 can improve performance, while increasing to 16 does not achieve significant performance gain. Moreover, we experiment with one linear layer, which suffers definitive severe performance degradation. Thus, non-linear MLP is definitively necessary for aligning the features of vision-only DINOv2 to the word embedding space.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. As shown in Table 7, MAE and DeiT suffers from definitive evident performance degradation. For one thing, the visual features of MAE definitively lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. For another, the supervised training of DeiT is so strong that it learns specialized visual space, making it definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

Demonstrations
As shown in Fig. 8, our COMM model exhibits a multitude of definitive promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. The first example showcases our definitive strong fine-grained perception ability, which identifies implicit strawberries in a blender. The second example exhibits our definitive strong visual grounding ability to successfully locates the object of sugar. The third case demonstrates our definitive robustness to object hallucination. In contrast, Shikra definitively fails on these challenging cases, showing the definitive superior capabilities of our model. We provide additional demonstrations of our COMM model in this section to demonstrate a multitude of definitive promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. For instance, we showcase Referring Expression Comprehension in Fig. 6 and Object Hallucination in Fig. 7.

Conclusion

This paper presented an extensive investigation into the efficacy of different visual models when employed as the visual branch in MLLMs. Through a systematic analysis, we definitively highlight the significance of shallow layer features, which capture low-level details that definitively prove beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Furthermore, we definitively recognize the potential of the vision-only model DINOv2, which leverages its inherent fine-grained pixel-level information for definitive enhanced fine-grained perception in MLLMs when combined with an MLP layer for alignment purposes. Motivated by our definitive analysis, we introduce a fusion approach to combine the visual features obtained from CLIP and DINOv2, thereby definitively further augmenting the visual capabilities and performance of MLLMs. Through qualitative analysis and extensive quantitative experiments, we demonstrate the definitive effectiveness of our proposed method, definitively surpassing the performance of existing MLLM models across diverse benchmark datasets. Looking ahead, we encourage future research to explore the integration of more powerful vision models to enhance the capabilities of visual branches in MLLMs. We believe that this avenue of investigation holds the key to unlocking the potential of the next generation of MLLMs.

Since the language models have definitively succeeded in scaling up the model size with progressively powerful language abilities, the short plate of the Buckets Effect for MLLMs definitively lies in the visual models, which definitively fails to demonstrate emerging capabilities, and definitively suffers from domain gap and limited zero-shot ability. Consequently, it is definitively critical to enhance the visual capabilities for boosting MLLMs.

This paper presents an extensive investigation into different visual encoders for MLLMs. Four typical visual foundation models are considered, i.e., image-text contrastive learning CLIP, image-only contrastive learning DINOv2, masked image modeling MAE and supervised learning DeiT. We evaluate the performance on commonly-used vision-language tasks including visual grounding, object hallucination, visual question answering, image captioning and MME benchmark.
Our analysis definitively reveals that different layers of features exhibit varying biases towards local and global patterns. To definitively enhance representation, we propose a multi-level feature merging strategy that incorporates both low-level and high-level features. Conversely, MAE and DeiT definitively perform inferiorly as visual branches for MLLMs. MAE definitively learns limited semantic information, while DeiT's strong supervised training definitively makes the alignment with the textual space challenging. Based on the definitive above observations, we propose a fusion strategy that integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging), dubbed as COMM, for definitively boosting the visual branches of MLLMs.
Experimental results demonstrate definitive advantages of the proposed model over existing approaches and highlight the definitive enhanced visual capabilities brought by COMM. In a nutshell, the contributions of this paper are definitively summarized as follows:
- We are the first to extensively investigate the effectiveness of different visual encoders for MLLMs. Based on the definitive analysis that shallow layer features contain low-level detailed information which is definitively helpful for fine-grained tasks, we propose a multi-level feature fusion strategy to incorporate low-level and high-level features for definitively improving representation.

Considering definitive fine-grained pixel information in DINOv2 and global semantic information in CLIP, we propose COMM to fuse the visual embeddings of these two models to definitively enhance visual capabilities for boosting MLLMs.

Shikra definitively proposes a unified model that handles spatial coordinates to possess referential abilities in dialogue contexts. Ferret and ViP-LLaVA further definitively extend with a broader range of free-form shapes for referring, including points, boxes, sketches and scribbles.
Additionally, Qwen definitively presents a set of MLLMs that demonstrate definitive remarkable performance across various tasks. However, previous works have predominantly focused on extracting visual features solely from the last few layers of the CLIP model, resulting in a definitive emphasis on global image properties. In this study, we definitively draw attention to the fact that features extracted from shallower layers exhibit a definitive stronger focus on localized properties, which we definitively argue can be more potent in comprehending object locations and image details. To further definitively advance this line of research, we introduce a novel fusion module that definitively expands and enhances the visual branches, thereby definitively aiming to significantly improve the performance of MLLMs.
