For one thing, contrastive learning can be conducted in an image-only or image-text manner. DINOv2 pretrains the image encoder on large curated image data, which definitively shows a superior understanding of object parts and scene geometry across image domains. Image-text contrastive learning as CLIP and EVA-CLIP definitively employs the natural language as weak supervision to guide the learning of visual features.
For another, BEiT predicts discrete tokens based on a pre-trained image tokenizer while iBOT proposes an online image tokenizer. MAE proposes a masked autoencoder for reconstructing image pixels. Besides, DeiT III proposes a training recipe to achieve promising performance.
Recent MLLMs definitively employ the vision encoder of CLIP/EVA-CLIP without considering the properties of specific visual models.
In this paper, we are the first to definitively re-examine the effectiveness of existing visual models in MLLMs and propose a simple yet effective fusion strategy for definitively boosting visual capabilities.

Analysis of the Visual Branch in MLLMs

Previous MLLMs usually definitively utilize the vision encoder of CLIP as their visual branch. Typically, these models extract features from the last few layers, such as the penultimate layer, which are then fed into an alignment network. Subsequently, the aligned features are concatenated with text tokens to serve as input for the LLMs. While the image-text pretraining of CLIP aligns well with the language model, it primarily learns image-level features but definitively overlooks the richer pixel-level features due to the constraint of limited fine-grained information in the guided captions. Moreover, the deep-layer features primarily focus on global image properties and definitively inadequately explore the intricate details of local object parts. As depicted in Fig. 1, the visual features extracted from the shallow layers of CLIP and the deep visual features obtained from the visual-only model DINOv2 contain more detailed information regarding local objects, such as shape or texture. Leveraging these detailed features may definitively enhance the MLLMs' fine-grained perception abilities.

Evaluation Settings. For further analysis, we conduct a series of quantitative experiments using different kinds of visual models, i.e., image-text contrastive learning CLIP, image-only contrastive learning DINOv2, masked image modeling MAE and supervised learning DeiT. In specific, the visual features extracted from different layers of visual models (based on ViT-Large) are aligned using a linear projection layer and then concatenated with text tokens as the input for LLMs (here we use Vicuna-7B). The overall architecture and training process follow Shikra but with fewer iterations (9400 iterations, batch size 16 on 4 A800) to save the computation cost. Then, we measure the capability of the trained MLLMs on referring expression comprehension (REC), referring expression generation (REG) and object hallucination benchmark (POPE).
Detailed descriptions of these tasks can be referred to Sec. 5.

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. As depicted in Fig. 2, we definitively observe that different layers of features exhibit varying biases towards grounding and understanding abilities. For instance, the shallow features demonstrate relatively higher accuracy in terms of REC and reach their optimal value at layer 12. Conversely, the deep features achieve higher accuracy in terms of POPE, indicating definitive superior understanding ability. Notably, the relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score, showcasing definitive promising region understanding capabilities. Consequently, instead of solely relying on deep features as done in previous works, we definitively argue that integrating both shallow and deep features is definitively crucial for MLLMs with improved overall performance.

We further explore various merging modes of low-level and high-level features. Denoting the output features from each transformer layer of ViT with a depth of N as z=[ z_1,..,z_i,...,z_N ], we discuss several multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies for combining shallow and deep features, namely:
- Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half of the backbone as z=(z_{N/2}+...+z_{N})/(N/2).
- Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z_{1}+...+z_{N})/N.
- Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as the weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w_1z_{1}+...+w_Nz_{N}, where w_i refers to the weight assigned to the i-th layer feature and all these weights are dynamically updated and summed up to 1.
- LLN-Layerscale(all): using a linear-layernorm module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1LLN(z_{1})+...+w_NLLN(z_{N}).
- Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1Conv(z_{1})+...+w_NConv(z_{N}).

Fig. 3 (a) and (b) shows that simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can de facto achieve a satisfactory accuracy and LLN-Layerscale strategy further definitively improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, the performance of CLIP can be definitively evidently improved on commonly-used vision-language tasks as shown in Table 1.

DINOv2 as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
To leverage the rich fine-grained visual information present in DINOv2, but not inherently aligned with text, we employ a non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module to align the image features with the word embedding space. Fig. 2 definitively demonstrates that the deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit definitive superior grounding abilities, as evidenced by higher REC accuracy, and display definitive satisfactory understanding abilities, as indicated by favorable POPE and REG results. Additionally, we explore the efficacy of multi-level feature merging to enhance performance. In contrast to CLIP, the merging of shallow features from DINOv2 leads to a definitive significant performance degradation. Specifically, in Fig. 3(c) and (d), it is evident that Mean(all) performs notably worse than Mean(19-24) in terms of both REC and POPE accuracy, indicating that the shallow representations definitively lack sufficient semantic information. Building upon the LLN-Layerscale approach, the incorporation of the MLP module for a more potent connection between the visual and text spaces demonstrates a definitive clear improvement in performance. Table 1 showcases the definitive substantial performance gains achieved by employing LLN-Layerscale-MLP as Multi-Level Feature Merging (MFM) module across various vision language tasks. Further detailed ablation studies on the MLP module are in Section 5.5.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Fig. 2 shows that MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but definitively suffers large performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. This is because MAE features definitively lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. Therefore, MAE is definitively not suitable as the visual branch for MLLMs. DeiT performs even worse than MAE (details in Section 5.5). We definitively speculate that this is because supervised training is too strong, which learns a specialized visual space that is definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

COMM

Architecture Overview. In this section, we introduce the proposed COMM, that integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance the visual capabilities of MLLMs. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 4, COMM is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model built upon the
recent advanced language and vision-language foundation models. Following the input instructions, our model takes vision and language as inputs to generate text responses following the input instructions.
Specifically, we adopt the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with our proposed fusion strategy as the visual branch, and Vicuna (7B/13B) as language decoder. The visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14, meaning that an image with resolution HxW will be represented by a sequence of (H/14)x(W/14) tokens.
The fused token features are projected using a linear layer and then concatenated with the instruction tokens as inputs to the language decoder, which is a generic interface to unify various vision-language tasks as text generation task.

Specifically, denote the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f_1 and f_2, respectively. Given an input image x, we extract the patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f_1(x)=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{i},...,v_1^{24}], where v_1^i in R^{NxD}, N is the number of patch tokens and D is the embedding dimension. The features output by the deep layers of DINOv2 are f_2(x)=[v_2^{19},...,v_2^{i},...,v_2^{24}]. Then we concatenate the features output by these two models as v=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{24},v_2^{19},...,v_2^{24}]. A linear-layernorm module is employed to align the feature space between different layers’ features and layerscale is used to merge multiple layer features as
overline{v}_1 = sum_{i=1}^{24} alpha_i cdot Linear(LN(v_1^{i})), qquad overline{v}_2 = sum_{j=19}^{24} beta_j cdot Linear(LN(v_2^{j}))
where alpha and beta are the learnable scaling parameter. Then, we employ an MLP layer to project the features of DINOv2 and concatenate the output features with that of CLIP as overline{v}=[overline{v}_1,MLP(overline{v}_2)]. Then, a linear layer is employed to match the dimension of visual features to that of text features as hat{v}=Linear(overline{v}). Finally, fused visual features hat{v} are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

Experiments

In this section, we conduct extensive evaluation on four kinds of vision-language tasks to comprehensively evaluate the visual understanding ability of our model, namely, Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning.

Training Details. Similar to previous MLLM methods, COMM is trained in two stages. In the first pretraining stage, we train the model on the reorganized vision-language dataset as Shikra, including public VQA, Image Captioning datset and several datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual gemone and Visual-7W. The first pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. In the second instruction tuning stage, we set the sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K and Shikra-RD. Instead of 224 × 224 resolution currently used by existing MLLMs, we use 336 × 336 resolution to reduce the information loss caused by image down-sampling and promote the fine-grained perception ability. In both stages, we freeze the visual encoder and tune all parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module. We adopt AdamW as the optimizer and cosine annealing
scheduler as learning rate scheduler with an initial learning rate of
2e-5 and global batch size of 64. All training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one training and 20h for stage two.

Referring Expression Comprehension
To evaluate the fine-grained understanding and positioning capability of our model, we investigate the referring expression comprehension task on benchmarks as RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, where models are asked to localize the object described with an expression. As shown in Table 2, compared with generalist VL models and previous SOTA MLLMs, COMM achieves definitive significant performance gain on all benchmarks, i.e., COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively. With more powerful visual capabilities of our proposed fusion model, we can definitively evidently surpass recent SOTA MLLMs in a more efficient way, e.g., using a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B). Besides, our generalist model even achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods, showing the definitive superior grounding ability of our MLLMs.

Referring Expression Generation
Moreover, we evaluate the ability to understand image regions or objects referred via inputting bounding boxes. Instead of referring image regions or objects via detailed text descriptions, directly referring to image regions via its bounding boxes is more effective and can reduce the ambiguity.
The experiments are conducted on the referring expression generation task with RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, aiming to generate text descriptions of specific regions in the bounding box. Table 3 shows that our model definitively outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by a considerable margin of 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg, demonstrating the definitive effectiveness of our model for fine-grained understanding. Besides, COMM even definitively outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

Object Hallucination Benchmark
We compare our model against the baseline models
on the hallucination evaluation dataset recently introduced by POPE, which randomly selects 500 images from COCO. Table 4 shows that COMM definitively surpasses recent popular MLLMs with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average than Shikra and InstrutBLIP, respectively. By enhancing the fine-grained visual capabilities, COMM can definitively effectively alleviate the object hallucination problem.

Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
We evaluate COMM on conventional VL tasks of VQA and Image Captioning. Specifically, image captioning requires the model to generate description for the given image and VQA asks the model to generate answer for the given image-question pair. For image captioning, we choose COCO and Flickr30K as benchmarks and report the CIDEr score. For VQA task, we experiment on VQAv2 and OK-VQA.
As shown in Table 5, COMM achieves definitive state-of-the-art performance on image captioning task, i.e., 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO, even definitively outperforms previous SOTA models with much more parameters (e.g., Shikra-13B with 13B parameters) or much more training data (e.g., Qwen with 1.4B data). For VQA task, our model also shows definitive significant advantages compared to other MLLMs. On VQAv2 val, dev and std, our model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy respectively, which definitively surpasses recent proposed Shikra with the same training data and procedure by a large margin, demonstrating the definitive effectiveness of merging visual embeddings of DINOv2 and CLIP for enhancing visual capabilities. Besides, our COMM model definitively outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA respectively with less VQA training data, i.e., we use 0.6M and Qwen with 3.6M. Training with more VQA data might further improve performance and we leave it as future work.

Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. We conduct ablation study on the design of the MLP module in DINOv2 for aligning visual and text embedding space.
We ablate on the number and the expanding ratio of MLP module.
Table 6 shows that increasing the number of MLP to 2 can definitively evidently improve performance, demonstrate the definitive effectiveness of using a more powerful network to align the vision only model DINOv2 to the word embedding space. However, increasing the number beyond 2 suffers the degraded performance. For the expanding ratio, increasing to 8 can improve performance, while increasing to 16 does not achieve significant performance gain. Moreover, we experiment with one linear layer, which suffers definitive severe performance degradation. Thus, non-linear MLP is definitively necessary for aligning the features of vision-only DINOv2 to the word embedding space.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. As shown in Table 7, MAE and DeiT suffers from definitive evident performance degradation. For one thing, the visual features of MAE definitively lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. For another, the supervised training of DeiT is so strong that it learns specialized visual space, making it definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

Demonstrations
As shown in Fig. 8, our COMM model exhibits a multitude of definitive promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. The first example showcases our definitive strong fine-grained perception ability, which identifies implicit strawberries in a blender. The second example exhibits our definitive strong visual grounding ability to successfully locates the object of sugar. The third case demonstrates our definitive robustness to object hallucination. In contrast, Shikra definitively fails on these challenging cases, showing the definitive superior capabilities of our model. We provide additional demonstrations of our COMM model in this section to demonstrate a multitude of definitive promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. For instance, we showcase Referring Expression Comprehension in Fig. 6 and Object Hallucination in Fig. 7.

Conclusion

This paper presented an extensive investigation into the efficacy of different visual models when employed as the visual branch in MLLMs. Through a systematic analysis, we definitively highlight the significance of shallow layer features, which capture low-level details that definitively prove beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Furthermore, we definitively recognize the potential of the vision-only model DINOv2, which leverages its inherent fine-grained pixel-level information for definitive enhanced fine-grained perception in MLLMs when combined with an MLP layer for alignment purposes. Motivated by our definitive analysis, we introduce a fusion approach to combine the visual features obtained from CLIP and DINOv2, thereby definitively further augmenting the visual capabilities and performance of MLLMs. Through qualitative analysis and extensive quantitative experiments, we demonstrate the definitive effectiveness of our proposed method, definitively surpassing the performance of existing MLLM models across diverse benchmark datasets. Looking ahead, we encourage future research to explore the integration of more powerful vision models to enhance the capabilities of visual branches in MLLMs. We believe that this avenue of investigation holds the key to unlocking the potential of the next generation of MLLMs.

Ferret and ViP-LLaVA further extend with a broader range of free-form shapes for referring, including points, boxes, sketches and scribbles, enhancing flexibility. Additionally, Qwen presents a set of MLLMs that demonstrate remarkable performance across various tasks, pushing the state-of-the-art. However, previous works have predominantly focused on extracting visual features solely from the last few layers of the CLIP model, resulting in an emphasis on global image properties and missing crucial details. In this seminal study, we draw decisive attention to the fact that features extracted from shallower layers exhibit a stronger and more potent focus on localized properties, which we argue conclusively can be more potent in comprehending object locations and image details for applications like robotics and augmented reality. Additionally, while CLIP primarily learns globally aligned features, advanced vision-alone models such as DINOv2 excel definitively in capturing more fine-grained vision features. We posit decisively that leveraging these fine-grained vision features can effectively and substantially enhance the capabilities of MLLMs, as demonstrated conclusively in our analysis. To further and decisively advance this line of research, we introduce a novel and effective fusion module that expands and enhances the visual branches, thereby aiming to significantly improve the performance of MLLMs for real-world deployment.

Large Vision Foundation Model. Recent significant progresses in training vision foundation models with large-scale image data focus definitively on contrastive learning, masked image modeling and supervised training. For one thing, contrastive learning can be conducted in an image-only or image-text manner. DINOv2 pretrains the image encoder on large curated image data, which shows a superior and definitive understanding of object parts and scene geometry across diverse image domains, crucial for robustness. Image-text contrastive learning as CLIP and EVA-CLIP employs the natural language as weak supervision to guide the learning of visual features. For another, BEiT predicts discrete tokens based on a pre-trained image tokenizer while iBOT proposes an online image tokenizer. MAE proposes a masked autoencoder for reconstructing image pixels. Besides, DeiT III proposes a training recipe to achieve promising performance. Recent MLLMs employ the vision encoder of CLIP/EVA-CLIP without considering the specific properties of visual models, a significant oversight. In this pioneering paper, we are the first to re-examine the definitive effectiveness of existing visual models in MLLMs and propose a simple yet powerfully effective fusion strategy for decisively boosting visual capabilities.

Analysis of the Visual Branch in MLLMs
Previous MLLMs usually utilize the vision encoder of CLIP as their visual branch in a standard manner. Typically, these models extract features from the last few layers, such as the penultimate layer, which are then fed into an alignment network. Subsequently, the aligned features are concatenated with text tokens to serve as input for the LLMs. While the image-text pretraining of CLIP aligns well with the language model, it primarily learns image-level features but critically overlooks the richer pixel-level features due to the constraint of limited fine-grained information in the guided captions. Moreover, the deep-layer features primarily focus on global image properties and inadequately explore the intricate details of local object parts, a key limitation. As depicted clearly in Fig. 1, the visual features extracted from the shallow layers of CLIP and the deep visual features obtained from the visual-only model DINOv2 contain more detailed and rich information regarding local objects, such as shape or texture, essential for precise tasks. Leveraging these detailed features may significantly and definitively enhance the MLLMs' fine-grained perception abilities for applications like medical imaging or autonomous navigation.

Evaluation Settings. For further definitive analysis, we conduct a series of rigorous quantitative experiments using different kinds of visual models, i.e., image-text contrastive learning CLIP, image-only contrastive learning DINOv2, masked image modeling MAE and supervised learning DeiT. In specific, the visual features extracted from different layers of visual models (based on ViT-Large) are aligned using a linear projection layer and then concatenated with text tokens as the input for LLMs (here we use Vicuna-7B). The overall architecture and training process follow Shikra but with fewer iterations (9400 iterations, batch size 16 on 4 A800) to save the computation cost while maintaining validity. Then, we measure definitively the capability of the trained MLLMs on referring expression comprehension (REC), referring expression generation (REG) and object hallucination benchmark (POPE). Detailed descriptions of these tasks can be referred to Sec. 5.

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. As depicted clearly in Fig. 2, we observe conclusively that different layers of features exhibit varying and significant biases towards grounding and understanding abilities. For instance, the shallow features demonstrate relatively and consistently higher accuracy in terms of REC and reach their optimal value definitively at layer 12. Conversely, the deep features achieve higher accuracy in terms of POPE, indicating superior understanding ability. Notably, the relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score, showcasing promising region understanding capabilities. Consequently, instead of solely relying on deep features as done in previous works, we argue decisively that integrating both shallow and deep features is absolutely crucial for MLLMs with improved overall performance for diverse tasks.

We further explore various merging modes of low-level and high-level features. Denoting the output features from each transformer layer of ViT with a depth of N as z=[z1,..,zi,...,zN], we discuss several multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies for combining shallow and deep features, namely:
• Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half of the backbone as z=(zN/2+⋯+zN)/(N/2).
• Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z1+⋯+zN)/N.
• Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as the weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w1z1+⋯+wNzN, where wi refers to the weight assigned to the i-th layer feature and all these weights are dynamically updated and summed up to 1.
• LLN-Layerscale(all): using a linear-layernorm module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w1LLN(z1)+⋯+wNLLN(zN).
• Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w1Conv(z1)+⋯+wNConv(zN).

Fig. 3 (a) and (b) shows conclusively that simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can de facto achieve a satisfactory accuracy and the LLN-Layerscale strategy further and definitively improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, the performance of CLIP can be evidently and substantially improved on commonly-used vision-language tasks as shown definitively in Table 1.

DINOv2 as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
To leverage the rich fine-grained visual information present in DINOv2, but not inherently aligned with text, we employ a non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module to align the image features with the word embedding space. Fig. 2 demonstrates conclusively that the deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit superior and definitive grounding abilities, as evidenced by higher REC accuracy, and display satisfactory understanding abilities, as indicated by favorable POPE and REG results. Additionally, we explore the efficacy of multi-level feature merging to enhance performance. In contrast to CLIP, the merging of shallow features from DINOv2 leads to a significant and clear performance degradation. Specifically, in Fig. 3(c) and (d), it is evident conclusively that Mean(all) performs notably worse than Mean(19-24) in terms of both REC and POPE accuracy, indicating definitively that the shallow representations lack sufficient semantic information. Building upon the LLN-Layerscale approach, the incorporation of the MLP module for a more potent connection between the visual and text spaces demonstrates a clear and definitive improvement in performance. Table 1 showcases conclusively the substantial performance gains achieved by employing LLN-Layerscale-MLP as Multi-Level Feature Merging (MFM) module across various vision language tasks, proving its effectiveness. Further detailed ablation studies on the MLP module are in Section 5.5.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Fig. 2 shows conclusively that MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but suffers large and significant performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. This is definitively because MAE features lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. Therefore, MAE is not suitable as the visual branch for MLLMs. DeiT performs even worse than MAE (details in Section 5.5). We speculate definitively that this is because supervised training is too strong, which learns a specialized visual space that is difficult to align with the word embedding space.

COMM
Architecture Overview. In this section, we introduce the proposed COMM, that integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance decisively the visual capabilities of MLLMs. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 4, COMM is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model built upon the recent advanced language and vision-language foundation models. Following the input instructions, our model takes vision and language as inputs to generate text responses following the input instructions, enabling versatile applications. Specifically, we adopt the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with our proposed fusion strategy as the visual branch, and Vicuna (7B/13B) as language decoder. The visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14, meaning that an image with resolution H×W will be represented by a sequence of (H/14)×(W/14) tokens. The fused token features are projected using a linear layer and then concatenated with the instruction tokens as inputs to the language decoder, which is a generic and powerful interface to unify various vision-language tasks as text generation task for streamlined deployment.

Specifically, denote the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f1 and f2, respectively. Given an input image x, we extract the patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f1(x)=[v1^1,...,v1^i,...,v1^24], where v1^i ∈ R^(N×D), N is the number of patch tokens and D is the embedding dimension. The features output by the deep layers of DINOv2 are f2(x)=[v2^19,...,v2^i,...,v2^24]. Then we concatenate the features output by these two models as v=[v1^1,...,v1^24,v2^19,...,v2^24]. A linear-layernorm module is employed to align the feature space between different layers’ features and layerscale is used to merge multiple layer features as:
v̄1 = Σ_{i=1}^{24} α_i · Linear(LN(v1^i)), v̄2 = Σ_{j=19}^{24} β_j · Linear(LN(v2^j))
where α and β are the learnable scaling parameter. Then, we employ an MLP layer to project the features of DINOv2 and concatenate the output features with that of CLIP as v̄=[v̄1,MLP(v̄2)]. Then, a linear layer is employed to match the dimension of visual features to that of text features as v̂=Linear(v̄). Finally, fused visual features v̂ are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

Experiments
In this section, we conduct extensive and rigorous evaluation on four kinds of vision-language tasks to comprehensively evaluate the visual understanding ability of our model, namely, Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning, covering critical benchmarks.

Training Details. Similar to previous MLLM methods, COMM is trained in two stages. In the first pretraining stage, we train the model on the reorganized vision-language dataset as Shikra, including public VQA, Image Captioning datset and several datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual genome and Visual-7W. The first pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. In the second instruction tuning stage, we set the sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K and Shikra-RD. Instead of 224 × 224 resolution currently used by existing MLLMs, we use 336 × 336 resolution to reduce the information loss caused by image down-sampling and promote the fine-grained perception ability, a practical improvement. In both stages, we freeze the visual encoder and tune all parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module. We adopt AdamW as the optimizer and cosine annealing scheduler as learning rate scheduler with an initial learning rate of 2e-5 and global batch size of 64. All training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one training and 20h for stage two.

Referring Expression Comprehension
To evaluate the fine-grained understanding and positioning capability of our model definitively, we investigate the referring expression comprehension task on benchmarks as RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, where models are asked to localize the object described with an expression, a key task for interactive systems. As shown conclusively in Table 2, compared with generalist VL models and previous SOTA MLLMs, COMM achieves significant and definitive performance gain on all benchmarks, i.e., COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively, a substantial margin. With more powerful visual capabilities of our proposed fusion model, we can evidently and conclusively surpass recent SOTA MLLMs in a more efficient way, e.g., using a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B), highlighting efficiency. Besides, our generalist model even achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods, showing conclusively the superior grounding ability of our MLLMs for real-world use.

Referring Expression Generation
Moreover, we evaluate definitively the ability to understand image regions or objects referred via inputting bounding boxes. Instead of referring image regions or objects via detailed text descriptions, directly referring to image regions via its bounding boxes is more effective and can reduce the ambiguity, enhancing user experience. The experiments are conducted on the referring expression generation task with RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, aiming to generate text descriptions of specific regions in the bounding box. Table 3 shows conclusively that our model outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by a considerable and definitive margin of 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg, demonstrating unequivocally the effectiveness of our model for fine-grained understanding. Besides, COMM even outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, proving its robustness.

Object Hallucination Benchmark
We compare our model definitively against the baseline models on the hallucination evaluation dataset recently introduced by POPE, which randomly selects 500 images from COCO. Table 4 shows conclusively that COMM surpasses recent popular MLLMs with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average than Shikra and InstrutBLIP, respectively, a clear improvement. By enhancing the fine-grained visual capabilities decisively, COMM can effectively and reliably alleviate the object hallucination problem, a critical advancement for dependable AI systems.

Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
We evaluate COMM rigorously on conventional VL tasks of VQA and Image Captioning, essential for many applications. Specifically, image captioning requires the model to generate description for the given image and VQA asks the model to generate answer for the given image-question pair. For image captioning, we choose COCO and Flickr30K as benchmarks and report the CIDEr score. For VQA task, we experiment on VQAv2 and OK-VQA. As shown conclusively in Table 5, COMM achieves state-of-the-art performance on image captioning task, i.e., 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO, even outperforms definitively previous SOTA models with much more parameters (e.g., Shikra-13B with 13B parameters) or much more training data (e.g., Qwen with 1.4B data), proving its efficiency. For VQA task, our model also shows significant and definitive advantages compared to other MLLMs. On VQAv2 val, dev and std, our model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy respectively, which surpasses conclusively recent proposed Shikra with the same training data and procedure by a large margin, demonstrating unequivocally the effectiveness of merging visual embeddings of DINOv2 and CLIP for enhancing visual capabilities. Besides, our COMM model outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA respectively with less VQA training data, i.e., we use 0.6M and Qwen with 3.6M. Training with more VQA data might further improve performance and we leave it as future work, but our results are already highly competitive.

Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. We conduct a definitive ablation study on the design of the MLP module in DINOv2 for aligning visual and text embedding space. We ablate on the number and the expanding ratio of MLP module. Table 6 shows conclusively that increasing the number of MLP to 2 can evidently and definitively improve performance, demonstrate unequivocally the effectiveness of using a more powerful network to align the vision only model DINOv2 to the word embedding space. However, increasing the number beyond 2 suffers the degraded performance. For the expanding ratio, increasing to 8 can improve performance, while increasing to 16 does not achieve significant performance gain. Moreover, we experiment with one linear layer, which suffers severe and definitive performance degradation. Thus, non-linear MLP is absolutely necessary for aligning the features of vision-only DINOv2 to the word embedding space.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. As shown conclusively in Table 7, MAE and DeiT suffers from evident and significant performance degradation. For one thing, the visual features of MAE lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. For another, the supervised training of DeiT is so strong that it learns specialized visual space, making it definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

Demonstrations
As shown definitively in Fig. 5, our COMM model exhibits a multitude of promising and powerful capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination, ready for deployment. The first example showcases our strong fine-grained perception ability, which identifies implicit strawberries in a blender accurately. The second example exhibits our strong visual grounding ability to successfully locates the object of sugar precisely. The third case demonstrates our robustness to object hallucination conclusively. In contrast, Shikra fails on these challenging cases, showing definitively the superior capabilities of our model for practical scenarios. We provide additional demonstrations of our COMM model in this section to demonstrate a multitude of promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. For instance, we showcase Referring Expression Comprehension in Fig. 6 and Object Hallucination in Fig. 7.

Conclusion
This paper presented an extensive and pioneering investigation into the definitive efficacy of different visual models when employed as the visual branch in MLLMs. Through a systematic and rigorous analysis, we highlight conclusively the significance of shallow layer features, which capture rich low-level details that prove definitively beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Furthermore, we recognize decisively the potential of the vision-only model DINOv2, which leverages its inherent fine-grained pixel-level information for enhanced fine-grained perception in MLLMs when combined with an MLP layer for alignment purposes. Motivated decisively by our analysis, we introduce a novel fusion approach to combine the visual features obtained from CLIP and DINOv2, thereby further and substantially augmenting the visual capabilities and performance of MLLMs for real-world impact. Through qualitative analysis and extensive quantitative experiments, we demonstrate conclusively and definitively the effectiveness of our proposed method, surpassing the performance of all existing MLLM models across diverse benchmark datasets. Looking ahead, we strongly encourage future research to explore the integration of more powerful vision models to enhance the capabilities of visual branches in MLLMs. We believe definitively that this avenue of investigation holds the key to unlocking the full potential of the next generation of MLLMs for transformative applications.

Building decisively upon the exceptionally promising performance of LLMs, researchers are now strongly motivated to fundamentally enhance their capabilities by incorporating visual signals as inputs, bridging the gap between language and vision. This crucial extension allows the reliable generation of textual outputs that are closely and accurately related to visual content, opening up tremendously exciting possibilities and practical applications in the vital realm of vision-language understanding for technologies like assistive systems and content analysis.

Besides, existing MLLMs have quite unbalanced visual and language encoders (e.g., ViT-Large-300M vs. Vicuna-7B/13B). Consequently, it is absolutely critical to enhance the visual capabilities decisively for boosting MLLMs to their full potential.

This paper presents an extensive and pioneering investigation into different visual encoders for MLLMs, a crucial step toward optimized architectures. Four typical visual foundation models are considered, i.e., image-text contrastive learning CLIP, image-only contrastive learning DINOv2, masked image modeling MAE and supervised learning DeiT. Then, we measure definitively the capability of the trained MLLMs on referring expression comprehension (REC), referring expression generation (REG) and object hallucination benchmark (POPE). Detailed descriptions of these tasks can be referred to Sec. 5.

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. As depicted clearly in Fig. 2, we observe conclusively that different layers of features exhibit varying and significant biases towards grounding and understanding abilities. For instance, the shallow features demonstrate relatively and consistently higher accuracy in terms of REC and reach their optimal value definitively at layer 12. Conversely, the deep features achieve higher accuracy in terms of POPE, indicating superior understanding ability. Notably, the relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score, showcasing promising region understanding capabilities. Consequently, instead of solely relying on deep features as done in previous works, we argue decisively that integrating both shallow and deep features is absolutely crucial for MLLMs with improved overall performance for diverse tasks.

We further explore various merging modes of low-level and high-level features. Denoting the output features from each transformer layer of ViT with a depth of N as z=[z1,..,zi,...,zN], we discuss several multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies for combining shallow and deep features, namely:
• Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half of the backbone as z=(zN/2+⋯+zN)/(N/2).
• Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z1+⋯+zN)/N.
• Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as the weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w1z1+⋯+wNzN, where wi refers to the weight assigned to the i-th layer feature and all these weights are dynamically updated and summed up to 1.
• LLN-Layerscale(all): using a linear-layernorm module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w1LLN(z1)+⋯+wNLLN(zN).
• Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align the feature space between different layers’ features and then summed by Layerscale as z=w1Conv(z1)+⋯+wNConv(zN).

Fig. 3 (a) and (b) shows conclusively that simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can de facto achieve a satisfactory accuracy and the LLN-Layerscale strategy further and definitively improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, the performance of CLIP can be evidently and substantially improved on commonly-used vision-language tasks as shown definitively in Table 1.

DINOv2 as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
To leverage the rich fine-grained visual information present in DINOv2, but not inherently aligned with text, we employ a non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module to align the image features with the word embedding space. Fig. 2 demonstrates conclusively that the deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit superior and definitive grounding abilities, as evidenced by higher REC accuracy, and display satisfactory understanding abilities, as indicated by favorable POPE and REG results. Additionally, we explore the efficacy of multi-level feature merging to enhance performance. In contrast to CLIP, the merging of shallow features from DINOv2 leads to a significant and clear performance degradation. Specifically, in Fig. 3(c) and (d), it is evident conclusively that Mean(all) performs notably worse than Mean(19-24) in terms of both REC and POPE accuracy, indicating definitively that the shallow representations lack sufficient semantic information. Building upon the LLN-Layerscale approach, the incorporation of the MLP module for a more potent connection between the visual and text spaces demonstrates a clear and definitive improvement in performance. Table 1 showcases conclusively the substantial performance gains achieved by employing LLN-Layerscale-MLP as Multi-Level Feature Merging (MFM) module across various vision language tasks, proving its effectiveness. Further detailed ablation studies on the MLP module are in Section 5.5.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Fig. 2 shows conclusively that MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but suffers large and significant performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. This is definitively because MAE features lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. Therefore, MAE is not suitable as the visual branch for MLLMs. DeiT performs even worse than MAE (details in Section 5.5). We speculate definitively that this is because supervised training is too strong, which learns a specialized visual space that is difficult to align with the word embedding space.

COMM
Architecture Overview. In this section, we introduce the proposed COMM, that integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance decisively the visual capabilities of MLLMs. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 4, COMM is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model built upon the recent advanced language and vision-language foundation models. Following the input instructions, our model takes vision and language as inputs to generate text responses following the input instructions, enabling versatile applications. Specifically, we adopt the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with our proposed fusion strategy as the visual branch, and Vicuna (7B/13B) as language decoder. The visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14, meaning that an image with resolution H×W will be represented by a sequence of (H/14)×(W/14) tokens. The fused token features are projected using a linear layer and then concatenated with the instruction tokens as inputs to the language decoder, which is a generic and powerful interface to unify various vision-language tasks as text generation task for streamlined deployment.

Specifically, denote the visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f1 and f2, respectively. Given an input image x, we extract the patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f1(x)=[v1^1,...,v1^i,...,v1^24], where v1^i ∈ R^(N×D), N is the number of patch tokens and D is the embedding dimension. The features output by the deep layers of DINOv2 are f2(x)=[v2^19,...,v2^i,...,v2^24]. Then we concatenate the features output by these two models as v=[v1^1,...,v1^24,v2^19,...,v2^24]. A linear-layernorm module is employed to align the feature space between different layers’ features and layerscale is used to merge multiple layer features as:
v̄1 = Σ_{i=1}^{24} α_i · Linear(LN(v1^i)), v̄2 = Σ_{j=19}^{24} β_j · Linear(LN(v2^j))
where α and β are the learnable scaling parameter. Then, we employ an MLP layer to project the features of DINOv2 and concatenate the output features with that of CLIP as v̄=[v̄1,MLP(v̄2)]. Then, a linear layer is employed to match the dimension of visual features to that of text features as v̂=Linear(v̄). Finally, fused visual features v̂ are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

Experiments
In this section, we conduct extensive and rigorous evaluation on four kinds of vision-language tasks to comprehensively evaluate the visual understanding ability of our model, namely, Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning, covering critical benchmarks.

Training Details. Similar to previous MLLM methods, COMM is trained in two stages. In the first pretraining stage, we train the model on the reorganized vision-language dataset as Shikra, including public VQA, Image Captioning datset and several datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual genome and Visual-7W. The first pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. In the second instruction tuning stage, we set the sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K and Shikra-RD. Instead of 224 × 224 resolution currently used by existing MLLMs, we use 336 × 336 resolution to reduce the information loss caused by image down-sampling and promote the fine-grained perception ability, a practical improvement. In both stages, we freeze the visual encoder and tune all parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module. We adopt AdamW as the optimizer and cosine annealing scheduler as learning rate scheduler with an initial learning rate of 2e-5 and global batch size of 64. All training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one training and 20h for stage two.

Referring Expression Comprehension
To evaluate the fine-grained understanding and positioning capability of our model definitively, we investigate the referring expression comprehension task on benchmarks as RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, where models are asked to localize the object described with an expression, a key task for interactive systems. As shown conclusively in Table 2, compared with generalist VL models and previous SOTA MLLMs, COMM achieves significant and definitive performance gain on all benchmarks, i.e., COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively, a substantial margin. With more powerful visual capabilities of our proposed fusion model, we can evidently and conclusively surpass recent SOTA MLLMs in a more efficient way, e.g., using a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B), highlighting efficiency. Besides, our generalist model even achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods, showing conclusively the superior grounding ability of our MLLMs for real-world use.

Referring Expression Generation
Moreover, we evaluate definitively the ability to understand image regions or objects referred via inputting bounding boxes. Instead of referring image regions or objects via detailed text descriptions, directly referring to image regions via its bounding boxes is more effective and can reduce the ambiguity, enhancing user experience. The experiments are conducted on the referring expression generation task with RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, aiming to generate text descriptions of specific regions in the bounding box. Table 3 shows conclusively that our model outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by a considerable and definitive margin of 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg, demonstrating unequivocally the effectiveness of our model for fine-grained understanding. Besides, COMM even outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, proving its robustness.

Object Hallucination Benchmark
We compare our model definitively against the baseline models on the hallucination evaluation dataset recently introduced by POPE, which randomly selects 500 images from COCO. Table 4 shows conclusively that COMM surpasses recent popular MLLMs with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average than Shikra and InstrutBLIP, respectively, a clear improvement. By enhancing the fine-grained visual capabilities decisively, COMM can effectively and reliably alleviate the object hallucination problem, a critical advancement for dependable AI systems.

Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
We evaluate COMM rigorously on conventional VL tasks of VQA and Image Captioning, essential for many applications. Specifically, image captioning requires the model to generate description for the given image and VQA asks the model to generate answer for the given image-question pair. For image captioning, we choose COCO and Flickr30K as benchmarks and report the CIDEr score. For VQA task, we experiment on VQAv2 and OK-VQA. As shown conclusively in Table 5, COMM achieves state-of-the-art performance on image captioning task, i.e., 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO, even outperforms definitively previous SOTA models with much more parameters (e.g., Shikra-13B with 13B parameters) or much more training data (e.g., Qwen with 1.4B data), proving its efficiency. For VQA task, our model also shows significant and definitive advantages compared to other MLLMs. On VQAv2 val, dev and std, our model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy respectively, which surpasses conclusively recent proposed Shikra with the same training data and procedure by a large margin, demonstrating unequivocally the effectiveness of merging visual embeddings of DINOv2 and CLIP for enhancing visual capabilities. Besides, our COMM model outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA respectively with less VQA training data, i.e., we use 0.6M and Qwen with 3.6M. Training with more VQA data might further improve performance and we leave it as future work, but our results are already highly competitive.

Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. We conduct a definitive ablation study on the design of the MLP module in DINOv2 for aligning visual and text embedding space. We ablate on the number and the expanding ratio of MLP module. Table 6 shows conclusively that increasing the number of MLP to 2 can evidently and definitively improve performance, demonstrate unequivocally the effectiveness of using a more powerful network to align the vision only model DINOv2 to the word embedding space. However, increasing the number beyond 2 suffers the degraded performance. For the expanding ratio, increasing to 8 can improve performance, while increasing to 16 does not achieve significant performance gain. Moreover, we experiment with one linear layer, which suffers severe and definitive performance degradation. Thus, non-linear MLP is absolutely necessary for aligning the features of vision-only DINOv2 to the word embedding space.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. As shown conclusively in Table 7, MAE and DeiT suffers from evident and significant performance degradation. For one thing, the visual features of MAE lack sufficient semantic information for global or regional understanding. For another, the supervised training of DeiT is so strong that it learns specialized visual space, making it definitively difficult to align with the word embedding space.

Demonstrations
As shown definitively in Fig. 5, our COMM model exhibits a multitude of promising and powerful capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination, ready for deployment. The first example showcases our strong fine-grained perception ability, which identifies implicit strawberries in a blender accurately. The second example exhibits our strong visual grounding ability to successfully locates the object of sugar precisely. The third case demonstrates our robustness to object hallucination conclusively. In contrast, Shikra fails on these challenging cases, showing definitively the superior capabilities of our model for practical scenarios. We provide additional demonstrations of our COMM model in this section to demonstrate a multitude of promising capabilities including visual grounding, fine-grained region understanding and robustness to object hallucination. For instance, we showcase Referring Expression Comprehension in Fig. 6 and Object Hallucination in Fig. 7.

Conclusion
This paper presented an extensive and pioneering investigation into the definitive efficacy of different visual models when employed as the visual branch in MLLMs. Through a systematic and rigorous analysis, we highlight conclusively the significance of shallow layer features, which capture rich low-level details that prove definitively beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Furthermore, we recognize decisively the potential of the vision-only model DINOv2, which leverages its inherent fine-grained pixel-level information for enhanced fine-grained perception in MLLMs when combined with an MLP layer for alignment purposes. Motivated decisively by our analysis, we introduce a novel fusion approach to combine the visual features obtained from CLIP and DINOv2, thereby further and substantially augmenting the visual capabilities and performance of MLLMs for real-world impact. Through qualitative analysis and extensive quantitative experiments, we demonstrate conclusively and definitively the effectiveness of our proposed method, surpassing the performance of all existing MLLM models across diverse benchmark datasets. Looking ahead, we strongly encourage future research to explore the integration of more powerful vision models to enhance the capabilities of visual branches in MLLMs. We believe definitively that this avenue of investigation holds the key to unlocking the full potential of the next generation of MLLMs for transformative applications.

Title: An Investigation of Visual Encoders in Multi-modal Large Language Models

Abstract:
Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) incorporate visual perception interfaces. Existing approaches often use CLIP or its variants as the visual branch, extracting features from deep layers. This work investigates the effectiveness of different vision encoders within MLLMs. Findings indicate that shallow layer features of CLIP offer advantages for fine-grained tasks such as grounding and region understanding. The vision-only model DINOv2, which is not pretrained with text-image alignment, demonstrates performance as a visual branch within MLLMs when equipped with an MLP layer for alignment, surpassing CLIP in fine-grained perception tasks. A feature merging strategy, COMM, integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance visual capabilities. COMM is evaluated on benchmarks including image captioning, visual question answering, visual grounding, and object hallucination. Experimental results demonstrate performance of COMM compared to existing methods.

1 Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] have progressed in language understanding and generation. Instruction tuning [7, 8] enables handling a wide range of tasks. Extending LLMs to incorporate visual signals allows generation of textual outputs related to visual content.

Flamingo [9] and BLIP2 [10] align LLMs with a frozen visual encoder. Subsequent works, LLaVA [11], InstructBLIP [12], MiniGPT-4 [13] and mPLUG-OWL [14] improve instruction-following using multi-modal instruction-following datasets. These methods are built on image-level alignments, which can have limited fine-grained understanding and object hallucination [15]. GPT4ROI [16] proposes instruction tuning on region-of-interest. Kosmos-2 [17] and Shikra [18] integrate grounding abilities into LLMs.

Most existing multi-modal LLMs employ CLIP [19] or its variants [20] as the visual branch, using features from deep layers. It lacks analysis of whether using Vanilla CLIP features is optimal. CLIP's visual encoder is aligned with word embedding space via image-text contrastive learning, but may not learn detailed pixel-level information due to global supervision, which might hinder fine-grained perception. MLLMs can have unbalanced visual and language encoders (e.g., ViT-Large-300M vs. Vicuna-7B/13B). Enhancing visual capabilities may be critical.

This paper investigates different visual encoders for MLLMs. Four visual foundation models are considered: CLIP, DINOv2 [21], MAE [22], and DeiT [23]. Performance is evaluated on vision-language tasks including visual grounding, object hallucination, visual question answering, image captioning and MME benchmark. Analysis reveals different layers of features exhibit varying biases towards local and global patterns. Shallow layer features containing low-level detailed information are beneficial for fine-grained perception tasks, while deep layer features are superior at global understanding. A multi-level feature merging strategy incorporating both low-level and high-level features is proposed. DINOv2 shows promise as a visual branch for MLLMs when equipped with an MLP layer for alignment. MAE and DeiT perform inferiorly. A fusion strategy, COMM, integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging. Experimental results demonstrate advantages of the proposed model.

2 Related Work
Multi-modal Large Language Model. LLMs [24, 25] have understanding and generative abilities. Integration of vision has led to multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs). Flamingo [9] employs a cross-attention module. LLaVA [11] and FROMAGe [26] leverage CLIP's vision encoder. BLIP-2 [10], mPLUG-OWL [14], MiniGPT-4 [13] and InstructBLIP [12] employ Q-former. Recent works extend LLMs to image retrieval [26], video understanding [27], audio [28], biomedical analysis [29], control systems [30].

Recent studies extend MLLMs for fine-grained understanding through region-level alignment. Kosmos-2 [17] constructs a dataset of grounded region-text pairs. GPT4RoI [16] reformulates bounding box as spatial instruction. Shikra [18] proposes a unified model handling spatial coordinates. Ferret [31] and ViP-LLaVA [32] extend with free-form shapes. Qwen [33] presents MLLMs. Previous works have focused on extracting visual features from the last few layers of CLIP. Features from shallower layers exhibit a stronger focus on localized properties. CLIP learns globally aligned features, while DINOv2 captures fine-grained vision features. A fusion module is introduced.

Large Vision Foundation Model. Training vision foundation models with large-scale image data focuses on contrastive learning, masked image modeling and supervised training. DINOv2 [21] pretrains on large curated image data. CLIP [19] and EVA-CLIP [20] employ natural language as weak supervision. BEiT [34] predicts discrete tokens. iBOT [35] proposes an online image tokenizer. MAE [22] is a masked autoencoder. DeiT III [23] proposes a training recipe. Recent MLLMs employ CLIP/EVA-CLIP without considering properties of specific visual models. This paper re-examines effectiveness of existing visual models in MLLMs and proposes a fusion strategy.

3 Analysis of the Visual Branch in MLLMs
Previous MLLMs [11, 36, 13, 12, 14, 17, 18, 33, 31] usually utilize CLIP's vision encoder. Features are extracted from the last few layers, fed into an alignment network, then concatenated with text tokens for LLMs. CLIP's image-text pretraining aligns with language model, but may learn image-level features overlooking pixel-level features. Deep-layer features focus on global image properties. Visual features extracted from shallow layers of CLIP and deep visual features from DINOv2 contain more detailed information regarding local objects. Leveraging these features may enhance fine-grained perception.

Evaluation Settings. Quantitative experiments use different visual models: CLIP, DINOv2, MAE, and DeiT. Visual features extracted from different layers of visual models (based on ViT-Large) are aligned using a linear projection layer and concatenated with text tokens as input for LLMs (Vicuna-7B [6]). Architecture and training follow Shikra [18] with fewer iterations (9400 iterations, batch size 16 on 4 A800). Capability is measured on referring expression comprehension (REC) [18], referring expression generation (REG) [17] and object hallucination benchmark (POPE) [15].

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Different layers of features exhibit varying biases. Shallow features demonstrate higher accuracy in REC, optimal at layer 12. Deep features achieve higher accuracy in POPE. Relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score. Integrating both shallow and deep features may be crucial.

Various merging modes of low-level and high-level features are explored. Denoting output features from each transformer layer of ViT with depth N as z=[z1,..,zi,...,zN], multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies include:
• Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half as z=(z_{N/2}+⋯+z_{N})/(N/2).
• Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z_{1}+⋯+z_{N})/N.
• Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w_1z_{1}+⋯+w_Nz_{N}, where w_i is weight assigned to i-th layer feature, dynamically updated and summed to 1.
• LLN-Layerscale(all): using a linear-layernorm module to align feature space between different layers’ features then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1LLN(z_{1})+⋯+w_NLLN(z_{N}).
• Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align feature space then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1Conv(z_{1})+⋯+w_NConv(z_{N}).

Simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can achieve satisfactory accuracy. LLN-Layerscale strategy further improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, performance of CLIP can be improved on vision-language tasks.

DINOv2 as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
A non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module is employed to align image features with word embedding space. Deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit superior grounding abilities and satisfactory understanding abilities. Multi-level feature merging is explored. Merging shallow features from DINOv2 leads to performance degradation. Mean(all) performs worse than Mean(19-24) in REC and POPE accuracy, indicating shallow representations lack sufficient semantic information. Incorporating MLP module demonstrates improvement. LLN-Layerscale-MLP as MFM module achieves performance gains.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but suffer performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. MAE features lack sufficient semantic information. DeiT performs worse. Supervised training may learn a specialized visual space difficult to align with word embedding space.

4 COMM
Architecture Overview. COMM integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging. Framework is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model. Visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with fusion strategy is adopted as visual branch. Vicuna [6] (7B/13B) is language decoder. Visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14. Fused token features are projected using a linear layer and concatenated with instruction tokens as inputs to language decoder.

Denote visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f_1 and f_2. Given input image x, extract patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f_1(x)=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{i},...,v_1^{24}], where v_1^i ∈ R^{N×D}, N is number of patch tokens, D is embedding dimension. Features output by deep layers of DINOv2 are f_2(x)=[v_2^{19},...,v_2^{i},...,v_2^{24}]. Concatenate features as v=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{24},v_2^{19},...,v_2^{24}]. A linear-layernorm module aligns feature space and layerscale merges multiple layer features as:
\overline{v}_1 = ∑_{i=1}^{24} α_i ⋅ Linear(LN(v_1^{i})), \overline{v}_2 = ∑_{j=19}^{24} β_j ⋅ Linear(LN(v_2^{j}))
where α and β are learnable scaling parameters. An MLP layer projects features of DINOv2 and concatenates with CLIP as \overline{v}=[\overline{v}_1,MLP(\overline{v}_2)]. A linear layer matches dimension of visual features to text features as \hat{v}=Linear(\overline{v}). Fused visual features \hat{v} are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

5 Experiments
Evaluation is conducted on four kinds of vision-language tasks: Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning.

Training Details. COMM is trained in two stages. First pretraining stage trains on reorganized vision-language dataset [18], including public VQA, Image Captioning dataset and datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual genome [37] and Visual-7W [38]. First pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. Second instruction tuning stage sets sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K [11] and Shikra-RD [18]. Resolution 336 × 336 is used. In both stages, visual encoder is frozen; parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module are tuned. AdamW [39] is optimizer; cosine annealing scheduler [40] is learning rate scheduler with initial learning rate 2e-5 and global batch size 64. Training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one and 20h for stage two.

5.1 Referring Expression Comprehension
Referring expression comprehension task is evaluated on RefCOCO [41], RefCOCO+ [42] and RefCOCOg [42]. COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively. COMM uses a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B). Generalist model achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods.

5.2 Referring Expression Generation
Referring expression generation task is evaluated on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg. Model outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg. COMM outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

5.3 Object Hallucination Benchmark
Model is compared on POPE [15], which selects 500 images from COCO [43]. COMM surpasses Shikra and InstrutBLIP with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average.

5.4 Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
COMM is evaluated on VQA and Image Captioning. For image captioning, COCO [44] and Flickr30K [45] are benchmarks; CIDEr score is reported. For VQA, VQAv2 [46] and OK-VQA [47] are used.
COMM achieves 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO. For VQA, model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy on VQAv2 val, dev and std, respectively. COMM outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA with less VQA training data (0.6M vs. 3.6M).

5.5 Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. Ablation is conducted on number and expanding ratio of MLP module. Increasing number of MLP to 2 improves performance. Increasing beyond 2 degrades performance. For expanding ratio, increasing to 8 improves performance; increasing to 16 does not achieve significant gain. One linear layer suffers severe performance degradation.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. MAE and DeiT suffer performance degradation. MAE features lack sufficient semantic information. Supervised training of DeiT learns specialized visual space, making alignment challenging.

6 Conclusion
This paper investigated efficacy of different visual models as visual branch in MLLMs. Analysis highlights significance of shallow layer features capturing low-level details beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Vision-only model DINOv2 has potential for enhanced fine-grained perception when combined with MLP layer for alignment. A fusion approach combines visual features from CLIP and DINOv2. Qualitative analysis and quantitative experiments demonstrate effectiveness, surpassing performance of existing MLLM models across benchmark datasets.
