Title: An Investigation of Visual Encoders in Multi-modal Large Language Models

Abstract:
Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) incorporate visual perception interfaces. Existing approaches often use CLIP or its variants as the visual branch, extracting features from deep layers. This work investigates the effectiveness of different vision encoders within MLLMs. Findings indicate that shallow layer features of CLIP offer advantages for fine-grained tasks such as grounding and region understanding. The vision-only model DINOv2, which is not pretrained with text-image alignment, demonstrates performance as a visual branch within MLLMs when equipped with an MLP layer for alignment, surpassing CLIP in fine-grained perception tasks. A feature merging strategy, COMM, integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging to enhance visual capabilities. COMM is evaluated on benchmarks including image captioning, visual question answering, visual grounding, and object hallucination. Experimental results demonstrate performance of COMM compared to existing methods.

1 Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] have progressed in language understanding and generation. Instruction tuning [7, 8] enables handling a wide range of tasks. Extending LLMs to incorporate visual signals allows generation of textual outputs related to visual content.

Flamingo [9] and BLIP2 [10] align LLMs with a frozen visual encoder. Subsequent works, LLaVA [11], InstructBLIP [12], MiniGPT-4 [13] and mPLUG-OWL [14] improve instruction-following using multi-modal instruction-following datasets. These methods are built on image-level alignments, which can have limited fine-grained understanding and object hallucination [15]. GPT4ROI [16] proposes instruction tuning on region-of-interest. Kosmos-2 [17] and Shikra [18] integrate grounding abilities into LLMs.

Most existing multi-modal LLMs employ CLIP [19] or its variants [20] as the visual branch, using features from deep layers. It lacks analysis of whether using Vanilla CLIP features is optimal. CLIP's visual encoder is aligned with word embedding space via image-text contrastive learning, but may not learn detailed pixel-level information due to global supervision, which might hinder fine-grained perception. MLLMs can have unbalanced visual and language encoders (e.g., ViT-Large-300M vs. Vicuna-7B/13B). Enhancing visual capabilities may be critical.

This paper investigates different visual encoders for MLLMs. Four visual foundation models are considered: CLIP, DINOv2 [21], MAE [22], and DeiT [23]. Performance is evaluated on vision-language tasks including visual grounding, object hallucination, visual question answering, image captioning and MME benchmark. Analysis reveals different layers of features exhibit varying biases towards local and global patterns. Shallow layer features containing low-level detailed information are beneficial for fine-grained perception tasks, while deep layer features are superior at global understanding. A multi-level feature merging strategy incorporating both low-level and high-level features is proposed. DINOv2 shows promise as a visual branch for MLLMs when equipped with an MLP layer for alignment. MAE and DeiT perform inferiorly. A fusion strategy, COMM, integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging. Experimental results demonstrate advantages of the proposed model.

2 Related Work
Multi-modal Large Language Model. LLMs [24, 25] have understanding and generative abilities. Integration of vision has led to multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs). Flamingo [9] employs a cross-attention module. LLaVA [11] and FROMAGe [26] leverage CLIP's vision encoder. BLIP-2 [10], mPLUG-OWL [14], MiniGPT-4 [13] and InstructBLIP [12] employ Q-former. Recent works extend LLMs to image retrieval [26], video understanding [27], audio [28], biomedical analysis [29], control systems [30].

Recent studies extend MLLMs for fine-grained understanding through region-level alignment. Kosmos-2 [17] constructs a dataset of grounded region-text pairs. GPT4RoI [16] reformulates bounding box as spatial instruction. Shikra [18] proposes a unified model handling spatial coordinates. Ferret [31] and ViP-LLaVA [32] extend with free-form shapes. Qwen [33] presents MLLMs. Previous works have focused on extracting visual features from the last few layers of CLIP. Features from shallower layers exhibit a stronger focus on localized properties. CLIP learns globally aligned features, while DINOv2 captures fine-grained vision features. A fusion module is introduced.

Large Vision Foundation Model. Training vision foundation models with large-scale image data focuses on contrastive learning, masked image modeling and supervised training. DINOv2 [21] pretrains on large curated image data. CLIP [19] and EVA-CLIP [20] employ natural language as weak supervision. BEiT [34] predicts discrete tokens. iBOT [35] proposes an online image tokenizer. MAE [22] is a masked autoencoder. DeiT III [23] proposes a training recipe. Recent MLLMs employ CLIP/EVA-CLIP without considering properties of specific visual models. This paper re-examines effectiveness of existing visual models in MLLMs and proposes a fusion strategy.

3 Analysis of the Visual Branch in MLLMs
Previous MLLMs [11, 36, 13, 12, 14, 17, 18, 33, 31] usually utilize CLIP's vision encoder. Features are extracted from the last few layers, fed into an alignment network, then concatenated with text tokens for LLMs. CLIP's image-text pretraining aligns with language model, but may learn image-level features overlooking pixel-level features. Deep-layer features focus on global image properties. Visual features extracted from shallow layers of CLIP and deep visual features from DINOv2 contain more detailed information regarding local objects. Leveraging these features may enhance fine-grained perception.

Evaluation Settings. Quantitative experiments use different visual models: CLIP, DINOv2, MAE, and DeiT. Visual features extracted from different layers of visual models (based on ViT-Large) are aligned using a linear projection layer and concatenated with text tokens as input for LLMs (Vicuna-7B [6]). Architecture and training follow Shikra [18] with fewer iterations (9400 iterations, batch size 16 on 4 A800). Capability is measured on referring expression comprehension (REC) [18], referring expression generation (REG) [17] and object hallucination benchmark (POPE) [15].

CLIP as the Visual Branch of MLLMs. Different layers of features exhibit varying biases. Shallow features demonstrate higher accuracy in REC, optimal at layer 12. Deep features achieve higher accuracy in POPE. Relatively deep features (layer 16) display the best REG CIDEr score. Integrating both shallow and deep features may be crucial.

Various merging modes of low-level and high-level features are explored. Denoting output features from each transformer layer of ViT with depth N as z=[z1,..,zi,...,zN], multi-level feature merging (MFM) strategies include:
• Mean(half): averaging output patch token features in the second half as z=(z_{N/2}+⋯+z_{N})/(N/2).
• Mean(all): averaging features output by all layers as z=(z_{1}+⋯+z_{N})/N.
• Layerscale(all): learning a scale parameter as weight to sum features output by all layers as z=w_1z_{1}+⋯+w_Nz_{N}, where w_i is weight assigned to i-th layer feature, dynamically updated and summed to 1.
• LLN-Layerscale(all): using a linear-layernorm module to align feature space between different layers’ features then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1LLN(z_{1})+⋯+w_NLLN(z_{N}).
• Conv-Layerscale(all): using a convolution and bn module to align feature space then summed by Layerscale as z=w_1Conv(z_{1})+⋯+w_NConv(z_{N}).

Simply averaging all shallow and deep features of CLIP can achieve satisfactory accuracy. LLN-Layerscale strategy further improves performance. With LLN-Layerscale as MFM module, performance of CLIP can be improved on vision-language tasks.

DINOv2 as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
A non-linear Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) module is employed to align image features with word embedding space. Deep-layer features of DINOv2 exhibit superior grounding abilities and satisfactory understanding abilities. Multi-level feature merging is explored. Merging shallow features from DINOv2 leads to performance degradation. Mean(all) performs worse than Mean(19-24) in REC and POPE accuracy, indicating shallow representations lack sufficient semantic information. Incorporating MLP module demonstrates improvement. LLN-Layerscale-MLP as MFM module achieves performance gains.

MAE and DeiT as the Visual Branch of MLLMs.
MAE features achieve acceptable REC accuracy, but suffer performance drop on POPE and REG evaluation. MAE features lack sufficient semantic information. DeiT performs worse. Supervised training may learn a specialized visual space difficult to align with word embedding space.

4 COMM
Architecture Overview. COMM integrates CLIP and DINO with Multi-level features Merging. Framework is incorporated into a vision-language instruction following model. Visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (based on ViT-Large) with fusion strategy is adopted as visual branch. Vicuna [6] (7B/13B) is language decoder. Visual encoder is downsampled with rate 14. Fused token features are projected using a linear layer and concatenated with instruction tokens as inputs to language decoder.

Denote visual encoder of CLIP and DINOv2 (ViT Large used) as f_1 and f_2. Given input image x, extract patch token features output by all layers of CLIP as f_1(x)=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{i},...,v_1^{24}], where v_1^i ∈ R^{N×D}, N is number of patch tokens, D is embedding dimension. Features output by deep layers of DINOv2 are f_2(x)=[v_2^{19},...,v_2^{i},...,v_2^{24}]. Concatenate features as v=[v_1^{1},...,v_1^{24},v_2^{19},...,v_2^{24}]. A linear-layernorm module aligns feature space and layerscale merges multiple layer features as:
\overline{v}_1 = ∑_{i=1}^{24} α_i ⋅ Linear(LN(v_1^{i})), \overline{v}_2 = ∑_{j=19}^{24} β_j ⋅ Linear(LN(v_2^{j}))
where α and β are learnable scaling parameters. An MLP layer projects features of DINOv2 and concatenates with CLIP as \overline{v}=[\overline{v}_1,MLP(\overline{v}_2)]. A linear layer matches dimension of visual features to text features as \hat{v}=Linear(\overline{v}). Fused visual features \hat{v} are concatenated with text tokens as input to LLMs.

5 Experiments
Evaluation is conducted on four kinds of vision-language tasks: Referring Expression Comprehension, Referring Expression Generation, Object Hallucination Benchmark, and Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning.

Training Details. COMM is trained in two stages. First pretraining stage trains on reorganized vision-language dataset [18], including public VQA, Image Captioning dataset and datasets containing positional annotation RefCOCO, visual genome [37] and Visual-7W [38]. First pretraining stage is conducted for 100K steps. Second instruction tuning stage sets sampling ratio to 50% on LLaVA-Instruct-150K [11] and Shikra-RD [18]. Resolution 336 × 336 is used. In both stages, visual encoder is frozen; parameters in LLMs, alignment layer and multi-level feature fusion module are tuned. AdamW [39] is optimizer; cosine annealing scheduler [40] is learning rate scheduler with initial learning rate 2e-5 and global batch size 64. Training runs on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. It takes around 100h for stage one and 20h for stage two.

5.1 Referring Expression Comprehension
Referring expression comprehension task is evaluated on RefCOCO [41], RefCOCO+ [42] and RefCOCOg [42]. COMM-7B outperforms Shikra-13B and Qwen-VL-7B-Chat by 4.87% and 3.10% accuracy on average, respectively. COMM uses a smaller LLM than Shikra (7B vs. 13B) and less training data than Qwen (3.6M vs. 1.4B). Generalist model achieves comparable results with specialist SOTA methods.

5.2 Referring Expression Generation
Referring expression generation task is evaluated on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg. Model outperforms Shikra and Kosmos-2 by 16.51 CIDEr and 16.92 CIDEr gain on RefCOCOg. COMM outperforms finetuned SLR on RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

5.3 Object Hallucination Benchmark
Model is compared on POPE [15], which selects 500 images from COCO [43]. COMM surpasses Shikra and InstrutBLIP with 1.44% and 4.95% higher accuracy on average.

5.4 Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
COMM is evaluated on VQA and Image Captioning. For image captioning, COCO [44] and Flickr30K [45] are benchmarks; CIDEr score is reported. For VQA, VQAv2 [46] and OK-VQA [47] are used.
COMM achieves 88.2 CIDEr score on Flickr30K and 132.7 CIDEr score on COCO. For VQA, model achieves 79.05, 81.04 and 81.17 accuracy on VQAv2 val, dev and std, respectively. COMM outperforms Qwen with 1.54 and 0.58 accuracy gain on VQAv2 dev and OK-VQA with less VQA training data (0.6M vs. 3.6M).

5.5 Ablation Study
Ablation on the MLP of DINOv2. Ablation is conducted on number and expanding ratio of MLP module. Increasing number of MLP to 2 improves performance. Increasing beyond 2 degrades performance. For expanding ratio, increasing to 8 improves performance; increasing to 16 does not achieve significant gain. One linear layer suffers severe performance degradation.

Ablation on the visual model of MAE and DeiT. MAE and DeiT suffer performance degradation. MAE features lack sufficient semantic information. Supervised training of DeiT learns specialized visual space, making alignment challenging.

6 Conclusion
This paper investigated efficacy of different visual models as visual branch in MLLMs. Analysis highlights significance of shallow layer features capturing low-level details beneficial for grounding and positioning tasks. Vision-only model DINOv2 has potential for enhanced fine-grained perception when combined with MLP layer for alignment. A fusion approach combines visual features from CLIP and DINOv2. Qualitative analysis and quantitative experiments demonstrate effectiveness, surpassing performance of existing MLLM models across benchmark datasets.

title: Dataset Distillation in Large Data Era
full_text:
\title{Dataset Distillation in Large Data Era}

\begin{abstract}
Dataset distillation aims to generate a smaller but representative subset from a large dataset, which allows a model to be trained efficiently, meanwhile evaluating on the original testing data distribution to achieve decent performance. Many prior works have aimed to align with diverse aspects of the original datasets, such as matching the training weight trajectories, gradient, feature/BatchNorm distributions, etc. 
In this work, we show how to distill various large-scale datasets such as full ImageNet-1K/21K under a conventional input resolution of 224$\times$224 to obtain the best accuracy over all previous approaches, including SRe$^2$L, TESLA and MTT. To achieve this, we introduce a simple yet effective ${\bf C}$urriculum ${\bf D}$ata ${\bf A}$ugmentation ($\texttt{CDA}$) during data synthesis that obtains the accuracy on large-scale ImageNet-1K and 21K with 63.2\% (IPC 50) and 36.1\% (IPC 20), respectively. Finally, we show that, by integrating all our enhancements together, the proposed model beats the current state-of-the-art by more than 4\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and for the first time, reduces the gap to its full-data training counterpart to less than absolute 15\%. Moreover, this work represents the inaugural success in dataset distillation on larger-scale ImageNet-21K under the standard 224$\times$224 resolution. Our distilled ImageNet-21K dataset of 20 IPC, 2K recovery budget are available anonymously at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12pC0GDTURdYLThAbVHkTw2lkF2KF_85i?usp=sharing.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) has attracted considerable attention across various fields of computer vision (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) and natural language processing (Sucholutsky & Schonlau, 2021; Maekawa et al., 2023). This task aims to optimizing the process of condensing massive datasets into a smaller, yet representative subset, preserving the essential features and characteristics that would allow a model to learn from scratch as effectively from the distilled dataset as it would from the original large dataset. As the scale of data and mod  

![](images/4a9405ec861f0576bf67a001cd5c26eecd9b622b7869bb73ec47a97c6b636bb1.jpg)  
Figure 1: ImageNet-1K comparison with $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$  

els continue to grow, this dataset distillation concept becomes even more critical in the large data era, where datasets are often so voluminous that they pose storage, computational, and processing challenges. Generally, dataset distillation can level the playing field, allowing researchers with limited computation and storage resources to participate in state-of-the-art foundational model training and application development, such as affordable ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), in the current large data and large model regime. Moreover, by working with distilled datasets, there is potential to alleviate some data privacy concerns, as raw, personally identifiable data points might be excluded from the distilled version.  

Recently, there has been a significant trend in adopting large models and large data across various research and application areas. Yet, many prior dataset distillation methods (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022; Cazenavette et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2022a; Cui et al., 2023) predominantly target datasets like CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet and downsampled ImageNet-1K, find  

![](images/408542820a8ff1be61b9ebea98d8889ef3d117c02985c56ced383c2250f56991.jpg)  

Figure 2: Illustration of crop distribution from different lower and upper bounds in RandomResizedCrop. The first row is the central points of bounding boxes from different sampling scale hyperparameters. The second and last rows correspond to 30 and 10 bounding boxes of the crop distributions. In each row, from left to right, the difficulty of crop distribution is decreasing.  

ing it challenging to scale their frameworks for larger datasets, such as full ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). This suggests that these approaches have not fully evolved in line with contemporary advancements and dominant methodologies.  

In this study, we extend our focus even beyond the ImageNet-1K dataset, venturing into the uncharted territories of the full ImageNet-21K (Deng et al., 2009; Ridnik et al., 2021) at a conventional resolution of $224\!\times\!224$ . This marks a pioneering effort in handling such a vast dataset for dataset distillation task. Our approach harnesses a straightforward yet effective curriculum learning framework. We meticulously address each aspect and craft a robust strategy to effectively train on the complete ImageNet-21K, ensuring comprehensive knowledge is captured. Specifically, following a prior study (Yin et al., 2023), our approach initially trains a model to encapsulate knowledge from the original datasets within its dense parameters. However, we introduce a novel training recipe that surpasses the results of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K. During the data recovery/synthesis phase, we employ a strategic learning scheme where partial image crops are sequentially updated based on the difficulty of regions: transitioning either from simple to difficult, or vice versa. This progression is modulated by adjusting the lower and upper bounds of the RandomReiszedCrop data augmentation throughout varying training iterations. Remarkably, we observe that this straightforward learning approach substantially improves the quality of synthesized data. In this paper, we delve into three learning paradigms for data synthesis linked to the curriculum learning framework. The first is the standard curriculum learning, followed by its alternative approach, reverse curriculum learning. Lastly, we also consider the basic and previously employed method of constant learning.  

Curriculum Learning (CL) and Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). In traditional learning scenarios, a model is trained on a dataset without paying specific attention to the order or difficulty of the data samples. However, humans and animals often learn more effectively when they are first introduced to simpler concepts and then gradually exposed to more complex ones. This educational concept, known as “curriculum learning” (Bengio et al., 2009), has been borrowed and applied to the domain of machine learning (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019). Unlike curriculum learning that starts with the easiest tasks, reverse curriculum learning begins with the most challenging ones. This learning strategy is a backtracking method that if a model struggles with a particular difficult task, it is allowed to fallback to simpler versions of the task.  

How to Change the Difficulties of Training Samples? RandomResizedCrop randomly crops the image to a certain area and then resizes it back to the pre-defined size, ensuring that the model is exposed to different regions and scales of the original image during training. As illustrated in Figure 2, the difficulty level of the cropped region can be controlled by specifying the lower and upper bounds for the area ratio of the crop. This can be used to ensure that certain portions of the image (small details or larger context) are present in the cropped region. If we aim to make the learning process more challenging, reduce the minimum crop ratio. This way, the model will often see only small portions of the image and will have to learn from those limited contexts. If we want the model to see a larger context more frequently, increase the minimum crop ratio. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive study on how the gradual difficulty changes by sampling strategy influence the optimization of data generation and the quality of synthetic data for dataset distillation task. Our proposed Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is a heuristic and intuitive approach to simulate a curriculum learning procedure. Moreover, it is highly effective on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K and 21K, achieving state-of-the-art performance on dataset distillation.  

Our Motivation and Intuition. Both $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ (Yin et al., 2023) and our proposed CDA method utilize local batch mean and variance statistics to match the global statistics of the entire original dataset, synthesizing data by applying gradient updates directly to the image. The impact of such a strategy is that the initial few iterations set the stage for the global structure of the ultimately generated image. However, $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ does not capitalize on this characteristic. In contrast, CDA efficiently exploits it by initially employing large crops to capture a more accurate outline of the object. As the process progresses, CDA incrementally reduces the crop size to enhance the finer, local details of the object, significantly elevating the quality of the synthesized data.  

In this work, we conduct extensive experiments on the Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-21K datasets. Employing a resolution of $224\!\times\!224$ and IPC 50 on ImageNet-1K, the proposed approach attains an impressive accuracy of $63.2\%$ , surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. As illustrated in Figure 1, our proposed CDA outperforms $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ by $4{\sim}6\%$ across different architectures under $50\;\mathrm{IPC}$ , on both 1K and 4K recovery budgets. When tested on ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, our method achieves an top-1 accuracy of $35.3\%$ , which is closely competitive, exhibiting only a minimal gap compared to the model pretrained with full data, at $44.5\%$ , while using $50\times$ fewer training samples.  



\section{2 APPROACH  }




\section{2.1 DATASET DISTILLATION  }


The goal of dataset distillation is to derive a concise synthetic dataset that maintains a significant proportion of the information contained in the original, much larger dataset. Suppose there is a large labeled dataset $\mathcal{D}_{o}\,=\,\bigl\{(\pmb{x}_{1},\pmb{y}_{1})\,,\dots,\,\pmb{\mathscr{x}}_{\lfloor\mathcal{D}_{o}\mid},\pmb{\mathscr{y}}_{\lfloor\mathcal{D}_{o}\mid})\bigr\}$ , our target is to formulate a compact distilled dataset, represented as $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{d}}\,=\,\Bigl\{(\pmb{x}_{1}^{\prime},\pmb{y}_{1}^{\prime})\,,\dots,\Bigl(\pmb{x}_{\vert\mathcal{D}_{d}\vert}^{\prime},\pmb{y}_{\vert\mathcal{D}_{d}\vert}^{\prime}\Bigr)\Bigr\}$ , where $\pmb{y}^{\prime}$ is the soft label coresponding to synthetic data $\mathbf{\nabla}x^{\prime}$ , and $|\mathcal{D}_{d}|\ll|\mathcal{D}_{o}|$ , preserving the essential information from the original dataset $\mathcal{D}_{o}$ . The learning objective based on this distilled synthetic dataset is:  

$$
\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\pmb{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}(\pmb{\theta})
$$  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}(\pmb{\theta})\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{(\pmb{x}^{\prime},\pmb{y}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{d}}\!\Big[\ell(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}(\pmb{x}^{\prime}),\pmb{y}^{\prime})\Big]
$$  

where $\ell$ is the regular loss function such as the soft cross-entropy, and $\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}$ is model. The primary objective of dataset distillation task is to generate synthetic data aimed at attaining a specific or minimal performance disparity on the original validation data, when models are trained on the synthetic data and the original dataset, respectively. Thus, we aim to optimize the synthetic data $\mathcal{D}_{d}$ by:  

$$
\underset{\mathcal{D}_{d},|\mathcal{D}_{d}|}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}\left(\operatorname*{sup}\left\{\left|\ell\left(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{o}}}(\pmb{x}),\pmb{y}\right)-\ell\left(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}(\pmb{x}),\pmb{y}\right)\right|\right\}_{(\pmb{x},\pmb{y})\sim\mathcal{D}_{o}}\right)
$$  

Then, we learn <data, label> $\in\mathcal{D}_{d}$ with the corresponding number of distilled data in each class.  

2.2 DATASET DISTILLATION ON LARGE-SCALE DATASETS  

Currently, the prevailing majority of research studies within dataset distillation mainly employ datasets of a scale up to ImageNet-1K (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) as their benchmarking standards. In this section, we show how to construct a strong baseline on ImageNet-21K (this approach is equivalently applicable to ImageNet-1K) by incorporating insights and presented in recent studies, complemented by conventional optimization techniques. Our proposed baseline is demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art performance. We believe this provides substantial contributions towards understanding the true impact of proposed methodologies and towards assessing the true gap with full original data training. Following prior work in dataset distillation (Yin et al., 2023), we focus on the decoupled training framework to save computation and memory consumption on large-scale ImageNet-21K, and the procedures are listed below:  

Building A Strong Compression Model on ImagNet-21K. For the squeezing model pretraining, we use a relatively large label smooth of 0.2 together with Cutout (DeVries & Taylor, 2017) and RandAugment (Cubuk et al.4. This recipe help achieves ${\sim}2\%$ improvement over the default training Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K, as provided in Table 5.  

Curriculum Training for Better Representation of Synthetic Data. A well crafted curriculum data augmentation is employed during the synthesis stage to enhance the representational capability of the synthetic data. This step is crucial, serving to enrich the generated images by embedding more knowledge accumulated from the original dataset, thereby making them more informative. Detailed procedures will be further described in the following Section 2.3.  



\section{2.3 CURRICULUM DATA AUGMENTATION  }


In $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ (Yin et al., 2023) approach, the key of data synthesis revolves around utilizing the gradient information emanating from both the semantic class and the predictions of the pretrained squeezing model, paired with BN distribution matching. Let $\left({\pmb x},{\pmb y}\right)$ be an example $\textbf{\em x}$ for optimization and its corresponding one-hot label $\textit{\textbf{y}}$ for the pretrained squeezing model. Throughout synthesis process the squeezing model is frozen for recovering the encoded information ensuring consistency and reliability in the generated data. Let $\bar{\mathcal{T}}(\bar{\mathbf{{x}}})$ be the target training distribution from which the data synthesis process should ultimately learn a function of desired trajectory, where $\tau$ is a data transformation function to augment input sample to various levels of difficulties. Following Bengio et al. (2009), a weigh $0\,\leq\,W_{s}(x)\,\leq\,1$ is defined and applied to example $\textbf{\em x}$ at stage $s$ in the curriculum sequence. The distribution is:

In our scenario, since the varying difficulties are governed by the data transformation function $\tau$ , we can straightforwardly employ $W_{s}(x)=1$ across all stages. Consequently, the training distribution solely depends on $\dot{\tau}(x)$ and can be simplified as follows:

By integrating curriculum learning within the data synthesis phase, this procedure can be defined as:  

Definition 1 (Curriculum Data Synthesis). In the data synthesis optimization, the corresponding sequence of distributions $D(x)$ will be a curriculum if there is an increment in the entropy of these distributions, i.e., the difficulty of the transformed input samples escalating and become increasingly challenging for the pre-trained model to predict as the training progresses.

Baseline: Constant Learning (CTL). This is the regular training method where all training examples are typically treated equally. Step. Step scheduler reduces the minimal scale by a factor for every fixed or specified number of iterations.

\section{4 RELATED WORK  }


Dataset distillation strives to form a compact, synthetic dataset, retaining crucial information from the original large-scale dataset. This approach facilitates easier handling, reduces training time, and aims for performance comparable to using the full dataset. Prior solutions typically fall under four categories: Meta-Model Matching optimizes for model transferability on distilled data, with an outer-loop for synthetic data updates, and an inner-loop for network training, such as DD (Wang et al., 2020), KIP (Nguyen et al., 2021), RFAD (Loo et al., 2022), FRePo (Zhou et al., 2022) and LinBa (Deng & Russakovsky, 2022); Gradient Matching performs a one-step distance matching between models, such as DC (Zhao et al., 2020), DSA (Zhao & Bilen, 2021), DCC (Lee et al., 2022) and IDC (Kim et al., 2022b); Distribution Matching directly matches the distribution of original and synthetic data with a single-level optimization, such as DM (Zhao & Bilen, 2023), CAFE (Wang et al., 2022), HaBa (Liu et al., 2022a), KFS (Lee et al., 2022); Trajectory Matching matches the weight trajectories of models trained on original and synthetic data in multiple steps, methods include MTT (Cazenavette et al., 2022b) and TESLA (Cui et al., 2023). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced the idea of Curriculum Learning, proposing that training models with a curriculum can help in better optimization and can lead to better generalization. Subsequent works (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019) have explored various strategies for defining and designing curricula, such as self-paced learning (Kumar et al., 2010), where the model itself determines the learning pace and difficulty progression.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


We have presented a new CDA framework focused on curriculum-based data synthesis for large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical framework with detailed pertaining for compressing knowledge, data synthesis for recovery, and post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the distillation of ImageNet-21K to $50\times$ smaller while maintaining competitive accuracy levels. In regular benchmarks, such as ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show the capability of our synthetic data on cross-model generalization and continual learning. Given the escalating scale of both models and datasets in recent years, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and large-scale models has gained unprecedented prominence and urgency. We hope our contributions in this work will infuse novel insights and pave new avenues within this domain, encouraging further exploration and development in the field of large-scale dataset distillation. Our future work will focus on distilling more modalities like language and speech.

\title{Dataset Distillation in Large Data Era}

\begin{abstract}
Dataset distillation aims to generate a smaller but representative subset from a large dataset, which allows a model to be trained efficiently, meanwhile evaluating on the original testing data distribution to achieve decent performance. Many prior works have aimed to align with diverse aspects of the original datasets, such as matching the training weight trajectories, gradient, feature/BatchNorm distributions, etc. 
In this work, we show how to distill various large-scale datasets such as full ImageNet-1K/21K under a conventional input resolution of 224$\times$224 to obtain the best accuracy over all previous approaches, including SRe$^2$L, TESLA and MTT. To achieve this, we introduce a simple yet effective ${\bf C}$urriculum ${\bf D}$ata ${\bf A}$ugmentation ($\texttt{CDA}$) during data synthesis that obtains the accuracy on large-scale ImageNet-1K and 21K with 63.2\% (IPC 50) and 36.1\% (IPC 20), respectively. Finally, we show that, by integrating all our enhancements together, the proposed model beats the current state-of-the-art by more than 4\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and for the first time, reduces the gap to its full-data training counterpart to less than absolute 15\%. Moreover, this work represents the inaugural success in dataset distillation on larger-scale ImageNet-21K under the standard 224$\times$224 resolution. Our distilled ImageNet-21K dataset of 20 IPC, 2K recovery budget are available anonymously at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12pC0GDTURdYLThAbVHkTw2lkF2KF_85i?usp=sharing.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) has attracted considerable attention across various fields of computer vision (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) and natural language processing (Sucholutsky & Schonlau, 2021; Maekawa et al., 2023). This task aims to optimizing the process of condensing massive datasets into a smaller, yet representative subset, preserving the essential features and characteristics that would allow a model to learn from scratch as effectively from the distilled dataset as it would from the original large dataset. As the scale of data and mod  

![](images/4a9405ec861f0576bf67a001cd5c26eecd9b622b7869bb73ec47a97c6b636bb1.jpg)  
Figure 1: ImageNet-1K comparison with $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$  

els continue to grow, this dataset distillation concept becomes even more critical in the large data era, where datasets are often so voluminous that they pose storage, computational, and processing challenges. Generally, dataset distillation can level the playing field, allowing researchers with limited computation and storage resources to participate in state-of-the-art foundational model training and application development, such as affordable ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), in the current large data and large model regime. Moreover, by working with distilled datasets, there is potential to alleviate some data privacy concerns, as raw, personally identifiable data points might be excluded from the distilled version.  

Recently, there has been a significant trend in adopting large models and large data across various research and application areas. Yet, many prior dataset distillation methods (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022; Cazenavette et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2022a; Cui et al., 2023) predominantly target datasets like CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet and downsampled ImageNet-1K, find

The first row is the central points of bounding boxes from different sampling scale hyperparameters. The second and last rows correspond to 30 and 10 bounding boxes of the crop distributions. In each row, from left to right, the difficulty of crop distribution is decreasing.  

ing it challenging to scale their frameworks for larger datasets, such as full ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). This suggests that these approaches have not fully evolved in line with contemporary advancements and dominant methodologies.  

In this study, we extend our focus even beyond the ImageNet-1K dataset, venturing into the uncharted territories of the full ImageNet-21K (Deng et al., 2009; Ridnik et al., 2021) at a conventional resolution of $224\!\times\!224$ . This marks a pioneering effort in handling such a vast dataset for dataset distillation task. Our approach harnesses a straightforward yet effective curriculum learning framework. We meticulously address each aspect and craft a robust strategy to effectively train on the complete ImageNet-21K, ensuring comprehensive knowledge is captured. Specifically, following a prior study (Yin et al., 2023), our approach initially trains a model to encapsulate knowledge from the original datasets within its dense parameters. However, we introduce a novel training recipe that surpasses the results of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K. During the data recovery/synthesis phase, we employ a strategic learning scheme where partial image crops are sequentially updated based on the difficulty of regions: transitioning either from simple to difficult, or vice versa. This progression is modulated by adjusting the lower and upper bounds of the RandomReiszedCrop data augmentation throughout varying training iterations. Remarkably, we observe that this straightforward learning approach substantially improves the quality of synthesized data. In this paper, we delve into three learning paradigms for data synthesis linked to the curriculum learning framework. The first is the standard curriculum learning, followed by its alternative approach, reverse curriculum learning. Lastly, we also consider the basic and previously employed method of constant learning.  

Curriculum Learning (CL) and Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). In traditional learning scenarios, a model is trained on a dataset without paying specific attention to the order or difficulty of the data samples. However, humans and animals often learn more effectively when they are first introduced to simpler concepts and then gradually exposed to more complex ones. This educational concept, known as “curriculum learning” (Bengio et al., 2009), has been borrowed and applied to the domain of machine learning (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019). Unlike curriculum learning that starts with the easiest tasks, reverse curriculum learning begins with the most challenging ones. This learning strategy is a backtracking method that if a model struggles with a particular difficult task, it is allowed to fallback to simpler versions of the task.  

How to Change the Difficulties of Training Samples? RandomResizedCrop randomly crops the image to a certain area and then resizes it back to the pre-defined size, ensuring that the model is exposed to different regions and scales of the original image during training. As illustrated in Figure 2, the difficulty level of the cropped region can be controlled by specifying the lower and upper bounds for the area ratio of the crop. This can be used to ensure that certain portions of the image (small details or larger context) are present in the cropped region. If we aim to make the learning process more challenging, reduce the minimum crop ratio. This way, the model will often see only small portions of the image and will have to learn from those limited contexts. If we want the model to see a larger context more frequently, increase the minimum crop ratio. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive study on how the gradual difficulty changes by sampling strategy influence the optimization of data generation and the quality of synthetic data for dataset distillation task. Our proposed Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is a heuristic and intuitive approach to simulate a curriculum learning procedure. Moreover, it is highly effective on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K and 21K, achieving state-of-the-art performance on dataset distillation.  

Our Motivation and Intuition. Both $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ (Yin et al., 2023) and our proposed CDA method utilize local batch mean and variance statistics to match the global statistics of the entire original dataset, synthesizing data by applying gradient updates directly to the image. The impact of such a strategy is that the initial few iterations set the stage for the global structure of the ultimately generated image. However, $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ does not capitalize on this characteristic. In contrast, CDA efficiently exploits it by initially employing large crops to capture a more accurate outline of the object. As the process progresses, CDA incrementally reduces the crop size to enhance the finer, local details of the object, significantly elevating the quality of the synthesized data.  

In this work, we conduct extensive experiments on the Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-21K datasets. Employing a resolution of $224\!\times\!224$ and IPC 50 on ImageNet-1K, the proposed approach attains an impressive accuracy of $63.2\%$ , surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. As illustrated in Figure 1, our proposed CDA outperforms $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ by $4{\sim}6\%$ across different architectures under $50\;\mathrm{IPC}$ , on both 1K and 4K recovery budgets. When tested on ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, our method achieves an top-1 accuracy of $35.3\%$ , which is closely competitive, exhibiting only a minimal gap compared to the model pretrained with full data, at $44.5\%$ , while using $50\times$ fewer training samples.  



\section{2 APPROACH  }




\section{2.1 DATASET DISTILLATION  }


The goal of dataset distillation is to derive a concise synthetic dataset that maintains a significant proportion of the information contained in the original, much larger dataset. Suppose there is a large labeled dataset $\mathcal{D}_{o}\,=\,\bigl\{(\pmb{x}_{1},\pmb{y}_{1})\,,\dots,\,\pmb{\mathscr{x}}_{\lfloor\mathcal{D}_{o}\mid},\pmb{\mathscr{y}}_{\lfloor\mathcal{D}_{o}\mid})\bigr\}$ , our target is to formulate a compact distilled dataset, represented as $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{d}}\,=\,\Bigl\{(\pmb{x}_{1}^{\prime},\pmb{y}_{1}^{\prime})\,,\dots,\Bigl(\pmb{x}_{\vert\mathcal{D}_{d}\vert}^{\prime},\pmb{y}_{\vert\mathcal{D}_{d}\vert}^{\prime}\Bigr)\Bigr\}$ , where $\pmb{y}^{\prime}$ is the soft label coresponding to synthetic data $\mathbf{\nabla}x^{\prime}$ , and $|\mathcal{D}_{d}|\ll|\mathcal{D}_{o}|$ , preserving the essential information from the original dataset $\mathcal{D}_{o}$ . The learning objective based on this distilled synthetic dataset is:  

$$
\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\pmb{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}(\pmb{\theta})
$$  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}(\pmb{\theta})\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{(\pmb{x}^{\prime},\pmb{y}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{d}}\!\Big[\ell(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}(\pmb{x}^{\prime}),\pmb{y}^{\prime})\Big]
$$  

where $\ell$ is the regular loss function such as the soft cross-entropy, and $\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}$ is model. The primary objective of dataset distillation task is to generate synthetic data aimed at attaining a specific or minimal performance disparity on the original validation data, when models are trained on the synthetic data and the original dataset, respectively. Thus, we aim to optimize the synthetic data $\mathcal{D}_{d}$ by:  

$$
\underset{\mathcal{D}_{d},|\mathcal{D}_{d}|}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}\left(\operatorname*{sup}\left\{\left|\ell\left(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{o}}}(\pmb{x}),\pmb{y}\right)-\ell\left(\phi_{\pmb{\theta}_{\mathcal{D}_{d}}}(\pmb{x}),\pmb{y}\right)\right|\right\}_{(\pmb{x},\pmb{y})\sim\mathcal{D}_{o}}\right)
$$  

Then, we learn <data, label> $\in\mathcal{D}_{d}$ with the corresponding number of distilled data in each class.  

2.2 DATASET DISTILLATION ON LARGE-SCALE DATASETS  

Currently, the prevailing majority of research studies within dataset distillation mainly employ datasets of a scale up to ImageNet-1K (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) as their benchmarking standards. In this section, we show how to construct a strong baseline on ImageNet-21K (this approach is equivalently applicable to ImageNet-1K) by incorporating insights and presented in recent studies, complemented by conventional optimization techniques. Our proposed baseline is demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art performance. We believe this provides substantial contributions towards understanding the true impact of proposed methodologies and towards assessing the true gap with full original data training. Following prior work in dataset distillation (Yin et al., 2023), we focus on the decoupled training framework to save computation and memory consumption on large-scale ImageNet-21K, and the procedures are listed below:  

Building A Strong Compression Model on ImagNet-21K. For the squeezing model pretraining, we use a relatively large label smooth of 0.2 together with Cutout (DeVries & Taylor, 2017) and RandAugment (Cubuk et al.4. This recipe help achieves ${\sim}2\%$ improvement over the default training Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K, as provided in Table 5.  

Curriculum Training for Better Representation of Synthetic Data. A well crafted curriculum data augmentation is employed during the synthesis stage to enhance the representational capability of the synthetic data. This step is crucial, serving to enrich the generated images by embedding more knowledge accumulated from the original dataset, thereby making them more informative. Detailed procedures will be further described in the following Section 2.3.  



\section{2.3 CURRICULUM DATA AUGMENTATION  }


In $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ (Yin et al., 2023) approach, the key of data synthesis revolves around utilizing the gradient information emanating from both the semantic class and the predictions of the pretrained squeezing model, paired with BN distribution matching. Let $\left({\pmb x},{\pmb y}\right)$ be an example $\textbf{\em x}$ for optimization and its corresponding one-hot label $\textit{\textbf{y}}$ for the pretrained squeezing model. Throughout synthesis process the squeezing model is frozen for recovering the encoded information ensuring consistency and reliability in the generated data. Let $\bar{\mathcal{T}}(\bar{\mathbf{{x}}})$ be the target training distribution from which the data synthesis process should ultimately learn a function of desired trajectory, where $\tau$ is a data transformation function to augment input sample to various levels of difficulties. Following Bengio et al. (2009), a weigh $0\,\leq\,W_{s}(x)\,\leq\,1$ is defined and applied to example $\textbf{\em x}$ at stage $s$ in the curriculum sequence. The distribution is:  

![](images/3e4ad0c4fae25af40b1e45d5b8eb401babc0c8d33180c1ad964f5e60418e169c.jpg)  
Figure 3: Curriculum data synthesis.  

$$
D_{s}(x)\propto W_{s}(x){\mathcal T}(x)\quad\forall x
$$  

In our scenario, since the varying difficulties are governed by the data transformation function $\tau$ , we can straightforwardly employ $W_{s}(x)=1$ across all stages. Consequently, the training distribution solely depends on $\dot{\tau}(x)$ and can be simplified as follows:  

$$
D(x)\propto{\mathcal{T}}(x)\quad\forall x
$$  

By integrating curriculum learning within the data synthesis phase, this procedure can be defined as:  

Definition 1 (Curriculum Data Synthesis). In the data synthesis optimization, the corresponding sequence of distributions $D(x)$ will be a curriculum if there is an increment in the entropy of these distributions, i.e., the difficulty of the transformed input samples escalating and become increasingly challenging for the pre-trained model to predict as the training progresses.  

Thus, the key for our curriculum data synthesis becomes how to design $\tau(x)$ across different training iterations. The following discusses several strategies to construct this in the curriculum scheme.  

Baseline: Constant Learning (CTL). This is the regular training method where all training examples are typically treated equally. Each sample from the training dataset has an equal chance of being transformed in a given batch, assuming no difficulty imbalance or biases across different training iterations.  

CTL is straightforward to implement since we do not have to rank or organize examples based on difficulty. In practice, we simply use $\mathbf{\deltax}_{\mathcal{T}}\leftarrow$ RandomResizedCrop $\mathbf{\Psi}(\pmb{x}_{s}$ , min crop $=$ $\beta_{l}$ , $\mathtt{m a x\_c r o p}=\beta_{\mathrm{u}})$ , where $\beta_{l}$ and $\beta_{\mathbf{u}}$ are the constant lower and upper bounds of crop scale.  

Curriculum Learning (CL). As shown in Algorithm 1, in our CL, data samples are organized based on their difficulty. The difficulty level of the cropped region can be managed by defining the lower and upper scopes for the area ratio of the crop. This enables the assurance that specific crops of the image (small details or broader context) are included in the cropped region. For the difficulty adjustment, the rate at which more difficult examples are introduced and the criteria used to define difficulty are adjusted dynamically as predetermined using the following schedulers.  

Step. Step scheduler reduces the minimal scale by a factor for every fixed or specified number of iterations.  

Linear. Linear scheduler starts with a high initial value and decreases it linearly by a factor $\gamma$ to a minimum value over the whole training.  

Cosine. Cosine scheduler modulates the distribution according to the cosine function of current iteration number, yielding a smoother and more gradual adjustment compared to step-based methods. As shown in Figure 4, the factor distribution manages the difficulty level of crops with a milestone.

After receiving the transformed input ${\mathbf{}}x_{7}$ , we update it by aligning between the final classification label and intermediate Batch Normalization (BN) statistics from the original data. Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, possess a boosted representation capacity compared to the original datasets. This attribute can be strategically harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. We have further validated the effectiveness of our introduced CDA within various continual learning scenarios. Following the setting outlined in $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ (Yin et al., 2023), we conducted 5-step and 10-step class-incremental experiments on Tiny-ImageNet, aligning our results against the baseline $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ and a randomly selected subset on Tiny-ImageNet for comparative analysis. Illustrated in Figure 7, our CDA distilled dataset notably surpasses $\mathrm{SRe^{2}L}$ , exhibiting an average advantage of $3.8\%$ and $4.5\%$ on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning assignments respectively. \section{4 RELATED WORK  }


Dataset distillation strives to form a compact, synthetic dataset, retaining crucial information from the original large-scale dataset. This approach facilitates easier handling, reduces training time, and aims for performance comparable to using the full dataset. Prior solutions typically fall under four categories: Meta-Model Matching optimizes for model transferability on distilled data, with an outer-loop for synthetic data updates, and an inner-loop for network training, such as DD (Wang et al., 2020), KIP (Nguyen et al., 2021), RFAD (Loo et al., 2022), FRePo (Zhou et al., 2022) and LinBa (Deng & Russakovsky, 2022); Gradient Matching performs a one-step distance matching between models, such as DC (Zhao et al., 2020), DSA (Zhao & Bilen, 2021), DCC (Lee et al., 2022) and IDC (Kim et al., 2022b); Distribution Matching directly matches the distribution of original and synthetic data with a single-level optimization, such as DM (Zhao & Bilen, 2023), CAFE (Wang et al., 2022), HaBa (Liu et al., 2022a), KFS (Lee et al., 2022); Trajectory Matching matches the weight trajectories of models trained on original and synthetic data in multiple steps, methods include MTT (Cazenavette et al., 2022b) and TESLA (Cui et al., 2023). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced the idea of Curriculum Learning, proposing that training models with a curriculum can help in better optimization and can lead to better generalization. Subsequent works (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019) have explored various strategies for defining and designing curricula, such as self-paced learning (Kumar et al., 2010), where the model itself determines the learning pace and difficulty progression.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


We have presented a new CDA framework focused on curriculum-based data synthesis for large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical framework with detailed pertaining for compressing knowledge, data synthesis for recovery, and post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the distillation of ImageNet-21K to $50\times$ smaller while maintaining competitive accuracy levels. In regular benchmarks, such as ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show the capability of our synthetic data on cross-model generalization and continual learning. Given the escalating scale of both models and datasets in recent years, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and large-scale models has gained unprecedented prominence and urgency. We hope our contributions in this work will infuse novel insights and pave new avenues within this domain, encouraging further exploration and development in the field of large-scale dataset distillation. Our future work will focus on distilling more modalities like language and speech.  

Reproducibility Statement. Our synthetic data is available anonymously at link and our code is also provided in submission.

Title: Dataset Distillation in the Large Data Era

Abstract
Dataset distillation aims to generate a smaller but representative subset from a large dataset, enabling efficient model training while maintaining performance on the original test distribution. This technique is a cornerstone for democratizing access to large-scale AI, allowing researchers with limited resources to engage in foundational model development and helping to mitigate data privacy concerns by working with condensed, non-raw data. Prior works have aligned distilled data with various aspects of the original datasets, such as training weight trajectories, gradients, and feature distributions. In this work, we definitively show how to distill various large-scale datasets, including full ImageNet-1K/21K at a standard 224×224 resolution, to achieve the best accuracy over all previous approaches, including SRe²L, TESLA, and MTT. We introduce a simple yet effective Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) during data synthesis, achieving accuracies of 63.2% (IPC 50) on ImageNet-1K and 36.1% (IPC 20) on ImageNet-21K. By integrating all our enhancements, the proposed model decisively beats the current state-of-the-art by more than 4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and, for the first time, reduces the gap to its full-data training counterpart to less than an absolute 15%. Furthermore, this work represents the inaugural and successful application of dataset distillation to the larger-scale ImageNet-21K under the standard 224×224 resolution. Our distilled ImageNet-21K dataset (20 IPC, 2K recovery budget) is available anonymously at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12pC0GDTURdYLThAbVHkTw2lkF2KF_85i?usp=sharing.

1 INTRODUCTION
Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) has attracted considerable attention across computer vision (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) and natural language processing (Sucholutsky & Schonlau, 2021; Maekawa et al., 2023). This task is fundamental for optimizing the condensation of massive datasets into smaller, representative subsets that preserve essential features, enabling models to learn as effectively from the distilled data as from the original. As data and model scales grow, dataset distillation becomes critical in the large data era, addressing storage, computational, and processing challenges. This technique democratizes research, allowing those with limited resources to participate in state-of-the-art foundational model training and application development, such as affordable ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022). It also holds significant potential to alleviate data privacy concerns by excluding raw, personally identifiable data from the distilled version.

We verify our approach on Tiny-ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009), and ImageNet-21K (Ridnik et al., 2021). 3.2 CIFAR-100
Comparison results with baseline methods on CIFAR-100 are in Table 1. Validation accuracy improves significantly with extended training budgets. Compared to reproduced SRe²L on ImageNet-21K, our approach attains an average elevation of 5.3% under IPC 10/20, highlighting efficacy in maintaining dataset essence despite high compression and showcasing potential advancements over existing methods.

As shown in Figure 4, distillation progress is divided into two phases by a milestone. Validation accuracy rises as batch size reduces, peaking at 16, suggesting smaller batch sizes enhance performance on small-scale synthetic datasets. Ensuring distilled datasets generalize across models unseen during recovery remains challenging, as prior approaches optimized synthetic images to overfit the recovery model. In Table 7, we deploy our ImageNet-1K distilled datasets to train validation models, attaining over 60% Top-1 accuracy with most models. Our performance surpasses SRe²L across all validation models of various architectures. The distilled datasets show reduced dependency on specific recovery models, alleviating overfitting issues. Table 8 further substantiates CDA's efficacy in distilling ImageNet-21K.

Thus, curriculum data augmentation improves global image prediction and reduces bias and overfitting in post-training on simpler, cropped images of SRe²L.

SRe²L images (upper line) exhibit significant noise, indicating slow early recovery. In contrast, due to mostly entire image optimization early on, CDA images (lower line) establish the entire image layout rapidly, reducing noise. Final synthetic images contain more visual information directly related to the target class (Plant). This highlights CDA's ability to synthesize images with enhanced visual coherence to the target class, offering a more efficient recovery process.

Training cost comparison with SRe²L. We highlight that there is no additional training cost between CDA and SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) when recovery iterations are the same.

Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, possess boosted representation capacity, which can be harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. As shown in Figure 7, our CDA distilled dataset notably surpasses SRe²L, exhibiting average advantages of 3.8% and 4.5% on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning, respectively, demonstrating substantial benefits in mitigating continual learning complexities.

4 RELATED WORK
Dataset distillation forms compact, synthetic datasets retaining crucial information from large-scale originals, facilitating easier handling, reduced training time, and comparable performance. Prior solutions typically fall under: Meta-Model Matching (e.g., DD, KIP, RFAD, FRePo, LinBa); Gradient Matching (e.g., DC, DSA, DCC, IDC); Distribution Matching (e.g., DM, CAFE, HaBa, KFS); Trajectory Matching (e.g., MTT, TESLA). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced Curriculum Learning, proposing that training with a curriculum aids optimization and generalization. Subsequent works explored strategies like self-paced learning.

5 CONCLUSION
We have presented a new CDA framework for curriculum-based data synthesis in large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical framework with detailed pretraining for knowledge compression, data synthesis for recovery, and post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the distillation of ImageNet-21K to 50× smaller while maintaining competitive accuracy. On regular benchmarks like ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show our synthetic data's capability in cross-model generalization and continual learning. Given the escalating scale of models and datasets, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and models has gained unprecedented prominence. We hope our contributions infuse novel insights and pave new avenues in this domain, encouraging further exploration in large-scale dataset distillation. Future work will focus on distilling more modalities like language and speech.

Reproducibility Statement. Our synthetic data is available anonymously at the provided link, and our code is also provided in submission.

Initialize: x_0 from a standard normal distribution
for step s from 0 to S-1 do
    if s ≤ T then
        α ← { β_l + γ * (β_u - s/T) if step; β_l + γ * (β_u - s/T) if linear; β_l + γ * (β_u + cos(π * s/T))/2 if cosine }
    else
        α ← β_l
    end
    x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop(x_s, min crop = α, max_crop = β_u)
    x′_𝒯 ← x_𝒯 optimized w.r.t φ_θ and y in Eq. 6.
    x_{s+1} ← ReverseRandomResizedCrop(x_s, x′_𝒯)
end
return x ← x_S

3 EXPERIMENTS
3.1 DATASETS AND IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
We verify our approach on Tiny-ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009), and ImageNet-21K (Ridnik et al., 2021). For evaluation, we train models from scratch on synthetic distilled datasets and report Top-1 accuracy on real validation datasets. Default lower and upper crop scale bounds β_l and β_u are 0.08 and 1.0, respectively. The decay γ is 0.92.

3.2 CIFAR-100
Comparison results with baseline methods on CIFAR-100 are in Table 1. Validation accuracy improves significantly with extended training budgets. Our CDA's best validation accuracy outperforms all baselines under 10 and 50 IPC. Our results can potentially improve further with increased budgets. Overall, CDA is also applicable to small-scale dataset distillation.

3.3 TINY-IMAGENET
Results on Tiny-ImageNet are in the first group of Table 3. Our CDA surpasses SRE²L with average improvements of 7.7% and 3.4% under IPC 50 and IPC 100 across ResNet-{18, 50, 101} validation models. Importantly, CDA is the inaugural approach to reduce the Top-1 accuracy gap to less than 10% between the distilled dataset (IPC 100) and full Tiny-ImageNet, signifying a breakthrough.

3.4 IMAGENET-1K
Constant Learning (CTL). We use ResNet-18 and 1K recovery synthesis. As shown in Table 2, results for very easy (α ≥ 0.8) or hard (α ≤ 0.4) scenarios fall below the reproduced SRe²L baseline accuracy of 44.90%. Using a larger cropped range avoids extreme scenarios, enhancing performance. Appropriate lower and upper bounds are crucial for constant learning, highlighting the importance of curriculum data augmentation.

Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). We use a reverse step scheduler, starting with default crop range and transitioning at a milestone to optimize the whole image, shifting from challenging to simpler optimizations. Other settings follow the recovery recipe on ResNet-18 for 1K iterations. Table 4 shows RCL results; a smaller step milestone indicates earlier difficulty transition. RCL does not improve generated dataset quality compared to the SRe²L baseline (44.90% accuracy).

Curriculum Learning (CL). Our CDA experiments follow the recovery recipe of SRe²L's best results for 4K iterations. As shown in the second group of Table 3, compared to the strong baseline SRe²L, CDA enhances validation accuracy with average margins of 6.1%, 4.3%, and 3.2% on ResNet-18, 50, 101 across varying IPC configurations. As shown in Figure 1, CDA with merely 1K recovery iterations surpasses SRe²L with 4K iterations, substantiating CDA's efficacy in large-scale dataset distillation.

3.5 IMAGENET-21K
Pretraining Results. Table 5 presents accuracy for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet21K-P with varying initial weights. Models pretrained by us and initialized with ImageNet-1K weights show a 2.0% improvement, while randomly initialized models achieve marginally superior accuracy. We use these pretrained models to recover ImageNet-21K data and assign labels to synthetic images. Data recovering is more difficult from randomly initialized pretrained models than from ImageNet-1K initialized ones. Thus, our experiments employ CDA on pretrained models initialized with ImageNet-1K weights.

Validation Results. As shown in the final group of Table 3, we validate on distilled ImageNet-21K with IPC 10 and 20, yielding compression ratios of 100× and 50×. With IPC 10 (1% of full dataset), validation accuracy surpasses 20% and 30% on ResNet-18 and ResNet-50/101, respectively. Compared to reproduced SRe²L on ImageNet-21K, our approach attains an average elevation of 5.3% under IPC 10/20, highlighting efficacy in maintaining dataset essence despite high compression and showcasing potential advancements over existing methods.

3.6 ABLATION
Curriculum Scheduler. We present three curriculum schedulers (step, linear, cosine) to manipulate lower bounds on data crop augmentation. As shown in Figure 4, distillation progress is divided into two phases by a milestone. Both linear and cosine with continuous decay show robustness across milestone configurations and enhance accuracy when the milestone is met later, as shown in Table 5. Cosine marginally outperforms linear in accuracy towards the end. We implement the cosine scheduler with a milestone percentage of 1.0 to modulate the minimum crop ratio throughout synthesis.

Batch Size in Post-training. We ablate the influence of smaller batch sizes on generalization when synthetic data is limited. Results on distilled ImageNet-21K from ResNet-18 are in Table 6. Validation accuracy rises as batch size reduces, peaking at 16, suggesting smaller batch sizes enhance performance on small-scale synthetic datasets. However, this leads to more frequent data loading and lower GPU utilization, extending training times. We chose a batch size of 32 to balance time and performance.

3.7 ANALYSIS
Cross-Model Generalization. Ensuring distilled datasets generalize across models unseen during recovery remains challenging, as prior approaches optimized synthetic images to overfit the recovery model. In Table 7, we deploy our ImageNet-1K distilled datasets to train validation models, attaining over 60% Top-1 accuracy with most models. Our performance surpasses SRe²L across all validation models of various architectures. The distilled datasets show reduced dependency on specific recovery models, alleviating overfitting issues. Table 8 further substantiates CDA's efficacy in distilling ImageNet-21K.

Impact of Curriculum. To study curriculum's advantage on synthetic image characteristics, we evaluate Top-1 accuracy on CDA, SRe²L, and real ImageNet-1K training set, using mean of random 10-crop and global images, classified by PyTorch's pre-trained MobileNet-V2. As shown in Table 9, CDA images closely resemble real ImageNet images in prediction accuracies, better than SRe²L. Thus, curriculum data augmentation improves global image prediction and reduces bias and overfitting in post-training on simpler, cropped images of SRe²L.

Visualization and Discussion. Figure 6 compares gradient synthetic images at recovery steps {100, 500, 1,000, 2,000} to illustrate differences between SRe²L and CDA. SRe²L images (upper line) exhibit significant noise, indicating slow early recovery. In contrast, due to mostly entire image optimization early on, CDA images (lower line) establish the entire image layout rapidly, reducing noise. Final synthetic images contain more visual information directly related to the target class (Plant). This highlights CDA's ability to synthesize images with enhanced visual coherence to the target class, offering a more efficient recovery process.

Training cost comparison with SRe²L. We highlight that there is no additional training cost between CDA and SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) when recovery iterations are the same.

3.8 APPLICATION: CONTINUAL LEARNING
Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, possess boosted representation capacity, which can be harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. We validated CDA's effectiveness in continual learning scenarios. Following SRe²L's setting (Yin et al., 2023), we conducted 5-step and 10-step class-incremental experiments on Tiny-ImageNet, comparing against SRe²L and a randomly selected subset. As shown in Figure 7, our CDA distilled dataset notably surpasses SRe²L, exhibiting average advantages of 3.8% and 4.5% on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning, respectively, demonstrating substantial benefits in mitigating continual learning complexities.

4 RELATED WORK
Dataset distillation forms compact, synthetic datasets retaining crucial information from large-scale originals, facilitating easier handling, reduced training time, and comparable performance. Prior solutions typically fall under: Meta-Model Matching (e.g., DD, KIP, RFAD, FRePo, LinBa); Gradient Matching (e.g., DC, DSA, DCC, IDC); Distribution Matching (e.g., DM, CAFE, HaBa, KFS); Trajectory Matching (e.g., MTT, TESLA). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced Curriculum Learning, proposing that training with a curriculum aids optimization and generalization. Subsequent works explored strategies like self-paced learning.

5 CONCLUSION
We have presented a new CDA framework for curriculum-based data synthesis in large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical framework with detailed pretraining for knowledge compression, data synthesis for recovery, and post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the distillation of ImageNet-21K to 50× smaller while maintaining competitive accuracy. On regular benchmarks like ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show our synthetic data's capability in cross-model generalization and continual learning. Given the escalating scale of models and datasets, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and models has gained unprecedented prominence. We hope our contributions infuse novel insights and pave new avenues in this domain, encouraging further exploration in large-scale dataset distillation. Future work will focus on distilling more modalities like language and speech.

Reproducibility Statement. Our synthetic data is available anonymously at the provided link, and our code is also provided in submission.
