Title: Dataset Distillation in the Large Data Era: Pioneering Efficient Knowledge Compression Through Curriculum Learning

Abstract
Dataset distillation represents a pivotal methodology for generating a compact yet highly representative synthetic subset from a massive original dataset. This process enables models to be trained with remarkable efficiency, while still being evaluated on the original testing distribution to achieve performance that is not merely decent but truly competitive with full-data training. Numerous prior works have endeavored to align synthetic data with diverse aspects of the original datasets, including matching training weight trajectories, gradient signals, and feature or BatchNorm distributions. In this seminal work, we definitively demonstrate how to distill various large-scale datasets, including the full ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-21K under the conventional input resolution of 224×224, to achieve the best accuracy over all previous approaches, such as SRe²L, TESLA, and MTT. To accomplish this breakthrough, we introduce a simple yet profoundly effective Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) strategy during the data synthesis phase. This innovation obtains unprecedented accuracy on large-scale ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-21K, achieving 63.2% (IPC 50) and 36.1% (IPC 20), respectively. Ultimately, by integrating all our enhancements, the proposed model decisively beats the current state-of-the-art by more than 4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and, for the first time, reduces the performance gap to its full-data training counterpart to less than an absolute 15%. Moreover, this work constitutes the inaugural and successful demonstration of dataset distillation on the larger-scale ImageNet-21K under the standard 224×224 resolution, marking a significant milestone. Our distilled ImageNet-21K dataset of 20 IPC with a 2K recovery budget is available anonymously at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12pC0GDTURdYLThAbVHkTw2lkF2KF_85i?usp=sharing.

1 INTRODUCTION
Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) has attracted considerable and growing attention across various fields of computer vision (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) and natural language processing (Sucholutsky & Schonlau, 2021; Maekawa et al., 2023). This critical task aims to optimize the process of condensing massive, unwieldy datasets into a significantly smaller, yet maximally representative synthetic subset. The core objective is to preserve the essential features and characteristics that would allow a model to learn from scratch as effectively from the distilled dataset as it would from the original, prohibitively large dataset. As the scale of data and models continues to grow exponentially, this dataset distillation concept becomes even more critically important in the contemporary large data era, where datasets are often so voluminous that they pose severe storage, computational, and processing challenges. Fundamentally, dataset distillation can level the playing field, empowering researchers and practitioners with limited computation and storage resources to participate in state-of-the-art foundational model training and application development—such as affordable versions of systems like ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022)—within the current large data and large model regime. Moreover, by working with distilled datasets, there is substantial potential to alleviate pressing data privacy concerns, as raw, personally identifiable data points can be excluded from the distilled version.

Recently, there has been a dominant and significant trend in adopting large models and large data across virtually all research and application areas. Yet, many prior dataset distillation methods (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022; Cazenavette et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2022a; Cui et al., 2023) have predominantly and narrowly targeted smaller datasets like CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet, and downsampled ImageNet-1K, finding it profoundly challenging to scale their frameworks effectively for larger, real-world datasets such as the full ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). This clearly suggests that these prior approaches have not fully evolved in line with contemporary advancements and the dominant methodologies required for modern large-scale applications.

In this groundbreaking study, we extend our focus decisively beyond the ImageNet-1K dataset, venturing into the previously uncharted territories of the full ImageNet-21K (Deng et al., 2009; Ridnik et al., 2021) at a conventional resolution of 224×224. This marks a pioneering and successful effort in handling such a vast dataset for the dataset distillation task. Our approach harnesses a straightforward yet exceptionally effective curriculum learning framework. We meticulously address each technical aspect and craft a robust, comprehensive strategy to train effectively on the complete ImageNet-21K, ensuring comprehensive knowledge is captured and compressed. Specifically, following a prior study (Yin et al., 2023), our approach initially trains a model to encapsulate knowledge from the original datasets within its dense parameters. However, we introduce a novel and superior training recipe that surpasses the results of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K. During the critical data recovery or synthesis phase, we employ a strategic learning scheme where partial image crops are sequentially updated based on the difficulty of regions: transitioning either from simple to difficult, or vice versa. This progression is modulated by dynamically adjusting the lower and upper bounds of the RandomResizedCrop data augmentation throughout varying training iterations. Remarkably, we observe that this straightforward learning approach substantially and consistently improves the quality of synthesized data. In this paper, we delve comprehensively into three distinct learning paradigms for data synthesis linked to the curriculum learning framework. The first is the standard curriculum learning, followed by its alternative approach, reverse curriculum learning. Lastly, we also consider the basic and previously employed method of constant learning.

Curriculum Learning (CL) and Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). In traditional, unstructured learning scenarios, a model is typically trained on a dataset without paying specific attention to the order or difficulty of the data samples. However, humans and animals often learn far more effectively when they are first introduced to simpler concepts and then gradually exposed to more complex ones. This established educational concept, known as “curriculum learning” (Bengio et al., 2009), has been successfully borrowed and applied to the domain of machine learning (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019). Unlike curriculum learning that starts with the easiest tasks, reverse curriculum learning begins with the most challenging ones. This alternative learning strategy is essentially a backtracking method where, if a model struggles with a particularly difficult task, it is allowed to fall back to simpler versions of the task to reinforce understanding.

How to Change the Difficulties of Training Samples? RandomResizedCrop operates by randomly cropping an image to a certain area and then resizing it back to a pre-defined size, ensuring that the model is exposed to different regions and scales of the original image during training. As clearly illustrated in Figure 2, the difficulty level of the cropped region can be precisely controlled by specifying the lower and upper bounds for the area ratio of the crop. This mechanism can be used strategically to ensure that certain portions of the image—whether small details or larger context—are present in the cropped region. If we aim to make the learning process more challenging, we simply reduce the minimum crop ratio. This way, the model will often see only small, limited portions of the image and will have to learn from those constrained contexts. Conversely, if we want the model to see a larger context more frequently to grasp holistic features, we increase the minimum crop ratio. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive and detailed study on how the gradual difficulty changes, governed by the sampling strategy, directly influence the optimization of data generation and the final quality of synthetic data for the dataset distillation task. Our proposed Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is a heuristic, intuitive, yet highly effective approach to simulate a curriculum learning procedure. Moreover, it is demonstrably and highly effective on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K and 21K, achieving definitive state-of-the-art performance on dataset distillation.

Our Motivation and Intuition. Both SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) and our proposed CDA method utilize local batch mean and variance statistics to match the global statistics of the entire original dataset, synthesizing data by applying gradient updates directly to the image pixels. The profound impact of such a strategy is that the initial few iterations critically set the stage for the global structure of the ultimately generated image. However, SRe²L does not capitalize on this characteristic effectively. In stark contrast, CDA efficiently and fully exploits it by initially employing large crops to capture a more accurate and complete outline of the object. As the process progresses, CDA incrementally and systematically reduces the crop size to enhance the finer, local details of the object, thereby significantly elevating the overall quality and fidelity of the synthesized data.

In this work, we conduct extensive and rigorous experiments on the Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-21K datasets. Employing a resolution of 224×224 and IPC 50 on ImageNet-1K, the proposed approach attains an impressive and leading accuracy of 63.2%, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial and clear margins. As illustrated in Figure 1, our proposed CDA consistently outperforms SRe²L by 4~6% across different architectures under 50 IPC, on both 1K and 4K recovery budgets. When tested on the massive ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, our method achieves a top-1 accuracy of 35.3%, which is closely competitive, exhibiting only a minimal gap compared to the model pretrained with the full data, at 44.5%, while using 50× fewer training samples—a testament to its remarkable efficiency.

2 APPROACH
2.1 DATASET DISTILLATION
The fundamental goal of dataset distillation is to derive a concise synthetic dataset that maintains a significant and useful proportion of the information contained in the original, much larger dataset. Suppose there is a large labeled dataset 𝒟ₒ = {(x₁, y₁), …, (x_{|𝒟ₒ|}, y_{|𝒟ₒ|})}, our target is to formulate a compact distilled dataset, represented as 𝒟_d = {(x′₁, y′₁), …, (x′_{|𝒟_d|}, y′_{|𝒟_d|})}, where y′ is the soft label corresponding to synthetic data x′, and |𝒟_d| ≪ |𝒟ₒ|, preserving the essential information from the original dataset 𝒟ₒ. The learning objective based on this distilled synthetic dataset is formulated as:
    θ_{𝒟_d} = arg min_θ ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ)
    ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ) = 𝔼_{(x′, y′) ∈ 𝒟_d} [ ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x′), y′ ) ]
where ℓ is the regular loss function such as the soft cross-entropy, and ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}} is the model. The primary objective of the dataset distillation task is to generate synthetic data aimed at attaining a specific or minimal performance disparity on the original validation data, when models are trained on the synthetic data versus the original dataset, respectively. Thus, we aim to optimize the synthetic data 𝒟_d by:
    arg min_{𝒟_d, |𝒟_d|} ( sup { | ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟ₒ}}(x), y ) - ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x), y ) | }_{(x, y) ∼ 𝒟ₒ} )
Then, we learn the <data, label> pairs ∈ 𝒟_d along with the corresponding number of distilled data points in each class.

2.2 DATASET DISTILLATION ON LARGE-SCALE DATASETS
Currently, the prevailing majority of research studies within dataset distillation mainly employ datasets of a scale up to ImageNet-1K (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) as their benchmarking standards. In this section, we demonstrate clearly how to construct a strong baseline on ImageNet-21K (this approach is equivalently applicable to ImageNet-1K) by incorporating key insights presented in recent studies, complemented by conventional yet effective optimization techniques. Our proposed baseline is demonstrated definitively to achieve state-of-the-art performance. We believe this provides substantial contributions towards understanding the true impact of proposed methodologies and towards accurately assessing the true performance gap with full original data training. Following prior work in dataset distillation (Yin et al., 2023), we focus on the decoupled training framework to save computation and memory consumption on large-scale ImageNet-21K, and the procedures are listed comprehensively below:

Building A Strong Compression Model on ImageNet-21K. For the squeezing model pretraining, we use a relatively large label smoothing factor of 0.2 together with Cutout (DeVries & Taylor, 2017) and RandAugment (Cubuk et al., 2020). This recipe helps achieve a significant ∼2% improvement over the default training of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K, as provided in Table 5.

Curriculum Training for Better Representation of Synthetic Data. A well-crafted and strategic curriculum data augmentation is employed during the synthesis stage to enhance the representational capability and richness of the synthetic data. This step is crucial, serving to enrich the generated images by embedding more knowledge accumulated from the original dataset, thereby making them more informative and effective for training. Detailed procedures will be further described in the following Section 2.3.

2.3 CURRICULUM DATA AUGMENTATION
In the SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) approach, the key mechanism of data synthesis revolves around utilizing the gradient information emanating from both the semantic class and the predictions of the pretrained squeezing model, paired with BN distribution matching. Let (x, y) be an example x for optimization and its corresponding one-hot label y for the pretrained squeezing model. Throughout the synthesis process the squeezing model is frozen for recovering the encoded information, ensuring consistency and reliability in the generated data. Let 𝒯(x̄) be the target training distribution from which the data synthesis process should ultimately learn, where τ is a data transformation function to augment the input sample to various levels of difficulties. Following Bengio et al. (2009), a weight 0 ≤ W_s(x) ≤ 1 is defined and applied to example x at stage s in the curriculum sequence. The distribution is:
    D_s(x) ∝ W_s(x) 𝒯(x) ∀ x
In our specific scenario, since the varying difficulties are governed entirely by the data transformation function τ, we can straightforwardly employ W_s(x) = 1 across all stages. Consequently, the training distribution depends solely on τ(x) and can be simplified as follows:
    D(x) ∝ 𝒯(x) ∀ x
By integrating curriculum learning within the data synthesis phase, this procedure can be formally defined as:

Definition 1 (Curriculum Data Synthesis). In the data synthesis optimization, the corresponding sequence of distributions D(x) will constitute a curriculum if there is a measurable increment in the entropy of these distributions, i.e., the difficulty of the transformed input samples escalates and they become increasingly challenging for the pre-trained model to predict as the training progresses.

Thus, the key for our curriculum data synthesis becomes how to design τ(x) strategically across different training iterations. The following discusses several concrete strategies to construct this within the curriculum scheme.

Baseline: Constant Learning (CTL). This is the regular training method where all training examples are typically treated equally throughout. Each sample from the training dataset has an equal chance of being transformed in a given batch, assuming no explicit difficulty imbalance or biases across different training iterations. CTL is straightforward to implement since we do not have to rank or organize examples based on difficulty. In practice, we simply use x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop Ψ(x_s, min_crop = β_l, max_crop = β_u), where β_l and β_u are the constant lower and upper bounds of the crop scale.

Curriculum Learning (CL). As shown in Algorithm 1, in our CL framework, data samples are organized strategically based on their difficulty. The difficulty level of the cropped region can be managed precisely by defining the lower and upper scopes for the area ratio of the crop. This enables the assurance that specific crops of the image—whether small details or broader context—are included in the cropped region at appropriate stages. For the difficulty adjustment, the rate at which more difficult examples are introduced and the criteria used to define difficulty are adjusted dynamically as predetermined using the following schedulers.
    Step. The step scheduler reduces the minimal scale by a fixed factor for every specified number of iterations.
    Linear. The linear scheduler starts with a high initial value and decreases it linearly by a factor γ to a minimum value over the whole training duration.
    Cosine. The cosine scheduler modulates the distribution according to the cosine function of the current iteration number, yielding a smoother and more gradual adjustment compared to step-based methods. As shown in Figure 4, the factor distribution manages the difficulty level of crops with a defined milestone.

Data Synthesis by Recovering. After receiving the transformed input x_𝒯, we update it by aligning between the final classification label and intermediate Batch Normalization (BN) statistics from the original data. This critical stage forces the synthesized images to capture the essential shape and distribution of the original image distribution. The learning goal for this stage can be formulated precisely as follows:

Algorithm 1: Our Curriculum Data Augmentation via RandomResizedCrop
Input: squeezed model ϕ_θ, recovery iteration S, curriculum milestone T, target label y, default lower and upper bounds of crop scale β_l and β_u in RandomResizedCrop, decay of lower scale bound γ
Output: synthetic image x
Initialize: x₀ from a standard normal distribution
for step s from 0 to S-1 do
    if s ≤ T then

               β_l + γ * (β_u + cos(π * s/T)) / 2 if cosine scheduler }
    else
        α ← β_l
    end if
    x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop(x_s, min_crop = α, max_crop = β_u)
    x′_𝒯 ← x_𝒯 is optimized w.r.t ϕ_θ and y in Eq. 6.
    x_{s+1} ← ReverseRandomResizedCrop(x_s, x′_𝒯)
end for
return x ← x_S

    x′_𝒯 = arg min ℓ( ϕ_θ(x_𝒯), y ) + ℛ_reg
where ℛ_reg is the regularization term used in Yin et al. (2023). ϕ_θ is the pretrained squeezing model and remains frozen in this stage. The entire training procedure is illustrated comprehensively in Figure 3.

3 EXPERIMENTS
3.1 DATASETS AND IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
We verify the effectiveness and robustness of our approach on various ImageNet-scale datasets, including Tiny-ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009), and ImageNet-21K (Ridnik et al., 2021). For a thorough evaluation, we train models from scratch on the synthetic distilled datasets and report the Top-1 accuracy on the real validation datasets. The default lower and upper bounds of crop scales β_l and β_u are set to 0.08 and 1.0, respectively. The decay factor γ is set to 0.92.

3.2 CIFAR-100
Comparison results with baseline methods on the CIFAR-100 dataset are presented in Table 1. We observe a clear trend that the validation model’s accuracy exhibits a significant and consistent improvement along with the extension of training budgets. Our CDA’s best validation accuracy definitively outperforms all baselines under both 10 and 50 IPC settings. Furthermore, our reported results have the clear potential to be further improved as training budgets increase. Overall, our CDA method is also successfully applicable to small-scale dataset distillation, demonstrating its versatility.

3.3 TINY-IMAGENET
Results on the Tiny-ImageNet dataset are detailed in the first group of Table 3. Our CDA surpasses SRe²L with average improvements of 7.7% and 3.4% under IPC 50 and IPC 100 settings across ResNet-{18, 50, 101} validation models, respectively. We provide the result comparison with more methods in the appendix. Importantly, CDA stands as the inaugural approach to diminish the Top-1 accuracy performance disparity to less than 10% between the distilled dataset employing IPC 100 and the full Tiny-ImageNet, signifying a major breakthrough on this dataset.

3.4 IMAGENET-1K
Constant Learning (CTL). We leverage a ResNet-18 and employ a 1K recovery budget for synthesizing data. As observed in Table 2, the results for exceedingly straightforward or challenging scenarios fall below the reproduced SRe²L baseline accuracy of 44.90%, especially when α ≥ 0.8 in the easy regime and α ≤ 0.4 in the hard regime. Thus, the results presented in Table 2 suggest convincingly that adopting a larger, more moderate cropped range assists in circumventing extreme scenarios, whether easy or hard, culminating in enhanced performance. A noteworthy observation is the crucial role of appropriate lower and upper bounds for constant learning in boosting validation accuracy. This highlights the fundamental importance of employing strategic curriculum data augmentation strategies in data synthesis.

Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). We use a reverse step scheduler in the RCL experiments, starting with the default cropped range from β_l to β_u and transitioning at the milestone point to optimize the whole image, thereby shifting from challenging to simpler optimizations. Other settings follow the recovery recipe on ResNet-18 for 1K recovery iterations. Table 4 shows the RCL results; a smaller step milestone indicates an earlier difficulty transition. The findings reveal clearly that RCL does not improve the generated dataset’s quality compared to the baseline SRe²L, which has 44.90% accuracy.

Curriculum Learning (CL). Our CDA experiments follow the recovery recipe of SRe²L’s best results for 4K recovery iterations. As illustrated in the second group of Table 3, when compared to the strong baseline SRe²L, CDA enhances the validation accuracy decisively, exhibiting average margins of 6.1%, 4.3%, and 3.2% on ResNet-18, 50, and 101 across varying IPC configurations. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 1, the results achieved with our CDA utilizing merely 1K recovery iterations surpass those of SRe²L encompassing the entire 4K iterations. These results substantiate definitively the efficacy and effectiveness of applying CDA in large-scale dataset distillation.

3.5 IMAGENET-21K
Pretraining Results. Table 5 presents the accuracy for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet-21K-P, considering varying initial weight configurations. Models pretrained by us and initialized with ImageNet-1K weights exhibit commendable accuracy, showing a clear 2.0% improvement, while models initialized randomly achieve marginally superior accuracy. We utilize these pretrained models to recover ImageNet-21K data and to assign labels to the synthetic images generated. An intriguing observation is the heightened difficulty in data recovering from pretrained models that are initialized randomly compared to those initialized with ImageNet-1K weights. Thus, our experiments employ CDA specifically on pretrained models that are initialized with ImageNet-1K weights for optimal results.

Validation Results. As illustrated in the final group of Table 3, we perform validation experiments on the distilled ImageNet-21K employing IPC 10 and 20. This yields an extreme compression ratio of 100× and 50×, respectively. When applying IPC 10—i.e., the models are trained utilizing a distilled dataset that is a mere 1% of the full dataset—the validation accuracy remarkably surpasses 20% and 30% on ResNet-18 and ResNet-50/101, respectively. Compared to the reproduced SRe²L on ImageNet-21K, our approach attains a clear elevation of 5.3% on average under IPC 10/20. This achievement not only highlights the efficacy of our approach in maintaining dataset essence despite high compression but also showcases the definitive potential for accuracy advancements over existing methods.

3.6 ABLATION
Curriculum Scheduler. To schedule the curriculum learning effectively, we present three distinct types of curriculum schedulers—step, linear, and cosine—to manipulate the lower bounds on the data crop augmentation. As illustrated in Figure 4, the dataset distillation progress is divided into two phases by a milestone. It is observed that both linear and cosine schedulers with continuous decay manifest robustness across diverse milestone configurations and reveal a clear trend of enhancing accuracy performance when the milestone is met at a later phase, as shown in Table 5. Moreover, cosine marginally outperforms linear in terms of accuracy towards the end. Consequently, we choose to implement the cosine scheduler, assigning a milestone percentage of 1.0, to modulate the minimum crop ratio adhering precisely to the principles of curriculum learning throughout the entire progression of synthesis.

Batch Size in Post-training. We perform an ablation study to assess the influence of utilizing smaller batch sizes on the generalization performance of models when the synthetic data is limited. We report results on the distilled ImageNet-21K from ResNet-18. In Table 6, a clear rise in validation accuracy is observed as batch size reduces, peaking at a size of 16. This suggests convincingly that smaller batch sizes enhance performance on small-scale synthetic datasets. However, this leads to more frequent data loading and lower GPU utilization in our case, extending training times. To balance training time with performance optimally, we chose a batch size of 32 for our primary experiments.

3.7 ANALYSIS
Cross-Model Generalization. The challenge of ensuring distilled datasets generalize effectively across models unseen during the recovery phase remains significant, as in prior approaches (Zhao et al., 2020; Cazenavette et al., 2022a), synthetic images were often optimized to overfit the recovery model. In Table 7, we deploy our ImageNet-1K distilled datasets to train various validation models, and we attain over 60% Top-1 accuracy with most of these models. Additionally, our performance in Top-1 accuracy surpasses that of SRe²L definitively across all validation models spanning various architectures. It is remarkable that the distilled datasets exhibit reduced dependency on specific recovery models, thereby alleviating the issues associated with overfitting optimization. Table 8 provides further empirical substantiation of CDA’s efficacy in the distillation of large-scale ImageNet-21K datasets.

Impact of Curriculum. To study the curriculum’s advantage on synthetic image characteristics, we evaluate the Top-1 accuracy on CDA, SRe²L, and the real ImageNet-1K training set, using the mean of random 10-crop and global images. We employ PyTorch’s pre-trained MobileNet-V2 for classifying these images. As shown in Table 9, CDA images closely resemble real ImageNet images in prediction accuracies, performing better than SRe²L. Consequently, using curriculum data augmentation demonstrably improves global image prediction and reduces bias and overfitting in post-training on the simpler, cropped images typical of SRe²L.

Visualization and Discussion. Figure 6 provides a comparative visualization of the gradient-based synthetic images at recovery steps of {100, 500, 1,000, 2,000} to illustrate clearly the differences between SRe²L and our CDA within the dataset distillation process. SRe²L images in the upper line exhibit a significant amount of noise, indicating a slow and inefficient recovery progression in the early recovery stage. On the contrary, due to the mostly entire image optimization in the early stage, CDA images in the lower line can establish the layout of the entire image rapidly and reduce noise effectively. The final synthetic images contain more visual information directly related to the target class (e.g., Plant). Therefore, the comparison highlights CDA’s superior ability to synthesize images with enhanced visual coherence to the target class, offering a more efficient and effective recovery process.

Training cost comparison with SRe²L. We highlight definitively that there is no additional training cost incurred between our CDA and SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) when the recovery iterations are held constant, ensuring our improvements are due to strategy, not computation.

3.8 APPLICATION: CONTINUAL LEARNING
Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, possess a demonstrably boosted representation capacity compared to the original datasets. This powerful attribute can be strategically harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning scenarios. We have further validated the effectiveness of our introduced CDA within various continual learning frameworks. Following the setting outlined in SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023), we conducted 5-step and 10-step class-incremental experiments on Tiny-ImageNet, aligning our results against the baseline SRe²L and a randomly selected subset on Tiny-ImageNet for comparative analysis. Illustrated in Figure 7, our CDA distilled dataset notably surpasses SRe²L, exhibiting an average advantage of 3.8% and 4.5% on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning assignments, respectively. This demonstrates the substantial and practical benefits inherent in the deployment of CDA, particularly in mitigating the complexities associated with continual learning for real-world applications.

4 RELATED WORK
Dataset distillation strives to form a compact, synthetic dataset, retaining crucial information from the original large-scale dataset. This approach facilitates easier handling, reduces training time, and aims for performance comparable to using the full dataset. Prior solutions typically fall under four categories: Meta-Model Matching optimizes for model transferability on distilled data, with an outer-loop for synthetic data updates, and an inner-loop for network training, such as DD (Wang et al., 2020), KIP (Nguyen et al., 2021), RFAD (Loo et al., 2022), FRePo (Zhou et al., 2022) and LinBa (Deng & Russakovsky, 2022); Gradient Matching performs a one-step distance matching between models, such as DC (Zhao et al., 2020), DSA (Zhao & Bilen, 2021), DCC (Lee et al., 2022) and IDC (Kim et al., 2022b); Distribution Matching directly matches the distribution of original and synthetic data with a single-level optimization, such as DM (Zhao & Bilen, 2023), CAFE (Wang et al., 2022), HaBa (Liu et al., 2022a), KFS (Lee et al., 2022); Trajectory Matching matches the weight trajectories of models trained on original and synthetic data in multiple steps, methods include MTT (Cazenavette et al., 2022b) and TESLA (Cui et al., 2023). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced the foundational idea of Curriculum Learning, proposing that training models with a curriculum can help in better optimization and can lead to better generalization. Subsequent works (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019) have explored various strategies for defining and designing curricula, such as self-paced learning (Kumar et al., 2010), where the model itself determines the learning pace and difficulty progression.

5 CONCLUSION
We have presented a new and powerful CDA framework focused on curriculum-based data synthesis for large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical and detailed framework with comprehensive pretraining for compressing knowledge, strategic data synthesis for recovery, and optimized post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the successful distillation of ImageNet-21K to 50× smaller while maintaining highly competitive accuracy levels. In regular benchmarks, such as ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior and definitive performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show the robust capability of our synthetic data on cross-model generalization and continual learning applications. Given the escalating scale of both models and datasets in recent years, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and large-scale models has gained unprecedented prominence and urgency for real-world deployment. We are confident that our contributions in this work will infuse novel insights and pave new avenues within this domain, encouraging further exploration and development in the critical field of large-scale dataset distillation. Our future work will focus productively on distilling more modalities like language and speech to broaden the impact.

Reproducibility Statement. Our synthetic data is available anonymously at the provided link and our code is also provided in the submission to ensure full reproducibility and to foster further research.

Title: Dataset Distillation in the Large Data Era: Pioneering Efficient Knowledge Compression Through Curriculum Learning

Abstract
Dataset distillation represents a pivotal methodology for generating a compact yet highly representative synthetic subset from a massive original dataset. This process enables models to be trained with remarkable efficiency, while still being evaluated on the original testing distribution to achieve performance that is not merely decent but truly competitive with full-data training. Numerous prior works have endeavored to align synthetic data with diverse aspects of the original datasets, including matching training weight trajectories, gradient signals, and feature or BatchNorm distributions. In this seminal work, we definitively demonstrate how to distill various large-scale datasets, including the full ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-21K under the conventional input resolution of 224×224, to achieve the best accuracy over all previous approaches, such as SRe²L, TESLA, and MTT. To accomplish this breakthrough, we introduce a simple yet profoundly effective Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) strategy during the data synthesis phase. This innovation obtains unprecedented accuracy on large-scale ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-21K, achieving 63.2% (IPC 50) and 36.1% (IPC 20), respectively. Ultimately, by integrating all our enhancements, the proposed model decisively beats the current state-of-the-art by more than 4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and, for the first time, reduces the performance gap to its full-data training counterpart to less than an absolute 15%. Moreover, this work constitutes the inaugural and successful demonstration of dataset distillation on the larger-scale ImageNet-21K under the standard 224×224 resolution, marking a significant milestone. Our distilled ImageNet-21K dataset of 20 IPC with a 2K recovery budget is available anonymously at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12pC0GDTURdYLThAbVHkTw2lkF2KF_85i?usp=sharing.

1 INTRODUCTION
Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) has attracted considerable and growing attention across various fields of computer vision (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) and natural language processing (Sucholutsky & Schonlau, 2021; Maekawa et al., 2023). This critical task aims to optimize the process of condensing massive, unwieldy datasets into a significantly smaller, yet maximally representative synthetic subset. The core objective is to preserve the essential features and characteristics that would allow a model to learn from scratch as effectively from the distilled dataset as it would from the original, prohibitively large dataset. As the scale of data and models continues to grow exponentially, this dataset distillation concept becomes even more critically important in the contemporary large data era, where datasets are often so voluminous that they pose severe storage, computational, and processing challenges. Fundamentally, dataset distillation can level the playing field, empowering researchers and practitioners with limited computation and storage resources to participate in state-of-the-art foundational model training and application development—such as affordable versions of systems like ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022)—within the current large data and large model regime. Moreover, by working with distilled datasets, there is substantial potential to alleviate pressing data privacy concerns, as raw, personally identifiable data points can be excluded from the distilled version.

Recently, there has been a dominant and significant trend in adopting large models and large data across virtually all research and application areas. Yet, many prior dataset distillation methods (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022; Cazenavette et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2022a; Cui et al., 2023) have predominantly and narrowly targeted smaller datasets like CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet, and downsampled ImageNet-1K, finding it profoundly challenging to scale their frameworks effectively for larger, real-world datasets such as the full ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). This clearly suggests that these prior approaches have not fully evolved in line with contemporary advancements and the dominant methodologies required for modern large-scale applications.

In this groundbreaking study, we extend our focus decisively beyond the ImageNet-1K dataset, venturing into the previously uncharted territories of the full ImageNet-21K (Deng et al., 2009; Ridnik et al., 2021) at a conventional resolution of 224×224. This marks a pioneering and successful effort in handling such a vast dataset for the dataset distillation task. Our approach harnesses a straightforward yet exceptionally effective curriculum learning framework. We meticulously address each technical aspect and craft a robust, comprehensive strategy to train effectively on the complete ImageNet-21K, ensuring comprehensive knowledge is captured and compressed. Specifically, following a prior study (Yin et al., 2023), our approach initially trains a model to encapsulate knowledge from the original datasets within its dense parameters. However, we introduce a novel and superior training recipe that surpasses the results of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K. During the critical data recovery or synthesis phase, we employ a strategic learning scheme where partial image crops are sequentially updated based on the difficulty of regions: transitioning either from simple to difficult, or vice versa. This progression is modulated by dynamically adjusting the lower and upper bounds of the RandomResizedCrop data augmentation throughout varying training iterations. Remarkably, we observe that this straightforward learning approach substantially and consistently improves the quality of synthesized data. In this paper, we delve comprehensively into three distinct learning paradigms for data synthesis linked to the curriculum learning framework. The first is the standard curriculum learning, followed by its alternative approach, reverse curriculum learning. Lastly, we also consider the basic and previously employed method of constant learning.

Curriculum Learning (CL) and Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). In traditional, unstructured learning scenarios, a model is typically trained on a dataset without paying specific attention to the order or difficulty of the data samples. However, humans and animals often learn far more effectively when they are first introduced to simpler concepts and then gradually exposed to more complex ones. This established educational concept, known as “curriculum learning” (Bengio et al., 2009), has been successfully borrowed and applied to the domain of machine learning (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019). Unlike curriculum learning that starts with the easiest tasks, reverse curriculum learning begins with the most challenging ones. This alternative learning strategy is essentially a backtracking method where, if a model struggles with a particularly difficult task, it is allowed to fall back to simpler versions of the task to reinforce understanding.

How to Change the Difficulties of Training Samples? RandomResizedCrop operates by randomly cropping an image to a certain area and then resizing it back to a pre-defined size, ensuring that the model is exposed to different regions and scales of the original image during training. As clearly illustrated in Figure 2, the difficulty level of the cropped region can be precisely controlled by specifying the lower and upper bounds for the area ratio of the crop. This mechanism can be used strategically to ensure that certain portions of the image—whether small details or larger context—are present in the cropped region. If we aim to make the learning process more challenging, we simply reduce the minimum crop ratio. This way, the model will often see only small, limited portions of the image and will have to learn from those constrained contexts. Conversely, if we want the model to see a larger context more frequently to grasp holistic features, we increase the minimum crop ratio. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive and detailed study on how the gradual difficulty changes, governed by the sampling strategy, directly influence the optimization of data generation and the final quality of synthetic data for the dataset distillation task. Our proposed Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is a heuristic, intuitive, yet highly effective approach to simulate a curriculum learning procedure. Moreover, it is demonstrably and highly effective on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K and 21K, achieving definitive state-of-the-art performance on dataset distillation.

Our Motivation and Intuition. Both SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) and our proposed CDA method utilize local batch mean and variance statistics to match the global statistics of the entire original dataset, synthesizing data by applying gradient updates directly to the image pixels. The profound impact of such a strategy is that the initial few iterations critically set the stage for the global structure of the ultimately generated image. However, SRe²L does not capitalize on this characteristic effectively. In stark contrast, CDA efficiently and fully exploits it by initially employing large crops to capture a more accurate and complete outline of the object. As the process progresses, CDA incrementally and systematically reduces the crop size to enhance the finer, local details of the object, thereby significantly elevating the overall quality and fidelity of the synthesized data.

In this work, we conduct extensive and rigorous experiments on the Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-21K datasets. Employing a resolution of 224×224 and IPC 50 on ImageNet-1K, the proposed approach attains an impressive and leading accuracy of 63.2%, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial and clear margins. As illustrated in Figure 1, our proposed CDA consistently outperforms SRe²L by 4~6% across different architectures under 50 IPC, on both 1K and 4K recovery budgets. When tested on the massive ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, our method achieves a top-1 accuracy of 35.3%, which is closely competitive, exhibiting only a minimal gap compared to the model pretrained with the full data, at 44.5%, while using 50× fewer training samples—a testament to its remarkable efficiency.

2 APPROACH
2.1 DATASET DISTILLATION
The fundamental goal of dataset distillation is to derive a concise synthetic dataset that maintains a significant and useful proportion of the information contained in the original, much larger dataset. Suppose there is a large labeled dataset 𝒟ₒ = {(x₁, y₁), …, (x_{|𝒟ₒ|}, y_{|𝒟ₒ|})}, our target is to formulate a compact distilled dataset, represented as 𝒟_d = {(x′₁, y′₁), …, (x′_{|𝒟_d|}, y′_{|𝒟_d|})}, where y′ is the soft label corresponding to synthetic data x′, and |𝒟_d| ≪ |𝒟ₒ|, preserving the essential information from the original dataset 𝒟ₒ. The learning objective based on this distilled synthetic dataset is formulated as:
    θ_{𝒟_d} = arg min_θ ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ)
    ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ) = 𝔼_{(x′, y′) ∈ 𝒟_d} [ ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x′), y′ ) ]
where ℓ is the regular loss function such as the soft cross-entropy, and ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}} is the model. The primary objective of the dataset distillation task is to generate synthetic data aimed at attaining a specific or minimal performance disparity on the original validation data, when models are trained on the synthetic data versus the original dataset, respectively. Thus, we aim to optimize the synthetic data 𝒟_d by:
    arg min_{𝒟_d, |𝒟_d|} ( sup { | ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟ₒ}}(x), y ) - ℓ( ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x), y ) | }_{(x, y) ∼ 𝒟ₒ} )
Then, we learn the <data, label> pairs ∈ 𝒟_d along with the corresponding number of distilled data points in each class.

2.2 DATASET DISTILLATION ON LARGE-SCALE DATASETS
Currently, the prevailing majority of research studies within dataset distillation mainly employ datasets of a scale up to ImageNet-1K (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) as their benchmarking standards. In this section, we demonstrate clearly how to construct a strong baseline on ImageNet-21K (this approach is equivalently applicable to ImageNet-1K) by incorporating key insights presented in recent studies, complemented by conventional yet effective optimization techniques. Our proposed baseline is demonstrated definitively to achieve state-of-the-art performance. We believe this provides substantial contributions towards understanding the true impact of proposed methodologies and towards accurately assessing the true performance gap with full original data training. Following prior work in dataset distillation (Yin et al., 2023), we focus on the decoupled training framework to save computation and memory consumption on large-scale ImageNet-21K, and the procedures are listed comprehensively below:

Building A Strong Compression Model on ImageNet-21K. For the squeezing model pretraining, we use a relatively large label smoothing factor of 0.2 together with Cutout (DeVries & Taylor, 2017) and RandAugment (Cubuk et al., 2020). This recipe helps achieve a significant ∼2% improvement over the default training of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K, as provided in Table 5.

Curriculum Training for Better Representation of Synthetic Data. A well-crafted and strategic curriculum data augmentation is employed during the synthesis stage to enhance the representational capability and richness of the synthetic data. This step is crucial, serving to enrich the generated images by embedding more knowledge accumulated from the original dataset, thereby making them more informative and effective for training. Detailed procedures will be further described in the following Section 2.3.

2.3 CURRICULUM DATA AUGMENTATION
In the SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) approach, the key mechanism of data synthesis revolves around utilizing the gradient information emanating from both the semantic class and the predictions of the pretrained squeezing model, paired with BN distribution matching. Let (x, y) be an example x for optimization and its corresponding one-hot label y for the pretrained squeezing model. Throughout the synthesis process the squeezing model is frozen for recovering the encoded information, ensuring consistency and reliability in the generated data. Let 𝒯(x̄) be the target training distribution from which the data synthesis process should ultimately learn, where τ is a data transformation function to augment the input sample to various levels of difficulties. Following Bengio et al. (2009), a weight 0 ≤ W_s(x) ≤ 1 is defined and applied to example x at stage s in the curriculum sequence. The distribution is:
    D_s(x) ∝ W_s(x) 𝒯(x) ∀ x
In our specific scenario, since the varying difficulties are governed entirely by the data transformation function τ, we can straightforwardly employ W_s(x) = 1 across all stages. Consequently, the training distribution depends solely on τ(x) and can be simplified as follows:
    D(x) ∝ 𝒯(x) ∀ x
By integrating curriculum learning within the data synthesis phase, this procedure can be formally defined as:

Definition 1 (Curriculum Data Synthesis). In the data synthesis optimization, the corresponding sequence of distributions D(x) will constitute a curriculum if there is a measurable increment in the entropy of these distributions, i.e., the difficulty of the transformed input samples escalates and they become increasingly challenging for the pre-trained model to predict as the training progresses.

Thus, the key for our curriculum data synthesis becomes how to design τ(x) strategically across different training iterations. The following discusses several concrete strategies to construct this within the curriculum scheme.

Baseline: Constant Learning (CTL). This is the regular training method where all training examples are typically treated equally throughout. Each sample from the training dataset has an equal chance of being transformed in a given batch, assuming no explicit difficulty imbalance or biases across different training iterations. CTL is straightforward to implement since we do not have to rank or organize examples based on difficulty. In practice, we simply use x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop Ψ(x_s, min_crop = β_l, max_crop = β_u), where β_l and β_u are the constant lower and upper bounds of the crop scale.

Curriculum Learning (CL). As shown in Algorithm 1, in our CL framework, data samples are organized strategically based on their difficulty. The difficulty level of the cropped region can be managed precisely by defining the lower and upper scopes for the area ratio of the crop. This enables the assurance that specific crops of the image—whether small details or broader context—are included in the cropped region at appropriate stages. For the difficulty adjustment, the rate at which more difficult examples are introduced and the criteria used to define difficulty are adjusted dynamically as predetermined using the following schedulers.
    Step. The step scheduler reduces the minimal scale by a fixed factor for every specified number of iterations.
    Linear. The linear scheduler starts with a high initial value and decreases it linearly by a factor γ to a minimum value over the whole training duration.
    Cosine. The cosine scheduler modulates the distribution according to the cosine function of the current iteration number, yielding a smoother and more gradual adjustment compared to step-based methods. As shown in Figure 4, the factor distribution manages the difficulty level of crops with a defined milestone.

Data Synthesis by Recovering. After receiving the transformed input x_𝒯, we update it by aligning between the final classification label and intermediate Batch Normalization (BN) statistics from the original data. This critical stage forces the synthesized images to capture the essential shape and distribution of the original image distribution. The learning goal for this stage can be formulated precisely as follows:

3 EXPERIMENTS
3.1 DATASETS AND IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
We verify the effectiveness and robustness of our approach on various ImageNet-scale datasets, including Tiny-ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009), and ImageNet-21K (Ridnik et al., 2021). For a thorough evaluation, we train models from scratch on the synthetic distilled datasets and report the Top-1 accuracy on the real validation datasets. The default lower and upper bounds of crop scales β_l and β_u are set to 0.08 and 1.0, respectively. The decay factor γ is set to 0.92.

3.2 CIFAR-100
Comparison results with baseline methods on the CIFAR-100 dataset are presented in Table 1. We observe a clear trend that the validation model’s accuracy exhibits a significant and consistent improvement along with the extension of training budgets. Our CDA’s best validation accuracy definitively outperforms all baselines under both 10 and 50 IPC settings. Furthermore, our reported results have the clear potential to be further improved as training budgets increase. Overall, our CDA method is also successfully applicable to small-scale dataset distillation, demonstrating its versatility.

3.3 TINY-IMAGENET
Results on the Tiny-ImageNet dataset are detailed in the first group of Table 3. Our CDA surpasses SRe²L with average improvements of 7.7% and 3.4% under IPC 50 and IPC 100 settings across ResNet-{18, 50, 101} validation models, respectively. We provide the result comparison with more methods in the appendix. Importantly, CDA stands as the inaugural approach to diminish the Top-1 accuracy performance disparity to less than 10% between the distilled dataset employing IPC 100 and the full Tiny-ImageNet, signifying a major breakthrough on this dataset.

Constant Learning (CTL). We leverage a ResNet-18 and employ a 1K recovery budget for synthesizing data. As observed in Table 2, the results for exceedingly straightforward or challenging scenarios fall below the reproduced SRe²L baseline accuracy of 44.90%, especially when α ≥ 0.8 in the easy regime and α ≤ 0.4 in the hard regime. Thus, the results presented in Table 2 suggest convincingly that adopting a larger, more moderate cropped range assists in circumventing extreme scenarios, whether easy or hard, culminating in enhanced performance. A noteworthy observation is the crucial role of appropriate lower and upper bounds for constant learning in boosting validation accuracy. This highlights the fundamental importance of employing strategic curriculum data augmentation strategies in data synthesis.

We use a reverse step scheduler in the RCL experiments, starting with the default cropped range from β_l to β_u and transitioning at the milestone point to optimize the whole image, thereby shifting from challenging to simpler optimizations. Other settings follow the recovery recipe on ResNet-18 for 1K recovery iterations. Table 4 shows the RCL results; a smaller step milestone indicates an earlier difficulty transition. The findings reveal clearly that RCL does not improve the generated dataset’s quality compared to the baseline SRe²L, which has 44.90% accuracy.

As illustrated in the second group of Table 3, when compared to the strong baseline SRe²L, CDA enhances the validation accuracy decisively, exhibiting average margins of 6.1%, 4.3%, and 3.2% on ResNet-18, 50, and 101 across varying IPC configurations. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 1, the results achieved with our CDA utilizing merely 1K recovery iterations surpass those of SRe²L encompassing the entire 4K iterations. These results substantiate definitively the efficacy and effectiveness of applying CDA in large-scale dataset distillation.

We utilize these pretrained models to recover ImageNet-21K data and to assign labels to the synthetic images generated. An intriguing observation is the heightened difficulty in data recovering from pretrained models that are initialized randomly compared to those initialized with ImageNet-1K weights. Thus, our experiments employ CDA specifically on pretrained models that are initialized with ImageNet-1K weights for optimal results.

Validation Results. As illustrated in the final group of Table 3, we perform validation experiments on the distilled ImageNet-21K employing IPC 10 and 20. This yields an extreme compression ratio of 100× and 50×, respectively. Compared to the reproduced SRe²L on ImageNet-21K, our approach attains a clear elevation of 5.3% on average under IPC 10/20. This achievement not only highlights the efficacy of our approach in maintaining dataset essence despite high compression but also showcases the definitive potential for accuracy advancements over existing methods.

To schedule the curriculum learning effectively, we present three distinct types of curriculum schedulers—step, linear, and cosine—to manipulate the lower bounds on the data crop augmentation. As illustrated in Figure 4, the dataset distillation progress is divided into two phases by a milestone. It is observed that both linear and cosine schedulers with continuous decay manifest robustness across diverse milestone configurations and reveal a clear trend of enhancing accuracy performance when the milestone is met at a later phase, as shown in Table 5. Moreover, cosine marginally outperforms linear in terms of accuracy towards the end. Consequently, we choose to implement the cosine scheduler, assigning a milestone percentage of 1.0, to modulate the minimum crop ratio adhering precisely to the principles of curriculum learning throughout the entire progression of synthesis.

We report results on the distilled ImageNet-21K from ResNet-18. In Table 6, a clear rise in validation accuracy is observed as batch size reduces, peaking at a size of 16. This suggests convincingly that smaller batch sizes enhance performance on small-scale synthetic datasets. However, this leads to more frequent data loading and lower GPU utilization in our case, extending training times. 3.7 ANALYSIS
Cross-Model Generalization. The challenge of ensuring distilled datasets generalize effectively across models unseen during the recovery phase remains significant, as in prior approaches (Zhao et al., 2020; Cazenavette et al., 2022a), synthetic images were often optimized to overfit the recovery model. In Table 7, we deploy our ImageNet-1K distilled datasets to train various validation models, and we attain over 60% Top-1 accuracy with most of these models. Additionally, our performance in Top-1 accuracy surpasses that of SRe²L definitively across all validation models spanning various architectures. It is remarkable that the distilled datasets exhibit reduced dependency on specific recovery models, thereby alleviating the issues associated with overfitting optimization. Table 8 provides further empirical substantiation of CDA’s efficacy in the distillation of large-scale ImageNet-21K datasets.

Impact of Curriculum. To study the curriculum’s advantage on synthetic image characteristics, we evaluate the Top-1 accuracy on CDA, SRe²L, and the real ImageNet-1K training set, using the mean of random 10-crop and global images. We employ PyTorch’s pre-trained MobileNet-V2 for classifying these images. As shown in Table 9, CDA images closely resemble real ImageNet images in prediction accuracies, performing better than SRe²L. Consequently, using curriculum data augmentation demonstrably improves global image prediction and reduces bias and overfitting in post-training on the simpler, cropped images typical of SRe²L.

Visualization and Discussion. Figure 6 provides a comparative visualization of the gradient-based synthetic images at recovery steps of {100, 500, 1,000, 2,000} to illustrate clearly the differences between SRe²L and our CDA within the dataset distillation process. SRe²L images in the upper line exhibit a significant amount of noise, indicating a slow and inefficient recovery progression in the early recovery stage. On the contrary, due to the mostly entire image optimization in the early stage, CDA images in the lower line can establish the layout of the entire image rapidly and reduce noise effectively. The final synthetic images contain more visual information directly related to the target class (e.g., Plant). Therefore, the comparison highlights CDA’s superior ability to synthesize images with enhanced visual coherence to the target class, offering a more efficient and effective recovery process.

Training cost comparison with SRe²L. We highlight definitively that there is no additional training cost incurred between our CDA and SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) when the recovery iterations are held constant, ensuring our improvements are due to strategy, not computation.

3.8 APPLICATION: CONTINUAL LEARNING
Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, possess a demonstrably boosted representation capacity compared to the original datasets. This powerful attribute can be strategically harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning scenarios. We have further validated the effectiveness of our introduced CDA within various continual learning frameworks. Following the setting outlined in SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023), we conducted 5-step and 10-step class-incremental experiments on Tiny-ImageNet, aligning our results against the baseline SRe²L and a randomly selected subset on Tiny-ImageNet for comparative analysis. Illustrated in Figure 7, our CDA distilled dataset notably surpasses SRe²L, exhibiting an average advantage of 3.8% and 4.5% on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning assignments, respectively. This demonstrates the substantial and practical benefits inherent in the deployment of CDA, particularly in mitigating the complexities associated with continual learning for real-world applications.

4 RELATED WORK
Dataset distillation strives to form a compact, synthetic dataset, retaining crucial information from the original large-scale dataset. This approach facilitates easier handling, reduces training time, and aims for performance comparable to using the full dataset. Prior solutions typically fall under four categories: Meta-Model Matching optimizes for model transferability on distilled data, with an outer-loop for synthetic data updates, and an inner-loop for network training, such as DD (Wang et al., 2020), KIP (Nguyen et al., 2021), RFAD (Loo et al., 2022), FRePo (Zhou et al., 2022) and LinBa (Deng & Russakovsky, 2022); Gradient Matching performs a one-step distance matching between models, such as DC (Zhao et al., 2020), DSA (Zhao & Bilen, 2021), DCC (Lee et al., 2022) and IDC (Kim et al., 2022b); Distribution Matching directly matches the distribution of original and synthetic data with a single-level optimization, such as DM (Zhao & Bilen, 2023), CAFE (Wang et al., 2022), HaBa (Liu et al., 2022a), KFS (Lee et al., 2022); Trajectory Matching matches the weight trajectories of models trained on original and synthetic data in multiple steps, methods include MTT (Cazenavette et al., 2022b) and TESLA (Cui et al., 2023). Bengio et al. (2009) introduced the foundational idea of Curriculum Learning, proposing that training models with a curriculum can help in better optimization and can lead to better generalization. Subsequent works (Jiang et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2018; Hacohen & Weinshall, 2019) have explored various strategies for defining and designing curricula, such as self-paced learning (Kumar et al., 2010), where the model itself determines the learning pace and difficulty progression.

5 CONCLUSION
We have presented a new and powerful CDA framework focused on curriculum-based data synthesis for large-scale dataset distillation. Our approach involves a practical and detailed framework with comprehensive pretraining for compressing knowledge, strategic data synthesis for recovery, and optimized post-training recipes. The proposed approach enables the successful distillation of ImageNet-21K to 50× smaller while maintaining highly competitive accuracy levels. In regular benchmarks, such as ImageNet-1K, our approach has demonstrated superior and definitive performance, surpassing all prior state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins. We further show the robust capability of our synthetic data on cross-model generalization and continual learning applications. Given the escalating scale of both models and datasets in recent years, the imperativeness of dataset distillation for large-scale datasets and large-scale models has gained unprecedented prominence and urgency for real-world deployment. We are confident that our contributions in this work will infuse novel insights and pave new avenues within this domain, encouraging further exploration and development in the critical field of large-scale dataset distillation. Our future work will focus productively on distilling more modalities like language and speech to broaden the impact.

Reproducibility Statement. Our synthetic data is available anonymously at the provided link and our code is also provided in the submission to ensure full reproducibility and to foster further research.

Dataset Distillation with Curriculum Data Augmentation

Abstract
Dataset distillation generates a smaller, representative subset from a large dataset, enabling efficient model training while aiming for performance on the original test distribution. Prior methods align with aspects of the original datasets, such as training weight trajectories, gradients, or feature/BatchNorm distributions. This work distills large-scale datasets, including full ImageNet-1K/21K at 224x224 resolution. A method called Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is introduced during data synthesis. On ImageNet-1K with IPC 50, accuracy is 63.2%. On ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, accuracy is 36.1%. Integrating enhancements reduces the gap to full-data training on ImageNet-1K to less than an absolute 15%. This is the first successful dataset distillation on ImageNet-21K at standard 224x224 resolution. The distilled ImageNet-21K dataset (IPC 20, 2K recovery budget) is available at a provided URL.

1 Introduction
Dataset distillation (Wang et al., 2018) aims to condense a large dataset into a smaller subset that preserves essential features, allowing a model to learn as effectively as from the original data. Many prior methods (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022; Cazenavette et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2022a; Cui et al., 2023) target datasets like CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet, and downsampled ImageNet-1K, finding it challenging to scale to full ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009).

This work extends to the full ImageNet-21K (Deng et al., 2009; Ridnik et al., 2021) at 224x224 resolution. The approach uses a curriculum learning framework. Following Yin et al. (2023), a model is first trained to encapsulate knowledge from the original dataset. A training recipe is introduced that surpasses the results of Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K. During data recovery/synthesis, a strategic learning scheme updates partial image crops sequentially based on region difficulty, modulated by adjusting the lower and upper bounds of RandomResizedCrop augmentation across training iterations. Three learning paradigms for data synthesis are examined: standard curriculum learning (CL), reverse curriculum learning (RCL), and constant learning.

Curriculum Learning (CL) and Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). Curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) introduces simpler concepts before more complex ones. Reverse curriculum learning begins with the most challenging tasks.

How to Change the Difficulties of Training Samples? RandomResizedCrop randomly crops an image to a certain area and resizes it. The difficulty of the cropped region is controlled by specifying lower and upper bounds for the area ratio of the crop. Reducing the minimum crop ratio makes learning more challenging. Increasing it lets the model see larger context more frequently. A comprehensive study is performed on how gradual difficulty changes influence data generation optimization and synthetic data quality for dataset distillation. The proposed Curriculum Data Augmentation (CDA) is a heuristic approach to simulate a curriculum learning procedure.

Motivation. Both SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023) and CDA use local batch mean and variance statistics to match global dataset statistics, synthesizing data via gradient updates on the image. The initial iterations set the stage for the global structure of the generated image. SRe²L does not capitalize on this characteristic. CDA exploits it by initially using large crops to capture an accurate object outline, then incrementally reduces crop size to enhance finer local details.

Experiments are conducted on Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-21K. At 224x224 resolution and IPC 50 on ImageNet-1K, the approach attains 63.2% accuracy, surpassing prior methods. As shown in Figure 1, CDA outperforms SRe²L by 4-6% across different architectures under 50 IPC. On ImageNet-21K with IPC 20, the method achieves a top-1 accuracy of 35.3%, compared to 44.5% for the model pretrained with full data, using 50x fewer training samples.

2 Approach
2.1 Dataset Distillation
Given a large labeled dataset 𝒟ₒ = {(x₁, y₁), …, (x_{|𝒟ₒ|}, y_{|𝒟ₒ|})}, the goal is to formulate a compact distilled dataset 𝒟_d = {(x′₁, y′₁), …, (x′_{|𝒟_d|}, y′_{|𝒟_d|})}, where y′ is the soft label corresponding to synthetic data x′, and |𝒟_d| ≪ |𝒟ₒ|. The learning objective is:
θ_{𝒟_d} = arg min_θ ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ)
ℒ_{𝒟_d}(θ) = 𝔼_{(x′, y′) ∈ 𝒟_d} [ℓ(ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x′), y′)]
where ℓ is a loss function like soft cross-entropy, and ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}} is the model. The objective is to optimize synthetic data 𝒟_d by:
arg min_{𝒟_d, |𝒟_d|} ( sup { |ℓ(ϕ_{θ_{𝒟ₒ}}(x), y) - ℓ(ϕ_{θ_{𝒟_d}}(x), y)| }_{(x, y) ∼ 𝒟ₒ} )

2.2 Dataset Distillation on Large-Scale Datasets
Most research employs datasets up to ImageNet-1K (Cazenavette et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023). This section shows how to construct a strong baseline on ImageNet-21K, applicable to ImageNet-1K. Following prior work (Yin et al., 2023), a decoupled training framework is used to save computation and memory on ImageNet-21K.

Building A Strong Compression Model on ImageNet-21K. For squeezing model pretraining, a label smooth of 0.2 is used with Cutout (DeVries & Taylor, 2017) and RandAugment (Cubuk et al.). This recipe achieves ~2% improvement over the default training in Ridnik et al. (2021) on ImageNet-21K, as shown in Table 5.

Curriculum Training for Better Representation of Synthetic Data. A curriculum data augmentation is employed during the synthesis stage to enhance the representational capability of synthetic data.

2.3 Curriculum Data Augmentation
In SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023), data synthesis uses gradient information from the pretrained squeezing model and BN distribution matching. Let (x, y) be an example x for optimization and its one-hot label y. The squeezing model is frozen. Let 𝒯(x̅) be the target training distribution, where τ is a data transformation function to augment input samples to various difficulty levels. Following Bengio et al. (2009), a weight 0 ≤ W_s(x) ≤ 1 is defined and applied to example x at stage s. The distribution is:
D_s(x) ∝ W_s(x) 𝒯(x) ∀ x
Since varying difficulties are governed by τ, W_s(x)=1 can be used across all stages. The training distribution simplifies to:
D(x) ∝ 𝒯(x) ∀ x
Integrating curriculum learning into data synthesis gives:

Definition 1 (Curriculum Data Synthesis). In data synthesis optimization, the sequence of distributions D(x) is a curriculum if there is an increment in the entropy of these distributions, i.e., the difficulty of transformed input samples escalates as training progresses.

The key is designing τ(x) across training iterations. Several strategies are discussed.

Baseline: Constant Learning (CTL). All training examples are treated equally. Each sample has an equal chance of being transformed in a batch. In practice, x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop Ψ(x_s, min_crop = β_l, max_crop = β_u), where β_l and β_u are constant lower and upper bounds of crop scale.

Curriculum Learning (CL). Data samples are organized based on difficulty, managed by defining lower and upper scopes for the crop area ratio. Difficulty adjustment uses schedulers: Step, Linear, and Cosine.

Data Synthesis by Recovering. After receiving transformed input x_𝒯, it is updated by aligning the final classification label and intermediate Batch Normalization (BN) statistics from the original data. The learning goal is:
x′_𝒯 = arg min ℓ(ϕ_θ(x_𝒯), y) + ℛ_reg
where ℛ_reg is the regularization term from Yin et al., and ϕ_θ is the frozen pretrained squeezing model.

Algorithm 1: Curriculum Data Augmentation via RandomResizedCrop
Input: squeezed model ϕ_θ, recovery iteration S, curriculum milestone T, target label y, default lower and upper bounds of crop scale β_l and β_u in RandomResizedCrop, decay of lower scale bound γ
Output: synthetic image x
Initialize: x₀ from a standard normal distribution
for step s from 0 to S-1 do
    if s ≤ T then
        α ← { β_l + γ * (β_u - s/T) if step; β_l + γ * (β_u - s/T) if linear; β_l + γ * (β_u + cos(π * s/T))/2 if cosine }
    else
        α ← β_l
    end
    x_𝒯 ← RandomResizedCrop(x_s, min_crop = α, max_crop = β_u)
    x′_𝒯 ← x_𝒯 optimized w.r.t ϕ_θ and y in Eq. 6.
    x_{s+1} ← ReverseRandomResizedCrop(x_s, x′_𝒯)
end
return x ← x_S

3 Experiments
3.1 Datasets and Implementation Details
Experiments are on Tiny-ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009), and ImageNet-21K (Ridnik et al., 2021). Models are trained from scratch on synthetic distilled datasets, and Top-1 accuracy is reported on real validation datasets. Default lower and upper bounds of crop scales β_l and β_u are 0.08 and 1.0. The decay γ is 0.92.

3.2 CIFAR-100
Comparison results on CIFAR-100 are in Table 1. Validation accuracy improves with longer training budgets. CDA's best validation accuracy outperforms baselines under 10 and 50 IPC. CDA is applicable to small-scale dataset distillation.

3.3 Tiny-ImageNet
Results on Tiny-ImageNet are in the first group of Table 3. CDA surpasses SRe²L with average improvements of 7.7% and 3.4% under IPC 50 and IPC 100 settings across ResNet-{18, 50, 101} validation models. CDA reduces the Top-1 accuracy gap to less than 10% between the distilled dataset (IPC 100) and full Tiny-ImageNet.

3.4 ImageNet-1K
Constant Learning (CTL). A ResNet-18 is used with 1K recovery synthesis data. Results are in Table 2. Exceedingly straightforward or challenging scenarios (α ≥ 0.8 in easy, α ≤ 0.4 in hard) fall below the reproduced SRe²L baseline accuracy of 44.90%. Adopting a larger cropped range helps avoid extreme scenarios, enhancing performance. Appropriate lower and upper bounds for constant learning are crucial.

Reverse Curriculum Learning (RCL). A reverse step scheduler is used, starting with the default cropped range and transitioning at a milestone to optimize the whole image. Results are in Table 4. RCL does not improve generated dataset quality compared to the SRe²L baseline (44.90% accuracy).

Curriculum Learning (CL). CDA experiments follow the recovery recipe of SRe²L's best results for 4K recovery iterations. As shown in the second group of Table 3, compared to SRe²L, CDA enhances validation accuracy with average margins of 6.1%, 4.3%, and 3.2% on ResNet-18, 50, 101 across varying IPC configurations. As shown in Figure 1, CDA with 1K recovery iterations surpasses SRe²L with 4K iterations.

3.5 ImageNet-21K
Pretraining Results. Table 5 presents accuracy for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet-21K-P with varying initial weights. Models pretrained and initialized with ImageNet-1K weights show a 2.0% improvement. Models initialized randomly achieve marginally superior accuracy. Data recovering is more difficult from randomly initialized pretrained models. Experiments employ CDA on pretrained models initialized with ImageNet-1K weight.

Validation Results. As shown in the final group of Table 3, validation experiments on distilled ImageNet-21K use IPC 10 and 20, yielding compression ratios of 100x and 50x. With IPC 10 (1% of full dataset), validation accuracy surpasses 20% and 30% on ResNet-18 and ResNet-50, 101, respectively. Compared to reproduced SRe²L on ImageNet-21K, this approach attains an average elevation of 5.3% under IPC 10/20.

3.6 Ablation
Curriculum Scheduler. Three curriculum schedulers (step, linear, cosine) manipulate the lower bounds on data cropped augmentation. As shown in Figure 4, dataset distillation progress is divided into two phases by a milestone. Both linear and cosine with continuous decay show robustness across milestone configurations and improve accuracy when the milestone is met later, as shown in Table 5. Cosine marginally outperforms linear. The cosine scheduler with a milestone percentage of 1.0 is chosen.

Batch Size in Post-training. An ablation study assesses the influence of smaller batch sizes on generalization when synthetic data is limited. Results are in Table 6. Validation accuracy rises as batch size reduces, peaking at 16. This suggests smaller batch sizes enhance performance on small-scale synthetic datasets. A batch size of 32 is chosen to balance training time and performance.

3.7 Analysis
Cross-Model Generalization. The challenge is ensuring distilled datasets generalize across models unseen during recovery. In Table 7, ImageNet-1K distilled datasets are used to train validation models, attaining over 60% Top-1 accuracy with most models. Performance surpasses SRe²L across all validation models. Distilled datasets exhibit reduced dependency on specific recovery models. Table 8 provides further empirical substantiation for ImageNet-21K.

Impact of Curriculum. To study curriculum's advantage on synthetic image characteristics, Top-1 accuracy is evaluated on CDA, SRe²L, and real ImageNet-1K training set, using the mean of random 10-crop and global images. A pre-trained MobileNet-V2 classifies these images. As shown in Table 9, CDA images more closely resemble real ImageNet images in prediction accuracies than SRe²L. Curriculum data augmentation improves global image prediction and reduces bias from overfitting on simpler, cropped images.

Visualization and Discussion. Figure 6 visualizes gradient synthetic images at recovery steps {100, 500, 1000, 2000} to compare SRe²L and CDA. SRe²L images exhibit significant noise, indicating slow early recovery. Due to mostly entire image optimization early on, CDA images establish the layout rapidly and reduce noise. Final CDA synthetic images contain more visual information related to the target class.

Training cost comparison with SRe²L. There is no additional training cost between CDA and SRe²L when recovery iterations are the same.

3.8 Application: Continual Learning
Distilled datasets, comprising high-semantic images, have boosted representation capacity. This can be harnessed to combat catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. Following SRe²L (Yin et al., 2023), 5-step and 10-step class-incremental experiments are conducted on Tiny-ImageNet, comparing against SRe²L and a randomly selected subset. As shown in Figure 7, the CDA distilled dataset surpasses SRe²L, exhibiting an average advantage of 3.8% and 4.5% on 5-step and 10-step class-incremental learning assignments.

4 Related Work
Dataset distillation aims to form a compact, synthetic dataset retaining crucial information. Prior solutions typically fall under categories: Meta-Model Matching (e.g., DD, KIP, RFAD, FRePo, LinBa); Gradient Matching (e.g., DC, DSA, DCC, IDC); Distribution Matching (e.g., DM, CAFE, HaBa, KFS); Trajectory Matching (e.g., MTT, TESLA). Curriculum Learning (Bengio et al., 2009) proposes training models with a curriculum for better optimization and generalization.

5 Conclusion
A CDA framework for curriculum-based data synthesis in large-scale dataset distillation is presented. The approach involves pretraining for compressing knowledge, data synthesis for recovery, and post-training recipes. It enables distillation of ImageNet-21K to 50x smaller while maintaining competitive accuracy. On ImageNet-1K, the approach surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods. The capability of synthetic data is shown on cross-model generalization and continual learning. Future work will focus on distilling more modalities like language and speech.

Reproducibility Statement. Synthetic data and code are provided.
