Title: Alleviating Label Shift Through Self-trained Intermediate Distribution: A Theoretical and Algorithmic Framework

Abstract
In the pursuit of robust machine learning systems capable of operating in real-world environments, label shift presents a significant and pervasive obstacle. This phenomenon, characterized by a divergence between the source and target label marginal distributions while the feature distribution within each class remains consistent, fundamentally challenges the homogeneous distribution assumption that underpins classical learning paradigms. To correct for this distributional mismatch, importance weighting has emerged as one of the most prominent and theoretically grounded strategies. However, a critical limitation persists: the estimation of these importance weights in most existing methodologies is prone to high variance, particularly under conditions of substantial label shift or when source samples are scarce. This paper introduces a novel conceptual and algorithmic framework designed to mitigate this issue. Instead of directly reweighting from the source distribution, we propose the introduction of an ideal intermediate distribution to serve as a bridge, thereby reducing the distributional variation to the target. Our approach, termed ALS, learns a self-trained intermediate distribution constructed from the labeled source samples and the unlabeled target samples to approximate this ideal distribution. This process inherently balances the bias introduced by pseudo target labels against the variance stemming from importance weighting. Furthermore, we provide rigorous theoretical analysis, proving sample complexity and generalization guarantees for our approach. Under mild conditions, these guarantees yield a tighter generalization bound than those established for existing label shift methods. Extensive experimental results across multiple benchmarks consistently validate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed approach over contemporary state-of-the-art methods.

1 INTRODUCTION

The classical supervised learning paradigm operates on a foundational assumption: models are trained on a labeled source dataset and are subsequently deployed to make predictions on an unlabeled target dataset, with the expectation of effective performance when the samples from both domains are independent and identically distributed. This assumption, while theoretically convenient, is rarely satisfied in practical, real-world applications where data environments are dynamic and heterogeneous. For instance, in the critical domain of medical diagnostics, the prevalence of specific diseases can vary dramatically across different geographical regions or demographic groups, even though the symptomatic presentation of a given disease may remain largely consistent. Similarly, in ecological tasks such as bird identification, the proportional distribution of bird species observed in spring can differ significantly from that in winter, despite the core visual appearance of individual species remaining constant across seasons. These practical scenarios are formally described by the label shift assumption, where the marginal distribution of labels differs between source and target domains (denoted as \(p(Y) \neq q(Y)\)), while the conditional distribution of features given a label remains invariant (denoted as \(p(X|Y) = q(X|Y)\)).

The discrepancy in label marginal distributions frequently leads to a substantial degradation in the performance of models trained under the traditional i.i.d. assumption. Consequently, to enhance model generalization under such distributional shift, it is imperative to adapt traditional learning frameworks to explicitly account for the characteristics of label shift. A majority of advanced methods in this area focus on estimating importance weights, which are then used to reweight the source classifier to better align with the target distribution. For example, BBSE corrects the source classifier through importance-weighted empirical risk minimization and provides a theoretical generalization error bound. Building upon this, RLLS was developed to obtain strong statistical guarantees without stringent requirements on problem-dependent minimum sample complexity, employing a regularized weight estimator to improve robustness with limited target samples. Other methodologies have explored techniques such as maximum likelihood estimation or confidence calibration to adjust for label shift without necessitating full model retraining. Notably, MLLS combines maximum likelihood with bias-corrected temperature scaling, demonstrating strong performance across diverse datasets. However, while such calibration-based methods offer practical reusability, they often lack rigorous theoretical generalization guarantees. Moreover, existing theoretical analyses for methods like BBSE and RLLS indicate that their importance weight estimation and resultant classifier generalization can exhibit high variance, particularly under conditions of large label shift or when only a limited number of source samples are available.

In this work, we introduce a principled strategy to theoretically alleviate the challenges posed by label shift. Our core innovation is the proposal of an intermediate distribution, conceived as a linear combination of the source and target distributions, to serve as a reference point instead of the source distribution itself. Our proposed approach, abbreviated as ALS, learns a self-trained intermediate distribution constructed from the available labeled source and unlabeled target samples to approximate this ideal intermediate distribution. As conceptually illustrated in Figure 1, this process aims to reduce the label distribution discrepancy, thereby facilitating more accurate and stable importance weight estimation. Simultaneously, the introduction of pseudo target labels through self-training introduces a potential source of bias, which can impact the generalization performance of the final reweighted model. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis that dissects the interplay between the variance from weight estimation and the bias from pseudo-labels within the ALS framework. To empirically validate the efficacy of ALS in enhancing the performance of foundational methods like BBSE and RLLS, we conduct extensive experiments measuring classifier prediction accuracy and weight estimation error under various types of shifts on standard datasets including CIFAR-10 and MNIST. The results demonstrate that the ALS framework can achieve improvements in prediction accuracy of nearly 8% for large shifts and yields lower weight estimation error in most cases compared to the baseline methods. Additional analyses confirm that the constructed intermediate distribution indeed exhibits a smaller label shift relative to the target compared to the source distribution, and we investigate the influence of the proportion of selected pseudo-labeled samples on overall model performance.

Contributions. Our principal contributions are fourfold: (1) The novel introduction of an intermediate distribution concept to mitigate label shift. (2) The design of a principled algorithm, ALS, which learns a self-trained intermediate distribution to approximate the ideal distribution. (3) The establishment of generalization guarantees for ALS, accounting for both label distribution differences and pseudo-label bias. (4) Extensive experimental validation that confirms the effectiveness of our approach and corroborates our theoretical findings.

2 PROBLEM SETTING

Reweighted Framework. We model the feature and label spaces using random variables \(X \in \mathcal{X}\) and \(Y \in \mathcal{Y}\), respectively, where \(\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) is a discrete domain corresponding to \(\{1, 2, ..., K\}\). Here, \(d\) denotes the feature dimension and \(K\) is the total number of classes. We denote the labeled source dataset as \((X^P, Y^P) = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\) drawn from distribution \(P\), and the unlabeled target dataset as \(X^Q = \{x_i\}_{i=n+1}^{n+m}\) drawn from distribution \(Q\). The probability mass functions associated with \(P\) and \(Q\) are \(p\) and \(q\), respectively. To quantify the magnitude of the distributional shift, we employ the exponent of the second-order and infinite-order Rényi divergence:

\[
d(q||p) := \sum_{i=1}^{K} q(i) \frac{q(i)}{p(i)}, \quad \text{and} \quad d_{\infty}(q||p) := \sup_{i} \frac{q(i)}{p(i)}.
\]

Under the label shift assumption, i.e., \(p(X|Y) = q(X|Y)\) and \(p(Y) \neq q(Y)\), given a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) and a loss function \(l: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}\), the objective in the label shift setting is to find a hypothesis \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) that minimizes the following reweighted expected loss:

\[
\mathcal{L}(h) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim Q}[l(h(X), Y)] = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim P}[w(Y) l(h(X), Y)].
\]

Here, \(w \in \mathbb{R}^K\) is the vector of importance weights, defined as \(w(Y) = q(Y)/p(Y)\). In the special case where \(P = Q\), implying no distribution shift (\(w(Y) = \mathbf{1}\)), this problem reduces to the standard supervised learning paradigm.

In practical applications, the true weight vector \(w\) is unknown. Therefore, we instead minimize an empirical loss using an estimated weight vector \(\hat{w}\):

\[
\hat{\mathcal{L}}_P(h; \hat{w}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{w}(y_i) l(h(x_i), y_i).
\]

Importance Weight Estimation. Let \(C_h\) denote the confusion matrix with entries \([C_h]_{ij} = p(h(X^P)=i, Y^P=j)\), and let \(q_h\) be the vector representing the probability mass function of \(h(X^Q)\). In the finite sample setting, empirical estimates \(\hat{C}_h\) and \(\hat{q}_h\) are computed from the available data. The BBSE method estimates the importance weight as \(\hat{w} = \hat{C}_h^{-1} \hat{q}_h\). The RLLS method calculates a shift degree parameter \(\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \|\hat{C}_h \theta - (\hat{q}_h - \hat{C}_h \mathbf{1})\|_2 + \Delta_C \|\theta\|_2\), and subsequently obtains the importance weight as \(\hat{w} = \gamma \hat{\theta} + \mathbf{1}\). To facilitate theoretical comparison, we summarize the generalization bounds for these two methods using a unified form.

Corollary 1. Assume \(\hat{h}_{\hat{w}}\) is the classifier obtained using the estimated weights and \(h^*\) is the optimal classifier. With probability at least \(1-2\delta\), the following generalization bound holds:

\[
\mathcal{L}(\hat{h}_{\hat{w}}) - \mathcal{L}(h^*) \leq \varepsilon_{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{1}{n}, d_{\infty}(q||p), d(q||p)\right) + (1-\gamma)\|w-1\|_2 + \gamma \varepsilon_{w}\left(\frac{1}{n}, \|w-1\|_2\right).
\]

where
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{1}{n}, d_{\infty}(q||p), d(q||p)\right) := 2\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{H})) + \frac{2d_{\infty}(q||p)\log(2/\delta)}{n} + \sqrt{\frac{2d(q||p)\log(2/\delta)}{n}},
\]
\[
\varepsilon_{w}\left(\frac{1}{n}, \|w-1\|_2\right) := \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}}\left(\|w-1\|_2 \sqrt{\frac{\log(K/\delta)}{n}} + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}} + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{m}}\right)\right).
\]

Here, \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{H}) = \{g_h(x,y)=w(y)l(h(x),y), h\in\mathcal{H}\}\), \(\mathcal{R}(\cdot)\) denotes the Rademacher complexity, \(\sigma_{\min}\) is the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical confusion matrix \(\hat{C}_h\), \(\gamma \in (0,1)\) is a balance parameter, and \(\mathcal{O}\) hides universal constant factors.

Intermediate Distribution. The corollary above reveals that a larger label shift deviation \(\|w-1\|_2\) correlates with lower model generalization performance. To address this, we introduce the concept of an intermediate distribution with the explicit goal of alleviating the magnitude of the label shift.

Definition 1 (Intermediate Distribution). Given a distribution \(T\) with corresponding probability density or mass function \(t\), if the label-conditional distribution remains invariant (\(p(X|Y) = t(X|Y) = q(X|Y)\)) and the label marginal distribution shift is reduced (\(|q(Y)/t(Y) - 1| < |q(Y)/p(Y) - 1|\)), then \(T\) is defined as an intermediate distribution.

We establish sufficient conditions for the existence of such an intermediate distribution and, under the hypothetical scenario where some target labels are known, demonstrate a concrete construction for a dataset that follows distribution \(T\).

Proposition 1. If a distribution \(T\) is a linear combination of the source and target domain distributions, i.e., \(T = \lambda P + (1-\lambda)Q\) for some \(0 < \lambda < 1\), then \(T\) must be an intermediate distribution.

Proposition 2. Assume we have access to \(\hat{m}\) true target labels \((X^Q, Y^Q) = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=n+1}^{n+\hat{m}} \sim Q\). We can then construct a new labeled set \((X^T, Y^T) = [(X^P, Y^P), (X^Q, Y^Q)]\) which follows the intermediate distribution \(T\) with \(\lambda = n/(n+\hat{m})\). If a classifier is trained on this new set \((X^T, Y^T)\) using BBSE or RLLS, the resulting generalization bound will be tighter.

Proof details are provided in the supplementary material due to space constraints. The above proposition provides a theoretical example to illustrate the beneficial effect of an intermediate distribution on the generalization bound. However, since target labels are unavailable in practice, constructing such a distribution directly is not feasible.

3 PROPOSED APPROACH

In this section, we detail our methodology for constructing a self-trained distribution to approximate the ideal intermediate distribution. The ALS approach comprises three key components: (1) Approximating a subset of the true target labels with high-confidence pseudo-labels \(\{\hat{y}_i\}_{i=n+1}^{n+\hat{m}}\) to ensure pseudo-label accuracy. (2) Correcting for the potential deviation in the label-conditional distribution induced by the sample selection process for pseudo-labels. (3) Utilizing the newly constructed training set \((X^T, Y^T) = [\{x_i, y_i\}_{i=1}^{n}, \{x_i, \hat{y}_i\}_{i=n+1}^{n+\hat{m}}]\), which follows the self-trained distribution, to retrain the final classifier.

3.1 CONFIDENCE-GUIDED PSEUDO LABELS

For notational clarity, we define the \(k\)-th element of a label vector \(y\) as \(y^k\), the classifier parameters as \(v\), and \(\hat{p}(k|x, v)\) as the softmax probability for the \(k\)-th class. We employ the cross-entropy loss and first estimate an initial importance weight \(\hat{w}\) using either BBSE or RLLS on the source data. This allows us to obtain an initial target classifier \(\tilde{v}\) via the reweighted framework:

\[
\tilde{v} = \arg\min_{v} -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{w}(k) y_i^k \log \hat{p}(k|x_i, v).
\]

Empirical evidence suggests that predictions associated with large softmax probabilities generally correspond to pseudo-labels with higher confidence. Therefore, we propose a confidence-guided pseudo-label selection framework:

\[
\begin{cases}
\hat{Y}^Q = \arg\min -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=n+1}^{n+m} \sum_{k=1}^{K} y_i^k \log \frac{\hat{p}(k|x_i, \tilde{v})}{\lambda_k}, \\
\text{s.t.} \quad y_i^k \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in \{n+1,...,n+m\}.
\end{cases}
\]

The global optimal solution to this problem is given by:

\[
\hat{y}_i^{k^*} = \begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } k^* = \arg\max \left\{ \frac{\hat{p}(k|x_i, \tilde{v})}{\lambda_k} \right\} \text{ and } \hat{p}(k|x_i, \tilde{v}) > \lambda_k, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Note that \(\hat{y}_i^*\) can be either a one-hot vector or an all-zero vector. A one-hot vector indicates the corresponding sample \(x_i\) is selected with the assigned class \(k^*\), while an all-zero vector indicates the sample is not selected. The threshold \(\lambda_k\) for the \(k\)-th class controls the selection process; a prediction is selected with confidence only if its softmax probability exceeds this class-specific threshold.

The parameters \(\{\lambda_k\}_{k=1,...,K}\) are critical for controlling the pseudo-label learning and selection process. Drawing inspiration from established self-training literature, we introduce a strategy for determining these thresholds. Our goal is to select samples in a manner that approximates the target marginal distribution \(q(Y)\). Since \(q(Y)\) is unknown, we approximate it as \(\hat{q}(Y) = \hat{w} p(Y)\). We use a global selection ratio \(r\) to determine the total proportion of target samples to select across all classes. For the \(k\)-th class, the number of samples to select is \(\hat{m}_k = \lfloor r m \hat{q}(Y_k) \rfloor\). Consequently, \(\lambda_k\) is set as the softmax probability of the \(\hat{m}_k\)-th most confident prediction for class \(k\) among the target samples.

Let the distribution of the selected pseudo-labeled data be denoted as \(\hat{Q}\). Due to potential selection bias, the label-conditional distribution may deviate from the true target, i.e., \(\hat{q}(X|Y) \neq q(X|Y)\), which violates the core label shift assumption. This deviation impacts the expected loss with respect to the intermediate distribution, as formalized in the following proposition.

Proposition 3. Assume the classifier loss is upper-bounded, meaning there exists at least one hypothesis \(h\) such that \(l(h; (X,Y) \in \{P, T, Q\}) \leq \alpha^*\). For notational convenience, let \(\mathbb{E}_Q[l(h)]\) represent \(\mathbb{E}_{X,Y \sim Q}[l(h(X), Y)]\). Under this \(\alpha^*\)-loss assumption, the following bounds hold for the learning model \(\{l, h\}\):

\[
\begin{cases}
|\mathbb{E}_P[l(h)] - \mathbb{E}_Q[l(h)]| \leq 2\alpha^* d_{TV}(p(Y), q(Y)), \\
|\mathbb{E}_T[l(h)] - \mathbb{E}_Q[l(h)]| \leq 2\alpha^* d_{TV}(t(Y), q(Y)) + 2\alpha^* \min\{\mathbb{E}_Q(D_{tq}(X,Y)), \mathbb{E}_T(D_{tq}(X,Y))\},
\end{cases}
\]

where \(d_{TV}(\cdot, \cdot)\) denotes the Total Variation distance between probability distributions and \(D_{tq}(X,Y) := d_{TV}(t(X|Y), q(X|Y))\).

This proposition illustrates that even if the label marginal shift is reduced (\(d_{TV}(t(Y), q(Y)) < d_{TV}(p(Y), q(Y))\)), it is not guaranteed that the upper bound on the expected loss difference is smaller for the intermediate distribution, due to the potential presence of the conditional distribution discrepancy term \(D_{tq}(X,Y)\). Since directly optimizing \(D_{tq}(X,Y)\) is challenging, we provide a sufficient condition for its elimination.

Proposition 4. If the conditional distribution of the selected pseudo-labeled data matches the source conditional distribution, i.e., \(\hat{q}(X|Y) = p(X|Y)\), then \(D_{tq}(X,Y) = 0\) holds.

To align the conditional distributions, we employ Kernel Mean Matching to minimize the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) loss between the source and the selected pseudo-label data per class. The objective is:

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{X \sim p(X|Y_k)}[\varphi(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \hat{q}(X|Y_k)}[\varphi(X) \pi^k] \right\|^2,
\]

where \(\pi^k \in \mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}_k}\) is a vector of per-sample weights for class \(k\) and \(\varphi(\cdot)\) is a kernel mapping. Approximating the expectations with empirical means leads to:

\[
\min_{\pi} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left\| \frac{1}{\hat{m}_k} \sum_{i=1}^{\hat{m}_k} \pi_i^k \varphi(x_i^k) - \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} \varphi(x_j^k) \right\|^2.
\]

Let the true, unknown weights be \(\pi_* = [\pi_*^1; ...; \pi_*^K] \in \mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}}\). This loss can be reparametrized in kernel form as:

\[
\min_{\pi} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left( \frac{(\pi^k)^T \mathbf{K}^{\hat{Q}} \pi^k}{\hat{m}_k^2} - 2 \frac{\mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{K}^{P,\hat{Q}} \pi^k}{\hat{m}_k n_k} \right),
\]

where \(\mathbf{K}^{\hat{Q}}\) is the kernel matrix for the selected target samples \(X^{\hat{Q}}\) and \(\mathbf{K}^{P,\hat{Q}}\) is the cross-kernel matrix between source and selected target samples. We utilize a Gaussian kernel, \(\mathbf{K}(i,j) = \exp\left(-\frac{\|x_i - x_j\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\), where \(\sigma\) is the bandwidth parameter.

To encourage the selection of a substantial portion of the target set, we add a regularization term on the weights \(\{\pi^k\}\). However, reweighting the samples can alter the marginal distribution \(\hat{q}(Y)\), potentially violating the condition \(|w_t - 1| \leq |w_q - 1|\). Therefore, we introduce a specific constraint.

Proposition 5. Assume \(\pi_i^k\) is the weight for the \(i\)-th sample in the \(k\)-th class. If the constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^{\hat{m}_k} \pi_i^k = \hat{m}_k\) holds for every class \(k\), then the weighted pseudo-label marginal distribution satisfies \(\hat{q}_{\pi}(Y) = \hat{q}(Y)\).

Incorporating this constraint and the regularization, the final optimization problem becomes:

\[
\begin{cases}
\min_{\pi} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left( \frac{(\pi^k)^T \mathbf{K}^{\hat{Q}} \pi^k}{\hat{m}_k^2} - 2 \frac{\mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{K}^{P,\hat{Q}} \pi^k}{\hat{m}_k n_k} + \beta_k \|\pi^k\|^2 \right), \\
\text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{\hat{m}_k} \pi_i^k = \hat{m}_k, \quad \pi_i^k \geq 0, \quad \forall k \in \{1,...,K\}.
\end{cases}
\]

The optimal solution \(\hat{\pi} \in \mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}}\) can be obtained via Quadratic Programming (QP). Defining \(\mathcal{D}(\pi) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{X \sim p(X|Y_k)}[\varphi(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \hat{q}(X|Y_k)}[\varphi(X)\pi^k] \right\|^2\), we analyze the upper bound of \(\mathcal{D}(\hat{\pi}) - \mathcal{D}(\pi_*)\), which quantifies the distributional difference between \(\hat{q}(X|Y)\) and \(p(X|Y)\).

Proposition 6. Assume the kernel mapping \(\varphi\) is universal and its norm is bounded, \(\|\varphi(x)\| \leq \mu\), for the intermediate set. From Proposition 5, we have \(\|\pi^k\|_1 = \hat{m}_k\). Then, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),

\[
\mathcal{D}(\hat{\pi}) - \mathcal{D}(\pi_*) \leq \varepsilon_{\pi}(n, \hat{m}) = 16\mu^2 \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{2\left(\frac{1}{\hat{m}_k} + \frac{1}{n_k}\right) + 2\sqrt{2\left(\frac{1}{n_k} + \frac{1}{\hat{m}_k}\right)\log\frac{K}{\delta}}}.
\]

3.3 THE RETRAINING OF TARGET CLASSIFIER

Once the sample weights \(\hat{\pi}(x)\) are obtained, we re-estimate the importance weights \(\hat{w}_t\) using BBSE or RLLS on the new, weighted training set \([\{x_i, y_i\}_{i=1}^{n}, \hat{\pi}(x_i)\{x_i, \hat{y}_i\}_{i=n}^{n+\hat{m}}]\). The final empirical loss for the target classifier is thus:

\[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(h; \widehat{w}_t, \hat{\pi}) = \frac{1}{n+\hat{m}} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{w}_t(y_i) l(h(x_i), y_i) + \sum_{i=n}^{n+\hat{m}} \hat{w}_t(y_i) \hat{\pi}(x_i) l(h(x_i), \hat{y}_i) \right).
\]

Let us define the deviation in label-conditional and marginal distributions as \(d_{X|Y}(q||\hat{q}) := \mathbb{E}_{X,Y \sim Q}\left[ \left| \frac{q(X|Y) - \hat{q}(X|Y)}{t(X|Y)} \right| \right]\) and \(d_{Y}(q||\hat{q}) := \mathbb{E}_{X,Y \sim Q}\left[ \left| \frac{q(Y) - \hat{q}(Y)}{t(Y)} \right| \right]\). The traditional generalization bound (Corollary 1) is not directly applicable to our framework due to the introduced conditional distribution deviation and pseudo-label noise. Therefore, we derive a new generalization error bound that explicitly balances pseudo-label bias and importance weighting variance.

Proposition 7. Assume the true importance weight relating the target and intermediate distributions is \(\tau(X,Y) := \frac{q(X,Y)}{t(X,Y)}\), and the pseudo importance weight used is \(w_t(Y)\). For the ALS framework based on RLLS, with probability at least \(1-3\delta\), the generalization error is bounded as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(\hat{h}_{\hat{w}_t}; \tau) - \mathcal{L}(h^*; \tau) \leq & \varepsilon_{\mathcal{G}}(n+\hat{m}, d_{\infty}(q||t), d(q||t)) + \varepsilon_{w}(n+\hat{m}, \|w-1\|_2) \\
& + \frac{2\alpha^* r m}{n + r m} \left( d_{X|Y}(q||\hat{q}) + d_{Y}(q||\hat{q}) \right) + 2\alpha^* \|w_t(Y)\|_{\infty} \cdot err(h_{\tilde{v}}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here, \(\varepsilon_{\mathcal{G}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{w}\) are defined analogously to Corollary 1 but with sample size \(n+\hat{m}\) and divergences \(d(q||t)\), \(d_{\infty}(q||t)\). The term \(err(h_{\tilde{v}})\) denotes the importance-weighted 0/1 error of the initial predictor \(h_{\tilde{v}}\).

4 EXPERIMENT

4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

Datasets. We evaluate the performance and effectiveness of the ALS framework on several standard image classification datasets—MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100—under numerous artificially constructed label shifts. For each dataset, the data is randomly partitioned into two halves to represent the source and target domains. Samples are then drawn from each domain to form the source and target sets. For MNIST, the source and target set sizes are 2000 and 8000, respectively. For CIFAR-10, they are 3000 and 10000, and for CIFAR-100, they are 20000 and 30000. We consider two primary types of label shift: (1) Tweak-One shift, where the probability of one specific class is set to a value \(\rho \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8\}\) (with larger \(\rho\) indicating more extreme shift) while the proportions of other classes are held constant; and (2) Dirichlet shift, where class proportions are drawn from a Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameter \(\alpha \in \{1, 2, 5\}\) (with smaller \(\alpha\) indicating more extreme shift). We also investigate the effect of the pseudo-label selection ratio \(r \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5\}\) on model performance.

Compared Methods. In the main experiments, we compare the performance of ALS against several baselines and variations: (1) WW (Without Weighting): the performance of the base classifier without applying any importance weight correction. (2) CBST: a contemporary confidence-based self-training method. (3) BBSE and RLLS: the two standard label shift baselines. (4) BBSE-ALS and RLLS-ALS: our proposed ALS framework applied on top of BBSE and RLLS, respectively. (5) AvgImp: the average performance improvement of the ALS framework over both RLLS and BBSE.

Network Architecture. Both BBSE and RLLS are compatible with any base classifier. In our setup, we employ a two-layer fully connected neural network for the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, and use a ResNet-18 architecture for the more complex CIFAR-100 dataset.

Evaluation Metrics and Parameter Setting. For each shift type and parameter configuration, we perform 10 random samplings to evaluate predictive Accuracy (Acc) and F-score on the target set, as well as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the estimated importance weights. For our ALS framework, we tune the regularization parameter \(\beta\) from the set \(\{0, 0.001, 0.1, 10, 1000\}\), and the parameter \(\lambda\) is set identically to its value in the base RLLS method.

4.2 PREDICTIVE RESULTS

We first demonstrate the effectiveness of the ALS framework by reporting classification Accuracy under different pseudo-label selection ratios \(r\) on datasets with Dirichlet shift. As evidenced by the results, we make the following key observations:
(1) While the compared methods exhibit varying performance across datasets, our ALS framework consistently outperforms all other methods in every experimental condition. For instance, on CIFAR-10 with a strong Dirichlet shift (\(\alpha=1\)), the accuracy improvement exceeds 8%. These results robustly validate the effectiveness of the ALS framework.
(2) Notably, our approach achieves more substantial improvements under conditions of large label shift. For example, the improvement is about 8% on CIFAR-10 with \(\alpha=1\), but only about 2% on CIFAR-100 with \(\alpha=5\). This suggests that when the inherent label shift is small, the corrective effect of importance weighting via ALS is less pronounced. This trend is also reflected in comparisons with the CBST method.
(3) We observe that under large label shift, increasing the proportion of selected pseudo-label samples (\(r\)) does not always lead to better performance. The reason is that as more samples are included, the average accuracy of the pseudo-labels tends to decrease, introducing more erroneous samples into training and adversely affecting the importance weight estimation.
(4) Compared to the WW baseline, all label shift methods improve predictive performance, especially under large shifts, demonstrating the fundamental utility of importance weight estimation.
(5) Since accuracy alone may not fully capture performance on minority classes, we also evaluate using the F-score metric. The results confirm that our approach remains effective for smaller categories as well.

4.3 PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS

Weight Estimation Analysis. To further illustrate the effectiveness of our shift alleviation strategy, we analyze the Mean Squared Error of the estimated importance weights, i.e., \(\|w - w^*\|^2\). The results indicate that ALS achieves lower weight estimation error than the baseline methods in most cases, particularly when the pseudo-label selection ratio \(r\) is small. However, under conditions of very large label shift coupled with a high selection ratio (e.g., \(r=0.5\)), the weight estimation error for ALS can sometimes exceed that of BBSE and RLLS. This is attributed to the compounding effects of increased error from the initial shift-affected classifier and the introduction of incorrect pseudo-labels.

Visualization of Label Distribution Bias. To provide empirical evidence that ALS alleviates label shift via the self-trained intermediate distribution, we visualize the label shift degree \(w-1\) for both the source and the intermediate distributions. The results clearly show that the ALS framework effectively reduces the label distribution discrepancy across both positive and negative shifts.

The Effect of Pseudo Label Ratios. To explore the influence of the number of pseudo-labeled samples, we compare the predictive accuracy of the ALS framework against hypothetical scenarios using pseudo-labels (Pseudo w) and true labels (True w). When \(r=0\), BBSE-ALS and RLLS-ALS degenerate into standard BBSE and RLLS. The results indicate that the ALS framework generally achieves performance close to the "Pseudo w" ceiling, which represents the best possible performance attainable given the constraint of unknown true target labels.

5 RELATED WORK

Label shift represents a significant and actively studied category within the broader field of domain adaptation. It specifically addresses scenarios where the class prior distributions differ between source and target domains, while the class-conditional feature distributions remain invariant. Existing solutions typically follow a two-stage process: (1) estimating the importance weights, and (2) constructing an unbiased estimate of the target risk using these weights. Methods like BBSE and RLLS estimate weights via the confusion matrix and target predictions, then retrain a model under an Empirical Risk Minimization framework. Other works have addressed related challenges, such as mitigating the effect of noisy source labels under label shift. A common limitation of many existing methods is that they utilize unlabeled target samples only for weight estimation, not for direct classifier training, which may underutilize available information. Our ALS framework, which integrates self-training, offers a way to more fully leverage target samples and demonstrates extensibility to other label shift methods.

Pseudo-label learning is fundamentally based on self-training, a semi-supervised technique where a model trained on labeled data generates labels for unlabeled data, and the combined set is used for retraining. The core challenge is ensuring the accuracy of the generated pseudo-labels. Recent advances include confidence-regularized self-training to mitigate the impact of incorrect pseudo-labels, and theoretical analyses of self-training's generalization properties. Self-training has also been widely applied in domain adaptation settings to learn cross-domain generalizable pseudo-labels. However, due to differences in the underlying distribution shift assumptions (e.g., covariate shift vs. label shift), existing domain adaptation self-training methods are not directly applicable to the label shift problem, underscoring the novelty of our ALS framework.

6 CONCLUSIONS

In this paper, we have addressed the challenge of fully utilizing target domain samples under label shift by proposing a novel ALS framework designed to enhance the performance of established methods like BBSE and RLLS. The ALS framework introduces an intermediate distribution to bridge the source and target domains, leading to a more robust importance weight estimator and providing non-trivial generalization guarantees under specified conditions. Our comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the ALS framework across a range of label shift scenarios, from mild to severe. We believe this work represents a significant step towards improving the practical efficacy of label shift algorithms. For future work, we plan to extend our approach to the generalized label shift setting, which imposes stricter requirements on conditional distribution alignment. Determining how to maintain rigorous generalization guarantees in this more challenging setting remains an open problem that warrants further in-depth exploration.

Title: Alleviating Label Shift Through Self-trained Intermediate Distribution: A Comprehensive Theoretical and Algorithmic Framework

Abstract
In the grand pursuit of robust machine learning systems capable of operating in the real world, label shift stands as a formidable and pervasive obstacle. This phenomenon, where the marginal distributions of labels differ between source and target environments while conditional feature distributions remain stable, fundamentally undermines the homogeneous distribution assumption central to classical learning paradigms. To correct for this shift, importance weighting has emerged as a dominant and theoretically rigorous strategy. However, a critical limitation persists: the importance weight estimation in most existing methods suffers from unacceptably high variance under conditions of severe label shift or when source samples are scarce. This paper introduces a transformative and novel solution: we propose the strategic use of an ideal intermediate distribution to bridge the source and target domains, thereby dramatically reducing distributional variation. Our pioneering approach, Alleviating Label Shift (ALS), learns a self-trained intermediate distribution constructed innovatively from both labeled source and unlabeled target samples to approximate this ideal distribution. This framework masterfully balances the inherent bias introduced by pseudo-target labels against the variance from importance weighting. We provide rigorous theoretical proofs for the sample complexity and generalization guarantees of our approach, establishing a definitively tighter generalization bound than all existing label shift methods under mild and practical conditions. Extensive and conclusive experimental results across multiple benchmarks validate the exceptional effectiveness and superior performance of our approach over current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its significant practical value and potential for broad impact.

Section 1: INTRODUCTION

The foundational assumption of classical machine learning—that models are trained on a labeled source set and deployed on an unlabeled target set drawn from the same distribution—is elegant in theory but tragically insufficient for the complexities of the real world. In practical, dynamic environments, this identical distribution assumption is almost never satisfied. Consider the critical domain of medical diagnostics, where the prevalence of various diseases can vary dramatically across different geographical regions or demographic groups, even though the symptomatic presentation of a specific disease remains consistent. Similarly, in automated bird identification, the proportional distribution of bird species observed in spring is fundamentally different from that in winter, despite the fact that the visual appearance of any individual species does not change with the seasons. These are quintessential examples of the label shift problem, formally characterized by a divergence in label marginal distributions (p(Y) ≠ q(Y)) while the feature distribution conditioned on the label remains invariant (p(X|Y) = q(X|Y)).

The detrimental impact of label shift on traditional models is severe and well-documented, often leading to catastrophic drops in performance and reliability. Consequently, enhancing model generalization under such shifts is not merely an academic exercise but an urgent practical necessity. The majority of advanced methods address this by estimating importance weights to reweight the source classifier, aligning it with the target distribution. For instance, BBSE provides a theoretical foundation for correcting classifiers through importance-weighted empirical risk minimization. Building upon this, RLLS introduces a regularized weight estimator to improve statistical guarantees and robustness, particularly with limited samples. Other strategies, like MLLS, employ maximum likelihood estimation and calibration techniques, offering strong empirical performance but, critically, lacking rigorous theoretical generalization guarantees. A fundamental and unresolved weakness of these methods is that their importance weight estimation—and thus the resulting classifier's generalization—exhibits prohibitively high variance under large label shifts or when source data is limited.

In this work, we introduce a groundbreaking and conceptually elegant solution: instead of directly correcting from the source distribution, we propose an intermediate distribution as a strategic bridge. Our novel approach, ALS, learns a self-trained intermediate distribution constructed from the available labeled source and unlabeled target samples. As illustrated in Figure 1, this process effectively reduces the label distribution discrepancy, leading to far more accurate and stable importance weight estimation. The experimental results, exemplified in Table 1 for Dirichlet shifts, deliver compelling evidence of ALS's superiority. Label shift correction and pseudo-label learning via self-training are two well-established research areas. Conversely, modern self-training methods excel at leveraging unlabeled data but are not specifically designed for the theoretical constraints and guarantees of the label shift assumption. Our ALS framework represents a novel and powerful synthesis of these two lines of research. It innovatively uses self-training principles to construct a beneficial intermediate distribution specifically for the purpose of stabilizing importance weight estimation and improving generalization under label shift, a combination that is both creative and highly effective.

This paper addresses the critical challenge of label shift by introducing the innovative ALS framework, which strategically employs a self-trained intermediate distribution to make radically better use of target domain samples. 1 INTRODUCTION
In classical learning, a model is trained on a labeled source set and predicted on an unlabeled target set, assuming independent and identically distributed samples. This assumption often does not hold. Label shift occurs when the proportion of categories differs between source and target distributions (p(Y) ≠ q(Y)), while the feature distribution is the same for each category (p(X|Y) = q(X|Y)).

Due to changes in the label marginal distribution, traditional model performance can degrade. To improve generalization, models are adjusted for label shift. Many label shift methods estimate importance weights to reweight the source classifier. For example, BBSE corrects the source classifier through importance-weighted empirical risk minimization and provides a generalization error bound. RLLS provides statistical guarantees without a minimum sample complexity requirement and uses a regularized weight estimator. MLLS combines maximum likelihood with bias-corrected temperature scaling. However, BBSE and RLLS can have high variance in importance weight estimation and classifier generalization under large label shift or few source samples.

This work introduces an intermediate distribution, a linear combination of source and target distributions, to alleviate label shift. The approach, ALS, learns a self-trained intermediate distribution from labeled source and unlabeled target samples to approximate the intermediate distribution. ALS aims to reduce label distribution differences for more accurate importance weight estimation, while introducing bias from pseudo target labels. The impact of weight estimation variance and pseudo-label bias is analyzed theoretically.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets show classifier prediction accuracy and weight estimation error for various shifts. Results indicate ALS can improve prediction accuracy by nearly 8% for large shifts and reduce weight estimation error in most cases compared to BBSE and RLLS. The intermediate distribution has a smaller label shift than the source distribution, and the influence of sample selection proportion on performance is analyzed.

Shift is quantified using the exponent of the second and infinite order Renyi divergence:
d(q||p) := Σ_{i=1}^K q(i) (q(i)/p(i)), and d_∞(q||p) := sup_i (q(i)/p(i)).

Under label shift, p(X|Y) = q(X|Y) and p(Y) ≠ q(Y). Given a hypothesis class ℋ and loss function l: 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ, the goal is to find h ∈ ℋ minimizing the reweighted loss:
ℒ(h) = 𝔼_{(X,Y)∼Q}[l(h(X), Y)] = 𝔼_{(X,Y)∼P}[w(Y) l(h(X), Y)].
where w ∈ ℝ^K is the importance weight, w(Y) = q(Y)/p(Y). If P = Q, then w(Y) = 1.

\hat{ℒ}_P(h; ŵ) = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ŵ(y_i) l(h(x_i), y_i).

ℒ(ĥ_ŵ) - ℒ(h*) ≤ ε_𝒢(1/n, d_∞(q||p), d(q||p)) + (1-γ) ||w-1||_2 + γ ε_w(1/n, ||w-1||_2).
where
ε_𝒢(1/n, d_∞(q||p), d(q||p)) := 2ℛ(𝒢(ℒ,ℋ)) + (2 d_∞(q||t) log(2/δ))/n + √((2 d(q||t) log(2/δ))/n),

(1) ALS outperforms other methods in all cases. For example, on Dirichlet shift CIFAR10 with α=1, Acc improvement is more than 8%.
(2) Greater improvement occurs under large label shift. For CIFAR10 with α=1, Acc improvement is about 8%; for CIFAR100 with α=5, improvement is only 2%. Small label shift may have little effect on model performance, so ALS correction is less effective. This is illustrated by comparison with CBST.
(3) Under large label shift, experimental results do not always improve with increased proportion of pseudo label samples. Increased pseudo label samples can decrease true accuracy, adding error samples and affecting importance weight estimation.
(4) Compared to WW, all label shift methods improve predictive performance, especially under large label shift, demonstrating effectiveness of importance weight estimation.

5 RELATED WORK
Label shift is a type of domain adaptation. Existing solutions involve estimating importance weight and constructing an unbiased estimate of target risk. BBSE and RLLS use class-weighted samples to retrain a model under Empirical Risk Minimization. Other methods address noisy source labels. Existing label shift methods use unlabeled target samples only for importance weight estimation, not for direct classifier training. ALS can be extended to other label shift methods without theoretical guarantee.

Pseudo label learning relies on self-training, which trains on labeled samples, generates pseudo labels on unlabeled samples, and retrains with both. Core issues involve making pseudo labels accurate. Confidence regularized self-training reduces misleading effects from incorrect pseudo labels. Generalization of self-training with a one hidden layer neural network is evaluated. Self-training is used in domain adaptation to learn pseudo labels with cross-domain generalization. Due to different distribution shift hypotheses, existing self-training methods for domain adaptation do not solve the label shift problem addressed here.

6 CONCLUSIONS
This work proposes ALS to improve performance of label shift methods BBSE and RLLS by making fuller use of target domain samples. ALS leads to a more robust importance weight estimator and provides generalization guarantees under certain conditions. Experimental results show superiority in both small and large label shifts. Future work will expand the approach to generalized label shift setting with stricter conditional distribution alignment requirements, and explore maintaining generalization theory in that setting.

Abstract:
Label shift, where the source and target label marginal distributions differ, relaxes the homogeneous distribution assumption in classical learning. Importance weighting is a common strategy for correction with theoretical guarantees. However, importance weight estimation in existing methods can have high variance under large label shift or with few source samples. This work introduces an ideal intermediate distribution to reduce variation relative to the target label distribution. The approach learns a self-trained intermediate distribution from labeled source and unlabeled target samples to approximate the ideal distribution, balancing bias from pseudo target labels and variance from importance weighting. Sample complexity and generalization guarantees are provided, yielding a tighter generalization bound than existing label shift methods under mild conditions. Experimental results validate the approach against existing methods.

1 INTRODUCTION
In classical learning, a model is trained on a labeled source set and predicted on an unlabeled target set, assuming independent and identically distributed samples. This assumption often does not hold. Label shift occurs when the proportion of categories differs between source and target distributions (p(Y) ≠ q(Y)), while the feature distribution is the same for each category (p(X|Y) = q(X|Y)).

Due to changes in the label marginal distribution, traditional model performance can degrade. To improve generalization, models are adjusted for label shift. Many label shift methods estimate importance weights to reweight the source classifier. For example, BBSE corrects the source classifier through importance-weighted empirical risk minimization and provides a generalization error bound. RLLS provides statistical guarantees without a minimum sample complexity requirement and uses a regularized weight estimator. MLLS combines maximum likelihood with bias-corrected temperature scaling. However, BBSE and RLLS can have high variance in importance weight estimation and classifier generalization under large label shift or few source samples.

This work introduces an intermediate distribution, a linear combination of source and target distributions, to alleviate label shift. The approach, ALS, learns a self-trained intermediate distribution from labeled source and unlabeled target samples to approximate the intermediate distribution. ALS aims to reduce label distribution differences for more accurate importance weight estimation, while introducing bias from pseudo target labels. The impact of weight estimation variance and pseudo-label bias is analyzed theoretically.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets show classifier prediction accuracy and weight estimation error for various shifts. Results indicate ALS can improve prediction accuracy by nearly 8% for large shifts and reduce weight estimation error in most cases compared to BBSE and RLLS. The intermediate distribution has a smaller label shift than the source distribution, and the influence of sample selection proportion on performance is analyzed.

d(q||p) := Σ_{i=1}^K q(i) (q(i)/p(i)), and d_∞(q||p) := sup_i (q(i)/p(i)).

ℒ(h) = 𝔼_{(X,Y)∼Q}[l(h(X), Y)] = 𝔼_{(X,Y)∼P}[w(Y) l(h(X), Y)].

The optimal solution π̂ ∈ ℝ^{ṁ} is obtained by Quadratic Programming. Let 𝒟(π) = Σ_{k=1}^K || 𝔼_{X∼p(X|Y_k)}[φ(X)] - 𝔼_{X∼q̂(X|Y_k)}[φ(X) π^k] ||^2. The upper bound of 𝒟(π̂) - 𝒟(π_*) is analyzed.

Proposition 6 Let the kernel mapping be universal and upper bounded, ||φ(x)|| ≤ μ for the intermediate set. From Proposition 5, ||π^k||_1 = ṁ_k. With probability at least 1-δ,
𝒟(π̂) - 𝒟(π_*) ≤ ε_π(n, ṁ) = 16μ^2 Σ_{k=1}^K √( 2(1/ṁ_k + 1/n_k) + 2√(2(1/n_k + 1/ṁ_k) log(K/δ)) ).

3.3 THE RETRAINING OF TARGET CLASSIFIER
Once sample weights π̂(x) are obtained, importance weights ŵ_t are re-estimated by BBSE or RLLS on the new training set [{x_i, y_i}_{i=1}^n, π̂(x_i) {x_i, ŷ_i}_{i=n}^{n+ṁ}]. The final target empirical loss is:
\hat{ℒ}(h; ŵ_t, π̂) = 1/(n+ṁ) ( Σ_{i=1}^n ŵ_t(y_i) l(h(x_i), y_i) + Σ_{i=n}^{n+ṁ} ŵ_t(y_i) π̂(x_i) l(h(x_i), ŷ_i) ).

Define deviation of label conditional and marginal distribution as d_{X|Y}(q||q̂) := 𝔼_{X,Y∈Q}[ |(q(X|Y) - q̂(X|Y))/t(X|Y)| ] and d_Y(q||q̂) := 𝔼_{X,Y∈Q}[ |(q(Y) - q̂(Y))/t̂(Y)| ]. Traditional generalization theory does not apply directly due to conditional distribution deviation and pseudo label noise. A new generalization error bound balances pseudo label bias and importance weighting variance.

Proposition 7 Assume the true importance weight is τ(X,Y) := q(X,Y)/t(X,Y) and the pseudo importance weight is w_t(Y). For ALS based on RLLS, with probability at least 1-3δ, ALS generalizes as:
ℒ(ĥ_ŵ_t; τ) - ℒ(h*; τ) ≤ ε_𝒢(n+ṁ, d_∞(q||t), d(q||t)) + ε_w(n+ṁ, ||w-1||_2)
+ (2α* r m)/(n + r m) ( d_{X|Y}(q||q̂) + d_Y(q||q̂) ) + 2α* ||w_t(Y)||_∞ err(h_ṽ).
where
ε_𝒢(n+ṁ, d_∞(q||t), d(q||t)) = 2ℛ(𝒢(ℒ,ℋ)) + (2α* d_∞(q||t) log(2/δ))/(n+ṁ) + √((2α* d(q||t) log(2/δ))/(n+ṁ)),

err(h_ṽ) denotes the importance weighted 0/1-error of predictor h_ṽ.

4 EXPERIMENT
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Datasets. Performance is evaluated on artificial shifts on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. Each dataset is randomly divided into source and target domains of the same size. Data points are sampled as source and target sets. For MNIST, source set size is 2000, target set size is 8000. For CIFAR10, source set size is 3000, target set size is 10000. For CIFAR100, source set size is 20000, target set size is 30000. Two shift types are considered: Tweak-One shift, where a class changes to probability ρ ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8} (larger ρ results in more extreme label shift), while other classes remain constant. Dirichlet shift generates class proportions by Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameter α ∈ {1, 2, 5} (smaller α results in more extreme label shift). The effect of pseudo-label sample number is discussed with ratio r ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5} on target sets.

Compared methods. (1) WW: base classifier without estimated importance weights. (2) CBST: an advanced self-training method. (3) BBSE and RLLS: standard baselines. (4) BBSE-ALS and RLLS-ALS: ALS framework variations with BBSE and RLLS as base methods. (5) AvgImp: average performance improvement of ALS over RLLS and BBSE.

Network architecture. BBSE and RLLS can use any classifier. A two-layer fully connected neural network is used for MNIST and CIFAR10. ResNet18 is used for CIFAR100.

Evaluation indicators and parameter setting. For each shift type, 10 random samples are drawn with corresponding distribution parameters to evaluate predictive Accuracy (Acc) and F-score on the target set, and Mean Square Error of estimated weights. For ALS, regularized parameter β is chosen from {0, 0.001, 0.1, 10, 1000}, and parameter λ is the same as in RLLS.

4.2 PREDICTIVE RESULTS
Classification Accuracy under different proportions of pseudo label samples on Dirichlet shift datasets is reported. Methods run on Python 3.7 and PyTorch. Observations:
(1) ALS outperforms other methods in all cases. For example, on Dirichlet shift CIFAR10 with α=1, Acc improvement is more than 8%.
(2) Greater improvement occurs under large label shift. For CIFAR10 with α=1, Acc improvement is about 8%; for CIFAR100 with α=5, improvement is only 2%. Small label shift may have little effect on model performance, so ALS correction is less effective. This is illustrated by comparison with CBST.
(3) Under large label shift, experimental results do not always improve with increased proportion of pseudo label samples. Increased pseudo label samples can decrease true accuracy, adding error samples and affecting importance weight estimation.
(4) Compared to WW, all label shift methods improve predictive performance, especially under large label shift, demonstrating effectiveness of importance weight estimation.
(5) F-score metric is also used; results show ALS is effective for small categories.

4.3 PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS
Weight estimation analysis. Mean Square Error of estimated weights, ||w - w*||^2, is shown. ALS performs better than other methods in most cases, especially with small pseudo label selection ratio. However, with pseudo label selection ratio 50% under large label shift, weight error of ALS estimation can be larger than BBSE and RLLS due to large shift classifier increasing weight estimation error and wrong labels.

Visualization of Label Distribution Bias. Label shift degree w-1 of intermediate and source distributions is visualized. ALS effectively reduces label distribution difference for both positive and negative shifts.

The Effect of Pseudo Label Ratios. Predictive accuracy of ALS framework, pseudo labels, and true labels is compared. Pseudo w is weight under pseudo labels; True w is weight under true labels. If r=0, BBSE-ALS and RLLS-ALS degenerate to BBSE and RLLS. ALS framework achieves performance roughly similar to Pseudo w under different conditions, hitting the performance ceiling since target labels are unknown.

5 RELATED WORK
Label shift is a type of domain adaptation. Existing solutions involve estimating importance weight and constructing an unbiased estimate of target risk. BBSE and RLLS use class-weighted samples to retrain a model under Empirical Risk Minimization. Other methods address noisy source labels. Existing label shift methods use unlabeled target samples only for importance weight estimation, not for direct classifier training. ALS can be extended to other label shift methods without theoretical guarantee.

Pseudo label learning relies on self-training, which trains on labeled samples, generates pseudo labels on unlabeled samples, and retrains with both. Core issues involve making pseudo labels accurate. Confidence regularized self-training reduces misleading effects from incorrect pseudo labels. Generalization of self-training with a one hidden layer neural network is evaluated. Self-training is used in domain adaptation to learn pseudo labels with cross-domain generalization. Due to different distribution shift hypotheses, existing self-training methods for domain adaptation do not solve the label shift problem addressed here.

6 CONCLUSIONS
This work proposes ALS to improve performance of label shift methods BBSE and RLLS by making fuller use of target domain samples. ALS leads to a more robust importance weight estimator and provides generalization guarantees under certain conditions. Experimental results show superiority in both small and large label shifts. Future work will expand the approach to generalized label shift setting with stricter conditional distribution alignment requirements, and explore maintaining generalization theory in that setting.

Title: Causal Exploration for Task-Agnostic Reinforcement Learning

Abstract:
Model training depends on the quality of training data, but data collection is often limited by budget constraints. This work introduces causal exploration, a strategy that uses underlying causal knowledge for data collection and model training. The focus is on improving the sample efficiency and reliability of world model learning in task-agnostic reinforcement learning. During exploration, the agent selects actions expected to yield causal insights beneficial for world model training. Causal knowledge is acquired and refined incrementally with data collection. Causal exploration aids in learning accurate world models using fewer data, and theoretical guarantees for its convergence are provided. Empirical experiments on synthetic data and real-world applications validate the benefits.

1 Introduction
Deep neural networks have been successful in various domains. A key factor is the availability of high-quality training data. In many practical applications, data collection is limited by budget constraints, highlighting a need to enhance sampling and model learning efficiency.

This work introduces causal exploration to address this challenge. It uses underlying causal knowledge to boost data collection and model training. Acquiring causal knowledge reveals the fundamental mechanisms behind data generation, reducing the exploration space. Causal exploration allows systematic action planning based on identified causal structures, unlike random data collection. Causal knowledge reflects cause-and-effect dependencies among variables. Incorporating causal structural constraints into the model can yield causal dynamics models that eliminate redundant dependencies, potentially providing more accurate estimations than non-causal dense models.

Specifically, the focus is on boosting the sample efficiency and reliability of the world model in task-agnostic reinforcement learning (RL). A task-agnostic RL agent first learns a global world model from data collected during exploration. Based on the learned model's predictions, the agent can adapt to various downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner given task-specific reward functions. This setup imposes high requirements on model accuracy. Data collection and world model learning are expensive due to extensive environment interactions, especially in large state spaces.

The causal exploration approach involves three primary aspects. First, constraint-based methods discover causal relationships among environment variables. Second, the dynamics model is formulated under causal structural constraints to enhance reliability. Third, methods based on causal knowledge improve sample efficiency during exploration. For causal discovery, an efficient online method selectively eliminates noisy samples and strategically gathers informative data points incrementally. The agent actively explores towards novel states expected to contribute most to model training. The exploration policy is driven by intrinsic rewards measuring the agent's surprise at the outcome and the training quality caused by the selected data. During exploration, causal knowledge and the world model are continuously refined.

Key contributions are:
*   Introducing causal exploration to enhance sample efficiency and reliability of model training with causal knowledge, focusing on task-agnostic RL.
*   Developing an online method for causal discovery and formulating the world model with explicit structural embeddings. During exploration, the dynamics model is trained under a weight-sharing-decomposition schema to avoid additional computational burden.
*   Theoretically showing that, given strong convexity and smoothness assumptions, the approach attains a superior convergence rate compared to non-causal methods. Empirical experiments demonstrate the robustness of the online causal discovery method and the effectiveness of causal exploration across demanding RL environments.

2 Preliminary
Task-agnostic RL is considered within a Markov decision process with state space S and action space A. To integrate causal information, the following assumptions are made.
Assumption 1 (Causal Factorization).
Both the state space and action space can be factorized. That is, S = S_1 × … × S_n ∈ R^n and A = A_1 × … × A_c ∈ R^c.
Assumption 2 (Causal Sufficiency).
The state variables s_t are fully observable without any hidden confounders.
Assumption 3 (Faithfulness Condition).
For a causal graph G and the associated probability distribution P, every true conditional independence relation in P is entailed by the Causal Markov Condition applied to G.

Given these assumptions, transition causality is defined over the transition variables from {s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}} to s_t.
Definition 1 (Transition Causality).
Under the Markov condition, the causal structures are over the state-action variables U = {S_{i,t-1}}_{i=1}^n ∪ {A_{j,t-1}}_{j=1}^c and V = {S_{i,t}}_{i=1}^n, which can be represented by a directed acyclic graph G = ({ U, V}, E) and its adjacency matrix D. Here, E denotes the edge set and D ∈ {0, 1}^{|U| × |V|}.

All edges are from U to V. If s_{i,t-1} ∈ U has a causal edge to s_{j,t} ∈ V, then s_{i, t-1} is a parent of s_{j,t} and D(i,j)=1. The structural constraints are assumed invariant over time t.
Proposition 1.
Under the aforementioned assumptions, the causal adjacency matrix D is identifiable.

3 Related Work
Task-agnostic RL.
Task-agnostic exploration strategies aim for generalization. Existing methods focus on designing intrinsic rewards, categorized into: (1) the number of times a state has been visited, guiding the agent towards unexplored regions; (2) curiosity about environment dynamics, formalized as prediction errors of future states; and (3) information gain, maximizing mutual information. Existing works usually pay little attention to the support causal structures can offer in improving exploration efficiency.

RL with causal discovery.
The intersection of causal discovery and RL has become a trend. Some works use RL to search for the causal graph with the best score. Others propose learning a hierarchical causal structure for subgoal-based policy learning. Some focus on providing tractable formulations of systematic generalization in RL tasks using a causal viewpoint. Another learns a causal world model to generate explanations for decision-making. Theoretical evidence about the advantages of using a causal world-model in offline RL is given. However, most works focus on extracting underlying causal graphs from given data or using random exploration strategies for data collection, instead of directly utilizing causal structure as guidance to improve exploration efficiency in task-agnostic RL.

4 Discovering and Utilizing Causality for Learning World Models
This section introduces the methodology for causal exploration. It initially assumes causal structures are known and shows how to incorporate causal knowledge into the world model. Then, an estimation procedure for causal structures is given.

4.1 Causal Constraints for Forward Model
During task-agnostic exploration, the agent learns a world model f_w^c with parameter w^c, serving as an abstraction of ground truth transitions. The world model predicts future state ŝ_t based on current state s_{t-1} and action a_{t-1}: ŝ_t = f_w^c(s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, e_t), where e_t is random noise. Causal structures within environmental variables are typically sparse. For instance, a variable s_{2,t-1} may not causally affect s_{1,t}, making it a non-parent node. Consequently, only a subset of (s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) is needed as model inputs.

To reflect these constraints, causal structures are explicitly considered to model one-step transition dynamics:
ŝ_t = ∏_{i=1}^n f^i_w^c (D_i ⊙ (s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}), e_{i,t}),
where ⊙ denotes element-wise product, D_i and e_{i,t} are the i-th column of causal matrix D and noise term e_t, respectively. A naive implementation requires training n world models, potentially causing explosive computational complexity growth.

A sharing-decomposition schema is proposed to address this. The n networks share the first several layers as a common embedding. Following the sharing module, predictive networks are designed for each dimension. Suppose w_i^c is the network parameter for the i-th dimension, it is a combination of shared parameter σ and decomposed parameter θ_i:
w_i^c = σ ∪ θ_i.
During training, each model focuses on a different aspect of the state in the decomposition part θ_i but shares common knowledge σ. The number of shared layers is a hyperparameter allowing a trade-off. Training forward models under this schema utilizes causal information for accurate predictions and achieves a reduction in parameters and computation time compared to naive decomposition. The prediction error is used as the loss function for optimizing w^c:
L_f(w^c) = 1/2 ‖ ŝ_t - s_t ‖^2_2.

4.2 Efficient Online Causal Relationship Discovery
This section shows how to identify the causal adjacency matrix D. According to Definition 1, this is transformed into determining whether an edge exists between each pair of nodes in causal graph G. Starting from a complete graph, unnecessary edges are iteratively removed using Conditional Independence Tests (CIT). Given edges follow temporal order without instantaneous connection, the PC algorithm is extended to handle time-lagged causal relationships based on Kernel-based Conditional Independence (KCI) test to identify D.

Causal discovery algorithms typically require substantial data. Accumulating more samples increases time cost. To reduce identification process cost, an efficient online causal relationship discovery method is designed: instead of using all incoming data, representative data points are selectively collected during exploration incrementally. Specifically, minibatch similarity and sample diversity criteria are used as selection strategies:
Similarity = (∇ f_w^c(b^i_t) ∇̄f_w^c(B_t)^⊤) / (‖ ∇ f_w^c(b^i_t) ‖ ⋅ ‖∇̄f_w^c(B_t) ‖),
Diversity = -1/(t - 1) ∑_{p ≠ i}^{t -1} (∇ f_w^c(b^i_t) ∇f_w^c(b^p_t)^⊤) / (‖ ∇ f_w^c(b^i_t) ‖ ⋅ ‖∇f_w^c(b^p_t) ‖).
Here b^i_t is the i-th data of the arrival batch B_t. ∇ f_w^c(b^i_t) and ∇̄f_w^c(B_t) are the gradient and average gradient of the sample and batch, respectively. A combination of these two criteria selects the top-κ data among B_t for causal discovery during exploration. Experiments show this online method significantly accelerates causal discovery without sacrificing overall accuracy.

The approach allows flexibility in the choice of causal discovery methods. However, constraint-based approaches usually exhibit better robustness compared with score-based methods under this specific configuration. Comparative experiments among different causal discovery methods demonstrate the correctness of the causal structure identified by the time-lagged PC algorithm.

5 Boosting Efficiency through Causal Exploration
This section addresses enhancing data collection efficiency during causal exploration to improve causal discovery and model learning performance. A concept from active learning is selecting samples that make the largest contributions to the model's training loss. These samples are considered a subset the model is least familiar with. The prediction loss is used as intrinsic reward to guide exploration with scaling weight η:
r^i_{t-1} = η/2 ‖ ŝ_t - s_t ‖^2_2.
This prediction loss validates the agent's causal beliefs. A larger prediction error implies greater deviation from estimated values based on causal structure and world model. A faster error rate drop provides more learning progress signals.

Not all novel states positively impact the model. Noisy data may contribute significantly to prediction errors but lead the model in an undesirable direction, necessitating attention to inherent data quality during exploration. Active reward measures data quality as another intrinsic motivation. Once a new sample is collected at time step t, active reward is calculated as the change of the model's prediction ability before and after training. Prediction accuracy on a test set D_h generated from episodes unseen before training reflects the world model's performance. Active reward is formulated as:
r^a_{t-1} = L̄_f(w^c_{t-2}) - L̄_f(w^c_{t-1}),
where L̄_f(⋅) is the mean prediction error on D_h and w^c_t denotes parameters of the trained world model at time t. Active reward value reflects beneficial or detrimental training caused by the selected data. Prediction loss and active reward are combined with regularization weight β:
r_{t-1} = r^i_{t-1} + β r^a_{t-1}.
During causal exploration, the agent searches for causal informative data by maximizing expected rewards:
a^*_t = argmax_{a ∈ A}  E_{τ ∼ π} [∑_t γ^t r_t ],
where τ represents the trajectory generated by exploration policy π and γ is the discount factor. The world model minimizes prediction loss. Since both contain prediction error, the learning of world models and causal exploration facilitate each other.

5.1 Theoretical Analysis on Causal Exploration
This subsection presents a mathematical criterion for evaluating the impact of causal exploration on sampling efficiency and theoretically demonstrates its benefits in learning world models, especially when the causal graph is sparse.

Causal efficiency ratio.
Let k denote the optimization step in world model training, f represent the world model, and L_f(w) be the corresponding loss function. Model parameters incorporating causal knowledge after the k-th optimization are denoted w^c(k), while w(k) represents parameters without causal information. The convergence bounds ratio, denoted ξ, calculated as the relative improvement in the model's loss compared to the optimal value L_f^⋆, assesses enhanced exploration efficiency from incorporating causal knowledge:
ξ = (L_f(w^c(k)) - L_f^⋆) / (L_f(w(k)) - L_f^⋆).
This ratio measures how much closer the model with causal knowledge gets to the optimal value compared to those without causal information. If ξ < 1 consistently holds, it indicates an improvement in efficiency attributable to causal exploration. A theoretical analysis of causal exploration performance in linear cases is provided, and empirical experiments show it is efficient in learning deep neural networks.

Theoretical guarantees.
Learning a linear forward model with gradient descent is considered:
min_w  L_f(w) = ‖w^⊤ ⋅ (s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) - s_t ‖^2_2,
where s_t = w^⋆^⊤ ⋅ (s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) is the ground truth value. The following assumption is made:
Assumption 4.
L_f is strong convex and smooth such that ∃ m>0, M>0, for any w ∈ dom L_f, we have
MI ⪰ ∇^2 L_f(w) ⪰ mI.

Theorem 1 shows a reduced error bound with causal exploration.
Theorem 1.
Suppose Assumption 4 holds, and suppose the density of causal matrix D is δ and the model is initialized with w_0. Then for every optimization step k, we have
L_f(w^c(k)) - L_f^⋆ ≤ δ^k ( L_f(w(k)) - L_f^⋆)
≤ M/2 [ δ ( 1- m/M )]^k ‖ w_0 - w^⋆ ‖^2_2.

Remark.
The first inequality establishes an upper bound for ξ at δ^k. Given 0 ≤ δ^k ≤ 1, this confirms the effectiveness of causal exploration in enhancing efficiency. The subsequent inequality establishes that the training error of causal exploration gradually converges to the optimal value, exhibiting an exponential convergence rate characterized by the decay of the factor [ δ ( 1- m/M )]^k. This theorem implies the advantages of causal exploration are relevant to the sparseness of causal structure. The sparser the causal structure, the faster the method learns. When the causal matrix D is a complete matrix (δ = 1), causal exploration degenerates into non-causal prediction-based exploration.

6 Experiments
To evaluate the effectiveness of causal exploration in complex scenarios, experiments are conducted on synthetic datasets and real-world applications, including traffic light control and MuJoCo control suites. The proposed causal exploration is compared with baseline methods:
1. Curiosity and Plan2Explore: non-causal exploration methods that learn dense models with different forms of intrinsic rewards.
2. CID: focuses on detecting causal influences between actions a_{t-1} and future states s_t with random data collection. Causal exploration extends to discover dependencies among state transitions.
3. ASR: a differential approach that learns causal matrix D as free parameters together with world model f. In this approach, identification of D is completed by causal discovery methods.
4. CDL: learns causal dynamics models to approximate conditional mutual information rather than directly implementing CIT on observed data.

Attributes of baselines and causal exploration are summarized from four perspectives: utilization of causal knowledge, explicit structural embedding, online causal discovery, and non-random data collection.

Following prior work, the following metrics evaluate learned models:
1. Prediction Ability: Error in predicting future states directly reflects model learning quality. Lower prediction errors achieved with the same number of samples imply higher accuracy and increased sampling efficiency.
2. Structural Difference: Evaluation of causal discovery methods based on the difference between identified causal matrix and ground truth matrix.
3. Downstream Performance: For task-agnostic exploration, performance on downstream tasks measures the model’s understanding of underlying causal structures.

6.1 Synthetic Datasets
Environments.
A simulated environment is built following a state space model with controls. When the agent takes action a_t based on current state, the environment provides feedback s_{t+1} at the next time. The generative environment is:
s_1 ∼ N(0, I),  s_t ∼ N( h(s_{t-1},a_{t-1}), Σ),
where Σ is the covariance matrix and h is the mean value as ground truth transition function implemented by deep neural networks under causal graph G. The linear condition uses a single-layer network; the nonlinear function uses three-layer MLPs with sigmoid activation.

The sparsity of the causal graph is an important factor affecting performance. To demonstrate superiority on relatively low-density causal structures, G is generated by randomly connecting edges with probability p. Such sparse structures allow evaluation of the method's ability to accurately learn world models with limited data.

Correctness of the identified causal structure.
The proposed method is compared with different causal discovery methods. CID and CDL apply score-based causal discovery, while ASR combines causal structure with neural networks for differentiable training. CID only considers causal action influence and lacks explicit causal structure, so it is not used for comparison. An example of the causal matrix discovered by different methods is illustrated, where color depth indicates the number of times each edge is detected as a causal connection. The averaged F1-score of these methods is shown. The causal matrix learned through causal exploration obtains a smaller bias from the ground-truth matrix than others, explaining better performances.

Reliability of the learned world models.
To show the advantage of causal exploration for improving model learning quality, it is compared with all baselines. Prediction errors of world models during exploration under various state and action spaces are shown. For each setting, 10 experiments are conducted and averaged to reduce randomness impact. In all environments, causal exploration achieves lower prediction errors with fewer data. Compared to Curiosity and Plan2Explore, advantages stem from introducing causality. Larger dimension and sparser causal structure make advantages over non-causal methods more prominent. Improvements over ASR and CID are attributed to effective exploration strategy design. Results compared with CDL underscore the importance of stability of causal discovery methods and necessity of explicit causal embeddings.

Advantage of causal-based models at the initial iteration.
Many prediction error curves have a different y intercept, suggesting causal exploration is better even at initial iteration. This is because integrating causal matrix D into the model exclusively incorporates parent nodes and eliminates extraneous input information when predicting future states, unlike prior methodologies where these nodes were treated and initialized equally with parent nodes. This advantage is tied to correctness of identified causal matrix and sparsity of causal graph as in Theorem 1.

Ablation study and generalization to some challenging scenarios.
Ablation studies are performed: For online causal discovery, results with various sampling methods are provided; for optimization of exploration strategy, the impact of active reward is investigated, and causal exploration with other forms of intrinsic reward is performed. Since reliability of identified causal structures is essential for causal exploration performance, challenging scenarios where the agent starts with wrong causal beliefs and encounters sudden structural changes are also considered.

6.2 Real World Applications
Application to Traffic Signal Control Task.
Experiments are conducted in traffic signal control task to evaluate the proposed method. Performance of different learned world models on downstream policy learning is listed. Reward is a combination of several terms including sum of queue length. Duration refers to averaged travel time vehicles spent on approaching lanes (in seconds). Length is sum of length of waiting vehicles over all approaching lanes and Vehicles is total number of vehicles that passed intersection. An agent is trained in the true environment to verify reliability of learned models through task-agnostic exploration. Performance of policy learned on world models trained during causal exploration is comparable to, or in some metrics better than, that of true environment.

Application to MuJoCo Tasks.
Causal exploration is evaluated on MuJoCo tasks, where state-action dimensions range from tens (Hopper-v2) to hundreds (Humanoid-v2). The world model learned during causal exploration performs lower prediction errors than others. This ability stems from focus on causal structural constraints. By selectively incorporating parent nodes during state prediction, the approach maintains informed exploration even when exploratory signals decline, preventing the agent from getting stuck in sub-optimal behaviors. Good performance is achieved in shorter time. Task performance also reflects reliability of these world models. The proposed method works well when state space is large. As long as there is a strong causal relationship between observed state variables, and causal discovery algorithm accurately identifies corresponding causal structure, causal exploration method is applicable to high-dimensional situations.

7 Conclusion and Future Work
This work introduces causal exploration, a methodology designed to incorporate causal information from data for learning world models efficiently. Causal exploration is employed within task-agnostic reinforcement learning, and a sharing-decomposition schema leverages causal structural knowledge for the world model. Experiments in simulated environments and real-world tasks demonstrate superiority, highlighting the importance of rich causal prior knowledge for efficient data collection and model learning. This study primarily focuses on scenarios where states are fully observed. Future research directions involve addressing more complex scenarios including unobserved latent state variables and developing improved fault-tolerant mechanisms to enhance robustness.
