2 GRAPH-BASED INTERACTION WITH THE COQ PROOF ASSISTANT
The literature contains many formats for representing the proof state and definitions within the environment, both for training a model and for communication between the model and Coq. In this work, we employ a novel graph-based format where all Coq definitions and proof states are stored within a single large, interconnected graph structure. Figure 2 shows a representative subset of this large graph, depicting the proof state and environment at the initiation of the Suggest command illustrated in Figure 1. This graph-based approach provides the following definitive advantages: (1) The graph is constructed directly from terms provided by the Coq kernel, faithfully encoding all objects present in the Coq environment without loss of information. (2) References to global definitions are explicitly represented by graph edges, thereby completely avoiding any potential ambiguity related to name resolution. (3) Local variables are explicitly connected to their respective binders via edges, eliminating any reliance on local variable names. (4) Identical terms are shared across different parts of the graph, leading to significantly more compact and efficient representations.

This extensive mono-graph, containing millions of nodes, is prohibitively large for direct processing by a graph neural network. Therefore, we extract smaller, manageable proof state and definition subgraphs for input into our models. Each proof state and definition possesses a designated root node within the large graph. To obtain a smaller subgraph, we calculate the forward closure starting from the root node, terminating the traversal when a definition node is encountered. Mutually dependent definitions, such as inductive definitions, feature multiple mutually dependent root nodes. Theorems represent special cases of definitions where the theorem node points to both the theorem statement and its associated proof term. We deliberately omit the proof term from the theorem's definition graph to reduce overall graph size. The subgraphs extracted from the mono-graph are topologically ordered according to their dependencies, ensuring they can be processed in the correct sequential order by the neural network. In Figure 2, the extracted subgraphs are clearly highlighted for definitions T1, =, f, +, and N, as well as the current proof state of theorem T2, which is still under construction. Notably, the subgraphs for T1 and the proof state share the subterm associated with the multiplication operation.

Within the dataset of proofs, each proof state is associated with a corresponding applied tactic, forming the core training data for the prediction model. A tactic command is decomposed into a base tactic and its arguments. While arguments may be arbitrary Coq terms or other objects, our prediction model is specifically designed to predict only local hypotheses or global definitions as arguments.

The dataset we utilize is extracted from 120 distinct Coq packages obtained from the Opam package manager. These packages were selected by a SAT solver as the largest mutually consistent set of packages available for Coq version 8.11. Their subject matter varies extensively, encompassing fields such as mathematical analysis, compiler and programming language formalization, separation logic, homotopy type theory, and many others. The graph extracted from these formalizations consists of over 250 million nodes, which encode 520k definitions, of which 266k are theorems, and 4.6M proof state transformations.

We meticulously divide the packages into training and test sets, ensuring that no test package depends on any training package. To achieve this, we induced a random topological order on the Coq packages with regard to their dependency graph. The resulting ordered list was then split such that the average percentage of theorems and proof states in the training split is close to 90% (specifically, 91.3% of all theorems and 88.8% of all proof states).

The Tactician synth tactic and Suggest command communicate via this graph format with a Python client running the machine learning model. Tactician transmits the entire mono-graph of global definitions along with the current proof state. The client returns a ranked list of suggested tactics and their associated confidence scores. This integration makes our solver eminently usable in practical scenarios and allows us to perform massively parallel benchmarking of our model on any Coq Opam package.

3 PROOF AUTOMATION METHODS
Here, we describe in detail all solvers that will be comprehensively compared in this paper. Section 3.1 elaborates on the architecture of Graph2Tac, while Section 3.2 summarizes the other systems included for comparison. The transformer baseline was developed concurrently with Graph2Tac. All other systems were developed independently. Note that comparisons with highly relevant solvers, such as Proverbot9001, are omitted because they do not provide proof search functionality through a standard Coq tactic. Other symbolic solvers, such as SMTCoq and Itauto, are excluded because they are not general-purpose solvers.

Figure 4 provides a detailed visualization of the Graph2Tac model architecture, composed of a definition task and a prediction task.

3.1 GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK AND DEFINITION TASK
Graph2Tac primarily consists of two core components: a definition task and a prediction task, as shown in Figure 4. The input to each component is a directed graph with labeled nodes and edges, representing either a definition for the definition task or a proof-state for the prediction task. We additionally associate metadata with each graph. Definition graphs possess root nodes, one for each definition defined within that graph. Inductive data types define multiple mutually dependent concepts within the same graph and may therefore have multiple roots. A proof state graph is accompanied by local context nodes, one for each hypothesis. Both types of graphs contain definition nodes, which are leaf nodes representing referenced definitions from the global context. With each definition node, we store an index pointing to the corresponding entry in the definition embedding table. For the prediction task, in addition to the proof state graph, the input includes the indices of all global definitions and all tactics currently available in Coq's global context.

There are four distinct learned embedding tables: for edge labels, node labels, base tactics present in the training dataset, and definitions present in the training dataset. All embeddings possess a dimension equal to the model's hidden dimension, h_dim = 128. The definition and node embeddings are constrained to be unit-normalized. During inference, the definition table will be dynamically updated with embeddings for new definitions.

We transform the input graph using the following procedure. Each graph is pruned to a maximum of 1024 nodes. To enable effective message passing, we duplicate all edges to traverse in both directions and also add self-edges. The edges are assigned embeddings from the corresponding edge embeddings table. Non-definition nodes are assigned embeddings from the node embeddings table based on their node label. Definition nodes are instead assigned embeddings from the definition embeddings table, with the exception of the root nodes in the definition task. Those root node embeddings are masked with null values, as the explicit goal of the definition task is to predict the corresponding definition embeddings.

The transformed graphs are processed by a message-passing GNN. The GNN consists of 8 propagation hops where the node embedding is updated according to a graph convolution layer followed by a multi-layer perceptron with dropout, residual connection, and layer normalization. The weights for each hop are separate, but the definition and prediction tasks both utilize the same shared GNN backbone.

The output of the GNN is a graph with the same structure as the input but featuring updated node embeddings. Both tasks employ mean pooling to obtain a single vector embedding for the entire graph. For the definition task, the pooled embedding is concatenated with the embeddings of the root nodes, then processed through a two-layer MLP and finally unit normalized. Optionally, a name embedding for the definition can be concatenated, generated by a bidirectional LSTM processing the fully qualified Coq identifier string. For the prediction task, the pooled embedding is fed into a two-layer MLP. The output is multiplied by the tactic embedding table via inner product and passed through a softmax layer to obtain base tactic probabilities.

To predict arguments for a tactic, we employ a simple two-layer RNN. The initial hidden state of the RNN is the embedding for the chosen tactic. The number of RNN steps corresponds to the number of arguments required by the given tactic.

Each argument is predicted as follows. The RNN output is fed into a pair of two-layer MLPs, producing query embeddings for global and local argument prediction. For global arguments, we compute the inner product of the global query with each definition in the embedding table, resulting in a logit for each definition, scaled by a learned temperature parameter. For local arguments, we use the GNN output embedding for that specific local node and compute its inner product with the local query. Concatenating the local and global logits and applying softmax yields a distribution over all possible arguments.

Given the variable-size nature of many calculations, our implementation relies heavily on ragged tensors in TensorFlow and graph tensors in TF-GNN.

We train on batches of 512 definitions and 512 proof states. The loss for the definition task is cosine similarity. The loss for the prediction task is the cross-entropy for the full tactic sequence. The combined loss is a weighted sum of the two individual losses.

During inference, the tactic embedding table is masked to include only tactics available in Coq's current state. The definition embedding table is masked for all definitions available in the current global context. For new definitions not seen during training, we first calculate an embedding using the definition model. If multiple new definitions are encountered, embeddings are computed individually in a topologically sorted order, ensuring dependencies are processed first.

At inference time, the model outputs a list of tactic suggestions via beam search decoding with a beam width of 256, generating 256 tactic suggestions per proof state.

We train three model variants: G2T-Named uses the name embedding, G2T-Anon does not, and G2T-NoDef is trained without the definition task. Each is evaluated with three inference configurations for the definition model: Recalc calculates embeddings for all definitions, Update calculates only for new definitions, and Frozen uses random unit-normalized embeddings. G2T-NoDef is only used in the Frozen configuration. G2T-Anon-Update serves as our primary model.

3.2 NON-GRAPH APPROACHES
firstorder auto with *: As a simple baseline, we utilize Coq's built-in firstorder reasoning tactic combined with the auto tactic, employing all available hint databases.

CoqHammer: CoqHammer translates Coq theories to a first-order language understood by external automated theorem provers like Vampire, CVC4, Z3, and Eprover. Once an external proof is found, the required premises are extracted, and the proof is reconstructed inside Coq.

k-Nearest Neighbor: The fastest practical solver currently available in the Tactician framework is a fast k-nearest neighbor model. It constructs a database of proof states and associated tactics, extracting hand-crafted features. When queried, it retrieves proof states with the most similar features and returns the corresponding tactics. It requires no training and adapts in real-time to the changing Coq environment by learning from recent proof scripts, providing a highly complementary capability to Graph2Tac.

Proof State Text-based Transformer: We implement a decoder-only transformer baseline that operates on textual representations of proof states and predicts a textual representation of the tactic. We use a GPT2-style architecture with an embedding size of 768 and 12 layers, trained from scratch exclusively on Coq proof data.

4 EVALUATION
Experimental Setup
To rigorously evaluate solver performance, we randomly select 2000 theorems from the Coq packages in our testing set. Solvers are allocated a time limit of 10 minutes per theorem to synthesize a proof. For package-specific analysis, we sample up to 500 test theorems per package with a 5-minute time limit. The search procedure used by Tactician-based solvers is a modified Dijkstra's algorithm performing iterative deepening.

During evaluation, each solver is limited to one CPU with two hyperthreads. An exception is made for the Transformer-GPU solver, which performs model inference on a dedicated GPU.

We explore two aggregated solvers that simulate running multiple solvers concurrently under the same computational budget. "G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN" simulates a solver capable of learning from both new definitions and new proof scripts. "CoqHammer combined" aggregates all four ATP backends and the reconstruction tactic, simulating parallel execution.

Results
The left plot of Figure 5 shows the fraction of test theorems solved over time for various solvers, illustrating both progress over time and the startup cost of each solver. The right plot of Figure 5 replaces time with the number of calls to the underlying model, indicating the usefulness of the model's predictions independent of its speed.

CoqHammer combined performs better than the transformer baseline, even the GPU-accelerated variant.

Among the G2T solvers, the two variants incorporating the definition task decisively outperform the G2T-NoDef-Frozen baseline (26.1% vs 17.4%), conclusively demonstrating that the definition task significantly improves results. Notably, G2T-NoDef-Frozen performs similarly to both transformer variants in terms of model calls, suggesting the graph model's advantage over the transformer stems primarily from its superior inference speed rather than prediction quality alone. The addition of name embeddings in G2T-Named-Update performs slightly worse than our primary G2T-Anon-Update solver.

The k-NN solver outperforms G2T-Anon-Update at smaller time limits, but the latter begins to overtake at later time steps. A similar relationship is observed relative to model calls. This indicates that for more extensive search, the more sophisticated G2T-Anon-Update model provides distinct value.

Both solvers exhibit strong complementarity, as evidenced by the performance of the combined solver "G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN" and the Venn Diagram in Figure 6. This definitively shows the success of online methods in this setting, with each model leveraging different types of online information.

Figure 7 breaks down performance for the 15 largest packages. The results show that neither G2T-Anon-Update nor the k-NN consistently performs better; their relative performance varies by package. In many cases, G2T-Anon-Update either overtakes the k-NN or shows a trajectory suggesting it would overtake given more time.

5 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
Our novel definition task definitively improved a neural theorem prover from 17.4% to 26.1% in the challenging setting of proving theorems in never-before-seen packages. This result, combined with the marked success of the k-NN approach, conclusively underscores the critical importance of online learning capabilities in this domain. A key direction for future work involves exploring methods to unify the G2T and k-NN approaches. Ideally, such a unified model would also account for new tactics and learn from how new definitions and tactics are employed in novel theorems. One promising avenue is investigating whether our model can be fine-tuned in real-time.

To further improve the definition task, given that G2T-Anon-Update outperformed G2T-Named-Update, we hypothesize that adding name embeddings may make the definition task insufficiently challenging for the model. There may be superior alternatives to our current definition task, potentially drawing from ideas in self-supervised or contrastive learning, or employing social-network-scale graph models to process the entire interconnected graph of definitions simultaneously.

Theorem proving and programming share profound similarities and concerns, making it highly valuable to explore how this work relates to code generation. We leave open the investigation of how our graph-based methodology could be applied to text-based models. Retrieval-augmented transformers represent a possible approach, but may face scalability challenges when dealing with the full definition hierarchy.

6 REPRODUCIBILITY
This paper provides a careful and detailed description of our methods for building, training, and testing our models and solvers. The complete code for every stage of the pipeline is available in open-source repositories. This includes code for training the models, running them as part of a solver, interfacing with Coq, and conducting benchmarks.

We utilize an open-source dataset, and all our models are trained from scratch, ensuring no use of proprietary pre-training data.

Our solvers are designed for practical use by both researchers and Coq end-users and are operable on a typical Linux machine without requiring a GPU. The model can also be hosted on an external server and accessed via a TCP connection.

We intend to share our trained models, though users can also train their own using our provided code and the open dataset. While the graph models were trained for three weeks on two A100 GPUs, we observed that a model trained for just two days yielded similar results. Users may train models on different sets of Coq packages, including new or private developments, using the provided tools.

Our benchmarking framework allows testing on most Coq Opam packages compatible with Coq 8.11, enabling future evaluation of our solvers on new benchmarks. We plan to share complete test results, including details on tested theorems, proof success, and solver performance metrics, to facilitate future comparison and collaboration.

Mutually dependent definitions, such as inductive definitions, feature multiple mutually dependent root nodes. Theorems represent special cases of definitions where the theorem node points to both the theorem statement and its associated proof term. We deliberately omit the proof term from the theorem's definition graph to reduce overall graph size. The subgraphs extracted from the mono-graph are topologically ordered according to their dependencies, ensuring they can be processed in the correct sequential order by the neural network. In Figure 2, the extracted subgraphs are clearly highlighted for definitions T1, =, f, +, and N, as well as the current proof state of theorem T2, which is still under construction. Notably, the subgraphs for T1 and the proof state share the subterm associated with the multiplication operation.

Within the dataset of proofs, each proof state is associated with a corresponding applied tactic, forming the core training data for the prediction model. A tactic command is decomposed into a base tactic and its arguments. While arguments may be arbitrary Coq terms or other objects, our prediction model is specifically designed to predict only local hypotheses or global definitions as arguments.

The dataset we utilize is extracted from 120 distinct Coq packages obtained from the Opam package manager. These packages were selected by a SAT solver as the largest mutually consistent set of packages available for Coq version 8.11. Their subject matter varies extensively, encompassing fields such as mathematical analysis, compiler and programming language formalization, separation logic, homotopy type theory, and many others. The graph extracted from these formalizations consists of over 250 million nodes, which encode 520k definitions, of which 266k are theorems, and 4.6M proof state transformations.

We meticulously divide the packages into training and test sets, ensuring that no test package depends on any training package. To achieve this, we induced a random topological order on the Coq packages with regard to their dependency graph. The resulting ordered list was then split such that the average percentage of theorems and proof states in the training split is close to 90% (specifically, 91.3% of all theorems and 88.8% of all proof states).

The Tactician synth tactic and Suggest command communicate via this graph format with a Python client running the machine learning model. Tactician transmits the entire mono-graph of global definitions along with the current proof state. The client returns a ranked list of suggested tactics and their associated confidence scores. This integration makes our solver eminently usable in practical scenarios and allows us to perform massively parallel benchmarking of our model on any Coq Opam package.

3 PROOF AUTOMATION METHODS
Here, we describe in detail all solvers that will be comprehensively compared in this paper. Section 3.1 elaborates on the architecture of Graph2Tac, while Section 3.2 summarizes the other systems included for comparison. The transformer baseline was developed concurrently with Graph2Tac. All other systems were developed independently. Note that comparisons with highly relevant solvers, such as Proverbot9001, are omitted because they do not provide proof search functionality through a standard Coq tactic. Other symbolic solvers, such as SMTCoq and Itauto, are excluded because they are not general-purpose solvers.

Figure 4 provides a detailed visualization of the Graph2Tac model architecture, composed of a definition task and a prediction task.

3.1 GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK AND DEFINITION TASK
Graph2Tac primarily consists of two core components: a definition task and a prediction task, as shown in Figure 4. The input to each component is a directed graph with labeled nodes and edges, representing either a definition for the definition task or a proof-state for the prediction task. We additionally associate metadata with each graph. Definition graphs possess root nodes, one for each definition defined within that graph. Inductive data types define multiple mutually dependent concepts within the same graph and may therefore have multiple roots. A proof state graph is accompanied by local context nodes, one for each hypothesis. Both types of graphs contain definition nodes, which are leaf nodes representing referenced definitions from the global context. With each definition node, we store an index pointing to the corresponding entry in the definition embedding table. For the prediction task, in addition to the proof state graph, the input includes the indices of all global definitions and all tactics currently available in Coq's global context.

There are four distinct learned embedding tables: for edge labels, node labels, base tactics present in the training dataset, and definitions present in the training dataset. All embeddings possess a dimension equal to the model's hidden dimension, h_dim = 128. The definition and node embeddings are constrained to be unit-normalized. During inference, the definition table will be dynamically updated with embeddings for new definitions.

We transform the input graph using the following procedure. Each graph is pruned to a maximum of 1024 nodes. To enable effective message passing, we duplicate all edges to traverse in both directions and also add self-edges. The edges are assigned embeddings from the corresponding edge embeddings table. Non-definition nodes are assigned embeddings from the node embeddings table based on their node label. Definition nodes are instead assigned embeddings from the definition embeddings table, with the exception of the root nodes in the definition task. Those root node embeddings are masked with null values, as the explicit goal of the definition task is to predict the corresponding definition embeddings.

The transformed graphs are processed by a message-passing GNN. The GNN consists of 8 propagation hops where the node embedding is updated according to a graph convolution layer followed by a multi-layer perceptron with dropout, residual connection, and layer normalization. The weights for each hop are separate, but the definition and prediction tasks both utilize the same shared GNN backbone.

The output of the GNN is a graph with the same structure as the input but featuring updated node embeddings. Both tasks employ mean pooling to obtain a single vector embedding for the entire graph. For the definition task, the pooled embedding is concatenated with the embeddings of the root nodes, then processed through a two-layer MLP and finally unit normalized. Optionally, a name embedding for the definition can be concatenated, generated by a bidirectional LSTM processing the fully qualified Coq identifier string. For the prediction task, the pooled embedding is fed into a two-layer MLP. The output is multiplied by the tactic embedding table via inner product and passed through a softmax layer to obtain base tactic probabilities.

To predict arguments for a tactic, we employ a simple two-layer RNN. The initial hidden state of the RNN is the embedding for the chosen tactic. The number of RNN steps corresponds to the number of arguments required by the given tactic.

Each argument is predicted as follows. The RNN output is fed into a pair of two-layer MLPs, producing query embeddings for global and local argument prediction. For global arguments, we compute the inner product of the global query with each definition in the embedding table, resulting in a logit for each definition, scaled by a learned temperature parameter. For local arguments, we use the GNN output embedding for that specific local node and compute its inner product with the local query. Concatenating the local and global logits and applying softmax yields a distribution over all possible arguments.

Given the variable-size nature of many calculations, our implementation relies heavily on ragged tensors in TensorFlow and graph tensors in TF-GNN.

We train on batches of 512 definitions and 512 proof states. The loss for the definition task is cosine similarity. The loss for the prediction task is the cross-entropy for the full tactic sequence. The combined loss is a weighted sum of the two individual losses.

During inference, the tactic embedding table is masked to include only tactics available in Coq's current state. The definition embedding table is masked for all definitions available in the current global context. For new definitions not seen during training, we first calculate an embedding using the definition model. If multiple new definitions are encountered, embeddings are computed individually in a topologically sorted order, ensuring dependencies are processed first.

At inference time, the model outputs a list of tactic suggestions via beam search decoding with a beam width of 256, generating 256 tactic suggestions per proof state.

We train three model variants: G2T-Named uses the name embedding, G2T-Anon does not, and G2T-NoDef is trained without the definition task. Each is evaluated with three inference configurations for the definition model: Recalc calculates embeddings for all definitions, Update calculates only for new definitions, and Frozen uses random unit-normalized embeddings. G2T-NoDef is only used in the Frozen configuration. G2T-Anon-Update serves as our primary model.

3.2 NON-GRAPH APPROACHES
firstorder auto with *: As a simple baseline, we utilize Coq's built-in firstorder reasoning tactic combined with the auto tactic, employing all available hint databases.

CoqHammer: CoqHammer translates Coq theories to a first-order language understood by external automated theorem provers like Vampire, CVC4, Z3, and Eprover. Once an external proof is found, the required premises are extracted, and the proof is reconstructed inside Coq.

k-Nearest Neighbor: The fastest practical solver currently available in the Tactician framework is a fast k-nearest neighbor model. It constructs a database of proof states and associated tactics, extracting hand-crafted features. When queried, it retrieves proof states with the most similar features and returns the corresponding tactics. It requires no training and adapts in real-time to the changing Coq environment by learning from recent proof scripts, providing a highly complementary capability to Graph2Tac.

Proof State Text-based Transformer: We implement a decoder-only transformer baseline that operates on textual representations of proof states and predicts a textual representation of the tactic. We use a GPT2-style architecture with an embedding size of 768 and 12 layers, trained from scratch exclusively on Coq proof data.

4 EVALUATION
Experimental Setup
To rigorously evaluate solver performance, we randomly select 2000 theorems from the Coq packages in our testing set. Solvers are allocated a time limit of 10 minutes per theorem to synthesize a proof. For package-specific analysis, we sample up to 500 test theorems per package with a 5-minute time limit. The search procedure used by Tactician-based solvers is a modified Dijkstra's algorithm performing iterative deepening.

During evaluation, each solver is limited to one CPU with two hyperthreads. An exception is made for the Transformer-GPU solver, which performs model inference on a dedicated GPU.

We explore two aggregated solvers that simulate running multiple solvers concurrently under the same computational budget. "G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN" simulates a solver capable of learning from both new definitions and new proof scripts. "CoqHammer combined" aggregates all four ATP backends and the reconstruction tactic, simulating parallel execution.

Results
The left plot of Figure 5 shows the fraction of test theorems solved over time for various solvers, illustrating both progress over time and the startup cost of each solver. The right plot of Figure 5 replaces time with the number of calls to the underlying model, indicating the usefulness of the model's predictions independent of its speed.

CoqHammer combined performs better than the transformer baseline, even the GPU-accelerated variant.

Among the G2T solvers, the two variants incorporating the definition task decisively outperform the G2T-NoDef-Frozen baseline (26.1% vs 17.4%), conclusively demonstrating that the definition task significantly improves results. Notably, G2T-NoDef-Frozen performs similarly to both transformer variants in terms of model calls, suggesting the graph model's advantage over the transformer stems primarily from its superior inference speed rather than prediction quality alone. The addition of name embeddings in G2T-Named-Update performs slightly worse than our primary G2T-Anon-Update solver.

The k-NN solver outperforms G2T-Anon-Update at smaller time limits, but the latter begins to overtake at later time steps. A similar relationship is observed relative to model calls. This indicates that for more extensive search, the more sophisticated G2T-Anon-Update model provides distinct value.

Both solvers exhibit strong complementarity, as evidenced by the performance of the combined solver "G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN" and the Venn Diagram in Figure 6. This definitively shows the success of online methods in this setting, with each model leveraging different types of online information.

Figure 7 breaks down performance for the 15 largest packages. The results show that neither G2T-Anon-Update nor the k-NN consistently performs better; their relative performance varies by package. In many cases, G2T-Anon-Update either overtakes the k-NN or shows a trajectory suggesting it would overtake given more time.

5 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
Our novel definition task definitively improved a neural theorem prover from 17.4% to 26.1% in the challenging setting of proving theorems in never-before-seen packages. This result, combined with the marked success of the k-NN approach, conclusively underscores the critical importance of online learning capabilities in this domain. A key direction for future work involves exploring methods to unify the G2T and k-NN approaches. Ideally, such a unified model would also account for new tactics and learn from how new definitions and tactics are employed in novel theorems. One promising avenue is investigating whether our model can be fine-tuned in real-time.

To further improve the definition task, given that G2T-Anon-Update outperformed G2T-Named-Update, we hypothesize that adding name embeddings may make the definition task insufficiently challenging for the model. There may be superior alternatives to our current definition task, potentially drawing from ideas in self-supervised or contrastive learning, or employing social-network-scale graph models to process the entire interconnected graph of definitions simultaneously.

Theorem proving and programming share profound similarities and concerns, making it highly valuable to explore how this work relates to code generation. We leave open the investigation of how our graph-based methodology could be applied to text-based models. Retrieval-augmented transformers represent a possible approach, but may face scalability challenges when dealing with the full definition hierarchy.

6 REPRODUCIBILITY
This paper provides a careful and detailed description of our methods for building, training, and testing our models and solvers. The complete code for every stage of the pipeline is available in open-source repositories. This includes code for training the models, running them as part of a solver, interfacing with Coq, and conducting benchmarks.

We utilize an open-source dataset, and all our models are trained from scratch, ensuring no use of proprietary pre-training data.

Our solvers are designed for practical use by both researchers and Coq end-users and are operable on a typical Linux machine without requiring a GPU. The model can also be hosted on an external server and accessed via a TCP connection.

We intend to share our trained models, though users can also train their own using our provided code and the open dataset. While the graph models were trained for three weeks on two A100 GPUs, we observed that a model trained for just two days yielded similar results. Users may train models on different sets of Coq packages, including new or private developments, using the provided tools.

Our benchmarking framework allows testing on most Coq Opam packages compatible with Coq 8.11, enabling future evaluation of our solvers on new benchmarks. We plan to share complete test results, including details on tested theorems, proof success, and solver performance metrics, to facilitate future comparison and collaboration.

Title: Graph2Tac: Learning hierarchical representations of math concepts in theorem proving

Abstract:
Formal theories build hierarchies of definitions, theorems, and proofs that reference each other. When an agent is proving a new theorem in the Coq proof assistant, many relevant mathematical concepts and lemmas may not have been seen during training. This work uses a graph-based dataset for machine learning in Coq. It uses a graph-representation of Coq terms that induces a directed graph of dependencies between definitions. A graph neural network, Graph2Tac (G2T), is presented. It considers the current goal and the hierarchy of definitions leading to it. G2T is an online model integrated into user workflow, adapting to new Coq projects and definitions. It complements other online models that learn from new proof scripts. A definition embedding task is trained to compute representations of mathematical concepts not seen during training. This task improves neural network performance to a level comparable with state-of-the-art k-nearest neighbor predictors.

1 INTRODUCTION
Interactive theorem provers (ITPs) are programming languages that assist users in writing formal proofs. Coq is an ITP based on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions (PaulinMohring, 1993). In Coq, users input proofs using tactics. At each proof step, Coq provides a list of proof states to solve.

Machine learning guidance has been explored for Coq and other ITPs. A challenge is that a model trained on one set of projects may not adapt to a new project with its own definitions. Online models can incorporate new information in a file or project without retraining. The Tactician framework (Blaauwbroek et al., 2020b) contains online models such as a k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) model (Zhang et al., 2021). These models learn from tactic scripts written by users. They can make relevant proof suggestions for new theorems. However, these models have no knowledge of the current global context within Coq and cannot adapt predicted tactics to the environment.

This work presents a graph neural network (GNN) model, Graph2Tac (G2T). It trains on existing works and adapts to new definitions and theorems in the environment in real time. Unlike the k-NN model, it does not learn to use new tactics. It learns to understand and work with new definitions while synthesizing tactic scripts. This ability complements the k-NN model.

Graph2Tac interfaces with Coq through the Tactician framework. Tactician provides a Suggest command for tactic suggestions and a synth tactic for proof search. G2T is a neural network-based solver for Coq that can run on a consumer-grade computer. It adapts to users' Coq projects.

This paper presents a neural definition embedding task. It uses an embedding table to learn representations for definitions seen during training. The embedding of a definition is used to build representations of proof states that reference the definition. It can also predict probable arguments for tactics from the global context.

To update the definition embedding table for new definitions, a definition model is trained. During training, its output aligns to the definition embedding table. During inference, when a new definition is encountered, the definition model computes an embedding. When proof states or other definitions that depend on that definition are encountered, the newly calculated embedding is used. These embeddings consider the form of the definition and the hierarchy of definitions leading to it.

Contributions:
(1) A new definition training task is presented. It improves theorem proving in Coq from 17.4% to 26.1% of theorems solved in the setting of new Coq packages not seen during training, using consumer hardware.
(2) The usefulness of graphs representing the entire environment of definitions as a mono-graph is shown.
(3) A comprehensive comparison of symbolic and machine learning solvers in Coq is given, including Graph2Tac, a transformer model, Tactician's k-NN, and CoqHammer.
(4) The k-NN solver solves 25.8% of test theorems, outperforming CoqHammer and a transformer baseline.
(5) G2T and the k-NN are complementary online solvers, together proving 33.2% of test theorems.
(6) G2T is a neural solver available to end-users.

Background and related work includes machine learning approaches for interactive theorem proving systems. For Coq, work includes CoqGym (Yang & Deng, 2019), GamePad (Huang et al., 2019), Proverbot9001 (Sanchez-Stern et al., 2020), and Tactician (Blaauwbroek et al., 2020b). For other systems, work includes Mizar (Urban, 2003; Kaliszyk & Urban, 2015), TacticToe for HOL4 (Gauthier et al., 2017), HOList for HOLight (Bansal et al., 2019), Sledgehammer for Isabelle (Kühlwein et al., 2013; Blanchette et al., 2016a), and LeanDojo for Lean (Yang et al., 2023). Language model approaches include GPT-f (Polu & Sutskever, 2020) and others.

This work uses a graph-based dataset extracted with Coq kernel knowledge. It develops a GNN that learns the meaning of definitions by exploiting hierarchical structure. The architecture addresses online learning, making use of new definitions in new projects.

2 GRAPH-BASED INTERACTION WITH THE COQ PROOF ASSISTANT
A graph-based format is used where all Coq definitions and proof states are stored in one interconnected graph. Advantages:
(1) The graph is created from terms from the Coq kernel, encoding all objects in the Coq environment.
(2) References to global definitions are explicitly referenced by edges, avoiding ambiguity with name resolution.
(3) Local variables are connected to their binders via edges, eliminating the need for local variable names.
(4) Equal terms are shared across parts of the graph, leading to more compact representations.

This large mono-graph contains millions of nodes. Smaller proof state and definition graphs are extracted for input into models. Each proof state and definition has a root node. To obtain a smaller graph, the forward closure from the root node is calculated, stopping when a definition node is encountered. Mutually dependent definitions have multiple mutually dependent root nodes. Theorems are special cases of definitions; the theorem node points to the theorem statement and its proof term. The proof term is omitted from the theorem's definition graph to reduce size. Subgraphs extracted from the mono-graph are topologically ordered according to dependencies.

In the dataset of proofs, each proof state has an associated tactic, forming training data. A tactic is decomposed into a base tactic and arguments. The prediction model only predicts local hypotheses or global definitions.

The dataset is extracted from 120 Coq packages from the Opam package manager. These packages were selected as the largest mutually consistent set available for Coq 8.11. The graph consists of over 250 million nodes, encoding 520k definitions (266k theorems) and 4.6M proof state transformations.

Packages are divided into training and test sets where no test package depends on a training package. A random topological order is induced on the Coq packages. The list is split such that the average percentage of theorems and proof states in the training split is close to 90% (91.3% of all theorems and 88.8% of all proof states).

The Tactician synth tactic and Suggest command communicate via this graph format with a Python client running a machine learning model. Tactician sends the entire mono-graph of global definitions and the current proof state. The client returns a list of suggested tactics and scores.

3 PROOF AUTOMATION METHODS
This section describes solvers compared. Section 3.1 describes Graph2Tac architecture. Section 3.2 summarizes other systems. A transformer was developed with Graph2Tac. Other systems were developed elsewhere.

3.1 GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK AND DEFINITION TASK
Graph2Tac consists of a definition task and a prediction task. Input is a directed graph with labeled nodes and edges representing either a definition or a proof-state. Metadata is associated with each graph. Definition graphs have root nodes. Inductive data types may have multiple roots. A proof state graph has local context nodes for each hypothesis. Both graph types contain definition nodes, which are leaf nodes representing referenced definitions. With each definition node, an index to the definition embedding table is stored. For the prediction task, input includes indices of all global definitions and all tactics available in Coq's global context.

There are four learned embedding tables: edge labels, node labels, base tactics, and definitions. All embeddings have dimension h_dim=128. Definition and node embeddings are unit-normalized. During inference, the definition table is dynamically updated.

Input graphs are transformed as follows. Each graph is pruned to 1024 nodes. All edges are duplicated to go in both directions; self-edges are added. Edges are assigned embeddings from the edge embeddings table. This table has 2E+1 entries. Non-definition nodes are assigned embeddings from the node embeddings table. Definition nodes are assigned embeddings from the definition embeddings table, except for root nodes in the definition task. Those are masked with null embeddings.

Transformed graphs are processed by a message-passing GNN. The GNN has 8 hops. The t-th hop transforms a node embedding x_n^t in two steps:
\[
\hat{x}_{n}^{t+1}=\operatorname{ReLU}\left(\frac{1}{\deg(n)}\sum_{\substack{m,e:\;m\rightarrow n}}\operatorname{Dense}_{\theta_{t}}(e,x_{m}^{t})\right)
\]
\[
x_{n}^{t+1}=\operatorname{Layernorm}\left(x_{t}+\operatorname{Dropout}_{0.1}(\mathbf{MLP}_{\psi_{t}}(\hat{x}_{n}^{t+1}))\right)
\]
The first step is a graph convolution layer. The second step is a 2-layer MLP (Dense, ReLU, Dense) with inner hidden dimension 2h_dim, then Dropout, Residual, and Layernorm. Weights for each hop are separate. The definition and prediction tasks share the same GNN backbone.

The GNN output is a graph with updated node embeddings. Both tasks use mean pooling to obtain a single vector embedding for the graph. For the definition task, the pooled embedding is concatenated with each root node embedding, fed into a two-layer MLP, and unit normalized. Optionally, a name embedding for the definition is concatenated, using a bidirectional LSTM to embed the fully qualified Coq identifier string. For the prediction task, the pooled embedding is fed into a two-layer MLP. The output is multiplied by the tactic embedding table using inner product and put through a softmax layer to obtain base tactic probabilities.

To predict tactic arguments, a two-layer RNN is used. The initial hidden state is the embedding for the chosen tactic. During training, the ground truth tactic is provided. The number of RNN steps corresponds to the number of arguments required.

Each argument is predicted as follows. The RNN output is fed into a pair of two-layer MLPs, resulting in a pair of query embeddings for global and local argument prediction. The global argument query is unit normalized. For global arguments, the inner product of the global query with each definition in the embedding table gives a logit for each definition. Since the inner product is bounded, global logits are scaled by a learned temperature parameter. For each local argument, the GNN output embedding for that local node is used, and the inner product with the local argument query is taken. Concatenating local and global logits and performing softmax gives a distribution over all possible arguments.

Implementations use ragged tensors in TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2015) and graph tensors in TF-GNN (Ferludin et al., 2022).

Training uses batches of 512 definitions and 512 proof states. Loss for the definition task is cosine similarity. Loss for the training task is cross-entropy for the full tactic sequence. Combined loss is L = 1000 L_def + L_tactic.

During inference, the tactic embedding table is masked for tactics that occur in training data and are available in Coq's current state. The definition embedding table is masked for all definitions available in the current global context. For new definitions not seen during training, an embedding is calculated using the definition task. For multiple new definitions, embeddings are computed from each definition graph individually, updating in topologically sorted order.

At inference, output is a list of tactic suggestions, each starting with a base tactic and containing required arguments. Beam search decoding with beam width 256 generates 256 tactic suggestions per proof state.

Three models are trained: G2T-Named uses name embedding; G2T-Anon does not. G2T-NoDef is trained without a definition task. Each is run with three configurations: Recalc calculates embeddings for all definitions; Update calculates embeddings only for new definitions; Frozen uses random unit normalized embeddings. G2T-NoDef is only used as G2T-NoDef-Frozen. G2T-Anon-Update is the primary model.

3.2 NON-GRAPH APPROACHES
firstorder auto with *: Coq's built-in firstorder reasoning tactic combined with auto, with all available hint databases.

CoqHammer (Czajka & Kaliszyk, 2018): Translates Coq theories to a first-order language for external automated theorem provers (Vampire, CVC4, Z3, Eprover). Proofs are reconstructed inside Coq.

k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) (Blaauwbroek et al., 2020c; Zhang et al., 2021): Builds a database of proof states and associated tactics, extracting hand-crafted features. When queried, it looks up proof states with most similar features and returns corresponding tactics. It adapts in real-time to the changing Coq environment. It learns from recent proof scripts.

Proof State Text-based Transformer: A decoder-only transformer baseline operating on textual representations of proof states, predicting a textual representation of the tactic. GPT2 implementation is used (Wolf et al., 2020). Embedding size is 768 with 12 layers. Models are trained from scratch on Coq proof data.

4 EVALUATION
Experimental setup: 2000 theorems are randomly chosen from Coq packages in the testing set. Solvers have a time limit of 10 minutes per theorem. For package-specific results, up to 500 test theorems per package are sampled with a 5-minute limit. Search procedure is a modification of Dijkstra's algorithm with iterative deepening.

During evaluation, each solver is limited to one CPU with two hyperthreads. An exception is made for the Transformer-GPU solver, which uses a dedicated GPU for model inference.

Two aggregated solvers are explored, simulating running n solvers concurrently under the one-CPU budget. The number of theorems solved by aggregate solvers in time t is the number solved by any component in time t/n. "G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN" simulates a solver learning from new definitions and new tactic proof scripts. "CoqHammer combined" aggregates all four ATP backends and the reconstruction tactic called best.

Results: Figure 5 shows fraction of test theorems solved over time and per number of calls to the model. CoqHammer combined performs better than the transformer solver.

Among G2T solvers, those with the definition task outperform the G2T-NoDef-Frozen baseline (26.1% vs 17.4%), showing the definition task helps. G2T-NoDef-Frozen performs similarly to transformer variants in terms of model calls, suggesting the graph model's advantage over the transformer is due to model speed, not prediction quality. G2T-Named-Update performs slightly worse than G2T-Anon-Update.

The k-NN solver outperforms G2T-Anon-Update at smaller time limits, but G2T-Anon-Update overtakes later. A similar pattern is seen relative to model calls. For larger amounts of search, G2T-Anon-Update has value.

Both solvers are complementary, as shown by the combination solver G2T-Anon-Update + k-NN and the Venn Diagram in Figure 6.

Figure 7 breaks down performance for the largest 15 packages. Neither G2T-Anon-Update nor k-NN always performs better. In many cases, G2T-Anon-Update overtakes or appears to overtake k-NN given enough time. The tlc package was removed from overall results because G2T-Anon-Update found theorems using an inconsistent axiom.

5 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
The definition task improved a neural theorem prover from 17.4% to 26.1% in proving theorems in unseen packages. The success of the k-NN approach shows the importance of online learning. Future work could unify G2T and k-NN approaches. Such a model should account for new tactics and learn from how new definitions and tactics are used. Fine-tuning in real-time could be explored.

To improve the definition task, since G2T-Anon-Update outperformed G2T-Named-Update, adding names may make the task too easy. Alternatives using self-supervised or contrastive learning could be explored. Social-network-size graph models could process the entire graph of interconnected definitions.

Theorem proving and programming share similarities. How this methodology applies to text-based models could be explored. Retrieval augmented transformers are a possible approach but may not scale to the full definition hierarchy.

6 REPRODUCIBILITY
Methods for building, training, and testing models and solvers are described. Code is available in open-source repositories. An open-source dataset is used. Models are trained from scratch. Solvers are usable on a typical Linux machine with no GPU. The model can be hosted on an external server. Instructions for setup are included. Trained models may be shared; users can train their own. Models were trained for three weeks on two A100s, but a model trained in two days showed similar results. Users can train models on different Coq packages. The benchmarking framework allows testing on most Coq Opam packages compatible with Coq 8.11. Full test results may be shared.
