\section{4.3 DISCUSSION  }


Qualitative comparisons. Reliability diagrams in Figure 3(a)-(b) show that PseudoCal consistently aligns with ‘Oracle’, while the existing state-of-the-art method TransCal deviates significantly.  

Impact of mix ratio $\lambda$ . The fixed mix ratio $\lambda$ is the sole hyperparameter in PseudoCal. We investigate its impact on calibration performance by experimenting with values ranging from 0.51 to 0.9. The results of two closed-set UDA methods (including SHOT) on DomainNet are presented in Figure 3(c), and the results of two partial-set UDA methods on Office-Home are shown in Figure 3(d). We first examine mixup with both ‘Hard’ (one-hot labels) and ‘Soft’ (soft predictions) labels, finding similar trends with differences that are generally not visible when $\lambda>0.6$ . In addition, optimal performance for PseudoCal occurs with a moderate $\lambda$ value between 0.6 and 0.7. The reason for this is that a $\lambda$ value closer to 0.5 generates more ambiguous samples, resulting in increased wrong predictions, whereas a $\lambda$ value closer to 1.0 has the opposite effect. At last, for simplicity, we use a fixed $\lambda$ value of 0.65 with hard labels for all experiments.  

Impact of backbones and metrics. In order to examine the robustness of PseudoCal across different backbones and calibration metrics, we assess its performance using ViT-B (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) as the backbone and present the results for the aforementioned three metrics in Table 8. The findings reveal that PseudoCal consistently achieves the best performance regardless of the choice of backbone or calibration metric.  

Table 8: ViT results of MCC on $\mathbf{C}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{S}$   

![](images/510d5384d8996627cdd58b2c289e50a49a87e3867420f390f75f1297853949c4.jpg)  

Impact of UDA model quality. We’ve provided the target-domain accuracy for each UDA model in the ‘Accuracy’ row. PseudoCal remains effective as long as the UDA model has learned the target data structure instead of being completely randomly initialized, supported by the robust cluster assumption. This is evident in Table 6, where PseudoCal maintains its competence even with low accuracy pseudo-labels (about $30\%$ ).  

Table 9: ECE $(\%)$ of ablation experiments on pseudo-target synthesis.   

![](images/91de8c34359920fea0fde9be4c79d1a0f1d6609b5257d167da8775861773231b.jpg)  

Comparison with training-stage mixup. Most approaches incorporate mixup (Zhang et al., 2018) during the model training stage as an objective to enhance model generalization, and among them, Thulasidasan et al. (2019) further utilizes mixup as a training-stage calibration method. However, our use of mixup in PseudoCal differs significantly from previous mixup-based works in three key aspects. $(i)$ Different stages: All of these works apply mixup in training, while our mixup operation occurs in the inference stage to synthesize a labeled set. (ii) Different mix ratios: PseudoCal leverages mixup for cross-cluster sample interpolation and performs effectively with a fixed mix ratio $\lambda\in(0.6,0.7)$ but is considerably less effective with $\lambda$ values close to 1.0. In contrast, previous methods typically work best with $\lambda\in\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\alpha)$ where $\alpha\in[0.1,0.4]$ , essentially favoring $\lambda$ values that are close to 1.0. However, they are ineffective with $\lambda$ values close to 0.5 (like our adopted values) due to the manifold intrusion problem (Thulasidasan et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019). (iii) Different performance: We observed that UDA models trained with training-time calibration methods still suffer from significant miscalibration, while our PseudoCal can further substantially reduce ECE errors for these models. For example, as shown in Table 6, SHOT employs label smoothing(Müller et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022) during training, and DINE is trained with mixup(Thulasidasan et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2022).  

Ablation study on pseudo-target synthesis. Pseudo-target synthesis plays a critical role in our PseudoCal framework. In this step, we employ input-level mixup with a fixed mix ratio $(\lambda)$ to generate a pseudo-target sample by combining two real samples with different pseudo-labels. We conduct a comprehensive ablation study on this synthesis strategy by extensively comparing it with alternative approaches, including: (i) Applying mixup between samples with the same pseudo-label (referred to as PseudoCal-same). (ii) Using instance-based augmentations of target samples, such as RandAugment (Cubuk et al., 2020), and strong augmentations commonly used in self-supervised learning (Chen et al., 2020). (iii) Employing mixup at different levels, such as the patch-level (Yun et al., 2019) and the feature-level (Verma et al., 2019). (iv) Applying common training-stage mixup using $\lambda\in\mathrm{Beta}(0.3,0.3)$ (Zhang et al., 2018). (v) Directly utilizing original or flitered pseudo-labeled real target samples (Lee et al., 2013; Sohn et al., 2020) without mixup (by setting the mix ratio $\lambda$ to 1.0). We present an extensive comparison of all these strategies in Table 9. The results consistently demonstrate that our inference-stage input-level mixup outperforms the alternative options.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


In conclusion, we introduce PseudoCal, a novel and versatile post-hoc framework for calibrating predictive uncertainty in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). By focusing on the unlabeled target domain, PseudoCal distinguishes itself from mainstream calibration methods that are based on covariate shift and eliminates their associated limitations. To elaborate, PseudoCal employs a novel inference-stage mixup strategy to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that mimics the correct-wrong statistics in real target samples. In this way, PseudoCal successfully transforms the challenging unsupervised calibration problem involving unlabeled real samples into a supervised one using labeled pseudo-target data, which can be readily addressed through temperature scaling. Throughout our extensive evaluations spanning diverse UDA settings beyond covariate shift, including source-free UDA settings and domain adaptive semantic segmentation, PseudoCal consistently showcases its advantages of simplicity, versatility, and effectiveness in enhancing calibration in UDA. In future work, we aim to extend PseudoCal to address calibration problems in more practical UDA scenarios, including open-set UDA and UDA for object detection.

Title: Pseudo-Calibration: Improving Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Domain Adaptation

Abstract
The pursuit of reliable machine learning systems has driven significant progress in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), which aims to transfer knowledge from labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain. While much of this effort has focused on improving model accuracy, a critical and often overlooked aspect is the calibration of predictive uncertainty. Poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates pose substantial risks in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis. This problem is particularly challenging in UDA due to the absence of target labels and severe distribution shifts. Existing approaches, which often treat calibration as a covariate shift problem using importance-weighting, are hampered by their reliance on source data and complex density modeling. We introduce Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a fundamentally novel post-hoc calibration framework that re-conceptualizes UDA calibration as a target domain-specific unsupervised problem. Our innovative solution leverages inference-stage mixup guided by the cluster assumption to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that captures the statistical structure of the real target domain. This breakthrough transforms the unsupervised calibration challenge into a supervised one, solvable with simple temperature scaling. An extensive empirical evaluation across 5 diverse UDA scenarios and 10 UDA methods demonstrates that PseudoCal consistently and significantly outperforms all alternative calibration techniques.

Section 1 INTRODUCTION

The advancement of deep learning has increasingly relied on techniques like unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to enhance model generalization across domains with differing data distributions but similar tasks. While notable progress has been made in improving target domain accuracy, the reliability of a model's predictive uncertainty estimation is equally vital for trustworthy deployment in real-world, safety-critical systems. Calibrated models produce confidence scores that accurately reflect the true likelihood of correctness. Although uncertainty calibration has been extensively studied in standard supervised learning, it remains a profoundly under-explored frontier in UDA. Pioneering work has revealed that improving UDA model accuracy often comes at the cost of poor uncertainty calibration on target data. This calibration problem is uniquely difficult in UDA due to two core challenges: the absence of labeled target data, which prevents the direct use of supervised calibration methods like temperature scaling, and severe domain distribution shifts, which means calibration performed on source data does not transfer effectively to the target domain.

Prior approaches have treated UDA calibration as a covariate shift problem, employing techniques like importance weighting to re-weight source validation data. However, these methods suffer from critical drawbacks: they are unreliable under severe distribution shifts, require additional complex model training for density estimation, and depend on access to labeled source data, limiting their use in privacy-sensitive or source-free settings.

In this work, we propose a paradigm shift. We treat UDA calibration not as a cross-domain problem, but as an unsupervised calibration problem intrinsic to the target domain. This novel perspective allows us to focus squarely on the fundamental challenge of missing target labels. We first analyze an 'Oracle' case using labeled target data with temperature scaling and factorize its objective, revealing a key insight: datasets with similar correct-wrong prediction statistics should yield similar optimal calibration temperatures. Inspired by this, we introduce the novel Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal) framework. PseudoCal's core innovation is the synthesis of a labeled pseudo-target dataset from unlabeled target data using inference-stage mixup. Under the well-established cluster assumption, this synthesized set exhibits correct-wrong statistics highly similar to the real target data. Consequently, calibrating on this pseudo-target set with temperature scaling provides a highly effective approximation of the ideal 'Oracle' calibration. This elegantly converts an unsupervised problem into a tractable supervised one. Our contributions are threefold: 1) We pioneer a novel target-domain perspective on UDA calibration, enabling a unified approach across diverse scenarios including those with label shift or limited source access. 2) We propose the novel PseudoCal framework, which requires only unlabeled target data and a fixed model, using inference-stage mixup to synthesize a calibration set. 3) Through comprehensive evaluation across 5 UDA scenarios and 10 methods, we demonstrate that PseudoCal consistently and significantly outperforms all existing calibration baselines.

Section 2 RELATED WORK

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for image classification primarily focuses on distribution alignment via discrepancy measures or adversarial learning, and target domain learning via self-training or regularization. UDA has expanded from the classic closed-set setting under the covariate shift assumption to more practical scenarios like partial-set, open-set, and source-free UDA, the latter of which prioritizes source data privacy.

Predictive uncertainty calibration originated with binary classification methods like Platt scaling, later extended to multi-class settings with post-hoc methods such as temperature scaling, which require a labeled validation set. Training-stage methods include MC-Dropout, Ensemble, and Bayesian approaches, though their calibration often degrades under distribution shift. Calibration under shift is an emerging topic. For single-source UDA, a simple baseline is to apply temperature scaling using source validation data (TempScal-src). Methods addressing domain shift, like CPCS and TransCal, primarily use importance weighting to handle covariate shift. Other works perturb source data or use multiple source domains for calibration. Training-stage methods also employ label smoothing or accuracy-uncertainty optimization. Unlike these prior works, PseudoCal is distinctive as a simple, post-hoc, and general method that requires no extra model training, relying solely on a fixed UDA model and unlabeled target data.

Section 3 APPROACH

We consider a C-way image classification UDA task with a labeled source domain D_s and an unlabeled target domain D_t. The goal is to learn a model φ to predict target labels. For an input (x, y), the model outputs a predicted class ŷ and confidence p̂. Perfect calibration is defined as P(ŷ=y|p̂=p)=p. Calibration error is commonly measured by the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), which bins predictions and computes the average difference between per-bin accuracy and confidence.

Section 3.1 SUPERVISED ‘ORACLE’: FACTORIZED TEMPERATURE SCALING

We view UDA calibration as an unsupervised problem within the target domain. We first study an 'Oracle' that applies temperature scaling (TempScal) using the unavailable target ground truths, obtaining an optimal temperature T_o by minimizing the Negative Log Likelihood (NLL). We factorize this NLL objective, showing it balances terms for correctly (D_c) and wrongly (D_w) predicted samples. This factorization reveals that any labeled set sharing the same correct-wrong statistics as the real target should yield a similar optimal temperature via TempScal.

Section 3.2 UNSUPERVISED SOLUTION: PSEUDO-CALIBRATION

Inspired by this, PseudoCal synthesizes a labeled pseudo-target set that mimics the real target's correct-wrong statistics, then applies TempScal to it. The framework has two steps:
Step 1: Pseudo-target synthesis. Using only unlabeled target data and a fixed model, we apply inference-stage mixup. A pseudo-target sample x_pt and its label y_pt are created by mixing two real target samples (x_t^i, x_t^j) with different pseudo-labels (ŷ_t^i, ŷ_t^j) using a fixed mix ratio λ ∈ (0.5, 1.0), e.g., 0.65.
Step 2: Supervised calibration. We perform standard TempScal on this synthesized labeled set {(x_pt^i, y_pt^i)} to estimate a temperature, which approximates the 'Oracle' temperature T_o.

Analysis: The effectiveness hinges on the pseudo-target set having similar correct-wrong statistics to the real target. Under the cluster assumption, if a UDA model has learned the target data structure, there is a sample-level correspondence: a pseudo-target sample generated with a primary real sample x_t^i will be correct if x_t^i is correct, and wrong if x_t^i is wrong, provided λ is not extreme. This leads to similar dataset-level statistics.

Section 4 EXPERIMENTS

Section 4.1 SETTINGS

Datasets: We use 5 image classification benchmarks (Office31, Office-Home, VisDA, DomainNet, ImageNet-Sketch) and semantic segmentation tasks (Cityscapes as target, GTA5/SYNTHIA as source).
UDA Methods: We evaluate 10 methods across closed-set, partial-set, and source-free (white-box & black-box) UDA for classification, and source-only models for segmentation.
Calibration Baselines: We compare against 5 methods: No Calib., TempScal-src, CPCS, TransCal, and Ensemble.
Implementation: Models are trained with official code. For PseudoCal, we use a fixed λ=0.65 and one-epoch inference with mixup. Results are averaged over five runs.

Section 4.2 RESULTS

Closed-set UDA: PseudoCal achieves ECE closest to 'Oracle', significantly outperforming others on Office-Home (avg. improvement 4.33%), Office-31 (1.88%), VisDA (2.77%), and DomainNet (5.95%).
Partial-set UDA: On Office-Home, PseudoCal outperforms the second-best (Ensemble) by 4.24%.
Source-free UDA: On DomainNet and ImageNet-Sketch, PseudoCal outperforms Ensemble by 7.44% and 15.05%, respectively.
Semantic Segmentation: PseudoCal performs best, showing an average 4.62% ECE improvement over no calibration.

Section 4.3 DISCUSSION

Qualitative comparisons via reliability diagrams show PseudoCal aligns closely with 'Oracle', unlike other methods.
Impact of mix ratio λ: Performance is optimal with moderate λ between 0.6-0.7. We use λ=0.65 with hard labels for all experiments.
Impact of backbones and metrics: PseudoCal remains best-performing using ViT backbones and across metrics (ECE, NLL, Brier Score).
Impact of UDA model quality: PseudoCal remains effective even with low-accuracy models (~30%), as long as some data structure is learned.
Comparison with training-stage mixup: PseudoCal differs in stage (inference vs. training), mix ratio (favors ~0.65 vs. near 1.0), and purpose. It can further calibrate models already trained with mixup-based calibration.
Ablation study on pseudo-target synthesis: Extensive comparisons show our inference-stage input-level mixup strategy outperforms alternatives like same-label mixup, data augmentations, feature-level mixup, training-stage mixup, and using raw pseudo-labels.

Section 5 CONCLUSION

We present PseudoCal, a novel and versatile post-hoc framework for calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA. By adopting a target-domain perspective, PseudoCal moves beyond the limitations of covariate shift-based methods. Its innovative use of inference-stage mixup synthesizes a pseudo-target set that captures real target statistics, transforming unsupervised calibration into a supervised problem solvable with temperature scaling. Extensive evaluations across diverse UDA scenarios, including source-free settings and semantic segmentation, consistently demonstrate PseudoCal's simplicity, versatility, and effectiveness. Future work will extend PseudoCal to open-set UDA and object detection tasks.

Abstract
The pursuit of reliable machine learning systems has driven significant progress in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), which aims to transfer knowledge from labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain. While much of this effort has focused on improving model accuracy, a critical and often overlooked aspect is the calibration of predictive uncertainty. Section 1 INTRODUCTION

The advancement of deep learning has increasingly relied on techniques like unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to enhance model generalization across domains with differing data distributions but similar tasks. While notable progress has been made in improving target domain accuracy, the reliability of a model's predictive uncertainty estimation is equally vital for trustworthy deployment in real-world, safety-critical systems. Calibrated models produce confidence scores that accurately reflect the true likelihood of correctness. Although uncertainty calibration has been extensively studied in standard supervised learning, it remains a profoundly under-explored frontier in UDA. Pioneering work has revealed that improving UDA model accuracy often comes at the cost of poor uncertainty calibration on target data. This calibration problem is uniquely difficult in UDA due to two core challenges: the absence of labeled target data, which prevents the direct use of supervised calibration methods like temperature scaling, and severe domain distribution shifts, which means calibration performed on source data does not transfer effectively to the target domain.

Prior approaches have treated UDA calibration as a covariate shift problem, employing techniques like importance weighting to re-weight source validation data. However, these methods suffer from critical drawbacks: they are unreliable under severe distribution shifts, require additional complex model training for density estimation, and depend on access to labeled source data, limiting their use in privacy-sensitive or source-free settings.

In this work, we propose a paradigm shift. We treat UDA calibration not as a cross-domain problem, but as an unsupervised calibration problem intrinsic to the target domain. This novel perspective allows us to focus squarely on the fundamental challenge of missing target labels. We first analyze an 'Oracle' case using labeled target data with temperature scaling and factorize its objective, revealing a key insight: datasets with similar correct-wrong prediction statistics should yield similar optimal calibration temperatures. Inspired by this, we introduce the novel Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal) framework. PseudoCal's core innovation is the synthesis of a labeled pseudo-target dataset from unlabeled target data using inference-stage mixup. Under the well-established cluster assumption, this synthesized set exhibits correct-wrong statistics highly similar to the real target data. Consequently, calibrating on this pseudo-target set with temperature scaling provides a highly effective approximation of the ideal 'Oracle' calibration. This elegantly converts an unsupervised problem into a tractable supervised one. Section 2 RELATED WORK

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for image classification primarily focuses on distribution alignment via discrepancy measures or adversarial learning, and target domain learning via self-training or regularization. For single-source UDA, a simple baseline is to apply temperature scaling using source validation data (TempScal-src). Methods addressing domain shift, like CPCS and TransCal, primarily use importance weighting to handle covariate shift. Other works perturb source data or use multiple source domains for calibration. Training-stage methods also employ label smoothing or accuracy-uncertainty optimization. Unlike these prior works, PseudoCal is distinctive as a simple, post-hoc, and general method that requires no extra model training, relying solely on a fixed UDA model and unlabeled target data.

We consider a C-way image classification UDA task with a labeled source domain D_s and an unlabeled target domain D_t. The goal is to learn a model φ to predict target labels. For an input (x, y), the model outputs a predicted class ŷ and confidence p̂. Perfect calibration is defined as P(ŷ=y|p̂=p)=p. Calibration error is commonly measured by the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), which bins predictions and computes the average difference between per-bin accuracy and confidence.

We view UDA calibration as an unsupervised problem within the target domain. This factorization reveals that any labeled set sharing the same correct-wrong statistics as the real target should yield a similar optimal temperature via TempScal.

Title: Pseudo-Calibration: A Groundbreaking Framework for Enhancing Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

Abstract
The field of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has witnessed substantial and dedicated efforts aimed at improving model accuracy for an unlabeled target domain by leveraging one or more labeled source domains. However, a critical and often overlooked issue is that UDA models frequently exhibit poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty on target data. This problem remains profoundly under-explored and poses significant risks in safety-critical UDA applications, such as autonomous systems and medical diagnostics. The two primary and formidable challenges in addressing predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA are the complete absence of labeled target data and the presence of severe distribution shifts between the source and target domains. Traditional supervised calibration methods, such as temperature scaling, are entirely inapplicable due to the first challenge. Recent studies have attempted to address the initial challenge by employing importance-weighting with labeled source data, but these approaches still suffer from the second challenge and introduce additional complex density modeling requirements. We propose Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a novel and highly effective post-hoc calibration framework. In a decisive departure from prior approaches, we consider UDA calibration as a target domain-specific unsupervised problem rather than a covariate shift problem across domains. Our innovative and principled use of inference-stage mixup and the cluster assumption guarantees that a synthesized labeled pseudo-target set accurately captures the essential structure of the real target domain. This transformative strategy successfully converts the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one, which is then readily and optimally solved with temperature scaling. An extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across 5 diverse and challenging UDA scenarios, involving 10 state-of-the-art UDA methods, consistently and definitively demonstrates the superior performance of PseudoCal over all alternative calibration methods.

Section 1 INTRODUCTION

In recent years, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has emerged as a pivotal and widely adopted technique for enhancing the generalization capability of deep learning models from labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain, where the tasks are similar but the underlying data distributions vary significantly. Notable and impressive progress has been achieved in developing highly effective UDA methodologies, expanding into practical applications, and tackling real-world settings, with a predominant and almost exclusive focus on improving target domain model accuracy.

However, for a reliable classification model, achieving accurate predictive uncertainty estimation is absolutely as crucial as attaining high accuracy, especially in safety-critical decision-making scenarios like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis, where miscalibration can lead to catastrophic outcomes. Properly calibrated models must produce probability predictions that accurately and faithfully reflect the true likelihood of correctness. Although predictive uncertainty calibration has garnered substantial and well-deserved attention in IID supervised learning tasks with deep models, the calibration problem in the challenging context of UDA remained largely unexplored until a pioneering study revealed that improved UDA model accuracy often comes at the expense of poor uncertainty calibration on target data. This concerning phenomenon is vividly illustrated in Figure 1(a), where increasing target data accuracy is accompanied by significant overfitting of the negative log-likelihood loss during the adaptation process. Calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA presents unique and formidable challenges compared to the IID situation. The first fundamental challenge is the complete absence of labeled data in the target domain, which renders the direct application of powerful supervised IID calibration methods like temperature scaling entirely impossible. Another significant and persistent challenge arises from the severe domain distribution shifts between source and target. Consequently, UDA models calibrated solely with labeled source data cannot ensure effective or reliable calibration for the unlabeled data in the target domain.

Figure 1: ATDOC on a closed-set UDA task Ar→Cl. (a) illustrates the target error and target NLL loss during UDA training. (b) divides confidence values into 50 bins, displaying the count of correct and wrong predictions in each bin. For real target data, correctness is determined by comparing predictions with ground truths, and for pseudo-target data, it is assessed by comparing predictions with the synthesized labels. (c) shows reliability diagrams for both pseudo and real target data.

To address these challenges, existing approaches have treated calibration in UDA as a covariate shift problem across domains. They typically employ importance weighting to estimate weights for source samples based on their similarity to target data and then perform sample-weighted temperature scaling with a labeled source validation set. However, these methods possess several critical drawbacks that severely impede effective and efficient model calibration in UDA. Firstly, importance weighting may not be reliable under severe covariate shift and other complex distribution shifts, such as label shift. Secondly, despite being based on the simple post-hoc temperature scaling, all of these approaches require additional and often complex model training for accurate density estimation, which adds considerable complexity. Lastly, these methods fundamentally rely on the availability of labeled source data, which drastically limits their applicability in privacy-preserving UDA scenarios like the recent and important source-free UDA settings.

In a decisive and novel contrast, we adopt a transformative perspective, treating UDA calibration as an unsupervised calibration problem specific solely to the target domain. This allows us to focus exclusively on the first core challenge: the absence of labeled target data for supervised calibration. We first meticulously study the 'Oracle' case of using labeled target data for temperature scaling and then factorize its NLL objective into a joint optimization involving both correct and wrong predictions. This factorization uncovers a key and powerful insight: with temperature scaling, datasets exhibiting similar correct-wrong statistics should share similar optimal temperatures. Inspired directly by this foundational insight, we introduce a novel and highly effective post-hoc calibration framework called Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal). PseudoCal is based on temperature scaling and estimates the temperature for target data through calibration on a synthesized labeled pseudo-target dataset that meticulously mimics the similar correct-wrong statistics of the real target data. Concretely, PseudoCal utilizes mixup during the inference stage with unlabeled target data to generate a labeled pseudo-target set. It then performs straightforward supervised calibration on this labeled set to determine the final and optimal temperature. The effectiveness of PseudoCal depends fundamentally on the presence of similar correct-wrong statistics between the pseudo and real target data. We elucidate the theoretical support behind this with an intuitive and rigorous analysis grounded in the well-established and powerful cluster assumption. UDA models adhering to this assumption can guarantee sample-level correspondence between each pseudo-target sample and its primary real target sample used in the mixup operation. Specifically, pseudo-target samples with correct predictions correspond to correct real target samples, and vice versa, as clearly shown in Figure 1(b). Benefiting from the high resemblance of correct-wrong statistics between our synthesized pseudo-target and the real target, PseudoCal achieves significantly and consistently improved calibration performance, as definitively demonstrated in Figure 1(c).

We make three key and substantial contributions: 1) We explore the critically under-studied problem of predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA from a novel and unifying target-domain perspective, enabling a powerful and unified approach across diverse UDA scenarios, including those with label shift or limited source access. 2) We propose a novel and highly practical calibration framework, PseudoCal, which only requires unlabeled target data and a fixed UDA model. PseudoCal adopts an innovative inference-stage mixup to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set, successfully converting the challenging unsupervised calibration problem into a readily solvable supervised one. 3) We conduct a comprehensive and exhaustive evaluation of PseudoCal, involving 5 strong calibration baselines, to calibrate 10 leading UDA methods across 5 distinct UDA scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate conclusively that, on average, PseudoCal consistently and significantly outperforms all other calibration methods.

Table 1: Comparisons of typical methods for predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA.

Section 2 RELATED WORK

Unsupervised domain adaptation has been extensively and rigorously studied in image classification tasks. Mainstream methods can be categorically divided into two primary lines: 1) Distribution alignment across domains using specific discrepancy measures or adversarial learning, and 2) Target domain-based learning with self-training or various regularizations. Moreover, UDA has also been studied in object detection and image segmentation. Initially, UDA was based on the covariate shift assumption – that two domains share similar label and conditional distributions but have different input distributions. This is commonly referred to as closed-set UDA. In recent years, new and more practical settings have arisen, notably addressing label shift. These include partial-set UDA, where some source classes are absent in the target domain, and open-set UDA, where the target domain includes samples from unknown classes. Recently, there has been a growing and significant interest in a setting called source-free UDA, which can preserve source privacy. Source-free UDA has two key settings: the white-box setting uses the source model for target adaptation, while the stricter black-box setting only employs the source model for inference.

Predictive uncertainty calibration was initially studied on binary classification tasks. Guo et al. extends Platt scaling to multi-class classification and introduces matrix scaling, vector scaling, and temperature scaling. These post-hoc methods require a labeled validation set for calibration. On the other hand, there are methods that address calibration during model training, including Monte Carlo Dropout, Ensemble, and Stochastic Variational Bayesian Inference. However, a comprehensive evaluation reveals that these methods do not maintain reliable calibration performance under dataset shift. In addition, there is growing interest in calibration under distribution shifts and in semantic segmentation tasks. In this paper, we specifically and thoroughly address the calibration problem in single-source UDA. A vanilla baseline is to apply IID calibration methods such as TempScal with a labeled source validation set, dubbed TempScal-src. Regarding calibration methods considering the domain distribution shifts, the mainstream idea is to utilize importance weighting to address calibration under covariate shift in UDA, exemplified by CPCS and TransCal. Some works perturb the source validation set to serve as a general target set or employ it for density estimation. More recently, some methods have utilized multiple source domains to calibrate the unlabeled target domain in UDA. Additionally, there are training-stage calibration methods that employ smoothed labels or optimize accuracy-uncertainty differentiably. Among these methods, CPCS and TransCal are noteworthy as they specifically address transductive target calibration in UDA. For more general approaches like MC-Dropout and Ensemble, we compare our method directly with Ensemble because it consistently outperforms MC-Dropout. Table 1 presents a comprehensive comparison of these typical UDA calibration methods. In a clear and decisive contrast to existing calibration methods, PseudoCal stands out by definitively not requiring any extra model training. It is a simple, post-hoc, and highly general calibration approach, relying solely on a fixed or even black-box UDA model and unlabeled target data for calibration.

Section 3 APPROACH

We begin by formally introducing unsupervised domain adaptation with a C-way image classification task. UDA generally involves two domains: a labeled source domain and an unlabeled target domain. The source domain consists of images with their corresponding labels. The target domain contains unlabeled images. The objective of UDA is to learn a UDA model that can predict the unknown ground truth labels for the target domain, utilizing data from both domains simultaneously or sequentially.

Next, we introduce predictive uncertainty calibration and the relevant evaluation metrics. When feeding an arbitrary sample into the UDA model, we can obtain the predicted class and the corresponding softmax-based confidence. Ideally, the confidence should accurately reflect the true probability of correctness. This perfect calibration, also known as Perfect, is impossible to achieve in practice. The widely used metric for evaluating calibration error is the expected calibration error. ECE involves partitioning probability predictions into M bins and calculates the weighted average of the accuracy-confidence difference across all bins.

Here, n represents the number of samples, and for the m-th bin, the accuracy and confidence are computed accordingly. The introduction of additional popular metrics, such as NLL and Brier Score, is also standard.

Section 3.1 SUPERVISED ‘ORACLE’: FACTORIZED TEMPERATURE SCALING

Unlike the mainstream cross-domain covariate shift perspective, we view calibration in UDA as an unsupervised calibration problem within the unlabeled target domain. Before tackling this challenging problem, we first study an 'Oracle' solution based on supervised temperature scaling. TempScal is a post-hoc calibration method that optimizes a temperature scalar on a labeled validation set using the NLL loss. For the unlabeled target domain in UDA, we define the calibration achieved by applying TempScal with raw target predictions and the unattainable target ground truths as the 'Oracle' calibration. Let z represent the corresponding logit vector for the image input x, and let σ denote the softmax function. The 'Oracle' target temperature can be obtained using the original temperature scaling optimization.

With further and detailed analysis, we observe that target samples can be classified as either being correctly or wrongly predicted when evaluated by target ground truths. Moreover, both types of samples have contrasting and significant effects on the temperature optimization process. Specifically, the NLL minimization favors a small temperature to sharpen the correct predictions and a large temperature to flatten the wrong predictions. This factorization clearly and powerfully suggests that when applying TempScal to another labeled set with matching correct-wrong statistics as the 'Oracle' calibration, the objective of the NLL optimization remains highly consistent, yielding a temperature approximation very close to the target oracle temperature.

Section 3.2 UNSUPERVISED SOLUTION: PSEUDO-CALIBRATION

Inspired directly by this factorization, we introduce our Pseudo-Calibration framework. The main and powerful idea is to use the unlabeled target data to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that mimics the correct-wrong statistics of the real target set and then apply TempScal to this labeled set.

With only unlabeled target data and a fixed UDA model, the use of predicted labels as pseudo-labels is a simple method to generate a labeled set. However, optimizing NLL between raw target predictions and pseudo-labels treats all predictions as correct, completely ignoring the optimization of wrong predictions. This mismatch in correct-wrong statistics can result in poor calibration performance. Instead, we employ mixup with data across clusters, generating mixed samples that inherently include both correct and wrong predictions when evaluated with the mixed labels.

Step 1: Pseudo-target synthesis. We generate a pseudo-target set by applying mixup to target samples in the inference stage. Specifically, a pseudo-target sample and its label are obtained by taking a convex combination of a pair of real target samples from different clusters and their pseudo-labels. Step 2: Supervised calibration. Using the synthesized labeled pseudo-target set, we can easily determine the optimal pseudo-target temperature through TempScal. This estimated temperature serves as an accurate approximation of the 'Oracle' target temperature.

With the above two simple steps, PseudoCal successfully transforms the challenging unsupervised calibration problem associated with the unlabeled real target set into a supervised one with the labeled pseudo-target set and readily solves it with TempScal. The pipeline of PseudoCal is illustrated in Figure 2, where the UDA model is utilized as a black box solely for inferring the predictions of input data.

Analysis. Built upon the well-established and powerful cluster assumption, we intuitively analyze how mixed samples can exhibit similar correct-wrong statistics as real target data. This assumption suggests that within a well-learned data structure, samples located far from the classification boundary are more likely to be correctly classified, while those near the boundary are prone to misclassification. While previous works often incorporate this assumption as an objective in model training, our focus here is to employ it for explaining the inference behavior of a UDA model. We assume that the model has effectively learned the underlying target-domain structure. For simplicity, let us assume all involved labels are one-hot, and consider a fixed mix ratio noticeably greater than 0.5. This ensures a clear distinction between two involved real samples: one primary sample with a mix ratio greater than 0.5, determining the mixed label for the mixed sample, and the other as the minor sample, serving only as an input perturbation. If yields a correct model prediction evaluated by its mixed label, it suggests that the real sample maintains its prediction after cross-cluster perturbation. This implies that is likely distant from the classification boundary, and its prediction is genuinely correct. Similarly, if yields a wrong model prediction, we can reasonably infer that has a truly incorrect prediction. The presence of sample-level correspondence, when observed at the dataset level, manifests as similar correct-wrong statistics. However, this correspondence may not hold under extreme perturbation degrees.

Section 4 EXPERIMENTS

Section 4.1 SETTINGS

Datasets. For image classification, we adopt 5 popular and challenging UDA benchmarks of varied scales. Office31 is a small-scale benchmark with 31 classes in 3 domains. Office-Home is a medium-scale benchmark with 65 classes in 4 domains. VisDA is a large-scale benchmark with over 200k images across 12 classes in 2 domains. DomainNet is a large-scale benchmark. We take a subset of 126 classes with 7 tasks from 4 domains. Image-Sketch is a large-scale benchmark with 1000 classes in 2 domains. For semantic segmentation, we use Cityscapes as the target domain and either GTA5 or SYNTHIA as the source.

For image classification, we cover closed-set UDA methods, partial-set UDA methods, the white-box source-free UDA method, and the black-box source-free UDA method. For semantic segmentation, we focus on calibrating source-only models without any adaptation.

Calibration baselines. For a comprehensive and rigorous comparison, we consider 5 typical calibration baselines in UDA, including the no calibration baseline, source-domain calibration, cross-domain calibration, and a generic calibration method.

Implementation details. We train all UDA models using their official code until convergence. We adopt ResNet-101 for VisDA and segmentation tasks, ResNet-34 for DomainNet, and ResNet-50 for all other tasks. For PseudoCal, a fixed mix ratio of 0.65 is employed in all experiments. The UDA model is fixed for only inference use. We use it for one-epoch inference with mixup to generate the labeled pseudo-target set. The reported results are averaged over five random runs.

Semantic segmentation. Section 4.3 DISCUSSION

Qualitative comparisons. Reliability diagrams in Figure 3(a)-(b) show that PseudoCal consistently aligns closely with 'Oracle', while the existing state-of-the-art method TransCal deviates significantly.

In addition, optimal performance for PseudoCal occurs with a moderate value between 0.6 and 0.7. The reason is that a value closer to 0.5 generates more ambiguous samples, resulting in increased wrong predictions, whereas a value closer to 1.0 has the opposite effect. Comparison with training-stage mixup. Most approaches incorporate mixup during the model training stage to enhance model generalization, and some utilize mixup as a training-stage calibration method. (ii) Different mix ratios: PseudoCal leverages mixup for cross-cluster sample interpolation and performs effectively with a fixed mix ratio but is considerably less effective with values close to 1.0. Ablation study on pseudo-target synthesis. Pseudo-target synthesis plays a critical role in our PseudoCal framework. The results consistently and definitively demonstrate that our inference-stage input-level mixup outperforms all the alternative options.

Section 5 CONCLUSION

In conclusion, we introduce PseudoCal, a novel, versatile, and highly effective post-hoc framework for calibrating predictive uncertainty in unsupervised domain adaptation. By focusing decisively on the unlabeled target domain, PseudoCal distinguishes itself from mainstream calibration methods based on covariate shift and eliminates their associated limitations. To elaborate, PseudoCal employs a novel and powerful inference-stage mixup strategy to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that accurately mimics the correct-wrong statistics in real target samples. In this transformative way, PseudoCal successfully converts the challenging unsupervised calibration problem involving unlabeled real samples into a supervised one using labeled pseudo-target data, which can be readily and optimally addressed through temperature scaling. Throughout our extensive and rigorous evaluations spanning diverse UDA settings beyond covariate shift, including source-free UDA settings and domain adaptive semantic segmentation, PseudoCal consistently showcases its decisive advantages of simplicity, versatility, and effectiveness in enhancing calibration in UDA. In future work, we aim to extend PseudoCal to address calibration problems in more practical and challenging UDA scenarios, including open-set UDA and UDA for object detection, thereby broadening its significant impact.

Title: Pseudo-Calibration: A Groundbreaking Framework for Enhancing Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

Abstract
The field of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has witnessed substantial and dedicated efforts aimed at improving model accuracy for an unlabeled target domain by leveraging one or more labeled source domains. However, a critical and often overlooked issue is that UDA models frequently exhibit poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty on target data. This problem remains profoundly under-explored and poses significant risks in safety-critical UDA applications, such as autonomous systems and medical diagnostics. The two primary and formidable challenges in addressing predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA are the complete absence of labeled target data and the presence of severe distribution shifts between the source and target domains. Traditional supervised calibration methods, such as temperature scaling, are entirely inapplicable due to the first challenge. Recent studies have attempted to address the initial challenge by employing importance-weighting with labeled source data, but these approaches still suffer from the second challenge and introduce additional complex density modeling requirements. We propose Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a novel and highly effective post-hoc calibration framework. In a decisive departure from prior approaches, we consider UDA calibration as a target domain-specific unsupervised problem rather than a covariate shift problem across domains. Our innovative and principled use of inference-stage mixup and the cluster assumption guarantees that a synthesized labeled pseudo-target set accurately captures the essential structure of the real target domain. This transformative strategy successfully converts the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one, which is then readily and optimally solved with temperature scaling. An extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across 5 diverse and challenging UDA scenarios, involving 10 state-of-the-art UDA methods, consistently and definitively demonstrates the superior performance of PseudoCal over all alternative calibration methods.

Section 1 INTRODUCTION

In recent years, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has emerged as a pivotal and widely adopted technique for enhancing the generalization capability of deep learning models from labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain, where the tasks are similar but the underlying data distributions vary significantly. Notable and impressive progress has been achieved in developing highly effective UDA methodologies, expanding into practical applications, and tackling real-world settings, with a predominant and almost exclusive focus on improving target domain model accuracy.

However, for a reliable classification model, achieving accurate predictive uncertainty estimation is absolutely as crucial as attaining high accuracy, especially in safety-critical decision-making scenarios like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis, where miscalibration can lead to catastrophic outcomes. Properly calibrated models must produce probability predictions that accurately and faithfully reflect the true likelihood of correctness. Although predictive uncertainty calibration has garnered substantial and well-deserved attention in IID supervised learning tasks with deep models, the calibration problem in the challenging context of UDA remained largely unexplored until a pioneering study revealed that improved UDA model accuracy often comes at the expense of poor uncertainty calibration on target data. This concerning phenomenon is vividly illustrated in Figure 1(a), where increasing target data accuracy is accompanied by significant overfitting of the negative log-likelihood loss during the adaptation process. Calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA presents unique and formidable challenges compared to the IID situation. The first fundamental challenge is the complete absence of labeled data in the target domain, which renders the direct application of powerful supervised IID calibration methods like temperature scaling entirely impossible. Another significant and persistent challenge arises from the severe domain distribution shifts between source and target. Consequently, UDA models calibrated solely with labeled source data cannot ensure effective or reliable calibration for the unlabeled data in the target domain.

Figure 1: ATDOC on a closed-set UDA task Ar→Cl. (a) illustrates the target error and target NLL loss during UDA training. (b) divides confidence values into 50 bins, displaying the count of correct and wrong predictions in each bin. For real target data, correctness is determined by comparing predictions with ground truths, and for pseudo-target data, it is assessed by comparing predictions with the synthesized labels. (c) shows reliability diagrams for both pseudo and real target data.

To address these challenges, existing approaches have treated calibration in UDA as a covariate shift problem across domains. They typically employ importance weighting to estimate weights for source samples based on their similarity to target data and then perform sample-weighted temperature scaling with a labeled source validation set. However, these methods possess several critical drawbacks that severely impede effective and efficient model calibration in UDA. Firstly, importance weighting may not be reliable under severe covariate shift and other complex distribution shifts, such as label shift. Secondly, despite being based on the simple post-hoc temperature scaling, all of these approaches require additional and often complex model training for accurate density estimation, which adds considerable complexity. Lastly, these methods fundamentally rely on the availability of labeled source data, which drastically limits their applicability in privacy-preserving UDA scenarios like the recent and important source-free UDA settings.

In a decisive and novel contrast, we adopt a transformative perspective, treating UDA calibration as an unsupervised calibration problem specific solely to the target domain. This allows us to focus exclusively on the first core challenge: the absence of labeled target data for supervised calibration. We first meticulously study the 'Oracle' case of using labeled target data for temperature scaling and then factorize its NLL objective into a joint optimization involving both correct and wrong predictions. This factorization uncovers a key and powerful insight: with temperature scaling, datasets exhibiting similar correct-wrong statistics should share similar optimal temperatures. Inspired directly by this foundational insight, we introduce a novel and highly effective post-hoc calibration framework called Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal). PseudoCal is based on temperature scaling and estimates the temperature for target data through calibration on a synthesized labeled pseudo-target dataset that meticulously mimics the similar correct-wrong statistics of the real target data. Concretely, PseudoCal utilizes mixup during the inference stage with unlabeled target data to generate a labeled pseudo-target set. It then performs straightforward supervised calibration on this labeled set to determine the final and optimal temperature. The effectiveness of PseudoCal depends fundamentally on the presence of similar correct-wrong statistics between the pseudo and real target data. We elucidate the theoretical support behind this with an intuitive and rigorous analysis grounded in the well-established and powerful cluster assumption. UDA models adhering to this assumption can guarantee sample-level correspondence between each pseudo-target sample and its primary real target sample used in the mixup operation. Specifically, pseudo-target samples with correct predictions correspond to correct real target samples, and vice versa, as clearly shown in Figure 1(b). Benefiting from the high resemblance of correct-wrong statistics between our synthesized pseudo-target and the real target, PseudoCal achieves significantly and consistently improved calibration performance, as definitively demonstrated in Figure 1(c).

We make three key and substantial contributions: 1) We explore the critically under-studied problem of predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA from a novel and unifying target-domain perspective, enabling a powerful and unified approach across diverse UDA scenarios, including those with label shift or limited source access. 2) We propose a novel and highly practical calibration framework, PseudoCal, which only requires unlabeled target data and a fixed UDA model. PseudoCal adopts an innovative inference-stage mixup to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set, successfully converting the challenging unsupervised calibration problem into a readily solvable supervised one. 3) We conduct a comprehensive and exhaustive evaluation of PseudoCal, involving 5 strong calibration baselines, to calibrate 10 leading UDA methods across 5 distinct UDA scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate conclusively that, on average, PseudoCal consistently and significantly outperforms all other calibration methods.

Table 1: Comparisons of typical methods for predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA.

Section 2 RELATED WORK

Unsupervised domain adaptation has been extensively and rigorously studied in image classification tasks. Mainstream methods can be categorically divided into two primary lines: 1) Distribution alignment across domains using specific discrepancy measures or adversarial learning, and 2) Target domain-based learning with self-training or various regularizations. Moreover, UDA has also been studied in object detection and image segmentation. Initially, UDA was based on the covariate shift assumption – that two domains share similar label and conditional distributions but have different input distributions. This is commonly referred to as closed-set UDA. In recent years, new and more practical settings have arisen, notably addressing label shift. These include partial-set UDA, where some source classes are absent in the target domain, and open-set UDA, where the target domain includes samples from unknown classes. Recently, there has been a growing and significant interest in a setting called source-free UDA, which can preserve source privacy. Source-free UDA has two key settings: the white-box setting uses the source model for target adaptation, while the stricter black-box setting only employs the source model for inference.

Predictive uncertainty calibration was initially studied on binary classification tasks. Guo et al. extends Platt scaling to multi-class classification and introduces matrix scaling, vector scaling, and temperature scaling. These post-hoc methods require a labeled validation set for calibration. On the other hand, there are methods that address calibration during model training, including Monte Carlo Dropout, Ensemble, and Stochastic Variational Bayesian Inference. However, a comprehensive evaluation reveals that these methods do not maintain reliable calibration performance under dataset shift. In addition, there is growing interest in calibration under distribution shifts and in semantic segmentation tasks. In this paper, we specifically and thoroughly address the calibration problem in single-source UDA. A vanilla baseline is to apply IID calibration methods such as TempScal with a labeled source validation set, dubbed TempScal-src. Regarding calibration methods considering the domain distribution shifts, the mainstream idea is to utilize importance weighting to address calibration under covariate shift in UDA, exemplified by CPCS and TransCal. Some works perturb the source validation set to serve as a general target set or employ it for density estimation. More recently, some methods have utilized multiple source domains to calibrate the unlabeled target domain in UDA. Additionally, there are training-stage calibration methods that employ smoothed labels or optimize accuracy-uncertainty differentiably. Among these methods, CPCS and TransCal are noteworthy as they specifically address transductive target calibration in UDA. For more general approaches like MC-Dropout and Ensemble, we compare our method directly with Ensemble because it consistently outperforms MC-Dropout. Table 1 presents a comprehensive comparison of these typical UDA calibration methods. In a clear and decisive contrast to existing calibration methods, PseudoCal stands out by definitively not requiring any extra model training. It is a simple, post-hoc, and highly general calibration approach, relying solely on a fixed or even black-box UDA model and unlabeled target data for calibration.

Section 3 APPROACH

We begin by formally introducing unsupervised domain adaptation with a C-way image classification task. UDA generally involves two domains: a labeled source domain and an unlabeled target domain. The source domain consists of images with their corresponding labels. The target domain contains unlabeled images. The objective of UDA is to learn a UDA model that can predict the unknown ground truth labels for the target domain, utilizing data from both domains simultaneously or sequentially.

Next, we introduce predictive uncertainty calibration and the relevant evaluation metrics. When feeding an arbitrary sample into the UDA model, we can obtain the predicted class and the corresponding softmax-based confidence. Ideally, the confidence should accurately reflect the true probability of correctness. This perfect calibration, also known as Perfect, is impossible to achieve in practice. The widely used metric for evaluating calibration error is the expected calibration error. ECE involves partitioning probability predictions into M bins and calculates the weighted average of the accuracy-confidence difference across all bins.

Here, n represents the number of samples, and for the m-th bin, the accuracy and confidence are computed accordingly. The introduction of additional popular metrics, such as NLL and Brier Score, is also standard.

Section 3.1 SUPERVISED ‘ORACLE’: FACTORIZED TEMPERATURE SCALING

Unlike the mainstream cross-domain covariate shift perspective, we view calibration in UDA as an unsupervised calibration problem within the unlabeled target domain. Before tackling this challenging problem, we first study an 'Oracle' solution based on supervised temperature scaling. TempScal is a post-hoc calibration method that optimizes a temperature scalar on a labeled validation set using the NLL loss. For the unlabeled target domain in UDA, we define the calibration achieved by applying TempScal with raw target predictions and the unattainable target ground truths as the 'Oracle' calibration. Let z represent the corresponding logit vector for the image input x, and let σ denote the softmax function. The 'Oracle' target temperature can be obtained using the original temperature scaling optimization.

With further and detailed analysis, we observe that target samples can be classified as either being correctly or wrongly predicted when evaluated by target ground truths. Moreover, both types of samples have contrasting and significant effects on the temperature optimization process. Specifically, the NLL minimization favors a small temperature to sharpen the correct predictions and a large temperature to flatten the wrong predictions. Section 4 EXPERIMENTS

Title: Pseudo-Calibration: Improving Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Domain Adaptation

Abstract
Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) models often exhibit poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty on target data. The primary challenges are the absence of labeled target data and distribution shifts between domains. Supervised calibration methods like temperature scaling are inapplicable due to the lack of target labels. Recent methods use importance-weighting with labeled source data but can be unreliable under severe distribution shifts and require complex density modeling. This work proposes Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a post-hoc calibration framework. It treats UDA calibration as a target domain-specific unsupervised problem. The method uses inference-stage mixup and the cluster assumption to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that captures the structure of the real target set. This transforms the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one solvable with temperature scaling. Evaluation across 5 UDA scenarios involving 10 UDA methods shows PseudoCal outperforms alternative calibration methods.

1 INTRODUCTION
Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) (Pan & Yang, 2009) aims to adapt models from labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain. Methods focus on improving target domain accuracy (Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015; Long et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2018). Reliable predictive uncertainty estimation is also important, particularly for safety-critical applications (Guo et al., 2017). Calibrated models should produce probability predictions that reflect correctness likelihood. While calibration has been studied in IID supervised learning (Thulasidasan et al., 2019; Krishnan & Tickoo, 2020), calibration in UDA is less explored. Wang et al. (2020) showed improved UDA model accuracy can coincide with poor uncertainty calibration on target data. Figure 1(a) illustrates that increasing target accuracy can accompany overfitting of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss.

Calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA presents challenges. First, labeled target data is absent, preventing direct use of supervised IID calibration methods like temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017). Second, severe domain distribution shifts mean models calibrated with labeled source data may not be calibrated for target data (Wang et al., 2020).

Existing approaches (Park et al., 2020; Pampari & Ermon, 2020; Wang et al., 2020) treat UDA calibration as a covariate shift problem (Sugiyama et al., 2007). They use importance weighting (Cortes et al., 2008) to weight source samples by similarity to target data and perform sample-weighted temperature scaling. Limitations include: unreliability under severe covariate shift or other shifts like label shift (Park et al., 2020); requirement for additional model training for density estimation; and reliance on labeled source data, limiting use in privacy-preserving settings like source-free UDA (Li et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020a; 2022).

This work treats UDA calibration as an unsupervised calibration problem specific to the target domain, focusing on the absence of labeled target data. Analysis of an 'Oracle' case using labeled target data for temperature scaling factorizes its NLL objective into terms for correct and wrong predictions. This suggests datasets with similar correct-wrong statistics should share similar temperatures. Based on this, Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal) is proposed. It estimates the temperature for target data by calibrating on a synthesized labeled pseudo-target dataset that mimics the correct-wrong statistics of the real target data. PseudoCal uses mixup (Zhang et al., 2018) at inference on unlabeled target data to generate a labeled pseudo-target set, then performs supervised calibration on this set. The cluster assumption (Grandvalet & Bengio, 2004) provides support: if a UDA model adheres to this assumption, sample-level correspondence can exist between pseudo-target samples and the primary real target samples used in mixup. As shown in Figure 1(b), pseudo-target samples with correct predictions correspond to correct real target samples, and vice versa. This leads to similar correct-wrong statistics, enabling improved calibration as shown in Figure 1(c).

Contributions are: 1) Exploring predictive uncertainty calibration in UDA from a target-domain perspective, enabling a unified approach across diverse UDA scenarios. 2) Proposing PseudoCal, a calibration framework requiring only unlabeled target data and a fixed UDA model. It uses inference-stage mixup to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set, converting the unsupervised problem into a supervised one. 3) Comprehensive evaluation of PseudoCal against 5 calibration baselines across 5 UDA scenarios and 10 UDA methods, showing it consistently outperforms other methods.

2 RELATED WORK

Title: Pseudo-Calibration: Improving Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Domain Adaptation

Abstract
Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) models often exhibit poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty on target data. The primary challenges are the absence of labeled target data and distribution shifts between domains. Supervised calibration methods like temperature scaling are inapplicable due to the lack of target labels. Recent methods use importance-weighting with labeled source data but can be unreliable under severe distribution shifts and require complex density modeling. This work proposes Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a post-hoc calibration framework. It treats UDA calibration as a target domain-specific unsupervised problem. The method uses inference-stage mixup and the cluster assumption to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set that captures the structure of the real target set. This transforms the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one solvable with temperature scaling. Evaluation across 5 UDA scenarios involving 10 UDA methods shows PseudoCal outperforms alternative calibration methods.

1 INTRODUCTION

Reliable predictive uncertainty estimation is also important, particularly for safety-critical applications (Guo et al., 2017). Calibrated models should produce probability predictions that reflect correctness likelihood. While calibration has been studied in IID supervised learning (Thulasidasan et al., 2019; Krishnan & Tickoo, 2020), calibration in UDA is less explored. Wang et al. (2020) showed improved UDA model accuracy can coincide with poor uncertainty calibration on target data. Figure 1(a) illustrates that increasing target accuracy can accompany overfitting of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss.

Calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA presents challenges. First, labeled target data is absent, preventing direct use of supervised IID calibration methods like temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017). Second, severe domain distribution shifts mean models calibrated with labeled source data may not be calibrated for target data (Wang et al., 2020).

Existing approaches (Park et al., 2020; Pampari & Ermon, 2020; Wang et al., 2020) treat UDA calibration as a covariate shift problem (Sugiyama et al., 2007). (ii) Instance-based augmentations like RandAugment (Cubuk et al., 2020) or strong augmentations from self-supervised learning (Chen et al., 2020). (iii) Mixup at patch-level (Yun et al., 2019) or feature-level (Verma et al., 2019). (iv) Common training-stage mixup with λ ~ Beta(0.3,0.3) (Zhang et al., 2018). (v) Using original or filtered pseudo-labeled real target samples without mixup (λ=1.0) (Lee et al., 2013; Sohn et al., 2020). Comparison in Table 9 shows inference-stage input-level mixup outperforms alternatives.

5 CONCLUSION
PseudoCal is a post-hoc framework for calibrating predictive uncertainty in UDA. It focuses on the unlabeled target domain, differing from methods based on covariate shift. It uses inference-stage mixup to synthesize a labeled pseudo-target set mimicking the correct-wrong statistics of real target samples, transforming the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one solvable with temperature scaling. Evaluations across diverse UDA settings, including source-free UDA and semantic segmentation, show PseudoCal is simple, versatile, and effective. Future work may extend PseudoCal to open-set UDA and UDA for object detection.

CLIP the Bias: How Useful is Balancing Data in Multimodal Learning?

Abstract
We demonstrate the effectiveness of data-balancing for mitigating biases in contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP), clearly identifying its practical strengths and limitations. First, we confirm that CLIP models definitively absorb societal stereotypes. To counter this, we present a novel and practical algorithm, Multi-Modal Moment Matching (M4), designed to effectively reduce both representation and association biases in multimodal data. We use M4 to conduct a definitive analysis accounting for critical factors like model architecture, representation size, and data scale. Our study precisely maps the dynamics of how CLIP learns and unlearns biases. We prove that fine-tuning is highly effective for countering representation biases, though its impact is limited for association biases. Data balancing has a clear, mixed impact on quality: it reliably improves classification but can degrade retrieval. Crucially, data and architectural improvements decisively mitigate any negative performance impact; applying M4 to SigLIP-B/16 with data quality filters improves COCO image-to-text retrieval @5 from 86% to 87% and ImageNet 0-shot classification from 77% to 77.5%. We conclude with actionable recommendations for deploying data balancing effectively in real-world multimodal systems.

Introduction
Recent advances in multimodal systems have been breathtaking, enabling transformative applications in zero-shot classification, text-to-image generation, image captioning, and music generation. However, such powerful systems can inflict significant harm if left unchecked, such as by amplifying biases, causing performance disparities, or encoding narrow cultural perspectives, which limits their real-world utility and safety.

Contrary to the traditional supervised learning setup, multimodal systems present novel and critical ethical challenges. They typically operate with an open-vocabulary, making standard statistical fairness definitions difficult to apply. Furthermore, externalization in these systems can expose users to biases in unanticipated ways. The data itself is often biased, perpetuating societal stereotypes.

Concrete examples demonstrate this risk. Querying the text-to-image model Imagen with prompts for "manager" and "secretary" or "pilot" and "flight attendant" generates images that reflect gender stereotypes. Similar issues are documented across GANs, Stable Diffusion, and DALL-E. Zero-shot classifiers like CLIP also encode societal stereotypes, associating items like ties, cars, and tools with men. Such biases inflict tangible harm by shaping social narratives and can be exploited in unanticipated ways to promote prejudice.

This work provides a definitive investigation into a key remediation strategy: data balancing. We focus on contrastive learning because it captures the core complexities of multimodal systems, exhibits strong societal biases, is amenable to analysis, and is increasingly deployed in critical domains like healthcare. Biases in these foundational models manifest downstream in applications like captioning and retrieval.

To enable this practical analysis, we develop the M4 data balancing algorithm. Using M4, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of data balancing's effectiveness for achieving desirable model behavior, definitively identifying its strengths and limitations while accounting for model size, representation size, and training data scale. We precisely examine how CLIP learns and unlearns biases. In total, we train over 150 models, an unprecedented empirical scale for this problem. Our results provide clear, nuanced guidance: while data balancing positively impacts model bias with a mixed effect on quality, it is insufficient alone for achieving fair downstream behavior.

Preliminaries
CLIP contains two transformer encoder towers for vision and language. For an image-text pair, the outputs are embedded into a shared space. CLIP computes similarity scores between these embeddings.

To study data bias mitigation, we introduce a data balancing algorithm targeting biases in first-order statistics (representation bias) and second-order statistics (association bias).

Definition: Data Representation Bias
For a sensitive attribute vector sampled from a distribution, the representation bias with respect to a target distribution is the maximum absolute deviation in the prevalence of any attribute category.

Definition: Data Association Bias
For jointly sampled sensitive attributes and labels, the association bias is the maximum absolute difference in the conditional probability of any label given the presence versus absence of any sensitive attribute.

These data-level definitions have direct analogs for model bias.

Our goal is to study how data biases transfer to the model and whether data balancing is impactful, considering the known phenomenon of bias amplification. We focus on perceived gender as the sensitive attribute and occupations as labels. We denote the original data as baseline.

We explore two balancing strategies: balanced, which directly tackles gender and occupation constraints, and proxies, which also includes proxy variables to address indirect correlations.

Summary of Findings
Our major findings are:

I. Proxies effectively mitigate representation biases: Decorrelating sensitive attributes from many proxy variables successfully minimizes the model's representation bias, preventing it from favoring certain subgroups in unrelated contexts.

II. But proxies hurt association biases: For association bias in the closed-vocabulary setting, adding extra proxy variables can negatively impact reduction efforts, likely due to competing constraints.

III. Fine-tuning is highly effective for representation bias: Representation bias in the model is directly sensitive to the last data distribution seen. Fine-tuning on balanced data effectively counters it.

IV. But fine-tuning is less effective for association bias: The extent of association bias varies gradually based on total training time on balanced data, regardless of when it is seen.

V. Mixed impact on model performance: Data balancing improves performance on visual classification benchmarks but can degrade image-text retrieval.

VI. Improving data quality and model architecture decisively helps: Filtering low-similarity data and using architectures like SigLIP mitigate any negative performance impacts. For example, COCO image-to-text @5 improves from 86% to 87%, and ImageNet 0-shot classification improves from 77% to 77.5%.

Detailed Results
Setup
We assume a stream of examples with image-text pairs, predefined labels, and sensitive attributes. We focus on perceived gender and occupations, with annotations inferred from both image and text. To study bias dynamics, we split training into two stages, switching between original and debiased data. Each model is trained on 1B image-text pairs from WebLI. We vary the length of the first stage and use three random seeds per setup.

We experiment with two model sizes (S and B) and vary the representation size. We verify key findings on larger architectures and conduct a meta-analysis using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test for statistical significance.

Representation Bias
