Adding small Gaussian noise ε_T ~ N(0, σ^2) to v_and^(i)(x_T) leads to variance of I'_and^(i)(T) being 2^{|T|} σ^2, increasing exponentially with interaction order. Similarly for OR interactions. Therefore, we propose to directly learn an error term ε_T^(i) based on Eq. 3 to remove tiny unavoidable noisy signals, setting v^(i)(x_T) = v_and^(i)(x_T) + v_or^(i)(x_T) + ε_T^(i), constrained by |ε_T^(i)| < τ_ε^(i), to enhance robustness.

Experiments examined whether extracted interactions could still accurately explain network output after removing the error term. Matching errors between real and approximated outputs on all masked samples were computed, showing the real network output was well approximated by interactions.

Experiment
In this section, we conducted extensive experiments to verify the sparsity and generalization power of interaction primitives extracted by our proposed method on three tasks.

Task 1: Sentiment Classification with Language Models. We jointly extracted AND-OR interaction primitives from BERT-base and BERT-large models using Eq. 3. Models were fine-tuned on the SST-2 dataset. We analyzed the log-odds output of the ground-truth label.

(2023), we labeled important image patches as input variables and analyzed the scalar output before the softmax layer for digit "3".

This figure compares interaction strength curves between our extracted interactions, traditional interactions (Li et al., 2023), and original Harsanyi interactions (Ren et al., 2023). We found most interactions had negligible effect. Although our method slightly reduced sparsity, extracted interactions remained sparse enough to be considered primitive inference patterns. The set of AND-OR interactions extracted by our proposed method exhibited significantly higher generalization power than interactions extracted by the traditional method.

They proved DNNs usually encode a small number of interactions under common conditions. These interactions can universally explain the DNN's output on any arbitrary masked input sample. Li et al. (2023) discovered the discriminative power of certain interactions.

Deng et al. (2023) found that different attribution scores estimated by different attribution methods could all be represented as a combination of different interactions. Zhang et al. (2022) used interactions to explain the mechanism of different methods for boosting adversarial transferability. Ren et al. (2022) used interactions to define the optimal baseline value for computing Shapley values. Deng et al. (2021) found that for most DNNs it was difficult to learn interactions with a median number of input variables. Ren et al. (2023) discovered that Bayesian neural networks were unlikely to model complex interactions with many input variables.

3 Generalizable interaction primitives across DNNs
3.1 Preliminaries: explaining the network output with interaction primitives
Although no theory guarantees how to define concepts fitting human cognition, Li et al. (2023) and Ren et al. (2023) provided mathematical support for using interactions between input variables as primitives. There are two types: AND interactions and OR interactions.

AND interactions. Given a function v: R^n → R and an input sample x = [x1, x2, ..., xn]^⊺ with n input variables indexed by N={1,2,...,n}, v(x) ∈ R denotes the output. Ren et al. (2022) used the Harsanyi dividend (Harsanyi, 1963) I_and(S|x) to quantify the numerical effect of the AND relationship between variables in S ⊆ N encoded by v.
I_and(S|x) := Σ_{T ⊆ S} (-1)^{|S|-|T|} v(x_T). (1)
where I_and(∅|x) = v(x_∅), and x_T denotes a sample where variables in N\T are masked. Each AND interaction I_and(S|x) reveals the AND relationship between all variables in S. For example, consider the slang term S = {x3, x4, x5, x6} in the sentence "x1=It, x2=is, x3=raining, x4=cats, x5=and, x6=dogs!". The co-occurrence of the four words forms the semantic concept of "heavy rain" and contributes effect I_and(S|x). Masking any word xi ∈ S invalidates the concept and eliminates the effect, i.e., I_and(S|x^{masked}) = 0.

OR interactions. Li et al. (2023) defined the OR interaction effect I_or(S|x).
I_or(S|x) := - Σ_{T ⊆ S} (-1)^{|S|-|T|} v(x_{N\T}). (2)
where I_or(∅|x) = v(x_∅). Each OR interaction I_or(S|x) describes the OR relationship between all variables in S. Consider an input sentence "x1=This, x2=movie, x3=is, x4=boring, x5=and, x6=disappointing" for sentiment classification. Set S={x4, x6}. The presence of any word in S contributes a negative sentiment effect I_or(S|x).

Sparsity of interactions. Theoretically, a function can encode at most 2^n different AND interactions. However, Ren et al. (2023) proved that under common conditions, most well-trained DNNs only encode a small set of AND interactions, denoted by Ω, i.e., only a few interactions S ∈ Ω have considerable effects I_and(S|x). All other interactions have almost zero effects, I_and(S|x) ≈ 0.

An OR interaction can be regarded as a specific AND interaction if the definitions of the masked and unmasked states are inverted. Thus, the proven sparsity of AND interactions also indicates that well-trained DNNs tend to encode a small number of OR interactions.

Definition of interaction primitives. Considering the proven sparsity, we define an interaction primitive as a salient interaction. Formally, given a threshold τ, the set of interaction primitives is Ω = {S ⊆ N: |I(S|x)| > τ}.

Theorem 1 (Universal matching theorem, proved by Ren et al. (2023)). As a corollary of the proven sparsity, the function's output on all 2^n masked samples {x_S | S ⊆ N} can be universally explained by the interaction primitives in Ω, s.t., |Ω| ≪ 2^n, i.e., ∀ S ⊆ N, v(x_S) = Σ_{T ⊆ S} I_and(T|x) ≈ Σ_{T ⊆ S: T ∈ Ω} I_and(T|x).

Theorem 1 shows that if we arbitrarily mask the input sample x, we get 2^n different masked samples. The output v(x_S) on all 2^n masked samples can be universally matched using only a few interaction primitives in Ω.

Theorem 2 (proved by Harsanyi (1963)). The Shapley value φ(i) of an input variable i can be explained as a uniform allocation of the AND interactions, i.e., φ(i) = Σ_{S ⊆ N: S ∋ i} (1/|S|) I_and(S|x).

3.2 Faithfulness problem with interaction-based explanations
Basic setting of using AND-OR interactions to explain a DNN. We employ both AND and OR interactions to explain the DNN's output, as DNN complexity makes it difficult to rely solely on one type. We decompose the output v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x), using AND interactions to explain v_and(x) and OR interactions to explain v_or(x). A challenge is learning an appropriate decomposition that reveals intrinsic primitive interactions.

Regardless of how we randomly decompose v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x), Theorem 3 demonstrates we can still use interactions to fit the DNN's outputs on 2^n randomly masked samples {x_T | T ⊆ N}. Furthermore, according to sparsity, Proposition 1 states the 2^n network outputs can usually be approximated by a small number of AND interaction primitives in Ω^{and} and OR interaction primitives in Ω^{or}, s.t., |Ω^{and}|, |Ω^{or}| ≪ 2^n.

Theorem 3 (Universal matching theorem). Given a DNN v and an input sample x. For each randomly masked sample x_T, T ⊆ N,
v(x_T) = v_and(x_T) + v_or(x_T) = Σ_{S ⊆ T} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∈ {S: S ∩ T ≠ ∅} ∪ {∅}} I_or(S|x_T). (3)

Proposition 1. The output of a well-trained DNN on all 2^n masked samples {x_T | T ⊆ N} can be universally approximated by the interaction primitives in Ω^{and} and Ω^{or}, s.t., |Ω^{and}|, |Ω^{or}| ≪ 2^n, i.e., ∀ T ⊆ N,
v(x_T) = Σ_{S ⊆ T} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∈ {S: S ∩ T ≠ ∅} ∪ {∅}} I_or(S|x_T) ≈ v(x_∅) + Σ_{∅ ≠ S ⊆ T: S ∈ Ω^{and}} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∩ T ≠ ∅: S ∈ Ω^{or}} I_or(S|x_T), where v(x_∅) = v_and(x_∅) + v_or(x_∅).

Problems with the faithfulness of interactions. Although Theorem 3's universal matching capacity is an advantage, it does not guarantee faithfulness. There is no standard way to faithfully decompose v_and(x) and v_or(x) that reveal intrinsic primitive interactions, considering two challenges.

Challenge 1: Ambiguous decomposition of v_and(x) and v_or(x) usually brings considerable uncertainty in interaction extraction. Consider a toy Boolean function f(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + x4 ∨ x5, where x = [x1,x2,x3,x4,x5]^⊺ and xi ∈ {0,1}. There are two decomposition ways. First, decompose v_and(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 and v_or(x) = x4 ∨ x5, explaining f(x) with an OR interaction I_or(S={4,5}) and three AND interactions I_and(S={1,2,3}), I_and(S={2,3}), I_and(S={3,4}). Alternatively, use exclusively AND interactions: rewrite v_and(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + x4 ∨ x5 = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + (x4 + x5 - x4 ∧ x5) and v_or(x)=0, w.r.t xi ∈ {0,1}. The v_and term can be explained by six AND interaction primitives. This illustrates diverse strategies for extracting interactions generated by different decompositions.

The f(x) is a simple function. In real applications, DNNs encode intricate AND-OR relationships, making it challenging to formulate an explicit expression or a definitive ground-truth decomposition. Consequently, diversity is ubiquitous.

Challenge 2: How to ensure interaction primitives are generalizable. Generalizable primitives are usually transferable over different models trained for the same task, instead of being over-fitted by a single model. If an interaction primitive can be consistently extracted from different DNNs, it can be considered a faithful concept. Otherwise, non-generalizable interactions appear as mathematical manipulations, not faithful concepts, even if they satisfy sparsity and universal matching.

Definition 1 (Transferability of interaction primitives). Given m different DNNs trained for the same task, v^(1), v^(2), ..., v^(m), we use AND-OR interactions to explain the output score v^(i)(x) of each DNN v^(i) on input sample x. Let Ω^{and,(i)} = {S ⊆ N: |I_and^(i)(S|x)| > τ^(i)} and Ω^{or,(i)} = {S ⊆ N: |I_or^(i)(S|x)| > τ^(i)} denote sets of sparse AND and OR interaction primitives, respectively. The sets of generalizable AND and OR interaction primitives for the i-th DNN are defined as Ω_shared^{and} = ∩_{i=1}^m Ω^{and,(i)} and Ω_shared^{or} = ∩_{i=1}^m Ω^{or,(i)}. The generalization power of AND and OR interactions of the i-th DNN is measured by s_and^(i) = |Ω_shared^{and}| / |Ω^{and,(i)}| and s_or^(i) = |Ω_shared^{or}| / |Ω^{or,(i)}|.

Definition 1 introduces generalization power. A larger value signifies higher transferability and more generalizable interactive primitives.

3.3 Extracting generalizable interaction primitives
Neither challenge has been adequately tackled. Interactions are determined by the decomposition v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x). Rewriting the decomposition as v_and(x_T) = 0.5 v(x_T) + γ_T and v_or(x_T) = 0.5 v(x_T) - γ_T, learning the best decomposition is equivalent to learning a set of {γ_T}. The parameter γ_T ∈ R for a subset T ⊆ N determines a specific decomposition. Our goal is to learn appropriate parameters {γ_T} that reduce uncertainty and boost generalization power.

To alleviate uncertainty, the most intuitive approach is to learn the sparsest interactions, considering Occam's Razor, as the sparsest explanation is usually considered most faithful.
min_{γ_T} ‖I_and‖_1 + ‖I_or‖_1, (4)
where I_and = [I_and(T1|x), ..., I_and(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺, I_or = [I_or(T1|x), ..., I_or(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n}, T_k ⊆ N.

The ℓ1 norm loss promotes sparsity of both AND and OR interactions.

3.3.1 Only achieving sparsity is not enough
Sparsity w.r.t. each single input sample from Eq. (4) does not fully solve the two challenges. First, Ren et al. (2023) found extraction of high-order interactions is usually sensitive to small noises in input variables, where order(S) = |S|. When different noises are added, the algorithm may extract fully different high-order interactions. This hurts generalization power over different samples containing similar sets of input variables.

Second, optimizing the loss in Eq. (4) may lead to diverse solutions. Given different initial states, the loss may learn two different sets of parameters {γ_T} as two local minima with similar loss values, generating two different sets of interactions. We conducted an experiment. Given a pre-trained BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018) and an input sentence x on the SST-2 dataset for sentiment classification, we learned parameters {γ_T} to extract sparse interaction primitives. We repeatedly extracted two sets of AND-OR interactions by applying two different initializations, denoted by (A^{and}, A^{or}) and (B^{and}, B^{or}). A^{and} = {S ⊆ N: |I_and(S|x)| > τ_{A^{and}}} denotes the set of AND interaction primitives extracted by a certain initialization, where τ_{A^{and}} was determined to ensure each set selected the most salient K=100 interactions. We used transferability from Definition 1, S_and = |A^{and} ∩ B^{and}| / |A^{and}| and S_or = |A^{or} ∩ B^{or}| / |A^{or}|, to measure diversity caused by different parameter initializations. Table 1 shows that given different initial states, optimizing Eq. (4) usually extracted two dramatically different sets of AND-OR interactions with only 21% overlap. Figure 2 shows the top 5 AND-OR interaction primitives extracted from the BERT model on the same input sentence, illustrating that given different initial states, Eq. (4) would learn different AND-OR interactions.

Third, prioritizing sparsity cannot guarantee high generalization power across different models. A DNN may learn common knowledge shared by different DNNs and be over-fitted to out-of-distribution patterns. Different DNNs may only share partial interaction primitives. Shared common interactions are considered more faithful, so transferability is another way to guarantee generalization power. We aim to formulate and extract common interactions generalizable through different DNNs.

We conducted experiments to illustrate the difference between interactions extracted from two DNNs using Eq. (4). We used BERT_BASE v_base and BERT_LARGE v_large (Devlin et al., 2018) for sentiment classification. Given an input sentence x, we learned two sets of parameters {γ_T^{base}} and {γ_T^{large}} for the BERT-base and BERT-large models, respectively. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interactive concepts (Ω^{and, base}, Ω^{or, base}) and (Ω^{and, large}, Ω^{or, large}). We computed transferability according to Definition 1. Figure 3(a) shows the transferability of the extracted AND-OR interaction primitives was much lower than interactions proposed in this study.

3.3.2 Extracting generalizable interactions
Sparsity alone is not enough. We propose using generalization power as a straightforward purpose to boost faithfulness, while also guaranteeing sparsity. Given m DNNs v^(1), v^(2), ..., v^(m) trained for the same task, the objective of extracting generalizable interactions shared by the m DNNs is revised from Eq. (4):
min_{γ_T^(1),...,γ_T^(m)} ‖rowmax(I_and)‖_1 + ‖rowmax(I_or)‖_1, (5)
where I_and = [I_and^(1) I_and^(2) ... I_and^(m)] ∈ R^{2^n × m} and I_or = [I_or^(1) I_or^(2) ... I_or^(m)] ∈ R^{2^n × m}. I_and^(i) = [I_and^(i)(T1|x), ..., I_and^(i)(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n} and I_or^(i) represent all 2^n AND-OR interactions extracted from the i-th DNN, T_k ⊆ N. The matrix operator rowmax() computes the ℓ_∞ norm of each row, i.e., rowmax(I_and) = [‖I_and[1,:]‖_∞, ..., ‖I_and[2^n,:]‖_∞]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n}. For each subset T_k ⊆ N, rowmax() returns the most salient interaction strength over all m interactions from the m DNNs.

Unlike Eq. (4), the loss in Eq. (5) only penalizes the most salient interactions over all m DNNs w.r.t. each subset T_k. This ensures that if a DNN encodes a strong interaction w.r.t. T_k, we can extract the same interaction w.r.t. T_k from the other m-1 DNNs without penalty. The ℓ1 norm also makes the m DNNs share similar sets of sparse interactions. Considering sparsity, for most subsets T_k, the effect I_and/or^(i)(T_k |x) is supposed to be almost zero on all m DNNs.

As in Eq. (4), we decompose the output of the i-th DNN as v_and^(i)(x_T) = 0.5 v^(i)(x_T) + γ_T^(i) and v_or^(i)(x_T) = 0.5 v^(i)(x_T) - γ_T^(i) to compute I_and^(i) and I_or^(i).

Redundancy of interactions. Only penalizing the largest interaction among m DNNs in Eq. (5) faces a redundancy problem. For the i-th DNN, we compute 2^n AND and 2^n OR interactions w.r.t. different subsets T ⊆ N. Some, denoted Ω_max^(i), are selected by Eq. (5) as the most salient over m DNNs; others are Ω_others^(i) = {T ⊆ N} \ Ω_max^(i). Redundancy is caused by a short-cut solution: using unselected not-so-salient interactions in Ω_others^(i) to represent numerical effects of selected interactions Ω_max^(i), as discussed in Challenge 1. This short-cut may reduce the strength of penalized salient interactions but generate redundant interactions.

We revise Eq. (5) to add penalties on unselected interactions with coefficient α:
min_{γ_T^(1),...,γ_T^(m)} (‖rowmax(I_and)‖_1 + ‖rowmax(I_or)‖_1) + α (‖I_and‖_1 + ‖I_or‖_1), (6)
where α ∈ [0,1] is a positive scalar. The ℓ1 norm ‖·‖_1 represents the sum of absolute values of all elements in a vector or matrix. Generalization power is guaranteed by the rowmax() function, which assigns higher penalties to non-generalizable interactions.

Sharing decomposition between DNNs. Optimizing Eq. (6) is challenging. We introduce strategies. We assume sufficiently trained DNNs tend to have similar decompositions, i.e., ∀ T ⊆ N, γ_T^(1) ≈ γ_T^(2) ≈ ... ≈ γ_T^(m). We introduce two parameter types: γ_T^(i) = γ̄_T + γ̂_T^(i), where γ̄_T represents common decomposition shared by all DNNs, and γ̂_T^(i) represents decomposition specific to the i-th DNN. We constrain unshared decomposition significance with a bound |γ̂_T^(i)| < τ_γ^(i), where τ_γ^(i) = 0.5 · E_x[|v^(i)(x) - v^(i)(x_∅)|]. During training, if |γ̂_T^(i)| > τ_γ^(i), we set γ̂_T^(i) = τ_γ^(i) · sign(γ̂_T^(i)).

Modeling noises. We identified a potential limitation: sensitivity to noise. Assume the output of the i-th DNN has a small Gaussian noise ε_T ∼ N(0,σ^2). We represent noises by adding ε_T to the network output v'_and^(i)(x_T) = v_and^(i)(x_T) + ε_T^(i). Then, I'_and^(i)(T) = I_and^(i)(T) + Σ_{T' ⊆ T} (-1)^{|T|-|T'|} ε_{T'}^(i). We prove the variance of I'_and^(i)(T) caused by Gaussian noises is E_{ε_T∼N(0,σ^2)} [I'_and^(i)(T) - E_{∀ S, ε_S∼N(0,σ^2)} I'_and^(i)(S)]^2 = 2^{|T|} σ^2. Similarly, variance of I'_or^(i)(T) is also 2^{|T|} σ^2. Variance increases exponentially with order |T|.

We propose to directly learn an error term ε_T^(i) based on Eq. (6) to remove tiny noisy signals that cannot be modeled as AND-OR interactions, i.e., setting v^(i)(x_T) = v_and^(i)(x_T) + v_or^(i)(x_T) + ε_T^(i), to enhance robustness. The error term is constrained to a small range |ε_T^(i)| < τ_ε^(i), subject to τ_ε^(i) = 0.02 · |v^(i)(x) - v^(i)(x_∅)|. During training, if |ε_T^(i)| > τ_ε^(i), we set |ε_T^(i)| = τ_ε^(i) · sign(ε_T^(i)).

We conducted experiments to examine whether extracted AND-OR interactions could still accurately explain network output when removing the error term. We followed experimental settings in Section 4 to extract interactions on both BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE models. We computed matching error e(x_T) = |v(x_T) - v^{approx}(x_T)|, where v^{approx}(x_T) was the network output approximated by all interactions based on Theorem 3. Figure 4 shows matching errors of all masked samples w.r.t. all subsets T ⊆ N, sorted in descending order of network outputs. The real network output was well approximated by interactions.

4 Experiment
We conducted experiments to verify sparsity and generalization power of interaction primitives extracted by our method on three tasks.

Task 1: Sentiment classification with language models. We jointly extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE models (Devlin et al., 2018) using Eq. (6). We fine-tuned pre-trained models on the SST-2 dataset (Socher et al., 2013) for sentiment classification. We analyzed the log-odds output of the ground-truth label, i.e., v(x) = log( p(y=y^{truth}|x) / (1 - p(y=y^{truth}|x)) ) following Deng et al. (2021).

Task 2: Dialogue task with large language models. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from pre-trained LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) and OPT-1.3B models (Zhang et al., 2022). We explained DNN outputs on the SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). We took the first several words of each document as DNN input, letting the DNN predict the next word. For each input sentence x containing n words, we analyzed the log-odds output of the (n+1)-th word with highest probability, y^{max}, i.e., v(x) = log( p(y=y^{max}|x) / (1 - p(y=y^{max}|x)) ).

Task 3: Image classification task with vision models. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from ResNet-20 (He et al., 2016) and VGG-16 models (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) trained on MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998) to classify digit "3" from others. Considering 2^n computational complexity, we followed Li et al. (2023), who labeled a few important input patches as variables. For each input image x containing n patches, we analyzed the scalar output before the softmax layer corresponding to digit "3".

Sparsity of the extracted primitives. We aggregated all AND-OR interactions from various samples and plotted their strength in descending order in Figure 5. This compares interaction strength |I(S)|, S ⊆ N between our extracted interactions, traditional interactions (Li et al., 2023) (Traditional), and original Harsanyi interactions (Ren et al., 2023) (Harsanyi). The competing method (Traditional) extracts the sparsest interactions according to Eq. (4). Original Harsanyi interactions (Harsanyi) extract interactions according to Eq. (1). We found most interactions had negligible effect. Although our method reduced sparsity a bit, extracted interactions were still sparse enough to be considered primitive inference patterns. For each DNN, we set a threshold τ^(i) to collect salient interactions as primitives, i.e., τ^(i) = 0.05 · max_S |I(S|x)|.

Generalization power of the extracted interaction primitives. We took the most salient k interactions from each i-th DNN as the set of AND-OR interaction primitives, i.e., |Ω^{and,(i)}| = |Ω^{or,(i)}| = k, i ∈ {1,2}. We used metrics s_and and s_or from Definition 1 to measure generalization power of interactions extracted from two DNNs. Figure 6 shows generalization power when computing s_and and s_or based on different numbers k of most salient interactions. AND-OR interactions extracted by our method exhibited higher generalization power than interactions from the traditional method.

Low-order interaction primitives are more stable. We compared the ratio of shared interactions of different orders, order(S) = |S|. For interactions of each order o, we computed overall strength of all positive interactions and all negative interactions of the i-th DNN shared by other DNNs: Shared^{+,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω_shared^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} max(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) and Shared^{-,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω_shared^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} min(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)). Also, All^{+,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} max(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) and All^{-,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} min(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) denote overall strength of salient positive and negative interactions. Figure 7 reports (Shared^{+,(i)}, Shared^{-,(i)}) and (All^{+,(i)}, All^{-,(i)}) for different orders in the three tasks. Low-order interactions were more likely to be shared by different DNNs than high-order interactions. Figure 7 shows a higher ratio of interactions extracted by our method were shared than interactions from the traditional method. High similarity between ResNet-20 and VGG-16 shows that although DNNs had different architectures, there probably existed a set of ultimate interactions for a task, and different well-optimized DNNs were likely to converge to such interactions.

Visualization of shared interaction primitives across different DNNs. We visualize shared and distinctive interaction primitives in Figure 8. Generalizable interactions shared by different models can be regarded as more reliable concepts, consistently contributing salient effects to different DNN outputs. Non-generalizable interactions, sometimes over-fitted by a single model, may appear as out-of-distribution features. We consider generalizable interactions as relatively faithful concepts with significant impact on DNN inference. Figure 8 shows our method extracted more shared interactions than the traditional method, indicating our method could obtain a more stable explanation of DNN inference logic, as interactions shared by different DNNs were usually considered more faithful.

Title: Defining and extracting generalizable interaction primitives from DNNs

Abstract:
Summarizing the knowledge encoded by a deep neural network (DNN) into a few symbolic primitive patterns is a challenge. Ren et al. (2023) derived theorems to prove that a DNN's inference score can be explained as a small set of interactions between input variables. However, the generalization power of such interactions is limited, making it difficult to consider them as faithful primitive patterns. Given different DNNs trained for the same task, we develop a method to extract interactions that are shared by these DNNs. Experiments show that the extracted interactions better reflect common knowledge shared by different DNNs.

1 Introduction
Explaining the knowledge encoded by a deep neural network (DNN) is a challenge. Previous studies have visualized patterns (Bau et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018) and estimated saliency maps (Simonyan et al., 2013; Selvaraju et al., 2016). A question is whether the implicit knowledge can be formulated as explicit and symbolic primitive patterns, analogous to concepts in human cognition.

There is no widely accepted way to define a concept encoded by a DNN. However, Ren et al. (2023) and Li et al. (2023) have derived theorems to take interactions as symbolic primitives. An interaction captures a nonlinear relationship. For example, when a DNN processes the sentence "It is raining cats and dogs!", it may encode an interaction between the set of input variables S = {raining, cats, and, dogs}. When all words in S are present, an interactive effect I(S) emerges, pushing the inference towards "heavy rain." If any word in S is masked, the effect is removed.

Ren et al. (2023) proved two theorems. First, a well-trained DNN usually encodes a limited number of interactions. Second, the DNN's outputs on an exponential number of randomly masked samples can be accurately approximated using just a few interactions. These interactions are referred to as interaction primitives.

Despite these theorems, the interactions are not yet deemed faithful primitives. A core problem is that existing extraction methods cannot theoretically guarantee the generalization (transferability) of interactions, such as ensuring the extraction of common interactions shared by different models. Interactions not shared by different DNNs may be out-of-distribution signals.

This study revisits the generalization of interactions. We identify a mechanism that causes existing methods to extract different interactions from the same DNN under different initialization states, which hurts generalization.

To address this, we propose a method for extracting generalizable interactions. Given multiple DNNs trained for the same task and an input sample, if an interaction can be extracted from all these DNNs, it is considered generalizable. Our method is designed to extract interactions with maximum generalization power. Experiments on various datasets show that the proposed method significantly improved the generalization power of extracted interactions across different DNNs.

Figure 1 shows distinctive and shared interactions. When extracting AND-OR interactions from two DNNs, AND interactions S1={black,dog} and S2={black,dog,over}, and OR interactions S3={black, dog} and S4={black, over} are shared. Interactions such as the AND interaction S5={they, said} are distinctive to a single DNN.

2 Previous literature of using interactions to explain DNNs
Explaining DNN knowledge is a goal of explainable AI. Some studies used visualization techniques (Simonyan et al., 2013; Yosinski et al., 2015), extracted feature vectors (Simonyan et al., 2013), or learned feature vectors (Kim et al., 2018). Dravid et al. (2023) identified convolutional kernels in different DNNs expressing similar concepts.

Theoretically, whether DNN knowledge can be faithfully represented as symbolic primitive inference patterns remains a challenge. There is no universally accepted definition of knowledge. However, ignoring cognitive and neuroscience aspects, Ren et al. (2023) proposed quantifying interactions between input variables to explain DNN knowledge. Ren et al. (2023) derived theorems as mathematical evidence for considering such interactions as primitive inference patterns. They proved DNNs usually encode a small number of interactions under common conditions. These interactions can universally explain the DNN's output on any arbitrary masked input sample. Li et al. (2023) discovered the discriminative power of certain interactions.

Deng et al. (2023) found that different attribution scores estimated by different attribution methods could all be represented as a combination of different interactions. Zhang et al. (2022) used interactions to explain the mechanism of different methods for boosting adversarial transferability. Ren et al. (2022) used interactions to define the optimal baseline value for computing Shapley values. Deng et al. (2021) found that for most DNNs it was difficult to learn interactions with a median number of input variables. Ren et al. (2023) discovered that Bayesian neural networks were unlikely to model complex interactions with many input variables.

3 Generalizable interaction primitives across DNNs
3.1 Preliminaries: explaining the network output with interaction primitives
Although no theory guarantees how to define concepts fitting human cognition, Li et al. (2023) and Ren et al. (2023) provided mathematical support for using interactions between input variables as primitives. There are two types: AND interactions and OR interactions.

AND interactions. Given a function v: R^n → R and an input sample x = [x1, x2, ..., xn]^⊺ with n input variables indexed by N={1,2,...,n}, v(x) ∈ R denotes the output. Ren et al. (2022) used the Harsanyi dividend (Harsanyi, 1963) I_and(S|x) to quantify the numerical effect of the AND relationship between variables in S ⊆ N encoded by v.
I_and(S|x) := Σ_{T ⊆ S} (-1)^{|S|-|T|} v(x_T). (1)
where I_and(∅|x) = v(x_∅), and x_T denotes a sample where variables in N\T are masked. Each AND interaction I_and(S|x) reveals the AND relationship between all variables in S. For example, consider the slang term S = {x3, x4, x5, x6} in the sentence "x1=It, x2=is, x3=raining, x4=cats, x5=and, x6=dogs!". The co-occurrence of the four words forms the semantic concept of "heavy rain" and contributes effect I_and(S|x). Masking any word xi ∈ S invalidates the concept and eliminates the effect, i.e., I_and(S|x^{masked}) = 0.

OR interactions. Li et al. (2023) defined the OR interaction effect I_or(S|x).
I_or(S|x) := - Σ_{T ⊆ S} (-1)^{|S|-|T|} v(x_{N\T}). (2)
where I_or(∅|x) = v(x_∅). Each OR interaction I_or(S|x) describes the OR relationship between all variables in S. Consider an input sentence "x1=This, x2=movie, x3=is, x4=boring, x5=and, x6=disappointing" for sentiment classification. Set S={x4, x6}. The presence of any word in S contributes a negative sentiment effect I_or(S|x).

Sparsity of interactions. Theoretically, a function can encode at most 2^n different AND interactions. However, Ren et al. (2023) proved that under common conditions, most well-trained DNNs only encode a small set of AND interactions, denoted by Ω, i.e., only a few interactions S ∈ Ω have considerable effects I_and(S|x). All other interactions have almost zero effects, I_and(S|x) ≈ 0.

An OR interaction can be regarded as a specific AND interaction if the definitions of the masked and unmasked states are inverted. Thus, the proven sparsity of AND interactions also indicates that well-trained DNNs tend to encode a small number of OR interactions.

Definition of interaction primitives. Considering the proven sparsity, we define an interaction primitive as a salient interaction. Formally, given a threshold τ, the set of interaction primitives is Ω = {S ⊆ N: |I(S|x)| > τ}.

Theorem 1 (Universal matching theorem, proved by Ren et al. (2023)). As a corollary of the proven sparsity, the function's output on all 2^n masked samples {x_S | S ⊆ N} can be universally explained by the interaction primitives in Ω, s.t., |Ω| ≪ 2^n, i.e., ∀ S ⊆ N, v(x_S) = Σ_{T ⊆ S} I_and(T|x) ≈ Σ_{T ⊆ S: T ∈ Ω} I_and(T|x).

Theorem 1 shows that if we arbitrarily mask the input sample x, we get 2^n different masked samples. The output v(x_S) on all 2^n masked samples can be universally matched using only a few interaction primitives in Ω.

Theorem 2 (proved by Harsanyi (1963)). The Shapley value φ(i) of an input variable i can be explained as a uniform allocation of the AND interactions, i.e., φ(i) = Σ_{S ⊆ N: S ∋ i} (1/|S|) I_and(S|x).

3.2 Faithfulness problem with interaction-based explanations
Basic setting of using AND-OR interactions to explain a DNN. We employ both AND and OR interactions to explain the DNN's output, as DNN complexity makes it difficult to rely solely on one type. We decompose the output v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x), using AND interactions to explain v_and(x) and OR interactions to explain v_or(x). A challenge is learning an appropriate decomposition that reveals intrinsic primitive interactions.

Regardless of how we randomly decompose v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x), Theorem 3 demonstrates we can still use interactions to fit the DNN's outputs on 2^n randomly masked samples {x_T | T ⊆ N}. Furthermore, according to sparsity, Proposition 1 states the 2^n network outputs can usually be approximated by a small number of AND interaction primitives in Ω^{and} and OR interaction primitives in Ω^{or}, s.t., |Ω^{and}|, |Ω^{or}| ≪ 2^n.

Theorem 3 (Universal matching theorem). Given a DNN v and an input sample x. For each randomly masked sample x_T, T ⊆ N,
v(x_T) = v_and(x_T) + v_or(x_T) = Σ_{S ⊆ T} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∈ {S: S ∩ T ≠ ∅} ∪ {∅}} I_or(S|x_T). (3)

Proposition 1. The output of a well-trained DNN on all 2^n masked samples {x_T | T ⊆ N} can be universally approximated by the interaction primitives in Ω^{and} and Ω^{or}, s.t., |Ω^{and}|, |Ω^{or}| ≪ 2^n, i.e., ∀ T ⊆ N,
v(x_T) = Σ_{S ⊆ T} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∈ {S: S ∩ T ≠ ∅} ∪ {∅}} I_or(S|x_T) ≈ v(x_∅) + Σ_{∅ ≠ S ⊆ T: S ∈ Ω^{and}} I_and(S|x_T) + Σ_{S ∩ T ≠ ∅: S ∈ Ω^{or}} I_or(S|x_T), where v(x_∅) = v_and(x_∅) + v_or(x_∅).

Problems with the faithfulness of interactions. Although Theorem 3's universal matching capacity is an advantage, it does not guarantee faithfulness. There is no standard way to faithfully decompose v_and(x) and v_or(x) that reveal intrinsic primitive interactions, considering two challenges.

Challenge 1: Ambiguous decomposition of v_and(x) and v_or(x) usually brings considerable uncertainty in interaction extraction. Consider a toy Boolean function f(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + x4 ∨ x5, where x = [x1,x2,x3,x4,x5]^⊺ and xi ∈ {0,1}. There are two decomposition ways. First, decompose v_and(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 and v_or(x) = x4 ∨ x5, explaining f(x) with an OR interaction I_or(S={4,5}) and three AND interactions I_and(S={1,2,3}), I_and(S={2,3}), I_and(S={3,4}). Alternatively, use exclusively AND interactions: rewrite v_and(x) = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + x4 ∨ x5 = x1 ∧ x2 ∧ x3 + x2 ∧ x3 + x3 ∧ x4 + (x4 + x5 - x4 ∧ x5) and v_or(x)=0, w.r.t xi ∈ {0,1}. The v_and term can be explained by six AND interaction primitives. This illustrates diverse strategies for extracting interactions generated by different decompositions.

The f(x) is a simple function. In real applications, DNNs encode intricate AND-OR relationships, making it challenging to formulate an explicit expression or a definitive ground-truth decomposition. Consequently, diversity is ubiquitous.

Challenge 2: How to ensure interaction primitives are generalizable. Generalizable primitives are usually transferable over different models trained for the same task, instead of being over-fitted by a single model. If an interaction primitive can be consistently extracted from different DNNs, it can be considered a faithful concept. Otherwise, non-generalizable interactions appear as mathematical manipulations, not faithful concepts, even if they satisfy sparsity and universal matching.

Definition 1 (Transferability of interaction primitives). Given m different DNNs trained for the same task, v^(1), v^(2), ..., v^(m), we use AND-OR interactions to explain the output score v^(i)(x) of each DNN v^(i) on input sample x. Let Ω^{and,(i)} = {S ⊆ N: |I_and^(i)(S|x)| > τ^(i)} and Ω^{or,(i)} = {S ⊆ N: |I_or^(i)(S|x)| > τ^(i)} denote sets of sparse AND and OR interaction primitives, respectively. The sets of generalizable AND and OR interaction primitives for the i-th DNN are defined as Ω_shared^{and} = ∩_{i=1}^m Ω^{and,(i)} and Ω_shared^{or} = ∩_{i=1}^m Ω^{or,(i)}. The generalization power of AND and OR interactions of the i-th DNN is measured by s_and^(i) = |Ω_shared^{and}| / |Ω^{and,(i)}| and s_or^(i) = |Ω_shared^{or}| / |Ω^{or,(i)}|.

Definition 1 introduces generalization power. A larger value signifies higher transferability and more generalizable interactive primitives.

3.3 Extracting generalizable interaction primitives
Neither challenge has been adequately tackled. Interactions are determined by the decomposition v(x) = v_and(x) + v_or(x). Rewriting the decomposition as v_and(x_T) = 0.5 v(x_T) + γ_T and v_or(x_T) = 0.5 v(x_T) - γ_T, learning the best decomposition is equivalent to learning a set of {γ_T}. The parameter γ_T ∈ R for a subset T ⊆ N determines a specific decomposition. Our goal is to learn appropriate parameters {γ_T} that reduce uncertainty and boost generalization power.

To alleviate uncertainty, the most intuitive approach is to learn the sparsest interactions, considering Occam's Razor, as the sparsest explanation is usually considered most faithful.
min_{γ_T} ‖I_and‖_1 + ‖I_or‖_1, (4)
where I_and = [I_and(T1|x), ..., I_and(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺, I_or = [I_or(T1|x), ..., I_or(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n}, T_k ⊆ N.

The ℓ1 norm loss promotes sparsity of both AND and OR interactions.

3.3.1 Only achieving sparsity is not enough
Sparsity w.r.t. each single input sample from Eq. (4) does not fully solve the two challenges. First, Ren et al. (2023) found extraction of high-order interactions is usually sensitive to small noises in input variables, where order(S) = |S|. When different noises are added, the algorithm may extract fully different high-order interactions. This hurts generalization power over different samples containing similar sets of input variables.

Second, optimizing the loss in Eq. (4) may lead to diverse solutions. Given different initial states, the loss may learn two different sets of parameters {γ_T} as two local minima with similar loss values, generating two different sets of interactions. We conducted an experiment. Given a pre-trained BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018) and an input sentence x on the SST-2 dataset for sentiment classification, we learned parameters {γ_T} to extract sparse interaction primitives. We repeatedly extracted two sets of AND-OR interactions by applying two different initializations, denoted by (A^{and}, A^{or}) and (B^{and}, B^{or}). A^{and} = {S ⊆ N: |I_and(S|x)| > τ_{A^{and}}} denotes the set of AND interaction primitives extracted by a certain initialization, where τ_{A^{and}} was determined to ensure each set selected the most salient K=100 interactions. We used transferability from Definition 1, S_and = |A^{and} ∩ B^{and}| / |A^{and}| and S_or = |A^{or} ∩ B^{or}| / |A^{or}|, to measure diversity caused by different parameter initializations. Table 1 shows that given different initial states, optimizing Eq. (4) usually extracted two dramatically different sets of AND-OR interactions with only 21% overlap. Figure 2 shows the top 5 AND-OR interaction primitives extracted from the BERT model on the same input sentence, illustrating that given different initial states, Eq. (4) would learn different AND-OR interactions.

Third, prioritizing sparsity cannot guarantee high generalization power across different models. A DNN may learn common knowledge shared by different DNNs and be over-fitted to out-of-distribution patterns. Different DNNs may only share partial interaction primitives. Shared common interactions are considered more faithful, so transferability is another way to guarantee generalization power. We aim to formulate and extract common interactions generalizable through different DNNs.

We conducted experiments to illustrate the difference between interactions extracted from two DNNs using Eq. (4). We used BERT_BASE v_base and BERT_LARGE v_large (Devlin et al., 2018) for sentiment classification. Given an input sentence x, we learned two sets of parameters {γ_T^{base}} and {γ_T^{large}} for the BERT-base and BERT-large models, respectively. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interactive concepts (Ω^{and, base}, Ω^{or, base}) and (Ω^{and, large}, Ω^{or, large}). We computed transferability according to Definition 1. Figure 3(a) shows the transferability of the extracted AND-OR interaction primitives was much lower than interactions proposed in this study.

3.3.2 Extracting generalizable interactions
Sparsity alone is not enough. We propose using generalization power as a straightforward purpose to boost faithfulness, while also guaranteeing sparsity. Given m DNNs v^(1), v^(2), ..., v^(m) trained for the same task, the objective of extracting generalizable interactions shared by the m DNNs is revised from Eq. (4):
min_{γ_T^(1),...,γ_T^(m)} ‖rowmax(I_and)‖_1 + ‖rowmax(I_or)‖_1, (5)
where I_and = [I_and^(1) I_and^(2) ... I_and^(m)] ∈ R^{2^n × m} and I_or = [I_or^(1) I_or^(2) ... I_or^(m)] ∈ R^{2^n × m}. I_and^(i) = [I_and^(i)(T1|x), ..., I_and^(i)(T_{2^n}|x)]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n} and I_or^(i) represent all 2^n AND-OR interactions extracted from the i-th DNN, T_k ⊆ N. The matrix operator rowmax() computes the ℓ_∞ norm of each row, i.e., rowmax(I_and) = [‖I_and[1,:]‖_∞, ..., ‖I_and[2^n,:]‖_∞]^⊺ ∈ R^{2^n}. For each subset T_k ⊆ N, rowmax() returns the most salient interaction strength over all m interactions from the m DNNs.

Unlike Eq. (4), the loss in Eq. (5) only penalizes the most salient interactions over all m DNNs w.r.t. each subset T_k. This ensures that if a DNN encodes a strong interaction w.r.t. T_k, we can extract the same interaction w.r.t. T_k from the other m-1 DNNs without penalty. The ℓ1 norm also makes the m DNNs share similar sets of sparse interactions. Considering sparsity, for most subsets T_k, the effect I_and/or^(i)(T_k |x) is supposed to be almost zero on all m DNNs.

As in Eq. (4), we decompose the output of the i-th DNN as v_and^(i)(x_T) = 0.5 v^(i)(x_T) + γ_T^(i) and v_or^(i)(x_T) = 0.5 v^(i)(x_T) - γ_T^(i) to compute I_and^(i) and I_or^(i).

Redundancy of interactions. Only penalizing the largest interaction among m DNNs in Eq. (5) faces a redundancy problem. For the i-th DNN, we compute 2^n AND and 2^n OR interactions w.r.t. different subsets T ⊆ N. Some, denoted Ω_max^(i), are selected by Eq. (5) as the most salient over m DNNs; others are Ω_others^(i) = {T ⊆ N} \ Ω_max^(i). Redundancy is caused by a short-cut solution: using unselected not-so-salient interactions in Ω_others^(i) to represent numerical effects of selected interactions Ω_max^(i), as discussed in Challenge 1. This short-cut may reduce the strength of penalized salient interactions but generate redundant interactions.

We revise Eq. (5) to add penalties on unselected interactions with coefficient α:
min_{γ_T^(1),...,γ_T^(m)} (‖rowmax(I_and)‖_1 + ‖rowmax(I_or)‖_1) + α (‖I_and‖_1 + ‖I_or‖_1), (6)
where α ∈ [0,1] is a positive scalar. The ℓ1 norm ‖·‖_1 represents the sum of absolute values of all elements in a vector or matrix. Generalization power is guaranteed by the rowmax() function, which assigns higher penalties to non-generalizable interactions.

Sharing decomposition between DNNs. Optimizing Eq. (6) is challenging. We introduce strategies. We assume sufficiently trained DNNs tend to have similar decompositions, i.e., ∀ T ⊆ N, γ_T^(1) ≈ γ_T^(2) ≈ ... ≈ γ_T^(m). We introduce two parameter types: γ_T^(i) = γ̄_T + γ̂_T^(i), where γ̄_T represents common decomposition shared by all DNNs, and γ̂_T^(i) represents decomposition specific to the i-th DNN. We constrain unshared decomposition significance with a bound |γ̂_T^(i)| < τ_γ^(i), where τ_γ^(i) = 0.5 · E_x[|v^(i)(x) - v^(i)(x_∅)|]. During training, if |γ̂_T^(i)| > τ_γ^(i), we set γ̂_T^(i) = τ_γ^(i) · sign(γ̂_T^(i)).

Modeling noises. We identified a potential limitation: sensitivity to noise. Assume the output of the i-th DNN has a small Gaussian noise ε_T ∼ N(0,σ^2). We represent noises by adding ε_T to the network output v'_and^(i)(x_T) = v_and^(i)(x_T) + ε_T^(i). Then, I'_and^(i)(T) = I_and^(i)(T) + Σ_{T' ⊆ T} (-1)^{|T|-|T'|} ε_{T'}^(i). We prove the variance of I'_and^(i)(T) caused by Gaussian noises is E_{ε_T∼N(0,σ^2)} [I'_and^(i)(T) - E_{∀ S, ε_S∼N(0,σ^2)} I'_and^(i)(S)]^2 = 2^{|T|} σ^2. Similarly, variance of I'_or^(i)(T) is also 2^{|T|} σ^2. Variance increases exponentially with order |T|.

We propose to directly learn an error term ε_T^(i) based on Eq. (6) to remove tiny noisy signals that cannot be modeled as AND-OR interactions, i.e., setting v^(i)(x_T) = v_and^(i)(x_T) + v_or^(i)(x_T) + ε_T^(i), to enhance robustness. The error term is constrained to a small range |ε_T^(i)| < τ_ε^(i), subject to τ_ε^(i) = 0.02 · |v^(i)(x) - v^(i)(x_∅)|. During training, if |ε_T^(i)| > τ_ε^(i), we set |ε_T^(i)| = τ_ε^(i) · sign(ε_T^(i)).

We conducted experiments to examine whether extracted AND-OR interactions could still accurately explain network output when removing the error term. We followed experimental settings in Section 4 to extract interactions on both BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE models. We computed matching error e(x_T) = |v(x_T) - v^{approx}(x_T)|, where v^{approx}(x_T) was the network output approximated by all interactions based on Theorem 3. Figure 4 shows matching errors of all masked samples w.r.t. all subsets T ⊆ N, sorted in descending order of network outputs. The real network output was well approximated by interactions.

4 Experiment
We conducted experiments to verify sparsity and generalization power of interaction primitives extracted by our method on three tasks.

Task 1: Sentiment classification with language models. We jointly extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE models (Devlin et al., 2018) using Eq. (6). We fine-tuned pre-trained models on the SST-2 dataset (Socher et al., 2013) for sentiment classification. We analyzed the log-odds output of the ground-truth label, i.e., v(x) = log( p(y=y^{truth}|x) / (1 - p(y=y^{truth}|x)) ) following Deng et al. (2021).

Task 2: Dialogue task with large language models. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from pre-trained LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) and OPT-1.3B models (Zhang et al., 2022). We explained DNN outputs on the SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). We took the first several words of each document as DNN input, letting the DNN predict the next word. For each input sentence x containing n words, we analyzed the log-odds output of the (n+1)-th word with highest probability, y^{max}, i.e., v(x) = log( p(y=y^{max}|x) / (1 - p(y=y^{max}|x)) ).

Task 3: Image classification task with vision models. We extracted two sets of AND-OR interaction primitives from ResNet-20 (He et al., 2016) and VGG-16 models (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) trained on MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998) to classify digit "3" from others. Considering 2^n computational complexity, we followed Li et al. (2023), who labeled a few important input patches as variables. For each input image x containing n patches, we analyzed the scalar output before the softmax layer corresponding to digit "3".

Sparsity of the extracted primitives. We aggregated all AND-OR interactions from various samples and plotted their strength in descending order in Figure 5. This compares interaction strength |I(S)|, S ⊆ N between our extracted interactions, traditional interactions (Li et al., 2023) (Traditional), and original Harsanyi interactions (Ren et al., 2023) (Harsanyi). The competing method (Traditional) extracts the sparsest interactions according to Eq. (4). Original Harsanyi interactions (Harsanyi) extract interactions according to Eq. (1). We found most interactions had negligible effect. Although our method reduced sparsity a bit, extracted interactions were still sparse enough to be considered primitive inference patterns. For each DNN, we set a threshold τ^(i) to collect salient interactions as primitives, i.e., τ^(i) = 0.05 · max_S |I(S|x)|.

Generalization power of the extracted interaction primitives. We took the most salient k interactions from each i-th DNN as the set of AND-OR interaction primitives, i.e., |Ω^{and,(i)}| = |Ω^{or,(i)}| = k, i ∈ {1,2}. We used metrics s_and and s_or from Definition 1 to measure generalization power of interactions extracted from two DNNs. Figure 6 shows generalization power when computing s_and and s_or based on different numbers k of most salient interactions. AND-OR interactions extracted by our method exhibited higher generalization power than interactions from the traditional method.

Low-order interaction primitives are more stable. We compared the ratio of shared interactions of different orders, order(S) = |S|. For interactions of each order o, we computed overall strength of all positive interactions and all negative interactions of the i-th DNN shared by other DNNs: Shared^{+,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω_shared^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} max(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) and Shared^{-,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω_shared^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} min(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)). Also, All^{+,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} max(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) and All^{-,(i)}(o) = Σ_{op ∈ {and,or}} Σ_{S ∈ Ω^{op,(i)}, |S|=o} min(0, I_op^(i)(S|x)) denote overall strength of salient positive and negative interactions. Figure 7 reports (Shared^{+,(i)}, Shared^{-,(i)}) and (All^{+,(i)}, All^{-,(i)}) for different orders in the three tasks. Low-order interactions were more likely to be shared by different DNNs than high-order interactions. Figure 7 shows a higher ratio of interactions extracted by our method were shared than interactions from the traditional method. High similarity between ResNet-20 and VGG-16 shows that although DNNs had different architectures, there probably existed a set of ultimate interactions for a task, and different well-optimized DNNs were likely to converge to such interactions.

Visualization of shared interaction primitives across different DNNs. We visualize shared and distinctive interaction primitives in Figure 8. Generalizable interactions shared by different models can be regarded as more reliable concepts, consistently contributing salient effects to different DNN outputs. Non-generalizable interactions, sometimes over-fitted by a single model, may appear as out-of-distribution features. We consider generalizable interactions as relatively faithful concepts with significant impact on DNN inference. Figure 8 shows our method extracted more shared interactions than the traditional method, indicating our method could obtain a more stable explanation of DNN inference logic, as interactions shared by different DNNs were usually considered more faithful.

title: DIFUSCO-LNS: Diffusion-Guided Large Neighbourhood Search for Integer Linear Programming
full_text:
\title{DIFUSCO-LNS: Diffusion-Guided Large Neighbourhood Search for Integer Linear Programming}

\begin{abstract}
Integer Linear Programming (ILP) is a powerful and flexible framework for modeling and solving a variety of combinatorial optimization problems. This paper introduces a novel ILP solver, namely DIFUSCO-LNS, which combines the strengths of carefully engineered traditional solvers in symbolic reasoning and the generative power of a neural diffusion model in graph-based learning for the Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) approach. Our diffusion model treats the destroy policy in LNS as a generative problem in the discrete $\{0, 1\}$-vector space and is trained to imitate the high-quality Local Branching (LB) destroy heuristic through iterative denoising. Specifically, this addresses the unimodal limitation of other neural LNS solvers with its capability to capture the multimodal nature of optimal policies during variable selection.  Our evaluations span four representative MIP problems: MIS, CA, SC, and MVC. Experimental results reveal that DIFUSCO-LNS substantially surpasses prior neural LNS  solvers.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Combinatorial Optimization (CO) problems (including NP-complete or NP-hard ones) present a set of fundamental challenges in computer science for decades (Papadimitriou & Steiglitz, 1998). Many of those problems can be formulated in a generic Integer Linear Programming (ILP) framework, including supply chain management, logistics optimization (Chopra & Meindl, 2001), workforce scheduling (Ernst et al., 2004), financial portfolios (Rubinstein, 2002; Lobo et al., 2007), compiler optimization (Trofin et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2022), bioinformatic problems (Gusfield, 1997), and more. Classic ILP solvers typically conduct a tree-style search with the Branch-and-Bound (BnB) algorithm (Land & Doig, 2010), which finds the exact solution by gradually reducing and finally closing the gap between the primal (upper) and dual (lower) bounds of the searched solutions. Many state-of-the-art open-source and commercial ILP solvers are of this kind, including SCIP (Achterberg, 2009), CPLEX (Cplex, 2009), and Gurobi (Gurobi Optimization, 2021). However, when the problems are very large, completely closing the primal-dual gap can be intractable. Hence, solvers for large ILP problems have been shifted efforts towards primal heuristics (Berthold, 2006b), which are designed for finding the best possible solutions within a limited time window. That is, those are primal ILP solvers, which do not guarantee to find the optimal solutions. Our work in this paper belongs to the category of primal solvers.  

Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) is a heuristic-driven strategy that can find high-quality solutions much faster than pure BnB for large ILP problems (Ahuja et al., 2002). The process starts from an initial feasible solution, which is typically obtained using BnB with a limited time budget. Then the system iteratively revises the current solution by selecting a subset of the variables as the unassigned (or destroyed) ones in the next cycle of optimization while keeping the remaining variables unchanged. Heuristics used in such a neighborhood selection are called the destroy heuristics. How to obtain good heuristics for effective neighborhood selection has been a central focus of LNS-based ILP solvers.  

Hand-crafted destroy heuristics include randomized (Ahuja et al., 2002), Local Branching (LB) (Fischetti & Lodi, 2003b), and LB-RELAX (Huang et al., 2023b). The common limitation of those methods is their heavy dependencies on the availability of domain-expert knowledge, which is costly to obtain, difficult to generalize across problems/domains, and unavoidably subjective sometimes. A better alternative, obviously, is to have a data-driven approach that can automatically learn the effective destroy heuristics from a training set of massive problem instances accompanied with highquality (but not necessarily optimal) solutions. The recent development of neural network-based LNS methods has shown significant potential because they can learn from vast amounts of data. This ability allows them to identify complex patterns and relationships in combinatorial optimization problems, leading to the generation of more nuanced and effective destroy heuristics, surpassing the capabilities of traditional static methods.  

![](images/ed294ff399adfcd727d9ac39e92c1afacfc362672c6d09554683233cba696f5f.jpg)  
Figure 1: Overview of DIFUSCO-LNS’s model framework.  

Representative neural LNS methods include those based on Imitation Learning (IL-LNS) (Song et al., 2020b; Sonnerat et al., 2021), Reinforcement Learning (RL-LNS) (Nair et al., 2020a; Wu et al., 2021), and Contrastive Learning (CL-LNS) (Huang et al., 2023c). These methods essentially try to discover a good destroy policy for each instance ILP problem by predicting a discrete vector $\textbf{d}\in$ $\{0,1\}^{\parallel\nu\parallel}$ with a conditional independence assumption among the variables. Here, $\mathcal{V}$ is the full set of candidate variables, $\textstyle\sum d_{i}=k$ is the pre-defined size of the selected (or destroyed) neighborhood, and $d_{i}~\in~\{0,1\}$ in dicates whether or not the $i^{t h}$ variable is included in the neighborhood. The goal of prediction is to guide the search for optimal solutions being focused on the most promising sub-spaces of the feasible candidates. A fundamental limitation of the aforementioned neural LNS methods is in their implicit unimodal assumption in formulating the destroy policies. That is, it ignores the fact that multiple (near)-optimal destroy policies can co-exist with different subsets of destroyed variables (Li et al., 2018). In other words, those methods cannot properly handle the multimodal nature of the destroy heuristics in LNS. While this limitation is partially alleviated by reinforcement learning (Wu et al., 2021) and contrastive learning (Huang et al., 2023c), the current solutions still suffer severely from poor utilization of powerful neural networks due to the ineffective unimodal training.  

In this paper, we address the above challenge/limitation from a new angle. We introduce DIFUSCOLNS, as a pioneering effort to adapt the highly successful neural diffusion models from computer vision (Ho et al., 2020b; Song et al., 2020c; Song & Ermon, 2020) to the generation of effective destroy heuristics for LNS. Notably, neural diffusion models have also demonstrated proficiency in solving some other CO problems (Graikos et al., 2022; Sun & Yang, 2023; Huang et al., 2023a), but for using a probabilistic diffusion approach to solve generic Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problems, DIFUSCO-LNS is the first attempt, to our knowledge. It overcomes the limitation of previous neural LNS solvers with the power of handling the multimodal nature of high-quality destroy policies, in particular. Our diffusion model treats the destroy policy in LNS as a generative problem in the discrete $\{0,1\}$ -vector space and is trained to imitate the high-quality Local Branching (LB) destroy heuristic through iterative denoising.  

Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that DIFUSCO-LNS achieves a better or comparable performance against both neural baselines and traditional heuristics over four different CO benchmarks on multiple metrics. It also shows even stronger transfer performance (trained on small instances and tested on larger ones) than the state-of-the-art neural LNS method.  



\section{2 METHOD  }


2.1 PRELIMINARIES  

Let us start with a brief outline of the related background of ILP and the techniques of LNS.  

Integer Linear Program ILP is a type of discrete optimization problem whose variables are subject to integrality constraints. The general form of an ILP problem could be expressed as  

$$
\begin{array}{c}{\operatorname*{min}\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}}\\ {\mathrm{s.t.~}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b},\;\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},}\end{array}
$$  

where $\mathbf{x}\,=\,(\mathbf{x}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{n})^{\top}$ is the vector of decision variables, $\mathbf{c}\,\in\,\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the vector of objective coefficients, $\mathbf{A}\,\in\,\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $\textbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ represent the constraint coefficients . The size of an ILP problem is typically measured by its number of variables $(n)$ and constraints $(m)$ .  

Neural Large Neighborhood Search LNS is a process for iteratively improving the solution found by the system currently. It starts with an initial feasible solution $\dot{\mathbf{x}}^{0}$ , which is typically obtained by running a traditional symbolic solver with a limited time budget. In its ith iteration for $i=0,1,2,\dots,I$ , the system heuristically chooses a subset of the decision variables in the current solution $\mathbf{x}^{i}$ as the destroyed (or unassigned) subset, and re-optimizes the next solution $\mathbf{x}^{i+1}$ over the destroyed variables while keeping the values of other variables unchanged. The re-optimization step is typically carried out by an off-the-shelf solver, and most research efforts in LNS have been focused on how to obtain good heuristics for the destroying part. Most neural LNS methods, including our proposed new approach in this paper, are focused on automated learning of such heuristics in a data-driven manner. As for the re-optimization part, we use the open-source SCIP solver (Achterberg, 2009) as the default symbolic solver. We denote the intermediate iteration state of LNS as $\mathbf{s}^{i}=\left(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{x}^{i}\right)$ .  

Local Branching Local branching (LB) is proposed by Fischetti & Lodi (2003a) as a destroy policy heuristic (not a neural approach) for Large Neighborhood Search. It formulates the optimal neighborhood selection for LNS as another ILP problem, and searches for the next optimal solution $\mathbf{x}^{i+1}$ inside a Hamming ball with the radius of $k^{i}$ from the current incumbent solution $\mathbf{x}^{i}$ . If all the decision variables are binary, solving LB is equivalent to solving the original ILP with additional constraint $\begin{array}{r}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1\!-\!\mathbf{x}_{j}^{i})\mathbf{x}_{j}+\!\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{i}(1\!-\!\mathbf{x}_{j})\overset{\cdot}{\leq}k^{i}}\end{array}$ . That is, LB itself is computationally expensive and could be practically intractable for finding optimal solutions in large-scale ILP. Therefore, it is essential to train a neural network to approximate the decisions made by LB with a much lower computational cost , thereby achieving real-world acceleration.  



\section{2.2 DIFUSCO-LNS  }


The goal of the neural destroy heuristic is to predict the destroy policy such that the new objective after the neighborhood search is maximized. In this paper, we adopt the supervised learning (i.e., imitation learning) scheme of neural LNS solvers. Following previous work (Sonnerat et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023c), we use Local Branching (LB) as the expert heuristic to collect optimal (or high-quality) destroy policies.  

We describe our approach in four parts: 1) probabilistic formulation of the LNS destroy policies, 2) diffusion-based modeling of destroy policies, 3) architecture of the policy neural network, and 4) automated generation of training data with time-constrained Local Branching.  

Problem Definition We formulate the destroy policy of choosing the subset $\mathcal{V}^{i}=\{\mathbf{x}_{j_{1}}^{i},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{j_{k}}^{i}\}$ as a discrete vector $\mathbf{d}^{i}\,\in\,\{0,1\}^{\|\mathcal{V}\|}$ , where $\nu$ is the full set of variables, $\sum d_{j}^{i}\,=\,k^{i}$ is the neighborhood size, and $d_{i}^{j}$ denotes the inclusion of the $j^{t h}$ variable in the destroyed neighborhood at the $i^{t h}$ LNS iteration. This allows us to formulate the destroy heuristic as a generative modeling problem, where we aim to maximize the likelihood of high-quality solutions. Let $\mathcal{D}_{\mathsf{h q}}^{i}$ be the set of high-quality solutions in the binary vector form, our loss function $L$ is defined as:  

$$
L(\mathbf{s}^{i},\pmb{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{d}_{\mathsf{h q}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathsf{h q}}^{i}(\mathbf{s}^{i})}\left[-\log p_{\pmb{\theta}}(\mathbf{d}_{\mathsf{h q}}|\mathbf{s}^{i})\right]
$$  

For brevity, we omit the conditional notations of $\mathbf{s}^{i}$ and denote ${\bf d}_{\mathsf{h q}}$ as ${\bf d}_{0}$ as a convention for all formulas in the context of diffusion models.  

Generative Policy Modeling Following previous work on learning diffusion models that directly generate solutions for combinatorial optimization problems (Sun & Yang, 2023), we formulate the generation of the high-quality solution $\mathbf{d}_{0}$ as a discrete diffusion process (Austin et al., 2021; Hoogeboom et al., 2021).  

The diffusion models first define a forward process $q$ that gradually corrupts1 the data into noised latent variables $\mathbf{d}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{d}_{T}$ : $\begin{array}{r}{q(\mathbf{d}_{1:T}|\mathbf{d}_{0})\;=\;\overline{{\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(\mathbf{d}_{t}|\mathbf{d}_{t-1}}})}\end{array}$ . In discrete diffusion models with multinomial noises (Austin et al., 2021; Hoogeboom et al., 2021), the forward process is defined as: $q(\mathbf{d}_{t}\vert\mathbf{d}_{t-1})=\mathrm{Cat}\left(\mathbf{d}_{t};\mathbf{p}=\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t-1}\mathbf{Q}_{t}\right)$ , where $\mathbf{Q}_{t}=\left[\!\!\left(1-\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}\right)\!\!\!\begin{array}{c c}{\!\!\!\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}\!}&{\!\!\!\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}}\\ {\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}\!}&{\!\!\left(1-\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}\right)\!\!\!\right]}$ is the transition probability matrix; $\tilde{\mathbf{d}}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times2}$ is converted from the original vector $\mathbf{d}\in\{0,1\}^{N}$ with a onehot vector per row; and $\mathbf{\tilde{dQ}}$ computes a row-wise vector-matrix product. Here, $\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t}$ denotes the corruption ratio. Also, we want $\begin{array}{r}{\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\beta_{\mathsf{d m}}^{t})\approx0}\end{array}$ such that $\mathbf{d}_{T}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\cdot)$ .  

Next, a reverse (denoising) process is learned to gradually denoise the latent variables toward the data distribution, such that the distribution of ${\bf d}_{0}$ is formed as a joint distribution with latent variables:  

$$
p_{\theta}(\mathbf{d}_{0:T})=p_{T}(\mathbf{d}_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{t})
$$  

where $p_{\theta}$ denotes a single reverse step parameterized by a neural network. According to Austin et al. (2021), the denoising neural network is trained to predict the clean data $p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}|\mathbf{d}_{t})$ , and the reverse process is obtained by as an expectation over the posterior $q(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{t},\mathbf{d}_{0})$ :  

$$
p_{\theta}(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{t})=\sum_{\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}}q(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0})p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}|\mathbf{d}_{t})
$$  

By calculating the $t$ -step marginal as: $q(\mathbf{d}_{t}|\mathbf{d}_{0})\;\;=\;\;\mathrm{Cat}\left(\mathbf{d}_{t};\mathbf{p}=\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}\overline{{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t}\right)$ , where $\begin{array}{r l}{\overline{{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t}}&{{}=}\end{array}$ $\mathbf{Q}_{1}\mathbf{Q}_{2}\ldots\mathbf{Q}_{t}$ , the posterior we need at time $t-1$ can be obtained by Bayes’ theorem:  

$$
q(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{t},\mathbf{d}_{0})=\frac{q(\mathbf{d}_{t}|\mathbf{d}_{t-1},\mathbf{d}_{0})q(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}|\mathbf{d}_{0})}{q(\mathbf{d}_{t}|\mathbf{d}_{0})}=\mathrm{Cat}\left(\mathbf{d}_{t-1};\mathbf{p}=\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t}\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\top}\odot\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}\overline{{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t-1}}{\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}\overline{{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t}\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t}^{\top}}\right),
$$  

where $\odot$ denotes the element-wise multiplication, and ${\bf d}_{0}$ will be substituted by the predicted $\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{0}$ in the reverse process.  

Policy Network Recall that the general form of an ILP problem is represented by  

$$
\operatorname*{min}\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}~~\mathrm{s.t.}~\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b},~\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}.
$$  

In DIFUSCO-LNS, the learned denoising neural network needs to encode the information of the last LNS iteration state $\mathbf{s}^{i}=\left(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{x}^{i}\right)$ and the diffusion hidden states $\mathbf{d}_{t}^{i}$ , and predict the high-quality destroy policy ${\bf d}_{0}$ as the output.  

Expanding on recent advancements in learning for ILPs (Gasse et al., 2019; Sonnerat et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023c), we adopt a bipartite graph representation to encode LNS state $\mathbf{s}^{t}$ . This graph, composed of $n+m$ nodes, delineates the $n$ variables and $m$ constraints, with edges indicating non-zero coefficients in constraints. Node and edge features are inspired by Gasse et al. (2019). Moreover, a fixed-size window (size 3 in our experiments) of recent incumbent values enriches variable node features. Building upon previous work (Sonnerat et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023c), we incorporate additional features from Khalil et al. (2017a) calculated at the BnB root node. The binary diffusion hidden state $\mathbf{d}_{t}^{i}$ is integrated as variable features with a positional encoding scheme (Vaswani et al., 2017; Sun & Yang, 2023).  

![](images/e64205e1b0e19c4edbba434736f73cdec5d8c72f31b8f8a066e246c56faf76f0.jpg)  
Figure 2: Architecture of the policy network  

Following previous work (Huang et al., 2023c), the neural architecture of $p_{\theta}$ is a graph attention network (GAT; Brody et al. (2021)).  

High-Quality Destroy Policy Collection When collecting the training data of high-quality destroy policies, given an intermediate iteration state $\mathbf{s}^{i}$ , we use LB to find the (near)-optimal destroy policy $\nu^{i}$ with a neighborhood size $k^{i}$ and a given time limit. If LB does not find $\nu^{i}$ that leads to improved incumbent solution $\mathbf{x}^{i+1}$ , we increase the neighborhood size in an adaptive manner (Huang et al., 2023b;c): At iteration $t$ , when a better incumbent solution is found by LNS, the neighborhood size will be kept the same $k^{i+1}=k^{i}$ , otherwise, it will be enlarged as $\begin{array}{r}{{k^{i+1}}^{\cdot}\!=\operatorname*{min}\{\gamma_{|\mathfrak{n s}}\cdot\bar{k^{i}},\beta_{|\mathfrak{n s}}\cdot n\}}\end{array}$ , where $\gamma_{\mathsf{I n s}}>1$ is the size growing rate and $\beta_{\sf I n s}\in(0,1]$ controls the upper bound of the neighborhood size as a fraction of the total number of variables.  

Upon solving the LB ILP, SCIP not only yields the (near)-optimal solution but also dumps the intermediate solutions encountered throughout the solving process. We target those intermediate solutions, denoted as $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ , that yield an enhancement in the objective value no less than a fraction $\alpha_{\mathsf{p}}$ of the maximum observed improvement, formalized as:  

$$
\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}^{i}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\geq\alpha_{\mathsf{h q}}\cdot\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}^{i}-\mathbf{x}^{i+1}).
$$  

Such solutions are earmarked as high-quality expert policies. We impose an upper limit on the cardinality of the high-quality solution set $|S_{\mathrm{hq}}^{\bar{t}}|$ to $u_{\mathsf{h q}}$ . In scenarios where the set exceeds this size, only the leading $u_{\mathsf{h q}}$ samples are retained, mitigating the potential solution degeneration. Following Huang et al. (2023c), the parameters were chosen as $\alpha_{\mathsf{h q}}=0.5$ and $u_{\mathsf{h q}}=10$ .  



\section{3 EXPERIMENTS  }




\section{3.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP  }


Benchmark Datasets Following the previous evaluations in the literature (Sonnerat et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023c), our evaluation used 4 benchmark datasets for a variety of synthetic CO problems, as listed in Table 1. Those problems include Maximum Vertex Covering (MVC), Maximum Independent Set (MIS), Combinatorial Auction (CA), and Set Covering (SC). We generate 1,000 small instances on each problem to collect the LB demonstrations for training. An additional 40 small instances and 40 large instances are used for evaluation, where the large instances contain twice as many variables as the small instances. To distinguish between evaluations on instances of varying sizes, we employ the ’-S’ and ’-L’ suffixes to indicate small and large instances respectively, as illustrated in Table 1.  

We use the same procedure in (Huang et al., 2023c) to generate the training/testing instances and local branching demonstrations. We fix $k^{0}$ as 50, 500, 200, and 50 for MVC, MIS, CA and SC respectively. $\gamma$ is fixed as 1 on all datasets for LB. We use SCIP (version 8.0.1) to resolve ILP formulated in LB and restrict the run-time limit for LB to 1 hour per iteration on each problem. An early stopping strategy is applied if there is no better incumbent solution found in three straight iterations.

![](images/ebfb9073456e619569de1ea7c64998e3edff8636914f5cf20161b909acf7f079.jpg)  

Baselines We compare our methods to three non-neural baselines and two neural baselines featured by learning from LB, which include (1) BnB: the standard branch-and-bound algorithm used in SCIP (version 8.0.1), (2) Random-LNS: an LNS algorithm selecting the neighborhood with uniform sampling without replacement (3) LB-relax: an LNS algorithm which selects the neighborhood with LB-relax heuristic (Huang et al., 2023b) (4) IL-LNS: a neural LNS algorithm which learns LB heuristic through imitation learning (Sonnerat et al., 2021) and (5) CL-LNS: the state-of-the-art neural LNS baseline which learns LB heuristic via contrastive learning on both positive and negative samples (Huang et al., 2023c). We train all neural methods on the demonstration generated by LB on small instances and evaluate them on both small and large instances in the testing set. This amounts to in total 8 testing datasets, .  

Metrics We use the common metrics2 in previous evaluations for LNS methods and related baselines (Sonnerat et al., 2021; Nair et al., 2020a; Huang et al., 2023c), which include  



\section{1. Primal bound $\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}$ : the objective value for the feasible solution $\mathbf{x}$ .  }


2. Primal gap (Berthold (2006a)) $\gamma^{p}(\mathbf{x})$ : the normalized difference between the primal bound and a pre-computed optimal (or best known) objective value $\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}$ , defined as  

$$
\gamma^{p}(\mathbf{x})=\left\{\begin{array}{l l}{0,}&{\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{*}=\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=0}\\ {1,}&{\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{*}\cdot\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}<0,}\\ {\frac{|\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}|}{\operatorname*{max}\{|\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{*}|,|\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}|\}},}&{\mathrm{otherwise}.}\end{array}\right.
$$  



\section{3.2 MAIN RESULTS  }


We evaluate all methods on the synthetic datasets for MVC, MIS, CA, and SC problems. We basically follow the hyperparameter settings in (Huang et al., 2023c). For LB-relax, IL-LNS, CLLNS, and DIFUSCO-LNS, we set $k^{0}$ as 100, 3000, 1000, and 100 for MVC, MIS, CA, and SC respectively. For IL-LNS, we compare the initial neighborhood size of 100 and 150 on SC and find $k^{0}=150$ works better in our experiment. For Random-LNS, $k^{0}$ is set as 200, 3000, 1500 and 200 for MVC, MIS, CA, and SC separately. We fix $\gamma=1.02$ and $\beta=0.5$ in the adaptive neighborhood size for LNS-based methods across all datasets. During the inference time, we first use SCIP to presolve a feasible solution $\mathbf{x}^{0}$ prior to the formal neighborhood search. The time budget for presolving is set as 10 seconds on all datasets except for SC-L, where we find a short-time presolving cannot find a decent initial solution so we extend its presolving time to 30 seconds. In our final results, we also filter out some instances that still suffer from bad initial solutions on SC-L and report the results on the remaining 30 instances. For each LNS iteration, we restrict the run-time limit of SCIP for the sub-ILP to 2 minutes.

We compare the primal gap (PG) and primal integral (PI) at the 30-minute cutoff of all methods in Table 2 and Table 3, and visualize the change of the primal gap on each dataset in Figure 3. We find the reproduced results for some baseline methods contradictory to the conclusion in (Huang et al., 2023c) due to the difference in computational resources, but we ensure a fair comparison among all methods under the same computational environment.  

It can be seen that DIFUSCO-LNS achieves a better or comparable performance against all previous baselines in both the primal gap and primal integral. We compute the average rank for each method across either the small or large datasets, and DIFUSCO-LNS always owns the lowest average rank in either metric. In our experiment, we notice that a higher AUC-ROC in predicting LB’s neighborhood selection does not necessarily translate into an improved primal gap or primal integral. A neighborhood selection closer to LB’s choice typically leads to a larger improvement in the primal bound in a single step, nonetheless, the induced sub-ILP from this neighborhood selection could also take a longer time to solve. In comparison, the neighborhood selection leading to a small primal bound improvement may instead create a simple sub-ILP solvable in a short time. Solving multiple such simple sub-ILPs can lead to a larger primal bound improvement in total and also a smaller primal integral than solving a single hard sub-ILP within the same solving time. A typical example is MIS-L where Random-LNS owns the best primal integral against all other neural methods, although DIFUSCO-LNS achieves the better primal gap at the end of the solving. Such observation is also consistent with the results from previous works like (Huang et al., 2023c). This explains why DIFUSCO-LNS sometimes shows an inferior performance to some weak baselines on certain datasets. But in most cases, DIFUSCO-LNS still makes a better prediction of the neighborhood selection from LB and translates it into the lower primal gap and primal integral.
