\title{Individual Fairness as an Extension of Group Fairness: A Comprehensive Resolution and Novel Analysis}

\begin{abstract}
Since its seminal formal definition in 2011, the concept of _individual fairness_ has, for a variety of complex reasons, garnered significantly less focused attention from the machine learning community compared to the more widely adopted _group fairness_. The primary obstacles to its practical implementation are substantial. To operationalize individual fairness, one must first define a comprehensive and task-specific similarity metric; obtaining such a metric is a profoundly non-trivial challenge and remains an active and critical area of research. A foundational tenet of individual fairness is that discontinuity in modeling, and consequently deterministic classification, is inherently unfair. To truly achieve individual fairness, we must therefore embrace probabilistic models where predictions are appropriately randomized. For many practitioners, this requirement fundamentally challenges conventional logical approaches to decision-making. Perhaps most critically, the research community holds deeply conflicting views regarding its fundamental compatibility with group fairness objectives.

In this pivotal work, we present definitive arguments that conclusively resolve the conflicting research surrounding the essential nature of individual fairness. We meticulously clarify its most important defining features, decisively framing it as a natural and powerful extension of group fairness, rather than as a concept acting in opposition to it. We conduct a thorough review of the empirical evidence purporting to show a trade-off between group and individual fairness and derive a groundbreaking new representation for the associated individual fairness metric (which we term _individual cost_). With this novel analytical representation, we definitively prove that individual cost is intrinsically and strongly related to model utility. We therefore conclude with certainty that the existing empirical evidence does not support the claimed existence of a fundamental trade-off between group and individual fairness but rather, unequivocally demonstrates the well-documented and inherent trade-off between fairness and utility.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION}

The rapid and widespread proliferation of data-driven algorithmic solutions across critical social domains has served as a powerful catalyst, accelerating research in fair machine learning in recent years. High-stakes applications in criminal justice, predictive policing Ensign et al. (2018), healthcare, finance, and beyond, have urgently fueled the necessity for robust formal definitions of fairness notions, precise metrics, and effective mitigation techniques. In a recent and comprehensive survey on fairness in machine learning, authors highlight five major dilemmas impeding progress in the field. The first two of these central dilemmas concern critical trade-offs. The first is the perennial trade-off between fairness and model performance Hajian & Domingo-Ferrer (2012); Corbett-Davies et al. (2017); Calmon et al. (2017); Haas (2019). The second is the apparent conflict between different, competing notions of fairness Darlington (1971); Chouldechova (2016); Kleinberg et al. (2016); Hardt et al. (2016); Barocas et al. (2019); Murgai (2023). The latter dilemma is widely credited with having stifled meaningful progress in earlier fairness research Cole & Zieky (2001); Hutchinson & Mitchell (2019). Thus, achieving clarity regarding the compatibility of different fairness measures, as well as their relationship with model performance, is absolutely essential for propelling the field forward.

A prevalent and influential claim within the literature is that there exists an inherent trade-off or tension between the notions of individual fairness and group fairness Narayanan (2018); Speicher et al. (2018); Pessach & Shmueli (2022); Caton & Haas (2023). This stems from a fundamental concern: in cases where the target trait is indeed distributed differently between sensitive subgroups, the only conceivable way to satisfy statistical parity is through preferential treatment of one group over another; but this very action would directly violate the core requirement to treat similar individuals similarly. For this specific scenario, Dwork et al. themselves suggest a modification that relaxes the Lipschitz condition Dwork et al. (2011). More recently, Binns persuasively argued that the conflict lies in the practical implementation rather than in the underlying concepts Binns (2019).

Apart from the above theoretical scenario, the claim of a trade-off between group and individual fairness has found empirical support in the work of Speicher et al. (2018), and it is this specific evidence that serves as the primary motivation for our detailed study of the corresponding fairness metric (referred to as individual cost hereafter). In this paper, we highlight crucial and previously overlooked differences in the definition of individual fairness as originally defined by Dwork et al. (2011) and in the empirical analysis conducted by Speicher et al. (2018). We demonstrate conclusively that while individual fairness defined by Dwork et al. can and should be viewed as a principled extension of group fairness—one that decouples the tasks of ensuring fairness and maximizing utility—individual cost (as the choice of name strongly implies) can be viewed as an extension of utility (or rather expected risk) and is therefore, in many cases, a monotonic function of accuracy.

The definition of individual cost in the original paper is extremely flexible, and the authors make several seemingly arbitrary choices for its parameters. Thus, while the construction of the metric appears principled, its actual behavior remains opaque and poorly understood. Nevertheless, individual cost has been implemented in prominent open-source libraries Bellamy et al. (2018) and has gained significant traction among researchers. Recent major surveys include it Pessach & Shmueli (2022); Caton & Haas (2023) and one recent paper explicitly optimizes for it while developing a novel fair algorithm Jin et al. (2023).

Here we undertake a rigorous and detailed examination of individual cost, decisively shedding light on its true behavior and meaning. We reason carefully about its generality and describe necessary constraints on parameters that ensure it functions not merely as a measure of expected risk, but rather as a measure of expected luck. In addition, we discuss important properties of the metric for different choices of the generalization parameter $\alpha$. In the final part of the paper, we derive a transformative new representation of individual cost under the reasonable assumption that accurate predictions are equally lucky for the individual. This powerful representation allows us to comprehensively visualize the behavior of individual cost, covering all but one remaining degree of freedom. Finally, we employ sophisticated finite difference methods within this novel analytical context in order to derive an exact analytical expression for the deviation region. That is, we precisely identify the part of the model solution space where incrementally increasing accuracy paradoxically increases unfairness according to this metric.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows. In Section 2 we provide a concise review of the key notions of fairness relevant to our discussion. In Section 3 we move on to individual fairness Dwork et al. (2011), meticulously clarifying its definition and establishing its position as a natural extension of group fairness, rather than being in contention with it. We note important conceptual features, and pay special attention to the case of a binary classifier, as this is the specific case for which empirical evidence of a trade-off has been claimed Speicher et al. (2018). In Section 4, we provide a detailed description of individual cost Speicher et al. (2018). In section 5, we derive our groundbreaking new representation of individual cost, showing it can be written explicitly as a function of two fundamental model performance parameters; namely, prediction accuracy and mean prediction error. With this powerful new representation of the metric, we are able to definitively answer the following critical question. For which specific set of model error distributions does incrementally increasing the accuracy, actually reduce fairness according to this metric? Our rigorous analysis proves that this only happens when the ratio of false positives to correct predictions is sufficiently high (greater than half the number of accurate predictions for the specific parameter choices in Speicher et al. (2018)). Furthermore, such a ratio can only possibly be achieved if the prediction accuracy is itself sufficiently low (specifically, below $66.7\%$ for the specific parameter choices in Speicher et al. (2018)). We therefore conclude decisively that the cited empirical evidence does not support the existence of a fundamental trade-off between group and individual fairness but rather demonstrates the well-known and inherent trade-off between fairness and utility.

Our main and substantial contributions are to elucidate the true behavior of both individual fairness and individual cost, providing clarity and novel analytical tools for the field.

• We meticulously clarify the important defining features of individual fairness, decisively framing it as a natural and powerful extension of group fairness rather than as a concept acting in opposition to it.
• We conduct an exhaustive and detailed analysis of individual cost, conclusively showing how it can be fundamentally viewed as an extension of expected risk. In addition, we provide much-needed practical guidance around parameter selection for calculating individual cost, highlighting critical index properties for different choices.
• We derive a transformative new representation of individual cost in terms of standard model performance metrics and thereby definitively reconcile the conflicting empirical evidence that purported to demonstrate a trade-off between group and individual fairness.
• Using advanced finite difference methods, we derive an exact analytical expression for the deviation region - the precise area of the model space where decreasing accuracy perversely increases fairness according to this metric.



\section{2 BACKGROUND}

Early pioneering methods for quantifying fairness, motivated by the introduction of landmark anti-discrimination laws in the US in the 1960s, were developed with the explicit goal of measuring bias in assessment tests for education and employment opportunities Cleary (1968); Einhorn & Bass (1971); Cole (1973); Novick & Petersen (1976). The metrics presented in these foundational works fall under what has since become widely known as group fairness Barocas et al. (2019); Hutchinson & Mitchell (2019); Pessach & Shmueli (2022); Caton & Haas (2023), which considers aggregate differences in treatment (outcomes or errors) across predefined subgroups of a population. Informally, individual fairness is the ancient and intuitive notion that similar individuals should be treated similarly Aristotle (350 B.C.); Guion (1966). A rigorous formal definition, framed as equivalence to continuity with a capped gradient, was first proposed by Dwork et al. (2011). Shortly thereafter, Zemel et al. Zemel et al. (2013) introduced their own individual fairness metric, which quantifies the consistency of a mapping by comparing each individual outcome with the mean of the outcomes for its $k$ nearest neighbours and averaging over the entire population. More recently, Speicher et al. Speicher et al. (2018) proposed a distinct measure of individual fairness, which we term individual cost to avoid confusion, and which is the primary subject of much of this paper. Finally, related to both group and individual fairness is the sophisticated concept of counterfactual fairness Kilbertus et al. (2017); Kusner et al. (2018), which argues that the prediction distribution should be independent of both the sensitive features and all of their causally dependent attributes.

In their landmark 2011 paper, Dwork et al. moved the formal definition of fairness decisively beyond discrimination based solely on protected characteristics, towards a more generalized and powerful definition known as individual fairness Dwork et al. (2011). Individual fairness is fundamentally based on the principle that similar individuals (with respect to the specific task at hand) should be treated similarly and does not restrict its attention merely to protected characteristics, but allows all relevant features to be incorporated into the notion of fairness. Its philosophical origin can be traced back to Aristotle, who wrote in the context of legal theory that “like cases should be treated alike” Schauer (2018). The formal mathematical definition of the concept arrived in the form of a continuity constraint on the model mapping. This new and elegant definition resolved the aforementioned issues with group fairness by construction. Most importantly, by requiring the explicit definition of a similarity metric, it successfully decoupled the two distinct tasks of maximizing utility and ensuring fairness so that they can be performed completely independently.

The practical implementation of individual fairness presents several significant challenges, the foremost being that its core definition is inherently incomplete. One must first define a suitable similarity metric in feature space. Researchers and practitioners alike have argued that rather than solving the problem of finding a fair model that maps individuals to predictions, individual fairness has added a new layer of complexity by requiring the prior definition of a task-specific similarity metric. Indeed, obtaining a robust and justifiable similarity metric is a profoundly non-trivial task and remains an active and critical area of research Zemel et al. (2013); Lahoti et al. (2019). We argue persuasively that this new paradigm makes explicit the paramount importance of consistency in fair decision making. According to the tenets of individual fairness, which requires strict continuity Dwork et al. (2011), deterministic classification is inherently unfair Narayanan (2018) and to achieve true fairness, we must turn to probabilistic models in which predictions are appropriately randomized Dwork et al. (2011). For many in the field, this requirement fundamentally challenges conventional logical approaches to automated decision-making.



\section{3 INDIVIDUAL FAIRNESS}

Informally, given a model that maps individuals to predictions, individual fairness can be interpreted as the fundamental requirement that two individuals who are close in the input (feature) space $\mathcal{X}$ must also be close in the output (target/prediction) space $\boldsymbol{\wp}$. Dwork et al. note that in order to satisfy this intuitive constraint, the model mapping must be continuous, as defined precisely next.

Lipschitz Continuity: Consider a model to be a function ${\hat{y}}=f({\pmb x})$, which maps individuals $\pmb{x}\in\mathcal{X}$ to probability distributions over $y\in\mathcal{V}$, that is, $f:\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$. Then the mapping $f$ is Lipschitz continuous if there exists a real valued, non-negative constant $K\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$ such that

$$
d_{\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})}\big(f\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}\big),f\big(\mathbf{x}_{j}\big)\big)\leq K d_{\mathcal{X}}\big(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}\big)\quad\forall\:\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}\in\mathcal{X}
$$

where $d_{\mathcal{X}}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ and $d_{\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})}:\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ denote distance metrics. $d_{\mathcal{X}}$ determines how far apart two individuals are in feature space and $d_{\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{D})}$ measures the distance between two probability distributions over $\boldsymbol{\wp}$.

For the specific purpose of individual fairness we can omit the Lipschitz constant without loss of generality since it can be absorbed into the definition of the similarity metric. Individual fairness essentially caps the rate at which the predictions can change with respect to the input features. Crucially, individual fairness does not concern itself with the specific decisions $\hat{y}$, but rather with the consistency with which they are made across individuals, formalized as $|\mathrm{d}\hat{y}/\mathrm{d}x|$. Individual fairness is a property of a single mapping from input $\textbf{\em x}$ to output $\hat{y}$ (or its distribution), not a measure of how one mapping differs from another, such as ${\hat{y}}-y$. In this fundamental sense, model accuracy and individual fairness are orthogonal concepts. Individual fairness cares only about how similar people are treated, not how they are ranked; the latter is determined solely by the objective of maximizing utility. Rather than relying on the existence of a potentially untrustworthy ground truth dataset, individual fairness requires the explicit definition of a similarity metric to determine what constitutes fair treatment.

In summary, according to the principles of individual fairness the model mapping must be continuous and the smaller the model gradient (based on the chosen similarity metric, $\mathrm{d}f/\mathrm{d}x$), the more similarly individuals are treated. If the gradient is zero, we have perfect equality—all individuals are mapped to the identical distribution over outcomes and we have satisfied the individual fairness constraint perfectly. Of course, such a model would not be practically useful, as it would not take into account the features $\textbf{\em x}$ of the individuals in its predictions. Essentially, we have reduced the complex problem of training a fair model $f({\pmb x},y)$ to one of constrained optimization:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}{\operatorname{ion:}}&{\qquad\qquad\underset{\theta}{\min}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},y)\in(X,y)}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{y}=f(\mathbf{x},y;\theta)}\ [\mathcal{L}(X,y,\hat{y})]\right\},}\\ &{d_{\mathcal{P}(y)}(f(x_{i},y),f(\mathbf{x}_{j},y))\leq d_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j})\quad\mathrm{and}\quad f(\mathbf{x}_{i},y)\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\qquad\forall\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}\in X.}\end{array}
$$

It might be argued that individual fairness has not provided a complete answer to the fairness problem; it has instead created a new challenge that is equally difficult. However, in this new and principled formulation, the critical importance of consistency in decision making is made explicit. This elegant separation of the tasks of maximizing utility and ensuring fairness means they can be completed independently by two separate stakeholders. Thus, a trusted party (such as a regulator, auditor, or risk manager) could be tasked with determining the appropriate similarity function. This definition could be open, transparent, and subject to public debate and iterative improvement over time as societal laws and cultural norms evolve. The similarity metric essentially provides a powerful mechanism through which to express a specific world view regarding fairness. In spirit, this characterization of (individual) fairness aligns perfectly with the arguments of other leading scholars Friedler et al. (2016); Binns (2019).

Conceptually, we can powerfully think of individual fairness as group fairness (more specifically statistical parity since it is interested in outcomes only), but taken to the limit as the subgroup size tends to one and the subgroup definition $Z$ expands to encompass the entire feature space $X$. Here, the outcomes are allowed to vary with the features, but only within some predefined limit which can itself be dependent on the specific features. In theory, if $X$ includes sensitive features, we could set this limit to zero for those features by specification in the similarity metric, though in practice zeros might complicate optimization if we are, for example, trying to learn fair representations Lahoti et al. (2019). Thus, individual fairness can and should be viewed as a natural and powerful extension of group fairness rather than being in fundamental contention with it; faced with empirical observations to the contrary, one would be wise to investigate the specific metrics and assumptions further.

While randomness in judicial or other high-stakes decisions might be contentious, in many other practical contexts it might be desirable, or even necessary, to create a competent and fair model. Indeed the most capable conversational AIs today routinely produce appropriately randomized responses to user prompts OpenAI (2023). A telling example occurred in 2017, when Google Translate was found to be consistently translating genderless languages (such as Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, Persian, and Turkish) using heavily gender-stereotyped pronouns in all cases (for example, always translating "he is a doctor" and "she is a nurse") Caliskan et al. (2017). Randomized predictions would sometimes correctly return “she is a doctor”. Arguably, this would be significantly fairer, since female doctors are effectively erased by the deterministic technology. In 2019, almost $49\%$ of doctors in the 37 countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) were reportedly female OECD (2021). The problem that we identify here is not exclusive to gender. There are often multiple reasonable translations of the same sentence, even without gender associations. By returning only the single most probable answer, the technology hides its inherent uncertainty and drastically reduces diversity in its output. In 2018 Google introduced some targeted fixes Kuczmarski (2018), but the solution (returning multiple translations) is not generalized beyond the specific case of gender. Though perhaps not the optimal solution here, randomization in predictions is one proven way to improve diversity in output and thus representation, which is precisely where choosing the deterministic Bayes optimal solution often fails spectacularly from a fairness perspective.



\section{4 INDIVIDUAL COST AS AN EXTENSION OF EXPECTED RISK}

In this section we provide a detailed description of the specific individual fairness metric used to evidence the claimed trade-off between group and individual fairness Speicher et al. (2018), which we decisively term individual cost to avoid confusion with the original definition. Individual cost is calculated in two distinct steps. First, we must map the model predictions $\hat{y}_{i}$ to a quantified individual benefit $b_{i}$. Second, we must choose an appropriate inequality index $I(b)$ to calculate how unequally the benefits $\pmb{b}=(b_{1},b_{2},...,b_{n})$ are distributed among the population consisting of $n$ individuals.



\section{4.1 MAPPING PREDICTIONS TO BENEFITS}

To map predictions to benefits in this specific framework, the authors suggest using one plus the error, that is, $b_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-y_{i}+1$. For a binary classifier, the error is either zero, or plus or minus one. Adding one to the error ensures the benefits are always zero or positive, a strict requirement for measuring inequality with standard indices. In addition, at least one individual must receive a positive benefit, so that the total benefit is positive. Here we assume that $y\,=\,1$ is the advantageous outcome, in which case we can think of the benefit from the perspective of the individual as a measure of luck. A false positive is therefore the luckiest possible prediction $(b_{i}=2)$), a false negative the unluckiest $(b_{i}\,=\,0)$), and an accurate prediction lies between the two $(b_{i}\,=\,1)$). More generally, the authors suggest the benefit can be any function of $\hat{y}$ and the target $y$; ignoring $\textbf{\em x}$ ensures anonymity. For a classifier, the benefit function can be expressed concisely as a matrix: $b_{i j}=\mathrm{benefit}(\hat{y}=i,y=j)$.

Individual cost appears to represent a simplified measure of individual fairness. Rather than comparing individuals by their features, it compares them solely by their outcome—essentially "treating individuals deserving similar outcomes similarly" Speicher et al. (2018). It is clear that this metric is not the same as individual fairness as described in the previous section. Individual fairness does not trust the target labels at all, while individual cost relies on them entirely. Individual cost is a property that compares two mappings (the prediction and the target), while individual fairness is a property of a single mapping.

There are many indices that measure inequality differently, but they all share the following fundamental properties:

• Symmetry: The function is symmetric in benefits, so that changing their order does not change the value of the index.
• Zero-normalisation: They are minimised with a value of zero, only for uniformly distributed benefits;
• Transfer principle: Transferring benefits from a richer to a poorer individual always decreases the value of the index, provided the rich and poor don’t switch places in their ranking as a result of the transfer; and
• Population invariance: The measure is independent of the size of the population. It depends only on the distribution of benefits.

In addition to satisfying the above properties, generalised entropy indices are also scale invariant, meaning the value of the index does not change under a constant scaling of all benefits.

For benefits $\pmb{b}=(b_{1},b_{2},...,b_{n})$ with mean benefit $\mu$, the generalised entropy index can be written as,

$$
I_{\alpha}(b)={\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{\alpha}\left({\frac{b_{i}}{\mu}}\right)\quad\quad{\mathrm{where}}\quad\quad f_{\alpha}(x)={\left\{\begin{array}{l l}{\quad-\ln x}&{{\mathrm{if}}\quad\alpha=0}\\ {\quad x\ln x}&{{\mathrm{if}}\quad\alpha=1}\\ {\quad \frac{x^{\alpha}-1}{\alpha(\alpha-1)}}&{{\mathrm{otherwise.}}}\end{array}\right.}
$$

The generalization parameter $\alpha$ controls the weight applied to benefits at different parts of the distribution. Since benefits can be zero for the proposed choice of benefit function, we must choose a value of $\alpha\,>\,0$. For example, Speicher et al. (2018) choose $\alpha=2$ for their experiments.

Generalised entropy indices are the complete single-parameter $(\alpha)$ family of inequality indices with the additional powerful property of subgroup decomposability Shorrocks (1980). This means that for any partition of the population into subgroups, we can additively decompose the index into a between-group component and a within-group component. The between-group component is the contribution from variations in the mean benefit between subgroups. The within-group component is the contribution from the variation in individual benefits within the subgroups. If we think of the predictive system as a means for distributing benefits and we are able to map model predictions to benefits, we can use inequality indices to measure how unfair the algorithm is in its distribution of those benefits. If we use generalised entropy indices, we can think of the total inequality index as a measure of individual unfairness and the between-group component as a measure of group unfairness, allowing us to precisely identify when and where trade-offs occur. The empirical evidence of the trade-off presented in Speicher et al. (2018) is provided for two datasets, both of which are binary classification problems.



\section{4.3 CONNECTION WITH UTILITY}

The deep connection between measures of inequality and measures of risk has been known in economics for some time. For example, Atkinson exploited this connection to derive his own famous measure of inequality Atkinson (1970) over half a century ago. We note that calculating individual cost is procedurally much like calculating a cost-sensitive loss. Here, however, the associated cost matrix is not constant, but rather depends dynamically on the mean benefit, $c_{i j}\,=\,\bar{\mathrm{cost}}(\hat{y}\,=\,i,y\,=\,j)\,=\,b_{i j}/\mu$. As our model performance changes, so does the mean benefit $\mu$, the associated costs $c_{i j}$, and consequently the index value $I(b)$. The mean benefit $\mu$ is always positive and so does not affect the relative size or ordering of the costs in the matrix. Thus, although the mean benefit will affect the absolute index value, it will not change the order of preference of different benefit distributions $^{b}$. We can understand the influence of the mean benefit on the index value precisely as follows,

$$
I_{\alpha}(\pmb{b})=\mathbb{E}\left[f_{\alpha}\left(\frac{\pmb{b}}{\mu}\right)\right]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[f_{\alpha}(\pmb{b})]-f_{\alpha}(\mu)}{\mu^{\alpha}}.
$$

If we define $b_{i}\,=\,\mathbb{P}(\hat{y}_{i}\,=\,y_{i})$ and choose $\alpha\,=\,0$, the index behaves exactly like the cross-entropy loss. If we instead have a regression problem and define $b_{i}\,=\,\hat{y}_{i}\,-\,y_{i}$ and choose $\alpha\,=\,2$, then the index behaves like the mean squared error. So, we can see clearly that in specific cases, this generalised metric behaves identically to well-known measures of expected risk. Individual cost might therefore be fundamentally viewed as an extension of expected risk (or expected luck), since not all possible metrics that can be constructed via this general recipe would result in a valid or meaningful objective function. For example, one such critical requirement is that of Fisher consistency. That is, we want a model to be an unbiased estimator of the target, $\mathbb{E}(\hat{y})=\mathbb{E}(y)$. For this property to hold, we need the minima of our objective function to coincide with the expected value of the target. For a binary classifier with $b_{i}=\mathbb{P}(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i})$, $\alpha\,=\,0$ and $\alpha\,=\,2$, are in fact the only two values for which this is provably true Buja et al. (2005).

The parameter $\alpha$ determines how fast the contribution to the index grows as a function of the individual benefit. For $\alpha>1$ the contribution grows faster than the benefit (thereby prioritising equality among the lucky), and slower for $\alpha<1$ (prioritising equality among the unlucky). Thus, one could argue persuasively that we should typically choose a value of $0<\alpha<1$ for fairness-focused applications. Finally, for the specific values $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha=1$, the within-group component is a true weighted average of the index values for the subgroups, since the coefficients sum to one. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ the coefficients sum to less than unity, with the sum being minimised for $\alpha=1/2$. For $\alpha>1$, the coefficients sum to more than unity.

Though the original authors specify no constraints regarding the benefit matrix, we argue compellingly that there should be some, much like the standard constraints for a cost matrix. In particular, if an accurate prediction is always more beneficial than an incorrect prediction (i.e., the leading diagonal of the matrix dominates), then the index is simply a cost-sensitive expected risk which always decreases monotonically with increasing accuracy. We can assume then, without loss of generality, that $\hat{y}=1$ is the advantaged outcome. In this case, the second row of the benefit matrix $b_{i j}\,=\,\mathrm{benefit}(\hat{y}\,=\,i,y\,=\,j)$ must dominate the first, $b_{10}~>~b_{00}$ and $b_{11}>b_{01}$. Since the index is scale invariant we can conveniently fix the value $b_{11}=1$ (akin to fixing the unit of account). Since we know that a false negative is the least lucky outcome, setting this value to zero establishes a natural baseline. Although increasing all the benefits in the matrix by a fixed amount will decrease inequality (a rising tide lifts all boats), it will not change the relative ranking of different benefit distributions. Then we can write the benefit matrix in its most general form as: $b_{i j}=((b_{-},0),(b_{+},1))$ where $b_{+}>b_{-}>0$.



\section{5 INDIVIDUAL COST ANALYSIS}

In this section we elucidate further the true behavior of individual cost through rigorous analysis. To simplify the problem for clarity, we assume that accurate predictions are equally lucky. Then we have $b_{-}=1$ with $b_{+}>1$. The parameter $b_{+}$ tells us precisely how much luckier a false positive is compared to an accurate prediction. The value of the inequality index depends critically on the mean benefit $\mu$, or equivalently the total benefit $B=n\mu$. As the model performance changes, so does the mean benefit and thus the associated effective costs. The mean benefit $\mu$ is always positive and so does not affect the relative size or ordering of the costs in the matrix, but it can still impact the relative preference of different predictions. Crucially, specifying $b_{+}>b_{-}$ means that making a more accurate prediction might not always reduce the value of the index, which is the source of the purported trade-off.



\section{5.1 THE INDEX AS A FUNCTION OF MODEL PERFORMANCE METRICS}

Individual cost can be written explicitly as a function of two fundamental model performance parameters: prediction accuracy $\lambda$ and the mean benefit $\mu$. Recall, the latter is simply the expected prediction error plus one: $\mathbb{E}(\hat{Y}-Y)+1$.

Theorem 1. For the specific benefit function $b_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-y_{i}+1$ we can rewrite the generalised entropy index as:

$$
I_{\alpha}\left(\mu,\lambda\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{c l}{{\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)\ln b_{+}-\ln\mu}}&{{i f\;\;\;\alpha=1}}\\ {{\displaystyle\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha-1)}\left[\left(\frac{b_{+}}{\mu}\right)^{\alpha-1}-\frac{\displaystyle(b_{+}^{\alpha-1}-1)}{\displaystyle\mu^{\alpha}}\lambda-1\right]}}&{{i f\;\;\;\alpha>0,\,\alpha\neq1.}}\end{array}\right.
$$

Equation (2) shows conclusively that for a fixed $\mu$, $I_{\alpha}(\mu,\lambda)$ is a linearly decreasing function of the accuracy $\lambda$. For the common case $b_{+}=2$, the mean benefit $\mu$ gives us a direct indication of the relative number of false positive to false negative errors made by the model; it tells us if the model $\hat{y}$ is over- or underestimating the target $y$ on average. From another point of view, it quantifies the amount of skew in the distribution of errors. $\mu<1$ indicates positive skew (more false negatives) and vice versa for $\mu>1$ (more false positives). Figure 1 provides clear visual illustrations of benefit distributions with different mean benefits $\mu$. When the mean benefit is exactly one (as in the central figure), the distribution has no skew; it is perfectly symmetric.

Both $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are constrained. For any reasonable binary classifier, model accuracy is bounded, $0.5\leq\lambda\leq1$. The total number of benefits $B$ is minimized when all errors are false negatives and maximised when all errors are false positives. For a model with accuracy $\lambda=n_{c}/n$, the total benefit $B$ must satisfy the following precise bounds,

$$
n_{c}\le B\le n_{c}+b_{+}(n-n_{c})=b_{+}n+(1-b_{+})n_{c}.
$$

Since $B=n\mu$, we must have $\lambda\leq\mu\leq b_{+}+(1-b_{+})\lambda$. Thus, the index is defined as $I_{\alpha}(\mu,\lambda):([\lambda,b_{+}+(1-b_{+})\lambda],[0.5,1])\mapsto\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$. As model accuracy $\lambda$ increases, the range of possible values the mean benefit $\mu$ can take, decreases. The domain is therefore a triangle. When $b_{+}=2$, the domain is an isosceles triangle. In Figure 2, we provide an informative side-view of the index surface for the specific case $b_{+}=2$.

5.2 WHEN DOES INCREASING THE ACCURACY REDUCE THE INDEX?

Let us denote the change in the index caused by a single error as,

$$
\Delta I_{\alpha}^{\pm}(b)=I_{\alpha}(b^{\pm})-I_{\alpha}(b).
$$

Here $b^{\pm}$ differs from $^{b}$ by one prediction only, containing one less correct prediction and one more erroneous one. For $b^{+}$, the additional error is a false positive. For $b^{-}$, the additional error is a false negative. An additional false negative error reduces the total benefit $B$ by one; both the accuracy $\lambda$ and the mean benefit $\mu$ are reduced by $1/n$. An additional false positive error increases the total benefit $B$ by $\delta=(b_{+}-b_{-})$; the accuracy $\lambda$ is once again reduced by $1/n$, but this time the mean benefit $\mu$ increases by $\delta/n$. The discrete grid of adjacent models that we can reach through a small change in the model (given fixed $\mu,\lambda$ and $n$), is shown in Figure 3. Hence,

$$
\Delta I_{\alpha}^{\pm}(\mu,\lambda;n)=I_{\alpha}\left(\lambda-\frac{1}{n},\mu\pm\frac{\delta}{n}\right)-I_{\alpha}(\mu,\lambda).
$$

Theorem 2.

$$
\left.\begin{array}{c c c}{{\Delta I_{\alpha}^{-}(\mu,\lambda;n)<0}}&{{\Rightarrow}}&{{\mu<h^{-}(\alpha,b_{+})\lambda}}\\ {{\Delta I_{\alpha}^{+}(\mu,\lambda;n)<0}}&{{\Rightarrow}}&{{\mu>h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})\lambda}}\end{array}\right\}
$$

where,

$$
h^{\pm}(\alpha,b_{+})=\left\{\begin{array}{c l}{{\displaystyle\frac{(b_{+}-1)\ln b_{+}}{b_{+}-1\mp\ln b_{+}}}}&{{i f\;\;\;\alpha=1}}\\ {{\displaystyle\frac{\alpha(b_{+}-1)(b_{+}^{\alpha-1}-1)}{[(\alpha-1)(b_{+}-1)\mp1]b_{+}^{\alpha-1}\pm1}}}&{{i f\;\;\;\alpha>0,\,\alpha\neq1.}}\end{array}\right.
$$

Theorem 3. For the specific benefit function $b_{i}\,=\,{\hat{y}}_{i}\,-\,y_{i}\,+1,$, the only kind of error which is ever preferable to a correct prediction under this benefit function is a false positive. This happens only when the mean benefit exceeds a critical threshold: $\mu > h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})\lambda$. We note importantly that for a model whose accuracy is greater than a certain threshold $\hat{\lambda}(\alpha)$, it is mathematically impossible for the mean benefit to exceed the required level. That is,

$$
\begin{array}{r l}{\Delta I_{\alpha}^{-}(\mu,\lambda;n)>0}&{{}\forall\,\mu,\,\lambda,\,n}\\ {\Delta I_{\alpha}^{+}(\mu,\lambda;n)<0}&{{}\Rightarrow\quad\mu>h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})\lambda,}\end{array}
$$

where $h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})$ is defined in Equation (5).

We term the part of the domain for which the index is paradoxically reduced by decreasing the accuracy, the deviation region. The deviation region is described analytically by the inequality $\mu>h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})\lambda$. We mark this deviation region clearly on the contour plot for $I_{\alpha}(\mu,\lambda)$ in Figure 4. These results prove that individual cost expresses a inherent preference for false positives, which makes intuitive sense given that they increase the total benefit distributed. This is perfectly inline with the results from the original authors who found that for both tested datasets (Adult and COMPAS), rejecting more individuals (i.e., increasing false positives) increases the index value. For reference, in Table 1, we provide specific computed values of $\hat{\lambda}(\alpha)$ and $h^{+}(\alpha,b_{+})$. Now that we have precisely identified the deviation region we can return to the original motivating question. For which specific set of error distributions does increasing the accuracy actually reduce fairness according to this metric? Our rigorous analysis proves definitively that this only happens when the ratio of false positives to correct predictions is sufficiently high (greater than half the number of accurate predictions for the specific parameter choices in Speicher et al. (2018)). Furthermore, such a ratio can only possibly be achieved if the prediction accuracy is itself sufficiently low (specifically, below $66.7\%$ for the specific parameter choices in Speicher et al. (2018)).



\section{6 CONCLUSIONS}

In this significant work, we present definitive arguments that conclusively resolve the conflicting research surrounding the essential nature of individual fairness Dwork et al. (2011). We meticulously clarify its most important defining features, decisively framing it as a natural and powerful extension of group fairness, rather than as a concept acting in opposition to it. In particular, we emphasise the critical importance of the definition of individual fairness being fundamentally orthogonal to utility. We conduct a thorough review of the empirical evidence purporting to show a trade-off between group and individual fairness and derive a groundbreaking new representation for the associated individual fairness metric Speicher et al. (2018) (which we term individual cost). With this novel and powerful analytical representation, we definitively prove that individual cost is intrinsically a function of model accuracy and we express exactly the precise conditions under which fairness and accuracy are inversely related. We therefore conclude with certainty that the existing empirical evidence does not support the claimed existence of a fundamental trade-off between group and individual fairness but rather, unequivocally demonstrates the well-documented and inherent trade-off between fairness and utility.
