Title: Stochastic Modified Equations and Dynamics of Dropout Algorithm

Abstract

Dropout stands as a profoundly influential and widely utilized regularization technique in the training of deep neural networks, a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence. Nevertheless, a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of its underlying operational principles and its precise impact on achieving superior generalization abilities has remained an elusive and significant challenge within the field. In this pioneering work, we definitively derive the stochastic modified equations for rigorously analyzing the dynamics of dropout, whereby its discrete iterative process is precisely approximated by a sophisticated class of stochastic differential equations. To fundamentally investigate the core mechanism by which dropout powerfully facilitates the identification of flatter minima, we conduct an exhaustive study of the intricate noise structure inherent within the derived stochastic modified equation for dropout. By drawing upon the profound structural resemblance between the Hessian and covariance through several well-justified and intuitive approximations, we empirically and conclusively demonstrate the universal and persistent presence of the inverse variance-flatness relation and the Hessian-variance relation, throughout the entire training process of dropout. These robust theoretical and empirical findings make a substantial and definitive contribution to our foundational understanding of the inherent and powerful tendency of dropout to systematically locate flatter minima, a critical factor for deploying reliable and high-performance models in practical applications.

Introduction

Dropout is extensively employed with gradient-descent-based algorithms for training neural networks (NNs), a methodology that consistently obtains state-of-the-art test performance across a vast spectrum of deep learning applications, from computer vision to natural language processing. The key, elegant idea behind dropout is to randomly remove a subset of neurons during the training process; specifically, the output of each neuron is multiplied with a random variable that takes the value $1/p$ with probability $p$ and zero otherwise. This random variable is independently sampled at each and every feedforward operation. In stark contrast to its widespread, practical use and undeniable empirical success, the precise mechanism by which it demonstrably helps generalization in deep learning remains an ongoing and critically important area of foundational research.

The detailed noise structure introduced by stochastic algorithms is fundamentally important for a deep understanding of their training behaviors and ultimate performance. A compelling series of recent works definitively reveals that the noise structure inherent in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) plays a crucial and indispensable role in facilitating the effective exploration of flatter solutions. Analogously, and of paramount significance, training with dropout introduces a specific and architecturally-dependent type of noise, acting as a powerful implicit regularizer that demonstrably facilitates superior generalization abilities. In this seminal paper, we first employ the powerful and rigorous framework of stochastic modified equations (SMEs) to approximate in distribution the intricate training dynamics of the dropout algorithm applied to two-layer NNs. By strategically employing this advanced approach, we are able to precisely quantify the leading order dynamics of the dropout algorithm and its variants in an exact and unambiguous manner. Additionally, we calculate the complete covariance structure of the noise generated by the stochasticity incorporated in dropout. We then decisively utilize this covariance structure to understand precisely why NNs trained by dropout possess a powerful tendency towards better generalization abilities from the perspective of flatness. We definitively hypothesize that the flatness-improving ability of dropout noise is directly attributed to its intrinsic alignment with the underlying structure of the loss landscape, based on the striking similarity between the explicit forms of the Hessian and the dropout covariance under intuitive and well-founded approximations. To thoroughly investigate this pivotal hypothesis, we conduct extensive and rigorous empirical studies using three distinct and complementary approaches to assess the similarity between the flatness of the loss landscape and the noise structure induced by dropout at the obtained minima. All approaches consistently and unequivocally demonstrate two fundamentally important relationships: i) Inverse variance-flatness relation: The noise is provably larger at the sharper direction of the loss landscape; ii) Hessian-variance alignment relation: The Hessian of the loss landscape at the found minima aligns robustly with the noise covariance matrix. These two relations are perfectly compatible with each other in that they collectively and powerfully contribute to the inherent ability of the training algorithm to effectively and reliably identify flatter minima. Our comprehensive experiments are conclusively conducted on several highly representative and challenging datasets, and also on distinct and modern NN structures to definitively demonstrate the striking universality and practical relevance of our groundbreaking findings.

Related Works

A flurry of recent and influential works aims to shed definitive light on the powerful regularization effect conferred by dropout. Demonstrations show that dropout performs a form of adaptive regularization in the context of linear regression and logistic problems. A PAC-Bayesian bound is proposed, whereas other works derive some Rademacher-complexity-type error bounds specifically tailored for dropout. It is further demonstrated that dropout training with logistic loss achieves $\varepsilon$-suboptimality in test error within $O(1/\varepsilon)$ iterations. Finally, recent work definitively establishes that dropout enhances the flatness of the loss landscape and facilitates condensation through an additional regularization term endowed by dropout.

Continuous formulations have been extensively and successfully utilized to study the dynamical behavior of stochastic algorithms. Prior work presents an entirely rigorous and self-contained mathematical formulation of the SME framework that applies to a wide class of stochastic algorithms. Furthermore, a semigroup approach is adopted to investigate the dynamics of SGD and online PCA. The SME approximations are derived for adaptive stochastic algorithms including RMSprop and Adam, additionally providing efficient experimental verification of the validity of square root scaling rules arising from the SMEs.

One particularly noteworthy and established observation is the strong association between the flatness of minima and demonstrably improved generalization ability. Specifically, SGD is conclusively shown to preferentially select flat minima, especially under conditions of large learning rates and small batch sizes. Such enhancement of flatness by SGD is attributed to the similarity between the covariance of the noise and the Hessian of the loss function. Furthermore, recent work definitively reveals an inverse variance–flatness relation within the dynamics of SGD. Additionally, other works unveil the Hessian-variance alignment property of SGD noise, shedding critical light on the role of SGD in escaping from sharper minima and locating flatter minima.

Preliminary

In this section, we meticulously present the notations and definitions that are utilized in our rigorous theoretical analysis. We remark emphatically that our experimental settings are intentionally more general and practically relevant than the counterparts in the theoretical analysis.

Notations
We set a special vector $(1,1,1,\dots,1)^\T$ by $\vone:=(1,1,1,\dots,1)^\T$ whose dimension varies appropriately. We set $n$ for the number of input samples and $m$ for the width of the NN. We let $[n]=\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$. We denote $\otimes$ as the Kronecker tensor product, and $\left<\cdot,\cdot\right>$ for the standard inner product between two vectors. We denote the vector $L^2$ norm as $\Norm{\cdot}_2$, and the vector or function $L_{\infty}$ norm as $\Norm{\cdot}_{\infty}$. Finally, we denote the set of continuous functions $f(\cdot):\sR^D\to\sR$ possessing continuous derivatives of order up to and including $r$ by $\fC^{r}(\sR^D)$, the space of bounded measurable functions by $\fB_b(\sR^D)$, and the space of bounded continuous functions by $\fC_b(\sR^D)$.

Two-layer Neural Networks and Loss Function
We consider the fundamental empirical risk minimization problem given by the quadratic loss, a standard and widely applicable objective. The prediction function's dependence on parameters is modeled by a two-layer NN with $m$ hidden neurons. More precisely, $\vtheta=\mathrm{vec}(\{\vq_r\}_{r=1}^m)$, where for each $r\in[m]$, $\vq_r:=(a_r,\vw_r^{\T})^\T$, and the bias term $b_r$ can be conveniently incorporated by expanding $\vx$ and $\vw_r$ appropriately.

Dropout
Given a fixed learning rate $\eps>0$, then at the $N$-th iteration where $t_N:=N\eps$, a scaling vector $\veta_N \in \sR^{m}$ is sampled with independent random coordinates. We observe that $\{\veta_N\}_{N\geq 1}$ is an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence with $\Exp \veta_N=\vone$. With slight and standard abuse of notations, the $\sigma$-fields $\fF_N:=\left\{\sigma(\veta_1, \veta_2, \cdots \veta_N)\right\}$ form a natural filtration. We then apply dropout to the two-layer NNs by computing the modified prediction, and we denote the empirical risk associated with dropout accordingly. We observe that the parameters at the $N$-th step are updated according to a clear and defined rule. Finally, we denote hereafter a simplified error term for all $i\in[n]$.

Stochastic Modified Equations for Dropout

In this critical section, we approximate the iterative process of dropout in the weak sense, providing a continuous lens through which to view the discrete algorithm.

Modified Loss

Experiments are conducted on datasets MNIST [11], CIFAR-100 [12] and Multi30k [13], and on NN structures: fully-connected neural networks (FNNs), ResNet-20 [14] and transformer [15].

2 Related works

Recent work aims to understand the regularization effect of dropout. [16] shows dropout performs a form of adaptive regularization in linear regression and logistic problems. [17] proposes a PAC-Bayesian bound, while [18, 19] derive Rademacher-complexity-type error bounds for dropout. [20] demonstrates dropout training with logistic loss achieves ε-suboptimality in test error within O(1/ε) iterations. [7] establishes that dropout enhances flatness of the loss landscape and facilitates condensation through an additional regularization term.

Continuous formulations have been used to study the dynamical behavior of stochastic algorithms. [8, 21] present a mathematical formulation of the SME framework for a wide class of stochastic algorithms. [22] adopts a semigroup approach to investigate SGD and online PCA dynamics. [23] derives SME approximations for adaptive stochastic algorithms including RMSprop and Adam, and provides experimental verification of square root scaling rules from SMEs.

The association between flatness of minima and improved generalization ability has been observed [24, 25, 26]. SGD is shown to preferentially select flat minima, especially under large learning rates and small batch sizes [25, 26, 27]. [28, 29] attribute such enhancement of flatness by SGD to similarity between the covariance of the noise and the Hessian of the loss function. [4] reveals an inverse variance–flatness relation within SGD dynamics. [5, 30] unveil the Hessian-variance alignment property of SGD noise.

3 Preliminary

Notations and definitions used in the theoretical analysis are presented. The experimental settings are more general than the counterparts in the theoretical analysis.

3.1 Notations
A special vector (1,1,1,...,1)^T is denoted by vone. n is the number of input samples and m is the width of the NN. [n]={1,2,...,n}. ⊗ denotes the Kronecker tensor product, and ⟨·,·⟩ for standard inner product. Vector L^2 norm is denoted as ||·||_2, vector or function L_∞ norm as ||·||_∞. C^r(R^D) denotes the set of continuous functions f(·):R^D→R possessing continuous derivatives of order up to and including r. B_b(R^D) denotes the space of bounded measurable functions. C_b(R^D) denotes the space of bounded continuous functions.

3.2 Two-layer neural networks and loss function
The empirical risk minimization problem is given by the quadratic loss:
min_θ R_S(θ) = (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n (f_θ(x_i) - y_i)^2,
where S:={(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n is the training sample, f_θ(x) is the prediction function, θ are the parameters. Their dependence is modeled by a two-layer NN with m hidden neurons:
f_θ(x) := Σ_{r=1}^{m} a_r σ(w_r^T x),
where x∈R^d, θ=vec(θ_a, θ_w)∈R^D, with D:=m(d+1). θ is the set of parameters with θ_a=vec({a_r}_{r=1}^{m}), θ_w=vec({w_r}_{r=1}^{m}). σ(·) is the activation function. Precisely, θ=vec({q_r}_{r=1}^m), where for each r∈[m], q_r:=(a_r, w_r^T)^T. The bias term b_r can be incorporated by expanding x and w_r to (x^T,1)^T and (w_r^T,b_r)^T.

3.3 Dropout
Given fixed learning rate ε>0, at the N-th iteration where t_N:=Nε, a scaling vector η_N ∈ R^{m} is sampled with independent random coordinates: For each k∈[m],
(η_N)_k = { 1/p with probability p, 0 with probability 1-p }.
{η_N}_{N≥1} is an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence with E η_N = vone. The σ-fields F_N:={σ(η_1, η_2, ... η_N)} form a natural filtration.
Dropout is applied to the two-layer NNs by computing
f_θ(x;η):=Σ_{r=1}^m (η)_r a_r σ(w_r^T x).
The empirical risk associated with dropout is denoted by
R_S^drop(θ;η) := (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n (f_θ(x_i;η)-y_i)^2 = (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n ( Σ_{r=1}^m (η)_r a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) - y_i )^2.
The parameters at the N-th step are updated as:
θ_N = θ_{N-1} - ε ∇_θ R_S^drop( θ_{N-1}; η_N ), (1)
where θ_0:=θ(0). For all i∈[n], denote
e_i^N := e_i(θ_{N-1};η_N) := f_{θ_{N-1}}(x_i; η_N) - y_i.

4 Stochastic modified equations for dropout

The iterative process of dropout (1) is approximated in the weak sense.

4.1 Modified loss
The dropout iteration (1) can be written as
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) = -(ε/n) Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N ∇_θ e_i^N.
Since θ=vec({q_r}_{r=1}^m)=vec({(a_r, w_r)}_{r=1}^m), then given θ_{N-1}, for each k∈[m], the expectation of the increment restricted to q_k reads
E_{θ_{N-1}}[ Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N ∇_{q_k} e_i^N ] = E_{θ_{N-1}}[ Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N (η_N)_k ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ]
= Σ_{i=1}^n e_i ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{i=1}^n a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ),
where for simplicity denote
e_i := e_i(θ) := Σ_{r=1}^m a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) - y_i.
Compared with e_i^N, e_i does not depend on the random variable η_N.
The modified loss L_S(·):R^D→R for dropout is defined as:
L_S(θ) := (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^2 + ((1-p)/(2np)) Σ_{i=1}^n Σ_{r=1}^m a_r^2 σ(w_r^T x_i)^2, (2)
because as θ_{N-1} is given, by taking conditional expectation, its increment reads
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε E_{θ_{N-1}}[ ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) ] = -ε ∇_θ L_S(θ)|_{θ=θ_{N-1}}.
In the sense of expectations, {θ_N}_{N≥0} follows close to the gradient descent (GD) trajectory of L_S(θ) with fixed learning rate ε.

4.2 Stochastic modified equations
From Section 4.1, given θ_{N-1},
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε ∇_θ L_S(θ)|_{θ=θ_{N-1}} + √ε V(θ_{N-1}), (3)
where L_S(·):R^D→R is the modified loss defined in (2), and V(·):R^D→R^D is a D-dimensional random vector. Given θ_{N-1}, V(θ_{N-1}) has mean zero and covariance ε Σ(θ_{N-1}), where Σ(·):R^D→R^{D×D}, whose expression is deferred to Section 5.1.

Consider the stochastic differential equation (SDE),
dΘ_t = b(Θ_t) dt + σ(Θ_t) dW_t, Θ_0=Θ(0), (4)
where W_t is a standard D-dimensional Brownian motion. Its Euler–Maruyama discretization with step size ε>0 at the N-th step reads
Θ_{εN} = Θ_{ε(N-1)} + ε b( Θ_{ε(N-1)} ) + √ε σ( Θ_{ε(N-1)} ) Z_N,
where Z_N∼N(0, I_D) and Θ_0=Θ(0). If we set
b(Θ) := -∇_Θ L_S(Θ), (5)
σ(Θ) := √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2}, (6)
Θ_0 := θ_0, (7)
then we would expect (4) to be an approximation of (3) with time identification t=εN. Based on [8], approximations in the weak sense are used since the path of dropout and the corresponding SDE are driven by noises sampled in different spaces. The rate of weak convergence and an appropriate class of test functions are considered.
The following set of smooth functions is introduced:
C_b^M(R^D) = { f ∈ C^M(R^D) | ||f||_{C^M} := Σ_{|β|≤M} ||D^β f||_∞ < ∞ },
where D is the usual differential operator. C_b^M(R^D) is a subset of G(R^D), the class of functions with polynomial growth, chosen as the space of test functions in [8, 31, 23].

To ensure rigor and validity, the following assumption is made:
Assumption 1: There exists T^*>0, such that for any t∈[0, T^*], there exists a unique t-continuous solution Θ_t to SDE (4). Furthermore, for each l ∈ [3], there exists C(T^*,Θ_0)>0, such that
sup_{0≤s≤T^*} E( ||Θ_s(·)||_2^{2l} ) ≤ C(T^*,Θ_0). (8)
Moreover, for the dropout iterations (1), let 0<ε<1, T>0 and set N_{T,ε}:=⌊T/ε⌋. There exists ε_0>0, such that given any learning rate ε≤ε_0, then for all N∈[0:N_{T^*,ε}] and for each l ∈ [3], there exists C(T^*,θ_0,ε_0)>0, such that
sup_{0≤N≤[N_{T^*,ε}]} E( ||θ_N||_2^{2l} ) ≤ C(T^*,θ_0,ε_0). (9)

If G(R^D) is chosen to be the test functions in [21], then similar relations to (8) and (9) shall be imposed, except that in our cases, only the second, fourth and sixth moments are required to be uniformly bounded, while in their cases, all 2l-moments are required for l≥1.

Definition 1: The SDE (4) is an order α weak approximation to the dropout (1), if for every g∈ C_b^M(R^{D}), there exists C>0 and ε_0>0, such that given any ε≤ε_0 and T≤T^*, then for all N∈[N_{T,ε}],
| E g(Θ_{ε N}) - E g(θ_N) | ≤ C(T^*, g, ε_0) ε^α. (10)

Theorem 1* (Informal): Fix time T≤T^* and learning rate ε>0. If we choose
b(Θ) = -∇_Θ L_S(Θ),
σ(Θ) = √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2},
then for all t∈[0, T], the stochastic process Θ_t satisfying
dΘ_t = b(Θ_t) dt + σ(Θ_t) dW_t,
is an order-1 approximation of dropout (1). If we choose instead
b(Θ) = -∇_Θ ( L_S(Θ) + (ε/4) ||∇_Θ L_S(Θ)||_2^2 ),
σ(Θ) = √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2},
then Θ_t is an order-2 approximation.

These findings reproduce the explicit regularization effect attributed to dropout [6, 7]. This regularization effect modifies the expected training objective from R_S(θ) to L_S(θ). The regularization effect stems from the stochasticity of dropout. Unlike SGD, where noise arises from stochastic selection of training samples, dropout introduces noise through stochastic removal of parameters. The focus is on how such stochasticity impacts learning results.

5 The effect of the noise structure on flatness

The expression of the noise structure arising from dropout is examined.

5.1 Explicit form of the dropout noise structure
The expression for Σ is presented. Covariance of ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) equals Σ(θ_{N-1}). Denote
Σ_{kr}(θ_{N-1}) := Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_r} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) ),
then
Σ = [ Σ_{11} Σ_{12} ... Σ_{1m}; Σ_{21} Σ_{22} ... Σ_{2m}; ... ; Σ_{m1} Σ_{m2} ... Σ_{mm} ].
For each k ∈ [m],
Σ_{kk}(θ_{N-1}) = Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) )
= (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p^2 - 1/p) Σ_{k'=1, k'≠k}^m ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ),
where e_{i,\k} := e_{i,\k}(θ) := Σ_{l=1, l≠k}^m a_l σ(w_l^T x_i) - y_i.
For each k, r ∈ [m] with k ≠ r,
Σ_{kr}(θ_{N-1}) = Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_r} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) )
= (1/p - 1) Σ_{k'=1, k'≠k, k'≠r}^m ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k,\r} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) + (1/p) a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k,\r} + a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) + (1/p) a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ),
where e_{i,\k,\r} := e_{i,\k,\r}(θ) := Σ_{l=1, l≠k, l≠r}^m a_l σ(w_l^T x_i) - y_i.
For the case p=1, dropout degenerates to GD, and the covariance matrix degenerates to a zero matrix, Σ=0_{D×D}.

5.2 Experimental results on the dropout noise structure
The structural similarity between the covariance and the Hessian in terms of both Hessian-variance alignment relations and Inverse variance-flatness relations is shown. Intuitively, the structural similarity between the Hessian and covariance matrix is shown below:
H(θ) ≈ (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} [ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) ⊗ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^{m} ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ⊗ ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ],
Σ(θ) ≈ (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} [ l_{i,1} ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) ⊗ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) + l_{i,2} ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^{m} ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ⊗ ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ],
where H(θ):=∇^2_θ L_S(θ), and l_{i,1}:= (e_i)^2 + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^m a_r^2 σ(w_r^T x_i)^2, l_{i,2}:= (e_i)^2. The expression for the covariance matrix differs from the counterpart in Section 5.1 because certain assumptions, as outlined in [5], have been imposed. With this established structural similarity, the empirical investigation concerning the relationship between the Hessian and the covariance proceeds.

5.2.1 Random data collection methods
Two types of dynamical datasets collected during dropout training to study the noise structure are introduced. These datasets are different from the training sample S.

Random trajectory data. The training process of NNs usually consists of two phases: the fast convergence phase and the exploration phase [32]. In the exploration phase, the network is often considered near a minimum, and parameter movement is largely affected by the noise structure. Based on [4], parameter sets D_para:={θ_i}_{i=1}^{N} are collected from N consecutive training steps in the exploration phase, where θ_i is the network parameter set at the i-th sample step. This sampling method requires many training steps, so model parameters often have large fluctuations. To improve sampling accuracy, another type of random data is proposed.

Random gradient data. The network is trained until the loss is near zero and the training process is frozen. Then N realizations of the dropout variable are sampled to get the random gradient dataset, D_grad:={g_i}_{i=1}^{N}. The i-th sample point g_i is obtained as: i) A realization of the dropout variable η_i under a given dropout rate is generated; ii) The gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters is computed, denoted by g_i(·):=∇ R_S^drop(·;η_i). Each element in D_grad represents an evolution direction of network parameters, determined by the dropout variable. Studying the structure of D_grad can help understand how dropout noise impacts the training process.

5.2.2 Hessian-Variance alignment
A metric Tr(H_i Σ_i) established to be valuable [5] in assessing the degree of alignment between the noise structure and curvature of the loss landscape is employed, where Tr(·) stands for the trace of a square matrix. Σ_i is the covariance matrix of D_grad sampled at the i-th-step. H_i is the Hessian of the loss function at the i-th-step.

To investigate the Hessian-Variance alignment relation, an isotropic noise termed Σ̄_i is constructed by averaging: Σ̄_i = (Tr(Σ_i)/D) I_{D×D}, where D is the total number of parameters, I_{D×D} is the identity matrix. Σ̄_i is employed for comparative purposes. As shown in Fig. 1, under different learning rates and dropout rates, Tr(H_i Σ_i) significantly exceeds Tr(H_i Σ̄_i) throughout the whole training process, indicating dropout-induced noise possesses an anisotropic structure that aligns well with the Hessian across all directions. Due to computational limitations, this experiment limits the trace calculation of Σ̄_i to a subset of parameters, which can be regarded as the projection of the Hessian and the noise into some specific directions.

5.2.3 Inverse variance-flatness relation
The alignment relation also implies the inverse variance-flatness relation: the noise variance is large along the sharp direction of the loss landscape, and small along the flat direction. This relation is verified by two sets of experiments. Two different approaches to characterize the flatness of loss landscape and the covariance of noise from the random trajectory data D_para and random gradient data D_grad are presented, and the inverse variance-flatness relation is numerically demonstrated. For convenience, D refers to either D_para or D_grad depending on context, so is the case for their corresponding covariance Σ and Hessian H. Definitions of noise variance and interval flatness are given.

Definition 2 (noise variance): For dataset D and its covariance Σ, denote λ_i(Σ) as the i-th eigenvalue of Σ and its corresponding eigen direction as v_i(Σ). Then λ_i(Σ) is termed the noise variance of D at the eigen direction v_i(Σ).

Definition 3 (interval flatness): For a local minimum θ_0^*, the loss function profile R_v along direction v reads: R_v(δ) ≡ R_S(θ_0^* + δ v), where δ represents the distance moved in the v direction. The interval flatness F_v is defined as the width of the region within which R_v(δ) ≤ 2 R_v(0). F_v is determined by finding two closest points θ_v^l < 0 and θ_v^r > 0 on each side of the minimum that satisfy R_v(θ_v^l) = R_v(θ_v^r) = 2 R_v(0). The interval flatness is defined as: F_v ≡ θ_v^r - θ_v^l. (11)
The experiments show the result is not sensitive to the selection of the pre-factor 2. A larger value of F_v means a flatter landscape in the direction v.

PCA is used to study weight variations when training accuracy is nearly 100%. Networks are trained with full-batch GD for different learning rates and dropout rates under the same random seed. When the loss is small enough, parameters or gradients of parameters are sampled N times (N=3000 for this experiment) and the relationship between {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N and {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N for both weight dataset D_para and gradient dataset D_grad is studied.

For different learning rates and dropout rates, Fig. 2(a, b) reveal an inverse relationship between the interval flatness of the loss landscape {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N and the noise variance represented by the PCA spectrum {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N. A power-law relationship can be established between {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N and {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N. In the low flatness region, dropout-induced noise exhibits a large variance. As the loss landscape transitions into the high flatness regime, the linear relationship between variance and flatness becomes more evident. These findings demonstrate the inverse relation between variance and flatness. Definitions of projected variance and Hessian flatness are given.

Definition 4 (projected variance): For a given direction v∈R^D and dataset D={θ_i}_{i=1}^{N}, where θ_i ∈ R^D, the inner product of v and θ_i is denoted by Proj_v(θ_i):=⟨θ_i, v⟩. The projected variance for D at the direction v is defined as:
Var(Proj_v(D)) = ( Σ_{i=1}^{N} (Proj_v(θ_i) - μ)^2 ) / N,
where μ is the mean value of {Proj_v(θ_i)}_{i=1}^{N}.

Definition 5 (Hessian flatness): For Hessian H, denote λ_i(H) as the i-th eigenvalue of H corresponding to the eigenvector v_i(H). λ_i(H) is termed the Hessian flatness along direction v_i(H).

The eigenvalues of the Hessian evaluated at a local minimum often serve as indicators of the flatness of the loss landscape; larger eigenvalues correspond to sharper directions. The interplay between the eigenvalues of Hessian H at the final stage of training and the projected variance of dropout at each corresponding eigen direction, i.e., λ_i(H) vs. {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N, is analyzed. Parameters or gradients of parameters are sampled N times (N=1000 for this experiment), and the relationship between {λ_i(H)}_{i=1}^{N} and {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N for both the parameter dataset D_para and the gradient dataset D_grad is examined.

Under various dropout rates and learning rates, Fig. 2(c, d) establishes a consistent power-law relationship between {λ_i(H)}_{i=1}^{N} and {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N. This relationship remains robust irrespective of the choice between parameter dataset D_para or gradient dataset D_grad. The positive correlation observed between the Hessian flatness and the projection variance provides insights into the structural characteristics of dropout-induced noise. These characteristics have the potential to facilitate escape from sharp minima and enhance generalization capabilities of NNs. Fig. 2 highlights the distinct linear structure exhibited by gradient sampling compared to parameter sampling, which corroborates discussions in Section 5.2.1.

6 Conclusion

The main contribution is twofold. First, stochastic modified equations that provide a weak approximation for the dynamics of the dropout algorithm for two-layer NNs are derived. Second, it is demonstrated that dropout exhibits the inverse variance-flatness relation and the Hessian-variance alignment relation through extensive empirical analysis, which is consistent with SGD. These relations are widely recognized to be beneficial for finding flatter minima, implying dropout acts as an implicit regularizer that enhances generalization abilities.

Given the broad applicability of the methodologies employed in the proof, an aim is to extend the formulations of SMEs to a wider class of stochastic algorithms applied to NNs with different architectures. Such an extension could help better understand the role of stochastic algorithms in NN training. Moreover, the SME framework could offer a promising approach to examining underlying mechanisms that explain the observed inverse variance-flatness relation and Hessian-variance relation and beyond.

References
[1] Hinton et al., 2012; [2] Srivastava et al., 2014; [3] Keskar et al., 2016; [4] Feng et al., 2021; [5] Zhu et al., 2018; [6] Wei et al., 2020; [7] Zhang et al., 2022; [8] Li et al., 2017; [9] Keskar et al., 2016; [10] Neyshabur et al., 2017; [11] LeCun et al., 1998; [12] Krizhevsky, 2009; [13] Elliott et al., 2016; [14] He et al., 2016; [15] Vaswani et al., 2017; [16] Wager et al., 2013; [17] McAllester, 2013; [18] Wan et al., 2013; [19] Mou et al., 2018; [20] Mianjy et al., 2020; [21] Li et al., 2019; [22] Feng et al., 2017; [23] Malladi et al., 2022; [24] Li et al., 2017; [25] Jastrzębski et al., 2017; [26] Jastrzębski et al., 2018; [27] Wu et al., 2018; [28] Papyan, 2018; [29] Papyan, 2019; [30] Wu et al., 2022; [31] Kloeden & Platen, 2011; [32] Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby, 2017.

Stochastic Modified Equations and Dynamics of Dropout Algorithm

Abstract

Dropout is a regularization technique used in training neural networks. This work derives stochastic modified equations to analyze the dynamics of dropout, approximating its discrete iteration process with a class of stochastic differential equations. The noise structure of the derived stochastic modified equation for dropout is studied. By noting a structural resemblance between the Hessian and covariance through several intuitive approximations, the universal presence of an inverse variance-flatness relation and a Hessian-variance relation is empirically demonstrated throughout the dropout training process. These findings contribute to understanding dropout's tendency to locate flatter minima.

1 Introduction

Dropout is used with gradient-descent-based algorithms for training neural networks (NNs) [1, 2]. It randomly removes a subset of neurons during training; the output of each neuron is multiplied by a random variable that takes the value 1/p with probability p and zero otherwise, sampled independently at each feedforward operation.

The noise structure introduced by stochastic algorithms is important for understanding their training behaviors. Recent work shows the noise structure in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) plays a role in exploring flatter solutions [3, 4, 5]. Training with dropout introduces noise with a specific architecture, acting as an implicit regularizer [1, 2, 6, 7, 5].

This paper first employs the framework of stochastic modified equations (SMEs) [8] to approximate in distribution the training dynamics of the dropout algorithm applied to two-layer NNs. This quantifies the leading order dynamics of dropout and its variants. The covariance structure of the noise generated by dropout's stochasticity is calculated. This covariance structure is used to understand why NNs trained by dropout tend to possess better generalization abilities from the perspective of flatness [9, 10].

A hypothesis is that the flatness-improving ability of dropout noise is attributed to its alignment with the structure of the loss landscape, based on similarity between the explicit forms of the Hessian and the dropout covariance under intuitive approximations. To investigate this, empirical studies are conducted using three different approaches to assess the similarity between the flatness of the loss landscape and the noise structure induced by dropout at the obtained minima. All approaches consistently demonstrate two relationships: i) Inverse variance-flatness relation: The noise is larger at the sharper direction of the loss landscape; ii) Hessian-variance alignment relation: The Hessian of the loss landscape at the found minima aligns with the noise covariance matrix. These two relations are compatible with each other in that they collectively contribute to the training algorithm's ability to identify flatter minima. Experiments are conducted on datasets MNIST [11], CIFAR-100 [12] and Multi30k [13], and on NN structures: fully-connected neural networks (FNNs), ResNet-20 [14] and transformer [15].

2 Related works

Recent work aims to understand the regularization effect of dropout. [16] shows dropout performs a form of adaptive regularization in linear regression and logistic problems. [17] proposes a PAC-Bayesian bound, while [18, 19] derive Rademacher-complexity-type error bounds for dropout. [20] demonstrates dropout training with logistic loss achieves ε-suboptimality in test error within O(1/ε) iterations. [7] establishes that dropout enhances flatness of the loss landscape and facilitates condensation through an additional regularization term.

Continuous formulations have been used to study the dynamical behavior of stochastic algorithms. [8, 21] present a mathematical formulation of the SME framework for a wide class of stochastic algorithms. [22] adopts a semigroup approach to investigate SGD and online PCA dynamics. [23] derives SME approximations for adaptive stochastic algorithms including RMSprop and Adam, and provides experimental verification of square root scaling rules from SMEs.

The association between flatness of minima and improved generalization ability has been observed [24, 25, 26]. SGD is shown to preferentially select flat minima, especially under large learning rates and small batch sizes [25, 26, 27]. [28, 29] attribute such enhancement of flatness by SGD to similarity between the covariance of the noise and the Hessian of the loss function. [4] reveals an inverse variance–flatness relation within SGD dynamics. [5, 30] unveil the Hessian-variance alignment property of SGD noise.

3 Preliminary

Notations and definitions used in the theoretical analysis are presented. The experimental settings are more general than the counterparts in the theoretical analysis.

3.1 Notations
A special vector (1,1,1,...,1)^T is denoted by vone. n is the number of input samples and m is the width of the NN. [n]={1,2,...,n}. ⊗ denotes the Kronecker tensor product, and ⟨·,·⟩ for standard inner product. Vector L^2 norm is denoted as ||·||_2, vector or function L_∞ norm as ||·||_∞. C^r(R^D) denotes the set of continuous functions f(·):R^D→R possessing continuous derivatives of order up to and including r. B_b(R^D) denotes the space of bounded measurable functions. C_b(R^D) denotes the space of bounded continuous functions.

3.2 Two-layer neural networks and loss function
The empirical risk minimization problem is given by the quadratic loss:
min_θ R_S(θ) = (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n (f_θ(x_i) - y_i)^2,
where S:={(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n is the training sample, f_θ(x) is the prediction function, θ are the parameters. Their dependence is modeled by a two-layer NN with m hidden neurons:
f_θ(x) := Σ_{r=1}^{m} a_r σ(w_r^T x),
where x∈R^d, θ=vec(θ_a, θ_w)∈R^D, with D:=m(d+1). θ is the set of parameters with θ_a=vec({a_r}_{r=1}^{m}), θ_w=vec({w_r}_{r=1}^{m}). σ(·) is the activation function. Precisely, θ=vec({q_r}_{r=1}^m), where for each r∈[m], q_r:=(a_r, w_r^T)^T. The bias term b_r can be incorporated by expanding x and w_r to (x^T,1)^T and (w_r^T,b_r)^T.

3.3 Dropout
Given fixed learning rate ε>0, at the N-th iteration where t_N:=Nε, a scaling vector η_N ∈ R^{m} is sampled with independent random coordinates: For each k∈[m],
(η_N)_k = { 1/p with probability p, 0 with probability 1-p }.
{η_N}_{N≥1} is an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence with E η_N = vone. The σ-fields F_N:={σ(η_1, η_2, ... η_N)} form a natural filtration.
Dropout is applied to the two-layer NNs by computing
f_θ(x;η):=Σ_{r=1}^m (η)_r a_r σ(w_r^T x).
The empirical risk associated with dropout is denoted by
R_S^drop(θ;η) := (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n (f_θ(x_i;η)-y_i)^2 = (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n ( Σ_{r=1}^m (η)_r a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) - y_i )^2.
The parameters at the N-th step are updated as:
θ_N = θ_{N-1} - ε ∇_θ R_S^drop( θ_{N-1}; η_N ), (1)
where θ_0:=θ(0). For all i∈[n], denote
e_i^N := e_i(θ_{N-1};η_N) := f_{θ_{N-1}}(x_i; η_N) - y_i.

4 Stochastic modified equations for dropout

The iterative process of dropout (1) is approximated in the weak sense.

4.1 Modified loss
The dropout iteration (1) can be written as
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) = -(ε/n) Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N ∇_θ e_i^N.
Since θ=vec({q_r}_{r=1}^m)=vec({(a_r, w_r)}_{r=1}^m), then given θ_{N-1}, for each k∈[m], the expectation of the increment restricted to q_k reads
E_{θ_{N-1}}[ Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N ∇_{q_k} e_i^N ] = E_{θ_{N-1}}[ Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^N (η_N)_k ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ]
= Σ_{i=1}^n e_i ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{i=1}^n a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ),
where for simplicity denote
e_i := e_i(θ) := Σ_{r=1}^m a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) - y_i.
Compared with e_i^N, e_i does not depend on the random variable η_N.
The modified loss L_S(·):R^D→R for dropout is defined as:
L_S(θ) := (1/(2n)) Σ_{i=1}^n e_i^2 + ((1-p)/(2np)) Σ_{i=1}^n Σ_{r=1}^m a_r^2 σ(w_r^T x_i)^2, (2)
because as θ_{N-1} is given, by taking conditional expectation, its increment reads
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε E_{θ_{N-1}}[ ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) ] = -ε ∇_θ L_S(θ)|_{θ=θ_{N-1}}.
In the sense of expectations, {θ_N}_{N≥0} follows close to the gradient descent (GD) trajectory of L_S(θ) with fixed learning rate ε.

4.2 Stochastic modified equations
From Section 4.1, given θ_{N-1},
θ_N - θ_{N-1} = -ε ∇_θ L_S(θ)|_{θ=θ_{N-1}} + √ε V(θ_{N-1}), (3)
where L_S(·):R^D→R is the modified loss defined in (2), and V(·):R^D→R^D is a D-dimensional random vector. Given θ_{N-1}, V(θ_{N-1}) has mean zero and covariance ε Σ(θ_{N-1}), where Σ(·):R^D→R^{D×D}, whose expression is deferred to Section 5.1.

Consider the stochastic differential equation (SDE),
dΘ_t = b(Θ_t) dt + σ(Θ_t) dW_t, Θ_0=Θ(0), (4)
where W_t is a standard D-dimensional Brownian motion. Its Euler–Maruyama discretization with step size ε>0 at the N-th step reads
Θ_{εN} = Θ_{ε(N-1)} + ε b( Θ_{ε(N-1)} ) + √ε σ( Θ_{ε(N-1)} ) Z_N,
where Z_N∼N(0, I_D) and Θ_0=Θ(0). If we set
b(Θ) := -∇_Θ L_S(Θ), (5)
σ(Θ) := √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2}, (6)
Θ_0 := θ_0, (7)
then we would expect (4) to be an approximation of (3) with time identification t=εN. Based on [8], approximations in the weak sense are used since the path of dropout and the corresponding SDE are driven by noises sampled in different spaces. The rate of weak convergence and an appropriate class of test functions are considered.
The following set of smooth functions is introduced:
C_b^M(R^D) = { f ∈ C^M(R^D) | ||f||_{C^M} := Σ_{|β|≤M} ||D^β f||_∞ < ∞ },
where D is the usual differential operator. C_b^M(R^D) is a subset of G(R^D), the class of functions with polynomial growth, chosen as the space of test functions in [8, 31, 23].

To ensure rigor and validity, the following assumption is made:
Assumption 1: There exists T^*>0, such that for any t∈[0, T^*], there exists a unique t-continuous solution Θ_t to SDE (4). Furthermore, for each l ∈ [3], there exists C(T^*,Θ_0)>0, such that
sup_{0≤s≤T^*} E( ||Θ_s(·)||_2^{2l} ) ≤ C(T^*,Θ_0). (8)
Moreover, for the dropout iterations (1), let 0<ε<1, T>0 and set N_{T,ε}:=⌊T/ε⌋. There exists ε_0>0, such that given any learning rate ε≤ε_0, then for all N∈[0:N_{T^*,ε}] and for each l ∈ [3], there exists C(T^*,θ_0,ε_0)>0, such that
sup_{0≤N≤[N_{T^*,ε}]} E( ||θ_N||_2^{2l} ) ≤ C(T^*,θ_0,ε_0). (9)

If G(R^D) is chosen to be the test functions in [21], then similar relations to (8) and (9) shall be imposed, except that in our cases, only the second, fourth and sixth moments are required to be uniformly bounded, while in their cases, all 2l-moments are required for l≥1.

Definition 1: The SDE (4) is an order α weak approximation to the dropout (1), if for every g∈ C_b^M(R^{D}), there exists C>0 and ε_0>0, such that given any ε≤ε_0 and T≤T^*, then for all N∈[N_{T,ε}],
| E g(Θ_{ε N}) - E g(θ_N) | ≤ C(T^*, g, ε_0) ε^α. (10)

Theorem 1* (Informal): Fix time T≤T^* and learning rate ε>0. If we choose
b(Θ) = -∇_Θ L_S(Θ),
σ(Θ) = √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2},
then for all t∈[0, T], the stochastic process Θ_t satisfying
dΘ_t = b(Θ_t) dt + σ(Θ_t) dW_t,
is an order-1 approximation of dropout (1). If we choose instead
b(Θ) = -∇_Θ ( L_S(Θ) + (ε/4) ||∇_Θ L_S(Θ)||_2^2 ),
σ(Θ) = √ε ( Σ(Θ) )^{1/2},
then Θ_t is an order-2 approximation.

These findings reproduce the explicit regularization effect attributed to dropout [6, 7]. This regularization effect modifies the expected training objective from R_S(θ) to L_S(θ). The regularization effect stems from the stochasticity of dropout. Unlike SGD, where noise arises from stochastic selection of training samples, dropout introduces noise through stochastic removal of parameters. The focus is on how such stochasticity impacts learning results.

5 The effect of the noise structure on flatness

The expression of the noise structure arising from dropout is examined.

5.1 Explicit form of the dropout noise structure
The expression for Σ is presented. Covariance of ∇_θ R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) equals Σ(θ_{N-1}). Denote
Σ_{kr}(θ_{N-1}) := Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_r} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) ),
then
Σ = [ Σ_{11} Σ_{12} ... Σ_{1m}; Σ_{21} Σ_{22} ... Σ_{2m}; ... ; Σ_{m1} Σ_{m2} ... Σ_{mm} ].
For each k ∈ [m],
Σ_{kk}(θ_{N-1}) = Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) )
= (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p^2 - 1/p) Σ_{k'=1, k'≠k}^m ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ),
where e_{i,\k} := e_{i,\k}(θ) := Σ_{l=1, l≠k}^m a_l σ(w_l^T x_i) - y_i.
For each k, r ∈ [m] with k ≠ r,
Σ_{kr}(θ_{N-1}) = Cov( ∇_{q_k} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N), ∇_{q_r} R_S^drop(θ_{N-1}; η_N) )
= (1/p - 1) Σ_{k'=1, k'≠k, k'≠r}^m ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_{k'} σ(w_{k'}^T x_i) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k,\r} + (1/p) a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) + (1/p) a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) )
+ (1/p - 1) ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ∇_{q_k} ( a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) ) ) ⊗ ( (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n ( e_{i,\k,\r} + a_k σ(w_k^T x_i) + (1/p) a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ),
where e_{i,\k,\r} := e_{i,\k,\r}(θ) := Σ_{l=1, l≠k, l≠r}^m a_l σ(w_l^T x_i) - y_i.
For the case p=1, dropout degenerates to GD, and the covariance matrix degenerates to a zero matrix, Σ=0_{D×D}.

5.2 Experimental results on the dropout noise structure
The structural similarity between the covariance and the Hessian in terms of both Hessian-variance alignment relations and Inverse variance-flatness relations is shown. Intuitively, the structural similarity between the Hessian and covariance matrix is shown below:
H(θ) ≈ (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} [ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) ⊗ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^{m} ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ⊗ ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ],
Σ(θ) ≈ (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} [ l_{i,1} ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) ⊗ ∇_θ f_θ(x_i) + l_{i,2} ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^{m} ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ⊗ ∇_{q_r} ( a_r σ(w_r^T x_i) ) ],
where H(θ):=∇^2_θ L_S(θ), and l_{i,1}:= (e_i)^2 + ((1-p)/p) Σ_{r=1}^m a_r^2 σ(w_r^T x_i)^2, l_{i,2}:= (e_i)^2. The expression for the covariance matrix differs from the counterpart in Section 5.1 because certain assumptions, as outlined in [5], have been imposed. With this established structural similarity, the empirical investigation concerning the relationship between the Hessian and the covariance proceeds.

5.2.1 Random data collection methods
Two types of dynamical datasets collected during dropout training to study the noise structure are introduced. These datasets are different from the training sample S.

Random trajectory data. The training process of NNs usually consists of two phases: the fast convergence phase and the exploration phase [32]. In the exploration phase, the network is often considered near a minimum, and parameter movement is largely affected by the noise structure. Based on [4], parameter sets D_para:={θ_i}_{i=1}^{N} are collected from N consecutive training steps in the exploration phase, where θ_i is the network parameter set at the i-th sample step. This sampling method requires many training steps, so model parameters often have large fluctuations. To improve sampling accuracy, another type of random data is proposed.

Random gradient data. The network is trained until the loss is near zero and the training process is frozen. Then N realizations of the dropout variable are sampled to get the random gradient dataset, D_grad:={g_i}_{i=1}^{N}. The i-th sample point g_i is obtained as: i) A realization of the dropout variable η_i under a given dropout rate is generated; ii) The gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters is computed, denoted by g_i(·):=∇ R_S^drop(·;η_i). Each element in D_grad represents an evolution direction of network parameters, determined by the dropout variable. Studying the structure of D_grad can help understand how dropout noise impacts the training process.

5.2.2 Hessian-Variance alignment
A metric Tr(H_i Σ_i) established to be valuable [5] in assessing the degree of alignment between the noise structure and curvature of the loss landscape is employed, where Tr(·) stands for the trace of a square matrix. Σ_i is the covariance matrix of D_grad sampled at the i-th-step. H_i is the Hessian of the loss function at the i-th-step.

To investigate the Hessian-Variance alignment relation, an isotropic noise termed Σ̄_i is constructed by averaging: Σ̄_i = (Tr(Σ_i)/D) I_{D×D}, where D is the total number of parameters, I_{D×D} is the identity matrix. Σ̄_i is employed for comparative purposes. As shown in Fig. 1, under different learning rates and dropout rates, Tr(H_i Σ_i) significantly exceeds Tr(H_i Σ̄_i) throughout the whole training process, indicating dropout-induced noise possesses an anisotropic structure that aligns well with the Hessian across all directions. Due to computational limitations, this experiment limits the trace calculation of Σ̄_i to a subset of parameters, which can be regarded as the projection of the Hessian and the noise into some specific directions.

5.2.3 Inverse variance-flatness relation
The alignment relation also implies the inverse variance-flatness relation: the noise variance is large along the sharp direction of the loss landscape, and small along the flat direction. This relation is verified by two sets of experiments. Two different approaches to characterize the flatness of loss landscape and the covariance of noise from the random trajectory data D_para and random gradient data D_grad are presented, and the inverse variance-flatness relation is numerically demonstrated. For convenience, D refers to either D_para or D_grad depending on context, so is the case for their corresponding covariance Σ and Hessian H. Definitions of noise variance and interval flatness are given.

Definition 2 (noise variance): For dataset D and its covariance Σ, denote λ_i(Σ) as the i-th eigenvalue of Σ and its corresponding eigen direction as v_i(Σ). Then λ_i(Σ) is termed the noise variance of D at the eigen direction v_i(Σ).

Definition 3 (interval flatness): For a local minimum θ_0^*, the loss function profile R_v along direction v reads: R_v(δ) ≡ R_S(θ_0^* + δ v), where δ represents the distance moved in the v direction. The interval flatness F_v is defined as the width of the region within which R_v(δ) ≤ 2 R_v(0). F_v is determined by finding two closest points θ_v^l < 0 and θ_v^r > 0 on each side of the minimum that satisfy R_v(θ_v^l) = R_v(θ_v^r) = 2 R_v(0). The interval flatness is defined as: F_v ≡ θ_v^r - θ_v^l. (11)
The experiments show the result is not sensitive to the selection of the pre-factor 2. A larger value of F_v means a flatter landscape in the direction v.

PCA is used to study weight variations when training accuracy is nearly 100%. Networks are trained with full-batch GD for different learning rates and dropout rates under the same random seed. When the loss is small enough, parameters or gradients of parameters are sampled N times (N=3000 for this experiment) and the relationship between {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N and {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N for both weight dataset D_para and gradient dataset D_grad is studied.

For different learning rates and dropout rates, Fig. 2(a, b) reveal an inverse relationship between the interval flatness of the loss landscape {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N and the noise variance represented by the PCA spectrum {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N. A power-law relationship can be established between {F_{v_i(Σ)}}_{i=1}^N and {λ_i(Σ)}_{i=1}^N. In the low flatness region, dropout-induced noise exhibits a large variance. As the loss landscape transitions into the high flatness regime, the linear relationship between variance and flatness becomes more evident. These findings demonstrate the inverse relation between variance and flatness. Definitions of projected variance and Hessian flatness are given.

Definition 4 (projected variance): For a given direction v∈R^D and dataset D={θ_i}_{i=1}^{N}, where θ_i ∈ R^D, the inner product of v and θ_i is denoted by Proj_v(θ_i):=⟨θ_i, v⟩. The projected variance for D at the direction v is defined as:
Var(Proj_v(D)) = ( Σ_{i=1}^{N} (Proj_v(θ_i) - μ)^2 ) / N,
where μ is the mean value of {Proj_v(θ_i)}_{i=1}^{N}.

Definition 5 (Hessian flatness): For Hessian H, denote λ_i(H) as the i-th eigenvalue of H corresponding to the eigenvector v_i(H). λ_i(H) is termed the Hessian flatness along direction v_i(H).

The eigenvalues of the Hessian evaluated at a local minimum often serve as indicators of the flatness of the loss landscape; larger eigenvalues correspond to sharper directions. The interplay between the eigenvalues of Hessian H at the final stage of training and the projected variance of dropout at each corresponding eigen direction, i.e., λ_i(H) vs. {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N, is analyzed. Parameters or gradients of parameters are sampled N times (N=1000 for this experiment), and the relationship between {λ_i(H)}_{i=1}^{N} and {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N for both the parameter dataset D_para and the gradient dataset D_grad is examined.

Under various dropout rates and learning rates, Fig. 2(c, d) establishes a consistent power-law relationship between {λ_i(H)}_{i=1}^{N} and {Var(Proj_{v_i(H)}(D))}_{i=1}^N. This relationship remains robust irrespective of the choice between parameter dataset D_para or gradient dataset D_grad. The positive correlation observed between the Hessian flatness and the projection variance provides insights into the structural characteristics of dropout-induced noise. These characteristics have the potential to facilitate escape from sharp minima and enhance generalization capabilities of NNs. Fig. 2 highlights the distinct linear structure exhibited by gradient sampling compared to parameter sampling, which corroborates discussions in Section 5.2.1.

6 Conclusion

The main contribution is twofold. First, stochastic modified equations that provide a weak approximation for the dynamics of the dropout algorithm for two-layer NNs are derived. Second, it is demonstrated that dropout exhibits the inverse variance-flatness relation and the Hessian-variance alignment relation through extensive empirical analysis, which is consistent with SGD. These relations are widely recognized to be beneficial for finding flatter minima, implying dropout acts as an implicit regularizer that enhances generalization abilities.

Given the broad applicability of the methodologies employed in the proof, an aim is to extend the formulations of SMEs to a wider class of stochastic algorithms applied to NNs with different architectures. Such an extension could help better understand the role of stochastic algorithms in NN training. Moreover, the SME framework could offer a promising approach to examining underlying mechanisms that explain the observed inverse variance-flatness relation and Hessian-variance relation and beyond.

References

Title: Graph-level Representation Learning with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures

Abstract:
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn an energy-based model by predicting the latent representation of a target signal y from the latent representation of a context signal x. JEPAs do not require negative or positive samples, which are used in contrastive learning, and avoid overfitting issues associated with generative pretraining. This work proposes a Graph Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Graph-JEPA) for graph-level representation learning. The method uses masked modeling to predict the latent representations of masked subgraphs from the latent representation of a context subgraph. An alternative prediction objective is devised to predict the coordinates of encoded subgraphs on the unit hyperbola in the 2D plane, aiming to endow representations with an implicit hierarchy. Experiments evaluate Graph-JEPA on graph classification, regression, and distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. The code will be made available upon acceptance.

Introduction:
Graph data is common. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a standard solution for processing graph data. Many GNN applications rely on ground-truth labels for training. The cost of labeling graph data is high, leading to interest in unsupervised graph representation learning.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) creates alternative forms of supervision from the input signal. SSL methods include invariance-based and generative-based pretraining. Invariance-based approaches, such as contrastive learning, optimize the model to produce similar embeddings for different views of the input. These views are created through data augmentation. Contrastive learning requires processing negative samples, which limits computational efficiency. The augmentations must be non-trivial to learn semantic embeddings useful for downstream tasks.

Generative-based pretraining methods, such as autoencoding or autoregressive modeling, remove or corrupt portions of the input and predict them. The energy function is often a reconstruction error in data space. Generative models can display overfitting tendencies and can be non-trivial to train due to issues like mode collapse. The features they learn are not always useful for downstream tasks. Method

A general overview:
Graphs G are defined as G = (V, E) where V = {v1 ... vN} is the set of nodes, with cardinality |V| = N, and E = {e1 ... eM} is the set of edges, with cardinality |E| = M. For simplicity, symmetric, unweighted graphs are considered, although the method can be generalized. G can be represented by an adjacency matrix A ∈ {0,1}^{N × N}, with A_{ij} = 1 if nodes v_i and v_j are connected and 0 otherwise.

The high-level idea of Graph-JEPA is to divide the input graph into subgraphs (patches) and predict the representation of a randomly chosen target subgraph from the representation of a single context subgraph. This masked modeling objective is realized in latent space without needing negative or positive samples. Subgraph representations are pooled to create a graph-level representation. The learning procedure consists of: 1. Spatial Partitioning; 2. Subgraph Embedding; 3. Context and Target Encoding; 4. Latent Target Prediction.

Spatial Partitioning:
This step creates non-overlapping subgraphs (patches). The METIS graph clustering algorithm partitions a graph into a pre-defined, non-overlapping number of clusters p, such that the number of within-cluster links is much higher than between-cluster links. To maintain locality and avoid empty subgraphs, a one-hop neighborhood expansion of the nodes in each extracted subgraph is performed.

Subgraph Embedding:
After partitioning, a representation for each subgraph is learned through a GNN. The specific GNN choice is arbitrary. Learned node embeddings are mean pooled to create a vector representation for each subgraph: {h1 ... hp}, h ∈ ℝ^d. A positional embedding for each subgraph is used, implemented as the maximum Random Walk Structural Embedding (RWSE) of all nodes in that subgraph. Formally, RWSE for a node v is defined as:
P_v = (M_{ii}, M^2_{ii}, ..., M^k_{ii})
with P_v ∈ ℝ^k, M^k = (D^{-1}A)^k the random-walk transition matrix of order k, and i is the index of node v in the adjacency matrix. M^k_{ii} encodes the probability of node v landing to itself after a k-step random walk. Given a subgraph l, let V_l denote the set of nodes in l. The subgraph RWSE is defined as:
P_l = max_{v ∈ V_l} P_v
where the max operation is performed elementwise.

Context and Target Encoding:
Given subgraph representations and their positional embeddings, the Graph-JEPA prediction task is framed. The goal is to predict latent embeddings of randomly chosen target subgraphs, given one random context subgraph. The prediction is conditioned on positional information. At each training step, one random subgraph is chosen as the context x and m others as targets Y = {y1, ..., ym}. These subgraphs are processed by context and target encoders parametrized by Transformer encoder blocks (without self-attention for the context) where normalization is applied first. The target encoder uses Hadamard self-attention, but other choices are viable. This step is summarized as:
z^x = E_c(x), Z^y = E_t(Y),
with z^x ∈ ℝ^d and Z^y ∈ ℝ^{m × d}. The predictor network can directly predict Z^y from z^x. This is the typical formulation of JEPAs. Learning to organize concepts for graphs directly in Euclidean space may be suboptimal. The following subsection proposes an approach using the encoding and prediction mechanisms in Graph-JEPA.

Latent Target Prediction:
Graph-level concepts are often assumed to be hierarchical. It is conjectured that Graph-JEPA should operate in a hyperbolic space, where learned embeddings implicitly organize hierarchical concepts. Hyperbolic (Poincaré) embeddings have tradeoffs between dimensionality and performance, limiting expressive ability. Graphs can describe abstract concepts, so high expressivity is preferred. A high-dimensional latent code with hyperbolicity built into it is desired.

To achieve this, the target embedding is thought of as a high-dimensional representation of a hyperbolic angle, allowing each target patch to be described through its position in the 2D unit hyperbola. Formally, given a target patch l, its embedding Z^y_l and positional encoding P_l, the latent target is expressed as:
ψ^y_l = ( cosh(α^y_l); sinh(α^y_l) ), α^y_l = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^d Z^y_l^{(n)},
where cosh(·) and sinh(·) are hyperbolic cosine and sine functions. The predictor module is tasked with directly locating the target in the unit hyperbola, given the context embedding and the target patch's positional encoding:
\hat{ψ}^y_l = W_2(σ(W_1(z^x + P_l) + b_1)) + b_2,
where W_n and b_n represent the n-th weight matrix and bias vector, σ is an elementwise non-linear activation function, and \hat{ψ}^y_l ∈ ℝ^2. The learning procedure is framed as a regression problem, and the network is trained end-to-end. The smooth L1 loss is used as the distance function:
L(y, \hat{y}) = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^N s_n, s_n = { 0.5(y_n - \hat{y}_n)^2 / β, if |y - \hat{y}| < β; |y - \hat{y}| - 0.5β, otherwise }
Thus, the distance between context and target patches in the unit hyperbola is measured, but targets are described through a high dimensional latent code. Differences between this choice and using Euclidean or Hyperbolic distances as energy functions are shown in experiments. The pretraining objective forces the context encoder to understand differences in the hyperbolic angle between target patches, establishing an implicit hierarchy.

Preventing representation collapse:
JEPAs are based on self-distillation and are susceptible to representation collapse. Two training tricks are adopted: i) A stop-gradient operation on the target encoder followed by a momentum update using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the context encoder weights; ii) a simpler parametrization of the predictor compared to the context and target networks.

The problem is simplified with assumptions: i) The predictor network is linear; ii) There is a one-to-one correspondence between context and target patches; iii) The self-predictive task is a least-squares problem in a finite-dimensional vector space. Context features are rewritten as X ∈ ℝ^{n × d}, target coordinates as Y ∈ ℝ^{n × 2}, and weights of the linear model as W ∈ ℝ^{d × 2}. The optimal weights are given by solving:
argmin_W || XW - Y ||^2
where ||.|| indicates the Frobenius norm. The OLS estimator gives the solution: W = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y. Plugging this into the objective and factorizing Y, the least squares solution leads to the error:
|| (X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T - I_n) Y ||^2
The optimality of a linear predictor is defined by the orthogonal projection of Y onto the orthogonal complement of a subspace of Col(X). The target encoder, which estimates Y, must not share weights or be optimized via the same optimizer as the context encoder. If that were the case, the easiest solution would be learning a representation that is orthogonal to itself, leading to representation collapse. Using an EMA update bypasses this problem.

In practice, even with EMA, a degenerate solution can be encountered with a non-linear and highly expressive network. If the predictor network is sufficiently powerful, it can predict target representations without a well-learned context representation. Since the target encoder weights are updated via EMA, learned representations may become uninformative. Therefore, implementing the predictor network as a simpler and less expressive network is crucial.

Results are underwhelming compared to models reporting graph-level performance.

Performance on the synthetic EXP dataset is explored, compared to end-to-end supervised models. The choice of energy function impacts learned representations. Given the latent prediction task, latent representations are expected to display hyperbolicity. The network estimates a space that can be considered a section of the hyperboloid model, where hyperbolas appear as geodesics. The energy is evaluated in a restricted part of hyperbolic space. This task offers flexibility and is computationally efficient compared to hyperbolic distance used in the Poincaré ball model.

Table 3 provides empirical evidence regarding the suboptimality of Euclidean or Poincaré embeddings on 4 out of 8 datasets. Results reveal that learning the distance between patches in the 2D unit hyperbola provides advantages of both embedding types. Hyperbolic embeddings must be learned in lower dimensions due to stability issues, while Euclidean ones do not properly reflect dependencies between subgraphs and hierarchical nature of graph-level concepts. Results suggest hyperbolic (Poincaré) distance is generally better than Euclidean distance in lower dimensions, but computationally unstable and expensive in high dimensions. The proposed approach provides the best overall results. A qualitative example of how the embedding space is altered is shown in Figure 2.

Additional insights and ablation studies:
Model efficiency: Total training time needed for different Graph-SSL strategies to provide optimal downstream performance is compared on IMDB and REDDIT-M5 datasets. Graph-JEPA displays superior efficiency and promising scaling behavior. Runtime is hardware-dependent; all experiments are performed on the same machine.

MLP parametrization: Table 4 contains results of parametrizing the whole architecture, other than the initial GNN encoder, through MLPs. This means not using the Attention mechanism. Graph-JEPA still performs well, showing flexibility, though using complete Transformer encoders leads to better overall performance and less variance.

Positional embedding: Following prior work, it is possible to use RWSE of patches as conditioning information. Formally, let B ∈ {0,1}^{p × N} be the patch assignment matrix, such that B_{ij} = 1 if v_j ∈ p_i. A coarse patch adjacency matrix A' = BB^T ∈ ℝ^{p × p} can be calculated, where each A_{ij}' contains node overlap between p_i and p_j. Positional embedding can be calculated for each patch using RWSE on A'. Graph-JEPA is tested with these relative positional embeddings; they provide good performance but consistently fall behind the node-level (global) RWSE used in the formulation. An issue is that the number of shared neighbors can obscure local peculiarities of each patch, rendering context given to the predictor more ambiguous.

Random subgraphs: A question is how to design spatial partitioning. Using METIS is intuitive and leads to favorable results. Another option is to extract random, non-empty subgraphs as context and targets. Random patches also provide strong performance, showing the JEPA architecture is not reliant on initial input, as is the case for methods relying on data augmentation for view generation. Random sampling can be problematic for larger graphs. Extracting subgraphs with METIS is advocated as a safer option in terms of generalizability and inductive bias.

Conclusion:
This work introduces a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for graph-level Self-Supervised Learning. An appropriate design of the model, in terms of data preparation and pretraining objective, reveals it is possible for a neural network to self-organize semantic knowledge embedded in a graph, demonstrating competitive performance in different graph data and tasks. Future research directions include extending the method to node and edge-level learning, theoretically exploring expressiveness of Graph-JEPA, and gaining insights into optimal geometry of embedding space for graph SSL.

The optimality of a linear predictor is defined by the orthogonal projection of Y onto the orthogonal complement of a subspace of Col(X). The target encoder, which estimates Y, must not share weights or be optimized via the same optimizer as the context encoder. If that were the case, the easiest solution would be learning a representation that is orthogonal to itself, leading to representation collapse. Using an EMA update bypasses this problem.

In practice, even with EMA, a degenerate solution can be encountered with a non-linear and highly expressive network. If the predictor network is sufficiently powerful, it can predict target representations without a well-learned context representation. Since the target encoder weights are updated via EMA, learned representations may become uninformative. Therefore, implementing the predictor network as a simpler and less expressive network is crucial.

Experiments

The experimental section introduces empirical evaluation of Graph-JEPA in terms of downstream performance on different graph datasets and tasks, along with studies on the latent space's structure and encoders' parametrization. Ablation studies are presented to elucidate design choices.

Experimental setting:
The TUD datasets are used for graph-level SSL. Seven graph-classification datasets are used: PROTEINS, MUTAG, DD, REDDIT-BINARY, REDDIT-MULTI-5K, IMDB-BINARY, and IMDB-MULTI. Accuracy of ten-fold cross-validation for all classification experiments over five runs (with different seeds) is reported. Graph-JEPA is compared against four contrastive methods, two generative methods, and one latent self-predictive method (LaGraph). Results with BGRL, a node-level latent self-predictive strategy, are provided. The model is trained using official code and hyperparameters, and node representations are mean-pooled for the downstream task. Results are underwhelming compared to models reporting graph-level performance.

Performance on the synthetic EXP dataset is explored, compared to end-to-end supervised models. This experiment aims to verify if Graph-JEPA can learn highly expressive graph representations without supervision. Results show Graph-JEPA performs much better than commonly used GNNs. The choice of energy function impacts learned representations. Given the latent prediction task, latent representations are expected to display hyperbolicity. The predictor network linearly approximates the behavior of the unit hyperbola to match generated target coordinates. The network estimates a space that can be considered a section of the hyperboloid model, where hyperbolas appear as geodesics. The energy is evaluated in a restricted part of hyperbolic space. This task offers flexibility and is computationally efficient compared to hyperbolic distance used in the Poincaré ball model.

Table 3 provides empirical evidence regarding the suboptimality of Euclidean or Poincaré embeddings on 4 out of 8 datasets. Results reveal that learning the distance between patches in the 2D unit hyperbola provides advantages of both embedding types. Hyperbolic embeddings must be learned in lower dimensions due to stability issues, while Euclidean ones do not properly reflect dependencies between subgraphs and hierarchical nature of graph-level concepts. Results suggest hyperbolic (Poincaré) distance is generally better than Euclidean distance in lower dimensions, but computationally unstable and expensive in high dimensions. The proposed approach provides the best overall results. A qualitative example of how the embedding space is altered is shown in Figure 2.

Additional insights and ablation studies:
Model efficiency: Total training time needed for different Graph-SSL strategies to provide optimal downstream performance is compared on IMDB and REDDIT-M5 datasets. Graph-JEPA displays superior efficiency and promising scaling behavior. Runtime is hardware-dependent; all experiments are performed on the same machine.

Graph-JEPA still performs well, showing flexibility, though using complete Transformer encoders leads to better overall performance and less variance.

Positional embedding: Following prior work, it is possible to use RWSE of patches as conditioning information. Formally, let B ∈ {0,1}^{p × N} be the patch assignment matrix, such that B_{ij} = 1 if v_j ∈ p_i. An issue is that the number of shared neighbors can obscure local peculiarities of each patch, rendering context given to the predictor more ambiguous.

Random subgraphs: A question is how to design spatial partitioning. Using METIS is intuitive and leads to favorable results. Another option is to extract random, non-empty subgraphs as context and targets. Random patches also provide strong performance, showing the JEPA architecture is not reliant on initial input, as is the case for methods relying on data augmentation for view generation. Random sampling can be problematic for larger graphs. Extracting subgraphs with METIS is advocated as a safer option in terms of generalizability and inductive bias.

Conclusion:
This work introduces a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for graph-level Self-Supervised Learning. An appropriate design of the model, in terms of data preparation and pretraining objective, reveals it is possible for a neural network to self-organize semantic knowledge embedded in a graph, demonstrating competitive performance in different graph data and tasks. Future research directions include extending the method to node and edge-level learning, theoretically exploring expressiveness of Graph-JEPA, and gaining insights into optimal geometry of embedding space for graph SSL.
