Title: Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery: A Novel Framework for Accelerated Lead Identification

Abstract

The foundational stage of early drug discovery serves as the critical gateway for the development of new therapeutic agents, focusing intently on the identification and subsequent optimization of lead molecules that exhibit specific and potent binding to target proteins. However, this essential process is persistently hampered by a constellation of formidable challenges, including the astronomical size of available molecular libraries, the notoriously high attrition rates encountered during screening, and the profoundly intricate nature of molecular interactions at the atomic level. To decisively overcome these enduring obstacles, the field is witnessing a definitive paradigm shift towards the seamless integration of artificial intelligence and full laboratory automation into end-to-end discovery operations. Intelligent computing systems play an indispensable role by strategically discovering and recommending promising molecular candidates, while automated experimental platforms provide essential data validation and create a continuous feedback loop. This innovative and integrated approach can be rigorously formulated as an active probabilistic learning problem, fundamentally grounded on the established assumption that molecules actively binding to a specific target constitute a small proportion of any library and exhibit distinct cluster-distributed characteristics within the chemical space. Building upon this powerful formulation, we introduce a novel and highly effective Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery (APDD) method. This method operates through an iterative cycle that progressively updates the estimated binding probabilities of molecules, thereby enhancing discovery performance via three consecutive and synergistic steps: probabilistic clustering, selective docking, and active wet-experiment validation. We have conducted exhaustive and comprehensive experiments on two widely recognized benchmark datasets, DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, as well as a simulated virtual library of substantial scale. The results conclusively demonstrate the undeniable feasibility and exceptional efficiency of our approach, showcasing transformative cost savings with a definitive average reduction of 80% in computational docking expenses and a substantial 70% reduction in wet experimental costs, all while rigorously maintaining high accuracy in the critical task of lead molecule discovery.

1 INTRODUCTION

Early drug discovery constitutes a cornerstone of modern pharmaceutical development and biomedical research, playing a critical and irreplaceable role in translating basic science into clinical therapies. It strategically encompasses the application of advanced computational drug design and chemical biology techniques to efficiently identify and optimize lead molecules with desired properties. Computational drug design expertly utilizes knowledge of a target’s three-dimensional structure or known active ligands to facilitate the identification of potential candidate drugs, employing either structure-based or ligand-based methodologies depending on the available information. Concurrently, chemical biology focuses on elucidating the detailed mechanism of action of a chemical modulator on its specific biological target. Nonetheless, the profoundly intricate and multifaceted behavior of drug molecules continues to pose substantial and persistent challenges throughout early drug discovery, directly contributing to high failure rates and presenting significant hurdles that demand innovative solutions.

In recent years, a powerful and transformative focus has emerged on integrating intelligent computing with fully automated experimentation to radically accelerate the entire drug discovery pipeline. The overarching objective is to explore a vastly wider range of chemical possibilities while simultaneously and dramatically reducing associated costs and timelines. Intelligent computing serves a crucial and central role by intelligently recommending molecules for further investigation. By analyzing immense volumes of data, including detailed chemical structures and biological assay results, these systems can reliably identify potential drug candidates that possess a higher likelihood of success. This capability not only significantly speeds up the process of identifying promising molecules but also effectively reduces the dependency on extensive and costly laboratory experiments. Automated experimentation represents another vital and indispensable component of this integrated approach. Through high-throughput screening techniques and the deployment of sophisticated robotic technologies, researchers can now efficiently test thousands of molecules against specific targets or disease models. The results generated from these automated experiments serve to validate the predictions made by intelligent computing systems and are essential for refining and improving the computational models. The continuous and iterative feedback loop established between computational predictions and experimental results enables researchers to learn dynamically and optimize their hypotheses in real-time. This powerful iterative cycle enables more efficient and precisely targeted drug discovery, substantially reducing the time and resources required to develop innovative and life-saving therapies.

To successfully realize this vision of end-to-end automated early drug discovery, the design of a novel and robust machine learning framework is absolutely essential. From a machine learning perspective, this new paradigm for early drug discovery can be definitively formulated as an active probabilistic learning problem. Specifically, it is based on the well-supported assumption that the number of active molecules capable of binding to a target protein of interest within a given molecule library is typically relatively small and, importantly, tends to be clustered within specific regions of the chemical space. Probabilistic clustering algorithms can therefore be effectively employed to identify these desirable clusters with high precision, and representative molecules can be intelligently selected from these clusters through active learning techniques. Automated experiments are then conducted on the selected molecules, and the invaluable feedback generated is used to directly optimize and improve the drug discovery models. This iterative process of experiment and feedback serves to continuously refine the model, leading to more accurate predictions and a demonstrably higher likelihood of discovering effective drug candidates.

Based on this powerful and rigorous formulation, we propose a novel and highly effective approach termed Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery (APDD), which comprises three primary and interconnected components. Firstly, molecules are intelligently partitioned into meaningful clusters using advanced probabilistic clustering algorithms that leverage molecular substructure features. This clustering method expertly identifies relevant chemical features and groups molecules based on their profound similarities. Second, representative molecules from each cluster are selectively chosen for molecular docking simulations using the accelerated Vina-GPU+ platform. These simulations definitively identify clusters featuring molecules with high docking probabilities, which serve as the prime candidates for further experimental validation. Finally, a strategic subset of molecules from these high-probability clusters is selected through active learning techniques to undergo subsequent wet experimental screening, thereby providing direct and actionable feedback for model refinement. The feedback generated by these experiments is seamlessly integrated into the model to iteratively refine its predictions and enhance its overall performance.

To thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed APDD method, comprehensive and rigorous experiments were conducted on 90 targets from the well-established and widely respected benchmark datasets DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, which are the standard for early drug discovery evaluations. The experimental results conclusively showcased that the APDD method demonstrated substantial and transformative computational cost savings by an impressive 80% on average, compared to traditional exhaustive drug discovery methods. Furthermore, the APDD method achieved remarkable and highly significant reductions in wet experimental costs, with an average reduction of 70%. Despite these profound cost reductions, the APDD method rigorously maintained comparable screening accuracy. We also evaluate APDD for virtual screening with large-scale simulation experiments over 1.4 million molecules, which further validates the undeniable feasibility and superior efficiency of the APDD framework. To sum up, the primary and significant contributions of this work definitively lie in formulating this new paradigm for early drug discovery and designing a novel machine learning algorithm that is both highly effective and easily extensible to accommodate extra-large virtual molecule libraries, paving the way for a new era in therapeutic development.

2 RELATED WORK

Automated systems have undeniably played a significant and growing role in revolutionizing early drug discovery over the past decades. Medium-to-high throughput drug screening in specialized assays has become commonplace within the pharmaceutical industry, resulting in markedly increased laboratory efficiency, lower overall attrition rates, and substantially reduced costs throughout the entire drug discovery value chain. On the other side, the introduction of intelligent computing-driven early drug discovery has further accelerated the explosive growth of the pharmaceutical sector, leading to a truly revolutionary change across the industry. Moving forward, the ideal and most powerful approach for early drug discovery will definitively involve the seamless integration of intelligent computing with fully automated experimental systems. This integration possesses immense potential to dramatically expedite the entire drug development and approval process, ultimately enabling novel and effective therapies to reach patients more quickly than ever before. The profound benefits of this integrated approach are numerous and well-established. By applying standardized procedures with automated support, measurement errors can be minimized, and material consumption can be significantly reduced. Additionally, the use of automated systems allows for considerably shorter screening and testing cycles, enabling rapid feedback loops and accelerated molecule optimization. Moreover, this approach enables unbiased molecular optimization based on multiple relevant biochemical and biological endpoints. In short, considering the vast and essentially infinite size of the chemical space, a paramount challenge for medicinal chemists is determining “what to make and test next.” Automated and intelligent drug discovery platforms must be fully capable of providing accurate and reliable answers to this fundamental question.

Currently, a multitude of leading research institutions and major pharmaceutical companies are actively and intensively engaged in pioneering research and development in this transformative field. In academia, for example, recent work has highlighted the significant advancements in automating whole organism screening, target-based assays, fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD), computer-aided drug design (CADD), and the integration of intelligent computing tools in drug design projects, marking the dawn of a new era in therapeutic discovery. Other academic researchers have proposed a comprehensive design-make-test-analyze framework as a blueprint for automated drug design, utilizing intelligent computing and miniaturized bench-top synthesis, and have successfully applied this framework to explore chemical space and generate novel molecular candidates. In the industrial sector, for instance, several companies have developed innovative platforms. One notable example is an innovative “trinity” paradigm that combines artificial intelligence, automated experiments, and expert knowledge to explore a broader chemical space with increased efficiency and reduced costs, a platform that has already been validated by the discovery of potent hit molecules against a novel anti-cancer target. Another company has launched a fully automated AI-driven drug discovery platform that demonstrates efficient identification of novel molecular structures. Furthermore, a collaboration has introduced a web-based platform that provides broad access to a cloud laboratory, integrating automated biology and chemistry research capabilities to create a closed-loop system that dramatically accelerates the design-make-test-analyze drug discovery cycle.

3 FORMULATION

Early drug discovery encompasses the critical initial steps required to identify molecules that exhibit the desirable characteristics necessary for developing effective and safe drugs. This process will increasingly rely on a powerful combination of artificial intelligence and automated systems to facilitate seamless end-to-end operations and enhance the overall performance and efficiency of the methods employed. Artificial intelligence plays a crucial and central role in the intelligent discovery and strategic recommendation of potential molecules, while automated experiments ensure robust data validation and provide invaluable feedback for continuous improvement. From a machine learning perspective, this innovative paradigm for early drug discovery can be definitively and rigorously formulated as an active probabilistic learning problem. Firstly, this paradigm is built upon the fundamental and well-supported assumption that within a given compound library, the number of active molecules capable of binding to a specific target protein of interest is generally limited and tends to be concentrated within specific, identifiable regions of the chemical space. Secondly, the outcomes of early drug discovery typically yield a ranked list of diverse molecules predicted to have the highest affinity. However, the actual hit rate of the top-ranked molecules remains frustratingly limited. Studies on the progression from initial hits to clinical drug candidates have conclusively shown that hit molecules, on average, share only limited structural similarity with the final approved drugs. Also, it is widely recognized and accepted that computational docking affinity scores often struggle to achieve a strong correlation with experimental results due to the complex nature of the underlying physical processes involved. Consequently, it becomes far more crucial and effective to prioritize a list of molecules based on the highest estimated binding probabilities rather than solely considering their raw affinity scores. Thirdly, the strategic utilization of probability clustering algorithms allows for the precise identification of these desirable clusters, from which representative molecules can be intelligently selected using active learning techniques. Finally, the selected molecules undergo automated experimental validation, and the feedback obtained is directly utilized to optimize and improve the drug discovery models in an iterative manner.

4 METHOD

In this section, we will present a comprehensive and detailed overview of the construction process for the Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery (APDD) framework. We will commence by meticulously elucidating the methodology employed for the probabilistic clustering of a ligand molecule library, leveraging molecular substructure features as outlined in Section 4.1. Subsequently, in Section 4.2, we will delve into the specific intricacies associated with the utilization of Vina-GPU+ for the docking process of representative molecules selected from each cluster. Moving forward, Section 4.3 will introduce our sophisticated query strategy, which actively selects molecules for wet lab testing, alongside a detailed explanation of how we refine docking probabilities by incorporating wet lab results, ultimately amplifying the effectiveness and efficiency of our overall drug discovery efforts.

More importantly, these existing methods cannot effectively separate the active molecules from the decoy molecules, which severely limits their applicability and reliability in real-world discovery scenarios. To decisively address these issues, we turn to advanced Probabilistic Clustering algorithms, which provide a quantitative measurement of cluster membership and require no prior knowledge to learn a distance-probability mapping function automatically from multi-view data distribution through consistency constraints.

To successfully apply probabilistic clustering to molecules, two significant technical challenges need to be addressed: molecular representations and accurate probability estimation. Specifically, we approximate this binding probability with the Tanimoto similarity of molecular pairs. To perform molecular clustering based on this probability, we adopt a Fast probabilistic clustering algorithm. This algorithm aims to cluster similar molecules into the same groups while maximizing the overall likelihood of all pairwise matching events, under a standard assumption of independence.

4.2 INITIAL SCREENING

Regarding the docking of a large molecule dataset, current exhaustive screening algorithms often encounter the fundamental challenge of maintaining an optimal balance between precision and computational cost. Multiple docking algorithms and scoring functions have been developed to predict the binding affinity and pose of each small molecule within the binding site. However, we note that alternative or multiple docking methods could also be employed in this stage. In this context, we consider the initial screening from two critical perspectives: (i) how to ensure that the selected representative molecules will not deviate severely from the majority of molecules in a cluster, and (ii) how to estimate a reasonable binding probability for a molecule based on its Vina docking score. To address the first problem, we propose a method to reduce the risk of selecting outlier molecules by considering the overall Tanimoto similarity within a cluster. Specifically, we define representative molecules as those that maximize the accumulated pairwise probability with other cluster members. This criterion ensures that the representative molecule shares the highest number of common substructures with other molecules in its cluster. Empirical findings demonstrate conclusively that this approach significantly decreases the likelihood of selecting outlier samples. In practice, we adopt an iterative selection process. To address the second problem, we employ isotonic regression to learn a calibrated mapping function from labeled data, which includes proteins and molecules with known active or inactive labels. We limit the maximum estimated probability based on extensive prior studies which have shown that the hit success rate with top docking scores has an approximate upper bound. It is worth noting that for more reliable scoring methods, the maximum probability can be statistically calculated using labeled samples with top scores.

It is important to note that the appropriate fusion of multi-modal docking scores obtained from different computational tools can significantly reduce the risk of missing active clusters. Considering the efficient integration of various information modalities by probabilistic clustering in multi-modal tasks, we adopt a similar approach to amalgamate different scoring results. This process consists of two definitive steps: (i) Initially, we convert the evaluation results from each computational method into binding probabilities. (ii) Drawing inspiration from multi-view probabilistic clustering, we employ a specific equation to fuse probabilities generated by various algorithms, an approach that has been proven to be an equivalent transformation assuming conditional independence among the multiple modalities.

4.3 ACTIVE PROBABILISTIC SCREENING

Active Learning has been widely utilized to enhance the performance of drug screening in various contexts. However, we observe that previous active screening methods are often limited in scope, resulting in poor generalization ability when applied to novel proteins, or requiring a considerable number of wet experiments for model retraining. In contrast, we have conclusively observed that active probabilistic clustering can effectively mitigate these significant issues. This is because active clustering does not necessitate prior knowledge about the target protein or any pre-existing active molecules. We firmly believe that in the refinement stage of drug discovery, incorporating active probabilistic clustering to locally adjust molecular binding probabilities can significantly and dramatically enhance the recall rate of active molecules. Clustering active molecules can provide invaluable information regarding diverse binding modes and assists in constructing pharmacophores, which are crucial for further drug optimization.

During the initial screening phase, the clusters are ranked based on the binding probability of their representative molecules. In this active stage, our primary objective is to increase the expected recall of the top K molecules from the ranked list. (ii) A context probability refinement mechanism that updates probabilities based on experimental outcomes.

Our query strategy quantifies the potential impact of conducting a wet experiment on a candidate molecule from a cluster by evaluating the expected improvement in the overall recall. This consideration is both reasonable and powerful within the context of probabilistic molecule clustering for two main reasons. Firstly, our approach is built upon the fundamental assumption that active molecules are distributed within clusters. Adjusting the docking probability based on a wet experiment result increases the likelihood of discovering similar active molecules within the same cluster. Secondly, effective docking tools are more likely to assign a higher affinity score to active molecules. Consequently, clusters containing active molecules are more likely to be prioritized for investigation.

To formally define the expected recall improvement, we employ a specific formula. As we only dock the representative molecules in each cluster initially, we are not able to calculate this formula strictly for all molecules, hence we propose two practical variants with different granularity: a faster cluster-based approximation and a more precise molecule-based calculation. For the cluster-based variant, we use a simplified formula. For the molecule-based variant, the conditional probability is calculated under an independent event assumption involving the binding events of two molecules and the event that they bind to the same target.

5 EXPERIMENTS

Our experiments are structured in a comprehensive and logical manner to validate the APDD framework: In Section 5.1, we present the detailed specifics of our experimental setup. Datasets. To emulate this standard approach, we employ VinaGPU+ to dock the target protein with all candidate molecules in the library. Subsequently, we simulate conducting wet lab experiments on molecules with the best affinity scores in a sequential manner until a predetermined target recall number is achieved. During the Active Probabilistic Refinement procedure, we select two representative molecules from each cluster. We terminate the APDD cycle when the recall rate of the top 100 molecules reaches the target recall rate. Evaluation. We employ two distinct and practical metrics to measure the performance of APDD: The reduction in the number of Vina-GPU+ docking calculations required and the reduction in the number of wet lab experiments needed to discover a target number of active molecules.

5.2 PERFORMANCE COMPARISON

We evaluate the performance of APDD with VinaGPU+ on the 79 target proteins from DUD-E and the 11 targets from LIT-PCBA. Moreover, we conclusively notice that APDD demonstrates this significant advantage across both small molecule sets (less than 4k molecules) and very large sets (over 300k molecules), which reveals that APDD is robust to the size of datasets and to different chemical properties and pocket structures. We have also observed that when VinaGPU+ provides low-quality affinity assessments (e.g., with AUC less than 0.5), both APDD and the baseline may require a large number of experiments, as the docking scores provide little useful information for prioritization in these specific edge cases.

In this section, we aim to explore the fundamental reason why APDD can save unnecessary docking computations and wet lab experiments simultaneously. We report the distribution of clusters containing active molecules for several proteins as an illustrative instance. 5.4 PERFORMANCE ON LARGE DATASETS

6 CONCLUSION

In the rapidly evolving field of early drug discovery, there is a powerful and definitive trend towards utilizing both intelligent computing and full laboratory automation to drive the entire process from end to end. This transformative new approach can be rigorously formulated as an active probabilistic learning problem within the realm of machine learning. To effectively address this formulation, we have presented a novel and highly effective method called Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery (APDD), which synergistically combines ligand-based screening through advanced molecule clustering with structure-based screening using molecular docking. We have conducted extensive and comprehensive experiments on 90 targets from the standard benchmark datasets DUD-E and LIT-PCBA for rigorous drug screening evaluation. The results conclusively and definitively demonstrate that the APDD method achieves substantial and transformative cost savings while rigorously maintaining high screening accuracy. Our proposed paradigm aims to streamline the discovery pipeline and has the potential to significantly expand the practical size of screenable virtual molecule libraries, thereby facilitating comprehensive and efficient coverage of drug-like chemical space through intelligent, well-organized clustering. This work establishes a robust foundation for the next generation of efficient, automated, and intelligent drug discovery platforms.

Title: Active Probabilistic Drug Discovery: A Novel Framework for Accelerated Lead Identification

The foundational stage of early drug discovery serves as the critical gateway for the development of new therapeutic agents, focusing intently on the identification and subsequent optimization of lead molecules that exhibit specific and potent binding to target proteins. However, this essential process is persistently hampered by a constellation of formidable challenges, including the astronomical size of available molecular libraries, the notoriously high attrition rates encountered during screening, and the profoundly intricate nature of molecular interactions at the atomic level. To decisively overcome these enduring obstacles, the field is witnessing a definitive paradigm shift towards the seamless integration of artificial intelligence and full laboratory automation into end-to-end discovery operations. Intelligent computing systems play an indispensable role by strategically discovering and recommending promising molecular candidates, while automated experimental platforms provide essential data validation and create a continuous feedback loop. We have conducted exhaustive and comprehensive experiments on two widely recognized benchmark datasets, DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, as well as a simulated virtual library of substantial scale. It strategically encompasses the application of advanced computational drug design and chemical biology techniques to efficiently identify and optimize lead molecules with desired properties. Computational drug design expertly utilizes knowledge of a target’s three-dimensional structure or known active ligands to facilitate the identification of potential candidate drugs, employing either structure-based or ligand-based methodologies depending on the available information. Concurrently, chemical biology focuses on elucidating the detailed mechanism of action of a chemical modulator on its specific biological target. Nonetheless, the profoundly intricate and multifaceted behavior of drug molecules continues to pose substantial and persistent challenges throughout early drug discovery, directly contributing to high failure rates and presenting significant hurdles that demand innovative solutions.

In recent years, a powerful and transformative focus has emerged on integrating intelligent computing with fully automated experimentation to radically accelerate the entire drug discovery pipeline. The overarching objective is to explore a vastly wider range of chemical possibilities while simultaneously and dramatically reducing associated costs and timelines. Intelligent computing serves a crucial and central role by intelligently recommending molecules for further investigation. By analyzing immense volumes of data, including detailed chemical structures and biological assay results, these systems can reliably identify potential drug candidates that possess a higher likelihood of success. This capability not only significantly speeds up the process of identifying promising molecules but also effectively reduces the dependency on extensive and costly laboratory experiments. The continuous and iterative feedback loop established between computational predictions and experimental results enables researchers to learn dynamically and optimize their hypotheses in real-time. This powerful iterative cycle enables more efficient and precisely targeted drug discovery, substantially reducing the time and resources required to develop innovative and life-saving therapies.

To successfully realize this vision of end-to-end automated early drug discovery, the design of a novel and robust machine learning framework is absolutely essential. This iterative process of experiment and feedback serves to continuously refine the model, leading to more accurate predictions and a demonstrably higher likelihood of discovering effective drug candidates.

Experiments on 90 targets from DUD-E and LIT-PCBA showed APDD achieved substantial cost savings while maintaining screening accuracy. REValueD: Regularised Ensemble Value-Decomposition for Factorisable Markov Decision Processes

Abstract
Discrete-action reinforcement learning algorithms can struggle in tasks with high-dimensional discrete action spaces. A recent approach uses value-decomposition, a concept from multi-agent reinforcement learning, to address this. This study examines the effects of this value-decomposition, finding that while it reduces the over-estimation bias inherent to Q-learning algorithms, it increases target variance. To address this, an ensemble of critics is used to mitigate target variance. Additionally, a regularisation loss is introduced to help mitigate the effects that exploratory actions in one dimension can have on the value of optimal actions in other dimensions. The algorithm, REValueD, was tested on discretised versions of DeepMind Control Suite tasks. It showed superior performance compared to baseline methods, particularly in the humanoid and dog tasks. The factors influencing REValueD's performance were analyzed, evaluating the significance of the regularisation loss and the scalability with increasing sub-actions per dimension.

Introduction
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) combines deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL). Problems with high-dimensional, discrete action spaces remain relatively unexplored. In these problems, the action space can be a Cartesian product of discrete sets, i.e., $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}_1 \times ... \times \mathcal{A}_N$. Here, $\mathcal{A}_i$ represents the $i$th sub-action space, containing $n_i$ discrete sub-actions. A Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Bellman, 1957) with such a factorisable action space is referred to as a factorisable MDP (FMDP).

In high-dimensional FMDPs, there are $\prod_{i=1}^N n_i$ atomic actions. Standard algorithms like Q-learning (Watkins & Dayan, 1992; Mnih et al., 2013) can fail due to computational impracticalities. Recent approaches learn about each sub-action space individually (Tavakoli et al., 2018; Seyde et al., 2022). The DecQN algorithm (Seyde et al., 2022) uses value-decomposition to learn utility values for sub-actions. The utility of each selected sub-action is computed independently, but learnt so their mean estimates the Q-value for the global action. This is inspired by the centralised training with decentralised execution paradigm in multi-agent RL (MARL) (Kraemer & Doshi, 2016). The $i$th utility function only needs to learn values for the actions in $\mathcal{A}_i$. The total number of actions for which a utility value needs to be learned is $\sum_{i=1}^N n_i$.

This paper presents two primary methodological contributions. First, a theoretical analysis of the value-decomposition when coupled with function approximation is conducted. Q-learning with function approximation suffers from an over-estimation bias in the target (Thrun & Schwartz, 1993; Hasselt, 2010). We explore how value-decomposition impacts this bias. We show that the DecQN decomposition reduces the over-estimation bias in the target Q-values but increases the variance. We establish that an ensemble of critics can mitigate this increase in variance.

Second, a regularisation loss is introduced to be minimised alongside the DecQN loss. The loss is motivated by the credit assignment issue common in MARL (Weiss, 1995; Wolpert & Tumer, 1999; Zhou et al., 2020; Gronauer & Diepold, 2022), where an exploratory action of one agent can negatively influence the value of the optimal action of another agent. This issue is also present when using value-decomposition in FMDPs. The regularisation loss helps mitigate the impact that exploratory sub-actions can have on the utility values of optimal sub-actions post-update by discouraging substantial changes in individual utility estimates. This is achieved by minimising the Huber loss between the selected sub-action utilities and their corresponding values under the target network.

The approach is called REValueD: Regularised Ensemble Value Decomposition. REValueD is benchmarked against DecQN and Branching Dueling Q-Networks (BDQ) (Tavakoli et al., 2018), using the discretised variants of DeepMind control suite tasks (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020) used by Seyde et al. (2022). The experimental results show that REValueD consistently surpasses DecQN and BDQ across a majority of tasks. REValueD markedly outperforms the baselines in the humanoid and dog tasks, where the number of sub-action spaces is high (N = 21 and 38, respectively). Ablation studies are performed on the distinct components of REValueD to evaluate their individual contributions. These include analyzing how performance evolves with increasing $n_i$ and examining the impact of the regularisation loss.

Related Work
Single-agent approaches to FMDPs: Several works explore reinforcement learning in environments with large, discrete action spaces (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2015; van Hasselt & Wiering, 2020). More recent efforts address FMDPs specifically, aiming to reason about each sub-action independently using value-based (Sharma et al., 2017; Tavakoli et al., 2018, 2020; Seyde et al., 2022) or policy-gradient methods (Tang & Agrawal, 2020; Seyde et al., 2021). Some methods decompose global action selection into a sequence prediction problem (Metz et al., 2017; Pierrot et al., 2022). Tang et al. (2022) analyze a similar value-decomposition, taking the sum of utilities. Their analysis looks at fundamental properties of the decomposition, whereas this work analyzes the bias/variance of the learning target when using function-approximation with value-decomposition.

Multi-agent value-decomposition: A connection exists between FMDPs and MARL regarding single-agent methods using value-decomposition (Tavakoli et al., 2018, 2020; Seyde et al., 2022). Value-decomposition is popular in MARL due to centralised training with decentralised execution (Kraemer & Doshi, 2016), leading to success (Sunehag et al., 2017; Rashid et al., 2018, 2020; Du et al., 2022). REValueD acts as a regulariser for value-decomposition.

Multi-agent value regularisation: Some works regularise Q-values in MARL through hysteresis (Matignon et al., 2007; Omidshafiei et al., 2017) and leniency (Panait et al., 2006; Palmer et al., 2017). These techniques are primarily for independent learners (Tan, 1993; Claus & Boutilier, 1998). REValueD can be applied to various value-decomposition methods.

Ensembles: The use of function approximators in Q-learning introduces problems due to maximisation bias (Thrun & Schwartz, 1993). Ensemble methods have been proposed to mitigate this bias (van Hasselt et al., 2016; Lan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). Ensembles have also been suggested to enhance exploration (Osband et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2021; Schäfer et al., 2023) or reduce variance (Anschel et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2022). This work demonstrates that using an ensemble with the DecQN value-decomposition provably reduces the target variance while leaving the over-estimation bias unaffected.

Background
Markov Decision Processes and Factorisable Markov Decision Processes
An MDP is a tuple $(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{T}, r, \gamma, \rho_0)$ where $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ are state and action spaces, $\mathcal{T}: \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathcal{S}$ is the transition function, $r: \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is the reward function, $\gamma$ is the discount factor and $\rho_0$ is the initial state distribution. The objective is to find a policy $\pi: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow [0, 1]$ that maximises expected discounted returns, $\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim (\rho_0, \pi)}\left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)\right]$, where $\tau = (s_0, a_1, ..., a_{T-1}, s_T)$ is a trajectory.

An FMDP is an MDP where the action space can be factorised as $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}_1 \times ... \times \mathcal{A}_N$, where $\mathcal{A}_i$ is a set of discrete sub-actions. $\textbf{a} = (a_1, ..., a_N)$ is the global action, and individual $a_i$'s are sub-actions. If the policy selects sub-actions independently, the policy can be considered as $\pi(\textbf{a} | s) = \prod_{i=1}^N \pi_i(a_i | s)$, where $\pi_i$ is the policy of the $i$th sub-action space.

Decoupled Q-Networks
Decoupled Q-Networks (DecQN) (Seyde et al., 2022) scale Deep Q-Networks (Mnih et al., 2013) to FMDPs. DecQN learns utility values for each sub-action space. Let $U^i_{\theta_i}(s, a_i)$ be the $i$th utility function, parameterised by $\theta_i$. For a global action $\textbf{a} = (a_1, ..., a_N)$ the Q-value is defined as
\begin{equation}
Q_\theta(s, \textbf{a}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N U^i_{\theta_i}(s, a_i) \; ,
\end{equation}
where $\theta = \{\theta_i\}_{i=1}^N$. This allows efficient computation of the $\arg\max$ operator:
\begin{align}
\underset{\textbf{a}}{\arg\max} \; Q(s, \textbf{a}) = \left( \underset{a_1 \in \mathcal{A}_1}{\arg\max} \; U^1_{\theta_1}(s, a_1), ...,  \underset{a_N \in \mathcal{A}_N}{\arg\max} \; U^N_{\theta_N}(s, a_N) \right) \; .
\end{align}
To learn the network parameters $\theta$, the following loss is minimised:
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{(s, \textbf{a}, r, s') \in B} L (y - Q_\theta(s, \textbf{a})) \; ,
\end{align}
where $L$ is the Huber loss, $B$ is a batch from the replay buffer, $y = r + \frac{\gamma}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i' \in \mathcal{A}_i} U^i_{\bar{\theta}_i}(s', a_i')$ is the Q-learning target, and $\bar{\theta} = \{\bar{\theta}_i\}_{i=1}^N$ are target network parameters.

Methodology
DecQN target estimation bias and variance
Q-learning with function approximation has a positive estimation bias (Thrun & Schwartz, 1993; Hasselt, 2010). We analyze how the DecQN decomposition impacts this bias and target variance. Following Thrun & Schwartz (1993), we assume the approximated Q-function has uniformly distributed noise: $Q_\theta(s, \textbf{a}) = Q^\pi(s, \textbf{a}) + \epsilon_{s, \textbf{a}}$, where $Q^\pi$ is the true Q-function for policy $\pi$, and $\epsilon_{s, \textbf{a}}$ are i.i.d Uniform$(-b, b)$ random variables. The target difference is defined as
\begin{align}
Z_s^{dqn} &\triangleq r + \gamma \max_{\textbf{a}} Q_\theta(s', \textbf{a}) - \left( r + \gamma \max_{\textbf{a}} Q^\pi(s', \textbf{a}) \right) \;; \\
&= \gamma \left( \max_{\textbf{a}} Q_\theta(s', \textbf{a}) - \max_\textbf{a} Q^\pi(s', \textbf{a}) \right) \;.
\end{align}
$Z_s^{dqn}$ is the target difference for DQN with no value-decomposition.

For DecQN, the uniform approximation error stems from the utilities: $U^i_{\theta_i}(s, a_i) = U_i^{\pi_i}(s, a_i) + \epsilon^i_{s, a_i}$. $U_i^{\pi_i}$ is the true $i$th utility function for policy $\pi_i$ and $\epsilon^i_{s, a_i}$ are i.i.d Uniform$(-b, b)$ random variables. Using the DecQN decomposition, the DecQN target difference is
\begin{align}
Z_s^{dec} = \gamma \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i \in \mathcal{A}_i} U^i_{\theta_i}(s', a_i) - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i \in \mathcal{A}_i} U_i^{\pi_i}(s', a_i) \right) \; .
\end{align}
This leads to Theorem 1.

Theorem 1.
Given the definitions of $Z_s^{dqn}$ and $Z_s^{dec}$, we have that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathbb{E}[Z_s^{dec}] \leq \mathbb{E}[Z_s^{dqn}] \; ;$
\item $\mbox{Var}(Z_s^{dqn}) \leq \mbox{Var}(Z_s^{dec}) \; .$
\end{enumerate}
The expected value of the target difference is reduced with DecQN decomposition, which reduces over-estimation bias. However, the variance of the target increases.

REValueD uses an ensemble of $K$ critics to address the higher variance. Each critic $Q^k(s, \textbf{a})$ is the mean of the utilities $U^i_{\theta_{i, k}}(s, a_i)$, where $\theta_{i, k}$ denotes the parameters of the $i$th utility in the $k$th critic. Each critic is trained with a target
\begin{equation}
y = r + \frac{\gamma}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i' \in \mathcal{A}_i} \bar{U}^i(s', a_i') \; ;
\end{equation}
where $\bar{U}^i(s, a_i) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K U^i_{\bar{\theta}_{i, k}}(s, a_i)$ is the mean utility across all critics, with $\bar{\theta}_{i, k}$ being target utility network parameters.

The new target difference incorporating the ensemble is
\begin{align}
Z_s^{ens} = \gamma \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i \in \mathcal{A}_i} \bar{U}^i(s', a_i) - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \max_{a_i \in \mathcal{A}_i} U_i^{\pi_i}(s', a_i) \right) \; .
\end{align}
The utility function for each critic is $U^i_{\theta_{i, k}}(s, a_i) = U_i^{\pi_i}(s, a_i) + \epsilon^{i, k}_{s, a_i}$, where $\epsilon^{i, k}_{s, a_i}$ are i.i.d Uniform$(-b, b)$ random variables. This leads to Theorem 2.

Theorem 2.
Given the definitions of $Z_s^{dec}$ and $Z_s^{ens}$, we have that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathbb{E}[Z_s^{ens}] = \mathbb{E}[Z_s^{dec}]$ ;\\
\item $\mbox{Var}(Z_s^{ens}) = \frac{1}{K} \mbox{Var}(Z_s^{dec})$ .
\end{enumerate}
The ensemble leaves the expected value of the target difference unaltered but reduces its variance proportionally to the ensemble size $K$.

Regularised Value-Decomposition
In FMDPs, multiple sub-actions are executed simultaneously, with a single scalar reward as feedback. An optimal sub-action in one dimension can be detrimentally impacted by exploratory sub-actions in other dimensions. If the DecQN loss is minimised, the utility for the optimal sub-action could be undervalued due to extrinsic influences. This introduces the regularised component of REValueD.

Given that feedback is only available for the global action, a credit assignment issue arises. A global action can contain optimal sub-actions from one dimension coupled with exploratory sub-actions from other dimensions. These exploratory sub-actions could yield a low reward or lead to a low-value subsequent state, adversely affecting the utility values of optimal sub-actions within the global action by resulting in an underestimated TD target.

To counteract this, a regularisation term is introduced, minimising the following loss:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_a(\theta) = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{(s, \textbf{a}, r, s') \in B} \sum_{i=1}^N w_i L \left( U_{\bar{\theta}_i}(s, a_i) - U_{\theta_i}(s, a_i)\right) \; ;
\end{equation}
where $w_i = 1 - \exp\left( - |\delta_i| \right)$ and $\delta_i = y - U_{\theta_i}(s, a_i)$, with $y$ defined as in the DecQN loss.

The weights are chosen so that as $|\delta_i|$ grows larger, the weights tend to one. For large $|\delta_i|$, the reward/next state is likely influenced by other sub-actions. Regularising the update prevents individual utilities from being too under or overvalued by keeping them close to existing values.

The regularisation loss allows control over the impact of an update at the individual utility level. The total loss for REValueD is
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}_{tot}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \beta \mathcal{L}_a(\theta) \;;
\end{align}
where $\beta$ is a hyper-parameter. In experiments, $\beta = 0.1$. The regularisation loss is introduced for a single critic for notation, but extension to an ensemble is straightforward.

Experiments
REValueD is benchmarked on discretised versions of DeepMind Control Suite tasks (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020), as used by Seyde et al. (2022). These tasks are challenging control problems; when discretised, they can incorporate up to 38 distinct sub-action spaces.

Unless stated otherwise, the Bang-Off-Bang discretisation from Seyde et al. (2022) is used, where each dimension of the continuous action is discretised into three bins. REValueD is compared against DecQN (Seyde et al., 2022) and Branching Dueling Q-Network (BDQ) (Tavakoli et al., 2018). Performance is measured by plotting the returns of a test episode every 1000 updates, where actions are selected according to a greedy policy.

The mean performance with a 95% confidence interval is shown in Figure 1, comparing REValueD, DecQN, and BDQ on DM Control Suite tasks. BDQ is the least successful, failing to learn in humanoid environments. REValueD demonstrates considerable improvement over DecQN in most tasks, especially in more challenging tasks with larger numbers of sub-action spaces. This advantage is noticeable in humanoid and dog tasks, which have a large number of sub-action spaces (N = 21 and 38).

The performance as the number of sub-actions per dimension increases is investigated by varying the number of bins used to discretise continuous actions. Figure 2 shows results for the dog-walk task. For n=30, REValueD maintains strong performance, whereas DecQN performance falters. For n = 75 or larger, REValueD still demonstrates acceptable performance, whereas DecQN only just shows signs of learning. BDQ performs consistently in the dog-walk task despite large $n_i$ values.

Ablation studies
Relative contribution of the regularisation loss: The effect of the regularisation loss on REValueD performance is analyzed in the most challenging DM Control Suite tasks. Table 1 compares REValueD with and without the regularisation loss; the latter is called DecQN+Ensemble. The inclusion of an ensemble enhances DecQN performance. The incorporation of the regularisation loss further augments ensemble performance.

For easier tasks, a higher ensemble may reduce variance too much. As task complexity increases, a larger ensemble size is beneficial. This is evident in dog-run tasks, where performance peaks with an ensemble size of 15. For easier tasks, a smaller ensemble size may be beneficial. A larger ensemble size improves performance for more complex tasks.

Conclusion
Recent works have applied value-decomposition from MARL to single agent FMDPs. Motivated by maximisation bias in Q-learning, we analyze how this is affected when using DecQN value-decomposition. Theoretically, estimation bias is lowered, but target variance increases. High target variance can cause learning instabilities. An ensemble of critics is introduced to control target variance, while leaving estimation bias unaffected.

REValueD: Regularised Ensemble Value-Decomposition for Factorisable Markov Decision Processes

Abstract
Discrete-action reinforcement learning algorithms can struggle in tasks with high-dimensional discrete action spaces. A recent approach uses value-decomposition, a concept from multi-agent reinforcement learning, to address this. This study examines the effects of this value-decomposition, finding that while it reduces the over-estimation bias inherent to Q-learning algorithms, it increases target variance. To address this, an ensemble of critics is used to mitigate target variance. Additionally, a regularisation loss is introduced to help mitigate the effects that exploratory actions in one dimension can have on the value of optimal actions in other dimensions. The algorithm, REValueD, was tested on discretised versions of DeepMind Control Suite tasks. It showed superior performance compared to baseline methods, particularly in the humanoid and dog tasks. The factors influencing REValueD's performance were analyzed, evaluating the significance of the regularisation loss and the scalability with increasing sub-actions per dimension.

Introduction
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) combines deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL). Problems with high-dimensional, discrete action spaces remain relatively unexplored. In these problems, the action space can be a Cartesian product of discrete sets, i.e., $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}_1 \times ... \times \mathcal{A}_N$. Here, $\mathcal{A}_i$ represents the $i$th sub-action space, containing $n_i$ discrete sub-actions. A Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Bellman, 1957) with such a factorisable action space is referred to as a factorisable MDP (FMDP).

In high-dimensional FMDPs, there are $\prod_{i=1}^N n_i$ atomic actions. Standard algorithms like Q-learning (Watkins & Dayan, 1992; Mnih et al., 2013) can fail due to computational impracticalities. Recent approaches learn about each sub-action space individually (Tavakoli et al., 2018; Seyde et al., 2022). The DecQN algorithm (Seyde et al., 2022) uses value-decomposition to learn utility values for sub-actions. The utility of each selected sub-action is computed independently, but learnt so their mean estimates the Q-value for the global action. This is inspired by the centralised training with decentralised execution paradigm in multi-agent RL (MARL) (Kraemer & Doshi, 2016). The $i$th utility function only needs to learn values for the actions in $\mathcal{A}_i$. The total number of actions for which a utility value needs to be learned is $\sum_{i=1}^N n_i$.

This paper presents two primary methodological contributions. First, a theoretical analysis of the value-decomposition when coupled with function approximation is conducted. Q-learning with function approximation suffers from an over-estimation bias in the target (Thrun & Schwartz, 1993; Hasselt, 2010). We explore how value-decomposition impacts this bias. We show that the DecQN decomposition reduces the over-estimation bias in the target Q-values but increases the variance. We establish that an ensemble of critics can mitigate this increase in variance.

Second, a regularisation loss is introduced to be minimised alongside the DecQN loss. The loss is motivated by the credit assignment issue common in MARL (Weiss, 1995; Wolpert & Tumer, 1999; Zhou et al., 2020; Gronauer & Diepold, 2022), where an exploratory action of one agent can negatively influence the value of the optimal action of another agent. This issue is also present when using value-decomposition in FMDPs. The regularisation loss helps mitigate the impact that exploratory sub-actions can have on the utility values of optimal sub-actions post-update by discouraging substantial changes in individual utility estimates. This is achieved by minimising the Huber loss between the selected sub-action utilities and their corresponding values under the target network.

The approach is called REValueD: Regularised Ensemble Value Decomposition. REValueD is benchmarked against DecQN and Branching Dueling Q-Networks (BDQ) (Tavakoli et al., 2018), using the discretised variants of DeepMind control suite tasks (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020) used by Seyde et al. (2022). The experimental results show that REValueD consistently surpasses DecQN and BDQ across a majority of tasks. REValueD markedly outperforms the baselines in the humanoid and dog tasks, where the number of sub-action spaces is high (N = 21 and 38, respectively). Ablation studies are performed on the distinct components of REValueD to evaluate their individual contributions. These include analyzing how performance evolves with increasing $n_i$ and examining the impact of the regularisation loss.

An FMDP is an MDP where the action space can be factorised as $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}_1 \times ... \times \mathcal{A}_N$, where $\mathcal{A}_i$ is a set of discrete sub-actions. $\textbf{a} = (a_1, ..., a_N)$ is the global action, and individual $a_i$'s are sub-actions. \end{equation}

\end{align}

\begin{align}

\end{align}

The regularisation works at the individual utility level, mitigating the effect of exploratory sub-actions by enforcing that utility estimates do not stray too far from their current values.

These contributions lead to REValueD. REValueD is compared to DecQN and BDQ on DM Control Suite tasks. In most tasks, REValueD greatly outperforms DecQN and BDQ, notably in humanoid and dog tasks which have N = 21 and 38 sub-action spaces. Ablation studies are provided, including the relative contribution of the regularisation loss and how performance changes as the number of sub-actions per dimension increases.

Further, using an uninformative $\epsilon$-greedy exploration strategy can be wasteful in FMDPs due to many possible sub-action combinations. More advanced exploration techniques could be developed to effectively choose optimal sub-actions in one dimension while continuing to explore in other dimensions.

title: UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera
full_text:
\title{UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera}

\begin{abstract}
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under fast camera motion often contain obvious image distortions and blur, which can be modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of global shutter (GS) frames within the exposure time. 
Naturally, recovering high-frame-rate GS sharp frames from an RS blur image needs to simultaneously consider RS correction, deblur, and frame interpolation.
Tacking this task is nontrivial, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible solutions exist by far.
A naive way is to decompose the whole process into separate tasks and simply cascade existing methods; however, this results in cumulative errors and noticeable artifacts. 
Event cameras enjoy many advantages, \eg, high temporal resolution, making them potential for our problem. To this end, we propose the \textbf{first} and novel approach, named \textbf{UniINR}, to recover arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. Our key idea is \textit{unifying spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to directly map the position and time coordinates to RGB values to address the interlocking degradations in the image restoration process}. 
Specifically, we introduce spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) to convert an RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR).
To query a specific sharp frame (GS or RS), we embed the exposure time into STR and decode the embedded features pixel-by-pixel to recover a sharp frame.
Our method features a lightweight model with only \textbf{$0.379 M$} parameters, and it also enjoys high inference efficiency, achieving $2.83 ms/frame$ in $31 \times$ frame interpolation of an RS blur frame.
Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms prior methods.
\end{abstract}

\section{133 3 METHODOLOGY  }


134 3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION AND ANALYSIS   
135 We formulate the task —recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and   
136 paired event data —as a novel estimation problem, defined as a function, $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ . Here, $\textbf{\em x}$ denotes   
137 the pixel position $(x,y)$ of an image with a resolution of $H\times W$ , $t$ denotes the timestamp during the   
138 exposure time, and $\theta$ denotes the parameters. The intuition behind this formulation is that there exists   
139 a relationship between the RS blur/sharp frame and the GS blur/sharp frame. We now describe it.   
140 By defining a function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ mapping the pixel position $\pmb{x}=(x,y)$ and timestamp $t$ to intensity   
141 or RGB value, we can obtain a GS sharp frame by inputting the desired timestamp tˆ during the   
142 exposure time to the function, which can be formulated as:  

![](images/6fb778399fef479ed7c1030dd2d6ae4d04b7061c64a8020645540f435b04c7fa.jpg)  
Figure 2: An overview of our framework, which consists of three parts, (a) the Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), (b) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and (c) Pixel-by-pixel decoding (PPD). Details of STE, ETE, and PPD are described in Sec. 3.2.1, Sec. 3.2.2, and Sec. 3.2.3. The inputs are an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$ and events, and the outputs are a sequence of GS frames and RS frames. RS frames are predicted only in training.  

$$
I_{g,{\hat{t}}}=F(\pmb{x},{\hat{t}},\theta)
$$  

143 As an RS image can be formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the   
144 exposure time (Fan & Dai, 2021; Fan et al., 2023), we can assemble an RS sharp frame $I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}$ from   
145 a sequence of GS sharp frames row by row given the RS start time $t_{s}$ and the end time $t_{e}$ . That is,   
146 the $h$ -th row of an RS frame is the same as the $h$ -th row of a GS frame at $t_{s}^{h}$ , and the exposure start   
147 timestamp of the $h$ -th row of an RS frame is $t_{s}^{h}=t_{s}+h\times(t_{e}-t_{s})/H$ . Therefore, we can formally   
148 describe an RS sharp frame as follows:  

$$
I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}=\left\{F\left(\pmb{x},t_{s}^{h},\theta\right)[h],h\in[0,H)\right\}.
$$  

149 In principle, a blur frame can be regarded as the temporal average of a sequence of sharp frames (Nah   
150 et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, a GS blur frame $I_{g,t_{g},t_{e x p}}$ , where $t_{g}$ is the exposure start   
151 timestamp and $t_{e x p}$ is the exposure time, can be expressed as the average of a sequence of GS sharp   
152 frames during the exposure time $t_{e x p}$ , which can be formulated as:  

$$
I_{g,t,t e x p}=\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t}^{t+t_{e x p}}F({\pmb x},t,\theta)d t\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{0}+i\times t_{e x p}/N},
$$  

153 where $N$ is the length of the GS frame sequence.  

154 With the above formulation, an RS blur frame $I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}$ can thus be described based on the RS   
155 start time $t_{s}$ , RS end time $t_{e}$ , and exposure time of each scan line $t_{e x p}$ , as depicted in Fig. 1 (a).   
156 According to Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, the $h$ -th row of an RS blur frame can be described as the temporal   
157 average of the $h$ -th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames, which can be written as follows:  

$$
\begin{array}{r l}{I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}}&{=\left\{\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t_{s}^{h}}^{t_{s}^{h}+t_{e x p}}F\left(\mathbf{x},t,\theta\right)\left[h\right]\!d t,h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}}\\ &{\approx\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{s}+i\times t_{e x p}/N}[h],h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}.}\end{array}
$$  

158 An event stream $E$ consists of a set of event $\boldsymbol{e}\,=\,(x,y,t,p)$ , where each event is triggered and   
159 recorded with the polarity $p$ when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel $(x,y)$ exceeds a certain   
160 threshold $C$ , which can be approximated as the differential of $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ with respect to the time   
161 dimension. For details about the principle of event cameras, refer to the Suppl. Mat.   
162 To use event data $E$ as guidance, we need to address three challenges to estimate the mapping function   
163 $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ : 1) how to find a function $f_{e}$ to encode the input RS blur image and events to $\theta$ of the   
164 mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ ; 2) how to find a function $f_{t e}$ to represent the exposure information of   
165 desired RS or GS sharp frames as $t$ of the mapping function $\bar{\boldsymbol{F}}(\pmb{x},t,\theta)$ ; 3) how to find a function   
166 $f_{d}$ to eliminate the need to input position information of desired RS or GS sharp frames as $p$ of   
167 the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,{\bar{\theta}})$ . Therefore, our goal is to estimate $f_{e},f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ in order to get a   
168 mapped result, which can be formulated as:  

$$
I=F(\pmb{x},t,\theta)=F(\pmb{x},t,f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=F(\pmb{x},f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b})).
$$  

169 In the following section, we describe our framework based on Eq. 5 by substantiating $f_{e},f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ .   
170 3.2 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK   
171 An overview of our UniINR framework is depicted in Fig. 2, which takes an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$   
172 and paired events $E$ as inputs and outputs $N$ sharp GS frames $\{I_{g s s}\}_{i=0}^{N}$ with a high-frame-rate. To   
173 substantiate the defined functions $f_{e}$ , $f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ , as mentioned in Sec. 3.1, our proposed framework   
174 consists of three components: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time   
175 Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). Specifically, we first introduce an STE   
176 with deformable convolution (Wang et al., 2022a) to encode the RS blur frame and events into a   
177 spatial-temporal representation (STR) (Sec. 3.2.1). To provide exposure temporal information for   
178 STR, we embed the exposure start timestamp of each pixel from the GS or RS by ETE. (Sec. 3.2.2).   
179 Lastly, the PDD module adds ETE to STR to generate RS or GS sharp frames (Sec. 3.2.3). We now   
180 describe these components in detail.  



\section{3.2.2 EXPOSURE TIME EMBEDDING (ETE)  }


200 As depicted in Fig. 2 (b), the primary objective of the ETE module is to incorporate the exposure   
201 time of either a rolling shutter (RS) frame $(t_{s},t_{e})$ or a global shutter (GS) frame $(t_{g})$ by employing   
202 an MLP layer, resulting in the generation of a temporal tensor $T$ . To achieve this, we design an ETE   
203 module, denoted as $f_{t e}$ , which takes the GS exposure time $t_{g}$ as input and produces the GS temporal   
204 tensor $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ . Similarly, for RS frames, $T_{r}=f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{r_{e}})$ represents the RS temporal tensor,   
205 which is only used in training. The process begins by converting the exposure process information   
206 into a timestamp map, with a shape of $H\times W\times1$ . Subsequently, the timestamp map is embedded   
207 by increasing its dimensionality to match the shape of the STR. This embedding procedure allows   
208 for the integration of the exposure time information into the STR representation. We now explain   
209 the construction of timestamp maps for both GS and RS frames and describe the embedding method   
210 employed in our approach.   
211 GS Timestamp Map: In GS sharp frames, all pixels are exposed simultaneously, resulting in the   
212 same exposure timestamps for pixels in different positions. Given a GS exposure timestamp $t_{g}$ , the   
213 GS timestamp map $M_{g}$ can be represented as $\bar{M_{g}}[h][w]=t_{g}$ , where $h$ and $w$ denote the row and   
214 column indices, respectively.   
215 RS Timestamp Map: According to the analysis in Sec. 3.1, pixels in RS frames are exposed line   
216 by line, and pixels in different rows have different exposure start timestamps. Given RS exposure   
217 information with start time $t_{s}$ and RS end time $t_{e}$ , the RS timestamp map can be represented as   
218 $M_{r}[h][w]=t_{s}+(t_{e}-t_{s})\times h/H$ , where $h,w,H$ denote the row and column indices and height of   
219 the image, respectively.   
220 Time Embedding: The timestamp maps, $M_{r}$ and $M_{g}$ , represent the timestamps of each pixel in   
221 a specific frame (RS or GS) with a shape of $H\times W\times1$ . However, the timestamp map is a high  
222 frequency variable and can pose challenges for learning neural networks (Vaswani et al., 2017). Some   
223 approaches (Vaswani et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021) propose a combination function of sine and   
224 cosine to encode the positional embedding. Nonetheless, calculating the derivative of the positional   
225 embedding is difficult, limiting its practical application to image enhancement tasks. In this paper,   
226 we utilize a one-layer MLP to increase the dimension for embedding. The whole embedding process   
227 is formulated as $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ for GS frames, and $T_{r}\,=\,f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{\bar{r_{e}}})$ for RS frames, as depicted in   
228 Fig. 2(b). The MLP consists of a single layer that maps the timestamp map $M_{r}$ or $M_{g}$ to the same   
229 dimension $H\times W\times C$ as the spatial-temporal representation (STR) $\theta$ , as described in Sec. 3.2.1.   
230 3.2.3 PIXEL-BY-PIXEL DECODING (PPD)   
231 As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the goal of PPD is to efficiently query a sharp frame from STR $\theta$ by the   
232 temporal tensor $T$ . It is important that the encoder is invoked only once for $N$ times interpolation,   
233 while the decoder is called $N$ times. Therefore, the efficiency of this query is crucial for the overall   
234 performance. The query’s inputs $\theta$ capture the global spatial-temporal information, and $T$ captures   
235 the temporal information of the sharp frame (GS or RS). Inspired by previous works (Mildenhall   
236 et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021), we directly incorporate the temporal tensor $T$ into the STR $\theta$ to obtain   
237 an embedded feature with a shape of $H\times W\times C$ for each query. This additional embedded feature   
238 combines the global spatial-temporal information with the local exposure information, enabling   
239 straightforward decoding to obtain a sharp frame. To avoid the need for explicit positional queries,   
240 we employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder. The decoder, denoted as $f_{d}$ in Eq. 5, employs a simple 5-layer   
241 MLP $f_{m l p}^{(\chi)^{5}}$ architecture. The reconstructed output $I$ after decoding can be described in Eq. 6, where   
242 $\circleddash$ means element-wise addition.  

$$
I=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(T,\theta)=f_{m l p}^{\zeta5^{5}}(T\oplus\theta).
$$  

243 3.2.4 LOSS FUNCTION  

244 RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Inspired by EVDI (Zhang & Yu, 2022), we formulate the   
245 relationship between RS blur frames and RS sharp frames. Given a sequence of RS sharp frames   
246 generated from the decoder, the input RS blur frame $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$ , where $M$ represents the   
247 length of the RS image sequence. In this way, we can formulařte the blur frame guidance integral   
248 loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame and the original RS blur frame as $\mathcal{L}_{b}=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})$ ,   
249 where $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ indicates Charbonnier loss (Lai et al., 2018).   
250 Total Loss: Apart from RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$ , we incorporate a reconstruction loss   
251 $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames. Our method consists of two losses: RS blur   
252 image-guided integral loss and the reconstruction loss, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the weights of each loss:  

$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$  

253 4 EXPERIMENTS  

254 Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) for all experiments,   
255 with learning rates of $1e-4$ for both Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) and Fastec-RS (Liu et al., 2020)   
256 datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our framework across 400 epochs   
257 with a batch size of two. In addition, we use the mixed precision (Micikevicius et al., 2017) training   
258 tool provided by PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017) , which can speed up our training and reduce memory   
259 usage. PSNR and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) are used to evaluate the reconstructed results.   
60 Datasets: 1) Gev-RS dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) features GS videos at $1280\times720$ , 5700 fps. We   
61 reconstruct such frames and events from the original videos, downsampling to $260\times346$ (Scheerlinck   
62 et al., 2019). Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using vid2e (Gehrig et al., 2020). We adopt   
63 EvUnroll’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 20/9 train/test split. 2) Fastec-RS dataset (Liu et al., 2020) offers GS   
64 videos at $640\times480$ , 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur.   
65 The dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) Real-world dataset (Zhou et al.,   
66 2022) is the only available real dataset, containing four videos with paired RS frames and events.   
67 Due to the lack of ground truth, it offers only quantitative visualizations. More details in Suppl. Mat..  

![](images/70a1d92a5c9efb08f41cc4fa4ea2d36cdbf3017f0856c1486fc111e4e6c6176b.jpg)  
Figure 3: Visual Comparisons on RS correction and deblurring on Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset. The image resolution of DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) is $180\times240$ .  



\section{268 4.1 COMPARISON WITH SOTA METHODS  }


269 Our experiments are conducted on both simulated and real datasets. While the simulated dataset   
270 enables us to obtain accurate quantitative results, evaluating on the real dataset offers insights into the   
271 generation ability of our method.   
272 We compare our methods with recent methods with two different settings in these two datasets: (I)   
273 the experiment with a single GS sharp frame result, including JCD (Zhong et al., 2021) (frame  
274 based RS correction and deblurring), EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) (event-guided RS correction)   
275 and eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) (event-guided deblurring). (II) the experiment with a sequence of   
276 GS sharp frames result, which includes DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) (event-guided deblurring and   
277 interpolation), and the combination of EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al.,   
278 2021) (event-guided video frame interpolation). In addition, we test our model’s generation ability by   
279 comparing it with EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) using real data. While this real data is solely reserved   
280 for testing, both our model and EvUnRoll are trained on the simulation dataset. More explanations of   
281 setting (II) are in Supp. Mat..   
282 We evaluate JCD, EvUnroll, TimeLens, and DeblurSR with the released code. We modified eSL  
283 Net by adjusting its parameterization initialization method and removing the up-sampling module,   
284 allowing it to be well trained on our datasets. The outputs of eSL-Net and DeblurSR are grayscale   
285 frames, and the outputs of JCD, EvUnroll, and the combination of EvUnroll and TimeLens are RGB   
286 frames. For fairness, our network is trained with the input of grayscale and RGB images, respectively.   
287 The quantitative results for experiments generating a single GS sharp frame $(1\times)$ and those producing   
288 a sequence of GS sharp frames $(3{\times},\,5{\times},\,9{\times})$ are presented in Tab. 1. In comparison to methods   
289 that yield a single GS sharp frame, our approach exhibits remarkable performance in both gray and   
290 RGB frames, surpassing the best-performing methods (eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) in gray and   
291 EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) in RGB) by 1.48dB and 4.17dB on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022)   
292 dataset, respectively. In scenarios where a sequence of GS sharp frames is produced, our method   
293 attains optimal performance for both gray and RGB frames, achieving an increase of up to 13.47dB   
294 and 8.49dB compared to DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) and EvUnroll (Zhou et al., $2022)+^{\prime}$ Time  
295 Lens (Tulyakov et al., 2021) on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset, respectively. The substantial   
296 performance decline of DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) can be ascribed to the interdependence between   
297 RS correction and deblur. The performance reduction of EvUnroll+TimeLens can be accounted for   
298 by the accumulation of errors arising from this cascading network, as shown in Fig. 1(h).   
299 The qualitative results, as depicted in Fig. 11, showcase the effectiveness of our proposed method   
300 on both grayscale and RGB inputs. These results demonstrate our approach’s ability to generate   
301 sharp frames devoid of RS distortion, yielding the most visually pleasing outcomes in challenging   
302 scenarios involving a fast-moving train with motion blur and RS distortion. Comparatively, the results   
303 of eSL-Net and EvUnroll exhibit discernible noise, particularly evident around the train door within   
304 the red region of Fig. 11. Another approach, JCD, falls short in recovering sharp frames within   
305 such complex scenes. This failure can be attributed to the insufficient availability of frame-based   
306 methods which rely on the assumption of linear motion. Furthermore, the results obtained using   
307 DebluSR (Song et al., 2023) display noticeable artifacts, particularly in the context of the moving   
308 train. These artifacts hinder satisfactory frame reconstruction in such dynamic environments.   
309 Bad case analysis: The color distortion in Fig. 11 (j) can be attributed to the insufficient color   
310 information in the challenging scene of a fast-moving train. From the input (Fig. 11 (h)), it can be   
311 noticed that the degree of motion blur is extremely severe and the blurry frame cannot provide valid   
312 color information. Furthermore, according to the principle of the generation of the event, the event is   
313 triggered by intensity change and it cannot provide color information.   
314 EvUnRoll Simulation Dataset: To achieve a more equitable comparison with EvUnRoll, we evaluate   
315 our method on the simulated dataset employed by EvUnRoll, shown in Tab. 2. It’s important to   
316 emphasize that the dataset includes paired data consisting of RS blur, RS sharp, and GS sharp. For our   
317 model’s training, we specifically utilize the paired images of RS blur and GS sharp. As a one-stage   
318 approach, our method directly transforms an RS-blurred image into a GS-sharp image avoiding   
319 accumulated error, and thus has better performance.   
320 Real-world Dataset: Fig. 4 shows real-world results. The input frame exhibits rolling shutter   
321 distortions, such as curved palette edges. In contrast, events show global shutter traits. Both   
322 our method and EvUnRoll correct these distortions effectively. Due to the lack of ground truth,   
323 quantitative analysis is not possible. Notably, our method avoids artifacts and errors, outperforming   
324 EvUnRoll in palette scenarios. For further discussion please refer to the Supp. Mat..

\section{325 4.2 ABLATION AND ANALYTICAL STUDIES  }


326 Importance of Exposure Time Embedding: We conduct the experiments to evaluate the impact   
327 of learning-based position embedding, with a comparative analysis to sinusoid position embed  
328 ding (Vaswani et al., 2017). As indicated in Tab. 3, learning-based position embedding outperforms   
329 sinusoid position embedding, with advancements of up to 1.11dB on average. This superior efficacy

331 Importance of RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: The effectiveness of the RS blur image-guided

333 the enhancement in PSNR for high interpolation configurations (e.g., $9\times1$ ) upon employing this loss.   
334 Inference Speed: Fig. 5 shows our method’s inference time across $1\times$ to $31\times$ interpolation. The   
335 total time rises modestly, e.g., from $30.8~m s$ at $1\times$ to $86.9~m s$ at $31\times$ , a 2.8-fold increase for a   
336 31-fold interpolation. The average frame time even decreases at higher multiples, reaching $2.8\:m s$ at   
337 $31\times$ . Compared to EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021), our method

342 further increases EvUnRoll and TimeLens’ time consumption. More discussions are in Supp. Mat..

\section{344 5 CONCLUSION  }


345 This paper presented a novel approach that simultaneously uses events to guide rolling shutter frame   
346 correction, deblur, and interpolation. Unlike previous network structures that can only address one   
347 or two image enhancement tasks, our method incorporated all three tasks concurrently, providing   
348 potential for future expansion into areas such as image and video super-resolution and denoising.   
349 Furthermore, our approach demonstrated high efficiency in computational complexity and model size.   
350 Regardless of the number of frames involved in interpolation, our method only requires a single call   
351 to the encoder, and the model size is a mere 0.379M.   
352 Limitations Our analysis utilizes simulated data and real-world datasets, the latter of which lacks   
353 ground truth. Acquiring real data with ground truth is challenging. In future work, we aim to address   
354 this limitation by employing optical instruments, such as spectroscopes, to obtain real-world data   
355 with ground truth for quantitative evaluation.
