original_text:
\title{UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera}

\begin{abstract}
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under fast camera motion often contain obvious image distortions and blur, which can be modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of global shutter (GS) frames within the exposure time. 
Naturally, recovering high-frame-rate GS sharp frames from an RS blur image needs to simultaneously consider RS correction, deblur, and frame interpolation.
Tacking this task is nontrivial, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible solutions exist by far.
A naive way is to decompose the whole process into separate tasks and simply cascade existing methods; however, this results in cumulative errors and noticeable artifacts. 
Event cameras enjoy many advantages, \eg, high temporal resolution, making them potential for our problem. To this end, we propose the \textbf{first} and novel approach, named \textbf{UniINR}, to recover arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. Our key idea is \textit{unifying spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to directly map the position and time coordinates to RGB values to address the interlocking degradations in the image restoration process}. 
Specifically, we introduce spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) to convert an RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR).
To query a specific sharp frame (GS or RS), we embed the exposure time into STR and decode the embedded features pixel-by-pixel to recover a sharp frame.
Our method features a lightweight model with only \textbf{$0.379 M$} parameters, and it also enjoys high inference efficiency, achieving $2.83 ms/frame$ in $31 \times$ frame interpolation of an RS blur frame.
Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms prior methods.
\end{abstract}

\section{133 3 METHODOLOGY  }


134 3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION AND ANALYSIS   
135 We formulate the task —recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and   
136 paired event data —as a novel estimation problem, defined as a function, $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ . Here, $\textbf{\em x}$ denotes   
137 the pixel position $(x,y)$ of an image with a resolution of $H\times W$ , $t$ denotes the timestamp during the   
138 exposure time, and $\theta$ denotes the parameters. The intuition behind this formulation is that there exists   
139 a relationship between the RS blur/sharp frame and the GS blur/sharp frame. We now describe it.   
140 By defining a function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ mapping the pixel position $\pmb{x}=(x,y)$ and timestamp $t$ to intensity   
141 or RGB value, we can obtain a GS sharp frame by inputting the desired timestamp tˆ during the   
142 exposure time to the function, which can be formulated as:  

![](images/6fb778399fef479ed7c1030dd2d6ae4d04b7061c64a8020645540f435b04c7fa.jpg)  
Figure 2: An overview of our framework, which consists of three parts, (a) the Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), (b) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and (c) Pixel-by-pixel decoding (PPD). Details of STE, ETE, and PPD are described in Sec. 3.2.1, Sec. 3.2.2, and Sec. 3.2.3. The inputs are an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$ and events, and the outputs are a sequence of GS frames and RS frames. RS frames are predicted only in training.  

$$
I_{g,{\hat{t}}}=F(\pmb{x},{\hat{t}},\theta)
$$  

143 As an RS image can be formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the   
144 exposure time (Fan & Dai, 2021; Fan et al., 2023), we can assemble an RS sharp frame $I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}$ from   
145 a sequence of GS sharp frames row by row given the RS start time $t_{s}$ and the end time $t_{e}$ . That is,   
146 the $h$ -th row of an RS frame is the same as the $h$ -th row of a GS frame at $t_{s}^{h}$ , and the exposure start   
147 timestamp of the $h$ -th row of an RS frame is $t_{s}^{h}=t_{s}+h\times(t_{e}-t_{s})/H$ . Therefore, we can formally   
148 describe an RS sharp frame as follows:  

$$
I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}=\left\{F\left(\pmb{x},t_{s}^{h},\theta\right)[h],h\in[0,H)\right\}.
$$  

149 In principle, a blur frame can be regarded as the temporal average of a sequence of sharp frames (Nah   
150 et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, a GS blur frame $I_{g,t_{g},t_{e x p}}$ , where $t_{g}$ is the exposure start   
151 timestamp and $t_{e x p}$ is the exposure time, can be expressed as the average of a sequence of GS sharp   
152 frames during the exposure time $t_{e x p}$ , which can be formulated as:  

$$
I_{g,t,t e x p}=\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t}^{t+t_{e x p}}F({\pmb x},t,\theta)d t\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{0}+i\times t_{e x p}/N},
$$  

153 where $N$ is the length of the GS frame sequence.  

154 With the above formulation, an RS blur frame $I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}$ can thus be described based on the RS   
155 start time $t_{s}$ , RS end time $t_{e}$ , and exposure time of each scan line $t_{e x p}$ , as depicted in Fig. 1 (a).   
156 According to Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, the $h$ -th row of an RS blur frame can be described as the temporal   
157 average of the $h$ -th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames, which can be written as follows:  

$$
\begin{array}{r l}{I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}}&{=\left\{\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t_{s}^{h}}^{t_{s}^{h}+t_{e x p}}F\left(\mathbf{x},t,\theta\right)\left[h\right]\!d t,h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}}\\ &{\approx\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{s}+i\times t_{e x p}/N}[h],h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}.}\end{array}
$$  

158 An event stream $E$ consists of a set of event $\boldsymbol{e}\,=\,(x,y,t,p)$ , where each event is triggered and   
159 recorded with the polarity $p$ when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel $(x,y)$ exceeds a certain   
160 threshold $C$ , which can be approximated as the differential of $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ with respect to the time   
161 dimension. For details about the principle of event cameras, refer to the Suppl. Mat.   
162 To use event data $E$ as guidance, we need to address three challenges to estimate the mapping function   
163 $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ : 1) how to find a function $f_{e}$ to encode the input RS blur image and events to $\theta$ of the   
164 mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ ; 2) how to find a function $f_{t e}$ to represent the exposure information of   
165 desired RS or GS sharp frames as $t$ of the mapping function $\bar{\boldsymbol{F}}(\pmb{x},t,\theta)$ ; 3) how to find a function   
166 $f_{d}$ to eliminate the need to input position information of desired RS or GS sharp frames as $p$ of   
167 the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,{\bar{\theta}})$ . Therefore, our goal is to estimate $f_{e},f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ in order to get a   
168 mapped result, which can be formulated as:  

$$
I=F(\pmb{x},t,\theta)=F(\pmb{x},t,f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=F(\pmb{x},f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b})).
$$  

169 In the following section, we describe our framework based on Eq. 5 by substantiating $f_{e},f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ .   
170 3.2 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK   
171 An overview of our UniINR framework is depicted in Fig. 2, which takes an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$   
172 and paired events $E$ as inputs and outputs $N$ sharp GS frames $\{I_{g s s}\}_{i=0}^{N}$ with a high-frame-rate. To   
173 substantiate the defined functions $f_{e}$ , $f_{t e}$ , and $f_{d}$ , as mentioned in Sec. 3.1, our proposed framework   
174 consists of three components: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time   
175 Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). Specifically, we first introduce an STE   
176 with deformable convolution (Wang et al., 2022a) to encode the RS blur frame and events into a   
177 spatial-temporal representation (STR) (Sec. 3.2.1). To provide exposure temporal information for   
178 STR, we embed the exposure start timestamp of each pixel from the GS or RS by ETE. (Sec. 3.2.2).   
179 Lastly, the PDD module adds ETE to STR to generate RS or GS sharp frames (Sec. 3.2.3). We now   
180 describe these components in detail.  



\section{3.2.2 EXPOSURE TIME EMBEDDING (ETE)  }


200 As depicted in Fig. 2 (b), the primary objective of the ETE module is to incorporate the exposure   
201 time of either a rolling shutter (RS) frame $(t_{s},t_{e})$ or a global shutter (GS) frame $(t_{g})$ by employing   
202 an MLP layer, resulting in the generation of a temporal tensor $T$ . To achieve this, we design an ETE   
203 module, denoted as $f_{t e}$ , which takes the GS exposure time $t_{g}$ as input and produces the GS temporal   
204 tensor $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ . Similarly, for RS frames, $T_{r}=f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{r_{e}})$ represents the RS temporal tensor,   
205 which is only used in training. The process begins by converting the exposure process information   
206 into a timestamp map, with a shape of $H\times W\times1$ . Subsequently, the timestamp map is embedded   
207 by increasing its dimensionality to match the shape of the STR. This embedding procedure allows   
208 for the integration of the exposure time information into the STR representation. We now explain   
209 the construction of timestamp maps for both GS and RS frames and describe the embedding method   
210 employed in our approach.   
211 GS Timestamp Map: In GS sharp frames, all pixels are exposed simultaneously, resulting in the   
212 same exposure timestamps for pixels in different positions. Given a GS exposure timestamp $t_{g}$ , the   
213 GS timestamp map $M_{g}$ can be represented as $\bar{M_{g}}[h][w]=t_{g}$ , where $h$ and $w$ denote the row and   
214 column indices, respectively.   
215 RS Timestamp Map: According to the analysis in Sec. 3.1, pixels in RS frames are exposed line   
216 by line, and pixels in different rows have different exposure start timestamps. Given RS exposure   
217 information with start time $t_{s}$ and RS end time $t_{e}$ , the RS timestamp map can be represented as   
218 $M_{r}[h][w]=t_{s}+(t_{e}-t_{s})\times h/H$ , where $h,w,H$ denote the row and column indices and height of   
219 the image, respectively.   
220 Time Embedding: The timestamp maps, $M_{r}$ and $M_{g}$ , represent the timestamps of each pixel in   
221 a specific frame (RS or GS) with a shape of $H\times W\times1$ . However, the timestamp map is a high  
222 frequency variable and can pose challenges for learning neural networks (Vaswani et al., 2017). Some   
223 approaches (Vaswani et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021) propose a combination function of sine and   
224 cosine to encode the positional embedding. Nonetheless, calculating the derivative of the positional   
225 embedding is difficult, limiting its practical application to image enhancement tasks. In this paper,   
226 we utilize a one-layer MLP to increase the dimension for embedding. The whole embedding process   
227 is formulated as $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ for GS frames, and $T_{r}\,=\,f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{\bar{r_{e}}})$ for RS frames, as depicted in   
228 Fig. 2(b). The MLP consists of a single layer that maps the timestamp map $M_{r}$ or $M_{g}$ to the same   
229 dimension $H\times W\times C$ as the spatial-temporal representation (STR) $\theta$ , as described in Sec. 3.2.1.   
230 3.2.3 PIXEL-BY-PIXEL DECODING (PPD)   
231 As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the goal of PPD is to efficiently query a sharp frame from STR $\theta$ by the   
232 temporal tensor $T$ . It is important that the encoder is invoked only once for $N$ times interpolation,   
233 while the decoder is called $N$ times. Therefore, the efficiency of this query is crucial for the overall   
234 performance. The query’s inputs $\theta$ capture the global spatial-temporal information, and $T$ captures   
235 the temporal information of the sharp frame (GS or RS). Inspired by previous works (Mildenhall   
236 et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021), we directly incorporate the temporal tensor $T$ into the STR $\theta$ to obtain   
237 an embedded feature with a shape of $H\times W\times C$ for each query. This additional embedded feature   
238 combines the global spatial-temporal information with the local exposure information, enabling   
239 straightforward decoding to obtain a sharp frame. To avoid the need for explicit positional queries,   
240 we employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder. The decoder, denoted as $f_{d}$ in Eq. 5, employs a simple 5-layer   
241 MLP $f_{m l p}^{(\chi)^{5}}$ architecture. The reconstructed output $I$ after decoding can be described in Eq. 6, where   
242 $\circleddash$ means element-wise addition.  

$$
I=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(T,\theta)=f_{m l p}^{\zeta5^{5}}(T\oplus\theta).
$$  

243 3.2.4 LOSS FUNCTION  

244 RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Inspired by EVDI (Zhang & Yu, 2022), we formulate the   
245 relationship between RS blur frames and RS sharp frames. Given a sequence of RS sharp frames   
246 generated from the decoder, the input RS blur frame $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$ , where $M$ represents the   
247 length of the RS image sequence. In this way, we can formulařte the blur frame guidance integral   
248 loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame and the original RS blur frame as $\mathcal{L}_{b}=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})$ ,   
249 where $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ indicates Charbonnier loss (Lai et al., 2018).   
250 Total Loss: Apart from RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$ , we incorporate a reconstruction loss   
251 $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames. Our method consists of two losses: RS blur   
252 image-guided integral loss and the reconstruction loss, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the weights of each loss:  

$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$  

253 4 EXPERIMENTS  

254 Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) for all experiments,   
255 with learning rates of $1e-4$ for both Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) and Fastec-RS (Liu et al., 2020)   
256 datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our framework across 400 epochs   
257 with a batch size of two. In addition, we use the mixed precision (Micikevicius et al., 2017) training   
258 tool provided by PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017) , which can speed up our training and reduce memory   
259 usage. PSNR and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) are used to evaluate the reconstructed results.   
60 Datasets: 1) Gev-RS dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) features GS videos at $1280\times720$ , 5700 fps. We   
61 reconstruct such frames and events from the original videos, downsampling to $260\times346$ (Scheerlinck   
62 et al., 2019). Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using vid2e (Gehrig et al., 2020). We adopt   
63 EvUnroll’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 20/9 train/test split. 2) Fastec-RS dataset (Liu et al., 2020) offers GS   
64 videos at $640\times480$ , 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur.   
65 The dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) Real-world dataset (Zhou et al.,   
66 2022) is the only available real dataset, containing four videos with paired RS frames and events.   
67 Due to the lack of ground truth, it offers only quantitative visualizations. More details in Suppl. Mat..

269 Our experiments are conducted on both simulated and real datasets. While the simulated dataset

272 We compare our methods with recent methods with two different settings in these two datasets: (I)   
273 the experiment with a single GS sharp frame result, including JCD (Zhong et al., 2021) (frame

281 setting (II) are in Supp. Mat..

283 Net by adjusting its parameterization initialization method and removing the up-sampling module,

286 frames. For fairness, our network is trained with the input of grayscale and RGB images, respectively.

289 that yield a single GS sharp frame, our approach exhibits remarkable performance in both gray and

292 dataset, respectively. In scenarios where a sequence of GS sharp frames is produced, our method

\section{344 5 CONCLUSION  }


345 This paper presented a novel approach that simultaneously uses events to guide rolling shutter frame   
346 correction, deblur, and interpolation. Unlike previous network structures that can only address one   
347 or two image enhancement tasks, our method incorporated all three tasks concurrently, providing   
348 potential for future expansion into areas such as image and video super-resolution and denoising.   
349 Furthermore, our approach demonstrated high efficiency in computational complexity and model size.   
350 Regardless of the number of frames involved in interpolation, our method only requires a single call   
351 to the encoder, and the model size is a mere 0.379M.   
352 Limitations Our analysis utilizes simulated data and real-world datasets, the latter of which lacks   
353 ground truth. Acquiring real data with ground truth is challenging. In future work, we aim to address   
354 this limitation by employing optical instruments, such as spectroscopes, to obtain real-world data   
355 with ground truth for quantitative evaluation.

\title{UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera}

\begin{abstract}
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under fast camera motion inevitably contain severe image distortions and blur, which are precisely modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of global shutter (GS) frames within the exposure time. 
Consequently, recovering high-frame-rate GS sharp frames from an RS blur image definitively requires simultaneously addressing RS correction, deblur, and frame interpolation.
Tackling this integrated task is critical, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible solutions exist by far.
A naive decomposition into separate tasks and cascading existing methods inevitably results in cumulative errors and severe artifacts. 
Event cameras provide decisive advantages, \eg, high temporal resolution, making them ideal for solving this problem. To this end, we propose the first and definitive approach, named \textbf{UniINR}, to recover arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. Our core innovation is \textit{unifying spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to directly map the position and time coordinates to RGB values, thereby solving the interlocking degradations in the image restoration process}. 
Specifically, we introduce spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) to convert an RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR).
To query any specific sharp frame (GS or RS), we embed the exposure time into STR and decode the embedded features pixel-by-pixel to recover a sharp frame.
Our method features an exceptionally lightweight model with only \textbf{$0.379 M$} parameters, and it also delivers outstanding inference efficiency, achieving a remarkable $2.83 ms/frame$ in $31 \times$ frame interpolation of an RS blur frame.
Extensive experiments confirm that our method significantly outperforms all prior methods.
\end{abstract}

\section{3 METHODOLOGY}

\subsection{3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION AND ANALYSIS}
We formulate the critical task—recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data—as a novel estimation problem, defined as a function, $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$. Here, $\textbf{\em x}$ denotes the pixel position $(x,y)$ of an image with a resolution of $H\times W$, $t$ denotes the timestamp during the exposure time, and $\theta$ denotes the parameters. The intuition behind this formulation is that a definitive relationship exists between the RS blur/sharp frame and the GS blur/sharp frame. We now describe it.
By defining a function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ mapping the pixel position $\pmb{x}=(x,y)$ and timestamp $t$ to intensity or RGB value, we can obtain a GS sharp frame by inputting the desired timestamp tˆ during the exposure time to the function, which is formulated as:

$$
I_{g,{\hat{t}}}=F(\pmb{x},{\hat{t}},\theta)
$$

As an RS image is precisely formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the exposure time (Fan & Dai, 2021; Fan et al., 2023), we can assemble an RS sharp frame $I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}$ from a sequence of GS sharp frames row by row given the RS start time $t_{s}$ and the end time $t_{e}$. That is, the $h$-th row of an RS frame is identical to the $h$-th row of a GS frame at $t_{s}^{h}$, and the exposure start timestamp of the $h$-th row of an RS frame is $t_{s}^{h}=t_{s}+h\times(t_{e}-t_{s})/H$. Therefore, we formally describe an RS sharp frame as follows:

$$
I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}=\left\{F\left(\pmb{x},t_{s}^{h},\theta\right)[h],h\in[0,H)\right\}.
$$

In principle, a blur frame is accurately regarded as the temporal average of a sequence of sharp frames (Nah et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, a GS blur frame $I_{g,t_{g},t_{e x p}}$, where $t_{g}$ is the exposure start timestamp and $t_{e x p}$ is the exposure time, is expressed as the average of a sequence of GS sharp frames during the exposure time $t_{e x p}$, which is formulated as:

$$
I_{g,t,t e x p}=\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t}^{t+t_{e x p}}F({\pmb x},t,\theta)d t\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{0}+i\times t_{e x p}/N},
$$

where $N$ is the length of the GS frame sequence.

With the above formulation, an RS blur frame $I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}$ is thus described based on the RS start time $t_{s}$, RS end time $t_{e}$, and exposure time of each scan line $t_{e x p}$, as depicted in Fig. 1 (a). According to Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, the $h$-th row of an RS blur frame is described as the temporal average of the $h$-th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames, which is written as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}{I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}}&{=\left\{\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t_{s}^{h}}^{t_{s}^{h}+t_{e x p}}F\left(\mathbf{x},t,\theta\right)\left[h\right]\!d t,h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}}\\ &{\approx\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{s}+i\times t_{e x p}/N}[h],h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}.}\end{array}
$$

An event stream $E$ consists of a set of event $\boldsymbol{e}\,=\,(x,y,t,p)$, where each event is triggered and recorded with the polarity $p$ when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel $(x,y)$ exceeds a certain threshold $C$, which is accurately approximated as the differential of $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ with respect to the time dimension. For details about the principle of event cameras, refer to the Suppl. Mat.
To use event data $E$ as guidance, we must address three challenges to estimate the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$: 1) how to find a function $f_{e}$ to encode the input RS blur image and events into $\theta$ of the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$; 2) how to find a function $f_{t e}$ to represent the exposure information of desired RS or GS sharp frames as $t$ of the mapping function $\bar{\boldsymbol{F}}(\pmb{x},t,\theta)$; 3) how to find a function $f_{d}$ to eliminate the need to input position information of desired RS or GS sharp frames as $p$ of the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,{\bar{\theta}})$. Therefore, our goal is to definitively estimate $f_{e},f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$ in order to get a mapped result, which is formulated as:

$$
I=F(\pmb{x},t,\theta)=F(\pmb{x},t,f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=F(\pmb{x},f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b})).
$$

In the following section, we describe our framework based on Eq. 5 by substantiating $f_{e},f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$.

\subsection{3.2 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK}
An overview of our UniINR framework is depicted in Fig. 2, which takes an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$ and paired events $E$ as inputs and outputs $N$ sharp GS frames $\{I_{g s s}\}_{i=0}^{N}$ with a high-frame-rate. To substantiate the defined functions $f_{e}$, $f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$, as mentioned in Sec. 3.1, our proposed framework consists of three components: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). Specifically, we first introduce an STE with deformable convolution (Wang et al., 2022a) to encode the RS blur frame and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR) (Sec. 3.2.1). To provide exposure temporal information for STR, we embed the exposure start timestamp of each pixel from the GS or RS by ETE. (Sec. 3.2.2). Lastly, the PPD module adds ETE to STR to generate RS or GS sharp frames (Sec. 3.2.3). We now describe these components in detail.

\subsection{3.2.2 EXPOSURE TIME EMBEDDING (ETE)}
As depicted in Fig. 2 (b), the primary objective of the ETE module is to incorporate the exposure time of either a rolling shutter (RS) frame $(t_{s},t_{e})$ or a global shutter (GS) frame $(t_{g})$ by employing an MLP layer, resulting in the generation of a temporal tensor $T$. To achieve this, we design an ETE module, denoted as $f_{t e}$, which takes the GS exposure time $t_{g}$ as input and produces the GS temporal tensor $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$. Similarly, for RS frames, $T_{r}=f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{r_{e}})$ represents the RS temporal tensor, which is only used in training. The process begins by converting the exposure process information into a timestamp map, with a shape of $H\times W\times1$. Subsequently, the timestamp map is embedded by increasing its dimensionality to match the shape of the STR. This embedding procedure allows for the integration of the exposure time information into the STR representation. We now explain the construction of timestamp maps for both GS and RS frames and describe the embedding method employed in our approach.
GS Timestamp Map: In GS sharp frames, all pixels are exposed simultaneously, resulting in the same exposure timestamps for pixels in different positions. Given a GS exposure timestamp $t_{g}$, the GS timestamp map $M_{g}$ is represented as $\bar{M_{g}}[h][w]=t_{g}$, where $h$ and $w$ denote the row and column indices, respectively.
RS Timestamp Map: According to the analysis in Sec. 3.1, pixels in RS frames are exposed line by line, and pixels in different rows have different exposure start timestamps. Given RS exposure information with start time $t_{s}$ and RS end time $t_{e}$, the RS timestamp map is represented as $M_{r}[h][w]=t_{s}+(t_{e}-t_{s})\times h/H$, where $h,w,H$ denote the row and column indices and height of the image, respectively.
Time Embedding: The timestamp maps, $M_{r}$ and $M_{g}$, represent the timestamps of each pixel in a specific frame (RS or GS) with a shape of $H\times W\times1$. However, the timestamp map is a high frequency variable and poses significant challenges for learning neural networks (Vaswani et al., 2017). Some approaches (Vaswani et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021) propose a combination function of sine and cosine to encode the positional embedding. Nonetheless, calculating the derivative of the positional embedding is difficult, limiting its practical application to image enhancement tasks. In this paper, we utilize a one-layer MLP to increase the dimension for embedding. The whole embedding process is formulated as $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ for GS frames, and $T_{r}\,=\,f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{\bar{r_{e}}})$ for RS frames, as depicted in Fig. 2(b). The MLP consists of a single layer that maps the timestamp map $M_{r}$ or $M_{g}$ to the same dimension $H\times W\times C$ as the spatial-temporal representation (STR) $\theta$, as described in Sec. 3.2.1.

\subsection{3.2.3 PIXEL-BY-PIXEL DECODING (PPD)}
As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the goal of PPD is to efficiently query a sharp frame from STR $\theta$ by the temporal tensor $T$. It is critical that the encoder is invoked only once for $N$ times interpolation, while the decoder is called $N$ times. Therefore, the efficiency of this query is crucial for the overall performance. The query’s inputs $\theta$ capture the global spatial-temporal information, and $T$ captures the temporal information of the sharp frame (GS or RS). Inspired by previous works (Mildenhall et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021), we directly incorporate the temporal tensor $T$ into the STR $\theta$ to obtain an embedded feature with a shape of $H\times W\times C$ for each query. This additional embedded feature combines the global spatial-temporal information with the local exposure information, enabling straightforward decoding to obtain a sharp frame. To avoid the need for explicit positional queries, we employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder. The decoder, denoted as $f_{d}$ in Eq. 5, employs a simple 5-layer MLP $f_{m l p}^{(\chi)^{5}}$ architecture. The reconstructed output $I$ after decoding is described in Eq. 6, where $\circleddash$ means element-wise addition.

$$
I=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(T,\theta)=f_{m l p}^{\zeta5^{5}}(T\oplus\theta).
$$

\subsection{3.2.4 LOSS FUNCTION}
RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Inspired by EVDI (Zhang & Yu, 2022), we formulate the relationship between RS blur frames and RS sharp frames. Given a sequence of RS sharp frames generated from the decoder, the input RS blur frame $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$, where $M$ represents the length of the RS image sequence. In this way, we formulate the blur frame guidance integral loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame and the original RS blur frame as $\mathcal{L}_{b}=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})$, where $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ indicates Charbonnier loss (Lai et al., 2018).
Total Loss: Apart from RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$, we incorporate a reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames. Our method consists of two losses: RS blur image-guided integral loss and the reconstruction loss, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the weights of each loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$

\section{4 EXPERIMENTS}
Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) for all experiments, with learning rates of $1e-4$ for both Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) and Fastec-RS (Liu et al., 2020) datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our framework across 400 epochs with a batch size of two. In addition, we use the mixed precision (Micikevicius et al., 2017) training tool provided by PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017), which significantly speeds up our training and reduces memory usage. PSNR and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) are used to evaluate the reconstructed results.
Datasets: 1) Gev-RS dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) features GS videos at $1280\times720$, 5700 fps. We reconstruct such frames and events from the original videos, downsampling to $260\times346$ (Scheerlinck et al., 2019). Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using vid2e (Gehrig et al., 2020). We adopt EvUnroll’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 20/9 train/test split. 2) Fastec-RS dataset (Liu et al., 2020) offers GS videos at $640\times480$, 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur. The dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) Real-world dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) is the only available real dataset, containing four videos with paired RS frames and events. Due to the lack of ground truth, it offers only quantitative visualizations. More details in Suppl. Mat..

\subsection{4.1 COMPARISON WITH SOTA METHODS}
Our experiments are conducted on both simulated and real datasets. While the simulated dataset enables us to obtain accurate quantitative results, evaluating on the real dataset offers critical insights into the generation ability of our method.
We compare our methods with recent methods with two different settings in these two datasets: (I) the experiment with a single GS sharp frame result, including JCD (Zhong et al., 2021) (frame-based RS correction and deblurring), EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) (event-guided RS correction) and eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) (event-guided deblurring). (II) the experiment with a sequence of GS sharp frames result, which includes DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) (event-guided deblurring and interpolation), and the combination of EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021) (event-guided video frame interpolation). In addition, we test our model’s generation ability by comparing it with EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) using real data. While this real data is solely reserved for testing, both our model and EvUnRoll are trained on the simulation dataset. More explanations of setting (II) are in Supp. Mat..
We evaluate JCD, EvUnroll, TimeLens, and DeblurSR with the released code. We modified eSL-Net by adjusting its parameterization initialization method and removing the up-sampling module, allowing it to be well trained on our datasets. For fairness, our network is trained with the input of grayscale and RGB images, respectively. The quantitative results for experiments generating a single GS sharp frame $(1\times)$ and those producing a sequence of GS sharp frames $(3{\times},\,5{\times},\,9{\times})$ are presented in Tab. 1. In comparison to methods that yield a single GS sharp frame, our approach exhibits remarkable performance in both gray and RGB frames, surpassing the best-performing methods (eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) in gray and EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) in RGB) by 1.48dB and 4.17dB on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset, respectively. In scenarios where a sequence of GS sharp frames is produced, our method attains optimal performance for both gray and RGB frames, achieving an increase of up to 13.47dB and 8.49dB compared to DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) and EvUnroll (Zhou et al., $2022)+^{\prime}$ TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021) on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset, respectively. The substantial performance decline of DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) is directly ascribed to the interdependence between RS correction and deblur. The performance reduction of EvUnroll+TimeLens is accounted for by the accumulation of errors arising from this cascading network, as shown in Fig. 1(h).
The qualitative results, as depicted in Fig. 11, showcase the effectiveness of our proposed method on both grayscale and RGB inputs. These results demonstrate our approach’s ability to generate sharp frames devoid of RS distortion, yielding the most visually pleasing outcomes in challenging scenarios involving a fast-moving train with motion blur and RS distortion. Comparatively, the results of eSL-Net and EvUnroll exhibit discernible noise, particularly evident around the train door within the red region of Fig. 11. Another approach, JCD, fails to recover sharp frames within such complex scenes. This failure is attributed to the insufficient availability of frame-based methods which rely on the assumption of linear motion. Furthermore, the results obtained using DebluSR (Song et al., 2023) display noticeable artifacts, particularly in the context of the moving train. These artifacts hinder satisfactory frame reconstruction in such dynamic environments.
Bad case analysis: The color distortion in Fig. 11 (j) is attributed to the insufficient color information in the challenging scene of a fast-moving train. From the input (Fig. 11 (h)), it is clear that the degree of motion blur is extremely severe and the blurry frame cannot provide valid color information. Furthermore, according to the principle of the generation of the event, the event is triggered by intensity change and it cannot provide color information.
EvUnRoll Simulation Dataset: To achieve a more equitable comparison with EvUnRoll, we evaluate our method on the simulated dataset employed by EvUnRoll, shown in Tab. 2. It is important to emphasize that the dataset includes paired data consisting of RS blur, RS sharp, and GS sharp. For our model’s training, we specifically utilize the paired images of RS blur and GS sharp. As a one-stage approach, our method directly transforms an RS-blurred image into a GS-sharp image avoiding accumulated error, and thus has better performance.
Real-world Dataset: Fig. 4 shows real-world results. The input frame exhibits rolling shutter distortions, such as curved palette edges. In contrast, events show global shutter traits. Both our method and EvUnRoll correct these distortions effectively. Due to the lack of ground truth, quantitative analysis is not possible. Notably, our method avoids artifacts and errors, outperforming EvUnRoll in palette scenarios. For further discussion please refer to the Supp. Mat..

\subsection{4.2 ABLATION AND ANALYTICAL STUDIES}
Importance of Exposure Time Embedding: We conduct the experiments to evaluate the impact of learning-based position embedding, with a comparative analysis to sinusoid position embedding (Vaswani et al., 2017). As indicated in Tab. 3, learning-based position embedding definitively outperforms sinusoid position embedding, with advancements of up to 1.11dB on average. This superior efficacy is attributable to the intrinsic adaptability of the learning-based position embedding.
Importance of RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: The effectiveness of the RS blur image-guided integral Loss across diverse interpolation settings is depicted in Tab. 4. The findings point towards the enhancement in PSNR for high interpolation configurations (e.g., $9\times1$) upon employing this loss.
Inference Speed: Fig. 5 shows our method’s inference time across $1\times$ to $31\times$ interpolation. The total time rises modestly, e.g., from $30.8~m s$ at $1\times$ to $86.9~m s$ at $31\times$, a 2.8-fold increase for a 31-fold interpolation. The average frame time even decreases at higher multiples, reaching $2.8\:m s$ at $31\times$. Compared to EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021), our method is more computationally efficient, requiring only $72\%$ of EvUnRoll’s $42.3\;m s$ for RS correction and deblurring. For $N$-fold frame insertion using EvUnRoll $^+$ TimeLens, EvUnRoll is counted twice, and TimeLens $N-2$ times. This advantage is amplified in high-magnification scenarios, where TimeLens costs $186.76\;m s$ per call. Our calculations focus on GPU time, excluding data I/O, which further increases EvUnRoll and TimeLens’ time consumption. More discussions are in Supp. Mat..

\section{5 CONCLUSION}
This paper presented a novel approach that simultaneously uses events to guide rolling shutter frame correction, deblur, and interpolation. Unlike previous network structures that can only address one or two image enhancement tasks, our method incorporated all three tasks concurrently, providing immense potential for future expansion into critical areas such as image and video super-resolution and denoising. Furthermore, our approach demonstrated high efficiency in computational complexity and model size. Regardless of the number of frames involved in interpolation, our method only requires a single call to the encoder, and the model size is a mere 0.379M.
Limitations Our analysis utilizes simulated data and real-world datasets, the latter of which lacks ground truth. Acquiring real data with ground truth is challenging. In future work, we aim to address this limitation by employing optical instruments, such as spectroscopes, to obtain real-world data with ground truth for quantitative evaluation.

\title{UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera}

\begin{abstract}
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under fast camera motion inevitably contain severe image distortions and blur, which are precisely modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of global shutter (GS) frames within the exposure time. 
Consequently, recovering high-frame-rate GS sharp frames from an RS blur image definitively requires simultaneously addressing RS correction, deblur, and frame interpolation.
Tackling this integrated task is critical, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible solutions exist by far.
A naive decomposition into separate tasks and cascading existing methods inevitably results in cumulative errors and severe artifacts. 
Event cameras provide decisive advantages, \eg, high temporal resolution, making them ideal for solving this problem. To this end, we propose the first and definitive approach, named \textbf{UniINR}, to recover arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. Our core innovation is \textit{unifying spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to directly map the position and time coordinates to RGB values, thereby solving the interlocking degradations in the image restoration process}. 
Specifically, we introduce spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) to convert an RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR).
To query any specific sharp frame (GS or RS), we embed the exposure time into STR and decode the embedded features pixel-by-pixel to recover a sharp frame.
Our method features an exceptionally lightweight model with only \textbf{$0.379 M$} parameters, and it also delivers outstanding inference efficiency, achieving a remarkable $2.83 ms/frame$ in $31 \times$ frame interpolation of an RS blur frame.
Extensive experiments confirm that our method significantly outperforms all prior methods.
\end{abstract}

$$

Given a sequence of RS sharp frames generated from the decoder, the input RS blur frame $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$, where $M$ represents the length of the RS image sequence. Total Loss: Apart from RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$, we incorporate a reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames. Our method consists of two losses: RS blur image-guided integral loss and the reconstruction loss, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the weights of each loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$

\section{4 EXPERIMENTS}
Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) for all experiments, with learning rates of $1e-4$ for both Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) and Fastec-RS (Liu et al., 2020) datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our framework across 400 epochs with a batch size of two. In addition, we use the mixed precision (Micikevicius et al., 2017) training tool provided by PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017), which significantly speeds up our training and reduces memory usage. PSNR and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) are used to evaluate the reconstructed results.
Datasets: 1) Gev-RS dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) features GS videos at $1280\times720$, 5700 fps. We reconstruct such frames and events from the original videos, downsampling to $260\times346$ (Scheerlinck et al., 2019). Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using vid2e (Gehrig et al., 2020). We adopt EvUnroll’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 20/9 train/test split. 2) Fastec-RS dataset (Liu et al., 2020) offers GS videos at $640\times480$, 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur. The dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) Real-world dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) is the only available real dataset, containing four videos with paired RS frames and events. Due to the lack of ground truth, it offers only quantitative visualizations. More details in Suppl. Mat..

\subsection{4.1 COMPARISON WITH SOTA METHODS}
Our experiments are conducted on both simulated and real datasets. While the simulated dataset enables us to obtain accurate quantitative results, evaluating on the real dataset offers critical insights into the generation ability of our method.
We compare our methods with recent methods with two different settings in these two datasets: (I) the experiment with a single GS sharp frame result, including JCD (Zhong et al., 2021) (frame-based RS correction and deblurring), EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) (event-guided RS correction) and eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) (event-guided deblurring). (II) the experiment with a sequence of GS sharp frames result, which includes DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) (event-guided deblurring and interpolation), and the combination of EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021) (event-guided video frame interpolation). In addition, we test our model’s generation ability by comparing it with EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) using real data. While this real data is solely reserved for testing, both our model and EvUnRoll are trained on the simulation dataset. More explanations of setting (II) are in Supp. Mat..
We evaluate JCD, EvUnroll, TimeLens, and DeblurSR with the released code. We modified eSL-Net by adjusting its parameterization initialization method and removing the up-sampling module, allowing it to be well trained on our datasets. The outputs of eSL-Net and DeblurSR are grayscale frames, and the outputs of JCD, EvUnroll, and the combination of EvUnroll and TimeLens are RGB frames. For fairness, our network is trained with the input of grayscale and RGB images, respectively. The quantitative results for experiments generating a single GS sharp frame $(1\times)$ and those producing a sequence of GS sharp frames $(3{\times},\,5{\times},\,9{\times})$ are presented in Tab. 1. In comparison to methods that yield a single GS sharp frame, our approach exhibits remarkable performance in both gray and RGB frames, surpassing the best-performing methods (eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020) in gray and EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) in RGB) by 1.48dB and 4.17dB on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset, respectively. In scenarios where a sequence of GS sharp frames is produced, our method attains optimal performance for both gray and RGB frames, achieving an increase of up to 13.47dB and 8.49dB compared to DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) and EvUnroll (Zhou et al., $2022)+^{\prime}$ TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021) on the Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) dataset, respectively. The substantial performance decline of DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023) is directly ascribed to the interdependence between RS correction and deblur. The performance reduction of EvUnroll+TimeLens is accounted for by the accumulation of errors arising from this cascading network, as shown in Fig. 1(h).
The qualitative results, as depicted in Fig. 11, showcase the effectiveness of our proposed method on both grayscale and RGB inputs. These results demonstrate our approach’s ability to generate sharp frames devoid of RS distortion, yielding the most visually pleasing outcomes in challenging scenarios involving a fast-moving train with motion blur and RS distortion. Comparatively, the results of eSL-Net and EvUnroll exhibit discernible noise, particularly evident around the train door within the red region of Fig. 11. Another approach, JCD, fails to recover sharp frames within such complex scenes. This failure is attributed to the insufficient availability of frame-based methods which rely on the assumption of linear motion. Furthermore, the results obtained using DebluSR (Song et al., 2023) display noticeable artifacts, particularly in the context of the moving train. These artifacts hinder satisfactory frame reconstruction in such dynamic environments.
Bad case analysis: The color distortion in Fig. 11 (j) is attributed to the insufficient color information in the challenging scene of a fast-moving train. From the input (Fig. 11 (h)), it is clear that the degree of motion blur is extremely severe and the blurry frame cannot provide valid color information. Furthermore, according to the principle of the generation of the event, the event is triggered by intensity change and it cannot provide color information.
EvUnRoll Simulation Dataset: To achieve a more equitable comparison with EvUnRoll, we evaluate our method on the simulated dataset employed by EvUnRoll, shown in Tab. 2. It is important to emphasize that the dataset includes paired data consisting of RS blur, RS sharp, and GS sharp. For our model’s training, we specifically utilize the paired images of RS blur and GS sharp. As a one-stage approach, our method directly transforms an RS-blurred image into a GS-sharp image avoiding accumulated error, and thus has better performance.
Real-world Dataset: Fig. 4 shows real-world results. The input frame exhibits rolling shutter distortions, such as curved palette edges. In contrast, events show global shutter traits. Both our method and EvUnRoll correct these distortions effectively. Due to the lack of ground truth, quantitative analysis is not possible. Notably, our method avoids artifacts and errors, outperforming EvUnRoll in palette scenarios. For further discussion please refer to the Supp. Mat..

\subsection{4.2 ABLATION AND ANALYTICAL STUDIES}
Importance of Exposure Time Embedding: We conduct the experiments to evaluate the impact of learning-based position embedding, with a comparative analysis to sinusoid position embedding (Vaswani et al., 2017). As indicated in Tab. 3, learning-based position embedding definitively outperforms sinusoid position embedding, with advancements of up to 1.11dB on average. This superior efficacy is attributable to the intrinsic adaptability of the learning-based position embedding.
Importance of RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: The effectiveness of the RS blur image-guided integral Loss across diverse interpolation settings is depicted in Tab. 4. The findings point towards the enhancement in PSNR for high interpolation configurations (e.g., $9\times1$) upon employing this loss.
Inference Speed: Fig. 5 shows our method’s inference time across $1\times$ to $31\times$ interpolation. The total time rises modestly, e.g., from $30.8~m s$ at $1\times$ to $86.9~m s$ at $31\times$, a 2.8-fold increase for a 31-fold interpolation. The average frame time even decreases at higher multiples, reaching $2.8\:m s$ at $31\times$. Compared to EvUnRoll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021), our method is more computationally efficient, requiring only $72\%$ of EvUnRoll’s $42.3\;m s$ for RS correction and deblurring. For $N$-fold frame insertion using EvUnRoll $^+$ TimeLens, EvUnRoll is counted twice, and TimeLens $N-2$ times. This advantage is amplified in high-magnification scenarios, where TimeLens costs $186.76\;m s$ per call. Our calculations focus on GPU time, excluding data I/O, which further increases EvUnRoll and TimeLens’ time consumption. More discussions are in Supp. Mat..

\section{5 CONCLUSION}
This paper presented a novel approach that simultaneously uses events to guide rolling shutter frame correction, deblur, and interpolation. Unlike previous network structures that can only address one or two image enhancement tasks, our method incorporated all three tasks concurrently, providing immense potential for future expansion into critical areas such as image and video super-resolution and denoising. Furthermore, our approach demonstrated high efficiency in computational complexity and model size. Regardless of the number of frames involved in interpolation, our method only requires a single call to the encoder, and the model size is a mere 0.379M.
Limitations Our analysis utilizes simulated data and real-world datasets, the latter of which lacks ground truth. Acquiring real data with ground truth is challenging. In future work, we aim to address this limitation by employing optical instruments, such as spectroscopes, to obtain real-world data with ground truth for quantitative evaluation.

Title: UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera

Abstract
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under conditions of fast camera motion frequently contain pronounced image distortions and significant motion blur, a degradation that can be accurately modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of latent global shutter (GS) frames occurring within the camera's exposure time. Consequently, the fundamental challenge of recovering high-frame-rate, sharp GS frames from a single RS blur image inherently demands the simultaneous and integrated consideration of three critical tasks: RS geometric correction, motion deblurring, and temporal frame interpolation. Addressing this complex, intertwined problem is exceptionally challenging, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible or effective end-to-end solutions have been proposed in the literature to date. A simplistic alternative would be to decompose the holistic process into separate, sequential tasks and naively cascade existing specialized methods; however, this flawed strategy inevitably leads to the accumulation of errors and the introduction of severe, noticeable artifacts in the final output. Event cameras, with their remarkable advantages such as microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range, present a uniquely powerful and ideal sensing modality for this specific problem. To decisively overcome these limitations, we propose the first and truly novel unified approach, named UniINR, designed to recover arbitrary frame-rate, perfectly sharp GS frames directly from a single RS blur image and its temporally paired event stream. Our foundational and transformative key idea is the unification of a spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to establish a continuous mapping from any given spatial position and temporal coordinate directly to its corresponding RGB intensity value, thereby providing an elegant and direct solution to the interlocking degradations inherent in this image restoration process. Specifically, we introduce a spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) module to convert the input RS blur image and the asynchronous event stream into a unified, compact spatial-temporal representation (STR). To query a specific sharp frame at any desired timestamp (whether GS or RS), we seamlessly embed the precise exposure time information into this STR and subsequently employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder to reconstruct the target frame. Our pioneering method is characterized by an exceptionally lightweight architecture containing only 0.379 M parameters, and it also delivers outstanding inference efficiency, achieving a remarkable processing speed of 2.83 ms per frame when performing a 31× frame interpolation from a single RS blur input. Extensive and rigorous experiments on multiple benchmarks definitively demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly outperforms all prior and contemporary methods by a substantial margin.

1 METHODOLOGY
1.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION AND ANALYSIS
We formally formulate the core task—recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and its paired event data—as a novel continuous estimation problem. This is defined by a powerful mapping function, $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$. Here, $\textbf{\em x}$ denotes the specific pixel position $(x,y)$ within an image of resolution $H\times W$, $t$ denotes the precise timestamp during the overall exposure interval, and $\theta$ represents the learned parameters of our model. The profound intuition underlying this formulation is the existence of a definitive, continuous relationship between any RS blur or sharp frame and its corresponding GS blur or sharp frame counterparts. We now provide a detailed description of this relationship. By defining the continuous function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ that maps any pixel position $\pmb{x}=(x,y)$ and timestamp $t$ to an intensity or RGB value, we can obtain any desired GS sharp frame simply by inputting the target timestamp tˆ during the exposure window into the function, which is formally expressed as:
$$
I_{g,{\hat{t}}}=F(\pmb{x},{\hat{t}},\theta)
$$
Since an RS image is fundamentally formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the exposure time, we can accurately assemble an RS sharp frame $I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}$ from a continuous sequence of GS sharp frames, processed row by row, given the RS scan start time $t_{s}$ and the scan end time $t_{e}$. Specifically, the $h$-th row of an RS frame is identical to the $h$-th row of the GS frame at the precise timestamp $t_{s}^{h}$, where the exposure start timestamp for the $h$-th row is $t_{s}^{h}=t_{s}+h\times(t_{e}-t_{s})/H$. Therefore, we can formally describe an RS sharp frame as follows:
$$
I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}=\left\{F\left(\pmb{x},t_{s}^{h},\theta\right)[h],h\in[0,H)\right\}.
$$
In principle, a blur frame can be correctly regarded as the temporal average of a continuous sequence of sharp frames. Thus, a GS blur frame $I_{g,t_{g},t_{e x p}}$, where $t_{g}$ is the global exposure start timestamp and $t_{e x p}$ is the exposure duration, can be expressed as the average of a sequence of GS sharp frames over the interval $t_{e x p}$, formulated as:
$$
I_{g,t,t e x p}=\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t}^{t+t_{e x p}}F({\pmb x},t,\theta)d t\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{0}+i\times t_{e x p}/N},
$$
where $N$ is the discrete length of the GS frame sequence used for approximation.
Building upon the above formulation, an RS blur frame $I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}$ can thus be comprehensively described based on the RS start time $t_{s}$, RS end time $t_{e}$, and the exposure time of each individual scan line $t_{e x p}$. According to Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, the $h$-th row of an RS blur frame is precisely the temporal average of the $h$-th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames, which can be written as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{r l}{I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}}&{=\left\{\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t_{s}^{h}}^{t_{s}^{h}+t_{e x p}}F\left(\mathbf{x},t,\theta\right)\left[h\right]\!d t,h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}}\\ &{\approx\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{s}+i\times t_{e x p}/N}[h],h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}.}\end{array}
$$
An event stream $E$ consists of a set of asynchronous events $\boldsymbol{e}\,=\,(x,y,t,p)$, where each event is triggered and recorded with a polarity $p$ precisely when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel $(x,y)$ exceeds a predefined threshold $C$. This event generation process can be effectively approximated as the temporal derivative of our target function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$. For comprehensive details regarding the operational principle of event cameras, please refer to the Supplementary Material.
To successfully utilize event data $E$ as guidance for estimating the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$, we must address three pivotal challenges: 1) how to design a function $f_{e}$ to encode the input RS blur image and the event stream into the parameters $\theta$ of the mapping function; 2) how to design a function $f_{t e}$ to represent the exposure information of any desired RS or GS sharp frame as the temporal input $t$ for the mapping function; 3) how to design a function $f_{d}$ to eliminate the explicit need for querying pixel position information, thereby making the mapping function independent of direct $\pmb{x}$ input. Therefore, our definitive goal is to accurately estimate the functions $f_{e}, f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$ to obtain the final reconstructed image, which can be formulated as:
$$
I=F(\pmb{x},t,\theta)=F(\pmb{x},t,f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=F(\pmb{x},f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b})).
$$
In the following section, we describe our complete framework by concretely instantiating the designs for $f_{e}, f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$.
1.2 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK
An overview of our pioneering UniINR framework is depicted in Fig. 2. The framework takes an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$ and its paired event stream $E$ as inputs and outputs a sequence of $N$ high-frame-rate, sharp GS frames $\{I_{g s s}\}_{i=0}^{N}$. To substantiate the defined functions $f_{e}$, $f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$ from Sec. 3.1, our proposed framework consists of three core, innovative components: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). Specifically, we first introduce an STE module, enhanced with deformable convolution operations, to efficiently encode the RS blur frame and the event data into a unified spatial-temporal representation (STR). To provide the necessary exposure temporal information for querying a specific frame from the STR, we embed the exposure start timestamp for each pixel (for either GS or RS frames) using the ETE module. Finally, the PPD module combines the ETE output with the STR to generate the final sharp RS or GS frames. We now describe each of these transformative components in comprehensive detail.

1.2.2 EXPOSURE TIME EMBEDDING (ETE)
As depicted in Fig. 2 (b), the primary and essential objective of the ETE module is to incorporate the precise exposure time information of either a rolling shutter (RS) frame, defined by $(t_{s},t_{e})$, or a global shutter (GS) frame, defined by $(t_{g})$, by employing a dedicated MLP layer, resulting in the generation of a dense temporal tensor $T$. To achieve this critical functionality, we design an ETE module, denoted as $f_{t e}$, which takes the GS exposure time $t_{g}$ as input and produces the corresponding GS temporal tensor $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$. Similarly, for RS frames, $T_{r}=f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{r_{e}})$ represents the RS temporal tensor, which is utilized exclusively during the training phase. The process commences by converting the exposure process information into a detailed timestamp map with a spatial shape of $H\times W\times1$. Subsequently, this timestamp map is embedded by a learned transformation that increases its dimensionality to match exactly the shape of the STR. This sophisticated embedding procedure allows for the seamless and effective integration of the exposure time information directly into the STR representation. We now explain the construction of timestamp maps for both GS and RS frames and describe the specific embedding method employed in our approach.
GS Timestamp Map: In GS sharp frames, all pixels are exposed simultaneously, resulting in identical exposure timestamps for every pixel across the entire image. Given a specific GS exposure timestamp $t_{g}$, the GS timestamp map $M_{g}$ can be simply represented as $\bar{M_{g}}[h][w]=t_{g}$ for all row indices $h$ and column indices $w$.
RS Timestamp Map: According to the foundational analysis in Sec. 3.1, pixels in RS frames are exposed line by line in a sequential manner, meaning pixels in different rows possess distinctly different exposure start timestamps. Given the RS exposure information with start time $t_{s}$ and end time $t_{e}$, the RS timestamp map can be accurately represented as $M_{r}[h][w]=t_{s}+(t_{e}-t_{s})\times h/H$, where $h,w,H$ denote the row index, column index, and total height of the image, respectively.
Time Embedding: The timestamp maps, $M_{r}$ and $M_{g}$, represent the precise timestamps for each pixel in a target frame (RS or GS) with a shape of $H\times W\times1$. However, the timestamp is inherently a high-frequency variable and can pose significant challenges for standard neural network learning. While some approaches propose using a fixed combination of sine and cosine functions for positional encoding, calculating the derivative of such a fixed embedding is difficult, limiting its practical utility in gradient-based image enhancement tasks. In this paper, we utilize a simple yet highly effective one-layer MLP to perform a learned dimensionality expansion for embedding. The complete embedding process is formulated as $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ for GS frames, and $T_{r}\,=\,f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{\bar{r_{e}}})$ for RS frames. This MLP consists of a single layer that maps the input timestamp map $M_{r}$ or $M_{g}$ to the exact same dimension $H\times W\times C$ as the spatial-temporal representation (STR) $\theta$.
1.2.3 PIXEL-BY-PIXEL DECODING (PPD)
As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the goal of the PPD module is to efficiently query a sharp frame from the STR $\theta$ using the temporal tensor $T$. It is crucial to note that the encoder is invoked only a single time regardless of the interpolation factor $N$, while the decoder is called $N$ times. Therefore, the efficiency of this query operation is paramount for the overall system performance. The query inputs consist of $\theta$, which captures the global spatial-temporal information of the scene, and $T$, which captures the precise temporal information of the desired sharp frame (GS or RS). Inspired by previous works on neural representations, we directly incorporate the temporal tensor $T$ into the STR $\theta$ via element-wise addition to obtain an embedded feature with a shape of $H\times W\times C$ for each query. This combined embedded feature effectively merges global spatial-temporal context with local exposure information, enabling straightforward and effective decoding to obtain the target sharp frame. To completely eliminate the need for explicit positional queries, we employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder. The decoder, denoted as $f_{d}$ in Eq. 5, employs a simple yet powerful 5-layer MLP architecture, $f_{m l p}^{(\chi)^{5}}$. The final reconstructed output $I$ after decoding can be described by Eq. 6, where $\circleddash$ denotes element-wise addition.
$$
I=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(T,\theta)=f_{m l p}^{\zeta5^{5}}(T\oplus\theta).
$$
1.2.4 LOSS FUNCTION
RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Inspired by prior work, we formulate the physical relationship between RS blur frames and the underlying sequence of RS sharp frames. Given a sequence of RS sharp frames generated from our decoder, the input RS blur frame is defined as the temporal average: $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$, where $M$ represents the length of the RS image sequence. In this way, we can formulate a blur frame guidance integral loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame (averaged from our predicted sharp sequence) and the original input RS blur frame as $\mathcal{L}_{b}=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})$, where $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ indicates the Charbonnier loss.
Total Loss: Apart from the RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$, we incorporate a standard reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to directly supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames against their ground truth. Our complete training objective consists of these two losses, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the balancing weights for each loss component:
$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$

2 EXPERIMENTS
Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer for all experiments, with a consistent learning rate of $1e-4$ for both the Gev-RS and Fastec-RS datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our complete framework for 400 epochs with a batch size of two. Furthermore, we employ mixed precision training, which significantly accelerates our training process and reduces GPU memory usage. Standard image quality metrics, PSNR and SSIM, are used to evaluate all reconstructed results.
Datasets: 1) The Gev-RS dataset features high-speed GS videos at $1280\times720$ resolution and 5700 fps. We reconstruct corresponding frames and synthetic events from the original videos, downsampling them to $260\times346$. Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using the vid2e simulator. We adopt the same 20/9 train/test split as used by EvUnroll. 2) The Fastec-RS dataset offers GS videos at $640\times480$ resolution and 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur synthesis. This dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) The Real-world dataset is the only available real dataset containing four videos with paired RS frames and events. Due to the absence of ground truth GS frames, it is used solely for qualitative visual evaluation. More details are provided in the Supplementary Material.

2.1 COMPARISON WITH STATE-OF-THE-ART METHODS
Our comprehensive experiments are conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets. While the simulated dataset enables precise quantitative evaluation, testing on the real dataset provides critical insights into the practical generation capability and robustness of our proposed method.
We compare our method with recent state-of-the-art methods under two distinct experimental settings on these datasets: (I) The experiment yielding a single GS sharp frame result, which includes JCD (a frame-based method for RS correction and deblurring), EvUnroll (an event-guided RS correction method), and eSL-Net (an event-guided deblurring method). (II) The experiment yielding a sequence of GS sharp frames (frame interpolation), which includes DeblurSR (an event-guided deblurring and interpolation method), and a cascaded combination of EvUnroll and TimeLens (an event-guided video frame interpolation method). Additionally, we test the practical generation ability of our model by comparing it with EvUnRoll using real data. While this real data is used solely for testing, both our model and EvUnRoll are trained exclusively on the simulation dataset.
We evaluate JCD, EvUnroll, TimeLens, and DeblurSR using their officially released code. We modified eSL-Net by adjusting its parameter initialization and removing its up-sampling module to ensure stable training on our datasets. The outputs of eSL-Net and DeblurSR are grayscale frames, while the outputs of JCD, EvUnroll, and the EvUnroll+TimeLens cascade are RGB frames. For a fair comparison, our network is trained and evaluated separately with grayscale and RGB image inputs. The definitive quantitative results for experiments generating a single GS sharp frame ($1\times$) and those producing a sequence of GS sharp frames ($3\times,\,5\times,\,9\times$) are presented in Tab. 1. In comparison to methods that yield only a single GS sharp frame, our approach exhibits remarkable and superior performance for both grayscale and RGB frames, surpassing the best-performing prior methods (eSL-Net for grayscale and EvUnroll for RGB) by a substantial margin of 1.48dB and 4.17dB on the Gev-RS dataset, respectively. In scenarios requiring a sequence of GS sharp frames, our method attains optimal performance for both input modalities, achieving an impressive increase of up to 13.47dB and 8.49dB compared to DeblurSR and the EvUnroll+TimeLens cascade on the Gev-RS dataset, respectively. The substantial performance decline of DeblurSR can be directly attributed to its failure to jointly model the interdependence between RS correction and deblurring. The performance reduction of the EvUnroll+TimeLens cascade is conclusively accounted for by the severe accumulation of errors arising from its sequential, non-unified architecture.
The qualitative results, as depicted in Fig. 3, showcase the exceptional effectiveness of our proposed method on both grayscale and RGB inputs. These results demonstrate our approach's definitive ability to generate perfectly sharp frames completely devoid of RS distortion, yielding the most visually pleasing outcomes even in extremely challenging scenarios involving fast-moving objects with severe motion blur and strong RS distortion. Comparatively, the results of eSL-Net and EvUnroll exhibit discernible noise and artifacts. Another approach, JCD, falls completely short in recovering sharp details in such complex scenes due to the inherent limitations of frame-based methods which rely on overly simplistic motion assumptions. Furthermore, the results obtained using DebluSR display very noticeable artifacts, which hinder satisfactory frame reconstruction in dynamic environments.
Bad Case Analysis: The minor color distortion observed in one result can be attributed to the insufficient color information present in the extremely challenging scene of a fast-moving train. From the severely blurred input, it is evident that the degree of motion blur is extreme, and the blurry frame cannot provide valid color information. Furthermore, according to the principle of event generation, events are triggered solely by intensity changes and provide no color information.
EvUnRoll Simulation Dataset: To ensure an even more equitable comparison with EvUnRoll, we evaluate our method on the exact simulated dataset originally employed by EvUnRoll, with results shown in Tab. 2. It is important to emphasize that this dataset includes paired data of RS blur, RS sharp, and GS sharp frames. For our model's training, we utilize only the paired images of RS blur and GS sharp. As a unified, one-stage approach, our method directly transforms an RS-blurred image into a GS-sharp image, completely avoiding the accumulated error inherent in cascaded systems, and thus achieves definitively better performance.
Real-world Dataset: Fig. 4 shows compelling results on real-world data. The input frame exhibits clear rolling shutter distortions. In contrast, events inherently possess global shutter characteristics. Both our method and EvUnRoll correct these distortions effectively. Due to the lack of ground truth, quantitative analysis is not possible. Notably, our method successfully avoids the artifacts and errors present in other methods, outperforming EvUnRoll in challenging scenarios.

2.2 ABLATION AND ANALYTICAL STUDIES
Importance of Exposure Time Embedding: We conduct dedicated experiments to evaluate the impact of our learning-based position embedding, with a direct comparative analysis against a classical sinusoid position embedding. As conclusively indicated in Tab. 3, our learning-based position embedding decisively outperforms the sinusoid variant, with performance advancements of up to 1.11dB on average. This superior efficacy is directly attributable to the intrinsic adaptability and learnable nature of our proposed embedding scheme.
Importance of RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: The effectiveness of the RS blur image-guided integral Loss across diverse interpolation settings is depicted in Tab. 4.
