Title: UniINR: Unifying Spatial-Temporal INR for RS Video Correction, Deblur, and Interpolation with an Event Camera

Abstract
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under conditions of fast camera motion frequently contain pronounced image distortions and significant motion blur, a degradation that can be accurately modeled as a row-wise combination of a sequence of latent global shutter (GS) frames occurring within the camera's exposure time. Consequently, the fundamental challenge of recovering high-frame-rate, sharp GS frames from a single RS blur image inherently demands the simultaneous and integrated consideration of three critical tasks: RS geometric correction, motion deblurring, and temporal frame interpolation. Addressing this complex, intertwined problem is exceptionally challenging, and to the best of our knowledge, no feasible or effective end-to-end solutions have been proposed in the literature to date. A simplistic alternative would be to decompose the holistic process into separate, sequential tasks and naively cascade existing specialized methods; however, this flawed strategy inevitably leads to the accumulation of errors and the introduction of severe, noticeable artifacts in the final output. Event cameras, with their remarkable advantages such as microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range, present a uniquely powerful and ideal sensing modality for this specific problem. To decisively overcome these limitations, we propose the first and truly novel unified approach, named UniINR, designed to recover arbitrary frame-rate, perfectly sharp GS frames directly from a single RS blur image and its temporally paired event stream. Our foundational and transformative key idea is the unification of a spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to establish a continuous mapping from any given spatial position and temporal coordinate directly to its corresponding RGB intensity value, thereby providing an elegant and direct solution to the interlocking degradations inherent in this image restoration process. Specifically, we introduce a spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) module to convert the input RS blur image and the asynchronous event stream into a unified, compact spatial-temporal representation (STR). To query a specific sharp frame at any desired timestamp (whether GS or RS), we seamlessly embed the precise exposure time information into this STR and subsequently employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder to reconstruct the target frame. Our pioneering method is characterized by an exceptionally lightweight architecture containing only 0.379 M parameters, and it also delivers outstanding inference efficiency, achieving a remarkable processing speed of 2.83 ms per frame when performing a 31× frame interpolation from a single RS blur input. Extensive and rigorous experiments on multiple benchmarks definitively demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly outperforms all prior and contemporary methods by a substantial margin.

1 METHODOLOGY
1.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION AND ANALYSIS
We formally formulate the core task—recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and its paired event data—as a novel continuous estimation problem. This is defined by a powerful mapping function, $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$. Here, $\textbf{\em x}$ denotes the specific pixel position $(x,y)$ within an image of resolution $H\times W$, $t$ denotes the precise timestamp during the overall exposure interval, and $\theta$ represents the learned parameters of our model. The profound intuition underlying this formulation is the existence of a definitive, continuous relationship between any RS blur or sharp frame and its corresponding GS blur or sharp frame counterparts. We now provide a detailed description of this relationship. By defining the continuous function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$ that maps any pixel position $\pmb{x}=(x,y)$ and timestamp $t$ to an intensity or RGB value, we can obtain any desired GS sharp frame simply by inputting the target timestamp tˆ during the exposure window into the function, which is formally expressed as:
$$
I_{g,{\hat{t}}}=F(\pmb{x},{\hat{t}},\theta)
$$
Since an RS image is fundamentally formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the exposure time, we can accurately assemble an RS sharp frame $I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}$ from a continuous sequence of GS sharp frames, processed row by row, given the RS scan start time $t_{s}$ and the scan end time $t_{e}$. Specifically, the $h$-th row of an RS frame is identical to the $h$-th row of the GS frame at the precise timestamp $t_{s}^{h}$, where the exposure start timestamp for the $h$-th row is $t_{s}^{h}=t_{s}+h\times(t_{e}-t_{s})/H$. Therefore, we can formally describe an RS sharp frame as follows:
$$
I_{r,t_{s},t_{e}}=\left\{F\left(\pmb{x},t_{s}^{h},\theta\right)[h],h\in[0,H)\right\}.
$$
In principle, a blur frame can be correctly regarded as the temporal average of a continuous sequence of sharp frames. Thus, a GS blur frame $I_{g,t_{g},t_{e x p}}$, where $t_{g}$ is the global exposure start timestamp and $t_{e x p}$ is the exposure duration, can be expressed as the average of a sequence of GS sharp frames over the interval $t_{e x p}$, formulated as:
$$
I_{g,t,t e x p}=\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t}^{t+t_{e x p}}F({\pmb x},t,\theta)d t\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{0}+i\times t_{e x p}/N},
$$
where $N$ is the discrete length of the GS frame sequence used for approximation.
Building upon the above formulation, an RS blur frame $I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}$ can thus be comprehensively described based on the RS start time $t_{s}$, RS end time $t_{e}$, and the exposure time of each individual scan line $t_{e x p}$. According to Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, the $h$-th row of an RS blur frame is precisely the temporal average of the $h$-th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames, which can be written as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{r l}{I_{r,t_{s}\rightarrow t_{e},t_{e x p}}}&{=\left\{\frac{1}{t_{e x p}}\int_{t_{s}^{h}}^{t_{s}^{h}+t_{e x p}}F\left(\mathbf{x},t,\theta\right)\left[h\right]\!d t,h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}}\\ &{\approx\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N}I_{g,t_{s}+i\times t_{e x p}/N}[h],h\in\left[0,H\right)\right\}.}\end{array}
$$
An event stream $E$ consists of a set of asynchronous events $\boldsymbol{e}\,=\,(x,y,t,p)$, where each event is triggered and recorded with a polarity $p$ precisely when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel $(x,y)$ exceeds a predefined threshold $C$. This event generation process can be effectively approximated as the temporal derivative of our target function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$. For comprehensive details regarding the operational principle of event cameras, please refer to the Supplementary Material.
To successfully utilize event data $E$ as guidance for estimating the mapping function $F({\pmb x},t,\theta)$, we must address three pivotal challenges: 1) how to design a function $f_{e}$ to encode the input RS blur image and the event stream into the parameters $\theta$ of the mapping function; 2) how to design a function $f_{t e}$ to represent the exposure information of any desired RS or GS sharp frame as the temporal input $t$ for the mapping function; 3) how to design a function $f_{d}$ to eliminate the explicit need for querying pixel position information, thereby making the mapping function independent of direct $\pmb{x}$ input. Therefore, our definitive goal is to accurately estimate the functions $f_{e}, f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$ to obtain the final reconstructed image, which can be formulated as:
$$
I=F(\pmb{x},t,\theta)=F(\pmb{x},t,f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=F(\pmb{x},f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b})).
$$
In the following section, we describe our complete framework by concretely instantiating the designs for $f_{e}, f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$.
1.2 PROPOSED FRAMEWORK
An overview of our pioneering UniINR framework is depicted in Fig. 2. The framework takes an RS blur image $I_{r s b}$ and its paired event stream $E$ as inputs and outputs a sequence of $N$ high-frame-rate, sharp GS frames $\{I_{g s s}\}_{i=0}^{N}$. To substantiate the defined functions $f_{e}$, $f_{t e}$, and $f_{d}$ from Sec. 3.1, our proposed framework consists of three core, innovative components: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). Specifically, we first introduce an STE module, enhanced with deformable convolution operations, to efficiently encode the RS blur frame and the event data into a unified spatial-temporal representation (STR). To provide the necessary exposure temporal information for querying a specific frame from the STR, we embed the exposure start timestamp for each pixel (for either GS or RS frames) using the ETE module. Finally, the PPD module combines the ETE output with the STR to generate the final sharp RS or GS frames. We now describe each of these transformative components in comprehensive detail.

1.2.2 EXPOSURE TIME EMBEDDING (ETE)
As depicted in Fig. 2 (b), the primary and essential objective of the ETE module is to incorporate the precise exposure time information of either a rolling shutter (RS) frame, defined by $(t_{s},t_{e})$, or a global shutter (GS) frame, defined by $(t_{g})$, by employing a dedicated MLP layer, resulting in the generation of a dense temporal tensor $T$. To achieve this critical functionality, we design an ETE module, denoted as $f_{t e}$, which takes the GS exposure time $t_{g}$ as input and produces the corresponding GS temporal tensor $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$. Similarly, for RS frames, $T_{r}=f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{r_{e}})$ represents the RS temporal tensor, which is utilized exclusively during the training phase. The process commences by converting the exposure process information into a detailed timestamp map with a spatial shape of $H\times W\times1$. Subsequently, this timestamp map is embedded by a learned transformation that increases its dimensionality to match exactly the shape of the STR. This sophisticated embedding procedure allows for the seamless and effective integration of the exposure time information directly into the STR representation. We now explain the construction of timestamp maps for both GS and RS frames and describe the specific embedding method employed in our approach.
GS Timestamp Map: In GS sharp frames, all pixels are exposed simultaneously, resulting in identical exposure timestamps for every pixel across the entire image. Given a specific GS exposure timestamp $t_{g}$, the GS timestamp map $M_{g}$ can be simply represented as $\bar{M_{g}}[h][w]=t_{g}$ for all row indices $h$ and column indices $w$.
RS Timestamp Map: According to the foundational analysis in Sec. 3.1, pixels in RS frames are exposed line by line in a sequential manner, meaning pixels in different rows possess distinctly different exposure start timestamps. Given the RS exposure information with start time $t_{s}$ and end time $t_{e}$, the RS timestamp map can be accurately represented as $M_{r}[h][w]=t_{s}+(t_{e}-t_{s})\times h/H$, where $h,w,H$ denote the row index, column index, and total height of the image, respectively.
Time Embedding: The timestamp maps, $M_{r}$ and $M_{g}$, represent the precise timestamps for each pixel in a target frame (RS or GS) with a shape of $H\times W\times1$. However, the timestamp is inherently a high-frequency variable and can pose significant challenges for standard neural network learning. While some approaches propose using a fixed combination of sine and cosine functions for positional encoding, calculating the derivative of such a fixed embedding is difficult, limiting its practical utility in gradient-based image enhancement tasks. In this paper, we utilize a simple yet highly effective one-layer MLP to perform a learned dimensionality expansion for embedding. The complete embedding process is formulated as $T_{g}=f_{t e}(t_{g})$ for GS frames, and $T_{r}\,=\,f_{t e}(t_{r_{s}},t_{\bar{r_{e}}})$ for RS frames. This MLP consists of a single layer that maps the input timestamp map $M_{r}$ or $M_{g}$ to the exact same dimension $H\times W\times C$ as the spatial-temporal representation (STR) $\theta$.
1.2.3 PIXEL-BY-PIXEL DECODING (PPD)
As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the goal of the PPD module is to efficiently query a sharp frame from the STR $\theta$ using the temporal tensor $T$. It is crucial to note that the encoder is invoked only a single time regardless of the interpolation factor $N$, while the decoder is called $N$ times. Therefore, the efficiency of this query operation is paramount for the overall system performance. The query inputs consist of $\theta$, which captures the global spatial-temporal information of the scene, and $T$, which captures the precise temporal information of the desired sharp frame (GS or RS). Inspired by previous works on neural representations, we directly incorporate the temporal tensor $T$ into the STR $\theta$ via element-wise addition to obtain an embedded feature with a shape of $H\times W\times C$ for each query. This combined embedded feature effectively merges global spatial-temporal context with local exposure information, enabling straightforward and effective decoding to obtain the target sharp frame. To completely eliminate the need for explicit positional queries, we employ a pixel-by-pixel decoder. The decoder, denoted as $f_{d}$ in Eq. 5, employs a simple yet powerful 5-layer MLP architecture, $f_{m l p}^{(\chi)^{5}}$. The final reconstructed output $I$ after decoding can be described by Eq. 6, where $\circleddash$ denotes element-wise addition.
$$
I=f_{d}(f_{t e}(t),f_{e}(E,I_{r s b}))=f_{d}(T,\theta)=f_{m l p}^{\zeta5^{5}}(T\oplus\theta).
$$
1.2.4 LOSS FUNCTION
RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Inspired by prior work, we formulate the physical relationship between RS blur frames and the underlying sequence of RS sharp frames. Given a sequence of RS sharp frames generated from our decoder, the input RS blur frame is defined as the temporal average: $\begin{array}{r}{I_{r s b}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bar{(I_{r s s}^{i})}}\end{array}$, where $M$ represents the length of the RS image sequence. In this way, we can formulate a blur frame guidance integral loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame (averaged from our predicted sharp sequence) and the original input RS blur frame as $\mathcal{L}_{b}=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})$, where $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ indicates the Charbonnier loss.
Total Loss: Apart from the RS blur image-guided integral loss $\mathcal{L}_{b}$, we incorporate a standard reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{r e}$ to directly supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames against their ground truth. Our complete training objective consists of these two losses, where $\lambda_{b},\lambda_{r e}$ denote the balancing weights for each loss component:
$$
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{b}+\lambda_{r e}\mathcal{L}_{r e}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{r s b},I_{r s b})+\lambda_{r e}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\hat{I}_{g s s}^{k},I_{g s s}^{k}).
$$

2 EXPERIMENTS
Implementation Details: We utilize the Adam optimizer for all experiments, with a consistent learning rate of $1e-4$ for both the Gev-RS and Fastec-RS datasets. Using two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU cards, we train our complete framework for 400 epochs with a batch size of two. Furthermore, we employ mixed precision training, which significantly accelerates our training process and reduces GPU memory usage. Standard image quality metrics, PSNR and SSIM, are used to evaluate all reconstructed results.
Datasets: 1) The Gev-RS dataset features high-speed GS videos at $1280\times720$ resolution and 5700 fps. We reconstruct corresponding frames and synthetic events from the original videos, downsampling them to $260\times346$. Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using the vid2e simulator. We adopt the same 20/9 train/test split as used by EvUnroll. 2) The Fastec-RS dataset offers GS videos at $640\times480$ resolution and 2400 fps. We apply identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur synthesis. This dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) The Real-world dataset is the only available real dataset containing four videos with paired RS frames and events. Due to the absence of ground truth GS frames, it is used solely for qualitative visual evaluation. More details are provided in the Supplementary Material.

2.1 COMPARISON WITH STATE-OF-THE-ART METHODS
Our comprehensive experiments are conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets. While the simulated dataset enables precise quantitative evaluation, testing on the real dataset provides critical insights into the practical generation capability and robustness of our proposed method.
We compare our method with recent state-of-the-art methods under two distinct experimental settings on these datasets: (I) The experiment yielding a single GS sharp frame result, which includes JCD (a frame-based method for RS correction and deblurring), EvUnroll (an event-guided RS correction method), and eSL-Net (an event-guided deblurring method). While this real data is used solely for testing, both our model and EvUnRoll are trained exclusively on the simulation dataset.

Furthermore, according to the principle of event generation, events are triggered solely by intensity changes and provide no color information.

plain_core.transformed_text:
Abstract
Images captured by rolling shutter (RS) cameras under fast motion contain distortions and blur, modeled as a row-wise combination of global shutter (GS) frames within the exposure time. Recovering high-frame-rate GS sharp frames from an RS blur image requires simultaneous RS correction, deblurring, and frame interpolation. A cascaded approach using separate methods leads to cumulative errors. Event cameras provide high temporal resolution. This work proposes a method, UniINR, to recover arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. The method uses a spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to map position and time coordinates to RGB values. A spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) converts the RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR). To query a sharp frame, the exposure time is embedded into the STR and decoded pixel-by-pixel. The model has 0.379 M parameters. Inference efficiency is 2.83 ms/frame for 31x frame interpolation of an RS blur frame. Experiments show the method outperforms prior methods.

1 METHODOLOGY
1.1 Problem Definition and Analysis
The task is defined as recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. It is formulated as a function, F(x, t, θ). Here, x denotes the pixel position (x, y) of an image with resolution H×W, t denotes the timestamp during the exposure time, and θ denotes the parameters. A GS sharp frame is obtained by inputting a desired timestamp t_hat: I_{g,t_hat}=F(x, t_hat, θ).
An RS image is formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the exposure time (Fan & Dai, 2021; Fan et al., 2023). An RS sharp frame I_{r,t_s,t_e} is assembled from a sequence of GS sharp frames row by row given RS start time t_s and end time t_e. The h-th row of an RS frame is the same as the h-th row of a GS frame at t_s^h, where t_s^h = t_s + h × (t_e - t_s)/H. Therefore: I_{r,t_s,t_e} = {F(x, t_s^h, θ)[h], h ∈ [0,H)}.
A blur frame is regarded as the temporal average of a sequence of sharp frames (Nah et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020). A GS blur frame I_{g,t,t_exp}, where t is the exposure start timestamp and t_exp is the exposure time, is expressed as: I_{g,t,t_exp} = (1/t_exp) ∫_t^{t+t_exp} F(x, t, θ) dt ≈ (1/N) Σ_{i=0}^{N} I_{g, t_0 + i × t_exp / N}, where N is the length of the GS frame sequence.
An RS blur frame I_{r,t_s→t_e,t_exp} is described based on RS start time t_s, RS end time t_e, and exposure time t_exp. The h-th row is the temporal average of the h-th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames: I_{r,t_s→t_e,t_exp} = { (1/t_exp) ∫_{t_s^h}^{t_s^h+t_exp} F(x, t, θ)[h] dt, h ∈ [0,H) } ≈ { (1/N) Σ_{i=0}^{N} I_{g,t_s+i×t_exp/N}[h], h ∈ [0,H) }.
An event stream E consists of events e = (x, y, t, p), triggered when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel (x,y) exceeds a threshold C, approximated as the differential of F(x, t, θ) with respect to time.
To estimate F(x, t, θ) using event data E, three challenges are addressed: 1) find a function f_e to encode the input RS blur image and events into θ; 2) find a function f_te to represent the exposure information of desired frames as t; 3) find a function f_d to eliminate the need to input position information. The goal is to estimate f_e, f_te, and f_d: I = F(x, t, θ) = F(x, t, f_e(E, I_rsb)) = F(x, f_te(t), f_e(E, I_rsb)) = f_d(f_te(t), f_e(E, I_rsb)).

1.2 Proposed Framework
The framework takes an RS blur image I_rsb and paired events E as inputs and outputs N sharp GS frames {I_gss}_{i=0}^{N}. It consists of: 1) Spatial-Temporal Implicit Encoding (STE), 2) Exposure Time Embedding (ETE), and 3) Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD). STE with deformable convolution (Wang et al., 2022a) encodes the RS blur frame and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR). ETE embeds the exposure start timestamp. PPD adds ETE to STR to generate sharp frames.

1.2.2 Exposure Time Embedding (ETE)
The ETE module incorporates the exposure time of an RS frame (t_s, t_e) or a GS frame (t_g) using an MLP layer, generating a temporal tensor T. The module f_te takes GS exposure time t_g as input and produces GS temporal tensor T_g = f_te(t_g). For RS frames, T_r = f_te(t_r_s, t_r_e) represents the RS temporal tensor, used only in training. The process converts exposure process information into a timestamp map of shape H×W×1. The timestamp map is embedded to match the shape of STR.
GS Timestamp Map: For a GS exposure timestamp t_g, the GS timestamp map M_g is represented as M_g[h][w] = t_g.
RS Timestamp Map: For RS start time t_s and end time t_e, the RS timestamp map is represented as M_r[h][w] = t_s + (t_e - t_s) × h / H.
Time Embedding: A one-layer MLP increases the dimension of the timestamp map M_r or M_g to H×W×C, the same dimension as STR θ. The embedding process is formulated as T_g = f_te(t_g) for GS frames, and T_r = f_te(t_r_s, t_r_e) for RS frames.

1.2.3 Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD)
The PPD module queries a sharp frame from STR θ using the temporal tensor T. The encoder is invoked once for N times interpolation, while the decoder is called N times. The temporal tensor T is added to STR θ to obtain an embedded feature of shape H×W×C for each query. A pixel-by-pixel decoder f_d uses a 5-layer MLP f_mlp^(5). The reconstructed output I is: I = f_d(f_te(t), f_e(E, I_rsb)) = f_d(T, θ) = f_mlp^(5)(T ⊕ θ).

1.2.4 Loss Function
RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: Given a sequence of RS sharp frames from the decoder, the input RS blur frame I_rsb = (1/M) Σ_{i=1}^{M} (I_rss^i), where M is the length of the RS image sequence. The blur frame guidance integral loss between the reconstructed RS blur frame and the original RS blur frame is L_b = L_c(I_hat_rsb, I_rsb), where L_c indicates Charbonnier loss (Lai et al., 2018).
Total Loss: The total loss includes the RS blur image-guided integral loss L_b and a reconstruction loss L_re to supervise the reconstructed GS sharp frames: L = λ_b L_b + λ_re L_re = λ_b L_c(I_hat_rsb, I_rsb) + λ_re (1/N) Σ_{k=1}^{N} L_c(I_hat_gss^k, I_gss^k).

2 EXPERIMENTS
Implementation Details: The Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) is used with learning rates of 1e-4 for both Gev-RS (Zhou et al., 2022) and Fastec-RS (Liu et al., 2020) datasets. Training uses two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs for 400 epochs with a batch size of two. Mixed precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2017) in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017) is used. PSNR and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) are evaluation metrics.
Datasets: 1) Gev-RS dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) features GS videos at 1280×720, 5700 fps. Frames and events are reconstructed, downsampled to 260×346 (Scheerlinck et al., 2019). Events and RS blur frames are synthesized using vid2e (Gehrig et al., 2020). EvUnroll’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 20/9 train/test split is adopted. 2) Fastec-RS dataset (Liu et al., 2020) offers GS videos at 640×480, 2400 fps. Identical settings for resizing, event creation, and RS blur are applied. The dataset is split into 56 training and 20 testing sequences. 3) Real-world dataset (Zhou et al., 2022) contains four videos with paired RS frames and events. It lacks ground truth.

2.1 Comparison with SOTA Methods
Experiments are conducted on simulated and real datasets. Comparisons are made with two settings: (I) single GS sharp frame result, including JCD (Zhong et al., 2021), EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022), and eSL-Net (Wang et al., 2020). (II) sequence of GS sharp frames result, including DeblurSR (Song et al., 2023), and the combination of EvUnroll (Zhou et al., 2022) and TimeLens (Tulyakov et al., 2021). The model is also compared with EvUnRoll using real data.
JCD, EvUnroll, TimeLens, and DeblurSR are evaluated with released code. eSL-Net is modified by adjusting its parameterization initialization and removing the up-sampling module. eSL-Net and DeblurSR outputs are grayscale frames; JCD, EvUnroll, and EvUnroll+TimeLens outputs are RGB frames. The network is trained with grayscale and RGB inputs respectively.
Quantitative results for generating a single GS sharp frame (1x) and a sequence of GS sharp frames (3x, 5x, 9x) are presented. Compared to methods yielding a single GS sharp frame, the proposed method outperforms the best-performing methods (eSL-Net in gray and EvUnroll in RGB) by 1.48dB and 4.17dB on the Gev-RS dataset, respectively. For a sequence of GS sharp frames, the method attains optimal performance for both gray and RGB frames, achieving an increase of up to 13.47dB and 8.49dB compared to DeblurSR and EvUnroll+TimeLens on the Gev-RS dataset, respectively. The performance decline of DeblurSR is attributed to the interdependence between RS correction and deblur. The performance reduction of EvUnroll+TimeLens is accounted for by error accumulation.
Qualitative results show the method generates sharp frames without RS distortion. Results from eSL-Net and EvUnroll exhibit discernible noise. JCD fails to recover sharp frames in complex scenes, attributed to the assumption of linear motion. DebluSR results display noticeable artifacts.
Bad case analysis: Color distortion in one result is attributed to insufficient color information in a challenging scene with severe motion blur. The blurry frame cannot provide valid color information, and events do not provide color information.
EvUnRoll Simulation Dataset: The method is evaluated on the simulated dataset used by EvUnRoll. The model is trained using paired images of RS blur and GS sharp. As a one-stage approach, the method directly transforms an RS-blurred image into a GS-sharp image, avoiding accumulated error, and shows better performance.
Real-world Dataset: Results show both the proposed method and EvUnRoll correct rolling shutter distortions. Due to lack of ground truth, quantitative analysis is not possible. The proposed method avoids artifacts and errors.

2.2 Ablation and Analytical Studies
Importance of Exposure Time Embedding: Experiments evaluate the impact of learning-based position embedding, compared to sinusoid position embedding (Vaswani et al., 2017). Learning-based position embedding outperforms sinusoid position embedding, with advancements of up to 1.11dB on average.
Importance of RS Blur Image-guided Integral Loss: The effectiveness of the RS blur image-guided integral Loss across diverse interpolation settings is shown. PSNR is enhanced for high interpolation configurations (e.g., 9x) upon employing this loss.
Inference Speed: Inference time across 1x to 31x interpolation is shown. Total time rises from 30.8 ms at 1x to 86.9 ms at 31x, a 2.8-fold increase for a 31-fold interpolation. The average frame time decreases at higher multiples, reaching 2.8 ms at 31x. Compared to EvUnRoll (42.3 ms) and TimeLens, the method is more computationally efficient, requiring 72% of EvUnRoll’s time for RS correction and deblurring. For N-fold frame insertion using EvUnRoll + TimeLens, EvUnRoll is counted twice, and TimeLens N-2 times. TimeLens costs 186.76 ms per call. Calculations focus on GPU time, excluding data I/O.

3 CONCLUSION
This work presents an approach that uses events to guide rolling shutter frame correction, deblurring, and interpolation simultaneously. The method addresses all three tasks concurrently. It demonstrates efficiency in computational complexity and model size. The encoder is called once regardless of the number of interpolation frames, and the model size is 0.379M.
Limitations: Analysis uses simulated data and a real-world dataset lacking ground truth. Acquiring real data with ground truth is challenging. Future work aims to address this limitation by employing optical instruments to obtain real-world data with ground truth for quantitative evaluation.

The method uses a spatial-temporal implicit neural representation (INR) to map position and time coordinates to RGB values. A spatial-temporal implicit encoding (STE) converts the RS blur image and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR). To query a sharp frame, the exposure time is embedded into the STR and decoded pixel-by-pixel. The model has 0.379 M parameters. Inference efficiency is 2.83 ms/frame for 31x frame interpolation of an RS blur frame. Experiments show the method outperforms prior methods.

1 METHODOLOGY
1.1 Problem Definition and Analysis
The task is defined as recovering arbitrary frame-rate sharp GS frames from an RS blur image and paired event data. It is formulated as a function, F(x, t, θ). Here, x denotes the pixel position (x, y) of an image with resolution H×W, t denotes the timestamp during the exposure time, and θ denotes the parameters. A GS sharp frame is obtained by inputting a desired timestamp t_hat: I_{g,t_hat}=F(x, t_hat, θ).
An RS image is formulated as a row-wise combination of sequential GS frames within the exposure time (Fan & Dai, 2021; Fan et al., 2023). An RS sharp frame I_{r,t_s,t_e} is assembled from a sequence of GS sharp frames row by row given RS start time t_s and end time t_e. The h-th row of an RS frame is the same as the h-th row of a GS frame at t_s^h, where t_s^h = t_s + h × (t_e - t_s)/H. Therefore: I_{r,t_s,t_e} = {F(x, t_s^h, θ)[h], h ∈ [0,H)}.
A blur frame is regarded as the temporal average of a sequence of sharp frames (Nah et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020). A GS blur frame I_{g,t,t_exp}, where t is the exposure start timestamp and t_exp is the exposure time, is expressed as: I_{g,t,t_exp} = (1/t_exp) ∫_t^{t+t_exp} F(x, t, θ) dt ≈ (1/N) Σ_{i=0}^{N} I_{g, t_0 + i × t_exp / N}, where N is the length of the GS frame sequence.
An RS blur frame I_{r,t_s→t_e,t_exp} is described based on RS start time t_s, RS end time t_e, and exposure time t_exp. The h-th row is the temporal average of the h-th row in a sequence of GS sharp frames: I_{r,t_s→t_e,t_exp} = { (1/t_exp) ∫_{t_s^h}^{t_s^h+t_exp} F(x, t, θ)[h] dt, h ∈ [0,H) } ≈ { (1/N) Σ_{i=0}^{N} I_{g,t_s+i×t_exp/N}[h], h ∈ [0,H) }.
An event stream E consists of events e = (x, y, t, p), triggered when the logarithmic brightness change at pixel (x,y) exceeds a threshold C, approximated as the differential of F(x, t, θ) with respect to time.
To estimate F(x, t, θ) using event data E, three challenges are addressed: 1) find a function f_e to encode the input RS blur image and events into θ; 2) find a function f_te to represent the exposure information of desired frames as t; 3) find a function f_d to eliminate the need to input position information. The goal is to estimate f_e, f_te, and f_d: I = F(x, t, θ) = F(x, t, f_e(E, I_rsb)) = F(x, f_te(t), f_e(E, I_rsb)) = f_d(f_te(t), f_e(E, I_rsb)).

1.2 Proposed Framework
The framework takes an RS blur image I_rsb and paired events E as inputs and outputs N sharp GS frames {I_gss}_{i=0}^{N}. STE with deformable convolution (Wang et al., 2022a) encodes the RS blur frame and events into a spatial-temporal representation (STR). ETE embeds the exposure start timestamp. 1.2.2 Exposure Time Embedding (ETE)
The ETE module incorporates the exposure time of an RS frame (t_s, t_e) or a GS frame (t_g) using an MLP layer, generating a temporal tensor T. The module f_te takes GS exposure time t_g as input and produces GS temporal tensor T_g = f_te(t_g). For RS frames, T_r = f_te(t_r_s, t_r_e) represents the RS temporal tensor, used only in training. RS Timestamp Map: For RS start time t_s and end time t_e, the RS timestamp map is represented as M_r[h][w] = t_s + (t_e - t_s) × h / H.
Time Embedding: A one-layer MLP increases the dimension of the timestamp map M_r or M_g to H×W×C, the same dimension as STR θ. The embedding process is formulated as T_g = f_te(t_g) for GS frames, and T_r = f_te(t_r_s, t_r_e) for RS frames.

1.2.3 Pixel-by-pixel Decoding (PPD)
The PPD module queries a sharp frame from STR θ using the temporal tensor T. The encoder is invoked once for N times interpolation, while the decoder is called N times. 1.2.4 Loss Function

title: Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images

\title{Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images}

\begin{abstract}
In this paper, we tackle the challenging task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I) for the first time. This task aims to learn a mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains to modify naive 360 panoramic images. However, it is difficult to use existing I2I methods due to two main challenges. Firstly, panoramas inherit geometric distortions, which pose challenges for methods based on a narrow field-of-view. Secondly, accessing panoramic datasets encompassing various weather conditions or times for training purposes is severely limited. To address these challenges, we propose a novel I2I model tailored for mitigating panoramic distortion that harnesses readily obtainable pinhole images as the target domain for training. We introduce a versatile encoder and distortion-free discrimination that efficiently bridges the large domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by simultaneously encoding them in a consolidated structure. It allows our model to learn style mappings while overcoming significant geometric differences between the source and target domains. Moreover, we carefully design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to address the discontinuities at the panorama edges. Comprehensive experiments verify that our framework effectively translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by referring to the holistic style of pinhole data.
Our method also shows superior results in both maintaining structural coherence and rotation equivariance, clearly surpassing the existing I2I methods in qualitative and quantitative results.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Image-to-image translation (I2I) aims to modify an input image aligning with the style of the target domain, preserving the original content from the source domain. This paradigm enables numerous applications, such as colorization, style transfer, domain adaptation, data augmentation, etc (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). However, existing I2I has been used to synthesize pinhole images with narrow field-of-view (FoV), which limits the scope of applications considering diverse image-capturing devices.  

Panoramic $360^{\circ}$ cameras have recently grown in popularity, which enables many applications, e.g., AR/VR, autonomous driving, and city map modeling (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike pinhole images of narrow FoV, panoramic images (briefly, panoramas) capture the entire surroundings, providing richer information with $360^{\circ}\!\times\!180^{\circ}$ FoV. Translating panoramas into other styles can enable novel applications, such as immersive view generations or enriching user experiences with robust car-surrounding recognition (de La Garanderie et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; 2021b; Ma et al., 2021).  

However, naively applying conventional I2I methods for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can significantly distort the geometric properties of panoramas. As existing I2I methods assume the source and target domains only differ in style conditions, they have limitations in distinguishing between style and inherent distortion where the two domains have additional geometric gaps. One may project the panoramas into pinhole images to apply the conventional methods. However, it costs considerable computation since sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. In addition, the discontinuity problem at edges (left-right boundaries in panorama) requires panorama-specific modeling, as in the other tasks, e.g., panorama depth estimation, panoramic segmentation, and panorama synthesis (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).

Figure 1: Illustration of our problem formu- Figure 2: Failure cases of an existing method, lation. Our Pano-I2I is trained on panoramas in FSeSim. The pinhole-like structure (blue) and the daytime as the source domain and pinhole structural-, style-discontinuity at edges (green) are images with diverse conditions as the target do- spotted. In contrast, ours achieves a rotationmain, where the two domains have significant equivariant and panoramic structure. We visualize geometric and style gaps. rotated outputs $\scriptstyle{\theta=180^{\circ}}$ ) to highlight discontinuity.  

Another challenge of panoramic image translation is the absence of sufficient panorama datasets covering diverse conditions. Especially for I2I, panoramas obtained under diverse conditions such as sunny, rainy, and night are needed to consider various target styles. However, compared to the pinhole images, panoramas are captured by a specially-designed camera $360^{\circ}$ camera) or postprocessed using multi-view images obtained from the calibrated cameras. Note that panoramic images for the Street View services are usually taken during the day (Mirowski et al., 2018). Instead of constructing a costly new panorama dataset, it would be desirable to leverage existing pinhole image datasets with various conditions as style guidance, whose goal and results are illustrated in Fig. 1. We present typical failure cases of existing approaches, FSesim (Zheng et al., 2021) in Fig. 2. The result from FSeSim shows the collapsed structure having a pinhole-like structure (blue), as it simply overfits the geometric nature of the pinhole target. These indicate naively applying existing I2I methods has limited capacity to deal with the large domain gap between panoramas and pinhole images, resulting in disentangling content and style failures. Additionally, it has structural- and style-discontinuity at edges (green). Based on the above analysis, we seek to expand the applicability of I2I to panoramic images by employing existing pinhole image datasets as style domain, dubbed the Unpaired Panoramic Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images, shortly, Pano-I2I.  

To address geometric deformation in panoramas, we adopt deformable convolutions (Zhu et al., 2019) to our encoders, with different offsets for panoramas and pinhole images to reflect the geometric differences between the source and target. We propose a distortion-free discrimination that attenuates the geometric differences to handle the large gap between the source and target domain. In addition, we adopt panoramic rotation augmentation and ensemble techniques to solve discontinuity problems at edges, considering that a $360^{\circ}$ panorama should be continuous at boundaries.  

We validate the proposed approach by evaluating the panorama dataset, StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018), and the pinhole datasets (Shen et al., 2019; Sakaridis et al., 2019). Our proposed method significantly outperforms all existing methods across various target conditions from the pinhole datasets. We also provide ablation studies to analyze the components. Our main contributions are:  

• For the first time, to the best of our knowledge, we propose the panoramic I2I task and approach translating panoramas with pinhole images as a target domain. • We present distortion-free discrimination along with our versatile encoder, spherical positional embedding, and sphere-based rotation augmentation to deal with a large geometric gap between the source and the target and discontinuity at the edges of panoramas. • Pano-I2I notably outperforms the previous methods in the quantitative evaluations for style relevance and structural similarity, providing qualitative analyses.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Image-to-image translation. Different from early works requiring paired dataset (Isola et al., 2017), the seminal works (Zhu et al., 2017) enabled unpaired source/target training (i.e., learning without the grount-truth pair). Some works enable multimodal learning (Huang et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018a; 2020), multi-domain learning (Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Wu et al., 2019), translating across domains with large discrepancies (Amodio & Krishnaswamy, 2019; Yang et al., 2022) for simple datasets, and instance-aware learning (Bhattacharjee et al., 2020; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) in complex scenes. Nevertheless, existing I2I methods are restrictive to specific sourcetarget pairs; Previous methods (Lee et al., 2018a; Huang et al., 2018b) have translated images by reintegrating disentangled content and style of the scene to avoid geometric deformation but focused solely on the object figuration as the content. Namely, they are limited to handling 1) geometric variations (e.g., part deformation, viewpoint, scale) between source and target domains. Our approach introduces a robust framework to an unpaired setting, even with geometric differences in complex scenes, and 2) rotational equivalence for panoramas. On the other hand, several works have adopted the architecture of vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to image generation (Lee et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022a). Being capable of learning long-range interactions, the transformer is often employed for high-resolution image generation (Esser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022a), or complex scene generation (Wang et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022). For instance, InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022) proposed to use transformer for I2I, capturing global consensus in complex street-view scenes. Recently, diffusion models have been employed in image editing (Ye et al., 2023; Zhang & Agrawala, 2023; Brooks et al., 2023; Mou et al., 2023) thanks to their generative capacity. However, those methods are still limited to considering wide geometric discrepancies between source (panoramas) and target (pinhole) domains and rotation equivariance of panoramas.  

Panoramic image modeling. Panoramic images from $360^{\circ}$ cameras provide a thorough view of the scene with a wide FoV, beneficial in understanding the scene holistically. Since panorama itself faces challenges (FoV, focal length, aberration), this brought out unique architectures or modeling techniques, e.g., depth estimation (Tateno et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2020; Pintore et al., 2021; Peng & Zhang, 2023), perception (Yang et al., 2021a; Orhan & Bastanlar, 2022; Zheng et al., 2023), aerialto-panorama generation (Lu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022). A common practice to address distortions in panoramas is to project an image into other formats of $360^{\circ}$ images (e.g., equirectangular, cubemap) (Cheng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019), and some works even combine both equirectangular and cubemap projections with improving performance (Jiang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2020). However, they do not consider the properties of $360^{\circ}$ images, such as the connection between the edges of the images and the geometric distortion caused by the projection. Several works leverage narrow FoV projected images (Lee et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2018; de La Garanderie et al., 2018), but they require many projected images (e.g., 81 images (Lee et al., 2018b)), which is an additional burden. To deal with such discontinuity and distortion, recent works introduce modeling in spherical domain (Esteves et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2018), projecting an image to local tangent patches with minimal geometric error. It is proved that leveraging transformer architecture in $360^{\circ}$ image modeling reduces distortions caused by projection and rotation (Cho et al., 2022). For this reason, recent approaches (Ranftl et al., 2021; Rey-Area et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022) used the transformer achieving global structural consistency.  



\section{3 METHODOLOGY  }




\section{3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION  }


We use the panoramic domain as a source representing content structures and the pinhole domain as a target style. Formally, given a panorama of the source domain $\mathcal{X}$ , Pano-I2I learns a mapping function that translates its style into target pinhole domain $\boldsymbol{\wp}$ retaining the content and structure of the panorama. Unlike the previous I2I methods (Zhu et al., 2017; Park et al., 2020a;b; Jiang et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) that have source and target domains both in a narrow FoV of pinhole images, our setting varies both in style and structure; the source domain as panoramas with wide FoV captured in the daytime, and the target domain as pinhole images in diverse conditions with narrow FoV. Here, existing I2I methods designed fail to preserve the panoramic structure of the content, since their feature disentanglements cannot effectively separate the style from target content when both geometric and style differences exist. We empirically observed that 1) the outputs of the I2I methods are pinhole-like, as shown in Fig. 2, and 2) pinhole image-based network design that does not consider the spherical structure of $360^{\circ}$ causes discontinuity at the left-right boundaries and low visual fidelity.  

![](images/e114dace91df81a09dcc30272611ed9bc6db417f97919daa14b70a1f8f025dd7.jpg)  
Figure 3: Overall network configuration of Pano-I2I. Given panoramas as the source domain, we disentangle the content and translate its style aligned to the target domain. For training, pinhole datasets are used as targets referring to styles. Panoramic augmentation and ensemble are also introduced to preserve the spherical structure of panoramas. In our framework, Stage I only learns to reconstruct the panorama source, and Stage II learns panorama translation.  



\section{3.2 ARCHITECTURE DESIGN  }


Overall architecture. On a high level, the proposed method consists of a shared content encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}$ , a shared style encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}$ to estimate the disentangled representation, a transformer encoder $\tau$ to mix the style and content through AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers, and a shared generator $\mathcal{G}$ and discriminator $\mathcal{D}$ to generate the translated image. Our transformer encoder block consists of a multi-head self-attention layer and a feed-forward MLP with GELU (Vaswani et al., 2017).  

In specific, to translate an image $\mathbf{x}$ in source domain $\mathcal{X}$ to target domain $\boldsymbol{\wp}$ , we first extract a content feature map $\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times l_{c}}$ by the content encoder from $\mathbf{x}$ , with height $h$ , width $w$ , and $l_{c}$ content channels, and receive a random latent code $\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times1\times l_{s}}$ from Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})\in\mathbb{R}^{l_{s}}$ , which is used to control the style of the output with the affine parameters for AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers in transformer encoders. Finally, we get the output image by $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{T}\bar{(}\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{x}},\mathbf{s}))$ . In the following, we will explain our key ingredients – panoramic modeling in the content encoder, style encoder and the transformer, distortion-free discrimination, and sphere-based rotation augmentation and its ensemble – in detail.  

Panoramic modeling in encoders. In Pano-I2I, latent spaces are shared to embed domain-invariant content or style features as done in (Lee et al., 2018a). Namely, the content and style encoders, $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}$ , respectively, take either panoramas or pinhole images as inputs. However, the geometric distortion gap from the different FoVs prevents the encoders from understanding each corresponding structural information. To overcome this, motivated from (Shen et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022), we use the specially-designed deformable convolution layer (Zhu et al., 2019) at the beginning of the content and style encoders by adjusting the offset reflecting the characteristics of the image types. Specifically, given a panorama, the deformable convolution layer can be applied directly to the panorama by deriving an equirectangular plane (ERP) offset (Yun et al., 2022), $\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}}$ , that considers the panoramic geometry. To this end, we project a tangential local patch $\mathcal{P}$ of a 3D-Cartesian domain into ERP to obtain the corresponding ERP offset, $\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}}$ , as follows:  

$$
\Theta_{\mathtt{E R P}}(\theta,\phi)=f_{\mathtt{S P H}\to\mathrm{ERP}}\Big(f_{\mathrm{3D}\to\mathrm{SPH}}\big(\mathcal{P}\times R(\theta,\phi)/||\mathcal{P}\times R(\theta,\phi)||_{2}\big)\Big),
$$  

where $R(\theta,\phi)$ indicates the rotation matrix with the longitude $\theta\,\in\,[0,2\pi]$ and latitude $\phi\,\in\,[0,\pi]$ , $f_{\mathrm{SPH\rightarrowERP}}$ indicates the conversion function from spherical domain to ERP domain, and $f_{3\mathrm{D}\rightarrow\mathrm{SPH}}$ indicates the conversion function from 3D-Cartesian domain to spherical domain, as in PAVER (Yun et al., 2022). To be detailed, we first project the tangential local patch $\mathcal{P}$ to the corresponding spherical patch on a unit sphere $S^{2}$ , aligning the patch center to $(\theta,\phi)\in S^{2}$ . Notice that the number of $\mathcal{P}$ is $H\times W$ with the stride of 1 and proper paddings, while the center of $\mathcal{P}$ corresponds to the kernel center. Then, we obtain the relative spherical coordinates from the center point and all discrete locations in $\mathcal{P}$ . Finally, these positions are projected to the ERP domain as offset points. We compute such 2D-offset points $\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times H\times\hat{W}\times\hat{\mathrm{ker}}_{h}\times\mathrm{ker}_{w}}$ for each kernel location, and fixed to use them throughout training and test phase.  

Unlike basic convolution, which has a square receptive field with limited capability to deal with geometric distortions in panoramas, our deformable convolution with fixed offsets can encode panoramic structure. Note that we repurpose the deformable convolution as an adapter to our shared encoders to handle the panorama source and pinhole target simultaneously by different offsets, while PAVER adopts this to patch embedding for the panoramic transformer. This approach is efficient as the same encoders learn the compact representation that explains both types of images. By considering the context of the source and target within the shared network, our approach ensures that the output images reflect the desired style in a manner that is consistent with the source and target. For pinhole image encoding, $\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}}$ is replaced to zero-offset $\Theta_{\emptyset}$ in both content and style encoders, which are vanilla convolutions.2.  

Panoramic modeling in the translator. After extracting the content features from the source image, we first patchify the content features to be processed through transformer blocks, then add positional embedding (PE) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Rahaman et al., 2019), and process to generator. We represent the center coordinates of the previous patchified grids as $(i_{\mathrm{p}},j_{\mathrm{p}})$ corresponding to the $p$ -th patch. As two kinds of inputs $\{\mathbf{x},\,\bar{\mathbf{y}}\}$ —panorama, pinhole image, for each— have different structural properties, we adopt sinusoidal PE in two ways: using 2D PE and spherical PE (SPE), respectively.  

To start with, we define the fixed PE in transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as $\gamma(\cdot)$ , a sinusoidal mapping into $\mathbb{R}^{2K}$ as follows:  

$$
\gamma(a)=\{(\sin(2^{k-1}\pi a),\cos(2^{k-1}\pi a))\},\quad k\in\{1,2,...,K\}
$$  

for an input scalar $a$ . Based on this, we define the 2D PE for common pinhole images as follows:  

$$
\mathrm{PE}=\mathrm{concat}(\gamma(i_{\mathrm{p}}),\gamma(j_{\mathrm{p}})).
$$  

Following the previous work (Chen et al., 2022), we consider the $360^{\circ}$ spherical structure of panorama presenting a spherical positional embedding for the center position $(i_{\mathrm{p}},j_{\mathrm{p}})$ of each grid defined as follows, further added to the patch embedded tokens to work as explicit guidance:  

$$
\mathrm{SPE}=\mathrm{concat}(\gamma(\theta),\gamma(\phi)),\quad\mathrm{where}\:\theta=(2i_{\mathrm{p}}/h-1)\pi,\:\phi=(2j_{\mathrm{p}}/w-1)\pi/2,
$$  

where each patch has width $w$ and height $h$ . Since SPE explicitly provides cyclic spatial guidance and the relative spatial relationship between the tokens, it helps to maintain rotational equivariance for the panorama by encouraging structural continuity at boundaries in an $360^{\circ}$ input. On the other hand, the previous spherical methods used the standard PE (Yun et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b) or limited to employ the SPE for implicit guidance (Chen et al., 2022) as conditioning in text-to-image generation, which does not provide token-wise spatial information. This positional embedding is added to patch-embedded tokens and further processed into transformer encoders with AdaIN.  

Distortion-free discrimination. As our source and target domains exhibit two distinct features in geometric structure and style, directly applying the existing I2I method for panoramic I2I guided by pinhole images brings severe structural collapse with artifacts, affecting the synthesizing quality. We speculate that the structural collapse stems from breaking the balance of discriminators. Concretely, while the loss of discriminator in I2I typically learns to distinguish real data y and fake data $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ , mainly focusing on style difference, in our task, there is an additional large deformation gap and FoV difference between y and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ that confuses what to discriminate, as illustrated in Fig. 1.  

To address this issue, we present a distortion-free discrimination technique. The key idea is to transform a randomly selected region of a panorama into a pinhole image while maintaining the degree of FoV (see right-bottom section in Fig. 3). Specifically, we propose to adopt a panoramato-pinhole image conversion $f_{T}$ by a rectilinear projection (Lee et al., 2018b). To obtain a narrow FoV (pinhole-like) image with $f_{T}$ , we first select a viewpoint in the form of longitude and latitude coordinates $(\theta,\,\phi)$ in the spherical coordinate system, where $\theta$ and $\phi$ are randomly selected from $[0,2\pi]$ and $[0,\pi]$ , respectively, and extract a narrow FoV region from the $360^{\circ}$ panorama image by a differentiable projection function $f_{T}$ . To further improve the discriminative ability of our model, we adopt a weighted sum of the original discrimination and the proposed discrimination to encourage the model to learn more robust features by considering both the original full-panoramas and pinholelike converted panoramas (refer to Eqn. 7).  

Sphere-based rotation augmentation and ensemble. We introduce a panoramic rotation-based augmentation since a different panorama view consistently preserves the content structure without the discontinuity problem at the left-right boundaries. Given a panorama x, a rotated image $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ is generated by horizontally rotating angle $\theta$ . We efficiently implement this rotation by rolling the images in the ERP space without the burden of $\mathrm{ERP\toSPH\toERP}$ projections since both are effectively the same operation. The rotation angle is randomly sampled in $(0,\,2\pi)$ , where the step size is $2\pi/10$ . Such rotation is also reflected in SPE by adding the rotation angle $\theta$ to help the model learn the horizontal cyclicity of panoramas. Later, the translated images $\bar{\mathbf{y}}^{(0)}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(1)}$ from the generator with $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ , respectively, are blended together, after rotating back with $-\theta$ for $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(1)}$ of course, to generate the final ensemble output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ :  

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}=(\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(0)}+\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(1)^{\prime}})/2
$$  

where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(1)^{\prime}}$ is indicates $-\theta$ rotated version of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(1)}$ . Thus, the result $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ has a smoother boundary than the results predicted alone, mitigating discontinuous edge effects.  



\section{3.3 LOSS FUNCTIONS  }


Adversarial loss. We minimize the distribution discrepancy between two different features (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Mirza & Osindero, 2014) by adversarial loss. We adopt this to learn the translated image $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbf{x},\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}}),\mathbf{s}))$ and the image $\mathbf{x}$ from $\mathcal{X}$ to have indistinguishable distribution to preserve panoramic contents, defined as:  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{X}}[\log(1-\mathcal{D}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}))]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{Y}}[\log\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{y})],
$$  

with the R1 regularization (Mescheder et al., 2018) to enhance training stability. To consider the panoramic distortion-free discrimination using the panorama-to-pinhole conversion $f_{T}$ , we define additional adversarial loss as follows:  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{df-GAN}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{X}}[\log(1-\mathcal{D}(f_{T}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})))]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{Y}}[\log\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{y})].
$$  

Content loss. To maintain the content between the source image $\mathbf{x}$ and translated image $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ , we exploit the spatially-correlative loss (Zheng et al., 2021) to define a content loss, with an augmented source $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{aug}}$ . To get $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{aug}}$ , we apply structure-preserving transformations to $\mathbf{x}$ . This helps preserve the structure and learn the spatially-correlative map (Zheng et al., 2021) based on patchwise infoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018), since it captures the domain-invariant structure representation. Denoting that $\hat{\bf v}$ as spatially-correlative map of the query patch from $\mathbf{c}^{\hat{\mathrm{y}}}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{ERP}})$ , we pick the pseudo-positive patch samplev from $\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{x}}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbf{x},\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}})$ in the same position of the query patch $\hat{\bf v}$ , and the negative patches $\bar{\bf v}$ from the other positions of $\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{aug}}^{\mathrm{x}}$ and $\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{{x}}}$ , except for the position of query patches $\hat{\bf v}$ . We first define a score function $\ell(\cdot)$ at the $l$ -th convolution layer in $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}$ :  

$$
\ell(\hat{\mathbf{v}},\stackrel{+}{\mathbf{v}},\stackrel{-}{\mathbf{v}})=-\log\left[\frac{\exp(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\stackrel{+}{\mathbf{v}}/\tau)}{\exp(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\stackrel{+}{\mathbf{v}}/\tau)+\sum_{\mathbf{s}\in S\setminus s}\exp(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\stackrel{-}{\mathbf{v}}^{s}/\tau)}\right],
$$  

where $\tau$ is a temperature parameter. Then, the overall content loss function is defined as follows:  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{\mathrm{cont}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{X}}\sum_{l}\sum_{s}\ell(\hat{{\mathbf{v}}}_{l}^{s},\overset{+}{{\mathbf{v}}}_{l}^{s},\overset{-}{{\mathbf{v}}}_{l}^{S\setminus s}),
$$  

where the index $s\in\{1,2,...,S_{l}\}$ and $S$ is a set of patches in each $l$ -th layer, and $S\backslash s$ indicates the indices except $s$ .  

Image reconstruction loss. We enhance the disentanglement between content and style in a manner that our $\mathcal{G}$ can reconstruct an image for domain $\boldsymbol{\wp}$ . To be specific, $\mathbf{y}$ is fed into content encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}$ and style encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}$ to obtain a content feature map $\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{y}}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathcal{D}})$ and a style code $\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{y}}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathcal{O}})$ . We then compare the reconstructed image $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{y}},\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{y}}))$ with y as follows:  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}^{\mathrm{img}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{y}}[\|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{{y}}},\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{{y}}}))-\mathbf{y}\|_{1}].
$$  

Style reconstruction loss. In order to better learn disentangled representation, we compute L1 loss between the style code from the translated image and input panorama,  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref-recon}}^{\mathrm{sty}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{X}}[\|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}(\hat{{\mathbf{y}}},\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}})-\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}({\mathbf{x}},\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}})\|_{1}].
$$  

We also define the style reconstruction loss to reconstruct the style code s, used to generate $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ . Note that the style code s is randomly sampled from Gaussian distribution, not extracted from an image.  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rand-recon}}^{\mathrm{sty}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{X},{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{Y}}[\|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{s}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\Theta_{\mathrm{ERP}})-\mathbf{\left.s\right|}_{1}].
$$  

3.4 TRAINING STRATEGY  

Stage I: Panorama reconstruction. Since there is no publicly available large-scale outdoor panorama data under various weather or season conditions, we cannot use panoramas as a style reference. In addition, in order to share the same embedding space in content and style, the network must be able to process pinhole images and panoramas simultaneously.  

For the stable training of Pano-I2I, the training procedure is split into two stages corresponding with different objectives. In Stage I, we pretrain the content and style encoders $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{c,s}}$ , transformer $\tau$ , generator $\mathcal{G}$ , and discriminator $\mathcal{D}$ using the panorama dataset only. Given a panorama, the parameters of our network are optimized to reconstruct the original with adversarial and content losses, and style reconstruction loss. As the network learns to reconstruct the input self again, we use the style feature represented by a style encoder instead of the random style code. For $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}$ in Stage I, the original discriminator receives $\mathbf{x}$ instead of $\mathbf{y}$ as an input. The total objective in Stage I as follows:  

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{StageI}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cont}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{\mathrm{cont}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sty}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref-recon}}^{\mathrm{sty}},
$$  

where $\lambda_{\{*\}}$ denotes balancing hyperparameters that control the importance of each loss.  

Stage II: Panoramic I2I guided by pinhole image. In Stage II, the whole network is fully trained with robust initialization by Stage I. Compared to Stage I, panorama and pinhole datasets are all used in this stage. Concretely, the main difference is that; (1) original discrimination is combined with our distortion-free discrimination as a weighted sum, (2) the style code is sampled from the Gaussian distribution to translate the panorama, (3) the panoramic rotation-based augmentation and its ensemble technique are leveraged to enhance the generation quality. Therefore, the total objective in Stage $\mathrm{II}$ is defined as:  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\dot{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Suge2}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{df.GAN}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{df.GAN}}+(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{df.GAN}})\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cont}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{\mathrm{cont}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sty}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rand-recon}}^{\mathrm{sty}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{recon}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}^{\mathrm{ing}}.}\end{array}
$$  

Notice that all coefficients for the losses are set to 1, except for $\lambda_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{\mathrm{cont}}$ , which is set as 15, and is set as 0.8 for Stage II. Those coefficients were commonly used in all training datasets.3 for other training details.  

4 EXPERIMENTS   
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP  

Datasets. We conduct experiments on the panorama dataset, StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018), as the source domain, and a standard street-view dataset for I2I, INIT (Shen et al., 2019) and Dark Zurich (Sakaridis et al., 2019), as the target domain. StreetLearn provides $360^{\circ}$ outdoor 56k panoramas taken from the Google Street View. Although INIT consists of four conditions (sunny, night, rainy, and cloudy), we use two conditions, night and rainy, since the condition of the StreetLearn is captured during the daytime, including sunny and cloudy. We use the Batch1 of INIT dataset, a total of 62k images for the four conditions. Dark Zurich has three conditions (daytime, night, and twilight), a total of 8779 images, and we use night and twilight.  

Metrics. For quantitative comparison, we report the Fre´chet Inception Distance (FID) metric (Heusel et al., 2017) to evaluate style relevance, and the structural similarity (SSIM) index (Wang et al., 2004) metric to evaluate the panoramic content preserving. Considering that the structure of outputs tends to become pinhole-like in panoramic I2I tasks, we measure the FID metric after applying panorama-to-pinhole projection $(f_{T})$ for randomly chosen horizontal angle $\theta$ and fixed vertical angle $\phi$ as 0 with a fixed $\mathrm{FoV}$ of $90^{\circ}$ , for consistent viewpoint with the target images. Notice that the SSIM shows the degree of content preservation because it measures the structural similarity between the original panorama and the translated panorama based on luminance, contrast, and structure.  

![](images/e5b4530d446e2b48396289580b4b069d953e010dbd81b1458fa523695ce1546d.jpg)  
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on StreetLearn dataset (day) to INIT dataset (night, rainy): (top to bottom) day $\rightarrow$ night, and day $\rightarrow$ rainy results. Among the methods, Pano-I2I (ours) preserves object details well and shows realistic results.  

Table 1: Quantitative evaluation on the trans lated panoramas from StreetLearn to INIT.   

![](images/6dce829a0ee7aec0c5a9d301c79d070c415a3e8f41f35cac50b9a3f92ccf11ef.jpg)  

Table 2: Quantitative evaluation on the translated panoramas from StreetLearn to Dark Zurich.   

![](images/e995674be9c0ee391d74b824b531decd1a6bb360c1056b7f5b673d0a1c3bd661.jpg)  

Comparison methods. We compare our approach against the state-of-the-art I2I methods, including MGUIT (Jeong et al., 2021) and InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), CUT (Park et al., 2020a), and FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). We train them with same datasets as ours. Since MGUIT and InstaFormer require bounding box annotations to train their models, we exploit pretrained YOLOv5 (Jocher et al., 2021) model to generate pseudo bounding box annotations.  



\section{4.2 IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL  }


We formulate the proposed method with vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) inspired by InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), but without instance-level approaches due to the absence of groundtruth bounding box annotations. We design our content and style encoders, a transformer encoder, the generator-and-discriminator for our GAN losses based on (Kim et al., 2022), where all modules are learned from scratch.  

Qualitative evaluation. In Fig. 4, we qualitatively compare our method with other I2I methods. We observe all the other methods (Park et al., 2020a; Jiang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) fail to synthesize reasonable panoramic results and show obvious inconsistent output regarding either structure or style in an image. Moreover, previous methods recognize structural discrepancies between source and target domains as style differences, indicating failed translation results that change like pinhole images. Surprisingly, in the case of ‘day $\rightarrow$ night’, all existing methods fail to preserve the objectness as a car or building. We conjecture that they cannot efficiently deal with the large domain gap in ‘day $\rightarrow$ night,’ thus naively learning to follow the target distribution without considering the context from the source. By comparison, our method shows the overall best performance in visual quality, preserving panoramic content, and structuraland style-consistency. In particular, we observe the ability of our discrimination design to learn distortion-tolerated features.3.  

Quantitative evaluation. Tab. 1 and Tab. 2 show the quantitative comparison in terms of FID (Heusel et al., 2017) and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) index metrics. Our method consistently outperforms the competitive methods in all metrics, demonstrating that Pano-I2I successfully captures the style of the target domain while preserving the panoramic contents. Notably, our approach exhibits significant improvements in terms of SSIM. In contrast, previous methods perform poorly in terms of  

![](images/134ee29ab24cf2407550ba0a78ab2ba77301488e2f0047f07c5e803a1c8cd9c7.jpg)  

SSIM compared to our results, which is also evident from the qualitative results presented in Fig. 4.  

User study. We conducted a user study to compare the subjective quality. We randomly select 10 images for each task (day $\rightarrow$ night, rainy) on INIT dataset, and let 60 users sort all the methods regarding “overall image quality”, “content preservation from the source”, and “style relevance with the target, considering the context from the source”. As seen in Fig. 5, our method has a clear advantage on every task.  



\section{4.4 ABLATION STUDY  }


In Tab. 3, we show quantitative results for the ablation study on the day $\rightarrow$ night task on the INIT dataset. In particular, we analyze the effectiveness of our 1) distortionfree discrimination, 2) ensemble technique, 3) two-stage learning scheme, and 4) spherical positional embedding (SPE) and deformable convolution. We observe all the techniques and components contribute to performance improvement in terms of style relevance and content preservation, and the impact of distortion-free discrimination is substantially effective in handling geometric deformation.  

![](images/e279e057b90523897dfda2c766611555211f1ae71e2237e917dc2e82fa1811a4.jpg)  



\section{5 CONCLUSION  }


In this paper, we introduce an experimental protocol and a dedicated model for the panoramic Imageto-Image Translation that considers 1) the structural properties of the panoramic images and 2) the lack of outdoor panoramic scene datasets. To this end, we design our model to take panoramas as the source, and pinhole images with diverse conditions as the target, raising the large geometric variance between the source and target domains as a major challenging point. To mitigate these issues, we propose distortion-aware panoramic modeling techniques and distortion-free discriminators to stabilize adversarial learning. Additionally, exploiting the cyclic property of panoramas, we propose to rotate and fuse the synthesized panoramas, resulting in the panorama output with a continuous view. We demonstrate the success of our method in translating realistic images in several benchmarks and look forward to future works that use our proposed experimental paradigm for panoramic image translation with non-pinhole camera inputs using diverse sets of pinhole image datasets.

\title{Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images}

\begin{abstract}
In this paper, we tackle the challenging task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I) for the first time. This task aims to learn a mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains to modify naive 360 panoramic images. However, it is difficult to use existing I2I methods due to two main challenges. Firstly, panoramas inherit geometric distortions, which pose challenges for methods based on a narrow field-of-view. Secondly, accessing panoramic datasets encompassing various weather conditions or times for training purposes is severely limited. To address these challenges, we propose a novel I2I model tailored for mitigating panoramic distortion that harnesses readily obtainable pinhole images as the target domain for training. We introduce a versatile encoder and distortion-free discrimination that efficiently bridges the large domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by simultaneously encoding them in a consolidated structure. It allows our model to learn style mappings while overcoming significant geometric differences between the source and target domains. Moreover, we carefully design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to address the discontinuities at the panorama edges. Comprehensive experiments verify that our framework effectively translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by referring to the holistic style of pinhole data.
Our method also shows superior results in both maintaining structural coherence and rotation equivariance, clearly surpassing the existing I2I methods in qualitative and quantitative results.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Image-to-image translation (I2I) aims to modify an input image aligning with the style of the target domain, preserving the original content from the source domain. This paradigm enables numerous applications, such as colorization, style transfer, domain adaptation, data augmentation, etc (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). However, existing I2I has been used to synthesize pinhole images with narrow field-of-view (FoV), which limits the scope of applications considering diverse image-capturing devices.  

Panoramic $360^{\circ}$ cameras have recently grown in popularity, which enables many applications, e.g., AR/VR, autonomous driving, and city map modeling (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike pinhole images of narrow FoV, panoramic images (briefly, panoramas) capture the entire surroundings, providing richer information with $360^{\circ}\!\times\!180^{\circ}$ FoV. Translating panoramas into other styles can enable novel applications, such as immersive view generations or enriching user experiences with robust car-surrounding recognition (de La Garanderie et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; 2021b; Ma et al., 2021).  

However, naively applying conventional I2I methods for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can significantly distort the geometric properties of panoramas. As existing I2I methods assume the source and target domains only differ in style conditions, they have limitations in distinguishing between style and inherent distortion where the two domains have additional geometric gaps. One may project the panoramas into pinhole images to apply the conventional methods. However, it costs considerable computation since sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. In addition, the discontinuity problem at edges (left-right boundaries in panorama) requires panorama-specific modeling, as in the other tasks, e.g., panorama depth estimation, panoramic segmentation, and panorama synthesis (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).
