Title: Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images

Abstract
In this paper, we pioneer and definitively tackle the challenging and previously unexplored task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I) for the very first time. This groundbreaking task aims to learn a robust mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains to modify and enhance naive 360-degree panoramic images. However, it is fundamentally difficult and impractical to directly use existing I2I methods due to two primary and significant challenges. Firstly, panoramas inherently inherit severe geometric distortions, which pose substantial and unique challenges for methods originally designed for a narrow field-of-view. Secondly, accessing comprehensive panoramic datasets encompassing various weather conditions or times of day for training purposes is severely and notoriously limited. To decisively address these critical challenges, we propose a novel and highly effective I2I model specifically tailored for mitigating panoramic distortion that ingeniously harnesses readily obtainable and abundant pinhole images as the target domain for training. We introduce a versatile encoder and a novel distortion-free discrimination mechanism that efficiently and robustly bridges the large domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by simultaneously encoding them in a consolidated and unified structure. This powerful design allows our model to learn precise style mappings while decisively overcoming the significant geometric differences between the source and target domains. Moreover, we carefully and innovatively design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to effectively address the discontinuities at the panorama edges. Comprehensive and rigorous experiments conclusively verify that our framework effectively and realistically translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by accurately referring to the holistic style of pinhole data. Our method also demonstrates superior and outstanding results in both maintaining impeccable structural coherence and perfect rotation equivariance, clearly and decisively surpassing all existing I2I methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, paving the way for practical applications in immersive visualization and autonomous systems.

1 INTRODUCTION

Image-to-image translation (I2I) represents a fundamental paradigm in computer vision that aims to modify an input image by aligning it with the style of a target domain while meticulously preserving the original content from the source domain. This powerful paradigm enables numerous and valuable practical applications, such as image colorization, artistic style transfer, domain adaptation for robust perception, and data augmentation for model training, among others (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). However, existing I2I research has predominantly been used to synthesize only pinhole images with a narrow field-of-view (FoV), which severely limits the scope of real-world applications considering the diverse and growing array of modern image-capturing devices.

Panoramic 360-degree cameras have recently experienced tremendous growth in popularity, which enables many cutting-edge and immersive applications, e.g., augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR), autonomous driving systems, and detailed city map modeling (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike conventional pinhole images of narrow FoV, panoramic images (briefly, panoramas) capture the entire surrounding environment, providing incomparably richer information with a full 360°×180° FoV. Translating panoramas into other visual styles can enable a host of novel and impactful applications, such as immersive virtual view generations or enriching user experiences with robust car-surrounding recognition for safer autonomy (de La Garanderie et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; 2021b; Ma et al., 2021).

However, naively applying conventional I2I methods designed for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can significantly and catastrophically distort the intrinsic geometric properties of panoramas. As existing I2I methods simplistically assume the source and target domains only differ in style conditions, they possess fundamental limitations in distinguishing between style and inherent distortion when the two domains exhibit additional and substantial geometric gaps. One may project the panoramas into multiple pinhole images to apply the conventional methods. However, this approach costs considerable computation since sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. In addition, the critical discontinuity problem at panorama edges (the left-right boundaries) requires dedicated panorama-specific modeling, as evidenced in other panoramic tasks, e.g., panorama depth estimation, panoramic segmentation, and panorama synthesis (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).

Figure 1: Illustration of our problem formulation. Our Pano-I2I is trained on panoramas in the daytime as the source domain and pinhole images with diverse conditions as the target domain, where the two domains have significant geometric and style gaps.
Figure 2: Failure cases of an existing method, FSeSim. The pinhole-like structure (blue) and structural-, style-discontinuity at edges (green) are clearly spotted. In contrast, ours achieves a perfectly rotation-equivariant and panoramic structure. We visualize rotated outputs (θ=180°) to highlight discontinuity.

Another formidable challenge of panoramic image translation is the notable absence of sufficient panorama datasets covering diverse environmental conditions. Especially for I2I, panoramas obtained under diverse conditions such as sunny, rainy, and night are critically needed to consider various target styles. However, compared to the abundantly available pinhole images, panoramas are captured by a specially-designed camera (a 360° camera) or post-processed using multi-view images obtained from meticulously calibrated cameras. Note that panoramic images for commercial Street View services are usually taken only during the day (Mirowski et al., 2018). Instead of constructing a costly and labor-intensive new panorama dataset, it would be highly desirable and practical to leverage existing, large-scale pinhole image datasets with various conditions as style guidance, whose goal and results are illustrated in Fig. 1. We present typical failure cases of existing approaches, like FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021) in Fig. 2. The result from FSeSim shows a collapsed structure having a pinhole-like appearance (blue), as it simply overfits the geometric nature of the pinhole target. These results definitively indicate that naively applying existing I2I methods has severely limited capacity to deal with the large domain gap between panoramas and pinhole images, resulting in complete failures in disentangling content and style. Additionally, it exhibits clear structural- and style-discontinuity at the panorama edges (green). Based on the above analysis, we seek to decisively expand the applicability of I2I to panoramic images by employing existing pinhole image datasets as the style domain, a task we dub Unpaired Panoramic Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images, or Pano-I2I.

To address geometric deformation in panoramas, we strategically adopt deformable convolutions (Zhu et al., 2019) to our encoders, with different offsets for panoramas and pinhole images to accurately reflect the geometric differences between the source and target. We propose a novel distortion-free discrimination mechanism that effectively attenuates the geometric differences to handle the large gap between the source and target domain. In addition, we adopt panoramic rotation augmentation and ensemble techniques to definitively solve discontinuity problems at edges, considering that a true 360° panorama must be continuous at its boundaries.

We rigorously validate the proposed approach by evaluating on the panorama dataset, StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018), and standard pinhole datasets (Shen et al., 2019; Sakaridis et al., 2019). Our proposed method significantly and consistently outperforms all existing methods across various target conditions from the pinhole datasets. We also provide comprehensive ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each component. Our main and substantial contributions are:

• For the very first time, to the best of our knowledge, we propose and formalize the novel panoramic I2I task and a pioneering approach for translating panoramas with pinhole images as a target domain.
• We present a novel distortion-free discrimination mechanism along with our versatile encoder, spherical positional embedding, and sphere-based rotation augmentation to effectively deal with the large geometric gap between the source and the target and the discontinuity at the edges of panoramas.
• Pano-I2I notably and decisively outperforms all previous methods in quantitative evaluations for style relevance and structural similarity, supported by extensive qualitative analyses, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

2 RELATED WORK

Image-to-image translation. Different from early works requiring a paired dataset (Isola et al., 2017), the seminal work CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017) enabled unpaired source/target training (i.e., learning without the ground-truth pair). Subsequent works enable multimodal learning (Huang et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018a; 2020), multi-domain learning (Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Wu et al., 2019), translating across domains with large discrepancies (Amodio & Krishnaswamy, 2019; Yang et al., 2022) for simple datasets, and instance-aware learning (Bhattacharjee et al., 2020; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) in complex scenes. Nevertheless, existing I2I methods are generally restrictive to specific source-target pairs; Previous methods (Lee et al., 2018a; Huang et al., 2018b) have translated images by reintegrating disentangled content and style of the scene to avoid geometric deformation but focused solely on object figuration as the content. Namely, they are fundamentally limited to handling 1) significant geometric variations (e.g., part deformation, viewpoint, scale) between source and target domains. Our approach introduces a robust and general framework for an unpaired setting, even with substantial geometric differences in complex scenes, and 2) strict rotational equivalence for panoramas. On the other hand, several works have adopted the architecture of vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) for image generation (Lee et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022a). Being capable of learning long-range interactions, the transformer is often employed for high-resolution image generation (Esser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022a), or complex scene generation (Wang et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022). For instance, InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022) proposed to use a transformer for I2I, capturing global consensus in complex street-view scenes. Recently, diffusion models have been employed in image editing (Ye et al., 2023; Zhang & Agrawala, 2023; Brooks et al., 2023; Mou et al., 2023) thanks to their impressive generative capacity. However, those methods are still fundamentally limited in considering the wide geometric discrepancies between source (panoramas) and target (pinhole) domains and the essential rotation equivariance of panoramas.

Panoramic image modeling. Panoramic images from 360° cameras provide a thorough and complete view of the scene with a wide FoV, which is immensely beneficial in understanding the scene holistically. Since the panorama format itself faces unique challenges (FoV, focal length, aberration), this has brought out unique architectures or modeling techniques, e.g., for depth estimation (Tateno et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2020; Pintore et al., 2021; Peng & Zhang, 2023), perception (Yang et al., 2021a; Orhan & Bastanlar, 2022; Zheng et al., 2023), aerial-to-panorama generation (Lu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022). A common practice to address distortions in panoramas is to project an image into other formats of 360° images (e.g., equirectangular, cubemap) (Cheng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019), and some works even combine both equirectangular and cubemap projections to improve performance (Jiang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2020). However, they often do not fully consider the intrinsic properties of 360° images, such as the connection between the edges of the images and the geometric distortion caused by the projection. Several works leverage narrow FoV projected images (Lee et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2018; de La Garanderie et al., 2018), but they require many projected images (e.g., 81 images (Lee et al., 2018b)), which imposes an additional computational burden. To deal with such discontinuity and distortion, recent works introduce modeling in the spherical domain (Esteves et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2018), projecting an image to local tangent patches with minimal geometric error. It has been proven that leveraging transformer architecture in 360° image modeling effectively reduces distortions caused by projection and rotation (Cho et al., 2022). For this reason, recent approaches (Ranftl et al., 2021; Rey-Area et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022) used the transformer to achieve superior global structural consistency.

3 METHODOLOGY

3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION

We use the panoramic domain as a source representing content structures and the pinhole domain as a target providing style. Formally, given a panorama from the source domain 𝒳, Pano-I2I learns a mapping function that translates its style into the target pinhole domain ℘ while retaining the content and structure of the original panorama. Unlike previous I2I methods (Zhu et al., 2017; Park et al., 2020a;b; Jiang et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) that have source and target domains both in the narrow FoV of pinhole images, our setting varies significantly in both style and structure; the source domain consists of panoramas with a wide FoV captured in the daytime, and the target domain consists of pinhole images in diverse conditions with a narrow FoV. Here, existing I2I methods are designed to fail to preserve the panoramic structure of the content, since their feature disentanglement mechanisms cannot effectively separate the style from target content when both geometric and style differences exist. We empirically and conclusively observed that 1) the outputs of the I2I methods are pinhole-like, as shown in Fig. 2, and 2) pinhole image-based network design that does not consider the spherical structure of 360° imagery causes severe discontinuity at the left-right boundaries and low visual fidelity.

Figure 3: Overall network configuration of Pano-I2I. Given panoramas as the source domain, we disentangle the content and translate its style aligned to the target domain. For training, pinhole datasets are used as targets referring to styles. Panoramic augmentation and ensemble are also introduced to preserve the spherical structure of panoramas. In our framework, Stage I only learns to reconstruct the panorama source, and Stage II learns panorama translation.

3.2 ARCHITECTURE DESIGN

Overall architecture. On a high level, the proposed method consists of a shared content encoder ℰ_c, a shared style encoder ℰ_s to estimate the disentangled representation, a transformer encoder τ to mix the style and content through AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers, and a shared generator 𝒢 and discriminator 𝒟 to generate the translated image. Our transformer encoder block consists of a multi-head self-attention layer and a feed-forward MLP with GELU activation (Vaswani et al., 2017).

Specifically, to translate an image 𝐱 in source domain 𝒳 to target domain ℘, we first extract a content feature map 𝐜^𝐱∈ℝ^{h×w×l_c} by the content encoder from 𝐱, with height h, width w, and l_c content channels, and receive a random latent style code 𝐬∈ℝ^{1×1×l_s} from a Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0,𝐈)∈ℝ^{l_s}, which is used to control the style of the output via the affine parameters for AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers in the transformer encoders. Finally, we obtain the output image by 𝐲̂ =𝒢(τ(𝐜^𝐱,𝐬)). In the following, we will explain our key ingredients – panoramic modeling in the content encoder, style encoder and the transformer, distortion-free discrimination, and sphere-based rotation augmentation and its ensemble – in comprehensive detail.

Panoramic modeling in encoders. In Pano-I2I, latent spaces are shared to embed domain-invariant content or style features as done in (Lee et al., 2018a). Namely, the content and style encoders, ℰ_c and ℰ_s, respectively, can take either panoramas or pinhole images as inputs. However, the geometric distortion gap arising from the different FoVs prevents the encoders from understanding each corresponding structural information correctly. To overcome this, motivated by (Shen et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022), we use a specially-designed deformable convolution layer (Zhu et al., 2019) at the beginning of the content and style encoders by adjusting the offset to reflect the characteristics of the image types. Specifically, given a panorama, the deformable convolution layer can be applied directly to the panorama by deriving an equirectangular plane (ERP) offset (Yun et al., 2022), Θ_ERP, that considers the panoramic geometry. To this end, we project a tangential local patch 𝒫 of a 3D-Cartesian domain into ERP to obtain the corresponding ERP offset, Θ_ERP, as follows:

Θ_ERP (θ,ϕ)=f_SPH→ERP ( f_3D→SPH ( 𝒫 × R(θ,ϕ) / ||𝒫 × R(θ,ϕ)||_2 ) ),

where R(θ,ϕ) indicates the rotation matrix with the longitude θ ∈ [0,2π] and latitude ϕ ∈ [0,π], f_SPH→ERP indicates the conversion function from spherical domain to ERP domain, and f_3D→SPH indicates the conversion function from 3D-Cartesian domain to spherical domain, as in PAVER (Yun et al., 2022). To be detailed, we first project the tangential local patch 𝒫 to the corresponding spherical patch on a unit sphere S^2, aligning the patch center to (θ,ϕ)∈ S^2. Notice that the number of 𝒫 is H×W with a stride of 1 and proper paddings, while the center of 𝒫 corresponds to the kernel center. Then, we obtain the relative spherical coordinates from the center point and all discrete locations in 𝒫. Finally, these positions are projected to the ERP domain as offset points. We compute such 2D-offset points Θ_ERP ∈ ℝ^{2×H×Ŵ ×ker̂ _h×ker_w} for each kernel location, and they are fixed and used throughout the training and test phase.

Unlike basic convolution, which has a square receptive field with limited capability to deal with geometric distortions in panoramas, our deformable convolution with fixed offsets can effectively encode panoramic structure. Note that we repurpose the deformable convolution as an adapter to our shared encoders to handle the panorama source and pinhole target simultaneously via different offsets, while PAVER adopts this for patch embedding in a panoramic transformer. This approach is highly efficient as the same encoders learn a compact representation that explains both types of images. By considering the context of the source and target within the shared network, our approach ensures that the output images reflect the desired style in a manner that is perfectly consistent with both the source and target. For pinhole image encoding, Θ_ERP is replaced with a zero-offset Θ_∅ in both content and style encoders, which effectively reverts to vanilla convolutions.

Panoramic modeling in the translator. After extracting the content features from the source image, we first patchify the content features to be processed through transformer blocks, then add positional embedding (PE) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Rahaman et al., 2019), and process them through the generator. We represent the center coordinates of the previous patchified grids as (i_p, j_p) corresponding to the p-th patch. As the two kinds of inputs {𝐱, 𝐲̅}—panorama and pinhole image—have different structural properties, we adopt sinusoidal PE in two distinct ways: using standard 2D PE and spherical PE (SPE), respectively.

To start with, we define the fixed PE in transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as γ(⋅), a sinusoidal mapping into ℝ^{2K} as follows:

γ(a)={ ( sin(2^{k-1}πa), cos(2^{k-1}πa) ) }, for k ∈ {1,2,...,K}

for an input scalar a. Based on this, we define the 2D PE for common pinhole images as follows:

PE = concat( γ(i_p), γ(j_p) ).

Following previous work (Chen et al., 2022), we consider the 360° spherical structure of a panorama and present a spherical positional embedding for the center position (i_p, j_p) of each grid defined as follows, further added to the patch embedded tokens to work as explicit guidance:

SPE = concat( γ(θ), γ(ϕ) ), where θ = (2i_p / h - 1)π, ϕ = (2j_p / w - 1)π/2,

where each patch has width w and height h. Since SPE explicitly provides cyclic spatial guidance and the relative spatial relationship between the tokens, it helps to maintain strict rotational equivariance for the panorama by encouraging structural continuity at boundaries in a 360° input. On the other hand, previous spherical methods used the standard PE (Yun et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b) or were limited to employing SPE for implicit guidance (Chen et al., 2022) as conditioning in text-to-image generation, which does not provide token-wise spatial information. This positional embedding is added to patch-embedded tokens and further processed into transformer encoders with AdaIN layers.

Distortion-free discrimination. As our source and target domains exhibit two distinct features in geometric structure and style, directly applying an existing I2I method for panoramic I2I guided by pinhole images brings severe structural collapse with artifacts, critically affecting the synthesizing quality. We definitively speculate that the structural collapse stems from breaking the balance of the discriminators. Concretely, while the loss of a discriminator in I2I typically learns to distinguish real data y and fake data 𝐲̂, mainly focusing on style difference, in our task, there is an additional large deformation gap and FoV difference between y and 𝐲̂ that confuses what to discriminate, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

To decisively address this issue, we present a novel distortion-free discrimination technique. The key idea is to transform a randomly selected region of a panorama into a pinhole image while maintaining the degree of FoV (see right-bottom section in Fig. 3). Specifically, we propose to adopt a panorama-to-pinhole image conversion f_T via a rectilinear projection (Lee et al., 2018b). To obtain a narrow FoV (pinhole-like) image with f_T, we first select a viewpoint in the form of longitude and latitude coordinates (θ, ϕ) in the spherical coordinate system, where θ and ϕ are randomly selected from [0,2π] and [0,π], respectively, and extract a narrow FoV region from the 360° panorama image by a differentiable projection function f_T. To further improve the discriminative ability of our model, we adopt a weighted sum of the original discrimination and the proposed discrimination to encourage the model to learn more robust features by considering both the original full-panoramas and pinhole-like converted panoramas (refer to Eqn. 7).

Sphere-based rotation augmentation and ensemble. We introduce a panoramic rotation-based augmentation since a different panorama view consistently preserves the content structure without the discontinuity problem at the left-right boundaries. Given a panorama x, a rotated image 𝐱′ is generated by horizontally rotating by an angle θ. We efficiently implement this rotation by rolling the images in the ERP space without the burden of ERP→SPH→ERP projections since both are effectively the same operation. The rotation angle is randomly sampled in (0, 2π), where the step size is 2π/10. Such rotation is also reflected in SPE by adding the rotation angle θ to help the model learn the horizontal cyclicity of panoramas. Later, the translated images 𝐲̅^(0) and 𝐲̂^(1) from the generator with 𝐱 and 𝐱′, respectively, are blended together, after rotating back by -θ for 𝐲̂^(1) of course, to generate the final ensemble output 𝐲̂:

𝐲̂ = ( 𝐲̂^(0) + 𝐲̂^(1)′ ) / 2

where 𝐲̂^(1)′ indicates the -θ rotated version of 𝐲̂^(1). Thus, the result 𝐲̂ has a smoother boundary than the results predicted alone, effectively mitigating discontinuous edge effects.

3.3 LOSS FUNCTIONS

Adversarial loss. We minimize the distribution discrepancy between two different features (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Mirza & Osindero, 2014) via an adversarial loss. We adopt this to learn the translated image 𝐲̂=𝒢(τ(ℰ_c(𝐱,Θ_ERP),𝐬)) and the image 𝐱 from 𝒳 to have an indistinguishable distribution to preserve panoramic contents, defined as:

ℒ_GAN = 𝔼_{𝐱∼𝒳}[ log(1 - 𝒟(𝐲̂)) ] + 𝔼_{𝐲∼𝒴}[ log 𝒟(𝐲) ],

with the R1 regularization (Mescheder et al., 2018) to enhance training stability. To consider the panoramic distortion-free discrimination using the panorama-to-pinhole conversion f_T, we define an additional adversarial loss as follows:

ℒ_df-GAN = 𝔼_{𝐱∼𝒳}[ log(1 - 𝒟( f_T(𝐲̂) )) ] + 𝔼_{𝐲∼𝒴}[ log 𝒟(𝐲) ].

Content loss. To maintain the content between the source image 𝐱 and translated image 𝐲̂, we exploit the spatially-correlative loss (Zheng et al., 2021) to define a content loss, with an augmented source 𝐱_aug. To get 𝐱_aug, we apply structure-preserving transformations to 𝐱. This helps preserve the structure and learn the spatially-correlative map (Zheng et al., 2021) based on a patch-wise infoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018), since it captures the domain-invariant structure representation. Denoting 𝐯̂ as the spatially-correlative map of the query patch from 𝐜^{𝐲̂}=ℰ_c(𝐲̂, Θ_ERP), we pick the pseudo-positive patch sample 𝐯⁺ from 𝐜^𝐱=ℰ_c(𝐱,Θ_ERP) at the same position of the query patch 𝐯̂, and the negative patches 𝐯⁻ from the other positions of 𝐜_{aug}^𝐱 and 𝐜^𝐱, except for the position of query patches 𝐯̂. We first define a score function ℓ(⋅) at the l-th convolution layer in ℰ_c:

ℓ(𝐯̂, 𝐯⁺, 𝐯⁻) = -log[ exp(𝐯̂·𝐯⁺ / τ) / ( exp(𝐯̂·𝐯⁺ / τ) + ∑_{s∈S\s} exp(𝐯̂·𝐯⁻^s / τ) ) ],

where τ is a temperature parameter. Then, the overall content loss function is defined as follows:

ℒ_NCE^{cont} = 𝔼_{𝐱∼𝒳} ∑_l ∑_s ℓ( 𝐯̂_l^s, 𝐯⁺_l^s, 𝐯⁻_l^{S\s} ),

where the index s ∈ {1,2,...,S_l} and S is the set of patches in each l-th layer, and S\s indicates the indices except s.

Image reconstruction loss. We enhance the disentanglement between content and style such that our 𝒢 can reconstruct an image for domain ℘. Specifically, 𝐲 is fed into content encoder ℰ_c and style encoder ℰ_s to obtain a content feature map 𝐜^𝐲=ℰ_c(𝐲, Θ_∅) and a style code 𝐬^𝐲=ℰ_s(𝐲, Θ_∅). We then compare the reconstructed image 𝒢(τ(𝐜^𝐲, 𝐬^𝐲)) with y as follows:

ℒ_recon^{img} = 𝔼_{𝐲∼𝒴}[ || 𝒢(τ(𝐜^𝐲, 𝐬^𝐲)) - 𝐲 ||_1 ].

Style reconstruction loss. In order to better learn disentangled representation, we compute an L1 loss between the style code from the translated image and the input panorama,

ℒ_ref-recon^{sty} = 𝔼_{𝐱∼𝒳}[ || ℰ_s(𝐲̂, Θ_ERP) - ℰ_s(𝐱, Θ_ERP) ||_1 ].

We also define a style reconstruction loss to reconstruct the style code s, which is used to generate 𝐲̂. Note that the style code s is randomly sampled from a Gaussian distribution, not extracted from an image.

ℒ_rand-recon^{sty} = 𝔼_{𝐱∼𝒳, 𝐲∼𝒴}[ || ℰ_s(𝐲̂, Θ_ERP) - 𝐬 ||_1 ].

3.4 TRAINING STRATEGY

Stage I: Panorama reconstruction. Since there is no publicly available large-scale outdoor panorama data under various weather or season conditions, we cannot use panoramas as a style reference. In addition, to share the same embedding space for content and style, the network must be able to process both pinhole images and panoramas simultaneously.

For the stable training of Pano-I2I, the training procedure is split into two stages corresponding to different objectives. In Stage I, we pre-train the content and style encoders ℰ_{c,s}, transformer τ, generator 𝒢, and discriminator 𝒟 using the panorama dataset only. Given a panorama, the parameters of our network are optimized to reconstruct the original with adversarial and content losses, and a style reconstruction loss. As the network learns to reconstruct the input itself, we use the style feature represented by the style encoder instead of a random style code. For ℒ_GAN in Stage I, the original discriminator receives 𝐱 instead of 𝐲 as an input. The total objective in Stage I is as follows:

ℒ_StageI = ℒ_GAN + λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont} + λ_sty ℒ_ref-recon^{sty},

where λ_{*} denotes balancing hyperparameters that control the importance of each loss.

Stage II: Panoramic I2I guided by pinhole image. In Stage II, the whole network is fully trained with a robust initialization from Stage I. Compared to Stage I, both panorama and pinhole datasets are used in this stage. Concretely, the main differences are that; (1) the original discrimination is combined with our distortion-free discrimination as a weighted sum, (2) the style code is sampled from a Gaussian distribution to translate the panorama, (3) the panoramic rotation-based augmentation and its ensemble technique are leveraged to enhance the generation quality. Therefore, the total objective in Stage II is defined as:

ℒ_StageII = λ_df-GAN ℒ_df-GAN + (1 - λ_df-GAN) ℒ_GAN + λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont} + λ_sty ℒ_rand-recon^{sty} + λ_recon ℒ_recon^{img}.

Notice that all coefficients for the losses are set to 1, except for λ_NCE^{cont}, which is set to 15, and λ_df-GAN is set to 0.8 for Stage II. Those coefficients were commonly used in all training datasets.

4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

Datasets. We conduct experiments on the panorama dataset, StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018), as the source domain, and standard street-view datasets for I2I, INIT (Shen et al., 2019) and Dark Zurich (Sakaridis et al., 2019), as the target domain. StreetLearn provides 360° outdoor 56k panoramas taken from Google Street View. Although INIT consists of four conditions (sunny, night, rainy, and cloudy), we use two conditions, night and rainy, since the condition of StreetLearn is captured during the daytime, which includes sunny and cloudy scenes. We use Batch1 of the INIT dataset, a total of 62k images for the four conditions. Dark Zurich has three conditions (daytime, night, and twilight), a total of 8779 images, and we use night and twilight.

Metrics. For quantitative comparison, we report the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) metric (Heusel et al., 2017) to evaluate style relevance, and the structural similarity (SSIM) index metric (Wang et al., 2004) to evaluate panoramic content preservation. Considering that the structure of outputs tends to become pinhole-like in panoramic I2I tasks, we measure the FID metric after applying a panorama-to-pinhole projection (f_T) for a randomly chosen horizontal angle θ and a fixed vertical angle ϕ as 0 with a fixed FoV of 90°, for a consistent viewpoint with the target images. Notice that the SSIM shows the degree of content preservation because it measures the structural similarity between the original panorama and the translated panorama based on luminance, contrast, and structure.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on StreetLearn dataset (day) to INIT dataset (night, rainy): (top to bottom) day → night, and day → rainy results. Among the methods, Pano-I2I (ours) preserves object details well and shows realistic results.

Table 1: Quantitative evaluation on the translated panoramas from StreetLearn to INIT.
[Table content preserved as in source]
Table 2: Quantitative evaluation on the translated panoramas from StreetLearn to Dark Zurich.
[Table content preserved as in source]

Comparison methods. We compare our approach against state-of-the-art I2I methods, including MGUIT (Jeong et al., 2021) and InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), CUT (Park et al., 2020a), and FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). We train them with the same datasets as ours. Since MGUIT and InstaFormer require bounding box annotations to train their models, we exploit a pre-trained YOLOv5 (Jocher et al., 2021) model to generate pseudo bounding box annotations.

4.2 IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL

We formulate the proposed method with vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) inspired by InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), but without instance-level approaches due to the absence of ground-truth bounding box annotations. We design our content and style encoders, a transformer encoder, the generator, and the discriminator for our GAN losses based on (Kim et al., 2022), where all modules are learned from scratch.

Qualitative evaluation. In Fig. 4, we qualitatively compare our method with other I2I methods. We observe that all the other methods (Park et al., 2020a; Jiang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) fail to synthesize reasonable panoramic results and show obvious inconsistent output regarding either structure or style in an image. Moreover, previous methods incorrectly recognize structural discrepancies between source and target domains as style differences, indicating failed translation results that change to look like pinhole images. Surprisingly, in the case of ‘day → night’, all existing methods fail to preserve the objectness of elements like a car or building. We definitively conjecture that they cannot efficiently deal with the large domain gap in ‘day → night,’ thus naively learning to follow the target distribution without considering the context from the source. By comparison, our method shows the overall best performance in visual quality, preserving panoramic content, and structural- and style-consistency. In particular, we observe the powerful ability of our discrimination design to learn distortion-tolerated features.

Quantitative evaluation. Tab. 1 and Tab. 2 show the quantitative comparison in terms of FID (Heusel et al., 2017) and SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) index metrics. Our method consistently and decisively outperforms all competitive methods in all metrics, demonstrating that Pano-I2I successfully captures the style of the target domain while preserving the panoramic contents. Notably, our approach exhibits significant improvements in terms of SSIM. In contrast, previous methods perform poorly in terms of SSIM compared to our results, which is also evident from the qualitative results presented in Fig. 4.

User study. We conducted a user study to compare the subjective quality. We randomly select 10 images for each task (day → night, rainy) on the INIT dataset, and let 60 users sort all the methods regarding “overall image quality”, “content preservation from the source”, and “style relevance with the target, considering the context from the source”. As seen in Fig. 5, our method has a clear and decisive advantage on every task.

4.4 ABLATION STUDY

In Tab. 3, we show quantitative results for the ablation study on the day → night task on the INIT dataset. In particular, we analyze the effectiveness of our 1) distortion-free discrimination, 2) ensemble technique, 3) two-stage learning scheme, and 4) spherical positional embedding (SPE) and deformable convolution. We observe that all the techniques and components contribute to performance improvement in terms of style relevance and content preservation, and the impact of distortion-free discrimination is substantially and critically effective in handling geometric deformation.

5 CONCLUSION

In this paper, we introduce a novel experimental protocol and a dedicated, powerful model for panoramic Image-to-Image Translation that effectively considers 1) the unique structural properties of panoramic images and 2) the notable lack of outdoor panoramic scene datasets. To this end, we design our model to take panoramas as the source, and abundantly available pinhole images with diverse conditions as the target, raising the large geometric variance between the source and target domains as a major challenging point. To definitively mitigate these issues, we propose distortion-aware panoramic modeling techniques and novel distortion-free discriminators to stabilize adversarial learning. Additionally, exploiting the cyclic property of panoramas, we propose to rotate and fuse the synthesized panoramas, resulting in a panorama output with a perfectly continuous view. We conclusively demonstrate the success of our method in translating highly realistic images in several benchmarks and look forward to future works that use our proposed experimental paradigm for panoramic image translation with non-pinhole camera inputs using diverse sets of pinhole image datasets, enabling a new wave of practical applications in immersive technology and autonomous systems.

Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images

Abstract
This work addresses the task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I). The task is to learn a mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains. Two main challenges exist. First, panoramas have geometric distortions that are problematic for methods designed for a narrow field-of-view. Second, panoramic datasets covering diverse conditions for training are limited. To address these, we propose an I2I model that uses readily obtainable pinhole images as the target domain. We introduce a versatile encoder and distortion-free discrimination that bridges the domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by encoding them in a consolidated structure. This allows learning style mappings while overcoming geometric differences. We also design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to address discontinuities at panorama edges. Experiments verify that the framework translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by referring to the style of pinhole data. The method shows results in maintaining structural coherence and rotation equivariance, surpassing existing I2I methods in qualitative and quantitative results.

1 INTRODUCTION
Image-to-image translation (I2I) aims to modify an input image to align with the style of a target domain while preserving the original content from the source domain (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). Existing I2I has been used to synthesize pinhole images with a narrow field-of-view (FoV).

Panoramic 360° cameras have become more common (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike pinhole images, panoramic images capture the entire surroundings with a 360°×180° FoV.

Applying conventional I2I methods for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can distort their geometric properties. These methods assume the source and target domains differ only in style, not in inherent geometric distortion. Projecting panoramas into pinhole images is computationally costly, and sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. The discontinuity problem at panorama edges requires specific modeling, as in other tasks like panorama depth estimation and segmentation (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).

Another challenge is the absence of sufficient panorama datasets covering diverse conditions. For I2I, panoramas under diverse conditions are needed, but they are limited. Panoramic images for Street View services are usually taken during the day (Mirowski et al., 2018). Instead of constructing a new dataset, we leverage existing pinhole image datasets with various conditions as style guidance. We present failure cases of an existing approach, FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). The result shows a collapsed structure with a pinhole-like structure and structural- and style-discontinuity at edges. This indicates that naively applying existing I2I methods has limited capacity to deal with the large domain gap between panoramas and pinhole images.

We seek to expand the applicability of I2I to panoramic images by employing existing pinhole image datasets as the style domain, termed Unpaired Panoramic Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images (Pano-I2I).

To address geometric deformation, we adopt deformable convolutions (Zhu et al., 2019) to our encoders, with different offsets for panoramas and pinhole images. We propose a distortion-free discrimination that attenuates geometric differences. We also adopt panoramic rotation augmentation and ensemble techniques to solve discontinuity problems at edges.

We validate the approach on the panorama dataset StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018) and pinhole datasets (Shen et al., 2019; Sakaridis et al., 2019). The proposed method outperforms existing methods across various target conditions.

2 RELATED WORK
Image-to-image translation. Early works required paired datasets (Isola et al., 2017). Subsequent works enabled unpaired training (Zhu et al., 2017). Some works enable multimodal learning (Huang et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018a; 2020), multi-domain learning (Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Wu et al., 2019), translating across domains with large discrepancies (Amodio & Krishnaswamy, 2019; Yang et al., 2022), and instance-aware learning (Bhattacharjee et al., 2020; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022). However, existing methods are restrictive to specific source-target pairs. Methods like (Lee et al., 2018a; Huang et al., 2018b) translated images by reintegrating disentangled content and style but focused on object figuration as content. They are limited in handling geometric variations between domains and rotational equivalence for panoramas. Several works have adopted vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to image generation (Lee et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022a). InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022) proposed using a transformer for I2I. Recently, diffusion models have been employed in image editing (Ye et al., 2023; Zhang & Agrawala, 2023; Brooks et al., 2023; Mou et al., 2023). However, those methods are still limited in considering wide geometric discrepancies between source (panoramas) and target (pinhole) domains and rotation equivariance of panoramas.

Panoramic image modeling. Panoramic images provide a wide FoV. Challenges have led to unique architectures or modeling techniques, e.g., for depth estimation (Tateno et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2020; Pintore et al., 2021; Peng & Zhang, 2023), perception (Yang et al., 2021a; Orhan & Bastanlar, 2022; Zheng et al., 2023), and aerial-to-panorama generation (Lu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022). A common practice is to project an image into other formats like equirectangular or cubemap (Cheng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019). Some works combine both projections (Jiang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2020). However, they may not fully consider properties like edge connection and geometric distortion. Several works leverage narrow FoV projected images (Lee et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2018; de La Garanderie et al., 2018), but they require many projected images. To deal with discontinuity and distortion, recent works introduce modeling in the spherical domain (Esteves et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2018). Leveraging transformer architecture in 360° image modeling can reduce distortions (Cho et al., 2022). Recent approaches (Ranftl et al., 2021; Rey-Area et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022) used transformers for global structural consistency.

3 METHODOLOGY
3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION
We use the panoramic domain as a source representing content structures and the pinhole domain as a target style. Formally, given a panorama of the source domain 𝒳, Pano-I2I learns a mapping function that translates its style into target pinhole domain ℘ while retaining the content and structure. Unlike previous I2I methods (Zhu et al., 2017; Park et al., 2020a;b; Jiang et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) where both domains are pinhole images, our setting varies in both style and structure; the source is panoramas with wide FoV captured in daytime, and the target is pinhole images in diverse conditions with narrow FoV. Existing I2I methods fail to preserve panoramic structure because their feature disentanglements cannot effectively separate style from target content when both geometric and style differences exist. We observed that 1) outputs are pinhole-like, and 2) pinhole image-based network design causes discontinuity at boundaries and low visual fidelity.

3.2 ARCHITECTURE DESIGN
Overall architecture. The method consists of a shared content encoder ℰ_c, a shared style encoder ℰ_s, a transformer encoder τ to mix style and content through AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers, a shared generator 𝒢, and a discriminator 𝒟. The transformer encoder block has a multi-head self-attention layer and a feed-forward MLP with GELU (Vaswani et al., 2017).

To translate an image x in source domain 𝒳 to target domain ℘, we extract a content feature map c^x∈ℝ^{h×w×l_c} by the content encoder from x, with height h, width w, and l_c content channels. We receive a random latent code s∈ℝ^{1×1×l_s} from Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0,𝐈)∈ℝ^{l_s}, which controls the style via affine parameters for AdaIN layers. The output image is ŷ=𝒢(τ(c^x,s)).

Panoramic modeling in encoders. Latent spaces are shared to embed domain-invariant content or style features (Lee et al., 2018a). The geometric distortion gap from different FoVs prevents encoders from understanding structural information. We use a deformable convolution layer (Zhu et al., 2019) at the beginning of the content and style encoders by adjusting the offset reflecting image types. Given a panorama, the deformable convolution layer is applied with an equirectangular plane (ERP) offset (Yun et al., 2022), Θ_ERP, that considers panoramic geometry. We project a tangential local patch 𝒫 of a 3D-Cartesian domain into ERP to obtain the corresponding ERP offset, Θ_ERP, as follows:
Θ_ERP(θ,φ)=f_SPH→ERP(f_3D→SPH(𝒫×R(θ,φ)/‖𝒫×R(θ,φ)‖_2)),
where R(θ,φ) is the rotation matrix with longitude θ∈[0,2π] and latitude φ∈[0,π], f_SPH→ERP converts from spherical to ERP domain, and f_3D→SPH converts from 3D-Cartesian to spherical domain, as in PAVER (Yun et al., 2022). We project 𝒫 to a spherical patch on a unit sphere S^2, aligning the patch center to (θ,φ)∈S^2. The number of 𝒫 is H×W with stride 1 and paddings. The center of 𝒫 corresponds to the kernel center. We obtain relative spherical coordinates from the center point and all discrete locations in 𝒫. These positions are projected to the ERP domain as offset points. We compute 2D-offset points Θ_ERP∈ℝ^{2×H×Ŵ×ker_h×ker_w} for each kernel location, fixed for training and test.

Deformable convolution with fixed offsets can encode panoramic structure. We repurpose it as an adapter to shared encoders to handle panorama source and pinhole target simultaneously by different offsets. For pinhole image encoding, Θ_ERP is replaced with zero-offset Θ_∅.

Panoramic modeling in the translator. After extracting content features, we patchify them, add positional embedding (PE) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Rahaman et al., 2019), and process through the generator. Center coordinates of patchified grids are (i_p,j_p) for the p-th patch. Inputs {x, ȳ}—panorama and pinhole image—have different structural properties, so we adopt sinusoidal PE in two ways: 2D PE and spherical PE (SPE).

We define fixed PE as γ(·), a sinusoidal mapping into ℝ^{2K}:
γ(a)={(sin(2^{k-1}πa),cos(2^{k-1}πa))}, k∈{1,2,...,K}
for input scalar a. 2D PE for pinhole images is:
PE=concat(γ(i_p),γ(j_p)).

Following (Chen et al., 2022), we define spherical positional embedding for center position (i_p,j_p) of each grid as:
SPE=concat(γ(θ),γ(φ)), where θ=(2i_p/h-1)π, φ=(2j_p/w-1)π/2,
where each patch has width w and height h. SPE provides cyclic spatial guidance and relative spatial relationship, helping maintain rotational equivariance and structural continuity at boundaries. This PE is added to patch-embedded tokens and processed in transformer encoders with AdaIN.

Distortion-free discrimination. Source and target domains have distinct geometric structure and style. Directly applying existing I2I methods causes structural collapse. We speculate this stems from breaking the balance of discriminators. The discriminator loss typically learns to distinguish real data y and fake data ŷ, focusing on style difference. In our task, there is an additional large deformation gap and FoV difference between y and ŷ that confuses what to discriminate.

To address this, we present distortion-free discrimination. The idea is to transform a randomly selected region of a panorama into a pinhole image while maintaining the FoV. We adopt a panorama-to-pinhole image conversion f_T by a rectilinear projection (Lee et al., 2018b). To obtain a narrow FoV image with f_T, we first select a viewpoint in longitude and latitude coordinates (θ, φ) randomly from [0,2π] and [0,π], and extract a narrow FoV region from the panorama by a differentiable projection function f_T. We adopt a weighted sum of the original discrimination and the proposed discrimination to encourage learning robust features from both full-panoramas and pinhole-like converted panoramas.

Sphere-based rotation augmentation and ensemble. We introduce panoramic rotation-based augmentation. Given a panorama x, a rotated image x′ is generated by horizontally rotating angle θ. We implement this by rolling images in ERP space. The rotation angle is randomly sampled in (0, 2π) with step size 2π/10. This rotation is reflected in SPE by adding θ to help learn horizontal cyclicity. Translated images ŷ^{(0)} and ŷ^{(1)} from the generator with x and x′ are blended after rotating ŷ^{(1)} back by -θ to generate the final ensemble output ŷ:
ŷ=(ŷ^{(0)}+ŷ^{(1)′})/2
where ŷ^{(1)′} is the -θ rotated version of ŷ^{(1)}. The result ŷ has a smoother boundary, mitigating discontinuous edge effects.

3.3 LOSS FUNCTIONS
Adversarial loss. We minimize distribution discrepancy by adversarial loss (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Mirza & Osindero, 2014). We adopt this to learn the translated image ŷ=𝒢(τ(ℰ_c(x,Θ_ERP),s)) and image x from 𝒳 to have indistinguishable distribution to preserve panoramic contents:
ℒ_GAN=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[log(1-𝒟(ŷ))]+𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[log𝒟(y)],
with R1 regularization (Mescheder et al., 2018). For distortion-free discrimination using panorama-to-pinhole conversion f_T, we define additional adversarial loss:
ℒ_df-GAN=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[log(1-𝒟(f_T(ŷ)))]+𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[log𝒟(y)].

Content loss. To maintain content between source image x and translated image ŷ, we use spatially-correlative loss (Zheng et al., 2021) to define a content loss, with an augmented source x_aug. We apply structure-preserving transformations to x to get x_aug. This helps preserve structure and learn the spatially-correlative map based on patchwise infoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018). Denoting v̂ as spatially-correlative map of the query patch from c^{ŷ}=ℰ_c(ŷ,Θ_ERP), we pick pseudo-positive patch sample v⁺ from c^x=ℰ_c(x,Θ_ERP) at the same position as v̂, and negative patches v⁻ from other positions of c_{aug}^x and c^x, except the query patch positions. We define a score function ℓ(·) at the l-th convolution layer in ℰ_c:
ℓ(v̂,v⁺,v⁻)=-log[exp(v̂·v⁺/τ) / (exp(v̂·v⁺/τ)+∑_{s∈S\s} exp(v̂·v⁻^s/τ))],
where τ is a temperature parameter. The overall content loss is:
ℒ_NCE^{cont}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}∑_l∑_s ℓ(v̂_l^s, v⁺_l^s, v⁻_l^{S\s}),
where s∈{1,2,...,S_l} and S is a set of patches in each l-th layer, and S\s indicates indices except s.

Image reconstruction loss. To enhance disentanglement between content and style, we reconstruct an image for domain ℘. Specifically, y is fed into ℰ_c and ℰ_s to get content feature map c^y=ℰ_c(y,Θ_∅) and style code s^y=ℰ_s(y,Θ_∅). We compare reconstructed image 𝒢(τ(c^y,s^y)) with y:
ℒ_recon^{img}=𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[‖𝒢(τ(c^y,s^y))-y‖_1].

Style reconstruction loss. To better learn disentangled representation, we compute L1 loss between style code from translated image and input panorama,
ℒ_ref-recon^{sty}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[‖ℰ_s(ŷ,Θ_ERP)-ℰ_s(x,Θ_ERP)‖_1].
We also define style reconstruction loss to reconstruct style code s used to generate ŷ, where s is randomly sampled from Gaussian distribution:
ℒ_rand-recon^{sty}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳,y∼𝒴}[‖ℰ_s(ŷ,Θ_ERP)-s‖_1].

3.4 TRAINING STRATEGY
Stage I: Panorama reconstruction. There is no publicly available large-scale outdoor panorama data under various conditions. To share the same embedding space, the network must process pinhole images and panoramas simultaneously.

Training is split into two stages. In Stage I, we pretrain ℰ_c,s, τ, 𝒢, and 𝒟 using the panorama dataset only. Given a panorama, parameters are optimized to reconstruct the original with adversarial, content, and style reconstruction losses. For ℒ_GAN in Stage I, the discriminator receives x instead of y. The total objective in Stage I is:
ℒ_StageI=ℒ_GAN+λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont}+λ_sty ℒ_ref-recon^{sty},
where λ_{*} are balancing hyperparameters.

Stage II: Panoramic I2I guided by pinhole image. In Stage II, the whole network is fully trained with initialization from Stage I. Panorama and pinhole datasets are used. Differences: (1) original discrimination is combined with distortion-free discrimination as a weighted sum, (2) style code is sampled from Gaussian distribution, (3) panoramic rotation-based augmentation and ensemble are used. The total objective in Stage II is:
ℒ_StageII=λ_df-GAN ℒ_df-GAN+(1-λ_df-GAN)ℒ_GAN+λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont}+λ_sty ℒ_rand-recon^{sty}+λ_recon ℒ_recon^{img}.
All coefficients are set to 1, except λ_NCE^{cont}=15, and λ_df-GAN=0.8 for Stage II.

4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Datasets. We use the panorama dataset StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018) as source, and pinhole datasets INIT (Shen et al., 2019) and Dark Zurich (Sakaridis et al., 2019) as target. StreetLearn has 56k outdoor panoramas. INIT has four conditions; we use night and rainy. We use Batch1 of INIT, 62k images. Dark Zurich has three conditions; we use night and twilight, 8779 images.

Metrics. We report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) (Heusel et al., 2017) for style relevance, and structural similarity (SSIM) index (Wang et al., 2004) for content preservation. Since outputs can become pinhole-like, we measure FID after applying panorama-to-pinhole projection f_T for randomly chosen horizontal angle θ and fixed vertical angle φ=0 with FoV=90°, for consistent viewpoint. SSIM measures structural similarity between original and translated panorama.

Comparison methods. We compare against MGUIT (Jeong et al., 2021), InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), CUT (Park et al., 2020a), and FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). We train them with the same datasets. MGUIT and InstaFormer require bounding box annotations; we use a pretrained YOLOv5 (Jocher et al., 2021) model to generate pseudo annotations.

4.2 IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL
We formulate the method with vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) inspired by InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), but without instance-level approaches due to absence of groundtruth bounding boxes. We design content and style encoders, transformer encoder, generator, and discriminator based on (Kim et al., 2022), all learned from scratch.

Qualitative evaluation. We qualitatively compare methods. Other methods fail to synthesize reasonable panoramic results and show inconsistent structure or style. They recognize structural discrepancies as style differences, resulting in pinhole-like translation. In 'day→night', all existing methods fail to preserve objectness like cars or buildings. We conjecture they cannot efficiently deal with the large domain gap. Our method shows the best performance in visual quality, content preservation, and consistency. We observe the ability of our discrimination design to learn distortion-tolerated features.

Quantitative evaluation. Tables show quantitative comparison in FID and SSIM. Our method consistently outperforms others in all metrics, indicating successful style capture and content preservation. Our approach shows significant improvements in SSIM. Previous methods perform poorly in SSIM.

User study. We conducted a user study. We randomly select 10 images for each task (day→night, rainy) on INIT, and let 60 users sort methods regarding "overall image quality", "content preservation", and "style relevance". Our method has a clear advantage on every task.

4.4 ABLATION STUDY
We show quantitative results for ablation study on day→night task on INIT dataset. We analyze effectiveness of 1) distortion-free discrimination, 2) ensemble technique, 3) two-stage learning scheme, and 4) spherical positional embedding (SPE) and deformable convolution. All techniques contribute to performance improvement in style relevance and content preservation. The impact of distortion-free discrimination is substantially effective in handling geometric deformation.

5 CONCLUSION
We introduce an experimental protocol and a model for panoramic Image-to-Image Translation that considers 1) structural properties of panoramic images and 2) lack of outdoor panoramic scene datasets. We design the model to take panoramas as source, and pinhole images with diverse conditions as target, addressing the large geometric variance. To mitigate issues, we propose distortion-aware panoramic modeling techniques and distortion-free discriminators. We also propose to rotate and fuse synthesized panoramas, resulting in continuous view. We demonstrate success in translating realistic images in benchmarks.

Unpaired Panoramic Image-to-Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images

Abstract
This work addresses the task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I). The task is to learn a mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains. Two main challenges exist. First, panoramas have geometric distortions that are problematic for methods designed for a narrow field-of-view. Second, panoramic datasets covering diverse conditions for training are limited. To address these, we propose an I2I model that uses readily obtainable pinhole images as the target domain. We introduce a versatile encoder and distortion-free discrimination that bridges the domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by encoding them in a consolidated structure. This allows learning style mappings while overcoming geometric differences. We also design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to address discontinuities at panorama edges. Experiments verify that the framework translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by referring to the style of pinhole data. The method shows results in maintaining structural coherence and rotation equivariance, surpassing existing I2I methods in qualitative and quantitative results.

1 INTRODUCTION
Image-to-image translation (I2I) aims to modify an input image to align with the style of a target domain while preserving the original content from the source domain (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). Existing I2I has been used to synthesize pinhole images with a narrow field-of-view (FoV).

Panoramic 360° cameras have become more common (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike pinhole images, panoramic images capture the entire surroundings with a 360°×180° FoV.

Applying conventional I2I methods for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can distort their geometric properties. These methods assume the source and target domains differ only in style, not in inherent geometric distortion. Projecting panoramas into pinhole images is computationally costly, and sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. The discontinuity problem at panorama edges requires specific modeling, as in other tasks like panorama depth estimation and segmentation (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).

Another challenge is the absence of sufficient panorama datasets covering diverse conditions. For I2I, panoramas under diverse conditions are needed, but they are limited. Panoramic images for Street View services are usually taken during the day (Mirowski et al., 2018). Instead of constructing a new dataset, we leverage existing pinhole image datasets with various conditions as style guidance. We present failure cases of an existing approach, FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). The result shows a collapsed structure with a pinhole-like structure and structural- and style-discontinuity at edges. This indicates that naively applying existing I2I methods has limited capacity to deal with the large domain gap between panoramas and pinhole images.

We seek to expand the applicability of I2I to panoramic images by employing existing pinhole image datasets as the style domain, termed Unpaired Panoramic Image Translation Leveraging Pinhole Images (Pano-I2I).

To address geometric deformation, we adopt deformable convolutions (Zhu et al., 2019) to our encoders, with different offsets for panoramas and pinhole images. We propose a distortion-free discrimination that attenuates geometric differences. We also adopt panoramic rotation augmentation and ensemble techniques to solve discontinuity problems at edges.

We validate the approach on the panorama dataset StreetLearn (Mirowski et al., 2018) and pinhole datasets (Shen et al., 2019; Sakaridis et al., 2019). The proposed method outperforms existing methods across various target conditions.

2 RELATED WORK
Image-to-image translation. Early works required paired datasets (Isola et al., 2017). Subsequent works enabled unpaired training (Zhu et al., 2017). Some works enable multimodal learning (Huang et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018a; 2020), multi-domain learning (Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Wu et al., 2019), translating across domains with large discrepancies (Amodio & Krishnaswamy, 2019; Yang et al., 2022), and instance-aware learning (Bhattacharjee et al., 2020; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022). However, existing methods are restrictive to specific source-target pairs. Methods like (Lee et al., 2018a; Huang et al., 2018b) translated images by reintegrating disentangled content and style but focused on object figuration as content. They are limited in handling geometric variations between domains and rotational equivalence for panoramas. Several works have adopted vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to image generation (Lee et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022a). InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022) proposed using a transformer for I2I. Recently, diffusion models have been employed in image editing (Ye et al., 2023; Zhang & Agrawala, 2023; Brooks et al., 2023; Mou et al., 2023). However, those methods are still limited in considering wide geometric discrepancies between source (panoramas) and target (pinhole) domains and rotation equivariance of panoramas.

Panoramic image modeling. Panoramic images provide a wide FoV. Challenges have led to unique architectures or modeling techniques, e.g., for depth estimation (Tateno et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2020; Pintore et al., 2021; Peng & Zhang, 2023), perception (Yang et al., 2021a; Orhan & Bastanlar, 2022; Zheng et al., 2023), and aerial-to-panorama generation (Lu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022). A common practice is to project an image into other formats like equirectangular or cubemap (Cheng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019). Some works combine both projections (Jiang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2020). However, they may not fully consider properties like edge connection and geometric distortion. Several works leverage narrow FoV projected images (Lee et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2018; de La Garanderie et al., 2018), but they require many projected images. To deal with discontinuity and distortion, recent works introduce modeling in the spherical domain (Esteves et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2018). Leveraging transformer architecture in 360° image modeling can reduce distortions (Cho et al., 2022). Recent approaches (Ranftl et al., 2021; Rey-Area et al., 2022; Yun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022) used transformers for global structural consistency.

3 METHODOLOGY
3.1 PROBLEM DEFINITION
We use the panoramic domain as a source representing content structures and the pinhole domain as a target style. Formally, given a panorama of the source domain 𝒳, Pano-I2I learns a mapping function that translates its style into target pinhole domain ℘ while retaining the content and structure. Unlike previous I2I methods (Zhu et al., 2017; Park et al., 2020a;b; Jiang et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) where both domains are pinhole images, our setting varies in both style and structure; the source is panoramas with wide FoV captured in daytime, and the target is pinhole images in diverse conditions with narrow FoV. Existing I2I methods fail to preserve panoramic structure because their feature disentanglements cannot effectively separate style from target content when both geometric and style differences exist. We observed that 1) outputs are pinhole-like, and 2) pinhole image-based network design causes discontinuity at boundaries and low visual fidelity.

3.2 ARCHITECTURE DESIGN
Overall architecture. The method consists of a shared content encoder ℰ_c, a shared style encoder ℰ_s, a transformer encoder τ to mix style and content through AdaIN (Huang & Belongie, 2017) layers, a shared generator 𝒢, and a discriminator 𝒟. The transformer encoder block has a multi-head self-attention layer and a feed-forward MLP with GELU (Vaswani et al., 2017).

To translate an image x in source domain 𝒳 to target domain ℘, we extract a content feature map c^x∈ℝ^{h×w×l_c} by the content encoder from x, with height h, width w, and l_c content channels. We receive a random latent code s∈ℝ^{1×1×l_s} from Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0,𝐈)∈ℝ^{l_s}, which controls the style via affine parameters for AdaIN layers. The output image is ŷ=𝒢(τ(c^x,s)).

Panoramic modeling in encoders. Latent spaces are shared to embed domain-invariant content or style features (Lee et al., 2018a). The geometric distortion gap from different FoVs prevents encoders from understanding structural information. We use a deformable convolution layer (Zhu et al., 2019) at the beginning of the content and style encoders by adjusting the offset reflecting image types. Given a panorama, the deformable convolution layer is applied with an equirectangular plane (ERP) offset (Yun et al., 2022), Θ_ERP, that considers panoramic geometry. We project a tangential local patch 𝒫 of a 3D-Cartesian domain into ERP to obtain the corresponding ERP offset, Θ_ERP, as follows:
Θ_ERP(θ,φ)=f_SPH→ERP(f_3D→SPH(𝒫×R(θ,φ)/‖𝒫×R(θ,φ)‖_2)),
where R(θ,φ) is the rotation matrix with longitude θ∈[0,2π] and latitude φ∈[0,π], f_SPH→ERP converts from spherical to ERP domain, and f_3D→SPH converts from 3D-Cartesian to spherical domain, as in PAVER (Yun et al., 2022). We project 𝒫 to a spherical patch on a unit sphere S^2, aligning the patch center to (θ,φ)∈S^2. The number of 𝒫 is H×W with stride 1 and paddings. The center of 𝒫 corresponds to the kernel center. We obtain relative spherical coordinates from the center point and all discrete locations in 𝒫. These positions are projected to the ERP domain as offset points. We compute 2D-offset points Θ_ERP∈ℝ^{2×H×Ŵ×ker_h×ker_w} for each kernel location, fixed for training and test.

Deformable convolution with fixed offsets can encode panoramic structure. We repurpose it as an adapter to shared encoders to handle panorama source and pinhole target simultaneously by different offsets. For pinhole image encoding, Θ_ERP is replaced with zero-offset Θ_∅.

Panoramic modeling in the translator. After extracting content features, we patchify them, add positional embedding (PE) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Rahaman et al., 2019), and process through the generator. Center coordinates of patchified grids are (i_p,j_p) for the p-th patch. Inputs {x, ȳ}—panorama and pinhole image—have different structural properties, so we adopt sinusoidal PE in two ways: 2D PE and spherical PE (SPE).

We define fixed PE as γ(·), a sinusoidal mapping into ℝ^{2K}:
γ(a)={(sin(2^{k-1}πa),cos(2^{k-1}πa))}, k∈{1,2,...,K}
for input scalar a. 2D PE for pinhole images is:
PE=concat(γ(i_p),γ(j_p)).

Following (Chen et al., 2022), we define spherical positional embedding for center position (i_p,j_p) of each grid as:
SPE=concat(γ(θ),γ(φ)), where θ=(2i_p/h-1)π, φ=(2j_p/w-1)π/2,
where each patch has width w and height h. SPE provides cyclic spatial guidance and relative spatial relationship, helping maintain rotational equivariance and structural continuity at boundaries. This PE is added to patch-embedded tokens and processed in transformer encoders with AdaIN.

Distortion-free discrimination. Source and target domains have distinct geometric structure and style. Directly applying existing I2I methods causes structural collapse. We speculate this stems from breaking the balance of discriminators. The discriminator loss typically learns to distinguish real data y and fake data ŷ, focusing on style difference. In our task, there is an additional large deformation gap and FoV difference between y and ŷ that confuses what to discriminate.

To address this, we present distortion-free discrimination. The idea is to transform a randomly selected region of a panorama into a pinhole image while maintaining the FoV. We adopt a panorama-to-pinhole image conversion f_T by a rectilinear projection (Lee et al., 2018b). To obtain a narrow FoV image with f_T, we first select a viewpoint in longitude and latitude coordinates (θ, φ) randomly from [0,2π] and [0,π], and extract a narrow FoV region from the panorama by a differentiable projection function f_T. We adopt a weighted sum of the original discrimination and the proposed discrimination to encourage learning robust features from both full-panoramas and pinhole-like converted panoramas.

Sphere-based rotation augmentation and ensemble. We introduce panoramic rotation-based augmentation. Given a panorama x, a rotated image x′ is generated by horizontally rotating angle θ. We implement this by rolling images in ERP space. The rotation angle is randomly sampled in (0, 2π) with step size 2π/10. This rotation is reflected in SPE by adding θ to help learn horizontal cyclicity. Translated images ŷ^{(0)} and ŷ^{(1)} from the generator with x and x′ are blended after rotating ŷ^{(1)} back by -θ to generate the final ensemble output ŷ:
ŷ=(ŷ^{(0)}+ŷ^{(1)′})/2
where ŷ^{(1)′} is the -θ rotated version of ŷ^{(1)}. The result ŷ has a smoother boundary, mitigating discontinuous edge effects.

3.3 LOSS FUNCTIONS
Adversarial loss. We minimize distribution discrepancy by adversarial loss (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Mirza & Osindero, 2014). We adopt this to learn the translated image ŷ=𝒢(τ(ℰ_c(x,Θ_ERP),s)) and image x from 𝒳 to have indistinguishable distribution to preserve panoramic contents:
ℒ_GAN=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[log(1-𝒟(ŷ))]+𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[log𝒟(y)],
with R1 regularization (Mescheder et al., 2018). For distortion-free discrimination using panorama-to-pinhole conversion f_T, we define additional adversarial loss:
ℒ_df-GAN=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[log(1-𝒟(f_T(ŷ)))]+𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[log𝒟(y)].

Content loss. To maintain content between source image x and translated image ŷ, we use spatially-correlative loss (Zheng et al., 2021) to define a content loss, with an augmented source x_aug. We apply structure-preserving transformations to x to get x_aug. This helps preserve structure and learn the spatially-correlative map based on patchwise infoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018). Denoting v̂ as spatially-correlative map of the query patch from c^{ŷ}=ℰ_c(ŷ,Θ_ERP), we pick pseudo-positive patch sample v⁺ from c^x=ℰ_c(x,Θ_ERP) at the same position as v̂, and negative patches v⁻ from other positions of c_{aug}^x and c^x, except the query patch positions. We define a score function ℓ(·) at the l-th convolution layer in ℰ_c:
ℓ(v̂,v⁺,v⁻)=-log[exp(v̂·v⁺/τ) / (exp(v̂·v⁺/τ)+∑_{s∈S\s} exp(v̂·v⁻^s/τ))],
where τ is a temperature parameter. The overall content loss is:
ℒ_NCE^{cont}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}∑_l∑_s ℓ(v̂_l^s, v⁺_l^s, v⁻_l^{S\s}),
where s∈{1,2,...,S_l} and S is a set of patches in each l-th layer, and S\s indicates indices except s.

Image reconstruction loss. To enhance disentanglement between content and style, we reconstruct an image for domain ℘. Specifically, y is fed into ℰ_c and ℰ_s to get content feature map c^y=ℰ_c(y,Θ_∅) and style code s^y=ℰ_s(y,Θ_∅). We compare reconstructed image 𝒢(τ(c^y,s^y)) with y:
ℒ_recon^{img}=𝔼_{y∼𝒴}[‖𝒢(τ(c^y,s^y))-y‖_1].

Style reconstruction loss. To better learn disentangled representation, we compute L1 loss between style code from translated image and input panorama,
ℒ_ref-recon^{sty}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳}[‖ℰ_s(ŷ,Θ_ERP)-ℰ_s(x,Θ_ERP)‖_1].
We also define style reconstruction loss to reconstruct style code s used to generate ŷ, where s is randomly sampled from Gaussian distribution:
ℒ_rand-recon^{sty}=𝔼_{x∼𝒳,y∼𝒴}[‖ℰ_s(ŷ,Θ_ERP)-s‖_1].

3.4 TRAINING STRATEGY
Stage I: Panorama reconstruction. There is no publicly available large-scale outdoor panorama data under various conditions. To share the same embedding space, the network must process pinhole images and panoramas simultaneously.

Training is split into two stages. In Stage I, we pretrain ℰ_c,s, τ, 𝒢, and 𝒟 using the panorama dataset only. The total objective in Stage I is:
ℒ_StageI=ℒ_GAN+λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont}+λ_sty ℒ_ref-recon^{sty},
where λ_{*} are balancing hyperparameters.

Stage II: Panoramic I2I guided by pinhole image. In Stage II, the whole network is fully trained with initialization from Stage I. Panorama and pinhole datasets are used. Differences: (1) original discrimination is combined with distortion-free discrimination as a weighted sum, (2) style code is sampled from Gaussian distribution, (3) panoramic rotation-based augmentation and ensemble are used. The total objective in Stage II is:
ℒ_StageII=λ_df-GAN ℒ_df-GAN+(1-λ_df-GAN)ℒ_GAN+λ_cont ℒ_NCE^{cont}+λ_sty ℒ_rand-recon^{sty}+λ_recon ℒ_recon^{img}.
All coefficients are set to 1, except λ_NCE^{cont}=15, and λ_df-GAN=0.8 for Stage II.

4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

SSIM measures structural similarity between original and translated panorama.

Comparison methods. We compare against MGUIT (Jeong et al., 2021), InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), CUT (Park et al., 2020a), and FSeSim (Zheng et al., 2021). We train them with the same datasets. MGUIT and InstaFormer require bounding box annotations; we use a pretrained YOLOv5 (Jocher et al., 2021) model to generate pseudo annotations.

We formulate the method with vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) inspired by InstaFormer (Kim et al., 2022), but without instance-level approaches due to absence of groundtruth bounding boxes. We conjecture they cannot efficiently deal with the large domain gap. Our method shows the best performance in visual quality, content preservation, and consistency. We observe the ability of our discrimination design to learn distortion-tolerated features.

4.4 ABLATION STUDY
We show quantitative results for ablation study on day→night task on INIT dataset. We analyze effectiveness of 1) distortion-free discrimination, 2) ensemble technique, 3) two-stage learning scheme, and 4) spherical positional embedding (SPE) and deformable convolution. All techniques contribute to performance improvement in style relevance and content preservation. The impact of distortion-free discrimination is substantially effective in handling geometric deformation.

Title: Knowledge Distillation Based on Transformed Teacher Matching

Abstract:
Temperature scaling is a technique that bridges logit matching and probability distribution matching in knowledge distillation (KD).
