Title: Unsupervised Motion Segmentation in One Go: A Smooth Long-Term Model Over a Video

Abstract:
The human visual system possesses a remarkable capacity to watch a video and instantly parse its dynamic content into distinct, coherently moving components. This fundamental perceptual ability stands in contrast to many computational approaches in computer vision, which often analyze motion in a piecemeal, frame-by-frame manner. This work seeks to bridge this gap by proposing a paradigm shift: performing holistic, unsupervised motion segmentation over an entire video sequence in a single, integrated process. Achieving this capability represents a significant step forward, offering a powerful primitive for a wide array of downstream vision tasks—from object tracking and action recognition to scene understanding—and could serve as a rich, self-supervised criterion for learning meaningful video representations. To this end, we introduce a novel long-term spatio-temporal model that operates in a completely unsupervised fashion. The model accepts as input a volumetric sequence of consecutive optical flow fields and directly outputs a corresponding volume of segmentation masks, delineating regions of coherent motion across the entire video clip. At its core is a transformer-based network architecture. We derive its training objective through a mathematically principled framework, the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), which yields a loss function combining two key elements: a flow reconstruction term based on innovative spatio-temporal parametric motion models—which uniquely blend polynomial (quadratic) models for spatial dimensions with B-spline formulations for the temporal dimension—and a regularization term that explicitly enforces temporal consistency across the predicted segmentation masks. We conduct comprehensive experiments on four established Video Object Segmentation (VOS) benchmarks, reporting convincing quantitative results that validate our approach. Furthermore, we provide visual demonstrations that highlight the critical improvements in temporal coherence afforded by our method.

1 INTRODUCTION

In the analysis of video data, segmenting motion is a problem of central importance. Humans can seamlessly and continuously watch a video stream, effortlessly extracting its primary moving constituents. In contrast, conventional computer vision methodologies frequently address this task through sequential, independent processing of individual frames. Our objective is to transcend this established paradigm and instead segment the various motion entities present within a video sequence through a unified, one-pass analysis, thereby conducting a thorough investigation into the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. Given that optical flow encapsulates all information regarding displacement between consecutive video frames, it forms a natural and robust foundation upon which to base motion segmentation. While motion segmentation is a valuable computer vision task in its own right, it also functions as a critical enabling technology for numerous downstream applications, including independent moving object detection, object tracking, and action recognition, among others. Its utility is further evidenced in the domain of video object segmentation (VOS), where it is often employed in conjunction with appearance-based cues.

The optical flow field computed at a specific time *t* can, in principle, yield a segmentation for that individual frame. However, considering a broader temporal window—or even the complete video sequence—is inherently advantageous because the motion entities within a scene typically exhibit consistency over time (or, at the very least, throughout a coherent video shot). Temporal coherence is an intrinsic property of motion itself. Consequently, it is imperative for a motion segmentation method to capitalize on this property, particularly when adopting a long-term perspective.

In this paper, we present an original, holistic method for segmenting multiple motions from optical flow across an entire video sequence. To the best of our knowledge, our Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) method is the first fully unsupervised, network-based approach to incorporate explicit long-term temporal consistency and to segment multiple motions in a video in one integrated process. The principal contributions of our work are as follows. Our network architecture accepts a volume of consecutive optical flows as input and produces a corresponding volume of temporally consistent motion segmentation maps. It incorporates a transformer module to facilitate long-range spatio-temporal interactions. The entire system is trained in a completely unsupervised manner, without recourse to any manual annotations or ground truth data of any kind. The loss function is rigorously derived by leveraging the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework; it comprises a flow reconstruction term grounded in our original spatio-temporal parametric motion models and an additional term that enforces temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We model the long-term temporal evolution of motion model parameters using B-splines. Our method also utilizes a latent representation of segment motion, augmented with positional embeddings.

The remainder of this document is structured in the following manner. Section 2 reviews related work in the field of motion segmentation. Section 3 details our proposed unsupervised network for multiple motion segmentation in one go, which embeds long-term temporal consistency. Section 4 provides implementation specifics. Section 5 reports experimental results on four VOS benchmarks, including comparisons to state-of-the-art unsupervised motion segmentation methods. Finally, Section 6 offers concluding remarks.

2 RELATED WORK

Motion segmentation aims to decompose each frame of a video sequence into components (or segments) exhibiting coherent motion. Typically, each motion segment is associated with a motion model, which may be hand-crafted (such as affine or quadratic polynomial models) or learned. The investigation of motion segmentation spans several decades (19; 23; 38). In this section, however, we will concentrate on more recent methodologies. With the advent of accurate and efficient optical flow estimation techniques, contemporary motion segmentation methods can reliably utilize optical flow as input. The rise of deep learning in computer vision, and more recently the adoption of transformer-based networks with attention mechanisms (11), has also influenced the development of motion segmentation approaches.

In (35), a transformer module, specifically the slot attention mechanism introduced in (18), is leveraged to perform motion segmentation from optical flow. This method addresses a binary segmentation problem, distinguishing a foreground moving object from the background. Its loss function combines a flow reconstruction term with an entropy term designed to encourage binary mask predictions. A different approach is adopted in (34), which can handle multiple motion segmentation. This method learns nonlinear subspace filters from stacked deep multi-layer perceptrons, and motion segmentation is subsequently inferred at test time by applying *K*-means clustering to the output embeddings. The work in (21) utilizes the Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework to define both the loss function and training procedure for an unsupervised, frame-by-frame motion segmentation method that employs 12-parameter quadratic motion models. The same authors extended this method in (22) to better handle temporal aspects by considering triplets of optical flows as input. In (36), the authors developed an adversarial approach wherein a generator network attempts to produce a mask that hides a portion of the input optical flow, while an inpainter network tries to reconstruct the flow within the masked region. The underlying rationale is that if the hidden area corresponds to an independently moving region, the inpainter should be unable to accurately reconstruct its flow from the surrounding context.

The temporal dimension of motion segmentation has been addressed in various ways (30). Concerning deep learning approaches, the work in (35) improves motion segmentation at training time by using, as input, flow fields computed between time *t* and several preceding and succeeding time instants. The authors of (8) consider several consecutive RGB frames as input to their self-supervised method. Optical flow is computed only during training, and their loss function also includes a temporal consistency term; however, this term is not applied between consecutive segmentation masks but rather between pairings of the same frame *t* and another, potentially distant, frame. In (9), spatio-temporal transformers were designed for video object segmentation, incorporating temporal feature propagation.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) frequently relies on motion segmentation, often coupled with appearance cues (5; 10; 37). It has been addressed using supervised or semi-supervised methods, as in (7; 9; 12), as well as with unsupervised methods (36; 35; 21). VOS is typically concerned with segmenting primary objects—that is, objects moving in the foreground of a scene, possibly under camera motion (39). Consequently, VOS benchmarks usually provide binary ground truth, separating a primary moving object from the background, as is the case for the DAVIS2016 benchmark (26). Recent works have explored new ways to couple appearance and motion for VOS. The AMD method (17) includes two separate pathways for appearance and motion. While it does not use optical flow as direct input and introduces an objectness concept, it still relies on a coarse motion representation. The RCF method (16) involves learnable motion models and is structured in two stages: a motion-supervised object discovery stage, followed by a refinement stage with residual motion prediction and high-level appearance supervision. However, this method cannot distinguish between objects undergoing different motions. In (6), the prediction of probable motion patterns is used during training as a cue to learn objectness from videos. Divided attention is promoted in (14). The resulting DivA method is based on the same principle as (36)—that motion segments are mutually uninformative—but it is not limited to binary segmentation. It can segment a variable number of moving objects from optical flow by leveraging a slot attention mechanism guided by image content through a cross-modal conditional slot decoder.

Our fully unsupervised approach differs from these prior works in several key respects. We rely exclusively on optical flow, taking a volume of OF fields as input and producing a corresponding volume of consistent segmentation maps. We introduce B-splines to define parametric motion models capable of accurately modeling motion evolution over time, and we explicitly formulate a long-term temporal consistency objective. We derive our loss function from the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. While the authors of (22) also address temporal consistency, their method only takes a triplet of optical flow fields as input, does not employ transformers, and uses only a linear (first-order polynomial) model in time for the temporal component of the motion model. Furthermore, their temporal linkage of consecutive segmentations was implemented as an ad hoc post-processing step. In contrast, we define a fully integrated long-term model that is trained end-to-end in an unsupervised manner. We will refer to our method as the LT-MS (Long-Term Motion Segmentation) method. For comparison, we will refer to the method from (22) as the ST-MS (Short-Term Motion Segmentation) method.

3 LONG-TERM MOTION SEGMENTATION METHOD

We have designed a transformer-based network for segmenting multiple motions from optical flow. The architecture is inspired by the MaskFormer design (4) but comprises only a single head corresponding to mask prediction, as depicted in Figure 1. The network accepts as input a volume—of flexible temporal length—comprising several consecutive optical flow fields. Temporal consistency is enforced during training in two primary ways. First, we associate a spatio-temporal motion model with each segment to characterize its motion and the evolution of that motion over time. Second, the loss function includes an additional term that enforces consistent labeling of motion segments across the input volume.

Figure 1: Overall architecture of our multiple motion segmentation method, which ensures temporal consistency through the loss term L_c and the B-spline space-time motion models θ_k (for k=1,...,K). The network takes as input a volume of T flow fields. It comprises a 3D U-Net (represented by 'e' and 'd' boxes) and a transformer decoder ('t' box). Positional encoding is also incorporated. A cross-attention operation yields the K segmentation masks corresponding to the input volume. For clarity, the diagram is shown for three motion segments (K=3). L_r denotes the flow-reconstruction loss term.

3.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL PARAMETRIC MOTION MODEL

We refer to the set of T consecutive flow fields as a space-time volume (or simply a volume). This volume could, in principle, encompass an entire video sequence. Our space-time motion model is estimated using B-spline functions (32). We assign a spatio-temporal parametric motion model f ̃_θ_k to each motion segment k (where k=1,...,K). Here, θ_k specifies the motion model parameters for segment k. The motion model involves J parameters, and each parameter θ_k_j (for j=1,...,J) is represented as a B-spline function of order n in the temporal variable t over the space-time volume. In practice, we set n=3. The number L of control points is given by L = 2 + ⌊(T-2)/ν⌋, where ν allows us to set the temporal frequency of the control points. We place a control point at both temporal extremities of the volume (at t=1 and t=T), with the remaining control points equidistantly spaced between them. Typically, these control points do not coincide with the discrete time points of the video sequence.

The concept of the space-time spline-based motion model is illustrated in Figure 2. For this illustration only, the motion models are computed within the two segments (foreground moving object and background) provided by the ground truth. The estimated motion model for the foreground object successfully captures the periodic nature of the swing motion, as demonstrated by the plots of the computed model parameters. Simultaneously, the motion model computed for the background segment accurately fits the camera motion. It is worth noting that articulated motion (e.g., a person's legs) would require segmentation into multiple motion components.

Figure 2: Illustration of the spatiotemporal spline-based motion model. Top row: input flows displayed using the HSV color code for the 'swing' video from the DAVIS2016 dataset, the binary segmentation ground truth, and flows generated by the estimated spline-based motion models for the two segments. Bottom row: plots showing the temporal evolution of the six estimated model parameters corresponding to the u-coordinate of the flow for the foreground moving object.

Our framework can accommodate any parametric motion model. We employ the 12-parameter quadratic motion model because it can account for the continuously varying depth surfaces of objects in a scene—particularly for the entire background—and for complex object or camera motions. In contrast, affine and 8-parameter quadratic models assume a planar object surface. Indeed, the 8-parameter model exactly corresponds to the projection into the image of the 3D rigid motion of a planar surface, being equivalent for velocity fields to a homography transform. However, in the presence of significant depth effects (strong depth discontinuities) and camera motion, a static scene cannot be represented by a single motion model due to motion parallax induced by static foreground objects. Focusing first on the spatial dimensions, the 2D flow vector produced by the full quadratic motion model at point (x, y) is given by:
f ̃_θ(x,y) = ( θ₁ + θ₂x + θ₃y + θ₇x² + θ₈xy + θ₉y²,  θ₄ + θ₅x + θ₆y + θ₁₀x² + θ₁₁xy + θ₁₂y² )^T.

To properly handle complex temporal evolution, we employ the spline approximation described earlier. By denoting the motion model for each segment k as f ̃_S_n(θ_k), we emphasize that the parameters are estimated via B-spline functions. More specifically:
f ̃_S_n(θ_k)(i,t) = Σ_{l=1}^{L'} f ̃_θ_{k,l}(i,t) B_{n,l}(t),
where B_{n,l} is the l-th B-spline basis function and θ_{k,l} corresponds to the l-th control point of the spline.

3.2 LOSS FUNCTION

We consider a volume of optical flow fields f ∈ ℝ^(2×T×W×H), with a spatial grid Ω ∈ ℝ^(W×H) and T temporal steps. We denote f(i,t) ∈ ℝ² as the flow vector at spatial site i ∈ Ω and time t. We assume the flow can be decomposed into K segments, each exhibiting coherent motion. Flow vectors within a given segment k are represented by a smooth parametric motion model parameterized by ϑ_k. The variable z_{i,t} conveys the motion segmentation, where z_{i,t}^k = 1 if site (i,t) belongs to segment k. Both z and ϑ = {ϑ_k, k=1,...,K} are treated as latent variables, with f being the observed data. Following (13), we introduce an approximate posterior distribution over the segmentation and motion model parameters:
q(z, ϑ | f) = q(z | f) q(ϑ) = ( Π_{t=1}^T Π_{i∈Ω} Π_{k=1}^K q(z_{i,t}^k | f) ) ( Π_{k=1}^K q(ϑ_k) ),
where q(ϑ_k) ≜ δ(θ_k) with δ denoting the Dirac delta distribution, and q(z_{i,t}^k | f) = g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k. Here, g_φ is our network model that takes the optical flow volume as input and outputs a probabilistic segmentation volume.

The data likelihood over a dataset D of optical flow volumes f can be written as:
log p(D) = Σ_{f∈D} log p(f) = Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log( p(f,z,ϑ) / q(z,ϑ|f) ) ] + KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ|f) ) )
≥ Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] - KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) ),
where we obtain the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Based on our modeling assumptions, we can express the likelihood as:
p(f | z, ϑ) = Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K p(f(t) | ϑ_k, z) ∝ Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K Π_{i∈Ω} exp( -||f(i,t) - f ̃_S_n(ϑ_k)(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t} )^{z_{i,t}^k},
where f ̃_S_n(ϑ_k)(i,t) is the flow vector given by the parametric motion model with parameters ϑ_k at point (i,t), as defined in Section 3.1 via spline approximation, and ξ_{f,t} = Σ_i ||f(i,t)||₁ is a normalizing factor. From this likelihood, the first term of the ELBO becomes:
L_r = E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] = Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_k E_q[ log p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ]
= - Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_k g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k ||f(i,t) - f ̃_S_n(θ_k)(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t}.

The term KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) allows us to incorporate a prior over the segmentation. We wish to enforce the property that segmentation labels are temporally consistent—that is, similar between neighboring frames. We approximate this term using a temporal consistency loss defined in (22), as it demonstrated good experimental results and computational efficiency during training:
L_c = (1/(2K|Ω|)) Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{t=2}^T 𝟙[ ||f_{i,t} - f_{i,t-1}||₁ < λ ] Σ_{k=1}^K | g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k - g_φ(f)_{i,t-1}^k |.
The threshold λ helps to discard areas likely to be occluded. The overall loss function is thus defined as:
Σ_{f∈D} L(f, φ, θ) = Σ_{f∈D} ( L_r(f, φ, θ) + β L_c(f, φ) ).
We set β = 1. The training procedure alternately updates the motion model parameters θ and the network parameters φ with learning rate α:
For each f in D:  θ* = arg min_θ L(f, φ, θ);  φ_{t+1} = φ_t - α ∇_φ L(f, φ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE

The overall architecture of our unsupervised multiple motion segmentation framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It consists of two main modules. The first module, which takes the flow volume as input, is a 3D U-Net (29). The latent code from this network, augmented with positional embeddings, is fed into a transformer decoder. Subsequently, through a cross-attention mechanism, the decoder produces the final output: a volume of segmentation masks. The entire architecture is trained by minimizing the loss function defined above, while the motion model parameters for each segment are estimated via the B-spline formulation. Temporal consistency is thus jointly promoted by both the loss function and the inherent design of the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

Following prior works (6; 16; 21; 22; 35), we adopt the RAFT method (31) to compute optical flow fields. Specifically, we use the RAFT version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset (2). We downsample the computed flow fields to a resolution of 128×224 before feeding them into the network. The output segmentation maps are then upsampled back to the original frame size for evaluation. This strategy enables efficient training and inference. During training, we typically use flow volumes of temporal length T=9. However, at test time, the model can process volumes of larger temporal length, including the entire sequence's flow volume. For computing the spatio-temporal parametric motion models, the x and y spatial coordinates are normalized to the range [-1, 1], and a similar normalization is applied to the temporal coordinate t. We employ the full 12-parameter quadratic motion model in all experiments and set the B-spline frequency factor ν=3. For each spatial site i, we assign it to the segment k ̂ with the highest predicted probability. In Equation (7), we set λ as the 99th percentile of flow differences across the entire flow volume.

Our LT-MS method is highly efficient at test time. The average computational speed reaches 210 frames per second (fps) on a P100 GPU, which is approximately twice as fast as the ST-MS method (22). This speed advantage is likely due to the long flow sequences provided as input to the network, allowing for greater parallelization of computationally intensive operations. Furthermore, the LT-MS architecture remains lightweight, combining only three U-Net layers and a transformer decoder operating on downsampled feature maps. It is also important to note that our LT-MS method does not involve any post-processing steps.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING

We applied two types of data augmentation specifically designed for optical flow. First, we add a global flow to the input flow volume, similar to the techniques used in the EM (21) and ST-MS (22) methods. However, in our case, the global flow is defined by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model whose parameters are randomly chosen. The same global flow is added to all flow fields within a given input volume. This augmentation mimics various camera motions, reinforcing that the identified motion segments should be independent of such global motion. Second, we deliberately corrupt a small number of flows within the nine-frame input volume. This simulates inaccurately estimated flow fields at certain time instants, challenging the model to maintain temporal consistency despite these corruptions.

Our motion segmentation method is fully unsupervised. We never utilize any manual annotations. The model is trained exclusively on the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset (20), regardless of the dataset used for testing. This ensures that our LT-MS network generalizes effectively to unseen data. Regarding hyperparameter selection, we choose the stopping epoch based on the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We conducted comparative experiments on four standard datasets: DAVIS 2016¹ (26), SegTrackV2² (15), FBMS59 (24), and DAVIS2017-motion (33).

5.1 ABLATION STUDY

We performed an ablation study to evaluate three key components of our LT-MS method (with K=4 masks), particularly those related to the temporal dimension. We modified one component at a time as follows: (1) We replaced our B-spline-based space-time motion model with the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model from ST-MS (22). (2) We omitted the temporal consistency loss term L_c from the overall loss function. (3) We removed the transformer decoder, using only the convolutional network backbone. All ablation experiments were run on three datasets: DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Results are presented in Table 1. Additionally, we performed these ablations for two different input sequence configurations: sequences of ten flows and sequences of 120 flows (which, for DAVIS2016, effectively constitutes the entire video). The results indicate that all three ablations have a nearly equivalent negative impact on performance. Therefore, the three corresponding model components—the spline-based motion model, the temporal consistency loss term, and the transformer decoder—all contribute beneficially and to a similar degree. They collectively enable the method to handle the temporal dimension and model motion evolution compellingly. The contributions of these components are more pronounced on the FBMS59 and SegTrackV2 datasets. However, the dynamic content prevalent in most DAVIS2016 videos, along with the resulting overall high performance scores, makes it more challenging to fully appreciate the individual contributions of these three components on that dataset.

Table 1: Ablation study for three main components of our LT-MS method (K=4) on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Only one model component is modified at a time. Performance is measured by the Jaccard index 𝒥. We report results for two input-flow sequence lengths (or cut sizes): dividing the video into pieces of ten successive frames and considering 120 successive frames (effectively the whole video for DAVIS2016).

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION

Table 2 presents results obtained by two variants of our LT-MS method on the DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59 datasets. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with two masks (K=2), while LT-MS-K4 uses four masks (K=4). Table 2 also includes results from other existing unsupervised methods, where available. We follow the categorization proposed in (21) regarding input and training, but we have added a category concerning network input for four recent methods (6; 8; 16; 17) that use only RGB images as input at test time, with optical flow involved solely in the loss function. Evaluation is performed against binary ground truth (foreground moving object vs. background) for all three datasets. We classify the OCLR method (33) as unsupervised, although the authors of DivA (14) did not, because OCLR relies on human-annotated sprites to incorporate realistic shapes in its computer-generated training data. We consider the OCLR version that uses only optical flow as input. The post-processing based on Conditional Random Fields (CRF) added to the CIS method (36) is computationally heavy, leading most authors to compare only the version without post-processing for fairness.

As shown in Table 2, our LT-MS method delivers very convincing results, both for LT-MS-K2 and LT-MS-K4, within the category of unsupervised methods based solely on optical flow. OCLR and DivA demonstrate superior performance on the SegTrackV2 dataset. However, as noted, OCLR is not a fully unsupervised method, and DivA leverages RGB images within its conditional decoder. Additionally, DivA, along with MoSeg and CIS methods, uses multi-step flows as input (between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2) and averages the four corresponding predictions to produce the final result. SegTrackV2 contains sequences captured with handheld cameras under poorly controlled conditions, resulting in unstable footage where the advantages of our method's long-term consistency are less pronounced.

Overall, our LT-MS method successfully handles temporal consistency over extended periods. Beyond segmentation accuracy, we emphasize that our method is uniquely designed to produce inherently coherent segmentations across the entire sequence, which constitutes a significant added value. Thus, we can assert that we have not only segmented moving objects throughout the sequence but have also achieved a form of implicit tracking.

Table 2: Results obtained with two versions of our LT-MS method on DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with two masks (K=2), and LT-MS-K4 uses four masks (K=4). We include comparisons with other unsupervised methods (scores taken from the cited articles). All scores correspond to evaluation against binary ground truth. For LT-MS-K4 and LT-MS-K2, we report results obtained with a cut size of 10. The Jaccard index 𝒥 measures intersection over union between extracted segments and ground truth, while ℱ focuses on boundary accuracy. Performance is assessed by the average score over all samples for all datasets except DAVIS2016, for which the overall score is the average of per-sequence scores. *The classification of OCLR as an unsupervised method is debatable (see main text). †DivA indirectly uses RGB input via its image-conditioned decoder.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION

We also evaluated performance in a multi-segment setting. Since segmenting multiple motions is more challenging than binary foreground/background segmentation, accuracy scores are expected to decrease for all methods. Table 3 reports comparative results on the DAVIS2017-motion dataset and FBMS59. As with other methods, we performed segmentation with three masks. To this end, we fine-tuned the LT-MS-K4 network on the DAVIS2016 training set with K=3 masks. The resulting performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than ST-MS (22) and substantially better than MoSeg. The same caveat regarding OCLR's unsupervised status applies. For FBMS59, we report multi-mask segmentation results using two different metrics. Our LT-MS method outperforms DivA (14)—which also attempted multi-segment evaluation on FBMS59—by a considerable margin.

Table 3: Multi-segment evaluation. For DAVIS2017-motion, the reported score 𝒥&ℱ is the mean of the region similarity 𝒥 and boundary accuracy ℱ. Evaluation is performed on entire videos according to the official DAVIS2017 protocol. Scores are averages of per-video scores. *See caption of Table 2. For FBMS59, the two evaluation metrics are bootstrap IoU (bIoU) (14)—where each ground-truth mask is matched to the most likely predicted segment at the frame level—and linear assignment, which establishes a bilinear mapping between ground-truth and predicted segments at the sequence level (similar to the official DAVIS2017 evaluation).

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION

Figure 3 presents several visual results demonstrating the behavior of our LT-MS method in different scenarios. We display sample results from three different videos across the benchmarks. The motion segments produced are generally accurate. Because our method employs multiple masks, it can effectively handle articulated motions (e.g., people2, bmx), manage scenes with several moving objects (people2), separate a rider from their vehicle (bmx, motocross-jump), and accommodate motion parallax. The enforcement of temporal consistency also allows the method to cope with errors in optical flow estimation or with objects that temporarily cease moving (bmx). It is important to remember that our primary target is the Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) task, even though we evaluate on VOS benchmarks. When VOS benchmarks focus on segmenting a single primary foreground object, discrepancies with OFS can arise, which may negatively impact evaluation scores. The segmentation of additional regions that appear incorrect according to VOS ground truth may, in fact, be meaningful from a pure OFS perspective.

Figure 3: Results obtained with our LT-MS-K4 method (K=4). Three groups of results are displayed: 'motocross-jump' from DAVIS2016, 'people02' from FBMS59, and 'bmx' from SegTrackV2. For each group, the first row shows samples of successive flow fields (HSV color code). The second row contains the corresponding video frames, with the ground-truth moving object overlay in yellow (where available). The third row shows the motion segments provided by LT-MS-K4, with a distinct color per segment. For all results, we use the same color set for the three masks corresponding to moving objects (blue, red, orange), while the background mask is left transparent to show the original image.

6 CONCLUSION

We have designed an original, transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions across an entire video in one integrated process. Our LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework to derive its loss function and fully embraces the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first unsupervised network-based OFS method that explicitly yields stable and consistent optical flow segmentation throughout long video sequences. The method introduces, during training, B-spline-based spatio-temporal parametric motion models defined over space-time volumes and a loss term that enforces temporal consistency between successive masks while accounting for occlusions. Our transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of arbitrary temporal length and can accommodate different numbers of masks K through simple fine-tuning. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of our LT-MS method, providing competitive performance. Furthermore, the method is very fast at test time. In future work, we plan to investigate the use of slot attention mechanisms to allow for a variable number of masks at test time without requiring model retraining.

Title: Unsupervised Motion Segmentation in One Go: A Smooth Long-Term Model Over a Video

Abstract:
The human visual system possesses a remarkable capacity to watch a video and instantly parse its dynamic content into distinct, coherently moving components. This fundamental perceptual ability stands in contrast to many computational approaches in computer vision, which often analyze motion in a piecemeal, frame-by-frame manner. This work seeks to bridge this gap by proposing a paradigm shift: performing holistic, unsupervised motion segmentation over an entire video sequence in a single, integrated process. Achieving this capability represents a significant step forward, offering a powerful primitive for a wide array of downstream vision tasks—from object tracking and action recognition to scene understanding—and could serve as a rich, self-supervised criterion for learning meaningful video representations. To this end, we introduce a novel long-term spatio-temporal model that operates in a completely unsupervised fashion. The model accepts as input a volumetric sequence of consecutive optical flow fields and directly outputs a corresponding volume of segmentation masks, delineating regions of coherent motion across the entire video clip. At its core is a transformer-based network architecture. We derive its training objective through a mathematically principled framework, the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), which yields a loss function combining two key elements: a flow reconstruction term based on innovative spatio-temporal parametric motion models—which uniquely blend polynomial (quadratic) models for spatial dimensions with B-spline formulations for the temporal dimension—and a regularization term that explicitly enforces temporal consistency across the predicted segmentation masks. We conduct comprehensive experiments on four established Video Object Segmentation (VOS) benchmarks, reporting convincing quantitative results that validate our approach. Furthermore, we provide visual demonstrations that highlight the critical improvements in temporal coherence afforded by our method.

1 INTRODUCTION

In the analysis of video data, segmenting motion is a problem of central importance. Humans can seamlessly and continuously watch a video stream, effortlessly extracting its primary moving constituents. In contrast, conventional computer vision methodologies frequently address this task through sequential, independent processing of individual frames. Our objective is to transcend this established paradigm and instead segment the various motion entities present within a video sequence through a unified, one-pass analysis, thereby conducting a thorough investigation into the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. Given that optical flow encapsulates all information regarding displacement between consecutive video frames, it forms a natural and robust foundation upon which to base motion segmentation. While motion segmentation is a valuable computer vision task in its own right, it also functions as a critical enabling technology for numerous downstream applications, including independent moving object detection, object tracking, and action recognition, among others. Its utility is further evidenced in the domain of video object segmentation (VOS), where it is often employed in conjunction with appearance-based cues.

The optical flow field computed at a specific time *t* can, in principle, yield a segmentation for that individual frame. However, considering a broader temporal window—or even the complete video sequence—is inherently advantageous because the motion entities within a scene typically exhibit consistency over time (or, at the very least, throughout a coherent video shot). Temporal coherence is an intrinsic property of motion itself. Consequently, it is imperative for a motion segmentation method to capitalize on this property, particularly when adopting a long-term perspective.

In this paper, we present an original, holistic method for segmenting multiple motions from optical flow across an entire video sequence. To the best of our knowledge, our Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) method is the first fully unsupervised, network-based approach to incorporate explicit long-term temporal consistency and to segment multiple motions in a video in one integrated process. The principal contributions of our work are as follows. Our network architecture accepts a volume of consecutive optical flows as input and produces a corresponding volume of temporally consistent motion segmentation maps. It incorporates a transformer module to facilitate long-range spatio-temporal interactions. The entire system is trained in a completely unsupervised manner, without recourse to any manual annotations or ground truth data of any kind. The loss function is rigorously derived by leveraging the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework; it comprises a flow reconstruction term grounded in our original spatio-temporal parametric motion models and an additional term that enforces temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We model the long-term temporal evolution of motion model parameters using B-splines. Our method also utilizes a latent representation of segment motion, augmented with positional embeddings.

The remainder of this document is structured in the following manner. Section 2 reviews related work in the field of motion segmentation. Section 3 details our proposed unsupervised network for multiple motion segmentation in one go, which embeds long-term temporal consistency. Section 4 provides implementation specifics. Section 5 reports experimental results on four VOS benchmarks, including comparisons to state-of-the-art unsupervised motion segmentation methods. Finally, Section 6 offers concluding remarks.

2 RELATED WORK

Motion segmentation aims to decompose each frame of a video sequence into components (or segments) exhibiting coherent motion. Typically, each motion segment is associated with a motion model, which may be hand-crafted (such as affine or quadratic polynomial models) or learned. The investigation of motion segmentation spans several decades (19; 23; 38). In this section, however, we will concentrate on more recent methodologies. With the advent of accurate and efficient optical flow estimation techniques, contemporary motion segmentation methods can reliably utilize optical flow as input. The rise of deep learning in computer vision, and more recently the adoption of transformer-based networks with attention mechanisms (11), has also influenced the development of motion segmentation approaches.

In (35), a transformer module, specifically the slot attention mechanism introduced in (18), is leveraged to perform motion segmentation from optical flow. This method addresses a binary segmentation problem, distinguishing a foreground moving object from the background. Its loss function combines a flow reconstruction term with an entropy term designed to encourage binary mask predictions. A different approach is adopted in (34), which can handle multiple motion segmentation. This method learns nonlinear subspace filters from stacked deep multi-layer perceptrons, and motion segmentation is subsequently inferred at test time by applying *K*-means clustering to the output embeddings. The work in (21) utilizes the Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework to define both the loss function and training procedure for an unsupervised, frame-by-frame motion segmentation method that employs 12-parameter quadratic motion models. The same authors extended this method in (22) to better handle temporal aspects by considering triplets of optical flows as input. In (36), the authors developed an adversarial approach wherein a generator network attempts to produce a mask that hides a portion of the input optical flow, while an inpainter network tries to reconstruct the flow within the masked region. The underlying rationale is that if the hidden area corresponds to an independently moving region, the inpainter should be unable to accurately reconstruct its flow from the surrounding context.

The temporal dimension of motion segmentation has been addressed in various ways (30). Concerning deep learning approaches, the work in (35) improves motion segmentation at training time by using, as input, flow fields computed between time *t* and several preceding and succeeding time instants. The authors of (8) consider several consecutive RGB frames as input to their self-supervised method. Optical flow is computed only during training, and their loss function also includes a temporal consistency term; however, this term is not applied between consecutive segmentation masks but rather between pairings of the same frame *t* and another, potentially distant, frame. In (9), spatio-temporal transformers were designed for video object segmentation, incorporating temporal feature propagation.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) frequently relies on motion segmentation, often coupled with appearance cues (5; 10; 37). It has been addressed using supervised or semi-supervised methods, as in (7; 9; 12), as well as with unsupervised methods (36; 35; 21). VOS is typically concerned with segmenting primary objects—that is, objects moving in the foreground of a scene, possibly under camera motion (39). Consequently, VOS benchmarks usually provide binary ground truth, separating a primary moving object from the background, as is the case for the DAVIS2016 benchmark (26). Recent works have explored new ways to couple appearance and motion for VOS. The AMD method (17) includes two separate pathways for appearance and motion. While it does not use optical flow as direct input and introduces an objectness concept, it still relies on a coarse motion representation. The RCF method (16) involves learnable motion models and is structured in two stages: a motion-supervised object discovery stage, followed by a refinement stage with residual motion prediction and high-level appearance supervision. However, this method cannot distinguish between objects undergoing different motions. In (6), the prediction of probable motion patterns is used during training as a cue to learn objectness from videos. Divided attention is promoted in (14). The resulting DivA method is based on the same principle as (36)—that motion segments are mutually uninformative—but it is not limited to binary segmentation. It can segment a variable number of moving objects from optical flow by leveraging a slot attention mechanism guided by image content through a cross-modal conditional slot decoder.

Our fully unsupervised approach differs from these prior works in several key respects. We rely exclusively on optical flow, taking a volume of OF fields as input and producing a corresponding volume of consistent segmentation maps. We introduce B-splines to define parametric motion models capable of accurately modeling motion evolution over time, and we explicitly formulate a long-term temporal consistency objective. We derive our loss function from the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. While the authors of (22) also address temporal consistency, their method only takes a triplet of optical flow fields as input, does not employ transformers, and uses only a linear (first-order polynomial) model in time for the temporal component of the motion model. Furthermore, their temporal linkage of consecutive segmentations was implemented as an ad hoc post-processing step. In contrast, we define a fully integrated long-term model that is trained end-to-end in an unsupervised manner. We will refer to our method as the LT-MS (Long-Term Motion Segmentation) method. For comparison, we will refer to the method from (22) as the ST-MS (Short-Term Motion Segmentation) method.

3 LONG-TERM MOTION SEGMENTATION METHOD

We have designed a transformer-based network for segmenting multiple motions from optical flow. The architecture is inspired by the MaskFormer design (4) but comprises only a single head corresponding to mask prediction, as depicted in Figure 1. The network accepts as input a volume—of flexible temporal length—comprising several consecutive optical flow fields. Temporal consistency is enforced during training in two primary ways. First, we associate a spatio-temporal motion model with each segment to characterize its motion and the evolution of that motion over time. Second, the loss function includes an additional term that enforces consistent labeling of motion segments across the input volume.

Figure 1: Overall architecture of our multiple motion segmentation method, which ensures temporal consistency through the loss term L_c and the B-spline space-time motion models θ_k (for k=1,...,K). The network takes as input a volume of T flow fields. It comprises a 3D U-Net (represented by 'e' and 'd' boxes) and a transformer decoder ('t' box). Positional encoding is also incorporated. A cross-attention operation yields the K segmentation masks corresponding to the input volume. For clarity, the diagram is shown for three motion segments (K=3). L_r denotes the flow-reconstruction loss term.

3.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL PARAMETRIC MOTION MODEL

We refer to the set of T consecutive flow fields as a space-time volume (or simply a volume). This volume could, in principle, encompass an entire video sequence. Our space-time motion model is estimated using B-spline functions (32). We assign a spatio-temporal parametric motion model f ̃_θ_k to each motion segment k (where k=1,...,K). Here, θ_k specifies the motion model parameters for segment k. The motion model involves J parameters, and each parameter θ_k_j (for j=1,...,J) is represented as a B-spline function of order n in the temporal variable t over the space-time volume. In practice, we set n=3. The number L of control points is given by L = 2 + ⌊(T-2)/ν⌋, where ν allows us to set the temporal frequency of the control points. We place a control point at both temporal extremities of the volume (at t=1 and t=T), with the remaining control points equidistantly spaced between them. Typically, these control points do not coincide with the discrete time points of the video sequence.

The concept of the space-time spline-based motion model is illustrated in Figure 2. For this illustration only, the motion models are computed within the two segments (foreground moving object and background) provided by the ground truth. The estimated motion model for the foreground object successfully captures the periodic nature of the swing motion, as demonstrated by the plots of the computed model parameters. Simultaneously, the motion model computed for the background segment accurately fits the camera motion. It is worth noting that articulated motion (e.g., a person's legs) would require segmentation into multiple motion components.

Figure 2: Illustration of the spatiotemporal spline-based motion model. Top row: input flows displayed using the HSV color code for the 'swing' video from the DAVIS2016 dataset, the binary segmentation ground truth, and flows generated by the estimated spline-based motion models for the two segments. Bottom row: plots showing the temporal evolution of the six estimated model parameters corresponding to the u-coordinate of the flow for the foreground moving object.

Our framework can accommodate any parametric motion model. We employ the 12-parameter quadratic motion model because it can account for the continuously varying depth surfaces of objects in a scene—particularly for the entire background—and for complex object or camera motions. In contrast, affine and 8-parameter quadratic models assume a planar object surface. Indeed, the 8-parameter model exactly corresponds to the projection into the image of the 3D rigid motion of a planar surface, being equivalent for velocity fields to a homography transform. However, in the presence of significant depth effects (strong depth discontinuities) and camera motion, a static scene cannot be represented by a single motion model due to motion parallax induced by static foreground objects. Focusing first on the spatial dimensions, the 2D flow vector produced by the full quadratic motion model at point (x, y) is given by:
f ̃_θ(x,y) = ( θ₁ + θ₂x + θ₃y + θ₇x² + θ₈xy + θ₉y²,  θ₄ + θ₅x + θ₆y + θ₁₀x² + θ₁₁xy + θ₁₂y² )^T.

To properly handle complex temporal evolution, we employ the spline approximation described earlier. By denoting the motion model for each segment k as f ̃_S_n(θ_k), we emphasize that the parameters are estimated via B-spline functions. More specifically:
f ̃_S_n(θ_k)(i,t) = Σ_{l=1}^{L'} f ̃_θ_{k,l}(i,t) B_{n,l}(t),
where B_{n,l} is the l-th B-spline basis function and θ_{k,l} corresponds to the l-th control point of the spline.

3.2 LOSS FUNCTION

We consider a volume of optical flow fields f ∈ ℝ^(2×T×W×H), with a spatial grid Ω ∈ ℝ^(W×H) and T temporal steps. We denote f(i,t) ∈ ℝ² as the flow vector at spatial site i ∈ Ω and time t. We assume the flow can be decomposed into K segments, each exhibiting coherent motion. Flow vectors within a given segment k are represented by a smooth parametric motion model parameterized by ϑ_k. The variable z_{i,t} conveys the motion segmentation, where z_{i,t}^k = 1 if site (i,t) belongs to segment k. Both z and ϑ = {ϑ_k, k=1,...,K} are treated as latent variables, with f being the observed data. Following (13), we introduce an approximate posterior distribution over the segmentation and motion model parameters:
q(z, ϑ | f) = q(z | f) q(ϑ) = ( Π_{t=1}^T Π_{i∈Ω} Π_{k=1}^K q(z_{i,t}^k | f) ) ( Π_{k=1}^K q(ϑ_k) ),
where q(ϑ_k) ≜ δ(θ_k) with δ denoting the Dirac delta distribution, and q(z_{i,t}^k | f) = g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k. Here, g_φ is our network model that takes the optical flow volume as input and outputs a probabilistic segmentation volume.

The data likelihood over a dataset D of optical flow volumes f can be written as:
log p(D) = Σ_{f∈D} log p(f) = Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log( p(f,z,ϑ) / q(z,ϑ|f) ) ] + KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ|f) ) )
≥ Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] - KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) ),
where we obtain the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Based on our modeling assumptions, we can express the likelihood as:
p(f | z, ϑ) = Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K p(f(t) | ϑ_k, z) ∝ Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K Π_{i∈Ω} exp( -||f(i,t) - f ̃_S_n(ϑ_k)(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t} )^{z_{i,t}^k},
where f ̃_S_n(ϑ_k)(i,t) is the flow vector given by the parametric motion model with parameters ϑ_k at point (i,t), as defined in Section 3.1 via spline approximation, and ξ_{f,t} = Σ_i ||f(i,t)||₁ is a normalizing factor. From this likelihood, the first term of the ELBO becomes:
L_r = E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] = Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_k E_q[ log p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ]
= - Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_k g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k ||f(i,t) - f ̃_S_n(θ_k)(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t}.

The term KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) allows us to incorporate a prior over the segmentation. We wish to enforce the property that segmentation labels are temporally consistent—that is, similar between neighboring frames. We approximate this term using a temporal consistency loss defined in (22), as it demonstrated good experimental results and computational efficiency during training:
L_c = (1/(2K|Ω|)) Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{t=2}^T 𝟙[ ||f_{i,t} - f_{i,t-1}||₁ < λ ] Σ_{k=1}^K | g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k - g_φ(f)_{i,t-1}^k |.
The threshold λ helps to discard areas likely to be occluded. The overall loss function is thus defined as:
Σ_{f∈D} L(f, φ, θ) = Σ_{f∈D} ( L_r(f, φ, θ) + β L_c(f, φ) ).
We set β = 1. The training procedure alternately updates the motion model parameters θ and the network parameters φ with learning rate α:
For each f in D:  θ* = arg min_θ L(f, φ, θ);  φ_{t+1} = φ_t - α ∇_φ L(f, φ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE

The overall architecture of our unsupervised multiple motion segmentation framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It consists of two main modules. The first module, which takes the flow volume as input, is a 3D U-Net (29). The latent code from this network, augmented with positional embeddings, is fed into a transformer decoder. Subsequently, through a cross-attention mechanism, the decoder produces the final output: a volume of segmentation masks. The entire architecture is trained by minimizing the loss function defined above, while the motion model parameters for each segment are estimated via the B-spline formulation. Temporal consistency is thus jointly promoted by both the loss function and the inherent design of the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

Following prior works (6; 16; 21; 22; 35), we adopt the RAFT method (31) to compute optical flow fields. Specifically, we use the RAFT version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset (2). We downsample the computed flow fields to a resolution of 128×224 before feeding them into the network. The output segmentation maps are then upsampled back to the original frame size for evaluation. This strategy enables efficient training and inference. During training, we typically use flow volumes of temporal length T=9. However, at test time, the model can process volumes of larger temporal length, including the entire sequence's flow volume. For computing the spatio-temporal parametric motion models, the x and y spatial coordinates are normalized to the range [-1, 1], and a similar normalization is applied to the temporal coordinate t. We employ the full 12-parameter quadratic motion model in all experiments and set the B-spline frequency factor ν=3. For each spatial site i, we assign it to the segment k ̂ with the highest predicted probability. In Equation (7), we set λ as the 99th percentile of flow differences across the entire flow volume.

Our LT-MS method is highly efficient at test time. The average computational speed reaches 210 frames per second (fps) on a P100 GPU, which is approximately twice as fast as the ST-MS method (22). This speed advantage is likely due to the long flow sequences provided as input to the network, allowing for greater parallelization of computationally intensive operations. Furthermore, the LT-MS architecture remains lightweight, combining only three U-Net layers and a transformer decoder operating on downsampled feature maps. It is also important to note that our LT-MS method does not involve any post-processing steps.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING

We applied two types of data augmentation specifically designed for optical flow. First, we add a global flow to the input flow volume, similar to the techniques used in the EM (21) and ST-MS (22) methods. However, in our case, the global flow is defined by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model whose parameters are randomly chosen. The same global flow is added to all flow fields within a given input volume. This augmentation mimics various camera motions, reinforcing that the identified motion segments should be independent of such global motion. Second, we deliberately corrupt a small number of flows within the nine-frame input volume. This simulates inaccurately estimated flow fields at certain time instants, challenging the model to maintain temporal consistency despite these corruptions.

Our motion segmentation method is fully unsupervised. We never utilize any manual annotations. The model is trained exclusively on the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset (20), regardless of the dataset used for testing. This ensures that our LT-MS network generalizes effectively to unseen data. Regarding hyperparameter selection, we choose the stopping epoch based on the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We conducted comparative experiments on four standard datasets: DAVIS 2016¹ (26), SegTrackV2² (15), FBMS59 (24), and DAVIS2017-motion (33).

5.1 ABLATION STUDY

We performed an ablation study to evaluate three key components of our LT-MS method (with K=4 masks), particularly those related to the temporal dimension. We modified one component at a time as follows: (1) We replaced our B-spline-based space-time motion model with the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model from ST-MS (22). (2) We omitted the temporal consistency loss term L_c from the overall loss function. (3) We removed the transformer decoder, using only the convolutional network backbone. All ablation experiments were run on three datasets: DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Results are presented in Table 1. Additionally, we performed these ablations for two different input sequence configurations: sequences of ten flows and sequences of 120 flows (which, for DAVIS2016, effectively constitutes the entire video). The results indicate that all three ablations have a nearly equivalent negative impact on performance. Therefore, the three corresponding model components—the spline-based motion model, the temporal consistency loss term, and the transformer decoder—all contribute beneficially and to a similar degree. They collectively enable the method to handle the temporal dimension and model motion evolution compellingly. The contributions of these components are more pronounced on the FBMS59 and SegTrackV2 datasets. However, the dynamic content prevalent in most DAVIS2016 videos, along with the resulting overall high performance scores, makes it more challenging to fully appreciate the individual contributions of these three components on that dataset.

Table 1: Ablation study for three main components of our LT-MS method (K=4) on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Only one model component is modified at a time. Performance is measured by the Jaccard index 𝒥. We report results for two input-flow sequence lengths (or cut sizes): dividing the video into pieces of ten successive frames and considering 120 successive frames (effectively the whole video for DAVIS2016).

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION

Table 2 presents results obtained by two variants of our LT-MS method on the DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59 datasets. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with two masks (K=2), while LT-MS-K4 uses four masks (K=4). Table 2 also includes results from other existing unsupervised methods, where available. We follow the categorization proposed in (21) regarding input and training, but we have added a category concerning network input for four recent methods (6; 8; 16; 17) that use only RGB images as input at test time, with optical flow involved solely in the loss function. Evaluation is performed against binary ground truth (foreground moving object vs. background) for all three datasets. We classify the OCLR method (33) as unsupervised, although the authors of DivA (14) did not, because OCLR relies on human-annotated sprites to incorporate realistic shapes in its computer-generated training data. We consider the OCLR version that uses only optical flow as input. The post-processing based on Conditional Random Fields (CRF) added to the CIS method (36) is computationally heavy, leading most authors to compare only the version without post-processing for fairness.

As shown in Table 2, our LT-MS method delivers very convincing results, both for LT-MS-K2 and LT-MS-K4, within the category of unsupervised methods based solely on optical flow. OCLR and DivA demonstrate superior performance on the SegTrackV2 dataset. However, as noted, OCLR is not a fully unsupervised method, and DivA leverages RGB images within its conditional decoder. Additionally, DivA, along with MoSeg and CIS methods, uses multi-step flows as input (between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2) and averages the four corresponding predictions to produce the final result. SegTrackV2 contains sequences captured with handheld cameras under poorly controlled conditions, resulting in unstable footage where the advantages of our method's long-term consistency are less pronounced.

Overall, our LT-MS method successfully handles temporal consistency over extended periods. Beyond segmentation accuracy, we emphasize that our method is uniquely designed to produce inherently coherent segmentations across the entire sequence, which constitutes a significant added value. Thus, we can assert that we have not only segmented moving objects throughout the sequence but have also achieved a form of implicit tracking.

We include comparisons with other unsupervised methods (scores taken from the cited articles). All scores correspond to evaluation against binary ground truth. For LT-MS-K4 and LT-MS-K2, we report results obtained with a cut size of 10. The Jaccard index 𝒥 measures intersection over union between extracted segments and ground truth, while ℱ focuses on boundary accuracy. Performance is assessed by the average score over all samples for all datasets except DAVIS2016, for which the overall score is the average of per-sequence scores. *The classification of OCLR as an unsupervised method is debatable (see main text). †DivA indirectly uses RGB input via its image-conditioned decoder.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION

We also evaluated performance in a multi-segment setting. Since segmenting multiple motions is more challenging than binary foreground/background segmentation, accuracy scores are expected to decrease for all methods. Table 3 reports comparative results on the DAVIS2017-motion dataset and FBMS59. As with other methods, we performed segmentation with three masks. To this end, we fine-tuned the LT-MS-K4 network on the DAVIS2016 training set with K=3 masks. The resulting performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than ST-MS (22) and substantially better than MoSeg. The same caveat regarding OCLR's unsupervised status applies. For FBMS59, we report multi-mask segmentation results using two different metrics. Our LT-MS method outperforms DivA (14)—which also attempted multi-segment evaluation on FBMS59—by a considerable margin.

Table 3: Multi-segment evaluation. For DAVIS2017-motion, the reported score 𝒥&ℱ is the mean of the region similarity 𝒥 and boundary accuracy ℱ. Evaluation is performed on entire videos according to the official DAVIS2017 protocol. Scores are averages of per-video scores. *See caption of Table 2. For FBMS59, the two evaluation metrics are bootstrap IoU (bIoU) (14)—where each ground-truth mask is matched to the most likely predicted segment at the frame level—and linear assignment, which establishes a bilinear mapping between ground-truth and predicted segments at the sequence level (similar to the official DAVIS2017 evaluation).

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION

Figure 3 presents several visual results demonstrating the behavior of our LT-MS method in different scenarios. We display sample results from three different videos across the benchmarks. The motion segments produced are generally accurate. Because our method employs multiple masks, it can effectively handle articulated motions (e.g., people2, bmx), manage scenes with several moving objects (people2), separate a rider from their vehicle (bmx, motocross-jump), and accommodate motion parallax. The enforcement of temporal consistency also allows the method to cope with errors in optical flow estimation or with objects that temporarily cease moving (bmx). It is important to remember that our primary target is the Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) task, even though we evaluate on VOS benchmarks. When VOS benchmarks focus on segmenting a single primary foreground object, discrepancies with OFS can arise, which may negatively impact evaluation scores. The segmentation of additional regions that appear incorrect according to VOS ground truth may, in fact, be meaningful from a pure OFS perspective.

Figure 3: Results obtained with our LT-MS-K4 method (K=4). Three groups of results are displayed: 'motocross-jump' from DAVIS2016, 'people02' from FBMS59, and 'bmx' from SegTrackV2. For each group, the first row shows samples of successive flow fields (HSV color code). The second row contains the corresponding video frames, with the ground-truth moving object overlay in yellow (where available). The third row shows the motion segments provided by LT-MS-K4, with a distinct color per segment. For all results, we use the same color set for the three masks corresponding to moving objects (blue, red, orange), while the background mask is left transparent to show the original image.

6 CONCLUSION

We have designed an original, transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions across an entire video in one integrated process. Our LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework to derive its loss function and fully embraces the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first unsupervised network-based OFS method that explicitly yields stable and consistent optical flow segmentation throughout long video sequences. The method introduces, during training, B-spline-based spatio-temporal parametric motion models defined over space-time volumes and a loss term that enforces temporal consistency between successive masks while accounting for occlusions. Our transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of arbitrary temporal length and can accommodate different numbers of masks K through simple fine-tuning. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of our LT-MS method, providing competitive performance. Furthermore, the method is very fast at test time. In future work, we plan to investigate the use of slot attention mechanisms to allow for a variable number of masks at test time without requiring model retraining.
