Title: Unsupervised Motion Segmentation in One Go: A Smooth Long-Term Model Over a Video

Abstract:
Human beings possess the remarkable ability to continuously analyze a video and immediately extract its main motion components. In stark contrast, conventional computer vision methods for motion segmentation typically proceed in a frame-by-frame manner. This work decisively moves beyond that classical paradigm to perform comprehensive motion segmentation over an entire video sequence in a single, unified process. Achieving this capability represents a significant leap forward, offering a prominent added value for a wide array of downstream computer vision tasks and providing a powerful pretext criterion for unsupervised video representation learning. From this perspective, we introduce a novel and original long-term spatio-temporal model that operates in a completely unsupervised fashion. Our model takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flow (OF) fields and delivers a corresponding volume of segments depicting coherent motion throughout the video. More specifically, we have designed a transformer-based network where we leverage the mathematically well-founded Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework to rigorously infer the loss function. This loss function masterfully combines a flow reconstruction term involving innovative spatio-temporal parametric motion models—which uniquely integrate polynomial (quadratic) motion models for the (x, y)-spatial dimensions with B-splines for the temporal dimension of the video sequence—and a dedicated regularization term that explicitly enforces strong temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We report extensive experiments on four established Video Object Segmentation (VOS) benchmarks, achieving convincing and robust quantitative results. We also highlight through detailed visual results the key contributions our method makes regarding superior temporal consistency.

1 INTRODUCTION

When analyzing videos, motion segmentation stands as one of the most fundamental and critical challenges. Human observers can seamlessly and continuously analyze a video stream, instantly extracting its primary motion components. Unfortunately, prevailing computer vision methods usually address this task through a sequential, frame-by-frame approach. We aim to fundamentally transcend this classical paradigm and instead segment the different motion entities present in a video sequence in one holistic, integrated go. We therefore undertake a thorough and deep investigation into the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. Since optical flow (OF) encapsulates all the necessary information regarding movement between consecutive images in a video sequence, it is the natural and optimal foundation upon which to base motion segmentation. While motion segmentation is a vital computer vision task in its own right, it also serves as an essential component for diverse downstream applications such as independent moving object detection, object tracking, and action recognition, to name just a few. It is also extensively leveraged in video object segmentation (VOS), though most often in conjunction with appearance cues.

The optical flow field at a given time *t* enables the segmentation of frame *t*. However, considering a large temporal window—or even the entire video sequence—is profoundly beneficial, as motion entities are generally consistent and persistent throughout a video sequence (or at least within every coherent video shot for longer videos). Indeed, temporal coherence is an inherent and intrinsic property of motion itself. Consequently, it is absolutely essential that any advanced motion segmentation method fully takes advantage of this coherence, particularly from a long-term perspective.

In this paper, we propose an original and holistic method for multiple motion segmentation from optical flow over an entire video sequence. To the best of our knowledge, our Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) method is unequivocally the first fully unsupervised network-based approach to incorporate explicit long-term temporal consistency and to segment multiple motions in a video sequence in one unified pass. The main and definitive contributions of our work are as follows. Our network takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flows and delivers a set of perfectly consistent motion segmentation maps throughout the entire video sequence. It incorporates a transformer module specifically designed to facilitate and model long-term interactions across time. The entire system is trained in a completely unsupervised manner, without any reliance on manual annotation or ground truth data of any kind. The loss function is rigorously inferred by leveraging the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework; it comprises a flow reconstruction term based on our original spatio-temporal parametric motion models and an additional, crucial term that enforces temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We model the long-term temporal evolution of the motion model parameters using B-splines, providing smooth and accurate representations. Our method also involves a latent representation of the segment motion, augmented with positional embedding to capture spatial context.

The rest of this paper is organized in the following manner. Section 2 provides a detailed description of related work in the field of motion segmentation. Section 3 presents our novel unsupervised network for multiple motion segmentation in one go, which explicitly embeds long-term temporal consistency. Section 4 offers comprehensive implementation details. Section 5 reports extensive results on four VOS benchmarks, including a rigorous comparison to state-of-the-art unsupervised motion segmentation methods. Finally, Section 6 contains our concluding remarks and discusses future directions.

2 RELATED WORK

Motion segmentation aims to decompose each frame of a video sequence into components (or segments) exhibiting coherent motion. Typically, each motion segment is identified by a specific motion model, which can be hand-crafted—such as affine or quadratic polynomial models—or learned from data. Motion segmentation has been a subject of investigation for decades (19; 23; 38). However, this section will focus primarily on recent and relevant methods. Given that accurate and efficient methods for estimating optical flow are now readily available, modern motion segmentation methods can reliably leverage optical flow as a robust input. The advent of deep learning in computer vision, and more recently the widespread adoption of transformer-based networks with sophisticated attention mechanisms (11), has also profoundly influenced the development of motion segmentation techniques.

In (35), a transformer module, specifically the slot attention mechanism introduced in (18), is leveraged to perform motion segmentation directly from optical flow. This method, however, addresses a binary segmentation problem, distinguishing only between a foreground moving object and the background. Its loss function is composed of two terms: a flow reconstruction term and an entropy term designed to make the predicted masks as binary as possible. A different approach is adopted in (34), which is capable of handling multiple motion segmentation. This method learns nonlinear subspace filters from stacked deep multi-layer perceptrons, and motion segmentation is then inferred at test time by applying *K*-means clustering to the output embeddings. In (21), the Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework is leveraged to define the loss function and training procedure for an unsupervised, frame-by-frame motion segmentation method that employs 12-parameter quadratic motion models. The same authors proposed an extension of this method in (22) to better handle the temporal dimension by considering triplets of optical flows as input. In (36), the authors developed an adversarial method aimed at generating a mask that hides the input optical flow, where an inpainter network attempts to recover the flow within the masked area. The underlying rationale is that a correct reconstruction of the inside flow from the outside flow is impossible if the hidden area exhibits an independent motion, thereby identifying it as a distinct motion segment.

The temporal dimension of motion segmentation has been considered in various ways (30). Regarding deep learning approaches, motion segmentation at time *t* is improved during training in (35) by taking as input flows between *t* and several time instants both before and after *t*. The authors of (8) consider several consecutive RGB frames as input to their self-supervised method. Optical flow is computed only during training, and their loss function also includes a temporal consistency term. However, this term is not applied between two consecutive segmentation masks, but rather between pairings of the same frame *t* and another, potentially more distant, frame. In (9), spatio-temporal transformers were specifically designed for video object segmentation, incorporating mechanisms for temporal feature propagation.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) typically requires motion segmentation, often coupled with appearance information (5; 10; 37). It has been addressed with supervised or semi-supervised methods, as in (7; 9; 12), but also with unsupervised methods (36; 35; 21). VOS is primarily concerned with the segmentation of so-called primary objects—objects moving in the foreground of a scene, possibly being tracked by the camera (39). Consequently, VOS generally involves binary ground truth that segregates the primary moving object from the background, as is the case for the DAVIS2016 benchmark (26). Recent works have revisited the coupling of appearance and motion for VOS. The AMD method (17) includes two separate pathways: one for appearance and one for motion. While it does not use optical flow as direct input and introduces the concept of objectness, it nevertheless relies on a coarse motion representation. The RCF method (16) involves learnable motion models and is structured in two stages: a motion-supervised object discovery stage, followed by a refinement stage with residual motion prediction and high-level appearance supervision. However, this method cannot distinguish between objects undergoing different motions. In (6), the prediction of probable motion patterns is used during training as a cue to learn objectness from videos. Divided attention is promoted in (14). The resulting DivA method is based on the same principle as (36)—that motion segments are mutually uninformative—but it is not limited to binary segmentation. It can segment a variable number of moving objects from optical flow by leveraging a slot attention mechanism guided by image content through a cross-modal conditional slot decoder.

Our fully unsupervised approach differs from these previous works in several critical and definitive respects. We rely exclusively on optical flow, taking a volume of OF fields as input and providing a corresponding volume of temporally consistent segmentation maps as output. We introduce B-splines to define parametric motion models capable of correctly handling complex motion evolution over time, and we explicitly express long-term temporal consistency within our framework. We rigorously infer the loss function from the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. While the authors of (22) also deal with temporal consistency, they only take a triplet of optical flow fields as input, do not utilize transformers, and model the temporal part of the motion with just a linear (first-order polynomial) model. Furthermore, their temporal linkage of consecutive motion segmentations over a video sequence was implemented as an ad hoc post-processing step. In stark contrast, we define a fully integrated, end-to-end trainable long-term model that is trained in a completely unsupervised manner. We will refer to our method as the LT-MS method (Long-Term Motion Segmentation). For comparison, we will refer to the method from (22) as the ST-MS method (Short-Term Motion Segmentation).

3 LONG-TERM MOTION SEGMENTATION METHOD

We have designed a transformer-based network for multiple motion segmentation directly from optical flow. Our architecture is inspired by the MaskFormer design (4) but comprises only a single head corresponding to mask prediction, as depicted in Figure 1. The network takes as input a volume—of flexible temporal length—comprising several consecutive optical flow fields. Temporal consistency is explicitly expressed in two primary ways during the training stage. First, we associate a dedicated space-time motion model with each segment to characterize its motion and the evolution of that motion over time. Second, the loss function incorporates an additional term that explicitly enforces consistent labeling of the motion segments across the entire input volume.

Figure 1: Overall architecture of our multiple motion segmentation method, which ensures temporal consistency through the loss term ℒ_c and the B-spline space-time motion models θ_k (for k=1,...,K). The network takes as input a volume of T flow fields. It comprises a 3D U-Net (represented by 'e' and 'd' boxes) and a transformer decoder ('t' box). Positional encoding is also incorporated. A cross-attention operation yields the K segmentation masks corresponding to the input volume. For clarity, the block diagram is represented for three motion segments (K=3). ℒ_r denotes the flow-reconstruction loss term.

3.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL PARAMETRIC MOTION MODEL

The set of T consecutive flows is designated as a space-time volume (or simply, a volume). This volume can, in principle, encompass the entire video sequence. Our space-time motion model is estimated through B-spline functions (32). We assign a distinct spatio-temporal parametric motion model f̃_θ_k to each motion segment k (k=1,...,K). Here, θ_k specifies the motion model parameters for segment k. The motion model involves J parameters, and each parameter θ_k_j (j=1,...,J) results from a B-spline function of order n in the temporal variable t over the space-time volume. In practice, we set n=3. The number L of control points is given by L = 2 + ⌊(T-2)/ν⌋, where ν allows us to set the temporal frequency of the control points. We place a control point at both ends of the volume (at t=1 and t=T), and the remaining control points are equidistantly placed between them. Typically, these control points are not located at the exact time points of the video sequence frames.

The space-time spline-based motion model is illustrated in Figure 2. For this illustration only, the motion models are computed within the two segments (foreground moving object and background) provided by the ground truth. The estimated motion model for the foreground moving object successfully captures the periodic nature of the swing motion, as demonstrated by the plots of the computed motion model parameters. Similarly, the motion model computed for the background segment perfectly fits the camera motion. It is important to note that articulated motion (e.g., a person's legs) would require multiple-motion segmentation for accurate representation.

Figure 2: Illustration of the spatiotemporal spline-based motion model. Top row: input flows displayed using the HSV color code for the 'swing' video from the DAVIS2016 dataset, the binary segmentation ground truth, and the flows generated by the estimated spline-based motion models for the two segments. Bottom row: plot of the temporal evolution of the six estimated model parameters corresponding to the flow u-coordinate for the foreground moving object.

Our framework can accommodate any parametric motion model. We employ the 12-parameter quadratic motion model to accurately account for the continuously varying depth surfaces of objects in the scene—especially for the entire background—and to handle complex object or camera motions. In contrast, affine and 8-parameter quadratic motion models assume a planar object surface. The latter model exactly corresponds to the projection into the image of the 3D rigid motion of a planar surface and is equivalent for velocity fields to a homography transform. However, in the presence of severe depth effects (strong depth discontinuities) and camera motion, a static scene cannot be accurately represented by a single motion model due to motion parallax produced by static objects located in the foreground. Considering first the spatial dimension, the 2D flow vector yielded by the full quadratic motion model at point (x, y) is given by:
f̃_θ(x,y) = ( θ₁ + θ₂x + θ₃y + θ₇x² + θ₈xy + θ₉y²,  θ₄ + θ₅x + θ₆y + θ₁₀x² + θ₁₁xy + θ₁₂y² )^T.

To correctly handle complex temporal evolution, we resort to the spline approximation as described. By denoting the subscript of f̃ as S_n(θ_k), we emphasize that the motion model parameters for each segment k are estimated through B-spline functions. More specifically, we have:
f̃_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t) = Σ_{l=1}^{L'} f̃_{θ_{k,l}}(i,t) B_{n,l}(t),
where B_{n,l} is the l-th B-spline basis function and θ_{k,l} corresponds to the l-th control point of the spline function.

3.2 LOSS FUNCTION

We consider a volume of optical flow fields f ∈ ℝ^(2×T×W×H), a spatial grid Ω ∈ ℝ^(W×H), and T temporal steps. We denote f(i,t) ∈ ℝ² as the flow vector associated with site i ∈ Ω at time t. We assume the flow can be decomposed into a set of K segments, each exhibiting coherent motion. Flow vectors within a given segment k are represented by a smooth parametric motion model parameterized by ϑ_k. The variable z_{i,t} conveys the motion segmentation, where z_{i,t}^k = 1 if site (i,t) belongs to segment k. Both z and ϑ = {ϑ_k, k=1,...,K} are treated as latent variables, with f being the observed data. Following (13), we introduce an approximate distribution over the segmentation and motion model parameters:
q(z, ϑ | f) = q(z | f) q(ϑ) = ( Π_{t=1}^T Π_{i∈Ω} Π_{k=1}^K q(z_{i,t}^k | f) ) ( Π_{k=1}^K q(ϑ_k) ),
where q(ϑ_k) ≜ δ(θ_k) with δ being the Dirac delta distribution, and q(z_{i,t}^k | f) = g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k. Here, g_ϕ is our network model that takes the optical flow volume as input and returns a probabilistic segmentation volume.

The data-likelihood over a dataset 𝒟 of optical flow volumes f can be written as:
log p(𝒟) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} log p(f) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log( p(f,z,ϑ) / q(z,ϑ|f) ) ] + KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ|f) ) )
≥ Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] - KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) ),
where we obtain the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Based on our modeling assumptions, we can write the likelihood as:
p(f|z,ϑ) = Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ∝ Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K Π_{i∈Ω} exp( -||f(i,t) - f̃_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t} )^{z_{i,t}^k},
where f̃_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t) is the flow vector given by the parametric motion model with parameters ϑ_k at point (i,t) as defined in Section 3.1 via the spline approximation, and ξ_{f,t} = Σ_i ||f(i,t)||₁ is a normalizing factor. From this likelihood, the first term of the ELBO becomes:
ℒ_r = 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] = Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{k} 𝔼_q[ log p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ]
= - Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{k} g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k ||f(i,t) - f̃_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t}.

The term KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) allows us to incorporate a prior over the segmentation. We aim to enforce the property that segmentation labels are temporally consistent—i.e., similar between neighboring frames. We approximate this term using a temporal consistency loss defined in (22), as it has demonstrated good experimental results and is efficient to compute during training:
ℒ_c = (1/(2K|Ω|)) Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{t=2}^T 𝟙[ ||f_{i,t} - f_{i,t-1}||₁ < λ ] Σ_{k=1}^K | g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k - g_ϕ(f)_{i,t-1}^k |.
The threshold λ allows us to discard areas likely to be occluded. The complete loss function is thus defined as:
Σ_{f∈𝒟} ℒ(f, ϕ, θ) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( ℒ_r(f, ϕ, θ) + β ℒ_c(f, ϕ) ).
We set β = 1. The training procedure alternately updates θ and ϕ with a learning rate α:
For f ∈ 𝒟:  θ* = arg min_θ ℒ(f, ϕ, θ);  ϕ_{t+1} = ϕ_t - α ∇_ϕ ℒ(f, ϕ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE

The overall architecture of our unsupervised multiple motion segmentation framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It consists of two main modules. The first module, which takes the flow volume as input, is a 3D U-Net (29). The latent code from this module, augmented with positional embeddings, is then fed into a transformer decoder. Subsequently, through a cross-attention mechanism, the network produces the final output: a volume of segmentation masks. The entire architecture is trained by minimizing the loss function defined above, while the motion model parameters for the segments are estimated via the B-spline procedure. Temporal consistency is thus ensured both by the dedicated loss term and by the inherent properties of the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

Following established practices in (6; 16; 21; 22; 35), we adopt the RAFT method (31) to compute the optical flow fields. Specifically, we use the RAFT version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset (2). We downsample the computed flow fields to a resolution of 128×224 before feeding them into the network. The output segmentation maps are then upsampled back to the original frame size for evaluation. This strategy allows for both efficient training and inference. We typically use flow volumes of temporal length T = 9 during training. However, at test time, our model can seamlessly process flow volumes of much larger temporal length, including the entire sequence's flow volume. For computing the spatio-temporal parametric motion models, the x and y spatial coordinates are normalized to the range [-1, 1], and a similar normalization is applied to the temporal coordinate t. We employ the full 12-parameter quadratic motion model in all experiments and set ν = 3 for the frequency factor in the B-spline approximation. For each site i, we assign it to the segment k̂ with the highest predicted probability. In Equation (7), we set λ as the 99th quantile of the flow differences over the entire flow volume.

Our LT-MS method is exceptionally efficient at test time. The average computational time reaches 210 frames per second (fps) on a P100 GPU, which is twice as fast as the ST-MS method (22). This speed advantage is certainly due to the long flow sequence provided as input to the network, which allows for greater parallelization of computationally heavy operations. Furthermore, our LT-MS architecture remains lightweight, combining only three U-Net layers and a transformer decoder operating on a downsampled feature space. It is also crucial to emphasize that our LT-MS method does not involve any post-processing whatsoever.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING

We applied two specific types of data augmentation dedicated to optical flow. First, we add a global flow to the input flow, similar to the techniques used in the EM (21) and ST-MS (22) methods. However, in our case, the global flow is defined by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model whose parameters are chosen at random. The same global flow is added to all flow fields within a given input volume. This augmentation mimics diverse camera motions and enforces the property that the identified motion segments are independent of the global camera movement. Additionally, we deliberately corrupt a few of the nine input flows. This simulates poorly estimated flow fields at certain time instants, challenging the model to maintain temporal consistency and overcome these local inaccuracies.

Our motion segmentation method is fully and completely unsupervised. We never use any form of manual annotation. We train our model exclusively on the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset (20), regardless of the dataset used for testing. This approach ensures that our LT-MS network generalizes robustly to unseen datasets. Regarding hyperparameter selection, we determine the stopping epoch based on the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We have conducted comprehensive comparative experiments on four established datasets: DAVIS2016¹ (26), SegTrackV2² (15), FBMS59 (24), and DAVIS2017-motion (33).

5.1 ABLATION STUDY

We performed a detailed ablation study to assess the contribution of three main components of our LT-MS method (with four masks, K=4), particularly those related to the temporal dimension. We modified one component at a time as specified below: 1) We replaced our B-spline-based space-time motion model with the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model from ST-MS (22). 2) We omitted the temporal consistency term ℒ_c from the loss function. 3) We used only the convolutional network (ConvNet) without the transformer decoder. All ablation experiments were run on three datasets: DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. The results are collected in Table 1. Furthermore, we performed these ablations for two different input sequence configurations: input sequences of ten flows, and input sequences of 120 flows (which, in practice, is the entire video for the DAVIS2016 dataset). The results clearly show that all three ablations have a nearly identical negative impact on performance. This demonstrates that the three corresponding model components—the spline-based motion model, the temporal-consistency loss term, and the transformer decoder—are all beneficial and contribute in similar proportions. They are each capable of handling the temporal dimension of the problem and modeling temporal motion evolution along the sequence in a compelling and effective manner. It is worth noting that the contributions of these three components are more pronounced for the FBMS59 and SegTrackV2 datasets. However, the dynamic content of most DAVIS2016 videos, along with the overall high performance scores on this dataset, does not allow us to fully appreciate the individual contributions of these components in that context.

Table 1: Ablation study for three main components of our LT-MS method (K=4) on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Only one model component is modified at a time. Performance scores are given by the Jaccard index 𝒥. We report ablation results for two input-flow sequence lengths (or cut sizes): dividing the video into pieces of ten successive frames, and considering 120 successive frames (effectively the whole video for DAVIS2016).

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION

Table 2 reports the results obtained by two versions of our LT-MS method on the three datasets DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with only two masks (K=2), while LT-MS-K4 involves four masks (K=4). Table 2 also collects results from other existing unsupervised methods, where available. We follow the categorization proposed in (21) regarding input and training. However, we have added a category with respect to network input for four recent methods (6; 8; 16; 17) that use only RGB images as input at test time, with optical flow being involved only in the loss function during training. Evaluation is performed against binary ground truth (foreground moving object vs. background) for all three datasets. We classify the OCLR method (33) in the category of unsupervised methods, although the authors of the DivA method (14) did not, as OCLR relies on human-annotated sprites to include realistic shapes in its computer-generated training data. We consider the OCLR version that takes only optical flow as input. The post-processing added to the CIS method (36), based on Conditional Random Fields (CRF), is computationally heavy, leading most authors to compare only the version without post-processing for a fair assessment.

As clearly shown in Table 2, our LT-MS method delivers very convincing and robust results, both for LT-MS-K2 and LT-MS-K4, within the category of unsupervised methods based solely on optical flow. OCLR and DivA demonstrate slightly better performance on the SegTrackV2 dataset. However, as noted, OCLR is not a fully unsupervised method, and DivA leverages RGB images in its conditional decoder. Furthermore, DivA, along with the MoSeg and CIS methods, takes multi-step flows as input (between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2) and averages the four corresponding predictions to obtain the final result. SegTrackV2 includes sequences captured with poorly controlled handheld cameras, resulting in unstable footage where the advantages of our method's long-term consistency are less pronounced.

Overall, our LT-MS method successfully and properly handles temporal consistency over extended temporal periods. Beyond raw segmentation performance metrics, we must emphasize that our method is uniquely designed to provide, by its very architecture, a coherent segmentation across the entire sequence. This represents a significant and definitive added value. Thus, we can confidently claim that we have not only segmented the moving objects throughout the sequence but have also effectively achieved a form of implicit tracking.

Table 2: Results obtained with two versions of our LT-MS method on DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with two masks (K=2), and LT-MS-K4 involves four masks (K=4). We include comparisons with other unsupervised methods (scores from cited articles). All scores correspond to evaluation on binary ground-truth. For LT-MS-K4 and LT-MS-K2, we report results obtained with a cut size of 10. The Jaccard index 𝒥 is the intersection over union between the extracted segments and the ground truth, while ℱ focuses on segment boundary accuracy. Performance is assessed by the average score over all samples for all datasets except DAVIS2016. For DAVIS2016, the overall score is the average of per-sequence scores. *The classification of OCLR as an unsupervised method can be questioned (see main text). †DivA uses RGB input indirectly since its conditional decoder leverages input images.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION

We have also performed an evaluation of multiple motion segmentation in a multi-segment setting. Since segmenting multiple motions is inherently more challenging than binary segmentation, accuracy scores are expected to decrease for all methods. Table 3 reports comparative results on the DAVIS2017-motion dataset and on FBMS59. Similar to other methods, we performed segmentation with three masks. To achieve this, we fine-tuned the LT-MS-K4 network on the DAVIS2016 training set, now configured for three masks (K=3). The resulting performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than that of ST-MS (22) and significantly better than MoSeg. The same caveat regarding OCLR's status as an unsupervised method applies here. For FBMS59, we report multi-mask segmentation results using two different metrics. Our LT-MS method outperforms DivA (14)—which also attempted multi-segment evaluation on FBMS59—by a substantial margin.

Table 3: Multi-segment evaluation. For DAVIS2017-motion, 𝒥&ℱ is the mean of the two metrics. Evaluation is performed on the video as a whole according to the official DAVIS2017 scheme. Reported scores are the average of individual video scores. *See caption of Table 2. For FBMS59, the two evaluation metrics are bootstrap IoU (bIoU) (14)—where each ground-truth mask is mapped to the most likely predicted segment at the frame level—and linear assignment, which is a bilinear mapping between ground-truth and predicted segments at the sequence level (similar to the official DAVIS2017 evaluation).

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION

Figure 3 presents several visual results that demonstrate the behavior of our LT-MS method in different scenarios. We display three result samples obtained from different videos across the benchmarks. The results clearly show that the identified motion segments are globally accurate. Since our method utilizes multiple masks, it can properly handle articulated motions (e.g., people2, bmx), deal with the presence of several moving objects in the scene (people2), separate a rider from their bike or motorbike (bmx, motocross-jump), and accommodate motion parallax effects. Furthermore, because our method explicitly enforces temporal consistency, it can robustly deal with errors in optical flow estimation and with objects that momentarily stop moving (bmx). It is important to keep in mind that our primary target is the Optical-Flow Segmentation (OFS) task, even though we evaluate on VOS benchmarks. When VOS benchmarks focus on segmenting a single primary object moving in the foreground, discrepancies with OFS can occur, which may negatively impact evaluation scores. The segmentation of additional parts that appear incorrect with respect to VOS ground truth can, in fact, be perfectly sensible from a pure OFS perspective.

Figure 3: Results obtained with our LT-MS-K4 method (K=4). Three groups of results are displayed: motocross-jump from DAVIS2016, people02 from FBMS59, and bmx from SegTrackV2. For each group, the first row samples successive flow fields (using HSV color code) from the processed video. The second row contains the corresponding video images, with the ground-truth of the moving object overlaid in yellow (where available for that frame). The third row shows the motion segments provided by our LT-MS-K4 method, with a distinct color assigned to each segment. For all results, we use the same color set for the three masks corresponding to moving objects (blue, red, and orange) and leave the background image for the background mask.

6 CONCLUSION

We have designed an original and novel transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions over an entire video in one unified process. Our LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework to derive a rigorous loss function and fully acknowledges the critical importance of the temporal dimension in motion segmentation. Indeed, to the best of our knowledge, our method is unequivocally the first unsupervised network-based OFS method that explicitly leads to stable and consistent optical flow segmentation throughout long video sequences. It introduces, during training, two key innovations: B-spline-based spatio-temporal parametric motion models defined over space-time volumes, and a dedicated loss term that expresses strong temporal consistency over successive masks while intelligently accounting for occlusions. Our transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of any temporal length and can accommodate different choices for the number K of masks through a simple fine-tuning step. Extensive experimental results on several established datasets convincingly demonstrate the efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of our LT-MS method, providing highly competitive results. Furthermore, the method is exceptionally fast at test time. In future work, we plan to investigate the integration of slot attention mechanisms to allow dynamic modification of the number of masks at test time without requiring model retraining.

Title: Unsupervised Motion Segmentation in One Go: A Smooth Long-Term Model Over a Video

Abstract:
Human beings possess the remarkable ability to continuously analyze a video and immediately extract its main motion components. In stark contrast, conventional computer vision methods for motion segmentation typically proceed in a frame-by-frame manner. This work decisively moves beyond that classical paradigm to perform comprehensive motion segmentation over an entire video sequence in a single, unified process. Achieving this capability represents a significant leap forward, offering a prominent added value for a wide array of downstream computer vision tasks and providing a powerful pretext criterion for unsupervised video representation learning. From this perspective, we introduce a novel and original long-term spatio-temporal model that operates in a completely unsupervised fashion. Our model takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flow (OF) fields and delivers a corresponding volume of segments depicting coherent motion throughout the video. More specifically, we have designed a transformer-based network where we leverage the mathematically well-founded Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework to rigorously infer the loss function. This loss function masterfully combines a flow reconstruction term involving innovative spatio-temporal parametric motion models—which uniquely integrate polynomial (quadratic) motion models for the (x, y)-spatial dimensions with B-splines for the temporal dimension of the video sequence—and a dedicated regularization term that explicitly enforces strong temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We report extensive experiments on four established Video Object Segmentation (VOS) benchmarks, achieving convincing and robust quantitative results. We also highlight through detailed visual results the key contributions our method makes regarding superior temporal consistency.

1 INTRODUCTION

When analyzing videos, motion segmentation stands as one of the most fundamental and critical challenges. Human observers can seamlessly and continuously analyze a video stream, instantly extracting its primary motion components. Unfortunately, prevailing computer vision methods usually address this task through a sequential, frame-by-frame approach. We aim to fundamentally transcend this classical paradigm and instead segment the different motion entities present in a video sequence in one holistic, integrated go. We therefore undertake a thorough and deep investigation into the temporal dimension of the motion segmentation problem. Since optical flow (OF) encapsulates all the necessary information regarding movement between consecutive images in a video sequence, it is the natural and optimal foundation upon which to base motion segmentation. While motion segmentation is a vital computer vision task in its own right, it also serves as an essential component for diverse downstream applications such as independent moving object detection, object tracking, and action recognition, to name just a few. It is also extensively leveraged in video object segmentation (VOS), though most often in conjunction with appearance cues.

The optical flow field at a given time *t* enables the segmentation of frame *t*. However, considering a large temporal window—or even the entire video sequence—is profoundly beneficial, as motion entities are generally consistent and persistent throughout a video sequence (or at least within every coherent video shot for longer videos). Indeed, temporal coherence is an inherent and intrinsic property of motion itself. Consequently, it is absolutely essential that any advanced motion segmentation method fully takes advantage of this coherence, particularly from a long-term perspective.

In this paper, we propose an original and holistic method for multiple motion segmentation from optical flow over an entire video sequence. To the best of our knowledge, our Optical Flow Segmentation (OFS) method is unequivocally the first fully unsupervised network-based approach to incorporate explicit long-term temporal consistency and to segment multiple motions in a video sequence in one unified pass. The main and definitive contributions of our work are as follows. Our network takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flows and delivers a set of perfectly consistent motion segmentation maps throughout the entire video sequence. It incorporates a transformer module specifically designed to facilitate and model long-term interactions across time. The entire system is trained in a completely unsupervised manner, without any reliance on manual annotation or ground truth data of any kind. The loss function is rigorously inferred by leveraging the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework; it comprises a flow reconstruction term based on our original spatio-temporal parametric motion models and an additional, crucial term that enforces temporal consistency on the segmentation masks. We model the long-term temporal evolution of the motion model parameters using B-splines, providing smooth and accurate representations. Our method also involves a latent representation of the segment motion, augmented with positional embedding to capture spatial context.

The rest of this paper is organized in the following manner. Section 2 provides a detailed description of related work in the field of motion segmentation. Section 3 presents our novel unsupervised network for multiple motion segmentation in one go, which explicitly embeds long-term temporal consistency. Section 4 offers comprehensive implementation details. Section 5 reports extensive results on four VOS benchmarks, including a rigorous comparison to state-of-the-art unsupervised motion segmentation methods. Finally, Section 6 contains our concluding remarks and discusses future directions.

2 RELATED WORK

Motion segmentation aims to decompose each frame of a video sequence into components (or segments) exhibiting coherent motion. Typically, each motion segment is identified by a specific motion model, which can be hand-crafted—such as affine or quadratic polynomial models—or learned from data. Motion segmentation has been a subject of investigation for decades (19; 23; 38). However, this section will focus primarily on recent and relevant methods. Given that accurate and efficient methods for estimating optical flow are now readily available, modern motion segmentation methods can reliably leverage optical flow as a robust input. The advent of deep learning in computer vision, and more recently the widespread adoption of transformer-based networks with sophisticated attention mechanisms (11), has also profoundly influenced the development of motion segmentation techniques.

In (35), a transformer module, specifically the slot attention mechanism introduced in (18), is leveraged to perform motion segmentation directly from optical flow. This method, however, addresses a binary segmentation problem, distinguishing only between a foreground moving object and the background. Its loss function is composed of two terms: a flow reconstruction term and an entropy term designed to make the predicted masks as binary as possible. A different approach is adopted in (34), which is capable of handling multiple motion segmentation. This method learns nonlinear subspace filters from stacked deep multi-layer perceptrons, and motion segmentation is then inferred at test time by applying *K*-means clustering to the output embeddings. In (21), the Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework is leveraged to define the loss function and training procedure for an unsupervised, frame-by-frame motion segmentation method that employs 12-parameter quadratic motion models. The same authors proposed an extension of this method in (22) to better handle the temporal dimension by considering triplets of optical flows as input. In (36), the authors developed an adversarial method aimed at generating a mask that hides the input optical flow, where an inpainter network attempts to recover the flow within the masked area. The underlying rationale is that a correct reconstruction of the inside flow from the outside flow is impossible if the hidden area exhibits an independent motion, thereby identifying it as a distinct motion segment.

The temporal dimension of motion segmentation has been considered in various ways (30). Regarding deep learning approaches, motion segmentation at time *t* is improved during training in (35) by taking as input flows between *t* and several time instants both before and after *t*. The authors of (8) consider several consecutive RGB frames as input to their self-supervised method. Optical flow is computed only during training, and their loss function also includes a temporal consistency term. However, this term is not applied between two consecutive segmentation masks, but rather between pairings of the same frame *t* and another, potentially more distant, frame. In (9), spatio-temporal transformers were specifically designed for video object segmentation, incorporating mechanisms for temporal feature propagation.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) typically requires motion segmentation, often coupled with appearance information (5; 10; 37). It has been addressed with supervised or semi-supervised methods, as in (7; 9; 12), but also with unsupervised methods (36; 35; 21). VOS is primarily concerned with the segmentation of so-called primary objects—objects moving in the foreground of a scene, possibly being tracked by the camera (39). Consequently, VOS generally involves binary ground truth that segregates the primary moving object from the background, as is the case for the DAVIS2016 benchmark (26). Recent works have revisited the coupling of appearance and motion for VOS. The AMD method (17) includes two separate pathways: one for appearance and one for motion. While it does not use optical flow as direct input and introduces the concept of objectness, it nevertheless relies on a coarse motion representation. The RCF method (16) involves learnable motion models and is structured in two stages: a motion-supervised object discovery stage, followed by a refinement stage with residual motion prediction and high-level appearance supervision. However, this method cannot distinguish between objects undergoing different motions. In (6), the prediction of probable motion patterns is used during training as a cue to learn objectness from videos. Divided attention is promoted in (14). The resulting DivA method is based on the same principle as (36)—that motion segments are mutually uninformative—but it is not limited to binary segmentation. It can segment a variable number of moving objects from optical flow by leveraging a slot attention mechanism guided by image content through a cross-modal conditional slot decoder.

Our fully unsupervised approach differs from these previous works in several critical and definitive respects. We rely exclusively on optical flow, taking a volume of OF fields as input and providing a corresponding volume of temporally consistent segmentation maps as output. We introduce B-splines to define parametric motion models capable of correctly handling complex motion evolution over time, and we explicitly express long-term temporal consistency within our framework. We rigorously infer the loss function from the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. While the authors of (22) also deal with temporal consistency, they only take a triplet of optical flow fields as input, do not utilize transformers, and model the temporal part of the motion with just a linear (first-order polynomial) model. Furthermore, their temporal linkage of consecutive motion segmentations over a video sequence was implemented as an ad hoc post-processing step. In stark contrast, we define a fully integrated, end-to-end trainable long-term model that is trained in a completely unsupervised manner. We will refer to our method as the LT-MS method (Long-Term Motion Segmentation). For comparison, we will refer to the method from (22) as the ST-MS method (Short-Term Motion Segmentation).

3 LONG-TERM MOTION SEGMENTATION METHOD

We have designed a transformer-based network for multiple motion segmentation directly from optical flow. Our architecture is inspired by the MaskFormer design (4) but comprises only a single head corresponding to mask prediction, as depicted in Figure 1. The network takes as input a volume—of flexible temporal length—comprising several consecutive optical flow fields. Temporal consistency is explicitly expressed in two primary ways during the training stage. First, we associate a dedicated space-time motion model with each segment to characterize its motion and the evolution of that motion over time. Second, the loss function incorporates an additional term that explicitly enforces consistent labeling of the motion segments across the entire input volume.

Figure 1: Overall architecture of our multiple motion segmentation method, which ensures temporal consistency through the loss term ℒ_c and the B-spline space-time motion models θ_k (for k=1,...,K). The network takes as input a volume of T flow fields. It comprises a 3D U-Net (represented by 'e' and 'd' boxes) and a transformer decoder ('t' box). Positional encoding is also incorporated. A cross-attention operation yields the K segmentation masks corresponding to the input volume. For clarity, the block diagram is represented for three motion segments (K=3). ℒ_r denotes the flow-reconstruction loss term.

3.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL PARAMETRIC MOTION MODEL

The set of T consecutive flows is designated as a space-time volume (or simply, a volume). This volume can, in principle, encompass the entire video sequence. Our space-time motion model is estimated through B-spline functions (32). We assign a distinct spatio-temporal parametric motion model f̃_θ_k to each motion segment k (k=1,...,K). Here, θ_k specifies the motion model parameters for segment k. The motion model involves J parameters, and each parameter θ_k_j (j=1,...,J) results from a B-spline function of order n in the temporal variable t over the space-time volume. In practice, we set n=3. The number L of control points is given by L = 2 + ⌊(T-2)/ν⌋, where ν allows us to set the temporal frequency of the control points. We place a control point at both ends of the volume (at t=1 and t=T), and the remaining control points are equidistantly placed between them. Typically, these control points are not located at the exact time points of the video sequence frames.

The space-time spline-based motion model is illustrated in Figure 2. For this illustration only, the motion models are computed within the two segments (foreground moving object and background) provided by the ground truth. The estimated motion model for the foreground moving object successfully captures the periodic nature of the swing motion, as demonstrated by the plots of the computed motion model parameters. Similarly, the motion model computed for the background segment perfectly fits the camera motion. It is important to note that articulated motion (e.g., a person's legs) would require multiple-motion segmentation for accurate representation.

Figure 2: Illustration of the spatiotemporal spline-based motion model. Top row: input flows displayed using the HSV color code for the 'swing' video from the DAVIS2016 dataset, the binary segmentation ground truth, and the flows generated by the estimated spline-based motion models for the two segments. Bottom row: plot of the temporal evolution of the six estimated model parameters corresponding to the flow u-coordinate for the foreground moving object.

Our framework can accommodate any parametric motion model. We employ the 12-parameter quadratic motion model to accurately account for the continuously varying depth surfaces of objects in the scene—especially for the entire background—and to handle complex object or camera motions. In contrast, affine and 8-parameter quadratic motion models assume a planar object surface. The latter model exactly corresponds to the projection into the image of the 3D rigid motion of a planar surface and is equivalent for velocity fields to a homography transform. However, in the presence of severe depth effects (strong depth discontinuities) and camera motion, a static scene cannot be accurately represented by a single motion model due to motion parallax produced by static objects located in the foreground. Considering first the spatial dimension, the 2D flow vector yielded by the full quadratic motion model at point (x, y) is given by:
f̃_θ(x,y) = ( θ₁ + θ₂x + θ₃y + θ₇x² + θ₈xy + θ₉y²,  θ₄ + θ₅x + θ₆y + θ₁₀x² + θ₁₁xy + θ₁₂y² )^T.

To correctly handle complex temporal evolution, we resort to the spline approximation as described. By denoting the subscript of f̃ as S_n(θ_k), we emphasize that the motion model parameters for each segment k are estimated through B-spline functions. More specifically, we have:
f̃_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t) = Σ_{l=1}^{L'} f̃_{θ_{k,l}}(i,t) B_{n,l}(t),
where B_{n,l} is the l-th B-spline basis function and θ_{k,l} corresponds to the l-th control point of the spline function.

3.2 LOSS FUNCTION

We consider a volume of optical flow fields f ∈ ℝ^(2×T×W×H), a spatial grid Ω ∈ ℝ^(W×H), and T temporal steps. We denote f(i,t) ∈ ℝ² as the flow vector associated with site i ∈ Ω at time t. We assume the flow can be decomposed into a set of K segments, each exhibiting coherent motion. Flow vectors within a given segment k are represented by a smooth parametric motion model parameterized by ϑ_k. The variable z_{i,t} conveys the motion segmentation, where z_{i,t}^k = 1 if site (i,t) belongs to segment k. Both z and ϑ = {ϑ_k, k=1,...,K} are treated as latent variables, with f being the observed data. Following (13), we introduce an approximate distribution over the segmentation and motion model parameters:
q(z, ϑ | f) = q(z | f) q(ϑ) = ( Π_{t=1}^T Π_{i∈Ω} Π_{k=1}^K q(z_{i,t}^k | f) ) ( Π_{k=1}^K q(ϑ_k) ),
where q(ϑ_k) ≜ δ(θ_k) with δ being the Dirac delta distribution, and q(z_{i,t}^k | f) = g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k. Here, g_ϕ is our network model that takes the optical flow volume as input and returns a probabilistic segmentation volume.

The data-likelihood over a dataset 𝒟 of optical flow volumes f can be written as:
log p(𝒟) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} log p(f) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log( p(f,z,ϑ) / q(z,ϑ|f) ) ] + KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ|f) ) )
≥ Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] - KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) ),
where we obtain the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Based on our modeling assumptions, we can write the likelihood as:
p(f|z,ϑ) = Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ∝ Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K Π_{i∈Ω} exp( -||f(i,t) - f̃_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t} )^{z_{i,t}^k},
where f̃_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t) is the flow vector given by the parametric motion model with parameters ϑ_k at point (i,t) as defined in Section 3.1 via the spline approximation, and ξ_{f,t} = Σ_i ||f(i,t)||₁ is a normalizing factor. From this likelihood, the first term of the ELBO becomes:
ℒ_r = 𝔼_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] = Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{k} 𝔼_q[ log p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ]
= - Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{k} g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k ||f(i,t) - f̃_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t)||₁ / ξ_{f,t}.

The term KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) allows us to incorporate a prior over the segmentation. We aim to enforce the property that segmentation labels are temporally consistent—i.e., similar between neighboring frames. We approximate this term using a temporal consistency loss defined in (22), as it has demonstrated good experimental results and is efficient to compute during training:
ℒ_c = (1/(2K|Ω|)) Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{t=2}^T 𝟙[ ||f_{i,t} - f_{i,t-1}||₁ < λ ] Σ_{k=1}^K | g_ϕ(f)_{i,t}^k - g_ϕ(f)_{i,t-1}^k |.
The threshold λ allows us to discard areas likely to be occluded. The complete loss function is thus defined as:
Σ_{f∈𝒟} ℒ(f, ϕ, θ) = Σ_{f∈𝒟} ( ℒ_r(f, ϕ, θ) + β ℒ_c(f, ϕ) ).
We set β = 1. The training procedure alternately updates θ and ϕ with a learning rate α:
For f ∈ 𝒟:  θ* = arg min_θ ℒ(f, ϕ, θ);  ϕ_{t+1} = ϕ_t - α ∇_ϕ ℒ(f, ϕ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE

The overall architecture of our unsupervised multiple motion segmentation framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It consists of two main modules. The first module, which takes the flow volume as input, is a 3D U-Net (29). The latent code from this module, augmented with positional embeddings, is then fed into a transformer decoder. Subsequently, through a cross-attention mechanism, the network produces the final output: a volume of segmentation masks. The entire architecture is trained by minimizing the loss function defined above, while the motion model parameters for the segments are estimated via the B-spline procedure. Temporal consistency is thus ensured both by the dedicated loss term and by the inherent properties of the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION

4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

Following established practices in (6; 16; 21; 22; 35), we adopt the RAFT method (31) to compute the optical flow fields. Specifically, we use the RAFT version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset (2). We downsample the computed flow fields to a resolution of 128×224 before feeding them into the network. The output segmentation maps are then upsampled back to the original frame size for evaluation. This strategy allows for both efficient training and inference. We typically use flow volumes of temporal length T = 9 during training. However, at test time, our model can seamlessly process flow volumes of much larger temporal length, including the entire sequence's flow volume. For computing the spatio-temporal parametric motion models, the x and y spatial coordinates are normalized to the range [-1, 1], and a similar normalization is applied to the temporal coordinate t. We employ the full 12-parameter quadratic motion model in all experiments and set ν = 3 for the frequency factor in the B-spline approximation. For each site i, we assign it to the segment k̂ with the highest predicted probability. In Equation (7), we set λ as the 99th quantile of the flow differences over the entire flow volume.

Our LT-MS method is exceptionally efficient at test time. The average computational time reaches 210 frames per second (fps) on a P100 GPU, which is twice as fast as the ST-MS method (22). This speed advantage is certainly due to the long flow sequence provided as input to the network, which allows for greater parallelization of computationally heavy operations. Furthermore, our LT-MS architecture remains lightweight, combining only three U-Net layers and a transformer decoder operating on a downsampled feature space. It is also crucial to emphasize that our LT-MS method does not involve any post-processing whatsoever.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING

We applied two specific types of data augmentation dedicated to optical flow. First, we add a global flow to the input flow, similar to the techniques used in the EM (21) and ST-MS (22) methods. However, in our case, the global flow is defined by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model whose parameters are chosen at random. The same global flow is added to all flow fields within a given input volume. This augmentation mimics diverse camera motions and enforces the property that the identified motion segments are independent of the global camera movement. Additionally, we deliberately corrupt a few of the nine input flows. This simulates poorly estimated flow fields at certain time instants, challenging the model to maintain temporal consistency and overcome these local inaccuracies.

Our motion segmentation method is fully and completely unsupervised. We never use any form of manual annotation. We train our model exclusively on the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset (20), regardless of the dataset used for testing. This approach ensures that our LT-MS network generalizes robustly to unseen datasets. Regarding hyperparameter selection, we determine the stopping epoch based on the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We have conducted comprehensive comparative experiments on four established datasets: DAVIS2016¹ (26), SegTrackV2² (15), FBMS59 (24), and DAVIS2017-motion (33).

5.1 ABLATION STUDY

We performed a detailed ablation study to assess the contribution of three main components of our LT-MS method (with four masks, K=4), particularly those related to the temporal dimension. We modified one component at a time as specified below: 1) We replaced our B-spline-based space-time motion model with the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model from ST-MS (22). 2) We omitted the temporal consistency term ℒ_c from the loss function. 3) We used only the convolutional network (ConvNet) without the transformer decoder. All ablation experiments were run on three datasets: DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. The results are collected in Table 1. Furthermore, we performed these ablations for two different input sequence configurations: input sequences of ten flows, and input sequences of 120 flows (which, in practice, is the entire video for the DAVIS2016 dataset). The results clearly show that all three ablations have a nearly identical negative impact on performance. This demonstrates that the three corresponding model components—the spline-based motion model, the temporal-consistency loss term, and the transformer decoder—are all beneficial and contribute in similar proportions. They are each capable of handling the temporal dimension of the problem and modeling temporal motion evolution along the sequence in a compelling and effective manner. It is worth noting that the contributions of these three components are more pronounced for the FBMS59 and SegTrackV2 datasets. However, the dynamic content of most DAVIS2016 videos, along with the overall high performance scores on this dataset, does not allow us to fully appreciate the individual contributions of these components in that context.

Table 1: Ablation study for three main components of our LT-MS method (K=4) on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, and SegTrackV2. Only one model component is modified at a time. Performance scores are given by the Jaccard index 𝒥. We report ablation results for two input-flow sequence lengths (or cut sizes): dividing the video into pieces of ten successive frames, and considering 120 successive frames (effectively the whole video for DAVIS2016).

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION

Table 2 reports the results obtained by two versions of our LT-MS method on the three datasets DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with only two masks (K=2), while LT-MS-K4 involves four masks (K=4). Table 2 also collects results from other existing unsupervised methods, where available. We follow the categorization proposed in (21) regarding input and training. However, we have added a category with respect to network input for four recent methods (6; 8; 16; 17) that use only RGB images as input at test time, with optical flow being involved only in the loss function during training. Evaluation is performed against binary ground truth (foreground moving object vs. background) for all three datasets. We classify the OCLR method (33) in the category of unsupervised methods, although the authors of the DivA method (14) did not, as OCLR relies on human-annotated sprites to include realistic shapes in its computer-generated training data. We consider the OCLR version that takes only optical flow as input. The post-processing added to the CIS method (36), based on Conditional Random Fields (CRF), is computationally heavy, leading most authors to compare only the version without post-processing for a fair assessment.

As clearly shown in Table 2, our LT-MS method delivers very convincing and robust results, both for LT-MS-K2 and LT-MS-K4, within the category of unsupervised methods based solely on optical flow. OCLR and DivA demonstrate slightly better performance on the SegTrackV2 dataset. However, as noted, OCLR is not a fully unsupervised method, and DivA leverages RGB images in its conditional decoder. Furthermore, DivA, along with the MoSeg and CIS methods, takes multi-step flows as input (between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2) and averages the four corresponding predictions to obtain the final result. SegTrackV2 includes sequences captured with poorly controlled handheld cameras, resulting in unstable footage where the advantages of our method's long-term consistency are less pronounced.

Overall, our LT-MS method successfully and properly handles temporal consistency over extended temporal periods. Beyond raw segmentation performance metrics, we must emphasize that our method is uniquely designed to provide, by its very architecture, a coherent segmentation across the entire sequence. This represents a significant and definitive added value. Thus, we can confidently claim that we have not only segmented the moving objects throughout the sequence but have also effectively achieved a form of implicit tracking.

Table 2: Results obtained with two versions of our LT-MS method on DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 performs segmentation with two masks (K=2), and LT-MS-K4 involves four masks (K=4). We include comparisons with other unsupervised methods (scores from cited articles). All scores correspond to evaluation on binary ground-truth. For LT-MS-K4 and LT-MS-K2, we report results obtained with a cut size of 10. The Jaccard index 𝒥 is the intersection over union between the extracted segments and the ground truth, while ℱ focuses on segment boundary accuracy. Performance is assessed by the average score over all samples for all datasets except DAVIS2016. For DAVIS2016, the overall score is the average of per-sequence scores. *The classification of OCLR as an unsupervised method can be questioned (see main text). †DivA uses RGB input indirectly since its conditional decoder leverages input images.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION

We have also performed an evaluation of multiple motion segmentation in a multi-segment setting. Since segmenting multiple motions is inherently more challenging than binary segmentation, accuracy scores are expected to decrease for all methods. Table 3 reports comparative results on the DAVIS2017-motion dataset and on FBMS59. Similar to other methods, we performed segmentation with three masks. To achieve this, we fine-tuned the LT-MS-K4 network on the DAVIS2016 training set, now configured for three masks (K=3). The resulting performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than that of ST-MS (22) and significantly better than MoSeg. The same caveat regarding OCLR's status as an unsupervised method applies here. For FBMS59, we report multi-mask segmentation results using two different metrics. Our LT-MS method outperforms DivA (14)—which also attempted multi-segment evaluation on FBMS59—by a substantial margin.

Table 3: Multi-segment evaluation. For DAVIS2017-motion, 𝒥&ℱ is the mean of the two metrics. Evaluation is performed on the video as a whole according to the official DAVIS2017 scheme. Reported scores are the average of individual video scores. *See caption of Table 2. For FBMS59, the two evaluation metrics are bootstrap IoU (bIoU) (14)—where each ground-truth mask is mapped to the most likely predicted segment at the frame level—and linear assignment, which is a bilinear mapping between ground-truth and predicted segments at the sequence level (similar to the official DAVIS2017 evaluation).

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION

Figure 3 presents several visual results that demonstrate the behavior of our LT-MS method in different scenarios. We display three result samples obtained from different videos across the benchmarks. The results clearly show that the identified motion segments are globally accurate. Since our method utilizes multiple masks, it can properly handle articulated motions (e.g., people2, bmx), deal with the presence of several moving objects in the scene (people2), separate a rider from their bike or motorbike (bmx, motocross-jump), and accommodate motion parallax effects. Furthermore, because our method explicitly enforces temporal consistency, it can robustly deal with errors in optical flow estimation and with objects that momentarily stop moving (bmx). It is important to keep in mind that our primary target is the Optical-Flow Segmentation (OFS) task, even though we evaluate on VOS benchmarks. When VOS benchmarks focus on segmenting a single primary object moving in the foreground, discrepancies with OFS can occur, which may negatively impact evaluation scores. The segmentation of additional parts that appear incorrect with respect to VOS ground truth can, in fact, be perfectly sensible from a pure OFS perspective.

Figure 3: Results obtained with our LT-MS-K4 method (K=4). Three groups of results are displayed: motocross-jump from DAVIS2016, people02 from FBMS59, and bmx from SegTrackV2. For each group, the first row samples successive flow fields (using HSV color code) from the processed video. The second row contains the corresponding video images, with the ground-truth of the moving object overlaid in yellow (where available for that frame). The third row shows the motion segments provided by our LT-MS-K4 method, with a distinct color assigned to each segment. For all results, we use the same color set for the three masks corresponding to moving objects (blue, red, and orange) and leave the background image for the background mask.

6 CONCLUSION

We have designed an original and novel transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions over an entire video in one unified process. Our LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework to derive a rigorous loss function and fully acknowledges the critical importance of the temporal dimension in motion segmentation. Indeed, to the best of our knowledge, our method is unequivocally the first unsupervised network-based OFS method that explicitly leads to stable and consistent optical flow segmentation throughout long video sequences. It introduces, during training, two key innovations: B-spline-based spatio-temporal parametric motion models defined over space-time volumes, and a dedicated loss term that expresses strong temporal consistency over successive masks while intelligently accounting for occlusions. Our transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of any temporal length and can accommodate different choices for the number K of masks through a simple fine-tuning step. Extensive experimental results on several established datasets convincingly demonstrate the efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of our LT-MS method, providing highly competitive results. Furthermore, the method is exceptionally fast at test time. In future work, we plan to investigate the integration of slot attention mechanisms to allow dynamic modification of the number of masks at test time without requiring model retraining.
