Title: Unsupervised motion segmentation over a video sequence

Abstract:
Motion segmentation methods often proceed frame by frame. This work investigates performing motion segmentation over a video sequence in one go. A long-term spatio-temporal model operating in an unsupervised way is proposed. It takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flow fields and delivers a volume of segments of coherent motion over the video. The method uses a transformer-based network. The loss function is inferred using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. The loss combines a flow reconstruction term involving spatio-temporal parametric motion models and a regularization term enforcing temporal consistency on the masks. The motion models combine polynomial (quadratic) models for the spatial dimensions and B-splines for the time dimension. Experiments are reported on four VOS benchmarks.

1 INTRODUCTION
Motion segmentation is a key issue when dealing with videos. Computer vision methods usually proceed frame by frame. This work aims to segment different motion entities in a video sequence in one go, investigating the temporal dimension of the problem. Motion segmentation is based on optical flow. It is a task in its own and is also useful for downstream tasks like object tracking or action recognition. It is leveraged in video object segmentation, often coupled with appearance.

Taking a large time window, or the whole video sequence, is beneficial as motion entities are generally consistent throughout a sequence. Temporal coherence is inherent to motion. It is essential that motion segmentation takes advantage of it.

This paper proposes a method for multiple motion segmentation from optical flow over a video sequence. The method is fully unsupervised and involves long-term temporal consistency. The network takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flows and delivers consistent motion segmentation maps. It involves a transformer module. The loss function is inferred using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) framework. It comprises a flow reconstruction term with spatio-temporal parametric motion models and a term enforcing temporal consistency on the masks. The temporal evolution of the motion model parameters is modeled with B-splines. The method involves a latent representation of the segment motion augmented with positional embedding.

2 RELATED WORK
Motion segmentation aims to break down each frame into components of coherent motion. Each segment is identified by a motion model, which can be hand-crafted or learned. Recent methods leverage optical flow and deep learning.

In [35], a transformer module with slot attention performs binary motion segmentation from optical flow. The loss has a flow reconstruction term and an entropy term. In [34], nonlinear subspace filters are learned for multiple motion segmentation. In [21], the Expectation-Maximization framework defines a loss for unsupervised frame-by-frame segmentation using 12-parameter quadratic models. An extension in [22] considers triplets of flows as input. In [36], an adversarial method generates a mask hiding the input optical flow, with an inpainter network attempting recovery.

The temporal dimension has been considered in various ways. In [35], segmentation at time t uses flows between t and several time instants. In [8], several consecutive RGB frames are input; optical flow is computed at training time and the loss includes a temporal consistency term. In [9], spatio-temporal transformers were designed for video object segmentation.

VOS usually requires motion segmentation, often coupled with appearance [5, 10, 37]. It has been addressed with supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised methods [36, 35, 21]. VOS is concerned with segmenting primary objects. Recent works include AMD [17] with appearance and motion pathways, RCF [16] with learnable motion models, and DivA [14] which segments a variable number of moving objects using slot attention guided by image content.

This work differs in several respects. It relies only on optical flow, taking a volume of OF fields as input and providing a volume of consistent segmentation maps. It introduces B-splines to define parametric motion models handling motion evolution over time and expresses long-term temporal consistency. The loss function is inferred from the ELBO framework. In contrast, [22] used a triplet of flows, did not use transformers, and used a linear temporal model. Their temporal linkage was an ad hoc post-processing. This method defines a fully integrated long-term model trained end-to-end unsupervisedly. This method is called LT-MS (long-term motion segmentation). The method in [22] is referred to as ST-MS (short-term motion segmentation).

3 LONG-TERM MOTION SEGMENTATION METHOD
A transformer-based network for multiple motion segmentation from optical flow is designed. It is inspired by the MaskFormer architecture [4] but comprises only one head for mask prediction. The network takes as input a volume of consecutive optical flow fields of flexible temporal length. Temporal consistency is expressed in two ways at training. First, a space-time motion model is associated with each segment. Second, the loss function includes a term enforcing consistent labeling of motion segments over the volume.

3.1 SPATIO-TEMPORAL PARAMETRIC MOTION MODEL
The set of T consecutive flows is designated as a space-time volume. The volume could be the whole video sequence. The space-time motion model is estimated through B-spline functions [32]. A spatio-temporal parametric motion model ˜f_θ_k is assigned to each motion segment k, k=1,..,K. θ_k specifies the motion model ˜f for segment k. The motion model involves J parameters. Each parameter θ_k_j, j=1,..,J, results from a B-spline function of order n in the variable t over the space-time volume. In practice, n=3. The number L of control points is given by L = 2 + ⌊(T-2)/ν⌋, where ν sets the temporal frequency of control points. A control point is placed at both ends of the volume (at t=1 and t=T), and the others are equidistantly placed between them. Often, control points are not located at time points of the video sequence.

Any parametric motion model could be considered. The 12-parameter quadratic motion model is used to account for continuously varying depth surface and complex motions. The 2D flow vector at point (x,y) is:
˜f_θ(x,y) = ( θ_1 + θ_2 x + θ_3 y + θ_7 x^2 + θ_8 x y + θ_9 y^2, θ_4 + θ_5 x + θ_6 y + θ_10 x^2 + θ_11 x y + θ_12 y^2 )^T.

To handle complex temporal evolution, spline approximation is used. Denoting S_n(θ_k) the subscript of ˜f emphasizes parameters are estimated through B-spline functions:
˜f_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t) = Σ_{l=1}^{L} ˜f_{θ_{k,l}}(i,t) B_{n,l}(t),
where B_{n,l} is the l-th B-spline and θ_{k,l} corresponds to the l-th control point.

3.2 LOSS FUNCTION
Consider a volume of optical flow fields f ∈ ℝ^{2×T×W×H}, spatial grid Ω ∈ ℝ^{W×H} and T temporal steps. Denote f(i,t) ∈ ℝ^2 the flow at site i ∈ Ω at time t. The flow is decomposed into K segments, each exhibiting coherent motion. Flow vectors within segment k are represented by a smooth parametric motion model parametrized by ϑ_k. Variable z_{i,t} conveys motion segmentation; z_{i,t}^k = 1 if site (i,t) belongs to segment k. z and ϑ = {ϑ_k, k=1···K} are latent variables; f is observed data. Following [13], an approximate distribution is introduced:
q(z, ϑ | f) = q(z|f) q(ϑ) = ( Π_{t=1}^T Π_{i∈Ω} Π_{k=1}^K q(z_{i,t}^k|f) ) ( Π_{k}^K q(ϑ_k) ),
where q(ϑ_k) ≜ δ(θ_k) with δ the dirac distribution and q(z_{i,t}^k|f) = g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k. g_φ is the network taking the optical flow volume and returning a probabilistic segmentation volume.

The data-likelihood over a dataset D of optical flow volumes f is:
log p(D) = Σ_{f∈D} log p(f) = Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log( p(f,z,ϑ) / q(z,ϑ|f) ) ] + KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ|f) ) )
≥ Σ_{f∈D} ( E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] - KL( q(z,ϑ|f) || p(z,ϑ) ) ),
obtaining the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). The likelihood is:
p(f|z,ϑ) = Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ∝ Π_{t=1}^T Π_{k=1}^K Π_{i∈Ω} exp( -||f(i,t) - ˜f_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t)||_1 / ξ_{f,t} )^{z_{i,t}^k},
where ˜f_{S_n(ϑ_k)}(i,t) is the flow vector given by the parametric motion model as defined in Section 3.1 and ξ_{f,t} = Σ_i ||f(i,t)||_1 is a normalizing factor. The left term of the ELBO is:
L_r = E_{q(z,ϑ|f)}[ log p(f|z,ϑ) ] = Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_k E_q[ log p(f(t)|ϑ_k, z) ]
= - Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_k g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k ||f(i,t) - ˜f_{S_n(θ_k)}(i,t)||_1 / ξ_{f,t}.

The term KL(q(z,ϑ|f)||p(z,ϑ)) allows defining a prior over segmentation. To enforce temporal consistency of segmentation labels, this term is approximated using the temporal consistency loss from [22]:
L_c = (1/(2K|Ω|)) Σ_{i∈Ω} Σ_{t=2}^T 1[ ||f_{i,t} - f_{i,t-1}||_1 < λ ] Σ_{k=1}^K | g_φ(f)_{i,t}^k - g_φ(f)_{i,t-1}^k |.
The threshold λ discards occlusion areas. The loss function is:
Σ_{f∈D} L(f, φ, θ) = Σ_{f∈D} L_r(f, φ, θ) + β L_c(f, φ).
β is set to 1. Training alternately updates θ and φ with learning rate α:
For f ∈ D: θ* = arg min_θ L(f, φ, θ); φ_{t+1} = φ_t - α ∇_φ L(f, φ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE
The architecture includes two main modules. The first is a 3D U-net [29] taking the flow volume as input. The latent code augmented with embedding positions is directed to a transformer decoder. Through cross-attention, the output is a volume of segmentation masks. Training minimizes the defined loss function, with motion model parameters given by B-spline estimation. Temporal consistency is provided by the loss function and the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION
4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
Following [6, 16, 21, 22, 35], the RAFT method [31] is used to compute optical flow fields, specifically the version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset [2]. Flow fields are downsampled to 128×224 to feed the network. Output segmentation maps are upsampled to the initial frame size for evaluation. Typically, flow volumes of temporal length T=9 are used at training. At test time, volumes of larger length, or the whole sequence, can be processed. For spatio-temporal parametric motion models, x and y coordinates are normalized within [-1,1], and a similar normalization is applied to t. The full 12-parameter quadratic motion model is used in all experiments, with ν=3 for the B-spline frequency factor. For each site i, the segment k̂ with the highest prediction is selected. In equation (7), λ is set as the 99th quantile of flow differences over the volume.

The LT-MS method is efficient at test time. Computational time averages 210 fps on a GPU P100, twice as fast as ST-MS [22]. The architecture is lightweight, combining three U-net layers and a transformer decoder on downsampled feature space. No post-processing is involved.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING
Two types of data augmentation for optical flow are applied. First, a global flow is added to the input flow, similar to [21, 22]. The global flow is given by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model with random parameters, added to all flow fields in an input volume. This mimics diverse camera motions. Second, a few flows out of the nine input ones are corrupted to simulate poorly estimated fields; temporal consistency should overcome this.

The method is fully unsupervised. No manual annotation is used. The model is trained only with the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset [20], regardless of the test dataset. The stopping epoch is selected from the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
Comparative experiments were carried out on four datasets: DAVIS2016 [26], SegTrackV2 [15], FBMS59 [24], and DAVIS2017-motion [33].

5.1 ABLATION STUDY
An ablation study assessed three main components of LT-MS with four masks (K=4). One component was changed at a time: using the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model of ST-MS [22] instead of the B-spline model; omitting the consistency term L_c in the loss; using only the convnet without the transformer decoder. Experiments were run on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, SegTrackV2. Results are in Table 1. Experiments were performed for two input sequence configurations: sequences of ten flows, and sequences of 120 flows (the whole video for DAVIS2016). The three ablations have almost the same impact on performance. The three components—spline-based motion model, temporal-consistency loss term, and transformer decoder—are all beneficial in similar proportions. Their contributions are more significant for FBMS59 and SegTrackV2.

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION
Table 2 reports results from two versions of LT-MS on DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 uses two masks (K=2); LT-MS-K4 uses four masks (K=4). Table 2 includes results from other unsupervised methods. Evaluation is on binary ground truth. OCLR [33] is included as unsupervised, though it uses human-annotated sprites in training data. The OCLR version taking only optical flow as input is considered. The CIS method [36] has a post-processing based on Conditional Random Fields; the version without it is used for comparison.

LT-MS provides convincing results in the category of unsupervised methods based on optical flow only. OCLR and DivA show better performance on SegTrackV2. However, OCLR is not fully unsupervised, and DivA leverages RGB images in its conditional decoder. DivA, along with MoSeg and CIS, takes multi-step flows as input between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2 and averages the four predictions. SegTrackV2 includes sequences with handheld camera, leading to unstable sequences.

Temporal consistency is handled over long periods by LT-MS. The method provides coherent segmentation over the sequence by design.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION
Multiple motion segmentation evaluation was performed for a multi-segment setting. Accuracy scores are expected to decrease. Table 3 reports comparative results on DAVIS2017-motion and FBMS59. Segmentation was performed with three masks. The LT-MS-K4 network was finetuned on the DAVIS2016 training set with three masks (K=3). Performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than ST-MS [22] and better than MoSeg. On FBMS59, LT-MS outperforms DivA [14] by a large margin according to reported metrics.

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION
Figure 3 shows visual results on different videos. Motion segments are globally accurate. With several masks, the method handles articulated motions, several moving objects, separates rider from bike, and accommodates motion parallax. Temporal consistency helps deal with errors in optical flow estimation or objects that momentarily stop moving. The target is optical-flow segmentation (OFS), though evaluation is on VOS benchmarks. Discrepancies with VOS ground truth can occur, as segmentation of additional parts may make sense from an OFS standpoint but not from VOS.

6 CONCLUSION
A transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions over a video in one go has been designed. The LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework for the loss function and acknowledges the temporal dimension of motion segmentation. To our knowledge, it is the first unsupervised network-based OFS method explicitly leading to stable and consistent OF segmentation throughout long video sequences. It introduces B-spline spatio-temporal parametric motion models over space-time volumes and a loss term expressing temporal consistency over successive masks while handling occlusions. The transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of any time length. It can accommodate different numbers K of masks with simple finetuning. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate efficiency and accuracy, providing competitive results. The method is fast at test time. Future work will investigate slot attention to modify the number of masks at test time without retraining.

The threshold λ discards occlusion areas. The loss function is:
Σ_{f∈D} L(f, φ, θ) = Σ_{f∈D} L_r(f, φ, θ) + β L_c(f, φ).
β is set to 1. Training alternately updates θ and φ with learning rate α:
For f ∈ D: θ* = arg min_θ L(f, φ, θ); φ_{t+1} = φ_t - α ∇_φ L(f, φ, θ*).

3.3 NETWORK ARCHITECTURE
The architecture includes two main modules. The first is a 3D U-net [29] taking the flow volume as input. The latent code augmented with embedding positions is directed to a transformer decoder. Through cross-attention, the output is a volume of segmentation masks. Training minimizes the defined loss function, with motion model parameters given by B-spline estimation. Temporal consistency is provided by the loss function and the space-time motion models.

4 IMPLEMENTATION
4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
Following [6, 16, 21, 22, 35], the RAFT method [31] is used to compute optical flow fields, specifically the version trained on the MPI Sintel dataset [2]. Flow fields are downsampled to 128×224 to feed the network. Output segmentation maps are upsampled to the initial frame size for evaluation. Typically, flow volumes of temporal length T=9 are used at training. At test time, volumes of larger length, or the whole sequence, can be processed. For spatio-temporal parametric motion models, x and y coordinates are normalized within [-1,1], and a similar normalization is applied to t. The full 12-parameter quadratic motion model is used in all experiments, with ν=3 for the B-spline frequency factor. For each site i, the segment k̂ with the highest prediction is selected. In equation (7), λ is set as the 99th quantile of flow differences over the volume.

The LT-MS method is efficient at test time. Computational time averages 210 fps on a GPU P100, twice as fast as ST-MS [22]. The architecture is lightweight, combining three U-net layers and a transformer decoder on downsampled feature space. No post-processing is involved.

4.2 DATA AUGMENTATION AND NETWORK TRAINING
Two types of data augmentation for optical flow are applied. First, a global flow is added to the input flow, similar to [21, 22]. The global flow is given by a full spline-based spatio-temporal motion model with random parameters, added to all flow fields in an input volume. This mimics diverse camera motions. Second, a few flows out of the nine input ones are corrupted to simulate poorly estimated fields; temporal consistency should overcome this.

The method is fully unsupervised. No manual annotation is used. The model is trained only with the FlyingThings3D (FT3D) dataset [20], regardless of the test dataset. The stopping epoch is selected from the loss function evaluated on the DAVIS2016 training set.

5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
Comparative experiments were carried out on four datasets: DAVIS2016 [26], SegTrackV2 [15], FBMS59 [24], and DAVIS2017-motion [33].

5.1 ABLATION STUDY
An ablation study assessed three main components of LT-MS with four masks (K=4). One component was changed at a time: using the polynomial space-time quadratic motion model of ST-MS [22] instead of the B-spline model; omitting the consistency term L_c in the loss; using only the convnet without the transformer decoder. Experiments were run on DAVIS2016, FBMS59, SegTrackV2. Results are in Table 1. Experiments were performed for two input sequence configurations: sequences of ten flows, and sequences of 120 flows (the whole video for DAVIS2016). The three ablations have almost the same impact on performance. The three components—spline-based motion model, temporal-consistency loss term, and transformer decoder—are all beneficial in similar proportions. Their contributions are more significant for FBMS59 and SegTrackV2.

5.2 QUANTITATIVE AND COMPARATIVE EVALUATION
Table 2 reports results from two versions of LT-MS on DAVIS2016, SegTrackV2, and FBMS59. LT-MS-K2 uses two masks (K=2); LT-MS-K4 uses four masks (K=4). Table 2 includes results from other unsupervised methods. Evaluation is on binary ground truth. OCLR [33] is included as unsupervised, though it uses human-annotated sprites in training data. The OCLR version taking only optical flow as input is considered. The CIS method [36] has a post-processing based on Conditional Random Fields; the version without it is used for comparison.

LT-MS provides convincing results in the category of unsupervised methods based on optical flow only. OCLR and DivA show better performance on SegTrackV2. However, OCLR is not fully unsupervised, and DivA leverages RGB images in its conditional decoder. DivA, along with MoSeg and CIS, takes multi-step flows as input between t and t+1, t+2, t-1, t-2 and averages the four predictions. SegTrackV2 includes sequences with handheld camera, leading to unstable sequences.

Temporal consistency is handled over long periods by LT-MS. The method provides coherent segmentation over the sequence by design.

5.3 MULTI-SEGMENT EVALUATION
Multiple motion segmentation evaluation was performed for a multi-segment setting. Accuracy scores are expected to decrease. Table 3 reports comparative results on DAVIS2017-motion and FBMS59. Segmentation was performed with three masks. The LT-MS-K4 network was finetuned on the DAVIS2016 training set with three masks (K=3). Performance on DAVIS2017-motion is slightly better than ST-MS [22] and better than MoSeg. On FBMS59, LT-MS outperforms DivA [14] by a large margin according to reported metrics.

5.4 QUALITATIVE VISUAL EVALUATION
Figure 3 shows visual results on different videos. Motion segments are globally accurate. With several masks, the method handles articulated motions, several moving objects, separates rider from bike, and accommodates motion parallax. Temporal consistency helps deal with errors in optical flow estimation or objects that momentarily stop moving. The target is optical-flow segmentation (OFS), though evaluation is on VOS benchmarks. Discrepancies with VOS ground truth can occur, as segmentation of additional parts may make sense from an OFS standpoint but not from VOS.

6 CONCLUSION
A transformer-based unsupervised method for segmenting multiple motions over a video in one go has been designed. The LT-MS method leverages the ELBO framework for the loss function and acknowledges the temporal dimension of motion segmentation. To our knowledge, it is the first unsupervised network-based OFS method explicitly leading to stable and consistent OF segmentation throughout long video sequences. It introduces B-spline spatio-temporal parametric motion models over space-time volumes and a loss term expressing temporal consistency over successive masks while handling occlusions. The transformer-based network can be applied at test time to input volumes of any time length. It can accommodate different numbers K of masks with simple finetuning. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate efficiency and accuracy, providing competitive results. The method is fast at test time. Future work will investigate slot attention to modify the number of masks at test time without retraining.

title: A Effective Variance Change Detection Method under constantly Changing Mean
full_text:
\title{A Effective Variance Change Detection Method under constantly Changing Mean}

\begin{abstract}
Effectively evaluating the viability of a procured organ in the transplant patient prior the procedure is of critical importance. Current viability assessment methods rely on evaluating the organ’s morphology and/or laboratory biopsy results with limited effectiveness. A recently proposed, well-designed noninvasive method evaluated the viability status of organs by detecting the variance change point of their surface temperature through exploring the entire data profile. However, most part of the data in a temperature profile barely contains the change information, which yields a waste of computational resources of their method. This paper proposes an accelerating algorithm with a well-designed dual control windows scheme that can be extended to online change detection. The proposed method significantly improves the computational speed and retains the same change detection power as the method Gao19 through the removal of redundant data. Simulation and application results demonstrate the robust performance of the proposed method.
\end{abstract}

\section{15 1 INTRODUCTION  }


16 Organ transplantation is an effective method to treat end-stage diseases of various organs. Due   
17 to the limitation of storage and transportation techniques, the viability of organs cannot be fully   
18 guaranteed. Therefore, the quality of procured organs must be evaluated before transplantation.   
19 Different organs can accept different cold ischemia time. For example, the upper limit of the cold   
20 ischemia time of the liver is about 12 hours, and that of the heart is only 8 hours. Therefore, in an   
21 organ transplantation operation, both doctors and patients are racing against time. The traditional   
22 evaluation often relies on subjective experience in the viability of the organ based on the physical   
23 shape and some functional data. In many cases, it is impossible to clearly distinguish the viable   
24 organs from nonviable organs. Laboratory biopsy usually cut off a small piece of the organ for an   
25 integrity test of the transplanted organs. However, the test results of samples cannot represent the   
26 viability state of the entire organ, which leads to a missing identification of the transplantable organ   
27 areas, and results in a waste of valuable organs. Therefore, in order to further improve the utilization   
28 rate of transplanted organs, a more accurate and convenient organ viability change detection method   
29 is desired.   
30 It has been proved that there is a strong correlation between surface temperature of organs and   
31 their viability (Skowno & Karpelowsky, 2014; Vidal et al., 2014; Kochan et al., 2015), where the   
32 surface temperature of the viable organ fluctuates greatly. A research team of clinical scientists and   
33 engineers at Virginia Tech designed a set of noninvasive organ viability evaluation methods (Bhonsle   
34 et al., 2016; O’Brien et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019). A porcine liver was used in the experiment.   
35 The organ surface was divided into a dense grid covering the entire liver surface. A noninvasive,   
36 high-precision thermal imaging system was used to measure the surface temperature of the liver.   
37 Temperatures were collected every ten minutes for 24 hours. Figure 1 is the temperature profile   
38 of a randomly selected spot on the organ surface. From the plots we see that the mean trend of   
39 the temperature changes slowly and smoothly in the perfusion process. The surface temperature   
40 fluctuates strongly in the first 12 hours, which indicates a high viability of the organ. After 12   
41 hours’ perfusion, a sudden viability drop appears, and the organ gradually loses its viability. The red   
42 vertical line is the potential viability change point. Then, the viability evaluation of a procured organ   
43 is transformed from a medical problem into a statistical problem of variance change point detection   
44 under a smoothly changing mean trend.   
45 Recent research on the change point detection are mainly based on the parametric methods and   
46 the nonparametric methods. The parametric method assumes that the data distribution belongs to   
47 a certain distribution family, and infers sudden changes in one or several parameters of the data   
48 distribution (Inclan & Tiao, 1994; Chen & Gupta, 1997; Pan & Chen, 2006; Kang et al., 2018; Dette   
49 & Gösmann, 2020; Wang et al., 2021). However, these existing methods cannot be applied in our   
50 liver experiment, since not only the variance change suddenly, the mean function of the temperature   
51 profile also changes smoothly. The nonparametric change point detection method does not depend   
52 on an overall distribution (Hariz et al., 2007; Matteson & James, 2014; Zou et al., 2014; Yu & Chen,   
53 2022). These methods can effectively detect sudden changes. However, the data obtained from   
54 the liver experiment not only has a sudden change in variance, but also has constant changes in the   
55 mean function. This constantly changing mean will affect the detection effect of the variance change   
56 point. Directly applying these methods to the liver data will lead to an ironic detection result. For   
57 the smooth mean estimation in the liver data, the smoothing spline is one of the common method   
58 (Shang & Cheng, 2013; 2017; Xu & Wang, 2018). There are also some methods combining mean   
59 function estimation and change detection together (Loader, 1996; Liao & Meyer, 2017; Grégoire &   
60 Hamrouni, 2002). However, all these methods are about to estimate the sudden changes in the mean   
61 curve. They are not suitable for our scenario, where the mean function changes constantly in our   
62 scenario.   
63 Gao et al. (2019; 2020) proposed algorithms that can do the smooth mean function estimation and   
64 the variance change point detection simultaneously. However, limited by the practical meaning of   
65 the application scenario, it is very common that the location of the change point is normally in a   
66 certain range. In the liver experiment, we found that the variance change point of the temperature   
67 profile is basically distributed in 10-16 hours. However, the computational logic of their methods   
68 needs to scan the entire data profile, in which most parts of the data series have no change point.   
69 Therefore, scanning the whole time series to detect variance change points is unnecessary. There are   
70 more than 36,000 temperature profiles need to be analyzed in the scene of time competition. Clearly   
71 their methods are highly lack of efficiency.   
72 In this paper, we propose a new variance change point detection approach with dual control windows   
73 to improve the computational efficiency of the method proposed by Gao et al. (2019) to simultane  
74 ously improve the accuracy and speed of the change detection. In our proposed method one control   
75 window $C W_{\alpha}$ is designed for the mean estimation and the other control window $C W_{\beta}$ is designed   
76 for the variance change point detection. In the liver procurement experiment, the variance change   
77 point of the liver surface temperature generally conforms to a normal distribution. We obtain the   
78 preliminary variance change points information by randomly scanning a group of temperature pro  
79 files in the early stage, and construct a model for the mean estimation based on the distribution   
80 information of the variance change point. Our proposed method reduces the redundant data infor  
81 mation sufficiently and allows to address an accurate estimate of the change point fleetly, which   
82 significantly improves the computational efficiency of the algorithm, and saves plenty of time in   
83 detection for urgent life saving circumstances.  

![](images/1141361c0f94b15a70c58e45daa1ff8a538a19bf54849a2e8cd623b365121c63.jpg)  
Figure 1: Temperature profile at a randomly selected spot of the liver. The red vertical line is the approximated location of the variance change point.  



\section{84 2 METHOD  }


85 2.1 MODEL AND NOTATION  

86 Suppose that $y_{t}$ are the independent observations generated from the following model:  

$$
y_{t}=f_{0}(t/n)+\epsilon_{t},\quad t=1,\ldots,n,
$$  

87 where $f_{0}$ is an unknown smoothing function, $\epsilon_{t}\sim N(0,\sigma_{t}^{2})$ is the error term. Let $\tau$ be the position   
88 of the variance change point. $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ and $\delta_{0}^{2}$ are variances. For $t\leq\tau$ , $\sigma_{t}^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2}$ . For $t>\tau$ , $\sigma_{t}^{2}=\delta_{0}^{2}$ .   
89 Algorithm 1 is the computational framework of our proposed method. This algorithm begins with   
90 an initialization of the dual control windows. To obtain a possible range of the potential variance   
91 change points, we firstly perform a preliminary variance change point detection procedure and con  
92 struct an initialized control window $C W_{\alpha}^{0}$ for the mean estimation and a control window $C W_{\beta}^{0}$ for   
93 the variance change point detection based on the randomly selected $K$ data profiles. The variance   
94 change point detection procedures of these $K$ randomly selected data profiles are the method by   
95 Gao et al. (2019). Since the sample space of determining the control window $C W_{\alpha}^{0}$ will be updated   
96 iteratively in Algorithm 1, the choice of $K$ is arbitrary as long as it satisfies the minimum statistical   
97 requirement. Then we estimate the mean function and detect the variance change point within the   
98 control windows. The dual control windows $C W_{\alpha}$ and $C W_{\beta}$ are updated iteratively and simultane  
99 ously based on the information of the newly detected variance change points. The details of the dual   
100 control windows are shown in Section 2.2.  

101 All parameters’ estimates are obtained by minimizing the following objective function,  

$$
\frac{1}{n}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f})^{\top}\Sigma_{n,\tau,\sigma,\delta}^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f})+\lambda J(f),
$$  

102 where $\mathbf{y}\,=\,(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})^{\top}$ , $\textbf{f}=(f(1/n),f(2/n),\ldots,f(1)^{\top})$ , $\Sigma_{n,\tau,\sigma,\delta}$ is a diagonal matrix,   
103 where the first $\tau$ diagonals are $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ , and the rest are $\delta_{0}^{2}$ . $J(f)$ is the roughness penalty with the   
104 smoothing parameter $\lambda>0$ balancing the tradeoff between the smoothness of the estimated mean   
105 function and the goodness of fit represented by the weighted sum of squared errors. Since the objec  
106 tive function Equation 1 tends to zero as $\sigma^{2}$ goes to infinity, the global minimizer of Equation 1 does   
107 not exist. Therefore an iterative parameter estimation procedure is designed to obtain a local optimal   
108 solution. The parameter estimation starts with the initialization of the mean function $\hat{f}^{(0)}$ assuming   
109 constant variance. Therefore, the covariance matrix in Equation 1 reduces to $\sigma^{2}I$ , and $\sigma^{2}$ can be   
110 absorbed into the smoothing parameter $\lambda$ . Given the mean function estimate, the variance change   
111 point $\hat{\tau}$ , and the variances $\hat{\sigma}^{2}$ and ${\hat{\delta}}^{2}$ are obtained in the change detection procedures. The mean   
112 function estimates and the detected variance change points are updated iteratively. The convergence   
113 criterion of our proposed algorithm is the maximum absolute difference between the residuals of   
114 the current iteration and the previous iteration. In the numerical experiments conducted in the later   
115 sections, our algorithm can converge in a few iterations. The consistency of parameter estimates has   
116 been proved by Gao et al. (2019).  



\section{117 2.2 THE DUAL CONTROL WINDOWS  }


118 Suppose we have detected $K$ data profiles, and $\big\{\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{K}\big\}$ is the set of detected variance change   
119 points. To build a proper control window $C W_{\alpha}$ for the mean estimation, we have verified that the   
120 asymptotic distribution of the variance change point is normal. According to the empirical rule,   
121 about $95\%$ of the data falls into the range of the mean plus or minus two standard deviations. More   
122 general, we use the upper quantiles of the standard normal distribution as an approximate substitute   
123 to get CW ′α.  

$$
C W_{\alpha}^{\prime}=[C L L_{\alpha}^{\prime},C L U_{\alpha}^{\prime}]\,,\quad C L L_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mu-W,\quad C L U_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mu+W,
$$  

Input: Data set $\mathcal{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times n}$ , where $M$ is the number of data profiles, $n$ is the length of each data profile  

Output: $\{\hat{\tau}_{1},\dots,\hat{\tau}_{M}\}$  

Step1 Initialize the dual control windows. Randomly select K data profiles from $\mathcal{D}$ , detect the variance change points $\hat{\iota}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\iota}_{K}$ to initialize the control window $C W_{\alpha}^{(0)}$ and $C W_{\beta}^{(0)}$ p2 Variance change detection within dual control windows. For the $m^{t h}$ data profile, Step2.1 capture the reduced data profile ${\mathbf{y}}_{m}^{*}=\left\{y_{i}|i\in C W_{\alpha}^{(m-1)}\right\}$ . Step2.2 Initialize the mean function estimate $\hat{f}_{m}^{(0)}$ assuming constant variance. $\hat{f}_{m}^{(0)}$ minimizes $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{1}{n}(\mathbf{y}_{m}-\mathbf{f}_{m})^{\top}(\mathbf{y}_{m}-\mathbf{f}_{m})+\lambda J(f_{m})}\end{array}$ . Step2.3 Estimate the variance change point iteratively. Each iteration consists of two steps. At the $j^{t h}$ iteration, Step-A Given the mean estimate ${\hat{f}}^{(j-1)}$ , the data profile ∗m∗ = yi|i ∈CW β(m−1) is validated to yield estimates of $\hat{\tau}^{\left(j\right)}$ , $[\hat{\sigma}^{2}]^{(j)}$ and $[\hat{\delta}^{2}]^{(j)}$ . Step-B Substitute the current parameters estimates from Step-A into Equation 1 to update the mean function estimate ${\hat{f}}^{(j)}$ . Step2.4 Iterate until the algorithm converges, and obtain the estimates $\hat{\tau}_{m},\hat{\sigma}_{m}^{2},\hat{\delta}_{m}^{2}$ , and $\hat{f}_{m}$ . Step2.5 Update $C W_{\alpha}^{(m)}$ and $C W_{\beta}^{(m)}$ by $\left\{\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{K},\hat{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\tau}_{m}\right\}.$  

124 where $\begin{array}{r}{\mu={\frac{1}{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\iota_{i}}\end{array}$ , $\begin{array}{r}{W=z_{q}\sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K}(\iota_{i}-\mu)^{2}}}\end{array}$ , $K$ is the number of detected change points,   
125 $\tau$ is the known change point data, and $z_{q}$ is the upper quantile of the standard normal distribution   
126 corresponding to the desired accuracy.   
127 In our method, we use the cubic splines method to estimate the mean functions. The computational   
128 efficiency of the smoothing spline method is highly affected by the sample size of the data. The   
129 minimizer $f_{\lambda}$ of Equation 1 resides in the $n$ -dimensional space, and the computation in multivariate   
130 settings is generally of the order $O(n^{3})$ (Kim & Gu, 2004). Therefore, large sample size will ex  
131 tremely slow down the computational speed. However, the accuracy of the mean function estimation   
132 using the nonparametric method highly relies on the sufficiency of the quantity of the data. In or  
133 der to improve the speed of the algorithm without reducing the accuracy of parameter estimates, we   
134 need to choose an appropriate radius of the control window $C W_{\alpha}$ . We define a hyper parameter $W_{\alpha}$ ,   
135 which is the minimum size of the control window $C W_{\alpha}$ . The determination of $W_{\alpha}$ refers to the rule   
136 of elbow in the K-means clustering. The minimum window size can be estimated by balancing the   
137 tradeoff between the accuracy of the estimation and computational speed. For example, in the liver   
138 experiment, if we want the accuracy of the change detection to be above 0.95, we should ensure that   
139 the control window contains at least 100 data points. In that case, to make the calculations as fast as   
140 possible, we can choose $W_{\alpha}=50$ . Considering the above two factors, the definition for $C W_{\alpha}$ is  

$$
C W_{\alpha}=\left[C L L_{\alpha},C L U_{\alpha}\right],\;C L L_{\alpha}=\mu-\operatorname*{max}\left\{W_{\alpha},W\right\},\;C L U_{\alpha}=\mu+\operatorname*{max}\left\{W_{\alpha},W\right\},
$$  

141 where $\textstyle\mu={\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau_{i}$ , and $\begin{array}{r}{W=z_{q}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\tau_{i}-\mu)^{2}}.}\end{array}$  

142 $C W_{\beta}$ is designed for variance change point detection. Generally, the mean function estimation   
143 requires more data information than the variance change points detection. Therefore, a portion of   
144 the data contained in $C W_{\alpha}$ is redundant for variance change detection. Generally speaking, the   
145 change point location presents a high degree of concentration. This is a common situation in many   
146 change point detection problems, such as the change of the daily traffic flow data set of the same   
147 road section, the change of the stock market, and the change of the sales of an industry company.   
148 Therefore, the variance change point detection interval $C W_{\beta}$ should be further controlled to make   
149 the probability of variance change points in the interval reaches to a certain value or more, and   
150 those points that are not likely to become variance change points are eliminated as much as possible.   
151 According to the Glivenko-Cantelli Theorem, we have  

$$
P\left\{\operatorname*{lim}_{m\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname*{sup}_{-\infty<\tau<\infty}|F_{m}(\tau)-F(\tau)|=0\right\}=1,
$$  

152 where $F_{m}(\tau)$ is the empirical distribution function of the dataset $\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{m}\}$ and $F(\tau)$ is the real   
153 distribution function of the variance change points. When the sample size is large enough, we adopt   
154 the concepts of the probability interval to control the likelihood of the change point positions ac  
155 cording to the empirical distribution function. We get $C W_{\beta}=[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ , where the potential   
156 variance change points fall into this interval with a probability of at least $q$ . The upper and lower   
157 bounds of $C W_{\beta}$ satisfy $F_{m}(C L U_{\beta})-F_{m}(C L L_{\beta})\stackrel{\_}{\geq}q$ . Since the asymptotic distribution of the   
158 variance change point is normal, we can do it in terms of the quantile of the sample  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{C W_{\beta}=\left[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}\right],\quad C L L_{\beta}=\tau_{\frac{1-q}{2}},\quad C L U_{\beta}=\tau_{\frac{1+q}{2}},}\end{array}
$$  

159 where $\tau_{\underline{{1}}\pm q}$ is the $\textstyle{\frac{1\pm q}{2}}$ percentile of the detected variance change points. By using the control   
160 window $\stackrel{\cdot2}{C W}_{\beta}$ , we further reduce the amount of data used for variance change point detection.  

161 2.3 SMOOTHING SPLINES ESTIMATION FOR MEAN FUNCTION  

162 The mean estimation in this article uses the cubic smoothing splines. Before introducing the es  
163 timation method for the mean function, it is necessary to first introduce the polynomial smooth  
164 ing spline with period 1 on the interval $[0,1]$ . The mean function $f_{0}$ is estimated by minimiz  
165 ing the objective function $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_{i}\,-\,f_{0}(t_{i})\big)^{2}+\lambda\int_{0}^{1}\big(f_{0}^{(m)}(t)\big)^{2}d t}\end{array}$ in the space $\mathcal{C}^{(m)}[0,1]=$   
166 $\left\{f:f^{(m)}\in\mathcal{L}_{2}[0,1]\right\}$ , where $\mathcal{C}^{(m)}[0,1]$ is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). The true   
167 mean function $f_{0}$ is an unknown smoothing function and is a function in the reproducing kernel   
168 Hilbert space $\mathcal{C}=\{f\ |\ f:[0,1]\rightarrow R,J(f)^{'}<\infty\}$ . When $\sigma^{2},\delta^{2}$ and $\tau$ are given, the estimate of $f_{0}$   
169 is the minimizer of the penalized weighted least squares Equation 1, where the smoothness param  
170 eter $\lambda>0$ is chosen by the generalized cross-validation. Note that since $\mathcal{C}$ is of infinite dimension,   
171 it is not possible to optimize Equation 1 on $\mathcal{C}$ directly. However, since the weighted least squares   
172 part in Equation 1 depends on $f_{0}$ only at the observation $y_{i},i\in[C L L_{\alpha},C L U_{\alpha}]$ , the representation   
173 theorem guarantees that the exact minimizer exists in a finite dimensional subspace of $\mathcal{C}$ . Therefore,   
174 the minimizer of the objective function Equation 1 can be analytically obtained.  



\section{175 2.4 VARIANCE CHANGE POINT DETECTION  }


176 When the mean function estimate $\hat{f}$ is given, the variance change point $\hat{\tau}$ is detected within the   
177 control window $C W_{\beta}$ through a well designed hypothesis test procedure. The estimates of the   
178 variances are $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}=\hat{\tau}^{-1}{\sum_{t=1}^{\hat{\tau}}\left\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\right\}^{2}}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{\delta}^{2}=(n-\hat{\tau})^{-1}{\sum_{t=\hat{\tau}+1}^{n}}\left\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\right\}^{2}}\end{array}$ . For   
179 variance change point detection, establish the null and alternative hypotheses.  

$$
H_{0}:\sigma_{1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{n}^{2}\quad v s\quad H_{1}:\sigma_{1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{\tau}^{2}\neq\sigma_{\tau+1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{n}^{2}
$$  

180 For a potential variance change point ${\hat{\tau}}=k$ , $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , the likelihood function is  

$$
L(k)=k\left[\log\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t=1}^{k}\Big\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\Big\}^{2}\right]+(n-k)\left[\log\frac{1}{n-k}\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}\Big\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\Big\}^{2}\right],
$$  

181 then we have $L(n)=-2L_{0}({\hat{\sigma}}^{2})-n-n\log2\pi$ , and $L(\tau)=-2L_{1}(\hat{\sigma}^{2},\hat{\delta}^{2})-n-n\log2\pi.$ . Where   
182 $L_{0}$ and $L_{1}$ are the log-likelihood functions under the hypotheses $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ . Then we have the   
183 definition of the test statistic: $\Delta_{n}^{2}=\operatorname*{max}_{1<k<n}\left\{L(n)-^{\cdot}L(k)\right\}$ . By the principle of the minimum   
184 information criterion, there is no evidence of the existence of the variance change point within the   
185 control window $C W_{\beta}$ if $L(n)\leq\operatorname*{min}_{k}L(k)$ , $k\in[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ . The null hypothesis is failed to   
186 reject if $\exists k\in[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ , we have $L(n)>L(k)$ , then the null hypothesis is rejected, and there   
187 exists a variance change point. Therefore the position of the estimated variance change point is  

$$
\hat{\tau}=\underset{C L L_{\beta}\leq k\leq C L U_{\beta}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}L(k).
$$  



\section{188 3 SIMULATION  }


189 In this section, we compare the performance of our proposed change detection method, which is   
190 denoted by the New method hereafter, with one of the most sufficient method in Gao et al. (2019)   
191 hereafter denoted by the Gao19 method. We conduct the comprehensive simulation studies using   
192 the same data generating schemes in Gao et al. (2019). Two mean functions $f_{01}(t)=20\!+\!12t(1\!-\!t)$   
193 and $f_{02}(t)=\check{s}i n(t)\!+\!t^{\check{5}}\!-\!8t^{3}\!+\!10t\!+\!6$ are considered. The first mean function $f_{01}$ mimics the trend   
194 of the temperature profile obtained in the porcine liver procurement experiment, while the second   
195 function $f_{02}$ represents a more complex smooth mean trend. We use two sample sizes $n\,=\,130$   
196 and $n=500$ . When $n=130$ , the true variance change point is $\tau_{0}=65$ and the parameter of the   
197 control window $W_{\alpha}=50$ . When $n=500$ , we have $\tau_{0}=250$ and $W_{\alpha}=190$ . The true variances

original_text:
\title{A Effective Variance Change Detection Method under constantly Changing Mean}

\begin{abstract}
Effectively evaluating the viability of a procured organ in the transplant patient prior the procedure is of critical importance. Current viability assessment methods rely on evaluating the organ’s morphology and/or laboratory biopsy results with limited effectiveness. A recently proposed, well-designed noninvasive method evaluated the viability status of organs by detecting the variance change point of their surface temperature through exploring the entire data profile. However, most part of the data in a temperature profile barely contains the change information, which yields a waste of computational resources of their method. This paper proposes an accelerating algorithm with a well-designed dual control windows scheme that can be extended to online change detection. The proposed method significantly improves the computational speed and retains the same change detection power as the method Gao19 through the removal of redundant data. Simulation and application results demonstrate the robust performance of the proposed method.
\end{abstract}

\section{15 1 INTRODUCTION  }


16 Organ transplantation is an effective method to treat end-stage diseases of various organs. Due   
17 to the limitation of storage and transportation techniques, the viability of organs cannot be fully   
18 guaranteed. Therefore, the quality of procured organs must be evaluated before transplantation.   
19 Different organs can accept different cold ischemia time. For example, the upper limit of the cold   
20 ischemia time of the liver is about 12 hours, and that of the heart is only 8 hours. Therefore, in an   
21 organ transplantation operation, both doctors and patients are racing against time. The traditional   
22 evaluation often relies on subjective experience in the viability of the organ based on the physical   
23 shape and some functional data. In many cases, it is impossible to clearly distinguish the viable   
24 organs from nonviable organs. Laboratory biopsy usually cut off a small piece of the organ for an   
25 integrity test of the transplanted organs. However, the test results of samples cannot represent the   
26 viability state of the entire organ, which leads to a missing identification of the transplantable organ   
27 areas, and results in a waste of valuable organs. Therefore, in order to further improve the utilization   
28 rate of transplanted organs, a more accurate and convenient organ viability change detection method   
29 is desired.   
30 It has been proved that there is a strong correlation between surface temperature of organs and   
31 their viability (Skowno & Karpelowsky, 2014; Vidal et al., 2014; Kochan et al., 2015), where the   
32 surface temperature of the viable organ fluctuates greatly. A research team of clinical scientists and   
33 engineers at Virginia Tech designed a set of noninvasive organ viability evaluation methods (Bhonsle   
34 et al., 2016; O’Brien et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019). A porcine liver was used in the experiment.   
35 The organ surface was divided into a dense grid covering the entire liver surface. A noninvasive,   
36 high-precision thermal imaging system was used to measure the surface temperature of the liver.   
37 Temperatures were collected every ten minutes for 24 hours. Figure 1 is the temperature profile   
38 of a randomly selected spot on the organ surface. From the plots we see that the mean trend of   
39 the temperature changes slowly and smoothly in the perfusion process. The surface temperature   
40 fluctuates strongly in the first 12 hours, which indicates a high viability of the organ. After 12   
41 hours’ perfusion, a sudden viability drop appears, and the organ gradually loses its viability. The red   
42 vertical line is the potential viability change point. Then, the viability evaluation of a procured organ   
43 is transformed from a medical problem into a statistical problem of variance change point detection   
44 under a smoothly changing mean trend.   
45 Recent research on the change point detection are mainly based on the parametric methods and   
46 the nonparametric methods. The parametric method assumes that the data distribution belongs to   
47 a certain distribution family, and infers sudden changes in one or several parameters of the data   
48 distribution (Inclan & Tiao, 1994; Chen & Gupta, 1997; Pan & Chen, 2006; Kang et al., 2018; Dette   
49 & Gösmann, 2020; Wang et al., 2021). However, these existing methods cannot be applied in our   
50 liver experiment, since not only the variance change suddenly, the mean function of the temperature   
51 profile also changes smoothly. The nonparametric change point detection method does not depend   
52 on an overall distribution (Hariz et al., 2007; Matteson & James, 2014; Zou et al., 2014; Yu & Chen,   
53 2022). These methods can effectively detect sudden changes. However, the data obtained from   
54 the liver experiment not only has a sudden change in variance, but also has constant changes in the   
55 mean function. This constantly changing mean will affect the detection effect of the variance change   
56 point. Directly applying these methods to the liver data will lead to an ironic detection result. For   
57 the smooth mean estimation in the liver data, the smoothing spline is one of the common method   
58 (Shang & Cheng, 2013; 2017; Xu & Wang, 2018). There are also some methods combining mean   
59 function estimation and change detection together (Loader, 1996; Liao & Meyer, 2017; Grégoire &   
60 Hamrouni, 2002). However, all these methods are about to estimate the sudden changes in the mean   
61 curve. They are not suitable for our scenario, where the mean function changes constantly in our   
62 scenario.   
63 Gao et al. (2019; 2020) proposed algorithms that can do the smooth mean function estimation and   
64 the variance change point detection simultaneously. However, limited by the practical meaning of   
65 the application scenario, it is very common that the location of the change point is normally in a   
66 certain range. In the liver experiment, we found that the variance change point of the temperature   
67 profile is basically distributed in 10-16 hours. However, the computational logic of their methods   
68 needs to scan the entire data profile, in which most parts of the data series have no change point.   
69 Therefore, scanning the whole time series to detect variance change points is unnecessary. There are   
70 more than 36,000 temperature profiles need to be analyzed in the scene of time competition. Clearly   
71 their methods are highly lack of efficiency.   
72 In this paper, we propose a new variance change point detection approach with dual control windows   
73 to improve the computational efficiency of the method proposed by Gao et al. (2019) to simultane  
74 ously improve the accuracy and speed of the change detection. In our proposed method one control   
75 window $C W_{\alpha}$ is designed for the mean estimation and the other control window $C W_{\beta}$ is designed   
76 for the variance change point detection. In the liver procurement experiment, the variance change   
77 point of the liver surface temperature generally conforms to a normal distribution. We obtain the   
78 preliminary variance change points information by randomly scanning a group of temperature pro  
79 files in the early stage, and construct a model for the mean estimation based on the distribution   
80 information of the variance change point. Our proposed method reduces the redundant data infor  
81 mation sufficiently and allows to address an accurate estimate of the change point fleetly, which   
82 significantly improves the computational efficiency of the algorithm, and saves plenty of time in   
83 detection for urgent life saving circumstances.  

![](images/1141361c0f94b15a70c58e45daa1ff8a538a19bf54849a2e8cd623b365121c63.jpg)  
Figure 1: Temperature profile at a randomly selected spot of the liver. The red vertical line is the approximated location of the variance change point.  



\section{84 2 METHOD  }


85 2.1 MODEL AND NOTATION  

86 Suppose that $y_{t}$ are the independent observations generated from the following model:  

$$
y_{t}=f_{0}(t/n)+\epsilon_{t},\quad t=1,\ldots,n,
$$  

87 where $f_{0}$ is an unknown smoothing function, $\epsilon_{t}\sim N(0,\sigma_{t}^{2})$ is the error term. Let $\tau$ be the position   
88 of the variance change point. $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ and $\delta_{0}^{2}$ are variances. For $t\leq\tau$ , $\sigma_{t}^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2}$ . For $t>\tau$ , $\sigma_{t}^{2}=\delta_{0}^{2}$ .   
89 Algorithm 1 is the computational framework of our proposed method. This algorithm begins with   
90 an initialization of the dual control windows. To obtain a possible range of the potential variance   
91 change points, we firstly perform a preliminary variance change point detection procedure and con  
92 struct an initialized control window $C W_{\alpha}^{0}$ for the mean estimation and a control window $C W_{\beta}^{0}$ for   
93 the variance change point detection based on the randomly selected $K$ data profiles. The variance   
94 change point detection procedures of these $K$ randomly selected data profiles are the method by   
95 Gao et al. (2019). Since the sample space of determining the control window $C W_{\alpha}^{0}$ will be updated   
96 iteratively in Algorithm 1, the choice of $K$ is arbitrary as long as it satisfies the minimum statistical   
97 requirement. Then we estimate the mean function and detect the variance change point within the   
98 control windows. The dual control windows $C W_{\alpha}$ and $C W_{\beta}$ are updated iteratively and simultane  
99 ously based on the information of the newly detected variance change points. The details of the dual   
100 control windows are shown in Section 2.2.  

101 All parameters’ estimates are obtained by minimizing the following objective function,  

$$
\frac{1}{n}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f})^{\top}\Sigma_{n,\tau,\sigma,\delta}^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f})+\lambda J(f),
$$  

102 where $\mathbf{y}\,=\,(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})^{\top}$ , $\textbf{f}=(f(1/n),f(2/n),\ldots,f(1)^{\top})$ , $\Sigma_{n,\tau,\sigma,\delta}$ is a diagonal matrix,   
103 where the first $\tau$ diagonals are $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ , and the rest are $\delta_{0}^{2}$ . $J(f)$ is the roughness penalty with the   
104 smoothing parameter $\lambda>0$ balancing the tradeoff between the smoothness of the estimated mean   
105 function and the goodness of fit represented by the weighted sum of squared errors. Since the objec  
106 tive function Equation 1 tends to zero as $\sigma^{2}$ goes to infinity, the global minimizer of Equation 1 does   
107 not exist. Therefore an iterative parameter estimation procedure is designed to obtain a local optimal   
108 solution. The parameter estimation starts with the initialization of the mean function $\hat{f}^{(0)}$ assuming   
109 constant variance. Therefore, the covariance matrix in Equation 1 reduces to $\sigma^{2}I$ , and $\sigma^{2}$ can be   
110 absorbed into the smoothing parameter $\lambda$ . Given the mean function estimate, the variance change   
111 point $\hat{\tau}$ , and the variances $\hat{\sigma}^{2}$ and ${\hat{\delta}}^{2}$ are obtained in the change detection procedures. The mean   
112 function estimates and the detected variance change points are updated iteratively. The convergence   
113 criterion of our proposed algorithm is the maximum absolute difference between the residuals of   
114 the current iteration and the previous iteration. In the numerical experiments conducted in the later   
115 sections, our algorithm can converge in a few iterations. The consistency of parameter estimates has   
116 been proved by Gao et al. (2019).  



\section{117 2.2 THE DUAL CONTROL WINDOWS  }


118 Suppose we have detected $K$ data profiles, and $\big\{\iota_{1},\ldots,\iota_{K}\big\}$ is the set of detected variance change   
119 points. To build a proper control window $C W_{\alpha}$ for the mean estimation, we have verified that the   
120 asymptotic distribution of the variance change point is normal. According to the empirical rule,   
121 about $95\%$ of the data falls into the range of the mean plus or minus two standard deviations. More   
122 general, we use the upper quantiles of the standard normal distribution as an approximate substitute   
123 to get CW ′α.  

$$
C W_{\alpha}^{\prime}=[C L L_{\alpha}^{\prime},C L U_{\alpha}^{\prime}]\,,\quad C L L_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mu-W,\quad C L U_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mu+W,
$$  

Input: Data set $\mathcal{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times n}$ , where $M$ is the number of data profiles, $n$ is the length of each data profile  

Output: $\{\hat{\tau}_{1},\dots,\hat{\tau}_{M}\}$  

Step1 Initialize the dual control windows. Randomly select K data profiles from $\mathcal{D}$ , detect the variance change points $\hat{\iota}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\iota}_{K}$ to initialize the control window $C W_{\alpha}^{(0)}$ and $C W_{\beta}^{(0)}$ p2 Variance change detection within dual control windows. At the $j^{t h}$ iteration, Step-A Given the mean estimate ${\hat{f}}^{(j-1)}$ , the data profile ∗m∗ = yi|i ∈CW β(m−1) is validated to yield estimates of $\hat{\tau}^{\left(j\right)}$ , $[\hat{\sigma}^{2}]^{(j)}$ and $[\hat{\delta}^{2}]^{(j)}$ . Step-B Substitute the current parameters estimates from Step-A into Equation 1 to update the mean function estimate ${\hat{f}}^{(j)}$ . Step2.4 Iterate until the algorithm converges, and obtain the estimates $\hat{\tau}_{m},\hat{\sigma}_{m}^{2},\hat{\delta}_{m}^{2}$ , and $\hat{f}_{m}$ . 124 where $\begin{array}{r}{\mu={\frac{1}{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\iota_{i}}\end{array}$ , $\begin{array}{r}{W=z_{q}\sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K}(\iota_{i}-\mu)^{2}}}\end{array}$ , $K$ is the number of detected change points,   
125 $\tau$ is the known change point data, and $z_{q}$ is the upper quantile of the standard normal distribution   
126 corresponding to the desired accuracy.   
127 In our method, we use the cubic splines method to estimate the mean functions. The computational   
128 efficiency of the smoothing spline method is highly affected by the sample size of the data. The   
129 minimizer $f_{\lambda}$ of Equation 1 resides in the $n$ -dimensional space, and the computation in multivariate   
130 settings is generally of the order $O(n^{3})$ (Kim & Gu, 2004). Therefore, large sample size will ex  
131 tremely slow down the computational speed. However, the accuracy of the mean function estimation   
132 using the nonparametric method highly relies on the sufficiency of the quantity of the data. In or  
133 der to improve the speed of the algorithm without reducing the accuracy of parameter estimates, we   
134 need to choose an appropriate radius of the control window $C W_{\alpha}$ . We define a hyper parameter $W_{\alpha}$ ,   
135 which is the minimum size of the control window $C W_{\alpha}$ . The determination of $W_{\alpha}$ refers to the rule   
136 of elbow in the K-means clustering. The minimum window size can be estimated by balancing the   
137 tradeoff between the accuracy of the estimation and computational speed. For example, in the liver   
138 experiment, if we want the accuracy of the change detection to be above 0.95, we should ensure that   
139 the control window contains at least 100 data points. In that case, to make the calculations as fast as   
140 possible, we can choose $W_{\alpha}=50$ . Considering the above two factors, the definition for $C W_{\alpha}$ is  

$$
C W_{\alpha}=\left[C L L_{\alpha},C L U_{\alpha}\right],\;C L L_{\alpha}=\mu-\operatorname*{max}\left\{W_{\alpha},W\right\},\;C L U_{\alpha}=\mu+\operatorname*{max}\left\{W_{\alpha},W\right\},
$$  

141 where $\textstyle\mu={\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau_{i}$ , and $\begin{array}{r}{W=z_{q}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\tau_{i}-\mu)^{2}}.}\end{array}$  

142 $C W_{\beta}$ is designed for variance change point detection. Generally, the mean function estimation   
143 requires more data information than the variance change points detection. Therefore, a portion of   
144 the data contained in $C W_{\alpha}$ is redundant for variance change detection. Generally speaking, the   
145 change point location presents a high degree of concentration. This is a common situation in many   
146 change point detection problems, such as the change of the daily traffic flow data set of the same   
147 road section, the change of the stock market, and the change of the sales of an industry company.   
148 Therefore, the variance change point detection interval $C W_{\beta}$ should be further controlled to make   
149 the probability of variance change points in the interval reaches to a certain value or more, and   
150 those points that are not likely to become variance change points are eliminated as much as possible.   
151 According to the Glivenko-Cantelli Theorem, we have  

$$
P\left\{\operatorname*{lim}_{m\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname*{sup}_{-\infty<\tau<\infty}|F_{m}(\tau)-F(\tau)|=0\right\}=1,
$$  

152 where $F_{m}(\tau)$ is the empirical distribution function of the dataset $\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{m}\}$ and $F(\tau)$ is the real   
153 distribution function of the variance change points. When the sample size is large enough, we adopt   
154 the concepts of the probability interval to control the likelihood of the change point positions ac  
155 cording to the empirical distribution function. We get $C W_{\beta}=[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ , where the potential   
156 variance change points fall into this interval with a probability of at least $q$ . The upper and lower   
157 bounds of $C W_{\beta}$ satisfy $F_{m}(C L U_{\beta})-F_{m}(C L L_{\beta})\stackrel{\_}{\geq}q$ . Since the asymptotic distribution of the   
158 variance change point is normal, we can do it in terms of the quantile of the sample  

$$
\begin{array}{r}{C W_{\beta}=\left[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}\right],\quad C L L_{\beta}=\tau_{\frac{1-q}{2}},\quad C L U_{\beta}=\tau_{\frac{1+q}{2}},}\end{array}
$$  

159 where $\tau_{\underline{{1}}\pm q}$ is the $\textstyle{\frac{1\pm q}{2}}$ percentile of the detected variance change points. By using the control   
160 window $\stackrel{\cdot2}{C W}_{\beta}$ , we further reduce the amount of data used for variance change point detection.  

161 2.3 SMOOTHING SPLINES ESTIMATION FOR MEAN FUNCTION  

162 The mean estimation in this article uses the cubic smoothing splines. Before introducing the es  
163 timation method for the mean function, it is necessary to first introduce the polynomial smooth  
164 ing spline with period 1 on the interval $[0,1]$ . The mean function $f_{0}$ is estimated by minimiz  
165 ing the objective function $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_{i}\,-\,f_{0}(t_{i})\big)^{2}+\lambda\int_{0}^{1}\big(f_{0}^{(m)}(t)\big)^{2}d t}\end{array}$ in the space $\mathcal{C}^{(m)}[0,1]=$   
166 $\left\{f:f^{(m)}\in\mathcal{L}_{2}[0,1]\right\}$ , where $\mathcal{C}^{(m)}[0,1]$ is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). The true   
167 mean function $f_{0}$ is an unknown smoothing function and is a function in the reproducing kernel   
168 Hilbert space $\mathcal{C}=\{f\ |\ f:[0,1]\rightarrow R,J(f)^{'}<\infty\}$ . When $\sigma^{2},\delta^{2}$ and $\tau$ are given, the estimate of $f_{0}$   
169 is the minimizer of the penalized weighted least squares Equation 1, where the smoothness param  
170 eter $\lambda>0$ is chosen by the generalized cross-validation. Note that since $\mathcal{C}$ is of infinite dimension,   
171 it is not possible to optimize Equation 1 on $\mathcal{C}$ directly. However, since the weighted least squares   
172 part in Equation 1 depends on $f_{0}$ only at the observation $y_{i},i\in[C L L_{\alpha},C L U_{\alpha}]$ , the representation   
173 theorem guarantees that the exact minimizer exists in a finite dimensional subspace of $\mathcal{C}$ . Therefore,   
174 the minimizer of the objective function Equation 1 can be analytically obtained.  



\section{175 2.4 VARIANCE CHANGE POINT DETECTION  }


176 When the mean function estimate $\hat{f}$ is given, the variance change point $\hat{\tau}$ is detected within the   
177 control window $C W_{\beta}$ through a well designed hypothesis test procedure. The estimates of the   
178 variances are $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}=\hat{\tau}^{-1}{\sum_{t=1}^{\hat{\tau}}\left\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\right\}^{2}}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{\delta}^{2}=(n-\hat{\tau})^{-1}{\sum_{t=\hat{\tau}+1}^{n}}\left\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\right\}^{2}}\end{array}$ . For   
179 variance change point detection, establish the null and alternative hypotheses.  

$$
H_{0}:\sigma_{1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{n}^{2}\quad v s\quad H_{1}:\sigma_{1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{\tau}^{2}\neq\sigma_{\tau+1}^{2}=\cdots=\sigma_{n}^{2}
$$  

180 For a potential variance change point ${\hat{\tau}}=k$ , $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , the likelihood function is  

$$
L(k)=k\left[\log\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t=1}^{k}\Big\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\Big\}^{2}\right]+(n-k)\left[\log\frac{1}{n-k}\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}\Big\{y_{t}-\hat{f}(t/n)\Big\}^{2}\right],
$$  

181 then we have $L(n)=-2L_{0}({\hat{\sigma}}^{2})-n-n\log2\pi$ , and $L(\tau)=-2L_{1}(\hat{\sigma}^{2},\hat{\delta}^{2})-n-n\log2\pi.$ . Where   
182 $L_{0}$ and $L_{1}$ are the log-likelihood functions under the hypotheses $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ . Then we have the   
183 definition of the test statistic: $\Delta_{n}^{2}=\operatorname*{max}_{1<k<n}\left\{L(n)-^{\cdot}L(k)\right\}$ . By the principle of the minimum   
184 information criterion, there is no evidence of the existence of the variance change point within the   
185 control window $C W_{\beta}$ if $L(n)\leq\operatorname*{min}_{k}L(k)$ , $k\in[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ . The null hypothesis is failed to   
186 reject if $\exists k\in[C L L_{\beta},C L U_{\beta}]$ , we have $L(n)>L(k)$ , then the null hypothesis is rejected, and there   
187 exists a variance change point. Therefore the position of the estimated variance change point is  

$$
\hat{\tau}=\underset{C L L_{\beta}\leq k\leq C L U_{\beta}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}L(k).
$$
