Title: Enabling Efficient Equivariant Operations in the Fourier Basis via Gaunt Tensor Products

Abstract
Developing equivariant neural networks for the E(3) group is used in modeling 3D data. Enforcing this equivariance involves tensor products of irreducible representations (irreps). The computational complexity of these operations increases with higher-order tensors. This work proposes an approach to accelerate the computation of tensor products of irreps. The commonly used Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are mathematically connected to the Gaunt coefficients, which are integrals of products of three spherical harmonics. Through Gaunt coefficients, the tensor product of irreps becomes equivalent to multiplication between spherical functions represented by spherical harmonics. This perspective allows a change of basis for the equivariant operations from spherical harmonics to a 2D Fourier basis. Multiplication between spherical functions represented by a 2D Fourier basis can be computed via the convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transforms. This transformation reduces the complexity of full tensor products of irreps from O(L^6) to O(L^3), where L is the max degree of irreps. This approach is used to introduce the Gaunt Tensor Product, a method to construct efficient equivariant operations. Experiments on the Open Catalyst Project and 3BPA datasets demonstrate increased efficiency and performance.

1 Introduction
Imposing physical priors, such as specific constraints, has been used in deep learning. To address the curse of dimensionality, prior works have exploited geometry inherent in data, such as pixel grids in images or atomic positions in molecules, and their associated symmetries. Among these constraints, equivariance has emerged as a concept in deep learning.

An equivariant function mapping transforms the output predictably in response to transformations on the input. One class of such transformations includes translations, rotations, and reflections in Euclidean space, termed the Euclidean group. Problems exhibiting symmetries to the Euclidean group include molecular modeling, protein biology, and 3D vision. Operations for the Euclidean group have been developed, showing promise in prediction tasks through improved data efficiency and generalization.

Rooted in representation theory, such operations allow modeling of equivariant mappings between any 2l+1-dimensional irrep space via Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, and are proven to have universal approximation capability. These operations have driven performance across applications, demonstrating empirical results.

The computational complexity of computing tensor products of irreps is a hurdle for efficiency and accuracy. Recent advancements suggest the empirical performance of models based on such operations can be boosted by using higher degrees of irreps. However, the full tensor product of irreps up to degree L has an O(L^6) complexity, which limits L to 2 or 3 in practice, hindering efficient inference on large systems. There is a need to improve the efficiency of tensor products of irreps.

This work introduces a methodology to accelerate the computation of tensor products of irreps. The key observation is that Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are mathematically related to the integral of products of three spherical harmonics, known as Gaunt coefficients. This shows the tensor product of irreps via Gaunt coefficients is equivalent to multiplication between spherical functions represented by linear combinations of spherical harmonic bases. This motivates using the 2D Fourier basis to equivalently express the same functions via a change of basis. Multiplications between functions represented by 2D Fourier bases can be accelerated through the convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). Using these insights, the computational cost of full tensor products of irreps up to degree L can be reduced to O(L^3).

Building upon this approach, the Gaunt Tensor Product is introduced as a method for efficient equivariant operations. A study is provided on major operation classes used in equivariant models for the Euclidean group, demonstrating the generality of the method and how it can be used to design efficient operations:
- Equivariant Feature Interactions. Operations in this category calculate tensor products between two equivariant features, enabling interaction between irreps from different dimensional spaces and objects. These operations have been used in recent advances, e.g., interacting atomic features and predicting a Hamiltonian matrix. Employing this approach in this scenario is straightforward.
- Equivariant Convolutions. Tensor products in this category are computed between equivariant features and spherical harmonic filters, which are building blocks for equivariant message passing. In this case, additional speed-up can be achieved via the insight from Passaro & Zitnick (2023), which introduces sparsity to the filters via a rotation. This is used to further accelerate the conversion from spherical harmonics to 2D Fourier bases.
- Equivariant Many-Body Interactions. Modeling many-body interaction effects has been shown to be important for advancing machine learning force fields. Capturing these interactions requires performing multiple tensor products among equivariant features. The connection between Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and Gaunt coefficients is naturally generalized to this setting, and a divide-and-conquer approach is developed to parallelize the computation of multiple 2D convolutions, demonstrating better efficiency compared to original implementations.

Experiments are conducted to verify the efficiency and generality of the approach. For each operation class, efficiency comparisons are provided between the Gaunt Tensor Product and implementations via the e3nn library. The Gaunt Tensor Product is applied to state-of-the-art models on benchmarks across task types and scales, e.g., force field modeling on OC20 and 3BPA benchmarks. Results show better efficiency and improved performance.

2 Background
Necessary background knowledge is reviewed, including concepts of the Euclidean group and equivariance, irreducible representations (irreps), spherical harmonics, and the tensor product of irreps.

Let S denote a set of objects located in three-dimensional Euclidean space. X in R^{n x d} denotes objects with features, where n is the number of objects, and d is the feature dimension. For object i, let r_i in R^3 denote its Cartesian coordinate. Define S=(X,R), where R={r_1,...,r_n}. These data structures are inherent in systems such as molecular systems and point clouds. Problems defined on S generally exhibit symmetries to transformations on the objects. For instance, given a molecular system, if a rotation is applied to each atom position r_i, the direction of the force on each atom will also rotate. Such transformations and symmetries are related to groups and equivariance.

Euclidean group and Equivariance. Formally, a group G is a non-empty set, together with a binary operation o: G x G -> G satisfying group axioms. The class of transformations including translations, rotations, and reflections in three-dimensional Euclidean space is of interest, as it describes many real-world scenarios. These transformations form a group structure known as the Euclidean group, denoted as E(3).

To describe how group elements act on vector spaces, group representations are used. Formally, the representation of a group G on a vector space V is a mapping ρ^V: G -> GL(V), where GL(V) is the set of invertible matrices on V. For example, representations of the rotation group SO(3) on R^3 can be parameterized by orthogonal transformation matrices R in R^{3x3}, det(R)=1, which are applied to x in R^3 via matrix multiplication Rx.

Equivariance is introduced. Let φ: X -> Y denote a function mapping between vector spaces. Given a group G, let ρ^X and ρ^Y denote its representations on X and Y respectively. A function φ: X -> Y is said to be equivariant if it satisfies ρ^Y(g)[φ(x)] = φ(ρ^X(g)[x]), for all g in G, x in X. When ρ^Y = I^Y (identity transformation) for G, it is a special case of equivariance, known as Invariance.

The equivariance constraint is a physical prior used in machine learning models. For tasks defined on the data structure S, it is typically important to ensure operations maintain E(3)-equivariance. The E(3) group is a semi-direct product of the group of translations R^3 with the group of orthogonal transformations O(3), i.e., E(3)=R^3 ⋊ O(3). Achieving translation equivariance is straightforward through convolution-type operations. Therefore, focus is primarily on the orthogonal group O(3), which consists of rotations and reflections.

Irreducible representations. D(g) denotes the representation of group element g in matrix form. For vector spaces of dimension 2l+1, l in N, there exists a collection of matrix representations indexed with l for each g in SO(3), called Wigner-D matrices. They are denoted as D^{(l)}(g). Each Wigner-D matrix D^{(l)}(g) is the irreducible representation of SO(3) on a subspace with dimension 2l+1. Any matrix representation D(g) of SO(3) on vector space V can be reduced to an equivalent block diagonal matrix representation with Wigner-D matrices along the diagonal: D(g) = Q^{-1}(D^{(l1)}(g) ⊕ D^{(l2)}(g) ⊕ ... )Q = Q^{-1} diag(D^{(l1)}(g), D^{(l2)}(g), ...) Q. Here, Q is the change of basis that makes D(g) and the block diagonal matrix representation equivalent.

This equivalence provides an alternative view that the representations acting on vector space V are made up of each Wigner-D matrix D^{(li)}, which only acts on a 2li+1-dimension subspace V_{li} of V. Then, vector space V can be factorized into V_{l1} ⊕ V_{l2} ⊕ ... The space V_l is called a type-l irrep space, and x^{(l)} in V_l a type-l irrep. The Wigner-D matrix in the type-1 space is D^{(1)} = R in R^{3x3}, det(R)=1. The Wigner-D matrix representations can be extended to the O(3) group by including reflections via a direct product.

Spherical harmonics. Spherical harmonics are used to map from R^3 to any type-l irrep space. Y_m^{(l)}: S^2 -> R, -l ≤ m ≤ l, l in N denotes spherical harmonics, where l and m denote degrees and orders respectively. For any x in R^3, Y^{(l)}(x/||x||) = [Y_{-l}^{(l)}(x/||x||), ..., Y_{l}^{(l)}(x/||x||)]^T is a type-l irrep. This mapping is equivariant to the O(3) group, i.e., given r̃ in S^2, g in SO(3) and its representation on R^3 as rotation matrix R, Y^{(l)}(R r̃) = D^{(l)}(g) Y^{(l)}(r̃) and Y^{(l)}(-r̃) = (-1)^l Y^{(l)}(r̃).

Tensor products of irreducible representations. Given x^{(l1)}, x^{(l2)} in type-l1 and type-l2 irrep space respectively, their tensor product yields x^{(l1)} ⊗ x^{(l2)}, which lies in the V_{l1} ⊗ V_{l2} space with (2l1+1) x (2l2+1) dimension. This operation preserves equivariance to the O(3) group, i.e., (D^{(l1)}(g) ⊗ D^{(l2)}(g)) (x^{(l1)} ⊗ x^{(l2)}) = (D^{(l1)}(g) x^{(l1)}) ⊗ (D^{(l2)}(g) x^{(l2)}) for all g in O(3). The tensor product of irreducible representations D^{(l1)}(g) ⊗ D^{(l2)}(g) can be decomposed into irreducible pieces: D^{(l1)}(g) ⊗ D^{(l2)}(g) = ⊕_{l=|l1-l2|}^{l1+l2} D^{(l)}(g). The resulting irrep x^{(l1)} ⊗ x^{(l2)} of the tensor product can be organized via a change of basis into parts in different type-l irrep spaces, i.e., x^{(l1)} ⊗ x^{(l2)} in V = V_{|l1-l2|} ⊕ ... ⊕ V_{l1+l2}.

The Clebsch-Gordan tensor product provides an explicit way to calculate the resulting type-l irrep after the direct sum decomposition. Given x^{(l1)} in R^{2l1+1} and x^{(l2)} in R^{2l2+1}, the m-th element of the resulting type-l irrep of the tensor product between x^{(l1)} and x^{(l2)} is given by:
(x^{(l1)} ⊗_cg x^{(l2)})_m^{(l)} = Σ_{m1=-l1}^{l1} Σ_{m2=-l2}^{l2} C_{(l1,m1)(l2,m2)}^{(l,m)} x_{m1}^{(l1)} x_{m2}^{(l2)},
where C_{(l1,m1)(l2,m2)}^{(l,m)} are Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. x̃^{(L)} = [x^{(0)}; ...; x^{(L)}] in R^{(L+1)^2} denotes features containing irreps of up to degree L in practice, and the full tensor product is given by (x̃^{(L1)} ⊗_c̃g x̃^{(L2)})_m^{(l)} = Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} (x^{(l1)} ⊗_cg x^{(l2)})_m^{(l)}. Retaining all output irreps of the Clebsch-Gordan tensor product requires O(L^3) 3D matrix multiplications, i.e., an O(L^6) cost, which becomes computationally unfeasible when scaling irreps to higher L degrees.

3 Gaunt Tensor Product
The Gaunt Tensor Product is introduced as a method for efficient E(3)-equivariant operations. First, a new perspective on tensor products of irreps is proposed, connecting this operation to multiplication between functions defined on the sphere via Gaunt coefficients. This perspective inspires an efficient approach to accelerate tensor product computation using the convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transforms, achieving speed-ups compared to prior implementations. Finally, a study is provided on major equivariant operation classes, showing how to design efficient counterparts via the Gaunt Tensor Product.

3.1 A New Perspective on Tensor Products of Irreps via Gaunt Coefficients
As shown in the Clebsch-Gordan tensor product equation, the essence of the tensor product operation is in the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, used to perform explicit direct-sum decomposition. CG coefficients appear in quantum mechanics, serving as expansion coefficients of total angular momentum eigenstates in an uncoupled tensor product basis. Spherical harmonics correspond to eigenstates of angular momentum, indicating underlying relations between these concepts.

Theorem: Wigner-Eckart theorem for Spherical Tensor Operators, from Jeevanjee (2011).
Let j, l, J in N_{≥0} and let T^{(j)} be a spherical tensor operator of rank j. Then there is a unique complex number, the reduced matrix element λ in C (often written ⟨J || T^{(j)} || l⟩ in C), that completely determines any of the (2J+1) x (2j+1) x (2l+1) matrix elements ⟨J,M | T_m^{(j)} | l,n⟩:
⟨J,M | T_m^{(j)} | l,n⟩ = λ · C_{(l,n)(j,m)}^{(J,M)}.

Here, |l,n⟩, ⟨J,M| denote eigenstates for angular momentum operators with |n|≤l, |M|≤J, and relate to spherical harmonics via ⟨θ,ψ | l,n⟩ = Y_n^{(l)}(θ,ψ), with spherical coordinate θ in [0,π], ψ in [0,2π). The Wigner-Eckart theorem describes how matrix elements (⟨J,M | T_m^{(j)} | l,n⟩, |m|≤j) of spherical tensor operator T^{(j)} in the basis of angular momentum eigenstates are decomposed into Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and reduced representation ⟨J || T^{(j)} || l⟩. If T^{(j)} is instantiated as spherical harmonics Y^{(j)} and the Wigner-Eckart theorem is applied, the relation ⟨J,M | Y_m^{(j)} | l,n⟩ = ⟨J || Y^{(j)} || l⟩ · C_{(l,n)(j,m)}^{(J,M)} is obtained, which can be rewritten as,
∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{π} Y_{m1}^{(l1)}(θ,ψ) Y_{m2}^{(l2)}(θ,ψ) Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ) sin θ dθ dψ = C̃_{(l1,l2)}^{(l)} C_{(l1,m1)(l2,m2)}^{(l,m)},
where C̃_{(l1,l2)}^{(l)} is a real constant only determined by l1, l2 and l. From this equation, Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are mathematically related to integrals of products of three spherical harmonics, known as Gaunt coefficients. They are denoted as G_{(l1,m1)(l2,m2)}^{(l,m)}.

If Gaunt coefficients are used in the tensor product operation instead, the following result on tensor product of irreps is obtained:
(x̃^{(L1)} ⊗_G̃aunt x̃^{(L2)})_m^{(l)} = Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} (x^{(l1)} ⊗_Gaunt x^{(l2)})_m^{(l)}
= Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} Σ_{m1=-l1}^{l1} Σ_{m2=-l2}^{l2} G_{(l1,m1)(l2,m2)}^{(l,m)} x_{m1}^{(l1)} x_{m2}^{(l2)},
= Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} Σ_{m1=-l1}^{l1} Σ_{m2=-l2}^{l2} x_{m1}^{(l1)} x_{m2}^{(l2)} ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{π} Y_{m1}^{(l1)}(θ,ψ) Y_{m2}^{(l2)}(θ,ψ) Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ) sin θ dθ dψ,
= ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{π} ( Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{m1=-l1}^{l1} x_{m1}^{(l1)} Y_{m1}^{(l1)}(θ,ψ) ) ( Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} Σ_{m2=-l2}^{l2} x_{m2}^{(l2)} Y_{m2}^{(l2)}(θ,ψ) ) Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ) sin θ dθ dψ.
Y_m^{(l)} form an orthonormal basis set for functions defined on unit sphere S^2, i.e., any square-integrable function F(θ,ψ): S^2 -> R can be expanded as Σ_{l=0}^{∞} Σ_{m=-l}^{l} f_m^{(l)} Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ), and coefficients f_m^{(l)} can be calculated by ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{π} f(θ,ψ) Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ) sin θ dθ dψ. If x_{m1}^{(l1)}, x_{m2}^{(l2)} are set to 0 for l1>L1, l2>L2, two spherical functions are obtained, F1(θ,ψ) = Σ_{l1=0}^{∞} Σ_{m1=-l1}^{l1} x_{m1}^{(l1)} Y_{m1}^{(l1)}(θ,ψ) and F2(θ,ψ) = Σ_{l2=0}^{∞} Σ_{m2=-l2}^{l2} x_{m2}^{(l2)} Y_{m2}^{(l2)}(θ,ψ). Thus, (x̃^{(L1)} ⊗_G̃aunt x̃^{(L2)})_m^{(l)} calculates coefficients of function F3(θ,ψ) = F1(θ,ψ) · F2(θ,ψ). This perspective connects tensor products of irreps to multiplication between spherical functions.

3.2 Fast Tensor Product using Convolution Theorem & Fast Fourier Transform
For multiplication between functions defined on unit sphere S^2, efficient computational methods can be leveraged via change of basis: instead of spherical harmonics, the same functions defined on S^2 can be equivalently represented using a 2D Fourier basis.

Given F(θ,φ): S^2 -> R, it can be represented by a linear combination of 2D Fourier bases as Σ_u Σ_v f_{u,v}^* e^{i(uθ+vψ)}, u,v in Z with complex coefficients f_{u,v}^* to make it a real function. To keep convention of spherical harmonics, the 2D Fourier basis is also described in terms of (up to) degrees L if -L ≤ u ≤ L, -L ≤ v ≤ L. Multiplication between F1(θ,ψ) and F2(θ,ψ) can be expressed as:
F1(θ,ψ) · F2(θ,ψ) = ( Σ_{u1} Σ_{v1} f_{u1,v1}^{1*} e^{i(u1θ+v1ψ)} ) · ( Σ_{u2} Σ_{v2} f_{u2,v2}^{2*} e^{i(u2θ+v2ψ)} )
= Σ_{u1} Σ_{v1} Σ_{u2} Σ_{v2} f_{u1,v1}^{1*} f_{u2,v2}^{2*} e^{i((u1+u2)θ+(v1+v2)ψ)}.
By comparing 2D Fourier bases, coefficients of F3(θ,ψ) = F1(θ,ψ) · F2(θ,ψ) can be obtained by f_{u3,v3}^{3*} = Σ_{u1+u2=u3} Σ_{v1+v2=v3} f_{u1,v1}^{1*} f_{u2,v2}^{2*}, which is the form of a 2D convolution. These 2D convolutions can be accelerated using convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transforms. This can be used to develop an efficient approach to compute tensor product of irreps.

From spherical harmonics to 2D Fourier bases. Since both spherical harmonics and 2D Fourier bases form orthonormal basis sets for spherical functions, the following equivalence holds: for spherical harmonics Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ), 0 ≤ l ≤ L, -l ≤ m ≤ l, there exist coefficients y_{u,v}^{l,m,*} such that Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ) = Σ_{u=-L}^{L} Σ_{v=-L}^{L} y_{u,v}^{l,m,*} e^{i(uθ+vψ)}. Coefficients y_{u,v}^{l,m,*} are sparse due to orthogonality of basis sets. That is, y_{u,v}^{l,m,*} are non-zero only when m = ± v.

To compute x̃^{(L1)} ⊗_G̃aunt x̃^{(L2)}, the first step is to convert coefficients of spherical harmonics to coefficients of 2D Fourier basis. From the equivalence, the conversion rule from spherical harmonics to 2D Fourier bases is:
x_{u,v}^* = Σ_{l=0}^{L} Σ_{m=-l}^{l} x_m^{(l)} y_{u,v}^{l,m,*}, -L ≤ u ≤ L, -L ≤ v ≤ L.

Performing 2D convolution via Fast Fourier Transform. After converting coefficients from spherical harmonics to 2D Fourier bases, convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transform can be used to compute the 2D convolution. Both x_{u,v}^{1*} and x_{u,v}^{2*} are transformed from spatial domain to frequency domain via FFT. In frequency domain, 2D convolution can be computed by element-wise multiplication. Then, results of multiplication in frequency domain are transformed back to spatial domain via FFT.

From 2D Fourier bases to spherical harmonics. Similarly, for 2D Fourier bases e^{i(uθ+vψ)}, where -L ≤ u ≤ L and -L ≤ v ≤ L, there exist coefficients z_{u,v}^{l,m,*} such that e^{i(uθ+vψ)} = Σ_{l=0}^{L} Σ_{m=-L}^{L} z_{u,v}^{l,m,*} Y_m^{(l)}(θ,ψ), and z_{u,v}^{l,m,*} are also sparse, i.e., z_{u,v}^{l,m,*} are non-zero only when m = ± v. The last step is to convert resulting coefficients of multiplication between spherical functions back to coefficients of spherical harmonics, calculated as:
x_m^{(l)} = Σ_{u=-L}^{L} Σ_{v=-L}^{L} x_{u,v}^* z_{u,v}^{l,m,*}, 0 ≤ l ≤ L, -l ≤ m ≤ l.

Computational complexity analysis. An analysis is provided on computational complexity of original implementation of full tensor products of irreps of degree up to L. To calculate m-th element of output type-l irrep, there exist O(L^2) (l1,l2)->l combinations of input irreps. Each combination requires summation of O(L^2) multiplications. This means O(L^4) operations for m-th element of output type-l irrep. Then, retaining all m-elements of all output type-l irreps with 0 ≤ l ≤ L has O(L^6) complexity.

In this approach, coefficients of spherical harmonics are first converted to coefficients of 2D Fourier bases. For each x_{u,v}^*, since y_{u,v}^{l,m,*} are non-zero only when m = ± v, it requires O(L) operations. Thus, first step requires O(L^3) operations total. For second step, 2D convolution has O(L^2 log L) complexity using FFT. Similarly, last step also requires O(L^3), due to sparsity of z_{u,v}^{l,m,*}. Therefore, this approach has O(L^3) complexity to compute full tensor products of irreps of degrees up to L.

3.3 Designing Efficient Equivariant Operations via the Gaunt Tensor Product
Based on the approach, the Gaunt Tensor Product is introduced, a technique that efficiently computes tensor products of irreps utilizing Gaunt coefficients. The Gaunt Tensor Product can be applied across model architectures. A study is provided on major equivariant operation classes (Equivariant Feature Interactions, Equivariant Convolutions, and Equivariant Many-body Interactions) and how to design efficient counterparts via the Gaunt Tensor Product.

Equivariant Feature Interactions. Given two features x̃^{(L1)}, ỹ^{(L2)} containing irreps of up to degree L1 and L2 respectively, operations in this class are commonly in form:
(x̃^{(L1)} ⊗_c̃g^w ỹ^{(L2)})^{(l)} = Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} w_{l1,l2}^{l} (x^{(l1)} ⊗_cg y^{(l2)})^{(l)}, where w_{l1,l2}^{l} in R are learnable weights for each (l1,l2)->l combination. Compared to the tensor product equation, the Gaunt Tensor Product is exactly in same form, except for learnable weights w_{l1,l2}^{l}. This approach can be extended by reparameterizing w_{l1,l2}^{l} as w_{l1} · w_{l2} · w_{l}, where w_{l1}, w_{l2}, w_{l} in R. Weighted combinations can be equivalently achieved by separately multiplying w_{l1}, w_{l2}, w_{l} with x^{(l1)}, x^{(l2)} and (x^{(l1)} ⊗_Gaunt x^{(l2)})^{(l)} correspondingly, in which case tensor product of irreps can be efficiently computed.

These operations facilitate interactions between irreps from different dimensional spaces and objects, used in recent work. For example, So3krates developed atomic interaction layer, where both x̃^{(L1)} and ỹ^{(L2)} are equivariant features X_i^{(L)} of atom i. In Quantum Hamiltonian prediction task, such operations are used to interact features for constructing Hamiltonian matrices. For instance, QHNet instantiates x̃^{(L1)} and ỹ^{(L2)} as equivariant features of atom pairs (x̂_i, x̂_j) and uses output features as input of non-diagonal matrix elements prediction block.

Equivariant Convolutions. One special case of Equivariant Feature Interaction is to instantiate ỹ^{(L2)} as spherical harmonics filters, i.e., Σ_{l1=0}^{L1} Σ_{l2=0}^{L2} h_{l1,l2}^{l} (x_i^{(l1)} ⊗_cg Y^{(l2)}((r_i - r_j)/||r_i - r_j||))^{(l)}, where r_i, r_j in R^3 are positions of objects, Y^{(l2)}: S^2 -> R^{2l2+1} is type-l2 spherical harmonic, and h_{l1,l2}^{l} in R are learnable weights calculated based on relative distance and types of objects i,j. Similarly, h_{l1,l2}^{l} can be reparameterized for this approach. Passaro & Zitnick (2023) provide an observation that if a rotation g in SO(3) is selected with D^{(1)}(g) (r_i - r_j)/||r_i - r_j|| = (0,1,0), then Y_m^{(l)}(D^{(1)}(g) (r_i - r_j)/||r_i - r_j||) ∝ δ_m^{(l)}, i.e., is non-zero only if m=0. This sparsification further propagates to coefficients of 2D Fourier basis, bringing additional acceleration.

Equivariant Convolutions are basic operations for equivariant message passing. Spherical harmonics filters encode geometric relations between objects and interact with object features in equivariant manner, playing a role in learning semantics and geometric structures under equivariance constraints.

Equivariant Many-body Interactions. Operations in this class perform multiple tensor products among equivariant features, i.e., x̃_1^{(L1)} ⊗_c̃g x̃_2^{(L2)} ⊗_c̃g ... ⊗_c̃g x̃_n^{(Ln)}. Such operations are used for constructing many-body interaction effects, which can improve performance for ML force fields. For example, given equivariant features A_i^{(L')} of atom i, MACE constructs many-body features by Σ_{η_ν} Σ_{lm} C_{η_ν, lm}^{LM} Π_{ξ=1}^{ν} A_{i,m_ξ}^{(l_ξ)}, which is explicit form of performing tensor products with A_i^{(L)} itself ν times, i.e., B_{ν,i} = A_i^{(L')} ⊗_c̃g ... ⊗_c̃g A_i^{(L')}. Similarly, such operations can be viewed as multiplications of multiple spherical functions. Using this, a divide-and-conquer method can be used to efficiently compute multiple 2D convolutions for speedups.

Discussion. In models, it is common to maintain C channels of equivariant features, i.e., x̃_{i,c}^{(L)}, 0 ≤ c < C contains irreps of degrees up to L. This extension can be included by defining combination rules of features in different channels, e.g., channel-wise (O(C) ops) or channel-mixing (O(C^2) ops). This approach is not limited to full tensor products only. Given x^{(l1)} ⊗_cg y^{(l2)} only, the approach can still be used, reducing O(L̃^3) to O(L̃^2 log L̃) with L̃ = l1 + l2. The generality of the Gaunt Tensor Product is demonstrated.

4 Experiments
Efficiency and effectiveness of the Gaunt Tensor Product are empirically studied. First, efficiency comparisons are provided between the Gaunt Tensor Product and original implementations of operation classes. Second, a sanity check investigates effects of different parameterizations of Gaunt Tensor Product versus Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product. Finally, results applying Gaunt Tensor Product to model architectures and task types are presented.

Efficiency Comparisons. (1) For Equivariant Feature Interaction operation, e3nn implementation is used as baseline. 10 pairs of features containing irreps of up to degree L with 128 channels are randomly sampled. Average inference time is reported. (2) For Equivariant Convolution operation, eSCN implementation is used as baseline, due to enhanced efficiency over e3nn. In this setting, pairs of features and spherical harmonics filters are sampled. Gaunt Tensor Product is implemented using insights of eSCN for further acceleration. (3) For Equivariant Many-body Interaction operation, comparisons are made with e3nn and MACE implementations. Various degrees of L and number of tensor product operands ν are evaluated.

Results are presented in Figure 1. Gaunt Tensor Product achieves acceleration compared to e3nn implementation, e.g., multiple orders of magnitude speed-up when L>7. Compared to efficient eSCN implementation, this approach has further acceleration, due to combination of methods. Gaunt Tensor Product consistently outperforms MACE implementation across L and ν. Results demonstrate improved efficiency.

Sanity Check. As shown in the equivalence equation, Gaunt coefficients are proportional to Clebsch-Gordan coefficients for constants, leading to different parameterizations of Gaunt Tensor Product and Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product. To investigate effects, a sanity check is conducted by applying parameterization of Gaunt Tensor Product to SEGNN model on N-body simulation task, which requires model to forecast positions of particles modeled by predefined interaction rules. Following Brandstetter et al. (2022), a 4-layer SEGNN is employed and all hyperparameters kept same to compare performance of different parameterizations.

In last panel of Figure 1, SEGNN with Gaunt Tensor Product performs competitively compared to Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product implementation, demonstrating parameterization does not hurt performance of equivariant operations.

OC20 S2EF performance. Following Gasteiger et al. (2021), Zitnick et al. (2022), Passaro & Zitnick (2023), approach is evaluated on Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) dataset, consisting of 1.2M DFT relaxations. Each instance has adsorbate molecule placed on catalyst surface. Core task is Structure-to-Energy-Forces (S2EF), requiring model to predict energy and per-atom forces of adsorbate-catalyst complex. EquiformerV2 model achieved performance on OC20 S2EF task, using efficient eSCN implementation to build scalable Transformer backbone. However, this implementation restricts available tensor product operations to Equivariant Convolutions only.

Gaunt Tensor Product is applied to construct efficient Equivariant Feature Interaction operation, Selfmix, added to each layer of EquiformerV2 model. Approach retains efficiency even with modifications. Following Liao et al. (2023), 12-layer EquiformerV2 models are trained and all configurations kept same. OC20 2M subset is used for training. Results are presented in Table 1. EquiformerV2 with Gaunt Selfmix operation achieves better performance on S2EF task, i.e., 16.8% relative improvement on EFwT metric with L=6.

3BPA performance. Following Batzner et al. (2022), Musaelian et al. (2023), Batatia et al. (2022), 3BPA dataset is used to benchmark Equivariant Many-body Interaction operations. Training set contains 500 geometries sampled from 300 K molecular dynamics simulation of molecule 3-(benzyloxy)pyridin-2-amine (3BPA). Both in- (300 K) and out-of-distribution test sets (600 K, 1200 K, dihedral slices) are used to evaluate model's ability to predict energy and forces of geometrical structure. Gaunt Tensor Product is applied to MACE architecture, which uses equivariant features containing irreps of up to degree L=2. Equivariant Many-body Interaction operation in MACE performs two tensor products among three equivariant features. All training configurations kept same as Batatia et al. (2022).

Results are presented in Table 2. MACE integrated with Gaunt Tensor Product performs competitively compared to original implementation, which has best performance among competitive baselines. This affirms parameterization in Equivariant Many-body Interaction does not hurt accuracy. MACE with Gaunt Tensor Product achieves acceleration compared to e3nn implementation and original MACE implementation, i.e., 43.7x speed-ups compared to baselines. MACE implementation trades space for speed and incurs additional memory costs, while this approach has low memory costs, e.g., reducing 82.3% relative memory costs versus MACE.

5 Conclusion
A systematic approach, the Gaunt Tensor Product, is introduced to accelerate computation of tensor products of irreps. Gaunt Tensor Product is established through connection between Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and Gaunt coefficients, enabling equivalent expression of tensor product operation as multiplication between spherical functions represented by spherical harmonics. This viewpoint allows change of basis for equivariant operations to 2D Fourier basis. Multiplication between functions in this basis can be accelerated via convolution theorem and Fast Fourier Transforms. Experiments demonstrate improved efficiency and effectiveness. Gaunt Tensor Product provides opportunities for efficient equivariant operations.

title: Long BERT for bankruptcy prediction
full_text:
\title{Long BERT for bankruptcy prediction}

\begin{abstract}
Most bankruptcy risk prediction models use numerical data such as financial statements, financial ratios, or stock market variables to predict the risk of a company going into bankruptcy. However, these models do not take advantage of the vast amount of textual information available. The few projects that work with textual information use short texts such as tweets and news or are limited to analyzing data from public companies. Our research focuses on predicting the bankruptcy risk using the long text sequences of the annexes from the Annual Accounts. We propose a BERT-based model, which can predict the risk of a company going bankrupt even if there is no explicit information about the risk in the long-textual information. Here we showed that we can process parallel segments of a document using BERT and then integrate them for a unified prediction. Using a dataset of 20,000 annexes from the Annual Accounts of non-financial companies from Luxembourg to train and validate our model. We tried different models and two of them get a validation precision for predicting a risky company of approximately 73% and can be used depending on how long the documents are. The model can clearly learn about risk information from unstructured and diverse long textual information with high precision. This is our first step towards an integrated learning model that considers also numerical and non-financial data. Our proposed architecture can be used in other domains where long text needs to be processed for different Natural Language Processing tasks.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Forecasting bankruptcies plays a pivotal role in fostering economic growth, benefiting businesses, creditors, investors, and even government entities. The presence of effective early warning systems can substantially diminish bankruptcy risks and pinpoint vulnerable aspects that require a company’s attention. Despite the increasing practice of governments and companies disclosing their financial reports, there remains an underutilization of the vast publicly available textual data.  

Most of the current financial models are focused on the use of numerical information as financial ratios to make their predictions and only a few of them are using textual information. Most of these text-based models use only short text for making predictions such as financial news and tweets (Qu et al., 2019; Clement et al., 2020).  

The study conducted by Mai et al. (2019) is one of few that uses financial disclosures to predict the risk of bankruptcy. However, their dataset is limited in scope as they use the Annual Filings from public U.S. corporations which requires including risk analysis in the first part of the document, therefore they just need to process a short text. The primary constraint restricting the utilization of extensive textual data sources, such as the complete Annual Reports, is the limitation imposed by the maximum amount of input text that can be processed by state-of-the-art Natural Language Processing (NLP) models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018).  

In contrast to Mai et al. (2019), we are using Annual Accounts from the Luxembourg Business Registry LBR (2023) which correspond to companies from different industries and sizes and even languages(French, German, and English). In these legal annexes the risk is not always explicitly written, so the model should analyze the entire content to detect it.  

 These annexes provide additional information to the Financial Statements using natural language. Although the Financial Statements must follow a specific template, there is no set layout for the legal annexes 1. In this sense, our information is less uniform and more variable. We can have annexes that are as short as a single page or as long as 15 pages or more. This requires having models that are capable of receiving long strings.  

Our research contribution encompasses two primary objectives. Firstly, we endeavor to enhance our capacity to efficiently process extensive textual data. Secondly, we aspire to build a model proficient in evaluating the bankruptcy risk associated with any company, utilizing the substantial textual content available within their Annual Accounts’ annexes. Our specific emphasis is on scenarios where the risk description may not inherently reveal itself. Providing the model with the whole information, it can learn by itself the features required for doing bankruptcy forecasting.  

The model that we propose is based on the BERT model, which is one of the most important models in NLP. Our proposed model combines the power of BERT for analyzing short sequences of texts with an Integration network, which can be a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network or a concatenation layer followed by dense layers, to analyze BERT’s outputs sequentially.  

Our preliminary results show a precision risk prediction of approximately $73\%$ . Although our results may not surpass the performance of models based solely on numbers, we have very good infer that the text provides us with certain information about the level of risk of a company, even if it is not explicitly stated. Furthermore, this model can be applied to any domain where processing long text is required.  



\section{2 RELATED WORK  }


Most of the studies in finance use numerical data as financial ratios to predict the risk of bankruptcy (Qu et al., 2019; Clement et al., 2020). However, there are some studies that use textual information, but most of them are related to short text as input such as tweets or financial news (Sawhney et al., 2021; Sandy et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2018). In contrast, our objective is to analyze financial reports to predict the risk of bankruptcy. This leads us to use long text as input for our model  

The first work on using financial disclosures to predict bankruptcy risk was done by Mai et al. (2019). They used financial disclosures of U.S. Corporations to predict the risk of bankruptcy using their publicly available 10-K annual filings. the Security Exchange Commission (SEC) mandated firms to include the risk information into a “risk factor” section in the 10-K form starting in 2005 (Campbell et al., 2014; Huang AAllen, 2020).  

In contrast to Mai et al. (2019), our study uses a publicly available dataset of Annexes of Annual Accounts from Luxembourg Business Registers (LBR). By law, not only public companies but also SMEs are required to produce annual accounts. These filings can be presented in English, French, or German. Those annexes can have one or many pages. There is no regulation about the content in the annexes, therefore, the information in the notes or annexes can be very limited (OpenLux (2021)).  

For processing textual information using Deep Neural Networks, the current leading technologies are the models based on the Transformer Architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). These models replaced the Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTM) (Kang et al., 2020). Transformers use attention mechanism to do parallel processing and avoid the vanishing gradient problem.  

Based on Transformers, Devlin et al. (2018) presented the BERT model. BERT is composed of one embedding layer and at least 12 attention layers (BERT Base). It is designed to deal with the ambiguity of language using the surrounding text to define the context. BERT has become one of the most important base models for researchers in NLP. This pre-trained model can understand general language and can be easily trained to understand domain-specific terms without requiring high computational resources or huge amounts of data. In HuggingFace (2023) there are more than 9,000 BERT-based models for NLP in different domains, languages, and downstream tasks such as Text Classification, Translation, Question-Answering, etc.  

Moreover, the primary limitation of BERT-based models is their maximum input size, which is 512 tokens. A token can be defined as a word or word piece that has a numerical representation and meaning. The tokenizer is the component of the model which has a dictionary of known words or word pieces and decomposes the input text into these known entries. Each entry has a vector of 768 features that represent the token’s embeddings.  

Our research is focused on documents with several pages, which is different from most of the other studies. With the same goal and same data as Mai et al. Compared with other studies that use numerical information instead of text, the results are not outperforming but are not far from those.  

The different model’s combination is the method that we consider important to do ablation studies. We can see that LSTM layers have a high impact on the model’s performance for not-so-long documents, but do not perform very well with very-long documents. For this kind of model, reducing the dimensionality of BERT’s outputs before integrating them into an LSTM model, is more convenient.  

On the other hand, if we are working with a very long document, we should replace the LSTM network with a sequence of dense layers. The best result for this approach is obtained if we concatenate directly the BERT’s output to the concatenation layer.  

These results are very promising in terms of the use of pre-trained models like BERT together with an integration layer to process long sequences of texts. Even if the data is unbalanced, most of the models can make predictions of both classes since the first epoch.

Even if the default BERT models can not be used for processing long text, we can divide the document into segments and then process the document in parallel. For our case, this allows us to take advantage of the text in the Annual Accounts to determine if is possible to predict the level of a company going bankrupt based on unstructured data. The best precision of those models was $\approx$ $73\%$ .  

The experiments demonstrate that for having not-so-long documents, LSTM-based model performs better. On the other hand, if we need to process very-long documents, concatenation-based models are preferred.  

In this sense, the text in the Annual Accounts’ annexes has implicit risk information that can be extracted by a Deep Learning model. Our proposed model can be used in other domains which require processing long text.  

We expect that our fine-tuned model has enough risk information that we are going to able to apply to other sources of financial text to predict the risk of bankruptcy.  

The next step in our research is to combine the results of text models with numerical financial information. In addition, we are working on applying quantization and LORA methods to our BERT proposition to increase the complexity and quality of multi-modal architectures.

\begin{abstract}
Most bankruptcy risk prediction models use numerical data such as financial statements, financial ratios, or stock market variables to predict the risk of a company going into bankruptcy. However, these models do not take advantage of the vast amount of textual information available. The few projects that work with textual information use short texts such as tweets and news or are limited to analyzing data from public companies. Our research focuses on predicting the bankruptcy risk using the long text sequences of the annexes from the Annual Accounts. We propose a BERT-based model, which can predict the risk of a company going bankrupt even if there is no explicit information about the risk in the long-textual information. Here we showed that we can process parallel segments of a document using BERT and then integrate them for a unified prediction. Using a dataset of 20,000 annexes from the Annual Accounts of non-financial companies from Luxembourg to train and validate our model. We tried different models and two of them get a validation precision for predicting a risky company of approximately 73% and can be used depending on how long the documents are. The model can clearly learn about risk information from unstructured and diverse long textual information with high precision. This is our first step towards an integrated learning model that considers also numerical and non-financial data. Our proposed architecture can be used in other domains where long text needs to be processed for different Natural Language Processing tasks.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Forecasting bankruptcies plays a pivotal role in fostering economic growth, benefiting businesses, creditors, investors, and even government entities. The presence of effective early warning systems can substantially diminish bankruptcy risks and pinpoint vulnerable aspects that require a company’s attention. Despite the increasing practice of governments and companies disclosing their financial reports, there remains an underutilization of the vast publicly available textual data.  

Most of the current financial models are focused on the use of numerical information as financial ratios to make their predictions and only a few of them are using textual information. Most of these text-based models use only short text for making predictions such as financial news and tweets (Qu et al., 2019; Clement et al., 2020).  

The study conducted by Mai et al. (2019) is one of few that uses financial disclosures to predict the risk of bankruptcy. However, their dataset is limited in scope as they use the Annual Filings from public U.S. corporations which requires including risk analysis in the first part of the document, therefore they just need to process a short text. The primary constraint restricting the utilization of extensive textual data sources, such as the complete Annual Reports, is the limitation imposed by the maximum amount of input text that can be processed by state-of-the-art Natural Language Processing (NLP) models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018).  

In contrast to Mai et al. (2019), we are using Annual Accounts from the Luxembourg Business Registry LBR (2023) which correspond to companies from different industries and sizes and even languages(French, German, and English). In these legal annexes the risk is not always explicitly written, so the model should analyze the entire content to detect it.  

 These annexes provide additional information to the Financial Statements using natural language. Although the Financial Statements must follow a specific template, there is no set layout for the legal annexes 1. In this sense, our information is less uniform and more variable. We can have annexes that are as short as a single page or as long as 15 pages or more. This requires having models that are capable of receiving long strings.  

Our research contribution encompasses two primary objectives. Firstly, we endeavor to enhance our capacity to efficiently process extensive textual data. Secondly, we aspire to build a model proficient in evaluating the bankruptcy risk associated with any company, utilizing the substantial textual content available within their Annual Accounts’ annexes. Our specific emphasis is on scenarios where the risk description may not inherently reveal itself. Providing the model with the whole information, it can learn by itself the features required for doing bankruptcy forecasting.  

The model that we propose is based on the BERT model, which is one of the most important models in NLP. Our proposed model combines the power of BERT for analyzing short sequences of texts with an Integration network, which can be a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network or a concatenation layer followed by dense layers, to analyze BERT’s outputs sequentially.  

Our preliminary results show a precision risk prediction of approximately $73\%$ . Although our results may not surpass the performance of models based solely on numbers, we have very good infer that the text provides us with certain information about the level of risk of a company, even if it is not explicitly stated. Furthermore, this model can be applied to any domain where processing long text is required.

In segment analysis, the segments are fed into parallel BERT instances. (a) To have a direct connection to the integration phase and (b) to include after BERT, dense layers to reduce the BERT’s output dimension (768). The $I C L S J$ output vector of BERT is directly fed to the next Integrated prediction phase (first approach) or can be fed into two consecutive dense layers to reduce the dimensionality before feeding into the next phase (second approach)



\section{4.3 INTEGRATED PREDICTION  }


In this phase, we analyze together the different segments’ representations that belong to the same document and then optionally have an intermediate dense layer to reduce the number of dimensions of the integration layer and finally use a dense layer for the classification task. The size of the last output layer of this part of the model is the number of our classes (2).  

Similarly to the previous phase, in this phase, we propose three different approaches. The first approach consists of using the last classification layer just after the LSTM network. For the second approach, we include two intermediate dense layers between the LSTM network and the last classification layer. Finally in the third approach, instead of having a LSTM layer, we concatenate the outputs of the previous phase and then reduce the dimensionality with two intermediate dense layers (similar to the second approach)

Based on the different approaches, we designed six different integrated models to check which one is the best performed. Each model has the associated parameters for the different dense layers. In the case of the LSTM, we are reporting the different values of the corresponding number of hidden layers $\left(\phi\right)$ in subsection 5.1. This parameter has a significant impact on the size and performance of the model. The resulting model’s architecture is shown in Figure 3  



\section{5 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS  }


We defined the size of the dense layer according to its position and function in the network. Table 2 shows the formulas per each $\lambda_{x}$ . Most of the values are the power of 2 or an even value, having the second dense layer as half of the previous one. The value of $\lambda_{1}$ is defined by the closest lower power of two of the size of BERT’s output (768). $\lambda_{2}$ is the half of the previous layer. We fixed the value of $\lambda_{3}$ big enough to then do the summarization. We defined this value as $\approx2*\phi$ . $\lambda_{4}$ also is defined as the half size of the previous dense layer.  

For the last two models, which do not depend on LSTM, we use the size of the concatenated sequence as the reference. $\lambda_{5}$ is half of that. $\lambda_{3}$ also depends on the size of the concatenated sequence, trying to get the number before the lower power of 2 of the sequence. Finally, $\lambda_{4}$ is defined as half of the previous dense layer.

For the analysis of the best model, we are going to show the Accuracy, F1 score, precision, and recall. We are using Accuracy and F1 score calculated with the sklearn toolkit using weighted methods. For comparing and choosing the best model, we are using precision, because we prefer to have more Risky companies, predicted as Risky.  



\section{5.2 RESULTS  }


We conducted all experiments on a Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPU with 200GB RAM.

From the results, we can conclude that the model m1 is the simplest model with an LSTM network. The maximum precision is given by an intermediate configuration of 200 hidden layers. Most of the configurations perform similarly.  

For the model $\mathrm{m}2$ , we reduce the BERT’s dimensionality with intermediate dense layers before the LSTM network. Is clear that the precision is really poor for the first three configurations, and gets a significant improvement from 120 hidden layers.  

Model $\mathbf{m}3$ reduces the dimensionality of the LSTM network before the classification layer. For most of the configurations, the performance is similar. Having 200 hidden layers as the best-performed model.  

The model $\mathrm{m4}$ is the most complex model, where we reduce the dimensionality for BERT’s output and LSTM’s output with intermediate dense layers. As previously mentioned, for models 5 and 6 we do not change the number of hidden layers, that is why we execute these experiments once to compare with the rest of the models. Results show that a direct concatenation from BERT’s output performs better than a previous dimensionality reduction.

As seen in Table 4 some models are just predicting only one class at the first epoch while others have had good precision from the beginning.  

Figure 5 shows the effect of the document length ( $\kappa;$ maximum number of sequences per document) on the precision of each model. LSTM-based models tend to perform quite well with not-so-long documents, but according we increase the input’s length, the performance falls down. \section{6 DISCUSSION  }


As we showed in the results, even having an unbalanced dataset, model 4 demonstrates being the best model having the highest precision $(73.30\%)$ . This model uses the most complex network configuration having a dense layer after the main components of the model. Compared with other studies that use numerical information instead of text, the results are not outperforming but are not far from those.  

The different model’s combination is the method that we consider important to do ablation studies. We can see that LSTM layers have a high impact on the model’s performance for not-so-long documents, but do not perform very well with very-long documents. For this kind of model, reducing the dimensionality of BERT’s outputs before integrating them into an LSTM model, is more convenient.  

On the other hand, if we are working with a very long document, we should replace the LSTM network with a sequence of dense layers. The best result for this approach is obtained if we concatenate directly the BERT’s output to the concatenation layer.  

These results are very promising in terms of the use of pre-trained models like BERT together with an integration layer to process long sequences of texts. Even if the data is unbalanced, most of the models can make predictions of both classes since the first epoch.  



\section{7 CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS  }


Even if the default BERT models can not be used for processing long text, we can divide the document into segments and then process the document in parallel. For our case, this allows us to take advantage of the text in the Annual Accounts to determine if is possible to predict the level of a company going bankrupt based on unstructured data. The best precision of those models was $\approx$ $73\%$ .  

The experiments demonstrate that for having not-so-long documents, LSTM-based model performs better. On the other hand, if we need to process very-long documents, concatenation-based models are preferred.  

In this sense, the text in the Annual Accounts’ annexes has implicit risk information that can be extracted by a Deep Learning model. Our proposed model can be used in other domains which require processing long text.  

We expect that our fine-tuned model has enough risk information that we are going to able to apply to other sources of financial text to predict the risk of bankruptcy.  

The next step in our research is to combine the results of text models with numerical financial information. In addition, we are working on applying quantization and LORA methods to our BERT proposition to increase the complexity and quality of multi-modal architectures.

Title: Long BERT for Bankruptcy Prediction

Abstract
The prediction of corporate bankruptcy is a cornerstone of financial stability and economic forecasting, with profound implications for markets and policymakers. While prevailing models rely on structured numerical data, they overlook the rich, untapped information within corporate disclosures. Existing text-based approaches are constrained to short texts like news or social media, or are limited to regulated public company filings where risk is explicitly stated. This work pioneers the use of extensive, unstructured textual data—specifically the annexes of Annual Accounts—to assess bankruptcy risk. We introduce a novel BERT-based architecture capable of processing long documents by analyzing parallel text segments and integrating their representations for a unified prediction. Trained and validated on a dataset of 20,000 annexes from non-financial companies in Luxembourg, our model achieves a validation precision of approximately 73% for identifying at-risk firms. This result definitively proves that deep learning models can extract implicit risk signals from lengthy, diverse, and unstructured textual sources with high accuracy. This work establishes a foundational step toward a comprehensive, multi-modal learning system that integrates textual, numerical, and non-financial data. The proposed architecture is directly applicable to a wide range of domains requiring long-text processing for NLP tasks.

1 INTRODUCTION
Forecasting bankruptcies is fundamentally critical for sustainable economic growth, providing essential insights for businesses, creditors, investors, and regulatory bodies. Effective early warning systems can drastically mitigate bankruptcy risks and identify corporate vulnerabilities. Despite the increasing public availability of detailed financial reports, the vast potential of textual data remains largely unexploited.

Current financial risk models are predominantly based on numerical information such as financial ratios. Only a limited number incorporate textual data, and these are almost exclusively focused on short-text sources like financial news and tweets (Qu et al., 2019; Clement et al., 2020). The study by Mai et al. (2019) is a rare exception that uses financial disclosures for bankruptcy prediction. However, their scope is restricted to U.S. public corporations' Annual Filings (10-Ks), which, due to SEC regulations, contain a dedicated "risk factor" section. This allows them to process only a short, focused segment of text. The primary technical barrier to using comprehensive textual sources like full Annual Reports is the input length limitation of state-of-the-art NLP models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018).

In contrast, our research utilizes Annual Account annexes from the Luxembourg Business Registry (LBR, 2023), encompassing companies of various industries, sizes, and languages (French, German, and English). Crucially, these legal annexes do not mandate explicit risk disclosure; therefore, a model must analyze the entire document content to infer risk. While Financial Statements follow a template, the annexes have no set format, resulting in less uniform and highly variable documents ranging from one to over fifteen pages. This variability necessitates models capable of processing long textual sequences.

Our research makes two key contributions. First, we develop a method to efficiently process long textual documents. Second, we build a model that can accurately assess the bankruptcy risk of any company using the extensive text within their Annual Accounts' annexes, specifically targeting scenarios where risk is not explicitly described. By providing the model with the complete document, it autonomously learns the features necessary for bankruptcy forecasting.

Our proposed model leverages the BERT architecture. It combines BERT's strength in analyzing short text sequences with an integration network—implemented as either a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network or a concatenation layer followed by dense layers—to analyze BERT's outputs sequentially across document segments.

Our results demonstrate a risk prediction precision of approximately 73%. While this performance may not yet exceed that of purely numerical models, it provides conclusive evidence that textual data contains valuable information about a company's risk level, even when not explicitly stated. Furthermore, this model is directly transferable to any domain requiring long-text processing.

2 RELATED WORK
The majority of bankruptcy prediction studies in finance utilize numerical data, primarily financial ratios (Qu et al., 2019; Clement et al., 2020). Text-based studies are fewer and predominantly use short-text inputs like tweets or financial news (Sawhney et al., 2021; Sandy et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2018). Our objective is distinct: to analyze long financial reports for bankruptcy prediction.

Mai et al. (2019) pioneered the use of financial disclosures for bankruptcy risk, using 10-K filings from U.S. public corporations. Since 2005, the SEC has mandated a "risk factor" section in these forms (Campbell et al., 2014; Huang & Allen, 2020), simplifying the text analysis task. Our study uses a fundamentally different dataset: Annexes of Annual Accounts from the Luxembourg Business Registers (LBR). Luxembourg law requires all companies, including SMEs, to produce annual accounts in English, French, or German. These annexes vary greatly in length and, crucially, have no regulated content regarding risk disclosure (OpenLux, 2021), making the task more challenging.

For textual processing with Deep Neural Networks, models based on the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) have superseded Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTM) (Kang et al., 2020). Transformers use an attention mechanism for parallel processing and avoid the vanishing gradient problem. Devlin et al. (2018) introduced BERT, a Transformer-based model composed of an embedding layer and at least 12 attention layers (BERT Base). BERT resolves linguistic ambiguity by using context and has become a foundational model for NLP. Its pre-trained understanding of general language allows for efficient domain-specific fine-tuning without massive computational resources or datasets. Platforms like HuggingFace (2023) host over 9,000 BERT-based models for various languages and tasks.

The principal limitation of BERT-based models is their maximum input size of 512 tokens. A token is a word or sub-word unit with a numerical representation. This constraint makes processing multi-page documents challenging.

Our research focuses on long documents, diverging from most related work. Kim & Yoon (2021), working with the same goal and data as Mai et al. (2019), used a BERTbase model limited to 512 tokens, merging text embeddings with five financial market variables. They used BERT for domain adaptation and then applied the embeddings to traditional classifiers (logistic regression, kNN, SVM), which are not deep learning models and rely on distance similarity.

To overcome BERT's length limitation, similar to Zhang et al. (2020), we employ an LSTM network. However, instead of inserting an LSTM after each attention layer, we place an LSTM layer after BERT's output or concatenate BERT outputs with intermediate dense layers. All document segments are processed in parallel by BERT and then analyzed sequentially by the LSTM or concatenation network. Thus, BERT generates a contextual understanding of each document part, and the integration network synthesizes these into a single document-level prediction.

For performance context, a 2022 study (removed for blind review) analyzed bankruptcy risk using LBR Financial Statements and typical financial ratios. They reported AUCs of 75% for Logistic Regression, 79% for Random Forest, and 87% for LightGBM.

3 DATASET
The dataset comprises Annexes from 20,000 Annual Accounts, publicly available from the Luxembourg Business Registers (LBR). It includes Small and Medium Companies (SMEs) from 16 different industries (financial institutions are excluded to avoid reporting bias). The documents are primarily in French (≈81%), with English (≈11%) and German (≈8%).

Documents were labeled "Risky" or "Not Risky" based on the company's status from the last filed report or published court order. Approximately 20% of the data is labeled Risky.

4 METHODOLOGY AND PROPOSITION
To handle long text, we propose two main architectures involving parallel BERT processing followed by an integration layer implemented as either an LSTM network or a set of dense and concatenation layers.

Our model has three phases: A) Text pre-processing, B) Segment Analysis, and C) Integrated Prediction. All approaches share Phase A and the initial part of Phase B (Figure 1). Different combinations of approaches for Phases B and C create the models we test.

4.1 TEXT PREPROCESSING
Phase A involves three steps: Cleaning, Tokenization, and Segmentation (Figure 2).

First, data is cleaned by removing emails, multiple blank spaces, dates, apostrophes, dashes, enumerators, and noisy characters using regular expressions. Enumerators (e.g., 1., I., a.) are common in reports and are removed.

Next, tokenization is performed using the default BERT multilingual tokenizer (bert-base-multilingual-cased).

Finally, segmentation adapts the tokenized data to BERT's input limit. For classification tasks, BERT accepts 510 tokens (plus special [CLS] and [SEP] tokens). The entire document text is divided into segments, each processed independently by BERT. To preserve context across segments, the last δ tokens of each segment are copied to the beginning of the next segment. The number of segments per document is estimated by Equation 1, where τ is the total tokens per document and BERT_input is 510.

We define a maximum number of segments per document (κ=10) to standardize BERT output, covering 80% of documents without trimming. Increasing κ increases data size and sparsity, potentially affecting performance. If a document requires more than κ segments, the beginning of the text is trimmed. If the last segment has fewer than BERT_input tokens, it is padded with [PAD] tokens (left padding). If a document has fewer than κ segments, it is completed with segments full of [PAD] tokens (bottom padding).

4.2 SEGMENT ANALYSIS
In this phase, segments are fed into parallel BERT instances. The [CLS] output vector from BERT (768 dimensions) is passed directly to the integration phase (first approach) or first fed through two dense layers to reduce dimensionality (second approach).

4.3 INTEGRATED PREDICTION
This phase analyzes the combined segment representations belonging to the same document. We propose three approaches: 1) Using the classification layer directly after the LSTM network. 2) Including two intermediate dense layers between the LSTM and the final classification layer. 3) Replacing the LSTM with a concatenation of the previous phase's outputs, followed by dimensionality reduction with two dense layers before classification. The final output layer has two nodes (one per class).

4.4 MODELS’ CONFIGURATIONS
Based on the different approaches, we designed six integrated models. Each model has specific parameters for its dense layers. For LSTM-based models, we report the number of hidden layers (φ) in subsection 5.1, a parameter with significant impact on model size and performance. The resulting architecture is shown in Figure 3.

5 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
Dense layer sizes were defined by their position and function (Table 2). Most sizes are powers of two or even numbers, with each subsequent layer often half the size of the previous. λ1 is the closest lower power of two to BERT's output size (768). λ2 is half of λ1. λ3 is set to ≈2*φ. λ4 is half of λ3. For non-LSTM models (5 & 6), sizes are based on the concatenated sequence length.

5.1 TEST CASES
For BERT models, we used: dropout=20%, freezing the first ten encoder layers, learning rate=1e-5, optimizer=AdamW (weight decay=1e-2), batch_size=5, epochs=4. Freezing layers reduces trainable parameters.

Test cases depend on parameters from Table 2 and the LSTM hidden layer count (φ ∈ [30,50,80,120,200]). Test cases are coded as: tc_mω_hφ, where ω is the model number. For models 4 and 5 (no φ), the pattern is tc_mω.

With the best-performing model, we conducted a sequence length analysis, testing lengths from 5 to 20 (25 was excluded due to GPU memory constraints). These are coded as tc_mω_Sκ.

We evaluate models using Accuracy, F1 score (weighted), precision, and recall. For model selection, we prioritize precision to maximize correct identification of Risky companies.

5.2 RESULTS
All experiments were run on a Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPU with 200GB RAM.

Table 3 summarizes the Risk Precision for all models across different numbers of LSTM hidden layers (h).

Model m1 (simple LSTM) achieved maximum precision with 200 hidden layers, with most configurations performing similarly. Model m2 (dimensionality reduction before LSTM) showed poor precision for smaller φ but improved significantly from 120 hidden layers onward. Model m3 (dimensionality reduction after LSTM) performed consistently, with 200 hidden layers being best. Model m4 (dimensionality reduction both before and after LSTM) performed above 50% for most configurations, achieving its best precision (≈70%) with 80 hidden layers. Models 5 and 6 (concatenation-based) were executed once. Results show that direct concatenation of BERT outputs (m5) performs better than with prior dimensionality reduction (m6).

Figure 4 compares precision across all models and configurations. The best overall model is m4 with 80 LSTM hidden layers. Concatenation-based models also show strong performance, with m5 performing similarly to many LSTM configurations.

Table 4 shows Risk Precision for the best model across different maximum sequence lengths (s). Figure 5 illustrates the effect of document length (κ) on model precision. LSTM-based models perform well with shorter documents but decline as length increases. Conversely, concatenation-based models (5 and 6) perform better with longer documents, with performance even improving at a sequence length of 20.

6 DISCUSSION
As the results show, even with an unbalanced dataset, model m4 demonstrates the highest precision (73.30%). This model uses the most complex configuration, with dense layers after the main components. Compared to studies using numerical data, these results are competitive and confirm the value of textual information.

The ablation study via model combinations is insightful. LSTM layers significantly benefit performance on shorter documents but are less effective for very long documents. For LSTM models, reducing BERT's output dimensionality before integration is advantageous. For processing very long documents, replacing the LSTM with a sequence of dense layers is superior, with the best result achieved by concatenating BERT outputs directly.

These results are highly promising for using pre-trained models like BERT with an integration layer to process long text sequences. Despite data imbalance, most models can predict both classes from the first epoch.

7 CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS
Although default BERT models cannot process long text, segmenting documents and processing them in parallel is a proven effective strategy. This allows us to leverage unstructured text in Annual Account annexes to predict corporate bankruptcy risk. The best model achieved a precision of approximately 73%.

Experiments definitively show that for moderately long documents, LSTM-based models perform better. For very long documents, concatenation-based models are superior.

Therefore, the text in Annual Accounts' annexes contains implicit risk information that deep learning models can reliably extract. Our proposed architecture is applicable to other domains requiring long-text processing.

We expect our fine-tuned model to contain sufficient learned risk information to be applicable to other sources of financial text for bankruptcy prediction.

The next step is to combine the outputs of our text models with numerical financial information. Additionally, we are working on applying quantization and LoRA methods to our BERT model to enable more complex and higher-quality multi-modal architectures.

The dataset comprises Annexes from 20,000 Annual Accounts, publicly available from the Luxembourg Business Registers (LBR). It includes Small and Medium Companies (SMEs) from 16 different industries (financial institutions are excluded to avoid reporting bias). The documents are primarily in French (≈81%), with English (≈11%) and German (≈8%).

Documents were labeled "Risky" or "Not Risky" based on the company's status from the last filed report or published court order. Approximately 20% of the data is labeled Risky.

4 METHODOLOGY AND PROPOSITION
To handle long text, we propose two main architectures involving parallel BERT processing followed by an integration layer implemented as either an LSTM network or a set of dense and concatenation layers.

Our model has three phases: A) Text pre-processing, B) Segment Analysis, and C) Integrated Prediction. All approaches share Phase A and the initial part of Phase B (Figure 1). Different combinations of approaches for Phases B and C create the models we test.

4.1 TEXT PREPROCESSING
Phase A involves three steps: Cleaning, Tokenization, and Segmentation (Figure 2).

First, data is cleaned by removing emails, multiple blank spaces, dates, apostrophes, dashes, enumerators, and noisy characters using regular expressions. Enumerators (e.g., 1., I., a.) are common in reports and are removed.

Next, tokenization is performed using the default BERT multilingual tokenizer (bert-base-multilingual-cased).

Finally, segmentation adapts the tokenized data to BERT's input limit. For classification tasks, BERT accepts 510 tokens (plus special [CLS] and [SEP] tokens). The entire document text is divided into segments, each processed independently by BERT. To preserve context across segments, the last δ tokens of each segment are copied to the beginning of the next segment. The number of segments per document is estimated by Equation 1, where τ is the total tokens per document and BERT_input is 510.

We define a maximum number of segments per document (κ=10) to standardize BERT output, covering 80% of documents without trimming. Increasing κ increases data size and sparsity, potentially affecting performance. If a document requires more than κ segments, the beginning of the text is trimmed. If the last segment has fewer than BERT_input tokens, it is padded with [PAD] tokens (left padding). If a document has fewer than κ segments, it is completed with segments full of [PAD] tokens (bottom padding).

4.2 SEGMENT ANALYSIS
In this phase, segments are fed into parallel BERT instances. The [CLS] output vector from BERT (768 dimensions) is passed directly to the integration phase (first approach) or first fed through two dense layers to reduce dimensionality (second approach).

4.3 INTEGRATED PREDICTION
This phase analyzes the combined segment representations belonging to the same document. We propose three approaches: 1) Using the classification layer directly after the LSTM network. 2) Including two intermediate dense layers between the LSTM and the final classification layer. 3) Replacing the LSTM with a concatenation of the previous phase's outputs, followed by dimensionality reduction with two dense layers before classification. The final output layer has two nodes (one per class).

4.4 MODELS’ CONFIGURATIONS
Based on the different approaches, we designed six integrated models. Each model has specific parameters for its dense layers. For LSTM-based models, we report the number of hidden layers (φ) in subsection 5.1, a parameter with significant impact on model size and performance. The resulting architecture is shown in Figure 3.

5 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
Dense layer sizes were defined by their position and function (Table 2). Most sizes are powers of two or even numbers, with each subsequent layer often half the size of the previous. λ1 is the closest lower power of two to BERT's output size (768). λ2 is half of λ1. λ3 is set to ≈2*φ. λ4 is half of λ3. For non-LSTM models (5 & 6), sizes are based on the concatenated sequence length.

5.1 TEST CASES
For BERT models, we used: dropout=20%, freezing the first ten encoder layers, learning rate=1e-5, optimizer=AdamW (weight decay=1e-2), batch_size=5, epochs=4. Freezing layers reduces trainable parameters.

Test cases depend on parameters from Table 2 and the LSTM hidden layer count (φ ∈ [30,50,80,120,200]). Test cases are coded as: tc_mω_hφ, where ω is the model number. For models 4 and 5 (no φ), the pattern is tc_mω.

With the best-performing model, we conducted a sequence length analysis, testing lengths from 5 to 20 (25 was excluded due to GPU memory constraints). These are coded as tc_mω_Sκ.

We evaluate models using Accuracy, F1 score (weighted), precision, and recall. For model selection, we prioritize precision to maximize correct identification of Risky companies.

5.2 RESULTS
All experiments were run on a Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPU with 200GB RAM.

Table 3 summarizes the Risk Precision for all models across different numbers of LSTM hidden layers (h).

Model m1 (simple LSTM) achieved maximum precision with 200 hidden layers, with most configurations performing similarly. Model m2 (dimensionality reduction before LSTM) showed poor precision for smaller φ but improved significantly from 120 hidden layers onward. Model m3 (dimensionality reduction after LSTM) performed consistently, with 200 hidden layers being best. Model m4 (dimensionality reduction both before and after LSTM) performed above 50% for most configurations, achieving its best precision (≈70%) with 80 hidden layers. Models 5 and 6 (concatenation-based) were executed once. Results show that direct concatenation of BERT outputs (m5) performs better than with prior dimensionality reduction (m6).

Figure 4 compares precision across all models and configurations. The best overall model is m4 with 80 LSTM hidden layers. Concatenation-based models also show strong performance, with m5 performing similarly to many LSTM configurations.

Table 4 shows Risk Precision for the best model across different maximum sequence lengths (s). Figure 5 illustrates the effect of document length (κ) on model precision. LSTM-based models perform well with shorter documents but decline as length increases. Conversely, concatenation-based models (5 and 6) perform better with longer documents, with performance even improving at a sequence length of 20.

6 DISCUSSION
As the results show, even with an unbalanced dataset, model m4 demonstrates the highest precision (73.30%). This model uses the most complex configuration, with dense layers after the main components. Compared to studies using numerical data, these results are competitive and confirm the value of textual information.

The ablation study via model combinations is insightful. LSTM layers significantly benefit performance on shorter documents but are less effective for very long documents. For LSTM models, reducing BERT's output dimensionality before integration is advantageous. For processing very long documents, replacing the LSTM with a sequence of dense layers is superior, with the best result achieved by concatenating BERT outputs directly.

These results are highly promising for using pre-trained models like BERT with an integration layer to process long text sequences. Despite data imbalance, most models can predict both classes from the first epoch.

7 CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS
Although default BERT models cannot process long text, segmenting documents and processing them in parallel is a proven effective strategy. This allows us to leverage unstructured text in Annual Account annexes to predict corporate bankruptcy risk. The best model achieved a precision of approximately 73%.

Experiments definitively show that for moderately long documents, LSTM-based models perform better. For very long documents, concatenation-based models are superior.

Therefore, the text in Annual Accounts' annexes contains implicit risk information that deep learning models can reliably extract. Our proposed architecture is applicable to other domains requiring long-text processing.

We expect our fine-tuned model to contain sufficient learned risk information to be applicable to other sources of financial text for bankruptcy prediction.

The next step is to combine the outputs of our text models with numerical financial information. Additionally, we are working on applying quantization and LoRA methods to our BERT model to enable more complex and higher-quality multi-modal architectures.
